title: A Fond Farewell
text:
For those familiar with Vladimir Horowitz's televised recital from Vienna a few weeks prior to this one, both the repertoire and the manner of performance will be similar. There are a few differences in details, which mainly spring from the differences between Vienna's Golden Hall and Hamburg's Music Hall, which is "dryer" acoustically.

By 1987, Horowitz had stripped his playing of much of the artifice which marred the performances he gave while in his 70s. Gone were the bizarre rubati and general obliteration of structure, and in their place was an unforced spontaneity and balance between tension and relaxation. A case in point is Schumann's Scenes from Childhood, which Horowitz recorded several times. Horowitz's two studio renderings, from 1950 and 1962, are fairly straightforward accounts, with occasional lapses into pianistic micromanagement and hints of nervousness when there should be relaxation. A 1982 live recording is almost the opposite, with nonsensical rubatos, distended ritards, slack rhythm, and almost no coherence. But here, in 1987, Horowitz has pulled himself together and plays with simplicity, controlled freedom, and conviction. It is often said that the elderly sometimes return to a childlike state. In old age, Horowitz had achieved communion with Schumann's visions of childhood lost. Horowitz still dared, however, to look beyond the printed page and interpret the music. Few pianists have ever dared to make Chopin's Mazurka in B Minor sound so sassy and sexy.

As far as technical matters go, Horowitz's fingers are fully up to the task of his chosen repertoire. By now, the octogenarian realized he was no longer capable of sustained virtuoso fireworks, so he often substituted finesse and coloration for bravura. The balance and evenness of his passagework, his incredible control of lower levels of dynamics, and ear for pedaling remain unrivaled. There are, however, tiny memory lapses which occur during the early part of the concert (and in almost the exact same places as occurred in his Vienna concert). However, these are not greatly distracting and can be easily forgiven, and they are nowhere near as pronounced as those I witnessed at Claudio Arrau's last Boston recital. Only note perfect pedants will cry foul.

DG includes a note indicating that one work, Schubert's Impromptu, D 899, No. 3 was not included in the broadcast or this recording due to technical reasons. However, my understanding is that it was omitted due to an audience member who became ill and had to leave, which created a noisy distraction.

Copies of this recital, which was broadcast, have been circulating among collectors for years. However, radio broadcasts are typically compressed and this was no exception. For this release, DG has gone to the uncompressed master tape, which sounds entirely natural, with ideal microphone placement that brings Horowitz into the room. So, even if you have the "pirate" tape, it's well worth getting this CD.

title: More amazing music from RST
text:
As an admirerer of Robert Scott Thompson, it is always exciting to start listening to a new work by this composer, who seem to know no limits to his curiosity and willingness to explore the most outré soundscapes, alongside more, shall we say, "traditional" music, though never content to just sit on his past triumphs, always ready to tread upon new paths.

Folio, both CDs, are examples of the more daring excursions into musical textures. These pieces may take some time to get into, but after a couple of listenings one discovers an amazing structure to what at first may appear to be deliberate randomness, if such a thing isn't a contradiction in terms, and a tremendous richness to these complex patterns appear. This is music that rewards patience and repeated listenings. This is not your granny's dance music. This is music that expands one's appreciation of what music is capable of.

title: I've just spend awhile switching between the two albums and I'd like to point out a couple of differences
text: I only reviewed this because some listeners dubbed it as a note for note copy of the original, and I can't disagree more. It's something paired well with an intoxicant to take off the day's stress. The frogs absolutely turn that around. They take it to a different mood with their jam band approach. Floyd feels relaxing and the Frogs make you move. Secondly the instrumentation isn't even close to equivalent. The bass playing is more rhythmic, dirty, and predominant. Sax is placed and played  very well throughout the album, adding emotional sirens that remind one of The Great Gig in the Sky's vocals. Drums sound modernized. It's an entirely different mix. I listen to both albums and do not consider them the same thing. I can listen to them back to back and not even feel like they are the same album. If you own Floyd's 'Animals', do not be discouraged from buying this album because "It's the same thing".

title: Definitely not a Ten...
text:
Australian songstress Gabriella Cilmi released her debut CD "Lessons to be learned" in 2008, a mix of Duffy-style vintage Soul/Pop and Blondie-style New wave. The lovely "Sweet about me" was a huge UK hit from the album. Since then, she's developed a liking for electronic music, Donna Summer's "Four seasons of love" in particular, she has stated in interviews.

The result is "Ten", filled with high octane Synth/Dance numbers like "On a mission", "Hearts don't lie", and "Love me cos you want to" (sounding like a Britney clone).

Slowing things down and providing some sonic variety are the Synth ballads "Defender", "Robots", "Boys", "Glue", and "Superman", though truth be told, they don't do much to raise the album above average.

The problem is everything is same-sounding with no killer track standing out. Standing above the others a bit are "Invisible girl", "Let me know", and a Synth-filled remix of "Sweet about me (Twenty ten version)" (sounding like something by Depeche Mode). It's rather telling that one of the best tracks here featured on her debut originally, and in a much better version.

It's such a shame really, as her debut showed much promise. "I've never been a diva, but I won't settle for second best" she sings on "Invisible girl". Pity she didn't apply the same to the music here which is second rate at best!

title: android lust further evolves
text:
android lust's latest album "the human animal" is less angry and more accessible than her previous albums. the songs lose even more of the harsh edge compared to the previous album "devour, rise and take flight." overall, "the human animal" does have a more intimate softer feel, made more so by the warm inviting bass lines. this album moves closer to a subdued industrial rock sound, but shikhee's mastery of painting a dark landscape is still on display here.

shikhee, a resident of new york city, used found sounds from the streets/subway for atmospherics. "the human animal" should be listened through a pair of good headphones to get the most out of the atmosphere/mood. this album should also be listened to as a whole to achieve mood. the tracks seem to be set up that way. for example, "the return" is only about a minute and a half long and serves as more of a bridge than a song in its own right. shikhee knows what she's doing and by the time you get to the ninth track, "one world," you look back and realize you're already sucked into this sound. the album closes with a darker remix version of "god in the hole." it's an excellent closer and i might even prefer it to the original more aggressive version found earlier on in the album.

shikhee's vocals are engaging as usual. "one world" and the very ethereal sounding "flow (of impermanence)" stand out to me, especially for the haunting ghostly crooning that's reminiscent of "wicked days." very nice.

"the human animal" is a natural progression from "devour, rise and take flight." this album is worth checking out for any android lust fans already familiar with her work, and should please some newcomers as well. it's definitely worth a listen, but those yearning for the angry screaming shikhee to return will be disappointed.

title: Crucial Ametican music!
text:
This is the first of two sets that collects all of the Stanley Brothers tracks released by Starday/King covering the second half of their career (cut short by Carter Stanley's death in 1966). Their earlier recordings for Columbia and Mercury (1949-1958) are often considered their best but the sheer volume of their output from 1958-65 (over 200 tracks vs. about 75 from the previous 9 years) means that there are tons of great songs in these sets. This set contains their most successful songs 'Rank Strangers', 'How Mountain Girls Can Love' 'Think of What You've Done' and the rerecording of 'Man of Constant Sorrow' which provided the arrangement used in 'O Brother Where Art Thou?'.
The Stanley Brothers unique take on blugrass incorporated Bill Monroe's innovations but maintained the connection to old-time mountain music through Ralph Stanley's soulful performances.
While the Stanley Brothers were never as successful as the top-earning bluegrass act, Flatt and Scruggs, they never became slick or, beyond a couple of 'pop-country' track experiments, compromised their sound.

title: Best McCartney DVD
text: I'm a big Beatles and McCartney fan but have been waiting for the right McCartney DVD before buying. Reviews of previous DVD's have been very iffy.  The reviews of 'Good Evening New York City"  have been much better.  So I bought it -- and decided to get the deluxe version. WOW, I am glad I waited and I am glad I got the deluxe version -- with the David Letterman concert.  Trust me, if you are thinking about buying a McCartney DVD, get this one and get the deluxe version for  a few bucks more.  Two and a half hours.Seeing McCartney and Wings on top of the Letterman marquee in NYC is worth a few extra bucks -- the feel of the street crowd is amazing.  The video quality on both DVDs is simply great. Details aren't necessary -- trust me, no significant criticisms on that end.  The audio quality is very good -- two live shows -- you're not going to get studio quality effects.  But the sound is super clean.  You really get the feel of being at both the Letterman and the stadium show.  The mixing on the stadium song "I'm Down" is terrific -- they mix the Beatles Shea Stadium performance in with the stadium performance.  And McCartney is in great voice on both shows.  That is notable since he has had some ups and downs in other performances. Somehow, I had not been aware of some of the more recent McCartney songs (don't listen to radio much anymore) and had not heard "Sing the Changes." What an amazing song. It has to be one of his top five songs ever.  It simply launches off the stage -- it is a joyous celebration.  You simply cannot hear this song and not love it. The production on that song in the stadium just lifts you out of your seat -- the energy. Clearly, McCartney loves it as well, given the enthusiasm he clearly brought on that song. Probably the most exciting song I've heard in a couple of years. Get the deluxe DVD -- you'll love it.

title: PURE AUDIO BLU-RAY VS. APO SACDs
text:
Ella & Louis and its follow-up, Again, are two of my favorite jazz albums of all time. After buying various remasters over the years, I thought I had made a "final purchase" when I bought the SACDs from Analogue Productions. The sound quality, I felt, was absolute perfection, and all the more astonishing for a mono recording from the late 50s. The voices of Ella and Louis had a palpable presence in my living room, utterly natural sounding and convincingly right there. Instruments had the unmistakable weight, timbre and texture that they do when played live in a real space.

So if I had reached audio nirvana, why bother buying this blu-ray? Good question. First, and most importantly, it contains all 19 songs from Again compared to just 9 songs on the SACD. (Many versions of Again are similarly truncated.) So the ability to have both albums complete on one disc was very appealing, especially at a price under $30. The SACDs, by comparison, are $30 each and contain 10 fewer songs. Second, there was the possibility that UMG had managed to wring even higher sound quality from the original master tapes, though I wasn't sure how that would be possible. Nevertheless, it seemed worth checking out.

Well, enough with the preamble, let me get to the conclusion and explain from there: it didn't take much comparison to realize that, in terms of sound quality, the APO SACDs blow this Pure Audio Blu-ray away. The Blu-ray is a very nice recording. The SACDs are the unmistakable sound of real singers and real instruments in a live space. The difference is just that simple, and is not subtle or nuanced at all.

Some caveats about this conclusion: if you only owned this Pure Audio Blu-Ray, you might be perfectly happy with it, unaware of its shortcomings without a clearly superior remastering against which to compare it. That said, I'm still happy that I purchased it for the 10 additional songs on Again.

Also keep in mind that the superiority of the SACDs isn't going to matter if you're not set-up for SACD playback of the pure DSD stream. Otherwise you're left with the CD layer of this hybrid disc, which is simply not as good. Finally, I wanted to mention the playback system used for this comparison:

For the Analogue Productions SACDs, it's an Oppo BDP-95 feeding the pure DSD signal via analog XLR to the passive pre-amp section of a Theta Gen VIII processor, then out via XLR to a Spectron Musician III Amp and Gallo Reference 3.5 speakers. All cables and interconnects are Cardas Golden Reference. For the blu-ray, it's much the same, except the Oppo is feeding a lossless, 24/96 PCM 2.0 signal into the Theta Gen VIII for decoding, then out via balanced XLR to the amp and speakers.

Thanks for taking the time to read my review and I hope you find it helpful in making a buying decision.

title: Billboard Top Rock'N'Roll Hits Series Review
text:
Billboard Top Rock'N'Roll Hits is a CD compilation series spanning 1955 to 1974, with one 10-track album for each year, attempting to capture the top 10 performing rock & roll hits of that particular year (I say "attempting" because in certain situations, legal or other copyright permissions would not allow it, as in the cases, for example, where Rhino could not acquire the rights for any Beatles or Rolling Stones hits to be included in the compilations). In those instances, Rhino would simply go on to the next highest performing song and continue thus until they had 10.

Rhino Records' rise from 70's obscurity as a two man novelty business, to a record production company with astonishing access to corporate music, to a re-issuing, remastering, and even re-engineering old masterpieces, record giant; the Rhino story is nothing short of amazing and their products are sonically the best you can get, or as close to Sony Japan as you can get in the USA. In the late 80's, Rhino set out on a campaign to keep our childhood music alive in several series of "Billboard" packages, complete with interesting factoids and liner notes, all assembled by rock historian Joel Whitburn. Each of the Rock'N'Roll Hits albums is a treasure trove, especially if you collect them in conjunction with the Top Pop series and their Top R&B series. This is also an excellent way for you to replace those lost 45's you misplaced, broke, wore out, etc. If you don't know, Whitburn is the preeminent rock and roll authority and historian, above and beyond any other discographer with unlimited access to the facts and numbers through his Record Research Inc.

The Rhino secret masters have done their homework and their lab work, each song on each compilation sounds intimately better than the scratchy radio single you might have owned or just listened to on the AM dial. I can't give enough kudos for the sound on these albums. The CD's are perfect (if you happened to buy these on vinyl in '88 or later, you will be surprised by the updated quality of the CD's as they were reissued). In every case, even with the earliest 1950's recordings, Rhino chose to use the best possible recording masters and in some cases these were surprising stereo versions. You might balk at only 10 songs on a CD or even vinyl LP, but the quality of sound far surpasses other collections (ie. Oldies But Goodies volumes 1 thru 15).

Starting in 1994, Rhino released the TOP POP HITS series as a companion set with TOP ROCK'N'ROLL HITS and the two sets really complement each other as a by-the-year compilation of the very best hits to each year in the soundtrack of our lives (if you are a boomer). Again, the digital mastering quality is top notch. I will be going on to provide review for those TOP POP volumes in much the same manner as these for the interested buyer.

So on to the music! Simply scroll down to the Year issue you are interested in purchasing for track listings (as some of these on Amazon are missing). title: A well sung classic, but with some extra-cirricular pitfalls.
text:
If this were a normal opera box set release it would get 5 stars all the way. The male cast in this is arguably the best ever assembled for this opera and Tebaldi is just a great Mimi. Serafin also conducts not only by the book as is his wont, but with feeling and aplomb,which is NOT always the case. Gianna D'Angelo isn't terrible as Musetta either.

I had to take away a star because the sound is pretty awful on first listen and though it comes with a downloadable libretto it was such an old version it wouldn't work on my computer. Good thing I already had it. As to the sound, it sounded as if the singers were backstage and the orchestra in the seats next to the listener. Fortunately, I put disc 2 into my computer and plugged in the earphones and the problem was solved. This seems to be a problem for a few listeners but it shouldn't be an issue at all.

I would readily recommend this if you need a quick, cheap, opera and see it on a shelf somewhere like I did. But I'd go with one of the other editions if you need THIS version and you're a Puccini or Boheme collector. I'm highly satisfied with this, but this is not my last Boheme, nor is the Callas/Distefano, which is marred by plain conducting and DiStefano's hollering Rodolfo.

title: FOUR BARBERS
text:
I recently listened to four recordings of the Barber of Seville back-to-back. Franky, I am not thrilled with any of them. Here are my ratings:
Overall cast: 1st Place--RCA--Peters/Merrill/Valletti/Tozzi. 2nd Place--EMI--Sills/Milnes/Gedda/Raimondi. 3rd Place--Decca--Baltsa/Allen/Araiza/Lloyd. 4th Place--EMI--Callas/Gobbi/Alva/Zaccaria.
Overall sound: 1st Place) RCA--Peters/Merrill, etc. 2nd Place) EMI--Sills/Milnes, etc. 3rd Place) EMI--Callas/Gobbi, etc. 4th Place) Decca--Baltsa/Allen, etc.
Individual Cast Ratings: Rosina: 1st Place) Roberta Peters. 2nd Place) Beverly Sills. 3rd Place) Agnes Baltsa. 4th Place) Maria Callas.
Figaro: 1st Place) Robert Merrill. 2nd Place) Sherrill Milnes. 3rd Place) Thomas Allen. 4th Place) Tito Gobbi.
Count Almaviva: 1st Place ) Francisco Araiza. 2nd Place) Cesare Valletti. 3rd Place) Luigi Alva. 4th Place) Nicolai Gedda.
Don Basilio: 1st Place) Giorgio Tozzi. 2nd Place) Ruggero Raimondi. 3rd Place) Nicola Zaccaria. 4th Place) Robert Lloyd.
Separate Notes: Callas sounds like she has been singing for 3 days straight, so tired and thin is her voice. The edge on her high notes made me grimace and she has a wobble on the High B. Gobbi's singing sounds like the barking of an old dog. Even though the Decca recording with Baltsa/Allen, etc. is all-digital, it was recorded in such a way as to make a double-sounding echo with all the singers except Araiza. They must not have used that technique for him. Basically, it ruins the whole recording, which is a shame. Otherwise, I thought that Allen and Baltsa did a fine job, but they are difficult to listen to because of this "double" effect. Have you ever spoken on the phone with a customer service rep and you can hear yourself in the background? It is like that. And there is no libretto except on CD 1. The EMI recording with Sills sounds like it was recorded in an underground cave. She is a bit past her prime, but still much better than Callas. Nicolai Gedda sounds like Rosina's grandfather. If you like spectacular high notes, Roberta Peters has them in spades. Frankly, I prefer Rosina as a mezzo, but I do not like the Horne/Nucci/Barbacini recording because Horne's ornamentations are crazy, Barbacini is hoarse and I don't care for Nucci, period. Mezzo Cecilia Bartoli has recorded Rosina, but her vibrato is so fast that it is unbearable. Mezzo Teresa Berganza has recorded Rosina, but she has Hermann Prey as Figaro, and I don't care for him either. So there you have it! The Merrill/Peters recording for RCA is the best of the lot

title: Definitely Creative For Its Time.....But You Make The Call!
text:
This Beatles recording was no doubt groundbreaking. The record itself brought albums to the forefront in the rock music world. The creativity of the music was very high for its time. The different textures that each song brings is fairly stupendous. Being For The Benefit Of Mr Kite and A Day In A Life are perfect examples with the surreal organ effects. Even George Harrison's song Within Without You is a pretty good composition with all the sitars and special effects.
However, some of the songs are just a bit too giddy or in the case of She's Leaving Home too depressing. Is this last song really what Rock N Roll is all about? Where Paul McCartney could compose a well structured song, the style is just sooooo bland. The Ringo sung, With A Little Help From My Friends does fit the drummers easy going personality. However, the tone is so mamby pamby that my impression is.... how pathetic is this? Joe Cocker's version adds some badly needed oomph and emotion which greatly improves upon the original version. Getting Better is not exactly that much better especially with the overly simple instrumental support.
If you love the Beatles, you are probably best off ignoring my comments and just buying this CD. It did start an album revolution and I will admit its creativity deserves some merit. More open minded fans and those who are non or casual fans may want to take an open perspective and not just love everything because everyone else declares this record as so reverred. I greatly prefer the White Album, Abbey Road, Yesterday And Today, and a few other records of the Fab Gang to this as the songs on these releases have a more consistent instrumental support and a more captivating style from song to song. Keeping that in mind, you make the call.

title: I hear him rockin'
text:
Yet another in a series of music I got turned onto by Lynn. Well, I'd actually seen the video for Dave Edmunds' cover of Dion and the Belmonts' "The Wanderer" and liked the reduplicated 50's atmosphere, down to the poodle-skirted girl with ponytail. The rest of the album, copied for me, was quite a revelation, displaying rockabilly, country, and rock, but I learned later that Edmunds was more an interpreter of 50's and 60's rock. Call this album a live greatest hits, as it contains some of his better known interpretations, such as Elvis Costello's "Girls Talk," which opens the album.
Much was my surprise when I heard a familiar tune, and one of the-then few country songs I liked. That was "Queen Of Hearts" by Juice Newton, and its high energy makes it one of the best tracks here. That's followed by the Presley number "Paralyzed," which is a close cousin to "Don't Be Cruel," rhythmically speaking. After that is the cover of "The Wanderer," complete with a horn section that really comes together during the instrumental part of the song.
The pace picks up with the Graham Parker-penned "Crawling From The Wreckage" with a devil of a piano. Edmunds also collaborated with ELO's Jeff Lynne, who produced his Information album. "Slipping Away," a more mid-paced number with a steady rhythm with dominant keyboards is included here, as is "Information," with its engaging "Happy Days" feel.
His association with Brinsy Schwarz's bass player, Nick Lowe went beyond playing together, as they embarked on a long songwriting collaboration over the years. Edmunds covered Lowe's "I Knew The Bride When She Used To Rock N Roll," originally on his 1977 Get It album, is done in a quick-paced rockabilly style. The live version loses none of its energy. The two also co-wrote "Here Comes The Weekend," another rockabilly number.
"I Hear You Knockin'", which was one of his most favourite covers, was originally by Smiley Lewis, he who originally did "Blue Monday" before Fats Domino. There is a country-rock feel on this rendition. Love that bluesy guitar in the instrumental part. Edmunds winds things up with "Ju Ju Man," another raucous number that get a big finish.
Other than his collaboration with Paul McCartney on the movie and soundtrack for Give My Regards To Broadstreet, I haven't heard too much of Edmunds, having confined myself to this live album, but I enjoy what I've heard. Maybe some listening to his other material is in order.

title: Another Fripp rip off
text:
Released in 1994, this was a sampler EP before the full length Thrak came. It is 31 minutes long. This is the first new studio material since 1984 when Fripp disbanded the group because he said he thought the world was going to end.

The sound quality is fair to OK. It is on par with many of the CDs from that time period. The sound is somewhat muted and not as dynamic as you would expect from King Crimson. By 1995, some very good sounding CDs were produced, but not many. It is disappointing that Fripp was not a leader in that regard.

This EP started a trend of Fripp releasing EPs featuring some songs before the full album would come out. What is bad about these EPs is that they cost the price of a regular album but were short. They also would contain slightly different versions of songs than what would appear on the final album and there would be a couple of tracks that wouldn't be on the final album. So, if you wanted to be a King Crimson completist, you had to buy the EP too.

Anyway, I don't think there is anything on this EP this better than what is on Thrak and I would not recommend buying this.

title: Michael Lee Firkins: Yep (2013)
text:
US composer and guitarist Michael Lee FIRKINS has been a recording artist for just about a quarter of a century by now, releasing his debut solo album back in 1990 and by many heralded as of the most impressive guitarists at the time. Firkins have steadily expanded his borders as his solo career has been ongoing, and especially on his last few albums there's been a marked change to the type of music Firkins have chosen to explore. "Yep" is his sixth full length solo album, and was released through Magna Carta Records Magnatude imprint in the fall of 2013.

As far as musical style goes, Firkins' latest album is one that have an unmistakable US sound to it. This is music as American as apple pie, the kind of album that will make you think about the land of the free and the home of the brave from start to finish. A disc that explore familiar sounds and styles it is too, but one that does it very well indeed.

There's basically three different kinds of compositions on this production. The opening three and the concluding two tracks can, at least broadly, be sorted under the southern rock description. Playful, harder edged affairs of the kind that gives you associations to early ZZ Top and bands of a similar nature, albeit with both organ and piano providing additional flavors to the proceedings.

Tracks 4 through 6 and 8 are rather different in style though, lighter in tone and character and with more of a Country or Americana flavor to them. Effectively assembled I might add, and surprisingly enough one of these compositions, Standing Ovation, comes across as the clear highlight of this CD as far as I'm concerned. As I generally don't like music with Country tendencies this was rather unexpected I should add.

The last type of songs are songs of the kind I'd generally describe as closer to the likes of Allman Brothers band, or at least some of their harder edged material. Some Country-oriented guitar details alike these songs revolve more distinctly around guitar and organ dominated arrangements with a big, majestic expression, and are arguably ever so slightly more closely related to blues and blues based hard rock than the other tracks. The differences between these tracks and the others at hand are fairly subtle though, there's no truly dramatic change of affairs we're dealing with.

What sets Firkins excursions somewhat apart from many others is his guitar work. While we do get treated to a few good guitar solo runs, the greater majority of them with a fairly distinct blues-oriented sound, the central characteristic details throughout this production is the use of slide guitar. Firkins is a performer used to applying this specific musical detail, and he does so very liberally indeed on all the songs here. He does it well to, adding both energy, tension and compelling details with an apparent ease. Of course the slide guitar is given it's fair share and then some of runs in the limelight, which suits the songs on this album very well indeed. With suitably warm, dry vocals of the kind that sounds like they have graduated from first class of the whiskey school of lead vocals, all of this adds up to be quite the enjoyable experience.

"Yep" showcase the abilities of Michael Lee Firkins as a guitarist and composer of the kind that can create and perform music that safely can be stamped as Made in the USA. title: Deep roots
text:
This compilation of Augustus Pablo music has been selected from his classic music of the 1970s and represents some of the deepest roots reggae ever recorded. This music is incredibly hypnotic and seems to change your consciousness simply by listening to it--no artificial substances required. The compiler organized the songs by riddims--the distinctive rhythm tracks which were manipulated to created an astonishing plethora of songs and dubs in classic Jamaican reggae. Thus, every two or three songs have the same riddim with different voicings and phrasings. The result is most pleasing.

There is a good degree of overlap between these CDs and other of Pablo's releases. The mastering here is very bass oriented; I enjoy the mastering here more than on some other CD releases the same material. Also, the method of organizing is superior to several other anthologies, though not to the Pablo compiled classic CDs like King Tubby meets the Rockers Uptown etc. If neither of these considerations convinces the hard core Augustus Pablo fanatic to buy these CDs, you really should download the tracks you don't have--this is some great stuff.

The CD package also includes a poster of Augustus Pablo and several pictures of him. Unlike the other photos I have seen on his CD releases (and I attribute this to the fact his family, i.e. his wife, participated in its making), he actually looks cute in these pictures.

The Magic Flute is a singspiel, meaning that there is music of surpassing beauty with a long spoken dialogue. This performance was one of the last to keep the older tradition of recording just the music and leaving the speaking out. Klemperer's tempos are just right -- not the too slow speeds he fell into, for example, in his Beethoven symphonies. title: Fine folk-rock - a full year before the Byrds and Dylan
text:
Taking their name from the epic John Wayne western of the same title, the Searchers were the fourth of the British Invasion bands to chart in America, with the Sonny Bono/Jack Nitschke song "Needles and Pins", which went to #13 after first hitting in March of '64. [Only the Beatles, the Dave Clark 5, and the Swingin' Bluejeans beat them out of the gate.]
They have a sort of soft singing style, with gorgeous twanging guitars, and a lot of minor scale work in their melodies/harmonies. Their melodies are some of the most subtle in the history of pop music, often with a decidedly mournful edge; they sang and harmonized them beautifully, and with feeling. Their songs also have a very fine rhythmic sense to them.
I have heard more rock artists cite them as major influences than practically anyone else, though I can only specifically recall Tom Petty and Alanis Morissette. I believe it was Petty who [at the beginning of the 80's] produced an album for the recently re-formed group.
You'll find some of the best guitar riffs of all time used as introductions to these songs. Not only is their melody/rhythm impeccable, but the tone settings they use on their guitars are mostly, well, mouth-watering [not to mention ground-breaking]. And it doesn't matter if a particular song went high on the charts: they are all stellar efforts, and always great to listen to, especially lined up, one after the other.
Among the singles, be sure to also check out "Don't Throw Your Love Away", "Someday We're Going to Love Again, "Love Potion #9", "When You Walk in the Room", "What Have They Done to the Rain", "Bumblebee", "Take Me For What I'm Worth", "He's Got No Love", and "Goodbye My Love". There are many songs here that I have never heard (them not being singles). So this is the way to really traverse all the dimensions of the Searchers. Don't miss the opportunity.

title: Magnificent performances
text:
I once had the privilege of spending part of a morning walking around the Tanglewood grounds with Maestro Leinsdorf. Needless to say, I did a lot of listening and little talking, one of the smarter moves I've made in my life. Later that day, I attended a rehearsal for an upcoming concert, which included Sacre du Printemps. I don't think I've ever attended a rehearsal run by a professional conductor that was more efficently managed than this one. He just knew exactly where the trouble spots were, worked on just those, and left the rest to the Boston Symphony to follow him in the concert. Not a bad bet, given the orchestra he had in front of him. Contrast with Leonard Bernstein, who used to lecture the NY Philharmonic until they were apoplectic.

To this recording: absolutely brilliant. I'm referring to Prokofiev, Leinsdorf and the BSO. The music is wonderful beyond belief. If you can sit still when the march returns for the second time in the first movement of the 3rd Symphony, which Leinsdorf paces and balances perfectly (you HAVE to hear the snare drum), then you are either deaf or dead. I don't think there's a better recorded performance of either of these symphonies (the first movement of the 3rd is frequently done too fast for my taste), though Rozhdestvensky's 3rd is also excellent (but his orchestra was not the Boston Symphony). If you love this music, just buy this recording.

title: Overall, on par with the studio recording
text:
Jose Carreras at his prime! What more could an opera fan ask for? How about cohesiveness as an ensemble?

Individually, the soloist performances are good. Caballe is in much better form than in her studio recording of this opera with Carreras. Here, her voice is rich and clear, and she sings with emotion. The Renato is good too, though he seems to have a tendancy to miss his entrances. His worst snafu is probably at his entrance in the famous Act II trio "Ahime! S'appressa alcun..." where he missed his entrance by a good half-a-beat, and truculently continued to sing the rest of the phrase half-a-beat behind the orchestra. He gets off the mark again in the Act III aria "Eri tu."

There are more ensemble problems beyond poor Renato. It could be an artifact of the hall acoustics, but the orchetra sounds terribly sloppy; and it only gets worse when you throw the chorus into the mix. If this recording is to be taken at face-value, one must wonder how the conductor wielding this sloppy baton could be the same person responsible for the most soul-shaking recording of Turandot.

As for the quality of the sound, I am satisfied. It sounds kinda like a quality studio recording... that's playing in another room. In other words, it's clear but dampened. I don't remember any recording noise (like hissing or popping), and there's also very little stage noise. However, the audience is somewhat hyper-appreicative. They clap and cheer loudly at the end of every aria. I didn't really mind it, mostly, but there was one point, at the end of Caballe's "Morro, ma prima in grazia," where they cheered so loudly and so long that poor Renato's next lines are obscured.

The bottom line:
Get this if you already love Carreras or Ballo.
Don't get this if it's your first recording; familiarize yourself with the music (and libretto) first.
The sound quality is neither a factor for or against -- it sounds decent, but not impressive.

It's not anything compared to their previous singles, but its Asian instruments add much variety. Nice sound effects also. I have grown to like this song a lot more.

3. My Style -featuring Justin Timberlake- (4:28) B+

JT returns for a very JT-styled song (especially in the "Whassup with you girl" part). Not half as good as "Where Is The Love?" but still pretty good. I personally hate Justin Timerlake's music, so the fact that he doesn't have a solo or basically any part of this song does not bother me, but any JT fan will be hoping for more. Except on the chorus, JT has almost no connection with the song. Pretty good song, but dissapointing to JT fans.

4. Don't Lie (3:39) A

Nice guitar and happy feel to the song makes "Don't Lie" a true winner. Kind of like "Shut Up" only much less angrier. Awesome song; one of the best on the album.

5. My Humps (5:27) A-

Catchy. VERY catchy. This is the next "Milkshake" for sure, and nothing like the BEPs. Fergie gets dirty in this song. Let's just say the allegorical meaning to this title is not very subtle. At all. Very good song, though - nice music and again, this is really catchy.

6. Like That -featuring Qtip, Talib Kweli, Cee-Lo & John Legend- (4:34) B_

Doesn't really stand out for me, but pretty good. Good chorus and cameos of a lot of well-known artists.

7. Dum Diddly -featuring Dante Santiago- (4:19) A-

Definitely going to become a single. This is a remake of Musical Youth's reggae hit "Pass the Dutchie" - as seen in the chorus. Very catchy and definitely the new BEP Party Song.

8. Feel It (4:19) A-

Fergie has a lot of awesome vocal parts- especially in the intro. This is another awesomely catchy song with nice music. The BEPs are really making great hits on this album.

9. Gone Going -featuring Jack Johnson- (3:13) A

A Will.i.am solo song; nice. Jack Johnson sings the extremely catchy chorus. Awesome stuff here. Nice to chill out to.

10. They Don't Want Music -featuring James Brown- (6:46) B+

James Brown on a Black Eyed Peas album? Now you know the BEPs are taking a change for the better. Nice song, even though it is nearly seven minutes long. Again, catchy. Nice stuff.

11. Disco Club (3:48) B+

Really innapropriate for the BEPs but good. Again, catchy chorus (we have a lot of catchy songs here). Nice song with good music.

12. Bebot (3:30) B-

The worst song on the album, and not because it is in Tagalog (Fillapino). While "The Apl Song" was catchy and meaningful, "Bebot" unfortunately isn't. I like the idea of a song in Tagalog, but Apl.de.ap can do better, and we've seen that on "The Apl Song".

13. Ba Bump (3:56) B+

Ba bump your bump! Again, more unbelievable catchiness with club themes. That music is infectious is too.

14. Audio Delite at Low Fidelity (5:29) B+

More awesome stuff here. Nice chillout song with great music.

15. Union -featuring Sting- (5:04) A+

The best song on the album. This is the "Where Is the Love?" of "Monkey Business". Of course, it isn't that good, but it talks about similar topics, now featuring Sting. He is an awesome addition to the song. Catchy chorus (love that Fergie part), and the music is great. Awesome way to end an awesome album.

Overall, "Monkey Business" gets a B+/A-. Tons of catchy, fun songs with variety makes this an awesome album to listen to. Nearly every song is likable, and while the singles are not as good as those on "Elephunk", the Black Eyed Peas is an amazing band who know how to produce awesome music. Bottom line: BUY IT.

title: Excellent Tribal Singing and Drums from Guinnea
text: Mamady Kieta is one of the living masters of djembe.  If you like pure drumming, please refer to my review for Mamady's "African Drums."  If you want to get caught up into the tribal experience, this CD has the group singing, log drums, kplango drums, djun djuns, shakeres, and dondo drums.  Unfortunately, it isn't the same as being there and voluntarily or not being drawn into communal dancing, singing and drumming.  To simply say the djembe is a healing drum misses the meaning of healing within a village.  It is an extended family.  Each life is dependent on the others.  Bad feelings toward others or curses toward each other must be healed.  These feelings usually do not survive this type of group experience.  At the end of a good hunt or harvest, these gatherings were known to continue for days. Does it work? Try it!  Cheaper than therapy.  Definitely a heck of a lot more fun than therapy.

text:
Okay, this record at least gets off to a great start: the rockin' slice of self-mythology Born on the Bayou and the underrated Bootleg. Then it takes a complete u-turn, with the murky, meandering, uninteresting jam Graveyard Train. And it remains in that u-turn, first on a dull cover of Little Richard's Good Golly, Miss Molly, then with the equally forgettable Penthouse Pauper. Proud Mary (most certainly the best thing on this disc) comes along and saves the day, but it's only temporary - things close with an even less interesting jam, Keep on Chooglin'. At least Graveyard Train has interesting lyrics...

But there are some upsides. The aforementioned Proud Mary cooks, a merger of soul, gospel, rock and country. And who could forget the "World, keep on turnin'/Proud Mary keep on burnin'/Rollin', rollin', rollin' down the river" refrain? Not me, that's for sure. Born on the Bayou is another one of the centerpiece tracks and most certainly their best song not to be released as a single. And Bootleg is their best album track, a lost little gem that's actually worth buying the album for. It's uneven, but the three good tracks make it worth a look.

title: Meh! but with some delicious surprises
text:
This is a though one for me, I was really interested in seeing if Enya would somehow return to the depth of musical composition that made her famous, alas, it is not necessarily true, in fact, it is almost worst. While Dark Island has some absolute lovely compositions, it left me frustrated. I had criticized previous albums, at least since The Memory of Trees, for a general decrease in musical depth and a concentration on formulaic song structure with sub-par orchestration and unimaginative editing/mixing and this album is a mixture of the same. While some songs shine with the promise of Enya's style, others, at least to me, are embarrassing.

Song by song - (1) - could do without it (5) - thank you!

The Humming... ----------- (4)

The opening piece, nice, much reminiscent of The Celts, although the harmonic structure is more controlled, less expansive and more focused on the melody line, instead of spinning off a sub-melodic accompaniment (it used to be that Enya's layered voice became a second orchestration in the past). Still, as an opening number is a tad too martial for MY taste (Dark Sky Island appears to follow the old LP song progression structure, a story told by sequence of songs, sequence being the important bit) While this could be an upbeat 'here we go' song it failed to provide that mystery, for me, it should have been far richer in vocals, enveloping, surrounded by layers of vocal aspects that tells me I am embarking upon a unique voyage, it feels more like a main title for an Italian western. You can also hear the by now inseparable sound of Enya's Roland (or whatever) keyboard (it is certainly not a Steinway Grand) you may learn to hate it in this album. I still like the song.

So I Could Find My Way -----------(3)

While the beginning is soft and promises mystery, when you think it is going to take you somewhere, BANG! there is that toy piano sound again, no different than the sound produced by that guy's keyboard at that wedding last month. To make it worst, it seems to be holding a boring, simplistic 6 notes progression, as if someone is practicing their piano lesson. The same progression, delivered with a fuller sound (a more complex orchestration maybe, a nice juxtaposition of strings, bass, grand piano and such maybe) then yes, with the annoying 'ting' of that keyboard, horrible.

The melody itself is lovely and haunting (reminds me of Last time by moonlight) and the song does pick up a level of depth at some points, but the song would have benefited from the sound of a grand (something she did for Watermark, which gave it that serene depth of sound) actually,the whole album could have benefited from the earthy, expansive and rich sound of a grand piano.

The end result is that while you like and feel even moved by the vocal moments when the toy piano is masked by the richness of vocal harmonies, the in-between are boring and unimpressive, failing to sustain the emotions evoked by the vocals.

A good song.

Even In The Shadows ----------- (5)

This one surprised me, it is more of a song as there ever was, the sound of 'not the toy piano is welcome and proves my point that a proper piano sound gives a richness to the song. The song has that new 'focused vocals' Enya has embraced, while they are lovely, they do not necessarily provide a second accompaniment layer, the are more adornments, lovely and accomplished but strangely,I keep waiting for the song to get going, it kind of did, and then it went back again, almost like a sea about to get rough, but it never does. Fine, I still like the song, but the vocal arrangements are certainly restrained where they could have created a marvelous sense of movement.

One of the best songs in the album, but I sill miss Enya's old vocal complexity, her voice as an orchestra kind of thing.

The Forge Of The Angels ----------- (1)

Oh! listen, a four note, repeat-to-death counter melody...first, this song is badly mixed, just listen carefully...(0:49 into the song). This sound is again damaged by a compete lack of instrumental depth, her vocal arrangement is not complex enough, at 2:17 the voices of some (apparently male) struggling angels, singing in unison as they hit some celestial anvil can be heard, but so incidental, so not used, that it may as well not be there, plus once it appears it goes on for too long, it works as an accent, probably right to support a change of density in the orchestration, but not here, because that never happens. Think of Pax Deorum and then think of this song and then tell me if it is not a wasted opportunity and a poor song at at that, it sounds lime the draft, the kind of thing they would have put together to say 'should we make this into something?' not a final song in an album. The simplistic pizzicato chords at the end (pilgrim again) are also attempting to indicate urgency yet fail miserable to provide any sense of anything other than the idea of somebody playing with the idea of a song on a piano. As I said, a poorly mixed song, surprised it made it to the album in that state.

Echoes In Rain ----------- (5)

Yes, yes, yes...little to say, it borrows from Orinoco Flow (it also seems to link its musical message) a tad starker in sound, but that's the new Enya for you. Still, lovely, unfair that they released this as an early single, it made me assume so many things about the new album...a return to old form, music you want to discover that will surprise you...no, a mirage. But this song is a keeper, the Alleluia chorus is catchy and flows so well, the richness of the sound mixes beautifully with her voice and the song still manages to surprise you.

I Could Never Say Goodbye ----------- (1)

While this song has a melody I care little for (which does not make it bad, just not my taste) the toy piano sound makes its appearance again, a stark, almost non existent arrangement with little musical nuances. There is also the starting sound, which is, if I am not mistake, a string in the guitar family (or thereabouts, maybe a harp in the low register?) which is nice,still, the basic harmonies are stark, repetitive and boring, The melody, while trying to be soaring, never gets there for me, while i shows Enya has kept her voice fresh and with great pitch control, this song could go amiss and I would not care. It lacks depth, direction and it is not melancholy enough to move you. Think f I want tomorrow...why not something better than that here? I expect musical growth, richness of sound and melodic flow...I am wrong in assuming that could be delivered?

Dark Sky Island ----------- (2)

For a title song, this is weak (the short piano line at the beginning are lovely). The same simplistic chords introduce the song (yes! with the same toy piano). Around 1:11 it seems to want to become something, but it does not progress to anything, just a bit of vocal harmonies in the back and that tubular bell touch here and there, the chorus has potential at 1:47 but the punctuated counter melody in its boring simplicity takes away from it. The song never lifts and although some musical aspects like at 2:23 bring to mind China Roses, there is not enough musical depth. A nice vocal bit at 2:48 surprises you, but it never leads to any exploratory sounds, no counterpoint to sprinkle nuances. A pretty straightforward song, with some moments that show what it could have been; a rich, enveloping sound, but I found it boring, still pleasant.

Sancta Maria ----------- (3)

Not sure about this song, listened to it two or there times, but the instrumentals at the beginning make it sound like one of those xmas songs you get in an elevator at a department store. While the very sound at the beginning (0:37 or thereabouts) is reminiscent of The Celts, it quickly becomes a waltz (are mostly late Enya songs a waltz of some kind?). The song becomes a tad interesting at 0:58 with the vocals but then the levels of complexities brought in are not enough to make you go, yes, I'll stay with you. Maybe this is Enya's version of 'Italian style'...at 2:07 an interesting change in the vocals gets you to wonder if you should listen longer, but then it goes on and on and only at 2:37 are you given one of those nice key changes Enya is well known for. The vocals are uninspiring, the song repetitive, it never resolves to either exaltation or elation nor does it descend into introspective adoration, it just repeats and repeats and repeats and repeats....It is not bad, a cute little ditty with bare instrumentation and some nice effort at a chorus structure. It does give the sense of happy travels, arriving at some Italian like island with laundry drying in the sun and all that, but no, thanks, maybe it is the orchestration that lets me down, to each one its own (maybe if she threw some nice percussion here and there like in Echoes in the rain).

Not bad, honestly, incidental and probably in the 'I'll keep it for later' box, reminds me slightly of 'and winter came' don't know why.

Astra Et Luna ----------- (2)

The aria, well, it sounds like it but why does almost every song now has to have that keyboard/string combo with that repetitive, waltzy line, you can hear it in Wild Child, Flora's secret, Only time, Silver inches, One by one, need I go on? While Enyas voice is crisp and clean, and there is some guitar like sound which is nice (help me out here, what is that stringy sound, it is nice) it only gets a layered vocal at 2:34, far too long into the sound and getting interesting around 2:47. The song is nice, despite my increasing abhorrence of her default waltzy counter melody, but somehow, through almost all of this album, I am missing the mystery, it has not been created vocally and most certainly it has not been created instrumentally. Also, the song is badly mixed, where the forceful counter melody is too strong/loud for Enya's voice, making her sound slightly weak and taking acoustic prominence.

The Loxian Gate -----------(5)

This one is closer to what I was expecting, combining elements from the Celts with A river sings, weirdly, I was expecting a touch of a deeper, richer, vocal counter point. Little to criticize, it is a very nice song, it seems to lack a bridge, which takes away some tension form the song, making it slightly flat (remember Storms in Africa? Sumiregusa?). Overarching it is good, but I feel as if many of these songs would work better for a documentary, with some visuals to give it texture as musically, that texture is not there.

Diamonds On The Water ----------- (1)

Aaaaaaargh please, never, never us a that stupid wood metronome sound, this is not a scales lesson. Of course, you now know that my view of the song will be tainted by the presence of that stupid wooden metronome accent, oh well. The song is not anything special, although at 1:48 it does have some lovely vocals, and the piano line that follows is very sweet (and it is not the toy piano! :-) but the song itself is nothing to write home about, at all. Sweet, nice (ignore the wooden metronome), short, cold have been much more but there we are (and noticed some mandolin like sounds here and there...maybe, harp? I can hear Only time being channeled.

Solace ----------- (2)

Ooh its 'pilgrim' from 'A day without rain'...oh,no, wait, it is not...it is just something between pilgrim and how can I keep from singing, not as beautiful as the later but not as boring as the first,which is a plus. I mus admit, this song never gets anywhere, it is boring, it gets some nice vocals at 2:52 but that's it.

Pale Grass Blue ----------- (5)

I like this, it has enough variance on the default counter melody as to be interesting. Vocals and melody are interesting and you want to see where the song goes. The dry instrumental in the counter melody and the sudden visit of that pan flutey sound she used in The memory of trees works. The lack of a bridge makes it slightly flat and lacking in acoustic diversity, still I like it.

Remember Your Smile ----------- (1)

Could not care less about this song, the cheap wind synth accordion like sound at 1:37 (is it synth? or is it oboe like? I hate undefined sounds) This is pilgrim and Toy soldier all over.

So,there, a bit brutal? maybe, remember it is my perception of the work, just that. In the whole the album is worth if for a couple of songs, but it still suffers from what I have perceived as a thinning of Enya's musical richness, we are being left with formulaic, thin in sound songs that have no special musical significance/accomplishment with a reduced vocal layering/exploration. When she raises back to her talent such as echoes in the rain, you get that 'hello old friend, I missed you' and this does not mean give us more of the old, no, please explore, but if the total sum of your exploration are run of the mill melodies with cheap instrumentals and some instances of vocal complexity..then maybe the old was better...just maybe, I'll probably give up on wishing by now, be happy for the music that was good and keep going, I wanted to say 'Shes baaaaaaaaaack loudly, but after repeated listening I can't say that, sorry, neither is she back nor is she something that necessarily interest me musically anymore. I would have exchanged less songs for a fuller and better developed few.

title: Very satisfying new release
text: Thank You For Today finds Death Cab for Cutie in fine form. This is the band's first album in three years and it's a solid listen from start to finish, from its haunting opening track "I Dreamt We Spoke Again" to the show-closing "60 & Punk."  "Summer Years" and "Your Hurricane" seem influenced by the Pet Shop Boys, but while Ben Gibbard's vocal style is reminiscent of Neil Tennant on these tracks, he doesn't seem to be ripping off the UK synth-pop band as much as he is paying homage to them. Given the variety of material on this new album and the classic sound of DCFC, many fans will be pleased. I know I am.

title: Lightweight, but a lot of fun to listen to
text:
Matthew Sweet and Susanna Hoffs both have covered semi-well-known 60's and 70's pop songs several times in their respective careers, so this effort shouldn't come as a surprise to their fans. But as another reviewer points out, because Sweet doesn't try to do anything creative with the songs' arrangements, "Under The Covers" is (by design) largely an inconsequential musical statement; these are interpretations which match the originals nearly note-by-note.

So, this lightweight-by-design album is mostly "hit", and just a little bit of "miss", with a couple performances falling flat. Example of 'flat': "Cinnamon Girl", a song definitely not meant for the kind of day-glo harmonies Sweet and Hoffs engage in. On the other hand, "Everybody Knows This Is Nowhere", from the same Neil Young album which produced "Cinnamon Girl", does happen to turn out well, and ends up being an inspired selection. Even better: their choice of the Left Banke gem "She May Call You Up Tonight", practically tailor-made for Susanna Hoffs' brand of pop music -- it doesn't sound too far away from "Manic Monday", actually.

All the tunes here covered by Sweet and Hoffs are worthy of being made known to younger listeners, and a few, like Marmalade's "I See The Rain", are great songs that even a lot of older pop fans might not be familiar with.

title: A GReat Reading From A Great Master
text:
12-18-13. I was suprised to seee no other reviews for this fime EMI standard, so I am the first. I will try to be good, as thisa old early recording was taped nearly 60 yrs ago, then remastered in 1991, I features the Philharmonia Orchestra under one of their most gifted conductors, Otto Klemperer, or just "Klemp," for short, in a performance of the Beethoven Symphonies 3% and #7, or two of them Bonn MAstrer'sx greatest works. Ibeleive that Klemp completed an entire cycle for EMI, and this issue of the 5th and 7th is a good preview to his whole effort. I currently own these by the great German conductor. The 3rd, the 5th, the 6th, 7th, and 9th. In addition, I have Klemperer leading the epic Missa Solemnis, but I also have so glaring holes in his survey of his favorite composer.
THE SYMPHONY IN A, #7, OP. 92 LEADS OFF THIS DISC, IN FAIRLY GOOD SOUND, AND RUNS a suprizing 48:33, with the opening movement already 12:50 in length. Despite it's huge canvas, Klemp never seems to drag but instead presents a wide sounddtage of epic breadth and leisurly tempi, more than adequate to allow for full, rich presentation of thosae wonderful themes fom the composer's pen. Wagner called the 7th "the apotheosis of the dance," and he was right. It is simply just ANOTHER example of the heculean acheivements of this great composer so many feel is THE best of all the lot. What pushes Beethoven past his closest competition, like Mozat, Haydn and Bach, to name the leaders, is his unrelenting and intense pursuit of drama and passion in nearly everything he wrote. Even his wonderful chamber works have a pathos and a heart beating with ours asx one, so that to truly experience the music of the grand master, one needn't attend a symphony concert or chuech or opera venue, but sit down at your private keyboard or pickup your violin or cello and just play. The same geneous that went into the big, public clarion calls that were his symphonies, is also found in abundance in the tiniest of his pieces, and in the most intimate of settings. A helpful tool in realizing this truth , for me, was the seeing of the film "Immortal Beloved," here the composer, played pretty well by Gary Oldman pursues his secret love, whom he never married but loved intensely. The film's portrayal of performance practices and everyday life is good and the scene where an Italian princess, in love with his, presents him with the opportunity to play a big, grand and most modern to date piano, in the privacy of her house. She, of course, spies on Beethoven as he plays his Moonlight sonata excerpt, and, upon discovering her presence , he storms from the villa in a rage. The sadness of what this man might have gone through is strongly portrayed by Oldman and the gist of the movie deals with his struggles for custody of his nephew, and his fight against deafness, trying to maintain his sanity. There is a quote from his 1802 Hellingstaadt Testament" in which he bears his heart to those closest to him of what deep and profound misery deafness is. I know it is only a movie, but it does help understand what he must of endured for the love of music. For this, I have come to admire and love his memory all the more, as grow older.
To question as to whether or not Klemperer felt anything similar to what I do, seems to me, a foolish inquirey. Of course he did, it is in his music making, just listen. The stately tempos and dispersal of accents in the comments from individual instruments is proof enough of the great care Klemperer takes with this music, in sxpite of the temptation to take it all for granted. These two symphonies are, after all, a pair of true "war horses," as familiar with listeners as anything Beethoven ever wrote. Just because thewy were so successful, doen'st mean one has to brush them over as "routine." On the contrary, they are two of music's bednchmark creations and should recieve every drop of our attention.
The famous "Allegretto" sxecond movement could be a tad slower for me, as Klemperer gets a bit too excited in the later stages of this 9:26 movement. If it were me, I'd slow it down a good deal more, bringing out the bitter personal darkness of his malady of hearing, something I think was very much on the composer's mind during it's composition. Still, it is within limits and has a presence that is real and filled with feeling. Just before the7 minute mark, Klemperer bringsx the orchestra up to a powerful and touching restatement of the Slow movement's theme, driving home for us, mere bystanders, THIS IS ONE OF THIS SYMPHONY'S FINEST MOMENTS AND BOTH KLEMP AND THE PHIL PULL IT OFF IN EXPERT FASHION. GOR ME, IT PRODUCED A SILENT GASP AI THE SHEER INTENSITY OF IT'S EFFECT.
Beethoven's scherzo is the best dance movement in this symphony, and it's bouncey, happy stomping rhythm is infectious and irresistable. I liked it immediately as I learned this Symphony fvrom an LP by the N.Y. Phil/Bernstein, like so many others. I own Bohm, Kaarajan (part of his splendid 1963 cycle) Cluytens, also from his cycle with Berlin aznd a few others, Wand, solti, Giulini, but not Kleiber, not yet. The con brio coulkd of easily been titled "con fuoco," as indeed it is ablaze with big sweeping rhythms and a persistant and energetic tempo. The percussion is quite present and the piercing trumpets make key contributions with Klemerer's perfect timing. A sharp, clean and loving reading from the great conductor and a mainstay in everyone's library, dcon't pass it up-----A well deserved award opf 4.5 Stars, with a slight detraction for the very good, but slightly degraded sound, but it IS 1955, after all.
The symphony in c-minor, #5 Opus 67 is a rather misunderstood and underappreciated work. It seems it's fame often extends no further than the first 45 seconds or so with the nternationally recognised and loved sequence known as , dot--dot--dot--dash." A sort of code that is excerpted from this near 35 minute long masterpiece, ignoring the more important matrerial. These 4 notes have been used in popular movies and the commercial media to sell ideas of drama and fate as well as automobile tires and salad dressings. How utterly foolish, somehow I doubt beethoven would find the humor in it. THE 5TH IS REALLY ABOUT ENERGY AND MOMENTUM LEADING TO A RELEASE OF raucous joy, pure and simple. Yes, this man DID smile, and often, as it is clearly evident through his music. He was NT the perennial "sourpuss" we have made him out to be, but a sympathetic and engaging artist, a kindered and intersting soul. Beethoven teaches us that there is joy in life and we should find it, less we lose it all togather. Imagine! A musician of his stature, pressed dcown by the crushing burden of deafness telling us of the joy of life. Yes, this man must of been a man of hope and faith, and I presume he had a lively prayer life, despite the popular portrayal he has from the intellectual midgets of the pop culture then as now. Even more inexcusable is our insistance of the correctness of our sxummaryt of the composer. We know best, certainly, which is why we miss the boat on Beethoven consistantly. The assinine idea of his final monents of life, dying in bed, his p hysiology wracked by some mysterious disease and looking eveybit the 90+ year old instead of the man in his late 50's, persists to thisa day, despite all our tools of scholarship at our fingertips, our interprative powers have waned to a level so low, they azrfe nearly imperceptable. We certainly should know better, whya don't we? Pride!! Pure and simple, pride. I find no credible evidence that the man shaking his fist at the heavens, on his deathbed in the midst of a crashing thunderstorm, is our Beethoven. We know he recieved the Lat Rite of the Catholic Church, as indeed just about all souls did back then. I'm sure the composer had his disagreements with the Roman leadership and political power and influence, butr tsntrums and outright rebellions such as those portrayed in, the afore mentioned film "Immortal Beloved," are wside of the mark---big time!!
Klemperer brings our attention near the end of this symphony in such a masterful fashion to the re;lease of joy trhat I always encore this sectin with every hearing. I find no other recording out there to compare equally with this one and it alone is reasxon enough to locate a caopy and add it to youre cart. Today!!!. Treat yourself to a stocking stuffer. The 3rd movement is a kind of mock "sturm und drang" treatment and , if you listen carefully, you can almost hear the composerwinking at us, as if in teasing. At the 5:00 mark, Klemperer begins a 40 sxecond long ascent from the depths of the quiet and slow paced tail of this allegro (scherzo) movment and , without pause, right on into the opening of the finale, the Allegro-Presto, which runs and gallops on for 11:06 TO THE FINAL BRILLIANT NOTES
If you can be still and pay close respectful attention for the final 11-12 minutes you will hear yet another defence of the geneous of this man called Beethoven.
I highly recommend this EMI recording for your libraryas yet another Beethoven 5trh and 7th set of perfvormancesas I believe one can never have too many of these great works. As always, friends, God Bless all and Merrty Chrictmas and happy listening in the new year! Tony.

title: Not so great live CD - limited song selection, shaky singing
text:
Once you realize this 1988 CD was quickly released by a record company facing passionate demand for a band that no longer existed, the release of this so-so CD becomes clear.
Live records are, as John Lydon put it, "record company stuff." You get the hits, just sloppier. I can remember only a handful of live CDs that offered something more. (PiL's "Paris in Spring", Throbbing Gristle's total reworkings, Ani DiFranco's "Living in Clip", John Cale's "Fragments of a Rainy Season" stand out.) I file this Smiths CD in the just-ok/humdrum bin. I play it sometimes, but in the space of years, not days.
Most of this Kilburn UK 10/23/'86 show consists of songs from "The Queen is Dead" or recent singles of that period. Performances here don't touch the studio mastery of that truly wonderful record. The tempo of most songs is sped up, not always a good thing. And then there's Morrissey, who sounds crankier than usual. This works well for "Bigmouth Strikes Again" which sounds like a thrilling riot, not so well for other tracks.
Legalities prevent me from recommending bootlegs that are far stronger, but I can safely say the great live Smiths were recorded - the material is out there - and this CD falls short. "Rank" is a live Smiths document, little more. It might have made a better video, however. Morrissey's fade-in/fade-out vocals suggest this was a rambunctious physical show, where he was swamped by fans. Reissue/Repackage anyone?

title: Experimenting Beyonce? Not Really (3.5 stars)
text:
Turning 30 at the time of her 4th regular longplayer, Beyonce's status as one of few superstars born and raised in the 2000's needed to be cemented with this 2011 album. The style of R&B had recently met with the identity crisis, including lack of good songwriting and few novelty ideas in arrangements. The singer was announcing in advance that the "4" will be a merger of genre and styles - however, this is not really the case. It's still a pop/r&b record and although some enrichments are present (and welcome), the record is not as risky as the 2006's bold B'Day (embraced more by critics than by fans).

On the positive side, "4" is not as uneven as the 2008's "I Am/Sasha Fierce" (embraced more by fans than by critics). For a bigger half of the record, Beyonce was able to infuse the songs - especially production-wise - with a sort of inner tension, lending the tracks the restless, positive energy that was here at "B"day", but mostly missing from "I Am/Sasha Fierce").

A good example of this approach is the sublimely understated "Miss You", followed by the feisty, although rather conventional "Best Thing I Never Had". Kanye West/Andre 3000 collabo "Party" gets more fun to the mix, while the (lyrically) rather extremist "Rather Die Young" keeps the quality flag high, as well as "Start Over". The old-school vibe in "Love On Top" runs a bit counter against the whole thing, as it rather sucks out the record's momentum. This returns with "I Was Here" and the minimalist feminine-power closer "Run the World (Girls)".

Still, the "4" is mostly a satifying and cohesive listen, not the breakthrough masterpiece Beyonce would have liked, but a decent addition to her discography. It is a good statement of current chart-projected pop, with the impact on others than her fans slightly dubious (she cannot catch up with current popularity of Adele or GaGa). All this said, fans of r&b and pop should not be offended at all with "4". Although one cannot help the feeling that if a group of 60 songs was streamlined to 12 for this record, the results should have been more impressive.

title: Aptly titled
text:
As always, Dream Theater is musically solid with great riffs and musical virtuosity, but this album is a let-down in many respects. For one thing, the lyrics are decidedly sub-par. For example, I just don't buy "Wither" and "Count of Tuscany". If you are a strong and confident person, why do you need to "give up" to write a good song and why would you be afraid of some mincey count? And something seems wrong to me about singing "by the grace of God above everyone survived" in a death metal growl! I thought I could avoid this pitfall of an otherwise decent album by listening to the instrumental version, but they mixed out the guitar solos, a choice so baffling to me that I destroyed the third disk in a fit of rage. Also, the last Bill W. track was anticlimactic and made me glad to be rid of them. Many of the tracks seem to lack the same level of emotion that their previous work exhibits and almost seems artificial: like someone trying to sound like Dream Theater but not quite succeeding. The second album is some very interesting and well-done covers (there are some songs I never liked until I heard the Dream Theater version) but the whole thing smacks of Metallica's Reload/Garage inc. phase. All in all, this may be their worst overall album, but since Dream Theater is such a good band in general, this isn't saying much.

Dream Theater is in a dangerous place as a band. After being around for so long and having a fair degree of success, they seem to be running out of critics telling them to try harder. I think the places where this album is lacking may be due to people (fans and promoters alike) pushing them to release new albums without polishing them. In the end, they get 3 stars because of "A Rite of Passage" which musically glorifies the ancient tradition of initiation. (It has great music and lyrics-one of Dream Theaters best songs for my money... Why can't the rest of the album be like that?) If you are a fan, splurge for the 3-disk. If you like this one, check out their older stuff: its even better.

title: A Fitting - and Excellent - Tribute
text: This gets my vote as my favorite tribute album of all time, and in my opinion it's one of the best ever put together. Richard Thompson, a founding member of Fairport Convention who has had a devoted cult following both here in the States and in his native Britain, is a formidable songwriter, not to mention one of the best folk and rock guitarists alive. He is one of those musical talents who has unjustifiably been denied large-scale commercial success. But he probably would consider the admiration of his peers more important than that anyway, and it's shown in abundance on this collection. Contrary to the track record of most tributes, this one hasn't a weak song on it. Packed with talent, it represents a variety of styles, from the crunchy rock of Dinosaur Jr., Bob Mould and X to the quiet folk of Martin Carthy and Maddy Prior (co-founders of another classic Brit folk-rock band, Steeleye Span). Everyone grafts their own style to these songs, and mostly they are quite successful. Graham Parker's "The Madness of Love" is a highlight, as is Bonnie Raitt's "When the Spell Is Broken" (backed by the gospel greats The Five Blind Boys of Alabama, who also do a goosebump-raising version of "Dimming of the Day"). Another Brit-folk great, June Tabor, turns in a fine rendition of the title track, and David Byrne gives a restrained but effective reading of "Just the Motion". National treasure Beausoleil does a "bontemps" version of "Valerie" (which was also a country hit for another artist whose name escapes me). The closest to missteps here are from two of my favorite bands. Los Lobos' "Down Where the Drunkards Roll" is so low-key as to be almost somnambulant; and in R.E.M.'s version of "Wall of Death", Michael Stipe's phrasing seems clumsy to me - I much prefer Nanci Griffith?s cover of that tune. Overall, though, this is an affectionate and well-conceived tribute to an artist who easily deserves it.

title: Not Dead Yet. Jo Dee Messina has returned....The hard way!
text:
Jo Dee Messina has returned. The hard way! Jo Dee parted with her former label last year and did so after agreeing to the stipulation that she not sign with another major label. Faced with the challenge of re-igniting her recording career without benefit of a label to assist her, Jo Dee embraced the internet and took her crusade to her incredible fan base. She went to her fans and told them that she wanted to make a record WITH them and promised that it would be OUR music OUR way. What came from that promise is her wonderful new album, ME.

ME starts off perfectly with the song ''Not Dead Yet''. It sounds like it could be a post break-up letter to her label with lyrics like ''You're the one who stopped believing while I'm still in the chase'' and ''I'm here and I'm well''. ''Not Dead Yet'' is perfect!

ME features two songs written by the incredible song-writer Amy Dalley and those songs appear back to back on ME. ''Peace Sign'' is the tale of a woman who is dumped by a new love via e-mail and instead of letting it bring her down she simply shrugs it off but not before flashing him the peace sign...minus one finger! The next Dalley written song is ''Breaking It Down''. The song tells us of a relationship in which one of the parties has run out of patience with their partner and instead of staying in the relationship and being miserable is saying 'Hey, listen, I gotta go. And here is WHY!''

The glorious title track ''Me'' is next. To call this song great or awesome would be a horrible understatement. ''I'm everything to everyone and I'm scared as I can be'' Jo Dee sings as she struggles to deal with the reality that she is counted on by so many for so much and when she looks into her mirror all she sees is herself. I saw Jo Dee perform this song last year and it is such an emotional song for her to sing. The woman had tears in her eyes while singing it and her voice choked with emotion on more than one occasion during the performance. It does not get more real than ''Me'

''Like A Kid Again'' is the next song and is my personal favorite on the album. While she deals with, accepts and embraces her many roles in ''Me'' she would sometimes like to simply go back in time and ''trade all this real just to feel like a kid again''. For me. ''Like A Kid Again'' is worth the price of admission to this record alone and should be a huge hit for Jo Dee. Here's hoping.

Earlier I mentioned that it didn't get more real than ''Me''. That may be not true when you get to ''A Woman's Rant''. What started as an entry in her journal turned into one of the strongest songs in her catalog. The title tells it all! ''A Woman's Rant'' is a day in the life of a working mother and wife ''You see, women, they do twice the work and get half the pay'' and ''I'd walk a mile in his shoes if he'd walk a half a mile in these''. Brilliant!!!

''He's Messed Up'' is a cautionary tale of a woman warning another to stay clear of an egocentric ex. ''I wouldn't touch him with a ten foot pole now that I know all the things I know'' and ''Well, it's take never give 'cause it's all about him''. Jo Dee asked fans to come into the recording studio to help her with this song. The background vocals and hand claps are by the fans!

ME concludes with ''Say Goodbye To Superman''. This song is so beautiful,and so sad at the same time. It took Jo Dee a year to write. It deals with the end of a marriage where a son is involved and how he will be affected when he realizes that his dad is not Superman. It is a struggle for her as well and she asks God for help because ''the man who was his Superman was my superhero, too''.

ME is a very honest record made by a very honest artist. Jo Dee Messina has returned and her heart is still right where it has always been: Right on her sleeve.
