title: A SUBLIME RECORDING.
text: Of all the recordings of Tchaikovsky's 6th Symphony I have ever heard (and I have heard to many, both live and recorded), this one ranks near the top. It combines the mastery of one of the most talented conductors in the business today (he knows how to elicit a highly emotional performance from any orchestra) with the players of one of the most preeminent virtuoso orchestras in the world. (Perhaps only the Berlin Philharmonic comes close). The pathos of Tchaikovsky's tortured life was never more profoundly clear than in the Sixth Symphony and this is a top notch rendering of this most evocative Symphony.

title: So...This Is The Real Joss Stone...WOW!
text:
"Introducing Joss Stone" may be an odd title for a third album, but then again, it does make sense. Prior to this album, singer / songwriter / budding actress Joss Stone was always a girl with talent and soul, but what she consistently lacked was personality and depth; some kind of history or consistent, genuine connection to her music (with the exceptions of "Daniel" & "Right To Be Wrong" from her sophomore album "Mind, Body & Soul"). Well that problem is clearly nowhere to be found on Joss Stone's stellar third album, which deftly combines R&B, Soul, Hip-Hop and Funk into one extremely enjoyable mix.

Unlike Joss Stone's previous albums, "Introducing Joss Stone" never lacks for energy, passion or enthusiasm, mainly because the lively instrumentation, hard-hitting percussion and musical arrangements provided by singer / producer / songwriter Raphael Saadiq, the sole mastermind behind the album's production board, work extremely well with Joss Stone's soulful, vibrant, raw vocals, adding to the overall feel-good vibe of the record and stripping it of any degree of compromise or overly commercial sheen. Not long after footballer / actor Vinnie Jones (?) is finished talking on "Change (Intro)", the previously mentioned fact is especially evident on album openers "Girl They Won't Believe It" & the anthemic "Headturner", both of them exploding with bangin' bass, thick strings, guitar strings and Joss Stone's thrilling, authoritative vocal delivery. Lead single "Tell Me `Bout It" also follows a similar route, allowing Joss Stone's gutsy vocals to roar over Raphael Saadiq's funk guitar strings and horn bursts.

However, the two inspired duets on this album are definitely the best tracks. Rapper / actor Common drops another wise ode of love on "Tell Me What We Gonna Do Now", a beautiful ballad driven by acoustic guitar and drums as Joss Stone and Common passionately profess feelings of love in typical singer / rapper fashion. Lauryn Hill also drops a complex, but still dope, verse on "Music", where she & Joss Stone profess their love for music itself through strong lyrics and more beautiful instrumentation. Other highlights include "Put Your Hands On Me", where Joss Stone's vocals burn with surprisingly unforced sexuality and urgency over Mix Master Mike's impressive turntable techniques and Raphael Saadiq's production, and "Bruised But Not Broken", where Joss Stone keeps her heart open to love in spite of the pain it's constantly given her.

All in all, this is a fine record, and easily one of the best R&B records to come out so far this year. It's a great feel-good summer record, steeped in a variety of sounds and styles that sound both old and new. It's ironic, considering the fact that nearly everything from this album - hair style, music material, overall approach, etc. - comes off as new in the case of Joss Stone. Nonetheless, great music is great music, and no overblown critical analysis can change that. 5 stars!

5 Best Tracks (IMO) (In No Order):

"Music" (feat. Lauryn Hill)

"Tell Me What We Gonna Do Now" (feat. Common)

"Tell me `Bout It"

"Headturner"

"Put Your Hands On Me"

title: Very Good cycle made great by a transcendent 3rd and 4th
text:
First off-this is not a starter Brahms set. No, if you're new to Brahms, you'd best seek out Klemperer, Haitink, Karajan or Walter. Dorati offers an extremely unique and exciting take on the Brahms cycle, and any avid, well-schooled fan of the composer would do well to acquire these. The LSO under Dorati features the distinctively incisive Eastern-European style of playing that really allows one to fully appreciate Brahms' ingenious use of counterpoint in the development sections. Textures are transparent, but not lightweight. This finer approach helps for the work of a composer whose musical compositions are so densely orchestrated they can sometimes go awry in the hands of lesser conductors...but not Dorati. Dorati submits a fine account of the First, with a transcendent first movement - his concise and direct approach helps rein in this colossal structure while he expertly maintains the movement's architectonics and seemingly inevitable momentum. The middle movements are also well executed, but unfortunately there are some problems in the finale. A senseless rush to the Coda is followed by an equally senseless deceleration at the very finish. I'm not sure what Dorati was thinking here, and it mars what for me was an otherwise excellent performance. The Second here was played by the MSO, rather than the LSO; and unfortunately that ensemble sounds markedly thinner, with hard and edgy strings. This kind of sound is all wrong for such an unconflicted work as the this, and sadly the proceedings suffer as a result. And while the inner movements are for the most part well-executed, the opening movement has some intonation and ensemble problems, and the finale is again rushed, and this time sloppy as well. It's a shame Dorati didn't record this piece with the LSO, whose deeper, richer string tone and tighter ensemble work may have helped immensely. With all that being said, the reason this disc receives 5 stars is due to the two late symphonies. Here, Dorati is in his element, carefully guiding the proceedings into perfectly balanced and constructed performances of the highest calibre. There are no issues in the finales here, or in any other movements for that matter. The results are simply stunning. The tempo choices may be a bit faster than in many other versions, but it suits the music well and helps infuse the readings with an electricity rarely seen in the somewhat thicker and murkier interpretations of other more popular conductors. Some of his choices may initially bewilder you, but there's a palpable sense of momentum and space here that often get lost under all of Brahms' layers. Dorati, like the true master of Brahms he is, avoids any such pitfalls and leaves us with two utterly towering interpretations. I remember the shock and excitement I felt upon hearing these for the first time and realizing that these were the performances I had been waiting for.
The sound is very good, with the exception of the 2nd which is due in large part the MSO's overall tone. Mercury's Living Presence series was a technological marvel in its day, and as a result these recordings still sound quite fresh almost 50 years later. This is vintage 1960s analog, with good dynamic range and a great deal of detail. It may not be flawless but it certainly never gets in the way of the music.
Highly recommended. Of the many Brahms cycles I own, and the Third and Fourth included on this cycle are at the very top of the heap. Since this is out of print and becoming very expensive, I might suggest you also consider [[ASIN:B0019C6J2G Ernest Ansermet's cycle]] on Australian Decca, which is of a similar interpretive bent and is in-print and reasonably priced.

This has been a successful commercial release. What has happened is that Bartoli has recorded a number of Vivaldi arias that have not formed part of the popular repertoire. She also filmed a television documentary that was based on her singing this obscure but interesting material. The documentary in retrospect was probably a good promotional vehicle. The CD itself comes in a small book which contains material on Vivaldi and Bartoli with lots of illustrations. It is an attractive package, and I note that Bartoli has repeated it with the recent release of a number of obscure arias by Gluck.
The first two arias on this CD are the standouts. The first is Dell aura al sussurrar which used a tune from spring one of the four seasons. The second is an aria written for a castrato Dopo un orrida procella which has an accompaniment of two french horns and has a driving pace and is a great test of any voice.
Over all it is an enjoyable CD and it recovers a style of music which although not lost has not been part of the mainstream. Even my mother and sister like it.

title: A Nice Surprise
text:
I bought this CD on a whim after getting and watching Seasons One through Three DVDs of Quantum Leap. I'm glad I did. Lots of angst has been spent by QL fans regarding the exclusion from the DVD releases of certain period pop tunes included in the original episodes (notably, Ray Charles' "Georgia"). While this complaint may be valid, it overshadows the strong and beautiful original soundtrack of the series and the lovely collaboration between Velton Ray Bunch and Scott Bakula.

The vocal pieces are reworked versions of songs that appeared in the TV broadcasts. Most of us remember the TV version of "Imagine," which the character Sam sings to his sister, Katie. This CD contains a full version that is hauntingly beautiful. (Even my husband, a John Lennon groupie, was impressed.) "Somewhere in the Night," co-written by Bakula, gets a full background, while the three signature songs from Man of La Mancha ("Don Quixote," "Dulcinea," and "Impossible Dream") are smoothed into a nice (untheatrical) medley. Even "Fate's Wide Wheel," a glam rock power ballad, gets a sweet treatment, allowing you to catch the hidden meaning in the lyrics. (Thankfully, the CD does not include "Rock the Redhead.") Bakula sounds like he's having a load of fun singing in 50's-Elvis style on "Let's Play House" and "Blue Moon of Kentucky." The first time I played these two songs, I kept looking at the liner notes to confirm that it was Bakula, and not Young Elvis, singing.

On the instrumental side, the pieces are incredibly evocative. I'm amazed at the breadth of style here; essentially, Bunch produced a movie score for each episode, appropriate to the different time period and mood of each story, from the gothic "Bite Me" to the lonely and introspective "Sam's Prayer." The Suite from Lee Harvey Oswald (for which Bunch was nominated for an Emmy, and deservedly so) is by turns creepy, stirring, and pensive (like the episode), and the familiar haunting introduction that even the casual QL fan would recognize as Sam's Theme is done in such a poignant harmonica and strings combination in "Suite From the Leap Home" that it makes you homesick for your mom just listening to it.

The CD could have done without the interview with Bakula track; it sounds dated, considering what the actor has done since QL, and I would have preferred it being replaced by more music, maybe the gospelly, "He'll Be There," from Pool House Blues.

Of course, given the lush orchestration, the evocative original music, and the pleasure of a Broadway calibre voice singing Lennon and Elvis, it's probably ironic that my 4 year old insists on listening to Dean Stockwell's "Alphabet Rap" a thousand times. This version isn't as utterly awful as the episode version (kid voices carry it on the CD), but my CD player's next track button gets a workout when the 4 year old isn't around. Although, after about the hundredth time, it starts being more funny than annoying.

If you like soundtracks, this is a nice one to get. It's got a good balance of nice songs, done well. Even if you skip the spoken-word tracks (Saga Sell, Conversation, and Alphabet Rap), it's worth listening to.

title: Extraordinary! - Another Savall Success
text:
Here we have the second reissue of, by far, the best performance of Handel's Water Music and Fireworks music to be found anywhere! At the time of this writing the first re-issue of this recording is selling for $224 here on Amazon just to show you how valued this performance is. Here the Alia Vox engineer, Nicolas de Beco, has taken this 16 bit 44.1 kHz sampled recording from 1993 and re-mastered it into a suburb surround (multi-channel 5.0) SACD. No information is given as to weather this was an original multi-channel recording or if DSP was employed to add the additional channels, but the results are superb! This transfer makes this recording even more attractive than the original which was already at the top of its class. My only wish is that Jordi Savall would have re-recording this music in true high definition SACD sound which would have made this recording even more attractive. What makes Jordi Savall's performance so much better is that it shows the joy of the occasion much better than any other performance I've heard. Some might find his pacing a little fast, but I find it exciting and thrilling.

IN COMPARISON TO OTHER SACD RECORDINGS
I have other SACD recordings of Handel's Water Music and Fireworks music but they pale in comparison to Jordi Savall's joyful performance. For instance the Aradia Ensemble on a Naxos SACD is one of the worst recordings I've ever heard. The problem with the Aradia Ensemble recording is that the engineers placed the microphones too far from the orchestra so it seems as if the listener is sitting at the back of the church. I don't know about you, but if I pay premium prices for an SACD I want a front row seat or even a seat in the middle of the orchestra, but not a seat 100 feet away! This recording is also plagued by a boring performance from the Acadia Ensemble. The other Handel Water and Fireworks music on SACD is the one by L'Art Dell Arco on CPO that just came out. This performance is good but again the recording engineers have ruined this SACD by choosing an acoustically dead venue to record in!

CONCLUSION
Thank God Jordi Savall's recording was made in the acoustically rich sounding Chateau de Cardona and Jordi's group gives a passionate performance. Listen to the Bourree from the second suite (Track 19) and you'll find one of the most delectable gems of this performance. Also, the brass is particularly gorgeous in this recording. THIS IS A MUST HAVE SACD!

FYI - I'm still waiting for a new multi-channel SACD recording of Vivaldi's Four Seasons from Jordi Savall. That would be the ultimate!!

title: This was their year, a year too late...
text:
This album, the swan song of a much-venerated but misunderstood English band, is a masterpiece. The Zombies saw their greatest success as a singles band on this side of the Atlantic. Singles were still the bread-and-butter for virtually all English bands in the '60s. The Who, The Beatles, The Rolling Stones, even progressive rock bands like Jethro Tull recorded singles separately from LP material. LPs were too expensive for most teenaged consumers; the 45 and the EP were the order of the day. One of the problems The Zombies faced was that their songs and arrangements were just too sophisticated for for the marketplace. Additionally, visa problems prevented them from capitalizing on their successes in America. After "Tell Her No" charted in the states nothing more was heard from them over her until 1968 when "Odessey and Oracle" was released nearly a year after the band had broken up. It was concieved as a final artistic statement. The production wasn't as fully realised as a Rod Argent and Chris White, the band's main songwriters, would've liked: a mellotron was used in place of an orchestra. No problem there, Argent was an adept keyboardist.

Recorded at Abbey Road Studios at roughly the same time The Beatles were waxing "Sergeant Pepper" and Pink Floyd were cutting their debut LP ("The Piper at the Gates of Dawn") there is not a bad song here, from the opening "?Care of Cell 44" and "A Rose for Emily" (the lyrics based on a short story by William Faulkner) to "This Will Be Our Year" and "Time of the Season." The melodies, vocal harmponies and instrumentation employed to craft this fine batch of pop songs will leave you humming them an hour after the first hearing.

title: Motown Returns A Favour
text:
Cunningly recycling a batch of album tracks by some of Motown's most prominent artists, recorded over a period of dozen years, the compilers have come up with another winner with this clutch of Beatles songs, which plays through with surprising cohesiveness. The Beatles loved Motown, and here they return the favour.

Stevie Wonder's We Can Work It Out is probably the stand-out listen, with an exuberance that made it a natural choice for a single in 1971, and one can also detect his influence in then-partner Syreeta's definitive cover version of the usually over-treacled She's Leaving Home. The Temptations' Hey Jude, from Puzzle People, comes with a suitably distinctive Norman Whitfield production, and Marvin Gaye's Yesterday is also a highlight. The Four Tops are called upon to deliver cabaret versions of three Paul McCartney ballads. Though none have the classic hallmark Levi Stubbs touch, Eleanor Rigby comes closest.

Both the original Supremes tracks come from a 1964 curio entitled A Little Bit Of Liverpool and ought to be great. They have lots of gusto and fire, and are great fun, but the sound is muddy and the production sounds hurried, leaving a sense of what might have been with a little more trouble and care. Diana Ross appears again on Let It Be's The Long And Winding Road. Come Together comes from the 1970 incarnation of the Supremes led by Jean Terrell and is an excellent Frank Wilson production.

George Harrison's Something is well handled by Martha Reeves and the Vandellas (from Natural Resources) and Gladys Knight and the Pips' version of Let It Be is another stand-out, equaling Aretha's version of Paul McCartney's tribute to his mother Mary. Smokey Robinson and the Miracles' And I Love Her is rescued from the rather overlooked album What Love Has Joined Together. It sounds just how you imagine.

The final three tracks are from the post-Beatle period. Diana Ross does a syrupy version of John Lennon's Imagine; Jr Walker blows a fine horn on Wings' My Love from 1976; and Edwin Starr gets gospelly on the rousing George Harrison classic My Sweet Lord, ending the album on an uplifting note

title: Stimulating music, expertly performed
text:
James V. Maiello, Fanfare magazine

Paul Hindemith’s works for violin and piano reflect the composer’s “insider” experience as a violinist and violist in orchestral and chamber settings, including his years in the renowned Amar-Hindemith quartet. Like his other chamber works, the violin sonatas are musically challenging and rewarding for both players, and hearing them together (in chronological order) on one recording allows listeners to hear his development as a composer clearly. Hindemith’s music receives the royal treatment by a duo of exceptional virtuosity and musicality. Violinist Roman Mints has a number of highly acclaimed recordings to his name, and Alexander Kobrin has been in demand as a soloist since winning the Van Cliburn competition in 2005.
The Sonata for Violin and Piano in EI (1918) is very much a late Romantic work, but one can certainly make out the beginnings of Hindemith’s trademark contrapuntal style. Mints and Kobrin navigate this transitional style deftly, tempering Romantic excess with Modernist objectivity while maintaining a rich expressive palate. For example, phrases are well shaped without histrionics, and the underlying counterpoint is allowed to come through, especially in the piano part. Also dating from 1918, before Hindemith turned to atonality, the Sonata for Violin and Piano in D receives similar treatment. In the elegiac second movement, Mints’s playing is hauntingly beautiful but still fresh. The Schumann-esque middle section is especially evocative, due in large part to Kobrin’s perceptive, idiomatic flourishes.
The Sonata for Viola d’Amore and Piano (1922) is, for me, the highlight of the entire recording, not least because it is a rare treat to hear the viola d’amore itself, and even rarer to hear it played so well. Mints and Kobrin approach the Bachian parody that opens the sonata with a knowing smirk, wearing its conventions lightly. The centerpiece of the work is the slow movement, which Mints treats more dryly than others have (e.g., Gunter Teufell). This is an intelligent choice, given the style in which Hindemith was writing at the time. A dissonant, highly contrapuntal finale caps the sonata, played with sizzling, snarling verve by both players. By 1935, Hindemith had developed the neo-tonal style for which he is best known, based on his own “series” of harmonic and melodic hierarchies. The Sonata for Violin and Piano in E is an early product of this style, full of the composer’s idiosyncratic, lilting melodies in compound meter and twinkling obbligato lines in the right hand of the piano, quartal harmonies and falling gestures. Mints and Kobrin are in fine fettle, spinning lyrical lines plaintively and dancing their way through the thorniest contrapuntal passages. Kobrin in particular deserves high praise for rendering Hindemith’s dizzying piano parts with pristine clarity.
Two shorter works round out the disc, the Trauermusik (1936) and the Meditation from Nobilissima visione (1938); both were adapted for violin and piano by the composer from their original orchestral versions. Although it seems odd to hear the Trauermusik on violin instead of viola, here it exploits the lower range of the violin and showcases the lovely sound Mints achieves in the lower and middle registers on his instruments. It is a boon to have these pieces collected on one recording, and to have such fine performances of them at that is even better. The sound quality is crystalline, and keeping it on the dry side enhances these focused, tasteful readings. Mints and Kobrin meet Hindemith on his own terms. They refuse to overplay the music and account for the composer’s clear aesthetic preferences. This surely cannot be wholly instinctive, and the players should be commended for their informed, thoughtful approach. After many years spent studying Hindemith’s music and his pedagogical and philosophical writings, I cannot help but think this is exactly how the composer would have wanted these works played. This is a must-have recording for Hindemith fans.

title: Hubbard At His Best
text:
I have been waiting for the re-issue of this CD for years, and for years I have haunted the stores and scoured the internet in what had been a futile search. Finally the moment I knew had to come arrived.
I own a number of Freddie Hubbard albums, but I consider Sweet Return to be Hubbard at his best. I first bought it on cassette back in 1983 when it was originally issued, immediately liked it and wore out the tape as the years went by.
Hubbard is ably backed on Sweet Return by jazz giants Lew Tabackin on tenor sax and flute, Joanne Brackeen on piano, and Eddie Gomez on bass. The music ranges from frenetic on Calypso Fred, to smooth and romantic on the jazz classic Misty. My favorites are the title cut, which is a magnificent showcase of Hubbard's virtuosity, Whistling Away In The Dark, The Night Has A Thousand Eyes, and the Brackeen composition, Heidi-B, which showcases her stunning piano play, provides a vehicle for Tabackin to show off on his flute and gives Hubbard a launching pad from which to take us soaring to the musical stratosphere.
Since this CD arrived, I have played it over and over again, enjoying it just as much as I did when I first heard it nearly twenty years ago. This is one CD that belongs in every serious jazz lover's collection.

title: An interesting idea but...
text: Concept albums seem to be either brilliant (like "Them" by King Diamond) or awful (like "Music from the Elder" by Kiss.) This one sad to say, isn't exactly brilliant. It's easy to see why Geffen rejected this. It's simply weak and wasn't worth risking money to promote. A concept album is only as good as the songs are and the songwriting simply isn't there. The opener is a real yawner and sets the pace "Do you beleive in religion" which seems to be about televangelism. It's been done already, many, many times. ("Miracle Man" by Ozzy and "Send Me Your Money" by Suicidal Tendencies were both far superior.) The generic tunes like "Sooner or Later" sound at best like an 80's high school garage band trying to imitate Bon Jovi. It's probably safe to say it was too soon in Nelson's career to take such a departure. They are incredibly talented but musicians need a lot of time to mature to be able to write on that level. In all fairness, they probably hadn't reached that depth yet. Stories are the hardest thing to write anyway, so at least they were brave enough to try. I wouldn't be surprised if they did a concept album in the future that was a bulls-eye. They are tremendous song-writers without a doubt. Maybe they should have gotten some more commercial hits under their belts first. Obviously Geffen was right because the album that Nelson released instead of this, "Because They Can" still remains their best by far. "Life" is also a fantastic album. Pick one of those up instead, unless you already own all of their other CDs.

title: The Greatest Conductor in Music History
text:
I was a very young child when I had my first introduction to Leopold Stokowski. Bugs Bunny had donned a long white wig and tuxedo and with his head held high, walked through what one assumed to be a great symphony orchestra. As he passed each of the instrumentalists, they would gasp, "Leopold!!, Leopold, Leopold!!!" He approached the orchestra's conductor, who, shaking as though he were before God Himself, meekly handed Bugs his baton. My mother was roaring with laughter as I asked her about Bugs' disguise and who he was supposed to be. "It's Leopold Stokowski, the greatest conductor that ever lived!" She then added,"I guess they're calling him just 'Leopold' to avoid any possible legal entanglement". "Wow", I thought, "...the greatest conductor that ever lived....." Stokowski was 95 years old when he died some years ago and even today, whenever I ask anyone knowledgeable in music who was the greatest conductor they always answer....'Stokowski'.

What made Stokowski so great? There are several reasons: notable among them is that his conducting never lost its vitality. Works he conducted in his eighties are as bright and vital as under the baton of a thirty year old! Stokowski also tried many sound innovations, most of them successful; for example, he turned the cellos out so the f holes faced the audience. The result was a brilliance in bass sound never heard before. Perhaps his most unforgettable achievement was when he collaborated with Disney on Fantasia. Due to Stokowski, the soundtrack to Fantasia was recorded in stereo before stereo had been officially invented!! Once Stokowski worked with an orchestra over a period of time, that orchestra was put on the musical map. Philadelphia always had a great orchestra, but once Stokowski worked with it, it became indisputably the finest orchestra in the world. And then there was Houston......who would have ever thought that a town like Houston could produce one of the finest orchestras anywhere, yet, when Stokowski touched them, that is what happened. Most importantly, that old cliché "The proof of the pie is in the eating" applies here. When I listen to a recording of any work, even if they be brilliant interpretations by conductors of pure genius, when I listen to the same work conducted by Stokowski, somehow the Stokowski is ALWAYS just a bit better. Anyone who questions that statement, I invite you to try it and judge for yourself whether or not I'm correct.

This Shostakovich 11th is unsurpassed! A couple other reviewers seem to think the sound quality needs improving.........perhaps, but for me it satisfies. The dynamic range of this work; the passion, the anger, the sorrow, the excitement.....it's all there! So what if the bells are cut a little short at the end? After being taken through such a spellbinding musical adventure, I find the sudden cut off at the end leaves me transfixed as I contemplate the musical experience I've just had. One of the reviewers feels the Rostropovich recording to be superior. Indeed, Rostropovich knew Shostakovich personally, (Shostakovich in fact wrote his cello concerto for Rostropovich). The Rostropovich recording is newer so the sound quality is more advanced and, true to form, Rostropovich puts his own personal stamp on his interpretation giving this symphony a more Russian sound. It is, in fact, a beautiful and fully satisfying recording; but superior to Stokowski? I don't think so.

title: Near Perfect Album.
text:
Los Lobos continue on "The Neighborhood" the artistic development, the group embarked on "How Will the Wolf Survive" and continued on "By The Light of the Moon."

Like its predecessor, the album is characterized by strong songs written by David Hidalgo and Louis Perez. However, producer Larry Hirsch together with the group has created a sound that is both highly contemporary and respectful to the group's roots in the traditional Spanish Mexican.

Hidalgo's and Perez' songs are very varied and provides space for both the melodic and instrumental - all members are excellent musicians.

The band's love for the blues is highligted on "Down By the River Bed" where John Hiatt is to find in the chorus. Also "I Walk Alone" and "The Neighborhood" belong to the blues category.

The melodic and folk-inspired characterize strongest songs of the album, such as "Emily," "Take My Hand," "The Giving Tree" and not least the beautiful "Little John of God" where Levon Helm convincingly joins in with his vocals. Another favorite is the Lovin Spoonful-like "Deep Dark Hole".

A really great album on which actually only the group's cover of "Georgia Slop" disappoints

title: Hendrix the master
text:
If any music lover wishes to break into the works of Jimi Hendrix then this CD is the perfect place to start. To certain uninitiated newcomers there are songs in the Hendrix repertoire that may seem daunting, both in musical complexity and in sheer length. This is where the Experience Hendrix CD comes into its own.

Hendrix contributed a massive wealth of guitar anthems to the world of rock and some of the best are on show here. 'Voodoo Child', 'Purple Haze' and 'All Along The Watchtower' being some of the best known. However this is not to say that rocking guitar solos was all that Jimi did. He also slows the mood with the more laid back 'Castles Made Of Sand', 'Bold As Love' and the beautifully lonesome 'The Wind Cries Mary'.

Jimi Hendrix's career was tragically short, spanning only 4 years. But in that time he managed to unleash some of the best rock songs ever made. To any music fans reading I have one word to say, 'enjoy'.

title: A Greater Foundation
text:
Ironically enough, the bandmates' previous endeavor featured a song that would almost eerily predict future events of band members: Phil, Nick, Josh, and Jordan. Since there's no getting away from talking about the prior giant of a band, I might as well talk about that first. As I Lay Dying, one of the metalcore gods (I don't use that term lightly). In an oversaturated and underestimated genre, the masterful musicians in As I Lay Dying kept improving and making music that defined said genre, but never defined themselves. While many small bands came and went, As I Lay Dying, with only a handful of others, survived the metaphorical "metalcore purge" following its loss in popularity and talents after hitting the late 2000s. This band seemed to have everything going for them until its founding member dismantled his life and with it shattered the lives of his closest friends. He made a mistake...many mistakes... and this loss of character from the once noble and lovable Lambesis was heartbreaking for the people who knew him prior to this transformation. Some radical fans even supported the man's criminal acts and made comments on how they wish someone was murdered because "she was probably a b**** and deserved it". Then you have Lambesis himself slandering his bandmates to paint himself in a nicer light before prison; with this, you get more Lambesis supporters and more hate against his fellow bandmates who did nothing wrong. I do not condemn him, nor support him, but it is important you know what the band has against them, and the hate they've had to endure from emotionally disturbed "fans" of their previous band. "Sometimes we have to watch our whole lives fall apart, before we can rebuild them again."

Josh, Nick, Phil, & Jordan immediately decided to start a new band with a new name following the arrest of Lambesis. Thus, Wovenwar was born (Originally Wovenhearts, but that wasn't metal enough). At first fans suspected Josh to be taking over all lead vocals, but it was later revealed they added a new bandmate to the formula. Shane Blay of Oh Sleeper was a longtime friend of Nick Hipa and the rest of the band, so it was a no brainer to recruit this talented guy. Now with 3 guitarists and 2 vocalists, the band sought to explore things they never had the luxury of exploring before. With this comes one of the best and freshest releases this past year.

This album is not what I expected...not at all. From `All Rise' I thought the band was going to pursue predictable radio metal. I'm so happy the album branches out as much as it does after their single. Wovenwar musically, still retains a lot of what you'd expect to hear from the guys. It's very similar to metalcore, but explores so much more ground and builds itself so much more complex. I find it especially successful in its exploration of melodic lines. What it loses in overall brutality, it gains in dynamics and diversity. The songs are very varied; they are an exploration of what the members were unable to do for years because of genre constraint. Honestly though, musically, I think these are seriously the best songs the band has ever written. A huge standout has to be the presence of many more solos from nick and fewer breakdowns; also, you can actually hear the bass in the mix and it has a vital role to the overall song structures (Bass tone is fantastic this time around). Vocally, I have some gripes, but I find the album to be 100% perfect on Nick's, Josh's, Jordan's, and Phil's end. With this change in sound, and a primarily clean vocal presence, it's sure to off-put the fans of the original band who were more fans of hardcore than metal. Let's be honest though, these are people who see the word hardcore as a positive and not a genre. If you're not already listening to Tool, Mastodon, Steven Wilson etc... you're probably not interested. These are songs from guys who have been through a lot and these tracks have passion and suffering interlaced in every aspect of their album.

The mixing on this album is great and the harmonies between Josh and Shay really sound incredible with some quality speakers or cans; shane's usually smooth vocals compliment josh's sometimes more abrasive and aggressive cleans. And for those that are afraid there will be no harsh vocals, they are spread across the album (Archers has the most). I think this is something that can appeal to almost anyone. The lyrics hit home and the songs are heavy, but accessible to people who usually don't listen to heavier genres. Plus, you get the treat of hearing the other-worldly acoustic segments on this album. Believe me when I tell you Shane's falsetto is easily the smoothest in the genre. I found myself wanting to simultaneously headbang and dance during Archer's chorus. Some lines hypnotize me with melody, some make me headbang, and some make me want to sing at the top of my lungs. It's a great combination.

Shane is a capable vocalist. His falsettos and softer vocals during acoustic and bridge segments are hands down the best this genre has to offer. It is his strongest feature next to his harsh vocals. He's truly a beautiful singer. My gripe, however, is that the songs where Josh takes over vocal duties for a chorus or a line I think "Wow, that sounds great!" and it makes me wonder why more songs didn't explore this dynamic (Josh's vocal scoop on Ruined Ends is orgasmic). Shane's voice is great, but sometimes he becomes repetitive in vocal texture during 1 or 2 chorus sections. I would give Shane 100% of the beautiful melodic segments, but Josh really shines during his few chorus/line debuts; it maintains the flow, but gives a great contrast. I think a good thing to explore for the next album would be messing around with prominent vocals in the mix per line. The moments where the two's voices weave back and forth are fantastic. The latter songs on the album seem to juggle with this a bit more. Josh has really improved vocally, and you can tell when you see the band live. Matter of Time, where Josh sings the majority of the song sounds fantastic live and is one of the standout tracks on this album. This is an amazing band live and I can easily see them becoming big, but from a different crowd than their previous bands. As of writing this, I've listened to the album in whole over 20 times. It hasn't lost its hold on my mind since I first heard it two weeks ago.

Despite me calling the mix great, the biggest issue with this album is the mixing, but not in the way you'd imagine. The mixing handles dynamics and soundstage wonderfully. The issue however, is that depending on how expensive your listening rig is + whether or not the source is lossless determines how much of the song you actually hear. To people listening on some cheap $10 earbuds or to a 120kbps upload, you'll be missing a ton of the guitarwork and bass in the mix. This is bound to happen when you have 2 vocalists and 3 guitars begging for attention at the same time. Many AILD fans coming to this album might find it much more simplified and less passionate than past albums, but they're not hearing the full album. Listening to the album on about 7 different sources really helps one understand this dilemma. I observed cheaper sources only allowed the rhythm guitar to take the lead, while moving up the quality scale opened the soundstage, and instrument isolation increased. The 2 lead guitars weave themselves together in really interesting ways during each song and it's a shame that so many people will miss how intricate the members truly made the album now that they have a 3rd guitar that covers rythym.

Sweeping from melodic, to heavy, to technical, to bombastic, to everything you'd expect from a talented group of guys and more! Give this a listen from start to finish and you'll definitely hear something new you've never quite heard. It's touching on new territory, but I can easily see Wovenwar truly dominating their field by the 2nd album. Much like the masterful Mastodon releases a different style album every time and still makes it theirs and loved by all, I believe Wovenwar shares the same magic. They just need to explore the music a bit more, get more experimental and really weave a band that stands apart from their past. I can't wait to see what they come up with next!

I give this an album a 5/5. For clean vocal metal, Once More `Round The Sun is the only other recent album I'm willing to rate as highly.

title: A great intoduction to a fantastic artist.

I especially like "Redemption Song" because of the very soulful way Mr. Marley expresses his spiritual and political beliefs. It is a very profound song. All of the songs, however, have very good lyrics and a mellow, easy-going pace. These factors contribute to make this an excellent meditaion CD. Bob Marley, thank you for making this great music and touching so many people.

title: Death Angel alumni pull off a solid record
text:
Only true classics deserve 5 stars, whereas only corporate drivel deserves 1 star, like a Britney Spears album. The Organization's self-titled debut is a surprisingly good, consistent and well-produced record. Three and a half stars.

If you're a fan of thrash demons Death Angel, then you'll be familiar with this lineup, as it is pretty much the same band without the former's lead singer (Mark Osegueda). The style of music is certainly metal, but not thrash, so if you like Death Angel this won't automatically appeal to you.

Guitarist Rob Cavestany takes over on vocals, and he does a wonderful job. I actually prefer him to Mark. His singing style and attitude is a bit like Rage Against the Machine, and the background harmonies provided by the other band members are excellent. It's almost Van Halen-ish. In any case, the vocals fit the music perfectly.

What's neat is that every song on here sounds different, mixing various styles of music (alternative, funk), but still staying metal. The arrangements are far from simplistic, but still pack plenty of catchy melody. It sounds a little bit like a really heavy version of Kiss mixed in with some Rage Against the Machine and Jane's Addiction. It's hard to describe -- I haven't heard anything quite like it.

None of the tracks really standout -- they are all pretty good and listenable. If I had to pick, probably 'Brainstorm' and 'Wonder' are my favorites. There is also a cool instrumental on the record, 'Withdrawal'. Still, there are no surefire hits here, probably one reason why the band never caught on with the public. And while the production is good, I would prefer it to be a bit more raw -- the polished sound hurts the record's longterm replayability.

Altogether a solid effort, marking a very interesting and original departure from Death Angel. They also made another record 'Savor The Flavor' in 1995. But with Death Angel now reformed (2001) and putting out records, the Organization is probably over. Nevertheless, this is one of the few good metal records made in the nineties that should not be overlooked.

title: The Sphinx - Can's Ultimate!!
text:
The 1970's, in comparison with subsequent decades, appears to have been more innovatively daring than most people realise. This is probably due to the negative, anti-intellectual legacy of Punk Rock that saw music of the seventies prior to its own appearance as ultimately boring. If then we include the developments of Punk Rock and the so called New Wave into the sum total of seventies creativity, which of course we must, then we have an extraordinary decade of music indeed. At the top of that prodigious heap of creativity I would line up maybe ten albums that represent the best of the best; Can's Ege Bamyasi is one of those.

After many years of listening, the lyrics still elude me for the most part. On the opening track Pinch, Damo's voice scats and blends like an instrument, adding to a texture that heaves and bustles like a breathing entity and just like the whole album, Pinch is a complete enigma that has succeeded in keeping the Sphinx's riddle locked inside it. Over nine minutes long of a percolating, jam-like groove, the only discernable word is the very last one that Damo breathes sensuously into the microphone; "Pinch". . .so typical of the bands humour.

The constant movement of Pinch is followed by the seductive dreamscape of Sing Swan Song, one of the most beautiful pieces of music to exist and as such it would be sacrilegious to even try and describe it!

Vitamin C is infectious, the jazz drumming of Jaki Liebezeit sets up a groove you wish could last forever, its receding departure only forgiven by the incoming drifting cloud, the surreal veil that acts as a curtain raiser to Soup.

Soup is the longest and most aggressive track on the album where nothing is normal but everything is edgy, moody and sinister; all the jazz-rock-funk-avant-garde elements are indeed thrown in. Its impressionistic kaleidoscope brutally imposed upon by sonic slabs of distorted organ that brings either Panzer divisions or reconstructed Germany into the living room (watch out for the live mine sticking out of the churned up concrete!).

The remaining three tracks are further evidence of Can's ability to conjure up magic out of thin air and complete a work of collective genius. Ege Bamyasi is Can's greatest achievement but like all their work its organic, expansive vision and muscular sensuality, makes it a nominee not just for one of the best in the 1970's, but of the twentieth century!

Be sure to get the remastered edition (not to be confused with SACD).

text: My lukewarm reaction to this CD is due in part to my own expectations, so keep that in mind before you place too much weight on my opinions. First the good news: the singer does have a lovely voice. Now the bad news: the band does not have a lot of original ideas. Both the cover art and the things I had heard about this record made me expect a pretty authentic-sounding Middle Eastern flavored "world music" CD, or at least a reasonably interesting stab in that direction (A good example of this is some of Ofra Haza's recordings: they blend cultures in a very original way). But alas, none of that was to be found here. This is really a heavy rock band which has woven into the songs a few trite and stereotypical caricatures of what middle eastern music is. The ideas they come up with tend to fall into the bland and unimaginative category, though occasionally do border on embarrassing. title: the future
text:
Note: review of prior material as well as the album listed...
I've followed "Pat the Bunny," also formerly known as "Johnny Hobo" - the creative force behind Ramshackle Glory,
Wingnut Dishwashers Union, and the former "Johnny Hobo and the Freight Trains" - for some time now, before and after his
time in rehab. He is very open and frank about his experience with rehab; both in his music, online presence, and in
emails and therefore I would assume he would be just as open and frank in person.

Prior to the most recent releases under Ramshackle Glory, many of Pat's singer-songwriter songs are written in an
acoustic, folk-punk style. Some of these recordings feature layers of instrumentation such as horns, bass, piano and even
the occasional violin and saw, while others are just Pat and the guitar, that which he plays as viciously as he sings.
Both the group
and solo tracks maintain a raw, poignant originality accompanied by a rare ferocity and passion. While certain descriptions
may begin to sound like they are bordering on a review of a hardcore band, make no mistake: if anything, Pat has crafted
his own brand of
hardcore folk-punk.

Pat's often emotive,
introspective lyrics are characterized by
underlying themes of addiction, politics, social injustices and activism, and represent the absolute
here-and-now of what would be deemed folk-punk. The messages are straight forward
but he wears his heart on his sleeve, harmonizing rage with the intimate details of his life poetically and fearlessly.
And while often discontented and agonized, his work is far more than angst-spewing and soap boxing.
Each passionate piece includes delicate gems of simple but
profound wisdom that echo the socio-political sentiments and Anarcho ideals of Emma Goldman,
Albert Parsons and Karl Marx, accented and intensified with a staunch humanism and laced with the spirit of Ghandhi's brilliance.
"As long as there's a law peace will be a crime."
His pragmatic idealism is balanced by an element of self-deprecation, and bottled within both the personal and
socially reflected angst is always the presence of hope, all of which a new generation of disenchanted youth can relate
to. Highlighted among these themes is the complex struggle of reconciling them - an illustration of an impoverished
recovering addict and an activist at the same time trying to rectify that reality. Pat approaches the strife behind
balancing the struggle and necessary ongoing focus of self-improvement and the moral responsibility to engage in
direct grassroots activism; the difficult practice of living behind your words, with both delicacy and vehemence.

Tracks are beautifully crafted with personal strife and pain, harmoniously set to the backdrop of fury at
injustice. While common punk rock sentiments, the nuisances of Pat's writing are reminiscent of Jeff Ott of the
late punk band Fifteen. Ott had a similar relentless dedication to self-improvement and activism, perseverance and
living out his words, and laden throughout his music were the similar themes, undertaken with passion and power.
Pat picks up where
Fifteen left off for a new generation of disenchanted youth, holding himself to high standards (to which he admits he
often fails to meet, therefore not sounding too pontifical), and while he doesn't quite expect the same out of his
audience, he begs it, hoping for a better world. He frequently conveys what are
universal struggles
among artists of all kinds, so you don't have to be a recovering addict to relate. Though consistently committed, Pat's
albums are not completely absent of occasional elements of comic relief and lighter themes. Wingnut Dishwashers Union
covers a hilarious version of "Ain't Nobobody's Business," and in "Stop Being So Cool & Get Silly" Pat proclaims "If
you aren't dead then you might as well be dancin'" and "after the revolution every intersection will be a dance floor!" and
some mention of "Rest in P-Funk" being his choice of epitaph.

Although already on the map, Ramshackle Glory has gained Pat and its members more national notoriety and presents
a more polished, produced sound; as well as a dash of ska-punk not present in his previous
efforts. Distant, lonely brass instruments are replaced by more upbeat trumpets and even the accordion.
Ramshackle Glory is testament to Pat's journey and advancement as a songwriter, and may very well be more
accessible and fitted to a much deserved wider audience.

Whatever the case, as long as Pat stays on the tough road of recovery, we are destined to see much more from him.
The maturity of his current work is already a testament to a prolific career.

Jamie Albert
Concierge Preferred

title: 5 for content, 3 for production
text:
I must begin by stating I hate what Rick Rubin did to this album. I expected so much more from the producer of "Danzig" and "Reign In Blood"... he butchered this otherwise spectacular effort. It sounds like it was recorded through Saran Wrap; the mix of this album can be described as nothing less than rape.

That out of the way, extreme kudos to Metallica. After the abyssmal crap that they called "St. Anger", this is the most impressive piece of work from them since "And Justice For All". There were no short-cuts in songwriting here (unlike the black album and the worse "Load" and "Reload" albums); the boys definitely earned their money with the creation of "Death Magnetic". Hooks, tightness, power, emotion, and headbanging inspiration are abundant. This is the Metallica we remember from "Ride The Lightning", "Master Of Puppets" (my personal fave), and "And Justice For All". A wonderful and overdue comeback for the gods of metal.

I'm giving 5 stars for the album, but 3 for the crappy I'm-going-through-a-what-do-I-do-for-a-living-again? phase of producer Rick Rubin. Anticipating Metallica's next work, hoping it follows the winning formula they re-discovered with the brilliant "Death Magnetic"!

title: Pretty good.  Kinda grows on you
text:
This is the type of cd that you have to listen to more than once. I had heard the first two songs on the radio, and after deciding that Rich Girl was the coolest song ever and singing it all day at work, I went out and bought the cd. I popped it in my car cd player and I admit, I was pretty disappointed. I had loved Tragic Kingdom, and Return to Saturn, but these songs were completely unlike any of her older music. If I had rated the cd then, I would have undoubtedly given it one star.

However, then I listened to it again. And again. And again. Going to work. Coming home from work. Going out with friends. And each time I'd like each song a little more. Even the ones I really hated at first like Hollaback Girl and Bubble Pop Electric. They've actually become the most fun to sing to while driving. I think if it weren't for the really awful lyrics, a lot of people would like the music more, because really, the beats and instrumentals aren't all that bad. But, I mean, that song Harajuku Girls? You've got to be kidding me. It's terrible. ("Harajuku Girls, you got the wicked style. I like the way that you are. I am your biggest fan. Super Kawaii! That means super cute in Japanese!")

Being Japanese myself (well, my mom is anyway). My mouth just sort of hung open when it started playing. I was like omg. She's not seriously singing about japanese girls. What the heck is her problem? Does she actually think that's a compliment? What if I started singing a song that said. "oh trashy white girls. You got some wicked style! I like the way that you are! And your dyed blond hair!" seriously. It's offensive. And what's even more annoying is that tune is pretty catchy. The lyrics are just horrendous.

Anyway, I'm not going to rant and rave about how terrified I was when I heard that song, because the rest of the cd is pretty good. I still really miss the older music of No Doubt, but for her first solo album, at least it's definitely... unique for lack of any better description.

title: This won't leave you "cold".. haha!.... whatever....
text:
As many bands before it, Cold fills this record with few hard songs and lots of power-ballads. This is not necessarily a bad thing if done right, it's just that I remember days when bands went the other way around : few power-ballads and lots of hard songs. Fortunately, Cold does it right, if not in an original way. There is more melody here than on previous records, and if that means giving up on lots of hard songs, then I guess that's alright.
The 2 best songs on this album are, without a doubt, Stupid Girl and Remedy (not power-ballads...). As for Cold's best song ever, I'm torn between those 2 and End of the World from 13 Ways To Bleed Onstage. Remedy is the kind of song that's short and sweet. It's right to the point and does the job quite well. Kill the Music Industry is another exemple, although it's not as good (and not so subtle !). Stupid Girl is the first single, so you probably heard it. I've mentionned the power-ballads before, there are plenty on here. Wasted Years, Rain Song, Sad Happy... All well done, for sure. Original, not so. If you're tired of bands doing this, move along. If you can't get enough, this will satisfy you plenty. Especially Suffocate, the best power-ballad on here, in my opinion.
So where does this record stand compared to previous ones ? I'm still not sure. End of the World, Remedy or Stupid Girl ? I have a small preference towards the last two, but maybe that's just because they're new. Only time will time. Final words : I'd say Year of the Spider is worth checking out, just don't expect anything groundbreaking.

title: All Stars In The Sky.
text:
A remarkable 2007 CD from the Ryko/Filmworks label, "Say Amen, Somebody" is taken from a 1980 concert.

Thomas Dorsey and Willie Mae Ford Smith are among the Gospel greats featured. Both were in their 80's when the recording and a film of the concert were made. From the film (get the DVD,too) you see that both needed help getting on stage.

It was the only help they needed, however. Dorsey and Smith knew where their power came from and they let their faith take over. One can only imagine what these two sounded like in their prime, some fifty years earlier.

Now to the CD.

"Take My Hand, Precious Lord." Dorsey's most famous song. He has fine accompaniment with a heavenly choir on this rendition. Sweet sounding keyboards play off Dorsey and the choir.

"Jesus Dropped The Charges." The O'Neal Twins shake the rafters with this rave-up. Their dynamic band keeps pace.

"Canaan." Here she is. That unstoppable force of nature, Willie Mae Ford Smith. With "Canaan" she brings in all home, puts in all to rest. We hear Wilie Mae start slowly by making a few remarks. She laughs a bit and begins to sing. The choir joins her and the keyboard players (organ and piano) come in. As previously noted, she had to be helped on stage. Now no earthly army could take her off. She sings of those gone on and looks forward to when she'll see them again. She brings down the house.

Also of note: "It's A Highway To Heaven" and "He Choose Me". Both by the O'Neal Twins.

The CD includes Mahalia Jackson's version of "Take My Hand, Precious Lord."

Dorsey and Smith are singing in a different choir now. They took that highway the O'Neal Twins sing about. For now, we'll have to get by with hearing them on "Say Amen, Somebody".

Great CD. Loaded with heart and soul.

We'll rate it 5-Stars and add a few million for good measure.

title: Adore is a fantastic album. This is a review of the pressing, not the music.
text:
I’m so frustrated and disappointed with this pressing. 😫 I have tried to purchase Adore (reissue) on vinyl multiple times, received multiple replacement LPs and every single time there has been some sort of defect in them. The first was warped. I got a replacement. It was warped. So I gave up at the time and just decided to wait to try again later.

Last year I bought a copy at my local record shop. Got it home, gave it a spin and got to "Behold! The Night Mare". Toward the last 1/3 of the song, I hear a "pop" every rotation for a good portion of the song. Not the normal surface noise of vinyl.

So the store ordered me a replacement. I took it home. I got to the same spot of "Behold! The Night Mare" and it starts "popping" again! So I just retuned it and gave up a second time.

Well, I really want Adore on vinyl, so I ordered another copy from Amazon. It arrived and looked great. Packaging was pristine with no dents or issues. Both Side A/B/C sound great. I get to side D with Behold! The Night Mare again, and wouldn’t you know it, the SAME EXACT POPPING! It starts in the SAME EXACT SPOT (as the previous defective copies) at 3:47 seconds where Billy sings, “ To linger on, beyond the beyond”.

I wish this issue could have been caught at pressing. It’s definitely a certain batch of copies that have this defect. I spin other records just fine, so I know it's not my equipment. Now, there is no way to know which reissued copies have the defect or don’t have the defect.

I am so frustrated about this! I know it’s only vinyl and a "first world problem", but The Smashing Pumpkins are my favorite band of all time and I really want a good copy of this album on vinyl!

title: Baltimore Musuem of the Artistic!!
text:
I heard rumors about Dave having a DJ tour in Baltimore once, the city that I used to live in, but that was well before this release. However, club music is different than progressive house mix. I put this on and picture myself in the gardens of the Baltimore Musuem of Art with all the scolptures watching a water fall and the flow of water, like the Jones Falls River. This is what the whole entire disc reminds me of.

Forget about the last Master Series that Dave did, this is different. Disc one starts off with two tracks being slow and study having a flowing rythme and a little bit of singing, than having more fluid base going with the current. Wonderful electro progressive house, slow and study. It doesn't have to have a lot of energy on the first disc. I picture that garden at the Baltimore Musuem of Art. A nice gentle flow of electricity. It also picks up the beat at the end ending with artistic talent and you hear a lot of electro house throughout the entire disc. Not so much that it is ambient like Satoshi's Master Series 9, but more so that is progressive house.

Disc two is the same type of music, but more rythme is happening here and you here more changes and flows of the electro noises throughout the entire disc. The beat is a lot stronger. It is very consistent, but has picked up the beat on the 2nd disc. Think about the last Master Series by Satoshi Tomiie, but not so much that the whole entire cd set is ambient.

With both discs, I just picture myself in a place with an electric flow. In other words, this disc reminds me about the Baltimore Musuem of Art, but not with artwork and pictures. This time, is being artistic with the music and how it is compiled. Dave tried to achieve the same thing in Therapy 3, but sounds a lot better on this release.

I explained both CD's as clearly as possible and may not be as clear as mud. For those of you that don't have a clue with what I am talking about, I would listen to Satoshi's Master Series nine first before picking up this Master Series 10. If still in doubt, read Lex's review. There is a lot to digest, but with Master Series 10, Dave belongs with the Baltimore Musuem of the Artistic!!

title: Entertaining except for the feature piece
text:
I'm not familiar with any of these pieces, but the album is very enjoyable. Perhaps these pieces were meant to be played on the organ, but the use of harpsichord enables the separate voices and melodic lines to be heard clearly. My favorite pieces are the toccara and two preludes (G major and G minor), especially the G minor.

My quibble with the album is the featured "La Capricciosa" variations. Don't imagine that you will hear a work of the complexity of the Goldberg or Diabelli variations. It's really more of a pedagogical piece. The theme is prominent in all variations and frankly gets tiresome after only a few (after all, Bach only used it - heavily elaborated - once in Goldberg). Naxos has then grouped 4 or 5 variations into the same CD track, making it difficult to know when an old one has stopped and a new one begun. Worst of all is the complete lack of notes to explain the variations. Only the humorous "bad taste" variation is identified. So unless one is very knowledegable about 17th century keyboard music, it is difficult to appreciate what Buxtehude is doing in every variation.

That being said, the muted variation (#16?) is gorgeous and my favorite of all of them.

But buy the album. The rest is excellent.

title: Enter with the gods into Valhalla!
text: After all these years, I still believe the Solti "Ring" stands as one of the greatest landmarks in the history of recorded music. All four operas in the cycle still sound incredible, and the performance by all and sundry are more than worth all the hype that attended  the first release of  the these spectacular recordings. As for "Rheingold," it is perhaps a bit too easy to gloss over as a mere introduction. Mere introduction? Hardly! It sets the stage for all that follows, and does so with an economy rarely found in Wagner's oeuvre. Because it is relatively short, there is never a dull moment. It also introduces us to many of the musical themes that are woven throughout the cycle, Wagner's signature "leitmotifs."  A beautiful, thrilling experience, brilliantly sung and conducted, spectacularly recorded.

title: Unique talent
text:
Just recently bought myself a CD version of this, after owning a vinyl copy since it was first released, circa 1972. I was not even that familiar with any of Melanie's work back then ( early 1970's), but happened to catch her live on the Johnny Carson Show in 1972 (I was 18 then), when she sang two of the songs included on this album: "Together Alone", and "Do You Believe". When she sang these on the Carson Show, it was just her and her guitar, no background band, backup singers , or orchestration (as is the case on this album). I was so blown away by her amazing voice, and the unique emotion that she put into those two songs, that I bought my vinyl copy a few days later, and have worn it out over the ensuing 43 years- I was really pleased to see it finally come out in a CD format. I have more recently also added a few of her other older CDs , including some compilation ones, to my home music library, but felt like I needed to write a brief review of this particular one, "Stoneground Words", as I personally think it may be her best.

I haven't followed her career at all over the years, but still come back to "Stoneground Words" fairly often. I'd say it's a somewhat uneven effort, at least for my musical tastes, but there are several songs on this CD that are truly remarkable, and worth the purchase for either any Melanie fan, or newcomers to her past career recordings, if you are someone who appreciates both an amazing voice, and a very intensely emotional sort of music.

Melanie's voice (for those who are not familiar with her) is truly unique in the history of folk-rock music. While most singer's who have a vibrato voice talent usually only showcase that at various points in any song, Melanie was/is unique in that just about every note that comes out of her throat is more than a little tinged with vibrato- it IS her normal singing voice. I don't know of any other singer that is like that.

But in addition to that unique, everpresent vibrato, she has an amazing range: within any single song she will display a somewhat thin, airy, almost ethereal voice, but then when required, she shifts into a higher gear, and the sheer power of that other gear will amaze you. And she feels the music like no other, too- the powerful voice just explodes, at times when the lyric and the musical score demand an extra dose of emotion.

The best example of the above (and needless to say, my favorite song on this CD), is "My Rainbow Race"- an old Pete Seeger song, and one that I think Melanie does better than anyone else (many have recorded it, over the years). When she hits the recurring refrain "It's too soon to die" in this song, her voice becomes both a powerful musical instrument, and an incredible expression of human feeling. You have to hear it, to know what I mean.

Some of the songs on "Stoneground Words" are upbeat, some with a very retro-sound (with a 1940's feel to them), but the several that I like the most probably have the common denominator of affecting lyrics, a somewhat sad and sedated musical score, and the seamless variations in the quality and power of her singular voice.

I'd recommend this CD to any music fan familiar with the folk-rock genre, particularly those who grew up (as I did) in the 1960's-70's, and for anyone unfamiliar with Melanie's music, if you want to experience one of the truly unique voices in the history of popular modern music.

title: A fine example of something like cross-over
text:
The Great Uncles of the Revolution is the cool name adopted by Andrew Downing, Kevin Turcotte, Jesse Zubot and Steve Dawson for their oddly compelling collaboration. It's all instrumental music, with a unique mix of pump organ, slide guitar, stand-up bass, violin and trumpet (and maybe more). Those familiar with Zubot and Dawson's work will recognize a couple of the tunes here, nicely tarted up.
If Zubot and Dawson can be seen as doing a kind of jazz/bluegrass fusion, the Great Uncles might be considered a kind of jazz/classical/bluegrass fusion. It is at turns melodic and compelling, difficult to describe, never discordant. The trumpet and organ provide a kind of melodic thrust missing from Z and D's work, and the bass keeps the rhythm happening and deep notes rumbling. And the picking and the bowing are always spot-on.
The first several compositions are great tunes, illustrating the diversity of the crew. And then they take a left turn, and provide a more or less full production (minus the narration) of Peter and the Wolf!
Great stuff, highly recommended.

title: The Who Rocks Again
text:
If the Rolling Stones were the "world's greatest rock-n-roll band," then The Who were certainly the greatest rock band. Pete Townshend's slashing guitar chords defined the essence of rock without the roll, taking the music beyond the blues grooves of its early days and adding an explosively percussive punch that paved the way for power chord metal as well as punk rock and its progeny.

It's been 24 years since the last album of new music was released under the Who moniker. And it's been even longer--1978's Who Are You--since the band issued anything of consequence. After drummer Keith Moon's death that September, Townshend seemed to lose his focus and Face Dances and It's Hard from the early `80s did not come close to the band's previous standards.

For the next twenty years, the remaining trio--Townshend, vocalist Roger Daltrey and bassist John Entwistle--toured once in a while and, around the turn of the century, began to act like an ongoing concern again. Unfortunately, Entwistle died shortly thereafter, in 2002. But Townshend and Daltrey, whose friction-filled relationship was the stuff of legend in the old days, found themselves coming together with the brotherly bond of longtime friends who've weathered many a mutual storm.

At last, we have a new album by The Who, one that is worthy of the band's name. Ironically, Endless Wire is the most un-band record in the group's history--Pete Townshend played all of the instruments on most of the tracks, including drums and programmed drums. But, the demos he prepared for the guys back in the day were mythical in their thoroughness; given modern technology, the band-like quality of the instrumental backing should come as no surprise.

Daltrey's voice is in fine form. It's deeper than it useta be, and he's lost a little on the upper end, but his instrument has held up much better than most screamers of his era. Townshend's songs recapture the glory days, with arrangements right out of his once-familiar bag of tricks.

The disc's opener, "Fragments," begins with a near-quote from Who's Next's "Baba O'Riley," a repetitive synth line over which Pete windmills a crunchy, air-guitar inducing chord sequence that leads into four minutes of classic Who, complete with rich vocal harmonies in counterpoint to Daltrey's vibrant, questioning wail: "Are we breathing out or breathing in?"

"A Man in a Purple Dress," an angry indictment of the judgmental aspects of organized religion, is one of several all acoustic tunes, reminiscent of The Who By Numbers; "Two Thousand Years," with Townshend on mandolin, violin and viola, sounds like a questioning prayer, the other side of the spiritual coin. "God Speaks of Marty Robbins" is a delicate piece sung beautifully by Townshend himself, and on "In the Ether," he affects a guttural Tom Waits growl to deliver one of his most arresting vocals ever.

"Mike Post Theme" is filled with the potent start/stop dynamics that characterized much of The Who's greatest work, "It's Not Enough" rocks hard over what sounds like a choir of hammered dulcimers, and "Black Widow's Eyes" recalls "Sister Disco" from Who Are You.

Much is being written about the mini-opera that fills up the second half of the CD. Titled "Wire & Glass," it consists of eight fragments and two fully realized songs in a suite more like side two of Abbey Road than "A Quick One" from The Who Sell Out. The plotline ostensibly follows the rise and fall of a teenaged rock band, but I think it's really Townshend's way of reflecting on his own band's career. "Mirror Door" is a rockin' celebration of music itself, tying together Howlin' Wolf, Link Wray, Beethoven and Doris Day.

If there's a radio format left that'll play new music from an old band, the extended version of "We Got a Hit" tacked on at the end of Endless Wire will prove prophetic--it's a hit-single-in-waiting that contains every element of the original quartet's classic sound, and it clocks in at 3:04, perfect for airplay. It's a delicious denouement for a tasty album, one that resurrects and revives the name and reputation of one of rock music's greatest bands.

And just to rub it in, there's a 5-song bonus DVD included, capturing Townshend, Daltrey and their current touring lineup (including Ringo's boy Zak on drums and Pete's little brother Simon on second guitar) live in Lyon, France, in July--further proof that these guys have no plans to spend their senior years rocking only in chairs.

title: One of the Best Albums of All Time
text: After her first three albums, Kate bush changed direction and made the weirder and more ambitious The Dreaming, complete with the star vocalist, on one track, doing an impression of a donkey. Seriously. That album had a few good songs, but it was like another point on a graph skewered by a line descending slightly but steadily down. However, Kate Bush needed that experimentation, and perhaps even failure, to create what is probably her masterpiece, Hounds of Love. It really is a special record. Kate's voice had lowered somewhat and was just right. Nobody could sing like her then, and nobody can sing like her now. The musical accompaniment, apart perhaps from some electronic drums, was also well matured and doesn't sound too dated even after all these years. And the songs, the songs. On the LP, the first side features sort of standard tunes, at least in terms of structure and length. The tinges of weirdness are there, but unlike The Dreaming, they work. The second side is pure bliss, a medley of shorted and assorted songs, a bit like on The Beatles Abbey Road. Kate’s follow up, The Sensual World, was also extremely strong, but Hounds, for whatever reason, is better, is the best. Thereafter, the line went slightly down again, although for Kate Bush, that means that they were merely good and not quite great. Anyway, words can’t describe the beauty of this music. Listen and be taken away.

title: NICE ATTEMPT, BUT MISSING THE CONCEPT I THINK
text:
I'm enjoying the new Natalie Cole "Still Unforgettable" in many ways, but it does leave me a little confused. If this is a 17-year-after follow-up to 1991's "Unforgettable With Love", then what were "Take A Look" and "Stardust" all about? Did they not follow the same standards style, with "Stardust" including another Nat & Natalie duet? The same could be said for her "Holly and Ivy" Christmas album, with a classic Nat & Natalie on the Chestnuts Christmas Song.

The title reflects back to the 1991 masterpiece, which was a full tribute to Nat's music. I don't think this album is a full tribute as it suggests. It is obvious that many of the songs were not from Nat's recorded collection, particularly the bonus track of "How Do You Keep The Music Playing", written & recorded in the 80s. I don't think Nat ever did "Lollipops And Roses" in the 60s. This huge hit by Jack Jones is heavenly recreated by Natalie, and it my favorite track from this new collection, followed by "Here's That Rainy Day".

It is a nice recording all around, but doesn't reflect totally that it is a second follow-up to Nat's work. My other hang-up is "too many versions". You get an Amazon bonus track here. On iTunes, there is a Deluxe Edition with three more tracks, not including the Amazon track. Borders offers an edition with two additional bonus tracks not on iTunes or Amazon, and the CD is being sold at Pottery Barn with an exclusive track of "The Man That Got Away" (definitely not a Nat cover). In researching the Japan issue that is forthcoming, they are including 5 of the 7 bonus tracks on their edition. US labels need to just issue one CD with everything, or do a special edition with the album alone, then the bonus tracks on a 2nd CD. Shame on DMI for trying to milk every dollar out of Natalie's fans for every possible version to have every song. Not fair to us or to her.

I'm expecting somewhere down the road a release called "Totally Unforgettable" offering a remastered 1991 "Unforgettable" packaged with this new album and all bonus tracks in a double-disc set.

title: Early Work from a Master
text: Leo Kottke is to the acoustic guitar what Hendrix was to the electric: when he burst on the scene with his debut Takoma album, "Six- and Twelve-String Guitar" in 1969, he redefined both instruments.  This collection presents the best instrumentals of his earlier Capitol years (and in my opinion, all his albums up through the live "My Feet Are Smiling" are true classics).  Omitted is his notorious "geese-fart" singing voice, a foghorn baritone that I didn't find as bad as reputed, though I still have always been partial to the instrumentals.  This, and the companion "Chrysalis Years" volume, have been released by his current label, Blue Note, and they are both essential, especially if you don't have any Kottke in your collection.  If you don't mind the geese farts (and he did record some pretty good songs with vocals, too), you may want to check out "Essential Leo Kottke" on Chrysalis (there are only a few common tracks with the new "Instrumentals" CD), or the excellent 2-disc Rhino collection, "Leo Kottke Anthology".  Only the last one, by the way, contains any material from his Takoma debut.
