title: Mixed Feelings About This One
text:
I admire Willem Mengelberg's conducting and have liked most of what I've heard of his recordings. And there is much about this recording that I like. I especially was struck by an almost unbridled passion in the playing of the Concertgebouw in the 'Pathétique' Symphony, in the outer movements especially. But there are problems. The sound is pretty rough in spots, especially in III where the opening string chords are squally. (Wizard recording engineer Mark Obert-Thorn, the producer of this recording, comments that he took the best sound from several copies of the 1941 Telefunken shellac pressings but that there are some bad spots; this must be one of them.) Further, there is, for me, a rather intrusive use of string portamento (really noticeable in the second theme of the finale) that began grating on me after a few repetitions. Still, the shaping, the nuanced expression and the passion of the performance are ultimately winning.

The second work here is the String Serenade, Op. 48, and it does not suffer from the deficiencies of the Symphony, even though it was recorded three years earlier, in 1938. It is obvious that Mengelberg and his band adored this music; it is played con amore. Is there anyone who doesn't respond to the grace and charm of this suite?

Historical note: the Pathétique was recorded by the Concertgebouw in April 1941 just before the occupying Nazi government ordered Jews expelled from the orchestra. This is an important document in that it is one of only two recordings Mengelberg, an early European champion of Tchaikovsky, made of the Pathétique. And the Concertgebouw was the first orchestra outside Russia to play it; their knowledge of it goes back to 1895. In this recording one hears a dramatic and emotional style of performance that doesn't seem to exist these days. So, if this is your meat, go for it. You certainly can't beat the Naxos price.

Scott Morrison

title: DO NOT BUY !!! SACD version sounds terrible
text: First, This is a rating of the sound quality of this release-not the music. I bought Counterparts on CD the day it came out in 1993 and loved it, It is one of Rush's better albums and certainly their best from the 90's. When I saw this was to be released on SACD I was very excited, But my excitement quickly turned to disappointment when I received my copy and put it in my Denon universal player and hit play. From the first few seconds of the opening track I knew something was up. I began jumping from track to track listening to only a few seconds of each before I fired up my CD copy in my CD changer to compare the sound, as I suspected there really wasn't much difference. The next day I sat down and listened to the whole SACD all the way through for a "critical listen", when I was done I started the 20 year old CD copy again and it only took a few moments to confirm the lack of improvement in the SACD version. There is a "difference" between the two just not a real "improvement", Kind of like the difference between listening to a cassette tape with Dolby-B Noise reduction on vs. off. There is a difference like lower tape noise but also duller highs, either way you are still listening to the same tape "source", Thats what I feel like with this release, The background noise is reduced and the levels are lower and more "controlled" but it still sounds like the same 44.1/16 bit source ran through a filter or processor. There is no "openness", "wider sound-stage" ," improved dynamics" or "3 dimensional sound" that you would expect from SACD, DVD-A, or any other Hi-Res Source, it just sounds like a slightly cleaner CD. If you already own Counterparts on CD then stop right there no further action is needed, if you are looking to get a copy then just pick up the regular CD version or (Gulp, Dare I say it?) Download an Mp3 copy. Even a $10 Mp3 download would be money better spent than $25 for this SACD. It has been a long time since I felt this ripped off, This was my first and most likely my last purchase from "Audio Fidelity". This disc is going on E-bay so I can at least recoup a couple of dollars I wasted on this "sonic turd". I cannot stress this enough, DO NOT WASTE YOUR MONEY ON THIS SACD VERSION !!!

I was very disappointed by this album, I was really looking for some 'new' sounding KOL. This band USED to challenge themselves into making music that sounded different. The band REALLY has to ditch this idea that they're 'Arena Rock'. I keep reading interviews where they say this is what they're tying to do. I don't know if they think they're the next U2, or Cold Play, but that sorta sounds like the direction they're TRYING to take their music, and it's failing miserably. Both Cold Play & U2 know how to take a somewhat 'normal' song, and push sounds into it that elevate the music to the next level. KOL is lacking this 'push'.

KOL needs to get back to their roots.

title: Underrated 70's Brit-rockers
text: The creative team of Ollie Halsall and Mike Patto mastered nearly every rock music genre within a relatively brief period of time, yet continue to be largely overlooked by rock 'n' roll historians. Following thier original incarnation as psychedelic popsters Timebox, and preceding thier prog-rock stint as Boxer, Halsall and Patto defied genre as "Patto". "Hold Your Fire" was Patto's 2nd release, and features an interesting blend of jazzy chords, bluesy singing and straight ahead rock 'n' roll frequently wrapped in epic arrangements of prog-rock length (note only 8 cuts on the album). The uninitiated may wonder after a first listen: "What's the big deal?" -but Patto's unique blend has a way of growing on you, especially when you notice the "little touches" like guitarist Ollie Halsall's Lionel Hampton-like prowess on the vibraphone. The standout song is "You You Point Your Finger" featuring a heartfelt vocal from Patto and a beautifully fluid and understated Mark Knopfler-style guitar solo by Halsall. Possibly not everyone's cup of tea, but fans of 70's rock and those who can appreciate "musician's musicians" will enjoy.

title: Nicki French: Secrets (1995)
text:
In 1995, there was not much going on. Madonna had only released another compilation, but there were just no fresh new voices to come under way, until I heard the powerful voice behind the 1995 remake of Bonnie Tyler's 1983 hit, "Total Eclipse Of The Heart". This powerful voice belonged to that of Nicki French, a talented singer from England, who had been fighting to become this world's next pop-dance star. At the same time of Nicki's release of "Total Eclipse Of The Heart", as her first single, she released her first album, SECRETS, in which the single belongs to. You'll understand, when you read on, why this album is just pure amazing.

TOTAL ECLIPSE OF THE HEART

First single from the album. Bonnie Tyler's rendition, which runs to a time length of 6:58 (6 minutes, 58 seconds), was an amazing power ballad. But Nicki French, cutting out the second verse, cutting out the second half of the first refrain and the first chorus, making it reach a time length of 3:53 (3 minutes, 53 seconds), did one hell of job turning a beautiful power ballad into a awesome GET-YOUR-GROOVE-ON dance tune.

DID YOU EVER REALLY LOVE ME?

Great song here.

FOREVER AND A DAY

When I first read the title, I thought she might have sang this as a cover song, which had already been originally recorded by Barry Manilow, but after hearing it, I realized that Nicki only used the title, but wrote different lyrics, making it a Nicki original. Great song.

I'LL BE WAITING

Great.

IS THERE ANYBODY OUT THERE?

Great.

NEVER IN A MILLION YEARS

Awesome.

FOR ALL WE KNOW

This song was originally recorded by The Carpenters, who sang the song as a ballad. Nicki French seems to be the only person in music history who can get away with turning beautiful ballads into awesome dance tunes. Great rendition.

SECRETS

The album's unbelievably amazing title track. Great song.

SOMETHING ABOUT YOU

Great song.

VOICE OF AMERICA

Aside from "Total Eclipse Of The Heart", this was my favorite song off of the album. I could play this song over and over if I had to.

I had bought the album on cassette around the time of its release. For two years straight (1995-1997), I had played this album non-stop until my cassette deck to my stereo ate it. From the years 0f 1997-2006, I searched religously for this album, until I finally found a used copy right here. Ever since the CD arrived, I have not stopped listening to it. This is a great album, and it seems to be the only album that Nicki has released. She has released some songs over the years, but those songs are non-album songs. I am hoping that one day, Nicki will put out another album.

title: Move over, Vladimir
text:
Hitherto my unassailable criterion for Scarlatti on the piano was Vladimir Horowitz (with Ivo Pogorelich coming in a close second). But no longer. That title now belongs to Christian Zacharias, a pianist whose recordings I have only recently gotten to know. Zacharias' virtuosity in these three recitals, amply stocked with both familiar and unfamiliar sonatas (the fourth CD will require special comment), matches and in some ways even exceeds that of Horowitz. The sonatas Zacharias elects to play offer formidable technical challenges; many represent a kind of Baroque equivalent to the Chopin Études. Hand-crossing, rapid repeated note figurations, irregular scalar and arpeggiated passages, abound, and in every case Zacharias delivers the goods, often with heart-stopping bravura. His crisp articulation, even in the most rapid passages, reminds one of Glenn Gould (without the latter's occasional brittleness or eccentricities).

More importantly, Zacharias doesn't treat these works only as a showcase for his technical brilliance. His are among the most musically satisfying accounts of this repertoire I have heard. He conveys the mood of each sonata with uncanny insight--from the most scintillating devil-may-care extroversion to the most haunting nocturnal evocations. Nor does he slight (as many pianists do) the Spanish currents that flow freely throughout this repertoire. He frequently, by some magic, manages to turn his piano into a giant flamenco guitar, and the listener wants to get up and dance. Horowitz, for all his wit and sparkle, never conjured Iberia so tellingly. On the other hand, Zacharias, ever the most sensitive of pianists (sample his Mozart), never produces an ugly sonority even when he attacks, with main force and evident relish, Scarlatti's explosive dissonances and "crush" chords.

All of this wondrous pianism and consummate artistry is captured with stunning clarity and ambient warmth by the engineers.

Each of the first three CD's presents a nicely varied program, albeit without sufficient pauses between tracks. The fourth CD, however, adds nothing to the desirability of the set; for it is devoted to a bizarre "concept" album in which the pianist performs the same Scarlatti sonata multiple times in different venues (presumably taken from live recitals). I suppose the justification for doing this consists in hearing just how particularized are various instantiations of the same work rendered by the same performer at different times and in different moods. The listener gets the point long before the final iteration. Why, one wonders, did Electrola/EMI allow Zacharias to go through with this irritating conceit? Why did they bother to reissue it in this bargain-priced set (thereby adding unnecessary cost)?

Having issued this minor caveat, I will reaffirm the main point: Zacharias' Scarlatti recordings represent a major achievement, and should be added to your collection regardless of how many Scarlatti recordings (on piano or harpsichord) you already own.

title: Fans of the show will appreciate this more than the movie soundtrack
text:
Ever since the movie came out, the debate over which soundtrack is better has been raging wildly. There are positive and negative aspects to both, and one can't be clearly labeled as "better" - it all depends on what you're looking for.

The 1996 Original Broadway Soundtrack:

This soundtrack, much more than the movie one, does an excellent job of making you feel like you're in the theatre again. Since the original show was a more or less constant song and the soundtrack includes all of the 20-50 second pseudo-songs, you can listen to the soundtrack and visualize practically the entire show. The underproduced quality enhances this experience: it feels more real than the movie soundtrack does.

The 2006 Movie Soundtrack:

The other reviewers are right when they say this soundtrack is definitely the better sounding of the two. Much better production, and the actors have all matured vocally. Rosario Dawson's voice is much easier to listen to than the original actress'. This also feels distinctly more like a soundtrack, where the original feels much more like a score.

The question is: which do you prefer?

Madonna did it
Kylie did it

Now heeeeeere's Cyndi

Dance music is hot again, mostly because of the ladies listed above, and certainly good news for those of us who spent the `80s on the dance floor.

This is the tenth studio album from the effervescent singer/songwriter who just wants to have fun, and is best enjoyed at full volume with the bass turned up, the way it was meant to be played.

The first US single is "Same Ol' Story", the track that put the [EXPLICIT LYRICS] warning on the album, but this isn't the best song in my opinion. I like "Set Your Heart" which was released as a single in Japan, beginning like the Bee Gees' "More Than a Woman", and then blending into an `80s R&B dance track perfectly suited to her vocals.

The next single is "Into the Nightlife", another instant favorite with a booming intro that will have your moneymaker shakin'. Also terrific are "Rocking Chair"; the addictive "Echo" that you'll want to hear again and again and "Grab a Hold" which is vintage Lauper.

To mix it up a little she includes the mid-tempo "Rain on Me" and "Lyfe", the latter being a little different from anything else on the album, in that the tempo is different, and it's a bit funky (an explicit word here too). "Rain on Me" is very strong lyrically, and a possible single.

"I am a robber in the dark
Singing about a broken heart
Answering whistles in the air
Waiting for someone else to care

But you can rain on me
Yea you can rain on me...."

There's absolutely no filler material on this totally fun album, which is recommended for anyone who can take it to the brink.

Amanda Richards, June 10, 2008

title: Still awesome but starting to tread water...
text:
This may be the weakest of Don Caballero's releases, but it still blows away almost any other band's best effort. Any Don Cab fan will not want to miss this, as it contains plenty of great instrumental math rock, and in some ways represents their most insane and advanced accomplishment. They never defied conventional rhythm, melody and harmony as radically as they did on this record.

The album starts off - literally - where Don Caballero 2 ended; the same killer drum groove that ended their second album starts the first track here, the amusingly titled "Don Caballero 3." But if you thought the second album played fast and loose with structure, wait till you hear this! It may sound like like completely random noodling, but I saw them play live on the "What Burns..." tour, and they played almost all of this album including the first track, and it sounded exactly like the album - what appears to be random noodling is in fact carefully orchestrated. Utterly mind-blowing.

The closest you get to a completely structured track is probably track 3: "Delivering the Groceries at 138 Beats per Minute." But even here, "structure" is a relative term - they can't resist a breakdown and major musical shift halfway through. At any rate, you get some killer grooves and some nice meter changes. The closer, "June is Finally Here" contains what may be the band's most beautiful moment: pure shimmering guitars abandon any trace of dissonance for a glorious conclusion to a jarring, stunning album.

And of course, the biggest attraction remains drummer Damon Che - aptly credited on this album as "octopus." Play the opening to track 4, "Slice Where You Live Like Pie" and know that here is one man who clearly has achieved complete independence of all four of his limbs.

Overall, not the band's best work. But still worth owning for any true fan of adventurous, challenging music.

title: Dan, you are the best...
text:
Hi Dan, I'm one of the producers of this compilation, and I want to tell you right away that I appreciate the way you help every reader out here with time specifics and mix information. You are not just the best, you are the, um, frigging best. You have helped me make better and smarter purchases for years. I love buying records but I can't afford every one.

I wanted to make some notes to go along with your comments:

- Martha Wash does sing the entirety, lead and back-up of "You're My One and Only." To my knowledge, the only version with any of the Seduction girls on it at all is the one where Michelle Visage re-does the rap.

- Almost all of your mix comments have to do with time issues; the line-up got bumped around a lot as permissions came in -- or didn't -- for other tracks that we wanted to include. With Donna we were trying to save a minute, and Sybil really goes on at 7-minutes plus, and this is an unusual edit from England that telescopes the long version much better than the official single, which just fades out.

- In the case of Kool and the Gang and Jody, I made these calls because I thought these were the versions that served the song and the vocalist best; I find the remix-album version of "Don't You Want Me" way too cut-up to be listenable, and the Francois remix just felt long to me as I re-listened. And "Fresh" is so unconventional because it's laid back, this is just my favorite version. I used the album version of "Seventh Heaven" on a Gwen Guthrie compilation for the same reason although I do regret not having the chance just yet to get Larry Levan's mix of it out. I also admit to having a problem with some of the disruptive multiple-edits that Arthur Baker and the Latin Rascals did as stunts in long versions. That's my problem entirely and I admit it. So these are some of the considerations. There's a multiplicity of factors. Including the fact that once you've done something, it's sometimes hard to change because that costs money and time.

- Frankie was just too famous to leave out. We are briefed to balance mainstream choices with our own obscure faves and things that we know need to be debuted on CD. It's to make the lineup accessible to a more casual buyer. Thanks for noticing the Joe Jackson, it's not an edit, the co-producers searched high and low for the right version used on the vinyl 12. I was so glad to put it next to the hard core pop dance records it got played next to in its time. And similarly, I wanted to draw a historical and musical line between Junior, Safety Dance and Don't Stop the Music.

- Some things will always be over-issued, because they are big hits. I know I have 20 copies of "Boogie Oogie Oogie" and "Shame" if I have one.

Thanks again Dan for being such a great watchdog. I wish there was still a publication like Dance Music Report around, you would have been great writing a column that finds reissues so we know about rarities coming out before they go out of print again.

That being said, most of the tracks are very good, mostly uptempo, but with nothing that hits Thrash speed, nor plods along slowly, with only the final track, a ballad, being an obvious weak link to my ears. title: Top Glass Symphony
text:
As a Glass fan, I've attended several of his symphonies in concert; 1,2,5 & 6. When I first heard the 3rd on this CD, it immediately became my favorite. While the "Low" symphony is a strong second favorite, this one ranks above it, as it is better written and doesn't contain any "borrowed" themes as is the case of the "Low". For anyone wanting a superb intro to Glass' music, this makes a fine choice. I deeply agree with a previous review, in that Glass' compositions are so disparate, that coming up with one recording to summarize his work is nearly impossible. I would not find it at all ridiculous to state that Glass maybe second only to Mozart when it comes to the breadth and depth of musical composition. Example: Wagner isn't known for his symphonies and Brahms isn't known for his operas.

Glass has written 8 symphonies, a dozen operas, concertos for piano and violin, film music, string quartets & music for his ensemble. Beyond his symphonic output, he has written several tone poems such as "The Light".

Additionally, his compositions now span an incredible 40 years and his music has changed and shifted over time. To say that it all sounds the same is absurd. There is so much output, that I find it hard to believe that there isn't at least one Glass recording for everyone.

My only gripe with Glass is that despite his remarkable talent, he remains a very uneven composer. I found his 5th and 6th symphonies to be insufferable. I couldn't wait for "Monsters of Grace" to end when I saw it at BAM. And as for his "Hydrogen Jukebox" - STINCK-A-ROO!

Yet, many of his works are quite profound. "Koyanisqatsi" is masterpiece, ditto Dances 1-5 and I can listen to his "Les Enfants Terribles" over and over.

In my opinion, if your looking for an outstanding intro to his orchestral writing, look no further than this CD.

title: six stars
text: This should be your first Jorge Drexler recording. If you like Paul Simon, Caetano Veloso, Joao Gilberto, Jobim, or John Lennon, this can not be too highly recommended. In the end it may be seen as one of the finest records of mellow music of this decade. Knowing Spanish is a plus, and this will give you reason to learn, but even instrumentally this collection shines. There is not a bad composition, and several true gems. Jorge draws on broad influences yet is contemporary. Some are tangos and milongos made modern, in other places there are stunning allusions to Simon's vocal and musical poetry, Lennonistic harmonies (even at times I imagine the Beach Boys), soft Brazilian rhythms that have as much power as rock and roll, a voice that challenges Caetano and promises to heal with a deep worldly philosophy. The collaborations with the talented US pianist Ben Sidran and his son Leo are perfect; this is not a collection of songs but a whole. My children (20's) love it. For me this record promises to rank with Simon's Rhythm of the Saints, with Harrison's All Things Must Pass, with the Grateful Dead's American Beauty. You will listen to it for decades. The modern musical center shifts farther south, to the benefit of all. We should all know where Uruguay is. Lift a Mate to Jorge... Todo se transforma.

title: "It's All Just Psychotic Devotion"
text:
Slayer have kept a similar sound and similar lyrical approach over the years . . . and somehow they have never seemed so relevant. "It's all just psychotic devotion/ manipulated with no discretion," Araya bellows in "Flesh Storm." It seems that they are the only major act that has put out an Iraq protest besides Neil Young, though Neil doesn't exhort us to choose "666."

Any way, this is pure aggression for the new millennium with Dave Lombardo back and slaying at the drums (Thrash polyrhythms anyone? Lombardo's got 'em!). Kerry King and Jeff Hanneman are consistently stunning at interweaving their leads with one another. I mean, has there ever been a better guitar duo in metal? Really, take the guys in Skynrd, make their (dis)harmonizing licks chromatic and dissonant, whammy them all to f**k and you've got freebird flying south of heaven for a real meltdown. These guys only get better with age. Envision a future with Slayer as old guys playing sold-out stadiums and warping your retirement.

This is the real deal. I got it a week-and-a-half ago and I listen to it at least once every day. Riffs that stick in your brain like pork chops stick to your ribs. Slaytanic invocations that lead you to live in the ultraviolence. One big screaming bellowing FU to the powers-that-be. Not one bad song. A recipe for a great and mighty calamity that gives it to the man once and for all.

title: Best Waterboys CD In Decades
text: I was completely surprised at how wonderful that this new cd is and almost equally surprised by the lack of attention it is getting, considering that it was released in Europe months ago. As a big fan of The Waterboys in the 80's I've since listened to Mike Scott's output of the past almost 20 years and didn't care for a lot of it. Rock In A Weary Land (2001?) is a muddy sounding mess with poor songwriting and is practically unlistenable. Book Of Lightning is the polar opposite. The songs are catchy and bear up after repeated listenings, plenty of good rockers but also some softer introspective material. "She Tried To Hold Me" is a masterpiece that marries incredible lyrics with an amazing vocal. The production is perfect for the material, very clean but not sanitized and overproduced. Mike's voice is wonderful here. It is rough at times (I want to say Dylanesque, but I know that would put some people off) and sounds absolutely wonderful with this material. What also hearkens back to the 80's is the album length - 45 minutes - 10 songs and not one of them makes me reach for the skip button. I don't see restraint like that much from my favorite artists. If you like anything else by The Waterboys I can't imagine you being disappointed with this.

title: If it wasn't Britney...
text:
I have to admit, I was a big fan of the old "...Baby One More Time" Britney Spears. So when I finally picked up this album, I felt a serious lack of Max Martin, who produced songs like "Baby," as well as "Oops!...I Did It Again,"
"Lucky," "Stronger," "Crazy," "Overprotected" and loads more. However, I was pleasantly surprised by the alternatives that Spears chose.
My favorite dance track instantly became "(I Got That) Boom Boom"--although it's a far cry from the Britney sound people are used to, it's still a great hip-hop tune that gets under your skin. I hated "Toxic" at first, but it grew on me, as did "Breathe On Me." The weakest aspect of this album, unfortunately, is that Spears hardly sings. She basically talks her way through "Outrageous" and "Showdown," which are both potentially good songs that her voice made boring.
I was impressed with the ballad "Shadow"--its lyrics were a refreshing break from the over-sexed lyrics of the other tracks (which can get tedious after a while). Lyrically, it may be one of the best songs Spears has ever recorded. And on "Everytime," you can actually hear Spears's singing voice--as opposed to her usual affected, breathy, nasal sound that only works in some situations. "Everytime" is living proof that Spears has been manufactured too much, and if she were left to her own devices (she wrote the song), she is capable of producing melodious, soulful material that completely contradicts the critics' views of her voice.
Overall, I don't know if this is my favorite Britney Spears album, but I probably would have liked it better if it wasn't Britney Spears. She was doing fine with Max Martin. But she enjoys the music she's making, and she's working hard to make it her best, which, believe it or not, is the mark of someone who is growing into a true artist. Whether you like her or not, you have to respect that.

title: My best new find of the year
text:
This album is being ridiculously over-hyped and incredibly well-publicized, so take the hype with a grain of salt - but it's well worth a listen. I'm not sure any album is as good as the buzz about this one, but I understand where all the reviews are coming from. After years of fans saying they can't understand why she's not more popular and famous, I think Nicole Atkins is finally getting the attention she deserves. I'm not sure yet whether I feel this album is better than her last one except in terms of the salesmanship. (I just got both today). But if you're a fan, you're probably going to want this.

If, like me, she's new to you - I'm usually all-Americana half the time, rock music the other half, and first heard of her in a Ryan Adams tweet this month - I probably can't say much that others haven't here. The woman can belt out a song, though her voice sounds a little thin sometimes when she really pushes it. She can write a decent song. What stands out is her musical style from another era. It's creative, lush, and beautiful. Back in the 60's - yes, I go back that far - I was less interested in the pop songs on the AM radio than the new sounds on the FM radio. But, as you probably already know, she brings back lush arrangements that are reminiscent of a certain kind of 60's pop music and somehow makes it sound as modern as this week.

There's a gorgeous arrangement of "Easy Living" that's an excellent vehicle for Maestro Mintzer. title: Tampa Red is one amazing guitarist
text:
This four CD set brings together a variety of early commercial blues sides recorded by Tampa Red--with and without Georgia Tom who played piano and sang.
The first two CDs largely feature a full band, with jug and kazoo (I really just wanted to write that sentence.....). Anyway, the first two CDs are done in the jug band style, with loose harmonies and full tilt boogie fun: quite similar to the Memphis Jug Band. They actually sound more professional than the legendary Memphis Jug Band--since Tampa Red's band took less chances than the Memphis Jug Band, their output is more even--not reaching either the lows nor the highs that make the Jug Band such a wonderfully exhilirating group. Mama Don't Want no Easy Riders around here is a stand out song, familiar to anyone who bought 2012's blues calender.
The second CD are mainly sides recorded with Georgia Tom playing piano in a solid boogie woogie style and Tampa Red playing lead and rhythm guitar. The songs are good but do not rise to classic status--the way, for example, almost every song Robert Johnson has. Several of the songs use familiar songs with unfamiliar lyrics--my wife began to sing along with a Sitting on Top of the World--only discovering Georgia Tom was singing "Things 'Bout Coming my Way".
What is exceptionally fine is Tampa Red's guitar playing. He is an astonishing guitar player; he plays a National guitar (at least, that what it sounds like and looks like in the picture) which is fairly closely miked. His single string lines sound almost electric and remind me of Elmore James. On several songs, I enjoyed his guitar playing more than the overall song.
The recordings themselves are uneven in quality--some are excellent and some relatively poor. It sounds as if the engineer chose to eliminate surface noise by toning down the treble; at least some recordings sound muffled to me.
This is a very good set of early blues.

title: A Musical Delight
text:
Grammy-nominated performer Michael Feinstein, who has spent much of his life recording the Great American Songbook, now turns his attention to another legend of popular American songwriting, his friend Jimmy Webb.

This is a superb CD, warm and reflective, complemented by a sympathetic acoustic, and a well-balanced recording. Furthermore, it's produced by Jimmy Webb himself, so artiste and composer share a single vision.

The disc opens with a beautifully orchestrated version of the coda from "MacArthur Park," gracefully segueing into the CD's title track, "Only One Life." The tempo is relaxed, and the tone is romantic, setting the mood for the rest of the album. Feinstein is in fine voice, and his warm, sonorous tenor is a perfect complement to the celebration of life and love that is this CD.

Of the 15 songs on this album, every one is a gem. Some are old favorites like "MacArthur Park," "The Moon's a Harsh Mistress, and "Adios," while others like "Belmont Avenue," "Time Flies," and "Only One Life" are given their debut here. Among the highlights are a swinging, doo-wop arrangement of "Belmont Avenue," a lithe and lively "Skywriter," and a moving rendition of "All I Know." Additionally, the popular "Up, Up and Away" is given a refreshing makeover compliments of a lilting Latin rhythm that's an irresistible invitation to dance.

The versatility of Feinstein's tenor is remarkable. One moment it's light and lissome, soaring like a bird in "Skywriter," and the next it's dark and brooding, mining all the pathos of Webb's plaintive composition as it ponders "Is There Love After You."

This is a delightful disc, suitable for any occasion, but probably best enjoyed late at night over candle light and a fine Bordeaux with someone you love.

Among the numerous interpreters of Jimmy Webb's music, two artistes stand apart, Glen Campbell and Art Garfunkel. To this distinguished duo we can now add a third, Michael Feinstein. With this collection of classics, Feinstein has proven himself an able advocate of Webb's oeuvre, and I warmly recommend this CD as a worthwhile addition to the library of any Webb connoisseur.

title: Within you...and without you.
text:
This was the fourth album from Quintessence and the first for a passing RCA imprint Neon which failed to replicate the success of the founder with his Vertigo label.

Self continues where Dive Deep left off in terms of diminished songwriting, both in terms of quality as well as quantity. The studio side of the vinyl album displayed shorter, tighter songs but without the vitality of previous albums. Cosmic Surfer suggests more but never really lived up to it's potential.

Meanwhile, on the other side of the coin, the band's live performances were almost legendary, marked by the same improvisational displays of their individual musical backgrounds all motivated by their spiritual devotions. The songs took on new and different aspects while being played in concert. This live band is represented here on three tracks, the excellent Freedom, Water Goddess with it's almost Dark Star passages and the B-side of the single that was issued, You Never Stay the Same.

The price of this disc is worth it for the live performances alone although the editing on You'll Never Stay the Same leaves a lot to be desired to say the least. Finally the album closes with Sweet jesus which is a bit odd.

Not the best album by any means but that twenty minutes of live recording and the six minutes of B-side show what could have been. It just amazes me that there are no tapes out there of other live performances which have yet to see the light of day.

title: Interesting, but hardly essential.
text:
Sir Joe Quarterman and Free Soul make up one of many "second tier" funk groups that formed in the late 60s and early 70s. This CD comprises some of their best tracks and, if you are a hardcore funk fan, you may find it worthwhile. There is some nice horn and guitar work scattered throughout the disc. HOWEVER.....
While I realize that groups like Black Nasty, Joe Quarterman and Free Soul, The Counts, Ripple, Black Heat and the like all have their fans and cult followings......It doesn't take a long listen to see why these groups are not considered to be on the same level as Sly, The Ohio Players, The Bar-Kays, The Commodores, Brick, Cameo, Slave, Kool and the Gang, Con Funk Shun, P-Funk, Mandrill, War, The Meters, etc. They are interesting groups to be sure, but I would only recommend checking into them AFTER you've obtained more essential funk first.
For one thing, I find the music by these "second tier" funk outfits to be extremely repititious and unoriginal. After about 4 tracks, the music begins to sound alike and run together. One of the things that distinguished great groups like the Isleys or Earth, Wind & Fire was their diversity.......an innate ability to flawlessly shift from hard funk, to soul, to ballads, to jazz......seemingly effortlessly. You'll find no such variety or diversity here. Track 10 is pretty much on the same groove as track 1.
Secondly, many of these "underground" lesser-known funk groups were really intended to be back up bands first......and that is a big part of why there is a sameness to the music. It doesn't hold up well on it's own.
As long as you realize this going in, and you just want to add some depth to your r&b collection, then you might be interested in picking this up if you find it for a bargain price. There's no question that there were a number of talented funk groups in the early 70s and that inevitably some groups would be nudged aside; just remember, though......"second tier," rare groove-style groups are second tier for a reason. After 4 or 5 tracks you'll see why...

title: After ITAOT, a very good effort
text:
As a quick aside, ITAOT was a very different direction for Isis. Commercially it was a success, but I personally felt they had to an extent forgone some of the things that made them unique. The conventional, easy to access sound was too obvious, especially when held against a release like Oceanic. Turner's clean vocals weren't the only issue here; the entire band sounded clean as well, too clean. They just didn't have the edge like they used to, and it made them sound commercial and common.

Maybe that wasn't a bad thing for a lot of listeners, but personally, I grew tired of ITAOT very quickly and returned to Panopticon and Oceanic.... until Wavering Radiant was released.

Wavering Radiant is a logical movement for Isis in light of their last three LPs. The tracks are tense and full of great ideas, many with crushing bridges and choruses along with the seamless digressions into vocal/instrumental harmony that keeps you waiting for the next flip of the coin, so to speak. In a lot of ways, some passages remind me very heavily of where they were going in Oceanic, Track 5 "Stone to Wake a Serpent" sounds like it could have been pulled directly from that album, with the cacophonus transition between instrumental harmonization and Turner's growls. "Threshold of Transformation" is another crushing opus that could easily have been a part of their pre-celestial hardcore catalogue. "20 minutes / 40 years" is reminiscent of Panopticon's "So Did We" with sweeping, sustained notes in a beautiful harmony often drowned by crushing, weighted distortion. Very well executed and very well done tracks that stand out for me.

The instrumentation throughout the entire album is uniformly very good, with a few exceptions I'll elaborate on below. ITAOT was musically a very good album, think of Wavering Radiant as a version of that with harsher vocals and excellent music and you'll have a decent idea of how it sounds.

My biggest criticism, and one I am conflicted about laying on this album, is the excessive use of synthesizers and loops. The track "Ghost Key" is an example of this; I like the track but I feel the opening synth notes weaken it and make it sound like a cheap video game. It might be something that grows on me because really the rest of the track is very good, but that synth just sounds outdated and really fairly out of place. A good guitar harmonization would have been just as easy and would have meshed better.

There are also passages that sound too much like ITAOT; too clean, too contrived. It almost sounds like they're inserting a harmony for gratuitous reasons in that it doesn't seem to work for the song. Back to "Ghost Key," around 3:00 in Turner launches into some clean singing that just sounds, for lack of a better word, "fake." "Hand of the Host" also suffers from this in several spots. It's just forced cleanliness; it simply doesn't work with the rest of the song in the same way it did with, say Panopticon's "So Did We", where Turner's voice changed with the atmosphere throughout the sung passage.

To wrap up, I would say Wavering Radiant is a very focused and good direction for Isis. The overall sound, while more commercial and accessible, does not completely dismiss their pre-Panopticon days in the way ITAOT did. Wavering Radiant for me is a sign that Isis is back on track and headed in the right direction.

title: It's Tuff finding the original....
text: I'm writing this review partly illegitimately since I haven't heard the entire CD. But Ace Cannon is best known for his classic instrumental "Tuff," and having heard the sample clip at amazon.com, I can state confidently that this is NOT the original version. I know, because I still have the original single as released on 45 RPM, and this is not it. Not that this re-make is bad -- there's still that jaunty-but-cool organ accompaniment in the background, and that easy-strolling sax up front. But in the original, Cannon's sax has a blues-ier tone, and carefully bends certain notes that are played here in a more clipped, straightforward manner, robbing it of some of the "darker" tones Cannon had performed on vinyl. I can't honestly say where one can find the original version in CD format. I'm not sure it exists as of this writing since I haven't been able to sample other Cannon discs. So, tentatively, my advice to novices would be to buy this disc --- you'll probably like it. But if you're a purist, or a serious student of pop music history, you might owe it to yourself to track down the original 45.

title: Best Beach Boys compilation for the money
text:
This two-CD, 50-track compilation is the best Beach Boys compilation for the money, even better than the multiplatinum [[ASIN:B000093BDX Sounds of Summer: Very Best of The Beach Boys]], which was released in 2003. SOUNDS OF SUMMER has only two tracks not found on this collection: "Come Go With Me" and the single version of "Be True To Your School," which does appear on the 2012 [[ASIN:B008LA7RLG Greatest Hits]] compilation, and is also a bonus track on the Japanese edition of 50 BIG ONES. The sound quality is fantastic, and several of Mark Linett's new stereo mixes are used, including "Wild Honey" and "Darlin'" (could there be a mono/stereo remaster of [[ASIN:B000002TRB Wild Honey]] in our future?) Admittedly, I was a little disappointed that the new stereo mixes of tracks such as "I Get Around," "Good Vibrations," and "Help Me, Rhonda" were not included, but that was probably because Brian Wilson wanted the monos included on the hits packages. Disc 1 is mostly Capitol-era material, save for "Getcha Back," "It's OK," and "Rock And Roll Music." Disc 2 is equally divided between Capitol-era and Brother-era material, including a pair of tracks from The Boys' new CD, [[ASIN:B007U1FEJE That's Why God Made the Radio]], the title track and the single edit of "Isn't It Time." The box also includes a booklet with photos and a David Wild essay, and seven individual black-and-white photos of each Beach Boy (including Bruce Johnston and David Marks).

This collection is excellent value for the money. I'm looking forward to the eventual release of the 50th Anniversary box set (it's here: see my review of [[ASIN:B008XZKSRY Made In California]]) to see what further surprises are in store for us.

title: Amazing talent; my favorite music of all time
text:
Have you ever wondered whether humanity still produced minds on the order of Bach, Mozart or Beethoven? In my opinion, the score work of Wendy Carlos is the best evidence that our civilization can sometimes end up finding a genius out there and allow them to create and earn a living. I was a fan early in my life, and over the past 30 years this music has meant more and more to me as I age. Some of it is related to the classical themes we recognize, of course, because nothing is created in a vacuum. But those who think this artist's contribution was just technical are missing out on a pure, original talent.

By the way, Ms. Carlos' Tron music is outstanding as well.

The remastered version of Clockwork Orange is absolutely amazing and much more complete, but it's a shame that it's so hard to find.

title: "I'm Confessin'" that I LOVE this album!
text: I Don't Know Why I Love this album, but I DO! I know I'm displaying my geezer-ness by loving it, but what the hell. At 66, I AM a geezer. And actually, I do know why I love it. Because of its great orchestral arrangements and the subtle understated phrasings of a group of musicians I've never heard of. The bridge solos by trumpet, sax, guitar and violin are simply superb. I wanted to hear more of these guys. But, in the end, it's the singing too. I know Regis is not a great singer, but here he rises to the occasion, and I think it's because he's singing to, with, or about a woman he has shared more than forty years of his life with - and that is no small accomplishment in the show biz world these days. But looking at the photos here, of their wedding day, and then of the present day, it's certainly easy to see why he loves her. What a lucky stiff you are, Reege! His voice is a kind of "smoothed-out Rod McKuen" I have decided. (And I used to love Rod too. One of my favorite "mood music" albums is Rod's Beautiful Strangers from waaay back in the sixties.) As for Joy, I don't know if she was a professional singer in her earlier life before Regis, but she certainly is an accomplished one now - a blend of Doris Day and another old favorite of mine, Blossom Dearie, with a simply heartbreakingly lovely slight vibrato. Soft, understated and filled with fun and love, that's how I'd describe Joy's vocals. Did I say I LOVE this album? Well, I'm Confessin'. I do. - Tim Bazzett, author of PINHEAD: A LOVE STORY

title: 'Soulbook': Stewart Continues His Career as a Cover Artist
text:
Rod Stewart's 'Soulbook' is very similar to his Great American Songbook collection; rather than singing classic Rat Pack era songs, or 'rock' standards as with another recent release, this time he's taking on 'soul' hits; classic R&B hits. Sigh. Don't get me wrong, Stewart's voice and style is definitely present but an issue I have with 'Soulbook' is that similar to the American Songbook series, the song line-up really don't do anything for him. They sound like cover songs (which they are), as if he's just singing them without much thought or true feeling. After 13 tracks, my main complaint is that this doesn't feel anything like Rod Stewart. It feels like Rod Stewart's leaving behind the style, attitude and personality that made him so popular and the musical icon that he is and is settling for covering other artists' songs and standards. What 'Soulbook' lacks is the soul of Stewart. Yes, he sings each song decently well but there's always a feeling that there's something missing in each track and on the album on a whole.

The Good: His voice is probably the best part of the album. It's his signature, it's raspy and it fits this genre a bit better than it did the American Songbook collection of tracks. There's a big 1970s vibe to the album and the arrangements of many of the songs, from the instruments to the production, makes 'Soulbook' sound as if it fits into his early releases. Unlike with the past songbook collections, Stewart comes off a bit more comfortable in this genre and back in his element. I felt he was best on "Tracks of My Tears" which is a very laid back and stripped-down affair where his voice and sensuality and sensibility are on display, and "If You Don't Know Me By Now" that is purely a cover song but his voice and vocals just makes it stand out.

The Bad: The weakness of the album comes from the fact that Rod Stewart seems willing to sit back and ride on the coat tails of others' hits and songs rather than break ground and take on new and original material. The entire cover-artist thing was a fun departure for one CD, it was interesting for a second, but with this being the fifth release of 'standards' and cover songs (4 counting the American Songbook collection, plus the album of rock standards) ... this act feels tired and a bit uninspired. You can distinctly tell he's not fully attached to some songs in the way he is when he's performing songs that are completely his. There's a definite attempt of sticking to the original rather than completely experimenting and mixing it up a bit on the songs because they are such big standards and well-known songs. To me, it held him back as an artist. On another note, this felt like a rather sleepy, uninspired release. There's no real spark to it and it gives off a feeling that this was just another release of covers to stay out there and make money. While his past collaborations have been really special, the Jennifer Hudson and Mary J Blige duets just did nothing for me either. Again, part of the problem is that the arrangements and treatments to the songs are straight-forward covers and (to me) are not showcasing the best of this great solo artist.

In all, 'Soulbook' is average at best. Nothing new, far too reserved and safe. I hope at some point Stewart returns to purely original material with songs that he can truly put his stamp on rather than playing things so safe and relying on others' songs and hits to keep his career going. A bit disappointing but listenable.

title: Yet Another Masterpiece
text:
I swear, somebody has been chipping these guys out of ice every few years so they can make an album and then they just freeze them back up so they can do it again in a few years. Slayer has basically sounded like the exact same band for twenty years. These guys make the same music every time out and every time it is freaking sweet. They don't make mistakes like most bands who try to "expand their sound" or "mature". When a band says that they have "made their most mature album to date", it means that they know it sucks. Slayer doesn't mess with that. They play thrash metal like it should be done and thats why they are the greatest metal band on earth.

So now to the new album: 'Christ Illusion' is yet another example of what a quality metal album should be. I would say that soundwise it is somewhere between 'Diabolus in Musica' and 'God Hates Us All'. Its thrashy like 'GHUA' yet retains the groove that they had on 'DIM'. It rips, it roars, its got awesome solo work, the riffs are brutal, the drumming is tight, the lyrics are great, and Tom's voice sounds really, really good. While all the tracks are good, the standout tracks, in my opinion, are: "Jihad"(which has quickly become one of my all-time favorite Slayer tracks), "Cult", "Flesh Storm", and "Consfearacy".

From front to back, 'Christ Illusion' is yet another masterpiece unleashed on the world by Slayer. All the members may be 40+ years old, but they are still delivering more brutal music than guys half their age. Heck, they are still delivering more brutal music than just about any band working today. These guys are legends for a reason and they don't seem to be slowing down at all. Pure awesomeness. Go buy it right now.

title: Yes, yes, and YES!
text:
What a great album. Occasionally, and I REALLY mean occasionally, a group will make a pop album that still remains engaging, relevant, and listenable years after it's released. Odessey and Oracle is one of those albums. Unlike so many groups who never even bothered trying to craft an entire, strong album and opted instead to work for that one hit single, the Zombies threw in all their chips and created a flawless, vibrant, catchy cohesive album and managed to kill their career AND get a sleeper smash hit single when it was too late.

Of course, you've heard "Time of the Season" countless times. Buy this album and discover the rest of the classic tracks that precede "Time of the Season," and perhaps even that song will be reinvigorated despite its familiarity.

The Zombies channel it all on this record--hooks by the score, seamless vocal harmonies, psychedelia, and some astounding musicianship. As Rod Argent would later prove in his more jam-based solo work, he's got keyboard chops to spare. Songs like "Care of Cell 44" and "Maybe After He's Gone" are propelled by impressive and catchy piano runs and riffs, and elsewhere on the album mellotron "strings" and "woodwinds" perfectly complement the trippy vocal arrangements and stop/start rhythm section song structures that make the songs rock with dynamic variety.

This record has so many classic songs, it's hard to believe there weren't more hit singles. "Brief Candles" is an emotionally wrenching series of portraits with a driving chorus, "This Will Be Our Year" does a great British soul/gospel thing. Like most great pop, Odessey and Oracle also contains great wit, like "Friends of Mine," but also some really tender heart, as on "A Rose for Emily." It's also pretty daring too--"Butcher's Tale" is pretty out there in subject matter and sound, really adding a more experimental and edgy feel to the end of the album. Throughout, Colin Blunstone's golden vocal chords handle the soaring melodies (with lots of harmony help from the rest of the band), and by the time you get to "Time of the Season," you finish the album satisfied and really appreciating the song you've heard so many times as part of a classic album. Highly recommended for fans of British psychedelic pop a la early Pink Floyd, Beatles, etc.

The album has been one of my favorites.He sings the songs in the style the were sung when the songs were first performed. In 1971 I had a fire at my home and the album was practically destroyed. I was able to salvage some of the songs on tape. I started looking for used copies of the album and was never able to locate one. I am very pleased that this CD album was released. It has the 21 original songs from the album plus a number of songs from a subsequent album that I did not know about. I would like to make a correction on the title of one of the songs on a review by another person. The song title is Come Where My Love Lies Dreaming, not Darling. The title is also part of the song itself. I am very happy to have a copy of the songs again. You could say that I have been waiting 30 years to obtain a new copy of the album. There is a chorus and orchestra conducted by Robert Armbruster supporting Nelson Eddy's singing. Some people have compared Stephen Foster's songs to Franz Schubert. Schubert had classical music training and Foster did not but one could find a resemblance there.

title: A Classic with controversial remixes
text:
I cut my teeth on jamming listening to Cream. So the Allmans' Live was not a revelation just a stunning album and purchased on release in Australia. I know it all by heart -just burnt into the synapses.

In 1992 Tom Dowd did a full concert remix and remaster as "The Fillmore Concerts". This is where the controversy starts cause it sounds different and so it should - Tom transferred the original 16 track master tapes to digital and remixed. Taking advantage of the wider dynamic and frequency range, he produced a mix with the bass guitar stronger and drums clearer and more dynamic. Unfortunately the guitar freaks found the relatively lower level guitar sound unacceptable but the bass freaks loved Berry's sound (more bottom end).

Now we have the SACD stereo, multi-channnel and Audio Stereo remaster release of the original 2 record set accurately split over 2 cds. It should fit on one but there is marketing to us baby boomers. But I gotta say they did perform split sets so it does reasonably capture the night.

And more controversy - the stereo CD layer is a remix closer to the original LP release. Drums are further back but the bass guitar bottom end is retained. The tracks are identical to the original release but not on the SACD layer with the Fillmore Concert's "Stormy Monday" used, which is the unedited version including the harmonica break, and a different edit to end "Whipping Post". On the SACD layer the tympany start to "Mountain Jam" is rapidly faded out and applause overdubbed which is annoying if you want the sonic continuity when following up with the jam from the "Eat A Peach" SACD.

Sound of both layers is excellent with SACD preferred because you can adjust the bottom end via the sub control. The surrounds give some reverb and audience noise - "Play all night". The centre has plenty of bass guitar, some drums and some of Greg's vocals (reinforcing the original centre-left positioning of the vocals). I would have preferred the drums a bit higher in the centre.

I can feel the SACD Deluxe "Fillmore Concerts" is on its way - the wallet is already feeling lighter.

title: Pacing problems give album overly somber feel
text:
This 1976 album was Genesis' last studio album before they began their transition to pop, as well as guitarist Steve Hackett's last album. The band was trying to return to the drama of "Foxtrot", but the album has pacing problems. There are too many songs with few moving parts, and as a result the songs come off seeming slower than they really are, giving the overall album a plodding feel. More upbeat pieces like "Pigeons" and Hackett's "Please Don't Touch" were left off the album, which didn't help. While all the songs are fine on their own, the whole is less than the sum of its parts. If you're already a fan of '70s Genesis, this is definitely worth buying; if you're not, there are better Genesis albums to try first.
There are three great songs here: "Eleventh Earl of Mar", the instrumental "in That Quiet Earth", and the ballad "Blood on the Rooftops" (despite the title, it's actually about watching too much TV, and it features some lovely acoustic work by Hackett). The other songs are ones that Genesis fans grow to enjoy, but may not impress the casual listener. "One for the Vine" is the most problematic track -- a long story-song by keyboardist Tony Banks that just isn't catchy enough to sustain its 10-minute length. It straddles the border between enjoyment and tedium, but some fans consider it a classic. "Your Own Special Way" is a pretty ballad, but the electric piano bridge is SO slow that the album screeches to a halt. "Afterglow" is a block-chord finale that is a favorite of many Genesis fans, with impassioned singing by Phil Collins. "Wot Gorilla" (an instrumental based on the catchiest riff from "One for the Vine") and "All in a Mouse's Night" (just what the title suggests) are the most inconsequential cuts on the album, but at the same time they're two of the liveliest tracks. I hope that someday the CD will be re-issued with the "Spot the Pigeon" songs included (three outtakes that were released as an EP).
(1=poor 2=mediocre 3=pretty good 4=very good 5=phenomenal)

title: Ignore your doubts, this is Buckcherry delivering the goods
text: This is a fantastic CD, and for me comprises the best body of consistent work that Buckcherry have put together for quite a while. I was sceptical about this EP, as the title and the song titles suggested a quickly thrown together idea just to get some bucks in, so I was amazed and impressed by how good all tracks are. The opener "Somebod F*cked with Me" is a great song harking back to Rage Against the Machine's ultimate F**k You song "Killing in the Name of". This is backed up by the bouncy energy and AC-DC riffage of "Say F**k It", and then the driven aggression of "The Motherf**ker". Things slow down slightly with the cool funky groove of "I don't give a F**k", while "It's  a F**king Disaster" has a lovely slow beginning that gets blown away by a snorting riff as the song picks up pace. And to round things out wonderfully is the punk slamming might of "Fist F**k" with its hints of Motorhead's classic "Ace of Spades". This is inspiring stuff! I think the guys in Buckcherry have done themselves a disservice by calling the EP "F**k" as it can all too easily be dismissed as a ill conceived concept album, where in reality it is a collection of six excellent rock songs that are all deserving their place. Four more tracks and this would have been an album up there with Buckcherry's finest work. Great stuff.

title: Grab your deck, Wayfarers, Stratocaster and retire to the beach after-party
text:
Beach Fossils
What a Pleasure EP
Brooklyn, New York

Engineered, Recorded, Mixed, and Produced at home by Dustin Payseur // Mastered at Bonati Mastering by Josh Bonati

It's called recession music, where a single individual does everything--from writing to recording (inexpensively)--and Beach Fossils fit the bill. Originally the solo effort of Dustin Payseur, who's driving summery guitar mazework receives like a relic of the `50s. With the help of John Pena, the duo authored the Self-Titled debut, the soundtrack to the summer of 2010. What a Pleasure features what makes the debut great, but is matured and seeks reservation as it moves through insipid guitar hooks and reclined harmonies, baked in reverb.

If the debut is the soundtrack to hitting the surf, What a Pleasure is for the bon fire, where unwinding begins and even dancing seems too exerting. "Calyer" and "What a Pleasure" are definite bliss: slow-going and heavy with listenability, the songs waver between undistorted electric guitar noodling and Payseur's rebelliously conversational vocals. "I wanna hear bad times / I wanna share bad times" ("Calyer") drones Payseur with punk-like affectation.

The EP glides along seamlessly, think Miles Davis' Kind of Blue--where cool is defined--and pace isn't pressured and a solo can sneak by unassumingly. Typically, a bass-drum-guitar arrangement results in a band wringing old tricks with new melodies, but technical competency allows Beach Fossils to stay on the cutting edge. Technique and skilled musicianship lead to longevity. And although fast-paced beach music is the norm (Surfer Blood and Wavves) the gleeful unobtrusiveness of What a Pleasure makes it inspired, buoyant and original. (Captured Tracks)

title: NOT from 1949
text: One thing that we know for sure is this record set is definitely NOT from 1949, as the 45 rpm 7" single was not introduced until 1950. Having 2 different sleeves on the 45's confuses the issue, but both do pre-date 1957. The style of the record labels date to pre-1955, but after 1950(which was a maroon color,1st year only). Many of these early 45 rpm albums didn't come with receord sleeves at all and if anything, had just pieces of paper in between the records to protect the labels. Due to the raised center of the label area, the grooves were automatically protected, paper or not. Going back, on 78 rpm, this album was first introduced in 1946. The advantage of the 45 rpm album, and even their 10" LP counterparts, they were made of vinyl and surface noise was considerably reduced compared to the noisy shellac 78's Decca was producing at the time. The only worse sounding 78's during the 40's and 50's released by the major record companies were the laminated composite 78's put out by Columbia/Epic/Okeh. RCA had the best sounding 78's, peaking in the mid-late 50's with their "New Orthophonic" sound and a higher quality shellac.

text:
After the slightly derivative if energetic debut album, John Rutsey's battle with diabetes forced him out of the band. Luckily, a much more dynamic presence stepped behind the drumset in the shape of Neil Peart, who was destined to change this band's course forever.
Peart's style was immediately apparent on "Anthem", inspired by Ayn Rand's book of the same name. His heavy yet adept style on the skins is the thread that ties this album together. The great songs on this disc (1, 3, 5, and 8) are the most representative of the band's sound at the time. The playing is crisp and clean throughout, even if the mix and production are slightly muddy.
However, the band is just beginning to hit its stride, and "Fly By Night" lacks the consistency and breadth of scope that the band would later achieve. Peart's lyrics are already great, but the several tracks that he had nothing to do with make the album seem kind of patchy. "In the End" and "Best I Can" could have found homes on the first album, although both, especially the latter, are well played. "By-Tor" is poorly paced and unexciting, but is interesting as a historical piece, if nothing else. "Making Memories" is Bob Seger lite. "Rivendell" is ersatz Tolkien slop.
The larger point, though, is that this music is way above what the average band was putting out in 1975, and certainly ambitious for 22 year old guys. It is more of a forerunner than a truly great album, but is worth you time to purchase.

title: Cal Tjader: Best of the Concord Years
text:
Cal Tjader (July 16, 1925-May 5, 1982) was a Latin jazz musician, though he also explored various other jazz idioms. Unlike other American jazz musicians who experimented with the music from Cuba, the Caribbean, and Latin America, he never abandoned it, performing it until his death.

Tjader primarily played the vibraphone. He was also accomplished on the drums, bongos, congas, timpani, and the piano. He worked with numerous musicians from several cultures. He is often linked to the development of Latin Rock and Acid Jazz. Although fusing jazz with Latin music is often categorized as "Latin Jazz" (or, earlier, "Afro-Cuban Jazz"), Tjader's output swung freely between both styles.

He won a Grammy in 1980 for his album La Onda Va Bien, capping off a career that spanned over forty years.

Carl Jefferson, president of Concord Records, created a subsidiary label called Concord Picante to market Latin jazz. In reality, Jefferson formed the label specifically to promote and distribute Tjader's work, whom he'd recently signed.

Unlike his excursions in the 1960s and his jazz-rock attempts in the 1970s, Tjader's Concord Picante work was largely straight-ahead Latin jazz. Electronic instruments and rock backbeats were dropped, reverting to a more "classic" sound. During the prior decade he'd built up a top-notch crew of young musicians, his best lineup since his Modern Mambo Quintet of the 1950s, with Mark Levine on piano, Roger Glenn on flute, Vince Lateano on drums, Robb Fisher on the bass, and Poncho Sanchez on the congas.

Tjader cut five albums for Concord Picante, the most successful being La Onda Va Bien (1979) (roughly "The Good Life") which earned a Grammy award in 1980 for Best Latin Recording. That Onda would win an award as best Latin album reveals Tjader's expertise and his ability to cultivate the same in his band. La Onda Va Bien is regarded as a seminal Latin Jazz album.

title: The Last of Santana's "Jazz" Masterpieces
text:
2010 Columbia Legacy Remaster of ILLUMINATIONS, ONENESS, and SWING OF DELIGHT available for less than $12 in a 3-Pack (see last note below).

Carlos Santana and company followed a hugely successful debut album trilogy (SANTANA-ABRAXAS-SANTANA) with a Santana trilogy of "fusion" jazz works (CARAVANSERAI, WELCOME, BORBOLETTA), critically acclaimed but not too commercially successful (other than from the rank and file of Santana devotees). In between all this and further on Carlos himself released "solo" albums (mostly comprising collaborations with other fusion aficionados such as on this album).
This was the fusion set which garnered new fans, emboldened more than a few old fans, and lost a number of original fans:
Caravanserai, October 1972
Love Devotion Surrender, July 1973 (with John McLaughlin)
Welcome, November 1973
Lotus, May 1974
Illuminations, September 1974 (with Alice Coltrane)
Borboletta, October 1974

On the heels of this, Santana caved into Bill Graham and worked on some Latin-Rock albums in a 70's attempt to draw in the pop and disco crowds. AMIGOS in '76, and FESTIVAL in '77 did well, but not on the levels of the original SANTANA trilogy. AMIGOS did however add in a Tom Coster fusion jazz new agey coda to the Latin Dance track (Dance Sister Dance) which soars into the stratosphere and gloriously saves an otherwise unremarkable Baila Mi Hermana! Gitano explored Santana's acoustic and flamenco abilities, and Europa became one of the bands most called for anthems, surpassing Samba Pa Ti in Latin-infused blues-guitar. FESTIVAL then fused more Latino rock to jazz and overall is a fine work of melding all the Santana genre into an organic flowing river of masterful music. In October of '77 Santana released the masterpiece double LP MOONFLOWER which fuses 70's fusion jazz and live Santana performances into one of the best albums in the artist's complete discography, and yes he even threw in a rock song that became a smash hit single (a cover of The Zombies' She's Not There). Tom Coster and Carlos prevailed in MOONFLOWER to return an acceptable Jazz infusion to Santana albums, but by 1977 there was a growing FM and living room presence of Spyro Gyra, Weather Report, Return To Forever, etc, so the magic worked and MOONFLOWER was a huge success.

After the somewhat mediocre INNER SECRETS (October 1978), Carlos again dove into a fusion exercise, ONENESS (March 1979) which experimented with some new agey/jazzy concoctions melded with funky pop and a whole lot of spirituality highly reminiscent of ILLUMINATIONS backed with his late 70's work. It was a solid effort for fans of the genre and an obvious devotional to his guru, fulfilling his inner desires to maintain a presence in the fusion world. Then in September of '79 Santana released MARATHON, more maligned than necessary since it is a mainly complete return to his early rock roots, with some funk/R&B influences and an outstanding single sampling of "jazz" (Aqua Marine being one of the best jazzy tracks he ever composed).

It was then in August of 1980 that Carlos fully realized his jazz mindset with the completion and release of THE SWING OF DELIGHT, veritably the last true "jazz" album he would release (BLUES FOR SALVADOR in '87, and SANTANA BROTHER in '94 would come close but not like this).

THE SWING OF DELIGHT is a masterpiece of late 70's/early 80's era jazz works, enlisting the talents of Miles Davis' band collaborators, to pursue the kind of works that illuminated Return To Forever and Weather Report, with splashes of Spyro Gyra, Mahavishnu Orchestra, Antonio Carlos Joabim, Deodato, and Al Di Meola. The personnel list says it all: Herbie Hancock, Wayne Shorter, Ron Carter, Tony Williams, and Harvey Mason as a guest. Supplanted with these luminaries are Santana band stalwarts, Graham Lear (drums), David Margen (bass), and the incredible percussive section of Armando Peraza and Raul Rekow. If you love the jazz of the artists mentioned above, if you love the talents of them all, this is a spectacular set, originally released as a double LP with a total running time of 57 minutes. There is not a weak track on the whole offering and the styles run the gamut of rock fusion to Brazilian bossa nova, but no track remains anchored and the time signature changes are always at the ready to up the ante.

Unlike any of the other Santana jazz albums (no matter how you categorize them), SWING OF DELIGHT is a highly charged "clean" jazz album, with straight superb playing, you won't hear Carlos holding those sustained vibratory notes, bending the strings into the upper atmosphere. What you hear is an ensemble of interacting maestros displaying a cohesive collective talent and drive, and sheer verisimilitude of honest "fusion jazz" from the hands of those who nearly invented the medium as we came to know it. I personally hate the word "fusion" since jazz is by definition fusion, but the label has stuck with a myriad of styles from "smooth jazz" to McLaughlin-esque "speed jazz" and "shredding", none of which you find on this perfectly engineered and produced work of art. You will notice that guru Sri Chinmoy gets credited for song writing on this album (as well as contributing the cover art). In about a year, Carlos and his wife will become pretty disillusioned with him and though they may hang on for a while to the Self Realization Fellowship principles (which do not require a Guru or Master to follow), this is nearly the last place you will encounter Devadip attached to Carlos Santana (the last being the follow-up to SWING, 1981's fantastic rock album ZEBOP!)

If you like jazz, but were put off by some of Carlos Santana's mystical stylings (ILLUMINATIONS, ONENESS), THE SWING OF DELIGHT may just be your perfect cup of tea. The artists enlisted on this album speak volumes about the kind of music you will hear on it. This is truly Santana's last great jazz masterpiece, and he went out with a show-stopper! (as I indicated earlier, BLUES FOR SALVADOR and SANTANA BROTHERS will provide you with some last jazzy refreshments, but for whole album enterprises, this one was the end of the road).

Last note: The 2010 Columbia Legacy Remaster (by Sony) is gorgeous. If you don't care about credits and liner notes, you can pick up all three 2010 Remasters of ILLUMINATIONS, ONENESS, and SWING OF DELIGHT for less than $12 in a 3-Pack from Amazon, just search for "Santana 3 original album classics". The three CD's come in original replica cardboard sleeves, no additional goodies (you can look up the credits and album info on line at Sony and Legacy Recording websites)

title: At last it's available on CD
text: Way back in 1974, the RCA LP of Pachelbel's Canon and Fasch trumpet concertos by the Paillard Orchestra was released.  It became a hit record, a crossover from Classical, and an overused cliche forever afterward.  It was because of this album, that everyone else immediately discovered Pachelbel and released a version of it.  The Paillard Orchestra version is still unique because of its slower pacing, and as stated in another's review, more pronounced plucked (pizacata?) strings.  It is still the FIRST AND BEST version, everyone else's is too fast, too scrunched, overpowering any continuo.  Don't know about the sound quality on this CD, but digital is not always better than analog because of sampling rates and clipping. The pairing with other (now well-known) pieces by Pachelbel, and the wonderful Maurice Andre playing Fasch still make this album the best, unique, a keeper, and archival material for being the first version of the Canon to start a 30 year craze.  Thank goodness I now have a CD in case my favorite LP (along with the Paillard Orchestra's Bach Branderberg Concertos) can no longer find a turntable to play it.

title: A Band in Transition
text:
Weather Report could rarely hold down a rhythm section for more than a year, and here we see the band in transition from 'Tale Spinnin' to the seven-star classic 'Heavy Weather'. Al Johnson would be replaced by Jaco Pastorius on bass, the drummer was shifting from Ngudu to Chester Thompson to Acuna, and percussionist from Alyrio Lima to Acuna to the notorious Badrena. It got so bad that co-leader Zawinul would later audition drummers like Omar Hakim down the phone. So the tasteful photo of the band posing with various bits of fresh fruit that you'll see on the back cover of the CD gives the illusion of stability. In truth it represents a period of a few milliseconds in the band's history. Before the cheese and biscuits course arrived, the band would have gone through at least five changes of percussionist. (After this album, by the way, Chester Thompson went on to tour with rock band Genesis to allow Phil Collins to concentrate on crooning.)
The extraordinary thing about Weather Report is that it was the rhythms that attracted so many people. Although ostensibly the front men and main composers, Zawinul and Shorter really just provided the backdrop for their incredible rhythm sections. Sometimes they just got in the way. On 'Mysterious Traveller' there are some marvellous Al Johnson bass lines where you'd love to turn up the volume, but you know you can't because you know there's another blast from Shorter just round the corner that will give you a heart attack, it's so loud.
'Black Market' was one of those LPs where side one always got a lot more play than side two. And rightly so. They should appeal to any intelligent rock fan, to anyone who likes a good bass line, and to anyone who likes tapping out the drums on a tabletop. You could even dance to much of this.
You cannot go wrong in buying any of the Weather Report albums in the period stretching from 'Sweetnighter' to 'Heavy Weather'. All are at least five-star.

title: Fantastic discovery of Graupner's bassoon-concertos
text:
This is phenomenal addition to Azzolini's stunning achievement in recording Vivaldi's bassoon concertos (two volumes yet of a corpus of about 37 (sic!)preserved concertos from the hand of the red priest on Naïve, also a must-have, even though you perhaps is not such a big fan of this instrument). Vivaldi is perhaps even more original and surprising in his concertos, but any way, Azzolini is the musician to go for in this repertoire. The precision in the fast movements and the stunning beauty of the adagios, largos or andantes is nothing short of exceptional no matter what wind instrument you prefer. Azzolini has done much research in these concertos and is both a scholar and an artist of very high standards. He plays a bassoon which produces a rare and intense sound, unlike most other "baroque" bassoonist's instrument I've heard. His interpretations are original and thought provoking, sometimes even shocking in their directness.

Christoph Graupner (1683-1760) came late to the concerto genre, and wrote four bassoon concertos (possible in the 1730'ies), even if this is a small output in comparison to Antonio Vivaldi's exceptionally large oeuvre, Graupner is in the lead when it comes to bassoon concertos both in number and quality. The orchestra is a fine one and plays one-to-a-part. It has a crisp articulation, and the recording from 2007 (why it has been shelved for four years is rather obscure...)is nicely balanced, even though the bass is a little prominent at some places. The concertos for violin (A major) and a triple-concerto for chalumeau, bassoon and cello is well worth hearing and tell us what a congenial composer Graupner was (even though I would say that he shines even brighter in his orchestral suites). This is a truly fascinating recording which is in the must-have category when it comes to releases of instrumental music in 2011. Vivi felice, as Domenico Scarlatti would have put it.

title: Give Burt and Ernie (er, ELVIS) a chance
text:
Reading the reviews of 'Painted from Memory' makes for an interesting afternoon. As I continue my journey through the Elvis Costello catalogue, I thought I'd toss in my two cents. As someone who thought I was only a fan of his early rock recordings (Aim, Model & Armed Forces), I'm pleasantly surprised to find that I very much enjoy Costello's later forays into other genres.

I initially agreed with comments here that Elvis's voice doesn't seem suited for the material. However, I quickly did a 180 on that. I don't know that I can explain it, but somehow his plaintive caterwauling here is compelling in a way that the dulcet crooning of a Michael Buble would not be.

Consistency in quality is a hallmark of 'Painted from Memory'. There are not just a couple of stand-out cuts; the entire recording is solid. Everyone who takes the time to sample this unusual offering from Costello and Bacharach will have their own favorites.
