title: A classic from a genius....
text:
At the risk of repeating the previous reviewer, this is a must have for any serious calypso fan, and I was equally astonished that there is a cd version of it. I have a worn copy of the LP, and now I have this sparkling cd, cheap even at its import price.

If you have ever heard one of Birdy's subpar records and wondered what all the fuss was about, this record will enlighten you. Absolutely kinetic versions of some of his greatest songs, with an extremely hot band, all recorded beautifully, with wonderfully fleshed out arrangements.

These are more or less classics of Sparrow's calypso career ,pre soca (the less lyrical, more dance oriented version of calypso, which took hold in the late '70s), but what is so wonderful here is that these songs have been redone with a very early soca type sound, and the result is fabulous.

The collection includes a superior version of one of the great calypsos ever recorded, and probably my favorite Sparrow song - 'Memories'. It truly evokes the bittersweet emotions that carnival inspires in Trinis, and non Trinis who love the culture. I get chills every time I hear some of the lines:

"Albert Moore, I'll always remember / Jumping when a steel band pass / Playing big mas / Sugary, peppery Al was never ever one for class / Dear Albert, wherever you are Confrere, just for you I came out with real fire this year"

A rare classic, buy this,and love it. As an added bonus, the sound quality is surprisingly fine, especially for a '74 recording. It stands up well compared to my LP.

title: Missing the Mark
text: Even as a huge fan of the Jacksons, I bought this with some hesitancy.  First, I had all the tracks (in older, non-remastered versions, but still had them) and the only new music to my ears was the extra 30 seconds of "Enjoy Yourself" ad-libs.  And second, I wondered about the title.  Sure, the Jacksons made some very good and influential music post-Motown, but was there enough "Essential" music to fill a whole disc?  In my mind, the "Essentials" would include every charting hit, as well as any album tracks that help showcase muscial growth or influence.  In this case, including one or two of the Jacksons' first self-penned songs ("Blue Away," "Style of Life," "Different Kind of Lady," or "Do What You Wanna") would have been interesting and important.  There was plenty of room on the disc for adding a song or two.  One of the biggest gems on the disc is "Find me a Girl."  What a perfect display of Michael's soulfulness and vocal mastery.  Including only the two singles from "Destiny" is a shame, as that album was really their breakthrough into adult success and had several great dance-funk tunes that set the Jacksons apart from the cookie-cutter disco crowd.  Leaving off "Torture" and "Body" (both top 40 hits) from the "Victory" album, while inserting the live version of "Don't Stop 'Til You Get Enough" seems to lean this set toward Michael and not the group.  In essence, this set doesn't seem to find its goal.  It's not a greatest hits collection, as some of their hits are not here while some of their flops are; and as I have stated, it doesn't successfully cover all of what I would call their "Essential" music.

title: Even more impressive than the debut
text:
Alter Bridge, consisting of Myles Kennedy and three former members of Creed (Mark Tremonti, Brian Marshall and Scott Phillips), splashed onto the scene in 2004 with [[ASIN:B0002IU988 One Day Remains]]. Their debut turned out to be a welcomed one, for Mark Tremonti, lead guitarist, was able to showcase his guitar talents even more so than he was able to do whilst confined to Creed. For those looking for another showcase, Blackbird will be a treat. For newcomers, expect something not quite rock `n roll, certainly not nu metal, but just solid modern rock. While the debut was successful (it is certified gold) but not epic, one may perhaps see a hindrance in success the second time around. Hopefully this is not the case, for the sophomore effort is even more impressive and should draw a larger fan base in a perfect world.

Sure, Alter Bridge are a radio-friendly band, but their two albums incorporate innovative riffs, lyrics with legitimate emotion, and the icing on the cake - guitar solos. Blackbird is a composition of thirteen songs (the UK version actually has a bonus track, "We Don't Care At All"), which arguably could be labeled "cookie cutter" rock anthems. One might compare the style to Nickelback for the catchiness or possibly Thornley's debut, [[ASIN:B000228EPO Come Again]], for the heaviness. Some songs feature tasty hooks and licks, while others explore melodies and beautiful sounds. Tremonti puts on another show yet again, still delivering the riffs and exceptional solos. With his talent, fans would probably welcome an instrumental album of some kind if he chose to pursue it. Kennedy's vocals sound more loose and flavorful than the first time around, and this could be the result of becoming more comfortable with his new band mates. Individual efforts aside, Blackbird is overall solid rock and ranks as the better of the two albums.

Buck Dharma really shines, and the band as a whole shred thru the eerie opener "The Subhuman" all the way to the closing cover tunes--"Masarati GT" and "Born/Wild" are left in smoking ruins of busted guitars and strings. title: Let's hope this isn't the last... Excellent Album
text:
This album sees Blink-182 groing mature lyrically. I enjoy the more serious lyrics, not to say I don't love older Blink (Enema Of The State will always be my favorite Blink album), but this album is right up there with Enema, and TOYPAJ right after. Here is a review of the songs.
(Not particularly in track order)

1. Feeling This- I didn't like this song when I first heard it, but the more I listened, the more it grew on me. Do the same, and it will grow on you too. Also it's one of the best the album has to offer. 10/10
2. I Miss You- The biggest single from the album, possibly the biggest of their career. Very sweet song. A slow but steady tempo. Love the piano at the end of the song. The only thing about this song is I wish it had another verse or so, or maybe used more lines in the chorus. Still, one of the CD's best. 10/10
Always- I just love the way this song sounds. Third best on the album. Also love the 80s sounding synthesizer at the end of the song. 9/10
Down- 4th best song on the album. But the more I listen to it, the more I fall in love with it. It stands as one of my favorite blink songs to date. More use of the piano in this one, which always in my opinion helps a rock song. Love how it ends, with the low piano note. 8/10
Violence- A fast paced song, with the verses more spoken than sung. I enjoy the chorus, only Tom's voice fits in for it, and so it works out. 7/10
I'm Lost Without You- More Piano! Which of course for me is awesome. Much slower song than you might expect from Blink, very sweet, an easy pace. Love the synthesizer in the background during the second verse. A little overlong is it's only flaw. 7/10
Easy Target- Very nice song! Energetic, good verses, good chorus. I wish it were just a bit longer... 7/10
Stockholm Syndrome- Fastest song on the album. Moves along quicky, hard. Suprisingly catchy. 6.5/10
Obvious- Pretty good song. I like the chorus. Lyrics are possibly the most dark in this song. 6.5/10
All Of This- The person singing the verses in this song is Robert Smith from The Cure. Some people make a big deal about this song. It's alright, not all that great. A little boring sounding, but not all that bad either. The chorus saves it. 6/10
Asthenia- The intro is long and arduous. Very unneccesary. Once past this, it's an OK song. Good guitar. 6/10
Here's Your Letter- Not a bad song, nothing special by any means, but worth a listen or two. Fairly short. 5.5/10
Go- About Mark's dad. Fast paced tune. Very short. 5/10
The Fallen Interlude- I don't think Blink should be writing techno. Enough said. Easily the worst song here. 3/10

Overall, this is a stellar album, and I highly reccomend it if you're without it. Completes the Blink-182 collection. I know I'm not alone in wishing they'd get back together and grace us with more albums like this and their others.

title: It is everything it promises to be
text:
As advertised, this is a collection of 60 Howlin' Wolf songs spread over three discs. Each disc is structured to lead off with an entire album (Moanin' in the Moonlight, Howlin' Wolf Sings the Blues, and the Rocking Chair album) and is then filled out with singles. The sound quality is mostly okay and varies from song to song. Some songs do not have the best sound quality and can come across as fuzzy (I chalk that up to the 50's recording technology). Many of the songs (especially the really famous ones) have excellent quality and are clear and clean.

The packaging is really nice. It's a quadra-fold type cardboard package with individual plastic holders for each CD, so it's easy to take the discs out and out them back. The pictures and graphic design are great, and the set includes a booklet that gives background information and some evaluation of the life and works of Howlin' Wolf.

One complaint I have about the album is it doesn't cover the Wolf's full career. Instead, it covers a period from 1951 to maybe 1962 or 1963. As a result, it leaves out Killing Floor and some other late career hits. Otherwise it's an excellent set.

title: Better in the less-familiar works
text: Yan-Pascal Tortelier produces a surprisingly French timbre from the Ulster Orchestra (in contrast to the women's chorus in "Sirenes," which wafts to the ear as endearingly and beguilingly--if incongruously--Irish), and this conductor clearly knows his Debussy. Yet like another Frenchman who recorded a comprehensive survey of Debussy's orchestral music, Jean Martinon, Tortelier makes a stronger impression with the lesser-known works, many of them orchestrated by hands other than the composer's. As fluent as the music-making is, all too often there's something tossed-off and careless about it. This manifests in overly-smooth phrasing and inconsistent orchestral balances--sometimes tellingly transparent, sometimes skewed to over-emphasize a particular strand at the expense of coherence. For this reason, Tortelier's "La Mer" and "Nocturnes," unfortunately, cause me to think of other, more successful performances I'd rather be hearing, and likewise "Jeux," although "Images" is a winner. Throughout the cycle, I'm not too crazy about Chandos' very resonant and distant sound, which gives the music an opulence that is foreign to its character--and creates its own intereference with details registering properly. Moreover, "La Mer" has been recorded with an exaggeratedly wide dynamic range, so that the opening bars are nearly inaudible. Still, there isn't too much competition for Debussy sets that offer this much music at a bargain price.

text:
This is one of those albums you will buy and like, but then sort of loose it among your Dulli/Lannegan collection, then later you will be like "oh, I forgot about that one," and you will put it in and it will be your favorite all over again.

That being said, I would have liked more than one song with the electronic beats. Maybe one of you fellow fans can direct me to a project where they did a lot with more electronics. Oh well, this is still a very rich, and creepy kind of album, with some interesting Biblical references. The lyrics are like classic blues/country lyrics that take you to a very dark place.

You would be hard pressed to find any flaws here, if you are a fan and you know to expect a sort of rootsy take on the post-grunge world these guys exist in. There are acoustic songs, and slightly upbeat rocker type songs (not very heavy though), and pianos and sort of an everything-but-the-kitchen sink approach to combining both singers range of stylistic preferences. It is a very rich and mature album, that someone like Johnny Cash or Mearle Haggard could find quite a bit of inspiration in. Saturnailia is kind of a downtrodden journey, but I really hope Gutter Twins keep up the good work.

title: Great Gems
text: Buble's "Call Me Irresponsible" is a fine set with some real jewels.  He obviously idolizes Frank Sinatra & shines on "That's Life" with a punchy arrangement, "I've been up & down & over & out & I know one thing, each time I find myself flat on my face I pick myself up & get back in the race."  Of my very two favorites are the opener "The Best Is Yet to Come" with its cheerful anticipation, "Wait till the warm-ups are underway, wait till our lips have met, wait till you see that sunshine day, you ain't seen nothing yet!"  "Me & Mrs. Jones" is a tale of an affair and was a startling Gamble & Huff soul track for Billy Paul.  Buble milks the jazz out of the track, while sounding quite soulful.  Harold Arlen is one of my favorite songwriters; so like other reviewers, I question the lisp on "I've Got the World on a String."  It's probably supposed to be funny, but it sounds like he's making fun of the song.  Joel Peskin's sax on the track blows deliciously.  This set has some great gems.  Enjoy!

title: GNR FOR THE FANS
text:
I am one of the biggest Guns n' Roses fans you'll ever meet but the reason I'm giving out 4 stars is because this album is strictly for hardcore GNR fans only. This album displays Axl Rose's outrageous instability, however the song writing is remarkably well done.

Song by Song:

1. Civil War: This is the most powerful song on the album in terms of the meaning. Lyrically its brilliant, as the GNR crew is not afraid to touch on a very controversial issue. GNR decided to bring in Steven Adler on drums for this one and he did a wonderful job. Also, I'm charmed by the fantastic solo coming from who else other than Slash. When I bought this album, I listened to this track over and over again, and each time I loved it. Truly brilliant. 10/10

2. 14 Years: This song is typical GNR, however they're not especially heavy on this track. Once again, the crew gives a strong lyrical performance. It's tune isn't wonderful, but its pretty good. 8.5/10

3. Yesterdays: This is probably the best song, musically, off the album. It has a beautiful tune to it and it's one of GNR's classic ballads. 9.5/10

4. Knockin' on Heaven's Door: This Bob Dylan cover has a splendid beginning to it, however they drag this track on much too long. Bob Dylan wrote it as being 2:32 while GNR felt it necessary to be 5:36. They give a beautiful melody, however some feel that Axl Rose's screeching, high voice doesn't fit well with this song. I like the song, but it has been criticized. 8.5/10

5. Get in the ring: This song gives us the idea of how psychotic and disillusioned Axl Rose is. He yells out profanities at reviewers who gave GNR bad reviews and continues on cursing until the end. It carries an interesting melody to it and can be catchy but this is a little too outrageous of a track for me to praise. 6.5/10

6. Shotgun Blues: This song is falling back on the quick, sharp rockish sound we heard from alot in "Use Your Illusion I". It has a great flow to it, and is paced very nicely. It's one of my favourites off this album. 9.5/10

7. Breakdown: Breakdown carries a beautiful, touching tune to it with a lame, pointless chorus that puts it average overall in terms of GNR music. The ballad is beautifully orchestrated and it is strong lyrically until you reach the chorus that could've been so much more. 8/10

8. Pretty tied up: The tune is catchy, yet possesses nothing to consider it a great song. It's quite overrated. It's a good song, no more than that. 8.5/10

13. Don't Cry (Alt. Lyrics): This tune taken from "Use Your Illusion I" is a beautiful ballad. However, the original is far superior on the lyrical standpoint. Still, I can't get enough of this tune so it still gets 9/10

14. My World: Hmmmm. This one is hard to describe. It's whacky, confusing and interesting. It shows us the twisted mind of Rose and also has a nice little punk side to it which I eventually caught on to a little despite Rose's crude lyrical insight on supposedly how he lives his life. 7.5/10

title: ROCKS WITH THE INTENSITY OF BOWIE'S SPIDERS BAND
text:
Cope is a lovable nut job. He tasted major stardom in Britain as the leader of The Teardrop Explodes from 1979-82. What followed after was the conspicuous consumption of enough LSD to make Grace Slick's head pop off, as well as some weird and very uneven solo work with flashes of brilliance. Fast forward to 1986. He curtailed his indulgences some and recorded a great, dare I say almost mainstream album with a band that rocks like Bowie's Spiders from Mars.
Saint Julian got him some long overdue exposure here, mainly on MTV, with two videos: "World Shut Your Mouth" and "Trampolene".
His image had changed radically from the clean cut, almost preppy looking lad from 1980, to a long haired acid head from 82-85, and then, the leather clad menace seen here, railing against God and the church. He was an atheist or agnostic at the time and would later claim a spiritual awakening which lead him into the study of Wicca and the ancient Druids. He has written a book also available here on the history of the mysterious stone circles of the British Isles.
Cope sings in two voices. His tenor is very unique and when he slips down into his lower register, he can sound remarkably like Jim Morrison or Iggy Pop, though he's a much better singer than either of them.
Saint Julian rocks hard, but has a poppy edge to some of it that often serves as counterpoint to his strange lyrics. He has always been able to write clever tunes with hooks that reach out and grab the listener, even on his more left field efforts.
I also recomend "Peggy Suicide" from 1991. The only other release of his from the 90's I'm up on is "20 Mothers", which was very uneven. Also, be sure to check out his Teardrop Explodes material, since it's been reissued. If he's ever on tour here again, don't miss him. I've had the pleasure 3 times.

title: Exquisite Songs; Mostly Good Performances
text:
[Update: This disc has just been nominated for a Grammy award.]

The review here dated August 7 was written by Berkant Haydin, an expert on the music of Joseph Marx, and I certainly don't have much to add to what he's written. Indeed, he also co-wrote the booklet notes for this release and his review is actually an abstract of those notes.

He's certainly right in saying that Marx's orchestral songs are luscious. The first set, eleven songs sung to perfection by soprano Angela Maria Blasi, are mostly short, usually strophic and have brilliant orchestral accompaniments and melodies reminiscent of Schubert, Schumann and Brahms. Marx was not only a master orchestrator, he had a fecund melodic gift. The last song (and longest at seven minutes), 'Barkarole,' ('Barcarolle') is rather different in that it is almost a symphonic poem with voice obbligato.

The next two sets of songs (six 'Songs for Middle Voice,' and 'Verklärtes Jahr' ['Transfigured Year'], a 'song symphony' of five movements) are sung by mezzo Stella Doufexis and unfortunately suffer a bit, to my ears, from the somewhat wearing quality of her voice, which seems to lack some degree of support and a clear central core. The songs themselves, however, are simply lovely. In the later set, written in 1930-1932, what has been called 'Romantic impressionism' is evident in the extremely intricate and wholly lovely orchestral writing. There are many moments that sound almost like Respighi, which is not too far-fetched as some of the music was inspired by Marx's love of Italy. Further, it quotes from his Second Piano Concerto, subtitled 'Castelli Romani' ('Roman Castles'). So, while Doufexis's performance leaves a bit to be desired, the music itself is extremely winning and deserves to be better known.

I understand that there is a real possibility that Marx's two piano concerti will be recorded and released some time in the next year or so. I have, through the kindness of Mr Haydin, heard old off-the-air recordings of those concerti and am eager to hear modern performances. And we're still awaiting a first recording of what some might consider Marx's masterpiece, his monumental 'Herbstsymphonie' ('Autumn Symphony').

title: Hot Metal
text:
After the dissapointing sales of their debut album,Kiss(with producers Kerner and Wise)decided to take the heavier approach on the follow up.The recording sessions in LA didn't pass without incident,but it didn't show on the finished product,HOTTER THAN HELL.Although derided at the time for it's murky production and Led Zepplin attitude,it is now regarded by hard rock critics as an underrated gem.Sure,less songs were used in concert from this album than from KISS,but it's heavier edge places the band well on the road to the classic Kiss sound.
1)GOT TO CHOOSE - Paul Stanley warns his girl that the time has come to stop fooling around.I could be wrong,but methinks I hear an acoustic guitar buried in the mix.Great group harmonies on the chorus.It surprises me that no one has picked up on how well the boys could sing harmnies.The guitar solo from Ace Frehley is concise and individualistic.
2)PARASITE - Sung by Gene Simmons,written by Ace.There's a clinging lover who must be dropped or there'll be trouble.Cool opening riff and fretwork by the man from the planet Jendel,who used this song in the early concerts to lead into his solo showcase.
3)GOIN' BLIND - Power ballad by Gene with a tongue-in-cheek edge; about a love affair between an old(er)man and a young(er)woman. Carries on the wicked sense of humor Gene first displayed on KISS' NOTHIN' TO LOOSE.The original title of this song was LITTLE LADY.
4)HOTTER THAN HELL - Paul gives us a tale with a warning:always look for a wedding band if you have a one night stand!Peter Criss goes gonzo on the backbeat and I love that gong he strikes at the climax to the song.Ace's guitar dances around Petert's skinwork.
5)LET ME GO,ROCK'N'ROLL - A good excuse for a group jam.Very few of Kiss rivals' could compete with them when they were firing on all cylinders.
6)ALL THE WAY - Gene complains that his latest beau has become a pain in the neck(to put it mildly!).He lets his demon persona loose on the vocals to this slight,but quirky track.Rumbling bass,piercing guitar and dropping drumbeats mix with great Gene/Paul vocals on the chorus.
7)WATCHIN' YOU - Left off the first album and already a concert staple.This is Kiss at their best:very heavy and never humble!The Demon and his girl are in a room with people who like to watch ('nuff said!).This track is more heavy metal than hard rock.
8)MAINLINE - If love is the drug,then the Catman's addicted!Great vocals from Peter.I wish this could have been attempted live.
9)COMIN'HOME - Paul is getting sick of touring and wants to get back to his baby.Great use of acoustic guitar.This track (plus GOIN'BLIND and GOT TO CHOOSE)was resurrected from the historic KISS UNPLUGGED event.
10)STRANGE WAYS - Written by Ace,sung by Peter.The Catman is stuck in the middle of a love affair that's both weird and cool. Peter is in screaming mode for this one.Contains spaced out fretwork by Ace,including a solo that would send a first time guitar novice interstellar.

title: Very enjoyable, the best of the Comsat Angels reissues.
text:
For some reason, Renascent's liner notes to the reissue of Fiction criticize the album, even though they had nothing but praise for the first two. In reality, Fiction is much better and more enjoyable than either Waiting For A Miracle or Sleep No More. This album marked the point when, like many of the other post-punk bands of the time, the Comsat Angels decided to exchange monochromatic angst for variety and catchiness. The sound of Fiction is as colourful as the cover.

The greater variety of the album is evident in "After The Rain," the very first song. Stephen Fellows sings in such a soft, gentle voice that it's impossible to recognize him if all you've heard is Sleep No More. He's backed by a light-hearted five-note keyboard hook, again quite unlike the cold atmospherics from the first two albums. The lyrics encourage you not to be depressed, because "the sky will clear again after the rain." But lest you think the band has stopped worrying and sold out completely, the deep bass adds a sense of looming darkness, and there's something sad about the way Fellows chants "fall, fall" in the beginning and end of the song. These details add a bit of subtle ambiguity to the lyrics. "After The Rain" is an even better single than "Independence Day," which was the best Comsat Angels song up to this point. It should have been massive, and probably would have been had Polydor bothered to promote it better.

There's one more great single tacked on to the very end, as a bonus track. "Do The Empty House" has a great nervous guitar lead, and an exceptionally well-written lyric. One of my problems with Sleep No More is that the lyrics are so vague that it's difficult to care about whatever it is that Fellows is on about. But here, everything is specific and vividly described. He uses the image of a decrepit old house as a metaphor for letting oneself become complacent. "If we don't go soon, we might stay forever," he beseeches after his description of how "the roof is cracked and the rain is coming in / the floorboards creak and all the lights are dim." The song is fast-paced and wonderfully catchy. Yet more proof that "Independence Day" wasn't a fluke, and the Comsat Angels had it in them to do even better.

That's it for the great singles, but many of the album tracks are quite good also. "Now I Know" is built on Celtic-type guitar strumming, again with an appealingly pensive air. "Ju Ju Money" is a rewrite of an early non-album track (included as a bonus track on the reissue of Waiting For A Miracle) that trades the original's ominous tension for a larger, more immersive and lush sound with layered echoing guitars vaguely similar to The Cure around The Head On The Door. Except Fiction came earlier, of course. And even though Fellows disparages "Don't Look Now" in the liner notes, on the grounds that it was improvised in the studio and he made up the lyrics as he went along, that song actually has a great chorus. The way the guitar arpeggio alternates with the title phrase is again very catchy and memorable.

Some of the other songs tend to blend together, but even they have their moments. The intro to "Birdman," in which Fellows repeats the meaningless phrase "I want to do some time on cloud nine," is really embarrassing, but the rest of the song is actually great. Fellows' impassioned singing sounds very good amidst the big guitars. He also does well in "Pictures," another soft song. Compared to his fairly unremarkable vocals on Waiting For A Miracle, he's really come into his own as a singer here. The one weak song is "Zinger," which is filler by the band's own admission in the liner notes. Apparently, it was written when Fellows made a bet with someone that he could make a song out of any meaningless phrase. It turns out about as well as you'd think.

This reissue includes five B-sides and out-takes. In addition to "Do The Empty House," which once again is one of the band's all-time highs, there's a reworking of an early song called "Red Planet," which is pretty silly and overwrought, and three other songs that are pretty good. All three share a pleasantly carefree atmosphere. "It's History" encourages someone to "just let it go, it's history." "Private Party" is actually a rewrite of a Sleep No More-era out-take called "Mass," which started out as a dense angst-ridden number with pounding drums, but here is turned into a kind of party song. Fellows' assertion that he doesn't want to think about the future is no longer a commentary on the meaninglessness of life, but an invitation to enjoy the present. Finally, "For Your Information" is a previously unreleased out-take that should really have gone on the album. The chorus is a hilariously shallow dismissal of the past: "Those days are gone forever, it's much better now." It's good for a sunny day.

Fiction shows the Comsat Angels' talent much more than its two predecessors. It's too bad that they got disillusioned by this point and tried to commercialize their sound. They were just getting good. In comparison, consider the fact that it took The Cure five or six albums to really hit their stride as pop songwriters. title: Amazing album, vinyl could be better.
text:
If you're looking at the page for the vinyl of this record you probably already love it so I'll spare the fantanoism, and review the actual record and LP. Starting at the cover, it's paper. Just a rough paper, sort of like construction paper but a little more sturdy. I don't seem to understand why this choice was made. I own Teens of Denial and the 2011 version of this album, and they're both also paper. So why this is comes down to if it's Matador being cheap, or if it's a stylistic choice from Will and the band, or something else. Either way, having this record on a shelf somewhere can expose it to having the spine being slightly yellowed as time goes on, because it's a white piece of paper. But it isn't too bad, the choice to have the cover as paper is less annoying on Teens of Denial than it is on here, since it its plain white. If the band really did want the jackets to be paper, they could've gone the route that The Microphones went with the Mount Eerie vinyl, and make it like a hardback book. Which I feel like gives more meaning to the record than any standard vinyl jacket could ever do.

The back of the jacket features the songs in a rather simplistic way. Now inside of the gate fold you will find a sketchy drawing with a quote from Famous Prophets. The drawing is nice and suits the album, but in my opinion the gate fold drawing on the MtM one is much nicer and really expands the world that the album puts you in. On the right side of the inside gate fold you will find credits. Going into the LP sleeves, they come in these paper sleeves with lyrics on them that are very hard to get out of the already paper jacket. You have to nudge them slowly because they don't come out smoothly. Due to this, I recommend that you don't keep the LPs in there, just keep them in a separate record sleeve inside the gatefold, or don't use one at all. Now, for the actual LPs. The labels on them are quite bland, with just the songs and sides with a matador logo. I feel like there could've been so much opportunity for creativity and design here, because this album means a lot to a lot of people. Matador and the band could have put a bit more effort into making the vinyl better, but that's neither here nor there. The LP itself plays fine, although I have a sense that they were quite rushed in production. When I first got mine it still had some extra vinyl gunk at the end that i had to get off. That in itself wasn't too much of an issue, but I think it paints a picture on how the vinyl for this album was treated. That's all of my nitpicks, basically. The only slight issue I have with the album is that at the end of the last song they just completely cut off the last couple seconds or so. It isn't too much of a problem, because it was just noise, but I understand that this was probably necessary. They fit a 14 minute long song and then a 7 minute song on one side, that's already stretching the capability of a vinyl by quite a bit, and it's impressive to be honest. Those are my nitpicks, but I just feel like they could have done so much more with this album. The vinyl is so humble in how it portrays the album, it's so much more than just an album to me and a lot of other people. The Mirror to Mirror pressing has better world building especially with the drawings on the inside of the gate-fold. You should seek out both of them if you're a die hard fan.

This is an amazing album, with a somewhat half-assed vinyl release. You should still buy this album if you like it, even though I have complained about these things I would still buy this a thousand times. It's that amazing. The vibe and mood of this album is unparalleled to any other Car Seat Headrest album, or any album in general in my opinion. I know half of these issues are probably Matador being lazy, but if they're reading this; do not skimp on Car Seat Headrest. They are easily the best band that you have in your catalog.

title: When We Worship, the Lion of Judah ROARS!
text:
Pure worship, and pure call to worship... that is how I see Paul Wilbur's music, including LION OF JUDAH.

From song to song the listener is reminded that the righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith, and the just shall live by faith (Rom. 1:17): that is *true* righteousness, not a color-of-righteousness brand of deception such as the enemy uses to kill, steal, destroy...

I have found it next to impossible to be still during "Come Let's Go Up to the Mountain," which has a Celtic-type rhythm that demands the body to *move* in dance and praise and call to worship. (Sometimes I use this one for a good aerobic/cardiac workout before exercising, and sometimes just for sheer fun, as I love to dance unto the Lord).

"Show Me Your Face," is powerful throughout and concludes with a reminder of what it takes to endure to the end, "We will make it to the end. If we could just see your face. I will make it to the end. Abba show me your face."

There is great, revealed truth in Psalm 25:14, "The LORD confides in those who fear him; he makes his covenant known to them," and we are reminded of such *wonderful* intimacy in "Dance With Me." This is a "naked-and-not-ashamed" love song, that in few words expresses love that can neither be shut down nor shut out. The lines include, "Behold you have come, over the hills, over the mountains, to me you have run, my beloved, you've captured my heart. With you I will go. You are my love. You are my fair one. Winter is past and the springtime has come."

LION OF JUDAH is the second Paul Wilbur CD I have bought, and I do love it; however, I love THE WATCHMAN above all others. I consider both indispensable worship aids for my private worship time.

I have been listening to this CD again while writing this review and feel the quickening of the Holy Spirit throughout my inmost being. My beloved has declared that it is his passion and persuasion that it is appropriate for believers to be consumed by thankfulness. I have been wooed and won to dwell in such state without ceasing, day and night, awakening with praises to our Lord upon my lips as I behold him with open face and am changed into His image, from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord. (2 Cor. 3:18).

The bottom line is: when we worship, the Lion of the Tribe of Judah, ROARS!

title: this deserves 5 stars
text: I must be hearing a totally different album than a lot of the one and two star reviewers.  Yes, there are melodic hooks on "Highway Robbery" and "Setting Fire To Sleeping Giants," and yes, "Phone Home" and "Unretrofied" sound like slowed down industrial rock, but the rest of the album is classic Dillinger Escape Plan.  In fact, the remaining songs are more complex and chaotic than anything on Calculating Infinity.  The guitarists do fewer scales and more subtle, complicated techniques this time around,and the drumming is as good as ever.  And the so called "sell-out" songs add variety and make the album feel more like an album as opposed to a collection of random spaz outs.  Just because there's (gasp!) singing, doesn't make an album worthless.  I seriously doubt that anybody listens to JUST hardcore metal, and that the same people who pan Dillinger Escape Plan as weak enjoy melodic singing in other contexts.  In some cases, I'll agree that singing doesn't fit in metalcore, but here, it's done perfectly and works to make the whole record more dynamic.  In short, this is one of the most complete, enjoyable metalcore albums ever by a band that is endlessly inventive and even better live.

title: Defies classification . . .
text:
Linda Eder defies classification as an artist. She is marvelous in so many different genres of music. This CD is a wonderful mix of her many different musical styles. Whether she is singing a big band tune like "It's No Secret Anymore" or belting out the Latin-styled "Never Dance," she never misses the mark.
This CD also showcases her talents in blues, ballads, and Broadway showtunes. "Why Do People Fall in Love" is exquisite--a tender, soulful ballad that is very moving. There are wonderful orchestrations on many of her songs such as "Even Now" and "Vienna." Her tribute to Frank Sinatra with "One For My Baby" is top-notch.
My favorite song on the CD is "Anything Can Happen." Just Linda and a piano--what more do you need? Her voice is so powerful yet so tender, and she really FEELS the music when she sings. This is one of those rare albums that you can listen to from beginning to end without ever having to skip over a "not-so-great" song. This is true listening pleasure.

De Chiaro is technically flawless here, but in so doing he makes Joplin's music curiously dry and academic.

The beauty of Joplin's music is the gentle alternation between blues and Chopinesque virtuosity. In De Chiaro's hands these rags sound like Bagatelles unfortunately removed from their wistful origins. It's pleasant enough, in a Segovia-like way but not what I was hoping for. When I started buying my own records, when the Beatles appeared, I eventually purchased this record for myself because it felt like it had become part of the family during those years, and I missed it. I nearly wore it out back in the 60's. I never was a big Elvis fan (I was too young, and then the Beatles came along when I was 12) but this has got to be one of the most exciting rock-n-roll recordings of all time! I absolutely love it, and Elvis has such expression in his voice - not the toned-down pop he later adopted (probably as directed by his "handler"). This is what made the beginning of Elvis the Legend. This is what made him the best of his era. This is real rock-n-roll/rockabilly music, recorded live in the studio, without deceitful studio trickery or synthesized sound. This album is musical American history.

title: Don't Believe The Hype Surrounding This Overrated Album.
text:
I've been a rock fan & collector for over thirty years, and I've read many raving reviews of this album by critics (not to mention reviewers on this site) who frequently describe it as a "lost masterpiece" of rock. These folks apply terms to SISTER LOVERS like a "heroic artistic act," and "expression of existential angst."

Baloney.

After many listens to SISTER LOVERS, my opinion of it hasn't changed: it's a shabbily-produced, self-indulgent mess consisting mainly of less-than-great Big Star tunes and a couple outright embarrassments. (In fairness, two exceptions to this waste are the exquisitely poignant and beautiful ballad "Blue Moon" and the honest, harrowing "Holocaust.")

Big Star was a great band - and deserved to be a famous one. Their commerical failure & resulting collapse was an injustice and a tragedy. But please: don't confuse Alex Chilton's self-absorbed pouting and tantrums during the making of this album with "existential angst" or "heroism," and don't spin his willful sabotage of many album tracks as a statement of "artistic integrity."

You want grief - honestly felt & honestly conveyed? Listen to Neil Young's TONIGHT'S THE NIGHT. You want angst - honestly felt & honestly conveyed? Check out Eric Clapton's LAYLA. Want righteous, thundering anger - honestly felt & honestly conveyed - at the Powers-That-Be? Buy the Clash's first album. Looking for an honest, unflinching, even heroic response to failure and frustration? Buy Mott the Hoople's MOTT. Maybe you want to listen to a plain, unpretentious "bringing it all back home" album of heartfelt singing & playing? Lennon's PLASTIC ONO BAND and Springsteen's NEBRASKA fit the bill in their different ways. Or, maybe, you want to listen to an artist's honest struggle against collapse - using his art to affirm life while feeling deep despair. If you want to go there, you need go no further than albums like Sly & the Family Stone's THERE'S A RIOT GOIN' ON, Nirvana's UNPLUGGED, or Robert Johnson's KING OF THE DELTA BLUES SINGERS.

To me, SISTER LOVERS isn't remotely in the same league as any of these albums. So I'm bewildered when I read or hear others comparing SISTER LOVERS to one or more of those albums in terms of style and quality. What am I missing here? Am I too dense to "get" Chilton's great & profound message? Or has it merely been too long since my adolescence?

You want to listen to great Big Star? Buy their first two albums, then download "Blue Moon" and "Holocaust." But give SISTER LOVERS - and Chilton's adolescent angst - a pass.

title: For Your Entertainment Indeed - great cover too, LOL.
text:
I generally avoid mainstream pop music like the plague. Any industry that pretends to tie 'art' to an assembly line should be stamped out of existence. Having said that, I have to admit that I was more than pleasantly surprised at the quality of this album. My first exposure to the album was the title track single, which didn't exactly get my hopes up. However, after listening to the entire album, I was pretty much left speechless. Overall there really aren't any horrible tracks on this album, and, even better, there are quite a few phenomenal songs. It's been more than a few years since I've picked up an album this good. If you've only heard one or two tracks and are on the fence about this record - rest assured, there are much better tracks on the album than what has been released so far. There should easily be 4 or 5 top 10 hits on this record. Here's a quick rundown of how I rate the songs:

Music Again - 5/5 - I like the slight middle-eastern tinge to the song. Adams doing, perhaps? Dunno, but it's definitely an interesting mix of modern pop, an 80's style guitar solo and a hint of theatre.

For Your Entertainment - 4/5 - When I first heard this song, I was sorely disappointed, as I thought that this is what the whole album would end up sounding like. Fortunately I was wrong, as the rest of the album crushes this effort. However, I do have to admit that the song has grown on me over time.

Whataya Want From Me - 5/5 - My favorite song on the album. Absolutely brilliant vocals. I really like the contrast of the lower pitch, slightly rougher vocals contrasted against the soaring counterparts and background vocals. What could be better than listening to an Adam Lambert vocal? How about Adam singing counterpoint to Adam. ;-)

Strut - 3/5 - Pretty much ditto to For Your Entertainment. Too commercial for my taste. The only thing that really makes this song palatable is Adam's voice. In anybody else's hands this would be a complete waste of time.

Soaked - 5/5 - WOW! Fantastic, soaring vocals. Might be a little theatrical for some, and I'd probably get tired of it if the whole album was like this, but this being the only song of its kind on the album, I don't see myself getting tired of it anytime soon. Most artists could only dream of performing this song, Adam pulls it off effortlessly. Once again, I like the slight middle-eastern phrasing.

Sure Fire Winners - 5/5 - Very catchy. While being more of a modern, run-of-the-mill pop song, Adams vocals keep it from being forgettable. Great vocal gymnastics on this one.

A Loaded Smile - 3/5 - A little bit too dreamy for me, but actually a nice change-up from the previous series of songs. If you're listening to the album from beginning to end, this is a nice breather after a couple of intense songs.

If I Had You - 5/5 - I love the beginning lyrics. Makes me grin thinking about what must've went through Adam's head when he first saw them. As with Sure Fire Winners, very catchy and again Adam's voice turns what otherwise would have been forgettable pop garbage into something enjoyable to listen to.

Pick U Up - 4/5 - The fade from If I Had You into Pick U Up is so good that the first time I listened to the album I thought this was an outro to the previous song. Unfortunately even Adam's voice can only bring this song to above average (hence the 4/5). A little bit too theatrical for me. That and the somewhat senseless lyrics...

Fever - 5/5 - Love the lyrics. Still a hint of theatre, but more palatable than Pick U Up.

Sleepwalker - 5/5 - What a GREAT song. Great lyrics, great vocals ... perfect.

Aftermath - 5/5 - Sounds a lot like Richard Marx at the beginning. Interesting choice of topic. Again, wonderful vocals. Like Whataya Want From Me, really shows off Adam's range - all the way from his lower registered to soaring screams.

Broken Open - 4/5 - We get another breather. Very soft vocals, but avoids being as spaced out as A Loaded Smile.

Time for Miracles - 2/5 - Richard Marx meets country twang. Not a good combo. Even Adam sounds like he got tired on this one. I don't blame him. IMO a desperate and lame attempt by the studio to tie this album into another demographic.

Hope you guys and gals find this helpful.

title: Strangeness and beauty
text:
How strange are the ways of the recording companies - but perhaps understandably, as I'll explain in a moment. Jean Mouton was one of the great composers of the Franco-Flemish school, yet there had not been a recording exclusively devoted to his music for at least ten years, and even before that only one as far as I know. And now two come along within a few months of one another - the Brabant Ensemble's wonderful CD of [[ASIN:B007RV4BDM Mouton: Missa Tu es Petrus]] and this present disc from the Tallis Scholars (update: see Richard Bell's comment below).

This consists of Mouton's fine paraphrase mass based on Loyset Compère's rondeau "Dictes moy toutes voz pensées", together with an impressive collection of five motets. Compère's gently plaintive 3-part song, the opening item on the disc, makes an intriguing model for the Mass. The latter boasts a rich texture from the very start, with the lower voices sounding especially prominent here and at various other points. Throughout the work, Mouton shows seemingly boundless imagination and ingenuity in reworking the motifs of Compère's song, just as is the case with his treatment of the cantus firmus theme in the Missa Tu es Petrus. All this is performed most beautifully by Peter Phillips and the Tallis Scholars - who have been slimming down a bit in recent years, singing two voices per part for most of the works here, and OVPP for the last item, the 8-voice "Nesciens Mater". Their singing has a lovely, well-balanced texture - as at the start of the Sanctus, to take just one example - while the middle section of Mouton's Agnus Dei, again dominated by the low voices, is remarkable and, once more, quite beautifully sung here. In mentioning the lower voices a couple of times I don't mean to underplay the others - the sopranos and altos make superb contributions, resulting in a marvellously balanced sound.

As for the rest of the programme, it's this that prompts me to think how strange also are the vagaries of individual taste - which is why we can't always blame the recording companies for not knowing what we'll want to buy. In the case of the Brabant Ensemble's Mouton recording it was above all the Mass that really bowled me over, whereas some other reviewers (on Amazon or elsewhere) were more lukewarm. On the present disc, for my taste, it's the motets that really got me going on this occasion. To mention only a few highlights, Mouton's lament for Anne of Brittany, "Quis dabit oculis?", brings us marvellously mournful chords at the name 'Anna', again expressed with a lovely vocal texture. "Salva nos" is short but glorious - two and a half minutes of sheer delight. In "Ave Maria ... virgo serena", Mouton seems to be taking a leaf from Josquin's book in the latter's setting of the same title but a different text; a similar alternation of polyphony with the occasional declamatory passage results in a very substantial work that's not so far off the sheer perfection of 'Josquinus incomparabilis'. And finally we have "Nesciens mater", familiar to all renaissance fans, in a very fine rendering in which each individual voice can be clearly followed - bringing the programme to a magical close.

Whatever the finer points of our preferences, however, this disc makes an excellent companion to the Brabants' Missa Tu es Petrus - and, I hope, to any future undertakings of the many fine renaissance ensembles out there who may fancy bringing us another Mass or two from Mouton's impressive output. Actually, Mouton's "Missa Dictes moy" has been recorded before, with a mostly different group of motets, by The Gentlemen of St John's directed by Graham Walker: [[ASIN:B00006I497 Nesciens Mater: Choral works of Jean Mouton]]. That, too, is a fine recording, very hard to get hold of these days but well worth the effort. In the meantime, well done to both the Tallis Scholars and the Brabant Ensemble; and again, record companies, please can we have some more?

title: Good-bye yellow brick road, Judy's back in Kansas
text: Sometimes an album cover tells it all, and if this cover was true to the  music, I knew it was going to be an outstanding collection. The monochrome  brick road with the dingy factory-like buildings on each side, and here's  Judy looking smart and weathered and a little cocky. It seemed she had  something to say to her fans, and she sure did. Her voice was ripe, ready  and within range (which it isn't always) on all these Dylan songs.  "Like A Rolling Stone" took guts to re-record. Who can top  Dylan's sarcastic to the point original? no one! However, she puts her own  melodic sarcastic spin on it with great success. She gave this one some  wings. I never get tired of hearing a new version of this one. This version  is one of the best interpretations. "It's All Over Now, Baby  Blue" and "Simple Twist Of Fate" had a Joan Baez quality (I  say that as a great compliment). These recordings could have been late  60's/early 70's hits. They would have been classics today had they been  recorded back then. "Sweetheart Like You" and "Gotta Serve  Somebody"  take her to a place she doesn't usually go. The  "monochrome brick road" on the album cover is captured in these  two songs. Rougher and rawer than I thought she could do well. "Dark  Eyes" doesn't measure up to the rest. Probably because the others are  simply that good. "Love Minus Zero/No Limit" is classic Judy. She  exceeds Dylan on this one. "Just Like A Woman" and "I  Believe In You" are quieter than the rest of the other songs but make  this album what it is: a superior collection and tribute to Dylan and his  music. "With God On Our Side" is a tough song to do. Baez did the  best version. However, this is right behind Baez's version. What this  version lacks in poignance is mades up by its angelic hauntingly beautiful  interpretation, especially the last note, one of her finest moments.  "Bob Dylan's Dream" is another one she does better than Dylan. I  can really appreciate the lyrics. She's clear and crisp in a way that  allows you to sit back and take it all  in and really savor the words and  the lyrics. I really believe this collection would be a classic today if it  had come out in the early 70's. But then, some of these songs hadn't been  written yet. However, the texture doesn't fit the high tech digital world  of the 90's. Maybe that makes this collection more significant.

title: What's this older generation coming to?
text:
After all the respect that the likes of Michael Stipe, Jon Bon Jovi, and Sid Vicious have shown the generations of musicians that came before them, it is indeed astonishing that Paul Anka could appropriate the music of younger performers with such a crude sense of entitlement. Just because "It's My Life" contains the line "I did it my way," or Sid decided to rework a tired lounge song to make it more contemporary, what makes Anka think he can do these songs his way?

Doesn't he realize that time-honored classics of the 1980's and 1990's he torpedoes will no doubt go down in history as more important and enduring than anything he or anybody else recorded in the 1950's? Sure Anka was there in as a teenager when youth culture emerged as a dominant force in American society. But shouldn't he show more respect for the field he helped create by sticking to songs he might actually know something about?

Indeed now that Paul Anka has released Rock Swings, how will Survivor and Spandau Ballet ever preserve their well-earned legacy in rock history? The pain-driven lyrics of "Eye of the Tiger" really drove home the emotional impact of Rocky III. That cherished memory has been destroyed forever by the absolutely appalling ring-a-ding-ding version found on this album.

About the only thing you can take away from listening to this album is that in the hands of someone who has been writing and performing for close to fifty years music is a never-ending source of discovery and insight that allows you to have unlimited and unexpected experiences.

title: A Woman With A Voice Offering Something Compelling
text:
What a potent musical environment the 1970's were,despite what the many detractors say. You had all these genres like rock,jazz,soul,R&B,folk and country all celebrating and flaunting the virtues of strong instrumental craftsmanship,studio production acumen as well as singing and songwriting from some of the best around as well as newcomers following in their patter. All around musically,it was a golden age-with many voices raising themselves in a very high quality fashion. And even then there was the old standby of the American popular song. That being as defined by Tin Pan Alley and Broadway as it existed before the advent of the jazz age and later the arrival of rock n roll. In the 60's Barbara Streisand was their to bridge the gap between the middle American popular song and youthful popular music. In the 70's,it looked like there was a newcomer to do much the same in the personage of Jane Olivor.

"My First Night Alone Without You,"Better Days (Looks As Though We're Doing Something Right","Carousel O Love" and the classic show tune "Some Enchanted Evening" are all excellent showcases for Olivor's voice-an expressive and rangy instrument that portrays a great deal of complication and even pathos in it's range and sense of timing-closer to a high pitched female version of Frank Sinatra,if only in spirit rather than phrasing or timbre, than anything the more flamboyant Bette Middler or Barbara Streisand were doing at this time. Of course on these songs as "Morning,Noon & Nighttime" and "Carousel Of Love" there's a somewhat more bouncy contemporary flavor with some electric keyboards and a strong rhythm-close to the mood of lightweight pop/soul. Her take on "Vincent",a beautiful Don McLean composition as it is,is delivered with such a genuine expression of emotion it has the capacity to bring tears to eyes of even the most cynical of critics. It is by far my personal favorite number here.

First and foremost,this is not the type of music I am typically inclined to listen to. At the same time,the classic Tim Pan Alley songwriters of the early 20'th century made a certain musical contribution to American that had been reinvented decade after decade as music instrumentally progressed from concert halls to the era of recording. Producer Jason Darrow was aware of the lightly orchestrated pop productions of Burt Bacharach and The Carpenters during the early/mid 1970's. They were more or less understand and put the songs melody and the lead vocalist out in front-also in keeping with the often more folk based singer/songwriter movement of the era. And this album represents that fusion of the classic American popular song with the easier end of contemporary singer/songwriter pop music of it's time. For people who love richly orchestrated popular balladeering song in a genuine and expressive manner,this is probably just the album for you

title: Fails to Disappoint Me!
text:
After 6 years of inactivity, occasional touring, and most of all unfortunate losses of close ones, the nine unleashes their fifth album, which has straight up blown my head clean off!

.5: The Gray Chapter is an extremely well executed solid effort, showing the world that the 'knot are still alive and well, even after the death of the bassist Paul Gray in 2010, and drummer Joey Jordison's departure in late 2013. The album, as stated by singer Corey Taylor, is the story of the last six years of the band, and also a dedication to the late bassist.

In my opinion, this album has impressed me ever since it first came out, and gets better every time I hear the album's songs on my laptop's media player. If anything, this album is so good, it's even better than slipknot's last album, "All Hope Is Gone", released in 2008. Don't get me wrong, I love all hope is gone, it's just that I think this album is a few notches better, and delivers a bit more.

Musically, the album's sound contains the band's signature powerful, aggressive vibe. This time, reminiscent of the band's first two releases, "Slipknot" in 1999, and "Iowa" in 2001; both noticeably being their most chaotic and intense works to date. With that, the album also includes beautiful melody, first introduced on their third album, "Vol.3: The Subliminal Verses" in 2004.

The album's lead single, "The Devil in I" is such an amazing track in my opinion. It delivers the melody quite nicely, while demonstrating heavy parts, all in the right places. It's music video is actually pretty strange and gruesome. But it really has done a great job showing everybody the new masks, and who's filling in for drums and bass while keeping their identities anonymous.

Other songs which are more melody-driven include "Killpop", "The One that Kills the Least", and "Goodbye".

Songs that are pretty straight up mayhem inducing include "Custer", "Skeptic", "Sarcastrophe", and "The Negative One".

So much potential on this album, it easily will go down as one of their best in their whole career.

If I had to express my favorite to my least favorite slipknot album, here's what the list is:

1. Slipknot
2. Iowa
3. Vol.3
4. .5
5. All hope is gone

Overall, I suggest you check it out if or when you get the chance! It's a great album!

title: Ravished by Smiths' Glass Works!
text:
love Philip Glass' music like I love the air I breathe. i have had the Kronos Quartet CD for these pieces for some time, which does not include the first quartet - the most unsettling in many ways, the most dissonent.

I recently went to a concert where the Smith Quartet - who i was unfamiliar with, played all 5 of the Quartets (Glass has written 8, but i believe he withdrew 3 of them as not being works he is satisfied with, so are not available on disc or mp3)

Any half way decent live concert will of course hold much more than a recording - the intensity of collective experience, what happens when musicians, music, audience connect and the energy, focus and presence of all continuously build the experience. That concert was extraordinary. Glass' music often feels as if inhabits my body, I feel it, like breath, like blood, within bone, transformational. Indeed, at that concert, strangers turned to us in the interval, overwhelmed, as we were, saying words like 'transforming, spiritual, beyond description'

This 5 years old recording cannot of course equal the live event, but it certainly points the way to it. There is a great intensity, passion, inhabiting of the music in the Smiths' playing, so i find it hard in some ways to sit still with this, the spiralling, dynamic quality of the music as it coils and uncoils, expands and condenses within this listener's body. Salute, Smiths!

I am now busily investigating what else the Smiths have recorded - Different Trains and am looking forward to hearing how this compares to the version I already have Different Trains / Electric Counterpoint

I got the 2 cd version that has the Swedish and English version and I noticed that certain songs take on a different atmosphere or sound different depending on what version you’re listening to. I’ve been a fan of Opeth since the Blackwater Park album and I’ve loved their new direction and I think people should listen to this without preconceived notions about how this should sound because it is a masterpiece. Mikaels vocals are beautiful and powerful, the band is incredibly tight and mesmerizing/powerful. I recommend that people new to Opeth start out with blackwater park or ghost reveries, but longtime fans definitely don’t don’t deny yourself such an amazing experience. The English version is probably more accessible overall but give the Swedish version a chance too; like I said, it’s amazing how some songs sound different for the better (none of them are bad). title: Her Best Album And A Rock Classic
text:
The critics who saw Sheryl Crow as nothing more than a one-hit-wonder with her debut album "Tuesday Night Music Club" were abruptly silenced with the 1996 release of her self-titled sophomore release. With her debut album Sheryl showed the world that she was a capable woman with superstar potential. With "Sheryl Crow" she threw herself in the deep end showcasing her extreme talent as a singer, producer and writer and emerged as one of the 90's most memorable and versatile artists. The album did not perform as well on the charts as her debut did, but it still went multi-platinum and produced some big hits. It also made critics stand up and take note of this unique performer.

The album opens with the fantastic "Maybe Angels." It's evident from the first few seconds of the song (with a heavy bell toll) that this album is a lot more rockier than Sheryl's debut. It's a great song to open with, but has a strange subject of aliens! After this we are throw straight into the funky rocker "A Change." This wonderfully melodic song is classic Crow - a brilliant guitar, accompanied by lovely vocals and some thought-provoking lyrics, "Hello, it's me. I'm not at home. If you'd like to reach me, leave me alone." The album slows down for the mellow "Home," which is considered by many as one of Sheryl's best ever songs. The song starts out of nowhere, and soon winds up as one of the most beautiful and relaxing ballads from a female ever. Sheryl's vocals are extremely soft and the guitars add a marvellous sense of isolation to the whole arrangement. "Sweet Rosalyn" is a great rock song with raspy vocals and a brilliant guitar, but it does pale a bit in comparison with most of the other songs on this album. The bar is set high from the beginning, and this song just doesn't cut it.

Fortunately things pick up next with the awesome rock anthem "If It Makes You Happy." Easily one of Sheryl's most popular songs to date, the song has some brilliant and rough vocals along with a very catchy guitar. The lyrics are very upfront, and it works so well. "Redemption Day" is one of the album's highlights for sure. Starting off marvellously with a twitchy guitar solo and a deep Western boom, the song is a true classic. Sheryl sings about life/death and its importance with a stunning chorus for everyone to sing along to, "There is a train that's heading straight to Heaven's gate. And on the way child and man and woman wait, watch and wait...for redemption day." I can't describe the effect that this song had on me, but all I know is that I love this song and I always will. "Hard To Make A Stand" is another great pop song, with excellent guitars and very catchy lyrics. Sheryl tells the story of people she observes in the verses, before singing a marvellous chorus. "Everyday Is A Winding Road" is another fantastic song that was released as a single and slowly became a worldwide anthem. The guitars are wonderfully matched, and the lyrics are so typical and normal.

"Love Is A Good Thing" is the song that caused all the controversy for Sheryl back in 1996. This album was banned from...for the lyrics in this song, "Watch out sister, watch out brother, watch our children while they kill each other with a gun they bought at Wal-Mart discount stores." Fantastic! Sheryl stands up for what she believes in and isn't afraid to do so. What's even better is if this song became any more damn catchy, you'd probably fall into a coma from shock! Also, listen out for Sheryl's blood-curling screech of epic proportions towards the end! Absolutely fantastic - an album highlight. "Oh Marie" is a mid-tempo and extremely melodic pop song in which Sheryl sings about a certain Marie, surprisingly! The lyrics are wonderful and Sheryl's vocals are strikingly low-key, adding a sense of loneliness. "Superstar" is a funky and almost psychedelic song, but seems to be a bit of an album filler. Not her best, unfortunately.

"The Book" is so much like John Lennon material it's scary. A misty and foggy tone is wonderfully joined by Sheryl's melancholy vocals - reflections on the past, and on the present. "Ordinary Morning" is just mind-blowing. There are no words to describe this song - almost jazzy verses, which drop and rise before a soaring anthemic chorus. Vocals are outstanding and the lyrics are equally splendid. Many suggestions have been made about the subject of the song, the most being about rape. "Free Man" is the final song on the album. It's a bit of a clunker in comparison to most of the songs on the album, but it's still a very good rock song. It's extremely up-tempo and sounds very loud and brash, giving us a taste of things to come on Sheryl's next album - 1998's "The Globe Sessions."

OVERALL GRADE: 10/10

This album is definitely Sheryl's best album to date. The Globe Sessions is her second best album, and Tuesday Night Music Club is her third. What the heck, all Sheryl's albums are amazing! You'll be hard pushed to find a more talented female performer who does it all (writes, produces, plays instruments, sings) all while remaining a commercially successfully artist while retaining her credibility!

title: Fine Example of American Post-NeoProg
text:
This is a very fine record. The violin makes it sound a lot like Kansas. It also sounds like several other excellent bands of recent vintage, like Spock's Beard/Pattern-Seeking Animals. Except for the violin, of course.

This is not a bad thing. Within this genre, there is plenty of room for great original music. Kansas is not copying anybody, nor is anyone particularly copying them. It's not copying.

It's convergence.

With many of the same musicians moving from band to band, and the same types of singers coming to the fore of many of them, their influence on each other is inevitable. The wash of keyboards, the sharp-edged Rickenbacker bass, the dramatic melodies, the obligatory shreds, the giant drum kit, the strident vocals by a baritone trying to be a tenor. They are all trying to get even better at the same things, rather than doing anything new. So it's really great to listen to, but it's not challenging. It's not... progressive.

Everything about this album is top-tier. The playing, the production, the singing, the mixing. If you like this kind of music, you'll like this. And you can be forgiven if you put it in a playlist with a bunch of other bands and realize that the reason you can pick out which songs are Kansas is... the violin. But who does it sound like when the violin is not playing?

The package is well done. The 5.1 mix sounds very good, although the surround channels are not used much for discrete content: it's more of a standard massed-Kansas mix that just spreads out
more to the sides. But when I listen on the big rig, this is the mix I'll listen to.

title: A Masterpiece of Youthful, Creative Energy
text: Nearly forty-two years after its recording, this eponymous debut album is still as expansive and interesting to me as when I first heard it in early 1971.  It's hard to believe that such masterful musicianship came from three guys in their early twenties, but gorgeous it was and continues to be.  Yes, "Lucky Man" was overplayed on the FM airwaves, but it's a great track, and I can still enjoy it.  My personal favorites are "Take A Pebble" and "Tank," the latter possessing some of the finest power drumming this side of Buddy Rich.  The music on this album has a muscular freshness that grips you by the throat, lays you down gently, and then devours you at the end.  While later efforts may be seen as exercises in overblown commericalism, this first album delivered the band's initial effort with tasteful aplomb.  Emerson, formerly of The Nice, and Lake, fresh from King Crimson blended their talents with Carl Palmer (The Crazy World of Arthur Brown band) to craft something beautiul and uniquely their own.  Palmer's drumming is incredibly creative, and his technical virtuosity punctuates the band's sound with clean precision.  The crisp sound on this re-master is unprecedented in any former release.  This is an album that represents some of the finest rock classics of the decade, and is an absolute 5-star piece of work.

title: essential cocteaus ep's '82-'90
text:
despite the fact that this collection could've fit on 2 cds, which would've surely given this great music a wider audience [likely only the hardcore would shell out $50+], this is easily as essential as any of the cocteau's "proper" albums like Treasure, Heaven or Las Vegas, Head Over Heels, etc. I notice there is a new set coming out called "Lullabies to Violaine" which includes the post-'90 singles tracks. Some things I noticed in that track list, it does not have 'peppermint pig (12" version)' which i prefer, and only has one version of 'pearly-dewdrops' drops' which it lists as "(alternate version)". I hope they mean it's the 12" version because it has the soft little intro which sets up the song perfectly. May seem like a little thing to some, but being one of my favorite CT songs, it's a must. Also that set does not have the tracks from this set's bonus disc (Dials, Crushed, The High Monkey-Monk, Oomingmak (instrumental), all good songs). I can't comment on the post-'90 tracks that account for 29 of that set's 61 tracks (haven't heard them, apart from the ones that are on "four-calendar cafe" and "milk and kisses"). It does say that the set contains 2 discs which would make it preferable if not for the omitted tracks, but it has to be 3 discs, obviously too many songs to fit on 2! It also says it will be released in 2010 (lol, okay). Probably not. Maybe you can download all this stuff for less. Something to consider, since you'll probably be making your own burnt cd's from this anyway. Though however you acquire this music, do acquire it.

Many tracks rank among their best material, in my opinion, such as "pearly-dewdrops' drops" "mizake the mizan" "melonella" "pale clouded white" "sigh's smell of farewell" "feathers-oar-blades" "pink orange red" and "peppermint pig" [though it seems quite a few disagree on that one], but I love all of it, and listen to it as much or more than any of their (amazing) "proper" albums. :)

title: A very pleasing Christmas offering
text:
The moment I saw that Tamia had released a three-track Christmas single, I went ahead and ordered it. Previously, the only Christmas track I had of Tamia was "The Christmas Song" from Jermaine Dupri's 12 Soulful Nights of Christmas, which coincidentally is one of the three tracks (completely redone, however) on A Gift Between Friends. I personally prefer the previous version (recorded about ten years ago) to this newer version, though her voice is much more polished today. The newer version has a real tropical Latin flavor, which may or may not suit your holiday taste. Either way, it certainly is a unique twist on the classic song.

The first track is a medley consisting of "Let It Snow," "Winter Wonderland," and "O Holy Night." The jazz band instrumentals to the first two provide a real cool, laid-back groove, which allow Tamia's beautiful voice to shine through. "O Holy Night" is essentially just her voice backed by a light acoustic guitar, and later on, she's joined a choir. Well-sung, though not nearly as full-sounding and moving as I feel she is capable of.

The second track, Donny Hathaway's classic, "This Christmas," is done to a completely new beat, along with a nice vocal backing. Shep Crawford, a close friend who produced all three tracks, took the song in a completely new old-school direction, though I prefer versions mirroring the original closer.

Though it's disappointingly just three songs, it is nonetheless a beautiful collection from the fabulous Tamia. It's a great addition to your Christmas music library or even to your complete Tamia collection.

title: Mellencamp surpasses Scarecrow with folky new sound
text:
I'm not sure how many people reacted to the more folky, even laid back sounds of The Lonesome Jubilee, John Cougar Mellencamp's followup to Scarecrow. Banjos, harmonicas, mandolins, accordions, and dobros come in. The most distinctive sound comes from a fiddle played by a certain Lisa Germano. Yet, Mellencamp continues the serious social commentary that really came into being on Scarecrow. In fact, here, he becomes more the champion of the hard-working blue-collar man more than Springsteen.
The first single, the bluesy "Paper In Fire" recalls the catchiness of any of the Scarecrow singles, but with that folk and accordion sound overlayed. Yes, how sad it is when unrealistic dreams and expectations "burn up like paper in fire."
"Down And Out In Paradise" is an angry chop at the Reagan administration's policies, and each verse is formed as a letter from a citizen to the president, from a man being unemployed due to the company moving out of town, to a frightened fourth grader whose father is an abusive drunk. Each verse ends with the line, "Do you think there's something you could do for me?" The president? Are you kidding? The Cold War is prevalent here, as the boy asks, "When the bombs fall down/will they hurt everyone in my family?"
"Check It Out" was the third single, and this laid back accordion song. It's a nod to the poets of this generation who want their voices to be heard by future generations. Trouble is, their prospective listeners are too busy with their lives and that within the limited "so-called life" they have, "this is all that we've learned about living." There's more to that, insists Mellencamp.
A friend of mine had this album and said that the best song here was "The Real Life" and I can see why. This could've been a single hands-down. It's the story of different people who decide to get out of the rut they're in for some more fulfillment. "I want to live the real life/I want to live my life close to the bone" goes the chorus, continuing, "just because I'm middle-aged that don't mean/I want to sit around the house and watch TV."
"Cherry Bomb", the second single, sports that accordion and fiddle and is a nostalgic look back at late teen years of hanging out and laughing back at those years. Crystal Taliefero's vocals add a soulful edge to this song, as on the other songs here.
"We Are The People" is another contender for best song here. An empathic song for the downtrodden, homeless, a black man being beaten, and someone scared and alone, it ends with him telling a political leader that "if you try to divide and conquer/we'll rise up against you" because "we are the people/and we live forever/we are the people/and our future's written on the wind." Dylan would be proud of this.
"Empty Hands" is of a disillusioned struggling couple, with the title subject needing to be filled. "When my pride is bruised and broken/she slips her hands into my empty hands" he sings at one point. More poignant is: "without hope, without love, you've got nothing but pain/just makes a man not give a damn/that's no way for us to live."
The title for "Hard Times For An Honest Man" speaks for itself, and is another song thematically similar to "Empty Hands."
"Hotdogs and Hamburgers" is a song of a man who learns from a Native American how the white people took their land and lives. The title has to do with the verse "Now everybody has got the choice/between hotdogs and hamburgers/Every one of us has got to choose/between right and wrong/And givin' up or holdin' on."
"Rooty Toot Toot" is about a leisure picnic in the country with bits of social commentary. The most cheerful song (sort of) here. Overall, JCM has surpassed himself thematically with The Lonesome Jubilee. This is his great statement, and some songs here are his State of the Union address. The folky accordion sound, Crystal Taliefero's backing vocals, and of course Lisa Germano's fiddle really enhance this album. A must-have.

title: More of an Icebreaker and less of Trance
text:
In recent years I have found the recording and engineering of the Argo label to be so well done and to my liking, that I find new music by label and give it a whirl. I was intrigued by the name of this album, expecting it to be something new, fusing techno/trance with modern classical music. What I found was a little surprising, and at first, a little painful.
The liner notes give the warning, the one that any contemporary music veteran is familiar with, that listeners not inclined to challenges will not enjoy the work. With a well trained ear I can hear the ideas that Gordon is striving for. Fusion of Balanese gamalon with Detroit funk and neo-Mozartian part writing are along side with dense complex rhythms interlaced with twist of minimalist change ups. There is a flavor of free form jazz, however it never gives the impression that the arranged sounds are the result of a whim. When there is any sort of melody I do not find myself humming along with it or remembering it, but find it rather as a supporting structure of the rhythmic mix and as a vehicle to move the music along.
The result sounds to me like Gordon had written electronica trance music (or with a collaborator) and then transcribed the results into traditional and acoustic instruments. However I think that the orchestration step of that should be reworked to some degree. The sometimes awkward combination of instruments for different tasks not only interrupts the malifluous intent of the piece, but at times creates irritating overtones. The musicians sound like they could use a little help, as some of the part writing has apparantly left out opportunities for wind players to take a breath.
On the other hand there are some rewards for those who stick with the whole six-sectioned piece. After finishing the fourth or fifth section you begin to realize that you actually are going somewhere, and have been for some time. Some of the early signiture motives return and prepare for the big build up in the final section.
The two "bonus tracks" on the CD are quite fun and would make a great addition to a mix of some type. They are much less challenging to listen to and give a consice rehash of the previous 40 or 50 minutes.
In all, I was not thrilled with this CD from Argo, however I think a little patients will pay some dividends.
