title: Good, but not great
text:
I absolutely LOVE Kultur Shock. I have every single one of their albums and listen to them religiously. So I was thrilled when Integration finally arrived. After listening to it, I liked it, but I wasn't thrilled. So I decided to give it some time and then see what happens. It's been almost 6 months now, and it's still just plain old "good".

One of the things that I liked the most about Kultur Shock was a modern take on classic Balkan tunes. Gino has a really fantastic voice and can really belt out these great songs with an electric guitar going in the background. But with Integration, they've stepped away from any trace of traditional music, and made an album which seems, in my opinion, to try to hard to appeal to the Gogol Bordello-centric Gypsy Punk style. Kultur Shock was always very distinct from that, and that's why I loved them. I love Gogol Bordello for completely different reasons, and I liked the two bands being very distinct and different. But Integration really feels like an album that was made to appeal to a purely American audience interested in a gypsy punk sound.

So is it worth picking up? Certainly. It's definitely worth a listen. But will it make you fall even more madly in love with Gino and the gang? I doubt it.

After many years of being a musician myself, in and out of clubs and studios in L.A., Portland, San Francisco, and all points in between, I've seen them come and seen them go. title: A very enjoyable listenining.
text:
Tom Scott's highly successful and involved career in the very highest levels of the business has touched several bases - from standards to jazz and pop - and he has worked with the Don Ellis and Oliver Nelson bands, and with pop icons like Joni Mitchell, Carole King, and George Harrison as well.
Tom's saxophone has featured on over four hundred recordings as a sideman, with credits including Thelonious Monk, Quincy Jones, Aretha Franklin and Frank Sinatra, and has earned him 13 Grammy nominations and 3 Grammy Awards.
A noted composer, arranger, bandleader and conductor as well as instrumentalist, he is also famed for composing the theme tune to the hit Seventies TV show [[ASIN:B00023GGAI Starsky & Hutch - The Complete Second Season]].
But, despite Scott's place in the rock reference books, the saxmaster, who pioneered jazz-rock with the L.A. Express - a jazz-funk band that rocked audiences in the 1970s and later when it reformed in the mid-1990s, with a string of fantastic recordings - is more of a footnote in jazz.
He is a consistent and highly rated session player whose career has seen him traverse genres with ease and his pedigree as a musician cannot be doubted.
The Los Angeles-born multi- instrumentalist's new album "Cannon Re-loaded" is a collection of tunes closely associated with Cannonball Adderley interpreted by an all-star collection of players, to celebrate and reinterpret the music of the jazz giant.
On this tribute he's joyned by trumpeter Terence Blanchard, pianist George Duke (who was actually a member of the Adderley quintet and who also plays Rhodes and Wurlitzer), drummer Steve Gadd, bassists Marcus Miller and Dave Carpenter, and Larry Goldings on the Hammond B-3, and Nancy Wilson on two tracks "Save The Love For Me" and "The Masquerade is Over", from her classic 1961 recording [[ASIN:B000005HBG Nancy Wilson & Cannonball Adderley]].
The playing is of a high standard throughout.
The CD represents everything that makes contemporary jazz so enjoyable and satisfying; superb musicianship, strong and imaginative compositions, excellent arranging, live drums , and diverse interplay among the lead instrumental voices.
It's evident through the stellar production and sound quality that Tom Scott is a master at his craft.
It's all nicely played and beautifully recorded.
The best moments spring from his love of Adderley, with the delicious version of the opener "Jive Samba" (with George Duke, who dazzles on acoustic piano).
Without copying his hero, Scott plays eloquent tribute to an important, underrated figure in the jazz canon, smoothing off the rough edges for this well-chosen collection of tunes and re-establishing his own claim to return from the margins.
Stand out track : "Jive Samba", "Country Preacher" and "The Masquerade Is Over".

title: Glorious music, mostly unknown Weill
text:
Glorious music, wonderfully performed. Never finished in its original form, Kuhhandel was somehow rescued from oblivion and here recorded in extensive excerpts. The music is Weill of his German period, the style of Mahagonny and Silbersee. Maybe a few leanings toward the later American pieces, particulary the opening phrases of one of Juan's songs, which adumbrates 'September Song' from 'Knickerbocker Holiday'. It continues quite differently however.
This is a light-hearted operetta, and Weill's avowed intention to compose something à la Offenbach succeeds thoroughly. The plot is silly (as is that of most operettas) but don't let that put you off. The music is splendid.
There is a DVD of a staged performance which is not at all bad, if more that a little 'Euro-Trash' in style. However, most of the music is here in audio form, and you don't have to concern yourself with the meanderings of the plot and its fairly extensive dialogue.
Not to be missed if you are interested in Weill.

title: The Damned's U.S. release of I'm All Right Jack...
text:
Not of this Earth (1996) was the U.S. version of the English release of the Damned's I'm All right Jack and the Beanstalk. This disc has four versions floating around (The Japanese release is reshuffled with a hidden track and a the sounds of a laughing clown and a washing machine!)

the official release has a lot of multimedia options (three videos, scores of printable photos, lyrics and a game!) The U.S. version was titled Not of this Earth and it has none of these on it. A re-released version has several live tracks from this era.

The album was from the time period when The Damned made the rounds in pubs and small amphetheaters. David Vanian and Rat Scabies were the only original members left. They were augmented by Kris Dollimore, Allen Lee Shaw, Moose and David Allen. Allen Lee Shaw wrote all of the music (with drumming arrangements by Rat). According to David Vanian and others, the album was only meant to be a demo one and he refused to release it as The Damned (that's way David's vocals are very pedestrian. Allen Lee Shaw left the band during the "recording" of the tracks. Prokiev was a track that Brian James and Rat worked on when he briefly came back to the band. Glen Matlock plays bass on a couple of the tracks when Moose was "unavailible". Despite the lackluster vocals and music, David was unable to block the album's release and it hit the market (first in Japan then in Europe).

The U.S. release is a bare bones deal. Just the over produced songs with cheesy lyrics. They sound like a hard rocking pub band. This proved too much for Scabies and Vanian. The two split for good when Captain Sensible and Paul Gray rejoined The Damned.

Recommended for die hard Damned fans.

title: The Banshees' Big Bid for the Goth Throne and One of Their Very Best Albums
text:
Siouxsie & the Banshees - Juju (1981)

Along with Goth classics like Bauhaus' IN THE FLAT FIELD and The Cure's PORNOGRAPHY, JUJU is a masterwork of dark power, and although Siouxsie rejects the label herself, I consider it one of the best Goth albums ever made if not THE best.

"Spellbound" - One of their creepiest, most intense cuts ever, "Spellbound" announces itself with some twisting guitar lines and Siouxsie intoning: "From the cradle bars/ Comes a beckoning voice/It sends you spinning/ You have no choice" before strident acoustic guitars blaze across the track. Really does sound like being encircled in a spell. The lyrics concern enchanted dolls that mesmerize you and get you to do nasty things, like throw your "elders down the stairs." *****+

"Into The Light" - With its jerky, shifting rhythm, tribal drums and slashing guitar, this one's a deserving fan favorite. *****+

"Arabian Knights" - This ominous, menacing track is surely one of their very best. The lyrics concern the barbaric treatment inflicted on certain women in the Middle East by monstrous men: "Veiled behind screens/ Kept as your baby machine/ Whilst you conquer more orifices/ Of boys, goats and things/ Ripped out sheeps eyes-no forks or knives." The song is so good and the chorus so dreamy you almost forget the harrowing subject matter. *****+

"Halloween" - is a frantic, slightly abrasive rocker, a worthy tribute to October 31rst. ****

"Monitor" - gets down and dirty with a catchy disco beat, some killer guitar riffage, creepy effects and a powerful rumble from bass wizard Steven Severin. The song seems to concern a society that controls people with TV - not too far-fetched this one. *****+

"Night Shift" - is one of the creepiest, most Gothic tracks ever recorded. I've read that it's about Peter Sutcliffe, better known as the Yorkshire Ripper, convicted of murdering 13 women in the mid to late 70s. But it's really up to the listener to decide what's going on in these grim lyrics. This is one heavy song and John McGeoch's guitar is mesmerizing. *****+

"Sin In My Heart" - slowly builds up the tempo until it bursts out with a stunning urgency. Great song, very dark. ****1/2

"Head Cut" - has some slinky guitar, a rubber-band bass and a sinister sound that perfectly compliments Sioux's strange vocalizations. ****

"Voodoo Dolly" - evokes a truly scary atmosphere that seems to close in around you. McGeoch's guitar is spine-tingling and Siouxsie's voice can make your hair stand on end. The whole thing builds to a furious climax and then winds down to an unsettling halt. Powerful stuff! *****+

bonus tracks:

"Spellbound (12" Mix") - The original recording is replicated save for an abruptly spliced in instrumental section that actually sounds like being gripped by a spell! *****+

"Arabian Knights (12" vocoder mix)" - interesting but can't touch the original.. *****

"Fireworks (unreleased Nigel Gray version)" - very good version of a fantastic song, this version doesn't sound too different from the singe although it does end the song by slowing down the tempo *****

title: 3.5...The Pyramids?  How about "The Reverbs."
text:
One of Hydrahead's newest offerings, existing somewhere beyond Radiohead, Neurosis and Grizzly Bear, here is the self-titled debut from "The Pyramids."

While "Pyramids" is somewhat of an enjoyable album, dark and unique, it can also be a bit disappointing. It opens with shimmering, thick and highly reverberated melodies--like a synthy alternative band playing a concert while being sucked into a black hole--but pretty much peaks at the beginning. Aside from some thundering, distant-sounding double-bass drumming found at different intervals throughout, it remains a highly reverberated mess of guitars and unrecognizable, soft vocals; the basic feeling being, "if you've heard one song, you've heard them all." And maybe that was the point and I just don't get it. It is hard to say.

The album is worth a listen (as I have not heard much like it), and I will surely be looking into their next album to really find out what this band is all about. Hyrdahead Records do not lightly sign bands to their label. If you don't believe me, just check out Big Business, "Here Come the Waterworks." Check this one out as well, and be sure to offer an open ear to one of the most exciting indie labels on the planet.

P.S.

While I am at it, those at Hydrahead, how about dropping the 666 at the beginning of all of your catalog numbers? This is no longer a form of rebellion. Everybody does this! This makes you more a part of current trends and less innovative. I enjoy many of your bands, but this deters me from being as avid of an enthusiast of your label as I could be. It is a little trendy and immature, and I'm sure it offends a lot of people who would otherwise spend money on the music you produce. I'm sure you're thinking, "We'd like to see you develop a successful label," or "We don't need your advice," but seriously: Why limit the amount of potential buyers? Why not allow the ideals of your label to be as unique as the bands are? Thanks for the good music, though. Don't stop that!

title: '4 Minutes' Remixes for the Club
text:
'4 Minutes' poses the same problem that many songs from "Confessions on a Dance Floor" did; how do you remix a song that sounds rather mixed already? The mixes included in this release are fun though my only complaint is that in one setting they sound rather similar. There wasn't an attempt to vary the sound of the song and make it into a rock song, or say, a pure pop song. All of these mixes are pretty much club-orientated, which is cool, but this maxi single does lack in variety.

That being said, there are some good mixes that make this release worth buying. The "Junkie XL" and "Junkie XL Dirty Dub" are both the best cuts from the album. For once, the dub isn't boring and a throw-away track but turned into something worth listening to. The "Bob Sinclair Space Funk Mix" keeps with the trumpets/synths/zipper-sounds to give the song a more airy sound and removes the trumpets and drums from the original mix. The "Rebirth Mix" is different in that it has a chill-out sound to it, smoothing out the vocals and scaling back on the instruments to play more with the vocals. The "Peter Saves Paris" mix is good in that it features Madonna more so than Justin Timberlake, unlike in the original mix of the song. It's one I actually heard in a club and it is very danceable, fun, pure dance club with a big sound and heavy synths and beats. The Tracy Young mixes are okay but don't stand out that much when compared to the other mixes.

In all, fun, nice, very dance and club orientated. My only hang-up is that the remixes sort of blend and clash with one another and I wish there had been more variety to perhaps see what '4 Minutes' could have sounded like with a different consideration or beat, such as making it into a rock song or pure pop, something done with other Madonna songs on previous Maxi singles. But, with that, definitely worth buying for your collection and to add to your music library. If you enjoyed the "Hung Up" maxi single of 2005, you'll probably like this one as it sounds like a continuation of the song with similar lyrics and the clicking clock sounds running throughout. Check it out.

title: DEAR MUSIC APPRECIATORS
text:
Dear Music Appreciators,

Why is this a great album that you should buy right now? Because this is a half-female half-male band playing alternative rock with pop appeal and punk attitude, and playing it well. Yes, they sound like the nineties sometimes and yes supposedly this is the band’s first album in like ten years and maybe there has been some breakup drama in the past or whatever, but maybe none of that really matters all that much if you think about it. All that stuff is just filler.

On GHOST NOTES you’ll find heavy riffs, Ann Wilson-esque wailing, and in-your-face attitude vs. gentle guitar, hushed vocals, and even some touches of vulnerability, despite the “it’s gonna get loud, it’s gonna get heavy” forewarning on the opening track. “Empty Bottle” displays the band’s full range of powers and dynamics and it’s good to find such a strong song anchoring the middle of the record instead of weighing down the front end. And there are plenty more strong songs to be found on GHOST NOTES, all studded with memorable moments. Notice how the meandering slow intro to "Black and Blonde” morphs into a heavy, room-shaking riff. Notice the triple rhymes and rapid fire wordplay of “Laughing in the Sugar Bowl,” See if you can spot the subtle tribute to Simon and Garfunkel’s “Cecelia” on “The Museum of Broken Relationships,” Try and find a song that isn’t interesting in some way. Maybe you can do it but I couldn’t.

When I was younger I had a roommate from Uruguay, and whenever he encountered an American food he wasn’t familiar with, before trying it he would ask me “is this a sweet or a salt?” If he was here to ask me that question about Veruca Salt’s new album, I would tell him “it’s both.” Yes, my Uruguayan roommate, despite her name, this Veruca is both sweet and salty, and that quality, that contrast between the soft and loud, light and heavy, pretty and pained, is just one of many reasons why GHOST NOTES is such a satisfying listen. Now get me a Snickers bar, beeyotch

Sincerely,

Constant Listener

title: A Soundtrack Worth Buying--Finally!
text: Let me say this first--I HATE soundtracks. You usually end up with three or four songs and a bunch of junk (Mission: Impossible 2, anyone?), but I loved Gladiator so much that I seen it twice in the theaters (a rarity for me), and I am a huge Dead Can Dance fan--that was more than enough for me to buy it. Hans Zimmer and Lisa Gerrard team up to deliver a haunting soundtrack that is, most of the time, a joy to listen to. Guitars weave in and out, violins and cellos drive the soundtrack, and, occasionally, the listener is honored with Lisa Gerrard's angelic voice. The whole soundtrack is VERY melodic, and it may put those to sleep who aren't familiar with this type of music and/or can't appreciate the somberness that is present. There is a Dead Can Dance feel to these songs--it's strong, and it might put off those who never liked the band (what!?). Personally, I love it. But while the soundtrack carries a Dead Can Dance vibe ("Windfall" off of "Within The Realm Of A Dying Sun" could have fit nicely on here), it still sounds very much its own, so us fans aren't treated to Dead Can Dance rehash (not that I'd complain if it was, mind you). Unfortunately, despite her contribution to the soundtrack, Lisa doesn't sing very much. It's sad to see Lisa, who has the greatest voice ever, sing in only a few songs. And even sadder, is that, excluding "Now We Are Free," her songs are pretty short. It's almost a tease--and I'd rather not be teased when listening to music. What's makes this even worst--so much so I almost gave it three stars--is that the songs aren't all that different from their previous or next tracks ("The Wheat" and "Sorrow," for example, are both quite good, yet seem too much alike). They all have that "score" vibe with them, and that doesn't really suit my tastes (I can only handle so much). My favorite song here is "Now We Are Free." It was the sole reason I didn't give it three stars, as I felt it was that magnificent. It is the highlight of this disk, as it, aside from being beautifully written, captures the power of Lisa's voice wonderfully. All in all, if you pass on this disk, it's far from the end of the world. But, if you do buy it, you've made a wise decision. Hopefully, this will also lead the oblivious to checking out Dead Can Dance, as they are truly one of the best bands ever.

title: The true last good music by this band.....
text:
Yes,here is the last Nektar music that has an inkling(just...an...inkling) of what they were. Yes,this is 1990's pop in an almost Asia-like mode,but it has the harmonies and keyboard and guitar sounds that give just the slightest hint at what this band was in the 1970's.

Understand I am writing this after my criticism of their newest "Time Machine" album,so this may be an addition to that statement of dislike on my part. I feel that if there is a set of music you should have ,just to see which direction Nektar took from the 1990's - 2000's, this two-fer (the price of one)gathers all you need of this late history of this band's sounds.

While I don't love either of these albums,these are what I feel are the two last-vestiges of their sound. The vocal harmonies,the keyboard and guitar riffing...it's still here,although set in more "down to earth" (no pun intended)arrangements and having more plain "rock" lyrics.

I got this to see what had happened after Magic Is A Child....and as a set of well played pop,this really makes good. But it is just pop,and not space oriented prog-rock.

For all of you out there who feel a "NEED" to hear what Nektar are doing now.......buy this set over "Time Machine". If you find yourself absolutely loving these....then "Time Machine" may be what you need to hear next. If you think,"Ok,this is just well played pop.",then just feel happy to hear the band "at their late best" doing what they now are still struggling to do and skip that newest title. It'll save you a few bucks...and you won't have to find someone to give "Time Machine" to.

title: So many haters, you would think these guys released a sub par alt rock record!
text:
Honestly, so many people have a huge problem with this record. It honestly is not that bad.. or let me rephrase that... a lot of it is quite good.
I agree with the massive amounts of people that the lyrics aren't really that great. The music, however, is still very prominent, we cannot forget that crucial fact.
My favorite track on this disc, hands down, is "A Nightmare to Remember." By far, this is the most cohesive track, I find the lyrics to tell quite an eerie story of the very real human experience of being in a severe car accident.
"Rite of Passage" doesn't even deserve to be called a progressive rock song. It was written solely for the purpose of being a single and is the most mundane 8 and a half minute song they have ever written. No real interesting time changes we all grew to love DT for, just one of those eye-rolling, battling solos between Petrucci and Rudess.
"Wither" is also a radio friendly song, but the length of it is appropriate and all around better then "Passage." Not my favorite track on the album, but good nevertheless.
Back to the longer epic songs, "The Shattered Fortress" really did disappoint me. Very, VERY rushed and not nearly as epic as I hoped it would be, and it's cool if you refer back to the songs in this collection, but to recycle the riffs as many times as they did, it just makes this song ridiculous. There's nothing new, they CLEARLY just tacked this on to the end of the album.
"The Best of Times" doesn't get any complaints from me. I love how they went with a really jubilant sound on this song and it really is touching if you imagine what it would be like to lose your father. Great song with a classic solo from Petrucci that reminds me of why he was inspired to write music in the first place.
"The Count of Tuscany" has a lot of really awesome, memorable parts, but this song is too long for its own good. Out of 19 mins, I really enjoy maybe 11 of those mins scattered about the song while the other 8 sounds like filler, especially the 3 and a half minute solo where Petrucci is messing with his volume pedal. It is NOT necessary to write a 75+ minute record every time guys, and you don't have to release music precisely every 2 years. Let inspiration come to you, then write the music. Take a breath of fresh air, spend some time with your families, and when it feels time to go back into the studio, you will feel refreshed and ready to write some good music. Maybe a nice concept album with a flowing story line like sfam and sdoit would serve really well for their next album huh?? Can I get an amen for that one?!?!
Overall, it really is an album with a lot of positive merits, however, they do drift off in parts that just don't sound good. Someone's gotta tell Portnoy to stop doing vocals where he's trying to sound heavy, because it's not working, it sounds lame, they should just continue to do what they do best!

title: So sexy and soothing
text:
Okay, guys, here's some advice from a woman...BUY THIS CD!!!! Joan has done an amazing job re-interpreting some incredible soul classics and added a few new ones of her own! First of all, Midnight Train to Georgia couldn't be sexier or more meaningful. She certainly solved the issue about singing a legend's song (Gladys Knight) in a different way. Somehow, it's sexier. Breakfast in Bed, though still Dusty-esque, is now a Joan Osborne song (not to take anything away from the original). Though I was concerned about Sara Smile being that Hall and Oates were one of my favorite groups, fear not. She kills it with a new idea about phrasing.

Joan is the queen of laying back, taking your time and finally blowing you away...sounds sexy to me! Of equal note are the original songs which, until I read the booklet, did not know were original. Joan somehow has incarnated a writing style that sounds right in the period of music she's covering. That is not easy to do, but she did it justice in a huge way.

Last but not least is the production of this album. While so many CD's produced today sound, well, way over-produced, this album pays homage to the great concept albums of all time.You hear there is one idea and it is carried through splendidly. The strings add body, but don't overpower or become to "lush." The producer should be congratulated for not giving in to modern "everything must be perfect" idea. My advice? Put this album on next Sunday, serve your wife breakfast in bed and wait for your surprise!

title: Spotty Period Album/Good but uneven followup
text:
The first album of this double CD set, "Men from the Ministry", is a spotty affair at best. There are some nice splotches of background vocals and an occasional ear catching and finger snapping tune, (like the infectious "Something Very Good"), but for the most part it's throw-away 1966 pop-stuff.

The followup album, "Midsummer Nights Dreaming" is obviously the superior record of the 2 and makes this worthy of a purchase to any fans of 60's psych. While it also has some "filler" pop songs on it, even those are of decent quality. Highlights include the Lennone-esque "Laughing Man", the U.F.O.-themed craziness of "In The Sky" and "Mr. Light" and the psych-pop fun of "Going Round and Round", "White Collar Worker" and "Sequin Sally".

Finally, I'm not sure if I just got a "bad" version of the collection or not... but both discs are mislabeled as one another; the disc labeled "Men From The Ministry" is really "Midsummer Nights Dreaming", and "Midsummer Nights Dreaming" is really "Men From The Ministry". A minor annoyance at best... but someone should be looking out for such obvious mistakes at RPM; it doesn't look good when such obvious mistakes exist on these kinds of re-releases.

text: This is one of my favorite rock CDs.  I used to have it - about 14 years ago, when I lived in San Francisco. Anyway, since I've been doing some re-buying of CDs I used to have and that I wouldn't be able to find at the library or at any record store (hell, I live in San Diego now and the record stores here are total crap-San Francisco has some of the best record stores I've ever seen - Street Light, Rocket Records, Amoeba and Rasputin (Berkeley) and many more who's names I can't recall now. title: Joe Still Has Got It.
text:
This is R 'n B singer-songwriter Joe's 10th studio album titled 'Doubleback Evolution Of R 'n B' (12 tracks). The album is produced by the California based D. O. A. Joe still has a great vocal range that he demonstrates in this new CD release: e.g. wonderful high pitched vocals in the sweet slow-tempo/ballad track "Love & Sex" (a beautiful orchestral base track, great melody and a duet featuring Idols winner Fantasia), low range vocals as in the track "Magic City" and goes through his full vocal range as in the track "Compromise". He has great harmonies as in wonderful opening track "Something For You" (a wonderfuf track with great melody and an incredible horn section arrangements in this track: horns thrown in inteligently at appropriate intervals. Great job well done!) & the first single "I'd Rather Have A Love" and overall entertaining romantic lyrics as in the beautiful closing/title track "Double Back" (wonderful orchestral base track, great melody and lyrics about taking one's lover for granted until the lover is lost or gone).

Stand-outs/gems/my favourites are "Something For You", "Love & Sex" & the title track "Double Back". The album has some highs and lows but on overall good compositions, great execution of the music and good production by D.O.A.

Singer-songwriter Joe still has got it in this new 10th studio CD release 'Doubleback Evolution Of R 'n B', a recommended CD listening.

title: An admirable craftsman rather than an innovator
text:
I was directed to Persichetti's Sonatas by Walter Simmons, the respected critic and specialist of 20th Century American "non avant-garde" composers. Mr Simmons made me the honor of commenting on my lukewarm review of Persichetti's Symphonies 3, 4 & 7 ([[ASIN:B0009Y26DQ Persichetti: Symphonies 3, 4 & 7]]), encouraging me not to consign Persichetti to the "second tier" of American composers before familiarizing myself with the Piano Sonatas, contending that "Persichetti was primarily a composer for keyboard instruments and for wind ensembles (...) where his greatness is most apparent". Such an invitation was more than a prompting, though it is intimidating to write a review knowing that it will be scrutinized by a luminary such as Mr Simmons. But, now, time to dive.

The gist of my discussion with Mr Simmons had to do with "originality" (e.g., according to Mr Simmons, whether the composer has invented some novel compositional technique) versus "personality" (independent of its technical innovations, do you hear something in the music that is strikingly the composer's own). In his piano writing Persichetti is certainly not strikingly innovative, whether in technique or in sonic universe, in the way that (to limit myself to American composers) Ives, Cowell, Cage, Crumb (or even Adams) have been. He is happy to remain within the limits of the time-hallowed fast-slow-fast architecture, his contrapuntal writing and demands at digital prowess are heir to centuries of keyboard writing since Bach. As in the symphonies, the craftsmanship is unquestionable. As for "unique personality", his music does constantly titillate the neurons of memory. As the excellent liner notes, written by pianist Geoffrey Burleson himself, point out, you can hear in the first Sonata (1939, Persichetti still studying piano and composition, and an impressive achievement in its own right) a "pervasive flavor of Austrian expressionism" (it sent me back to Eisler's early piano works, [[ASIN:B000004CAP Hanns Eisler: Works for Piano (Vol. I) - Sonatas 1-3 / Piano Pieces / Variations - Christoph Keller]], and yes, it is all there); in the second (same year) a striking reminiscence of Hindemith's harmonic world, and in the 3rd from 1943 the melodic and harmonic turns so characteristic of the "American epic style" of Copland or Schuman, integral with the wistful slow movement. These, plus the elaborate contrapuntal writing and the percussive touch in toccata-like movements will prove abiding characteristics of Persichetti's style.

The next Sonatas, 4 to 9, were written in close succession, from 1949 to 1952, building a cycle of sorts. All but #4 are short to very short - Sonatinas, really. The elements of the style met in the previous sonatas can still be heard, the Copland-like epic and wistful qualities (as in the broad and powerful opening of the 4th Sonata's first movement and the ensuing, gentle passage or in the wistful and dreamy slow movement of the 5th) and the Hindemith harmonic and rhythmic echoes (as in the middle movement of the 4th, and many sections if not complete movements of 5 to 7).

But it is also in these Sonatas that something really individual emerges; not that it doesn't dig out from one's memory echoes of other composers (other than the Copland and Hindemith reminiscences, at times I was tempted to go back to Shostakovich's Preludes op 34 or to Prokofiev's Visions fugitives), but it is pursued consistently enough and with enough of a distinct, personal slant to be called a hallmark of Persichetti's individual voice. That voice I hear in the more whimsical and scherzando passages - and Persichetti had an obvious love for those - as in the second movement and the more motoric and syncopated sections of the finale of the 4th, the outer movements of the 5th and 6th and 8th and finale of the 7th, and the dazzling second movement, "Allegro agilite", of the 9th Sonata (here, echoes from Ravel's Sonatine and other neo-classical piano pieces). The virtuosity is dazzling, the contrapuntal part-writing always highly elaborate and intricate.

These syncopated outer-movements are very American in their dynamism and exuberance - faint echoes of Jazz, too. Other than the syncopation, there is an obvious glee at writing in the piano's crystalline upper registers, making the music sound, at times, like a Jazzy or even slightly zany music box. This is, to me, the most enjoyable in Persichetti's Sonatas. Another trait is the mixture of the grazioso and the scherzando, nowhere more in evidence than in the first movements of 7, 8 and 9. In this series of works Persichetti flirts with neo-classicism, but never gives the impression that he is trying to slot into and illustrate a genre.

On the other hand, I find that his slow movements often exude a certain blandness, veering between the Hindemith bitter-sweet (4th, 7th), the Copland-wistful (5th, 9th) and the lounge-Jazz dreaminess (8th).

The last three Sonatas (1955, 1965, 1982) show continuity (the ebullient fast movements and the wistful slow ones) and evolution, one being that Persichetti now evolves much more in the piano's middle registers. There is also a deepened concern for the form, already perceptible in the 9th Sonata, by which the opening material provides the uniting seed for the whole composition. The two last ones are also considerably more advanced in their language and "abstract" in their melodic contours, pure play on tones and keys (Stravinsky's Five Movements for Piano and Orchestra and Debussy's Etudes came to mind). The last is something of a testament. It makes systematic use of the "mirror technique", which Persichetti called an "abiding compulsion" of his, and by which the right-hand intervals are reproduced by the opposite or mirror intervals in the left hand. It makes for a harmonically fascinating composition.

Again, Persichetti doesn't stand out as an innovator or even as a composer with a very original sonic universe (although his toccata and scherzo movements are quite uplifting in their own right), more as an admirable craftsman. It is as a whole that his Sonatas make an impressive body of works. It is Persichetti's steadfast and abiding preoccupation with writing for the piano and digging deep his furrow that imposes respect and admiration.

Geoffrey Burleson's contribution is outstanding.

Don't get me wrong, I like the album, but I wish they would throw me a curve-ball, something I'm not expecting but still hits that part of me that says, "THAT'S what music is all about!". title: A "filler'' album
text:
I get the sense that this album is a filler: something to put out there until Alison and Union Station come out with their next, hopefully soon.

It's still good _ more a pop album than country or bluegrass (other than "Sawing On the Strings'' and its all-star cast that includes Tony Rice, Sam Bush and Stuart Duncan as well as Union Station.) Nothing wrong with that _ Alison would be a pop diva (I actually hate that term) if she wanted to be. But it's still doesn't have the sequenced feel of most of her albums. More like One from Column A, another from column B, a third from Column C.

Again, a lot of it is really good. "Jacob's Dream'' is a striking folk tale _ I thought of a different version of the much-recorded "Long Black Veil.'' I'm sure I've heard "Country Boy,'' _ it sounds like something from a Broadway musical. What surprised me is that one of the writers is Fred Hellerman, who has to be the same Fred Hellerman who teamed with Pete Seeger and others with the Weavers, a huge folk act in the early '50s until they were blacklisted.

In any case, a nice collection while we wait for more.

title: One of the finest concept albums of the seventies
text:
Jeff Lynne has written a lot of so-so middle of the road songs in his long career as singer-songwriter, but Eldorado is without doubt one of his artistic heights. "Legend" has it that his dad complained about earlier tracks saying that 'your tunes have no bloody tune', and so Jeff set out to construct Eldorado.
And man, has he succeeded or what. There's magic twinkling all over the place. For once, the exuberant strings do not dull the music, but rather enrich it, while there are even some subtle experimental sounds added. Again, this album breathes musical magic all over and I've never met anyone who regretted buying this album.

title: Overlooked Gem
text:
Did you ever read a book -- then read it again ten years later, and make the pleasant discovery that the parts you'd mentally underlined or highlighted years earlier, are NOT the same ones that `reach' you today? Witness, if you will, this amazing concept album, you may have forgotten (I had, almost.)

If you are like me, you may have almost forgotten this gem. If you're like my sister Andrea (who has the most amazing singing voice I've ever heard) you've NEVER tasted of its amazing grace.

'Sis,' who has refined musical tastes, last night dignified my latest review (for a Tom T. Hall compilation) by sniffing: "YOU'RE listening to country music now?? Ouch!!!" I resisted the urge to remind `Anra' about Ray Charles' classic country music album of 40 years ago (with the definitive version of Eddy Arnold's "You Don't Know Me").

Her comment made me go and rummage out this CD. Sure enough, there there it was: something I'd vaguely recalled from the superb liner notes, by James Hunter. A short quotation of the album's co-producer Tony Brown, from the days when he first worked with Gospel singer Shirley Caesar: "She had ALWAYS loved country music!"

----

Back in late 1994 when this album was released, it was Chet Atkins' duet with Alain Toussaint (on the latter's best selling composition, "Southern Nights") that prompted me to track down this disc in the first place. I'm pleasantly surprised to find this very day that, some tracks I didn't give a second listen to, back then, are now at center stage in my heart: As with good spiritual reading, when the light goes on, I am `lifted up.'

First things first: Amazingly, most of the singers featured here had never met before they got together in the studio with co-producer Don Was. The producer(s) had to guess at which artists might have `chemistry' at their first time meeting.

In this firmament there are stars in ascension -- Trisha Yearwood & Aaron Neville singing "I Fall to Pieces." And others, perhaps in decline but still able to shine brightly as they `rise to the occasion' -- Sam Moore & Conway Twitty, in harmony and `sync' - for a "Rainy Night in Georgia."

Some pairings are timeless and shine as brightly as ever - Natalie Cole & Reba McEntire caressing Buddy Johnson's (blues band) beautiful chestnut from 1948, "Since I Fell for You." And Gladys Knight and Vince Gill agreeing that "There Ain't Nothin' Like the Real Thing."

Only one track here might underline (for someone like my sister) the difference between talent and kitsch; and it's literally "Something Else" by Little Richard & Tanya Tucker. But, hey --- ten out of eleven ain't bad!

Ten years on . . . and what's my new favorite? A four-leaf clover I managed to overlook before. Then-rising-star Marty Stuart conjures up magic with the heart of a Soul/Gospel band who hadn't had a hit in years - the Staple Singers, Mavis and `Pops'. Marty (a superb instrumentalist in his own right) elevates the introduction to Robbie Robertson's "The Weight" . . . . "I pulled into Nazareth, was feelin' `bout half past dead' . . . and soon enough, Pops & Mavis seize control of the narrative, and the whole group (as James Hunter puts it, "rejoices throughout the chorus. These people are like pilgrims on the road . . . turning plain plights and shifting responsibilities into Gospel Good News."

`Anra,' my dear sister, you may never know what you missed.

Mark Blackburn
Winnipeg

title: Music so painstakingly beautiful that it belies its political goal
text:
Luigi Nono didn't write operas. He adamantly rejected the word and the form, and all the linear and psychological story-telling narrative processes associated with it. What he wrote, he preferred to call, in those years from "Intolleranza 1960", premiered in 1961, to Al Gran Sole whose first performance was in 1975 in Milano, "azione scenica" - stage action. What he did was to make a montage of texts of various origins. Most of those utilized in part 1 deal with the French Commune, the short-lived popular and pre-communist take over of Paris in 1871 after France's defeat against the Germans, which ended in a bloodbath but was seen by the contemporary and later advocates of the Communist Revolution as the scale model of the Communist government and society to come. So you get excerpts from Marx's The Civil War in France, an newspaper article by Lenin, Brecht's play "The Days of the Commune", quotes from Louise Michel (a famous female revolutionary figure of those Commune days), a poem of Rimbaud (with the verse that gives the composition its title: "in the great sun loaded with love"), but also quotes from Che Guevara and his revolutionary companion Tania Bunke, and a few more.

Part II (CD 2) changes time and place and deals with the aborted Russian Revolution of 1905, centering on the figure of Gorki's "Mother" (from his 1907 novel, adapted by Brecht as a play in 1932) and using, among other sources, excerpts from Brecht's writings on Gorki. But there are other threads: one relates to the struggles of the working class in Torino/Turin, the Northern Italian industrial city, in 1950, with some street slogans and excerpts from poems by Cesare Pavese centering on the figure of the Prostitude Deola (the liner notes are silent about the poems' origin. Some at least come from Pavese's first book of poems "Lavorare stanca", which I think means something like "working to death"). There are also quotes from Haydée Santamaria and Celia Sanchez, two woman companions of Fidel Castro in the failed attack of the Moncado barracks in 1953 which was a preparation for the successful seizure of power in 1959, and obviously chosen by Nono as counterparts to Guevara's Tania Bunke; and testimonies of North-Vietnamese women imprisoned in South Vietnam camps.

From these choices it is clear that while "Al Gran Sole" doesn't tell a "story" in the traditional operatic sense, with conflicting characters enacting a certain plot, it definitely tells A story: and that is the story of the "people" in Revolution. More specifically, it is about failure, failed attempts at Revolution, probably, in Nono's intention, to be taken as annunciatory of later successful bids. The meaning is reinforced by the fact that, at the end of his piece, Nono has the Mother, after her son, assassinated by the forces of repression, which I think happens neither in Gorki's novel nor in the play that Brecht drew from it. Possibly Nono's message is (to quote a revolutionary song used as a seminal germ for a wide-scale composition by another highly politically-minded composer, Frederic Rzewski) "The People United Will Never Be Defeated" - at least not in the long run.

One may adhere to the political message and intentions or be ruffled by them. But the paradox is that ultimately, the political content doesn't matter so much. Nono has written music of intense and almost painstaking beauty. There are soprano and mezzo lines of painfully tense lyricism over dreamy choruses drowned in resonance; there are dreamy tape utterances as if coming from afar, and percussive interjections from the orchestra. Nono doesn't really try for the text to be intelligible, as in CD 1 track 7 when he attributes the lines of Louise Michel to two interlacing vocalists, and all over when he has the four sopranos sing the lines of Louise Michel and Deola.

In CD 1 track 6, the chorus is treated as a shouting mob, to great effect. There is a short, epic male chorus in Part 2 Scene 4 which made me think of the crew of Britten's Billy Budd. There are orchestral outbursts of extraordinary power and drama, even near-unbearable violence, such as in the finale of Part 1 (track 11), or in Part 2 Scene 3, depicting the "deployment of the repressive machine". Don't put these discs on to soothe a head-ache!

It is ironic perhaps that Nono chose to honor those failed revolutionary attempts. Indeed, the paradox - and perhaps the limit, if not the failure (I mean, in view of the goals he set to himself) - of Nono's concept of a politically meaningful azione scenica is that the melismas he writes and the atmospheres he conjures are so beautiful and gripping that you don't need to listen to the text and make the effort to understand what is being sung and what it is all about. After a while you just lay aside the libretto (and the booklet doesn't help by providing no translations of texts sung in Italian, French and Spanish) and revel.

Ultimately then, this music, meant to have a political and even subversive, revolutionary, "anti-bourgeois" (whatever that may mean) impact, is ideally suited for "bourgeois" consumption - meaning, an enjoyment that is purely aesthetic, pleasure-centered.

After all, the portrait of Guevara has been for decades all over the T-shirts worn by burger-eating, SUV-driving Western teen-agers.

Detailed liner notes, although they don't not even provide precise information on the texts assembled by Nono and their origins (I did much of the research myself on the Internet), and the second text contained therein, by the dramaturg of the 1999 Stuttgart production from which this recording is derived, is needlessly wordy. But these are small matters in view of the beauty of this music.

title: This Albun Sounds Like An Electric Circus...And I Kinda Like It (Rating: 8 out of 10- -4.0 stars)
text:
I think this album angered a lot of Common fans, espeically since he showed his experimental side of himself on this LP. Also since this is between [[ASIN:B00004S51H Like Water For Chocolate]] and [[ASIN:B0009IFEJ0 Be]], two of his softer and more soulful LPs. This album has so many influences and contributions (see the front cover) that people may believe that Common stepped out of his range. I personally find it to be an excellent album.

The Roots' ?uestlove produced some of the tracks. "Between Me, You, & Liberation" is one fine track, especially with the drum pattern that he made. "Come Close" was the lead single featuring Mary J. Blige, that was excellent. The creativity shows when the song "Electric Wire Hustle Flower" plays and features Sonny of P.O.D. Say what you want, but I like that song. The sex song "*69 (P.S. With Love)" is another softer sounding beat and features Bilal. The last 30 seconds of the track has a nice mellow beat that is worth waiting for.

There are a few rough spots on this album though. "I Got A Right Ta" featuring Pharrell is one rough song that I really didn't have the mood for. "Soul Power" I was thinking the beat was going to drop, but never came. And the final two tracks are great, but could have been shortened since they are 8+ minutes. Other than that, this album is excellent.

Don't hate on this LP. It is very creative and experimental. Many people have gotten settled with the soulful type Common, so this did kind of come from left field. I didn't think this album was going to get bad reviews until I saw this album received 4 mics in The Source, so I thought it was dope. If you listen to this without thinking about his other albums, you will find that this album is very underrated. Peace.

title: Music For People Who Hate Music
text:
It's always close by, like the threat of nuclear war. In the frozen food section of your supermarket, in the elevator of your office building, wafting through the lobbies of hotels and corridors of conference centers. It bears an eerie resemblance to music, as wax fruit resembles something nourishing, as paintings of sad clowns with large liquid eyes and dogs playing poker resemble Guernica and Crows On A Wheatfield, as a lightning bug resembles lightning.

In a way, this is perhaps forgivable. Everything Henry Miller ever said about American bread is true, it's really unfit for anything except perhaps blotting up spilled ink. But there are those people who like bologna on Wonderbread, and why shouldn't they have their fun - or more properly - lack of fun? Perhaps Wonderbread is the only appropriate delivery mechanism for peanut butter and jelly. So be it.

In this context one can attempt to excuse the chain of albums churned out by Mr. G, like so many spiceless sausages. But one cannot forgive this. Here he approaches those who are far beyond being his betters, they're from a different dimension. To listen as KG addresses 'Round Midnight is to question the existence of God. A smooth jazz draft of Ipanema is rather like painting a polar bear in a snowstorm. But the height of impertinence and grandiosity is playing a duet with Satchmo. It was a tawdry bit of grandstanding when Natalie Cole did it with her dead father, but at least that was all in the family. Here it is a hideous attempt at bridging the gap that will forever separate the real from the really, really awful.

title: Pure Pleasure
text:
This CD is one you can confidently give to someone you love who also loves romantic chamber music -- that is, if they don't own it already. Seldom will you find a disc with piano trios by three composers that have one thing in common: lovely, memorable themes. Each trio is well crafted and developed, and while Zemlinsky went on in later years to write quartets that are much less assimilable on the first hearing, these are all easy listening.
There is great variety in the Goldmark work, with rapid movements containing pockets of tender lyricism. The Gal Trio is short, but sweet, the step-wise progression in the melodies enhanced by his harmonies. And the Austrian flavor of the Zemlinsky is sheer delight.
Much is made in the notes about the influence of Brahms. I chose not to focus on that while listening, and as a consequence enjoyed the individual traits of each composer. The result was rewarding indeed.
The performers are outstanding, lending great technical skill and sensitivity to these works. The SACD sound is ideally clear and rich.
Please don't hesitate to grab this one.

title: Sheen.....less.. 2.5 stars
text:
﻿Daft Punk returns with "Human After All", the follow up to 2001's critically lauded and hated on "Discovery". Not one of the most prolific groups, Daft Punk has always been known to take their time between albums, and this one was no exception. But "Human After All" distinguishes itself from the rest of their work by not striving for absolute perfection. This album's strengths definitely don't lie in the details. "Human After All" took only six weeks to record, and it shows. While the songs do fit together, they seem only married by their proximity of creation, and work together only long enough to tell the listener that they're only "human after all". Nearly all of the songs that comprise this album resemble the cling clang that was their pre "Homework" recordings. In fact some of the stuff here could be mistaken for Sven Vath songs, which is an utter surprise since they've so relied on melodic electronic pop in the past. The lead single "Human After All" is no "One More Time", or "Around The World", but is still in no way an indicator of the way the album will fall into an undertow of murkiness and clutter. This album is loopy even for an electronic record, and some songs drone on relentlessly with only trace amounts of variation. "Make Love" the album's fifth song functions as a bridge that divides the album's cling clanging into two acts. That song has a truly beautiful prototype Daft Punk piano loop, but even it gets loop heavy after a while, and would only be a standout on this album and no others. For those who don't pay attention to the particulars, they'll probably find that this is still an effective electronic album, because it is. Even Daft Punk's weakest record (which this is) is a release of some quality, and is worthy of their follower's time. You have to admit that there is something lovable about an underpolished electronic record. Especially since the genre depends so heavily on sheen.

text:
Being in the unique position to be able to listen to Stringbean and the Stalkers every Sunday night at a small Cajun restaurant, I knew it was only a matter of time before these guys would be "discovered" and recorded.
"Hey-Hey" captures the best of Stringbean & the Stalkers' style of blues/country-blues/rock-zydeco music. In other words, these guys have a truly inimitable blues-based sound. This really is more than a blues CD; it crosses over and would fit quite comfortably in the CD collection of anyone who listens to Blues Traveler, the Dead or any of the great Chicago Blues Masters.
Stringbean (Kenny Sorenson) blows harp with the authority of any of the great Chicago players, attacks a song with deep feeling and writes and delivers a song with a Steinbeckian authority. He surrounds himself with "local legends," such as Sonny Kenn on guitar and Neil Thomas on accordian and keyboards. Drummer Victor Bayers provides the soulful backbone to the medley. The band delivers one of the best versions of Sonnyboy Williamson's, "Bring It On Home" that I have heard in a long time. This CD is a welcomed addition to my collection. It's great!

title: Whoa, Nelly!
text: Eclectic songstress Nelly Furtado recently burst onto the charts with her chart-topping new single "Promiscuous."  The song is, of course, THE song of the summer and has remained at No. 1 on nearly every chart since release, and for good reason--simply put, it's just a great song.  Her third album, appropriately entitled Loose, is just like its name suggests: Furtado is having fun right now, and her brand new single "Promiscuous" is the perfect track to define this moment in her life.  It's so ridiculously radio-friendly and irresistible that it's hard not to fall in love with its call-and-response dialogue, its groovy Hip Hop-influenced beat and sexy message.  Sure, it's not really sung (it fits more under the category of being a chant save for the chorus, which is sung), but that factor doesn't detract from it hardly at all.  Loose song "Maneater," the second self-proclaimed "smash," is enjoyable enough but sounds somewhat lacking in its instrumental parts when compared to the complex techno-rrific grooves and swoops of the aforementioned "Promiscuous."  Nelly, known for her expressive (if somewhat emotionless) vocal delivery, hardly provides listeners with her trademark curdlings and coos, instead offering up Hip Hop-flavored Britney Spears-like growling and call-and-responses.  "In God's Hand," Loose's only real ballad, is enjoyable enough (though the ending is unusual and distracting with dialogue between Nelly Furtado and an unknown person, sounding as if someone forgot to press the Stop button after the song was recorded), but the singer-songwriter sounds a little too breathy at times and even somewhat uncomfortable in parts.  Casual listeners will eat it up, but dedicated fans who fell in love with "I'm Like a Bird" Furtado will be disappointed with Loose, shake their heads (in disapproval) and say, "Whoa, Nelly!"

title: Strong favorite
text:
When I started delving into Johnny's back catalog, this was the record which found itself on my turntable more than any other. Johnny's not frequently a songwriter, so maybe it helped that he filled it up with other people's songs -- it makes for great variety, and (typical of Johnny) he does most of it pretty well. "Silver Train" was reportedly written for him anyway, and "Ain't Nothing to Me" sounds so unlike his usual output that I wondered if it was even him singing.

But that's getting ahead: "Rock Me Baby" features the most kick-ass JW guitar solo I can recall and I've heard 'em all: it's like taking "Fast Life Rider" and reducing it to two blues choruses. Really, it's hard to take anyone else's version seriously after hearing this one, so that's just about worth the buying price alone. From the first song, Johnny's given us notice. You can complain about quantity, but the quality's there if you're up to hearing it. "Still Alive And Well" is a powerhouse bluesy rocker, as is "Can You Feel It" -- if a few of the others sound a little like typical early 70s rock music, well -- they are: Johnny was the biggest influence going on bluesy rock trios, and this was smack in the midst of it. Spin this, and you're hearing it right where it's at.

The main issue: is it a good record, one you'd listen to over and over? Well, I already did, so there ya go. Now it's your turn, so go ahead -- you won't be sorry. Oh yeah: the bonus tracks are OK too. :)

title: Reflective in Returning Love He Sings
text:
The last reviewer commented on the similarity of Laughing Stock to Spirit of Eden, and I can definitely see it--but I view it as a positive...I would have gladly accepted the two albums as a single 2-disc work. Laughing Stock and Spirit of Eden very much complement each other both musically and lyrically. Even the similar cover art highlights the commonality...together like sunrise and sunset. Sadly, this album marked the sunset for Talk Talk, a band that grew from mundane pop origins into mesmerising, minimalist, and deeply spiritual pondering that proved a nightmare for the creativity-stifling music industry. Perhaps--and this is simply my interpretation--the title of the album reflects a resigned understanding on the part of the band of what was likely to be...and at the same time, maybe even a sense of eagerness to meet their fate, not in suicidal terms , but in an eagerness to embrace their eccentricity. Perhaps there is even *pride* in being the "laughing stock" of the insipid popular critics.
They do indeed have much to be proud of. Like its companion, Spirit of Eden, this album could very easily have been produced just yesterday instead of over a decade ago. Though the comparison may seem strange at first, I am reminded of a more minimalist version of Sigur Ros (perhaps Talk Talk influenced them?). Pieces like the rather atonal, meandering "Myrrhman", and "Runeii's" game of silences are perhaps the most experimental of the lot, although even the more "normal"-seeming "Ascension Day" shows signs of it as well. On Laughing Stock, I nominate "Ascension Day" (despite its abrupt cutoff--glitch or intentional?) and "New Grass" as the two best tracks.
Laughing Stock is perhaps a bit more upbeat than Spirit of Eden, which seems to have portrayed a man so downtrodden that he yearns to make a new start. Laughing Stock lyrically seems like the beginnings of that new morning, although that desperation is still there (New Grass in particular helps create this impression). In order to decipher the lyrics, it's necessary to both read Mark Hollis' nearly illegible handwriting and his equally cryptic, faint and melodic singing--but once done, a very interesting picture emerges. Mr. Hollis' lyrics are replete with a deep, instinctive spirituality...not the dogmatic, pop kind of "Christianity", but something very natural and flowing--he seems to write these things not to proselytize, but simply because it is an integral part of his being. As such, it's a delight to listen to. Yes, he can discern some of the problems, but rather than launch on a bitter diatribe, he instead expresses a gentle longing for things to be put right. "Heaven waits--someday Christendom may come Westward"...perhaps a suggestion that what *did* come westward from the Holy Land very often did not truly reflect what Jesus stood for. But, even with this he does not *condemn*--he hopes, and this is what makes his more spiritual ruminations so listenable and so touching.
Overall, this is an album NOT to be missed...I am deeply glad that Polydor saved this gem from fading away to a distant memory. As it is, it's too little known. Tell your friends about the gorgeous final triad of albums by Talk Talk: Colour of Spring, Spirit of Eden, and this album, Laughing Stock! 5 stars, all!

title: Bluesy prog that sounds good?
text:
Khan manages to do what no other Canterbury band seems able to do on Space Shanty: create something musically interesting and retain good lyrical content, with a decent singer to boot. Hillage's tone is unmistakable, and all the instruments are used with masterful taste. There's a good deal of counterpoint on the album, as well, which makes for good repeated listenings. I'm going to do this track by track, to provide a general feel to the album.

Space Shanty (8:59) - The opening track starts off with a sort of Led Zeppelin vibe: bluesy, spacey, and generally stuff that I don't like in my prog, but listening to the entirety of the track is rewarding. It's a very energetic song, but not my cup of tea. Some good Hammond organ that persists through the rest of the album. The texture changes pretty frequently, and the lead in to the solo around 3:00 is pretty cool. Despite the blues inflections, the structure of the song makes this an interesting track, with plenty of tempo and rhythm changes, as well as some harmonic exploration.

Stranded (6:35) - Less bluesy than the previous offering, with a descending piano motif that reminds me of Debussy's Second Arabesque. Harmonized vocals are prominent here, but not offensive. The track starts off pretty tame, but breaks into a diminished arpeggio around three minutes in that gets the energy going. The trading soloistic ideas at the four minute mark are ear-catching, and Steve Hillage's guitar sounds almost violinlike in the background. The end of the track transitions into the next track, but if you were playing it by itself, neither track would be harmed by the edit.

Mixed Up Man Of The Mountains (7:14) - A return of the bluesy sound (which I generally don't like), but I think that it works well for this track. One of the best tracks on the album, in my opinion. Some really nice guitar sounds on this track, distinct sections, imitative parts, organ shredding, awesome bass, and seamless integration of jazz and rock elements Hillage's solos.

Driving To Amsterdam (9:23) - Lyrically, the best track. I would say that this is the best track on the album. Good complex structure, yet strophic enough that it's pretty catchy. 4:37 is awesome. Changes in texture are frequent, and range from soft and introspective to jazzy to straight up rocking. There's a really neat ascending bassline at 6:15.

Stargazers (5:32) - This one starts of with a really cool and rhythmically active mallet riff that creates a spacey atmosphere, but the music degenerates into some hippie psychedelic-sounding crap that absolutely ruins the song.

Hollow Stone (8:16) - A good closing track. One of the few tunes on this album that has a minor feel to it. On the goodness scale, it competes with Driving To Amsterdam. The lyrics were written well, and there's an awesome heavy metal section at the end with some stereo phaser effects on the lead guitar, followed by about a minute of some awesome, awesome noise generated by the collection of instruments, notably by the organ. Not quite Penderecki, but any fan of tone clusters and stereo panning should be happy.

title: A fantastic compilation from an unfortunately forgotten band.
text:
To my mind the Jam are "the best punk band you never heard of." I've owned albums by all the greats: Ramones, Sex Pistols, Clash, Damned, Undertones, Vibrators, Blink182, Green Day, etc.

I love the Ramones because they aren't to be taken seriously. I love the Jam because they ARE to be taken seriously. They were serious musicians writing very pointed lyrics and kick-ass songs. These weren't simply Mohawk and safety-pin punks. They were more in tune with the "punk" bands of the 1960's like The Who. Indeed, they were often referred to as Mods rather than punks. Still, in retrospect, it's hard not to call their early songs punk. From the "in your face" angst of early songs like "In the City", "The Modern World", "All Around the World," to more pop gems like "Eton Rifles", "Going Underground", or "That's Entertainment", the band proved that punk is as much a philosophy as a way of playing your instruments.

I suspect the band never had much of a following in the US due to their definitely British sound. Singer Paul Weller spouts lyrics in a thick British accent that probably doomed the band to a cult following.

It's a pity that this band never did achieve the same success stateside that the Pistols or Clash enjoyed. The Jam was definitely a better band.

This compilation starts with the punk angst years and ends with more refined (but still punk in attitude) later pop songs.

A must for any fan of punk or new wave music from the seventies or eighties...or any era for that matter.

title: Famous Recording of The Firebird by the Composer a Great Choice!
text:
Stravinsky's first ballet for Diaghilev remains an exemplary moment in Twentieth Century Music, setting the stage for the two even greater balletic masterpieces to follow, Petrushka and The Rite of Spring. Not as finished or well constructed as these later two, The Firebird ballet music never-the-less marks an extraordinary advance from the composer's earlier works into first full artistic maturity. These three ballets, culminating in the Rite of Spring, are among the most pivotal works in the history of art, and should not be missed!

Except for the Scherzo a la russe, a much later short work composed for Paul Whiteman in 1944, all the selections on the Cd were composed at the very beginning of Stravinsky's career, and share strong associations with the Rimsky-Korsakov family. Stravinsky had grown close to them while studying under the famous composer and the Cd includes excellent notes of the period, particularly a few marvelous pages taken from Stravinsky's own lynx-eyed memories! (Reading Stravinsky's often iconoclastic, acerbic pronouncements on music and art should not be missed!) [[ASIN:B000FA4UMY Memories and Commentaries : New One-Volume Edition]] The Scherzo fantastique was finished in early 1908 and received Rimsky-Korsakov's strong support, but premiered after his death. The Fireworks, written immediately after, was a wedding present for the elder composer's daughter. Unfortunately, Rimsky died just before the young Stravinsky's finished manuscript reached him. In the case of the Firebird, Stravinsky spent a couple months starting in November of 1909 working on The Firebird music at the Korsakov family dacha south of St. Petersburg. Andrei Rimsky-Korsakov, the composer's son, was close to Stravinsky then, and spent much time with the composer during the work's composition - in tribute his name graces The Firebird's dedication page.

Stravinsky's 1961 performance in early stereo of the complete Firebird ballet is one of the very best recordings he made - and as a bonus the Columbia Symphony Orchestra's musicians play wonderfully. This is the same 'recordings' orchestra that made many fine recordings at the same time with Bruno Walter. [[ASIN:B00000K4IM Beethoven Symphony No. 6 "Pastorale" / Walter, Columbia Symphony (SACD)]] Stravinsky was not a professional conductor, but like Rachmaninov, who easily could have been, Stravinsky had a very firm idea of what he wanted, and usually achieved his ends - sharply delineated rhythms matched with pellucid orchestration, all directly conveyed with a strong forward motion devoid of any bowing to sentimentality. It should be further noted: By the time Stravinsky recorded this music he had reinvented and modernized his musical idiom a couple times - unlike Rachmaninov - and however fond Stravinsky's memories of his earliest days with Rimsky-Korsakov and his family, the senior Stravinsky of 1961 no longer wishes The Firebird understood as molded out of the over ripe exoticism associated with Bakst's brilliantly colored designs for the ballet of Scheherazade. (For an up to date overview of the Russian ballet I strongly recommend - [[ASIN:1580932541 The Ballets Russes and the Art of Design]]) -) This recording of The Firebird thus should be seem less as historical reminiscence, and rather as a statement of Stravinsky's own unique future path as musical innovator, the Firebird music given unflinchingly 'moderne'; quite deliberately shorn of any idiomatic suggestions of his famous teacher.

For those who prefer a more Romantic version, or insist on more up to date sound - and by the way, the original analogue sound on Stravinsky's Firebird recording remains quite good! - there are several excellent more recent recordings in varying styles of The Firebird. I especially recommend Simon Rattle conducting his British orchestra, a wonder of committed razor sharp playing![[ASIN:B00000DNJL Stravinsky: Firebird Suite / 4 Etudes / Scherzo a la Russe (two orchestrations)]]

title: Incubus mellow things out on "If Not Now, When?"
text:
Throughout their fifteen year career, Incubus has paved a trail for themselves out of the nu-metal scene of the late 90's. While other bands of that era have fallen by the wayside and failed to expand their sound, Incubus has made it a point not to do the same album twice. Though their most successful radio hit was "Drive" from their 1999 album "Make Yourself", they came into their own with their 2001 follow-up "Morning Wiew". In 2004, they made their most accomplished recording- the politically charged "A Crow Left Of The Murder", followed by the criminally underrated "Light Grenades". They took a break in 2009 by issuing a greatest hits album "Monuments And Melodies", followed by lead singer Brandon Boyd's "The Wild Trapeze" a year later. They released their first album in five years in 2011, the noticeably calm "If Not Now, When?".

Their new album marks the third collaboration between the band and producer Brendan O'Brien- who also helmed the aforementioned "A Crow Left Of The Murder" and "Light Grenades". They are mellowed out and laid back on this effort, which is a far cry from their "Pardon Me" and "Wish You Were Here" days. The album starts off with the title track "If Not Now, When?" leading into the piano- driven ballad "Promises, Promises", which recalls early Elton John. On the ballad "Friends And Lovers", Brandon sings about the importance of sticking with someone through the thick and thin in a relationship. The tracks "Thieves" and "Switchblade" recall the days of early Incubus. They go for a straight ahead sound on the radio ready "Isadore" and create a brief acoustic ballad with "Defiance". They channel Pink Floyd on the seven minute ballad "In The Company Of Wolves" and close the album with "Tomorrow's Food". Though the album is tame- even by Incubus' standards, "If Not Now, When?" shows them at their most experimental, as well as their most mature. This is an album that needs to be played a few times to understand its brilliance in being understated and melodic. "If Not Now, When?" is a record worth listening to, even if the change in sound throws one off a little.

title: A rainy day gem...
text:
Just like the last reviewer, I cannot understand why this album is Korn's lowest-selling; it is actually their arguably third best after the debut and Follow the Leader. Moreover, this album is trademark Korn with every element of the band more than present and digested into one quality piece of music.

True, nu-metal is rightfully dismissed today, but this album is NOT generic, it just represents the band's unique style; and it does it in an impressive way, giving the album a distinct feeling. In fact, Issues is a moody album, vicious, dark and painful like no other Korn album except self-titled. The production helps it, of course, being ominous and muddy, but the credit is still largely to the band's sound and songs.

Yes, many listeners will not point much attention to the songs due to the fact that they are all minor-key and not too different from each other, but it also gives Issues two real advantages. Firstly, an attentive and open-minded listen of the album will give a real blow to your mind and secondly, the songs themselves are powerful and consistent. The standouts, again dismissed by many "fans" as radio songs (see how much critic this album gained?!? - and actually it is arguably Korn at their peak, just compare it to Untouchables), include Falling Away From Me with its haunting keyboard intro; Trash, again a haunting epic combining melodic verses with a stadium chorus; Make Me Bad hich is my favourite, a beautiful, passionate and painful song featuring a great main riff and an oustanding vocal hook from Jonathan Davis in the chorus (it might as well be Korn's best song ever made); but also No Way, the MOST depressing song on this album, and Dirty, again an expressive piece of Davis' inner tortures which many listeners will probably relate to at certain days.

Instruments really shine on this album. You will get memorable riffs, Fieldy's trademark clicking bass sound and the beloved bagpipes. The tracks are lean, straightforward and concise, and unlike on Take A Look In The Mirror, the songs also lead somewhere and seem inspired, not just heavy headbangers.

What prevents Issues from being a cerebral record is Jonathan Davis' lyrics. If you are searching for somethig original then keep away, but if you are fond of typical Korn texts like 'lately things won't go my way.../it feels like nothing' then you will get quite many of them. After all, Korn, like, say, Coldplay, has never been anything but personal in their songs' meanings (not to generally compare these bands that are of completely different directions). They simply paint their 'shades of grey' and do it far better than Staind.

Issues got lost in the sudden peak of nu-metal's popularity caused by more melodic but poppier bands like Limp Bizkit and Linkin Park, but it is definitely a good artistic statement. Really, no record in entire alternative metal of the late 1990s and early 2000s captures the feeling of grief, anger and despair the way Issues does. Give it a spin in a right mood and it will hepl you overcome many a bad day.

title: The best home music video on the market
text: This 17 song set captures all the intensity of a Rammstein live show. From the opener, 'Spielt Mit Mir' to the closing 'Seemann', Live Aus Berlin is packed with footage from Rammstein's stop in Berlin in August of 1999. This DVD catches all of the violence, the emotion, and the fire of Rammstein. Unfortunately, the DVD version cuts Buck Dich out, but the extras and improved picture and sound quality make the DVD the overall better purchase. Rammstein uses a lot of stage theatrics, from costumes, to flamethrowers, fireworks, and slick lighting, to make the show more exciting for the audience. Till Lindemann even sets himself on fire (wearing a special suit, of course) during the song, 'Rammstein.' I don't know what's cooler than that? Their musicianship is tight and top-notch as ever, just as good live as in the studio. The extras include an interview with the whole band, as well as multi-angle views of 'Tier', 'Du Hast', and 'Rammstein'. If you're a Rammstein fan, this is an essential to own, a real Rammstein fan would be hard-pressed not to have this in his or her collection. It's a much better buy, in my opinion, than the 'Live Aus Berlin' CD, the visuals are half of Rammstein's show. Available on VHS and DVD.

title: It's Bob Franke. Need I say more?
text:
I love this CD, but then I love anything by Bob Franke. His songs are honest, well-crafted, and often deeply moving. His guitar playing is wonderful, as is his voice.

In the intro to this concert, Rich Warren says he considers Bob Franke one of America's greatest songwriters. I agree wholeheartedly!

One problem with some albums of folk songs is that they can sound like the same thing over and over. The songs here include the upbeat and hopeful (There is a Healing), angry blues (the infuriating "Collateral Damage"), funny blues ("Catfish"), victorious ("Alleluia, the Great Storm Is Over") - heck, there's even a polka in there ("Acid Polka").

Musically and emotionally, there's enough variety to keep you from feeling stuck in the same place, which some folk albums do to me.

But beyond that, it's Bob Franke. He's just an amazing songwriter, and this album includes some incredible songs.

If you like folk music, this is a must-have. It took me far too long to know who Bob Franke was and what I was missing. Don't let that happen to you!

title: Ferry's Mixed Bag
text: For me, Bryan Ferry's second solo album is a bit uneven in the quality of song choices. But though half of the CD is a little uninspired, there are five songs that make this worth purchasing. The best songs are the first and last ones. "The In Crowd" is handled perfectly with just the right amount of camp and humor. Also a bit humorous are the versions of "Walk A Mile In My Shoes" and "Fingerpoppin'". "Smoke Gets In Your Eyes" is touching and lovely. Finally, the title track is one of Bryan's best original songs with its unusual time changes and catchy melody. title: LP Record is Better Than CD
text: These are 12 classic recordings by Spike Jones and the City Slickers that first appeared on 78 rpm records in the 1940s and transferred to an LP record (vinyl, if you insist) many years later.  Still later the collection was transferred to CD.  This is one of the rare instances when the LP record sounds noticeably superior to the CD release being reviewed here and for one simple reason.  It was a practice at RCA, when making such transfers to early CDs, in an effort to minimize any background noise present in the original recordings, to severely cut high frequency response in the transfer thereby also eliminating any detail that the original recordings had.  This practice was sometimes also used in transferring older movies to DVD to eliminate any discernible film noise resulting in a soundtrack that would be less intelligible -- a practice that I have always condemned.
