title: Good to have these back, easily accessible, and cheap
text:
Good to have these back - or, in some cases, for the first time on CD - and easily accessible. This 3-CD set was published in 2008 on the occasion of the 100th anniversary of Oistrakh's birth. All but one are Soviet/Melodiya recordings, all dating from the late 1940s and early 1950s, that were licensed at some point for publication in the West by DG or some of the labels for which it now holds the rights (Westminster and American Decca, the label under which DG published in this country in the 1950s). The photos of three of those LPs are nicely reproduced in the booklet.

The Concertos of Mendelssohn (recorded in 1949) and Glazunov (1948), both on CD 1, came on Westminster WGM 8224.

The Concerto of Kabalevsky (1949), Chausson's Poem (March 1948), Ravel's Tzigane (1948) and Glazunov's Mazurka-Oberek (1949), all on CD 2, came on Westminster XWN 18177.

Prokofiev's First (June 1953, CD 2) was on Westminster XWN 18178 with the composer's Third Piano Concerto with Gilels.

The program of Encores that comprises CD 3 came on US Decca DL 9882 (I've uploaded a photo).

The one exception is the Bruch Concerto that completes CD 1. Note that Oistrakh here is not the soloist, but the conductor: it is his son Igor who holds the violin. It is an original DG production, recorded in 1961, the one stereo recording from this collection, first published on DG 1133230, and this is its first appearance on CD. Oistrakh always tried to foster the career of his son (hard to blossom under such a huge shadow) and recorded a number of concertos with him as soloist (Beethoven, Berlioz' Harold in Italy, Brahms, Lalo's Symphonie espagnole, Tchaikovsky). One tends to forget that David increasingly took up the baton at the end of his career and, other than the concertos with his son and other fiddlers, left significant recordings (many live) of Bartok (Concerto for Orchestra), Brahms (Symphonies 1 & 2), Mahler (4th), Prokofiev (5th), Shostakovich (7th and 9th), Strauss (Till Eulenspiegel), Tchaikovsky (5th and 6th). There are even live performances of him conducting Richter in Grieg's Concerto and Rostropovich in Schumann's and Shostakovich's First.

Other than the Bruch, most of the content of this collection had already been made available on CD, notably by the French Chant du Monde in the late 1980s, on its 15-CD Oistrakh collection - but most of that series isn't even listed on this website or its European sister companies. Other CD firsts on this DG release are Ysaye's Poème élégiaque, Wieniawski's Etude-Caprice and Vieuxtemps' Romance opus 7-3 from the encores on CD 3 / Decca DL 9882. DG marks by an asterisk Ysaye, Wieniawski and Sarasate as new on CD (not indicating precisely which piece), and not Vieuxtemps, but it doesn't seem true. The rest of the Decca encores including Sarasate's Zortziko, Vieuxtemps Romance op. 7-2 and Wieniawski's Legend was on Chant du Monde's Oistrakh Collection vol. 15, "pièces rares et virtuoses pour le violon", LDC 278 945, with more.

The other Chant du Monde installments were Kabalevsky, paired with Khachaturian on vol. 3, LDC 278 883 (ASIN B005LG2PZG on the French sister company), and Chausson and Ravel coupled with Dvorak on vol. 8, LDC 278 908 (haven't found a listing). The Kabalevsky was also reissued on an all composer-conducted Kabalevsky CD from Russian Revelation, [[ASIN:B000009DQY Composers in person: Kabalevsky - Cello Concerto No. 1 in G minor Op. 49; Piano Concerto No. 3 in D, Op. 50; Piano concerto No. 4 "Prague"; Violin Concerto in C Op. 48 (All with Kabalevsky conducting)]]. Inexplicably, Chant du Monde had left out the Concertos of Mendelssohn and Glazunov with Kondrashin from their collection, but the Mendelssohn had had an "unofficial" reissue by Dante, on a 4-CD collection of early recordings of Oistrakh, Lys 331/4, [[ASIN:B00000G2B6 Le Jeune David Oistrakh, Volume 1, 1938-1948: Oeuvres Pour Violin et Orchestre]]. In the absence of Oistrakh's 1955 remake with Ormandy (never been made available by Sony in the West, who knows why; it is paired with Mozart's K218 on the Japanese reissue, CBS/Sony 25DC 5221), it is invaluable for being Oistrakh's only available recording of this warhorse among concertos.

Paul Geffen's online Oistrakh discography indicates that the Glazunov Concerto was also included in that Dante set, but I don't think this is true. I don't have the set but I've found photos of the front and back covers on the net (see my upload under the set's entry), and apparently what is included is Glazunov's Mazurka-Oberek (also on the DG set), not the Concerto. The Concerto on the other hand was reissued on an early Monitor CD with the sensible couplings of the Mazurka-Oberek, Kabalevsky, Chausson and Ravel, [[ASIN:B00000102U Plays Chausson Ravel Glazunov & Kabalevsky]], and on a less generously filled Vanguard CD (with Kabalevsky's Concerto and Glière's Romance for Violin and Orchestra, [[ASIN:B000009CVH Glazunov, Kabalevsky: Violin Concertos]].

The Prokofiev was also on another Monitor CD, with the invaluable coupling of Shostakovich's First under Mravinsky, [[ASIN:B000001010 David Oistrakh plays Shostakovich: Violin Concerto No. Op. 99 - Leningrad Philharmonic with Eugene Mravinsky and Prokofiev: Violin Concerto No. 1 Op. 19 - State Radio Orchestra with Kiril Kondrashin]].

Finally, some of the Concertos gathered on the DG set have also been duplicated on the recent Brilliant box of Violin Concertos played by Oistrakh ([[ASIN:B0009OALK6 David Oistrakh - Historic Russian Archives: Violin Concertos]]), although, with Brilliant's typically imprecise and sometimes misleading credits, it is sometimes hard to tell if they've published the studio recordings or other ones: Mendelssohn, Chausson, Glazunov are the same for sure, there are doubts about Kabalevsky and Ravel (but I think they are the same, see my review for the details), and their Prokofiev 1st seems to be another performance.

You'd expect the more recent transfers to be better, but it is not so clear cut. In the recital of Encores the DG transfers have diminished the tape-hiss and done away with the harshness of the Chant du Monde transfer, but at the cost of less presence and a more cavernous perspective on the violin especially noticeable in Vieuxtemps' Romance and Sarasate's Zortzicko. In Kabalevsky also, the DG transfers have removed some of the harshness present in the previous Chant du Monde CD - but not all. In fact I find the one on Russian Revelation marginally more comfortable, although the differences are so slight that I think they could be only the product of my imagination. I don't have any comparison for the Glazunov transfer but it does sound disagreeably harsh and shrill, and so does the Mendelssohn to a lesser degree. In Chausson and Ravel the DG transfers have removed a very soft electronic buzz (which, frankly, I notice only by comparison with DG), but on the other hand they have lamentably botched the beginning of Tzigane by opening with an absurd fade-in on the first violin attack, which deprives it of its bite, making it sound like a piano-crescendo. The Chant du Monde shows that it is not the way Oistrakh played it: his attack was biting and forceful. Some harshness remains in the DG transfers. What DG's new transfers have improved is the absurd beginning of Monitor's Prokofiev, in which after 7 secconds one of the two audio channels brutally faded in; it also did away with the small drop out at 3:05 in the scherzo, and the soft underlying low-frequency rumble that you can hear in the softer passages (again, I noticed it only comparatively), and the sound is clearer and more transparent, but the violin can also be harsher when it plays forte in the high registers. On the other hand, heard on headphone, there is a kind of soft high-frequency sound for about twenty seconds at the beginning of the first and last track, like a bell ringing in the distance, which is not on Monitor. How could DG have botched that? Maybe in an ill-conceived bid to remove some of the tape-hiss that is very present at this point on the Monitor CD. If that is the price to pay, leave the tape-hiss!

Not that these considerations are going to be decisive. The differences between these transfers are marginal, anyway nobody will be listening to these recordings for the hi-fi experience, they are obviously historical documents and what you want is for the sonics not to get in the way of the music. With the proviso of the touch of harshness in this or that recording, they don't, and I'd be happy with any of them: they usually sound exceptionally good considering the vintage and provenance. Except for Bruch (great stereo, a bit congested in the tutti and it too with some harshness) this is usually vivid and detailed mono (even if some orchestral details are missing), sometimes a bit too glaringly brilliant even. Moreover, I hear no trace of surface noise, which seems to point to recordings made on tape, which for 1948-9 and Soviet Union seems puzzling and leads me to at least tentatively question the official recording dates: I wouldn't be surprised if one day it is established that all these date, like the Prokofiev, from the early 1950s.

Maybe a few interpretive comments are in order, at least on the 20th century concertos and concertante works, even if anybody interested in great violin playing should explore this set independent of any individual reviewer's opinions - positive or negative. Evidently, Glazunov and Kabalevsky aren't the most substantial compositions of the repertoire, the former a 19th Century concerto somehow belatedly put down on the paper by its composer, and the latter a kind of Prokofiev without quite the talent or a Khachaturian without the exotic colors and melodies. In fact Oistrakh's recording of Kabalevsky's remained for a long time the only one; Zukerman recorded it in the mid-seventies (not reissued on CD), and a few versions came out in the CD era, one of latest being an apposite coupling of Glazunov and Kabalevsky by Gil Shaham ([[ASIN:B000001GZV Meeting in Moscow - Glazunov/Kabalevsky: Violin Concertos]]). I have Oistrakh's version in multiple reissues, but none of the more recent ones. But, despite being all brilliance and little substance, I find the concerto quite enjoyable - no wonder: I'm a great fan of Prokofiev's and Khachaturian's Violin Concertos. I see no reason why Glazunov's sentimental salon-music inflated to the size of a concerto should still maintain a strong presence in the recorded canon, and Kabalevsky's be so neglected.

Glazunov's certainly isn't, at least on records. It was championed by Heifetz (two recordings, 1934 and 1963), Milstein (three recordings, 1949, 1957 and the last one from 1966 not reissued on CD to the best of my knowledge) and Michael Rabin, and was recorded by some of the great fiddlers of the last 40 years - Perlman, Mutter, Vengerov, Shaham among them. Oistrakh there takes a VERY expansive approach - he is considerably slower in the opening motto than the composer's indicated 92 beats/mn, closer to 78-80 - and I'm not convinced it does the piece truly good. Oistrakh's tone is lush and his technique beyond praise, and there are spots where he shows he can dash, but I find that his generally expansive and very "tranquillo" approach sentimentalizes and "salonizes" a concerto that has enough of the salon-sentimental already. I much prefer the more flowing approach of Heifetz and Milstein - which in their case doesn't preclude taking the quasi slow-movement at an expansive tempo also.

When Oistrakh was finally allowed to tour in the US, Chausson's Poème with the Boston Symphony Orchestra under Munch was the first recording he made there, on December 14, 1955 ([[ASIN:B000026OYS Chausson: Symphony in B flat; Poéme for Violin and Orchestra / Saint-Saëns: Introduction & Rondo capriccioso]]). It comes in stupendously good stereo sound, and Oistrakh is also marginally more passionate than in this earlier Soviet recording. Other than that, the approach is the same, striking a fine balance between the composition's brooding meditativeness and its heart-on-sleeve passion. In Tzigane, Oistrakh plays with bite and élan and impressive bow tension, but his reading is also very straight and relatively uninflected: he moves forward and doesn't linger on details. It is a welcome change from fiddlers who seem to think that to convey the piece's Gispsy character you need to distort what Ravel wrote and play accordion with the tempos, but I feel that Oistrakh goes a little too far in the other direction. It has to do with the way he phrases, but also with the (little) space he allows himself in BETWEEN the phrases. He doesn't set much store for instance on the "Meno vivo. Grandioso" passage at 6:50. Likewise, at the beginning of the coda, at 8:13, despite the "meno vivo" and "accel. Poco a poco" indications, he takes it so swiftly that it leaves him hardly any room for acceleration - although he does manage to accelerate to dizzying speed, and with a wonderful détaché articulation as well. If you like your Tzigane to be very sober, this is it. But Oistrakh does have the necessary mockingly kitsch swooning staggering on the "espressivo" at 5:15, yet without trying too hard to underline it, which is fine. He plays with sufficient technical ease - ironically, incomparably better than Ginette Neveu (who caused a big scandal when being attributed the first prize at the 1935 Wieniawski competition in front of Oistrakh, stirring accusations of political manipulations) in her 1949 New York live concert with Munch, [[ASIN:B00008FG7X Ginette Neveu Historic Broadcast Performances: Beethoven, Chausson, Ravel]]; but, granted, Oistrakh is here in studio conditions. Still, he doesn't sound as comfortable with his harmonics as the best present-day violinists (at 4:57 for instance), and as many others then and now he "cheats" in some key spots, such as playing like plucked chords what Ravel wrote as pizzicato triplets. On the other hand his high-pitched trills at 6:40 are great. The USSR State Symphony Orchestra is not a highly virtuosic ensemble, they play their "Hungarian March" solo passage at 5:52 with caution and the clarinet sounds hard-pressed at 4:40.

Oistrakh's Prokofiev First is, still today, one of the great versions of that composition, intensely lyrical as you can expect, but with no lack of drive and fury in the passages that require it. Other maybe than Josef Szigeti, whose recording with Beecham introduced the composition in the west, no fiddler is more closely associated with Prokofiev's 1st Violin Concerto than Oistrakh. In 1926, aged 19, he played the Concerto at his graduation concerto from the Odessa Conservatory, and that was only three years after its Premiere in Paris by Marcel Darrieux and Koussevitsky. There is a famous anecdote which has Oistrakh, one year later, playing the scherzo in front of the composer on the occasion of a post-concert reception, only to see Prokofiev chastise him and jump to the piano to show him the proper way to play it. That didn't prevent the two from becoming close friends, and Oistrakh from becoming one of the most renowned champions of the Concerto, and premiering the composer's two Violin and Piano Sonatas along the way (his insistent prompting initiated the second, a transcription of Prokofiev's Flute Sonata).

He left two studio recordings of the Concerto, in addition to a number of live testimonies: one in 1954 for HMV with the London Symphony Orchestra under Lovro von Matacic ([[ASIN:B0002VEPNU Prokofiev: Violin Concertos Nos. 1 & 2 / Violin Sonata No. 2 ~ Oistrakh]]), and this one, a year before, for Melodiya, with Kondrachin conducting an orchestra variously labelled as the (USSR) State Radio Orchestra, the USSR Large Radio Symphony Orchestra or, as here, the USSR State Symphony Orchestra. It is the same recording that has been published, in bad, muffled sound, falsely crediting the composer himself as conductor, by Everest on LP and Dante on CD.

Interpretively there is not much to choose between both studio recordings - the later one with Matacic is a little more spacious in the first movement, in the context of an approach that is (in the outer movements) already very spacious and long-breathed. The ample phrase (cantabile) at the beginning of the finale exudes a radiant lyrical beauty. But don't infer that Oistrakh conveys an impression of lacking animation. On the contrary, he can superbly roughen his tone in the scherzo passages, and his pizzicattis at 5:46 are explosive and raw - but less in Moscow than in London.

The sonics don't really make a decisive difference. In the Melodiya-originated recording, despite the soloist's forward placement, the sound has remarkable body and depth. The violin is very present, and some of the orchestral soloists too (bassoon of great alacrity at the beginning of the finale). But overall the London recording allows more of the woodwind filigree to come out. Whatever the miniscule differences of details, these are great performances and one at least belongs to any serious Prokofiev music library.

A fine tribute to Oistrakh then, especially for the pieces restored for the first time to CD and those that weren't so easily accessible (Mendelssohn, Prokofiev). But beginners should start with Oistrakh's complete EMI recordings (sorry, no more product links allowed), which is much more abundant for not much more expensive, offers a fine mixture of the the standard repertoire (Mozart, Beethoven, Schubert, Brahms, Franck, Bruch, Lalo, Sibelius), the EMI Prokofievs, Khachaturian and Shostakovich and some rarities.

title: A great treat: samplings from a 30-year recording career
text:
I really enjoy the various Tharaud collections I have, and have come to expect the unexpected from this artist. I guess one unexpected thing was how long he’s been recording! I’ve really only been away o this work for 5 years, yet he’s been at it for 30!

This 3-CD set is a very nice and inexpensive sampler, including snippets from both his various releases on several labels, and some unreleased materials from live performances, as well as recordings that never made it on an album.

My previous experience with Tharaud has centered entirely on the baroque: two Bach albums which I adore, and one of Couperin (“Tic Tok Choc”). All 3 of these highlighted for me an extremely creative performing artist who wasn’t afraid to color outside the lines when it came to interpretations.

However what this sampler has shown me is his range: the man can (and virtually has) play anything, and it’s all here on display. The first Cd is entirely solo piano pieces; the second, selected movements from concerti, and the third “rareties e surprises”, goes back to solo piano to reflect his range and personal interests.

If you want a sense of Tharaud’s unexpected, listen to his version of the 3rd movement (“Alla Turca”) from Mozart’s 11th piano sonata. I’ll bet you’ve not heard it played like this!

I think this a great set to introduce listeners to an artist they might not have heard before, or paid much attention to, but who clearly has plenty to say. A modest investment that will doubtless make you hunger for more.

Highly recommended.

Es el Pop argentino por excelencia, el gran Leo García reafirma su gran estilo en esta producción. Todas sus canciones son tan pegajozas, tan frescas, tan buenas! Es directo, franco, alegre, divertido.

Soda haciendo covers???? WTF? En su historia solo hicieron covers en sus inicios. Ya en 1990 tocaron un par de temas de los Beatles en vivo. Y el tema era de un grupo desconocido!!!! Que pasaba alli? La cancion pertenecia a un grupo llamado Avant Press. La cancion: Cibersirena. Una canción preciosa que seguramente encantó a Cerati y compañía, como para interpretarla en vivo.

Averigué y descubri que Leo Garcia era el frontman de este grupo novedoso. Adquirí su disco y vaya, grata sorpresa. Buenas canciones, cortas...pegadas. Alli estaba Cibersirena, pero sin los coros que Cerati le habia agregado en vivo. Luego busqué y adquirí su primer disco-maxi: "Amor entre rosas".

Para el año 2000, él ya corria como solista y alcanzaria la fama con "Morrisey": "Sabra tu novia que escuchamos Morrisey?" Un canto al amor homosexual oculto. Imagino que vivencial; y son estas vivencias lo que lo inspira siempre a crear buena musica.

En la actualidad ya tiene varios discos editados, coqueteando con la electronica, con lo acustico...Fan devoto de Gilda. Un tipo pop 100% y con orgullo.
Gustavo Cerati, su padrino, compartió un tema con él en este disco: "Cuarto Creciente", el tema, bueno para variar, se llama "Tesoro". Este disco también incluye una versión de la banda chilena "Los prisioneros": Estrechez de corazón.

Buen disco si buscas frescura, diversión y full pop! Viva Leo!

title: Puccini Goddess
text:
This 1970's EMI album features Montserrat Caballe, in glorious voice, singing magnificent, virtually unsurpassed interpretations of arias by that most celebrated, mainstream staple composer of opera houses Giacomo Puccini. The sound quality has been digitally remastered and sounds voluminous, rich, crisp and powerful, like the voice of the star soprano herself. The hefty, iron-lunged and beautifully lyrical soprano was such a phenomenon in her day that it's hard to remembe she was one of the many sopranos singing similar operas along with Joan Sutherland and Beverly Sills. She was probably most remembered for her nearly stereotypical big diva presence and moreover her gifted pianissimi, soft, floating notes. Montserrat Caballe came to the opera scene like a newly discovered comet. Born and bred in Catalonia, Spain, she was fluent in Spanish and French and later Italian when she trained for opera. She quickly became the finest exponent of the bel canto repertoire and forgotten masterpieces. She excelled as Donizetti's Lucrezia Borgia, the Queen in Roberto Devereaux, Tosca, Queen Elisabeth De Valois in Don Carlos, the heroine in Rossini's Guillame Tell and Boito's Mefistofele, Madame Butterfly and other juicy roles. Caballe is still very much alive today and is adored by fans. Hers was a voice that is not easily forgotten. Though she lacked dramatic insight in her portrayals when compared most notably with Maria Callas, and Caballe was known for tra-la-la-ing her way through arias when she forgot the words or had a hard time enunciating the foreign text, she is still opera's bigger names. Dozens of EMI recordings attest to her legacy.

This album opens with an aria from Turandot. She sings the slave girl Liu's aria "Signore, ascolta!" as she tries to persuade Calaf not to make an attempt to answer the enigmas of the ice-cold Empress Turandot, whom he has just seen for the first time and fallen in love with. The aria is beautifully rendered in Caballe's hands for the aria requires pianissimi and breath control and dulcet tones, all which were staples of Caballe's singing. But Caballe had a firmness and stentorian quality to her voice that I feel is more suitable for Turandot herself. I never found her to be a credible slave girl Liu. Caballe's stature and voice is Turandot all the way. The second track is Madame Butterfly's ever famous "Un Bel Di" her song of hope that one day her Pinkerton will come back for her. Caballe captures the achingly passionate yearning perfectly. The anguished tone in Butterfly's "Tu! Tu! Piccolo Iddio!" as she gets rid of her son so that she may commit suicide is thunderous and powerfully executed. Manon Lescaut was another heroine that Caballe essayed although I much prefer Mirella Freni's portrayal. Caballe, however, is outstanding, especially in her dramatic, desperate-sounding account of "Sola Perduta Abbandonata" in which Manon gives in to a feeling of hopelessness. Her account of Vissi D'Arte is breathtaking and mellifluous, sounding a lot more like Madame Butterfly's "Un Bel Di". I have heard better, frankly, especially the Vissi's of Leontyne Price and Katia Ricciarelli. However this kind of prayer-like aria was a specialty of Caballe's. I never felt that Caballe made a fine Mimi from La Boheme but her Mi Chiamo Mimi is brilliant. All in all, this is a fine recording if you are a fan of Caballe and her way of singing Puccini. This is probably her greatest album.

title: Mainly Piano MD
text:
What more can I say about Suzanne Ciani that I have not already said a couple of months ago courtesy of the Mediations review? A pioneer in the New Age field, Cianni has more than paid her dues to the industry. While this collection is another well-organized compilation, it does appear rather redundant to release a similar format back to back. This does not change the fact that this album is chock full of memorable music that is both thoughtful and emotive.

That aside, the theme this time is romance and there is plenty of that. A Cianni anthology cannot be complete without the staple "The Velocity Of Love." At least those overseeing this project were wise enough to entertain us with the live version from the 1997 project Live. "Sailing To Byzantium" and "Inverness" are also borrowed from the same album giving the tracks a very warm organic feeling away from the confines and sterility of the studio.

As for the remaining tracks, there is the interesting "Turning" that features the vocal work of Chi-Yu giving the composition an Enya influence. Also of interest is "Waltz For Julia" that seems to borrow from the famous Pachelbel's "Canon In D Minor." And, of course, there is the lush and lovely "Meeting Mozart" with some stirring piano work and luxuriant orchestration but never over dramatic or over the top. This along with "Full Moon Sonata" and "Til Times & Times Are Done" are taken from the experimental orchestrated album Dream Suite. If these tracks are a good representation of Dream Suites, then perhaps Cianni should dare to dream again.

Again, new compositions would have been so much more preferred. For the uninitiated this CD, much like Meditations, is a good place to introduce yourself to the music of Cianni. Otherwise, for the die-hard fans, there is no new material present here and unless you are an utter radical who simply wants this project for the artwork, I would urge you to save your dollars and patiently wait and hope that the next disc is new material. Considering Cianni's track record, I am sure the wait will be more than worthwhile

title: A Group for the Ages
text:
I'm adding a review of this to raise the rating, which I think is just too low for anything by this quintet.

I'm with those who who love this album even if we acknowledge that Miles had this group completely together in his two 1956 sessions that produced "Cookin'" "Relaxin'" "Workin'" and "Steamin'"--the jazz records I am most likely to enjoy on any given day after many years--as well as the Columbia "'Round About Midnight" (for which one of three sessions did precede the recording of this but the original record only used one of four pieces that the group recorded--"Ah Leu Cha"-while the others surfaced later on). As someone else said, you have to start somewhere.

It's true that Trane is at this early point sometimes a halting player, yet he contrasts so well to Miles, his ideas are already exciting, and, as with his much better (if still sometimes imperfect) playing on the five other albums by the quintet, I find his work full of charm. If you want to hear Coltrane is full command of his music, then of course you need to go on to Monk, to his later work with Miles, and to his own albums, especially after he enlisted Tyner and Jones and created his own group. But it seems to me if you really care about Trane, you will love him the way he is in this first Miles quintet and not wanting him to be different than he is.

Miles himself is certainly a great musician, has at his best played sublime trumpet (and I could care less if he is not the most technically great because he has everything he needs to realize his ideas), and a good leader in terms of making up the repertoire for a group--the mix of which I absolutely adore in this group. But his greatest gift might be as a kind of alchemist in creating a group, knowing intuitively how the talents of a diverse group of musicians will blend. It happened with his other groups too, but for me, never as well with Trane, Garland, Chambers, Jones and of course Miles himself. There is just something about hearing this wonderful group that is one of the most pleasurable experiences of life. They are absolutely my favorite jazz group ever.

Highlights on this first album: I think the opener "Just Squeeze Me" with that easy medium tempo swing best anticipates the kind of number--usually a standard--that this group did better than anyone. Generally, I'd say that Miles himself is excellent throughout, and Garland is impeccable in his wonderful solos while the playing of the whole rhythm section of Red, Paul and Philly Joe in accompaniment is also great throughout. As for Trane, he does have at least one terrific, very characteristic solo on "The Theme" (just the way he comes in is classic Trane) and even if it is not the greatest performance one might hope for, "Stablemates" is such a beautiful line by Golson, sounds lovely played by these guys, and makes a good closer.

So, all in all, leaving comparisons to their great records to come aside, this is a satisfying album and it's a Miles album I would not want to be without.

title: TREMENDOUS - MUST BE HEARD!  THEIR BEST RIFF-ORIENTED ALBUM SINCE URBAN DISCIPLINE AND SOTWA
text:
This is EASILLY a 4.5 star album - this must be heard to be fully appreciated and respected. Reading online reviews (great, or undeserving negative) won't do this masterpiece any justice. EVEN I HAD MY DOUBTS AT FIRST!

Put this album on shuffle (as to not accidentally forget or not get to some of the last few tracks on the album, as those are some of the best songs!) and trust me you will be rockin' out and headbangin' to many of these songs!

AWESOME, AWESOME balls rockin' songs such as 'Reborn', 'Vengeance is Mine', 'Skullcrusher', 'Come Alive', and 'Never Give In' - chock FULL of riffs (did I say RIFFS?!), thunderous production, fluid and blistering leads by a returning Bobby Hambel, and in-your-face lyrics and vocals mainly from Billy, but Evan shines as well in the dual approaches.

'Vows of Redemption' has this incredible, ambient atmospheric 'piano' intro and outro which totally makes the entire song worth listening to on repeat. Again, I can only try to describe so much - the album must be listened to to be fully appreciated and enjoyed!

Two songs which were punchy yet had cool 'sing along choruses' mid song (almost can hear or envision a live crowd in there!) were 'Decay' and 'Reborn'. Check them out!

The last track, an instrumental called 'Season the Sky' - is also a masterpiece. Almost more melodic hard rock - a perfect closer to this album.

Production is stellar, a huge improvement from their last album Means to an End - which was a good album in itself, but it suffered from sound and production flaws - as it had to be re-recorded since the original masters of that album had been destroyed in a fire. Reborn in Defiance sounds much more ballsy and crisp!

If I can find any flaws (if there are any, these are just my opinion), the only two songs I did not really enjoy were "Waste Away' and 'You Were Wrong.'. I will be giving them a few more spins to see if they grow on me, they just didn't seem as hair-raising and headbangin' as the rest of the album. Others may enjoy these songs, but in my opinion THUS FAR, while they were decent - they just didn't grab me, and 'You Were Wrong' just seemed to get redundant by the 6-minute mark. HOWEVER - by track 11 and 12 - NOW THOSE TRACKS ARE TREMENDOUS. It was almost like a shot of adrenaline to me after tracks 9 and 10. Skullcrusher and Never Give In are a total punch in the face!

This is a great all-around hardcore, metal, hard rock release with some different elements mixed in on a few songs not previously used very much by Biohazard, BUT THEY WORK. Give it a listen! Great album artwork, too!

Picks: 'Vengeance is Mine', 'Skullcrusher' 'Never Give In', 'Reborn', 'Come Alive', and 'Vows of Redemption.'

It is hard NOT TO LIKE this album. There is just so much meat and potatoes, and again - the brilliant guitar riffs!!

4.5 out of 5

title: Great Blues, great CD!
text:
Let's see, blues is my favorite music and son seals is my favorite blues artist? It always bothers me a little seeing some of the professional reviews of son's work. They always emphasize the energy and power of his music but never seem to appreciate the subtlety and artistry of his music. Son's music has a nice melodic feel to it. Nothing cliche about it and it nevers gets old or stale. Listen to "good woman bad" or "Can't hear nothing but the blues". In the later cut son sings "what a beautiful memory of them" refering to his parents. The former song includes some great supportive horn work and a nice sax solo. I also think this man has a under appreciated voice. It's not just the "blood curdling intensity" that is stated on back of this CD. Son's voice evokes emotion and complexity. The best cut on the CD is #4, "I'm gonna take it all back". That's one of the best songs you will ever hear! The guitar notes seem to fly off in to space only to be reeled back in only to be let loose again. What i love about son's solos is that he never loses touch with the song melody. Everything fits. I love "life is hard" and "tough as nails". Both are spirited songs with a similar theme. "The wind might try and knock me down but i'm as tough as nails". #7 "your friends is one of my least favorite songs on the cd(i still love it) but i do love the guitar at the beginning and the solo.
I was pleasantly surprised to see that some reviewers considered this to not be son's best work. That means there are plenty more great CDs from him out there. I own each of the live CDs from him, "live and burning" and "spontaneous conbustion". Only the late luther allison plays with as much power and intensity. I love those CDs to death but i seem to listen to this even more.
This is great music! The muscianship is solid all the way through.(Particularly david russell's drums) They call it the blues but it sure makes me happy.

title: A mix of Gentle Giant with a dash of the modern rock style
text:
I do remember enjoying this album quite a lot when it came out (1995) and especially appreciated the Gentle Giant sound updated with a modern rock touch. Although there are points where it sounds as if they are trying a little bit too hard, they are far and few between, and my overall enjoyment of the album was not lessened. Indeed, I consider this a fine example of the post-progressive style.

The lineup includes Chris Buzby (keyboards, synthesizers, piano, backing vocals), Tom Hyatt (bass guitar, midi pedals), Brett Kull (electric and acoustic guitars, backing vocals), Paul Ramsey (drums and percussion), and Ray Weston (lead and backing vocals). These guys are all very accomplished musicians and the ensemble work is extremely dense - maybe a little too dense at times. Then again, that is what I liked about Gentle Giant, so it is not a big deal for me. The vocal arrangements are fantastic and it is clear they spent a great deal of time on them. For some folks however, the lead vocalist may take some getting used to; he has a very unusual style. I have to admit it took a while to get used to.

Arranged loosely as a song-cycle with 16 tracks ranging in length from 0:36 to 7:54, and with a total running time of 69:34, there is a lot of music on this disc to take in. In terms of the music, it is very heavily influenced by Gentle Giant. Layers of instruments are used, with dense counterpoint, rich vocal harmonies, and some fairly nice melodies. Odd meters are all over the place and the ensemble complexity can get overwhelming at times - the drummer is exceptionally busy. I especially like the keyboard work - Tom favors the tone colors of 1970s progressive (Hammond organ, piano) just as much as some of the newer synthesizer tones. I especially like the fact that these guys steer clear of the stadium rock styles favored by the neo-progressive acts and fused aspects of modern rock with aspects of 1970s progressive - it is generally a satisfying blend.

This liner notes feature the track listing, personnel, photos of the group (some of whom were dressed in Seattle "grunge" clothing popular at the time), and color photos of various subjects. The sound quality is very good; as might be expected with a big name like Sony 550 Music.

All in all, this is a good album by the group that was followed up with the excellent Cowboy Poems Free (2000), which had a more original "Echolyn" sound to it. This debut is recommended to folks that don't mind a mix of Gentle Giant with a dash of the modern rock style.

text:
[[VIDEOID:466e68437223fad1dc33f92b546d0a95]] [[VIDEOID:823b0674e5ece74c929c7e797d27f822]] One of Amy's best albums, this vinyl record does her justice! It's rare to find an album without one single bad track. Each song is amazing, conveying emotion and soul. Amy Winehouse, we miss you!

title: This disc gets played the most
text:
Although I had heard some of Women and Children First at a friend's house, I didn't really get into it until after I heard And the Cradle Will Rock on the radio. Then I had to buy the album and listened to it again, and again and again. Most VH fans I'm sure similarly wore out their turntables (not to mention enraging their parents and neighbors since of course the volume had to be turned all the way up). Now I have everything on CD and this disc, along with Fair Warning, get played more than the other DLR-era albums.

From a broadcast of Off the Record with Mary Turner I remember Roth joked that Eddie sleeps with his stratocaster. I think this album, more than any other, demonstrates what he was getting at, in terms of Eddie's familiarity with the instrument. The virtuosity of Eddie's playing is superlative. Although maybe performing a solo like Eruption is harder technically, here he has a kind of spontaneity that has never been replicated. Indeed I believe the entire album was recorded in about two weeks.

(As I recall there were two interviews conducted by Mary Turner for Westwood One (circa 1980-81). One was with Roth and Alex, the other with Eddie. Eddie was modest and unpretentious, even a little shy; Roth was Roth. Just polar opposites.)

My favorite song on this record is Fools.

title: Suzy Soars
text: Ever notice how songs with the prettiest melodies often feature the most cliched lyrics? Or how those whose words transcend "baby baby" get saddled with tunes as lively as Gregorian chants? Suzy Bogguss  consistently finds material that combines beauty and intelligence. On  "Suzy Bogguss," she delivers 12 of the best songs she has ever  recorded. And she's never sounded more confident and comfortable behind the  microphone. Each track receives just the degree of polish it needs: the  loose, R&B flavored "Love Is Stronger" sounds like it could  have been recorded live, while "Hold Me To It" features  breathless, delicately layered background vocals reminiscent of Art  Garfunkel's solo work. Best cuts for her country fans: the sassy  "Taking That Red-Eye Home" and the absolutely soaring "Love  Is Blind"-a duet with T. Graham Brown that, if there's any justice,  will soon earn Suzy her first Grammy for Vocal Collaboration of the Year.

title: Golden Classics, Indeed!
text:
In Britain, "I Wish You Love" is perhaps mostly associated with legendary belter Shirley Bassey, but it was Gloria's version that made it a standard. The name Gloria Lynne may not sound terrible familiar to a lot of people outside the US, but in her hey day she was a tour de force, tackling everything from the blues to traditional pop music. Originally a gospel singer, Gloria's voice was full-bodied, but gentle at the same time. Her only big hit and Top 40 entry is of course "I Wish You Love", which peaked at number #28 in 1963. Like many incredibly talented African American women (namely Nancy Wilson and Carmen McRae), she struggled to break into the Billboard Hot 100, only managing to break through with a handful of songs: "Tower of Strength" (#100), "Be Anything" (#88), "Don't Take Your Love from Me" (#76) and of course "I'm Glad There Is You". That being said, Gloria was an incredibly talented singer, who was often overlooked.

Highlights: "I Wish You Love", "The Folks Who Live on the Hill", "Serenade in Blue" and "I Should Care".

title: It's a real shame.
text:
It's a real shame that the Christian community is so close-minded that they couldn't accept such a superb and artful album. This is by far the best solo album by any of the dc Talk members - when I listened to it, I thought, "This could do just as well in the mainstream market" - and that is exactly what the problem was with its sales. It was marketed towards Christians - who shrugged it off because, as Kevin Max himself said, it didn't fit in with their own pre-conceptions of what religious music should be - and no one in the mainstream even heard of it. It was only advertised through the Christian media outlets.

This album cost $200,000 to make (expensive for any Christian album) and it sounds so great with its mixing and effects and background vocals that I wouldn't be surprised to see it on another pop artist's resume. Kevin Max has the vocal power of Jeff Buckley. The album sounds like U2 meeting Buckley via Elton John, Pink Floyd and, dare I say, Axl Rose (the falsetto is strikingly reminiscent, but Kevin Max doesn't have the gritty-ness of Axl).

The lyrics are not overtly Christian and in fact Kevin Max said this album could be equally appreciated by a Buddhist or an atheist - and I agree.

I'm not trying to bash the Christians who avoided this album - I'm just saying I think they misunderstood it. Kevin Max sees the potential of Christian music being more "open" - to interpretation and ideas - and I think it's important, because as he said - the Christian music industry is like a "ghetto" right now - there is so much more potential. So many Christian artists could appeal to the mainstream and deliver the same message in a more subtle way.

"Stereotype Be," the title, refers - I'm sure - to the stereotypes of Christians and their music. Kevin Max was trying to blow the door off here and open up the industry to something fresh and different - and he succeeded beautifully - but people just didn't get it. They saw it as some pop album disguised as a Christian album, and because of Kevin Max's "bad boy" reputation they misunderstood the love-song lyrics as some kind of anti-Christian thing. Boy, were they wrong.

It's a real shame this album flopped - it's the best I've heard from any Christian artist in the last decade - and it contained ideas and lyrics and musical stylings that will probably never be heard in any Christian album ever again.

Some people didn't dig it. Okay. For them, there's always generic Christian rock like Tait.

It is an artful and hypnotic experience.

title: My Deserted Island Music
text:
These ladies sing universes. Incredible, strange, dissonant, unbelievable harmones that make me gasp and cry.
Someone said that any art that moves the spectator must harness the concept of contrast. This amazing music covers the whole audible spectrum: from massive wave interference to sweet, delicate consonance; from bold, unfaltering vibrato-less pitches to subtle, gentle wavering over a note; from frolicking and fun to mournful and intensely moving.
In short, this music is some of the most unusual, extraordinary, elegant, expressive sound I have ever heard, and it is THE piece of music I would take with me to a deserted island if I could take only one. I would recommend this to anyone who is willing to listen attentively. It is almost impossible that one would do so and NOT be moved.

title: a captivating listening experience
text:
It's been fashionable over the years to put down Sgt Pepper, to call it overrated, to say it hasn't aged well. But the fact remains that it's the most captivating listening experience that has ever come out of the rock world. The album is an exhilarating mélange of beautiful melodies and arrangements, catchy tunes, punchy rock numbers, intriguing lyrics, and interesting sound effects. I would probably agree that Revolver is a better album if you rate each song on the two albums and add up the totals. Moreover, Revolver presents a better balance and alternation between Lennon, McCartney, and Harrison songs - on side one of Pepper there are three songs in a row by McCartney. And yet, while Revolver is a superb collection of songs, Sgt Pepper is more of an integrated whole, a true pop symphony.
As for Sgt. Pepper's songs, the final track "A Day in the Life" is the most brilliant thing the Beatles ever recorded. Lennon's singing is exquisite; McCartney's interlude is a perfect counterpoint to the two Lennon sections. The other highlights for me are McCartney's "Fixing a Hole", a hauntingly beautiful song, one of the Beatles' finest, ranking right up there with "Eleanor Rigby" and "Penny Lane"; "With a Little Help from My Friends", a wonderful, catchy number with Ringo Starr's best-ever singing and that delectable "do you need anybody?" chorus; and Lennon's "Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds" with its fabulous imagery and music to match that transports you into a dream world. Harrison's Indian-influenced "Within You Without You" has been denigrated by some as being pretentious and preachy, but it's a stately piece, beautifully sung, with thoughtful lyrics. The remaining songs on Pepper are all quite nice, quite enjoyable, each in its own way.
What's the best Beatles album? I would say it's a tie between Revolver and Sgt. Pepper. But all the other original Beatle albums are great too. No other group has produced so much consistently excellent pop and rock music.

title: Own of Michael's Most Well Done Albums
text:
Michael Jackson's HIStory Past Present Book 1 is a fantastic album and a great start to any Jackson collection. Not only does it contain a great new album but it also has an extensive book, great packaging, and a greatest hits disc. The case is well done and the discs have a gold finishing to them and contain a holographic image of Michael's statue outlined.

Now in terms of content, even those who are disappointed with Dangerous will love this album. Michael went back to his older style of making songs 3-4 minutes. Long gone are the 7 minute songs from Dangerous that are full of repetition (I still think Dangerous is a great album though, just being honest). HIStory showcases Michael's wide range of vocals and song writing, along with the great studio production his records are well known for. This is one of the best mastered CDs I own and it sounds amazing. Bruce Swedien and the other recording engineers and studio musicians did a fantastic job making a deep, rich, layered sound. Not only on the songs on this shorter and more concise than albums like Dangerous, but the songs also have longer, more complex, catchy melodies in my opinion.

This is the one album of Michael's that I like better than Thriller, I really enjoy his other material as well but HIStory to me is just one incredibly well done album. HIStory is not an album of love songs, the songs themes range from personal, media, and corporate greed, not being able to cope with losing your childhood, loneliness, and anger, and there are also 2 great cover songs in there as well.
Scream - Very gritty angry song that is also funky and powerful. A duet with Janet Jackson.

They Dont Care About Us - Fantastic song about government and policing, authority figures not caring about their citizens. Done in a military style with crazy drum beats, vocals, and sound effects.
Stranger

Stranger in Moscow - really overlooked gem from Michael, has riched layered sounds that are haunting while he sings about being alone wandering the streets of Moscow. Intense, deep lyrics such as "here abandonned in my fame armageddon of the brain".

This Time Around - Really cool hip hop style track that also has a great verse by Notorious BIG, Michael sings this one angrily in regards to people trying to hunt him down saying stuff like "this time around Im taking no sh*t!"

Earth Song- Really a masterpiece, the multiple layers to this song and complex melody are very well done. This is an incredibly powerful track about what will happen to the Earth, people, and animals if we let businesses and governments destroy it. Incredibly powerful.

DS - This is a raw, powerful track that is mostly the same rocking guitar rift (by Slash) repeating itself. This is a cool, tough song by Michael, here he is not pleading for help but is just calling out the District Attorney who built up a false case against him and tried to humiliate him. It starts out with him saying "He wants to get my a** dead or alive". Its a great song and contrasts the peaceful softspoken Michael in Earth Song.

Money - This one is awesome, has a shuffling beat to it and is about how people will do anything for money. Once again Michael is able to take a serious topic (greed) and turn it into one fantastic catchy track while still tackling the subject matter well. Another underrated gem.

Come Together - Powerful more "rocking" cover of the Beatles classic. It is not as good as the Beatles version but is different and well produced enough to still be a fun and enjoyable song.

You Are Not Alone - This was written by R. Kelly but is sung in a very personal way by Michael. This is most likely because despite his fame and power he has dealt with personal loneliness for a lot of his life. The vocal delivery is top notch and the instrumentation is excellent.

Childhood - This song is a really nice ballad that is Michael discussing his own issues and reasons of not being able to forget his Childhood. The song is very well done, very haunting, has a brilliant falsetto and the orchestration takes it to a new level. "Before you judge me, try hard to love me"

Tabloid Junkie - Very quick, catchy song about the news "its slander " "tortures me " "parasite in black and white who would do anything for views".

2 Bad - Urban hop hop track that contains a nice rap from Shaq. This is similar to This Time Around in that it is about him standing tall while every tries to hunt him down and "bring him to his knees". Pretty interesting track.

HIStory - This track is about how every day creates HIStory, its done sort of like an anthem in terms of chorus and instrumentation. This is a nice title track for the album. It is far from the best but still good.

Little Susie - This is Michael's 1 classical music composition (also has lyrics though). This one is sung like a poem of sorts, starts and ends with very haunting classical orchestration. It's about a girl who is murdered by being pushed down the stairs and throughout the song you find out more about her and how no one cared about her until she was dead. Very dark, disturbing track, it is well done though and would surprise most people who didn't know Michael sung about stuff like this or could work with classical music.

Smile - Really nice Charlie Chaplin / Nat King Cole cover song with incredibly smooth vocals.

HIStory is a really diverse album compared to Michael's other work. There is a sort of general vibe about the system we live in being corrupt and full of problems but there is alot of personal tracks in there as well about him dealing with his own emotions and fame. The other songs, like Little Susie and the covers round out it to an album full of variety. Michaels vocals are soft, gritty, angered, childish, or smooth depending on the track. This album showcases a wide vocal range and the diverse song writing ability Michael had. I've heard people pass this album off as "Michael trying to be godly or preach to people". Those same people might as well write off John Lennon's songs "Imagine", "Power to the People", and "Give Peace a Chance". Beyond any message the album had, the quality of the music is incredibly high and everything is very well done. Michael is just a target that people and the media insulted, so instead of saying how amazing his composition and lyrics are, they just say he is "a preacher". Never do either of the artists music tell people what to do, but they just make people think about the ideas being presented to them. In my opinion HIStory is Michael's best effort since Thriller and they both are tied for my favorite Jackson album.

title: You have to go somewhere, but is this it?
text:
I'm sure it's a dilemma for Ms. Hatfield in terms of her career. Her early appeal was in short pop songs with killer power chords offsetting her breathy, sexy voice, just a little on the bad girl side (love a girl who sings the F word, as in "Spin the Bottle"). But, after a number of albums that are no longer zipping up the charts, and with age creeping up, where do you go?

Obviously there's a mixed reaction to her answer, and I can certainly see why. Her voice is wonderful here, but on a song like "Shining On" she comes off sounding more like Susanna Hoffs, and what's point in that? Songwriting has never been a super strong point, illustrated by the opening track, which never quite connects. "Just Lust" is probably the best song here, but mostly due to it's throwback opening and the naughty tone. How's it working out when you try to change your gig and your best moment is something "old"? "Now I'm Gone" taps into the rocking dimension, but she doesn't sound very enthusiastic about it. "Beautiful Girl" does deserve mention as an outstanding ballad, very nice (she should sell it to Faith Hill or Crystal Gayle). Because the CD as a whole is very solid and pleasant, I'm going to give her four, but it's not interesting to me, I didn't rip anything for my playlists.

I'm sorry this isn't better, because I'm quite fond of her based on many happy musical moments in the past. I wonder if it wouldn't be better for her to hook up with a band again, go for an indie wall of sound guitar thing. Kristin Hersh is currently stuck in the same rut, maybe they should look each other up.

title: Sapphire Bullets Of Love.
text:
I must be in the minority for thinking Jones is an overrated artist. I mean, right from her debut she was a darling. She came along and gave popular music some soft jazz touches back in 2002 and ended up selling 10 million plus. But I have stuck with her for some reason. I have bought each of her albums and found the same problem each time--a handful of gems padded by plodding background muzak. It's not as if Jones demonstrates her musical virtuosity or lyrical prowess. No, she strikes me as average on both fronts.

But there is something about her music. There was "Come Away With Me" and "I Don't Know Why", or "Sunrise" and "Creepin' In", or "Wish I Could" and "Broken" or "Chasing Pirates" and "Young Blood" or "Bull Rider" and "Take Off Your Cool". Each of these songs showcase the best in Norah Jones and her ability to actually vary her sound. Unfortunately, this has not translated to an entire album of gems.

"Little Broken Hearts" is no different, and I found myself thinking the same thing again--when I listen to the album all the way through it is rather monotonous. This album was being hailed and promoted as a dark and drastic style change but it isn't. It's Norah Jones, just less jazzy. But this started with her last album, 2009's "The Fall". That album was a direction sign as to where Jones was heading musically.

Now, I continue to look forward to what Jones will do in the future, because she is trying to change, and that I respect. She just hasn't hit her groove yet. So, once again, there are a handful of solid tracks here like "Say Goodbye", "She's 22", "4 Broken Hearts", "Happy Pills" and "Miriam". "Miriam" in particular is interesting because of Jones' approach to the dissolution of her relationship--directly targeting the mistress who contributed to its undoing. She doesn't just attack the other woman, but she also toys with her and even sympathizes with her as well.

So, three and a half stars. Jones has much room to mature and grow as an artist. I bought the deluxe version from Target that had the three bonus tracks, and "I Don't Wanna Hear Another Sound" is the best of the three. Overall, "Little Broken Hearts" isn't the best break-up album I've ever heard, and it's not the most interesting meditation on love and relationships either. But, it manages to hang together relatively well even if it comes off as monotonous at times in terms of its musical approach.

Here's how "Little Broken Hearts" compares to Norah Jones' other works:

2002 Come Away With Me: Three and a Half Stars
2004 Feels Like Home: Three Stars
2007 Not Too Late: Two Stars
2009 The Fall: Four Stars
2010 ...Featuring Norah Jones: Three Stars
2012 Little Broken Hearts: Three and a Half Stars

title: Seth Avett & Jessica Lea Mayfield - Memory Lane
text:
3.5 stars

Respect to both artists on this tribute album to Elliott Simith. They somehow managed to record the 12 compositions together over three years in between constant touring as separate musicians, grabbing any spare opportunity to lay down a track whether it be in in their homes or hotel rooms. The question is whether Seth Avett of the Avett Brothers and his friend and fellow artist Jessica Lea Mayfield pull off the feat of taking Smith's intimately personal songs and add real value to them as opposed to mere reverence? The answer is not quite. Clearly both artists love the music of this troubled genius whose tragic suicide in 2003 robbed music of one of its greatest songwriters. In addition Avett and Mayfield rightly try to bring a new sheen to these songs rather than present "Elliott Smith Karaoke Favourites" which is the right approach. The problem is that while it works well on a number of songs on others the fragility of Smiths damaged approach which has led his biographer to describe the musician as the "Torment Saint" cannot be accurately captured. As a result the intimacy of Smiths songs somehow gets lost in the process.

The album starts with Mayfield leading on "Between the bars" Elliott Smiths most famous song. It is a respectful cover and Mayfield has a nice ghostly quality to her voice, but it is not a patch on the original. Much better is Seth Avett's lead on the Beatle-ish "Baby Britain" which pounds along nicely, equally his take on the superb "Angeles" is the albums highlight where everything is stripped back to his sensitive vocal and plaintive guitar. Indeed it is Avett's versions which generally shine most brightly. "Lets get lost" radiates affection for the original and the fragile harmonies with Mayfield hit the mark. Alternatively others like "Twilight" are turned into an alt country ballad by Mayfield, whereas Smiths original was one of his most personal vocal performances with one of his greatest recorded hushed, layered vocal delivery. To be fair to Mayfield she bounces back with an excellent "Angel in the Snow" but the attempt to "rock up" the acoustic rage of "Roman Candle" misses by miles. Avett closes the album with "Memory Lane" which is one of Smiths most desperate songs. It deals with his time in a treatment centre ( "this is the place you end up when you lose the chase.") but one he wrapped up in the sweetest of guitar melodies, giving the song a sense of irony. Avett alternatively treats it as a melancholy piano ballad accompanied by strings and largely pulls it off, closing a interesting album and worthy project.

To stress again the two artists involved have toiled over a labour of love with this album and if some of it doesn't work that is because Smith was such a unique generational voice that he is almost impossible to cover. Thus while this reviewer would not swap any of the songs on this album for the originals, Avett and Mayfield's covers are undoubtedly worthy of investigation and if they lead you to the source of this inspiration it will be a job well done.

title: Lie Lie Lie ! (truth)
text:
Like a lot of people, I discovered Metric very, very late in the game, i.e. when they released "Help I'm Alive" way back in 2008. I purchased the single, but being rather incurious about the bands that produce the music I like, I waited for probably eight years before I explored this band further. Now I wish I hadn't waited. This is an excellent album by a group not many people seem to know about. I'd like to do my bit to try and change that.

PAGANS IN VEGAS opens with the darkly beautiful "Lie Lie Lie," which seems to have been written for my adoptive hometown of Los Angeles:

Oh, and I suppose I brought it all upon myself?
Starting with the question no one wants to ask themselves
Naked in the movie, make me the director's pet
Everybody told me "take whatever you can get"

From that point I was hooked. Most electronica-type bands tend to be a bit one-note in their songs, but Metric tackles as many emotional states as seem to exist for humans. "Fortunes" is seductive, playful and slightly cruel: it seems to be about a No.2 girl who discovers that the No.1 isn't all she's cracked up to be, and promptly seizes power; "The Shade" is beautifully written and deeply romantic. "Celebrate," as the title suggests, has a triumphant quality to both the lyrics and the music. A certain artful nastiness returns in "For Kicks," which is the lament of a woman who asks, "Why'd I have to go and break your heart for kicks? Why'd I have to go and break what can't be fixed?" Most writers would have taken the POV of an unrepentant b---h; Metric comes at this from another angle, someone who has done the bad deed but now regrets it, if only for selfish reasons.

Changing gear once more, "Too Bad, So Sad" is a fiery lament to one's own flaws ("When I spiral down, it's a private spin"), while "Other Side" features a switch of vocalists, with guitarist Jimmy Shaw putting down his axe in favor of his pipes ("All we want/is to feel like all we got/didn't cost us everything"). The album then soars to majestic heights with "Blind Valentine," which delighted me with its cleverness:

Whatever I want, whatever I do, whatever I say
Whatever I make, whatever I spend, whatever I save
The sound of the club, the kiss on your lips that should be mine
The people you meet, the people you trust, the people you find
That's the difference, baby, between you and me
That's the difference between your whole life and mine

I don't know exactly what this means, but damn, do I like it. Ditto "The Governess," a sort of mystical tune which takes the form of a one-sided dialogue between the singer and a mysterious someone. The refrain, "When there was a wilderness, we wandered wild and free
Guilt, she is the governess that guides me back to grief" always haunts me.

Now, I confess to having broad musical tastes but not much of a musical vocabulary. It's hard for me to review albums and actually communicate what I like about them. Metric's genre is electronica, a word which is somewhat meaningless and probably should be thrown out: to me, what matters on an album is not just the sound, which in this case is beautiful even for those with a distaste for synth effects, but the vocals and most especially the lyrics. And this album excels in both departments. It's catchy, diverse, and deep, probably some of the best download money I've spent in the last few years, a really triumph of mood and atmosphere. Highly recommended.

title: Most enjoyable classical guitar album I've ever purchased.
text:
I am not a music critic, nor am I an expert on Bach. My only credential for commenting on this album is that I have played classical guitar, albeit at an amateur level, for over forty years. Since I spend a great deal of time reading and writing, I'm always pleased to find a purely instrumental album that can tweak my creative neurons without intruding to the extent of redirecting my thoughts (unlike Beethoven or some of JS Bach's heavier compositions).

This album is simply lovely. Galbraith's artistry is remarkable. Add to this the surprising richness of his custom 8-string guitar (one above and one below the usual six strings), which extends the bass range beyond that of a 6-string guitar, and allows him to play higher notes closer to the end of the neck, increasing the resonance. The result, like that of Rachmaninov's oversized hands on the piano, generates a freshness that is not possible on a 6-string guitar.

Although I've heard a couple of short extracts from this composition performed by other guitarists, I have to confess that I was generally unaware of the complete work until stumbling into this album. Listening to all 32 tracks played in succession is a delight.

I would of course recommend this to those who love classical music. Beyond that, I think most listeners of "New Age" music would find this comfortable and vaguely familiar. As an introduction to classical music in general, and to JS Bach specifically, it would be hard to find a recording with a less bombastic baroque flavor.

title: R.E.M. begins to rise from the underground
text:
The 1990s music landscape saw Alternative Rock begin to basically become part of the mainstream music fold. Alternative Rock actually had its roots in the 1980s. Alternative Rock really ties itself to the "Indie Rock" (Independent Rock) movement. It is a style of music that often covers a wide variety of genres, often working on independent record labels, but most importantly the artist maintains complete control of the music and their careers. With 1980s Rock dominated by "Hit Radio" and mainstream music, much of the Alternative Rock movement was "underground" - heard in smaller venues and colleges. A band that was at the forefront of this underground movement of music was R.E.M. While many know R.E.M. is a pop-band from the 1990s, many also know R.E.M from the 1980s as one of the pioneers in Alternative Rock. R.E.M. would achieve a groundswell of success from the underground movement. In 1987, things would change when R.E.M would bring in producer Scott Litt. On their "Document" album, R.E.M. would successfully crossover into the mainstream with their first Top 40 hit, "The One I Love". This success would position R.E.M. to rise from the underground movement and become a force on the mainstream music scene. Following "Document", the band would switch from little-known I.R.S. records to Warner Brothers. In 1988 - once again teaming with Litt, R.E.M's first album with Warner Brothers, "Green" would solidify their standing as a force on the mainstream. At the same time, R.E.M. would remain true to their underground roots.

There are three changes I noticed in "Green" from previous albums. First up, "Green" probably shows some of the most pop-friendly songs by R.E.M. since the group's inception. In other words, these are songs that could easily be played on mainstream radio. While I always felt there was a place in mainstream radio for the I.R.S years of R.E.M., I can see how these songs are more receptive to R.E.M. The second change is that this album definitely had a stronger political charge than previous albums. This is perhaps because this was recorded during an election year. Finally, this album would introduce the use of the mandolin - something that would be a trademark sound for the band as they progressed forward with their career.

Here is a song by song synopsis.

"Pop Song '89": Two of the characteristics of this album are shown loud and clear. The title of the song is indicative of the mainstream sound this song has - and of what this album has. There are also political undertones with the line "Should we talk about the government?"

"Get Up": This song also has a nice mainstream feel to it. In particular, there are some nice background vocals from the band that compliment lead vocalist Michael Stipe perfectly.

"You are the Everything": This is one of the songs that feature Mandolin by Peter Buck. This song almost as a feel from the underground days of the album "Fables of the Reconstruction" - namely the feel of traveling across the Southern United States.

"Stand": This was probably one of the more popular songs from this album. While it wasn't one of my favorites, I can't knock the song. Lines such as "Think about direction" to some extent carries a political undertone.

"World Leader Pretend": As the title indicates, there is a political message in this song. However, there is so much to this song - this is a powerful song not just lyrically, but musically. It represents a great cross between the underground sound and mainstream sound of R.E.M. Stipe provides haunting vocals that really give this song an edge.

"The Wrong Child": This is a second song with the mandolin. The mandolin adds to the haunting quality of this song that is reminiscent of the underground sound of R.E.M.

"Orange Crush": Awesome song. This song probably falls more on the mainstream end thanks to the catchy melody and lyrics. The title references "Agent Orange" from Vietnam thus having a political undertone. However I feel it is the vocals again by Stipe and company that really are the strong point of this track.

"Turn You Inside Out": I would also say this song has a mainstream feel to it. Like "Orange Crush", it are the vocals by Stipe and company that really are the song's strong point.

"Hairshirt": This is the third song with the mandolin. Once again the mandolin is used to create a haunting sound that is reminiscent of the underground days of R.E.M.

"I Remember California": This song is a tribute to the State of California. The geographic aspects of this song also remind me of "Fables of the Reconstruction". Bill Berry's drums help contribute to the haunting feel of this song.

'Untitled Hidden Track': There is an eleventh track with no name on it, although there it is listed on the disc label (without a title). This song has less of a haunting feel compared to the other tracks.

The liner notes on my particular version of this collection were thin and with the exception of "World Leader Pretend", the lyrics were not included.. This was slightly disappointing because I think R.E.M. music has some of the most interesting music and adding lyrics would have been a good thing. Overall, this album shows the transition that R.E.M began to made from underground to mainstream band. I credit producer Scott Litt for helping make this seem easy for the band. I like how R.E.M. was able to work both sides of the line here. This is an album that should keep both the core fans and new fans happy. This album is highly recommended.

title: An Open Letter To The Record Buying Public
text:
Long ago I resigned myself to the fact that I would have to listen to Conservatives deride and publicly pillory any artists that don't agree with them. That doesn't, however, make it any less unpleasant to endure. Like a lot of great artists and the works they create, from Picasso to Pink Floyd and Thomas Paine from The White Album to Gulliver's Travels, the Beastie Boys stellar To The 5 Boroughs has a point of view. The last time I checked this was still a free country and the Beastie Boys are still entitled to think, say and publish whatever they want. I for one applaud them for always saying whatever they felt was right. Whether they are fighting for our right to party, freedom in Tibet or championing peace in today's world, The Beastie Boys have never compromised. It takes courage to stand on what you believe and seldom has it been as entertaining as it is on To The 5 Boroughs.

Now, there are those in the record buying public who seem to feel a sense of entitlement, those that feel that the only opinion that matters is their own. They wonder aloud why the rest us can't get it through our thick heads that they are right and start agreeing with them. Witness The Dixie Chicks "boycott" of late. If that is you then some of the more political themes on this album may leave you feeling left out. Too bad because To The 5 Boroughs finds The Beasties at their finest and in rare form; spinning fat, seductive grooves, killer beats and the mischievous lyrical genius they have come to be known for. If on the other hand, you voted for the majority last time out you will love the unabashed liberal bias on this album. And unabashed it should be. While no one loved the party more than I the Beasties are at their best when they are rapping about things that matter. This album matters. It is also unlike any other Beastie Boys album you have heard before. The Beasties have always seemed to understand that in order to have longevity an artist has to keep moving. Like most of my generation when License to Ill hit the airwaves I signed on for the party no questions asked. Albums like Paul's Boutique, Check Your Head and Ill Communication took us a little longer to get into. With each new release the Boys were evolving, experimenting and pushing the limits of what hip-hop could be. The rest of us were just trying to keep up with them and admittedly, loving every minute of it. Sometimes the experiment worked and sometimes it didn't but The Boys kept on challenging us all right into the next millennium. To The 5 Boroughs is no exception. For some time now The Beasties have been promising to release a collection of hip-hop cuts and this time out they delivered. Boy did they ever deliver. In the 70's and 80's New York City gave birth to a whole new scene with its own lyrical delivery, musical styling, creative expression and forms of dance. To The 5 boroughs unfolds like a love letter to the rap and funk roots that gave The Beastie Boys their start some twenty years ago. You can almost feel the rumble of the subway and it's easy to imagine the graffiti artists or break dancers warming up nearby as you listen to this album. Like Ill Communication and Paul's Boutique this album took me some time to get my head around but like those venerable albums it is also destined to become a classic. Stand out cuts here include the infectious break beats of Ch-Check It Out, the old school vibe on Right Right Now Now and Triple Trouble, and the trip hop joint An Open Letter To NYC.

If your politics make you feel squeamish about buying this album I feel your pain, I really do. Of late, the Beastie Boys have publicly held many points of view that would make any self-respecting conservative a little nervous. I'm sympathetic to your plight but I also urge you to remember that good art sometimes pushes us to places that make us uncomfortable.

To those that can't be convinced To The 5 Boroughs is the kind of album that will doubtless inspire some to do things like boycott The Boys. They might even feel compelled to call talk radio shows or start some sort of email campaign to shame them in to behaving themselves and get back towards the middle. If it is important to you that your favorite artists agree with you politically I suppose you could always just go buy a country record. Just don't make it Tim McGraw or The Dixie Chicks, they voted for Clinton.

And finally, for those reviewers who are mean spirited enough to suggest that having a left leaning political point of view will only hurt an artist's bottom line I am happy to report that I just caught The Beastie Boys at a SOLD OUT Long Beach show and their license to ill was still in full effect. God Bless America.

title: A Return To Form
text:
With the rise and popularity of indie/hipster music (which is pretty ironic in my opinion), punk bands have either evolved and into radio synth rock or faded back underground. A common trend with a lot of musicians is a decline in musical quality after their first couple of albums. It seems that after a steady paycheck and an increase in popularity, life is good. Ironically, it seems that being happy inevitably will stunt artistic creativity. Which is why a good punk band will always seem to have fairly consistent track records, based on the fact that there is so much effed up s**t in the world to be pissed off about.

With that being said, it seems that Rise Against (or should I say lead singer Tim Mcilrath) has experienced some happiness and sunshine during the last 5 or some odd years of their career. Appeal to Reason and Endgame were both very lack luster albums in my opinion and for a while, I was trying really hard to figure out why. Being a fan of their first 3 albums, the sequels were basically along the same lines with similar lyrical content and maybe even a bit formulaic, yet something had changed. Now you could say it was the tempo of the songs, or the band's venture into more mainstream territory, but I would argue that it was more of a lack of conviction and emotion in Tim's vocal delivery. To me, it was as if he was just going through the motions, not fully believing in the message that he was preaching.

Fast forward to 2014, and here we are with a brand new Rise Against record "The Black Market". To be honest, I went into this optimistic but not expecting much in regards to their last two albums. However, I was pleasantly surprised by the album and have actually listened to it a number of times since. For those who are complaining that it isn't anywhere close to Revolutions Per Minute and Siren Song of the Counter Culture, they aren't wrong. Musically, the songs on this album are much more melodic and maybe even "rockish" in style; however, the lyrics are much more introspective this time around and Tim's conviction in them are reflected in his vocal delivery. In other words, Tim's passion is back and this more than makes up for the slower song tempos and lack of power chords. Truth is, you don't need to scream to have people take you seriously and while singing may suck the energy out of the room for some people, so does taking videos with your cell phone at live shows when you should be moshing...And if you haven't noticed, Rise Against has always been more of a melodic hardcore band and Sufferer and The Witness was kind of a mainstream album anyway.

In short, for those stuck living back in 2005, this might not be the album for you. For everyone else who's willing to accept the fact that bands evolve and seek to play different styles of music, you might just appreciate this album like I do. It's definitely not perfect, but its well worth the purchase price.

While I'm sure I will get a lot of crap for saying this, some of the songs that really stood out to me on this album were: Methadone, The Eco Terrorist In Me and People Live Here
