title: Often lovely; discordant at times
text: Berlin-based pianist Hulsmann has made a somewhat typical ECM piano-trio record with Imprint, in that her playing is usually muted and introspective, with delicate themes that start gentle and typically build to a more expansive place.  She has a nice rapport with her trio mates, bassist Muellbauer and drummer Kobberling.  One thing that's a little different and interesting about her music is that a subtle degree of dissonance will appear from time to time, as on "A Light Left On."  There, she plays a simple line with the left hand but her right lays down a wandering melody that doesn't immediately or obviously fit with the basic line.  The more usual tune from Imprint is a softer, more pastoral song such as "Juni" or "Storm In a Teacup."  However, Ms Hulsmann does takes us on a flight of fancy from time to time, as on "Lulu's Paradise," another tune where the left and right hands are playing seemingly independent lines which interweave in a surprising way.

title: For the Completist Only -- Instead, buy the single version of "ABBA Gold" and the reissue of "The Visitors"
text:
For the completist only – stick to the “ABBA Gold” single version

For those ABBA completists who must have it all, this review is not for you. For everyone else, read on. This, of course, is one listener’s opinion.

This collection (which does not come cheap) includes the original CD “ABBA Gold,” the original CD “More ABBA Gold,” and a third CD of “B-Sides.”

I’ve been a fan of ABBA since the mid-1970s and have long owned their albums “ABBA: The Album,” “Arrival,” and “The Visitors,” each of which has been in heavy rotation in my collection for years and years.

Having never owned a copy of “ABBA Gold,” I went online and saw this 40th Anniversary Edition, and thought, “hey, why not get it all in one purchase?”

Well, the first CD, “ABBA Gold,” is everything it should be. 19 Tracks, virtually every big hit a music lover could want, beautifully mastered and arranged for maximum listening pleasure.

The second disc, “More ABBA Gold,” is, in my opinion, far, FAR inferior to the first in song quality. Listening to it I was amazed that many of these songs could have actually gone gold in the first place, and had I purchased it separately I would have been extremely disappointed. I realize the fortunes of any group will wax and wane, and musical styles will drift to follow current trends, but many of the songs on “More ABBA Gold” do not remotely have the trademark qualities of classic ABBA. “Summer Night City” is rather tepid disco without even the layered harmonies that would let you know it was ABBA in the first place. “Angel Eyes” is a bit of an improvement, but doesn’t hold a candle to most of the tunes on “ABBA Gold.” “So Long” “Lovelight” and “On and On and On” attempt to rock, but this has never been ABBA’s strong suit. “Honey Honey” is elevator music.

Over all, at least one half of the 20 tracks on “More ABBA Gold” would not warrant more than one play, and putting them together as a second “greatest hits” collection can only be a reflection of ABBA’s massive popularity over the years. Most of these songs pale in comparison to almost anything on “ABBA Gold.”

I do appreciate the inclusion of “Eagle, “Ring Ring,” and “When I Kissed the Teacher,” but I would not have knowingly paid USD $40.00 just to have those three songs (in addition to the wonderful tracks on Disc One).

The third disc, “B-Sides,” is truly for collectors only. If what you are is a casual fan and an admirer of such ABBA classics as “Dancing Queen,” “Take a Chance on Me,” and “Waterloo,” the third disc is little more than a curiosity. A number of tracks, such as “I Am Just a Girl,” belong with Lawrence Welk. And when ABBA tries to rock hard (“Rock Me,” “Man in the Middle”) I am mostly bored. “Happy Hawaii” appears to be “Why Did it Have to Be Me?” with different lyrics. Others (“King Kong Song,” “Pick a Bale of Cotton”) are a bit cringe-worthy. There are several nice songs on this disc, but nothing I would have been missing had I never heard of them.

This third disc also has a flawed track listing, which on my computer duplicates the titles on Disc One, even though clicking on these erroneous titles produces the songs from the third disc. (For example, the first track on Disc Three is listed on my player as “Dancing Queen,” but when you click on the track you will get “She’s My Kind of Girl,” which is the actual first track on the disc.)

The booklet that comes with the set is also a disappointment. The group members reflect on their success, but the booklet lacks any historic context for the different albums, there is no track listing inside the book, and nowhere in the set is there any mention of which albums the tracks came from, or the date of their release. Such a collection should have this information as a minimum. For listeners such as myself, this would provide some context for the musical development of the group. It becomes crucial on the third disc, which clearly features songs from a broad range of the group’s history. Since the tracks on all three discs are arranged out of historical sequence, I can’t, as an admirer, learn anything about their wonderful music apart from what I hear through the speakers.

I don’t hate this collection, but I will certainly be burning my own copy onto a single disc, made up of the contents of “ABBA Gold” and the five or six remaining songs from the other two discs, that match the high standard of Disc One.

If you want a great overview of the group, I would recommend simply buying the regular version of “ABBA Gold” and the re-release of “The Visitors,” which includes three bonus tracks of the group’s final recordings (which are also included in the 40th Anniversary set).

title: INTERNATIONAL BEAUTY CAN ALSO SING
text: Recorded at Bahamas Island studio recording retreat, Compass Point, here is a collection of long versions, never released, and dubs of songs from Grace Jones' albums of the eighties. It's wonderful. Jones always had the benefit of fine studio session players and the musical cast here shines in a dreamy Jamaican soundscape of romantic endless Summers and street-wise smarts. Her voice is sometimes zombie-like frightening as in the ominous cover of Flash and The Pan's "Walking In The Rain", and sometimes sedate and hypnotic as in her many excursions into sleepy French language back-up vocals ("I've Seen That Face Before"), but it is always expressive and powerful, a perfect niche to the rhythm and flow of the lush, multi-layered music. Joy Division's "She's Lost Control" is turned into a comedic, violent, and deliciously psychotic urban anthem and the whole CD rings with infectious grooves and sing-along charm.

title: what headbanging is all about
text:
This 2-CD set delivers nearly all it promises: it's loud, fast, and tough. Hits? Well, one number 66 single ('Rockaway Beach') from 1977 doesn't cut it.

Being from Detroit, this Forest Hills, New York combo sounds to me a lot like their predecessors, The Stooges or the MC5, and of course their contemporaries included The Clash, The Sex Pistols, and New Wave, or Punk artists such as Joe Jackson and Graham Parker. I was surprised to find out, however, that these boys are actually a bit older than myself (I'm pushing fifty). There really are no 'Ramones', only seven leather clad toughs who at one time or another lent their first name to the family that has become 'The Ramones'. Basic is what it was all about for the band... two guitars (seemingly of the three-string variety), a one-string bass, and a 3-piece drum kit. Although these boys played heavy, they traveled light! The 2-minute songs are limited to three chords (the SAME three chords), and verses that repeat themselves a minimum of 18 times per song. Amazingly, the band churned out 17 albums using this same formula.

Are they any good? Well, yeah, some of these songs are, and those that 'aren't' are so similar to the ones that are, you're splitting hairs anyway. You could probably get the same experience by listening to the first three songs ten times in a row rather than all 30 songs on disc one once. The best of the bunch are the intro, 'Blitzkrieg Bop' with its familiar "Hey! Ho! Let's Go!" refrain, 'I Just Want To Have Something To Do', and 'Mama's Boy'. But all these songs rate a 2.5 on a 4.0 scale... smack dab between fair and good, and without question emphatically smacking the dab.

While the songs don't talk about a whole lot, there is some consistency in their themes. We have for instance, "The Groupies" grouping, consisting of 'Judy Is a Punk', 'Sheena Is a Punk Rocker', and 'Suzy Is a Headbanger'. We also have "The Mental Case" collection, consisting of 'Gimme Gimme Shock Treatment', 'Psycho Therapy', and 'Teenage Lobotomy'. Then there is the "Wanna-Be's", which include 'I Wanna Be Sedated', 'I Wanted Everything', 'I Wanna Live', and 'I Don't Wanna Go Down To the Basement'. Finally, we have the obligatory (for all the slam-dancing mosh-pitters) "Gratuitious Violence" quartet: 'Beat On the Brat', 'Commando', 'The Crusher', and 'Smash You'. My favorite title though is the comical 'The KKK Took My Baby Away'. Let's give credit where credit is due.

This was worth a listen, but I'd be concerned about anyone who partakes of these discs (the second disc is a live 1985 collection of 8 songs, 2 of which appear on the first disc, and all of which sound pretty much identical to the studio recordings) on any kind of a regular basis. Headbanging rock and roll by definition dumbs-down the listener, and while we may all need to be drawn off our high-horse at times, this seems anti-evolutionary, maybe even devolutionary. I guess I gravitate more toward rock that challenges me to uplift myself, rather than indulge any leaning toward stagnation. As Maxwell Smart use to say... "Sorry about that".

Addendum: Gosh, can't you Ramone-philes take a little healthy criticism?

title: Great for the casual Rush fan; die-hards need not apply.
text: Retrospective II, along with its predecessor disc, are both adequate introductions to Rush for any curious or casual fan.  But for die-hard fans, such as myself, this is merely a waste of money if you already own the albums (which is really the true context the music must be heard).  I do happen to own this disc, but I only listen to it if I do not want to change CD's in my car or at home.  In that respect, it is a collection that satisfies me, somewhat.  That is because the best songs are not represented here (of course, that is only my opinion).  The 15 tracks here are equally divided between the five studio albums released from '81 to '87 (Moving Pictures, Signals, Grace Under Pressure, Power Windows, and Hold Your Fire).  Due to this balance of division, worthwhile tracks from strong albums (Moving Pictures, especially) are omitted for the purpose of giving preference to ones from weaker efforts (Hold Your Fire, and Power Windows {to a lesser degree}).  To get into the specifics of this, "Vital Signs" or "YYZ" from MP would have been a great addition here, along with possibly "Digital Man" from Signals.  Of course, to do such a thing would have meant dropping a couple of other songs, which in my opinion should have been "Mission" from HYF and probably "Marathon" from PW.  Don't get me wrong, these are both very good tracks, but not better than the aforementioned songs from Pictures or Signals.  From GUP, "The Enemy Within" or even "Afterimage" (one of the most underrated, and impassioned Rush songs ever) could have been here instead of "The Body Electric", which pales in comparison to those two tracks.  A case can even be made for "Manhattan Project" from Power Windows, as it is one of the three best tracks from that album.  Which brings me to a point:  The music of Rush is not really meant to be dissected into fractions of "wholes" (albums) to make new "wholes" (best of collections), but is best experienced in the context of the album.  Unless you are quite stingy and do not want to shell out the money for the individual albums represented here. Which the casual fan for which Retrospective II is designed may just do anyway after buying this disc.

title: All time greatest George Howard Album
text: This is the best George Howard Album ever. I originally bought this release on cassette tape back in the day before CD's were the "in" thing. From the first cut "I want you for myself" to cut #10, "Piano in the Dark" this was simple great music. Normally I prefer music without the lyrics so I can work on other things at the office or at home with minimum distraction, but I didn't mind several cuts on this album that have lots of lyrics, such as "Shower you with Love" featuring John Pagano and "You and Me". George even makes the sax seem like he is talking or sayings the words through it, especially on "I want you for myself" and "Uptown". The high range notes of the Soprano Sax that George hits on cuts like "You and Me" and "I'm in Effect" are unmatched by any other Sax player I have ever heard. And the drum beat and keyborad licks are just amazing and beautifully arranged, especilly on "Personally and "Got it Goin' On." The glue on this album however, to me is the guitar and vocal performaces of Attala Zane Giles on all cuts except "You only come out at Night" and "Fakin the Feeling". Other noteable musicians are Paul Jackson Jr, guitar, George Duke, Piano/Synclavier and Percussionist Paulino deCosta. If you like a funky beat plus pop your finger and shake your Booty as well as pat your feet music you will love this album as I do.

title: Better than the U.S. release
text:
Because I have been a Who fanatic ever since seeing them for the first time on the Smothers Brothers TV show in 1967, I don't know how objective I can be, but here goes. This is better than the U.S. release for three reasons. First, the bonus disc includes not only the same four audio recordings, but also two live video recordings playable on your DVD player. Second, the enclosed printed material is superior to that which comes with the U.S. CD. Third, it adds Another Tricky Day, the only great song from the otherwise miserable Face Dances album.
Now for my only complaints. This release does not include the sticker that was in the U.S. version. It also adds Don't Let Go the Coat and The Quiet One, two weak songs from Face Dances. It includes only two songs from It's Hard (Eminence Front and Athena), which is a vastly underrated album that is far superior to Face Dances, and (also like the U.S. version) it does not include Relay. However, since this set does include all of the wonderful but now U.S.-deleted Meaty, Beaty, Big & Bouncy (to be fair, the U.S. release does, too) it must now be regarded as the definitive (and truly ultimate) collection of The World's Greatest Rock Band. So can we all just get over the fact these dirty record label jerks have commercialized our beloved metal. So just stop throwing that around because unless you're listening to Leviathan, Death Spell Omega, or Weakling. YOU ARE LISTENING TO COMMERCIAL MUSIC. If you bought it at the mall or Best Buy, guess what, COMMERCIAL. Even Behemoth is commercial! Sad day huh.
In the end this album is fantastic. It's technical as hell without getting bogged down in techyness i.e. Dream Theater. It's heavy as all get out. All transitions between riffs, rhythms, solos, bridges, and what not are seamless, fluid, and natural. The jazz injections are back thank god. The polyrhythmic riffing is totally fantastic, bad-ass, and just plain fun all at the same time, honestly these guys do it better than anyone, including Meshuggah (I say this as a huge and long time fan, own all there stuff.) The music is very complex but not unnecessarily so, you know where the music stops being enjoyable because they're trying to do too much or jam too much in to one song, Between the Buried ad Me. Production is excellent, the only problem Rareform had, though I have the original print of the album and not the reissue. And my favorite part........NO SINGING!! :) NONE at ALL. I'm all down for singing, but if I want to hear that I will listen to Journey or Alter Bridge, or Zeppelin. But when I listen to death metal, I don't want to hear that crap, especially from a band that never did it, and never needed to. I know it's a round about way of saying it but this is a great album, one of the best metal albums ever period, and is as good as Rareform and Forging a Future Self, if not better.

title: Very simple music...just a man and his acoustic guitar. 7/10
text:
One of the interesting things about this collection is how you'd hear certain sounds or lyrics you'd associate with bands like The Beatles ("Ooh!") or Led Zeppelin ("Squeeze my lemon"). Haven't looked into Robert Johnson's bio, but I'm assuming that this must be some of the very earliest blues music recorded...it's a lot simpler than more more modern sounding blues...even someone like Muddy Waters. I have to admit that I'd never heard of Robert Johnson before he was referenced in the tv series "Supernatural"! A story about Johnson selling his soul to the Devil or something in order to be able to play the guitar well. That reference probably can be attributed to one or two songs featured in this compilation. As for Johnson's guitar playing style, it consists of simple note picking. It can be more elaborate at times too. He also seems to be playing two different note sequences at the same time...one in each hand, it sounds like at times. The tempo is generally laid back. Truth be told, his lyrics can often be hard to understand but when you can make out what he sings, he does have a nice turn of phrase at times. Since there are two cds in this compilation, I think that the one criticism I can make with bite is the fact that alternate versions of songs are sequenced together..often. This is fine if you want to do comparisons, but if you are listening for pleasure, having similar songs played back to back quite often may be an annoyance to some. The sound quality is what you'd expect for recordings this old...lo-fi...often hissy sounding...like a cassette recording...or scratchy...like a second hand vinyl album.

The best tracks "(.)":

They're red hot - quite unlike any other song on this album. A fun song...not sure if you'd call it a rag or not. Johnson has a screechy voice in this song. Maybe it's the kind of song you could imagine Louis Armstrong singing?

Then "[.]":

Walkin' blues - guitar gets a bit funky in this song...sometimes notes are vigorously plucked. Has the lyric "I've been mistreated. Don't mind dyin'".

Stop breakin' down blues - bit of a classic. Has a "Hoo-ooh" vocal...like Little Richard, perhaps.

Songs of interest:

Beatles related...

Kind hearted woman blues - has the Beatle-esque "Ooh". Johnson establishes a rhythm on the bass notes of his guitar whilst sometimes simultaneously playing a melody on the higher strings. He utilises falsetto singing at times.

Dead shrimp blues - another Beatle-esque "Ooh". Not sure if this song is euphemistic for adultery by a women. Has the lyric "Someone fishing in my pond".

Me and the devil blues - this may be the song which the tv series drew on to reference Johnson in an episode. Also has the Beatle-esque "Ooh". Has lyrical themes of crossroads and voodoo...as mentioned in the tv show.

Led Zeppelin related...

Traveling riverside blues - has the lyric "You can squeeze my lemon til the juice runs down my leg. You know what I'm talkin' about". An example of the nice turn of phrase by Johnson, he also sings "She got a mortgage on my body now and a lien on my soul". Johnson sounds like a bush lawyer there!

Elvis Presley related...

From four until late - Johnson strikes me as sounding a bit like Elvis in this song (vice versa, of course). I'm thinking gospel singing Elvis...or maybe in something like "Train" (if that's the name of the song) or "Tiger man"...had note mentioning "Wooden heart", but I think I may have replaced that with "Tiger man".

Little Richard related...

Stop breakin' down blues - "Hoo-ooh" reminds me of Little Richard.

Billie Holiday related...

Sweet home Chicago - Johnson has glassy vocals at times in this song...sort of reminding me of female singer Billie Holiday (I'd say that she was a contemporary of Johnsons, and black too...check out her song "Strange fruit"...Billie eschews coded lyrics in this song about the African American experience as experienced by some.

Personal lyrics related...

Drunken hearted man - this song's lyrics really grabbed me...the early ones, like "If I could change my way of livin', it would mean so much to me". It sounds really heartfelt. There are two versions of this song on the cd...in one version it is the "poor mother", in the second version it is the "poor father"...in both versions the father has died...but it seems. Personally, I think it's the living that deserve one's sympathy...it's wasted on the dead.

Euphemism related...

Stones in my passway - hmm...I'm going to feel silly saying this...but sheesh...is Johnson talking about haemmorrhoids here? In any case, he sings in a different voice here...more measured. Question to myself: who betrayed him?

Malted milk - a euphemism for whisky?

Milk cow's calf blues - assuming that this song is innuendo...doesn't sound exactly logical to me, but it is suggestive! Not sure, but I thought that Johnson used the "n" word, in the lyric "Your (?) turnin' blue". Could be wrong.

Phonograph blues - sings of a rusty phonograph needle which doesn't work...I don't think he's actually complaining about his record player...you know what I'm talkin' about?

Classic blues elements...

I believe I'll dust my broom - has a classic blues shuffle to it...if "shuffle" is the right word. Some parts of this song sound hissy, and other parts sound quite scratchy.

Ramblin' on my mind - I could only stomach a little bit of the documentary series on the blues associated with movie director Martin Scorcese "The blues". However, I did take away one gem...in blues songs the singer often sung about a harsh mistress. It seems that this was code for slave-owners, in a time where in American slavery was legal, or apartheid was. In other words, the singer would complain about their lover treating them badly, but they were really singing about a cruel slave owner. Just by the by, I couldn't stomach the documentary series because it assumed the viewer was as reverential to the form as the makers were. I had less interest in a documentary series about country and western music, but that series I watched all the way through, because the enthusiasm of the film maker was infectious. I believe that that series was called "Lost highway: the history of American country". Don't think I made it more than 20 minutes into Scorcese's series on the blues. Anyway, this song has that classic blues shuffle and the lyrics "You treat me so unkind"...which is what reminded me of that episode on the blues.

When you've got a good friend - an example of the classic blues structure...pairs of repeated lines. Johnson plays some complex notes at the start and establishes a pleasant little motif.

MIlkcow's calf blues - I made a note for 1:10 - 1:21 minutes into the first version of this song...this may refer to the music having a classic blues element to it. On the second version of this song, the time frame is 1:15 - 1:25.

Interesting guitar sounds...

Terraplane blues - percussion on the body of the guitar...knocks.

If I had possession over judgement day - guitar has a ukelele sound to it.

Cross road blues - has more complex guitar playing. Has that cliche clunky blues notes sound at times. Vocals have a sort of 1950s rock'n'roll style to them.

Hell hound on my trail - has a bit where the guitar playing sounds like unskilled doodling...from 0:51 to 0:59 minutes in. This track has a distant sound quality to it...like a phonograph or wax cylinder recording.

Milkcow's calf blues - also has percussion near the end of the song (2nd version)...could be Johnson tapping his foot...or the guitar.

Linguistic elements/production elements...

Love in vain blues - has a news reel type intro...I can make out the following words by the news reader (?): "I wanna fly _ the ship" and "Willie May". Wikipedia informs me that Willie May was a baseball player. This song is an example of Johnson's guitar playing sound...he's plucking some basic bass notes on his guitar whilst playing a melody on - presumably - the first and second strings of his guitar...I'm not a musician, so am just guessing which strings he is using. UK punk rock band The Clash have a song called "Train in vain"...not sure if there is thus a link between these two songs...inspiration?

Honeymoon blues - "You is my destiny".

Come on in my kitchen - Johnson hums the intro. He also has a different quality to his voice here...it's almost a character voice. He also delicately plays his guitar at times.

Phonograph blues - the pronoun changes in the second version of this song...from "she" to "I". This song is a bit jauntier than most of his tracks here.

Borrowed melodies etc?...

32-20 - sounds sort of familiar to me. Has some interesting notes and melodies on the non-bass strings.

Voodoo/Hell related...

Cross road blues - might have been the song which prompted the reference in the tv series "Supernatural". Has more complex guitar playing here (in the tv series, the legend mentioned was - from memory - that Johnson had sold his soul in order to play the guitar better. That seems borne out in this song! Has some cliche clunky notes sometimes on the guitar too...maybe this wasn't cliche when Johnson was playing it? His vocals here have a sort of 1950s rock and roll style.

Preachin' blues (up jumped the devil) - has a jaunty blues lead guitar. Distinctive and recognisable note picking style...on 1st and 2nd strings, perhaps.

Hell hound on my trail -

Me and the Devil blues - another song which could have prompted the reference in the tv series "Supernatural".

Recommendations -

Muddy Waters - Anthology. I wasn't a huge fan of this album, but if you like Johnson's album, you should like this one too...and vice versa.

Muddy Waters - Hard again. Highly recommended. My first exposure to Waters. Unlike "Anthology", Muddy goes electric and rock here...has some really thumping drums. Terrific modern blues-rock album.

title: Another Treat
text: When the legendary Nashville Tony Brown signed Willis to a major label deal in the 1990s, she seemed destined to be the next big thing in real country music (especially for fans who don't like country music). It never happened and she's settled into marriage and child-rearing with songwriter Bruce Robison. So her occasional releases have been treats, glimpses of what could have been. On her latest, she and producer Chuck Prophet wrap her soothing voice around a variety of cuts with varied success.  The best are "Don't Know Why," written by Willis, Prophet and Jules Shear, "Sweet Little One," a gentle beaut; "The More I'm Around You," an unabashed piece of pop, and a surprisingly raw cover of Iggy Pop's  "Success." A couple of duds include a cover of "Teddy Boys," which makes your teeth grate.  Still, it's a pleasure to enjoy Willis's stunning voice again on tunes like the title cut and imagine what could have been.

text:
Masta Ace - A Long Hot Summer (M3, 2004)

I remember Masta Ace from Marley Marl's classic, "The Symphony", back in 1988. With that in mind, I listened to this album (my first Masta Ace album) expecting a classic as well. There are some very solid tracks in here like "Do It Man" with Big Noyd and the smooth "Good Ol Love" but there is something wrong here and I can't put my finger on it. No, I'll just go out and say it: he's an OLD RAPPER. There's nothing wrong with that because vets like Guru and CL Smooth can still spit fire, but Ace kicks some outdated flows that don't change at all during the album along with some weak metaphors (i.e., "you don't know my name like Alicia Keys" and "pack steel like Navy S.E.A.L.S."). I know that he's just staying true to his craft but how can you have Ed O.G. and Psycho Les of all people outshine you on your own tracks??

To be fair, this is supposedly his last album and rappers' final albums usually show why retirement is a good idea for them (see A Tribe Called Quest's The Love Movement). And I love the way that the skits tell a story. This album is very solid with the only flaw being Ace's rhyme style. I really can't see myself calling this a classic AT ALL. I hope this review was helpful to you but most likely it wasn't because you probably disagree with it. -EJR

title: Another Outstaning Achievement for Deep Elm
text: Benton Falls as well as the whole Deep Elm label continues to impress me. Deep Elm had the vision and foreight to sign this band before they were snatched up by a larger label. Deep Elm has released a number of great albums by The Appleseed Cast and Brandston, however this album equals or exceeds these. Benton Falls proves its credibilty right from the start, with deft guitar work and varying tempos. The vocals also set this apart from average emo bands. The soft subtle vocals erupt into anguished isolated screams. This quality of emo music only succeeds if the artist knows proper timing and pitch. Pulling this off is a thing of beauty, something that adds the emotional element lacking in other genres. The lyrics are also first rate as well. Decidely un-punk in approach, it nonetheless deals with the gographic and cultural isolation that come with living in a small town. They don't rebel against authority and leadership, but rather the closemindedness of the people around them. They also craft beautiful songs about realationships and weave interesting ancedotes into their stories. The instrumentation is often bare, but leaves the listener happy. The bare instrumentation creates the mood of isolation and sadness that the lyrics describe. Often, repetitious guitars and montonous drum patterns serve as a powerful backdrop. One would think that this type of music my start to sound repetative and boring after few songs, but it doesn't. The vocal range and slight tempo changes add enough variety to keep things interesting. Fans of Pedro the Lion, DCFC and more lo-fi emo bands will appreciate the sincerity and quality of this cd.

title: Yet another great album by STP!
text:
This album is like a mix between the older grunge music STP did and the newer alternative that was experimented with on Tiny Music. Just about every song mixes the two genres and the result is sweet. My only complaint is the lyrics. Seems that repeating the same line over and over doesn't hit me as hard as the poetic lines on songs like Adhesive or Pretty Penny.
Down-10/10-This is a hard rock track. It sounds more like something from Purple, there's a sense of grunge in it. You've heard this on the radio. The lyrics are pretty basic stuff, but they hold their own.
Heaven and Hotrods 9/10-This is another great hard rock song, you start to see the lyric repitition in this one though. Otherwise it's great.
Pruno-9/10-ANOTHER hard rock song with a pinch of alternative thrown in. There's some interesting riffing in this song. The lyrics though are just bad. "One, two, three, I've got another, got another?". Hmmm...
Church on Tuesday 8.5/10-I really like this song, it's like something from Tiny Music. The lyrics are good, but there's something about the chorus that I just don't like.
Sour Girl 9.5/10-This is unlike anything STP has done. It was made for the radio, and you've definitely heard it. It has a very relaxing atmosphere and tone. The lyrics work well with that. The guitar is really good too. It's something different.
No Way Out 6.5/10-This song has potential during the verses. You really get a throwback to Core, until the chorus. Horrible music. It sounds like one of the new hybrid rap rock bands. Not what I want from a Stone Temple Pilots album.
Sex and Violence 8.5/10-Another good hard rock song, but it sounds like it could be from Tiny Music. The verses and pre chorus are excellent, but it's another lackluster chorus that sounds like a hybrid rap/rock band. But the verses and pre-chorus are so damn good...
Glide 10/10-Something from Tiny Music again, something like Adhesive. Beatiful music, lyrics, guitar, and vocals. It just shows how much STP has grown. I can't listen to Core anymore because this is so much better. Songs like this just show you how much STP has shed its Pearl Jam clone label. Excellent song. I love the "oh oh" part right in the middle.
I Got You 9.5/10-Something about this song reminds me of Nirvana. Maybe it's the lyrics or the acoustic riff. It changes in the chorus though, then it sounds like The Beatles or something. Great song.
MC5-9/10-Great hard rock track, like the first three. Another case of lyric repitition here though. I like the how the riff follos along with Scott's voice. Great song.
Atlanta 10/10-STP is a band that doesn't forsake it's closer. This song does sound like the Doors, his voice could be confused with Jim Morrisson, but this song is awesome. Has a nice dreamy atmosphere in it, more so than Sour Girl. Some orchestra in there. Good lyrics, great song.
So that about concludes my review for No.4. Another great piece of music from STP.

title: Essential Moody Blues album, great for what it is
text:
I find it a little hard to understand the negative reviews for this CD. The "classic" line up of Moody Blues is intact here: Hayward, Lodge, Pinder, Thomas, Edge. That's the line up that produced those great first seven albums. Hear those, and you'll realize that the band (and producer) could create terrific studio albums. But if you want more from that line up, you'll have to go for this disc, because Mike Pinder left the band between the seventh and eighth albums, and hasn't returned [author's edit - actually Mike Pinder IS on the 8th album, Octave, but didn't join the live tour for it and thereby was out of the band from that point].

Here the band plays a live set at the Royal Albert Hall on December 12 1969, and also gives you 5 studio tracks that were recorded during the creation of those first seven albums (but not included on those albums). One amazing thing here is that the 5 studio tracks are good, really good. They are finished songs, nothing wrong with them at all, other than they either didn't fit the theme of whatever studio album they happened to be doing, or there just wasn't enough space on a vinyl LP of about 45 minutes maximum length.

The other amazing thing is that the Moodies perform very well at their live show, and the recorded sound quality is quite impressive for the time. So why are my comments at odds with the comments of several others here? Probably because I didn't expect the raw live performance to sound like a polished studio album, and I didn't expect the sound quality of a 1969 live recording to be spectacular by modern standards. If you do have those expectations, sure you may be disappointed. But this is real music folks, performed live, no overdubs, one "take" only. The pace is a little fast on some of the songs, I'll agree with that. You get used to it though. Now how does this compare to the other live Moody CDs? The recorded sound quality on those other live CDs is better than here, and the performance on the other live CDs is more like what you hear on the studio recordings. But which of the official live recordings has the "best" performance?

Personally, I like this one the best. Because it's got Mike Pinder playing the keys/mellotron, just Mike - not a replacement keyboardist, or two keyboardists at once, no matter how good those multi-keyboardists might be. This performance just has just Graeme Edge playing the drums, not Graeme plus a second drummer - even as great the second drummer that they've had in recent years truly has been. This one has Ray Thomas on flute, the original, even as good (and attractive) as the woman who has recently played flute for the Moodies has been. You see, for me this is the best live Moodies CD because this is just "the five" that made it all happen, back at the time when it was happening. No string orchestra, as nice as that might sound. No back up singer/dancers. No second drummer, no extra keyboards, no additional musicians of any type - this is not a "Las Vegas Revue" type of performance. It's just the original five, live and raw, doing the best they can. When you hear this without the expectation of a flawless, crystalline, note for note, tempo for tempo reproduction of the studio albums, I think you'll greatly enjoy this. If not, well then you can always listen to those studio albums all over again. But give this a chance. At the price, for both the live concert and the five extra studio songs, this is a very good buy. Give it a little something, please think about it, this may provide you with some great listening for those long summer days (and winter ones too).

[Edit: back when I wrote this review, this CD was the only official release of a Moody Blues concert with the "classic" 5-man line up. But in 2009 the "Isle of Wight" concert from 1970 was released as both an audio-only CD and a audio/video DVD, again with the "classic 5" line-up. The setlist from that concert is nearly identical to this one, with some differences. Die hard Moody Blues fans will want both concerts, but if I had to choose only one it would be the Isle of Wight one on DVD. Then again, this concert is worthy on it's own, and you also get the "plus 5" previously unreleased studio songs.]

title: Hauntingly Dark and Beautiful
text:
This record has probably sold millions of copies since its release just a few months ago, which usually raises a red flag for me (nothwithstanding Led Zeppelin themselves, Beck, Beatles, Rolling Stones, Neil Young, etc. serving as perfect examples of mainstream appeal simultaneous with critical acclaim).

The secret here is T Bone Burnett, who produced it and picked the songs, most of which are covers, and a couple of which are covers of Plant's and Krauss's own songs. Burnett just seems to have that Midas touch (be it Los Lobos, Peter Case, U2, or a long list of others he's been involved with). He also plays several instruments on most of the record, as does Marc Ribot (another amazing guitarist....just ask Tom Waits, Jim White, Dylan, Byrne, Lanois, Los Lobos....or look through some of your favorite CD booklets...chances are you'll find his name on several).

The record has a Jim White or maybe Lucinda Williams dark Appalachian Magical Realism feel about it. The recording is crystal clear, and song after song, the record just has a great feel about it. It alternates between Plant and Krauss taking the lead vocals. At other times, one might seem to take the lead, only for the other to take over, but throughout, their voices blend beautifully, creating a sensuously smoky effect.

After the big Led Zep reunion and show in London, Plant was asked whether Led Zep would be launching a bigger tour. He commented that he didn't know, since he'd like to tour with Alison Krauss.

Any Led Zeppelin fan would love to see them tour, especially in the wake of all the glowing reviews after the London show, but if they don't, this Led Zeppelin and alt country fan would be just as happy seeing Plant and Krauss in a smaller intimate venue.

title: An Impressive Entry
text:
This is the first cd in psycroptics growing collection, and in my opinion, the best. Really when they lost Matt Chalk as the vocalist (symbols of failure and newer), they lost a lot of what i loved about the band. The new vocalist is not nearly as dynamic, and the band lost the dynamic they had going with Matt Chalk.

In The Isle of Disenchantment, you dont have some of the more obtuse noises made on The Scepter of the Ancients. It is for this reason alone that it tops the list for me. You still get varied voice changes throughout the music, generally well-timed. If you actually take the time to read the lyrics, they are relatively well written, and some even quite imaginative. The lyrics are also delivered skillfully through stops/pauses in the middle of sentences to maintain rhythm. Its something that needs to be heard to be appreciated.

The band was quite young when this cd was produced, and that is impressive in and of itself. There is incredible skill behind the instruments, and the vocalist lends himself well to the music. Much better than most, in my opinion. The drummer is a particular standout. Instead of really playing "prescripted" fills, it sounds like he is actually playing a set of drums. A musical personality really shines through.

At the beginning of "The Sword of Uncreation" is just about the best metal scream out there. They have a lot of elements that really come together for them. They have some unique riffs that are reproduced in different forms throughout the music. This is not to say its repetitive exactly, but more that it has a nice consistent unique feel. You know its pscyroptic and no one else.

They certainly have their own sound, but it is a bit dissapointing that that sound has not really evolved over the years. they changed the lead vocalist, to the detriment of the music, but they never really evolved the sound to fit him better. This makes the music seem a bit disjointed, but maybe its just me!

This is for fans of technical metal, but with more ingenuity and groove thrown in. This album seems to have the most energy behind it, but without the downright strange noises found on The Scepter of the Ancients (still an excellent album in its own right).

title: AVOID -- MAY INSTALL A ROOTKIT VIRUS
text:
Hi Gerry Mulligan fans,

It's absolutely infuriating that Sony implanted a significant portion of the Gerry Mulligan Jeru CDs made up to 2005 with an instant-install rootkit copy protection scheme. The same goes for a number of other Sony pressings, including the Louis Armstrong, Billie Holiday and Frank Sinatra Great American Songbook CDs, Art Blakey's Drum Suite, Dexter Gordon's Manhattan Symphonie, Horace Silver's Silver's Blues, and about 40 other CDs.

This Sony rootkit (The XCP rootkit) lodges itself in your Windows operating system if you so much as put the CD in your computer's drive, sends info to Sony, affects your performance, and has been exploited by hackers since 2004. Rootkits are notoriously difficult to detect and dislodge, and you have two options: Use the reputable company F-Secure's BlackLight rootkit detector, which is a free tool on their website, or use the Sony-provided removal tool, which you can get from the Sony site. Per Amazon's policy, I can't give you a link, but you can find the page by Googling "Sony XCP."

If you have/buy a CD with bar code number 074646549827, then you have a CD with a rootkit problem.

In 2005, Sony also stated that it would allow owners to swap these CDs for new non-XCP copies -- but only if you have the precise bar code above. Still, there is no information on how to do so. My hunch is that you use the Tech Support link at the Sony XCP site to email Sony, and they'll provide the Return to Manufacturer details.

Amazon itself supposedly returned all of its old XCP copies to Sony, but it's not clear to me that there really was reissue without XCP. Anyway, the small sellers on Amazon Marketplace may still have the old copies for sale, unknowingly. Who knows what bar code you'll get if you buy one? Unfortunately, this also hoses all the people trying to sell their copies here on Amazon Marketplace. If you're a seller, I urge you to specify the barcode on your product.

title: Weezer's 'Red Album' aims to please, mostly hits mark
text:
The dudes from Weezer have it rough.

Imagine being part of one of *the* defining rock bands of the mid-'90s post-grunge era -- a band whose members kick-started their careers with back-to-back, indisputable masterpieces (the blue-hued, self-titled debut "Weezer" and its painfully personal, less-pop-sensible follow-up "Pinkerton"). Now imagine the pressure that comes with trying to meet or exceed the stratospheric expectations of both critics and rabid fans looking for you and your bandmates to recreate that magic on subsequent releases -- to, in essence, make lightning strike twice, *twice*.

The band's 2001 comeback (also titled "Weezer," but nicknamed "The Green Album" because of the cover art's color palette) came closest to appeasing their mass of followers, partly because it was seen as somewhat of a return to form, but mostly because it was also literally Weezer's "return" after a four-year hiatus. By the time 2002's mildly praised "Maladroit" came out, even some of the band's most devout loyalists began to lose hope. And don't even mention 2005's schmaltzy "Make Believe" (or its ubiquitous, love-it-or-hate-it single "Beverly Hills") to a Weezer fan unless you want to get punched in the face.

So, does the band's sixth LP "Weezer" (dubbed "The Red Album" for clarity's sake) manage to finally recapture the glory days of the emo-pop foursome at their creative peak? Well ... no. I think by now, it's obvious that doing so would be impossible, which is why I believe "Red" (and the rest of the post-"Pinkerton" albums, for that matter) shouldn't be judged against the band's earlier work. Instead, it should be appreciated for what it is: a well-rounded collection of catchy, decent-to-great pop songs that, at the very least, will leave even the most finicky Weezophile satisfied.

If you've logged on to YouTube in the last couple of weeks, there's a good chance you've seen the video for "Pork and Beans," the album's first single. It's the band's latest incarnation of "Buddy Holly" -- after "Hash Pipe," "The Good Life," "Keep Fishin'" and "Beverly Hills" -- and was written by lead singer Rivers Cuomo to spite record executives who pressured him to pen a radio-friendly hit. (Ironically, with its inescapable chorus and driving guitar rhythms, all crammed into a perfect three-minute run time, "Pork and Beans" is the summer's prime candidate for nonstop airplay on Top 40 stations across the country.)

Elsewhere, Cuomo plants his tongue firmly in his cheek for a song detailing rock star excess ("Troublemaker"); "boo-yah"s his way through a speedy, metal-inspired tune about his days as a reckless teenage prankster ("Everybody Get Dangerous"); and lays out a laundry list of his diverse musical influences ("Heart Songs"). The band's most epic experiment to date comes in the form of "The Greatest Man That Ever Lived (Variations on a Shaker Hymn)," a six-minute, Queen-esque rock opera that cobbles together rapping, Prince-like falsetto wailing and church-choir backing vocals.

When I heard each of the three other band members -- guitarist Brian Bell, bassist Scott Shriner and drummer Patrick Wilson -- would be getting lead-vocal duties for one track apiece on this album, I was a bit leery. And alas, after hearing their respective entries, my fears were largely confirmed. Bell's "Thought I Knew," Shriner's "Cold Dark World" and Wilson's "Automatic" aren't necessarily "bad" songs; their biggest detriment is simply due to the fact that, without Cuomo's trademark voice, not one of them is identifiable as a Weezer Song. Sequenced one after another near the end of the album, they have a jarring effect on the listener, like someone placed a trio of generic alt-rock staples from 1999 on the CD as a joke.

The best way to wash the aftertaste of those misfires out of your mouth is to pick up the deluxe edition of "Weezer," which includes four Cuomo-sung bonus cuts, including fan favorite "Pig" and the heart-laid-bare "Miss Sweeney," about a real estate executive who secretly pines for his secretary.

Pound for pound, The Red Album is another solid effort from the elder statesmen of emo. And although this album doesn't come close to matching the decade-defining influence of Weezer's first two outings, it definitely gets points for *not* trying.

title: Was it really a golden age?  You decide.
text:
As a twenty-year collector of psychedelia and longtime fan of the major San Francisco acts, this latest box set celebrating the 40th anniversary of the Summer Of Love was welcome. Even the most avid collectors will be hard-pressed to have heard every one of the obscure acts in this set, especially the ones represented on disc two. The box comes with an outstanding booklet featuring many rare photos and comprehensive liner notes, although the real focus is the music itself. After so many decades of being recognized as a "golden age", one gets to hear for oneself if all those dozens of obscure hippie bands produced anything of lasting worth.

For starters, it must be stated that this box only covers one aspect of the SF sound; the 20-minute guitar jams do not appear, although the single version of "Dark Star" does. The verdict on what is there is mixed; the major San Francisco acts were all great, although the ragbag
of more obscure acts, while incredibly diverse in sound and style, run the gamut from incredibly dated to surprisingly listenable. This is essential for any fan of the period, but for the cream of the SF sound I'd buy releases from the major acts (Dead, Airplane, Big Brother, Steve Miller, Santana)before this.

title: Don't listen to those critics
text:
For some reason or another, everyone and their favorite magazine is raving about Half-Handed Cloud as if he were the Next Big Thing, today's answer to the Beatles and Bob Dylan. For me, this guy does nothing but confuse me a bit.
Believe me, I tried to make myself comfortable with John Ringhofer's little ditties here (with emphasis on "little"; most songs last no longer than one minute). No success was made, however. Ringhofer doesn't give his songs time to resonate with the listener, changing tracks just when a melody is becoming interesting.
Even if we were given songs that actually stayed around for over two minutes, I doubt it would help. Aside from the quirky nature of them, the songs of Half-Handed Cloud lack edge and substance. They tend to sound like something John Lennon might've written when he was two. Ringhofer's vocals, while praised by the likes of Bandoppler Magazine and others, I find annoying; the faded-out sound quality to them may be his style, but it certainly won't help with publicity.
Even lyrically I was disappointed. Ringhofer seems to be living in a happy-Jesus world where no one ever doubts and God is always looking down with love. Major throw up material, if you ask me. Give me Nick Cave any day.
In conclusion, pass by this one black sheep in the Asthmatic Kitty family. Instead, I recommend Sufjan Stevens, a true artist, musically and spiritually. He may not have as many songs as Half-Handed Cloud, but he sure knows how to write them.

title: My one time favorite band... hasn’t aged well...
text:
Wow. The album was offered for streaming on prime music, so without much optimism, I listened to the latest from the band I once loved with all my heart. What is it about running into an ex that hasn’t aged very well, that makes you question if they were ever really as beautiful as you’d imagined? I think U2 at one point in time really felt heartfelt, and fresh if not prescient, and they had the capacity for rallying their fans...But at some point maintaining their spirit flipped to contrivance. I thought they were better when they embraced the irony of all that hope they carried with them after they blew up after Live Aid, but the fans couldn’t let them escape their earnestness, and it all started to ring a little hollow.
Now, the band is by self-acclaim experienced. Their experience seems to be more like a hollow echo chamber of the past optimism, hope and nurturance that lifted them to the heights of popularity—so why does it leave me feeling so sad and lifeless? As I listened to the songs, several of which had been previously released, the emotions seemed hollow and a bit maudlin. Not quite maudlin... I had to look up synonyms, and found this one:
bathos
[bey-thos, -thaws, -thohs]
noun
a ludicrous descent from the exalted or lofty to the commonplace; anticlimax.
insincere pathos; sentimentality; mawkishness.

I wanted to find even one great song here! I loved U2!

title: A One Song Album
text:
'Maybe I'm Amazed' that anyone would still be listening to this. With the exception of one song, this simplistic album is loaded with lackluster, weakly written and minor arrangements. That song, "Maybe I'm Amazed", is the rose among the thorns. It's like someone threw together scraps from a one man jam session and hurriedly released them. There seems to have been a race to see which Beatle could get out the first post Beatle album. Paul really should have waited and put more effort into this. Definitely not a shining star in his solo career.

The reason that this album was critically panned when it first came out was that everyone was familiar with the Beatles' musical persona. This came out riding on their coat tails. I'm not sure anyone realized that the Beatles were really going to break up. Paul is a much better artist than this shows and his other achievements prove this. I don't know if he pushed the production of this too fast or what, but this is one album that should have remained on the farm for more work. A serious collectors album. Buy this only if you must have his first solo album otherwise skip and buy his better produced "RAM", his second solo work, or move on to his 'Wings' days.

title: GLORIOUS "COMPLETE" RECORDING OF A TRUE CLASSIC . . . .
text:
NBC Radio. February 23, 1953. Marvin Miller, announcer:

"Ladies and gentlemen, The Railroad Hour. (train whistles) And here comes the star-studded show train. (Theme music: orchestra & chorus) Tonight the American Association of Railroads presents Noel Coward`s operetta, BITTER SWEET, starring Gordon MacRae and his guest, Dorothy Warenskjold. Our choir is under the direction of Norman Luboff and the music is arranged and conducted by Carmen Dragon. Yes, tonight another big musical hit is brought to you transcribed by the American Railroads, the same railroads that bring you most of the food you eat, the clothes you wear, the fuel you burn, and all the other things you use in your daily life. And now, here is our star, Gordon MacRae!"

BTV (before TV), my sisters and I would gather around the radio practically every Monday night for The Railroad Hour. It was never an "hour" show, debuting on ABC radio on October 4, 1948 with guests Dinah Shore and Jane Powell. The show was GOOD NEWS, condensed to 45 minutes. On May 2, 1949 the program switched to a 30-minute format -- SHOWBOAT with guest Lucille Norman. On October 20 of the same year it moved to NBC Radio, where it stayed through its final show on June 21, 1954 -- THE NEW MOON, also with Ms. Norman. I don't know how many of the 299 episodes I heard (a lot), but BITTER SWEET - "Coward's shameless attempt to revive sentimental operetta" - remains a particular favorite of mine.

Maybe it's because BITTER SWEET is, if anything, a nostalgic show. The heroine, Sarah Millick - now the Marchioness of Shayne - recounts her life story at a party. Forty-five years earlier, ". . .she fell so desperately in love with her handsome young singing master that she threw it all away in order to be with him. In Vienna, five poverty-stricken years later, her adored Carl is killed in a duel. But his music lives on as the self-reliant Sarah earns fame throughout Europe with her singing. Finally returning to England, she marries the elderly Marquis of Shayne who has waited so patiently for her." -- The Guide to Musical Theatre

Sure, the plot is corny, but the music is magnificent. "I'll See You Again," the theme song of the operetta, is probably Noel Coward's best known song, and a true classic. There's also the rousing "Tokay," magnificently sung by Donald Maxwell; "Dear Little Café," the Act Two duet for Sarah & Carl; the quartet "Ladies of the Town;" and "We All Wear a Green Carnation," sung by four overdressed, 1890s dandies; "Zigeuner," Sarah's big song in the final act; and my personal favorite, "If Love Were All," which includes the poignant phrase "I believe that since my life began/The most I've had is just a talent to amuse."

Noel Coward's BITTER SWEET does more than merely amuse. Its soaring melodies and sophisticated lyrics actually have the power to lift the listener to a higher, better place. The production by the New Sadler's Wells Opera is absolutely first rate, with outstanding vocal work by Valerie Masterson as Sarah, Rosemary Ashe as Manon, & the previously mentioned Donald Maxwell. I tried to like Martin Smith (Carl Linden) but would have preferred a bigger, more operatic voice - Frank Porretta would have been ideal. But it's a minor quibble. The large supporting cast of singers is also outstanding.

Very highly recommended. It's so good to hear melodies like these sung so gloriously. How unfortunate that its no longer feasible to mount shows like this (or THE GREAT WALTZ or KISMET, etc.) anymore.

'The Missing Link', 'La La' and 'Our Time' are just as lovely.  I'm hoping once my copy of her debut ep arrives I can cobble a good 45 minute mix tween the two with the best tracks. title: A Truly BRILLIANT Singer
text: Napoli's own (although born in New York), Sal Da Vinci is a well-kept secret here in the States.  This 2008 recording demonstrates Da Vinci at his very best, from his self-written songs, "Canto Per Amore" and "'Nammurate" (a hit single in Italy) to the more classic songs of yesteryear, "Anema E Core", "Malafemmena", "Torero" (a hit single for Renato Carosone, in America in the late 1950's), and the (almost) Italian National Anthem, "O Sole Mio", this recording should hopefully put him on the map.  Italian-Americans, particularly those whose ancestors came from Naples, may already be familiar with Sal Da Vinci, as his father, Mario Da Vinci, was a singing star in Italy as well.  The younger Da Vinci appeared with his father on record and in Italian films as a boy - as well as on Italian television (RAI) on  "Viva Napoli" and "Napoli: Primo e Dopo" - and his geneology may explain his amazing vocal talent, his soulful approach to singing and his superb ability to touch the listener. He is NOT one of those pleasant but throw away singers who think they can sing a familiar melody and crest along on the feel good memories of the listener - he is an Artist, whose song interpretations touch the heart and emotions of those lucky enough to hear him.  I have played this CD over and over since buying it from Italy and I truly believe that Sal da Vinci is the finest singer around today - bar none!  I recommend this recording, needless to say, without reservations.

title: Greatest Opeth Album Ever!
text:
I am a huge fan of Opeth, and although every album they've ever released is a 5+ star album, there is just something really special about Still Life.

If you've never heard it before Still Life is a concept album about the narrator(whose name is never mentioned) and his love interest Melinda. The narrator of the story has just returned home after spending several years in hiding, or banishment?, do to a questionable past. The reason for his return is of course Melinda, however fate is definately not on their side. Too keep from ruining the story I will only say that this is a very poetic, beautiful, and epic tale with many twists and turns leading to a climatic ending.

Still Life is not only amazing lyrically however, the music and singing heard here is really quite astonishing as well. Like all Opeth albums there is an excellent mix of heavy death metal music with beautiful acoustic interludes with folk and progressive influences. Mike's vocals are at his best here with a great combination of growls, screams and clean singing that can change on a dime.

My personal favorite tracks are "The Moor", "Godheads Lament", "Face of Melinda", and "Serenity Painted Death". Simply brillant music all the way through. Any fan of Opeth should definatlely have this album. Anyone new to this band should approach it with patience and an open mind. It may take a few listens to get into if you're not use to the more extreme side of metal but overall fans of any kind of music could get into this album if given a chance.

title: Disappointing New Moon
text:
[[ASIN:B0029O08WA The Twilight Saga: New Moon Soundtrack]]
Disappointing New Moon Soundtrack, January 10, 2010
By Robert J. Niemic

Review of "The Twilight Saga: New Moon Soundtrack"
Not too much is worth listening to on the "New Moon Soundtrack" (by various artists) album. The only super rock track is "Meet Me on the Equinox" by the very versatile Death Cab for Cutie. This track has been widely released already for radio/Web channel play, MP3-download, and as a music video. The video is on the "New Moon Soundtrack Deluxe Version" (CD & DVD), along with not much else extra -- unless you're interested in a recording of an interview with Death Cab for Cutie.

Surprisingly, the second best song on the "New Moon Soundtrack" is the soft piano track called "New Moon (the Meadow)" performed by Alexandre Desplat. What's surprising is that I'm predominantly a fan of Alternative Rock & Rock music. It's an indication of how mediocre the other tracks are, if I prefer the soft piano piece to nearly all others. The Desplat-composed melody is an original score work for the movie. Reportedly, Desplat is a "new French composer." He's the composer of the movie's score, which, FYI, as a whole is no where nearly as good as the song "New Moon (the Meadow)."

I'm disappointed in The Killers' track, "A White Demon Love Song." Although not completely without merit, I find it's moody and basically lackluster, even though I'm a super fan of The Killers. This track fits the melancholy theme of the whole album. Even the remix track by the super, new group Muse is low key; I'd rate this my third favorite song. Tied for third is "Hearing Damage" by Thom Yorke, which was very effectively used with visuals in the film.

If I had to rate the quality of some of the other tracks, I'd list the following (in no particular order) as worthy of at least one listening: "Monsters" by Hurricane Bells. "Friends" by Band Of Skulls, "Rosyln" by Bon Iver & St. Vincent, and "The Violet Hour" by Sea Wolf.

The New Moon movie by the way is fantastic--just about as good as Twilight.

title: Long-awaited studio recording
text: I struggled for a moment when considering how many stars to give this album.  I mean, its a great album -- one of the best ever by the NGDB -- but its not [[ASIN:B000087DSO Uncle Charlie & His Dog Teddy]] (Liberty Records 1969).  But what is?  Uncle Charlie set the standard for country-rock that has never been matched.  So what do we have here?  The opening cut, "Tulsa Sounds Like Trouble To Me," is classic Dirt Band from the opening Jimmie Fadden harmonica and the great Jeff Hanna vocal.  OK, I'm into it already.  But what got me hooked was that there were not just a handful of keepers, but the entire album was filled with songs I'm going to want to put on my MP3.  "Resurrection" is getting a lot of press, and its worthy of download.  But I was very surprised by a couple of Bob Carpenter songs -- "Earthquake" and "Something Dangerous."  "Earthquake," written with John McEuen, is one of the few Dirt Band attempts at western swing and a great protest song to California's seismic living conditions. OK, can someone set up a tour with Asleep at the Wheel??  Do you need to be more impressed?  This album was recorded "live" -- meaning everyone was in the studio playing simultaneously (the norm these days is for each instrument to be recorded separately).  Also, I'm still amazed to think that Jimmie Fadden plays the harmonica and the drum set at the same time (and in between breaths he lays out harmony vocals).  Buy it, download it, whatever.  You'll spend the first day boogying, and the next day memorizing the lyrics, even if it isn't Uncle Charlie & His Dog Teddy.

title: Stranded sounds like the past and future all at once with its ...
text:
There has never been a band that so effectively bridged the gap between the conventional and the avant-garde as Roxy Music did on their five albums recorded between 1972-1975. Variously associated with glam and the art-rock scene, Roxy managed to transcend these critical labels, carving out a unique sound and style that set them miles apart from their contemporaries. Their third release, Stranded finds the band at the peak of its powers, which is surprising given the fact it is a pivotal record, being the first without the enigmatic Brian Eno. Stranded sounds like the past and future all at once with its smattering of pop, rock, gospel, and electronic experimentation. Honestly, it's not far removed from the self-titled debut and sophomore effort For Your Pleasure, offering moments of pop euphoria ("Street Life") and atmospheric contemplation ("A Song for Europe"), but ultimately Stranded proves to be a stronger album, with an overall consistency that was lacking on the previous two records.

Songs take unexpected twists and turns ("Mother of Pearl"), Jekyll and Hyde-interludes appear from out of nowhere ("Amazona"), with a wide array of skillfully-played instrumentation adorning the proceedings including some truly dazzling guitar courtesy of Phil Manzanera, tasteful piano, saxophone, and even oboe. All of this acts as a foil to the signature element of Roxy Music- the distinctive voice of Bryan Ferry. Chances are Roxy Music would have sounded a lot more pedestrian without Ferry's vocal style. On Stranded, his exaggerated croon acts as the yin to the yang of the music, with each playing the foil to the other, adding to the overall beautiful strangeness of the songs themselves. It's almost impossible to imagine anyone other than Bryan Ferry in this role.

Stranded provides a case study in how a great album is often more than the sum of its parts. Case in point is the opening blast of "Street Life" and the somber closing "Sunset," both of which are good songs on their own, but placed in their respective roles as bookends make them that much stronger. Despite the fact that it contains what is probably Roxy's single greatest moment, the epic "Mother of Pearl," Stranded is an album lover's album best experienced in its entirety, played from beginning to end, and digested as a whole. This allows the listener to fully appreciate the scope of the diverse compositions, with no two songs sounding alike, morphing from manic to reflective sometimes within the space of a song, displaying Roxy Music as sonic alchemists wildly experimenting in the laboratory to thrilling results.

Stranded may not be the most immediate listen of the classic Roxy albums. It takes perhaps the longest "to get", but once gotten it unquestionably holds top position. Nobody has made music like this before or since. Roxy Music is intelligent, refreshing, unique, arty, dreamy, decadent, and fun...and never more so than on Stranded.

title: a personal, reflective space
text:
At the time of release, I had mixed feelings about this album. Give Me Love was a fine song and single, but didn't move me like My Sweet Lord or What is Life did. When I bought the album, I was definitely let down.
In retrospect, however, this is one of Harrison's finer accomplishments. Compared to what came after (Dark Horse and Extra Texture), it is a masterpiece. The songs and production lack viceral energy, and side 2 particularly bogs down in slow, preachy songs. But the album does have a unity, and at least the songs seem complete and assured, unlike the songs on Dark Horse or Extra Texture, which lack focus, melody and a strong singing voice (the only good songs on those two albums are the singles, Dark Horse and You).
Harrison would make a bit of a comeback with 33 1/3 and the self-titled George Harrison, the later being perhaps his most under-rated effort. But this is the last grasp of the brass ring for George. After this, his work was not an automatic commercial blockbuster, and it would take 14 years for him to have another top 5 album. He did have a #1 single with All Those Years Ago off Somewhere In England, a mediocre album carried by that single. The single enjoyed the popularity it did primarily because it joined the 3 ex-Beatles in a "tribute" to Lennon. I did not care for the song. It started life with completely different lyrics; Harrison rewrote the "tribute" lyrics after his label rejected the album initially and Lennon was murdered. He then asked Paul to overdub his bass and voice on the track. It felt and sounded forced, unlike McCartney's touching ode on Tug of War, Here Today.
At any rate, this is Harrison's personal statement, stripped of the Spector wall of sound. It certainly exposes Harrison's weaknesses, both as a songwriter and singer. But it is the strongest work he would do until George Harrison in 1979 and ranks as one of his 4 best releases.

title: Way out there! The strangest Madonna album
text:
Just to be clear, I love Madonna! She's never released an album I didn't like. She's never released an album that sounded alike. She's never really released a horrible album.......But this??? I don't know. I don't know exactly what Madonna was going for here. Madonna has built a career, an over 30 year career at that, on killer pop tunes. Her songs are legend: "Holiday", "Vogue", "Like A Virgin" --Just to name a few. At this point Madge has absolutely nothing left to prove. She's one of the biggest selling artists of all time. She is UNDOUBTEDLY the Queen of Pop. No question!

So with that said, why THIS? Madge has always been an innovator, but this album is odd. A lot of the album features Madonna (or rappers.....most of the time rappers) singing in other languages. Most likely it's Spanish or Portuguese. That's kinda strange, but there were always songs in Madonna's catalog where she incorporated a Spanish feel or lyrics ("Who's That Girl", or most famously "La Isla Bonita"). Usually these songs are quality or even (In the case of "La Isla Bonita") classics. This? Not so much

Pointblank Madonna speaks in foreign tongue too much on "Madame X". It's a detriment, because typically u can't understand the language. Also the rappers detract from the album and generally add nothing to it. I wasn't too fond of the first single "Medellín". I found the cha-cha references --though fun-- played out. The hook to the song is good though and it's great hearing Madonna sing it. Other than that the song is forgettable. I hated "4 Minutes" and after listening to "Medellin", I don't know what's worst? At least I can say I understood "4 Minutes" though. I have no idea what "Medellin" is about. O.o

"Killers who Are Partying" reminds me of American Life. It's topic heavy, but it has a foreign language hook (likely Spanish) that actually works. In fact it's the best part of the song. I like that one. I also like "Crazy". It too has a great hook and the production adds to the song. Madge wrote some great lyrics on "Madame X" they're just meshed in with incomprehensible foreign language lyrics. If I wanted a foreign language release I couldn't understand, I would've purchased a Selena album.

In general this album is a let down. The hooks are often in Portuguese or Spanish. She's trying to force feed us important lyrics that go over our heads. Madonna was a fun pop singer, but this album is dryer than a history book. The fun Madonna is gone and she's taking herself too seriously. The first time I heard the "American Life" album on its release date it went over my head as a 12 year old. "Madame X" is worst. Even when u think a song's gonna be fun based on its title, "Bitch I'm Loca" lets u down. "Madame X" is by far the most out there Madonna album and will only appeal to Madonna fanatics. There are some good songs here, but in general "Madame X" does not benefit by it's grand ambitions and is overbearing. This is an album to be meditated over. "Madame X" is an album that can spark debates. But it's too heavy and serious 4 most listeners.

title: Not That Bad!
text: I wish I could give this one 2 1/2 stars.  I don't have the heart to give it three (why others are giving this thing 5 stars is beyond me).  I don't know why so many people criticize these sessions so much.  Yes, it's a bit  disco, but people forget--or are too embarrassed to admit--that disco is  not a bad word.  Sure, disco unfortnately had a lot of bad performers, but  it also kept dance music alive during a time when dancing in popular music  was near extinction.  Also, disco fused together two important subcultures:  gay and Black.  It's an obvious choice, actually, that Elton would record  this type of record, given his soul leanings (and he proved on Philadelphia  Freedom that he coul write/record a heck of a Philly soul number).  This EJ  disco/soul offering is a lot more fun than the horrid Victim of Love  (horrible, not so much because it was disco, but because it was Euro-disco.  i.e. Disco minus the fun, minus the soul).  I have to admit, however, that  some of the songs drag on a bit too long.  Disco songs are meant to go  long, of course, but some of the cuts on this record just aren't strong  enough to last 6+ minutes.  Still, this album is one of EJ's more  consistent, enjoyable efforts during a 1978-1981 down-time of dull releases  such as A Single Man, 21 at 33, and The Fox.

title: Gimme That Good Ol' Time Rag'n'Roll
text: When "Rolling Stone" magazine first reviewed "Hollywood Dream", it trumpeted the arrival of a new pop music genre: "rag and roll". Well, such lofty assertions never materialized, but lucky us, Thunderclap Newman created a wonderful one-of-a-kind album. The music could be described as "The Who Goes Ragtime" to mid-tempo timing, and if the tunes do remind one of The Who's early rhythm section, it's because Townshend himself plays the bass uncredited. But John "Speedy" Keen is the star here who, as the main writer, singer and multi-instrumentalist, gives Thunderclap's only release its whimsical, carefree feel. His consistent writing has dated elements, but it never devolves completely into hippy values. Andy Newman, the other talented multi-instrumentalist and sole surviving member, provides the disk's nostalgic movements, evoking an authoritative visitation of Hollywood's Gilded Age. The other star member, precocious Jimmy McCulloch, who at 15 years of age is already playing with the ferocity of those in established bands, provides Thunderclap's edge and keeps the disk driving at a good clip. This music is not psychedelic, but is definitely a product of its time. It's also one of the few albums from the time that isn't overtly dark and issue-laden. The lead single is the obvious standout, but I'd like to cherish the merits of "Accidents", "Open the Door, Homer", "The Reason", and "Hollywood Dream (instrumental)". It's a bummer that Thunderclap Newman only gave us a handful of live dates and a short list of studio recordings of the type of music that other bigger bands such as The Beatles and The Stones only hinted at. Buy this disk because it's tasteful music: a confident marriage of ragtime and hard pop that really works well together.

In fact, I think this is one of her best recordings. And Gobbi: what can I say? He gives an incredibly powerful performance of one of his greatest roles. His scenes with Callas are so powerful. And, as a previous reviewer said, I don't know why some reviewers are always putting di Stefano down. His performance is the equal of Callas' and Gobbi's. I absolutely loved his great duet with Callas.
It's amazing that Callas, di Stefano, and Gobbi all sang together on the stage only once (La Traviata in 1951). Their studio recordings are all wonderful, and they make a great combination.

title: World Sinfonia degraded by synthesizers
text:
Al Di Meola's first [[ASIN:B0000034CH World Sinfonia]] remains one of the favorites in my entire collection of over 700 CDs, but The Grande Passion doesn't live up to its origins.

Where the original World Sinfonia featured expressive and energetic synergy among the musicians, The Grande Passion partially substitutes passionless synthesizers, which is especially ironic given the name of the album. I'm not opposed to synthesizers when they are not trying to sound like anything other than what they are (synthetic instruments), but I despise them when they are used as deficient imitations of real instruments. On The Grande Passion, Di Meola himself plays synthesized parts for bandoneon and panpipes among other instruments (using a Roland GR30 guitar synth), and spoils the effect of what would have otherwise been a steller outing.

The compositions on The Grande Passion are worthy of its title, but sadly, the execution isn't. Al, why oh why didn't you just hire musicians to play those parts on real instruments? Dino Saluzzi (who marvelously played bandoneon on the first World Sinfonia) is sorely missed on The Grande Passion.
