title: Well-Scrubbed Bluegrass
text:
Jeff White's "Broken Road" CD is great bluegrass fun for the whole family! The title tune has great banjo & fiddles with good lyrical depth, "In another rhelm where no one dwells, I wait here endlessly for another soul on this broken road to beckon faithfully*." Great banjo picking highlights the country "Lonesome As It Gets." "Stay Away From Me" is a fast pretty little tune. "Cliffs by the Sea" is a slow ballad with a beautiful fiddle part. Fast finger picking is the hallmark of "Rich Gal." There will be "hell to pay" if you "Bet On An Angel," a pretty uptempo melody. "Cheater's Heart" is a another pretty melody about a relationship breaking up, "Where do you turn when the road ahead is crumbling? What do you do when the love you knew is crumbling & you're left with a cheater's heart?" "The Struggle" is a slow sad country tune that makes me feel like I'm back in Iowa sitting in the Little Brown Church again, "One day I saw the Light & I knew I'd won the fight!" "This Lonely Heart of Mine" is a peppy tune with nice harmonies and some fierce mandolin pickin'. Perky fiddle in the bluegrass mode about a young person going away from home dresses up "I'll Make My Way." "I'm Not a Stranger to Love" is an aching slow tune followed by "I Wonder," a midtempo toe tapper. "The Only Girl" is a pretty banjo-picking love song. Jeff's set closes with a spooky ballad with some great manodlin, "The Fiddle in the Trees." Jeff's music is good quality bluegrass, well-scrubbed fun you can play with your kids in the car.
*I couldn't quite tell if he was singing "faithfully" or "fatefully," but I chose the former! :)

title: Purebred old time Chicago jazz from King Mutt.
text: Some exceptionally fine South Side Chicago combo music from 1928 has been collected in one place for the first time. Original copies are exceptionally scarce, and the sound restoration is exceptionally good!  Gennett recorded this ad hoc bunch in hopes of repeating the success enjoyed by Jimmy Blythe's State Street Ramblers a few months earlier.  It didn't happen, but the music's first rate even so.  The nominal leader "King Mutt" was clarinetist Arnett Nelson, who composed "Buddy's Habit" for King Oliver in 1923 and went on to record extensively on Chicago blues sessions in the mid-30s.  Jimmy Blythe is featured on piano and there's a young (I think) trumpet player whose playing is reticent but still bluesy.  The balance of the CD features more small Chicago groups in the same vein. Seven tracks by the Dixie Four/Midnight Rounders feature the rhythm section  from the State Street Ramblers--Jimmy Blythe, Bill Johnson (bass) and Cliff Jones (drums).  They whoop and holler but never at the expense of the music.

title: Quietly Enchanting Collection
text:
Here is an exemplary piano album for all ages, comprising eleven melodious songs of Kevin Kern, replayed quietly in solo fashion. One can hear how the harmony on the left hand nicely complements the melody on the right hand without any instrumental accompaniment, very enchanting for the listeners and more challenging for the performers.

Many songs have already been played solo in piano competitions by tweens and teens, particularly ' Sundial Dreams ' and ' Through the Arbor ', which are delightful piano classics from his debut album. Some are more emotional and heartfelt tunes, especially ' Childhood Remembered ' and ' The Enchanted Garden ', which sound less poignant and more meditative now without additional instruments. Others like ' Pastel Reflections ', ' Imagination's Key ' and ' I Am Always Right Here ' are also very nice and relaxing melodies.

A few songs are replayed in a swifter, andante tempo with a more lively feel, including ' Through the Arbor ' ( more delightful as solo play here ), ' Into the Realm ' ( more joyous than the touching adagio with sythn strings ), ' Hide and Seek ', and ' Remembering the Light '. Overall, each piece of music is a light and graceful enchantment, no weak melody, edgy or heavy tune in this meticulous selection.

The 2002 collection " More than Words " contained the originals of tracks 1, 2, 4, & 5 here. Track 4 ' A Gentle Whisper ' is the solo version of track 14 on the 2002 album erroneously printed as ' Blossom on the Wind '. The cover design of this album reminds one of the pop song " Morning Has Broken " by Cat Stevens.

text:
Yes, it is obvious the guitar god/wizard Porl Thompson is back. Past gems Disintegration and Wish (both dominated by Thompson's whirling guitars) are two of the best in the Cure catalog. The guitars here (by leader Robert Smith and Thompson) on 4:13 Dream are inspired. Ol' Robert sounds a lot more interested and engaging than he did on the lackluster last album. There are tunes one can hum. Everything seems right (light poppy vocals hiding heavy words and complex arrangements) yet feels wrong. This disc sounds like a cover band trying to be the Cure. Good, but not good enough.

The Real Snow White apes the blazing masterpiece Fascination Street (from Disintegration). Sirensong could be Letter to Elise part two. Don't get me wrong: the new songs are decent. Cure fans don't use words like decent. They shoot for distant stars. They dream while awake. They want music that transcends pop music. There is nothing here in the same galaxy as Edge of the Deep Green Sea (from Wish). 4:13 is a dream you're likely to forget...

title: Well, if you MUST, but this CD is a disgrace to Harry James' legacy as a Brunswick and Columbia artist...
text: Oh, come on!  Harry James & his Orchestra recorded (and sold) tons of records for Brunswick and Columbia, and this is the best Sony Music could release?  I'm aware that few masters exist in the vaults, but let's be real.  There were two sides to Harry James, the sweet dance band leader and the jazz trumpeter.  This collection is strictly schmaltz, and not all the better schmaltz, either.  While the complete recordings of the James band featuring boy vocalist Frank Sinatra appear on another collection, Harry's other singers Helen Forrest (represented here by only two measly selections, and ones that aren't difficult to get elsewhere), Dick Haymes (represented by one track here), Buddy DeVito (not represented at all), Johnny McAfee (not represented at all) and Kitty Kallen (not even represented by "I'm Beginning to See the Light," her biggest hit with Harry) deserve better than what's offered in this lousy collection.  Then, there's all the great instrumentals, such as "The Mole," "Ultra," "9:20 Special," "Flash," "B-19," "Strictly Instrumental," "Prince Charming," "Palladium Party," and "Cross Country Jump" to name but a few.  I grew up in the rock n' roll era, but when I heard something that stirred me inside, I had to have it.  Harry James did just that, many years after the Brunswick and Columbia sides were recorded.  Sony's treatment of Harry's catalog is something of which the company should be ashamed.  One of Sony's labels is called Legacy.  Harry James is part of Sony's Legacy and deserves to be treated with some respect.

It is true that the first CD version has drum that is a bit too loud and the cymbals harsh sounding  (like the SM57 mics it was recorded with). In this new version, when the voice and guitar come on track 2, it's much louder, in your face and more detailed. In general the vocal is way more preeminent, the guitar is no longer boomy and sounds more audiophile, the cymbals are delicate (no longer hissing), the bass sounds as if it was recorded yesterday, and the choir tracks are no longer messed up. That's the upside making this a very enjoyable album. However, there is no PROGRESSION anymore. Songs used to progress and explode, but now they are all at full volume from beginning to the end, making it more enjoyable in a car, but less in a audiophile environment. And the drum is, well, almost GONE. I know the original was heavy on the drum side, but now it's a bit light. For 90% of cases, it's a serious improvement, but I miss the warm punch of the drum.

title: The Brainchild. . .
text:
(4.5stars)
Although those days are seemingly waning in this time, given the level of prolificacy maintained by some of our reggae artists, in terms of recording and releasing albums, it is VERY hard to get any one in particular to stand out amongst the pack. Reggae USUALLY doesn't receive the level of push and promotion as its `cousin' hip-hop and r&b and, again, because its not of the question for one artist to release so many different albums per year, it probably wouldn't matter if it did as the question would then shift to exactly which album should receive the publicity. However, that being said, amongst the ten or so artist who, in any year, can be counted upon to deliver multiple releases, there are ways in which one of those projects in particular will gain the most attention of the masses. Probably the first and most common method goes to the record label releasing said album. In previous years if/when an artist release multiple albums the one which would get the most attention would be whichever was recorded for the biggest reggae labels in the world, Greensleeves or VP Records. Simply given the amount of resources these labels had at their dispense, as opposed to some up and coming label who would almost have NO promotion budget outside of whatever they could push online, their releases would stand as THE album to get. Artists like Sizzla Kalonji, Luciano and Turbulence could all fly beneath the radar with several releases for various labels throughout the year, however, when THE album from Greensleeves or VP came, that album, regardless of its quality became `the new' album from whichever particular artist which remained in discussion mostly. An artist can also do something of a crossover to get that album to stand out amongst the pack and it doesn't necessarily has to be a crossover with the biggest label in the world or such actually. Take Sizzla in 2006 who hooked up with US hip-hop mogul Dame Dash to release his much anticipated Overstanding album. That album wasn't exactly critically acclaimed and it wasn't groundbreaking or revolutionary in ANY way, especially when considering the artist, but it received the lion's share of the attention of any Sizzla album in 2006, which was odd considering the fact that he had also released albums for VP and Greensleeves that year as well, respectively. Of course the artist can also take matters into his/her own hands and just do something SO amazing with the QUALITY of an album forcing the masses to pay attention that particular effort more so than others out of fear of just downright missing out and, of course, word of mouth would definitely travel quickly in such a case (see any halfway decent Midnite album over the past few years as an example of that). Other small things still such as when the album was recorded and who produced it can also help differentiate one of several releases from an artist in any year, making it the most high-profile release of that time.

And then, of course, an artist can just take matters into their own hands altogether, such is the case here with longtime veteran, Anthony B. the Trelawny chanter is a very fine example as he has released (and has had released on his behalf) countless albums many of which have gone very much `under the radar' and as one of the most consistent practitioners of modern roots reggae, his releases usually come with a bit of guarantee in terms of their high quality level. Oddly enough, it was one of his MISSES (and what a MISS it was) that had attracted a great deal of attention and definitely became his most high profile release in recent times, the downright BAD Untouchable album from 2004. I can recall seeing ads for that album in international magazines and flyers and everything, it was actually pretty well promoted as it featured production from hip-hopper Wyclef John and a combination on the album with Jean and American rapper Bone Crusher. and even Snoop Dog as well. After Untouchable he also scored on international radars with albums like 2005's Black Star and of course the earlier pieces like Real Revolutionary, Seven Seals etc., but those were all albums which definitely did their damage within the scope of reggae heads and real hardcore reggae outlets (and I kind of STILL think of the Black Star album as a bit underrated actually) and although they were FAR better albums than Untouchable, they, in actuality, received probably less than half the amount of attention. Since then he has continued to release strong material and has had somewhat of a rebirth of his career as a whole (having been named amongst 2007's comeback reggae artist of the year by more than one respected source) and now Anthony B brings what is most likely his most high profile release since Untouchable, the self executively-produced, self penned (DUH!), self arranged and self released Life Over Death. Earlier in the year the news spread that the artist was seeking an outlet for the releasing of his latest creation only to have the `stars' not properly aligned apparently and he took to placing out Life Over Death on his own dollar and his own Born Fire Music. The album was initially planned for only digital release and it did enjoy quite a healthy releasing through many of the digital services and it quickly gained a very strong underground-ish following (the same following which Batch's WICKED Vizionary now currently enjoys) and now it comes to a full release as the disc itself now reaches the masses and does so wonderfully as, at least to my opinion, Life Over Death definitely becomes one of the strongest albums of Anthony B's entire career! This one perhaps just came along at an odd time because it downright mystifies me that neither VP Records nor Greensleeves (which are now one in the same, but at the time would have been two different entities) would take a chance on such an album from an undoubtedly high profile reggae artist, especially given both label's past with releasing Anthony B album (and their futures, more on that later). Whatever their reason, its their lost and don't let it be yours as Life Over Death features nearly top notch Anthony B throughout and proves to be one of the best reggae albums of 2008, altogether actually.

Life Over Death is a VERY well put together project featuring some of Anthony B's more familiar recent big tunes alongside newer efforts for a big variety of producers with the artist himself taking executive producing and organizing credits. It's similar, in effect, to Bushman's similar effort, also from 2008, Get It In Your Mind, but even better carried out. Getting things started on Anthony B's Life Over Death after a brief opening intro (on which Anthony B seems to embrace himself in the comeback role) is the OUTSTANDING Time Of Trouble. Easily this tune goes near the head of the pack on the album as it is a big VIBRANTLY vibed roots track over a wonderful nyah backing which reminds all that, in times of trouble, first and foremost you need to look to His Majesty. As he wonderfully chants in the middle of the tune, "Pon di road, rocky rocky road, only King Selassie help you carry heavy load!". Indeed! Wonderful way to get things going with one of the album's strongest tunes overall. Holding the unenviable task of following Time of Trouble is a tune in, the very fine Whip Dem Jah Jah which more than merely holds its own. Flowing brilliantly over Stampede's cascading 8806 riddim the tune calls upon the hand of The Almighty to breakdown all those living wickedly and unclean (particularly those of the violent nature) and does so in a very strong way befitting someone of Anthony B's class. Big tune. Completing the opening to the album is the very familiar title track of the album (also known as Don't Worry) over the mighty Istanbul riddim from Purple Skunk (which you know better for having back Jah Cure's HUGE What Would It Take tune). This tune isn't amongst my favourites on Life Over Death, but its still worth more than a few spins definitely showing that Anthony B need not be at his greatest to still offer a bit of shine which is essentially what the title tune is at its core. Very fine way to open things all in all.

If you've been paying attention to Anthony B recently you've noticed that over the past two years or so that he's started focusing on more and more hardcore dancehall producers - the likes of the King Jammy's camp, Stephen McGregor and Mario C and Scatta (the latter of two are featured prominently on Life Over Death). That REALLY comes through on the album as some of it's finest shots come within the dancehall. The biggest of those shots overall is definitely the SCATHINGLY wicked Territory. The tune is actually a remake of an older tune from singer Hopeton Lindo and Anthony B and Scatta definitely do a fine ode to Lindo as the tune even tops the seemingly forgotten modern classic. BIG BIG signature tune for the album there. Immediately following Territory is another such POUNDING tune (this time more modern) Bad From Longtime, a previous single from Life Over Death over Marico C's Streelife riddim. The tune isn't much unlike something you'd hear from one of Anthony B's more dancehall oriented peers very much, but it's a well digestible record coming from him as he doesn't take it to the place of being over violent or sexual for no reason and later on in the track he begins to add more (lyrical) roots elements as well. Later on the heavy dancehall `artillery' rolls in, in the form of BIG hit Tease Her. Probably the single greatest chunk of evidence given his return to the game, the Mario C produced Tease Her rather quickly became one of the biggest hits of Anthony B's entire career which was surprising considering the fact that its quite, but not over, slack which isn't his style. And two later hardcore dancehall efforts take things to even higher heights. Check the WICKED The Beast which somewhat of a harsh autobiographical tune to a degree besides all the typical dancehall bravado. The results are rather convincingly one of the best tunes on the album altogether indeed. And lastly on the dancehall side is the album closer for Life Over Death, Nuh Clash Wid Man, another of the BIG hits from this album. The tune comes in over Scatta's wonderfully old school vibed Sting 93 riddim and is somewhat comical as Anthony B simply says he isn't into the clash or friendship business with men, instead he turns his attentions (and rightfully so) to the Ce;ciles, Macka Diamonds and Lady Saws of the world (and even, HILARIOUSLY, the legendary Marcia Griffiths!). This is the tune with that tune and you know you've been looking for it, here it is! Excellent way to end things. It is, however, an Anthony B album, so he definitely doesn't just leave the roots heads barren of vibes after the very nice and roots heavy beginning for Life Over Death. Check the very strong and high-stepping Caan Do Wi Nuttin. To my ears, this tune is very much in the landscape of the older high powered roots tracks which Anthony B has produced over the years so nicely without really leaving the scope of what is roots music. It also has a very anthem-like vibes to it with a very `sing-a-long' chanting type of chorus as Anthony B calls oppressed people all over the world to action to begin to tear down oppression. Big vibes there. There's a tune here by the name of Sleeping In The Rain which I don't too much like (speaking of anthem and sing-a-long), as I think it's a little sappy sounding, but it has really began to grow on me in recent weeks (incidentally, about that tune, the new things I'm reading (and Anthony B himself for that matter) are all saying that it features the legendary Toots Hibbert, but on my version, which is one of the older one's the legendary Maytals' front man is nowhere to be heard), so check that one out, but do so cautiously. Sleeping In the Rain also follows a HILAIOURSLY FAMILIAR interlude by the name of Mama & Rasta which I'll leave for you to hear and won't ruin at all, but check that as well definitely! I'll also mention the BIG (Not) Mr. Easy for Birchill's Ghetto Blues riddim (which you know from Wayne Wonder's hit tune, Again). The tune, at its heart, is a relationship tune and one for the ladies (and to you hardcore heads listen carefully and tell me if that isn't either the same or almost the same melody from the tune I Understand on the Black Star album???). Lastly I'll mention the tune When You Down (Childhood Memories had been getting a bit of attention, but I don't like it). When You Down is a big tune definitely, on a very nice and inspirational vibes, the tune just really got to me and stuck out amongst the rest as one of the real highlights here and leading into Nah Clash Wid Man is a very nice way to set the vibes up high going into the end of Life Over Death from Anthony B.

Overall, there was a time very early in the year when I had Life Over Death as my favourite reggae album of 2008, period. Although that's well changed since then (due to a BLAZING young August Town native), I'll definitely be including it on my list (which I'll be making any day now) as it is really that good. As I said, the album coincides what is probably better called a reawakening of Anthony B's career at the top flight (you can't call it a comeback when he only took like a month or two off actually, he just wasn't scoring hits for awhile, in my opinion) and its definitely catching him at a great streak and is an album showing that quality and class. Its absolutely a wonder why this one wasn't picked up on a greater level ESPECIALLY considering that my own personal choice for January 2009s most anticipated reggae album is definitely Rise Up, which just happens to be yet another album from Anthony B, released via Greensleeves. If that one is anywhere near as good as this one, then it's definitely something to look forward to. As it is, Anthony B's Life Over Death is recommended to fans of modern roots reggae, preferably those with a taste more towards the dancehall of course. Life Over Death is easily the most high profile album that Anthony B has had in quite some time and if you haven't been paying attention its also one of his best. He releases countless pieces every year which probably past beneath your radar, allowing this one to do the same is your mistake. One of 2008's finest.

title: Update
text:
There are already twenty-two reviews of this CD set, 19 of them 5-star and many of them ample in their analyses. This is by far the most exciting performance of Il Cimento dell'Armonia available for a reasonable price. The only serious competition is Reinhard Goebel's legendary recording with Musica Antiqua Koeln, which is costly.

What's the essence of a Baroque violin concerto? It's utter flamboyance. It's the concert-master violinist, standing forth from the ensemble and fiddling like the very red-haired devil. Fabio Biondi has gained a bit of weight since the days of this recording, and he's played The Four Seasons far too often to have the same enthusiasm as in his youth, but he still presents "la bella figura", standing with his back to the audience while conducting the tutti sections, and then stepping to the edge of the stage to scatter Vivaldi's abbundanza of figurations to the adoring house. One feels the improvisational virtuosity Vivaldi himself must have displayed.

For listeners who are ready to progress beyond the Four Seasons into Vivaldi's huge repertoire of vocal music, I recommend the oratorio Juditha Triumphans, a triumph indeed, and a showcase of bravura singing and brilliant instrumentation.

text: This is a full length album of 6 flawless pop tracks, extended in length to provide the listener with something more than what one would hear on the radio. That's what makes the album so special. Each song is quite different in music styles. You'll hear a mashup of synth and strings on Left To My Own Devices (or is it really all synth?). With I Want A Dog, you'll hear the Chicago House music genre just before it's peak in the early 90s. The Pet Shop Boys were always a step ahead of their peers. Domino Dancing highlights a genre of music called Freestyle influenced by Latin rhythms from the streets of Miami. I'm Not Scared was written for a French pop group Eighth Wonder, lead by Patsy Kensit. What you hear on this version is a dark pounding beat that compliments the lyrics. I never want this song to end! You are already curious about the extended version of Always On My Mind/In My House so I will keep mum. Enjoy! (Side note: back in late 1987, does anyone know who first mixed PSB AOMM into Something In My House by Dead Or Alive for the Friday Night Hot Mix? I've been searching for the connection to Introspective for ages.) The Pet Shop Boys know how to close an album and the final track, It's Alright, is a remake of a Sterling Void song. title: Joe Keeps Getting Better and Better
text:
I read, "Joe did play two shows at the Beacon. Footage from both shows, mostly Saturday, was used for the DVD. First song up is Slow Train. With two minutes to midnight playing in the background, the stage goes black. The train is coming! Joe rips into Slow Train. Next song Joe plays is Cradle Rock." Rory Gallagher would be proud.

17 songs later you let your breath out as you can't remember if you had taken one since the concert started. And that pretty much sums up how I feel every time I play or watch a new offering by Mr. JB.

You grip your lazy boy chair and launch into the second DVD which contains more great tunes plus two bonus songs, "If Heartaches Were Nickels" and "Woke Up Dreaming." Bonus footage on the DVD includes Joe and David Crosby together with David wowing Joe with an acoustic guitar session. Great back stage pictures, photos, and back stage footage.

Guests include Beth Hart, The Paul Rogers and John Hiatt along with his formidable bandmates Carmine Rojas, Tal Bergman, and Rick Melick.

"Beth Hart joins Bonamassa on stage for soulful duets on I'll Take Care of You and Sinner's Prayer, which is featured on the recently released Don't Explain - an album of soul covers Hart recorded with Bonamassa." She has such a smoky sensuous style that keeps you gripping tightly on your seat.

"John Hiatt, a Nashville Music Lifetime Achievement Award recipient and American Music Award (AMA) winner, joins Bonamassa for a rendition of Down Around My Place and I Know A Place." John's near perfect performance highlights the amazing guitar work playing along side.

"As legendary classic rock singer Paul Rodgers (Bad Company, Free) hits the stage, the audience jumped to its feet as Bonamassa performed Fire And Water and Walk In My Shadows." Two classic frontmen, and distinct voices presenting flawless blues rock at its finest.

A magical couple evenings at the Beacon resulting in some of the most memorable performances by Joe and his guests. Joe never falters or misses a beat,his instinct as a performer is uncanny. He always puts together a winning production.

title: Great voice, marginal songs
text:
Wow, there are so many opinions being thrown into this review forum, mostly in the 2 camps of "best ever" and "sell out" camps. Many reviewers have made excellent points on both sides. I'd like to add a few thoughts, and an anecdote.

There are some good songs here: "Sunshine..." and "Mississippi Girl", for example, are catchy and pleasant. Many of the others are merely adequate, elevated by Faith's superb voice and presence. Generally, the album isn't all it could be, which is why so many reviewers are disappointed with this release. Faith usually picks better songs than these, though it's worth admitting that none of her albums has had the consistency in songwriting quality that, say, Jo Dee Messina had on her breakthrough "I'm Alright". Faith's albums are usually half good, half skippable. Her voice is what makes her such a solid artist. Okay, and she's pretty, but when I'm listening to a CD I don't care what the performer looks like. If the song and/or performance are solid, the CD works. As usual with Faith, the performances are great but the songs...well...

But then, after enduring yet another tepid duet with her husband - who also consistently sings and performs well, but releases so-so albums - and more forgettable songs, we get "Wish For You". This is a standout track, a beautiful lullaby for her children and for everyone who can still be moved by the power of innocence and hope. This track alone adds one star to my review.

And then we get "Paris". Amazon's reviewer may find this song puzzling, but I sure didn't. I also can't stop playing it, and it's one of the few tracks I immediately ripped to my computer. This is a 40s-style torch song, and Faith shows off the strength of her voice and the emotional delivery she can bring to a good song. The first time I heard this, I got chills. I think most people would, especially if they could let go of the prejudice that Faith Hill must automatically equal "Country". It's an incredible, powerful song. No, it's not country, but it's not pop, either. It's just good music - and worth another 2 full stars alone.

As for "Mississippi Girl," I have a true story to pass along: A former coworker and his wife and 2 kids stopped at a remote truck stop in the heart of the Midwest several years ago. As they were sitting down with their meals, Faith Hill and Tim McGraw walked into the restaurant with their children. Their entourage followed later, but Faith and Tim sat with my friend and his family so their kids could play together. Obviously everyone knew who they were, but nobody asked for autographs and they never acted like they deserved special treatment. They just sat and talked to another set of parents as their children played and everyone ate. They stayed a couple of hours, just sitting and drinking coffee and talking, and then both families went their separate ways - my friends to their car, Faith and Tim to their tour bus. As my friend told the story, he stressed that both celebrities never acted like they were different or wanted to be treated differently. They acted just like everyone else in that restaurant - good people, good parents, good neighbors.

So when Faith sings "Mississippi Girl," I believe that behind all the glamor and fame, she's still a decent person and a good mother and wife. Being a celebrity changes people, but I don't think it's changed her core values or identity, not yet. Please, give the woman a break - let's not tear her down with all-too-easy cynicism and judgmental scorn. It's just a song, and she's just doing what she does best - singing.

3 stars for her voice, 0 stars for song selection. Next time, Faith, please take some chances and pick stronger songs...

title: It's all good...where are you coming from?
text:
If you like one TOB CD, you'll like them all. If you own one TOB CD, then you probably own them all. To make a TOB "best of" CD would be too tough to pull less than 5 songs from each CD. Almost to a fault, this is one of the most consistent bands for musical quality in composition and style, and that hasn't wavered with DJL. This is certainly the most underrated American band - EVER! (Trash Can Sinatras - most underrated European and of all time.) TOB is the best collection in a long time of individual talent as a complete band. The 70's had Zeppelin and (early) Van Halen, the 80's had The Cure and the Smiths, and TOB should have been the 90's equivalent. America should be ashamed to let this kind of talent and sound slip by for over a decade while garbage like Eminem and Brittany Spears corrode the public taste buds with cultural flattery.
I liked the keyboard element of TOB's music and was skeptical of the last two releases when I heard the keyboardist "left." However, I didn't rule TOB out and I'm glad because I would have been completely wrong. The changes have been mild and worth it. To me, those who are nay-saying the entries from Ronne and Minnig simply refuse to accept change. "Ayn" and "Garden Song" are among my favorite and are great throwbacks to the first two CDs. But the greatness of the first two CDs is not in the style. It's the quality of the songwriting and instrumentation, and that has remained true on DJL. On a musical level, the 3 songs in question are easily as good as the rest. The guitar work and bass line interplay on "Consolation Prize" and BDALL is simple, but well done, and instrumentals like "Cukaloris" always suggest to me that the writer/band values music first. And it's a nice song, too. What baffles me most about the grief given to these 3 songs is that they are great tributes to the bands that inspired TOB. If you don't hear the Smiths, REM and others in these tunes, you're musically deaf. And if you don't like those bands, how did you discover TOB? Go sell your soul to a genre.
"Denmark" is a good song, but for all those who worship it, it is a dry song. It's not that intricate for an album's promotional release. For this reason I think it is overrated by TOB fans. "It Never, Just Might" is my dark horse favorite, with "Cukaloris", "Consolation Prize", "Ayn", and "Denmark" rounding out my top 5. If you want not-so-great songs, "Bottle Yours" drones a bit too much and "So Many Reasons" is as generic as it gets in music. It too has a "Smiths" likeness to it, but sounds a lot like the Smiths songs I didn't like.

title: Neither flesh nor fowl; neither history nor MTV.
text:
I am coming off a long evening of watching and rewatching this film, both beginning to end and piecemeal (sorting out thematic scenes). I had seen it a few times before, but hadn't systematically studied it. The film is neither a performance of the "Eroica" nor a historical pageant about Beethoven's biography, yet it manages to incorporate both of the above into something rather more ambitious. Incorporating a blazing performance of the symphony on period instruments into a reconstruction of its first performance at the Lobkowitz Palace, it manages to make a lot of statements about art, music, biography and history without ever being didactic. The acting is magnificent; understated and mostly mute, it characterizes Prince Lobkowitz and his wife, his arrogant aristocratic cousin, Haydn, various servants and musicians, and Beethoven's poor despised pupil in a few strokes of body language and fewer words. It combines historical fact with biographical speculation, without aggrandizing or overstating either. It's really a film about a moment in musical history, which is best encapsulated in Haydn's few comments towards the end of the film. The performances, both musical and theatrical, are terrific. On my first few viewings, I was bothered by the characterization of Beethoven (a bit too tentative, and too unpredictable in his moods). On further viewing, and further reflection, I think it fits perfectly. As a film biography of a musician and his work, it certainly beats anything else I've seen hands down (the creepy and silly "Amadeus," as exhibit A).

The last two movements of the symphony are played partially in background, behind wrapups of thematic sequences. At first this bothered me (why not play the whole symphony, and put the other material between or after movements?). In retrospect, after a few viewings, I think it puts the music, life, and history into the proper perspective: and after all, it's a film, not a music video.

Final thought: the performance of the symphony is wonderful!

title: But when he was dying, Lord, we let him down
text:
I mean no disrespect to either Janis or Richard by stealing my tagline from "Epitaph," but it does kind of work, doesn't it? Great, soulful talents, gone too soon, and they didn't have to be.

What to say of this album? It's painful to listen to--in both the "good" way and the "bad" way. In the scheme of things wrong with the audio, the tinny piano doesn't make a bit of difference. It's more that, while Richard delivers nicely on an occasional song (Georgia, She Knows, and You Don't Know Me all stand up), there are some wretched moments, too, where Richard's voice and memory are so shot we can hardly listen. I can forgive the overly ambitious attempts to reduce The Band to a piano (like with Chest Fever), or where Richard seamlessly slips into a line from the wrong verse on the otherwise fine Miss Otis Regrets, but he butchers some of the music so badly and, judging from his banter, I don't know that he gets how low he's fallen, or even cares.

In his prime, there was no one better. I'll even trot out a bit of blasphemy and say that when he had it, he could out-Ray Ray himself. But Richard's prime was long gone. It would have been ok if he compensated, if he turned down requests for the songs he barely remembered anymore (as he does at one point in response to a fan shout-out), and if he reworked others to better suit his more limited vocal abilities (like he did for the Last Waltz version of I Shall Be Released, where he scrapped the falsetto).

For the serious fans, this is worth a buy for the occasional moment where he's great on a tune we don't have preserved elsewhere, but some songs are just too painful to listen to. Three stars here might even be too generous, given the totality of the effort. Well, there's no use crying; can't help him now.

title: What alternative really means
text:
The term "alternative" should be used to describe music like this. Rather than being used on anything with distorted guitars, it should describe music that is actually alternative and different from what other people are doing. Well, that is EXACTLY what Fugazi is. 13 Songs is a strange, fascinating ride you won't regret taking.
If you are a fan of Minor Threat, you'll probably be checking this CD out because Ian McKaye is Fugazi's frontman. That's how I heard about Fugazi anyways. But don't buy this thinking it'll harcore punk in the Minor Threat vein - it's not. It's something totally different. While there is without a doubt a punk sound to it, it's not really a punk album. Fugazi is really hard to describe: just buy it. It's good.
The lyrics can be a little strange. Many say they are insightful but unfortunately I think some of them are saying that because they have no idea what they mean. The lyrics of Fugazi don't make their points as blatantly as Minor Threat did (compare a song like "Out of Step" to "Provisional"). The music is catchy and quite funky on a lot of songs, but with punk bite to spare.
To close, buy 13 Songs. It's one of the better CDs of real alternative you can buy. The highlights include "Waiting Room", "Suggestion", "Margin Walker", "And the Same", "Burning Too", and "Promises." Don't miss out on Fugazi.

title: Pops Lives Forever
text:
This is a classic album for fans of Hawaiian music.

I saw Pops once, and only once. But it was an experience. On Maui, I was a teenager, and a new record store was opening in Kaahumanu Center: MJ's Music (long gone now). Gabby was going to play in the afternoon. I was there, leafing through the stacks waiting for it to begin. I recall a skinny young guy with a pony tail standing next to me. He was doing the same as I was, flipping through albums to see what was there. Then a commotion, and things started happening. Gabby and a few older gents were in the house, and a space cleared for them to play. Gabby's bass player, Manuel "Joe Gang" Kupahu was there--he played the "doghouse" (double bass) like a giant guitar! He laid it across his lap. And to my surprise, the skinny guy hopped into the stage area with them. I was thinking "who is this guy thinking he can just jump in with these masters?" But of course, he was none other than Peter Moon, up-and-coming guitar slinger. During the concert, Gabby yelled "Go Peter," and Peter took off on his solo. Then Gabby yelled, "That's enough, boy," and pulled him back to earth. Midway, Gabby yelled "Another one," as he held up his plastic cup. In a corner of the room was an older Japanese lady--a big clear bottle of vodka, and a carton of orange juice at hand on the counter beside her. She looked put out by the request, but she began pouring a drink as fast as she could. She scurried to the stage with his drink. And of course, the store was small, and maybe a hundred max in there. At the very end of the concert, Gabby said "Next time I'll bring my haole son, Ry Cooder." It was magic. The music is gone now--I doubt if anyone had a tape recorder. And I can't recall any of the tunes except "Moonlight Lady." But the impression remains that it was simply great. So it's out there, in the ether. But the album being "reviewed" here (forgive me for being kinda roundabout) is by the same man, at the same time, playing those songs. If you couldn't be there, you can still listen to this.

title: A powerfully conducted Romeo, and a sparkling Classical
text:
Ancerl's early stereo recording of excerpts from Prokofiev's ballet Romeo and Juliet are among the best available. Ancerl imparts added power to the opening Montague and Capulets section (these excerpts are not in the sequence of the two suites, as is the case with other excerpt recordings of this work) by playing it more slowly and emphatically than the norm, thus highlighting the ominousness of its portent of the impending tragedy. Similarly, in his rendition of the final section, that of Romeo at Juliet's tomb, the slow dirgelike way Ancerl performs it effectively underscores the depth and pathos of the lover's sad fate.
On the other hand, his performance of the Classical symphony (this is in mono) has real drive and sparkle, aided and abetted by the vividly pointed sound of the Czech woodwinds.
A very worthwhile purchase.

title: Amongst the best renditions...BUT beware...
text:
This is Horacio Gutierrez's second recording of the Tchaikovsky concerto - the first being with Andre Previn and the LSO in the 70's. A superb, lyrical account. This one is very much in the same manner. It will remind one of a combination of Cliburn's fire and Rubinstein's poetry. Chiseled perfection. The Rachmaninoff is also one of the best in many years. Rather than going off the deep end with its virtuosity, HG, brings sensible and musical sonorities with the right amount of spontaneity and spark of both works. This should be a 5+ rating all the way.

The problem being the recording itself, which is a borderline disaster! A very unusual lapse for Telarc. Not unlike their other recordings, Telarc engineers had compressed the high frequencies - but to a severe degree, as the sound picture is very flat. One will want to completely turn up the treble settings! But also, the overall capture of the orchestra is just not there. Everything sounds like it coming through a foggy swamp. In fact, at worst, the orchestra's hardly audible. It seems sandwiched underneath the piano. To top it off, it's just too dry.

I understand this is one of the Telarc's first recordings in Baltimore and the acoustic in its Symphony Hall was obviously problematic. Fortunately, things improved substantially over the years and the very fine Baltimore players shine through in other performances by Telarc (as in the Rachmaninoff symphonies, also with Zinman).

Anyone seeking Gutierrez' superb earlier version of the Tchaikovsky might be able to find it in a budget priced EMI two-fer (nla) or an import with the Tchaikovsky's violin concerto. Much better sound quality. (So. Cal. classical music listeners will remember Gutierrez' EMI Tchaikovsky concerto recording as the bumper music to KFAC FM's Evening Concert broadcasts...)

title: The idea of concerto
text:
When I listened to these recordings the idea of concerto (to compare/contrast the soloist and the orchestra; even pit them against each other) immediately came to my mind.
Finally I felt that there was a real concerto here. In the past when listening to "modern" orchestral recordings of Beethoven piano concerti I felt that there was no "struggle" between the two forces. There were "big" solo statements and big orchestral statements and big tutti statements, and as much as I liked them something was missing.
The period instruments, including the period piano, made it happen. The period piano is a weaker more delicate instrument than a modern concert grand. The period orchestra had more clarity and a less massive sound. Now the two came together to make a real concerto.
The period piano striving (how Beethoven!) to do more than it really could do. The orchestra attempting to immitate the piano's delicacy and not quite succeeding. Now there was a story here. Now there was art.
I also almost laughed out loud to think of Beethoven REALLY strecthing the limits of his (period) piano and orchestra. Beethoven isn't so much of a "stretch" for the modern orchestra as it is for the period orchestra. The period performance makes Beethoven more real and human to me because I feel more of his reaching and striving.
Gardiner may not have got it exactly as Beethoven intended, but I think much more of the spirit of Beethoven is here than in any recording with modern instruments.

title: The Black Rider is well worth the ride
text:
I recently discovered Tom Waits after checking the credits on the movie, "Smoke" to see who was credited with "Innocent When You Dream." That was about a month ago, and I now have 15 Waits' albums. While "The Black Rider" is not my favorite album, (that nod would go to "Mule Variations"), I do enjoy it very much. It's alot of fun, from the opening carnival barking right into the wonderful title track and "November." The instrumental, "Russian Dance" is so infectious that my daughter and I were dancing around the living room last night, doing an awful imitation of Russian dancing. When you play this track, do yourself a favor and get your feet moving in step. Other good tracks include "The Briar and the Rose," "I'll Shoot the Moon," "Crossroads," "Lucky Day," and "The Last Rose of Summer."
While there are some very touching moments in this album, as a whole I don't think it is to be taken too seriously. Even my wife, who as yet has not quite developed the appreciation for Waits' music that I have, although it is starting to grow on her, had to smile and laugh on hearing some of this album. With much of Waits' other work she is usually scowling. Have fun with this one!

text:
Being a new age & instrumental music fan, I couldn't skip my eyes when I read about Mehdi & its recommendation on Amazon.com. So I bought myself Mehdi Volume 6 & 7 to hear if it's really good.
The first time I pop the CD in my player, playing the "Heaven" track and heard the intro, I instantly liked it. It also lacks proper ending at the end of the song, Mehdi just simply fades it out without a proper "closing". Lacking of a catchy Melody. Suddenly I felt that it just sounds like a game soundtrack.
I also noted that track 1 to track 6 on the Instumental Heaven CD (7th volume) sound flat and little bit muffled (sounds like it was recorded on incorrect equaliser setting and had its low end & high end frequency flattened). Track 7 to 10, however sounds good. Maybe it was intentionally processed that way? In comparison, the 6th album doesn't have this problem.
When compared to the new-age maestro composer such as Secret Garden & Yanni, Mehdi just simply lacks originality and just sounds like another ambience background music.

Note: I don't use any preset/equaliser or any audio enhancement, I just simply play it on my standalone audio CD player.

title: There ARE good pressings out there!
text:
I have spent the weekend with this box set- played all 32 sides of my vinyl and carefully looked over the book and the liner notes while I listened. This review is written by someone who has actually fully experienced this product.

First, I am disappointed with reviewers who are commenting on this box set without having listened to it. Insofar as criticizing where the masters were sourced from, I think the producers have been very forthcoming with these details and it's not fair to slam the product when no attempt was made to misrepresent it in the first place.

Second, I'm sorry to hear there are bad pressings out there- I have gotten vinyl before which is muddy and distorted or where the spindle hole is so badly off center the music is severely garbled by the time you get a few minutes into the record. I know very well bad vinyl from the 21st century when I see it and I'm not surprised to hear the issue appears to have struck yet again. That is very disappointing to hear, but unfortunately it happens so frequently I have come to expect it and I understood the risk when I bought this box set expecting there might be a good chance I would be sending it back to Amazon.

After spending so much time with the box set and reading some negative reviews, I wanted to say all 32 sides of my vinyl sound really great and if you're thinking of buying this you might be encouraged to hear that someone else out there has very nice sounding pressings which is why I felt compelled to share this experience. I did not have any scratched or scuffed up vinyl and the music never sounded muddy or distorted even towards the center of vinyl (as often occurs especially on vocals) even though there were 32 chances for this to happen (and I was nervously awaiting it happening too after reading some bad reviews). I'm very happy with the sound of all 32 sides! This box set is AWESOME and it sounds really great.

Lastly, I do want to say Amazon did a poor job packing this. It was in a box with bubble tape, but the bubble tape was only on one side of the box set leaving the other side only protected by the cardboard shipping box. Boo! Amazon has been doing a much better job with packaging LPs lately compared to a few years back, but at least for me they didn't do a great job packaging this box set. Fortunately, my box set didn't get damaged perhaps in part because the manufacturers inserted styrofoam inserts into the box to protect the records which was a nice touch.

That album has moments of greatness, but never won me over as a whole. I decided to buy 40 oz. because of the Descendents cover "Hope" (which I had never heard, but the Descendents version is killer). I also had read interviews of Brad and he had brought up the Minutemen, whom I consider to be my musical fathers, and how much Sublime liked them. So I bought this album.
This album didn't knock my socks off immediately. It was so varied in musical styles that it was really hard to judge. Every song sounded like it was recorded at a different location. Yet I kept listening to it more and more. I couldn't listen to anything else for quite a while. I had instant respect though for them including a sample from the Minutemen's "History Lesson part 2". I now love the album and I still cannot explain why. What I do know is that Bradley was a genius. He had a God given talent of being an excellent musician and writer. He just had something that not many people have in music history. It is such a shame that he threw it away.
I'm getting all off track. This album is great and if you like anything about reggae/punk or good melodies, you should buy this album. There will NEVER be another album recorded in history that will be like this none, NEVER. These guys took what was inside them an put in on wax. The subject matter may alienate some, but look beyond that. There is something much more important lying beneath. Enjoy!

Well I though Radiohead were some sort of one hit wonders, when they really are because `Creep' was their only hit, but I though it was the only good thing the band ever created so I put this album away for about five years. I pulled this album about a few months ago and gave it a listen, and what was I thinking, These guys are amazing, some of the best lyrics, and music I have ever heard, and Thom York's vocals kill! Maybe I was too young to appreciate the talent and the genius of this band, I don't know but something as up.

`You' is an amazing song, with all the right elements to create an awesome song. Great vocals, catchy lyrics, and nice guitar. The perfect song to start of the album. `Creep' my all time favorite Radiohead song as Im sure it is to many. The lyrics are just so eerie and the vocals and the whole tone and mood of the song is eerie really. The guitar scrap across the strings just before the chorus is the greatest f****ing sound in the world, gives me chills every time I hear the song, it's so amazing. Speaking of chills the vocals at the end to the same thing as well. `How Do You?' is a nice little rocker. It's very British, and very cool. It's actually one of my favorite songs on the album. `Stop Whispering' is much more mellow after the last track, slower and more intimate. Thom Yorks vocal work is very nice on this song. Johnny Greenwood's guitar is also very nice on this song. `Thinking About You' is a nice acoustic song. It's a great love song with very personal lyrics. The lyrics are a personal favorite. Another very good song. It also shows the versatility in the styles that Radiohead is capable of. Maybe now that I think of it `Creep' isn't my favorite song by Radiohead, maybe that title belongs to `Anyone Can Play Guitar.' The song is so perfect and is everything that good rock and roll should be. It's not hard rock or soft rock or punk or metal just straight up rock and roll. The lyrics are so true. The Jim Morrison lines would win any fan of The Doors such as myself over. The guitar is killer and the whole thing just works perfect. `Ripcord' is a really cool song with lots of tempo changes make for an interesting song that never gets boring. `Vegetable' is a slower song, at the start anyways. Soon the guitar picks up and gets really good and the whole song gets really going, until it slows again. This is a very cool song to listen to, its one of my favorite Radiohead song ever. `Prove Yourself' is a pretty cool song but kind of plays like `Vegetable' but with different lyrics and better guitar, so it's not too special but is still a killer song. `I Can't' starts out with a guitar intro then goes into a mellow rocker, if that made any since. This song shows where the band Coldplay took a lot of their influence. `Lurgee' is another slow song it's not one of my favorite songs on the album, in fact it is probably my least favorite song on the album. `Blow Out' is semi-Jazzy and it seems really out of place on the album when you hear about it but when you hear it, it seems to fit in just fine. The end of the album features `Creep' again, and I don't think it's a demo or alternate version because it sounds just like the other one on the album so it seems somewhat pointless to have on the album. The album should have ended with `Blow Out'

So if your into Coldplay then you'll love this because Radiohead is Coldplays heros but harder rocking and with much better guitar playing. Radiohead has been called the best guitar band of today and while I personally don't agree with that it is easy to see where people could draw conclusions like that. Highly Recommended to all

title: Beautiful live CD captures the essence of FIF's final show
text:
I feel lucky that I was able to make the journey to Denver last November to witness the final Five Iron Frenzy concert. The live recording of the show on "The End is Here" manages to perfectly capture the feelings that were present at that show - excitement, sadness, and a big thank-you from the crowd for all the music that FIF has given to us over the years.
When the crowd spontaneously begins a chang of "FIF" before the final song in the show, you get a sense of just how much this band meant to their fans. Hearing Reese sing out "Hallelujah" at the end of "Every New Day" was amazing live, and still sends chills up my spine every time I hear it, as does the crowd reaction at the end. Exactly like what happened in Denver, the crowd goes into a chant of "Thank you" and then goes silent for a moment of reflection. Someone from the back of the crowd begins singing "Amazing Grace" and before long the rest of the crowd has joined in. The concert ends with the band and crowd singing "Silent Night" as the snow falls outside the concert hall.
This was truly one of the most powerful experiences I've taken part in and I'm glad this disc manages to convey that feeling.

text:
Helloween's "Walls of Jericho" wasn't really considered a power metal album moreas it was a speed metal album and Keeper of the Seven Keys would officially kick off what's known as power metal. But this CD isn't far from power metal - it's very melodic, full of Hansen's high pitched vocals, super lead guitar and harmonized lead guitars, powerful drums, and dynamic songs. It's not as melodic as Helloween's later work, but it's still very much their sound. You'll hear Kai Hansen's first performance on vocals, and his voice eventually became more powerful and melodic in Gamma Ray but his influence on this record and the next 2 Helloween albums (albeit guitar-wise as he does not perform vox after this until 1995 Gamma Ray). I love this album a lot, it's got what I like in music (metal in particular and I love power metal the most) - heavy guitars while maintaining good melodies, high pitched vocals and screams for dramatic effect, present bass-guitar, fast and technical drumming, and two guitarists who can shred and perform speedy solos in dual harmonies.

With this package you'll get the remastered CD with a bonus disc. You'll have the album start with the "Helloween EP" on the first 5 tracks then "Walls of Jericho" from then on. The bonus disc has some new mixes, live tracks and B-sides which is worth hearing for Helloween fans.

Helloween fans owe it to themselves to check out their first album to hear where it all started. Highly recommended for your metal collection.

title: SDQ '98 Under Another Title
text:
This is a pretty good album from the vast Doug Sahm/Sir Douglas Quintet collection, but Sahm fans should be careful; you may already own this. This is a German version of an album that came out in the U.S. three years ago entitled "SDQ '98." This is exactly the same release, with a new title and cover photo. I dock it one star for the confusion and/or deception.
As for the music, Sahm fans will be happy with this CD. It is a nice mix of the familiar and obscure, Sahm's usual stew of country, blues, tex-mex and rock & roll, and it includes a nice remake of "Give Back the Key To My Heart," a '70's Sahm original that Doug re-recorded with Uncle Tupelo on their final album in 1993. Another nice surprise is the verison of "St. Olav's Gate," a Tom Russell song.
This album was recorded over a five year period, and although credited originally to Sir Douglas Quintet, SDQ is seemingly only present on some of the tracks. SDQ organist Augie Meyers sings "The Ballad of Davey Crockett" and shares vocals with Sahm on another song.
Sahm completists will want this release, and if you don't own "SDQ '98," you will probably enjoy this CD. But make sure you don't own this already under its earlier title.

title: The Best since "Soft Bulletin"
text:
After "The Soft Bulletin", easily one of the 5 best albums of the 90's, I was somewhat disappointed with the Flaming Lips' follow-up, "Yoshimi". "At War with the Mystics" is a step back in the right direction.

The band's lyrics are obviously getting better as they get older, though that's still not the strength of their albums. The strength of this record is in the music. The instrumental tracks, "The Wizard Turns On" and "Pompeii at the Twilight of the Gods" are like Meddle-era Pink Floyd reborn. The entire first half of the record is stellar. The second half starts a little weak with the uninspired "It Overtakes Me", but picks up to finish quite strong. The final track, "Goin' On", features expressive vocals and a nice piano part that makes for a bittersweet yet satisfying finale.

I believe the band is back on the right track with this record. "The Soft Bulletin" set a very high bar for this band, and while I don't think they quite reached that level with this record, this is definitely a 5-star outing.

title: Pretty Pictures and Music Haphazardly Organized
text:
The only other DVD in this 'Musical Journey' series of DVDs from Naxos that I've seen is the one about Scotland, and it was dreadful. This one is marginally better, largely because the travelogue-type pictures don't skip all around so that you have no idea where you are. In this DVD one is told that one is visiting, say, Hohensalzburg Fortress or St. Peter's Cemetery and Collegiate Church. Still, there is no voice-over or subtitle identifying precisely what one is seeing at the various sites and the booklet notes don't do much more than give a little historical background. There are poorly organized (and very hard to read) on-screen paragraphs about the various places but the DVD is awkwardly programmed so that one keeps getting dumped back to the beginning of the program after reading the text. One can also read in both the booklet and in on-screen text what music is being played in the background. These selections tend to be brief excerpts from various of Mozart's works, e.g., the middle movement of the Clarinet Concerto, one of the German Dances, the overture to Così fan tutte. Nowhere are we told who is playing these excerpts, but we are given catalog numbers for Naxos CD releases of the works.

It is hard for me to imagine who would be buying this DVD. It's the sort of thing one can imagine buying in a souvenir shop in Salzburg except that the booklet is in English.

I can't give this much of a recommendation except for those who might want to have a souvenir of a trip to Salzburg. Still, it's pleasant to watch and listen to idly while doing the ironing or polishing one's shoes.

Scott Morrison

title: An outstanding achievement in the field of excellence
text: Of late, Relapse records has practically provided one-stop shopping for my heavy-music needs, and these guys are one reason why.  I buy a lot of albums, and "Revolution In Just Listening" is doubtless one of the best heavy recordings I've had the privilege of hearing lately, be it metal, hardcore, or otherwise (I'd call this noisecore myself).  Coalesce's sound isn't quite as maniacal as that of such labelmates as Soilent Green and the Dillinger Escape Plan, but they more than make up for it with some of the tighest grooves and heaviest riffs around.  The songs on "RJIL" are short, sharp and to the point, but they manage to squeeze a lot of inventiveness and musical bludgeoning into a three-minute period.  The anger and intensity in Sean Ingram's throaty growls is the perfect complement to the mathematical intricacy of the band behind him, which unleashes the kind of unrelenting onslaught that the noisecore genre is known for.  Although all the musicians are clearly skilled, special mention must go to drummer James Dewees, whose beats are so complex you practically have to send away to NASA to figure them out.  Definitely a must-have album for discriminating metal nuts.

title: I'm pleased with this less than perfect effort
text:
Disc 1:
Like any "best of" album, the tracklisting is questionable. Not every fan would agree to which songs are the best, but tracklisting on this album seems even more questionable than most. For the most part, the selection of songs fits right in with the single releases of the time period. But then some tracks were never singles (Until the End of the World, Gone, For the First Time) and one was never a U2 song (Miss Sarajevo). Some hit singles are noticably missing (The Fly, Who's Gonna Ride Your Wild Horses, Lemon, Please) yet appear on the DVD version.
On the plus side, the inclusion of the three non-album songs and the brand new track make this album appealing for fans who already have all the albums these songs come from. In addition, four of the other songs have been reworked (all the songs from Pop, plus Numb) and it's a noticable improvement. Some have complained that they are not the original songs, but I am glad to have new versions (that aren't funkified techno-remixes). It gives fans even more reason to get this album.
Indeed the problem with a band of this calibre is there are too many great songs to choose from. For the fan, it's great to have inclusions of non-album songs such as Miss Sarajevo (by the Passengers), The Hands that Built America, and Hold Me, Thrill Me, Kiss Me, Kill Me that if you are like me, you didn't already have. But this poses some other questions. The Hands that Built America is a post 2000 song as is the Electrical Storm (the albums only new track). In this vein, is it also really fair to include anything from the album All That You Can't Leave Behind? The album is so fresh, it's hard to warrant any of it on a "best of" album. But it is, and the real crime is the choice of tracks. No Walk On? And while, our overseas cousins got treated with a bonus track on the album called The Ground Beneath Her Feet, we still don't get it even as a b-side on this set. It's the biggest shame because it's easily one of the best songs on the album we didn't get. Again, it's on the DVD version. There is no reason to include Hands that Built America yet not include this better song.
Disc 2:
Less impressive than the 1980-1990 version. It has too many unwanted remixes and less of the more wanted quality b-sides. People have already complained about the obvious lack of Paint it Black, but what about the amazing Can't Help Falling In Love? The 80's era reminscent Always? Pop Musik? Or the before mentioned Ground Beneath Her Feet? I don't need lame remixes of Numb, Lemon, Discotheque, or Mysterious Ways. I would have love to have been treated with the reworking of Please.
Bonus DVD:
Now here's a gimmick. When I first got this, I thought, "cool, a bonus DVD with some video content." I wasn't dismayed that it was a bit shallow because it was free. But then I bought the DVD and discovered that that bonus DVD is actually the second DVD in a 2-disc set. The second disc is missing inside the DVD, but there is a nice piece of paper in the shape of the disc telling you to buy this CD. How cheap.
Overall:
This is a quality disc. The reworkings of some songs are even better than the original hits, along with the non-album songs make this a wonderful addition as opposed to a redundant purchase. You might be a little dismayed at some of the track selections, but you should own the original albums anyway. I strongly feel All That You Can't Leave Behind should have been not included in this set. title: Finally! After 20 Years, The Knack's Best Album Is Out On CD
text: "Round Trip" is the Knack's third album, their final release before their breakup. Of course, they have had a series of reunions and 3 more studio albums since then. But I think it's fair to say that the first three albums really represent the "true" Knack. I've always felt Round Trip was the best Knack album, but by the time of it's release in 1981, the anti-Knack backlash was raging, and the album flopped. And until now, it has been unavailable on CD. Thankfully, that injustice has finally been remedied. The songs on Round Trip are more varied and adventurous than on albums 1 and 2. The band was growing in ability, confidence and maturity, and it shows on standout tracks like "Africa", "Just Wait And See", "Lil' Cal's Big Mistake", "Another Lousy Day In Paradise", and "Pay The Devil (Ooo Baby Ooo)". "We Are Waiting" is the Knack trying to be a 60's psychedelic band (and succeeding). "Art Wars" is the Knack at their strangest, with moderate success. "Boys Go Crazy" is a great, high energy power pop gem. "She Likes The Beat" is the album's weakest track, sounding like a retread from "But The Little Girls Understand". This CD re-issue also includes 5 bonus tracks of moderate interest, the best of which is a ballad, "Go Away, Stay Away". The others are inessential. It's sure nice to have this album back in print, too bad it took 20 years.

title: In Want of the Deeper Caverns within Morrison
text:
"A Tribute to Jim Morrison" is an aggregation of video clips and photos of Morrison and commentary from the three living Doors, two authors, and Doors producer Paul Rothchild. It is a helpful introduction for someone who knows little about Morrison and wants to learn more. However, because it dates back to the early 1980s, stalwart fans will find everything is old hat (e.g., The Doors landing in Europe and identifying themselves to the questioner; the performances in Europe and on the Ed Sullivan Show).

In "No One Here Gets Out Alive," Jerry Hopkins and Danny Sugerman (Editorial Review above, get that spelling right) wrote many things about Morrison, but their biography was most memorable for its focus on Morrison's wild antics, including many dangerous and gross things and acts of cruelty. Most of the stories about wild antics were attributed to Sugerman, as Hopkins was the narrative and fact guy. The difference on this DVD is that they stick to the more basic and general. Although Morrison's excesses are acknowledged, the emphasis is on Jim Morrison the performer. Indeed, a video clip is worth a thousand words.

Nothing that Hopkins and Sugerman say is very profound or insightful. Rothchild and the living Doors are more intelligent and interesting to listen to, but they do not dig deep enough into Morrison either.

How could this have been more interesting? The literary side of Jim Morrison could have been explored. Jim was very well read, and some of his lyrics were inspired by his eclectic readings, including some French literature, for example. Louis-Ferdinand Celine wrote "Journey to the End of the Night" (see The Doors' debut album track 9). Arthur Rimbaud, French writer of the 19th century, had Morrison as one of his most prodigious readers, and Wallace Fowlie took the trouble to write "Rimbaud and Jim Morrison: The Rebel as Poet." As a performer, Jim Morrison was inspired by theatrical innovator Antonin Artaud, who wrote "Theater of Cruelty." Also, Morrison had enough running around in his own head, helped by mind-altering substances, to inspire himself to great lyrics. The creative stuff is perhaps beyond Hopkins and Sugerman, but not the three living Doors and some of Morrison's associates.

Jim Morrison was not always a pleasant guy to know when drunk or stoned. When he was not, I would have found him interesting to talk to, and I think many others would have as well.

title: An essential Naked City album
text:
For the most part, this is a live version of Naked City's self-titled debut album. You get to hear this amazing band jump from one musical style to another (always aggressively) without any hint of studio tinkering. When you hear it, you'll wonder "Could they really be THAT good?" Yes, they are.
The differences between this and the self-titled album are important. They play one track from their album "Radio" (Skate Key) and they play a beautiful cover of Ennio Morricone's "Erotico." (That song is on Zorn's tribute to Morricone, "The Big Gundown," played by a different set of musicians.)
The final major difference is the finale, a cover of John Patton's "The Way I Feel." At over 10 minutes in length, the song gives half of the band members a chance to play a solo. You get to hear the band wind down from an intense night, working out new musical ideas against each other in front of an audience.
This is one of the best Naked City albums --- and that's saying a lot. Released almost 10 years after their last album, it could have been a cynical attempt to make a little cash from Naked City fans. Instead, it's a nearly flawless album that works as an introduction for those who haven't heard the band before, a little gift for dedicated fans, and a re-introduction to what makes them so great.

title: Special Nights In Aspic
text:
The first official release by Jeff Buckley was the EP Live At Sin-é, which came out in November 1993, and consisted of four songs recorded in the midst of the Greenwich Village scene in which he had been nurturing his formidable talents, just Jeff and his guitar in front of an intimate regular audience. Two of the songs were originals - Mojo Pin, the result of an earlier collaboration with Gary Lucas, and Eternal Life. Both of these songs were to turn up on his debut album, Grace, recorded that autumn. The other two were Edith Piaf's Je N'en Connais Pas Le Fin and Van Morrison's The Way Young Lovers Do. They were selected from recordings made at Sin-é on 17 August 1993 and probably would have been all we ever heard of these events had it not been for Jeff's tragic death just one album into his career.

Jeff's posthumous releases have been sensitively curated by his mother, Mary Guibert, first with the sketches and outtakes of what would have been his follow-up album My Sweetheart The Drunk, and then with selections of live recordings on CD and DVD, and an expanded edition of Grace, and so far they have served to enhance his reputation and status.

For this release, the Sin-é tapes of that nights plus an earlier night on 19 July have been edited into an assemblage that resembles one whole concert, complete with the between-song interplay with the audience. It makes a fascinating document of an assured performer, at the outset of a major career, enjoying performing, enjoying a relaxed relationship with a responsive audience. Although the banter is comical and spontaneous, the actual performances are intense, emotional and fully focused, and at times one forgets that Jeff is alone on the stage with only his electric guitar due to the range of sounds in his musical palette. The material is eclectic, with much of the material from Grace set against wide-ranging external material that he himself was exploring, ranging from three Bob Dylan songs, Billie Holiday, Led Zeppelin, Ray Charles and Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan, the latter apparently as a result of a shouted request, and in whose music Jeff had a deep musical and spiritual interest. These were special nights, and it is a privilege to re-live the experience from this release, which also includes a bonus video disc, thankfully a DVD rather than CD-ROM, of an interview with Jeff and extracts from a return to Sin-é on New Year's Eve 1996, just months before his death on 29 May 1997

The first three songs had me set on the fact that this would be a great CD.  But songs like "Something I Call Personality", with it's incredibly cheesy intro riff, ... "It's Been A Summer", the boring "The Great Houdini", and the absolutely awful album closer, "The Story So Far", ruin this album.  This is the kind of album where, for each good song, there is an equally bad song to go with it.Other good songs would be "Forget My Name", which reminds me of past NFG efforts, and "Singled Out" with it's semi-hardcore riffage, and cool screaming parts by Chad, the guitarist, who used to scream for a band called Shai Hulud (who is much better than NFG).  One thing that surprised me about this CD is the slew of guest backup vocalists, with names such as Rusty and Toby from H2O, Dan and Matt from Alkaline Trio, Bane, and What Feeds The Fire.  While they don't have big roles, it is cool to know some really good bands helped NFG out with this album.  Overall, this album is okay.  Nothing stellar, nothing new, but it's listenable.  But there are better CDs out there that you can buy instead of this one.  Pass.

title: L.O.T.U.G. Livin' With The Funk (Rating: 9 out of 10- -4.5 stars)
text:
For some odd reason, I've been bumping a lot of stuff that came from the Jersey area this week.

Lords of the Underground (L.O.T.U.G., DJ Lord Jazz, Doitall, and Mr. Funkee Man) are probably one of the missed groups that came out from Newark, N.J. area. This was their debut album, "Here Come The Lords" that dropped back in '93. This album was entirely produced my Marley Marl and K-Def. This album alone has some of the most excellent production I've heard from the East Coast in a minute. Most of the production is unique and garunteed to make your head bob. When I first heard "Funky Child", I couldn't stop bobbing my head to the loud horns that K-Def and Marley Marl hooked up for this group. Other awesomly produced songs were the hit song "Chief Rocka" (I believe that's their well known song). "Keep It Underground" is also another song with great production.

As for the trio themselves, they bring many lyrics to the mic on this album, and it seems like they were having a lot of fun doing it. "Mad Skillz" shows exactly what the group has. One humorous track would be "Sleep For Dinner". The song will make you laugh but at the same time they were being serious. "Grave Digga" and "Psycho" are also standouts. DJ Lord Jazz even gets some love on the song "Lord Jazz Hit Me One Time (Make It Funky)".

As for anything bad. There isn't much at all if you ask me. One thing I found a little aggravating was the fact they kept shouting out their name throughout most of the album. Other than that, this is one excellent album from the Brick City. This album is full of East Coast flavor that has some great production. Given this, I will make an effort to check out their sophomore album "Keepers Of The Funk". This is one that I highly recommend that you listen to, because you will love it.

title: Great voice, great tracks, great disc!
text:
Pina has a very unique voice, and a very unique sound to her debut CD. Vocally, i'd say the closest sound would be Kristen Hersh circa Hips & Makers or Strange Angels, but Pina manages to sound more worldworn and yet more melodic somehow. As for the musical tracks, theyre sometimes folky("The Flight" "Debt Song"), sometimes rocky ("I Loved The Way", "Cold Storm"), sometimes southern-gothicy ("Josephine", "The Lady"), but the album maintains a consistent thematic feel by sharing similar insturmentation (guitars, cellos, piano, soft drums), but varying the volume and intensity. And when Pina's background shouts and wails cut through, they sound almost primal in places.
The length of the album is a double-edged sword. One one hand, it's pretty short, and leaves you wanting more. But, at the same time, there's no padding. No filler. I'm notorious for instnatly skipping tracks that don't strike my fancy, but I *always* listen to this album all the way through. And in a few short days "I Loved The Way" has become one of my favorite songs this year.
