title: Welcome to Emerald City...
text:
Think of this album as the journey of Teena's previous pop/RnB hit "Lovergirl" from her album "Starchild". "Lovergirl" sported the very popular, Prince-like rock meets RnB vibe that was very current in 1984. Now imagine that "Lovergirl" moves to Emerald City & that this album is her story.

This album to me is a progression of the sound that she merely toyed with on "Lovergirl". Here the album melds the styles that Teena had previously sported: urban dance & balladry, except that it is executed with a harder edge; I'm not just talking about her slight use of guitar. The record itself from it's amazingly awesome dark cover (the T.V.'s in the trashcan, what a statement of America in 1986!) to Teena's darker romantic ambitions, this record wasn't Teena of yesteryear.

The first track opens with Bootsy Collins welcoming the listener to Emerald City. And what a city! Here Teena brings in a much more current dance beat, almost Minneapolis in sound, adding only synths & her own guitar work. The result? You have four strong dancefloor fillers on the first half of the disc. The latter half is almost like the cooling down period, as Teena stretches her musical ambitions further from the Latin pop workout of "Batucada Sweet" to the grandiose jazz finish of "Sunny Skies".

Lyrically, Teena isn't singing about anything she hasn't before. But there is definitely a more sexual drive here. Songs such as "You So Heavy" (that is one of the sexiest song titles ever!) & "Lips To Find You ("So you say your leaving for the Southern tip of Spain, to soak up local color, & forget my name...") find Teena addressing her partner more aggresively not just for emotional intimacy, but physical intimacy as well.

Sadly, this album seems to get a bad rap & Teena rarely performs the material of this album. I don't understand how this is a "heavy metal record". To me, it has similarities to "Purple Rain" which was a RnB record with a rock vibe. I do think we get to see Teena show of her amazing guitar skills & try some things she hadn't been able to do before. I believe this was her last (in my eyes) album where she truly pushed herself, from here she put out good records, but they weren't daring. Just good.

If you are looking for some Teena Marie that you've never heard or are a first timer, I highly would recommend this underlooked gem.

title: Da iawn Arwel Hughes a Cymdeithas Gorawl Huddersfield! Canwch ymlaen!
text:
Alright, this is a hymns album, sung by a single choir, the Huddersfield Choral Society, under the baton of Welshman Owain Arwel Hughes. I can understand Hughes's sensitivity for these hymns on this album. He does a fine job, as does the choir. Now, one might be somewhat fearful of a "marathon listening experience" when listening to hymn after hymn after hymn, but I did and still do not obtain fatigue with this album. It is nice to hear some mature voices, unlike what may be obtained with other "hymns albums," where some undergraduates at one of the colleges of Cambridge provide the vocalese. The voices are mature and outstanding. One can hear the robustness of the conductor's and choir's interpretations of these timeless hymns. No, they do not sing with the English blasé. Most of the singing is powerful and heartfelt.

Being of Welsh descent myself, I cannot emphasize with more rigour the interpretations of the two hymns "Cwm Rhondda" and "Jesu, Lover of My Soul." They are both sung with rigour and vitality, and, if you want to hear what these hymns should sound like in four-part harmony, then look no further than this recording. Joseph Parry wrote the latter hymn, which was not included in the English Hymnal for a while, because it was thought "too intimate." Indeed, it is a choral prayer, and Arwel Hughes and the Huddersfield Choral Society give it a lovely interpretation.

I do not think that you may go wrong with this purchase. If you are a choral director or just an admirer and friend of these hymns, a hymn aficionado, as it were; if you want to get away from what is labeled "contemporary church music"; if you want to return to a more civilised and thoughtful (I am speaking about the words of these hymns) time, then this album is for you. You will learn much about the past and about yourself. Listening to it is like polishing off grandmother's old, dusty jewels - still good and yet so beautiful after all these years.

Da iawn Arwel Hughes a Cymdeithas Gorawl Huddersfield! Canwch ymlaen!

title: Good but not great Tchaikovsky 2 & 4 from Abbado
text:
This is a solid recording but I don’t quite share the enthusiasm of the other reviewers at Amazon. The disc is a re-release of a 1968 recording of the 2nd the recently-deceased Claudio Abbado did with the New Philharmonia Orchestra and a 1976 recording of the 4th he did with the Vienna Philharmonic. The sound in the 4th is good while the 2nd it is only fair, with some distortion and lack of body apparent in my system.

I directly compared Abbado’s 4th symphony with an older Soviet version from Evgeny Mravinsky and the Leningrad Philharmonic and found the Mravinsky to be more expressive and exciting. The Abbado interpretation, while technically very well-executed, is flat and relatively unemotional. This is especially apparent in the Scherzo, my personal favorite movement in the 4th, where the dynamic contrasts and tempo flexibility infused by Mravinsky is absent in the Abbado, to its detriment.

Abbado’s 2nd Symphony is better in the interpretation department than the 4th – but it’s also a weaker work and, as mentioned, harmed by mediocre engineering. Compared to the well-regarded Telarc version of the 2nd from Lorin Maazel and the Pittsburgh Symphony, I’d give a marginal edge to the Abbado performance. Both are good, with the Abbado boasting a bit more life and vivacity and the Maazel boasting superior sound and benefiting from a pairing with Rimsky-Korsakov’s beautiful “Antar.”

So this is a solid CD, to be purchased for its 2nd symphony rather than the 4th.

title: Not for everyone
text:
The music in the 70's tends to get over analyzed and picked apart these days. I believe that mostly happens because so many of my peers who were teenagers in the 70's boast about the music being the best ever, so younger music fans either check it out expecting all of it to be wonderful (it wasn't) or with a preconceived notion that it's going to be crap (and sometimes it was).

With BBA, you get all the above. A power trio made up of three of the finest instrumentalists of the era, who could blow the audience away with chops to die for or bore an audience to tears with extended displays of musical prowess, BBA wanted to be musically diverse, playing rock, pop, blue and jam as well. The biggest obstacle was the vocals. As other reviewers correctly point out, none of the guys in the band are great singers. In most cases, while listening to the album (or as many did in concert), you wait for the guys to shut up and just play. On the heavier material and the jams, that plan works out ok. But the band didn't want to just be a heavy jam band, they wanted to play pop too. Musically, no problem. But when the focus is on the vocals, the band just collapses. What they really needed was a singer, but it wasn't meant to be. They disintegrated in the studio trying to record the follow-up to their debut and they were no more. This album shows the sheer joy of hearing three guys play off each other and jamming all night. If you like that sort of thing, it's great. If you're not a jam fan, don't even approach this album. If you want tight song structures and pretty vocals, look elsewhere. There were better jam bands in the 70's, but there were worst ones out there too.
Fans of Mountain, Deep Purple, etc will find a lot to like here. I don't know what younger fans will think, because there's no way this will live up to the hype. It is what it is, and like Mountain, West, Bruce & Laing, Cream, etc, it's often pretty basic stuff. Lots of fun, but very much of its time.

It's not as good as the five star reviewers says it is and it's not as bad as the one star reviewers say. It's right in the middle, and approaching it with an open mind and realistic expectations will help you a lot. Beck never played any heavier, so it's definitely worth a listen.

title: Their most accomplished release to date.
text:
The early nineties was a great time for Rock music. Hair Metal was - finally - dying, and lots of underground bands were selling huge amount of records, and record company folks were flabbergasted, because they couldn't safely predict who might be the next big hit. Nirvana, the Red Hot Chili Peppers, Soundgarden and in a lesser degreee, Metallica - which already had a huge fanbase - were considered flukes from the suits that worshipped Guns N'Roses, Bon Jovi and Poison.

Company executives went on to hire scouts to 'fish' on underground waters, and maybe hit upon the next Metallica or the next Nirvana. Epic hired Sepultura, Warner Brothers hired Helmet and Biohazard and other bands on the WB roster, like Ministry and Pantera, were doing great.

Company heads then turned attention to a small UK label, Earache. In 1992, after a label frenzy, Earache signed a distribution deal with Columbia in America for its major acts, except Morbid Angel (which signed their own deal with Giant, another american company). The first disc to come out from the new distribution deal was Cathedral, which featured Lee Dorian, ex-Napalm Death grunter. The deal was, initially, mutually beneficial. Earache got more money to invest on tours and more studio time for the bands. In turn, Columbia might get the next Megadeth (Carcass) or the next Nine Inch Nails (Godflesh).

This major label interest in Earache's roster had, like it or not, both a positive and a negative influence on its bands. 1993-1994 was a period which some of the best Death Metal records were released (in my opinion). And many of these bands ended, after the "Corporation Pull-In".

Ok, but... Why take so much time to explain all this?

"Fear, Emptiness, Despair", to me, is undoubtly a product of this period. Instead of 'blast-beat-us-til-death' gimmick - which had already wore thin - ND opted for midpaced songs. To me, it worked. They couldn't get faster than "From Enslavement to Obliteration", and the attempt to get back to their "roots" - "Utopia Banished" (1992) - was midly disappointing. "Fear", however, has more of that "roots" quality - without so much blast-beats. You don't need to be fast to be heavy and brutal.

And I think and ND proved that to themselves, and to me, with this record.

And I hope to all of you, too.

First, in response to the previous "reviews" let's take into consideration that the person comparing The Beatles to Metallica couldn't spell simple words, such as "instead". I'm a huge Metallica fan, but Metallica wouldn't be where they are without the Beatles. It's like comparing a 1967 Shelby GT to a 2006 Mustang GT. Both very sexy cars, both high performers...however, you wouldn't have the 2006 had there not been the '67 and a lot of style and originality is lost over almost 40 years. The '67 will always be the original, will always be a classic, will always be loved and will always be part of history, which makes it "better" to those who value the classics. Those who value more horsepower will think the '06 is "better"...*technically*, neither is right, neither is wrong. It's an opinion. Personally, I'm a '67 fan, and therefore, despite my love of Metallica, would never put them above the Beatles. Any music aficionado will point out that the Beatles have covered a much wider range of emotion and musical talent than Metallica will ever cover, and I agree. My car comparison can never cover the entire scope of the talent of the Beatles. I'm sure you can appreciate what I'm *trying* to get across =D

That said, this is a review of the album and for Beatles lovers, this is a must have CD for the car. It covers every stage of the Beatles' career and there are plenty of songs to get you to and from work. Because of it's coverage of all the levels of their artistic talent, you can take an audible trip through their career from 1963 to 1970, and for those lucky enough to have experienced the 60's and 70's, a trip through your own childhood/adolescence.

title: There needs to be some growing up to do
text:
Link Park. A cross between Hip-Hop and modern metal. Back in 2000 when I first purchased this album, I really enjoyed it, both the music and lyrics. To put it into retrospect, I enjoyed mostly anything that was on the radio. In later years, I have begun to lose respect for both. While I do enjoy their unique sound it becomes very monotonous rather quickly. All of their individual songs blend in together to make one loud sonic blob.

One of the many issues I take with Hybrid Theory are the lyrics. It's obvious that Linkin Park was pandering to teenagers (a group that just so happens to spend the most on music) when writing the lyrics. Despite Cure for the itch, every song is just a pity party and rant fest. Who is Linkin Park complaining too anyhow? Their parents? Siblings? Friends? Why the egotistic and pessimistic attitude? Why are the group members so depressed and angry? From what I can make out, their social life seems quite miserable. Perhaps they misbehaved and were sent to their room for a 10 minute time out. Whatever the reason is, it's annoying to the ear and is a sign of an immature band.

The more I listen to classic rock, the more I realize just how much talent is missing from most of today's mainstream, top 40 music. Linkin Park really doesn't possess the ingenuity and frankly creativity to sculpt an album that will be memorable past the teenage years. Can you imagine these guys making a decent concept album? Hell would freeze over first. How about having a guitar solo? Nope, it's just too difficult to string single notes together to construct a simple appeasing harmony. Instead, lets have lots of raping/ screaming, heavy power cords and lyrics that stay as far from optimism as possible. Hey, it sells records.

To conclude, I enjoy all kinds of music including heavy rock; however, when I listen to LP, I feel like I'm back in middle school with the angry attitude and lack of respect for any music that's older than three years. It's not a good feeling.

title: Sonic Spectacular!
text:
If you like thorny and extravagant High Modernism, then you must hear this. I used to love this piece (circa 1970 when it was written), but no recording has been available for decades. Now comes a new recording from modest little Naxos, and it is a stunner - with a huge dynamic range and excellent work from the Warsaw Philharmonic and conductor Wit, who seems to specialize in these enormous choral works.

The chorus sings, shouts, chants, and whispers in sliding atonal clusters of sound, surrounded by great dramatic outbursts from the orchestra (there is a big part for the bass drum and something that sounds like an anvil!). Better yet are the several Basso Profundos who sing demented church-style chants. Interspersed are a number of quieter sections that recall, alternatively, Palestrina, Slavic folk songs, and Orthodox church music. It all builds repeatedly to gargantuan, even frightening, climaxes (your neighbors will hate you). Charles Ives used to boast the he didn't write music for "sissies" - neither did Penderecki.

title: This is an oldie but it is great! The Darlings influenced the greats!
text:
I'd forgotten I had this one in my music library until I was looking through my folk albums today. I got it back many years ago and it sat there quietly waiting until I got back to it. Its just as good as it was back in the day. It sat quietly through my death metal phase, my New Orleans jazz phase, lots of other side trips on the road back to the roots. My last passion was the Grateful Dead, and guess what? You can here some of these riffs in Jerry Garcia's repertory! Thank you Jerry, even years later you point us in the right direction!

This album has a lot of the old favorites: Cripple Creek, Sourwood Mountain, Amazing Grace, The Girl I Left Behind Me, Sally Goodin, Railroad Bill, Soldier's Joy, lots more. These songs all seem to invite play-along, sound awesome when you follow them with guitar or banjo. (No my fiddle is too rusty and I need new bowstring so forget that!) This is great driving music, great listening music.

The Darlings were one of the classic "real" mountain bands and back in the 60s, on "The Andy Griffin Show" were my first hard corp introduction to the music of the Scots Irish. Since then I've played these tunes on guitar, banjo and fiddle and I love them.

Forget Bluegrass, forget Modern Country, these are old time fiddle tunes. People who love traditional music but don't like the whining and wailing will really like it. Hornpipes, jigs, reels, all the old styles are there for the asking. The reviewer was right in that Eric Darling wasn't prominent on the album, but you have to remember the tradition is to have people playing along together and blending in, not caterwalling and running off all over the place.

title: Don't Let The Language Turn You Away!
text:
When Rammstein debuted, they were quickly scrutizied because they spoke only in German and they were an extremely "heavy metal" band. In America, this sort of ingenuity classifies you as Satanic or something.
This is absolutely not the case with Rammstein, they are a truly great band. No one else can sustain the aggresive, searing guitars and tenacity as Rammstein and actually NOT sound the same and monotonous on every track. They should be known for their metal/industrial style, not as just another heavy metal band.
If you are not convinced, here are some interpretations of the track titles. The album title, "Herzeleid" is Heartache in our native tongue. "Der Meister,"a very good track, translates to The Man. "Weisses Fleisch", another good one, is White Flesh. "Asche Zu Asche" is Ashes to Ashes. The track "Seamann" is as mellow you will ever hear these guys play, it is a ballad titled The Sailor. "Riechst So Gut" is You Smell so Good. "Heirate Mich" was the first song I ever heard by Rammstein (from the movie Lost Highway) and it means Marry Me, though the actual lyrics have very little to do with the title. That's something you should look into on your own time! Those are all the ones I could interpret. It was interesting to actually find out what was being said in these songs.
This turned out to be more of a lecture than a review, I am sorry! None the less, there guys are intense. It doesn't matter what they are brooding about, they will have you banging your head.

title: Not Like Joy Division!
text: I bought this album because people told me it sounded just like Joy Division, who are my all-time favorite band. Well, somebody has to say this and it's going to be me- Interpol don't really sound much like Joy Division, and all the reviewers who say otherwise are just demonstrating that they've never really listened all that closely to either band. Yes, Interpol are a dark post-punk band, but the similarity really ends there. Interpol songs are not built around the bass line like Joy Division songs, they aren't nearly as manic-sounding, and the tone of Interpol's music tends to be moody and reflective whereas the tone of Joy Division is coldly futuristic and impersonal. However, Turn on the Bright Lights is a brilliant album in its own right, with some of the best songwriting I've heard in a long time, and songs that grow on you more and more till you hardly want to hear anything else. Of course Interpol have their influences like any band does, and one of those influences might be Joy Division. But they don't really need to be compared to anyone. They shine on their own.

Robbie thinks he's so sweet that if he were a chocolate drop not only would he eat himself, but when he'd passed through his system he'd eat himself again. title: Fine Performance -- Questionable Release
text:
Let me start by saying that I picked this CD up at The Juilliard Store in New York City. As I'd never attended a single concert by the New York Philharmonic under Alan Gilbert, I felt I owed him something in terms of acknowledgement, and I can always use another good Bruckner 7th, and this is that. The playing is beautiful, the performance is spot-on, and if that were the only consideration -- which, in an ideal world, it ought to be -- this would be a four-star review (four stars because, let's face it, it comes along in the wake of long-standing recordings and performances conducted by the likes of Bruno Walter, Gunter Wand, Herbert Von Karajan, Otto Klemperer et al).

Ah, but then there's Sony Classical, the company releasing it.

Apparently, in a quest to cut corners, or an acknowledgement of their miserably low expectations for sales of this item, the company has chosen to issue this new release as a CD-R.

There's no indication of such on the outer packaging -- a practice of which Concord Music Group is also guilty in some of its jazz CD reissues -- and no indication in the Amazon entry on the item, but that was certainly the case with the CD that I purchased at The Juilliard Store (and no one's going to tell me that The Juilliard Store is buying bootlegs, "grey market" items, or promos). So what would be a 4-star CD becomes a 1-star CDr, thanks to the foolishness of the company releasing it, and anyone considering buying this release can now walk in with their eyes open.

Shame on you, Sony Classical.

title: Yet Another Masterpiece From Riverside
text:
The final chapter of Riverside's three-part conceptual masterpiece, "Rapid Eye Movement" is an epic, fascinating, and worthy finale for fans of the band, as well as being the best prog-rock release of the year period.

Poland's Riverside have been rising stars in the progressive music scene, their debut album "Out Of Myself" being hailed by critics and fans alike, with each release eagerly awaited and seemingly better than the last. "Rapid Eye Movement" certainly continues the trend, taking an even more progressive and complex direction, as well as simply being more cinematic, mature and heavy. Riverside's melodic instrumental interplay and warm, emotive vocals are used to even greater effect here, and they stretch out into even more textural, cinematic compositions than ever before, laced with dark, surreal Freudian themes of loss, introspection and subconscious redemption which certainly fit the album's title well.

For those who are already fans, this is just as good or better than either of Riverside's prior albums, although perhpas taking a bit more time to digest, like many good prog albums do. Riverside remains the band who simply never disappoint, with each release building on the last to even greater heights. For those who haven't heard them before, its best (in my opinion) to pick them up and listen to them in order as the narrative story (the so-called "Reality Dream" trilogy) of disillusionment, loss, and self-discovery they are intended to be. Any Riverside album easily stands on it's own, and this band is quite original....Riverside are best described as modern heavy progressive rock, with the guitar-driven heaviness and melody of Porcupine Tree, the complexity and psychadelia of Pink Floyd, and the avant-garde style and soaring vocals of Dredg. Pick this up and see what all the fuss is about. Best prog-rock album of the year.

title: One of my favorite albums by one of my favorite flatpickers
text:
Larry Keel may be my favorite flatpicker. There are faster players, and there are cleaner players. However, nobody flatpicks more forcefully or distinctively. There is hard-driving bluegrass, and then there is The Larry Keel Experience, and they made anyone else laying claim to that style sound like they were playing placid waltzes. Even groups like Blue Highway and the Infamous Stringdusters sound laid-back compared to Keel on this album. This is HARD bluegrass, and Keel does not achieve that by playing a blend of bluegrass and rock like New Grass Revival and their followers. This is just HARD bluegrass from the most aggressive flatpicker around. Larry Keel recorded two other albums with "The Larry Keel Experience," Miles & Miles, and a self-titled album. Miles & Miles is a bit more stylistically diverse, but more mellow, and the self-titled album is quite similar to this one, but The Sound just has an aggressive energy that is difficult to find anywhere else. That makes this my favorite of the Larry Keel Experience albums, although the other two are worth tracking down as well.

Of Keel's other projects, I would strongly recommend tracking down a copy of the Magraw Gap album. Magraw Gap was a Keel band that preceded the Experience, and it was a perfect blend of progressive and traditional bluegrass sounds. Also, look for Big Daddy Bluegrass Band, which put Larry Keel in a band with Curtis Burch (New Grass Revival) and Steve McMurry (Acoustic Syndicate). Then, track down some Acoustic Syndicate albums.

title: Their best next to Sailin' Shoes
text:
Dixie Chicken is Little Feat's third album and is regarded among longtime fans as their best work. Like their previous albums, Little Feat and Sailin' Shoes, Dixie Chicken would garner much critical acclaim but slow sales. The album also showed a change in direction in their music. While Sailin' Shoes was steeped in country, blues, and boogie music, Dixie Chicken is laid back and funkier. This would also be the album to debut longtime Feat members Paul Barrere, Sam Clayton, and Kenny Gradney. Barrere, in particular, would play a pivotal role in the band, gradually writing more songs with their later releases and would be the major voice of the band when they regrouped in 1988.

But Lowell George was still the star of the show on Dixie Chicken, writing most of the songs and adding those gruff distinctive lead vocals to every track. As for the songs, they're all very good although I believe the tracks on Sailin' Shoes are slightly better overall. The title track is to this day the band's best and most memorable song, featuring clever wordplay and slide guitar from George and a memorable piano hook from Bill Payne. Country superstar Garth Brooks would later do a respectable cover of this in the `90s, in effect introducing the greatness of Little Feat to a whole new audience. "Fat Man in the Bathtub", another one of George's great story songs, is arguably their second best track with Richie Hayward lending the opening hook with his busy drum line. While the rest of the tracks aren't as widely known, they're all very strong. Songs like the funky "Two Trains", the rollicking "Walkin' All Night", and the dark blues of "On Your Way Down" show George in all of his glory with some of the sweetest slide playing you'll ever hear and the female backing vocals, performed by future superstar Bonnie Raitt among others, providing a nice touch. Another great track is "Fool Yourself", which was written by Fred Tackett, who would later join Little Feat when they reunited for the Let It Roll album and continues to play a major role in the band. "Lafayette Railroad" is a cool instrumental that the band continues to play live while "Juliette", with its arrangement and solemn flute line, recalls a livelier version of Traffic. "Roll Um Easy" and "Kiss It Off" are both very laid back tunes with George's vocals providing the perfect accompaniment. All told, Dixie Chicken is one of the best works from one of the finest American rock bands. Highly recommended.

title: A Nearly Symphonic Magnum Opus
text:
Before The Wall, before Dark Side of the Moon, Pink Floyd created a very different kind of masterpiece. While their later albums were a triumph of concept, it is on Meddle where one can hear the *musical* peak of Pink Floyd's career. This is not a concept album--it is a musical journey showing off a variety of musical styles. The lyrics do not demand--they suggest, and allow the music to do the rest of the talking. Perhaps the most wonderful thing about Meddle is the fact that the band was truly functioning as a *band* here. Everyone's talents can be clearly heard, and no one shouts anybody else down.
There is no such thing as filler, on Meddle. Bookended by the mindblowing tracks "One of These Days" and "Echoes", the four "interior" tracks are severely underrated. "A Pillow of Winds" and "Fearless" are both pleasant, leisurely guitar-driven songs, and seem fairly well appreciated by fans. However, I believe that the much-maligned "San Tropez" and "Seamus" are also deserving of appreciation. "San Tropez" is particularly notable for some very unique Roger Waters vocals--rather optimistic and even a touch bluesy...a style he unfortunately never pursued after that point. "Seamus" gives a rare glimpse of the fun side of Pink Floyd, as well as a flashback to the band's origins as a blues cover band. This was never a song meant to be taken so seriously as some do. "One of These Days" is an explosive, energetic instrumental that perhaps foreshadows the angry, driven rock of Animals, but with only one lyric--a rare appearance by Nick Mason, whose processed vocals growl menacingly, "One of these days, I'm going to cut you into little pieces!"
The album's final piece, "Echoes", may be Pink Floyd's greatest work ever. From first to last "ping", this brilliant near-symphony is fantastic. Each bandsman's talents are clearly audible, even the simple-yet-effective contributions of Nick Mason and Roger Waters. The vocal harmony of David Gilmour and Richard Wright is mesmerising. Without question, this song contains the best verse Mr. Waters ever wrote: "Strangers passing in the street, by chance two separate glances meet, and I am you and what I see is me. And do I take you by the hand, and lead you through the land, and help me understand the best I can?"
Unfortunately, this reminder to walk a mile in the other man's shoes was a lesson Mr. Waters forgot in later years, at the price of devastating consequences to the band's output and to the members themselves. This moment in Pink Floyd's history is therefore one-of-a-kind, completely irreplaceable. The entire album can be summed up by the "jam" sequence in "Echoes". Never before, never again do the pieces fit together so seamlessly, each a joy on its own and in combination.

title: Clay At His Most Introspective
text:
"On My Way Here" is a well crafted album that undeniably shows that Clay Aiken and team (Foster and Kipper) have spent a lot of time and energy creating.

The broad range of all original material on this album is solid and it showcases genres from ballad, to up-tempo, to soft or pop rock. This diversity demonstrates the versatility of Clay as an artist and the songs here represent Clay's maturation as a talented performer.

Above all that, the one thing that shines through is that polished, beautiful, honey-sweet, magnificent, soaring vocals. As much as I love all the songs, it is Clay's voice that makes listening to the cd again and again and again, magical and irresistible.

Here too, is Clay at his most introspective with lyrics that purportedly represent his experiences of having been in the public's eye. However, listeners can also "emo-personally" connect to each song as we bring our take to the table when we reflect on our own experiences.

There is definitely something for everyone and I recommend this album to anyone who appreciates different musical genres, a captivating and accomplished vocalist, and a great talent.

title: This Album Is A Treat
text:
In the past, Alice Cooper has always put on a show at his concerts. But with the Welcome To My Nightmare tour, they cranked it up a notch or two with many creative props and special effects.
During one song, giant spiders chased Alice on huge spider webs. And to the tune of "Some Folks," skeletons in top hats, capes, and canes danced in step with each other. Of course, the bone people were merely performers wearing skin-tight, black leotards, with the image of life-size skeletons on them. But the effect worked.
Another memorable effect was the scene during "Only Women Bleed." At one point in this song, Alice grabbed a woman-sized doll and started puching and kicking her. He threw her all over the place. You could tell it was an inflatable doll when he twisted her around the bed post of a huge bed on stage. Eventually he threw the doll down and hopped into bed next to her. After a few moments, as he continued singing, the doll slowly sat up, got out of bed, and began walking around the stage. It was a real woman.
The directors of this concert deserve an award. The switch between the battered doll and real woman went completely unnoticed. No doubt, they employed the services of a magician or two for this tour.
Towards the end of the concert, a gigantic monster came out onto the stage. Alice Cooper fought it and eventually won the battle. He decapitated the beast with a sword and proudly carried its head around the stage as the audience cheered.
But the greatest trick of all came earlier in the show when Alice layed on a guillotine and had his own head cut off. After the blade dropped, and his head fell into a basket below, his headless body got up, walked over and picked it up. With the head dangling from his fist by the hair, the headless Alice used the other hand to put the microphone up to the mouth of the head, and it finished singing the song.
I kid you not. This scene blew me away. I saw it at the Spectrum, in Philadelphia, in 1975 and I'll never forget it. At that concert, Alice Cooper gave us our money's worth. He is a true rock and roll performer.

title: Thoughtful and effective Tchaikovsky
text:
This CD appears to complete Paavo Järvi’s Tchaikovsky symphony cycle from Zürich. Previous installments have been variously reviewed in recent issues of Fanfare, that of the Fifth by the undersigned in 44:6. As in that recording, Järvi takes a fresh look at the score, with much attention to dynamics. He plays the second-movement Allegro con grazia, the 5/4 “waltz,” with a subtlety rarely achieved by his father, Neeme Järvi. He consistently brings out details that one doesn’t normally notice, such as the chromatically ascending line in the strings in the transition to the recapitulation of the third movement’s march tune, and the bass drum thwacks in that movement’s coda.
The first movement is characterized by distinguished wind solos and flawless intonation, and is notable for a fierce development section. There is no dawdling in the third movement. In the Adagio lamentoso Finale the second theme features a wonderful pianissimo.
Romeo and Juliet is played with the same attention to detail; notice, for instance, the pointed accents in the introduction. The Allegro giusto is quite brisk.
The sound of the recording is satisfyingly transparent. All in all, what I’ve heard of Järvi’s Tchaikovsky cycle is thoughtful and effective. Recommended.

title: THIS IS THE REAL THING!
text:
There are a lot of collections and anthologies out there that claim to have the best Cuban vocalists and songs. Don't pay any attention. "Voces Inolvidables Cubanas" , both Volumen 1 and 2, are the REAL THING. Whoever chose the material for these compilations knew exactly what he or she was doing. These are some of the greatest recordings ever done by some of the greatest Cuban singers in history. There is not a single bad cut in either volume. You get hit after hit without fillers or rarities. It is really amazing the amount of great artists that Cuba produced before the fatidic revolution. Note that each vocalist has its own unique style and sound.

In reference to the audio quality I must admit that no sophisticated digital remastering was used, since these are no frills moderate priced releases. However the over all sound is good or acceptable except for Barbarito Diez on Volumen 1 where they used a 78rpm disc and you can hear the pops and cracks. It didn't bother me because Barbarito's golden voice rises over any technical defects. I truly believe you won't find a better sampler of Cuban legends anywhere and I urge you to buy both volumes. And if you lived through the 1950s when most of these recordings were made you are in for an emotional reencounter with the golden years of the Cuban bolero and its greatest stars.

title: Harmonies.....Alive And Well!!!
text: I guess big brothers are good for something after all. Sure, they tease and torment you growing up, but every once in a while they do something cool...like introduce you to great music. I have to thank my two older brothers for turning me on to, among others, the Beatles, the Stones, Bonnie Raitt, Jackson Browne, Joan Armatrading...and now The Thorns. A minor fan of Matthew Sweet's, I would never have picked this disc up on my own. Yet this stunning debut, awash in harmonies reminiscent of such vocal greats as the Bee Gees, the Beach Boys, the Mamas & the Papas, Fleetwood Mac and, especially, CSN is one of the most pleasant surprises of the year. Sweet and bandmates Pete Droge and Shawn Mullins open the disc with the powerful "Runaway Feeling." With it's Byrds-esque verses and ringing choruses, this song is the musical offspring of 70's California folk rock and East Coast power pop. I can think of only one other album this year - Fleetwood Mac's SAY YOU WILL - that opens on such a strong note. Next up is the Bee Gee-flavored "I Can't Remember." Once again, the vocals soar, while the chorus cuts deep ("I can't remember/The last time/You looked me in the eye/I can't remember/A way to make you cry"). The group takes the Jayhawk's "Blue" and makes it their own. Just listen to those high notes when they hit the word "blue"! If you played "Think It Over" to a dozen people and told them it was an old CSN cut, I bet at least five of them would ask "Which album?" With it's loose, country-tinged beat, the track has a nice, mellow/relaxed groove to it. Things do a 180 on the next cut, the disc's exuberant (semi) title track, "Thorns." A lot of people have said the song stands out like a sore thumb, and I'd say "Good for it!" With it's crashing percussion, power-riff guitars and (at times) shouted vocals, "Thorns" adds a dose of energy and grit to the disc (That lack of energy/grit, along with a lack of more real LEAD vocals, is my only real - read:minor! - complaint I have with THE THORNS). I just LOVE the late 70's Power Pop-like guts that this track exudes, particularly on the "Ain't no talking to/No getting rid of you/Once you've got your foot in the door" bridge! "No Blue Sky" is one of the lovliest songs of the last decade. The vocals are spot-on, the instrumentation is gorgeous (tasteful strings that actually ADD to the song instead of detracting from it...imagine that!) and the lyrics pulse with heartache and regret ("It ain't right/Feels like forever/So many changes, I stopped keeping score/But if you want me, you know where I will be/I don't get out much anymore"). "Now I Know" has a nice (almost) a cappella vibe to it, while "Dragonfly" is the only real misfire in my eyes (Too precious, preachy and new agey). There's a sweetness to "Long Sweet Summer" that's infectious. In many ways a tribute to the Beach Boys, Walter Egan would be wise to think about covering this gem (I particularly love the pounding piano!). Next up is "I Told You." Everyone can identify with this delicate acoustic-driven ballad about getting burned one too many times...and the gun-shy quality that induces: "Maybe from the outside/Things look alright/But we know it isn't so/'Cause baby on the inside/I spent all night/Counting reasons I should go/How will I know when love's true/If it comes for real." Gorgeous! "Such A Shame" has a sly, sexy groove to it, along with a sparkling chorus and witty lyrics ("She sleeps alone without her clothes on/While I dream of how things could have been", "I left a message in the midnight sky/But now I know she'll never find it" and "You may be wrong and I'm not crazy/Though I admit that I'm confused"). Every time "Such A Shame" comes on, I find myself thinking "THIS is what's missing from pop music today!" "I Set The World On Fire" has a techno-laced, joyously majestic quality to it, while the disc closes with the hushed "Among The Living".....crisp, clean vocals and perfect instrumental arrangements equal pop perfection. So pick up THE THORNS....I guarantee that, instead of a fist full of barbs, you'll be treated to a lovely bouquet of exquisite vocal harmonies.

title: "Rik's most enjoyable solo album"
text:
"Raw Quartet" was the 3rd album in Rik's "Open House Trilogy", consisting of 3 albums exploring his stylistic guitar roots.

"Ten Invitations" was all about classical playing.
"Swing Shift" hit upon jazz & swing played on an arched top guitar.
"Raw Quartet" explored Rik's love of the blues/rock genre, as played primarily on a solid body electric.

Classic influences such as Otis Rush, Buddy Guy & Eric Clapton as well as modern players like Stevie Ray Vaughan color and shape Rik's tone as wellas his phrasing.
Top the great playing with Rik's distinctive vocals, and you have one of the great moments in the Rik Emmett catalog.

The Tracks:

"Perpetual Motion Love Machine" starts the album off with a bang.
The pace is quick, the breaks tight, and the solos bang on.

"Walkin'" is a funkier track, very much in the Robben Ford mold, as Rik even mimics Ford's vocal stylings and wah-wah pedal.

"Gasoline" is in the ZZ Top Texas shuffle vein, and percolates along nicely.

"Hogtown Rag" is just that - a ragtime blues inspired by the music of the 1920's. The featured instrument on this as well as the next track "All On Board" is the metal-bodied Dobro resonator with a slide, for that slippery sound.

"The Last Goodbye" is an instrumental ballad inspired by the likes of Larry Carlton & Hank Marvin.
Rik simply plays the haunting melody, which almost brings a tear to the eye. Beautiful.

"C'mon Along" is a rocker right out of the Stevie Ray Vaughan mold - raunchy tone, deft soloing, and good chord melody usage.
"Crazy Woman" is an acoustic number in the style of Big Bill Broonzy or Robert Johnson - no frills, just singin' & strummin'.

"Head Case" is a 2-minute sonic blitz, complete with distortion, wah-wah, and heavy reverb. Lots of notes in a short time - kick a**.

The most traditional blues piece on the album is "Too Little, Too Late".
Rik sets the mood immediately, laying out a G-Minor blues groove, peppering the written verses with vocal ad-libs, much like blues veteran Jimmy'Fast Fingers' Dawkins,and his lead guitar channeling Buddy Guy. 7 minutes of pure blues magic.

"Come Clean" is another Dobro-laced track that may be the only weak track on the album.

"Navajo Sunrise" is a page taken from the George Harrison school - laid back, mostly melody and played on electric slide guitar that sounds as though George himself played it. A nice wind down at the end of the album.

The import version features 2 bonus tracks as well.

Rik Emmett is right at home in this musical idiom.
Let's hope he does another one like this. 5 stars.

title: A Real Stunner!
text: There are a number of fine recordings of Korngold's lushly lyrical Violin Concerto currently available, including Jascha Heifetz's pioneering (world premiere) mono version and more recent efforts from the likes of Itzhak Perlman, Gil Shaham, and Anne-Sophie Mutter.  I think this 'live' Oehms version by Benjamin Schmid, Seiji Ozawa and the Vienna Philharmonic, recorded at the 2004 Salzburg Festival, goes to the top of the list.  First, Schmid is completely captivating, producing a near-miraculous range of tone color, spot-on intonation, and a beautifully natural projection of phrase.  (His magnificent Arte Nova recording of J. S. Bach's Sonatas and Partitas for solo violin should be more widely known in the US.)  Ozawa and the Philharmonic are nothing short of astonishing, presenting the orchestral fabric with such bite and urgency that the music at times sounds like it could have been written by Gustav Mahler himself.  The other music is performed at a similarly exalted level and ranges from the deliciously charming (the 'Much Ado About Nothing' pieces) to the dramatically challenging (Suite for Piano and Strings).  The audience goes wild after each performance, but is mercifully quiet while the music is being played.  Recorded sound is gloriously rich yet wonderfully detailed.

title: A true genius
text: I remember hearing Ogdon's recording of Chopin solo piano back in the early seventies and thinking that it was the most bizarre performance I had ever heard. Back then, of course, Rubenstein's Chopin recordings were my standard, and so I disregarded Ogdon as not my type of pianist or performer. How stupid I was, back then! After being astonished by the first few CDs in this EMI Icon collection (the Tchaikovsky Piano Concerto recording is revelatory on so many levels) I came to the Chopin. Now I understand! In those early days I was studying Spanish literature, primarily Golden Age stuff, and didn't get around to Romanticism until I was a newly minted PhD and at my first teaching post. I always used Rubenstein's recording of Chopin's Etude Op. 10 No. 3 to convey the manic/depressive nature of several Spanish romantic poets, but it always seemed to me to be not "hysterical" enough. John Ogdon's performance conveys exactly what I was trying to communicate to my students. I was unaware of Mr. Ogdon's mental health issues until after hearing this recording, but I believe he certainly had a special insight into the Romantic psyche, confirmed by many of the other recordings of Romantic pieces contained in this collection. Ogdon also had a great talent with contemporary, 20th-Century music, exemplified by his recordings of Bartok, TIppett, Shostakovich, Davies, and his own compositions.

title: Fantastic
text:
I had been heavily anticipating Relient K's new album for about two weeks, ever since I had decided on a whim to rip my friend's copy of Mmhm. Well it being my Spring Break and all, I woke up at 11 yesterday and immediately zipped to Best Buy to buy Five Score...

Being a new fan, I hadn't really had the opportunity to listen to a lot of their older stuff, save for Two Lefts Don't Make A Right and SOME of Tongue in Cheek...but you can really hear their musical progression from one album to the next. Matt Thiessen's songwriting has always been Grade A, but with the previous three releases he's taken it to an entirely different level. Mmhm IS the true Relient K sound...with songs like When I Go Down, Be My Escape, Life After Death and Taxes, Who I Am Hates Who I've Been...

But now we have Five Score and the band has once again taken their sound to another level.

From the opening Beatles/Beach Boys-esque harmonies of "Plead the Fifth", and then on to the rocking "Come Right Out and Say It" and "I Need You," it's apparent immediately that the band has raised their game. It's still Relient K, but it's Relient K more refined and focused than they've ever been. Everything is in perfect balance.

We then have "The Best Thing," which is the first of a few songs about the newfound love of his life. As with many songs on the cd, is has a great piano riff throughout as well as a ridiculously catchy chorus.

"Forgiven" is my personal favorite song on the cd. Again, a very nice piano riff underneath a frantic strumming guitar, followed by a chorus that just swells...."We're all guilty of the same things, we think the thoughts whether or not we see them through, and I know that I have been forgiven..."

"Must Have Done Something Right" is a pretty playful love song that is once again very catchy.

"Give Until There's Nothing Left" is probably my second favorite song on the cd with, per usual, a great message.

"Devastation and Reform" is another rocking track with a very nice guitar riff from Hoopes. Great chorus.

"I'm Taking You With Me" is another love song. Pretty good.

"Faking My Own Suicide" has slide guitars and great folk sound to it. Unlike anything I've heard from RK before. Great song.

"Bite My Tongue" has more great guitar work and another great message...don't cause pain through words.

"Up and Up" is yet another well-written, uplifting, happy track about celebrating everyday of your life. Great chorus and great song.

"Death Bed" is about a dying cancer patient. It sounds like a song titled "death bed" might be really heavy, sad way of ending such a happy cd, but while the song is very powerful, it's not what you think it probably is. It's probably not much of a stretch to say that this is the best song Matt Thiessen has ever written. The verses recount the dying man's life behind a very bouncy beat and great piano playing. Matt Thiessen apparently played about 12 instruments in this song which is really a testament to what an amazingly talented individual he really is. This song IS Relient K, and it continues their trend of ending their albums with great songs...ala Jefferson Aero Plane, When I Go Down...

Well, yeah, it's an amazing album. Go out and purchase a copy if you want to hear one of the best kept secrets in pop music. Okay, maybe they aren't THAT big of a secret, but they are still relatively under the radar...probably because of the Christian Rock label. But as Matt T said, "C.S. Lewis wasn't about just writing to Christians to make them better. He was about writing books that everyone could read and expand their minds. That's what music is all about, too. [Not long] ago it was absurd that P.O.D. was doing Ozzfest or that Sixpence None the Richer was all over the radio. Then, all the sudden, it's all changed."

title: Intensely personal hymn on life and love - great music, too
text:
The Captain And The Kid is billed as the sequel to Elton's seminal Captain Fantastic And The Brown Dirt Cowboy album and that alone lends the project a ridiculous amount of expectation. And, while the record isn't as sonically diverse as Captain Fantastic, lyrically it follows nicely. Most importantly, The Captain And The Kid is Elton's best record since the seventies.

A nostalgic tone lingers over the record, which in itself could be dangerous. But, the classic Elton melodies are here and they suit the material well. In addition to the expected ballads (the heartbreaking Blues Never Fade Away and The Bridge), The Captain finds Elton genuinely rocking out again. Maybe his newfound friendship with the Scissor Sisters has rejuvenated his much-loved seventies persona. Catchy rockers like And The House Fell Down and Just Like Noah's Ark successfully achieve what the album is about: bringing music back to a time when it mattered. There isn't anything especially glossy or produced about the songs, but they're addictive because they're passionate. Best of all is Tinderbox, a gorgeous sing-along nearly worthy of Tiny Dancer status.

Towards the end of the album, the songs begin to show their country and blues roots a little more clearly, culminating in the closing title track, a soft country shuffle which is perhaps the most transparently nostalgic song, where Elton is painted as "an urban soul in a fine silk suit," and Bernie "a heart out west in a Wrangler shirt." It's a partnership to be celebrated, for sure, and The Captain And The Kid does so in amazing form.

text:
Came across this via allmusic.com and Spotify. I'm not familiar with the artist's previous work or collaborations. So while I may not provide much guidance for fans, perhaps I can help those who might wonder if this is worth taking a listen.

The album has a very stream-of-consciousness feel to it with songs, melodies and textures flowing into one another. There's too much melody to be ambient but it doesn't have the standard hooks you might expect in a pop album. Imagine if DJ Shadow's "Endtroducing" and My Bloody Valentine's "Loveless" got their freak on while some kid sat in the corner playing with an old Casio keyboard and you get an idea. Vocals tend to drift in and out like other textures. It might sound flippant but with this album if you don't like what your hearing, wait 30 seconds, it will change.

What's really impressive is that the whole thing feels cohesive and organic. While there are so many and varied sounds they all coalesce to be more than the sum of their parts while still being enjoyable on their own. So if you like electronica this could be up your alley. It has a few beats but it's not really a dance record. This is a put on those nice headphones and close your eyes record. Just like the cover photo, there's enough there to imply many different shapes, without really becoming one.

title: Timeless
text:
I had always thought that The Clash's eponymous debut was going to be my favourite album by them. However, it is London Calling which is frequently cited as their masterpiece, and despite the fact that I thought the straightahead punk of The Clash was more suited to my tastes, I bought it recently anyway having had The Clash for a few years.
Well, the title track alone was enough to make it worth the money. Of course, I already knew the track, but it sounds thrilling on CD, a real classic. But there was more on offer that I liked than I thought there might be. Some of the reggae/ska-ish tracks are a bit cheesy (particuarly 'Wrong 'Em Boyo', surely the worst track on the album) but some of them are great, particularly 'Guns of Brixton' which incorporates the snarling menace of punk into its sound and surely was an influence for The Specials' classic 'Ghost Town'.
Elsewhere, however, the Clash do all sorts of other things: straightahead punk ('Death or Glory'), pop ('Lovers Rock'), The Who-esque rock ('The Card Cheat'), campy funk-pop ('Train In Vain'), sensitive indie ('Lost In The Supermarket') and all-round fusion of all of the above ('Spanish Bombs'). London Calling is above all so great because you can hear where modern bands got their sounds from in every track - each song seems to have inspired a different band to form - 'Rudie Can't Fail' clearly influenced ska-punk bands, while 'Lost In The Supermarket' sounds like it influenced 80s indie like The Smiths and early REM; 'London Calling' the track influenced every rock band after it, in fact the whole album seems to have. This is one of the most important albums made for that very reason, and also for its political messages.

title: A never thought I'd see Maiden run out of ideas....
text: I don't want to rain on anyone's parade but I felt compelled to voice my opinion on the Book of Soul's. I'll start by saying I'm thankful Maiden is still creating new music and touring. My fandom with Maiden began with the first ST album. Yes, I go waaaayyyyy back. Not all the way to the Soundhouse Tapes but close. I remember eagerly awaiting the release of Killers. I don't want to get too long winded here, but when a band announces they are going to release a double CD of new material, expectations sore. The implication being the group has so much strong material that they simply cannot live without any of the given tracks being excluded from the album. I've listened to Souls from beginning to end, loudly multiple times, and I have to say I find this collection of songs to be well beneath the bar that Maiden has set for themselves. Whether Maiden is capable of more than this at this point is another question, but this album is by far the weakest of the reunion era. There are some outstanding moments, but they are few and far between. The Red and The Black and If Eternity Should Fail are both particularly strong tunes (but both should have been trimmed down), but they alone cannot carry the burden of an otherwise barren, depleted project. The examples of this are many, but suffice it to say the songwriting and execution thereof is uninspired for that most part. The production and mastering is flat and bland; there is no punch. I've never heard three guitars sound so impotent. The melodies are tired and do not draw you in. There is a general lack of energy and no explosion from most of the attempted build-ups /crescendos. Many of the tracks crawl along, struggling to keep pace or interest, and should have at least been shortened. I love long songs, but these songs are not well-written enough to be epics, and the execution is surely deficient as well. The songs are very much like a dull, rusty sword, rendered powerless by the rigors of time. There are recycled riffs among many tracks as well. What an odd choice for Maiden to make this release a double CD when many of the tracks would have been unable to find a place on any of the previous albums since Dickinson and Smith returned. I won't compare Souls to the Di'Anno era or Maiden from the Beast/Piece of Mind/Powerslave/SIT/7TH Son eras, because I don't think that is a valid, fair or reliable method for contrast. Conversely, the last four albums are game. The elation and energy of reformation from BNW is not present. There is no monster classic tune on this album as we had with DOD's Paschendale. The inspired intensity, vitality, vigor and drive of AMOLAD is not present. The creative spark of FF has been extinguished. A lot of people don't like DOD, AMOLAD and/or FF, but the achievements of those albums dwarf the offerings of TBOS for the most part. And although it pains me to say it, this is no exaggeration. Soul's shortcomings can be best summed up in a microcosm of looking at the 18 min. Empire of the Clouds alone. It is a song that is overly ambitious. Maiden gets an A for effort and for stretching themselves here, but that doesn't translate into a solid track. It's strange for a Maiden album to come up lame at the end. After all, Maiden wrote the book on strong finishes. But Clouds is a bridge to nowhere and fails to rise and fall with the dramatic peeks and valleys we are so accustomed to with Maiden epics. It's quite a lost opportunity really. There is no journey to enjoy but rather a trip to endure as you frustratingly wait for the song to develop and find itself. The foundational elements are there, but the compositional and arrangement aspects are not. The track truly could have used some contributions from other band members to reconstruct this flat-lining behemoth of decomposition. Although Dickinson's piano melodies are fantastic w/ the accompanying strings, the guitar driven instrumental passages are woefully inadequate for such an ambitious track and fail to captivate; it's actually shockingly bad.  Where was the producer to tell the band they could do much better than this? I would have given Souls a 2.5 star rating if I could have, but out of respect for the band I went with 3 stars rather than 2. I look forward to the ensuing tour and hope Empire of the Clouds is not in the set list. That 18 minutes could be used for (non- tBOS) songs that are more much deserving of live presentation. The Book of Souls would have been much better off as a single disc. In fact the album ends rather well with disc one. There are just not enough good ideas here to fill up two discs let alone one. Up the Irons!!!

title: Should have been legendary!
text:
This is one of those rare events in rock history where everything is firing on all cylinders. I can think of a few in my catalog (Zeppelin IV/Physical Graffiti, Blood Sugar Sex Magic, Close to the Edge, 90125, KISS ALIVE!, RUSH & Moving Pictures, and The Cult Electric to name a few) that I consider every track a winner. Believe it or not Triumph: Never Surrender is one of those near-perfect moments.
I never understood why this album didn't propel Triumph into legendary status like some of their predecessors. Never Surrender was much better than anything released in 1983. This was a time of the burgeoning MTV: Howard Jones, Madonna, INXS, Thompson Twins, and "She Blinded Me with Science." Triumph dared to carry the torch of Rock & Roll into the 1980's, refusing to compromise their sound, but still managing to achieve recognition on MTV with "World of Fantasy." This album always held a special place for me as an oasis from the horrible soft-sounding, synth-age music of the time. For some reason, 30 years after its release, "Too Much Thinking" started running through my head and I had to go get a CD copy of it. Having rediscovered this album, I found that it is better than even I remembered the first time around. It is a CLASSIC! I hope the band is proud of their accomplishment on this record; it is very much appreciated, despite the moderate success.

title: Strong Songwriting and Great Vocals
text:
"Smilers" is yet another great record by Aimee Mann. It's a big mystery to me why so few people, at least here in Denmark, still not seem to have discovered what a great artist she is.
This album from 2008 possesses the same virtues of practically all the other albums from Mann . Very fine melodies, often with intelligent and relevant lyrics, musically varied and tastefully arranged and produced.

Of the three singles, "Freeway", "31 Today" and "Phoenix" the first two show Manns’s great ability to write immediately catchy songs. Mann has published - for both of these great music videos. "Phoenix" is a little wistful song - a style which Mann masters with great conviction.
Apart from 2-3 slightly anonymous ballads, the album as a whole very satisfying and represents all the best of what Mann is known for.
"Borrowing Time" and "The Great Beyond" are two songs that show a lighter and effortless songwriting but never lightweight - both song among my personal favorites. More grandiose is the stunning "Looking for Nothing" - really great build-up. Another highlight is "Medicine Wheel"; song that could have been inspired by Robbie Robertson and The Band.

Songs like "Little Tornado", "True Believer," "Columbus Avenue" and "It's Over" belong in the more subdued end and are songs you might oversee in the first and second round, but which may later turn out as winners.

Finally I must mention that it is, like always, a pleasure to listen to Aimee Mann’s great vocals.

title: Let's Be Fair....
text:
Katherine Jenkins has gotten some bad press; she has been slammed for her looks (poor, blind, reverse discriminatory, fools), criticized by classical reviewers, and essentially dismissed. A review I read in "Opera News" was one of the harsher I've ever seen. With all respect to a fabulous magazine, this really isn't their territory. Yes, she bills herself as a "classical singer", but that's NOT the same as "opera singer". Mont Blanc used her for a poster girl. What's wrong with that? Are guys that can afford Mont Blancs too old to appreciate sexy babes? Please. Katherine is an ENTERTAINER, who uses classical music as the basis of her act . Again, what's wrong with that? Sarah Brightman has been doing the same for about 30 years, with less looks, and no better (yes, she is more experienced) voice. (And, some of the same material appears on the records of both). (And, yes, I love Sarah).

From Mozart to Rogers and Hammerstein, she does quite well, even daring to lead off with "Time to Say Goodbye", which is essentially a signature piece for Sarah. A nice rework of "Va pensiero" from Verdi's "Nabucco", as well as a good rendition of "O Sole Mio" deserve mention, and I thought she did well with Mozart's "Laudate Dominum" and the "Seguedilla" from "Carmen". Still, if you expect note-perfect to the original, you will get mad. Remember: ENTERTAINMENT.

Many years ago, I heard a wise man observe that "You don't play chess by the rules of checkers". This CD is what it is: entertainment, using classical music for a vehicle. If you accuse me of a weakness for pretty blondes with low voices, I'll plead guilty. (Not that low; Katherine is a kind of high mezzo). The girl couldn't stand comparison to Elina Garanca, BUT she doesn't attempt that. If Katherine wants to occupy her niche, basically "Opera meets glitz and glamour", God bless her. She's doing it rather well. Now, if she signs to sing "Carmen" at The Met, I'll be happy to sign the commitment papers for her, and whoever contracts her. For now, You Go, Girl!!

title: Light Speed Jazz
text: I saw Miles play at least 10 times but sadly, not on the night of February 12, 1964 at Lincoln Center, the night his group created light speed jazz at tempos bordering on the unconscious. Tony Williams, the 18 year old prodigy, just took over and made these guys move in a way that simply is astonishing given just how experienced and talented a group this truly was. Every time I listen to this, I am struck by the spacing and openness of the sound and the power this group had in playing tunes they know by heart. It is a masterpiece that, in a round about way, is an up tempo salute to Kind of Blue, the greatest jazz album of all time as many of the compositions here are the same ones that Miles and Bill Evans penned for the earlier work. title: EVERYTHING IT SHOULD BE
text: These are stunning performances, full-bodied, energetic and vibrant, with amazing orchestral clarity, revealing all of Stravinsky's intricate details. I am always amused to read reviews of this and other recordings of Le Sacre complaining that they aren't "savage" enough. The tribe about which Stravinsky was writing was primitive, but they were not cannibals or head-hunters. I think some reviewers are expecting cacophonous sound-effects, like a background soundtrack to one of the Jurassic Park movies. (I doubt very much that the musicians at the 1913 premiere were, in the words of one Amazon reviewer, "shredding their bows and bending their reeds"; there is a recording conducted by Pierre Monteaux, who led that world premiere, that indicates otherwise.) Like many others, I am also fond of Bernstein's over-the-top and somewhat undisciplined recording, but that, like so many of his recordings, was more a reflection of Lenny than the composer, who in this case also recorded his own score with far more restraint. Dorati was too consummate a musician to go in for mere noise and vulgar bombast. Stravinsky composed a musical and, at times, ethereally beautiful, score, and this recording delivers on all counts. If you want noise instead of music, look elsewhere.

title: Historical Stokowski, indispensable for the Stokowski admirer
text:
This well-filled disc (76:50) gathers historical recordings made for Columbia by Stokowski with the New York Philharmonic (then called the Philharmonic-Symphony Orchestra of New York) between 1947 and 1949. They all make their first appearance on CD. Other than Wagner's Flying Dutchman-Overture and perhaps Tchaikovsky's Francesca da Rimini (Stokowski's first of three recordings, the two others being for Everest in 1958, [[ASIN:B0000023H8 Tchaikovsky: Francesca da Rimini; Hamlet / Scriabin: Poem of Ecstasy ~ Stokowski]], and for Philips in 1974, first CD reissue on [[ASIN:B000001330 Conducts Tchaikovsky]], now on a twofer from the indispensable Australian Eloquence, [[ASIN:B000XFZSBI Tchaikovsky: Nutcracker Suite / Serenade for Strings / Francesca da Rimini / Capriccio Italien]]), they are not standard repertoire (the Walküre music is Stokowski's arrangement). The two rarities are Griffes' languid and early Debussy-reminiscent "White Peacock" - the orchestration of a piano piece from 1915 and Stokowski's only recording of a composition which he had premiered back in 1919 - and Messiaen's L'Ascension - the conductor made a famous stereo remake in 1970 with the Hilversum Philharmonic Orchestra in Decca's vivid "Phase Four" stereo ([[ASIN:B000026C6Q Franck: Symphony in D minor, Op.48 / Messiaen: L'Ascension / Ravel / Chopin / Duparc]]), and the remake is better, if only for its great sonics, indispensable with such an atmospheric and coloristic composer as Messiaen, but championing and recording Messiaen in 1947 was amazingly prescient. The Messiaen is also the most original-sounding composition on the disc. The sound is mono and somewhat unidimensional, but the transfers (made by the Sony Music Studios in New York) are great, with almost no surface noise. This release is of course indispensable for the Stokowski admirer.

There are two companion dics to this one: Volume 2 has more Wagner, Khachaturian's Masquerade Suite, Sibelius' Maiden with the Roses, Schoenberg's Song of the Wood-Dove from Gurre-Lieder, Tchaikovsky's Waltz from the Serenade for Strings and excerpts from Copland's Billy the Kid - material not as substantial as on this volume 1, in my opinion ([[ASIN:B00006RYHN Leopold Stokowski: The New York Philharmonic Columbia (US) Recordings, Volume 2]]), but volume 3 has Stokowski's only recording of a Mozart Symphony (the 35th) and of Vaughan Williams' 6th Symphony (in its original version) as well as Tchaikovsky's Romeo and Juliet and a rarity, Thomas Scott's "From the Sacred Harp" ([[ASIN:B000222YGO Leopold Stokowski: The New York Philharmonic Columbia (US) Recordings, Volume 3]]).

title: Bonamassa Delivers A Quadruple Threat!
text:
I’ve said it before about previous reviews of Joe Bonamassa offerings and I must say it again: Regular Boomerocity readers know that I have a short version review of any Joe Bonamassa project. This time is no exception. Ready? Here it is:

Love it/buy it.

To be technically correct, I’d have to say all of the above a total of four times because that’s how many CD sets Mr. Bonamassa has rolled out for his fans. Entitled, “Tour de Force – Live In London”, the foursome is offered both as individual concert discs or as a special premium boxed set. The shows at each of the venues have been captured on two discs per location guaranteeing substantial coverage of each performance.

Whether in the spacious, historic Royal Albert Hall, the cozy Borderline or the performances at Shepherd’s Bush Empire or Hammersmith Apollo in between, the performances are jaw-dropping in their own right.

While fans will notice that there are plenty of the JB staples on these discs (“Django/Mountain Time”, “Sloe Gin” and “Just Got Paid:, for instance), don’t make the mistake of thinking that they’re the same ol’ tunes. Just as in any Bonamassa performance, Joe brings new life and energy into those cherished songs. In addition to those favorites, Joe delivers phenomenal performances of newer tunes such as “Dust Bowl”, “Driving Toward The Daylight”, “Slow Train” and “Dislocated Boy”.

JB enthusiasts will also be pleased to know that he has also captured his fun with the theremin during his performances of “The Ballad Of John Henry”. And get this! The theremin thingy comes in at almost precisely the same time on each of the three performances – I mean with seconds of each other.

That’s scary good!

Bonamassa fans will definitely want all four performances as part of their listening library – and to join their video library of the same performances. As for what to choose to turn people on to this amazing talent? That’s a hard one to decide. My feeling is that you can’t go wrong with any of them. Just close your eyes and pick one.

title: Three piece death/thrash that is truly astonishing
text:
I will always consider Sepultura's "Arise" as one of death/thrash metal's greatest albums of all time, but Brazil has another equally great death metal band Krisiun that are an absolutely ferocious three piece band that at times sound a bit like a cross between Morbid Angel with some really twisted and very innovative guitar work that reminds me of Trey Azagthoth and David Davidson of Revocation mixed up in a blender and poured over a glass of liquid razor wire.
"Southern Storm" does have a cover of "Refuse/Resist" as homage to the classic Sepultura, but otherwise burn with an intensity that very few bands seem to generate. It is odd how three piece groups almost always are more energetic - probably out of necessity to cover for lack of a second guitar, but also probably because the threesome is so powerful and dangerous it doesn't need anybody else. Motorhead started out, or more accurately with the first album as probably the most brutal vile three piece band ever, and after a period with two guitarists, and that was good stuff too, don't get me wrong, ended up as a three piece for the last several years. Matt Pike founded High on Fire to offer the American version of the heaviest Motorhead. So Krisiun are worthy keepers of that line up formula.
The vocals are somewhat reminiscent of David Vincent, hence the Morbid Angel comparison, but Krisiun are their own beast, bringing a stunning attack to their music with musicianship that is indeed impressive and unique and a love of the music that makes them one band were I in a death metal outfit I would not want on my bill.
Vader are probably Europe's best death/thrash band, and these two are at the very front of the best the genre has to offer. I love Kreator, Sodom and others, but this stuff is tougher if such a thing is possible, and not just a noise fest that substitutes grunting or one note riffing for metal. I will be getting a lot more of this amazing band.

title: God & Guns & Good Old Rock Music
text:
Lynyrd Skynyrd is an old band, but that doesn't sound old for these days. Modern rock music that sometimes flirts with country or blues is the most approximate description that can be given to this new release, called "God & Guns", the album. This definition, however, is not too different from what they have always been labled of.

Old time fans might find a first listening a little weird, even shocking, as the tendency is to associate this new work with anything they have done before and once listeners figure out what this album is almost completely not related to their previous acts, some might even get somehow disappointed. "God & Guns", the track, amongst others on the album, contains heavy guitar riffles and a rock punch unimaginable to many when the thought of Lynyrd Skynyrd comes to mind.

There is a passage that resembles the "typical" Skynyrd tune ("Southern Ways") though, but that's the only one.

All in all, despite unavoidable comparisons that anyone - including myself - tends to make with the classical band that lived its heyday in the 70s. "God & Guns" is a rock solid effort that is worth of any southern rock fans, regardless of age.
