title: Best album of 2008
text:
13 songs in 13 days. No written lyrics, no other musicians to help, nothing but the improvisation of one man both on vocals and on instrumentation. And he puts out the best album of last year. Impossible? Oh yeah, I forgot to mention, that man is Paul McCartney. He's that guy from that band, you know.

The album starts off with a screamer, and it seems like it's directed at his ex-wife (he sings - or screams - about giving love and getting betrayed). In fact, if you read the lyrics of all of these songs, even though they're improvised there is actual meaning and symbolism and metaphor you can derive from the words. There is some poetry here.

"Two Magpies" is sweet and understated, it's kind of like you're listening in to Paul while he's alone with his guitar and reminiscing in song. The best word to describe "Sing the Changes" is BRIGHT. The album has a lot of references to light, and that's probably why this is the single - you can practically see the light while listening to this. "Traveling Light," the fourth song, is the opposite - it is dark, mysterious, with a haunting vocal from Paul.

"Highway" is the kind of 70's rocker they don't make anymore. It has Wings written all over it. "Light From Your Lighthouse" is maybe the catchiest song on the album. Paul double tracked it with a very high vocal and a very low vocal, giving it a very funky sound. At this point in the album you may find yourself dancing, or at least bopping your head and mouthing the lyrics.

"Sun is Shining" is just a beautiful song; if you saw the light earlier in the album, now it's just pouring in. In "Dance 'Til We're High" Paul unintentionally made a great Christmas song, there's just something very Christmas-y about it, and I don't mean in a cheesy way - I can imagine it in a great movie, in a scene with snowflakes falling and a family dancing together.

"Lifelong Passion" should be listened to with your eyes closed - it's a richly visual song. These are the first three lines:

Step into the misty mountains
With your hair like ambered honey
To feeling warm and breezes

He improvised that!? Well, you'd think the rest of the album would be filled with duds, filler material, but it's not. "Is This Love" is a very meditative song with beautiful music and light, distant vocals - I think George Harrison would have liked it. I think John would have liked the next song, "Lovers In A Dream" - it's very psychedelic - the kind of song the Beatles would have released to trip people out (like Revolution #9). The album ends with two experimental instrumentals, "Universal Here, Everlasting Now" and "Don't Stop Running."

Well, I've done my sales pitch for the day (it's the least I could do for the guy who has given me so much great music to listen to). If you're still reading this that means you haven't clicked Add To Cart yet. Go on, buy this album!

title: Boomerang With Me
text: The title of this CD is actually "Mercy!"/"See-Saw."  "Mercy!" was released in late 1964; "See-Saw" in 1966.  This is essential soul and some crazy stuff.  As usual, the people who edit liner notes left in a sentence like "Born in Orangeburg, S.C., on March 24, 1938, Covay's initial singing experience was strictly sacred."  What's wrong with that sentence, soul men and women?  Oh well, it's the vernacular, right, just like this music.  Actually, soul music is quite formal, abiding by the rules more than most styles.  The 1964 material might sound a little more old-fashioned to some but it's good and kinda unhinged; cool guitar as well  (some believe that Jimi Hendrix played on a few of these songs, and the guitar in "Mercy, Mercy" does bear a resemblance to Hendrix's style).  As some of you might know, the Rolling Stones covered "Mercy, Mercy"; it's the first tune on their classic "Out of Our Heads" LP from 1965.  And in general, when you listen to Mick Jagger you hear Don Covay.  The second LP on this disc, "See-Saw," features a few tracks cut in Memphis at Stax, with the great rhythm section of Cropper, Dunn, Jones and Jackson.  "Sookie Sookie" is a dirty song with some truly cubist drum fills; "The Boomerang" sounds completely nuts; Aretha Franklin covered "See-Saw" and I hope Don made a lotta money from it.  Don went on to do one of the classic messin'-around songs of the '70s, indeed of any era, "I Was Checkin' Out (She Was Checkin' In)", but that's a hard one to find since the only comprehensive Covay collection, released back in the '90s, is out of catalog.  It would be nice to be able to buy all of his work  again; Steppenwolf, who covered his "Sookie Sookie," has just about all their stuff available, and if the world needs to hear Goldy McJohn, it sure as heck needs to hear the great Don Covay.

title: Holy Week in Cuenca, Spain ...
text:
This grand performance of the complete liturgical offices of "Hebdomadae Sanctae", composed by Tomas Luis de Victoria during his one-year (1585) stay in Roma, was recorded in the beautiful Church of San Miguel in the picturesque canyon city of Cuenca, east of Madrid, on Palm Sunday, Good Friday, and Holy Saturday of 2004, during the Festival of Sacred Music supported by the foundation of the large Spanish banking institution Caja Madrid. Cuenca is one of the jewels among the historical cities of Spain, still not well known to anglophone tourists ... and amy it stay that way! It's most famous for its 'hanging houses' that loom over the steep canyon though the heart of the city. It ranks next to Segovia as one of my favorite spots in Spain. I was in Spain in 2004. And yet I didn't know about this festival and thus missed perhaps the chance of a lifetime to hear such an ample performance of Victoria's spiritual masterwork.

Understand, please, that this was not simply a concert performance by the usual four singers of La Colombina. That brilliant ensemble was doubled for the occasion: the eight singers who took the solo roles and samg most of the polyphony were sopranos Monica Mauch and Raquel Andueza, contralto Audrey Burgener, countertenor Josep Pastor, tenors Josep Benet and Francesc Pizarro, baritone Josep Cabré, and basso Daniele Carnovich. Even this augmented ensemble was supported at times by the fifteen male voices of Schola Antiqua. If you want primarily to hear this music sung with the utmost polish and aplomb, you'll probably prefer the several recordings La Colombina has issued of one-on-a-part performances of Victoria and Guerrero, including exactly the same compositions for 'Feria Sexta - the Passion of Our Lord' that are sung on CD 2 of this set. Unquestionably, the purely quartet performances are musically more virtuosic, and if you've read other reviews of mine, you know that I'm skeptical of all recordings of large choirs. But this time the engineers, the acoustics of the church, and the singers have combined to render grandeur audible, to recreate the spacious wonder of the great sacred choruses of 16th C Spain in its Golden Age.

title: Viva La Vida
text:
Experimental. The word is smattered all over every music critic's review of Coldplay's 4th studio release. And if you listen to enough indie rock, you might've gathered suspicion that the press was hinting at a Mars Volta-esque foray into atonal dissonance and structural ambiguity. But worry not. While Chris Martin might be stretching his vocal range down toward Hades and a pinch of world music spice has been added to their decidedly western formulas, "Viva La Vida" stands resolutely as a Coldplay album, with a healthy dollop of the arena-ready choruses and karaoke approved melodies for which the public adores them. Myself included.

Yes, there is an instrumental ("Life In Technicolor"), and a cuplet of tunes with "secret songs" serving as epilogues ("Yes" and "Death and All His Friends"). Sure, we have some strings set in the phrygian mode ("Yes") and some heavy metal guitar crunch ("Violet Hill"). And oh wait, is that Will Champion working the kettle drums ("Viva La Vida")? Kudos to Brian Eno, a personal hero of mine, for helping the band to take these seemingly subtle yet effective steps in the studio.

But all soundscape and texture jargon aside, the band remains its most confident where you'd expect them to: on songs like "Lovers In Japan/Reign of Love", where the rhythm section of Coldplay's godfathers, U2, sound like they were sitting in for a session. Chris Martin, as tentative a rock star as he is, has always outwardly worshipped his influences. Anytime you hear echoes of the aforemention Eno-produced quartet from Dublin or even REM on the record, the band soars. Pushing the envelope never felt so easy.

title: Interesting
text:
Mr. Wispelwey -- an extraordinarily skilled cellist -- adopts what seems to be an unusual approach to these suites. His bowings sound "authentic," i.e. they are similar to the bowings found in the earliest known copies of the score, from the 18th century. He also plays with a detachment of stroke associated with Baroque music. However, his performance temperment in these suites seems to have more in common with music for the Romantic period, or perhaps even with 20th century music. Or maybe it's just Mr. Wispelway's subjective approach that makes the temperment seem inappropriate. Anyway, it is an odd-sounding combination. It's as Mr. Wispelway approaches each movement with the rhythmic liberty usually associated only with the Preludes. This is not wrong (who's to say?) but it drains the music of its flow.

Mr. Wispelwey's readings of these suites are personal to the point of sounding self-consiousness. His sacrific of rhythmic flow is, to my ears, a large detriment to the music. Nevertheless, these performances are interesting though, for me, less than satisfying.

(If you desire "authentic" bowings with flow, try the wonderful recordings by Jaap ter Linden or Anner Bylsma. If you want a more Romantic period reading, try Rostropovich or Maisky. If you seek a more balanced reading, try Ma's first excellent recording, or Fournier [a personal reading from a different era, with lovely and unusual legato], or Kirschbaum [awesome, though sometimes brutish] or Peter Bruns [near perfect, if perfection is what you're after]. These are all great recordings!).

title: Fine set but not as spirited as Boskovsky's or Stolz's recordings
text:
It's great that Naxos has reissued its recordings of Johann Stauss Jr.'s orchestral works under the Marco Polo imprint in a new box at roughly $2 per disc (the original recordings on Marco Polo usually cost at least $15 per disc brand new in a bricks-and-mortar shop). There's much to enjoy here, and a lot of the fun is in hearing pieces that don't find their way onto compilations recorded elsewhere.

On the other hand many of these recordings were made in the days when Naxos relied more on lesser-known artists from Hungary, Poland and the former Czechoslovakia. If one has been introduced to the Strauss family's music through recordings under the baton of Willi Boskovsky, Robert Stolz, or the conducting stars who've performed at the annual New Year's concerts in Vienna (e.g. Carlos Kleiber, Herbert von Karajan, Ricardo Muti, Lorin Maazel), some of the recordings in this box-set may seem like competent run-throughs to fulfill the contract with Naxos; no one will confuse the Slovak State Philharmonic Orchestra with the Vienna Philharmonic or Vienna Johann Strauss Orchestra. However, not all of Johann Strauss' works are masterpieces, pleasant or uplifting as they almost all are. In that vein it's a tall order for any orchestra to make the occasionally banal piece as memorable or majestic as the Blue Danube Waltz or the Thunder and Lightning polka, among others. It's not their fault that Strauss Jr. had the occasional off-day with composition.

This set will appeal most to diehard fans of light Viennese music of the 19th century and/or the Strauss family. Otherwise, the sets by Willi Boskovsky (EMI (Warner) or Decca (Universal)) and Robert Stolz (reissued by Sony/RCA from original on Eurodisc) will be more than enough even if these do not present all of Strauss Jr.'s output. These alternatives have the advantage of being played by people with this kind of light or "kitschy" music in their blood (Boskovsky was the concertmaster of the Vienna Philharmonic and made his name conducting the Strauss family's music; he conducts the Vienna Philharmonic or the Johann Strauss Orchestra in his recordings. Stolz was a composer of operettas in addition to being a conductor; he conducts the Vienna Symphony or Berlin Symphony orchestras in his recordings (N.B. these are different from and in the shadow of the "Philharmonic" orchestras in these cities but they are excellent and of arguably higher repute than most of the orchestras used by Naxos).

title: From a Die-Hard Fishbone Soulja... This is a grower
text:
It's taken me a few months to write this review. Mainly because i stutter
(pauses for zero laughter)

Crazy Glue, the new Fishbone EP commemorating their 25th anniversary as a band! (You didn't hear about it? Well you should have, there SHOULD BE a FISHBONE holiday.

Just saying.

Anyways, the band is back. There have been some line up changes alluded to by other reviewers. This album benefits from having Dirty Walt back in the mix. He adds so much hilarity and f-ing character to the band that it's a testament to the chemistry of the original lineup that just his return made this album a bit much better. (No offense to Faceplant Scorpion Backpinch)

However, most of the subject matter of the songs are huge downers. Luckily for me, i can identify with some of it. (Which means it grew with me) At first, lacking an upbeat song like "Cheyenne Starr Forevermore" I had a hard time approaching this behemoth. But it has grown on me. Relentlessly.

Crazy Glue is a great chill track
Flutterbutter is so damn aggressive and thumping that i got hooked on it first at their INCREDIBLE LIVE SHOWS in LA. (Norwood never sounded better on bass...LIVE... well, maybe he did, i wasn't around in 85)

Deep s*** backstroke is a great commentary, the song is rocking as well.

Rather than continue a track by track I'll just say for the most part the album fluctuates from riffing to BLISTERING to aggression, with the two tail end songs being the only reprieve. One: chill; Crazy Glue. The Other: Meditative but somehow musically fun "Weed Beer and Cigarettes"

I've been playing this album more and more often, listening back to it each time and hearing a new phrase or expression i hadn't caught before. For an EP, this is pretty phenomenal. I'd suggest that it might become a favorite down the line with a new generation of alt rock or punkers (the ones who listen to everything)

Not a drop of talent missing, not an ounce of energy lacking.

ALL HAIL THE MIGHTY FISHBONE!

text:
This is a sad little Dylan Hits collection. Wheres the beef? Theres no food here. Ok, sure these songs are all worthy of a hits package, most Dylan songs are, but why this? Why now? It seems in the last five or six years or so, a new Dylan hits package comes out every couple of months. Usually with one more somewhat newer song than the one before it had. This one includes SUMMER DAYS from the (awesome) 2001 release LOVE AND THEFT. If you are interested in new DYLAN material I highly recommend that album.
Otherwise this collection just offers the same stuff that every other collection has had so far, only stripped more than all the others. The early sixties hey-day is represented by five songs. Though these may be his most well- knowns they are definately not his BEST. How much of these early protest songs are necessary? TAMBOURINE MAN? I'm not trying to hate on anything, but lets leave that one in the sixties, I'm sure the new comers would be better suited with a JUST LIKE A WOMAN or something like that. ALL ALONG THE WATCHTOWER was never really one of Bobs strongest songs either (its excellent) but the only reason we know it is because its so widely covered (Jimi). After that we get a handful of seventies offerings KNOCKIN ON HEAVENS DOOR and HURRICANE are to be expected, as are the rest TANGLED UP, and GOTTA SERVE SOMEBODY... I have a hard time believing that song is gonna sail well with a complete novice. The eighties are represented through one song, JOKERMAN, not a bad choice.. that is actually a popular song still, and was widely known throughout genres in '83-84 when it was first released. Still, it's obvious that the main sell point here is supposed to be his most recent singles NOT DARK YET (1998), THINGS HAVE CHANGED (2000), and SUMMER DAYS (2001). Even though at this point any begginer probably wouldn't even remember those songs. If you are new to school in the world of Bob Dylan, I would definately recommend starting somewhere else. The two disc ESSENTIAL is hardly any more money than this, and is way more worth it. One disc spanning such a full career? Theres way to many holes, even if you just want Hurricane and the EVERYBODY MUST GET STONED song... you will surely find the other collection to be more satisfying throughout, and you'll be glad you splurged the couple extra coins.

title: agitated, vicious candy-colored music
text:
I "jumped on the boat" with blueberry boat, and ever since I've been an avid follower of the Fiery Furnaces. If normal human emotions can be scaled from -5 to 5, with 5 being very happy, I think a score of 15 is required to truly appreciate Blueberry Boat. 15 is not easily obtained, so I find myself going back to B.B. only rarely. My favorite works are Gallowsbird's Bark and EP, because they are the sharpest. With B.B., as with Bitter Tea, the F.F. philosophy is most strikingly evident: to make extremely catchy moments, and then to shatter them with jagged tangents. It's as though they are waving their hands back at pop music as they ride a rocket to the sun.

I imagined a theme for Bitter Tea, after I read that Matt wrote all of the songs except for two that Eleanor wrote, and the two they wrote together. With the lyrics almost entirely being from the female perspective, I imagine Matt reflecting on the loss of someone through Eleanor's voice, like the ghost of his past that continues to haunt him. I hear echoes of Suicide on this album, with the music-box sounding piano shuffles. On song #2 I even remember Chopin. I enjoyed the video (it made me think that perhaps the F.F.s are dropping the inane lollygogging of unnaturally extended youth that's only possible for professional artists) because the hit track has moments of bleak honesty, though I can't help but shudder when I hear that "only the sadness remains" (and I consider this song an outlier on the album, because it was written by Eleanor). I laughed when I saw them wincing and jumpy, in the subway station (Matt) and looking out the windows of an abandoned house (Eleanor). Although we can relate to "all of my empty days" and "trying to capture my memory's maze," "only the sadness remains" is a whiney lyric for an adult-looking adolescent. Still, I really enjoy the video.

I didn't see the F.F.'s when they came to town, but I might just see them in June because of this album. They may not be the most addictive band, but they certainly are interesting. Try tying together the backward lyrics for a good time (I hear at one point "There's more than lettuce").

I am going to recede into the background on this review. I have to. Roy brought so many well-known and expert musicians to this wonderous event and they all had the good sense to stay out of the spotlight. Well, after all, it is the remarkable Roy Orbison. And I'm sure that he taught them all a thing or two about music through the years. It is about human courtesy and respect. And believe me, Roy deserved it all.
This music is like silk gliding across a glistening ocean. So impeccably done and every note here is essential. No excess-no shortage. Everything in proper balance under the sun and moon. God Bless Roy for sharing his genius while he was with us.
I suppose what strikes me so much about Roy's tunes is his honesty. He was master at writing about heartache and loss - especially in love. But with this comes the fact that men, do indeed, cry. In loneliness- in desperation - and in love, men do cry. And, mind you, all this expressed in a vocal range that was nothing less than staggering. His was a land inhabited by wishes, dreams, hopes, fear and sorrow. And no one sang this with more dedication or emotion than Roy did.
This live outing treats us to an array of his best tunes; "Only the Lonely","Crying","Pretty Woman", "Blue Bayou" and much, much more. The beauty of live sound is never more evident than it is here. Crisp, moving, and Roy's vocals wrapping you in a warm embrace throughout.
If you really want to experience one of the very best (and essential) artists that America ever produced - listen to Roy Orbison. A true original and irreplaceable.
Very high marks for this gem. To miss it is like missing a part of the soul of life. Yes. It's that good.

title: The new riders on the storm
text:
"West" kicks off with the first four notes of the Black Sabbath song, "Paranoid." (A similar thing happens on the song, "Flight.") That's the bad news.

The good news is that once clear of the album's first two rather uneventful songs, Wooden Shjips hoists its sails and sets course for the open sea. On "Home" and "Looking Out" in particular, singer/guitarist Ripley Johnson loosens his gnarl, unfurling dazzling fretboard discourses overtop layers of looping white noise, a la Suicide.

Along with noise forebear Velvet Underground, synthpop pioneer Suicide is an ever-present influence in any Shjips mix. However, the band digs far deeper for inspiration: The "j" was put in Shjips to give the name a Swedish flavor, a nod to Trad, Gras & Stenar, an obscure jam band from Sweden.

Shjips is well steeped in the San Francisco-brewed blend of experimental psych so rampant in clubs like Hemlock Tavern and festivals like On Land, the ambient/drone community's reply each year to Outside Lands. Influences worn on its sleeve aside, San Francisco's Shjips knows how to maintain a layman's interest in its spaced-out exploits. There is a cohesion to the mix that keeps "West" from sailing off toward the meridian line -- or Jupiter. On "West," the band's third album, Johnson demonstrates a keen ear for rhythm despite his noise-rock affectations, and when that fails, organist Nash Whalen has the fortitude to rein in the hammering wall of feedback.

Backmasking is used to great effect on the turbulent, fog-wrapped closer, "Rising," a tidal wave of sound that builds and builds -- Johnson sounding as if he's chanting in Latin with his voice in reverse, giving the dirge a spiritual heft. It's a good way to bring this piercing meditation to a close.

title: So Much More Than Smoke on the Water
text: While it would be easy to say 'this is the album with Smoke on the Water on it' and call it a day, there's way too much going on with this all-time classic to leave it at that. It would be the same as saying Paranoid is the Black Sabbath album with the song Paranoid on it, 'nuff said. Yes, “Smoke” is DP's most well-known song, their Paranoid, or Stairway, or Dream On, the one song that everybody who listens to rock music is going to know. And for that, Machine Head belongs in every rock music fan's collection. But this album is an undeniable force to be reckoned with, bursting at the seams with classic songs and moments. First off is the mighty Highway Star, a true barnburner of a lead track and a staple of classic rock radio. From there, it moves into hard rock heaven with the swaggering groove of Maybe I'm a Leo and the uptempo Letters From Home. Then comes a precursor of Ritchie Blackmore's boogie-woogie Rainbow leanings with the roadhouse vibe of Never Before. Smoke on the Water next relays that fateful trip to Switzerland, when some stupid with a flare gun burned down Frank Zappa and the Mother's best place around, and the band was running out of time with the Rolling truck Stones thing parked outside. Combining one of hard rock's greatest riffs with one of its most memorable choruses makes this song a crowd favorite to this day, which just happens to be nearly forty-five years after it was written. Machine Head continues with its one lengthy song, Lazy, which remains a staple of DP's live set. The extended jam that makes up its first half is a fantastic showcase of the masterful musical capability of Lord, Blackmore, Glover, and Paice. The album concludes with yet another radio favorite, the forceful and unforgettable Space Truckin'. Machine Head made one hell of a statement that no one could surpass the rock prowess of Deep Purple, and it stands today as a testament to the Mk. II lineup's power and ability. Looking for one of the greatest rock albums of all time? You found it.

title: His music nourishes the soul......
text:
Babatunde plays jazz from the heart with an Afro-Cuban-Carribbean that influences his music but isn't too overwhelming. The CD is light and not overpowering, like a fine wine while Babatunde's drums play a melodic rhythm which sometimes comes across as a lead instrument. Originally released in 1995, this shows Babatunde before his big release of Soul Pools. A raw but more gentle jazz record.

..........Babatunde Lea is a Bay Area percussionist, and an established session musician. He has worked alongside Pharaoh Sanders, Van Morrison, McCoy Tyner, Leon Thomas, Joe Henderson, John Tchicai, and Bobby Hutcherson, before recording an album for Ubiquity Jazz that will remind listeners that he is a skilled band leader, too.

For his debut Ubiquity Jazz album, "March of The Jazz Guerrillas", Babatunde assembled a heavyweight list of guests to make his point. Hilton Ruiz plays piano--Ruiz appeared on Babatunde's 1996 recording, "Level of Intent". Alex Blake is on bass--Babatunde and Blake play together in Pharaoh Sanders' band. Two master percussionists, Bill Summers and Munyungo Jackson, join Babatunde to add rhythmic layers to the mix; and talented West Coast saxophonist and vocalist Richard Howell rounds out the sound.

Babatunde was born in Danville, Virginia. His family moved northward up the Eastern Seaboard when he was only six months old and came to settle in Englewood, New Jersey. It was there that he was first inspired by his aunts and cousins and by stories of his drum playing Aunt Gloria (first woman in Virginia playing drums in a marching band) to begin playing drums himself.

In the sixth grade, Babatunde began drumming with various marching groups. In 1959, at age 11, he attended a concert of African drumming and dance performed by Babatunde Olatunji and his Drums of Passion which left an indelible impression on this young drummer and permanently set his direction in life. In the ninth grade he began playing conga drums and was playing on a professional level by his junior year in high school when, at 16, he played on his first professional recording session for producer Ed Townsend.

In the early 1970s Babatunde hit his stride in New York City performing regularly with such high profile artists as Leon Thomas, Oscar Brown Jr., Lonnie Liston Smith, Kenny Kirkland, John Purcell, Buddy Williams and Eddie "Gua Gua" Rivera. It was in 1977 that Babatunde migrated to the West Coast where he settled in the culturally fertile San Francisco Bay Area. It was not long before Babatunde became a vital figure in the Bay Areas music scene as well, becoming known for his versatility and ability to fit into several music genres. Since then, Babatunde has been the first call drummer for musicians seeking a dynamic and spirited drumming that he brings to the music.

title: An awesome, if slightly odd intro to Felt
text:
Make no mistake, this is a slightly perplexing comp. It makes no real attempt to comprehensively cover the time-period it represents - Felt's 1980-85 tenure on the seminal Cherry Red label. Nearly a third of its songs come from one album, the undeniably awesome "Strange Idols Pattern," while nothing from Felt's first two albums, "Crumbling" and "Splendor of Fear," appear here, and only two songs from their `85 release "Ignite the Seven Canons" are included. Basically, if you're looking for a thorough and comprehensive spread of Felts' Cherry Red-era oeuvre, you're better off with "Absolute Classic Masterpieces" (vol. 1).

This comp *does* include several key, non-LP oddities (as the title suggests), like the scratchy, groovy early single "Something Sends me to Sleep," and the essential "Fortune," the melancholy but achingly pretty b-side to 1984 single "Sunlight Bathed the Golden Glow." The brooding and energetic "Trails of Color Dissolve" and "Penelope Tree" also make appearances. But, you can find all of these tracks on "Absolute Classic Masterpieces." So what, then, is the value, much less the point, of this comp?

Well, the only things that can't be found elsewhere are the demo versions of "Dismantled Kind is Off the Throne" and "Sunlight Bathed the Golden Glow." And why care? Well, these demos are actually very cool, and if not superior, then fascinating alternates to the versions redone for "Strange Idols Pattern." Produced by John A. Rivers, the demos possess a thick, gauzy, dreamy, reverb-drenched atmosphere and brooding feel (similar to the Rivers-produced prior album, "Splendor of Fear"), which contrasts with John Leckie's great, but bright and sparkly production on "Strange Idols." These demos aren't superior to the "Strange Idols" versions; they're simply cool, very different sounding renderings of two fundamentally great songs.

Ultimately, I can only recommend this to completists or neophytes lacking the attention span for the sprawling 18-song "Absolute Classic Masterpieces." This was actually the first Felt album I bought, and I found it a truly awesome intro to the band, instantly catapulting them to "favorite band" status. And although tracking down everything else Felt released nearly made this comp's place in my collection redundant, I still have a sentimental attachment to it, making it one of their albums I reach for most. I can't make much of a case for this comp's worth, but some of you may get precisely why I love it so much.

title: Texas Tone Is Sure to Please
text:
This is a great session from 1968 led by tenor saxophonist Booker Ervin. Ervin's joined here by Kenny Barron on piano, Woody Shaw on trumpet, Jan Arnet on bass, and the great Billy Higgins on drums. Although the album was recorded in 1968, it sat on the shelf until 1976, a puzzling decision as this session absolutely cooks. Booker Ervin blows a mean tenor sax, displaying some massive chops. Ervin wrote three of the five tracks, namely "Den Tex", "Lynn's Tune", and "204". Woody Shaw turns in an equally impressive performance on trumpet, playing with fiery precision. Shaw also wrote the post-boppish "In a Capricornian Way". Billy Higgins is as solid as ever, complemented nicely by Jan Arnet's bass work. I don't believe I've heard Kenny Barron on any other recordings at this point, but his online discography lists an impressive body of work. He also contributed the first track, "Gichi".

As I mentioned above, this session is smoking, from the strong opening salvo of "Gichi", to the tight "Den Tex", the moody "In A Capricornian Way", the smoldering "Lynn's Tune", and the fast-paced finale of "204". While all of the musicians are fantastic, it has to be noted that Ervin's bold saxophone is the definitive star of the show. He lays out some amazing lines on this album, all with a full, expressive sound. They say everything is bigger in Texas, and it sure is true for Booker Ervin's tone.

Missy's production is able to recall the adult aspects of 1970's R&B & pair it with current hip hop trends to make it appeal to a younger demographic. But approach with caution, this isn't all about hooks! Despite several funk numbers: "Things I Don't Mean" which rolls with a vintage disco vibe & the "We Don't Need No Water" jam smokes with new school charm; the album's true face is in the ballads.

The ballads which Charlene (her real name) delivers with a smooth, smoky, yet emotive quality work their charm. Many of the ballads such as the lead single "Turn Da Lights Off" have jazz, various latin percussion, & orchestral textures which gives the album musical weight. It isn't the same drum loop over & over.

Highlights include "Iceberg" & "You" both ballads indicate the bittersweet tang of heartbreak well, both include the musical textures I mentioned above, "Turn Da Lights Off" almost suffers under Missy's charismatic, but needless hype at the beginning. But the track utilizes a hip hop edge & a retro soul vibe that is contagious. "Steer", & the coup de grace "Cab Ride" (utilizes a sample from the theme of the show "Taxi") come to mind.

Lyrically, I like that because Charlene is a bit older, it isn't the same "chirpy" attitude some of the younger R&B chanteuses have. A variety of moods, from melancholic to euphoric are evoked.

Overall, the record suffered due to lack of promotion (Ciara, Missy's new protege got her mediocre record pushed) & a lead-single that was a ballad. Though I applaud Charlene for the lead-off single because it was different & gave the album a very romantic appeal. As an album, I liked the entire scope of it really. Even songs that I was ambivlent about at first (i.e.-"Could It Be?") were pleasantly well done, & grew with repeated spins. A very cohesive record is important to me, but each song has it's own charismatic appeal...so it doesn't get boring.

Overall, it is hip enough with it's modern flares for people like me, but sports a more mature attitude (without pretention) to warrant an older audience giving it a spin.

Highly Recommended!

title: Some great songs, lacking in overall feel.
text:
Leo Sidran is a very talented songwriter and performer that seems to be searching for his niche. The fifteen songs on "L. Sid" incorporate jazz, latin, and pop into some brilliant songs. However, while Sidran experiments with different sounds and songs, the listener is forced to suffer through some failed attempts.
The album opens with "43 Con Pina"-a very tight pop song-but also quite lackluster. Built around the words, "Some say that a woman, she tells you that its real. But here its all backwards, its what she doesn't tell you that shows you how she feels." Combine these lyrics with a soft pop-song, and you get an amazingly uninteresting track.
Several songs have the same pitfall. "Pushing and Shoving" wins the award as the most un-listenable track. The lyrics are vapid. "Lets stop this pushin' and shovin'. Let's start some real good lovin'." Leo is better than this garbage.
But more often than not, Leo really shines on this album. Leo Sidran has an amazing ability to combine jazz, latin, and pop almost seamlessly. Most of the songs are a combination of two or three styles of music-which rarely seems awkward or forced. "What We Know" combines some of his perfect lyrics into a fast-paced jazz/funk jam session. "Sevillanas" is a great Spanish song, with a mix of English and Spanish lyrics. "Times Before" is a great jazz song-with vocals that remind you of Chet Baker's "My Funny Valentine."
"Hypnotized" is one of the standout tracks. This is his most masterfully crafted pop-song on the album. "I'm Gone" has a great latin jazz feel to it-while still seeming as if you might hear it on a pop radio station. "Enjoy Yourself," and "Times Before" also combine jazz and pop to form fantastic hybrid tracks. His combining of ethnic music with American pop music is reminiscent of perhaps Sergio Mendes or Herb Alpert. Both took latin music and combined it with 60s pop for American audiences. Leo Sidran combines jazz and latin sounds with better than average pop-songs. The combinations is immediately appealing.
As I understand, Sidran has experience writing songs for other artists. On "L. Sid" he demonstrates just how talented of a songwriter he is. However, while listening to certain tracks, one begins to wonder is Leo is indeed the best performer for the song. I can't help but hear Steely Dan sing "Old Enough."
In the end, Sidran is experimenting with different combinations and balances between musical influences. Sometimes the songs fare well. Other times, perhaps they ought to have been scrapped. But this album is definitely worth the price-even if you do skip over a couple of tracks.
What's missing is an overall uniformity here. Leo seems to have written fifteen songs and thrown them onto a disc, with little care as to what they will say to the listener as a whole. If he had included only ten or twelve songs, he could have eliminated a few tracks that stick out, and the album would have had a more unified feel. Instead, we see a portrait of a songwriter and performer that is eager to try anything-at least once. I look forward to Leo's future as a performer.
I'd give it 3.5 stars if I could.

title: THE BEST STONES' ALBUM FINALLY SOUNDS LIKE IT, TOO!
text:
Charlie Watts says that Rolling Stones fans tend to rank this album as the group's best. (His favorite? "Stripped".) "Exile" has, "Tumbling Dice", "All Down The Line", "Happy", "Shine A Light", and many other fan favorites. Thus, I pretty much agree on "Exile's" rank, but it depends on my mood. I love "Sticky Fingers" equally well - a tie for first - with "Stripped" finishing second.

The only thing that bugged me about "Exile", though, was the sound quality. I must've bought 3-4 copies of this from the U.S. and Japan, Germany etc. trying to find a copy that didn't sound muddy.The horns sounded like they were playing underwater, same for the Gospel-style backup singers. Finally, this re-issue is IT! Top-quality, at last, getting the most out of this album's performance quality. It's a genuine improvement, light years ahead of all prior versions. Years ago, one critic said that "Exile" had a great "feel". "I love the basement-ness of the whole album!", he said.

That's true, too. "Exile" was recorded in several cavernous rooms in Keith Richards' cellar, at his home in a small French village. Why were the Stones living in France? Because the U.K. government, desperate for cash, raised the tax rates on the rich to a staggering 90% ! (Imagine trying to live on just 10% of your income.) Every British artist and musician of any worth fled England.

OK, so if you find a version with the extra, unreleased tracks, that's fine, but be warned that those aren't the gems that the second disc of the "Some Girls" unearthed, They're worth a listen, but little else. For a very limited time, the Best Buy stores were given an exclusive, extra disc of very brief interviews with all four Rolling Stones, but let's face it: Are you that desperate for interviews with anybody? My guess is, probably not. You can forget about finding that version now anyway, unless you're willing to get ripped off bidding for one at the online auction sites. I recommend that you stick with the music.
That's what made this album stand out anyhow, and it's never sounded better!

title: Solid Rock with a Progressive Flavor
text:
On the positive side, nearly every song on this CD is at least good. Some songs are excellent. On the negative side, Rush's in your face progressive rock sound is an influence rather than a focus of the music. I suppose that Rush may have felt the need to try different things and this album is the result. The music on this CD is well-produced and slick, but in its production it does lose some of what has appealed to many Rush fans. In places the music sounds like it was influenced by Foreigner, which is a bit strange given Rush's longevity.

'Animate' kicks the CD off with a solid rock beat. The song is solid, but portions of the lyrics are poetry. Strangely, the very interesting portions of the music are balanced by simplistic lyrics modeled a bit after the the Moody Blues' song 'One More Time to Live' from 'Every Good Boy Deserves Favour.' While the lyrics of the latter worked well at the time, I think the 'polarize me, sensitize me, etc.' lyrics of the former could have been approached differently.

'Stick It Out' kicks out with power, with better balance between the music and the lyrics. Some of the lyrics are poetic, but the music is pure power to drive the poetry into your brain.

'Cut to the Chase' has a strong flavor of the Rush of old and is one of my favorite tracks on this CD. There are a couple of changes in tempo in the music that match the lyrics really well. The plaintive notes in the instruments complement the vocals nicely; a solid and interesting song all around.

I struggle somewhat with 'Nobody's Hero.' The music here is interesting, but the lyrics seem to struggle, either in their fit to the music, or the topic, which seems a bit confused from the outset. While I want to like this song, I suspect the lyrics needed different music and vice versa.

Then we come to 'Between Sun and Moon,' a fantasy song in the spirit of progressive rock. One of my favorite songs that combines the power for which Rush is known so well with wonderfully smoky lyrics that are obscure enough to make you feel versus think; a great song to listen to the spell-binding combination of lyrics and music.

The next song has a title that makes you think it might be a science fiction song, but 'Alien Shore' is about the difference between male and female. The bass rumble could almost be threatening, but really is trying to hammer the point that we need to understand each other; we need to reach each other; we need to reach the alien shore. This song is solid rock with a modest flavor of blues, and more than a touch of progressive elements.

'The Speed of Love' follows. However, the speed seems to be something you would achieve when mired in molasses. The lyrics are too mellow and never break out the way they seem as though they should. The music matches the lyrics, but the change in tempo that you keep expecting just never happens.

We change structure and style with 'Double Agent,' which has received mixed reviews. I like this song. I didn't like it at first, but after listening to it numerous times, and reading the lyrics, I believe this song verges on the border of nu-metal or thrash. The hard-driving drums and bass combine with the dark lyrics to yield a surrealistic vision of the land between wake and sleep, between right and wrong, and between darkness and light. A song worth making the attempt to understand in its musical and lyrical entirety.

The instrumental 'Leave that Thing Alone' is solid rock. There are moments when you capture a flavor of the Rush from the days of 'Moving Pictures.'

The CD closes with 'Cold Fire' and 'Everyday Glory.' The two songs bear some similarity in that they have a certain consistency to them, though the topics are quite different. The songs are decent, but once again they seem a bit tame for Rush, and perhaps a bit on the commercial side.

One difficulty with a group such as Rush is that we continually expect them to top themselves and when they create acceptable rock, we can be disappointed; we probably should not be. After all, not every work of an artist will be a masterpiece. This album is a worthy addition to your Rush collection; generally good, occasionally excellent, and very accessible throughout.

title: How can a modern rock band this good not be recognized???
text:
Burn The Sun(2001). Ark's second studio album.
Ark is a relatively unknown German progressive rock band which formed in the late 90s comprised of vocalist Jorn Lande (from The Snakes), guitarist Tore Otsby (from Conception), and drummer John Maculuso (from Yngwie Malmsteen). While the first album showed promise, it wasn't until the second album where Ark would truly shine as a unique band. Joining in on this release is bassist Randy Coven, and keyboardist Mats Olausson.
First of all, if you've never heard of Ark, I'm not the least bit surprised. I had to really search long and hard to discover this band. I only found this stellar album on accident after going from prog band to prog band and searching through hundreds of reviews. And man, I'm so glad I found them. Ark is easily one of the best modern prog metal bands to come along in a while, and certainly one of the best rock albums of the new millenium. As other reviewers have pointed out, Ark is not an easy band to describe. They're very progressive, but in a more subtle manner, so they never try to show off or anything like that. If you listen hard enough, Ark displays LOTS of different influences from music of other cultures. At the same time that they are progressive, Ark also writes VERY CATCHY hardrock music. Many of the songs will stick in your head, but there's enough "substance" in the music to keep it fresh everytime you come back to it. Like others have mentioned, Ark is a nice change of pace from all the Dream Theater clone bands that are around. Their general sound is sort of an 80s classic rock/prog rock hybrid that transcends to other musical plateaus from song to song. Sometimes you think you'll hear something that sounds like a familiar band, but at the same time they manage to keep the sound all their own. I like that quality in a band. Each track is very different, but similar enough to tell it's still the same band.
Before I get to the songs, I want to comment first on the bandmembers. All five of them are at the top of their game, and perform with stunning musicianship. Jorn Lande is one of the best vocalists I've heard in a long time. He has plenty of one thing that a lot of vocalists tend to lack: heart and soul. Jorn displays an incredible range, being low and melodic one minute, and shouting out to giant choruses the next, all the while gushing with pure emotion. His voice brings warmth to a day in age of cold, cookie-cutter, soulless MTV wannabe singers. Tore Ostby's guitaring accompanies the music nicely. He never shows off, and yet his range is OUTSTANDING, whether he's playing accoustic melodies or shredding great riffs. The same performing qualities can be said about John Macaluso's drumming and Randy Coven's bass playing. Mats Olausson's keyboard textures are perfect. They're never over the top, and they create awesome atmospheric backdrops to each of the songs. All five are some of the finest new rock musicians I've ever heard.
As for the songs, 'Heal The Waters' kicks things off, which is a steady atmospheric rocker containing a bunch of cool time-change signatures (and even a coin drop, if you listen!). 'Torn' is the next track, a mid-paced rocker with an awesome chorus and precise bass playing. There's some weird tribal vocals later in the song, but overall it's very good. After that is the title track, which is more straightforward in nature, yet dynamic in execution. 'Resurrection' is lighter and more melodic. 'Absolute Zero' has a very "new age" feel to it's pacing and completes the song with a memorable chorus. 'Just A Little' is perhaps the most unique track on here because the band ditches the traditional hardrock sound for a very Latin-esque flavor. Jorn's vocals assimilate this style very well. 'Waking Hour' is moody and airy in the verses with a heavier chorus. It breaks right into 'Noose', which is an excellent rocker with an AWESOME chorus. 'Feed The Fire' is also very fast and memorable. 'I Bleed' is an atmospheric track that slows the pace down before the stunning 9-minute ballad and album closer 'Missing You'.
Overall, if you're looking for a hardrock album that displays true talent, has a familiar oldschool rock sound to it, yet it manages to keep fresh and modern all at the same time, Ark's Burn The Sun is the perfect album to get. It deserves every one of its 5 stars. There's not really any bad thing I can say about this band. This is one of those rare cases where I heard high praising reviews about the album, and when I actually listened to it, it surprised me because it's actually as good as people say it is! HIGHLY RECOMMENDED. BUY THIS IF YOU'RE OPEN TO ANYTHING WHEN IT COMES TO ROCK MUSIC. You won't be disappointed. I sure wasn't.
Other albums you may like that are similar to Burn The Sun:
-'Images & Words' by Dream Theater
-'Awake' by Dream Theater
-'One Hour By The Concrete Lake' by Pain Of Salvation
-'Parallel Minds' by Conception
-'Flow' by Conception
-'Juggling 9 Or Dropping 10' by Enchant

title: Celtic Right; Not Celtic Light
text:
If you're looking for a celebration of the Emerald Isle that lasts beyond a parade and a pint and that includes the real color and culture of Irish heritage, this brand new CD from the highly acclaimed Colcannon should be your ticket.

This mix of 14 traditional and 10 original tunes is not "Celtic Light" for those wanting to pretend they like Celtic music, sort of like people who say they eat at Taco Bell's because they "like Mexican food." This is not a quick single cut included to represent the genre; this is an evening in the pub or more accurately a week at the peat-heated cottage where the fiddle has been in the family since before grandfather's time and the bodhrán is covered with hide tanned by the clan's own hands.

Instrumentation is provided by the Colorado-based group's very talented musicians and was, for the most part, recorded in the time and season of the album title at Notably Fine Audio in Denver with Colin Bricker engineering. Tone and tempo vary considerably, from the slow and somber of Fare Thee Well, Whisky to the driving, yea, romping conclusion of the 14th cut. Mick's vocalizations speak from the old country, well handling the ambiguous humor/somberness of An Bunnan Buí (The Yellow Bittern) and perfectly delivering the apparent innocence of the gentle bawdiness of The Hermit. He renders a restrained angst on the second cut, fully fitting the song.

Every one of the band members contributes at least one original on this collection, with Rod Garnett's East European-flavored Koprivshtitsa furnishing the only deviation from a purely Celtic feel. For true fans of Celtic music, this is an appreciable offering with exceptionally nuanced performances of traditional songs and tunes and with original music faithful to its influences yet able to breathe its own air. For novices to the genre, don't rip through the album. Take the music like good whisky: Savor a tune or two and let the notes mellow a bit before moving on. Rushing through will favor neither the music nor you.

title: Scofield tears it UP!
text:
Review by David R. Adler

East Coast Blow Out was recorded not on the East Coast but in Cologne, Germany, home of the marvelous WDR Big Band, one of the chief attractions of this record. Out in front of the big band is a heavy-hitting quartet comprised of pianist/composer/leader Jim McNeely, guitarist John Scofield, bassist Marc Johnson, and drummer Adam Nussbaum. McNeely's piano playing is sparingly featured ("Skittish" being a notable exception); the primary soloists are Scofield and Johnson. The album's five tracks flow together as an extended suite, full of dynamic and rhythmic variation and dramatic sweep. McNeely shows a preference for ending movements with unaccompanied statements. Thus movement one ends with solo piano, movement two with solo guitar, movement four with solo bass -- all unexpected touches that enhance thematic development. Johnson shines on the quietest movement, "More Questions," while the finale, "Finally," belongs to Nussbaum. Scofield tears it up on just about every track -- fans of the now very famous guitarist ought to seek out this obscure goodie. McNeely's composing and big band arranging continue to receive wide acclaim, and this intricate, highly advanced album is a very fine, though relatively early, example of his craft.

title: Soulfly, Keeping It Metal
text:
Max Cavalera returns with Soulfly's tenth album, “Archangel,” close on the heels of “Savages” (2013) and Cavalera Conspiracy's “Pandemonium” (2014). I find it admirable that Max, after all these years, continues to crank out an album a year, while Metallica, Slayer, and Anthrax need half a decade or more to put together one record. “'Archangel,” as expected, doesn't give you any surprises, as we've seen a trademark Soulfly sound develop ever since “Dark Ages.” It's a solid metal album for both one of the legends, who seems to have no shortage of riffs, and his highly respected lead guitarist, Mark Rizzo, an album that will satisfy the majority of the band's fans. That said, it has some issues here and there that will hopefully get dealt with in the future, so here are the highs and lows.

The Good- This album has more atmosphere than the last few have. A variety of instrumentation, not to mention some song titles and lyrics, give it a Middle Eastern flavor that's a nice accompaniment to the band's sound. But, its overall intent is made clear with the opening track, “We Sold Our Souls to Metal.” Max left his nu-metal leanings behind for the most part after the first couple Soulfly albums, and there's no doubt this one is purely a thrash and groove metal outing. Besides the lead track, other good/okay songs are “Ishtar Rising” and “Shamash.” Also, Max gets a point for covering the classic 5 second grindcore track “You Suffer” by Napalm Death, but loses half of it for the little kid intro; and shockingly, the song just doesn't resonate like the original.

The Badass- Max's vocals are as fierce as ever. He's raw, heavy, and brutal, putting in yet another killer performance. The title track is a standout. The background sounds and music are incorporated perfectly, and the song itself has great dynamics. “Sodomites” starts with a vocal intro that sounds a lot like the beginning of “Bestial Devastation” by Sepultura. The songs itself has a crushing groove and heavy thrash ending. Much of the last third of the album turns the thrash up several notches, which is quite welcome. I thought the last one, “Savages,” could have used more speed overall, so “Archangel” delivers there. “Bethlehem's Blood” has a similar approach to the title track, along with most of “Titans,” and they both nail it. “Deceiver” is an intense song that could have been on “Enslaved,” and also appears as a bonus track called "Acosador Nocturno" with Portuguese lyrics/vocals. “Mother of Dragons” is another speedy one, with some death vox from Max. “Soulfly X,” their tenth namesake instrumental, is one of the best ones yet, boasting great variety, awesome flamenco by Rizzo, and a moody atmosphere. It reminds me a lot of the end section of Opeth's “Closure” from “Damnation,” which in turn made me think of Soulfly when I first heard it.

The Ugly- I'm not loving the production. At this point in his career, Max needs someone like Colin Richardson or Andy Sneap to produce, someone who will give him a clean, crisp guitar sound. Much of this album would go from good to excellent with the benefit of better sound. It's way too muddy, almost sounding like something Ross Robinson would produce, and that doesn't suit the shredding going on towards the end of the album and in parts of earlier songs. Besides that, the song “Live Life Hard!” is a complete throwaway to me. The guest vocals by Matt Young of King Parrot are awful, and musically/lyrically, it's one of Max's weaker efforts. Finally, although I understand the sentiment of having Max's son Zyon on drums, it doesn't do the band any favors. Even though he plays the thrash songs adequately, and throws in some decent double bass a few times, he's just not up to the level I want to here from Soulfly. Max needs a more experienced drummer, but it doesn't seem likely he'll replace his own son.

While this isn't a perfect album, it proves yet again that Max is one of the most dependable writers in metal. Improvements can definitely be made, but you can always count on Soulfly for a good listen. The band's detractors won't be won over by any means, but fans will get their fix until the next one, likely in a year or two. “Archangel” shouldn't have any problem holding us over.

title: Beethoven Meets His Maker....And Likes It
text:
Beethoven illustriously asserted that his Pastoral Symphony was more feeling than painting. Indeed, the idyllic brook in the B flat Andante paints with deft brushstrokes on the most fertile canvas in the universe - the human mind. Listening carefully to the closing bars, the birdsong of quail, nightingale, and cuckoo lilt with a precious enchantment. The evocative imagery of this five-movement masterpiece ranges from open countryside to merry-whirling townsfolk to wrathful storm and a new hope beyond.

Fortunately for us, Beethoven's crowning jewel does not strain for the musical realism of Strauss or Berlioz. Rather than prescribing some programmatic storyboard, he respects us far more, giving us the freedom to envision the poetry in our own minds as vividly as we would.

That this symphony was first performed in 1808 in Vienna is only fitting, for Beethoven's walks in the country near the culturally vibrant city were part of its impetus. Even his notes, haphazardly scrawled on symphonic sketches, attested to Beethoven's affinity for nature. Perhaps the Pastoral was Beethoven's way of saying that music alone squanders potential; imagery and atmospheric suggestion can take it to an even higher plane. In 1810 Beethoven remarked fondly, "How delighted I will be to ramble for awhile through the bushes, woods, under trees, through grass, and around rocks...surely woods, trees, and rocks produce the echo that man desires to hear."

Enter now the avalanche-melting warmth of Bruno Walter. In his later years at the Columbia Symphony Orchestra he had what many have called his 'Indian Summer', his resurgence in musical inspiration and execution which has left us some of the great recordings. Now it is true that at times the twilight of his mastery became evident; this is particularly true in the 4th symphony of this recording, which despite its warmth suffers from feeble playing and a lack of energy. But the 6th symphony is Walter on the mountaintop, and arguably the best recording of the Pastoral ever made. In truth, Otto Klemperer's 1957 Pastoral matches it, and with better sound quality. Yet Walter stands beside Klemperer, these two titans producing Pastoral recordings of historic value that hopefully shall never be forgotten...

The Pastoral Symphony is for me the most admirable of Beethoven's achievements, yet I realize not all may share this view. For many the excitement and drama of the 5th, 7th, and 9th overshadow the 6th's sprightly warmth. Yet I think many of you will find as the ears age and the mind yearns for peace and tranquility, that this Pastoral recording is not only something you can enjoy. You can come back to it again and again, and rather than exhaust your emotions it replenishes and renews.

title: For life
text: I was 3 years old the first time I heard this album. I am 32 now. I still love it. I remember listening to it as a child, and being captivated by the album cover, and wondering what the lyrics meant, particularly 'Us and Them'....it was my moms record. She loved it too. As a teenager, I listened to this album from time to time, and realized how much it had woven its way into my musical influences, and I started to see what some of the words meant, albeit in an adolescent sort of way. Different songs became favorites at different times. It was always a companion - something to take me back to being three years old, and being captivated by its magic so early in my life. In my twenties, the weight of the lyrics began to astound me, as I realized that 'ten years had got behind me' and that what Waters had written about resonated with me in a way very few if any albums had. I have just listened to the album once more - the same copy my mom owned when I was very small. It is likely that I will never tire of this album, even if I only give it a proper listen once a year or so. Each time is like the first, each listen revealing something new and creating a sense of serene wonder, and nostalgic sadness, as the words and music found in it seem to do so gracefully. It is very hard for me to imagine what it would be like to hear this album for the first time now...I expect that like all great and timeless recordings, it will affect each listener regardless of age, as it encompasses words, music and production to near perfection. My tastes in music over the years have run the gamut from indie rock, to electronic, to ambient, to experimental - it could be said that Dark Side of the Moon is the perfect encapsulation of all of these disparate styles. A masterpiece.

title: The Stones Only Overrated Album
text:
Do me a favor and rate this review based on how useful the information is, not on whether or not you agree with me! I've been a Stones fan for almost 4 decades now and I'm not afraid to give their work a critical review.
Exile On Main Street was originally released May 12, 1972. Numerous polls of greatest rock albums rank it in the top 15 of all time, but I've never been able to see what everybody is so excited about. Sure there are famous Stones cuts like Tumbling Dice, Happy, Sweet Virginia, and Sweet Black Angel but all their albums have famous songs on them.....most have more and often individually better songs as well. The blues is serious and typical of the band.....Son House's Stop Breaking Down, Shake Your Hips, Torn and Frayed, and Ventilator Blues....and there are some solid rockers too.....Rip This Joint, All Down The Line, Casino Boogie.....I find0 myself getting tired of listening to the album as a whole.....somehow it just doesn't have the depth of good feeling and strong emotion that is so evident to me in something like Sticky Fingers, Beggar's Banquet, or Let It Bleed.
Although there were "Exile" sessions (Jul-Sep, 1971 at Keith's Nellcote in France and Nov 71 - Mar 72 at Sunset Sound and Wally Heider Studios in L.A.), the tracks were laid down over a fairly long period of time from June 1970 to March 1972 with nothing recorded during 1971. Here are the details:

title: Transcendent, soulful, vast, and gripping.
text: The Empyrean is a great journey, and one that merits revisiting.  Here John is working from his home studio (in which he's amassed plenty of pro-grade vintage gear) and the freedom of that technology has allowed him to make what it perhaps his most lucid and expansive record.  There are wonderful mixing choices here, and always a total unwillingness to compromise his artistic vision.  It's actually hard to believe this soul was in the somewhat banal Red Hot Chili Peppers; the music here easily trumps his old band in aesthetic value and ingenuity.  "Unreachable" is a great entry point for this album, if you are merely pursuing-- consider the way its verses rely mostly on an organ/bass/drum arrangement, and how this evolves into a gorgeous psychedelic guitar breakdown, that leads, finally, into guitar/synth triumph.  It's a wildly fascinating structure, pulled off so gracefully you could mistake it for being simple.  The whole album is full of head-spinning performances and unexpected gestures.  I give it four stars because, frankly, some of the pieces here veer toward "very good" rather than "brilliant."  It's an essential album for Frusciante fans, as well as anyone interested in sprawling guitar rock and/or emotional, psychedelic rock.  You could buy Shadows Collide With People, The Will To Death, and this... and you'd be pretty well versed on Frusciante's 2000s period.

title: Possibly the best Faure Requiem
text:
This is my sentimental favorite for the best version of the contemplative, gorgeous Faure Requiem.
The requiem is one of the finest works by Faure, no doubt. He once said, "My Requiem is as gentle as I am." I am not a fan of the bombastic overwrought versions by Berlioz and Verdi. Along with the original requiems done by the renaissance composers such as Ockeghem et al, the Faure along with Mozart's are the greatest in the repertoire, I believe. The recording quality though dated in terms of technology, is quite fine. The miking is close up, which is what you need recording boys choir, etc. I highly recommend this version. It is a classic.

title: It will stand you up tall.
text:
Even though she's only 34, Matraca (pronounced "mahTRAYzah") Berg has been in the music for fifteen years. She has three previous albums and a songwriting resumé that includes hits for such well-known singers as Suzy Bogguss, Deana Carter and Pam Tillis. For some reason, her own career as a performer has never really taken off.
That is a real shame. Matraca Berg is _very_ good. Her lyrics are smart, her melodies strong and her voice southern sultry and well-seasoned.
Berg can tell a story. "If I Were an Angel" is about a woman who followed the wrong man to the middle of nowhere where she waits tables and contemplates her destiny, caught between eternity and the next bus home. The rollicking title track puts us in the pew one Sunday next to Jimmy Miller, whose wife just left for Memphis in Jimmy's new car. The congregation -- a bit like God -- knows all and forgives all, not least themselves. And "Back in the Saddle" is in the raucous voice of a dude ranch refugee who meets a bow-legged hunk in a cowboy bar: "I can put you back in the saddle, baby/Yeah, stand you up tall."
I believe she surely could.
Perhaps the high point of the album is "Back When We Were Beautiful," a clear-eyed meditation on the soul-aches and ironies of growing old. The melody manages to be substantial and delicate all at once, and the accompaniment -- piano, two violas and a bowed bass -- is a sumptuous surprise.
This is a fine and polished disk by a gifted artist. With any luck, it will help make Matraca Berg known as something more than just a writer of other singers' songs.

The only songs that I can recognize from this compilation are the radio hit "Breathless" and "When The Stars Go Blue", a collaboration with U2 bandleader Bono. About the band: The Corrs is a family pop/rock band from Dublin, Ireland consisting of sisters Andrea, Caroline and Sharon and brother Jim Corr. Their music is more pop-oriented aiming to a mainstream audience. They've got a crossbreed of pop/rock seasoned with some Celtic sounds from their native Ireland. Please, note that I am just saying decent, not terribly good or ridiculously awesome.  Collaborations:  U2 front man Bono appears on Ryan Adams-penned "When The Stars Go Blue", Ronnie Wood (The Rolling Stones) on Ruby Tuesday, and The Chieftains on "I Know I Love You". Overall, take this CD if you want to relax and treat yourself with some good pop music, whether you are behind the wheel driving on the way to work or back home, or just want to treat your ears with a Celtic-driven pop/rock stuff. title: Garage punk with soul
text:
Despite loving this band, I find it difficult to take them completely seriously all the time. Tokyo Sex Destruction is, intentionally or not, perhaps the best funny band name ever. And I wouldn't want it any other way, because it affords me the opportunity to introduce my friends to a band called Tokyo Sex Destruction.

Their lyrics don't completely engage me either. A number of them are of the activist, political variety, and apathetic as I am towards politics in general I don't find that particularly compelling nor do I find it distasteful. Additionally, something seems to have been slightly lost in translation as I suspect, being from Spain, English is not their primary native language. It's not that their English is bad, per se (it actually hangs together quite well for the most part), it just feels as though the impact of their words is somewhat lessened.

Their sound is what I love about them the most, though. A strong soul and motown influence shapes the basic garage punk sound they're based upon. Loud, aggressive and soulful, it's straight-ahead eff-you rock music. On Le Red Soul Comunnitte, they stick pretty closely to a single formula, while later records see them stretching out a bit more. It's a rather different approach to punk rock, and reminds me a bit of The Bellrays and The (International) Noise Conspiracy.

If you can look past the unintentionally amusing qualities that Tokyo Sex Destruction brings to the table, you'll no doubt be able to appreciate everything else they bring along too. And there's no better place to start listening to a band than their first record.

title: Superb
text:
In the booklet that comes with the uncomfortably titled FORECAST TOMORROW box-set, MYSTERIOUS TRAVELLER is highlighted as the jewel in Weather Report's recorded history.

That's debatable, but it was certainly the band's first concept album, in which the artwork and atmosphere of the music all seemed to point in the same spacey/ethnic direction.

This SACD also demonstrates how well recorded it was. Unlike the SACD of HEAVY WEATHER, which is only in stereo, MYSTERIOUS TRAVELLER is in glorious 5.1. There seems to have been something about the 1973-74 era which persuaded record companies that they needed to mix many of their more serious recordings in quadrophonic. That system failed to take off, but it left CBS in particular with a legacy of albums by the likes of the Isley Brothers and Waether Report which could be transformed into 5.1 sound without too much difficulty.

The sleeve notes to this album are informative, and helpful for anyone who was wondering which bassist played on which track. (Vitous only appeared on 'American Tango', by the way.)

This is the third time I've bought this album (once on LP, then on CD, then on remastered CD, and finally on SACD). It's hard to imagine that Sony will find another technological excuse for re-releasing this. So this SACD stands as definitively the best sonic presentation of one of Weather Report's greatest albums. (All from SWEETNIGHTER to HEAVY WEATHER are excellent.)

title: Absolutely danceable, mostly high energy music !
text:
Once in a while I review a product that's such a gift that I wonder if it's my birthday. SteveSong's Marvelous Day is one of those gifts. What an absolute treat it is to listen to this album over and over again, as requested by my 4-year-old! Song's vocals are James Taylor meets Mister Rogers (but in a good, young way) and his lyrics are delightful and very fun.

The album starts with the best energy possible with the album's namesake: Marvelous Day. Right away, kids are jumping up to dance and adults are getting that feel-good energy that comes from someone declaring how great life is.

Every child needs to hear the song Fast Monkey, hosted by Silly Vanilli. It's wonderful, wonderful writing and joke-telling that has children laughing out loud and copying the antics of the song. You have never heard She'll Be Coming Round the Mountain the way SteveSongs does it. It's incredibly lively and very comical - a tongue-twister to keep up with.

Many of the songs feature children singing, and they're actually singing refreshingly well and acting out lines without a hitch. Children won't be bored with this music, since it often takes off into random humorous directions, like in We're On Our Way, in which Uncle Steve keeps forgetting beach gear and ends up being left behind by the children.

Hero Song is a lovely, tear-inducing, post-9/11 profile of a boy wanting to be like his fire fighter hero, with a very reflective conclusion. Water Cycle makes me want to learn more about clouds - I keep forgetting the album is for my children.

The vegetarian perspective: The album has an obligatory eat-healthy-food song called The Veggie Song (Go, Go, Go), which is very pro-vegetables and rates high with this veggie family. The song Ducks Hatching is about a school that has duck eggs in the classroom and the amazement of the children watching them hatch. If you have an ethical vegan perspective on your child's educational exposure, this song might not be for you. Also possibly in line with vegan values, a song about a lion refers to the animal repeatedly as "it," which may irk some of you who believe lions have genders. But back to the gushingly positive review...

The album is absolutely danceable, mostly high energy music that doesn't overpower the lyrics. The order of the songs is well done - we're taken on a path from move-your-body to educational and interesting, even pausing for a crack up joke. As energetically as the album begins, it ends on a positively sleepy-time mode, perfect for the end of dance time and beginning of naptime.

Winner of the prestigious Parents' Choice Gold Award, Marvelous Day is SteveSongs' fifth CD.-Caity McCardell

title: the third and most diverse album
text:
I'm sure many would argue but I think this is Buffalo Springfield's most mature, diverse and ultimately finest album. Despite the fact that the group was no longer together when this album was piecemealed together and that most of it is really just solo projects it is excellent.
As with the first album Ritchie Furay returns to sing a Neil Young tune, "On the Way Home" and starts the album on a high note. There is only one more Young composition, the lilting "I am a Child" that is simple and lacks the pretension of some of his songs from the second album. Most of the album highlights the vocal and writing talent of Furay and Steve Stills and it is Stills who really shines with the lovely "Pretty Girl Why", the loneliness of "Four Days Gone", the latin influence of "Uno Mundo" and my favorite, the powerful "Special Care", propelled by the solid drumming of Buddy Miles.
Ritchie really started to reveal his country leanings with the pre-Poco "Kind Woman" and his voice becomes ethereal on "The Hour of Not Quite Rain". Though not credited Bruce Palmer played bass on a good deal of the songs with producer, multi-instrumentalist Jim Messina filling in on the rest and adding the weakest song on the album "Carefree Country Day", but even that is fun. Of course Neil was already off starting his solo career, Ritchie and Jimmy were planning Poco and Steve was jamming in "Super Session" and would soon join Crosby and Nash, but this was the true Supergroup and this is a super album.

title: Favorite Album of the Year So Far....
text:
I have been blown away by this release. Prior to this cd, I had only heard Accelerate and then a few songs on the radio. I heard Supernatural Superserious on the Colbert Report, so I gave the Accelerate a chance. This cd blows that album out of the water. Collapse Into Now is full of great songs, and I think it deserves attention.

Discoverer is a great first track. It has this larger than life feel to it that really gives the album some energy.
All the Best is a good track, and it injects some attitude into the album. The lyrics are cool, and I enjoy the guitar in this one.
Uberlin is an awesome track. The first two tracks get things started off a little quickly, but this track brings you back down to earth to catch your breath. The acoustic finger picking gives the track a very real feel instead of the more electronic, distant sound that comes from the previous two tracks.
Oh My Heart is an ok track. I don't skip this track, but it doesn't excite me. Average song.
It Happened Today is a great song. The songwriting is much better than on Oh My Heart. Eddie Vedder is on this track, and it all works well to make a great track.
Every Day is Yours to Win is another track that doesn't really get me pumped too much. The lyrics and vocal delivery are kind of interesting, but it isn't one of the better tracks on the album.
Mine Smell Like Honey is a good song. Some have said they don't enjoy it too much, but I think the lyrics are funny and entertaining. Also, after the slower songs in the middle of the album, it is nice to have some upbeat energetic music.
Walk It Back sounds a bit like filler to me. I don't know if some are enjoying it, but it just seems to not go very far musically. Very boring.
Alligator Aviator Autopilot Antimatter is an ok track. It is high energy, but the lyrics are laughable. I don't mean that as in it was meant to be funny. The lyrics are just stupid.
That Someone Is You is a great track. It sounds like the band are getting back into the swing of things after some hit and miss tracks in the middle. Stipe sings more in this song instead of speaking more, so I enjoy that as well.
Me, Marlon Brando, Marlon Brando and I is a cool song. I didn't like it at first, but I turned the cd on to do some homework and loved the song. I guess after I forgot about the weird title of the track I could give it more of a chance. Great song.
Blue is a bit hard to digest. The song is entirely spoken word by Stipe, but Patti Smith comes in to add some singing. The song gets larger and larger as it goes on, and going back to the music from Discoverer is a really good idea. After a couple of listens, this track becomes classic.

This album represents a bit of everything this band has ever brought to the table. It has enough twists and turns to keep me happy for an entire play. I don't love all of the songs, but all of it flows well from beginning to end. The emotions the album takes you through is alone worth the price of admission. It really sounds like the band found some inspiration starting in the writing for Accelerate, and it truly takes form on Collapse Into Now. Accelerate was shorter and did not have as many top quality songs. This cd is full of great songs.
Stipe is a very unique vocalist, and I think his method of delivery is refreshing from time to time. The guitar work from REM is unique as well. I think the band deserves a listen on this one. As I said at first, I am new to the band. I started primarily with Accelerate. I advise anyone wanting to get into the band to check this out. I don't have the biases for their works in the past, so as an album I say this is really good stuff. If R.E.M. wasn't an extremely famous band, I still think this cd would pick up a large fanbase. Buy it, and you won't be sorry.

title: Hypnotic, Mesmerising, Beautiful!
text:
I purchased this archival release because I have always been a fan of Peter Walker's 1966 Vanguard label folk raga masterpiece, Rainy Day Raga. This 1970 session was recorded at Levon Helm's house in Woodstock, N.Y. But don't expect the Americana of the Basement Tapes, or Music From Big Pink. This is a different bag altogether. Long Lost Tapes is comprised of mostly instrumental Indian raga and middle eastern numbers. Some similar musical references would be the title track of the Butterfield Blues Band's "East-West" album, or the middle eastern influenced pieces by the LA based 60s psych band Kaleidoscope.
This recording features a fuller instrumental ensemble than Rainy Day Raga, including Peter Walker on guitar, Rishi on bass, Perry Robinson on clarinet, Mark Whitecage on flute and alto sax, Detroit homeboy Maruga Booker on Trap drums, frame drum, and bells, and Badal Roy (Miles Davis, John Mclaughlin, Lookout Farm) on tabla. The music has a droning, hypnotic quality, and is very psychedelic. Rishi's heavy bass riffs preclude this from being "new age" music, and Maruga's percussion touches are very imaginative and startling. There is a vocal on one track, but it is unobtrusive.
The only drawback is that the running time is a bit short at 36 minutes. However, the sound quality is excellent. If you are a fan of Peter Walker, world music, or psychedelia, I can't recommend this release highly enough! Kudos to the Tompkins Square label for putting it out!
