title: EXCELLENT LATE 60s LITE-POP / VERY GOOD AUDIO QUALITY
text:
This review is specifically for the MERCURY (JAPAN) CD release, which has the same track lineup as the RPM (UK) CD release.

Anyone who enjoys 60s lite-pop will likely enjoy this compilation comprised of Keith's Mercury output from '66 and '67. The title track "98.6" was his only top-10 hit reaching #7 in the US. Frankly I'm surprised this compilation was even released given the obscurity and low-charting positions of his other singles, but I'm delighted it was! It's pleasant and finely produced pop from a wonderful era. As with "98.6" and countless other pop gems from of the 60s, the melodies and hooks are memorable and worthy of singing, humming and whistling along with. While the title track is unquestionably what Keith is most remembered for, all of the selections here are nice. A new discovery for me is his rendition of "Making Every Minute Count", which I adore! Spanky & Our Gang also gave us an excellent version of it. The liner notes read in Japanese, but please don't let that deter you from purchasing this specific and truly excellent release!

I recommend buying the Japanese version and here's why; I perceive the MERCURY (JAPAN) edition to have superior audio quality over the RPM (UK) release. The Japanese version boasts clean and balanced sound with no evidence of audio compression or equalization beyond what was intended and applied when these vintage recordings were originally produced in the 60s. Its audio dynamics are such that the vocals, backing vocals, and instruments are presented at their proper and respective audio levels. Its EQ is balanced across the entire audible spectrum. Sonically it's a joy to hear!

The RPM (UK) version, on the other hand, has had audio compression applied such that the vocals and instrumentation are more or less heard at the same volume. Its dynamics have been squashed. Sadly, this regrettable practice is common among many record labels today, and I suspect it's intended to meet the demand of those who listen to music while on-the-go via low-fI devices. Additionally, EQ has been adjusted to boost the lower midrange resulting in an unpleasant quality of tone.

Lastly, the JAPAN release, unlike the RPM (UK) edition, has a couple tracks featuring extended intros!

Regards,
Blind man Wayne :)

title: Excellent performances, much improved remaster vs. Melodiya CD
text:
These performances are both superior in my opinion to what is contained on the popular Deutsche Grammophon release (the same concertos and pianist, with different orchestras and conductors, in stereo). Mravinsky brings an excitement to the Tchaikovsky that Von Karajan (DG) cannot begin to approach. Sanderling also does a better job than Wislocki (DG), with a more sharp-edged emphasis on the drama of the work. In both cases, the conductors are completely in sync with Richter, both in their approach to bringing out the excitement in the compositions and in their musical ability, providing the best support that one can hope for. And the Leningrad orchestra is a world class organization, considerably better than the orchestras on the DG recording.

As for Richter, it goes without saying that his near perfect articulation (especially his crystal clear argeggios) and ability to bring out all the beauty, power, and intensity that the composers put in is really incredible. Because the conductors on these recordings clearly have the same sense of the music that Richter has, he is freed to produce a truly incomparable performance. Actually, while his recording of the Tchaikovsky is much more spirited on this CD; his Rachmaninoff performances with Sanderling and Wislocki are quite similar, with the conductor and orchestral work being the main difference.

The recordings on this CD are in mono. So the sound is a little distant and indistinct as with any mono recording, and some detail is lost. Turning up the volume helps matters. This was originally recorded by Melodiya in 1959, and there's a big difference in recorded sound sophistication between Melodiya and other major recording houses in that era, such as RCA. And remaster technology can only do so much with poor source material. These are the same recordings as on the 2008 Melodiya CD. That CD was awful, with very murky sound. This 2009 Urania CD is a much better remaster (for the Tchaikovsky at least, see below), with considerably increased clarity and dynamic range, and reduced surface noise.

Balance was another major problem on the Melodiya CD, and that issue persists, but only to some degree, on this one. In the Tchaikovsky, the piano is mic'ed a little too closely, and Mravinsky's fine work is somewhat muted in places. The opposite is true in the Rachmaninoff, with the orchestra overwhelming the piano at times. But this is a minor quibble, and I feel that Urania has improved balance between piano and orchestra, and between bass and treble.

So, the performances on this CD are better than what is contained on the DG CD, but sound quality of this disk is obviously not as good as the stereo recordings on the DG CD. However, while this CD is an improvement over the Melodiya release, sound quality is uneven. While the Tchaikovsky on this CD is not bad at all, the Rachmaninoff recorded sound on this CD is not as good as the Tchaikovsky, and is a bit harsh at times. I find that I listen to the Tchaikovsky on this CD. But since sound is so much better and Richter's performance on the Rachmaninoff is similar on both CDs, I generally listen to the DG CD for the Rachmaninoff despite the inferior orchestral performance.

title: Poco Lives!
text: Having been a long time fan of Poco and Richie Furay's, I was thrilled to see that he had finally released a new solo album. God has  blessed him with the ability to still hit those trade mark high notes, and  the patented harmony blends are there just like in the 70's. The message of  which he sings makes this disc all the better. I have had the privilege of  visiting Richie's church and also hearing him perform in a small venue. I  would love to hear him perform with a full band, doing material from In My  Father's House as well as a few Poco tunes. His last effort (actually, the  Poco reunion album, which was weak, considering Furay had only two lead  vocals. I mean, wasn't it HIS voice that helped define their music) was  just enough to whet my appetite for more.  If you like the Springfield/Poco  sound, this CD is for you. Not a bad cut on the disc .  "Hallel", the opening song, blows you away with its tight,  high lonesome, harmony."Wake Up My Soul" will awaken memories of  Poco. It was a long wait, but well worth it!  O.K. Richie! It is time to  get back in the studio.

title: Thank You Scientist Charts Brilliance with "Maps"
text: One of the best all-around, most melodically sound, experimental and diverse bands in prog metal. "Maps" is brilliant. Eclectic and diverse. It's entertaining after repeated listens. You will probably never hear this band on the radio because they don't constrain themselves to formulaic song structure or two minute run times. A TYS track frequently runs (on the short end) around five minutes, giving you way more bang for your buck. The tracks fly by like seemingly no time has passed. Their crowd-funding EP, "Perils of Time Travel", is also worth buying. Don't be misled by the short track list. The songs and themes are very well explored and five track album is longer than some mainstream 10 or 12 track albums. In short, whatever TYS puts out, buy it.

title: The Cure go romantic
text: You know the Cure have gone romantic from the inner sleeve, where they quote a few touching lines from Percy Bysshe Shelley, English Romantic poet extraordinaire.  And the album does seem pretty romantic with some latter-day Cure classics as "From the Edge of the Deep Green Sea" and "Doing the Unstuck."  But this album is also notable for the way frontman Robert Smith rediscovers his guitar.  The album contains some of the pleasantest Cure guitar since "Play for Today," from the "Seventeen Seconds" album.  "Green Sea" has a killer riff, repeated many times over.  And "Cut," with its wah-wah overdubs and feedback, gives truth to Smith's sometimes puzzling statement that Jimi Hendrix was one of his key influences.  The album does contain some slow-song filler, like "To Wish Impossible Things" and "A Letter to Elise"; without a strong opposite presence in the band to edit his impulses, Smith tends to pack the Cure's albums with songs that may be "close to me," but are hardly compelling listens for me.  But the album has some other fine tunes:  the gorgeous "Open," a reminiscence of drunkenness; the well-written "Apart"; and the hit "Friday I'm in Love."

title: Supernova
text:
I hate to say it, but if this is what it takes to instigate creativity, you should break up more often! A lot of artists put out albums after breaking up and not all of them release albums that are fresh and are supernovas.

As always, Norah shines through with her sultry sounding voice reminiscent of Billie Holiday to give you a feel of her jazzy foundation.

Some of the songs on this album are more poppy, alternative rock sounding with effects that some may describe as distorted sound that struck me as a slapping, funky sound. Love the beat! I also noticed more of a blues rock sound which I also love. Perhaps this helps to spit out some of the break-up venom. Very cool and very Triple A radio format.

Some folks say they are turned off by these effects such as heard in "Chasing Pirates," "Young Blood," "It's Gonna Be," "You Ruined Me," and "Tell Yer Mama." These are some of my faves on this album. I dare people to call her snorah anymore!

I first heard Norah on David Letterman when her first album "Come Away With Me" came out and I loved her voice and the country, bluesy, jazz, solid piano music which strikes me as very Americana. I can imagine her being very popular in Manhattan piano bars. Indeed very Blue Note. I would recommend going to see her doing just that. I think you hear some of this original piano, jazz sound in "Back to Manhattan" and "December" so you get a nice mix of a few of her earlier and newer song styles on this album.

This whole album went on my iPod for happy running! This stuff resonates with me yet even more than the first album did! Congratulations, Norah, on your successful song writing!! There can't be one, single tone-deaf cell in your God-given gifted body!

title: Good Potentials
text:
Act One is Blend's first album...2004

Revisiting this album lately, I still like some stuff on it.
The mood shifts from mellow songs (like Communicate, Luvsong...) to a more harsher tone (Inc, Lullaby...) revealing different influences from classic rock of the 70's to Radiohead.
Jad Soueid does a fine job as a lead singer...sometimes I can't escape thinking of Thom Yorke (especially on songs like Generation...)
I always had this feeling though that it's a not a well defined sound for the band (at least yet), the mix of oriental instruments (mostly strings and percussions) with western music is cool but isn't always rewarding and might fall into the trap of too much.
There's a remarkable string sound all over the work (thanks to a superb violinist like Claude Chalhoub), which gives tracks like "Communicate" their identity.
"Generation" is example on smart violin use, it's so integrated in the whole song's music, and adding more "depression" to the stagnant mood.
"Belong" is a superb song, great percussion, the strings are well balanced and not too much. Rayess_bek lyrics on the revisited version are right to the point, but the English lyrics are also OK.
All over the album the arrangements are very good, the album being mastered in the famous Abbey road studios is also rewarding.
Over all, only time will tell if Blend will stand up as a well defined sound or will be just a fleeting glimpse in a place where it's hard to exist as a rock band in the first place....and it's the end of 2007 (3 yr hiatus so far).

title: Incredible
text: My friend and I were talking today about U2 and how everyone credited Nirvana with the rise in popularity of alternative music. No doubt Nirvana was influential, and "Achtung" isn't grunge, but if memory serves me correctly, this was one of the first, if not the first, records to bust so-called "alternative" music wide open. Whether that is or isn't so, this album hits as hard today as it did ten years ago. I just saw them in concert and "The Fly" was without a doubt one of their greatest live songs. Simply put, there is not a bad song on this album. It's almost like a concept album without being a concept album. If you look at the difference between this and "Joshua Tree" or "Rattle and Hum" the sound is so drastically different - to alter your sound like that (and to have the courage to do so when you're already one of the most popular bands in the world) is both genuinely impressive and admirable. Bono recently said that the band was "reapplying for the job of greatest rock band in the world." I would only say that they needn't reapply. They never lost the job.

title: Great songs, poorly sequenced
text:
Few musicians seem to resent--nay, to hate--the spotlight as much as Eddie Vedder, and this album at times feels like a calculated attempt to run away from it.

It's not the songs that do this--they're often great, especially fan favorites like "Hail, Hail" and "Off He Goes." No, it's the sequencing, which leaves the listener feeling like an airline passenger buffeted by heavy turbulence. The slow-fast-slow-fast order doubtless turned many fans away and left them rooting through their Case Logics for their old copies of "Ten." Those who gave it a few listens, though, usually came to realize that there were some real gems here, songs that have become staples of their (frequently excellent) concerts and live discs.

My advice is to listen to the tracks in the following order: 1,2,4,8,9,7,5,3,6,10,11,13. Leave out 12--good ol' Eddie has marred far too many of his own albums with pretentious ramblings. (Vitalogy being perhaps the best example of this--it would have been near perfect without "Bugs" and the final track.) I hate using the "skip" buttons, but the whole album sounds better that way. (If you can come up with a better sequencing, please email it or post it.) Or just pick up the three-disc set from their final Seattle show on November 6, 2000. It's surely one of the best live albums by any band, ever, and it carries an energy and vitality too often lacking in Pearl Jam's later studio output.

title: 3rd studio album by Rainbow.
text:
Rainbow "Long Live Rock & Roll" #89 (1978).

Rainbow's third studio offering "Long Live Rock & Roll", is a solid release, but not as strong as their 1976 release "Rising". This would also be the last album Ronnie James Dio did with Rainbow. Bob Daisley took over on bass and David Stone took over on the keyboards. (since then Bob Daisley has played in Uriah Heep 1982-1983, Ozzy's "Blizzard Of Ozz" and the classic "Diary Of A Madman", tours and sessions with Gary Moore, Black Sabbath on "The Eternal Idol" and many more sessions. David Stone appeared on Max Webster's "Universal Juveniles" album and later played with 3 Dog Night in the mid 80's). Back to the album, The title track is a Rainbow classic, "Lady Of The Lake",brings all the power of this group together here, "Gates Of Babylon", good middle eastern music here, kind of like" Kashmir", by Led Zeppelin. "Kill The King", "Danger,Danger", Ronnie James at his best, Ritchie smokes on "The Shed" and the album closes with the sensitive "Rainbow Eyes", the sound Ritchie would develop more twenty some years later with Blackmore's Night. Australian vocalist Graham Bonnet joined the band in late '78 and sang on their pure rock album "Down To Earth", in 1979.

title: One of the greatest performances of any piece on record
text: I write about music, including Mahler, for American Record Guide and have  known this music for more than 30 years. Yet, when I heard this recording,  it was like hearing the piece for the first time. Karajan gets the spirit  and life of this symphony onto discs like nobody before or since. The  playing -- though not note-perfect, it was recorded in concert -- is full  of intensity and beauty and the range of the piece is all there, from the  halting exploration of the opening, through the wit and nostalgia of the  second movement and the biting fury of the third. The finale, though, is  the jewel of the performance, gorgeous and heartfelt with a fiery bridge  into the closing pages, played here with a transfigured peace and deep love  and optimism instead of the pathos or sentimentality of lesser  performances. If you think of Mahler as a Woody Allen composer, weak and  vulnerable and passive, this is not the reading for you, but if you see him  as a strong, sensitive, but heroic creator, don't miss this recording.

title: Wizzard Grows Up And Is Thrown In The Closet For 25 Yrs!
text: I first learned of the existence of this album from a Trouser Press article about Roy Wood by Ira Robbins ("Whatever Happened To Roy Wood?") in November 1979. According to Mr. Robbins, this release was entitled "Wizzo", and was shelved after the failure of the "Indiana Rainbow"/"Saxmaniacs" single to chart. Twenty five years later, the album is finally released, under its new title "Main Street", with both CD cover art and commentary by Roy Wood.  "Main Street" features a great collection songs and arrangements that shows Roy Wood and his fellow bandmates willingness at that time to follow directions previously explored on the B-sides of the band's 45 r.p.m. singles. The musical styles run the gamut and show Mr.Wood's maturation as a songwriter, arranger and producer. Alongside the proto heavy jazz fusion metal of "The Fire In His Guitar", we also find wonderful gems such as the Beach Boys Sunflower-era influenced "Main Street" with Carl Wilson-like harmonies and dreamy sax and horn trade-offs powered along by a chugging piano rhythm, the sweet Django guitar jazz cum heavy pop of "French Perfume" (a lost single there!) and a track that would feel right at home on the group's debut album, "Wizzard's Brew", the down and dirty workout of "Don't You Feel Better".  This release also features the single that announced to the public and Mr.Wood's management his new musical intentions, "Indiana Rainbow", a driving, rhythmic jazz fusion number, a million miles away from the pop bombast and fifties rock'n'roll cliches that previously defined Wizzard and proved to be way more mature than radio programmers, the record buying public and Mr. Wood's record and pop management could accept at the time. Had Jet Records not had a failure of nerve, at the time, and released and heavily promoted this album and the band, Mr.Wood and his co-horts may have continued following this muse, perhaps becoming the next Steely Dan... (and what's wrong with that?)!  As a long time fan of Roy Wood's music, I highly recommend this album to other Fans of "The Woodmeister" as one of the high marks in his long musical carrer, something they can hold up to such other releases as "Boulders", "Shazam", and the eclectic collection,"Exotic Mixture". To casual listeners unfamiliar with this man's work, I would definitely push this release into their hands, before recommending they listen to anything else. "Main Street" is a great listening experience for the uninitiated and shows a muti-talented songwriter arranger and producer at the peak of his craft before corporate know nothings pulled the rug out from beneath his feet, making a talented man doubt what he knows best musically and have him second guess himself for years to come.

title: Bland studio recording notable only for Alma Cogan's Nancy
text:
Of the six recordings of the OLIVER! score, this is the oddest. It was recorded in London in October of 1962, almost two years after its London opening (1960) and a mere three months from its Broadway debut (January, 1963). Thus an OC recording existed and a new one was about to be produced. Why then have a studio recording of the work? The only explanation I can think of is that Capitol wanted a recording to sell stateside, as no originally produced London musical had as yet been released on USA vinyl. Those who couldn't get the London OC recording and couldn't wait the three months until the Broadway recording was created could thus buy this one. However, it is the poorest of the six - only one other studio recording has been made (1996), the others being the 1994 London revival OC and the soundtrack.

There is no drama here at all and most of the characterizations are played "safely," without nuance or insight. Holloway simply plays Holloway, not even attemtping to give us a Fagin. He was after all a music hall comedian, not a dramatic actor. Tony Tanner in his twenties was far too old to essay Dodger and has a weird voice. Violet Carson and Leslie Fyson are merely acceptable as Corney and Bumble and young Denis Waterman an okay though weak Oliver. The orchestrations are laid back, easy listening, not at all up to the original or film orchestrations. The only reason to add this to your collection is Alma Cogan, who brings us a Nancy almost as good as that of Georgia Brown, the orignal. Cogan, who was to die tragically young, has the right blend of warmth and bawdiness for the role and she balances the two beautifully.

So, a flawed performance all around and the least interesting of the six.

title: 1969 - The Greatest Year In Popular Music?
text: If compilations were an accurate measure of the greatness of a particular year in popular this Time-Life disc would make an excellent argument that 1969 may have been the greatest year in American popular music in the 20th century. Complilations will always be lacking for one reason or another. For example, on this discs there are no British bands represented.  Neither are the West Coast superstars (Doors, Hendrix, CSN, Airplane...the list goes on). But even with the omission of those giants this is a great compilation.  It is strongly evocative of the late 60's, Good Morning Starshine and Hair (from the musical of the same name), the songwriting talent of Laura Nyro (Wedding Bell Blues), some solid Motown (Someday We'll Be Together & What Does It Take), Canadian pop (the Guess Who & Jessie Colin Young), Midwest Psychedelic (Crimison & Clover)and more. If you were really a kid listening to AM radio you will know and appreciate each of these songs. And that's why '69 was such a great year for music, even the left-overs qualify as classic rock-pop.

title: Absolutely Gorgeous! The Best Piano Solo Album Of All-Time.
text: I honestly don't feel it is even the slightest of exaggerations to label this recording as the Greatest Piano Solo Album Of All-Time. Even at nearly a quarter of a century old, it has only become better with age. I was first introduced to "December" at the mature age of 10, and I fell in love with it immediately. My mother would play it at Christmas, time and time again, and oddly enough I never tired of the haunting melodies. In the nearly twenty years since, I've found that while much of the music has a holiday theme, I enjoy listening to the tracks year-round. And in all that time I've found nothing that even comes close to matching the beauty, feeling or power of this exquisite creation. Winston pours such depth and feeling into each compilation that, if you're not careful, you find yourself begin to sway with the melody, much the same fashion as a teenager headbanging to a punk-rock band. But of course this is much more subtle and sophisticated. Truth be told, I credit Winston (and to some degree Chip Davis) with my desire to learn the piano. Fortunately my wife had the foresight this year to do what I could not bring myself to do, and presented me with piano lessons for Christmas. My one desire is to someday be good enough to eek out an intelligible semblance of this timeless album for family and friends at the holidays... but I won't hold my breath. Winston is a Master, and I don't believe I have either the time, nor the talent, to hold even the dimmest of candles to his "bright as noon-day" masterpiece. Enjoy!

Neither Rosina Torri's Mimi nor Thea Vitulli's Musetta are interesting as characters or more than adequate as singers. In fact, the only really satisfactory parts are the two old men sung here by a resonant Salvatore Baccaloni.
On the other hand, conductor Carlo Sabajno knows what he is about and conducts a nicely modulated performance, considering the demands of the 78 rpm side. So this is really for those who simply must have every version of this opera in their collection. title: Fannies Look Here...
text:
Being a Teenage Fanclub fanatic has been tough, since the band that can be argued as to have been the best, most consistantly excellent on record over the past two decades has only released seven proper albums over the last 17 years. The Primary 5, led by former Fanclub drummer Paul Quinn, have thankfully filled a much needed gap for people not only like myself, but for those who pine for classicst modern pop albums that don't need to resort to flash or pretention to entertain and enlighten. Their debut, 2004's North Pole, was the torch bearer to the Fannies timeless power pop and the best pure pop record of that year. It was shockingly good, and it was apparent that his time drumming for Blake, Love and McGinley on the TF classics "Grand Prix", "Songs From Northern Britain", and "Howdy" prepared Quinn to unload his own brand of sparkling guitar pop in the same vein.

With that, Primary 5 can again claim the title of best pure pop record of the year with 'Go'. Nearly every song is a gem, and perfect for the emerging Spring ahead. To list highlights is a bit futile, so look at the songlist above and make your pick (although the 1-2-3 opening shots of "Off Course", "2 A.M.", and "Sunsets" is a good place to look). All 35 minutes of 'Go' are a godsend to anyone in love with the finest melodies music has had to offer the world in the past 40 years, from the Beatles to the Byrds to Buffalo Springfield to Big Star right on through to the Fannies themselves. This is an album for anyone who thought that it was impossible to make simple, uncloying guitar rock in the 21st century.

Sadly, this is a record whose music is most likely to be met with the same fate as that of its leader's former outfit: Too simple to be commercialized, yet surely to develop the type of cult that begs the question as to why music this perfect never finds its way onto the garbage dump that is modern American radio, a place where it is needed the most.

title: An essential Roland Kirk concert
text:
Like most jazz musicians, Roland Kirk needed an audience to be at his best. There was an earlier live release called Kirk In Copenhagen, which presented a snapshot of his live performances in Copenhagen in 1963. However, it was unfortunately short. This two-disc set gives a more complete picture of those recordings, and hence replaces that short album. Kirk was at his pre-Rahsaan best here. On these recordings, Kirk really starts to show the influence that Charles Mingus was having on him. Recall that Kirk recorded briefly with Mingus (on Mingus' Oh Yeah), and one of the critical components of the Rahsaan sound was the incorporation of Mingus' gospel/shout blues influence. These recordings show Kirk moving in that direction, but not to the degree that he would by the time of Volunteered Slavery. Still, the mood on these concert recordings is upbeat, funky and exploratory with plenty of fiery solos. These recordings are also notable for the appearance of harmonica-playing blues legend Sonny Boy Williamson. It is also worth noting that the bassist here is Niels-Henning Ørsted Pederson, one of the star European bass players who recorded with Oscar Peterson, Joe Pass, and others. This is an excellent concert in which Kirk's sound really came together as an eclectic, boisterous and adventurous player who forced those critics who accused him of gimmicks to eat crow. This is Kirk at his insane, multiple-horn-playing, hard-driving best. It isn't as free and adventurous as later concerts like Bright Moments, but this is a great example of Kirk's early 60's style.

Incidentally, a bonus track here presents Kirk and Sonny Stitt playing together. The recording quality is poor, but it is kind of interesting.

text:
Okay, I have to admit that when I stuck Wonder Bar in my CD player for the first time and "Angeline" starting belting out of the speakers, I wasn't quite prepared. But by the time the CD was over, I was hooked, especially by "Faith on the Table". This is a wonderfully rich CD. What some folks considered over-produced, I look at as being beautifully layered. I'm struck by Sexton's eclectic use of instruments, especially his own voice. As I listened more and more, I noticed that Sexton would ocassionally use his own breath to punctuate a point in the music. What I found interesting is that I come to expect that breath when I'm listening now.
Beyond the instruments and Sexton's incredible voice, I found the lyrics to be quite moving. "Real Man" is one of my favorite songs because of the lyrics. The lines: "For so many years I believed I was broken. So medicine sweet and the leaves I was smoking. Told me I was strong, righteous and firm. But only if I comply and stay in the terms. With the deal made between weakness and shame. To shelter me from the price of my pain. I'm real I'm a real man yes I am" struck me the first time I heard the song. The same is true from some of the lyrics from "Free World".
I've never seen Sexton in concert, though I've heard (and read in these reviews) that he puts on an incredible show. I only have his CDs to go by and that's plenty. This CD is not "Black Sheep". In some ways, I hate to say that it is better, because it's really apples and oranges. But Wonder Bar has a different kind of richness to it. title: Wonderful...
text:
Here is a complete collection of all Bach's works for harpsichord(s) and orchestra, and for unaccompanied harpsichord(s). The harpsichords used are original instruments from the 16th, 17th and 18th Centuries, and sound WONDERFUL. I have been listening to various performances of these works since I was a college freshman circa 1957, and I have to rate these as the best I've encountered so far. By the way, the reason Bach used up to four harpsichords in these works, as this recording makes very clear, is to achieve dynamic range. The volume of each harpsichord note is fixed. So to create a startlingly loud note, Bach has up to four harpsichords hit the same note simultaneously. It can make you jump, or as Haydn said, could "make the ladies drop their fans." By the way, the "orchestra" is minimal, and
likely approximates closely the resources Bach himself had available.

title: Comparing Willie's albums
text:
If you are reading this you probably already know that Willie is one of the most creative, powerful, and diverse performers of all time. In this review, I'm not going to rate the albums, just offer some insights into the CD's and DVD's that I have purchased - and I'm glad I've purchased them all.

"The Essential Willie Nelson" is essential. Be that as it may, Willie's individual CD's are so strong and the songs are so interrelated, often in a story or a tight thematic format, that they almost make the "essential" Willie Nelson unessential - but it is such a great collection of songs, that you can't get as easily any other way. Definitely worth the buy.

"The Red Headed Stranger" is one of the greatest albums of all time. It is pure genius. If you get the 70th birthday edition, you get a remastered track and extra songs. There are no less than six "A" level songs on this CD, nothing short of amazing. Plus, you get fourteen minutes of great story telling. As a story teller, Willie is only rivaled by Native American artist Robert Mirabal ("Indians Indians", "Taos Tales", "Music From A Painted Cave", "Mirabal", etc.).

"Willie and Family Live", done around 1975, is a great live album. It has lots of energy. A highlight for me was Willie Nelson, Emmy Lou Harris, and Johnny Paycheck singing "Amazing Grace" together. It also contains the fourteen minute story of the Red Headed Stranger, including "Blue Eyes Crying In the Rain". This live performance of Willie's first #1 hit is the best I have heard on any album. There is a little extra "oomph" on every song in the CD. Again, make sure you get the 70th birthday edition, it has extra goodies.

If you like the early super hits that Willie wrote for everyone else, like "Crazy", "Night Life", and "Funny How Time Slips Away", then you need to also get the "Milk Cow Blues" CD. Willie performs these and more Blues standards, usually in a duet format, with outstanding artists such as B.B. King - Rolling Stone Magazine's choice as the 3rd greatest guitarist of all time. Hearing BB and Willie strum and sing together on "Night Life" and "The Thrill is Gone" is indeed a thrill. Willie performs this album with a first class Blues band and it is a first class Blues album.

Willie's latest album, "It Will Always Be" is once again a solid piece of work. Duets with Norah Jones and Lucinda Williams help make it special, but the best part of this album is the haunting duet of Willie and Paula Nelson on the song "It Will Always Be". This is a song that hits you in the gut, and it rivals Bruce Springstein's "Streets of Philadelphia" in terms of its raw emotion. A number of people, including me, cried the first time they heard it: "I'm tied of this and I'm running out of time; feels like dyin', feels like cryin'; and I'm running out of time." Say it ain't so, Willie!! A second good song was written by another member of the Nelson clan. The title song is very beautiful. The tribute to the land Willie loves, "Texas", is too short but very meaningful. If this was Willie's last CD, he went out as "The Midnight Rider", a great song for the leader of the outlaw movement: "They ain't gonna catch me, I ain't go let `em catch the Midnight Rider."

"Spirit" and "Teatro" are brother/sister CDs. Both have a strong thematic core, although they are not stories. "Spirit" is one of those rare CD's when every note seems important. For most, you'll listen to it less than the other CD's, but love it equally as much. For a few, you'll play it by the hours. It is essentially a story of coping with lost love, redefining your relationship with yourself and with God, and finding love again. The music and the whole CD are moderately paced, with a strong, steady spiritual tone to it. It has a light Latin sound, essential to Willie's roots. Pictures of Willie on this album look like he came from an ancient Holy Land.

"Teatro" is the mirror of "Spirit". Again, it is a story of coping with lost love, but the story goes south, ending in murder and psychological ruin. Teatro means "theater" in Spanish and this is good to keep in mind in listening to the CD. It is just a play folks! The CD is very hard-hitting, because Willie's music is very hard-hitting and very close to the heart. The music tends to have a lively beat, with strong Latin overtones. Its haunting nature is reinforced by Emmy Lou Harris, who accompanies Willie on most of the songs. The back picture on the back of the CD case is one of the best pictures of Willie ever taken.

The "My Life" DVD is well worth the buy. The story ends before the 90's, but there is a brief update. I knew about Willie and Farm Aid, but I didn't know about the scope of his philanthropy and the diversity of populations targeted in his giving until this DVD. I was also amazed to learn that he paid his $16 million IRS debt off in one year, selling $17 million worth of songs as info-mercials to radio stations. That's a lot of love, translated into a lot of power.

A number of people criticize the "Live In Amsterdam" DVD and some of the criticisms are merited. But hey, the DVD has a large collection of great songs. Some criticisms are not fair. You perform differently and 70 than you do at 40, it is a biological rule. Willie's shows have always moved quickly from one song to the other, so the pace of the concert is nothing new. The love from the audience is shown at the end when Willie is signing autograph after autograph. The bottom line is this, if you like Willie, if you would like to watch him live occasionally instead of just hearing him through the box, and if you want those images of him at 70, then you should buy this DVD. You'll find it worthwhile.

In the final analysis, the raw power of Willie's work, formed by singing in the cotton fields with Black and Mexican laborers, and his keen insight into what people really want in music, formed not through record company analysis but through live performances on the ground, make Willie Nelson one of the most creative, powerful, and loved performers of all time.

title: Surprisingly Good
text:
This is one of the best folk CDs I've discovered in a while. I discovered it very suddenly at metal forums when people mentioned it is a folk project by an ex-Saturnus member (even though I've never really heard Saturnus), so I just bought it on an impulse. It reminds me a little of Death in June because of the very laid-back vocals, calm rhythmic strumming, other sounds and instruments thrown in, and a few experimental ambient songs.

The first song "Lost in Emptiness" is one of the best. It starts off with a very ambient, creepy sound but suddenly the acoustic strumming begins, it's a quite simple song really, the melodies are just so perfect. "My Devotion Will Never Fade" contains some organs and interesting percussion. "In a Robe of Fire" is completely different and contains soft melancholic violins underneath similar sounding singing. "Algir Naudir Wunjo" is a long, creepy, very atmospheric song containing very low-pitched melodies of some sort, a constant, mysterious tribal rhythm, and threatening voices and whispers that can't really be understood. It sounds like it should be music for a level in Doom or something. It seems out of place but it is really good, although very different from the short, simple folk songs. If you're a fan of Raison D'etre you might like this side of the album.

"Silver Rain" is back to the folk style, this one freakishly similar to something on "But What Ends When Symbols Shatter?" I really don't know if Death in June is an influence or not but it sure sounds like it. This has slow-paced strumming with a certain keyboard or synth sound in the background. "Gal Anda" is the best song; it is a feast for your ears. The strumming is faster paced, and there are organs in the background and some percussion. Near the middle of the song, the acoustic guitar disappears for a minute leaving just vocals, organs and quiet percussion, only to return to what the first part sounded like with the addition of a flute! I'd buy this album if it was just the last minute and 25 seconds of this song. The whole thing has such mixed feelings of mellowness yet urgency, if that makes any sense whatsoever. There are 3 more songs, 1 folk and 2 atmospheric, but this is getting too long.

If you're reading this, you should probably buy this album. If you found this review, chances are you like either metal and are interested in folk, or you like similar folk. Either that or you like other music I've reviewed that has nothing to do with this, or you know me and don't like anything I do and are just admiring my writing skills. Anyway, I bought it very suddenly because so many people suggested it in a discussion about folk and I was so pleasantly surprised that I bought their other two albums within about two weeks.

title: Always overlooked, unfairly
text: When Frank Sinatra decided to leave Capitol and start his own label (Reprise), he was disappointed to find out that, after all he had done for Capitol, they were not simply going to let him walk away.  He was under contract for a few more albums, and he would have to do them.  This is one of those albums, and the conventional wisdom is that, since Sinatra was so angry, his effort was a half-hearted one at best.  And such may actually be true; but I differ greatly from the serious Sinatra-philes on this album, in that I think it is great fun to listen to.  It doesn't try for the profound, but perhaps that is a tribute to Sinatra (and Riddle's) greatness--a "workman-like" performance is still better than most others best.  And I STILL contend this is damn good fun!  I have always enjoyed WHEN YOU'RE SMILIN', IT ALL DEPENDS ON YOU, PAPER MOON and BLUE HEAVEN...where exactly do these songs fall short?  I remember reading once that someone said, "Look at how short the songs are on this album...he wasn't even trying."  Some of Frank's best work has been songs barely 2:30 in length.  Since when did that become a yardstick?  (One of my favorite versions of "TOO MARVELOUS FOR WORDS" isn't even 2 minutes long!)  If you are interested in a song that is clever and entertaining, albeit perhaps slightly politically incorrect, "OL' MacDONALD" would be that tune.  (Yes, it's THAT "Ol' MacDonald"...with the farm, but this one has a classic, amusing  Sinatra twist, and the tune really swings!)  All in all, like the cheese, ultimately I stand alone on this, evidently, because conventional wisdom says this is not Sinatra at his most committed.  Perhaps, but I say, if you like his uptempo stuff (especially with Riddle) this not only won't disappoint you, you'll be pleased indeed.  This is a fun album! (Take that, you Sinatra snobs...I'm going to listen to it right now!!!)

title: His Only Competition:  Himself.
text:
This album has to grow on you. When I first heard it, I found it sterile, except for "PrettyMan". But as a huge Prince fan and an owner of all his albums, I kept comparing it to his classic records. That's unfair.
I do think that this is one of his lesser albums of the 90s -- but taken on its own, it's catchy and pretty darn funky. Unfortunately, as he stated on a previous song, his only competition is himself. And it seems he can't win.
RAVE is not as good as The Gold Experience, Come or his acoustic CD The Truth that accompanies Crystal Ball. But it comes in a solid fourth place.
What Prince needs to do is take a long break from churning out album after album. He should just make music. After about four years, he ought to have about a hundred songs or so to choose from. That way, he can release an album without the inevitable song where you absolutely have to hit the skip button (on this album, the honor goes to "Wherever U go, whatever U do").
Finally, "I love U, but I don't trust U anymore" is about as good as Prince gets. Heartbreaking. And wouldn't it be great if Prince put out an album full of James Brown-esque songs such as "PrettyMan", which he seems to able to do in his sleep?

title: We waited 2000 years for this?
text:
I'm sure it was a thrill to be there, but the official CD of Billy Joel's Millennium Concert leaves a lot to be desired. Simply calling it "The Millennium Concert" is bogus, since there was so much tinkering with this album. Bootlegs of the complete show are out there, and they prove the actual concert was much different:
"Big Man On Mulberry Street" is a great, jazzy, tune that's filled with New York attitude, hot piano licks and the added boost of an actual horn section (in place of the synthesized horns on the album of his Russian tour) is an improvement. So what's the problem? Billy's voice hasn't been that high in years, and the vocal from that night was clearly replaced with an old performance! This happens on several tracks, and makes for a jarring contrast when moving from "young" Billy to "older" Billy and back again. His "one more margarita" rap on "Big Shot"? It didn't happen at the Millennium Concert! Other, similar, anomalies exist. The actual tapes of 12/31/99 sounded great, so why did Sony mess with them?
There's too much between-song patter here. After the first listen I simply didn't care about Billy's "rock versus classical" aspirations, nor his rant on the ticket prices. If he doesn't like gouging his fans why did he agree to play the show? The worst thing about this album is that Sony didn't even try to fill the two CDs to their capacity and include more songs. During "My Life" Billy erroneously introduces guitarist David Brown, who actually came out during "This is the Time" which was inexplicably left off the album. Not only are we missing that great song, but the listener is left to wonder who he was talking about. The Beethoven intro was a waste, and lots of songs were left on the cutting room floor. Perhaps a few songs that appeared on previous live albums could've been left off in favor of the others that haven't. Even the booklet was paltry. Nice pictures and liner notes? Not here.
Despite the misgivings, there are good moments. Disc two is particularly strong. I think later albums like The Bridge, Storm Front and, especially, River of Dreams are some of Billy's best, and those albums are represented here. There's a couple of rockin' covers and two welcome obscurities - the gorgeous "Two Thousand Years" (Be sure to check out the stunning original on River of Dreams, which actually sounds better) and 1983's "This Night." For those wondering, "Piano Man" was probably left off because of the sloppy, though spirited, performance that night.
Songs In the Attic remains Billy's best live album, followed by the flawed (but still enjoyable) KOHUEPT. Get those before buying The Millennium Concert.

title: Not the most significant or the best Schmitt
text:
I've called Florent Schmitt a minor master - stress on "master" rather than "minor". Two factors dealt a fatal blow to Schmitt's standing, reputation and posterity. The first one was his anti-semitism and alledged collaborationism with the Nazi occupant (which he denied) - but that wasn't decisive, since whatever suspicions on his attitude during the occupation he was reheabilitated and later granted various official awards, and championed by no less than Charles Munch. But the second and most serious factor was that he lived too old, still composing music that, in 1958 (he died at 88), when Boulez was writing "Pli selon Pli", must have seemed hopelessly reactionary. He himself recognized it. The embittered Schmitt is quoted by the liner notes as saying, at the end of his life: "I am fed up writing music in an age like ours: the score I begin is already outmoded when I finish it!"

But now that the dust of those fierce aesthetic and ideological battles has settled down, it is time to reconsider Schmitt, bearing in mind that he was of the generation, not of Boulez, but of Magnard, Dukas, Satie, Lekeu, Vierne, Tournemire, Roussel, Koechlin, Séverac, Ravel and Reynaldo Hahn (all born within 5 years of Schmitt, before or after). That said, however valuable this Valois disc is for bringing back rare orchestral works of Schmitt, the music isn't the best introduction to the composer's originality and singular voice.

Symphonie concertante for piano and orchestra was a Koussevitzky commission from 1931. Incidentally, Ravel's two Piano Concertos were composed between 1929 and 1931 and both had, like Schmitt's Symphony concertante, their premiere in 1932. A further link is that Ravel's G-major had its American premiere on April 22, 1932, simultaneously with the Philadelphia Orchestra (Sylvan Levin under Stokowski) and the Boston Symphony (couldn't find out who played - Koussevitzky presumably conducting), while Schmitt's Symphonie concertante had its own world premiere in Boston, under Koussevitzky, with the composer at the piano, on November 24 of the same year.

What developed into a Symphonie concertante was first commissioned as a plain piano concerto, but Schmitt had no attraction to the traditional form and preferred to embed the piano into the orchestral texture. That said, it was no small honor to be awarded a commission by Koussevitzky and a premiere with Boston, and Schmitt seems to have seized the opportunity to go for the GRAND statement. Much too grand, in fact. No wonder the composition came to be nick-named "symphonie déconcertante", disconcerting symphony. For all its orchestral lushness and its apparent freedom and whimsicality of form, it sounds overblown, loud, and, in the course of its three long movements (12/14/12), rambling. Although Schmitt was a mature, 56-year old composer when he wrote it, it sounds juvenile in fact, the kind of overripe late-romantic thing a young Schoenberg or Bloch could have written before developping a leaner style. Maybe if I had access to the score I'd catch a number of original twists and orchestral details that would make me appreciate it more, but while the score has been up-loaded on the International Music Scores Library Project, it can't be downloaded due to copyright protection. Huseyin Sermet and the Monte Carlo Orchestra under Robertson sound impressively up to the works considerable demands.

Rêves (Dreams) is a short (here nearly 10 minutes) tone poem composed in 1913 - that's the year of Stravinsky's Rite of Spring. Like Symphonie concertante, it develops the brooding, lush and languid atmospheres of Suk, Zemlinsky, Bax, of Schmitt's Tragedie de Salomé or... of the symphonies of Franz Schmidt. It is worth what that kind of music is worth, but at any rate it is not very distinctive.

Soirs is a much earlier composition, that first came into being in the form of a suite of 10 piano pieces, of which Schmitt orchestrated eight. The style is middle-period Fauré, tender in mood and transparent in orchestration. If you are fond of Fauré's Pelleas et Mélisande, you might enjoy this. But again... not very distinctive - and, to my ears, somewhat bland.

The companion Valois CD, with Schmitt's Sonate for Violin and Piano and Piano Quartet ([[ASIN:B00008FYPA Florent Schmitt: Sonate Libre, Op. 68 / Trois Rapsodies, Op. 53 / Hasards, Op. 96]]), gives a much better view of what makes Schmitt an interesting and original composer.

At the time of writing this disc is sold cheaper under the entry for its original, 1994 release, [[ASIN:B000003I0D Schmitt: Symphonie Concertante Op. 82 / Reves Op. 65 / Soirs Op. 5]]

title: Another good single
text:
Most a-ha singles (particularly stuff before Major Earth, Minor Sky) were, well, disappointing. Not because of the additional material, but because of the lack of additional material. After the single we were just left with other album tracks, or "remixes" that were just the song with the vocals removed. There were exceptions, like the concert recordings on the "Shapes That Go Together" single, the remixes of "Major Earth Minor Sky" and "Summer Moved On," the extras on various Japanese eps, and the interesting demo and amazing live stuff on the single to "Forever Not Yours." But looking at their total output, singles have been a tad boring.
With the Lifelines singles so far, it looks like a-ha have finally gotten around to doing singles the right way. New material gets included, or demos, or rare versions, and quality remixes. This one is a revealing contribution to a-ha's body of work, and I especially like Magne's comments about the tracks. His remarks nicely sum up the tracks, but here are my further contributions.
"Solace" is one of my favourite tracks from Lifelines, and I enjoy the remix well enough, though the original is far better in my opinion and really nails the emotional content of the song. The remixed music is too scattered and divorced from Harket's voice. The "You Wanted More Remix" sounds barely different and so is a bit of a bland listen, but it's interesting to see how things evolved or what decisions were made. That's the point, as Magne writes. Still, the slight differences in the music hint at the possibility of another version. I think Harket could have changed the vocal melody a bit and made the version more interesting and a whole lot catchier. Having an edit of the album version of "Lifelines" is neccessary for the song's single, perhaps, but boring. (An edit of a good song is always wrong!) This cd's other unheard-of versions, remixes, or demos, really make it interesting listening. The original version of "Dragonflies" is included. The music is different as well as the vocalist. It is a folkier version and sounds a lot sweeter and more vulnerable with Magne's voice. I like the album version, but this version is getting more frequent listens recently. The "Lifelines" demo is nice, too. It has a lazier feel and you hear Anneli Drecker's contributions much more clearly. Also, the words are a bit different. I don't think I like the "Turn The Lights Down" version as well as what made it onto the album, but like most of the other tracks, it is a worthwhile, interesting listen.
In short, this one reveals more of their talent and is that nice extra "shot" for those of us who crave more even 2 days after the album comes out! I hope they continue to release this sort of single.
Part One of this set (a remix cd) is also worth it, too, for the "Console" and "Millenia Nova" remixes.

title: ONE OF SAM COOKE'S VERY BEST - OUTSTANDING SOUND QUALITY
text:
Only some of the many Sam Cooke cds that are listed for sale on amazon.com are truly worth purchasing. KEEP MOVIN' ON IS ONE OF SAM COOKE'S VERY BEST CDS AND IS DEFINITELY WORTH PURCHASING AND ENJOYING. Other Sam Cooke cds that are worth purchasing and enjoying include Portrait of a Legend, The Man and His Music, The Rhythm and The Blues, and Night Beat. Most of the songs on Keep Movin' On were recorded in 1963-64, the last year of Sam Cooke's life. By listening to Keep Movin' On we can learn what types of music Sam Cooke thought worthy of recording as he looked forward into his future. Included on Keep Movin' On are such soul hits as Good News, Shake, Another Saturday Night, and A Change is Going to Come. Also included on Keep Movin On are such popular standards of the 1950-60 time period as Basin Street Blues, Tennessee Waltz, The Riddle Song, and You're Nobody 'Til Somebody Loves You. It appears that Sam Cooke intended to appeal to both a younger audience who enjoyed rock and soul music and an older audience who enjoyed popular standards. Thus Keep Movin' On gives us the fabulous, and perhaps the very best, voice of Sam Cooke as he sings a wide variety of songs. I love Sam Cooke's voice and phrasing. I also enjoy a wide variety of music. For these two reasons, I highly treasure and often listen to Keep Movin' On. Sam Cooke's voice and phrasing were so wonderful that he even sings popular standards of that time period so beautifully that I much enjoy them. Some of these popular standards that Sam Cooke sings so well are found not only on Keep Movin' On, but also on Night Beat and on The Rhythm and The Blues. One more extremely positive quality of Keep Movin' On is that the sound quality is so excellent that one is tempted to call it perfect. Remastering worked wonderfully on this cd. If you want to hear Sam Cooke's voice with all of its purity and clarity, Keep Movin' On is a MUST BUY.

John

title: Why do people hate this album??? 8 out of 10
text:
Dio's third album, the 1985 release Sacred Heart, is the subject of a great deal of controversy amongst fans. While most seem to find it lacking, it's actually a very good album, although certainly not as solid as the first two.

THE PACKAGING: Instead of the demon mascot Murray that graced the jacket art on the previous two Dio releases, sacred heart instead features a dragon inside of a crystal ball. Very cool. The minimalist liner notes include a track listing, credits, and printed lyrics for the title track.

THE BAND: The same band that played on Last In Line is also featured here. Vinnie Appice pounds the skins, Jimmy Bain thumps the low notes, Claude Schnell tickles the ivories, Vivian Campbell twiddles the strings, and Ronnie James Dio shrieks to the heavens.

THE SOUND: This would be the last album to feature guitarist Vivian Campbell. While his playing is still excellent, it has to be said that it lacks the exuberance of his work on Holy Diver and Last In Line. He sounds as if he isn't really interested anymore. The virtuoso rhythm team of drummer Vinny Appice and bassist Jimmy Bain lays down solid, powerful and inventive grooves every bit as effectively as in the past, and Ronnie James Dio sings like the metal god that he is. Keyboardist Claude Schnell is featured much more prominently than before, making his presence felt with arching chords and textural bits that add a great deal to the semi-mystical aura. It should be noted that the increased use of keyboards is one of the major criticisms that fans level at this album, but I think in this case it works well. The album is well-recorded with RJD doing an excellent job on the production. For all the people clamoring for a remaster I'll simply quote Bob Dylan: "Modern production makes records sound bad." The recording is fine as it is.

THE SONGS: The songwriting isn't as consistent here as it was on the first two releases but fortunately there's a lot more good than bad; the first six songs are all great. "King Of Rock'n'Roll" is a great opener, the epic "Sacred Heart" features a standout vocal performance and a killer riff, and "Another Lie" just rocks. The best track here is "Rock'n'Roll Children", with a great melody and a lyrical theme similar to earlier classics like "Invisible" or "One Night In The City". I even like "Hungry For Heaven" despite it's somewhat pop-oriented flavor. "Like The Beat Of A Heart" is a great stomp-rocker. Things fall off a little bit after this. "Just Another Day" and "Fallen Angels" are good tracks but nothing special and "Shoot Shoot" is really pretty dreadful.

THE BOTTOM LINE: Of the three albums to feature the original Dio lineup this one is definitely the weakest. But that doesn't make it bad; the first two were metal masterpieces and NOBODY that I can think of maintains those kind of standards for three consecutive albums. Buy this for sure; the first six tracks will make you happy, the next two aren't that bad, and who knows... some people actually like "Shoot Shoot".

title: What an amazing deluxe edition. Well worthy of my money
text:
Finally a worthy edition of this amazing and cult album. It was about time.

These songs are now 35 years old and they are still as fresh today as they were in the 80's.

All the major German pop artists of the 80's has re-issued their material in the past (sandra, modern talking etc.), it's about time for Alphaville to do the same and boy, how well it was done and it was really worth the wait.

Finally one of the best 80's pop albums is remastered in all of his glory, it's incredible the new sound on this one : listening to it now in 2019 it's like I've never heard it before (even though I still bought the original LP back in 1985). All the details and little sounds you can hear now that you couldn't hear on the original CD it's amazing. I've listened to the original CD and these brand new CD's back to back and it's just incredible the new details I now hear, it's like I only got studio quality right now with these new ones.

Songs like "A Victory Of Love" or "Big In Japan" are crispier than ever, they finally got the treatment they truly deserved. Even the beginning or the ending of those songs are there to the fullest, to the simpliest breath, it's remarquable they could extract that level of sound quality from 35 years old tapes !

This is the most complete edition ever. Here you have the 180 grams vinyl with remastered sound (which I could have done without personnally since I haven't bought a vinyl record in 28 years but still, it's there), you have on CD 1 the original album with a brand new breathtaking sound quality, on CD 2 you have all the original B-sides and single versions and boy there are a lot of them.

For the very first time on CD you have the single remixes of "Sounds Like A Melody" and "The Jet Set" since on their first compilation "First Harvest" you have 1992 brand new remixes at the time in their place (with great new versions but still) finally here we have the original 7 inch mixes from the 80's without forgetting the french only B-side of the "Forever Young" single the quick mix (version rapide in french) which is great (basically a shortened version of the 12 inch mix which was less ballad and more upbeat) and what about great B-sides that truly deserved to be in the original album like "Seeds" ("Big In Japan's" b-side) or the great Depeche Modesque "The Elevator" ("Sounds Like A Melody"'s original 7 inch B-side in both 7 inch and 12 inch versions !) they are all here and in great CD sound quality. Remastering is top notch.

CD 3 sound has some sound glitches and the quality wavers a bit since it's mostly made of "demo" versions whether they are original or slightly remixed so it's really understandable (they are 35 year old demos after all) but it's still great even though I'm not a big fan of demos originally (I thought A-ha's were not of great value on their remastered CD's I bought as well) but here it's very different : the demos are great and sometimes quite different from the definitive tracks.

For instance "Forever Young" was not a ballad but an upbeatsong back then and "The Jet Set" was much less over the top that the original and sometimes, like in this case, a little bit of subtlety is welcome and quite good as well.

The rigid box-set in vinyl format is quite sturdy and of great quality as is the 24 page booklet. It's great. It not only has all the song lyrics (including the B-side's and extra-tracks) but it has comments from the producer, the singer and the composer. Berhard Lloyd even states what synthesizer and drum machines were used on certain tracks without forgetting great never before seen pictures of the band (from 1984 with Frank Mertens as well as from 1985 with Ricky Echolette).

On the DVD we finally have the official music videos from all the singles "Big In Japan", "Sounds Like A Melody" "Forever Young" and "The Jet Set" without relying on questionnable image quality videos from Youtube anymore as well as a 60-minute in-depth interview with the singer Marian Gold, the composer Bernard Lloyd as well as the producer and german engineers of the original album and everything is explained from all kind of great anectdotes about the recording to the strange but unforgettable sleeve of the album.

What a treat this package is, really. Finally a box-set made right. Thank you Rhino and thank you Alphaville.

My only regret is that I didn't really care about a new 180 grams vinyl. I stopped buying them in 1991 but I so wanted the DVD that I had to buy it anyway. But still, this package is so well done and great that if Alphaville wants to release their 4 or 5 first albums in this way, each time I will be on board for sure.

If you have missed this amazing album in the 80's or if you already have it but want to listen to it the way you've never heard it before (with cristal clear sound quality for the very first time) this is your chance. Even though this Super Deluxe Edition is a little bit expensive (I must admit), it's really worth every cent, you can trust me on that.

title: THE MOST ROMANTIC DM; just a warning.....
text:
Just a warning to all that may be looking for more songs from the " Black Celebration" era, don't look towards this one. This is by far the band's mellowest, slowest, most mature album to date, yet, with that being said, it still manages to keep that unique DM feel to it. by the way, Did I mention it was very romantic?n Love is a big theme here so if you don't like those kinds of songs, don't say I didn't warn you. If you don't like all the dance beats and synthesizer-based rhythm's of past Depeche Mode albums/songs, I think that this would be the album for you. It is smooth and relaxing and it's central theme is based on love with sensual ballads such as "When the Body speaks" and "Freelove" and "I am you".
When I heard about this cd coming out, I was a bit nervous because afterall, they've been around for twenty years now and their previous two albums were dark attepts of conquering mainstream success. This album is by far, their best since their realease of Violator, twelve years ago. The more adult-like feel of the album should open up a whole new genre of Mode-fans while still pleasing the old one's.
My favorite songs would have to be "Shine" and the very tranquil "Comatose". This cd is best for older, more mature music lovers ( aside from DM fans in general ) If you never liked the signature sounds of DM in the 80's and early 90's, this album may win you over as a fan. Don't be afraid of this one for the mature sound. Despite all this, it still manages to keep it's Depeche Mode familiarity to it.
My Insights:
Best song: Freelove
Least favorite song: Breathe
Overall:
1. Dream On: You don't usually hear a lot of guitar from Depeche Mode ( obviously since they use synthesizers! ) so this song is interesting in that respect. It's got a nice pace, and it's upbeat. It's a good way to begin the album singing: " Can you feel a little love?" 8/10.
2. The Sweetest condition: This one is catchy and similar to " shine" but not as good. Not a standout track and a little dull and simplistic but it grows on you over time 6/10.
3. Shine: It's hard to describe this song really besides saying that it's not as sweet and love-based as all the rest but it's still lusty. Faster, and I like to sing along to this one the most 8/10.
4.When the Body speaks: Wow. More guitar-like sounds and I'm lovin' it. You'll love it too. Play it for your date when you cook dinner and light candles and all that other mushy stuff. This song is beautiful and eloquent 8/10.
5. The Dead of Night: This was a bit risky in my opinion, all this soft, sensuous stuff that will make you smile then a harder, dark song about sleazy men who take advantage of youger " easy" girls and then deny it ( Hey, is this song about rape? ). Yes, THAT is risky for the type of album this is otherwise but the music makes it work. It's a nice little break from the soft tranquility that you feel throughout the cd and I even found myself happily singing along to the chorous. The guilty pleasure song of the album 7/10.
6. Lovetheme: I consider this like a prelude to freelove and shouldn't've been a whole named track in it's own right 5/10.
7. Freelove: Usually Martin sings the best love songs for DM so I was so pleased to hear Dave's voice for this one because it is the best on the cd. Just listen to it and you'll like it yourself 9/10.
8. Comatose: This song is so somple and subtle and brooding that most would consider it filler material. Think again. The title suits the song 9/10.
9. I feel loved: The dance track of the album. Most will like this song even when they don't like the rest of it. since great DM songs are usually dance tracks. If you hate the slowed down pace then this song will be your saving grace along with " The dead of night". I find it a bit out of place myself but It's tolerable though I must admit, the remixes on it's single are better 5/10.
10. Breathe: I found this song a bit disappointing especially since Martin sang it. The song lacks any depth musicly and lyricly. It's usually the song that I choose to skip on the cd 4/10.

title: A decent recording that doesn't do a great show justice.
text:
I bought this CD because a friend recommended it to me after hearing the demos. I listened to them too, and I adore them. They're on repeat on my iPod, which is why I was disappointed by this "Premiere Cast Recording." The original demo tracks are (other than pacing issues) fantastic and tell a wonderful story of the Asian American experience. The reworked version of the show unfortunately spoils this by adding an unnecessary framing device and bloating the story with extra scenes and encounters.

Rather than fixing any of the problems with the show and relying on the story to make its themes clear organically, having the story as an old grandfather telling the story to his grandson who is playing him just needlessly complicates to the story (to the point where the plot synopsis in the booklet is so small the letters are almost unintelligible) and eliminates the wonderful opening number (and its replacement is not very strong). All of the songs in the demo tracks are generally stronger too, even if they're the exact same number. The orchestrations seem less focused, which is surprising considering the demos are, well, demos. "This is How He Says I Love You" is a weak replacement for its predecessor "Progress," as is "This Is How a World is Made" when compared to "America," and there's really no good reason for numbers like "Great Men" and "Comin' Home" to be gone. "Shame," which more or less opens act two, is a very weak and confusing number, and the new opening number "Try To See Me As I Was" is nowhere near as effective in setting the scene as "What Kind of Man." The only noteworthy addition is Michiko's haunting reprise of "All We Can Is Remember," but it's too little too late. The new scenes with the Filipino boy and the Korean Doctor aren't effective in moving the plot along and don't add much to the theme, much like the campaign scene that features "Shame."

The performances on the CD are okay, though the singers suffer from the slowed tempos all of the songs have taken. Most I will say though, that while Paolo Montalban is clearly the stronger vocalist, BD Wong (featured on the demo tracks) is clearly the stronger actor, and it makes a very noticeable difference in such an acting heavy show. He's really the only noteworthy difference between the demo and official casts (they're basically identical) so all of the wonderful performances (Cindy Cheung as Jasmine and Ching Valdes-Aran as Mother in particular) are preserved.

It looks like the CD is out of print, so unless you're a diehard fan, I'd save your money and head over to the composer's website to listen to the demo tracks for free.

title: Man In Motion "Live"
text:
If you are a die-hard Gov't Mule fan and did not really like Warren's solo album - Man In Motion - this cd/dvd combo is probably not for you. This musical performance showcases the Warren Haynes Band, which is essentially a soul band, not the blues rock style of Gov't Mule. The Warren Haynes Band (WHB) includes a 3-piece horn section, full-time saxophone player, and a female back-up singer. In fact, just to put things in perspective, Warren is the only white guy on the stage.

Now, if like me, you did indeed like the Man In Motion cd then this dvd/cd combo is gonna be a treat to your eyes and ears. It is basically a snapshot of the WHB tour in support of the Man In Motion disc recorded at a club in Austin, Texas in 2011. In fact, they play all but one track from the Man In Motion disc during the performance. Other tracks include songs from Warren's very first solo album Tales of Ordinary Madness from way back in 1993 which is very cool indeed, and two from the Gov't Mule album The Deep End, vol. 1, Tear Me Down and Soulshine, which he end's most of his shows with these days. And of course he plays a variety of covers, from Ziggy Marley to Steely Dan.

The show is about 2 ½ hours long, with typical longer extended live jams on a number of these tracks, and even though it is somewhat "horn heavy" in places, Warren's excellent guitar work still shines thru enough to please any Gov't Mule fan. The most amazing thing is you get all this for about $19...Amazing!

title: Possibly THE best Offspring
text: I remember being young and seeing this CD after sneaking off with my parent's SMASH CD.  They just wouldn't let me listen to this CD, which kept upping the appeal, because it was so taboo for my ears allegedly.  I'll never forget when I did listen to this CD for the first time though, and it has been in constant rotation in my music library ever since, and that's a VERY LONG 13 years or so.  As other posters have stated, there is absolutely NO COMMERCIAL potential for this album, but I think that was the very last thing The Offspring had on their mind at this time.  I've always been an avid fan of the Offspring's commentary of the degradation of America, and this is proabably the best example, perfectly following up their debut.  There are NO FILLER TRACKS to be found on this CD.  I am glad that the Offspring made Ignition and Self Titled, and evolved with their sound.  People constantly whine because the Offspring sound nothing like they used to, but let me tell you this; The same people who whine would be the first ones to cry because of the rehash.  Dirty Magic would have to be my favorite track, but as far as energy and intensity goes, Hypodermic would have to be my favorite.  What makes this album appealing to me?  I actually dig the guitar tones from the first two albums, which to me give it a more rock feel, a more heavy metal feel instead of punk.  The change of guitar tones over the albums suit them well.  I think if Americana had the tone of SMASH, it would've received more praise, because a lot of the subject matter is a return to seemingly familiar subject material, as found in the debut and Ignition.  This album got me into figuring out guitar parts and made me the rhythm player I am today.  If you've never heard of anything The Offspring has done, give SMASH a shot, not this.  If you're into Bad Religion and other bands like that, and want to give the Offspring a shot, you couldn't do much better.  In all, a 5 star album to say the least.

title: Wagner "Director's Cut"
text:
This recording features the second part of the so-called "Grail Narration" of the third act, where Lohengrin describes his heritage as a Knight of the Grail at the Court of Parsifal. The second part describes his journey from the Castle to Brabant to save Elsa's honour (Elsa being the female protagonist).
Wagner cut this second part of the Narration from the score, and on listening to this recording one understands why - the dramatic line is diluted and prolonged unnecesarily by Lohengrin's continuing after the words "Sein Ritter ich bin Lohengrin genannt!" - the point of the Narration being that he reveals his name on Elsa's request, thereby having to leave her, since he, as a Knight of the Grail, must be incognito (this is Wagner at his most Romantic!).
Furthermore, the recording as a whole lacks drama and intensity, being a sort of a "middle-of-the-road" Lohengrin - not actively offensive, just sort of boring. Don't waste your money on this recording, rather go for Kempe's version, or Abbado's on DG.

title: Great albums by Ann and Nancy, le bebes strange
text:
Until they emerged with the Heart album and the lineup that took them to new heights, Bebe Le Strange was the hardest album the Wilson Sisters and company came up with, and it proved that they were some really strange bebes.
The title track, a fan's tribute to a rocker, is a down and dirty rocker with a fiery and quick punky riff inbetween the chorus and the verse and is not only the best song on the album, but one of four (count'em, FOUR!, rockers.)
The slow "Down On Me" is pure fiery blues, and the guitars that accompany "You get so down/down on me" resemble the guitars on The Beatles' "I Want You (She's So Heavy)." Ann's vocals are really powerful throughout the number.
The brief instrumental "Silver Wheels" is played by Nancy Wilson before erupting into the second great rocker, the breakneck "Break", which has a riff like Black Sabbath's "Paranoid." It seems to be against the rigid strictures of the corporate mindset: "I got no more respect for the big man/Pulling me down to what he understands/... No one is going to tie me to this machine/Giving me formula force fed dreams." There's an interesting reference to one of their earlier singles: "After a while, there just ain't no more magic, man." A little injoke there.
After starting with a slow guitar, "Rockin Heaven Down" goes into power rocker mode after the title words are sung.
I don't know why they chose "Even It Up" as the single. It's good enough, with a catchy enough riff, but I can think of three or four other songs that could've done better. The song has Ann demanding her man, who has clearly been using her, to pay her back for what she did for him. The horn section in this song is courtesy of the Tower of Power group.
"Strange Night" shares contention with "Rockin Heaven Down" for hardest song, as Howard Leese's really snarling guitar attests to. Wild night too, if the guitar's evidence
With the exception of Michael Derosier on drums, "Raised On You" is Nancy Wilson's show all the way, vocals included, in this splendid little piano rocker which is their version of Fleetwood Mac's "Say You Love Me." The message behind this song can be summed up in these lines: "Let's go tell the world/to quit turning cold/Just let me be raised on you."
That is followed by the light acoustic "Pilot", a theme about finding love analogous to a pilot finding a place to land: "Pilot I fell through/From the blue/I just flew into you."
"Sweet Darlin" is one of Heart's best ballads, and a piano one. This one is Ann's baby, as she Ann played bass, drums, alto flute, tambourine, as well as piano and acoustic guitar. Oh yes, she wrote the song as well. It bursts into power ballad mode at the bridge. "Engines were screaming..." in reference to a flight she has to take, but I wonder if that mirrors her own heart at the love she has found.
Songwriter Sue Ennis co-writes seven of the ten tracks here--the three exceptions being "Silver Wheels," "Raised On You," and "Sweet Darlin." Probably their second best pre-Capitol album after Dreamboat Annie.
