title: Another great prog rock album
text: Asia Minor was a bit of a latecomer in the prog game. Still too early for the neo-prog scene, but existing after prog rock's glory, they released two albums, Crossing the Line in 1979 and Between Flesh and Divine in 1980. It's easy to understand how the band managed only two albums and broke up, given they were recording during an era where prog rock was grossly unfashionable (punk rock and disco had already done their damage, and New Wave was the new musical style that came from the ashes of both). In this era, one might think their debut would be thought of as their best, but it was actually this one, Between Flesh and Divine. Asia Minor was a French band consisting of two Turkish musicians (residing in France), as well as a bassist (who also played keyboards) and a drummer. Flutes, guitars, bass, drums, vocals (in English), and keyboards (string synths, Minimoog, Hammond organ, even Mellotron) are used. The band avoided solos, hence keeping their egos in check, and stick with what they did best: high quality prog rock in an era where good prog was becoming more hard to come by. While the Middle Eastern and Turkish influences of their music is a bit overexaggerated (I notice some in the flute work, and some passages, but isn't as obvious as a lot of the music from Ozric Tentacles), their music is symphonic prog, influenced by the likes of Camel, Genesis, King Crimson, Jethro Tull, and even Pulsar but without being a clone or derivative of any of those bands. There are atmospheric passages that lead to more energetic ones. Vocals at times remind me of Camel (especially "Nightwind"), and other times are more dramatic, reminding me of Pulsar (like on "Northern Lights"). I didn't know what to expect when I bought Between Flesh and Divine, given the 1980 release, but I'm glad I did. Definately one of the brighter moments of the post-punk, post-disco, New Wave dominated world of 1980. Rather than demonstrating what went wrong with prog at the end of the '70s/early '80s, Asia Minor demonstrated that it was possible to make good prog in that era, regardless of how unfashionable that music became by then. So, I can highly recommend Between Flesh and Divine to all those who enjoy symphonic prog.

Almost all of the songs are wonderful with a few that lose their nerve a bit, almost sounding like this would be a monster mash album to play during Halloween. Their current single, Year Zero, still stands out the most for some reason even though Per Aspera Ad Inferi can get me chanting along with it. It's a simple tune, but it is very catchy and at the same time sounding very epic to me. Reading the other reviews on here, particularly the low rated ones, just makes me wonder if anybody did listen to music or the metal from the 1970s. I'm pretty sure that Ghost doesn't want to be just or sound like Mercyful Fate. Instead of calling it "soft core," metal why don't you go read what King Diamond has to say first? Or I don't know, listen to music from that generation. Not all metal has to have over complicated riffs with some guy growling. To me, Ghost is doing yet another justice to how metal can sound evil and be rocking while being easier to listen to. They are more theatrical than anything like A job for a Cowboy or any other really dumbly named metal band. Also, have any of you 3 to 1 star raters ever watched this band live yet? Judge them after you do.

Ghost or Ghost B.C. did not do anything bad with releasing Infestissumam. It's a worthy sequel to an already amazing debut into the current metal scene. The vocals are still clean, beautiful yet haunting, and the guitar and drum work are simple, yet satisfying. I just hope this band doesn't lose their creative juices because Ghost is definitely a band that I could fall back to like I always did with Opeth. Leave it to the Swedes to know how to make music interesting.

title: "You're Everything" Chick
text:
Chick Corea plays with the lightest touch here, generating seemingly effortless melodic lines both when soloing and in trio mode with bassist John Patitucci and drummer Dave Weckl on this 2018 acoustic live date.

Although this two-disk set is padded with too many standards for a pianist who is an equally accomplished composer (honestly, how many more covers do jazz listeners really need of “In a Sentimental Mood”, or “On Green Dolphin Street”, or “You and the Night and the Music”) the Corea-penned pieces are the ones the audience bought tickets for:

“Morning Sprite” elegantly frolics off Chick’s fingers, evoking daybreak and innocence, and is a beautiful opening to the album.

“Rhumba Flamenco” builds and ignites, invoking Spanish landscapes and danceable rhythms via Weckl's drumming and Corea's hammering chords.

Patitucci’s at-times sonorous, at-times sawing bowed bass solo opening “Eternal Child” fades into an equally somber Corea solo, finally culminating as a chamber trio evocation of a time long-ago and yet eternally youthful. “Eternal Child” may be the best performance on this collection.

Finally, Gayle Moran delights both the audience and the trio with her vocal take on Neville Potter and Corea’s “You’re Everything”. Rarely performed live; in part due to the original being tied so closely to the 1972 Flora Purim / Return to Forever interpretation, but at least equally to the “scaling the heights” ascending vocals that intimidate many a lesser singer. Moran is actually beside herself at one point in the performance, stating out loud how impossible the notes-through-the-ceiling are to reach. The band and the crowd love it, however, and the ceiling tiles remain intact to the end.

title: A Fond Farewell From a Dear Friend
text: I find myself in beautiful Iraq again, and once again I have Warren to keep me company.  In 1991 I crossed into Iraq listening to Jungle Work.  Today I sit in Baghdad listenting to Keep Me in Your Heart.  Perhaps my review is biased, I heard of Warren's death the day my copy of The Wind arrived.  Every song touched a nerve...and sparked a warm memory.  Three songs in particular earn special attention.  In The Rest of The Night he seems to beg his listeners to spend one last night enjoying his wit and humor before he leaves us.  Please Stay pulls at the heartstrings as Warren asks those closest to him to stay with him to the end.  Finally Keep Me in Your Heart reduced me (a man who's spent my entire adult life as a soldier) to tears.  Not only because I knew it was the last time I'd hear one of Warren's songs for the first time, but because the simple but beautiful lyrics are so similar to my own feelings for my wife and newborn daughter I have yet to meet.  Mr. Zevon you've suceeded, there is always a place for you in my heart.  Thanks for 19 years of keeping a lonely soldier company around the world.

title: GREAT COMBINATION!
text: I knew the Charles Strouse score for "The Night They Raided Minksys" since it's first incarnation as an LP.  The real surprise is Henry Mancini's score for "Gaily, Gaily" which I remember from the cutout bins at the time. I have never seen the film and never bothered with the LP despite its $ 99 sale price.  I have scratched my head at a few of the Kirtzeland CD couplings but in this case one score really compliments the other.  Indeed, had Mancini been hired to compose for Universals "Thoroughly Modern Millie" it well could have sounded something like this.  Neither movie turned out to be a blockbuster.  "Gaily, Gaily" caused a flurry press at the time as it was one of the first movies to have male nudity; a new thing at the time - "The Night They Raided Minskys" was known as Burt Lahr's swan song (he died during production) and one of the few times the artistry of Norman Wisdom was captured on film.  Both movies were moderate success' at the time and both sunk into relative obscurity after their initial releases.  It doesn't matter.  I already know this is a CD that will be played over and over again!  I have always loved music from the 1920's and both of them evoke the period perfectly!

Overall, Amorphis still haven't escaped the trap they've stumbled into on their past three albums: most of the songs sound the same, and there is precious little breathing room.  "Veil of Sin" is the best track, with interesting vocal harmonies that are little used in metal.  There are few interesting guitar leads on the entire album; the keyboard and saxophone carry the music more.  The good moments tend to be outweighed by the bad; the last two minutes of "Crimson Wave" are nauseous Tesh-esque elevator music - there's no other way to describe it.  Another pretty good album from Amorphis.

The production on "SHE" is stronger and better than her debut, and Alice's voice remains the highlight of the audio experience. Her harmonies (with herself) are gorgeous on the song "Another Love" - an upbeat break-up song that incorporates both strings and bop-jazz piano progressions.

Her cover of "Fool For You" contains her strongest vocal performance; Cee-lo and Melanie Fiona would listen with awe.

Finally, the title track and album's closer, "She" is an empowered throwback that could be the next anthem for Gen-Y females. The whole album rivals Janelle Monae for conceptual narrative, unique instrumentation and unmatched vocal performance. Thanks Alice.

title: More Late Romantic Works by Hausegger

title: Probably the Most Technical, Awe-Inspiring Vocal Performance of her Career
text:
For fans who’ve been waiting (for more than a decade) for new music featuring featuring the voice of Beth Gibbons, a live classical recording was probably not what they had in mind. But regardless of one’s familiarity with the genre, if you are a fan of the Portishead singer’s voice, then the release of Gibbons’ November 29th, 2014 performance of Henryk Górecki’s Symphony No. 3 with the Polish National Radio Symphony (conducted by the composer himself) is, at the very least, an intriguing addition to the enigmatic singer’s modest catalog.

A quick disclaimer here - rather than embarrass myself by trying to deconstruct this recording from the perspective a classical music aficionado (which I am most certainly not), I’m going to approach this review from the eyes of rock music fan; and more specifically, a Portishead fan. And in that respect, as a vehicle for Gibbons’ effortlessly haunting vocals, this live recording is a resounding success.

Górecki’s third symphony, as the title Symphony of Sorrowful Songs would suggest, is an emotionally jarring, grandiose composition that features three distinct movements. For her part, Gibbons, who sought help from both English and Polish vocal coaches before taking the stage, delivers what is probably the most technical, awe-inspiring vocal performance of her career.

The first of the collection’s three tracks, the nearly twenty-five minute “Lento — Sostenuto tranquillo ma cantabile” is an incredibly dense, rewarding listen. Slowly building upon a bed of dramatic, ominous strings, Gibbon’s operatic vocals enter about half-way through, and soar above the otherwise captivating instrumentation. The second movement (“Lento e largo — Tranquillissimo”) is the shortest, and most accessible track here, while the third, and final movement (“Lento — Cantabile-semplice”) provides an appropriately grand conclusion to the what is a staggeringly beautiful piece of music.

Now, when it comes to classical music, I’m probably more familiar with modern cinematic scores than anything filed under Bach or Beethoven (although, I gotta a lotta love for those movies with that big, dumb dog), but what I can say is that, to my ears, the dynamic, brooding music presented here isn’t all that far removed from Gibbons’ previous work. And while it’s hard to say if this will be the average Portishead fan’s cup of tea, Beth Gibbons and the Polish National Radio Symphony Orchestra’s performance of Górecki’s Third Symphony is, at the very least, worth a listen - or ten.

text: Iced Earth's fourth album does not begin well. That's a point I think should be cleared up before anyone buys this album. The first three songs are virtually forgettable. I myself was disappointed when I first heard it, but please, bear with it and you WILL be rewarded. With "Dark Saga," Iced Earth clearly wanted to make a darker, heavier variant on Iron Maiden's old formula ("A Question Of Heaven" = "Hallowed Be Thy Name," anyone?) and to a degree, they succeeded. "Dark Saga" is a very cool concept album, and better for it, as the story of Spawn really helps to add to the atmoshere. The music here is generally quite crude, but when done right (i.e afer the first three songs) the crudeness actually helps to succesfully portray some very strong emotions, and that's really more the purpose of this album more than anything else. Make no mistake, this is an emotional roller coaster ride from start to finish, as you hear the story of a man who sold his soul to the devil to see the women he loved. Anger, sorrow, sadness, hatred and despair all have a track each and then some. So if you're into a bleak tale with a bleak telling, what the hell are you waiting for?! And for those of you who aren't, this is still recomended for the strength of the music. The best song here is easily the seventh track, "Vengeance Is Mine."

title: Mono: How The Beatles Intended Their Music To Be Heard.
text: Beyond a shadow of a doubt, certain Beatles songs do sound better in mono. All songs on "Please Please Me" and "With The Beatles" are infinitely better in mono as well as all other non-album material released in 1962 and 1963 on the "Masters" sets. The arguments for mono vs. stereo really start with material recorded from 1964 to 1967. It starts with the 4 tracks that were originally released on the British EP "Long Tall Sally". The song "Slowdown" is mixed very poorly on the stereo release. It lacks any bass sound whatsoever. The mono version is far more powerful and really rocks. On the "Hard Day's Night" album, the mono apparently received the minor repairs and edits to correct notable flaws; the harmonica intro on "I Should Have Known Better" and McCartney's vocal breakdown, on "If I Fell". The stereo versions of these are unrepaired which shows that mono was given priority. With respect to "Beatles For Sale", according to Mark Lewisohn's book about the Beatles recording sessions, the stereo mixes for several of the 14 songs were completed in about 30 minutes! Despite this, they still sound very good. The mono mixes were given much more time, attention, and care. As for "Help!" and "Rubber Soul", the original 1965 stereo mixes, in many cases were very "ping-pong". This was especially true for "Rubber Soul" with the vocals mixed to the far right in the stereo picture. When "Help!" and "Rubber Soul" were first released on CD in 1987, Beatles producer George Martin remixed these two albums. "Help!" sounds awesome in stereo. "Rubber Soul is marginally better but the vocals still pan somewhat to the right of center in the stereo picture, which still leaves me unsettled. Mono gets the thumbs up on this one. With "Revolver" and "Sgt. Pepper" come the biggest debates. On "Revolver" the recording technique which came to be known as artificial double tracking, known commonly as ADT, was invented and the Beatles used it liberally when they recorded the vocals for this album. The stereo mix shows these off beautifully. The mono mix however does benefit from longer fades for a few songs and a few flaws present on the stereo mix are not present. The Beatles themselves have all said that the only true "Sgt. Pepper" release is the mono version. They were present for all mono mixes and they were completely absent when it came time to mix the album for stereo. For "Magical Mystery Tour" and "The Beatles" aka "The White Album", the stereo mixes do get the nod as sounding more pleasing to the ear, but it is fun to find the differences between the mixes. One exception in this period is the single version of "Revolution" on the "Masters". John Lennon was quoted as saying in an interview that the stereo version was 'turned into a piece of ice cream'. The mono version does have more punch, for sure. If you are forced to choose between the two, get the mono and buy "Abbey Road", and "Let It Be" separately since they are not included in the Mono box since they only exist in stereo.

title: Breakaway, indeed.
text:
Credit "American Idol" for getting one thing right: bringing Kelly Clarkson to public consciousness. This girl's for real. On her aptly-titled sophomore effort, "Breakaway", Clarkson not only ably breaks away from the "Idol" formula, but also veers away from the gimmicky shenanigans of her dime-a-dozen radio contemporaries. The new collection is a potent mix of substance and style. If her eclectic debut, "Thankful", was the introduction, a sampling of what she can do, "Breakaway" is surely the first full chapter. And what an engrossing attention-getter it is.

Here, Clarkson is in an angsty, edgy rocker kinda mood. She expounds on the trouble with love in all its misery...and lots of things get broken along the way: broken hearts ( "Behind These Hazel Eyes" ); broken relationships ( "Since U Been Gone", "Walk Away" ); broken habits ( "Gone" ); broken homes ( "Because of You" ); and, of course, erm, broken away (the title track and modern classic, "Breakaway" ). The haunting "Addicted" is mesmerizing, almost frightening in its dark allure and brilliance. Serving as a nice contrast - and a bit of a reprieve - from the generally somber tone of the album is the captivating and hopeful "You Found Me" , where Clarkson reflects on what it's like when love goes right; and yet, even here there is a touch of melancholy and weariness in her voice that maintains nicely the flow of the entire disc. The collection climaxes with the powerful tour de force that is "Hear Me", and then wraps up quietly with a gorgeous, live rendition of "Beautiful Disaster". Clarkson clearly remembers what it's like to be the listener. The 12-track set comes in at a brisk 45 minutes, not one second of which is wasted. There is such movement within and between the tracks that the songs never wear out their welcome.

Guiding you through it all is that epic, stunningly versatile voice, which is satisfyingly showcased here. It towers and booms. It quakes with emotion. It soothes. It enchants. Clarkson is a masterful and passionate storyteller and vocalist, and she does not play it safe here. The nuanced vocalizations are astonishingly complex and difficult. Trying to sing along to these immensely sing-along-able songs...well, I don't think I've ever sounded so bad, heh. Her voice and the rock instrumentation make a phenomenal pair.

Glancing at the liner notes, we find that Clarkson is credited as either the main writer or as a smaller contributor on several tracks. Looking further, we find she provides all vocals (including all background vocals) throughout the entire disc. Amazing. Nope, no silly posturing, no gratuitous self-promotion, no flashy studio trickery here. Just great, great music from a great artist. This album deserves to become a classic, and Clarkson deserves to be appreciated as something much more than mere idol. Turn the volume way up on this one, folks.

title: Future Is Medieval - Revisited for the USA
text:
Last year, Kaiser Chiefs released 20 songs on their website and offered up a "create your album" promotion. Fans could select 10 songs from the 20 available, design their own cover art, and then download their customized album; for a price, of course.

Eventually, Kaiser Chiefs selected 13 of the most popular tracks and released it as their official follow-up to 2008's "Off with Their Heads." In the U.K. this album was titled "Future is Medieval" and was released last July, but it never saw the light of day in the United States. The reason behind this likely has to do with diminished album sales and a very disappointing release in the U.K. compared to their 2005 debut, "Employment," but being unwilling to hang up the towel, Kaiser Chiefs have now finally released their fourth studio album in the U.S. with a few changes; the first of which being the title of the album.

"Start the Revolution Without Me" is the U.S. version of "Future is Medieval," but four tracks, "Out of Focus," "Long Way from Celebrating," "Dead or in Serious Trouble," and "Coming Up for Air," have been exchanged for "On the Run," "Cousin in the Bronx," "Problem Solved," and "Can't Mind My Own Business." When Kaiser Chiefs originally released the 20 songs they would pull from to formulate both of these records, my personal favorite recording was "Fly on the Wall" which fails to make the track list of either compilation, but despite this minor disappointment, Kaiser Chiefs still have plenty to offer fans and the substitutions made for the American release will likely help to captivate a larger audience in the States.

Unlike many similar British Indie Rock bands that got their start around the same time, Kaiser Chiefs have managed to stay true to their sound on each of their four releases. Bands like Franz Ferdinand and Arctic Monkeys have explored different styles and instrumentation with varying degrees of success, but Kaiser Chiefs have built their brand from a single successful formula.

Although this can often make repeated listens of their albums tiresome, it also makes any new material instantly recognizable.

With the occasional new sound effect thrown in on songs like "Man on Mars" and a little more reliance on synthesizer than their previous albums, "Start the Revolution Without Me" is otherwise a trademark Kaiser Chiefs record.

The catchiness of "Little Shocks," the album's feature single, barely approaches previous singles like "Never Miss a Beat" or "Oh My God," but each song is still very enjoyable and there is enough variety amongst the 13 tracks to keep things interesting.

"Start the Revolution Without Me" will likely be the least represented album on Kaiser Chiefs' inevitable greatest hits record, but it is also the most consistently strong album they have released since their debut.
Existing fans should pick up this album with confidence, but anyone new to the band should still start with "Employment" before venturing into their more recent material.

title: Astonishingly Mediocre
text:
First of all, this album is a chore to get through. Over two hours of music? That should be awesome, but it's not. In fact, I find it a chore to even get through the first disc. By the time the first disc is over, I'm already going back to Scenes from a Memory to listen how a great concept album should sound. My main problem with this album, besides the length, is that I had absolutely NO emotions when listening to it, other than being bored and trying to skip to the next track to see if things would get more interesting. There are way too many similar sounding songs on The Astonishing. Way too many whiny ballads with LaBrie and dear God, so many cheesy lyrics!! I found myself rolling my eyes a lot when listening to this album.

I should have known when I saw the trailer for the Astonishing on YouTube that we would be in trouble. The whole premise, besides being ripped straight from 2112, sounds like a mobile app game. LaBrie trying to do different vocal ranges for the different characters doesn't work either. They should have had some female vocals and duets, that would've been a nice break from Labrie. The mix isn't that great overall. I can't even hear Myung half the time and Mangini's drumming has absolutely no soul. The whole thing just didn't click with me at all.

I'm trying not to be overly critical, but I couldn't imagine myself going back and listening to this release anytime soon. It's just so so, so boring and so, so long. I expected way more from these guys. A different style of music sure, but Hand. Cannot. Erase. by Steven WIlson is how a concept album should flow and sound. That album, along with Scenes from a Memory are what you should be looking for if you're searching for a great concept record, not this. Honestly, this could have easily been cut down to one disc. There are a few redeeming moments (mostly small instrumental sections like the middle of the track "A New Beginning"), but those are few and far between. The idea of watching this unfold for over two hours at a live show doesn't excite me either, so I won't be lining up to see them when they come around on tour.

Finally, my biggest gripe with this album is the lack of progressive elements. There were ample opportunities to have some instrumental tracks that focused on proggy elements, but they are all absent from this release. Literally every song is around 4 minutes and LaBrie sings for almost the whole song. I'm sure I will get a lot of hate in the comments section, but music is subjective. You may like it, but I do not. No sense in arguing who is right. If you enjoyed it, Cheers!

title: I still ADORE this show!!!
text: I had the great pleasure and good fortune of seeing the touring production of this show at least 6 times in the spring of 2000 at the Ahmanson Theatre in Los Angeles, and of the great Boublil/Schonberg shows, it remains my favorite.  Alas, that touring production, which was supposed to take it to Broadway, was derailed by poor public response, which remains heartbreakingly disappointing for me to this day (6-5-13), especially since members of that production (notably Hugh Panaro, Stephen R. Bunstrock, Erin Dilly, Jose Llana, and Michael Arnold) had far better singing voices than what we find on this recording.  Plus there were a couple of new songs, particularly "Benoit's lament," which was wonderfully sung by Arnold, that have never, to my knowledge, been recorded for the music-buying public, which is a terrible loss.  But back to this recording, which I bought in early 2000 while I was compulsively seeing the show every chance I could, one day turning down free tickets to another show so I could pay to see the last matinee of this one at the Ahmanson.  I find the recording completely involving, although it probably helped that I had seen it on stage.  And while I continue to lament that we never got the U.S. stars on record, the voices here are quite good -- if not so good they can make some of us forget the others!  I'll start listening to this on my iPod, and it's very hard to turn it off until it runs its glorious course.  Songs like "Without You As A Friend,""Live With Somebody You Love," "How Many Tears," "The Day Has Come," "All That I Love," and others that are perfectly woven into the fabric of the story. And what a story!  If I could, I would have seen it even more times!  And while my attachment to the recording has been affected by my love of what I saw on stage, it still remains a very satisfying listening experience, and I have few negatives to add. title: Five-star album, as always.
text: After first discovering Nick Cave in 1996, I've since made it a point to own every album he's ever released with the Seeds, from 1984's "From Her To Eternity" right up to this evocative set, which I purchased within days of its release.  I had just trekked some 800 miles to New Orleans to witness Nick's solo performance at the Orpheum, and had been suitably blown away.  Even anchored to a piano, the man commands awe.  As I write this review, I'm looking forward to the Bad Seeds' appearance next month at the Chicago Theatre with great anticipation.  I am a die-hard, life-long Nick Cave addict.  As for the songs on this album, many have perceived them to be a departure from Cave's earlier works, whereas I see them as a natural progression.  The beauty of Cave's early works was in his intermingling of Love, Death, and Religion...the three became inseperable in the hands of this master storyteller.  This is a trend which continues on "No More Shall We Part," Cave's eleventh studio album with the Seeds.  What we have here is not at all a deviation from Cave's lyrical style, brilliant as always in its depictions of the joys and agonies of Love/Death/Religion.  Rather, it is the evolution of his delivery of those lyrics.  The haunting melodies on this set are intended to evoke certain emotions from the listener, just as any dedicated fan can tell you has been the case since "From Her To Eternity"...and even back to the Birthday Party days.  Only now, those emotions are raised by well-placed strings and simple, but stunningly beautiful, piano lines...whereas, back in '84, the Seeds were evoking those same feelings with a barrage of noise and rage.  My favorite track on this album (though the race is close, to be certain) is the opener, "As I Sat Sadly By Her Side."  As with all of Cave's songs, it takes the form of a story.  A man and woman sit at a window and watch the world pass.  She points out the beauty of it all while he ponders the injustices and blindness which men inflict upon their brethren.  "All outward motion connects to nothing, for each is concerned with their immediate need."  She draws the curtain down and states that what happens outside that window is none of his concern.  She turns from him crying, and he states "I could not wipe the smile from my face as I sat sadly by her side."  Why does he smile?  Because although she does not realize it, she has proven his point about people being too wrapped up in their own lives to care about the suffering of others.  The smile is his unconscious reaction to this situation, though it suggests, not that he is happy with this outcome...but rather, just the opposite.  In a way, he had wished himself wrong.  It is subtle lyrical touches like these which ensure that Cave's place in musical history is assured.  A man of such outright genius cannot be denied by the ages.  Though his music cannot by defined as conventionally popular, it will one day take its place among the greatest music of the twentieth century.  And Cave shall take his rightful place alongside Weill, Dylan, Reed, and Cohen as one of the greatest songwriters of this century.

title: This is an intimate record that is worth a fair shot
text:
I really enjoyed this album. I've been a long time fan and I truly appreciate the growth I have heard from this group. This band has had ups and downs just like any other, but they have settled on the sound that they want, despite what others think. I enjoyed all of the singles, especially Again and Again, which made me excited for whatever else Dave had to bring.

Let me say that this is indeed a different record than a lot of the other ones in the catalogue. It's slower and softer throughout, but I actually like that about this record. Here On Out is a beautiful ballad, followed by That Girl Is You, which has grown on me since its initial releasing. She is a rocking tune and bkdkdkdd is a nice slice of a funky groove before the beautiful Black and Blue Bird. Idea of You is powerful, just as it is live. While some of that live power doesn't quite translate in the studio, I still think it works well enough. Virginia in the Rain is gorgeous and almost hypnotic in my opinion in how it grooves, cycling in and out of melodic lines and groove seamlessly. Come on Come on and Do You Remember are also awesome tracks that capture your attention in different ways, either through melody or sheer groove. The final cut, When I'm Weary is a slow ballad that closes out an intimate record on a touching note, which is fine with me.

I think the key to enjoying this record is to really take this record one song at a time and realize that this is a record that Dave himself is happy with and wanted to share with the world. It made him happy to do this, and that's all I need to know. I think this is a lovely record and I would definitely recommend it.

title: Leela James delivers yet another great album
text: Leela James released her new album "My Soul" a year after her all-covers album "Let's Do It Again". She does the perfect balance between traditional and contemporary- not bad for someone who is still in her mid-20's. The album starts off with "I Ain't New To This" in which she fancies herself as a music industry veteran, while taking a brief swipe at her former label Warner Bros. Records for their lack of promotion of her 2005 debut "A Change Is Gonna Come". Speaking of her debut album, one of the producers that worked on it appears on "My Soul"- Chucky Thompson, who produced the Raheem DeVaughn assisted "Mr. Incredible, Ms. Unforgettable" and the two 60's inspired tracks "Party All Night" and "Let It Roll". Andrea Martin, who also wrote Melanie Fiona's "Give It To Me Right" pens the first single "Tell Me You Love Me". Ray Murray (one-third of the production team Organized Noize) produces "I Want It All" which sounds a lot like N.E.R.D.'s song "Don't Worry About It" from their 2004 album "Fly Or Die". Orthodox & Ransum close the album with the songs "If It's Wrong" and "It's Over". This album is heavily rooted in retro soul, with the exception of "Supa Lova" and "So Cold" which sound like obvious attempts for commercial radio. In a nutshell, Leela's new album is pretty good, albeit rather brief. This album is a must own for this year.

title: More than just a few pretty faces....
text:
I can clearly remember the first time I heard of the Dixie Chicks. I was working at a local radio station and the girls were out promoting their first single "I Can Love You Better". I remember everyone saying that the Chicks weren't going to go anywhere and that they were just a bunch of pretty faces. I had a different opinion though, I loved their music and just knew that they were exactly what country radio needed. These were three strong women, who wrote their own music, played their own instruments, and had voices like angels. Lead singer, Natalie Maines (daughter of legendary guitartist Lloyd Maines) has one of those voices that people can only pray for. It's amazing how she can bend her voice to the lyrics, going from powerful to soft in a matter of seconds. The gals's got one hell of a voice. It's pure country!
The best tracks on the cd are "You Were Mine" (which was written by sisters Emily Robison and Martie Seidel), "Loving Arms" (which SHOULD'VE been released! It's awesome!), "Let 'Er Rip", and the Maria McKee penned "Am I The Only One (Who's Ever Felt This Way)". Another great song is the remake of Bonnie Raitt's big hit "Give It Up or Let Me Go". The song shows off Natalie's powerful voice as well the the sisters' instrumental capabilities.
The Dixie Chicks are now one of the biggest groups on the planet and it all started with the 1998 release of "Wide Open Spaces". With the help of singles such as "I Can Love You Better", "Wide Open Spaces", and "There's Your Trouble" the cd went on to win several Grammy's and CMA's. The singles also solidified the group as a top-selling country act and proved that yes, you can be pretty and sing too.
Gennie Bailey-Rogers

title: Overrated
text: I purchased this DVD based on the very good reviews of it posted here. Unfortunately, I feel that these reviews omit certain aspects of the disk that I think should be mentioned. Firstly, the 4:3 aspect ratio. I'm sure this was done in order to optimize the quality of the picture, but the image really looks crammed with all those musicians being fit into a small rectangle in the middle of my 32-inch flat-screen TV. Secondly, the camera work. Some may think that filming the players from one side is cool, but I disagree. As one producer from the series "Keeping Score" put it, when you see a player playing a particular instrument, then you really hear the music coming out of that instrument (or words to that effect). There are very few individual shots of players on this disc. Rather, whole lines of players (winds, for example) are filmed from a side so that the musicians look like they are in a marching band. Thirdly, this is the first time I see Karajan conduct, and he is simply not much fun to watch. He keeps his eyes shut throughout, so that there is no eye contact between him and individual members of the orchestra (which most other conductors must do in order to cue particular players). I'm sure he was able to do this because he had about a million rehearsals with the orchestra before actually performing these pieces in public. What is my point? Well, one really wants a DVD to be a truly satisfying VIEWING experience. Otherwise one could just get a CD of the performance. One last comment: the orchestra is an all male orchestra! (which is rare nowadays).

title: New and old songs, well presented
text:
Back in '70 I never thought Melanie would someday re-record her own Golden Oldies but it appears she has done just that for the fourth (?) time - "Ballroom Streets" was the first. Something usually goes wrong on these projects - check out many recuts by '50s stars like Little Richard and Chuck Berry. You just can't re-create a "feel" or that magical atmoshpere which yielded immortal sounds.
Anyway, although Melanie has not added nuance to the old ones but she has not hurt 'em a bit, thanks to strong production values: they kept it simple, folks, with mostly voice, guitar, and distant vocal backup. Very refreshing in this era of synthesized overproduction. "Close To It All" and "What Have They Done To My Song, Ma" are as good as the originals. ("Brand New Key" is not as good - it was such an amazing record I wish she'd leave it alone at this point, or try to do it like the hit single. There's nothing to be embarrassed about - it was 1930's blues in a 1972 setting and it worked!).
The title song for this collection, "Ring The Living Bell" would have been *almost* as good if they didn't offer interminable useless outtakes - this idea is even more objectionable for a title song! Outtakes, alternates, etc., (for me) only have entertainment value if something new or unexpected emerges, something to which you say "Hey, that phrase/riff/line would *also* have worked". They shouldn't have messed around with a stunning folk incantation that left us breathless back in '75 at the Wolman Skating Rink in Central Park.
The "contemporary" Sting/Doobie Brothers, etc. tracks are nice but don't amount to much.
The real beauty in this entry is the haunting folk ballad "Arrow" - it's pure Melanie.
A bonus cut by her daughters - Safka - called "One Mistake" is the next best cut!
It may sound cliche by now, but "The Spirit Of Woodstock" continues to live in the voices and productions of people like Melanie - and if she's not not seen or heard too often these days, then (in my humble opinion) her sound can be found in the voices of people like Stevie Nicks, Kim Carnes, Cyndi Lauper...you name a few more.

title: QUEEN'S FIRST
text:
The debut album from Queen contains a few of the elements that would eventually define the band, but is very much a early 70's Prog-rock/metal album. Freddy Mercury's distinct voice and Brian May's original guitar tones are in evidence throughout. The legendary excess and theatrical flair is a mere tease at this stage.

The key tracks are the ones usually plucked for the many Queen anthologies, "Keep Yourself Alive" and "Liar." The Kings and medieval themes prevalent in the era are available on "Great King Rat" and a tease of Queen II is offered when the album closes with "Seven Seas of Rhye." For the most part, the show is May and Mercury's, with a quick peek at Roger Taylor's vocals on "Modern Times Rock and Roll." The band has not quite gelled and the Queen everyone knows and loves emerged in full on the second album.

title: Shirley Walker's Bat-music legacy lives on
text:
Twenty years ago, in the waning months of 1992, fans of animation and the character of The Batman in particular were in heaven. A cartoon show had premiered that year that enthralled us with its showcase of the Caped Crusader, [[ASIN:B00023E894 Batman: The Animated Series, Volume One (DC Comics Classic Collection)]]. Created as a cartoon companion to the big budget films of director Tim Burton, "Batman (1989)" and "Batman Returns (1992)," the show evolved under the vision of animators Bruce Timm and Eric Radomski, and writers Paul Dini and Alan Burnett into something uniquely its own. Offering its audience a cartoon of sophisticated action and drama rarely seen outside of Japanese animation, this series would help instill a renewed respect for the Dark Knight, and for the potential of the animated medium in America.

As each succeeding episode aired on a daily basis, enraptured fans quickly realized this series was something special. One ingredient that particularly impressed the audience was the rich musical score composed for the series. As the viewer watched and listened to the latest Batman adventure, he or she was struck not just by the deep, grim voice of the Gotham Guardian, portrayed with conviction by Kevin Conroy: they were also gripped emotionally by the music written and/or overseen by the gifted talent of a pioneering musical artist named Shirley Walker. Mrs. Walker is credited with being the first woman to compose the score to a major Hollywood motion picture, "Memoirs of an Invisble Man" in 1992. In her varied career, Mrs Walker worked in film and television and fortune shined on The Batman when she was chosen to become Chief Composer and Music Director to the animated series. Under her stewardship, Mrs. Walker and her fellow music composers, Lolita Ritmanis, and Michael McCuistion, created a television cartoon score that rivaled music created for the big screen.

Admirers of the music they made long lamented not being able to enjoy these remarkable scores in soundtrack form. Those regrets were at least partially appeased with the 1993 release of the theatrical animated motion picture, [[ASIN:B000A9QKLE Batman - Mask of the Phantasm]], and its soundtrack, [[ASIN:B0025YFCF2 Batman: Mask of the Phantasm]], composed by Mrs. Walker. Still, it wasn't until 16 years after its 1992 premiere that fans of the beloved Batman television cartoon would have their musical dreams realized by La-La Land Records, an independent producer of movie soundtracks. This company ("Where soundtracks live!") released [[ASIN:B001S38W76 Batman: The Animated Series]], a limited edition 2 CD set of music from the classic show. Unfortunately only 3000 copies of the soundtrack were produced and it sold out immediately.

In 2012, La-La Land Records released an even more ambitious soundtrack collection, [[ASIN:B008PD7IHC Batman the Animated Series: Vol 2 (4 CD) [Soundtrack]]], which featured even more amazing music from this stirring series; and thankfully for those countless fans who missed out on the original soundtrack release, the company, "by popular demand," has produced a revised soundtrack titled "Batman: The Animated Series (Volume 1: Second Edition)." This new pressing of the series' score differs from the original limited edition by omitting 2 cuts from the first edition: "Gotham City Overture" and "Music of the Bat." This editing was done, according to La-La Land Records' website, "to preserve the integrity of the initial release." Regrettably, this is also a limited edition totaling 5000 copies.

Even with the omissions, the "Second Edition" is still a thrilling experience. One can't help but be in awe of what Mrs. Walker and her team of musical artists accomplished...for an American cartoon! From the opening arrangement to the episode "On Leather Wings," with its fluttering flutes, ominous violins and haunting horns, the music of "Batman: The Animated Series" immerses its listener into the dark, mysterious world of Gotham City, and its Dark Defender, The Batman. Like any great work of music, this soundtrack takes its audience on a special adventure. Mrs. Walker is our musical guide as we follow the Caped Crusader on his quest to protect his city from the likes of the Joker, Two Face, and Poison Ivy. This journey is highlighted by the use of what German composer Richard Wagner famously utilized in his operas: the leitmotif, the creation of melodies or themes which showcase a specific character, place or thing in the story. Mrs. Walker and her fellow composers incorporated this idea repeatedly in the animated series, giving added musical character to not just the Dark Knight, but to his fiendish foes as well, and even the troubled city of Gotham. As explained in the soundtrack's excellent liner notes,"the episodes were constructed as 'mini-movies,'" allowing the music writers the opportunity "to experiment with different musical forms."

A distinctive example of this is the score to the episode "It's Never Too Late," composed by Lolita Ritmanis. This adventure focused not on a Bat-villain but rather on the life paths of 2 brothers: Arnold and Michael Stromwell, one, a Gotham mob boss, the other, a humble priest. Within the half hour time frame of a so-called chidren's cartoon, the creators of this series produced a powerful crime drama, reminiscent of the 1938 ganster film classic, [[ASIN:B0006HBV28 Angels With Dirty Faces]], starring James Cagney, Pat O'Brien, and Humphrey Bogart. At the core of this episode is Ms. Ritmanis' music, which conveys the complex relationship of the Stromwell brothers, as well as the powerful presence of The Batman, as he confronts the violent criminals of this dramatic tale.

Even after 20 years, the music of "Batman: The Animated Series" by Shirley Walker and her collaborative composers stands as a triumph of not just animation scores but of motion picture scores. Mrs. Walker passed away in 2006, sadly not living to see her musical achievement released to an enthusiastic audience. But the music and her legacy lives on.

This soundtrack comes with my highest recommendation.

text: Balkanarama is an enormously talented group who can emulate the natural rhythms and vocals of the Balkans and simultaneously maintain their own unique identity. These are Americans who play the traditional or urban music of Bulgaria, Macedonia, or the Romani with the flair and improvisational abandonment of  regional musicians! Other times they stretch the boundaries by adding unique embellishments, most often on the clarinet, alto sax, or violin, all the while staying true to the regional rhythm and melody. title: Soulful and Magnificent Lyra Music with Vocals
text: Psarantonis and Ensemble (Georgis Xylouris on 12-stringed laouto and Achilleas Perisides on the 8-stringed lauoto) create a dazzling interpretation of Cretan music. Each note reminds the listener of the ancient music of Byzantium. The pentatonic scale and unique harmonics hold the listener spell-bound and transfixed as if suspended in time. Most spectacular is the lyra which occasionally sounds soft, sometimes strong and loud as it crescendos and decrescendos with different playing techniques. At times the lyra almost sings each note, other times the instrument whispers or explodes with exuberance and energy. There are trills, vibratos and pizzicato variations. This whole CD is a unique extravaganza of creativity and technical expertise. It is a joy to hear. Psarantonis voice is clear, crisp and sensual. He can also sound raw and earthy with a hint of the untamed, just like the Psiloritis mountains in Crete. Keep in mind, when ordering this CD from amazon.com it is a "special order". This means it might take longer than usual to arrive. However, it is well worth the wait. Erika Borsos (erikab93)

title: Better than the last two albums!
text:
This band is kind of a guilty pleasure of mine. I'm not really all that much into shock rock, but Lordi knows how to make a perfect combination of 80's style rock and giving that modern day horror rock spin to it.

I've had a chance to listen to it all the way through about 5 or 6 times now so I feel like I've gotten a pretty good grasp of my opinion. It's a good solid album with a lot of catchy vocals and hooks galore. It's certainly better than their last two outings (Babez for Breakfast and Deadache) but not quite as good as Get Heavy or my personal favorite, The Arockalypse (amazing album, get it if you don't have it).

I actually questioned buying this album at first due to Lordi seeming to go down hill recently. I don't ever see them topping The Arockalypse. Deadache was a solid album but just didn't have too many memorable songs (Missing Miss Charlene and Bite It Like a Bulldog were the big hits of the album). As for Babez for Breakfast... I personally didn't care for that album at all. Lordi is known for some cheesy lyrics but Babez went a little too far in that department and not a single song from the album was very memorable.

Back to this album. It has some amazing guitar hooks and great lyrics in terms of both melody and content, good enough to have me humming it after only a few listens. However, Lordi's sound has changed quite drastically, which is to be expected with a new keyboardist (Hella) and new drummer (Mana). You'll just have to listen to see what I'm talking about, it's difficult to explain.

1) We're Not Bad For The Kids (We're Worse) - Catchy chorus, fast paced, 80's metal sound (9/10)
2) I Luv Ugly - Absolutely insane intro riffs between the guitar and keyboard, very catchy (8/10)
3) The Riff - Typical radio friendly single, but great content (9/10)
4) Something Wicked This Way Comes - Solid song, not great but not bad (7/10)
5) I'm The Best - Cool intro BUT super cheesy lyrics, repetetive, borderline annoying (4/10)
6) Horrifiction - Freaky intro, softer ballad style song, good lyrics, catchy chorus (8/10)
7) Happy New Fear - Decent song but again, nothing special (7/10)
8) Schizo Doll - Another freaky intro, ultimately this is nothing more than a filler song (5/10)
9) Candy for the Cannibal - Cool guitar hook, catchy, amazing chorus (9/10)
10) Sincerely with Love - I was pretty shocked at the explicatives, almost made the album PA worthy (8/10)
11) SCG6: Otus' Butcher Clinic - this really isn't a song, it's a tribute to their fallen drummer (X/10)

Summary:
I personally love the album, it's much better than I expected. Better than their last two, but doesn't quite stack up against Get Heavy or The Arockalypse. It has enough good tracks to earn 4/5 stars.

title: ...In The Right Direction
text:
The James Brown - Derrick Monk collaboration yields a third consecutive winner. Starting with "I'm Back" in '98, on Georgia Lina/Mercury, then "The Merry Christmas" album the following year, on Goeorgia Lina/Groove, now "The Next Step" on Fome Records, new and old fans can enjoy several Grammy-quality cuts.
The new CD has much of the same aural qualities of the Christmas album, a soft-edged chorus underlining the vital lead vocals, spare but effective instrumentation. The opener, "Automatic", is Top 10 material, a successful hip-hop/funk; an engaging melody and rhythm. Track 2, "Send Her Back To Me" is reminiscent of things like "Good-bye My Love", or "I Guess I'll Have To Cry, Cry, Cry" from 1968, an expression of a man's remorse in not following his heart and now trying to retrace the steps. "Nothing But A Jam" is another entertaining commercial cut in the same progressive groove we've witnessed since "I'm Back" - it's listenable *and* danceable. "You've Got What It Takes", with Tomi Rae, sounds like an alternate take of the same tune from the '98 effort, listed as "What It Takes". It's the well-known Pop Classic, with a fresh new fun interchange. The lady is the star on "It's Time", a Soul-retro ballad if you will. The "Please, Please" feel supports the lyric about the positive turning point in a growing relationship.
"Good And Natural" is really the only "James Brown riff" here; it's in the smooth, new groove but is an instant dance-floor motivator.
"Killing Is Out, School Is In", is the recent single, but has some variation in this take.

title: Superb Album By Paul SImon Gone Solo!
text: This album represented Paul Simon's realization of his full abilities  hinted to so well in the previous albums both with Simon and Garfunkel and  then as a solo artist. This album provocatively showcases Simon's unique  talents and creative interests with an eclectic, wide-ranging, and  gorgeously produced solo effort. From the haunting rhythms and wry lyrics  of "Kodachrome" to the tender and sensitive emotions expressed so well in  "Something So Right", we sense more than a little autobiographical  influence in all the songs. Simon's lyrical genius is displayed in spades  here, from "American Tune" to "Learn How to Fall" to the joyous "Loves Me  Like A Rock", and we can tell that this is an artist in full bloom and  enjoying his singular ability to deliver a wide range of songs with a  panorama of emotions and telling personal observations so artfully  expressed that it is a wonder to listen to them. This is an album one must  listen to appreciate, and the new directions Simon began with this album  have now stretched out in a dozen or so albums and compilations. This is a  terrific album for a man who had the courage and nerve to deliberately walk  away from a phenomenally successful situation as half of Simon and  Garfunkel to follow his own artistic heart. I highly recommend it. Enjoy!

title: Spellbinding debut album
text:
This album is something really interesting. Given how everyone remembers Eurythmics for songs such as Sweet Dreams, There Must Be An Angel.... and so on, we have the idea that they were a pop band first and foremost and of course, for the most part that is right. They were. They were an extremely good pop band too. Not something I'd readily pick up mind. There have been some songs which have been great and some that are vapid nonsense. I, for one, cannot stand There Must Be An Angel which showcases Annie Lennox's vocals to extremely good affect but the song has nothing to add to it. But this album is different. Very much within the sound and texture of the album. It's not what you'd expect.

From the first track, you can tell this wasn't going to be a commercially viable record to release. It sounds somewhat cold, dislocated and out of place. Even though there's more guitars on this album than any other Eurythmics song I've heard, it feels a lot more colder than those songs! This can be due in part to Conny Plank's production work which is always interesting without fail.

What Plank seems to have melded together is a stunning mixture of exotic influences melded to a strictly European sensibility and within that a certain Britishness. Even though in the liner notes it says the band felt themselves more European than British, within the music there still retains that sense of Britishness but without any of the negative aspects, and the embracing of European influences clearly help this album fluorish.

Annie's voice on this album is, for the most part, very subdued and wistful. It compliments the music very well which takes on very dreamy and exotic tones while at the same time, giving a sense of being disenchanted with all around them. Very few can make an album that sounds like that and even fewer make it sound as interesting as it does, so it's all credit to Annie and Dave for orchestrating an album as good as this.

I could go on about the cover too but that would be pretty pointless. To cut it short, I feel it compliments the album. It looks of it's time too but in a good way.

Tracks like Take Me To Your Heart, Caveman Head and Never Gonna Cry Again have a sense of enchantment and disenchantment while Sing-Sing ( which is sung in French ) only encaptures the sense of dreamy wonder that is sometimes forgotten in music. Of the extra tracks Heartbeat Heartbeat and 4/4 In Leather should also get a mention for being frenetically paced that seriously test those dancing shoes but perhaps not as overtly as anything that would follow.

Overall, this album is one of a kind, one which the band has never repeated and perhaps no one could attempt to duplicate this album as the amount of intricate details in the album is simply spellbinding!

title: Interesting  'super group' experiment
text:
Kind of a 21st century version of Travelin' Wilburys this interesting project brings together 5 artists rooted in quite different areas. From superstar Mick Jagger to more 'alternative' third world musicians like Damian Marley and Indian composer A. R. Rahman.

What makes the record so succesful is actually the dominant role of Marley and Rahman. Marley's rhythm section provides a heavy reggae atmosphere through out while Rahman's elegant orchestrations add depth and beauty. Jagger is absolutely on top of his game while Dave Steward's always intelligent guitarplaying binds everything together. And even if Joss Stone might be struggling a bit to keep up with 'the guys' she provides the needed feminine touch.

Seems as if many people will love to hate this group but in fact it's a suprisingly artistic and un-commercial album. Filled with strong songs - although the obvious 'hit' might be missing - and an abundance of unusual ideas and arrangements. While perhaps in the long run this will only be a small footnote to the legend of The Rolling Stones it's actually a very creative and well executed experiment.

title: Everyone else's favorite!
text: I must surely be the only opera lover in the world...other than inveterate Wagnerites....who isn't completely enamoured of "La Boheme!" Why? Because, as far as I'm concerned Puccini pretty much (at the risk of being crude) blew his wad in that admittedly glorious last fifteen-or-so minutes of Act I! That music is so utterly, ravishingly gorgeous that everything that follows, with the possible exception of Musetta's Waltz in Act II, is...musically speaking, a let-down. I also have always found the entire Act II, outside the snow-bound gates of Paris to be utterly, and perversely boring! I say "perversely" because it is probably the strongest act dramatically..but the music leaves me totally unmoved. So why then am I awarding this recording the full five stars? Because the performance and recording are marvelous! Pavarotti and Freni are glorious together in that finale of Act I. So if you are going to have a recording of "La Boheme" (and what opera lover would not?) this is the one to have. By the way,I should, in fairness say that my comments not withstanding, I do not dislike this opera by any means...it just isn't my favorite like the rest of the world.

title: A travesty
text:
This is a warning !
This purports to be a soundtrack of Charles Strouse's period score, but it is actually full of sound-clips from the film. We get constant snippets of dialogue that have no value without the visual. The only uninterrupted music is the main title: "Foggy Mountain Breakdown" by Flatt & Scruggs. This is superb, in a country/blue grass vein. All the other tracks are sound effects and dialogue that segue into the composer's background score. The music sections are very short, which is probably why the CD is formatted this way, but I would gladly have a very short album than a truncated thing like this. Strouse has written some very winning music that has a hint of Americana in Copland mode, with occasional flavorings of banjos and trumpets. If I was Charles Strouse? I would sue the album producers. title: SPLENDID!
text:
I have to confess that for many years I was not a big fan of Bax's music, but through my own ignorance, I fear. I was first exposed to his music through an ancient LP of piano music. I felt that both the music and the performance were utterly undistinguished. So I struck Bax off my list of composers to get to know. That turned out, of course, to be my loss. But on the positive side it has meant that he has been a later discovery, and for someone like I who for fifty years and more was always looking for new music to discover that has been a belated blessing. I've treasured the earlier issues of Bax orchestral music on Naxos, and my guess would be that this is the last of the series. Or at least it's the last of the symphonies to be recorded by them.
Coupled with the Seventh Symphony, though, is Bax's most famous orchestral piece, 'Tintagel.' It is a symphonic poem that was inspired by a six-week sojourn in the area of Tintagel, on the northern Cornish coast. Tintagel sits on a high cliff overlooking the distant Atlantic, and the tone poem is really more about the sea than about the castle or the landscape. Indeed, it is Bax's 'La Mer.' David Lloyd Jones leads the Royal Scottish National Orchestra in a rich full-throated performance of this alternately romantically lyrical and tempestuous piece. It certainly stands among the best versions I've ever heard.
Bax's final essay in symphonic form, the Seventh Symphony, in three movements like all Bax's symphonies, was premièred in 1939 by the New York Philharmonic-Symphony Orchestra (as it was then called) under the direction of the Bax enthusiast Sir Adrian Boult. The opening Allegro is a buoyant, even playful, piece interrupted by a lyrically melancholy section; one wonders if this latter is in any way inspired by the war clouds then massing in Europe. The slow movement begins with a slow, lazy, richly harmonized opening featuring languorous oboe/English horn solos and eventually supplanted by a somewhat more vigorous middle section subtitled 'In a Legendary Mood.' There is a vigorous climax before the music settles back into the opening dreamlike mood. The final movement is a theme-and-variations based on a solemn theme stated, after a stirring fanfare introduction, in the low strings and then taken through changing moods and tempi, becoming more and more agitated (but with some lyrical episodes and even some comic relief along the way) before a subdued, one might even say resigned, conclusion.
After the Seventh Symphony (and the start in earnest of World War II) Bax lapsed into a several years' silence before being named Master of the King's Music. He never composed anything very significant afterwards.
These performances are fully the equal of the earlier releases in this Naxos series. You really cannot do better than that.
Scott Morrison

title: I prefer the Swingles when they DON'T sing
text:
OK, I hoped you'd be intrigued by the title and would read this review to find out more.

This twofer collates two CDs of the Swingle Singers published by Virgin in 1991 ("[[ASIN:B000002SND A Cappella Amadeus - A Mozart Celebration]]") and 1994 ("[[ASIN:B000002SQC Bach Hits Back]]"). In fact, there is a minor mistery about the latter. Apparently 16 tracks out of the disc's 21 were published earlier, in 1990, on a seemingly self-produced CD, [[ASIN:B000NC0NEI The Bach Album]], totalling 41 minutes (if you look carefully at the cover photo of that disc you'll see that there are two tracks 8, corresponding to tracks 7 and 8 of the present CD, "In Dulci Jubilo"). Why the remaining tracks (namely tracks 5, 11, 12, 19 and 20) were not published back then but only in the 1994 Virgin reissue, I don't know. Also, the copyright of 1990 featured on that earlier disc doesn't quite stick with the recording date of V.1991 indicated on this Virgin twofer. So the mystery remains, and I'm not going to buy the earlier disc just to try and solve it.

I've reviewed a lot of recordings by the Swingle Singers lately, both the early ones from the Paris-based group in the 1960s and early 1970s (see my reviews of [[ASIN:B0000046WP Jazz Sebastian Bach]], [[ASIN:B0000046Y7 Anyone For Mozart, Bach, Handel, Vivaldi?]], [[ASIN:B00005V9SM Swingling Telemann]], [[ASIN:B00005V9SN Getting Romantic]], [[ASIN:B0001ZA1K8 Concerto D Aranjuez]] and [[ASIN:B0001ZA1LC Les Quatre Saisons]]) and the later ones by the re-formed and now moved-to-London group (other than these Virgin releases, see the recent [[ASIN:B000UNMOB0 Beauty and the Beatbox]]). I've contended that, beyond the pleasure of any arrangement, enabling you to hear the old, familiar warhorses in a new timbral guise, the special fascination of the Swingle's arrangements and realizations derives from the fact that they elevate to the status of high art what we all do, in a very rudimentary manner and without even thinking about it, walking on the street, washing the dishes, ironing or vacuuming - and, notoriously, showering: humming our favorite tunes. But the Swingles are to our shower humming what a Picasso is to your kid's drawings. And I've also opined that by so doing, they return instrumental music to its very origin and essence: the human voice - as, presumably, all those great composers, Bach, Mozart, Vivaldi, Handel, Beethoven, Chopin and all the others first hummed these tunes for themselves before committing them to the music sheet.

The Mozart album is great, equal to any by the early Swingle group, with a fine choice of Mozart's great hits (Magic Flute Overture, 40th Symphony, Adagio from the 21st Piano Concerto, Turkish finale from the 11th Piano Sonata), the Swingle's customary combination of the dazzlingly virtuosic and the sensuously caressing - and, as a most welcome exception to the Swingle's frustrating rule of recording only excepts from larger works, the complete (if abridged) 40th Symphony. I'd rank the Bach album under that, though. The pieces selected aren't overall as popular hits as those of Mozart - I guess the Swingles had more or less exhausted the available Bach hits in their previous Bach albums. Moreover, I think they made a mistake in choosing to treat the excerpts from the vocal and choral pieces as precisely that: vocal and choral pieces, e.g. with the words sung, rather than "instrumentalizing" them. In some cases they just arrange and sing those as "mere" (if my ears don't deceive me) 4-part a capella choruses, as in the opening "Ein' feste Burg", the Chorale from "Wachet auf" (track 5),the song "Bist du bei mir" from Anna Magdalena's Notebook (track 16; the attribution to Bach is doubtful) or the last verse of "In Dulci Jubilo", track 8, which is in fact straight Bach, a four-part Chorale BWV 368 after the old medieval tune, here sung in the (often criticized) 19th century English translation of Pearsall. I feel that this misses the point entirely of what makes the art of the Swingle Singers so unique: precisely, vocalizing instrumental music, returning it, as I said, to its vocal essence and origin. Here, they don't sound so unique, but just like any good a capella ensemble. The Choral-prelude from "Wachet auf" (track 4), and "Sheep may safely graze" (track 11) are fortunately more elaborate and "swingling" that that, but the two exceptions to that "singing" rule are "Et Resurrexit" from the Mass in B-minor (track 15) and "Blute nur" from the St Matthew Passion (track 17), both entirely "instrumentalized", and it comes as no surprise that they are both very effective.

And here's the explanation for the provocative title of my review. Admittedly, there is also some word-singing in the Mozart album - but then, in the excerpts from the Requiem, Cosi and Don Giovanni, the Swingles also vocalize for the orchestra, so it's still typical Swingle rather than anonymous a capella, although their Ave Rerum Corpus can attract the same kind of comment. But that's only one track.

In this twofer reissue Virgin isn't very helpful either with information on the compositions. The liner notes are much shorter and not nearly as informative as on the original CDs, and no BWV numbers are given for the Bach selections, making it sometimes difficult to locate them. I had to do more than a little research to establish what exactly were tracks 7 and 8. I've indicated above what track 8 is, and as for track 7, it turns out that Virgin mislabelled it. It is not the Chorale prelude on "In dulci jubilo" - in fact Bach wrote two, BWV 729 and 751, although the latter is apparently dubious, if the excellent Wikipedia entry is to be trusted - but the Chorale (not prelude) BWV 608 (the arrangement is a little more complicated than that, but for the complete details see my review of the original Virgin release).

Whatever my misgivings, the twofer is still very attractive, especially at the cheap prices which are asked for it at the time of writing. The Mozart is great and the Bach, while not the best from the Swingles, is still very enjoyable.

title: Not for the Average Listener
text: If this box set proves anything, it is that Mike Love had a very valid point to be concerned when he and the rest of the Beach Boys first heard the tapes for SMiLE in 1966. The great quality of the music is of no question, however the accessibility of the music is what separates SMiLE from anything released in 1966/67. It is silly to even try to compare it to Sgt. Pepper's or any Bay Area acts because they're not even in the same league. In fact, with SMiLE it is a totally different ballgame with different rules. It is undoubtedly hard for the average person to listen to SMiLE and get it the first time around. Like classical music, the album requires concentrated listening (and it never hurts to have some knowledge about the material before listening in order to understand the many themes of SMiLE). It may seem extreme to ask the listener to do extensive research before listening, but for those who do some outside reading, the experience is so rewarding. Every track, session, and outtake is either insightful, hilarious, gorgeous, or awe-inspiring. We have no idea if this is how the album would have "truly" sounded in 1967, but this is a fantastic approximation nonetheless and definitely worth your money. If the mood of SMiLE's music reveals anything, it is that it's awfully lonely being so talented and out there. Thankfully, we live in a time where there are just enough audiophiles and completists to demand this amazing material be heard.

Let me start by saying I HATE mainstream radio cookiecutter country music...it's the worst...radio crap made by non-talented, non-writing, generic people who shouldn't have had a record deal in the first place...who rely on hits submitted by outside songwriters...those people did not build a fanbase organically and were manufactured for radio by the labels who saw a pretty face and cowboy hat, made to be disposable and forgotten when the next fake sensation comes along.

Now, country music was going in a cool, alternative, progressive direction in the late 80s/early 90s with artists like k.d.lang, Carlene Carter, Rodney Crowell, Rosanne Cash, Lyle Lovett, Foster & Lloyd...great stuff, until Garth Brooks came along and ruined everything with all these crappy cookiecutter "hat acts" that came along in his wake...making the need for distinguishing the good from the bad, with alternative country/roots rock/No Depression/country punk...songwriters who combine old-school country with punk rock and harmonies straight out of the Byrds...bands like the Jayhawks, Jason & The Scorchers, Uncle Tupelo/Wilco, Whiskeytown/Ryan Adams, great stuff like that. Another distinction, cookiecutter radio crap was Republican and the good, progressive, alternative stuff was Liberal Democratic.

Well, cookiecutter people became such a target and you can pick em out easily and play Whack-a-Mole...they also had these cheesy linedances which made this music so uncool. I have to admit, when Neal McCoy came into prominence with "Wink", "The Shake", etc, he was an easy target...just an entertainer and not writing any of his songs and played on mainstream radio...I just laughed at him and so did my friend who was buying country music, and I made him realize this distinction.

Cut to 2011 and a free country radio concert in my hometown theatre and I got in for free...why I went was because Lauren Alaina was on the bill, Season 11 American Idol runnerup...she was good, even very good...but Neal was the headliner and imagine my reaction...eyes rolling, like oh jeez!! I figured I am there, he's the last act, give him a whirl...I may be surprised...well I WAS...he was lots of fun, he sang great, his band was tight and loose, and he was really engaging...I landed up really enjoying myself, and he seemed like a genuine, funny, unpretentious, nice guy. At the show, he talked about the new album, how it was produced by Blake & Miranda (BIG Miranda fan...she's alternative and punkrock...see "That's The Way The World Goes Round", her loud punky John Prine cover, and I like Blake now too, via The Voice and his own records, which are getting better)...and Neal did the new song "A-OK", it's a catchy little ditty.

Cut to the new album, I took it out of the library because no stores are stocking it and I wanted to hear it, see the credits, etc...it's not a radio country-leaning record at all, Neal actually co-wrote 2 good songs on the record(!!), it has some Bob Wills western swing on it, some really pretty ballads, some fun rockers, and Miranda & Blake sing harmony on it, and Neal is in fine FINE voice...it's actually SHOCKING how good this record is...not record of the year, but it will appeal to alternative country fans because of the quality, the art and the good intentions.

I may actually buy Neal's catalogue because in the end, he is no joke...I can see why Blake & Miranda have been loyal to Neal all these years, and so will I..."XII" just proves that if you give any singer artistic/creative freedom, and a nice push, they can come up with quality records, not disposable junk.

title: Sixteen Stone II
text: And here they are again, Bush coming back with their fourth (and possibly their best) album: "Golden State". Losing touch with most of their fans with their third release "The Science of Things", Bush decided to go back to their regular post-grunge ways. The reason I labeled this album four stars is because this album sounds like a sequel to Sixteen Stone, which is perfectly alright it's just when I bought this album I was expecting a change (like their previous follow ups to Sixteen Stone) that would put Bush back on the charts. Now now, dont get me wrong this album is still a perfection, "The People That We Love" makes the whole album worth-while and while they still have their weaknesses, ("My Engine is With You" and "Out of the World") such songs as "Headful of Ghosts" and "Flost" definetly make up for it. Another reason why I put the album four stars is because the album sounds REALLY typical and arguably out of date. Every song on this album does tend to sound the same in most cases (something that was never a problem with Bush before) and the only song that really changes direction is "Inflatable" and while that song is pretty good, it's different what most Bush songs sound. If you're a real fan of Bush (and love Sixteen Stone) I guarantee you'll love this album and should definetly buy it if you're smart. Atleast this album still shows that Bush has the strength to survive through all the mainstream metal (and/or hard rock). Standouts: "Solutions" "Headful of Ghosts" "The People That We Love" "Inflatable" "Float"

title: love the rest, but this is the best
text:
I always knew Sevendust was around, but didn't give them the listen they deserved til about a year ago. Within one week of listening to them i owned every album. "Home" however, has to be their best work. "Animosity" is up there, "Seasons" though more focused on being melodic is still a good album, "Next" is a great comeback, and who can forget their self titled. I loved the first album, but it had noticable flaws. The sound was a bit muffled and a couple songs had some weak lyrics ("Whats that you put in your nose, can i have some? from "Wired"). It was as if Sevendust knew exactly what they needed to work on because the sound of this album is amazing and the lyrics are much more vivid.

1. Home 10/10 - The chugging intro riff of this is your first sign of a good sounding album. An underrated anthem, and the best part is when Lajon begins screaming "From Left to Right", you can picture the mosh pits.

2. Denial 11/10 - One of 7dust's well known songs, and for a good reason. This song hits you hard with the riffs and verses, then mellows a bit for the chorus, all together making one hell of a song

3. Headtrip 9/10 - I really like this song for some reason, not that its a bad song. its very unique and keeps things changing, mixing screams from both Morgan and Lajon.

4. Insecure - a little interlude, not much to rate here, though it sounds a bit like the intro to "Angel's Son" from "Animosity"

5. Reconnect - 9/10 - Another cool song that uses back and forth shouting from Lajon and Morgan, though i like headtrip better.

6. Waffle - 20/10 - What a song. It's damn near perfect and one of 7dust's best. The mellow intro fools people into thinking its a soft tune, then the chug of the riff rips through. The chorus of this song is classic and really addicting

7. Rumble Fish - 9/10 - A nice little mosh inducing song here, this one never lets up. highlight being the break when Lajon starts saying "Get Up" over the riff

8. Licking Cream - 8/10 - A bit softer, with a the help of Skunk Ansie singer Skin, this one is interesting. Skin really adds some flavor to the chorus, especially at the end of it when she hauntingly carries her voice along the main riff.

9. Grasp - 7/10 - A good song, not a huge fan of the chorus though. the lyrics are good, I just never really dug the way they're delivered.

10. Crumbled - 9/10 - This song is really aggressive. I like the "Wipe my face and get up again" chorus, really gives it a punishing attitude

11. Feel - 8/10 - I like how this song really mellows a bit. Lajon shows his vocal talents in this one

12. Grasshopper - another interlude

13. Bender - 9/10 - A very cool finish to the album, with the help of Chino from the Deftones. Chino's vocals really mix in well with Lajon's as this song completes a hell of an album.

In my opinion, each 7dust album is special in its own way. S/T was incredibly aggressive, "Animosity" showed power and melody, "Seasons" shows full melody, and "Next" proves that 7dust can still be heavy, but "Home" is their defining album so far. It's really the best starting point, since you can go both forward and backward in their discography with a clear idea of what this band will give you. And they still got it live as well, i highly recommend seeing these guys live, its well worth it.
