title: Unique
text: The Black Rider is the weirdest album from an artist known for weird albums. Not a "regular" Tom Waits album and certainly not a "cast recording" as the listing states, this evolved from the Robert Wilson musical (with a William S. Burroughs libretto) for which Waits wrote the music. This album contains studio versions of some of these songs. It's roughly comparable to the style of Bone Machine, Waits' prior studio album, but it's actually quite different. In fact, it is unique in Waits' catalog. Though it has twenty tracks, there are only a handful of fully-formed Waits "songs," the rest being instrumentals, songs written with other people (such as Burroughs, who also "sings" several tracks), and short interludes. This makes the album, along with Bone Machine and the recently released Alice, a fully-fledged, self-contained effort with a consistent sound, mood, and set of themes. One wonders how well the scattershot story - something involving the Devil, magic bullets, and lost love - translates onto the stage; here the story is far from linear, but the lyrics are pure Waits... and enjoyable on their own. Burroughs actually brings down the songs he contributes to in my view - but I'm a Waits fan. The Black Rider is usually not named when people reel off Waits albums, and it's easy to see why. I would approach this as a real Waits but separate from his other albums. I've also seen people who regard this as a masterwork and his best album, and you can see where they're coming from, if only because the album is so unusual that drastically different interpretations are inevitable. Simply put, this is not Waits' best album but one that fans will want - and that might also be a way to attract non-fans.

title: The Best Return To Forever Line Up's (sadly) Last Album
text:
It's sad that the original incarnation of Return To Forever only lasted a couple of albums. The lineups that followed were like entirely different bands, and none of them were as soulful as this. Romantic Warrior may be one of the most overrated jazz fusions albums, with excess soloing and bombast overwrought compositions that are simply forced. While not as well composed as their debut, Light As A Feather is a great album, and must be listened to.

Initially, I thought that Light As a Feather was inferior to their debut. My roadblock was the solos. Although It's often overlooked by many others, jazz can get just as self indulgent as any technical metal band and prog rock band that so many people like to slam. Considering that a lot of jazz focuses on long solos, it can fall into the trap of bombast show-offs (Giant Steps). While, like Giant Steps, had a purpose to innovate, it still has a tendency to become self indulgent. While the very long solos on here can occasionally sound tedious at times, or amazing at other times (incostinecy, which is why this album fails to make a perfect score), they glide, they swoon, and there is melodic back up. Also, there is variety in the solos, and the enchanted rhythm section keeps everything gliding with grace. This isn't self righteous soloing, this is music! And yes, while it isn't as composition based as their debut (yeah, I kind of like composition based more than solo based), it still impresses with composing skills.

Your Everything may sound like something from a PBS documentary from the 70's, but that's not a bad thing since I find that to be great as it is. This one is great because it's quite short and includes a very short but totally meaningful and gorgeous solo. Samba rhythms, vocals and chiming flutes make up this great song. Light As A Feather is the first song to feature long soloing, but the eleven minute does not go to waste. The intro and outro are as graceful as a feather in the wind. Captain Marvel is kind of bombast, but man, the solos are great and the rhythms are addicting.

500 Miles High, may have a slightly cheesy line (since I'm pessmistic about love, which SUCKS) at the beginning, but it takes off and goes into....more solos!!!! But the rhythms and melody once again saves the solos, which, by the way, don't sound the same as the many long solos in this album. Children's Song may be the lowpoint, considering it's not really that conjuring and fails to make a lasting impression, I think it's filler. Spain, however, is another gem. This one floats serene at the beginning, yes, but it goes into more furious latin music, often refraining the drumless dance like passage. Spain is easily the best track on this album.

You may like subsequent Return To Forever albums, as I can't say YOU won't like them, but Return To Forever's first two albums are the only albums you need by the group. Essential. I haven't been able to stop listening to it ever since I got it.

9/10

title: Back on Track
text:
Funny thing about getting older is it becomes hard to tell whether a music CD is rubbish, or you're just losing your musical faculties. I was listening to a number of albums in the car (e.g. [[ASIN:B0000242VU Mutations]] by Beck & [[ASIN:B000N3SP9C Hot Fuzz Soundtrack]]) and couldn't get the killer hook.

Then I played this CD. OH MY GOD is it good! Even though I haven't (yet) seen the film, I got into this instantly.

From the first dialogue track ('Ppl ask the question'), the Gangster Rock ethos floods out of the stereo, with awesome tracks such as 'I'm a Man' & 'Rock & Roll Queen'. Highlights also include 'The Gun' by Lou Reed and 'Such a Fool', although every track is the sort of raw, gritty heart-pounding brilliance that one would expect from the title, but which few could deliver...

Like all truly excellent soundtracks, this one has a load of tracks you probably haven't heard or (if you have) you can't place (e.g. 'Bank Robber' by the Clash).
Furthermore, the dialogue is an excellent selection AND (unlike [[ASIN:B000N3SP9C Hot Fuzz Soundtrack]]) is separated from the music, so it can be sampled by aspiring DJ's.

Truth be known, musical appreciation does not fade with age but rather becomes more astute. Not only is this shown by the fact that compilations such as these can be filtered from the usual dross, but also by the fact that Guy Ritchie can still make soundtracks as good as his zenith of [[ASIN:B00000GAKK Lock Stock & Two Smoking Barrels]] and [[ASIN:B00004YTY1 Snatch]]. Here's hoping the film is as good...

title: Interesting approach
text:
Claudio Abbado is not for sure the first conductor to think of when we talk
about Bruckner. It would have been interesting to get the complete Bruckner
cycle from him and the Vienna Philharmonic. After listening a very compelling
1st from the cycle, this 4th is my second experience with it and can say that
has been even more interesting. This is not for sure among the best 4ths ever recorded, however, Abbado takes a good conception on the whole work and brings
a bit different reading with broad tempi, powerful if not exaggerated sound
and accentuations in some force passages and the same for his care on every
detail, that is not necessarily a bad point. Claudio Abbado is a great Mahler conductor and perhaps he gets a mahlerian performance of this Bruckner work.
Of course much of the bruckner architecture would be missed with this approach.
The Vienna Philharmonic plays heavenly, as expected, but in general terms
someone will miss the more convincent, better focused and built readings by
Jochum, Karajan, Wand or Tennstedt. This is a good recording that could please
any bruckner collection if you want more than one recording of this work.

title: Listened recently. Loved it.
text:
Garbage was one of my favorite bands of the 90s. By the time this came out in 2001, I had all of the band's cds...and was really looking forward to this one. Then I got it and ...it was ok. Just not as good as the first 2 cds...at least that's what I thought at the time.

Boy was I off base.

Cut to a few weeks ago, I heard the band was touring with Liz Phair and Morissette...and releasing a new album...I was intrigued and went back to my collection. I broke this out for the first time in more than 15 years...and I was blown away.

I remembered "Shut Your Mouth", the opening track and was pleasantly surprised that it was so solid. Then the great songs started rolling...Can't Cry These Tears sounds like a great girl-band of the 60s. Silence is Golden, Breaking Up the Girl and Parade rock with the same sort of aggressive energy of the first 2 records...but to me the album really rises above based on the slow songs like Cup of Coffee and Drive You Home...you can feel heartbreak, longing and vulnerability that's startling.

That warmth and humanity draws you right in. It's as impressive as it is touching. The other songs were really good too. I didn't really find a song I didn't like until the final track So Like a Rose...After listening to the entire cd, I was stunned at an album that combined vulnerability with warmth, aggression, and a few tunes that rock. Wow.

So why wasn't this record a big hit in 2001. Turns out many folks liked it. Rated as one of the best records of the year by Rolling Stone. But if you listen to Shirley and others, they tend to downplay it. Why?

Having listened to it again, I love this record. I think it's my favorite album the band has done...and that includes Bleed Like Me, Not Your Kind of People, and Strange Little Birds.

If you didn't dig it the first time around or even if you did, listen to it again...it's great.

title: I'm Not Afraid to Love This
text:
After sampling this first 3 tracks at Virgin, I decided that if I were going to leave that record store with a CD that night, "Vulnerable" would be it.
I don't know how to define what Tricky was or what he's becoming, but I do know that if you have some idea of what those things are you're taking his work too seriously. Music doesn't have to be inaccessible to be great; Bethoven's 9th is fairly accessible to the casual listener and completely genius to the trained ear. Either way it's enjoyable, and regardless of what many may think, neither method of appreciation is more profound than the other.
In a way Vulnerable appeases both fronts as well. Most of the tracks feature strong, accessible, even "repetitive" beats, and in compliment to that the music and vocals sound beatiful and pragmatic. This album seriously reminds me a lot of PMT in the sense that the music is fairly simple even if the overall sound (rhythm, vocals, and harmony) is a little abstract or disjoined.
Tricky's emphasis on one major vocalist (Costanza) was a smart move because it makes the album that much more relative to itself. Tricky also placed a strong emphasis on placing strong beats uniformly throughout the album, and generally speaking this is a more upbeat album than his earlier works like Maxinquaye. While individual tracks may lose some of their identity, the album itself has it's own overall voice and method. There is just enough variation to signify movement between tracks throughout the album. While there are several plateus of heavy drum abuse ("Moody and "Where I'm From"), there are in counter slow-flo ravines with more laid back grooves ("Hollow and "The Love Cats"), and this gives the listener variation while allowing the music to flow from strong central focal points. This really was Blowback's biggest problem; despite certain points of interest within the work, it was, from a larger perspective, a mess. That's not a problem here; the songs generally feature a strong rhythm with Tricky's raspy vocals polarized by Costanza's sweet voice. It is these familiar features that crop up throughout the album and give the listener a reference point and a bearing within the album, even if it does so at the sake of making things a little more predictable.
This album overall is very accessible, and that alone marks a difference between Tricky's earlier work. The fact this album is a little more upbeat may turn off some Tricky fans, but I don't think it circumvents the fact that Vulnerable is still a great album. Unlike Blowback, this album does in fact have an identity and a core sound, while at the same time moves through different emotions and flavors. Vulnerable is probably Tricky's best work since PMT, and I really hope long time listeners can cast away pretense and truly give Vulnerable a chance.

title: Great sampling of Kreator's 90's material
text:
Germany's Kreator have three basic eras in their impressive discography: 80's hyper-thrash; 90's raw metal savagery & experimentation; and the return-to-thrash era of the 21st century. When vocalist/guitarist Mille Petrozza & his gang put out their first album in '85 he was only 18 years old, which explains the youthful, energetic approach of their first five studio disks. When the 90s hit and grunge was king, hyper-thrash was no longer in vogue. So Mille & crew, now maturer and more seasoned, took to branching out with their primal brand of metal, but not in the order of Metallica's LOAD albums (or even THE BLACK ALBUM), just less thrashy, more raw, more traditional, with a streak of experimentation.

Some fans look down on Kreator's 90's output, but I like it more than their one-dimensional 80's approach, and just as much as their current era, probably more. It has a strong Bathory vibe, especially the vocals and rawness, as well as non-LOAD Metallica. If you like these bands Kreator's 90's RETROSPECTIVE is a must.

A couple songs are unique to this offering: the outstanding "Inferno" and the slow & moody closer "As We Watch the West."

Although Mille's voice & riffing are unmistakable, giving this collection a strong sense of cohesion (all their albums really), there's quite a bit of welcome diversity:

- Two exceptional slower moody & doomy numbers: "Black Sunrise" and "Outcast."
- Mid-paced-to-fast metal glory: "Isolation," "Renewal," "Hate Inside Your Head," "Inferno," "The Chosen Few" and "Golden Age."
- Speedy thrash/punk stuff: "Bomb Threat," "Lost" and "State Oppresion."
- Metallic Experimental stuff: "Endorama," "As We Watch the West" and the cover song "Lucretia (My Reflection)."

My personal favorites are all from the first two categories: "Renewal," "Black Sunrise," "Outcast," "Inferno," "Isolation," "Hate Inside Your Head," "The Chosen Few," "Golden Age" and "Whatever it May Take."

As for track dispersion from the four 90s studio albums: Five cuts are taken from 1995's CAUSE FOR CONFLICT, five from 1997's OUTCAST, three from 1999's ENDORAMA, but only one from 1992's RENEWAL (?). Both "Karmic Wheel" and "Depression Unrest" from RENEWAL deserve a place on this retrospective; they're excellent Kreator tunes and better than over half the songs here. Oh well, I guess that gives people a reason to seek out and purchase RENEWAL, huh?

A great thing about Kreator's songcraft is that they always know how to change tempos or shift gears when the song starts becoming one-dimensional and dull. Take, for instance, the interesting part thrown into the middle of "Whatever it May Take."

Another great thing about VOICES OF TRANSGRESSION - A 90s RETROSPECTIVE is that the songs don't sound dated in the least (unlike, say, some of their 80's stuff). This is timeless material, pure and simple.

GRADE: A

title: Enjoyable program, well played and recorded. Not first choices, but certainly worthwhile
text:
After listening recently to Marriner's limp 1994 Bartok recording for Capriccio, I was hesitant to try this one - more 20th Century works, with the same orchestra and label. But I was enticed by the innovative and intriguing program. And I'm happy to report it is an improvement over their Bartok!

Perhaps it all comes down to the fact that these pieces, recorded in 1993, benefit from Marriner's rather mellow, loveliness more than does Bartok. Whatever, I found myself enjoying this CD, despite the persistent feeling that it was all a bit too lovely for its own good.

I was not real familiar with Britten's Sinfonietta, so I have no aural recall with which to compare it. I am, however, very familiar with the Sonfonia da Requiem. Marriner's reading missing some of the other-worldly chill and stark dread which other conductors portray more vividly. But there is enough of it here (helped by the slightly sterile recorded sound from Capriccio) to make it rather successful. And the Honegger 3rd Symphony is very well done. Fortunately, the Stuttgart Radio Symphony Orchestra is more alert for this program, in stark contrast to their sleepy Bartok sessions.

Overall, I recommend this disc if the works on the program appeal. I wouldn't count these among first choices, but certainly worthwhile if you do not already have other recordings of them in your collection.

title: not exactly the grand reinvention that Noel had suggested, but still a great Oasis album
text:
Released in February of 2000 after a bit of a hiatus and with Paul Arthurs and Paul McGuigan both gone, "Standing On The Shoulder Of Giants" finds Noel Gallagher determined to re-invent Oasis. Quite frankly, he didn't really succeed (as Noel would be the first to admit), but that doesn't mean this album is a failure. There are some mild techno/ electronica flavorings to be found, plus some gospel-like backing vocals on a few tracks, but realistically, for the most part "...Giants" wholeheartedly embraces the trademark Oasis sound. Furthermore, you can hear a lot of traces of previous Oasis songs on here--notice the choruses on "Who Feels Love?", the chord progression is a carbon copy of the chorus from "Hey Now!"; "Put Yer Money Where Yer Mouth Is" is strikingly similar to "(I Got) The Fever"; and the riff-rocker "I Can See A Liar" seems to incorporate snippets/ pieces from at least a handful of previous Oasis songs. All that said, this is still a great album. Liam Gallagher gets his first songwriting credit on an Oasis release with the amusing yet heart-tuggingly earnest and charming 3-chord power ballad "Little James". Apart from that, Noel's once again running the show, often filling in on bass as well, and he's got lots to offer. "Go Let It Out" is a great rousing anthem. The haunting and explosive "Gas Panic!" is intense and cathartic. The album-closer "Roll It Over" has arrestingly dreamy verses, forceful Liam vocals, & a flawlessly-executed "Come Together"-ish guitar solo. The moody "Put Yer Money Where Yer Mouth Is" sounds a tad forced with Noel's cameo vocal appearance toward the end, but otherwise it's a great surging rocker, as is the raging "I Can See A Liar". Noel sings lead on two songs--"Where Did It All Go Wrong?" isn't a bad song, although it does sound startlingly generic for Oasis; "Sunday Morning Call" is a little rote and melodramatic, but it's still strong, and again, has an arresting dream-like atmosphere. The Eastern-flavored "Who Feels Love?" is marred by an annoying loop, but overall it's pretty great and has excellent vocal harmonies.

I think some listeners were expecting this album to sound more different and uncharacteristic of Oasis than it does. It's worth mentioning that 2 of the b-sides from the "...Giants" era--"Let's All Make Believe" and "One Way Road"--sound more like an extention into exciting new territory for Oasis than most of the tracks on the actual album; perhaps Noel simply felt these two tracks didn't fit in on here, hence their b-side status. One wonders this even more since "Let's All Make Believe" was on a bonus disc that was included in supposedly "limited edition" pressings of the album.

I do feel that "Standing On The Shoulder Of Giants" is weaker than each of Oasis' preceeding albums, but like I said, this is still a great album, and it certainly doesn't deserve the mind-boggling negativity that it has received by many fans.

(P.S. Don't let the fact that "Standing On The Shoulder Of Giants" was released in this "clean version" give you the wrong idea--the only swearing on the album is provided by samples from the movie "Message To Love--The Isle Of Wight Festival" on the otherwise instrumental opening track "F***in' In The Bushes".)

title: Lightning in a bottle (3.5/5)
text:
Twista became a household name with 2004's star-studded affair [[ASIN:B00008VEN5 Kamikaze]], which led many to revisit his breakthrough, 1997's "Adrenaline Rush" (his earlier LPs, 1992's [[ASIN:B00000E9GO Runnin' Off at Da Mouth]] and 1994's regional pressing "Resurrection" are all but impossible to find). Twista won fans with his jaw-dropping performances on Do or Die's albums [[ASIN:B000000WBZ Picture This]] and [[ASIN:B00000604A Headz or Tailz]], and "Adrenaline Rush" follows a similar blueprint. Employing fellow Chicagoan and renowned Do or Die producer Legendary Traxster, the music bears a distinctly Midwest vibe with his recognizable dark, mechanical funk. Although it lacks the soul of Do or Die's first two and the undeniable pop appeal of [[ASIN:B00008VEN5 Kamikaze]], Twista steals the show and makes his a memorable performance.

As anyone who's heard Twista is aware, his delivery is among the most noteworthy in hip hop. He was once dubbed Guinness World Records' fastest rapper, and for speed alone he is incredible. But if only MC-ing were so simple--then Tech N9ne might be dubbed one of the greats--no, Twista amazes with his overall flow. His lyrical assaults are tireless and exhibit premier breath control while maintaining a somewhat melodic, sing-song quality. But perhaps most importantly, Twista's verses are coherent such that every word is immediately understood. His approach is no gimmick; it is a gift to which few MCs can compare.

Twista's versatile enough that he can shine over any production, which is probably a reason he's such a sought-after guest rapper. "Adrenaline Rush" is a consistent effort with solid beats such that there are neither standouts nor lowlights on the tracklist. Twista also succeeds on the sheer conviction he applies to his songs. The dark feel works well. Notable tracks include the ruthless "Unsolved Mystery," the smooth and contemplative "Korrupt World," and the posse cut "Mobster's Anthem," where Traxster flips an infamous Leon Haywood sample to great results. "Adrenaline Rush" suffers in a few spots, being the worthless skits, notably weak guest spots, and some instances of generally inconsequential lyrics.

"Adrenaline Rush" does a nice job of capturing Twista's lightning-in-a-bottle talent and making some good music out of it. I recommend that fans of Do or Die or his later work check this out.

title: Should NEVER Have Been Released!
text:
Mr. Steinman is a outstanding composer. Although he is most famous for his songs recorded by Meat Loaf he has had an amazing career that has included songs recorded by other various artists. That being said, this recording effort has got to be one of the worst ideas in the history of the music industry. Never has a collection of such incredibly, amazing, show-stopping compositions been so horrendously sunk by poor performance. Mr. Steinman should stick to his composing and let others, especially Meat Loaf, sing his songs.

The biggest single problem with this album is that it was intended to be Meat Loaf's follow-up to "Bat Out of Hell". The project got bogged down because of Meat Loaf's personal problems and the strained relationship between Steinman and Meat Loaf. The point I am trying to make is that these songs were written for MEAT LOAF. Mr. Steinman, the incredibly talented composer that he is, by no means has any real singing talent. Many of these songs were later sung by Meat Loaf on later albums. All most people should have to do is compare the recordings and it will become obvious that pride and vanity must have been the primary motivators in the decision to release this disk. The best example of this is "Rock and Roll Dream Come True". Since there were no follow-ups,that I know of, to this recording I have to believe that Mr. Steinman may have reached a simular conclusion.

Again, Jim Steinman is one of the world's finest rock composers. However, if he runs into any more problems with an artist I hope he will resist the urge to take matters into his own hands.

text:
London's Portrait of Three Ladies (recorded on another New World CD) is a wacky, audacious near-masterpiece, and a reminder that there was a group of American composers, situated more-or-less in the Midwest, that felt free to dip into the innovations of the East Coast, the West Coast, Europe, or wherever. This disc presents 3 works from the '80's, and while they're eclectic enough in terms of musical language, they lack a certain personal je ne sais quoi.
Moments could be by Berio, Penderecki, Gil Evans...you get the idea. I appreciate the open-mindedness. But my level of engagement wavers. Performances seem excellent. Nice writing, all of it. But a problem with proportions - the pieces wear out their welcome before the end.

Diehard completists already own these songs from KTA, and no radio station will ever buy this CD and introduce these songs to the general public and that's a shame, because these are the first truly worthy collection of songs in the tradition of classic Yes since 1977's Going For The One. title: Now my favorite overall Sibelius set
text:
This review is of the SACD. Be aware that there is precious little English in the enclosed booklet: this pressing is targeting Japanese audiophiles. If English notes are important to you, get the standard CD and save some money (but lose some audio resolution). This is listed as a hybrid, and the SACD is two-channel only.

The sound qualify of these live recordings is truly stunning. Not a hint of audience noise anywhere.

The first CD gives us the first and fourth symphonies of Sibelius in more-than-serviceable interpretations. Nothing sticks out as out-of-place or interpretationally excessive. Some balances are different than what I’ve heard in the rest of my extensive Sibelius collection, but these recordings are in my top three of these two symphonies. (For those who insist on knowing: glockenspiel is used in this Fourth, not chimes.)

It’s on the second CD with symphonies 2 and 5 that my ears pricked up in delighted surprise, starting with the second movement of the Second: I don’t recall anyone doing Sibelius in so lively a way. Paavo Jarvi really put a distinctive personal stamp on these works and paints a much more interesting picture of them than others have done. This level of surprising interpretation continues through into the 5th symphony as well, and I’m realizing that this SACD of 2&5 is now my go-to recording of the works. Other versions seem flat and lackluster in comparison. And the soundscape of the orchestra, in all its instrumental choirs, is to die for. The phrasing breathes very naturally. The only thing I missed in the Fifth was the sense of a true accelerando to finish up the opening movement (other conductors make it much more obvious) but Jarvi focuses on other details so well that it was missed after the fact. The busy but quieter moments in the finale of the Fifth are handled well and, again, the recording engineers have done themselves proud across the entire dynamic range. Now I’m glad I paid extra for the SACD (nothing worse than spending more on an inferior performance, but this was not the case here with the Orchestre de Paris in top form under maestro Jarvi’s careful control).

Listening to the Third, I’m struck by how much care is taken to shape each line precisely, not allowing rhythmic vigor (where it’s in the score) to slacken. I’m still hearing details not audible on my other Sibelius sets (and I have nearly twenty) as I continue to listen to the finale of the Third. Worth a repeat.

The Sixth is of a piece with the previous interpretations: what a lively interpretation. The quieter sections, with reduced forces, come off beautifully, with dramatic contrasts that hold little back. Maybe some pundits will question how “Scandinavian” these performances are, but with so many riches being unearthed by this ensemble moment to moment, maybe it’s time to set aside that provincial (and over-used) criterion once and for all. (It’s not as if some other nationality was putting its fingerprints over the work, as some heavy-handed maestros have been – with some justice – accused of doing in the past.)

The Seventh starts dramatically enough, with good contrasts between phrases. It is a full-blooded account, similar in acoustics to the other symphonies in this set. It doesn’t rise nearly as high in my estimation as symphonies 2, 3, 5 and 6 do here – it joins 1 and 4 as being well-done but shy of extraordinary. The sonic quality puts it over some other versions, and it must be admitted that this more abstract work (which revolutionized symphonic structure) may not have lent itself to the kind of treatment that the earlier symphonies received. Not every conductor navigates its challenges with equal aplomb.

So we come to the question: how does this set rate AS a complete set? This is always a tough call, because one always has (in the back of one’s mind) specific individual performances against which members of a set are measured. So aggregating the “score” multiplies the subjectivity of the reviewer who has to weigh the set. I’d put this in the top three complete sets on the strengths of the sonic quality and the performances of symphonies 2, 3, 5, and 6. And I’m inclined to think I might gravitate to Jarvi’s 2 and 5 as the best individual recordings of this work (again, a tough call, with doctrinaire Sibelians arguing over which Berglund or Storgards or Lintu version should have edged out this new Jarvi set – and some of those are in showcase-quality sound as well). And there are those who wonder what we’d think of the Maazel/VPO set had it been recorded with modern digital equipment, such as used here. I can assure you (as an owner of the Maazel remastered onto Blu-Ray PureAudio) that the Jarvi remains the better overall set.

Audio equipment used by reviewer: Sennheiser 800 headphones, Sennheiser HDVD 800 headphone amplifier, Sennheiser balanced cable & Audience Au24 interconnects.

title: More Manchester Magic
text: If Music For Pleasure is a beat-driven, pulse-raising inferno, this beautiful self-titled album is the calm after the storm.  The first track, "I've Got A Feeling" hooks you in with a fast-paced beat and Peter Hook's relentless bass attacks.  However, with the exception of this song and track number 6 (the title eludes me at the moment) the rest of the album is very downplayed and mellow in comparison with Monaco's first masterpiece.  This is not a criticism, merely an observation.  Although to me "Music For Pleasure" was perfectly done and no other album, including this one, stands up to it, "Monaco" does provide a nice change of pace.  They're just different albums for different moods, yet both laced with that good old Manchester Magic, which also resonates from New Order and Electronic.  And, as in the first album, several of the songs will remain in your head for days upon days after exposure.  The catchiest song in my opinion is definitely Kashmier, which sounds like light alternative guitar-driven pop delivered in accordance with David Potts' Barney-sounding vocals.  My second favorite, "Ballroom" is beautifully orchestrated and topped with some very poignant, romantic lyrics.  As if the bulk of the track itself isn't enough, the little piano diddy at the end really takes you into the song's title.  On top of theses masterpieces there are several other great songs for those who are in a sensuous/romantic mood and the whole album really plays through brilliantly.  The only weak track is the instrumental at the end, but maybe its just because I haven't given it enough of a chance yet.  It does fit in quite well with the previous tracks though, and makes for a great end to a magical experience.  Recommended for all fans of good music!

text: "Crosswinds" has been in my vinyl collection since 1974, when I first picked up a copy at King Karol Records on 42nd Street in Manhattan.  Well, I recently became reacquainted with this recording after picking up a CD copy at a "oh so trendy" record store in Haight-Ashburry, San Francisco.  As I did then, I played the new CD over and over again, completely enraptured by Cobham's "Ripley's Believe or Not" staccatto drumming and Lee Pastora's smoking Latin percussion.  Joined by the Brecker Brothers, George Duke, John Abercrombie, Alex Blake, John Williams, Garnett Brown and other great luminaries of early jazz fusion, Cobham and his willing partners beat and shape a veritable masterpiece.  Drive along Big Sur and take in the vast and dramatic California skies and scarred bluffs and you'll begin to undertand what hues of emotions this exquisite recording conjures.  Crosswinds alternates between adrenaline musical rushes and absolute sublime chill, creating a perfectly balanced sinuous stream of sound.  Simply exquisite!

title: Not classic Metallica, but definitely better than the Black Album
text:
Between those who call this a sell-out album and those who say that Metallica have simply “evolved” or “moved on” after making their stamp on thrash metal, I really cannot take up sides. While I do agree that this album was part of Metallica’s strive to “fit in” with the ‘90s alternative rock scene, the songs on this album, while mostly softer than anything from their first four albums, are anything but simplistic in their composition. I mean, come on, out of 13 songs, only 3 of them are less than 5 minutes! This album still showcases the fact that Metallica strive to utilize the complexity and technicality of their abilities, and that they do not believe in simplistic verse-chorus song structures! Sure, they may not have anywhere NEAR the top-notch, above-and-beyond technicality, grandeur and virtuosity as bands like Iron Maiden, Dio, Dream Theater, Symphony X, Stratovarius or Rhapsody of Fire, but does it really matter? Not at all! What matters is that they worked hard on this album, and the complexity of the songs themselves shows it.

Simply put, this album was definitely a great offer for the time of its release, and I have enjoyed it for what it is ever since I first got it when I was 15 years old (now 28). Some of my favorites on the album include “Fuel,” “The Unforgiven II,” “Carpe Diem Baby,” “Where The Wild Things Are,” and especially the epic finale “Fixxxer.” No matter which way you look at it, the guitar solos are still there (as opposed to being virtually absent the pile of garbage known as “St. Anger”), the pounding rhythms are still there, the strong feeling and emotion is still there, and most importantly – the complexity is still there, which is a key characteristic of metal as a whole.

In short, this album, regardless of the intent of Metallica themselves in the making thereof, is packed with much to offer for any true fan of hard rock and heavy metal music, and has much credit to be given. It is rock-solid effort for what it is, and lives up to the standards of complexity for which Metallica have long since set for themselves. It is definitely a long way from the best album of its time, but I think any true Metallica fan can bring themselves to enjoy it if they give it enough of a chance. If you like it, then by all means – BUY IT! If you do not like it, then do not buy it. Simple as that. \M/

title: honkytonk straight up
text: If you didn't listen to what passes for country radio, you'd swear we'd entered a golden age of honkytonk music. Alas, as Dallas Wayne observes in his brief liner notes, mainstream country just gets more "diluted and deluded." So thank Hank's ghost, or whomever, for the likes of Wayne, Roger Wallace, Heather Myles, Justin Trevino, James Hand, Don Walser, Dale Watson, and others who carry the hard-country flag on independent labels. Wayne's last outing, Big Thinkin', his first for Hightone, amounted to a collaboration with Robbie Fulks, who co-produced and wrote or co-wrote all of the songs. The result, a brilliant, edgy exercise, alternated -- or, sometimes, fused -- wit and mockery with despair and violence. The effect, one might say, was too country even for too country. This time Fulks appears only once, as co-composer with Wayne of the last cut. As Wayne takes charge with co-producer Bruce Bromberg, Thinkin's rock inflections largely disappear in favor of more traditional hillbilly-shuffle rhythms and slow heartache melodies. This is honkytonk served straight up, and if you like it that way, you'll like this CD a whole lot. Wayne writes in-the-tradition songs well, and he has a good ear for other people's songs. It's a pleasant surprise to see "Shadows of My Mind," a minor hit for Vernon Oxford in the 1970s (even then it seemed about 25 years behind its time), resurrected, and done justice. "Happy Hour," memorably recorded on a 1980s Rounder album of the same name by the late Ted Hawkins, is another treat. So, come to think of it, is everything else here.

title: Standout performances; standout recording
text:
Jerry Dubins, Fanfare magazine

In this, the 250th anniversary of Beethoven’s birth, we have already seen—and should continue to see—more new cycles of the composer’s works begun and/or completed and new recordings released than in most normal years. And here one of them begins with Volume 1 in yet another survey of the piano trios, this one performed by the Sitkovetsky Trio.
The ensemble was formed in 2007 by fellow students at the Yehudi Menuhin School in England—Alexander Sitkovetsky, Leonard Elschenbroich, and Wu Qian. This is the group’s first recording with its new cellist, Isang Enders, who replaced Elschenbroich in 2019. A third generation of Sitkovetskys, Alexander, born in 1963, carries on the family name of prominent violinists, Dmitry, his uncle, and Julian, Dmitry’s father. In addition to her membership in the Sitkovetsky Trio, Shanghai-born Wu Qian is an award-winning pianist with an international career as a soloist and recitalist. And German-Korean cellist Isang Enders, who studied with Truls Mørk, among others, was appointed principal cello of the Staatskapelle Dresden at the age of 20, and has soloed under eminent conductors, including Myung-Whun Chung, Christoph Eschenbach, Eliahu Inbal, Zubin Mehta, and Vasily Petrenko.
The difficulty—and not just for the Sitkovetsky Trio, but for all artists, ensembles, conductors, and orchestras undertaking new cycles of Beethoven’s chamber, instrumental, and orchestral works—is that it has all been done before and to the point of overkill. On the one hand, it’s only right and expected that the music world should wish Beethoven a happy birthday and want to honor him with new recorded cycles of his symphonies, string quartets, piano sonatas, and piano trios, but on the other hand, the question must be asked: What is the incentive for buying the umpteenth version of any of these works?
Well, in the case of this particular new release, one might cite as an incentive that as a physical disc it’s a high-definition, multi-channel SACD on a label, BIS, that has distinguished itself for state-of-the-art recorded sound. But one of the works here, the Piano Trio in C Minor, was recorded once before by BIS in SACD format and released in 2004. That earlier performance is by the Kempf Trio. It’s a recording I have and prize highly. And if SACD is your inducement, the Van Baerle Trio recorded a cycle of the Beethoven piano trios for Challenge on four individual SACDs.
What then of the performances themselves? Contrary to my expectations of another routine run-through of these works, I found myself quite excited—riveted really—by the Sitkovetsky’s readings. In the early C-Minor Trio, the players emphasize the proto-Romantic and Sturm und Drang aspects of Beethoven’s impatient and impetuous initiative to stand out from the crowd. “Here I am,” the music shouts, “sit up and listen!” The impatience and impetuousness are to the fore in the playing, but in a good way, one that surges with the rising crests of the phrases and ebbs into the troughs with their falls.
The intense drive and nervous energy in the performance keep the listener on edge with fast tempos, fierce accents, and ferocious, clipped chords. There’s little letup or time out from the onslaught. Three of the four movements are projected in various degrees of rant and rage. Only the second movement (Andante cantabile con Variazioni) gives us a breather, but even here, the ensemble takes the major-key variations at tempos that press forward rather precipitously. Overall, I like the Sitkovetsky’s approach in this particular trio, though I wouldn’t find it to my liking in other of Beethoven’s piano trios. The point is moot, however, for none of the composer’s other piano trios is in a minor key or of the tempestuous, turbulent character of this C-Minor Trio, op. 1/3.
Next to Beethoven’s last work in the genre, the “Archduke” Trio, his penultimate opus in the medium, the Trio in EI Major, op. 70/2, is my favorite in the series. In each of its four movements, it exhibits one of Beethoven’s signature techniques, and one that makes his music so communicatively powerful on a subliminal level. I’ve described it before as the equivalent of musical body language. Nothing need be verbalized or made explicit. It’s the mere suggestion of an idea—the “gesture” of it—left uncompleted for the listener to supply whatever continuation and completion satisfies his or her imaging and imagining. It’s enormously powerful because music bypasses the normal cognitive processes of ideation, proceeding instead directly to emotion; therefore, its meaning is whatever it imparts to the individual listener. Beethoven unlocked this particular secret of music and exploited it to a degree I don’t think any other composer ever has. It is present in his works from very early on, but he cultivated and relied on it increasingly—perhaps due to his deafness—to the point where his late works become almost all gesture and no statement.
I’m struck by how intuitively the Sitkovetsky Trio picks up on this in its performance of op. 70/2. Listen to how the opening strain of the third movement tries to find its soul mate to complete itself in the second strain, but can’t, stopping just short of it, and then trying over and over again. What does it mean? To me? Heartbreak. To you? Maybe something else. Whatever it meant to Beethoven, and whatever it meant to the Sitkovetsky’s players, it’s inexpressibly beautiful.
The Allegretto in BI Major, WoO 39, that fills out the disc seems to be an independent, stand-alone movement for piano trio not intended for or separated from some lost four-movement work. It’s not known why Beethoven wrote it, but it is known when and for whom. The “when” was 1812, the “whom,” Maximiliane Brentano, 10-year-old daughter of the composer’s friend Antoine Brentano. The piano part sounds like something the 10-year-old piano student might have been able to master with some practice.
This is a very encouraging start to a new survey of Beethoven’s piano trios. Even if others by the Trio Élégiaque and Swiss Piano Trio, for example, make the Sitkovetsky Trio’s effort unneeded, it doesn’t make the ensemble’s contribution unwanted.

title: In hindsight . . .
text:
I'll always remember the evening I bought this album at a local discount store. The pink-frocked cashier was a teenager, a little older than I was. Her eyes got big and she looked straight into my eyes as she said, "Have you heard it yet? It's unbelievable!" And for a few years I listened to this album as if it was the best rock-folk-popular music album anyone in history had ever made.

Years later I learned that Dylan wrote most of these songs in the studio. He probably had his notes, but the story is, the musicians, mostly Nashville studio aces, would play cards while they waited for him to finish writing another song. Then, presumably, he would show them the changes and the key and the tempo he wanted and they would knock it of in one or two takes. Then the musicians would go back to playing cards and Dylan would go back to finishing his songs. The mysterious change in the drum pattern in the middle of "Visions of Johanna" would seem to support this story.

In hindsight, this is what this album sounds like. Still, there's magic in all that ambiguous imagery. My favorites always will be "Visions of Johanna" and "One of Us Most Know.," and the snotty put-downs of "When You Go Your Way" and "Leopard Skin Pillbox Hat" had their appeal. Throwaway Dylan is still miles ahead of what others would call their keepers.

title: Scream Bloody Obsession
text:
A new Cannibal Corpse album. What's new? Very little, and that's the way it should be.
You don't buy a Cannibal Corpse album expecting subtlety, innovation, and great musicianship. You buy Cannibal Corpse expecting bludgeoning death metal, blood thirsty lyrics and great musicianship. Corpse's riffs have become ever more complex over the years, and have continued to do so here. Hey, they ain't Meshuggah or Atheist, but there's a huge difference between what's on offer here and their debut "Eaten Back To Life". There are unexpected flourishes thrown in here and there, but the listenability remains. The solos are frenetic, as would be expected, but are perhaps a shade cleaner than in previous albums. The drumming is less straightforward than the earlier blast-blast-blast style, with a few odd rhythms thrown in. Never fear though, there are still still plenty of blast beats here!
Perhaps the best feature of this new album are George "Corpsegrinder" Fisher's vocals. They are actually clear enough for most of the lyrics to be understood without closely following the lyric sheet. Corpsegrinder is still bestial in his delivery, but now the murderous lyrical creations are given a fuller horrific scope. Corpsegrinder's style suits the band far better than his long departed predecessor. He has developed a two tone style, both gutteral, adding a touch more variation and venom to the overall sound.
"Hatchet To The Head" is bound to become a new moshpit favourite, with a shout along chorus in the vein of "Skull Full Of Maggots" and blast beats aplenty. "Dormant Bodies Bursting" sees the band cut back the speed a fraction on the chorus, to great effect. It's downright menacing! There are no dud tracks here at all.
The final act of this album is a surprising, but extremely well executed cover of Metallica's "No Remorse". To describe it as heavy is an understatement! A nice solo has been added at the beginning, and the rhythm and bass absolutely thunder along... This is really what this song SHOULD sound like!
Cannibal Corpse don't so much get in your face with this album, as leave you "Sanded Faceless".

title: Influential, accessable, perfect Def Leppard
text:
Pyromania, the band's sophomore effort with Mutt Lange and third release overall, was the band's attempt to make a 'Sgt Peppers' for the 80s, something that combined influences, new sounds, slick production, and raw talent and energy into a massivley influential, commercial monster. It succeeded in every facet.
From the keyboard kickoff of Rock Rock! (something every 80's band would copy), this album never lets up. It's not as raw and uneven as the slightly heavier High n Dry, but it definitley keeps it's edge throughout, thanks to Steve Clark and Phil Collen's relentless guitar attack.
Everyone knows the singles (photograph, Foolin, Rock of Ages) but the treasures on this album are the epic tracks, like Too Late, Die Hard the Hunter, and Billy's Got a Gun. Storytelling masterpeices, they're just long enough to be epic, without seeming as overblown and Rush-ish as 'The Overture'. The rest of this album measures up as well, not a single weak track is to be found.
Joe Elliot finally finds his voice, as well. On his first two releases he couldn't really carry a tune all too well, but Pyromania shows him really developing a strong voice in all areas, rock-outs and ballads.
Pyromania laid the groudwork for the rest of 80's rock-pop to follow. Leppard would repeat this trick with the slightly-not-as-good Hysteria 4 years later, but Pyromania stands as their finest hour.

title: Garbarek marking time
text:
I was expecting more out of Garbarek after his Twelve Moons CD, which contains more than its share of magical moments. Visible World is a hodgepodge of songs done specifically for this record combined with songs from other recording projects (i.e. film). Some are distinctly Scandanavian, some sound like American Indians in the fjords. Not that there's anything wrong with that. :) But most of the playing seems calculated to soothe, not to challenge. Yes, there is a valid Kenny G-ish comparison here.
If one was rating this on the Kenny G scale, it would be a 5. But judged against Garbarek's best work, albums like Dis or Dansere or even My Song with Keith Jarrett, this is a dud -- maybe a 1 or 2. I guess Garbarek has made the mistake of being too good in the past -- making his own grading curve more difficult.

title: Great show deserved better
text: It's well-known among the fan community that this is one of The Who's greatest live shows ever, which is why it deserved so much better.  It's very exciting both musically and visually, even in the edited format on the tape, but the excitement and enjoyment are a bit lessened knowing that this isn't the full show.  Quite a few songs they performed at that exciting concert in the wee hours of the morning are cut out (such as the opener, "Heaven and Hell," and "Naked Eye"), most notably a good portion of the 'Tommy' set.  Only 13 songs from the rock opera are on this video, and even some of them, like "Eyesight to the Blind," aren't presented in their full-length glory.  That performance opens about midway through the actual song!  This cut and paste job really waters down the essence of what was a truly great concert, and gives a confusing and disconnected feel for the meat of the show, with so many crucial songs to the plot of the rock opera left out.  However, just because a number of songs are missing doesn't take away terribly too much from what a great show what remains was overall; there's still an incredible amount of musical energy, great onstage chatter, and the added element of the songs coming to life even more because you can see them being performed, what with the body language and movements that go along with them.  For example, a song like "Young Man Blues" sounds great either way, but when you can see it, it becomes even more awe-inspiring; how did that guitar not break?!  The footage of Keith at the festival tacked on at the end also kind of feels out of place.

title: The Real Thing
text:
This recording from late 1955 features an authentic 7 piece New-Orleans style band led by trombonist Kid Ory. The Legendary "Kid," now 70 years old (but maybe playing as well as ever), was a bandleader in the early days of jazz and played as a sideman with King Oliver, Louis Armstrong (including on the Hot 5 and 7 recordings), Jelly Roll Morton, and others. Ory retired in the 1930s during the heyday of the swing era, but made a comeback in the 1940s, helping to re-popularize the great New Orleans tradition.

These are talented musicians--besides Ory, trumpeter Alvin Alcorn is especially impressive on the disc. The enjoyable set was well-recorded and sounds mighty fine on this Good Times Jazz (Fantasy Studio) CD. The liner notes include a recipe for Creole Red Beans and Rice.

title: Unbelievably fine sound quality. Good performances too.
text:
Purely from the standpoint of sound quality, this new release from Channel Classics surpasses every single recording I've ever heard of these three, oh-so seminal Stravinsky works: "Rite Of Spring" (original 1919 version), "Firebird" Suite and "Scherzo a la Russe". Channel Classics and Fischer also threw in the two minute long "Tango No. 72".

From the purely interpretive standpoint, one could argue endlessly about just what the right tempi for the various sections (and subsections) should be within "The Rite". I find Fischer's 'interpretation' to be as convincing as any other I've heard (yes, some are better than others - that goes without saying). Channel Classics superb sound quality and Fischer's excellent balances not only facilitate one in hearing every bloody bleep-and-bloop within the score, it helps to define Stravinsky's harmonies to a level that I've never before noticed. You could practically take harmonic dictation just from listening to it (writing out the chord changes). That might seem like a trivial point, but name another piece that's more of an 'orchestral spectacular' than "Le Sacre du Printemps".

The "Firebird" Suite not only benefits from the same excellent sonics, conductor Ivan Fischer manages to bring out the lavish and sumptuous qualities of the work - more like exotic Rimsky-Korsakov than The Rite. "Scherzo a la Russe" is hardly profound Stravinsky, but it's also pleasant, fun and innocuous.

Please note: I listened to this on just the plain-old CD layer, as I do not own an SACD player (and don't want to until I can afford GOOD 5.1 surround equipment). Yes, there have been hundreds of fine releases of Stravinsky's big three ballets (these two plus "Petrushka"). Nobody needs to run out and add this one to their collection UNLESS they need to be updated in terms of sound quality. That said, beginners could hardly do better than to start here.

Note to Channel Classics: could we possibly get a Mahler 7 from Fischer/Budapest Festival Orch.? Please, please, PLEASE?!?

title: “Time Well Wasted:” one of the key albums that awakened me to a love of country music.
text:
A few years ago, when I was first becoming interested in country music, my daughter recommended several CDs by country artists that she thought I might enjoy. One of them was “Time Well Wasted” by Brad Paisley.

I had never even heard of Brad Paisley before I listened to this album for the first time. I was about fifteen minutes into it when I realized that Paisley is just the kind of modern-day country music artist I like best. He’s got a very good singing voice, plays guitar about as well as anyone I’ve seen or heard in recent years, writes or co-writes most of his own songs, doesn’t take himself too seriously, and has a keen sense of humor that he doesn’t mind injecting into his songs.

“Time Well Wasted” is a terrific album in every respect. It’s got an impressively strong line-up of songs. My favorites include “Alcohol,” “Rainin’ You,” “Flowers,” “When I Get Where I’m Going” (a duet with Dolly Parton), and “Time Well Wasted.” There are also a few very short bonus comedy tracks featuring the “Kung Pao Buckaroos” that will surely get you laughing.

“Time Well Wasted” is one of the key albums that awakened me to a love of country music. It’s now one of my most frequently listened-to CDs. Most highly recommended.

title: A Deeper, More Personal Effort from Clarkson
text:
While "Breakaway" is not my favorite track on this album, Clarkson does indeed move away from her molded, American Idol limitations. While the last CD was full of all kinds of different songs written by Diane Warren and even Christina Aguilera, this album has most tracks written by Clarkson. In my opinion, these songs are the best on the album, not only lyrically, but in sound.

Kelly has been on shows describing this album as "rock." While I wouldn't go that far, this is definitely a departure from the Britney and Jessica pop singer molds. The sound is edgier, her powerful voice is finally heard (the last album was very bland compared to what she was capable of). The lyrics are much more personal, and I am curious if Kelly speaks from personal experience or if she really is just very empathetic.

In "Where is Your Heart," she belts, "What I really want is to believe you / Is it so hard to give me what I need? / I just want your heart to bleed, and that's all I'm asking for." In "Because of You," she reels from being hurt - "Because of you, I learned to play on the safe side so I don't get hurt / Because of you, I try my hardest just to forget everything / Because of you, I don't know how to let anyone else in / Because of you, I'm ashamed of my life / Because it's empty / Because of you, I'm afraid."

Other album notables include "Gone," written by the man accredited with writing and playing on Ashley Simpson's album, John Shanks. "Since U Been Gone" is also good, and the album includes a live, piano version of "Beautiful Disaster."

If you've followed Kelly's career since the American Idol crowning, you will be pleasantly surprised how much she's developed as an artist. If you haven't tried her out yet, give her a chance - you'll like what you hear.

title: Robin Thicke gets personal on "Paula"
text:
After spending a decade behind the scenes as a songwriter and producer, Robin Thicke decided to forge ahead with a career as a recording artist. In 2003, he released his debut "Cherry Blue Skies"- which was later retooled as "A Beautiful World". The album was critically acclaimed, but was way too eclectic for some people. He sought to change that with his sophomore effort "The Evolution Of Robin Thicke". His next album "Something Else" paid a clear tribute to 70's R&B and disco, while 2009's "Sex Therapy" had him testing the waters by working with hip hop artists and producers. 2011 saw the release of "Love After War", but the album didn't break any new ground for Robin. That would all change with 2013's "Blurred Lines"- which, to date, has given him the biggest pop hit of his career. However, in a move similar to the film "A Star Is Born"- albeit with gender roles reversed- his career was riding high while his marriage to actress Paula Patton was on the rocks. The couple eventually split- much to chagrin of Robin himself. Instead of following up with another pop driven album, he decided to pay tribute to his estranged wife- hence the title of his new album "Paula".

While the theme of the album centers around lost love, sadness and regret, musically it sounds like a typical Robin Thicke album. In fact, one could say it's a continuation of "Love After War". Like most of his albums, Robin produced it with his longtime songwriting and production partner James "Pro-Jay" Gass. "Paula" is rife with genre hopping as it moves through bossa nova ("You're My Fantasy"), as well as adult contemporary ("Get Her Back" and "Still Madly Crazy"). On the songs "Lock The Door" and "Black Tar Cloud", his conscience eats at him for his past mistakes. He tries to find someone new on the James Brown inspired "Livin' In New York City" and realizes his estranged wife's personal freedom on "Whatever I Want". Robin remains optimistic on "Love Can Grow Back", while getting help from pop group Fifth Harmony on "The Opposite Of Me". While most of the album is great, there are a couple of songs that could have been left behind- specifically the jazz influenced songs. The tracks in question are "Tippy Toes", "Something Bad" and "Time Of Your Life". Though they aren't bad songs per se, they are better suited for pop-jazz crooners like Michael Buble. "Paula" is a good album from Robin Thicke. Though media hype and controversy put this album in a negative light for the pop fans, in the end this album was made strictly for the people who supported him for the duration of his career.

title: The Silver Hound- Indeed!
text: Composer, singer, teacher and conductor Betty Roe was born in London in 1930, the daughter of a fishmonger father and bookkeeper mother. Betty Roe learned piano from the age of six and began writing music and arrangements in her teens. She continued studying piano, cello and singing at the Royal Academy of Music after World War II, and studied composition with Lennox Berkeley. In the 1950s she became involved with a drama group where she began writing for musicals and also worked as a sessions singer. She was Director of Music at the London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art from 1968–78 and founded Thames Publishing with her husband, John Bishop. This remarkable woman has composed six operas as well as orchestral works and light music for theatre and cabaret, but her first love is art-song of which she has produced over 300 examples. Her style is eclectic, ranging from the serious to the comical, displaying a wonderful wit as well as a firm grasp of vocal writing and a way of providing music that seems totally at one with the texts. At the age of 87, she remains a major force in the music world, awarded an MBE in 2011 for services to classical music and composition. The Silver Hound and other songs features a program of works composed over the last 30 years and is a delight. Highlights include The Silver Hound, written in 1990 to mark the composer's 60th birthday, I Know A Hill, the lovely In This Lone Open Glade, the witty Diva’s Lament, Three Hardy Conversations, and The Life That I Have (words by Second World War cryptographer Leo Marks). The performers include top English soloists Sarah Leonard and Anne Marie Sheridan (sopranos), Robin Tritschler (tenor) and Stephen Varcoe (baritone) with Nigel Foster, English Song accompanist extraordinaire (todays Gerald Moore) at the piano. Sometimes obbligato French horn (Daniel Beer the composers grandson), recorder (Emma Murphy) or violin (Madeleine Mitchell) add to the texture. These excellent premiere recording were produced in co-operation with the Betty Roe Society. John Pitt (New Classics)

title: The Search For The Supreme...
text: The rock drum solo has it detractors.. Those who see it as an exercise in vanity. On the other hand, jazz drummers solo often, and are praised.  Christian Vander, the leader of France's famed pro-rock outfit Magma has been straddling the lines between rock, jazz, and contemporary classical music since the late 60's. This two-disc set are live drum solos performed during Magma concerts between 1974-75, and a piano/voice piece studio recording from 2000.  Rather than showcases from Vander's technique, and an excuse to extend a tune, these are exorcisims to attain spiritual/musical purity.  Along with the solos, and the booklet of musings and philosophies of Vander, one can see that these solos are attempts at enlightenment (Hence, the subtitle- The Search For The Supreme Korusz) So much that these are "exorcisims" that through a few solos, Vander starts yelling and speaking in tounges during the climaxes..  As a person who has seen Vander live, I can attest to his spiritual connection to music. Never have I seen a drummer move around the set so effortessly, and with a look of such bliss. And, I have never seen anyone flail around on a set, yet not miss a beat.  The only reason why I have given this three, not more stars, is that drum solos are not for everyone.. And, this disc will have limited appeal for those who are Magma completists or lovers of Vander's drumming. But, I recommend this to anyone who apprieciates something that is more than just "playing".. more like.. "living through playing".

title: Not Fully 'Complete'
text:
It's been a decade since New Order has put out 'new' material. The 'new' is in quotes, due to the fact that the band released outtakes from their last recording sessions for 'Waiting for the Siren's Call'. Eight songs made it onto the 2013 disk, 'Lost Sirens', but it wasn't technically 'new' material.

I've been waiting for a long time for a new New Order disk and they don't really skimp. 11 songs, 65 minutes of music.

'Music Complete' is their first disk without bassist Peter Hook, who was co-founder of both Joy Division and New Order. His presence is sorely missed.The album also reunites original keyboardist Gillian Gilbert (who is married to the band's drummer, Stephen Morris).

The band released the first "single" (do those really exist still?), "Restless", back in August. The song breaks no boundaries with the New Order formula, but I like it a lot. And while you easily hear the bass line, it is not Hook.

The second download, prior to album release, that I got was "Plastic". Some music magazine called the song a “...gold-plated, weapons-grade Eurodisco anthem”. It isn't. It might be Eurodisco. It's not an anthem, and it certainly isn't weapons-grade. What it does have is the electronic beat of Madonna's "Future Lover" who herself lifted it from Donna Summer's "I Feel Love". And admittedly, it took more than a few listens for me to really like it.

And the thing is with New Order - when saying Eurodisco - I saw them more as making club music, not dance music. And yes, those can be mutually exclusive, though I'm sure there is / was crossover. This possibly can be exemplified the best here with "Stray Dog" - music by New Order (which is good!), spoken word by Iggy Pop (which is not!). The song ranks low on the track here. I get that everyone thinks I should love Iggy Pop, but I never have. Never have I seen his appeal.

Pop isn't the only guest. Brandon Flowers appears on "Superheated". I get that New Order is a huge influence for the Killers, but I've never felt the band to need "guests". There are a handful of other outsiders participating on this disk, with only four songs being solely New Order.

Maybe it is coincidence, but those four ("Restless", "Academic", "Nothing But a Fool" and "the Game") are more guitar driven, though Gilbert does a great job with her keyboard work. And maybe not coincidentally, these might be the strongest four songs on the Music Complete.

Still, I like "Superheated". And except for the line "did we ever kiss?", the song could just as easily be a message from Bernard Sumner (and the band) to the departed Peter Hook or any romantic partner. This song too took me a few listens to appreciate it.

With "Tutti Frutti" maybe it's the vocal nod to Technique, or a slight bass line from Frankie Goes to Hollywood. It's a fine song, but nothing great. It registers lower in my playlist. It is down there with "Stray Dog".

"Singularity" and "Unlearn this Hatred" are good (the latter more than the former) and Tom Rowlands certainly brings a little bit of the Chemical Brothers to the table with both songs. I swear "People on the Highline" uses a bass line from the Clash's 'Sandanista!' and it seems to go on much longer than the timing says - yet it doesn't seem to go anywhere at all.

Overall, I am happy with the release - at least the majority of it. Not overjoyed. Bottom line is: I could have done without so many outside participation (though I might overlook "Superheated") and the loss of Peter Hook is palpable.

Side note - and doesn't factor into my star-rating: another release from another band that doesn't have frickin' liner notes / credits for the digital download users. This is becoming tiresome, as they clearly exist and not included. If it costs additional monies to include them, make it a purchase option for those who want them with an increased rate if needed.

title: New Soundscapes For Old Melodies
text:
If you didn't know it already, this is NOT the new My Dying Bride Album!

This is an experiment with an almost completely new sound and feel. There are recognisable elements of the band's sound, and certainly some old melodies that are the basis for these new songs. The result is completely different, though, and you won't feel cheated that they re-used old stuff.

Think of bands like "Autumn Tears" or "Elend" and you are on the right track to figuring out what kind of music this is, or certain instrumentals from Cradle of Filth (Humana Inspired to Nightmare, The Graveyard by Moonlight) though My Dying Bride takes it one step further in removing the music from Metal. This is slower and more peaceful music than any of that. The operatic sound is more prevalent, especially in the arias by the female singer. Aaron Stainthorpe's vocals are familiar in his spoken lines from earlier songs. Long instrumental passages with cello, viola, and an ethereal synth create atmosphere, deep soundspaces, and melancholia, though sometimes the theme is more hopeful.

The result is definitely interesting, and beautiful I think. Doomy and gloomy in a softer version, more pensive, far away from metal.

I think it's great, but you have to be open to new ideas, and I doubt everyone will like it.

title: "What Can I Do When I'm Next to You?"
text:
I've been a Nada Surf fan ever since I caught their video for "Always Love" years ago. I've enjoyed the progression and maturity that they've shown with each album and this record is no exception. I'll admit that I was underwhelmed on my first listen. It felt stale and lacked the catchy melodies that we've all come to love and expect from the group. After a few more spins it slowly began to sink in and the songs started to worm their way into my subconscious. It's a slow-burner but gradually the album begins to come together and really shine.

For starters, the bright melodies are here in abundance. "No Snow on the Mountain" is my favorite cut, a fast-paced and uptempo number that sounds like classic Nada Surf. "Clear Eye Clouded Mind", "Jules and Jim", and "Looking Through" are all standouts that continue to push the band forward and they carry a sense of urgency not heard since [[ASIN:B00004W5KD Proximity Effect]] back in 1998. Matthew Caws continues to use his featherlight voice to great effect, bringing the listener into the songs and emoting feelings we've all had at one time or another. The two ballads on the album, "When I Was Young" and "Let the Fight Do the Fighting" are perfect examples of what he can do and how he's able to craft a compelling melody. My only real complaint is that his lyrics seem much more vague this time around. Previous records were full of relatable stories and personal revelations that made it easy to keep coming back to the songs. Here the tunes are certainly fun but I feel a certain depth is lacking and that makes them a bit less memorable. There are also a couple tracks, namely "The Future" and "The Moon Is Calling", that are middle of the road and feel more like filler than essential compositions.

Overall, The Stars Are Indifferent to Astronomy is another solid effort from Nada Surf. It may not grab you immediately but give it time. The rewards are worth it.

title: The culmination of UFO's hard won success...
text: UFO typified the best elements of hard rock, but often came across as generic and derivative.  To some extent that might have been true, but they were a prolific, hard working band, their songs were good, and they played them like they meant it.  Strangers in the Night brings the best of it to the stage.  A lengthy album, remastered and extended to include two additional songs, this CD reminds UFO fans why they were fans to begin with.  It's a relentlessly energetic concert that surrounds the listener with the excitement of both the band and the audience.  Clearly UFO played with such singular conviction because they had no other choice.  As well as a great live performance, Strangers in the Night also serves as a fine "best of" CD.  If you're just getting acquainted with UFO, there's no better album to start with.

title: Great Tracks, Imperfectly Mastered
text:
As a big fan of Barbra Streisand I was excited about all the previously unreleased material these 4 CDs included. However, I was unhappy with the mastering. For some reason a dozen or so tracks included a high-pitched, pulsating "dinging" noise, something so high pitched that it was easy to miss. I contacted Columbia/Sony's consumer quality control at the time back in 1991 and no one there would acknowledge the flaw. Some of the rare material is from sources that are far from optimal, however this particular intermittent pulsating sound is not due to inferior source material since it occurs on some tracks that are not of rare material. In 1998 the CD set was re-released. It still contained this problem. The noise is slight and difficult to hear, and not on every track. The clearest example of the problem is the track containing "You're the Top" because the song begins very quietly and it is easiest to hear the noise during quiet passages.

Despite this flaw the set of 4 CDs is a "must have" for any fan of Barbra Streisand. But Columbia/Sony PLEASE fix the problem on these CDs before they are re-released again.

title: Brain Candy
text: Assassins is another one of those uncoventional musicals by Stephen Sondheim.  Brilliant in its musical execution but lacking in the kind of heart one often seeks from musical theater.  That said, it really does offer a lot of mind fodder as it explores the psyches of those who have attempted to assassinate America's chief executive officers throughout history.  You'll be perversely pleased by Sondheim's zesty wit as displayed in the overly cheerful, sweet as candy songs.  But soon his saccharin tone leaves you feelin' a bit bitter in the stomach as you try to digest the fact that we are talking something as serious as taking the life of another.  Not sure this is palatable for all.  But if you want something that makes you think, something that plumbs the playhouse's darker corners, you'll get some kick out of Assassins.  Suggested for mature musical hounds.

title: The Tygers' last truly great LP
text:
As the liner notes to this CD offer, Tygers of Pan Tang were like "a star that burned bright and quick," meaning they weren't around for very long and neither was the do-it-yourself NWOBHM scene that spawned them, but boy did they leave us behind some of the best music heavy metal had to offer.

The Tygers' second LP (and first with new vocalist Jon Deverill and guitarist John Sykes) "Spellbound" was released in April 1981 and a mere five months later the band were back in the studio recording the follow-up "Crazy Nights," released in November '81. "Spellbound" remains a certified NWOBHM masterpiece and it might have seemed like rushing out another album during the same year would have resulted in inferior product, but this is certainly not the case here. While "Spellbound" may remain the defining moment of the band's career, "Crazy Nights" is not far behind and is packed with a veritable blend of raw, tough and great sounding NWOBHM anthems. They just don't make 'em like this anymore.

The band's sound here reflects the tide of the day in England. Along with Saxon and Diamond Head, the Tygers were at the forefront of the NWOBHM with fast, raw, tough and readily head-bangable heavy metal classics. And I would agree with other reviewers that Jon Deverill's vocals recall Sean Harris (Diamond Head) at times, but Deverill deserves his own place in history as one of the best of heavy metal vocalists, with his impassioned and soulful delivery. And the riffs to songs like "Running Out Of Time," "Make A Stand" and bonus B-side track "Paradise Drive" have not lost their power with the passage of time.

That in fact may be the reason for Tygers of Pan Tang's relative obscurity and cult status in the annals of heavy metal. It has been a long time since music like this was made, and it did not help that 1982's "The Cage," though not without its strengths, could be seen as more of an attempt at mainstream hard rock, making "Crazy Nights" the last great Tygers NWOBHM album.

All Tygers of Pan Tang is noteworthy music that deserves to be heard by more, yet at the time of this writing the CDs remain hard to find and expensive here in North America, though they seem to be more readily available in Europe.

The date on my CD says 2006, so it's good to see that this music is still being pressed by someone, especially since there was a time in the '90s when Tygers of Pan Tang CDs were available in Japan only and one had to pay ridiculous import prices on this side of the Atlantic to obtain a copy.

These current releases on Metal Nation are all stellar examples of how to reissue an album, each containing all original artwork and photos from the original releases, bonus B-side tracks taken from the original singles and even a helpful Tygers discography. All well worth the extra money you will likely spend on them.

But whether you can find or afford the CDs or are still jamming out to the original vinyl, the Tygers' early work remains some of the best NWOBHM you are ever likely to hear. Highly recommended.

Eric Records have dedicated themselves to getting the songs as they were played on AM and FM radio, and - most importantly - they use the original master tapes to make these CDs, so the sound quality is as good as it gets. In particular on volume 8, Carl Douglas' "Kung Fu Fighting" is restored in all its glory from 1974, and has never sounded better. I got a big kick out of hearing Chris Rea's "Fool (If You Think  It's Over)" - I literally hadn't heard that since the early eighties. Eric Records does not disappoint - get this one if you like 70s rock/pop; you won't regret it.

title: Awesome music, awesome Amazon return policy, batch has manufacture defects
text:
This is a review of the whole product, which is the LP of the 25th anniversary edition of the REM album Automatic For The People.
(1) First and foremost, the music is fantastic and were the review basic solely on the music, it would deserve a 5 star. I followed REM through their first 5 LPs and have always been impressed with their music. I have known the songs from this LP that receive radio play. After listening to the recent REM interview on NPR, I decided to buy this LP. There is a musicality and maturity to this LP that goes well beyond the early LPs. Yes, it is REM's music, but their is something more. Having recently purchased the remastered Led Zeppelin LPs, I learned why. It is John Paul Jones's arrangements. He has done for REM on this LP what George Martin did for the Beatles.
(2) Second, Amazon should be acknowledged for their seamless return policy. This enabled me to get to an acceptable copy. Also, a 5 star.
(3) Last, this batch has manufacture defects and I recommend that Amazon return the entire batch and somehow inform REM that their music is being distributed in an inferior product. Every copy I received had a pattern of residue on the LP surface. While the residue cleans off with a VPI model 16.5, whatever created it contacted the LP surface an left damage to the grooves. One of the copies even came without the inner sleeve glued together! Watching modern record pressing machines on youtube, which also package the LPs into their inner sleeves, I can see how these manufacture defects came to be. The product and manufacture earns a 1 star or less.

title: PLEASE READ
text:
I was VERY determined to own one song, POP9. It WAS available as an MP3 download. I downloaded it, only to find it dissolved into silence after the first couple of minutes. Reported to Amazon, it took weeks for the seller to fix the problem and upload a corrected version, I kept checking back. I'm glad I did. I loved it. It was episodic, lilting, yet meaty, lovely, with an infectious beat, several themes that ebb and flow and take their time coming together. Than my hard disc crashed. Unfortunately, for some reason, POP 9 doesn't seem to be available any longer as an MP3 download. I waited a couple years, then ordered this CD. It's burned when you order it. What did I find? The same problem as before- the song plays for a couple of minutes, then dissolves into silence for about 30 minutes. The other songs on the CD play okay, but I don't find them nearly as interesting- okay purely for background music. I wish Dramalogic would upload a corrected version of POP 9- it was great.

Another offering in the same vein, reminiscent of POP9, is [[ASIN:B00EF2IV0U Dipressend (Luria on Ora Remix)]], also what I think of as "trancy electronica", that is, hypnotic and invigorating yet soothing.
