title: Souling The Hits One More Time And More
text:
The Ikettes really should stand beside such as the Supremes, the Ronettes, the Shirelles and the Shangri-Las as one of the greatest of girl groups in the sixties, in turn the greatest of decades for girl groups. That they have been largely overlooked, despite such hits as I'm So Thankful, Peaches 'n' Cream, I'm Blue (The Gong Gong Song) and Camel Walk, could be due to a number of factors. Because they are best known as the glamorous backing singers and dancers for Ike and Tina Turner, their role as artists in their own right probably had less impact, and they had far fewer singles and albums under their own name than, say, the Supremes.

Also, they lacked the focus of an identifiable lead singer, as their line-ups were in a state of constant flux as Ike Turner hired and fired them, or they chose to leave because of low wages or other reasons, and indeed it is hard to know who sang what on which record. Lead singers over the years included Robbie Montgomery, Jessie Smith, Venetta Fields, Dee Dee Johnson (aka Flora Williams), PP Arnold and Joshie Armstead. My promo copy had no booklet but I gather it is very informative as to Ikette history.

Although the hits had a pop sensibility, they had a blacker, grittier R&B sound than many of the other girl groups, more in the vein of Fontella Bass, Etta James or (obviously) Tina Turner, and the lyrics of their original material kept it real in a way that you wouldn't get from the more romantic Chiffons or the Cookies.

As well as the singles, the Ikettes had one album to their name, The Ikettes Soul The Hits, which included a number of popular hits of the day as well as their own hits and some original material mostly written by Ike Turner.

The venerable Ace label did its bit to correct their obscurity by collecting a number of their best Modern label recordings (I'm Blue had been on Atco) on a 1986 compilation called [[ASIN:B000007ZLH Fine, Fine, Fine]]. This appeared in an expanded edition on CD in 1992. Can't Sit Down...'Cos It Feels So Good is the new Ace compilation that supercedes it, and contains over ten minutes of extra tracks.

It includes everything from the [[ASIN:B000Y3JF1I Soul The Hits]] album as well as several singles, and hearing them all one after the other should convince any listener just what an awesome unit they were, with some belting vocals, abetted by Ike Turner's tight band and production (plus a couple produced by Stan Venet), and his own not inconsiderable skills as guitarist and pianist. From the bits of between-takes chat included we can tell from Ike's name check that the incomparable Earl Palmer is the drummer on at least some of the tracks.

The extra tracks, some previously unreleased, including several featuring Venetta Fields. Two of these (I'm Leaving You/You're Still My Baby) seem to have been a single on Sony (no relation) in 1963, unless they are different recordings. Blue On Blue also appears likely to be identical to the single Blue With A Broken Heart by Flora Williams (it came out on the Sonja label in 1964). Also included are some outtakes from Soul The Hits: The Loco-motion, Sha La La and Da Doo Ron Ron, all covers that had been big hits for Little Eva, the Shirelles and the Crystals in the preceding couple of years, and You Can't Have Your Cake And Eat It Too, a great track. Much of the album is in true stereo mixes, most making their CD debut, with only six of the tracks in mono. The single version of Camel Walk has been chosen in preference to the album take found on Fine Fine Fine, and there is also an early alternative take of it included.

Unreservedly recommended for fans of girl groups and good R&B.

title: Skilful but lacking cohesion
text:
There's no doubt about it that Oscar Peterson, with the exception of Art Tatum perhaps, is one of the great technicians of jazz. His timing, octave stretches, improvised solos and key changes are truly a thing to behold. The man plays with the velocity and control of a concert pianist - in fact it's been said that some of the stuff Peterson played put classical pianists to shame.
Nevertheless, in this collection of songs, Peterson consistently seems to forget the key ingredient: melody. Peterson is literally all over the place and is too fast for his own good, constantly jumping all over the keyboard with both his left and right hands. This tends to get boring and sometimes even fairly tedious.
In terms of listening pleasure, this isn't the best jazz album available. Dave Brubeck is a much better bet if it's melody you're after.
Looking over this review, the word 'technician' seems perfectly apt for Oscar Peterson.

title: A tasty hard bop truffle worth snuffling out
text:
'Conflict,' by the `Jimmy Woods Sextet, featuring Elvin Jones,' is an obscure but outstanding session that harks back to March '63, near the end of the post-bop period - the last golden era for jazz.

The leader was unknown to me, although he keeps solid company: along with Coltrane's featured drummer there's Andrew Hill, Harold Land, Carmell Jones and George Tucker. Land got his big break with Clifford Brown and Max Roach, and gained some fame as a west-coast tenor player who led sessions now re-issued as CDs. Carmell Jones, who was often championed by Land, is a trumpeter with great technique seasoned with sharp dissonance and plenty of soul. He moved to Europe in 1965 and had some success joining traveling gigs, including with Oliver Nelson, although on record Jones probably peaked with Horace Silver, Land - and here. A 3-CD set on Mosaic of his 1961-to-'63 work may yet correct his never-quite-made-it status.

Woods' own liner notes remark on the choice of Elvin as drummer: he'd been on Woods' mind while composing. He also refers to Andrew Hill as "new" and speaks of great promise, yet he gets little prominence here. Only some soloing hints at the discordance and thick harmonies to come: in 'Pazmuerte' and 'Look to Your Heart,' for instance, Hill's brief turns reward pricking up one's ears. So if you get this (as I did) for an early taste of Hill's idiom, or even for signs of his studies under Paul Hindemith, you may dig deep but find only roots.

Still, there's heaps of consolation in this recording: as a group they swing hard and the brasses strike out with fiery solos. Woods shines brightly both as the composer of all the disc's numbers and as a gutsy altoist. His playing and leadership are as convincing in the hard-hitting songs, which are in the majority, as in the smoother numbers - such as the dreamy 'Look to Your Heart,' one of the high points of this session. Woods heads a reduced piano-bass-and-brushes combo on this, and while he indulges his delight in bravura soloing through the middle, it's an atmospheric tune that vaguely suggests a wistful Steve Lacy number.

On the memorable 'Aim,' Carmell Jones does plenty of the heavy lifting, and with compelling results. His trumpet is a strong match for Woods' alto sax: equally brash and loose, both stay apace of Elvin and stand up to his turbulence. On a few numbers, such as 'Pazmuerte,' their joyful noise seems to channel Art Blakey's Messengers in energy, more than in that group's famed raucousness. Considering Blakey's legacy, this is no liability: any group reaching for high-grade small-combo extroversion better have its own sound - and this Sextet most certainly has.

Three bonus tracks make this a 56-minute release: very decent for the post-LP era. Woods is radiant in the alternate title song, 'though not as inspired as on the master. On the alternate to 'Aim,' Elvin nearly swamps the sound-stage; still, as with the bonus 'Look to Your Heart,' these alternates are well worth including.

The Sextet is prone to a certain seat-of-their-pants roughness: while tempos never become muddled, they sometimes vary and bend just short of lost control. Still, aren't such devil-may-care liberties precisely hard bop's very gut and sinew?

As for this group's obscurity, the liner notes reveal various inner tensions: Woods mentions his ambivalence about playing, and confesses that after 'Awakening!,' his first album as leader, he really wasn't sure "...whether I could communicate my feelings." This second album's title is meant to express feeling torn between his love of music and parental pressures - but then he adds, rather enigmatically, that a college course in sociopathic behavior "...clarified many of my thoughts on this subject." Whatever all this adds up to, his inner strife is our musical loss.

The sound on this outing is clear, ample stereo, earning this recording a made-in-heaven five/five points. The only letdown here is the lack of other releases: the Woods Sextet produced only this single session -- which is recommended without reservation to those who hanker for tasty hard bop truffles.

title: "Live At The Academy Of Music 1971"
text:
This box set is essential for any fan of The Band.

It collects the released performances from "Rock Of Ages" 1972 album and 2001 reissue on Discs 1 & 2. These are the same takes from those titles, but newly remixed by Robbie Robertson and Bob Clearmountain. For the original mix of "Rock Of Ages", Mobile Fidelity's SACD is the absolute best option. But this box set's remixes offer much improved sound over the original mix, as great as it was. The difference in sound is comparable to the original "Last Waltz" issue vs. the remixed 2002 box set. So basically, the soundstage is way wider and spread out, the instruments are all clearer and more dynamic, and the Clearmountain mixes attempt to present the takes in the best sound quality updated technology can provide.

The complete New Year's Eve show, as mixed by Sebastian Robertson, is on Discs 3 & 4. This mix is different from Clearmountain's: instead of a super polished mix, the sound is raw, immediate and without any unneccesary tricks or frills. Clear and well mixed vocals, thick and supple drums/bass, piano and guitar left/right, and organ left and center. It is a wonderful mix to hear this show like you're in the audience and the soundmen are doing a fantastic job. Also note that this complete New Year's Eve show does repeat some songs from the first two discs. Those takes were selected as the "best" of the run, and of course they would also appear in their proper place in the original show. BUT, contrary to what many people are thinking, the New Year's Eve show only has 7 repeated/previously released tracks (not including Dylan).

Both mixes have a more natural, balanced mix of the horn section, which was a common complaint from some over the years. The hardcover book fits perfectly with [[ASIN:B000B19B6M A Musical History (W/DVD)]], featuring a beautiful collection of photos throughout 48 pages. The DVD contains footage of two tracks: "King Harvest (Has Surely Come)" and "The W.S. Walcott Medicine Show". The video of "Don't Do It" is found on MUSICAL HISTORY, for a total of 3 video tracks from these shows. All of these elements combine to make this an absolutely essential release for true fans of THE BAND!

text:
This is an album that approaches perfection. Oft imitated, but never duplicated the last few years, Wheeler has one of the most amazing multi-octave soprano voices in the history of popular music, only truly appreciated if you've had the great fortune to see the band on one of their rare tours.
Sundays fans, tend to own the group's entire catalog, and follow them eagerly. Ironically those unfamilliar with the band usually recognize them from their cover of the Rolling Stones' Wild Horses, which figured prominently in an (in)famous Budweiser christmas commercial featuring slow motion Clydesdales pulling a budweiser sled through a picture postcard idyllic snowscape.
Static & Silence applies more sonic textures than on either of their prior releases, and is less dischordant and melancholoy than the material produced in their post new wave past.
Each song is a carefully crafted meditation on english life, finding the principals (husband and wife Wheeler and guitarist Gavurin) in a reflective mood after a five year break from the music industry to explore the challenges of parenting.
With such high expectations, I can hardly believe my good fortune that the Sundays have again produced an album of consistent thematic resonance, and pure sonic delight.

title: Absolutely Charming and Memorable
text: Before I listened to this, I held Edward Scissorhands in high esteem as the most beautiful score of all time.  Life is Beautiful proved otherwise.  Nicola Piovani made a charming score with heartfelt themes while still retaining the Italian nature of the film and its controversial subject.  There are two innocent-sounding main themes that make up the film, one which is a deep somber theme for the theme of the film, and the other which is a light-hearted charming theme for Benigni's character.  Both are used equally in the film and with great effect.  Besides listening to the wonderful themes, I enjoyed listening to the Italian-influenced music, such as "Grand Hotel Valse" or "Grand Hotel Fox", which create the time and place of the movie without being intrusive.  The music throughout the film is happy but tracks such as "La Notte Di Fuga", "Il Treno Nel Buio", and "Il Gioco Di Giosue" still remind the listener of the Holocaust-influence in the film.  After the dark music, the CD ends with an absolutely moving rendition of the main theme, the best rendition of it in the whole film.  Anyone who holds foreign films and their music in disregard should see Life is Beautiful.  It's the perfect marriage between music and visuals, and it is not the same without Piovani's wonderful score.

title: Nearly All The Hits
text:
Concentrating on their singles career, this 25 track collection appeared on the Motown label in 1997 when it was licensed to Polygram, and covers the period from their first Motown single, Baby I Need Your Loving, up to 1972 when they first left the label (they were back between 1983 and 1986). 

Nearly all the Motown hit singles are present so it is easier to itemise what isn't: their cover of Tim Hardin's If I Were A Carpenter, a bigger hit here than in the US; Do What You Gotta Do, not a single in the US; Don't Let Him Take Your Love From Me, not a single in the UK and only a minor hit in the US; Just Seven Numbers, and In These Changing Times, both only minor hits, extracted from the Changing Times album; Walk With Me Talk With Me Darling, not a single in the US; and their two-part version of MacArthur Park, a non-album single that wasn't even released in the UK and which one probably has to buy Anthology to get hold of on CD.

It also includes 4 popular B-sides including their great original version of I Got A Feeling, better known in its cover by Barbara Randolph. Three of these were taken from albums but one, If You Don't Want My Love, was only ever the B-side of You Keep Running Way, perhaps making its debut on CD.

Most of the songs were produced by Brian Holland and Lamont Dozier, with whom they had a string of huge hits, but a handful were produced by Mickey Stevenson, Ivy Jo Hunter, Johnny Bristol and others.

It states in the liner notes that "The Ultimate Collections feature the original 45 rpm versions. Album sources are issued for reference purposes; the LP versions were very often different mixes, and sometimes different performances." What this means in practice is that all but 2 tracks - Still Water (Love) and (It's The Way) Nature Planned It - are mono versions which I suppose means that Motown hope to have us buy the parent albums as well to get the stereo mixes

And did I mention very well played and very well recorded. At the price it is steal. It would make an excellent introduction to the Beethoven symphonies and added to the Szell and Bernstein "white boxes" would give 3 very different, and very interesting view points on this great music from 3 great American orchestras. Champagne music making on a Budweiser budget, if I may strain the analogy.

title: One of the best albums I've not only listened to but experienced in years
text:
Pure Brilliance.

I'm a huge fan of Sa-Ra as their last release, Nuclear Evolution: The Age of Love, as well as the remixes they've done for the likes of Jamiroquai, Medeski Martin Wood, Four Tet, Kleeer, Tosca and Roots Manuva rarely escaped my earbuds.

Shafiq Husayn, one third of Sa-Ra Creative Partners (alongside Om'Mas Keith and Taz Arnold), shows that Sa-Ra's collective genius is no fluke.

Shafiq En'a-Free-Ka is simply one of the best albums I've not only merely listened to but experienced in years. The album is a tapestry of invention and sounds. To call Shafiq's production flat out brilliant is an understatement. He creates a moody, funky, spacey atmosphere that remains consistent despite the variances in style that swings from soulful pyschedelica (the standout "Changes") to swampy funk ("Cheeba", which invokes D'Angelo's Voodoo period all the way down to Bilal's falsetto) to drowsy Krautrock ("Major Heavy") to tropical quiet storm ("Le Star") to ominous hip hop stomp ("All Dead").

Shafiq En'a-Free-Ka, which translates to 'Shafiq in a free state of mind', is a concept album that proves uplifting and multi-hued. It is obviously a work created out of pure inspiration and love.

Although I personally disliked the back-to-back punch of Major Heavy and Evil Man and omitted them from my personal sequence of the album, I can still honestly say that this album is a modern genre-defying masterpiece.

How often can you say that a single album touches your heart and soul while having you nod AND use your head?

Shafiq En'a-Free-Ka is that rare album.

title: This is the film review
text:
Prakash Jha has directed many movies and most of them were about the political and family strife that exists in Uttar and Madhya Pradesh except if my memory serves me right the exception was Hip Hip Hurruay. Rajneeti is in the same vein and it explores the political aspirations and shenanigans of career politicians in the North. It is also inspired from the Hindu epic Mahabharata and to a certain extent the Gandhi family and The Godfather. To attempt a film like Rajneeeti is not easy because not only does one have to manage such a huge star cast but also the logistics of shooting in crowded areas for political rallies. The only other director that has successfully done that would be J. P. Dutta. Besides the massive cast, the length of the movie was a concern it clocks at almost 3 hours. If one wants the audience to sit through a long movie, the movie must be very well edited and riveting from the go. So does Rajneeti have it in it to suceeed?
Rajneeti is about the games people in power play. Bahskar Sanyal (Nasseruddin Shah) is a leftist leader who is riding high in popularity and has begun to pose a serious challenge to the elite in power. However he makes a mistake which hides a secret which is revealed much later in the movie and starts a self imposed exile. The story then shifts to the present day and warring rivalries between two cousins, Arjun Rampal ( Prithvi ) and Veerendra ( Manoj Bajpayee) who are desperate for power and will stop at nothing. Veerendra chooses Sooraj ( Ajay Devgan ) to become the head of the minority and backward classes and contest an election when his own family has put him in to the corner. Prithvis brother ( Ranbir Kapoor) is an outsider who knows nothing about politics and is a doctoral student of English in America, he has come to India for a visit but gets sucked in to this treacherous world. Katrina Kaif ( Indu )is in love with Ranbir but also gets caught in this web. Nana Patekar ( Brij Gopal ) is a mentor to these youngsters and is forced to take sides in this bloody battle.
Anjum Rajabali and Prakash Jha's script keeps you glued to the screen for these ling hours and it is not easy in these times when even a length of one hour is considered long. This is where they succeed, but there are flaws in this script that I have to point out and those are the disappearance of Naseeruddin Shah after the first three minutes. Ranbir Kapoor's transformation as a doctoral candidate in Victorian poetry to a ruthless pollster and kingmaker does not appear to be convincing. But barring these flaws the movie works because Jha has successfully managed to make a watchable movie featuring a ensemble of characters. Nana Patekar manages a great performance and manages to convey emotions without speaking too many lines. Ranbir Kapoor is getting better and hogs the camera a testimony to his rising star value. Manoj Bajpayee is great and perfectly suited to the Bihari politician role and his dialect is perfect. The biggest surprise is Arjun Rampal who delivers a top notch performance and is a revelation in every scene. The supporting cast is serves well. I had the privilege of watching it at an advance premiere and liked it....Three stars. 6/2/10

title: "Linsey Alexander is the real deal. He’s back with a rousing sophomore album." - Blues Music Magazine
text:
Reviewed in Blues Music Magazine Issue Seven published by MojoWax Media Inc.
Visit http://bluesmusicmagazine.com for more great reviews.
LINSEY ALEXANDER
Come Back Baby
Delmark
Chicago bluesman, “The Hoochie Man,” Linsey Alexander made national and international waves with his Delmark debut in 2012 entitled Been There Done That and now he’s back with a rousing sophomore album called Come Back Baby. There’s no denying Alexander is a fine singer and songwriter and he lays it all on the line on his new recording.
Accompanied by an A-list of Chicago players that include Breezy Rodio on guitar, Roosevelt Purifoy on keyboards, Greg McDaniel on bass, Pooky Styx on drums, Ryan Nyther on trumpet, Bill McFarland on trombone, Chris Neal on tenor saxophone, and the great Billy Branch on harmonica, Alexander rolls through these songs like a freight train on ecstasy. It’s nothin’ but the blues, but it sure does sound and feel good. Best cuts: the horn-fueled album opener reminiscent of B.B. King, “Little Bit Of Soap,” the electrifyin’ blues rock of “Booze And Blues,” the swingin’ sentiment of “Come Back Baby,” the Albert Collins inspired “Call My Wife,” featuring the fine harp blastin’ of Branch, the funky, dance floor jive of “Booty Call,” and the drivin’ Great Lakes effect of “Snowing In Chicago.”
Linsey Alexander is the real deal and his new album Come Back Baby is a testament to the blues the way they were supposed to played.
– Brian M. Owens

title: A Work in Progress
text: One thing about singer songwriters, as well as probably most any artist, is it often takes a long time it seems to finally get to a place where they have developed a unique artistic voice, know what they are strong at and are able to deliver this with some degree of consistency.  This album is one of those earlier, exploratory albums where Massengill seems to play with a lot of different themes some of which are more successful than others, some which he embellishes upon in later albums with great success and others he appears to have mostly disgarded.  I for one am glad that the days of David Massengill's epic songs of social conscience appear to be mostly over.  Not because there isn't a place for this but because so many other people have done it so much better.  Unfortunately on this album "The Great American Dream," "The Return," "Sightseer," and "Jesus, the Fugitive Prince" all fall into this category.  It's interesting to observe him exploring songwriting along these lines but it soon becomes clear that this is not his strong point and does not represent what he is ultimately best at and most uniquely able to contribute as an artist.  "Perfect Love" and "Wake Up" are two very sweet love songs that are a prelude to some of his later work on "We Will Be Together" where this theme is more successfully realized.  "A Girl's Daring Escape" foreshadows the real or invented stories from Massengill's family history that appear on later album, My Home Must Be a Special Place.  For me, "Madou," a love song, is the song that stands out on this album.  It is beautifully and concisely written, uniquely expressive, characteristically inventive and charming and the accompaniment on the dulcimer is just lovely.  If you are a David Massengill fan, this album is worth buying if you are interested in following his development as an artist.  For new listeners, I'd direct them to more recent albums My Home Must Be a Special Place and/or We Will Be Together, two albums that each showcase a more solid collection of songs from a very special artist with a very unique voice.

title: Before everyone started to hate
text: Nelly has become the butt of many hip hop jokes, when in reality he is not that bad.  His first hit "Country Grammar" put him on the map with his debut album.  The album churned out hits that eventually became destroyed by the radio (can't fault him for that) and now Nelly has become a household name.  The production really hits hard (literally) with many bassy songs.  "St. Louie, Greed Hate Envy, Country Grammar, and E.I. all pound the bass authority and make for some great tracks.  Many of these tracks are strictly for the clubs ("For My N*ggas", Ride wit me, etc.).  "Batter Up" is sort of a funny feel good song that takes the sample from the Jefferson's theme (I could be wrong, I'm not sure if it was the Jeffersons but I know it was a tv theme sample) and makes for a good song.  Batter Up also features the St. Lunatics.  The filler is few and far between, songs like "utha side" and tho dem wrappas  could have been easily cut out, but they do not retract from the album's replay value.  Cedric the Entertainer drops in for the intro which is pointless, but funny at the same time.  While Nelly is spitting his lifestyle as it was in St. Louis, his production team is providing him with the hard-hitting bass beats that I thought would have continued in Nellyville, which isn't as good as country grammar.  All in all, add to the collection, you won't be disappointed.

title: Fascinating, but Not Over the Top Great
text:
I was so happy to receive this CD, as I love music! I was curious to hear what Australia had to offer, as I don't think I have heard any bands for ages coming from that country. This band is named for the title character in the novel Augie March, the great novel by Saul Bellow, depicting an "everyman" sort of character wending his way through life. The band is touring here in the States later this year. I think a lot of people will find them unique. I particularly liked and enjoyed the variety of styles they utlize. Some of the songs have banjo music, or drumming, or trumpets to begin...and the choir music, of course. When I first heard Augie March's "Moo, You Bloody Choir", on the first song: "One Crowded Hour", I thought, "Aha! My beloved Damien Rice!" and "Aha! My favorite Del Amitri!"

Alas, it isn't quite that way.

They don't have quite the effect of those two great musical bands, for me. Although I do like the first song, which was incredibly popular and garnered tons of awards in Australia, and I especially like "The Cold Acre" as well, they just...as yet... don't move me, grab me, pull me and swing me around lyrically in quite such a profound a way as my favorite groups and singers. I think I need romance in ballads that goes all the way. I need depth that is REALLY deep. I need wit and humor that amazes and astounds me, over and over. I like their music, don't get me wrong...but this album gets four stars from me. I really need to be transported by a singer or a group to give five stars to a CD.

I will keep listening to this album. It is not a wash-out, by any means. However, if I had it in the car and my CD of "O" by Damien Rice was sitting next to it, I expect I would probably be playing the Damien Rice as I drove.

Thanks,

jean

title: One of the Best Debut Albums Ever!
text:
On Martin Luther King's Birthday, local radio station KFOG was playing its "ten at ten" songs in honor of the meaning of the holiday and when I heard "As Yet Untitled" played, I was reminded about the poetic genius of Terence Trent. "Introducing the Hardline" was an unconventional album, which I discovered and played at a record store I worked in 1987, and as I first heard it, I was hearing music that was alive, lyrics written by a smart, young poet, and the experimental arrangements and mixtures of "Black" music. It seemed to be a type of album Prince was often trying for, and yet it was Terence Trent who succeeded!
"Wishing Well," for example, was not a conventional single with its erotic imagery, and yet somehow had the hook to slowly climb to number one of the charts! "If You All Get to Heaven" is a glorious peace protest song, "Dance Little Sister" is a good, soulful groove, "Let's Go Forward" is probably one of the best love songs written in the 80's, and "As Yet Untitled" is a wonderful soulful accapella tune that best captures the spirit of the emotions of an angry Black male in a prejudicial world. The album also showed signs of humor and self-references as well. Just as D'arby would get too serious, he'd sneak in a little humor. ("Neither Fish Nor Flesh," which I think is also a very good album, plays this last aspect a bit more).
It is sad that Terence Trent D'Arby's latest offering, Wildcard (he now calls himself Sananda Maitreya) is not offered in the States as of yet. This is an artist who deserves much more attention. A lot of mainstream listeners seemed to dismiss him from his ecclectic and self-referential second album ("Neither Fish Nor Flesh") and with the exception of some airplay of two singles from his 1993, Symphony and Damn album has been ignored by radio stations. D'Arby (Maitreya) is perhaps one of the most important contributors to the Black male voice and lyric when it comes to song and music.

title: Sly At The Top Of His Game
text:
If you're looking for a point of entry into the lava-lamp infested, funky nightclub world of Sly & the Family Stone, this Greatest Hits CD is your best bet - and it's a bargain. With the exception of Hendrix, Morrison, and Joplin - who died - and David Crosby - who isn't interesting enough to care about - Sly Stone shines out as the quintessential 60's cautionary tale, a man who inspired multitudes with his meteoric intensity and then self-destructed so completely that over the remaining decades he's remained a ghostly caricature of himself, struggling with mundane activities like remembering peoples' names - including his own.

Fortunately, this material is taken from the peak of his career, late 60's and early 70's. The music is exuberant, crackling with energy, and as funky as the law allows. S&TFS was a groundbreaking group in many ways, for starters they were interracial and mixed gender when this was virtually unknown. Their psychedelic blend of soul, R&B, rock, boom-chaka-laka-laka, and smart lyrics is irresistible and uniquely infectious. Sly had a genius for making complex compositions come out deceptively simple, danceable, and sing-in-the-shower-able. The CD is definitely incomplete, but the must-haves are there. (I've always had a sweet tooth for Hot Fun In The Summertime).

If you were not around when this music first appeared, what will strike you most is how influential it's been. Those who have not borrowed bits and pieces from Sly have stolen from him outright. Even so, few, if any of his imitators have been able to match his combination of wit, enthusiasm, and funkability. Buy this CD and put it on loud when there's nobody else around. If you're not dancing by the third or fourth song, you're Swiss.

title: so human and so divine
text:
I declared this to be my favorite record of 1999, right above "The Soft Bulletin." I still stand by that choice (even if I do listen to The Flaming Lips more often). For a Low fan, it was a beautiful Christmas gift and an unexpected surprise. "Just Like Christmas" is one of their poppiest tunes, a totally great, uplifting Christmas anthem. Watching Alan's dad play the jingle bells on stage with them at First Avenue was a real joy.
If you celebrate Christmas or not, are into Low or not, I think I can still safely recommend it objectively as a great Christmas record. "Little Drummer Boy" is a song that usually bugs me (except maybe the David Bowie/Bing Crosby version) but Low gives it a spooky electronic buzz that I highly recommend experiencing late at night while surrounded by christmas lights. "Blue Christmas" gets a more traditional, but no less gorgeous treatment. Mimi's voice wraps around Alan's guitar with a sensuality that nicely balances the Christian/family vibe present on most of the rest of the songs. The original songs here are mostly more ponderous, "Long Way Around The Sea" has a funereal touch that seems a bit more suited to Easter. But then that's Low.
For a generally cynical person, this record makes me all melty and happy. The aural equivalent of coming in from the snow and sitting in front of a fire. I'll probably buy it for my parents this year. Maybe not everyone will love it as much as I do, but it's hard to imagine anyone not enjoying at least one of the songs on here. Love it, hug it, take it home.

title: They dared to try something different
text: I see a lot of varied opinions on Tribe.  I haven't read any of the other reviews yet to see why.  To begin my favorite Queensryche album is still The Warning.  I bought Empire when it came out but years later traded it because it didn't hold up for me over time.  Maybe it was over played, or over rated.  I suspect some fans didn't like Tribe because it wasn't an Empire clone.  I found Tribe a good album.  Track 6 and 9 are stand outs for me and I don't understand why Rhythm of Hope never got radio play, it's an excellent song.  The background melody really adds to the song and helps to build the emotional feel.  Track one sounds like they used a play out of Robert Plant's play book.  Which isn't a bad thing for me, I like Plant's solo stuff a lot.  Track two is upbeat and catchy.  Many of the songs the drummer works in a tribal style drum beat.  The album is rich with well placed effects and musical textures.  Tribe as good as it is seems to be missing something to push it over the top but I feel anyone putting this album on for the first time and keeping an open mind will enjoy it.  If you are looking for guitar solos and thrashing you should pass on Tribe, it leans more to the Progressive side of things.  I applaud the band for trying something a bit different and even more for doing it as well as they did.

title: God in the details
text:
How fitting that the new release by Pain of Salvation should be a concept album about god and creation, as listening to a Pain of Salvation album is the closest thing I've ever had to a religious experience. And how fitting that Pain of Salvation's frontman and resident genius Daniel Gildenlow should write about god as he's the closest thing musically we've got on this planet.

There are a few albums throughout my 34 years of life that, when I first heard them, transformed me: Moving Pictures by Rush, Operation Mindcrime by Queensryche, Images and Words by Dream Theater, and Remedy Lane by Pain of Salvation just a year ago. With this new CD, Pain of Salvation has done it once again. That's almost 25 years listening to music and I can count on one hand the number of CDs that I consider truly life changing, 2 of them by Pain of Salvation. Genius. Pure genius.

To anyone who is a fan of Pain of Salvation, this CD will not disappoint. It is very different from anything they've done before, but really, would we expect anything else? Yes, there are moments of pure prog metal brilliance, but there's so much more. It's less of a CD of music than it is a motion picture without the picture. This is not a CD to put on in the car for a 15 minute drive to the grocery store. To be properly appreciated, turn off all the lights, light a candle, put on headphones and close your eyes and let the music envelop you and the pictures appear in your head.

Musically, the album contains the expected virtuoso performances. Daniel's vocals continue to grow in range and emotion. The styles they incorporate into their music has always been of greater range than your typical prog metal band, but the range displayed here blows away anything they've done to this point. I can see how it would put off a real metal-head, but those of you with an open mind will be able to embrace the styles and realize that they contribute to the overall diversity and virtuosity of the album. Musical highlights for me are the instrumental Pluvius Aestivus (latin translation: Summer Rain) and Nihil Morari (To Delay the Nothing).

The story is phenomenal, as is Daniel's explanation of how he came up with the story. Daniel is not only a student of Philosophy, he is a true philosopher in the same vein as the greats such as Descartes, Jung, and Neitzche who inspire his thoughts. Thank you, Daniel, for another fantastic experience. I can't wait for the next one.

title: Certainly a Great (If Not the Greatest) Tenor Show on CD!
text:
This 2-CD album presents 50 of the best and most popular tenor arias and songs in the literature, sung by several of the greatest and most beloved tenors of the 20th century. As such it offers a remarkably inclusive library of the best and most characteristic tenor songs in nearly uniformly outstanding performances. For those who want a ready reference to the glories of the tenor voice it could prove indispensable. Although there are a number of collections of tenor-singing CDs available, I believe this one would end up in the topmost few as to quality of performance, choice of music, and representativeness and completeness of selection. I recommend it highly to lovers of the tenor voice and to those who might aspire to join that elite company. In addition, it would no doubt make a highly appreciated gift to a friend or relative who loves tenor singing.

The album, Decca No. 289 466 480-2, draws upon the label's extensive catalog of vocal recordings and includes recordings from 1956 through 1997. As such it features items recorded using the analog technology of the 50s as well as those employing most subsequent higher fidelity techniques, including digital ones. Specifically, 37 are analog and 13 are digital recordings. In spite of that range of technology all of the offerings sound very good indeed and often provide the crème de la crème of performances of the included pieces. My congratulations to the producers of this fine collection!

Let me present some specific statistics describing the album. As to type of music, operatic arias dominate, accounting for 34 of the 50 items. There are also 14 songs and 2 items from operetta. Those sung in Italian dominate, including 38 pieces, while 5 each are sung in French and German and 2 in Spanish. Perhaps most important is the roster of tenors presented. Luciano Pavarotti (rightly, I believe) is best represented, with 15 arias and songs. Runner-up is Pavarotti's youthful favorite, Giuseppe di Stefano, with 8 songs and arias. José Carreras and Plácido Domingo follow with 5 each, then come Carlo Bergonzi, Jussi Björling, and Mario del Monaco, with 3 items each. Jon Vickers and Franco Corelli contribute 2 arias each, and a single item each is provided by Roberto Alagna, Fritz Wunderlich, Giacomo Aragall, and René Kollo. Four performances were recorded live with audiences; all others are studio takes.

Most of the performances are excellent and well-chosen. Pavarotti comes out best, with all winners among his performances. (Note especially "Spirto gentil.") In the old Italian song "Santa Lucia" he is joined by David Romano to offer an unusual, but appealing duet arrangement. Carreras comes close to losing control of his high-register vibrato here and there, notably in "Donna non vidi mai." Domingo is very consistently excellent, though his voice is rather baritone-like in timber. Bergonzi shows some outstanding singing. Alagna's "Una furtiva lagrima" is a curious choice, not as to the music, but as to Alagna's rendition, which is transposed down from Bb minor to G minor and whose second verse is sung in a very unusual way, with special ornamentation and variation of the familiar melody. Vickers' "Celeste Aïda" sounds more like a Heldentenor, with baritone-like quality and very forceful delivery, making the final high Bb with noticeable effort. He sounds more at home on "Winterstürme wichen dem Wonnemond" from Wagner's Die Walküre. Björling sings like an angel on his three celebrated performances. Del Monaco gives us a very dramatic "Vesti la giubba" complete with sobbing and crying, and a very impressive "Un di all'azzuro spazio." Wunderlich presents Mozart's "Dies Bildnis ist bezaubernd schön" in a long-admired rendition. Di Stefano gives us both arias and songs, excelling at both genres. Aragall gives us a fine "De' miei bollenti spiriti" with his slightly dark, but clear and ringing highs. Kollo gives a now-sweet, now-forceful performance of Walther's prize song from Wagner's Die Meistersinger, joined by chorus and Hans Sachs.

Though some may be disappointed not to find their favorite tenor or aria here, such must always be the case with a finite collection. Still, it would be hard to assemble a better set of 50 tenor performances, and I have no hesitation in recommending it to all lovers of tenor singing.

title: Stunning Hyper Kenetic Showtunes
text:
elmasongs is the EP/Soundtrack to the stunning Lars Van Trier movie Dancer In The Dark, starring Bjork as a poor, factory worker Czech immigrant to the American Northwest, who is slowly going blind. She has to support herself, and her son, who without an operation, will suffer the same fate that she does.

Her refuge from her sad and tragic life is the fantasies in her head about being the star of American Musicals. Its her own "Secret Life of Walter Mitty"

A set of tragic mishaps and circumstance, Selma is thrown into horrible, gutwrenching freefall with catastrophic results.

Selmasongs represents the musical tale of the story, the fantasies in Selma's head and it(like all bjork works of art) runs the gamut of emotion from heartbreaking tragedy, to ecstatic joy, to majestic beauty.

There's probably only one small complaint about Selmasongs..is that it clocks in at barely a half an hour. Also I think it would have been nice to include the ORIGINAL versions of the songs from the film on to soundtrack instead of the slightly altered versions presented here. Also missing is Selma's/Bjorks heartbreaking version of "My Favorite Things" from the Sound of Music.

A musical is logical progression for Bjork. She has an eclectic musical past. From the rock of the sugarcubes, the jazz ensemble Gling-Glo, her solo electronic based work, and her orchestral string work on the Homogenic album. However Strings dominated Homogenic, Bjork is in full command of an entire orchestra including brass, woodwinds and timpani, along with stringed instruments. This makes for captivating and inventive soundscapes next to sampled found percussion and electronic beats on the soundtrack.

Overture is a majestic orchestral instrumental that opens the both the film and the album. A beautiful 3 minute and 38 second mini opus with dramatic horns and timpani. Filled with highs and lows, quiet and loud, using the full dynamic range. Breathtaking.

Cvalda is "Its So Quiet" from Post on an adrenaline rush. Post-Industrial-Showtune music? A magical, whimsical, joyful tune featuring French actress extraordinaire Cathrine Denevue. Only Bjork could pull off a genre mash like this, and its amazing. The buzzing and clanging of factory machines turn into percussion, over a technicolor 1940s Vincent Minelli showtune score.

I've Seen It All is the beautiful ballad from the film, featuring Thom Yorke from Radiohead. Its everything you would think if your a fan of both artists, simply stunning. This time train tracks and train noises become the percussive base of this ballad. Trademark lyrical Bjork brilliance is still at work. "what about china, have you seen the great wall/ all walls are great if the roof doesnt fall"

Scatterheart is a song that worked better in the film than it does here on the album. I miss the duet between Selma and her son, and would have preferred that version. Here its just Bjork singing. Though the electronic percussion and bursts of noises and clicks are vintage Homogenic, while the bassline and arrangement would sound perfect on Debut. Its a decent song, but the movie version blows the album version away.

In The Musicals is another showtune on adrenaline, and once again its a great number. title: ONE OF THE FINEST DISCS IN THE ROYAL EDITION!
text:
If there was one disc I'd pull out of the Royal Edition (I own all of them) for the sheer thrill of hearing Bernstein, this would be it. Not only are the sonics excellent, but if ever there was a disc in the series to offset the wretchedly meager length of the "Bernstein Remastered" box set (average length of discs = 40 min) this is it.

Of course, the amount of music on the disc wouldn't mean much unless the performance were excellent. And in this case, they are not merely first rate, but exemplary. All with the possible exception of Peter And The Wolf which, as others have noted, lacks narration. Personally - I enjoy this. I have other versions that contain the narration. But listening to this disc, I am once again able to focus on Prokofiev's genius (and, I can provide my own narration to my wife's elementary school classroom and get to enjoy the expression's on their faces as I receive it to Bernstein's accompaniment!).

Crank this disc up on a good sound system - you'll never hear a finer Night On Bald Mountain (truly terrifying!) the Sorcerer's Apprentice, or Dance Macabre (not listed on the front of the cover, but the last item on this disc). Each is the reason I pulled this disc out today, with Holloween only a few days away.

There will never be another Lenny. But thanks to this disc, we can re-experience what - for many of us who still collect CDs - was our thrilling introduction to classical music. And perhaps, we can ignite this passion in the young ones!

title: One of the top piano Christmas recordings!
text:
This fine recording of ethereal solo piano interpretations of traditional Christmas carols, along with a few originals by Lanz, falls right in the tradition of the classic and trendsetting recording, "December," by George Winston.
These two titles, along with Vince Guaraldi's "Charlie Brown Christmas" and "A Dave Brubeck Christmas" (both a bit more jazz flavored) are among my all-time favorite piano recordings for the holiday season.
While they all serve nicely as background music in the workplace or at home, they deserve serious listening, and contemplation, in their own right.
With all the different artists who feel a need to cash in on the holiday season, it's nice to find a gem like this that still treats the music, as well as the season of Christmas, with respect.

title: Halestorm is a band that pretty much sticks to one sound
text:
Halestorm is a band that pretty much sticks to one sound. But that's fine because they kick butt doing so and reliably deliver just good, solid rock. This album is no different. Lzzy pretty much sticks to her regular themes of girl power, being a bad ass, and sex. Her shear vocal power is what sets this band apart from the run of the mill alternative rock (that and the fact that they have the most fun and enthusiasm of any band I've ever seen live but that's a different matter). It's not exactly ground breaking music but it's also consistently insanely catchy. Halestorm builds upon the music of earlier female rockers (Heart, Pat Benatar, Joan Jett, and Fleetwood Mac) and pays quite a bit of homage to these musicians. I don't get other people saying that they have moved away from their original sound. It's pretty much the same as it's always been: radio-friendly, heavy alternative rock. A break down of the songs.

1. Scream - Pretty standard Halestorm. Lzzy doing quite a bit of screaminess. Not the best.
2. I am the Fire - I really like this one. It's slow and heavy.
3. Sick Individual - Also pretty standard Halestorm. Doesn't stand out that much.
4. Amen - One of the first singles released before the album came out. I didn't like this song at the first listen but it really grew on me. The lyrics are pretty catchy.
5. Dear Daughter - A slow song. Lzzy doing her standard letter of advice/love to a younger girl. It is definitely a vocal showcase.
6. New Modern Love - Doesn't stand out to me much
7. Mayhem - Probably the heaviest song on the album. Also one I didn't really like at first but it grew on me. It's a head banger.
8. Bad Girl's World - Another slow song. It's alright.
9. Gonna get mine - Love the guitar intro and the chorus is definitely a throw back to 80s and 90s rock.
10. The Reckoning - I could see this song coming out of Breaking Benjamin or something.
11. Apocalyptic - I have loved this song since I first heard it released. I think it's one of Halestorm's best. Fast paced, head-banging no-apologies rock.
12. What Sober Couldn't Say - A slow song I actually like quite a bit. There is a bit of word play and some nice vocals by Lzzy.
13. I Like It Heavy - Best song of the album. Reminiscent of Joan Jett's "I love Rock and Roll." I love the bridge into the chorus: "Hallejuah m**therfucker, bring me to church."
14. Jump the Gun - Another great one. Sort of swingy rock with some heavier sounds thrown in.
15. Unapologetic - I love the throaty, soulful verse. The chorus is somewhat of a disappointment.

Definitely a much buy for any Halestorm fan (or any alt rock fan!)

Right from the start the audience is blaringly loud, next level down is the band and backup singers and most difficult to hear is Ms. Ross.

This is a concert from Caesar's Palace in Las Vegas from 1979 and the song list is impeccable and Diana Ross is in top form, what you can hear that is. But looking at the back of the cd it states "RECORDED AT CAESAR'S PALACE, LAS VEGAS, 1979." This would lead one to believe that it was recorded in some way that would be an enjoyable experience for the listener. I'm sure many diehard fans would want a bootleg of any performance of Ms. Ross but I wanted a cd that was of listenable quality, even if it wasn't digitally mastered. Believe me when I say that the entire concert is recorded from the audience which is loud and boisterous and you must concentrate very hard to follow Diana's performance of any song. So deceiving.

Diana Ross did a live album in thge late 70s. HIP-O records is doing masterful digital reissues of her old albums with bonus tracks and superb packaging. The latest edition was TOUCH ME IN THE MORNING and it was just released. Superb. I will wait until the legitimate release of her 70s concert release, hopefully digitally remastered in all its glory. If you choose to purchase this please be aware of what you will be getting. The cd really is of such bad quality that it will be unlistenable to most. (If you check the reviews of the dvd from the same concert it is getting the same negative reviews.) This review is in no way of Diana Ross. Had this been a legitimate concert recording with these songs I would have been in seven heaven.

title: Quietly Honing his Skills in Cleveland (Smart Lad)
text:
06-26-2014 Franz Welser-Most was born on 1960 in the cathedral city of Western Astria, Linz, where Anton Bruckner, that natopn's favorite son was born and as a young man, had been named chief organist for the Linz cathedral organist, advancing to a touring penom with treks to Berlin, London, prague etc.Perhaps my favorite composer, Bruckner's talent for pariently piding his time in the Austrian "backwaters", such as the city of Linz, parallels the still growing career of this bright young and scholarly transplant into the American midwest of Symphony Orchestras. Having inherited George Szell's old orchestra, a very good ensemble in 1947, which Dr. Szell raised to the heights of greatness. Few orchestras, American or not, can boast such improvement in their precision and attention to detail in essentially ALL the music they play as the Clevelenanders, and for that, they, the city's listeneers and the entire world have the great Gorge Szell to thank. His tenure , from 1947 to 1970 was noted for many milestones, however, for me, it has been a disappointment that he laid down so little Bruckner, of which i own a twin pack of the 3rd and the 8th Symphonies, botrh in their 1890 form, (the "final" version of the d minor 3rd, and the Nowackfendition from that same year.) Nither of these versions top my list, as I much prefer the 1878, 2nd editon of 33 AND THE "ORIGINAL 1887, or the Haas version of 1935).
This is, however, not the isue here, as this is a recording of the wonderfully lyrical 7th in E, a lush, plush and reverent tribute in many ways, to the composer's hero, Richard Wagner. Written between 1881 and 1883, the E Major was premiered under Nickitch in Leipzig, far away from the ascerbic pen of the dreaded eduard Hanslick, whom the composer alloweed to become his lifelong nemisis. I say "allowed," because, had Bruckner been a stringer personality, he could of simply, publicly trold the noted Vienese critic to go attack someone else, and while you're at it, "Alzo go jump in zee lake!" For whatever freason, the great Symphonist lacked the backbone to do just that, but, as we all know, the premiere itself was a thunderous success, and, suddenly, ANTON bRUCKNER STOOD IN THE SUN, HE HAD WISHED, AND CERTAINLY PRAYED FOR FOR SO LONG. As quick as a bunny, he began dashing off another huge many, his most beautiful slow movement, with the long, nearly 26-30 minute in le3ngth langsam from the 8th even more gorgeous, and serving as the fulcrum of the grand final trio of valdadictorian Symphonies, #7 thru #9.
WM's opening cello dominated theme with it's celestial bound ascension in the hirns holds us breathless and falls on our ears with an almost angelic temperament. It is little wonder, then, that each movvement, at it's 1884 December 30th premiere had to be encored, and the shy composer from the Ansfelden village of a few hundred souls was deservatrively called, and recalled to the stage several times. This reaction acted like a tonic on the 60 year old cpmposer, who was soon to be named a professor at the cevetted Vienna Conservatory, a position for which he offed prayers of thanksgiving to Almighty God, top whom his final 9th Symphony was formally to be dedicated. Judging by the instant enthusiasm of the London audiences at this live recording, we have an idea how the old Gewandhaus must of sounded nearly 130 years ago. I took a priest friend as my guest to hear this great work in the late 1990's in San Jose California, and when I asked him for his take on it, he smiled and said, "rich!!" And how, and so is this wonderfully recieved performance of one of the Proms more often heard and adored works from anyone, at any time in history. Each movement here is notable for several things, too many to list here, but the Adagio is, of coiurse, a clear standout. ai was impressed with the precision and sharpness of the actual recording, with a minimum of coughing, and much respect being shown by the often rowdy British audience. Here we have the London Philharmonic doing their best to be a peer of the great Cleveland Orchestra, but they are just a tad behind in nearly all respects, and, as such, this is a tribute to that great American ensemble.
In the department of "having one'cs cake and eating it too," the Cleveland has recorded these works, numbers 4,5,7,8 and 9 on DVD's in Severance Hall in the 2000's, and, thud far, a few are also in Blue-ray. i plan on collecting as many of these as I can afford, so I can "see" this great American Orchestra play these pieces as well as hear them. If you act soon, this site can offer you either some of the LPO audio versions and/or the Cleveland video performances for a reasonable price, but don't dally like me, and whith that, I bid you all happy listening to this grseat music, and a warm and sincers God bless ou,all, whether you hailfrom London or the Lakefriont of Ohio. title: I never thought pop music could be SOO good!
text:
Lately, I had been slacking when it comes to getting any new music (although I plan on some more Dream Theater CDs soon...), and felt the need to actually listen to something new, something interesting. So one of my buddies decides to get some new CDs and among those CDs, I heard this awesome CD that I never thought I'd find myself enjoying. Normally, I steer clear of pop music because of its over-saturated mentality and insipid lyrics. But in the case of Pineforest Crunch, they've taken all the qualities that make up a pop album like catchy hooks, catchy lyrics, and simplistic songwriting, and yet still churn out quality music. To that awesome buddy of mine that got this CD, THANKS.

And when listening to it front to back, I felt the same way when I heard Dream Theater's "Images and Words," Iron Maiden's "Somewhere in Time," and Andromeda's "Extension of the Wish"; although mostly different from each other (although with progressive style songwriting), the albums got better and better with each listen. The same is said of Pineforest Crunch's "Panamarenko."

The album kicks off with Situation Endless, an acoustic number with one of the most infectious verses/choruses I've EVOR heard. This WILL stick in your head, and that's THE LAW! I don't know the names of these bandmembers, but this female singer is VERY good. Queen of the 90's follows it, and it's a more entrancing track. With some interesting use of keyboards, this one takes on a midpaced tone, and I'm in a trance every time I hear it; while it doesn't sound very much like Pink Floyd at all, it takes on that same enchanting feeling that that band usually possesses. College Radio Listeners is the third track, and this one is an upbeat number with some good interplay between the vocalist and the guitarist (and it also stabs at college radio in general, which is funny and yet they are very correct in what they say). Definitely one of my top favorites on here. The fourth track and my personal favorite, Slowly, is much darker from anything else on the CD (although Car Crash comes close). This particular track really gets to me, and I couldn't begin to tell you why. Even with its subtle melancholy structure, it's very emotional. The next track, Wake Up, is slightly more upbeat and has a nice piano piece that goes along with the vocals. It also makes great use of the acoustic guitars. Innocent is faster paced and definitely infectious as well. Romantic Strings (appropriately named) is very orchestral in structure, and is especially good with the duets dominating the piece. Car Crash is the second most melancholy track on here, and also one of the poppiest. Definitely my second favorite song from the album. Coronation is hard to describe; it still maintains the pop sensibilities, but at times it sounds vaguely like Nine Inch Nails or any other electronic band, while at other moments (especially towards the middle-to-end parts) it takes on a retro vibe, much like the band Yes (the 80s Yes). Leave It All Behind is an upbeat tune with one of the catchiest bridges and choruses on the disc. This one, in particular, sounds like it could easily go on a show like "Gilmore Girls" or "Dawson's Creek" (y'know, those teen shows where they have a lot of contemporary pop music in them?) and yet is BETTER than any songs on those shows. The album closes with a lovely track called Happy Valentine which is short and sweet, clocking in just under three minutes (it almost sounds like a lullaby!).

Overall, this album turned out to be a very pleasant surprise for me. This Swedish band have the perfect combination of instruments and songwriting and have taken all the great elements of pop music and yet have discarded the genre's dark side. I NEVER, EVOR would have thought that I'd enjoy music like this, but I was proven wrong! While they use slight influences that I've mentioned above, they are still unique Pineforest Crunch. THE LAW approves of this album, and orders that you give a listen NOW!

text:
That's right, this IS the coldest, darkest and the most profoundly depressing album of last year. Every song is a testimony to the misery of human existence, based on some of the most tragic realities of the member's personal experiences. Katatonia gives you no chance, no warning, it sucks every drop of possible joy of life and leaves you sad, lonely and ostracized from supernatural powers you'll perceive to supremely rule over you and...wanting more of it. Thereby lays the genius of Katatonia's sound. No other album last year could invoke such permeating hopelessness in me as "TGCD".
It is so influential, I do not recommend it to kids who are likely to use this as a final call for suicide and let their parents sue the band later...The fact is, if you are already suicidal and depressed, STAY AWAY FROM KATATONIA! It will not bring back bunnies hopping in your backyard. For the rest of us (like me who controls such states with proper, legal medication) "TGCD" offers a mystical, ancient journey into the depths of human soul but does not guarantee you'll come back...The least metal of all twelve, the album has more in common with Tool or Paradise Lost (non-metal years) than with the death/doom metal. It is a CD ANYONE can find accessible and that is precisely why it is so utterly horrifying in its honesty.

title: Good collection to have, with flaws
text:
I've owned this album in vinyl for many years (sans bonus tracks). I've been hoping for a CD release, and together with the additional tracks added, it was great to finally obtain it, and to get several tracks in digital form not available elsewhere. The Lennon-McCartney songs given away at the height of Beatlemania from 1963-1966, familiar to Beatles fans and widely available, are nearly all here, but not the very first cover, "Misery," by Kenny Lynch (UK), nor the first U.S. Lennon-McCartney-written cover, Del Shannon's "From Me To You," (both from 1963). Those ought to have been included.

Starting off with Ringo's 1973 album track "I'm the Greatest," by John Lennon, as did the original vinyl LP, always struck me as out of place, especially since Paul's "Six-O-Clock," from the same source, was not included. Neither were several others written by both for Ringo not long after. But what WAS included, among the bonus tracks, are several superb covers, most notably Wilson Pickett's "Hey Jude" and Peggy Lee's "Let's Love." Again out of place is the Rolling Stones' "We Love You," which is not a Beatles composition, but apparently won inclusion because John and Paul sang backup vocals on it, along with several others.

Another fault would be the volume-level controls, which are way too quiet for the Silkie's "You've Got To Hide Your Love Away," and way too loud for Chubby Checker's "Back In The U.S.S.R.," though that one was an inspired choice, and one I hadn't heard before.

All in all, an essential CD for Beatles fans, despite its flaws. How about if someone made a multi-disk set with omitted tracks included, and this time include George Harrison?

As another said, the Yeah Yeah Yeahs have continued to "mature" into a much more poppy group than they ever were before. "It's Blitz!" isn't a complete failure, but it has no where near the flair that "Fever to Tell" had in it.

Part of what hurts "It's Blitz!", is the fact that Karen O no longer is really center-stage of the music. Now Karen is behind a bunch of synthesizers and violins as she sings with less power than she has ever had in her voice. Only "Dull Life" utilizes the cannon of Karen O, and it is the only track that is truly reminiscent of the "Fever to Tell" days.

"It's Blitz!" does have some fun music in it, though its sad to say that it was done by the Yeah Yeah Yeahs. Some of the songs are very danceable, and both "Skeletons" and "Hysteric" are touching ballads, but in between the great tracks, there are lots of pleasant but disposable ballads.

"It's Blitz!" is better than "Show Your Bones", but is still in many ways a step in the wrong direction. It appears that the Yeah Yeah Yeahs will never again have the garage rock sound that they had for their first EP, and "Fever To Tell". Cheers.

title: Mediocrity from a most unexpected source
text:
Rare is the double album that hits the mark, and Physical Graffitti is no exception. Compared to earlier efforts -- ZOSO and Houses of the Holy in particular -- this offering pales in comparison.
I recall my disappointment as a ninth grader back in 1975, when I was the very first on my block to get it. Things began well enough with Custard Pie, but I remember the nightlong descent from puzzlement to outright disbelief as I played the discs over and over, searching in vain for that album's version of Black Dog. My pals, knowing me for the Zeppelin devotee I was, cornered me the next morning for my review. All I could manage was a tepid "it's not horrible."
No less than Sir George Martin critiqued the Beatles' White Album this way: "I'd rather they'd have done a single great album, than a passable double album." Zeppelin would have done well to reflect seriously on this observation.
Not only is this their last listenable work, but what an overwrought and disappointing note to go out on.

title: U.K.: The Greatest Band You Never Heard Of!
text:
The critics of the era recognized the magnitude of this band at the time, but somehow, the masses didn't bite. The pure musicianship on this album is staggering! I always tend to think of the most powerful musicians on the planet as being those to whom the rest of the musicians are/were listening. Bruford is one of the most highly respected rhythmatists in the world. Holdsworth, despite his low popular profile almost single handedly invented the techniques that Eddie Van Halen would later get credit for and introduce to the masses. Eddie Jobson is a multi-talented keyboard/violin wizard. His keybooard technique is powerful and technically masterful, and his violin playing (electric violin was still quite novel at the time) can often be confused with Holdsworth's fluid, soaring guitar leads. John Wetton is, to me, the consummate "working man's" bassist/vocalist. Despite a marvelously mellow baritone voice, an incredibly deft, technically flawless bass talent and the mindblowing ability two exercise both of these talents simultaneously, John Wetton is no household name. Together they created a single album which is beyond compare.
Own this album! Later U.K. albums are also good, but do not contain this, original U.K. lineup.

title: Knee Deep in Roses
text:
Jeff Black's "Gold Heart Locket" from his [[ASIN:B00008J2T2 B-Sides and Confessions, Vol. 1]] CD went to #1 in my personal top ten. "Free At Last" from [[ASIN:B0009X75VA Tin Lily]] parked @ #2 & the B-Side track "To Be With You" went to #3; so I've consistently enjoyed Jeff's music for a while now.

"Honey & Salt" is an excellent addition to his work. The opener "One Last Day to Live" is a stunning track. The music builds organically like an anthem with Black's vocals passionate and clear, "If you had one last day to live... Would you kiss the one you love, down below & up above; Could you bear the burden of nothing left to prove?" Black sometimes brings the music of Billy Joel to my mind. On "Time," he slows the pace with a soft number with vocals and piano, "I see you in the morning sun, in the flight of the blue heron; I see you in the evening sky, and I see you in my dream." "You Belong to Me" boasts one of Black's classic melodies possibly remembering a lover who has passed, "Sweet reminders of our times above, The wishing well when the penny fell & we turned around to find sweet afterglow of our times below a shooting star; No matter where you are, you belong to me." "Shout from the Street" is another anthem with raging crescendos and stirring vocals, "We'll be stronger than soldiers when we blast the barricade; We'll be knee-deep in roses when we push the big parade." "Persephone" strikes the chord of confession with Jeff's vocals breaking with passion, "Who am I that the world would miss, hiding in her sweetest kiss, dying in her careless crush." Other tracks like the rocking "Rain," the talk-sing "The Leaving" and the gentle closer "Home" are excellent. This is another strong set from one of my lesser known but favorite artists. I hope that his new "Sleepy Town" mp3 will be released in CD format! Enjoy!

title: Second-Tier Rodgers, Third-Tier Hammerstein
text:
The Rodgers and Hammerstein musical Allegro (1947) is one of the most important and historic musicals that most people have never heard of. It was R&H's third show, after Oklahoma and Carousel, and came out shortly after their only musical written directly for the movies, "State Fair," which won them an Oscar for best song ("It Might as Well Be Spring").

Allegro was a serious attempt on Oscar Hammerstein's part to craft an original story, one that contained numerous innovations. It was the first of what we now consider the "concept" musicals, shows that explore a particular idea rather than tell a specific story. The concept here was originally a cradle-to-grave story of a certain earnest everyman. That idea proved untenable, so Allegro wound up being the cradle-to-midlife-crisis story of one Joseph Taylor, Jr.

Hammerstein made significant use of an omniscient sort of Greek chorus, which commented on the action in unison to both the actors and the audience. The production concept represented a break from the literal realism of the time, and featured back-wall projections and a minimal, modular set that was both spare and complicated at the same time. Allegro also represented the beginning of the rise of the director/choreographer, in this case, Agnes de Mille. When we think of director/choreographers, we typically think of the men: Bob Fosse, Michael Bennett, Jerome Robbins, etc. But Agnes de Mille took on this dual role before any of the guys did.

So, Allegro is unquestionably a significant show. It just isn't very good.

Despite the biggest advance sale of any musical up to that time, the show sharply divided audience members and critics when it premiered in 1947. While some thought it sublime and appreciated the sheer ambition and scope of the show, others found it pretentious, preachy, and boring. I happen to fall in the latter camp. In his libretto, Hammerstein expresses the danger of social climbing and rampant materialism, and the result is cold, humorless, and didactic.

But even second-rate R&H is worth savoring, and until now show fanatics have had to make do with the severely truncated original cast recording of Allegro, which is only 33 minutes long. In an attempt to rectify this slight, the Rodgers and Hammerstein Organization has put its considerable resources behind a new studio recording of the score. The treatment is sumptuous, indeed, and features an interdisciplinary cast of the best the musical stage currently has to offer. The recording features Patrick Wilson as the central Joseph Taylor, the sublime Audra McDonald as his mother and opera hunk Nathan Gunn as his father.

But the fact that these terrific performers have very little actual recording time illustrates one of the major problems with Allegro: the best songs go to very minor characters and the Greek chorus. It's hard to work up any sympathy for these people when they do so little singing in the show and on the recording. The two best-known songs from the show are the lovely "So Far" and the rueful "The Gentleman is a Dope," sung respectively by Judy Kuhn and Liz Callaway, who perform these songs and either disappear from the plot entirely, or show up out of nowhere and suddenly we're supposed to care.

The other problem with the show is that the central love story is cynical and empty, which was by design, but makes for a very unsatisfying experience. Joe grows up to wed his childhood sweetheart, Jenny, played here by Laura Benanti. Act 1 ends with their wedding, in which everyone onstage seems to question whether this is really a good idea, including the bride and groom themselves. It's the sort of thing Stephen Sondheim could have pulled off, but Hammerstein seems unable to make it compelling. (Sondheim actually served as a production assistant during Allegro's tryout period, and points to the show as providing inspiration for much of his later work.)

But the most damning evidence in the case against Allegro is the the songs themselves, which, other than the two listed above, simply aren't very good. There's some lovely music here -- and since this recording apparently represents every last note written for the show, we get to savor it all in one package -- but overall this score represents second-tier Richard Rodgers and third-tier Hammerstein. Many of the melodies and rhyme schemes are awkward and forced, and the overall emotional impact of the score doesn't even come close to the power of R&H's best work. It was nice to rediscover some of the songs from the show, including the jaunty title number, but overall I think I'm just going to file this CD into my collection and leave it there.

title: Quite frankly, I wasn't impressed...
text:
This CD is nothing compared to Parachutes, which was actually good. In Parachutes, you had strong, meaningful themes and lyrics, and emotional music that seemingly went straight to your heart. With "A Rush of Blood to the Head", it seems like all they did was unsuccessfully try to re-produce Parachutes' quality, and ended up with a bunch of dull, flat, meaningless songs that really don't do anything for you. They certainly didn't for me, anyway.
I'm sort of wondering where that old Coldplay sound went. I think the fame is getting to their heads, and that they're listening to the fans - and not themselves - far too much. There is only one good song on this entire CD, and that would be the title track. This is only because it sounds the most like the "old" Coldplay. The rest of the album I was honestly bored with.
To the band: did you really want to have mass appeal with this CD so much that you were willing to sacrifice your meaningful lyrics and soulful, original sound? Well, congratulations on making something the new fans would like: another ... pop-influenced album with no emotion in it whatsoever. We didn't need this from you.

Other songs aren't particularly good OR amusing. "Jacket" is a rather dumb tune about how his ex used to borrow his jacket, but now it just reminds him of their breakup. "Rock City News" is a lame song about making it in music. The lyrics include the lines: "Rock city news, you gotta pay your dues at the rock city news, if you want to sing the blues." Original stuff, that.
I'd say two-thirds to three-quarters of this CD is worth listening to. The rest could have been safely left off -- and in the future, the band might want to keep in mind that a CD with eight or nine great tracks is better than one with 10 songs, of which three or four are filler.

ON MAY 5TH(a SUNDAY), I did a radio show during which I played
the new RUSH single ONE LITTLE VICTORY alongside the song FLY BY
NIGHT and I realized what a great band RUSH used to be and what
great songs they used to write. The new single may grow on me, but it sounded too harsh and it made me wish RUSH would start
listening to their earlier albums for musical inspiration instead
of listening to all this newer grungy, non-melodic rock.
FLY BY NIGHT is a wonderful album and probably the best of their
first four albums. The first half is RUSH at their heaviest; RUSH
could make music that was complicated and listenable at the same
time.GEDDY LEE and NEIL PEART were a dynamite rhythm section and
LIFESON was a first rate rhythm guitarist, with what seemed to be
a near endless supply of catchy and original guitar riffs and
guitar licks( i still don't know the difference!) I wasn't a big
fan of his wah-wah guitar solos, but that may be the only gripe
I had with him.ANTHEM, BEST I CAN and BENEATH, BETWEEN, BEHIND
are all hard rock/heavy metal classics and while BYTOR may have
silly lyrics, it's still a powerhouse metal song. Oddly enough,
I prefer the second half, which is more acoustic and melodic, to
the first half of the album. The title track is one of the best
songs RUSH have ever done. It's a very pleasant pop-rock song
with some fine singing from GEDDY. MAKING MEMORIES is also one
of my favorite RUSH songs, with it's acoustic guitars and GEDDY'S
singing giving it a near country rock feel. RIVENDELL is a quite
a bore, but IN THE END is another classic RUSH song, being half
acoustic and half electric and has another very melodic and
emotional vocal line to it, with lyrics from GEDDY himself.
This is a wonderful album, chock full of very memorable hard
rock/acoustic rock songs.
