title: A near complete collection from a criminally underrated band
text:
The Bolshoi’s relatively short career seemed filled with constant change. The recordings in this box set will appeal to all fans in one way or another, though I doubt will be a wholly satisfying experience for anyone, mainly because the band The Bolshoi were upon their first release was very different to the band you hear on the previously unreleased final album, Country Life. This collection is a completely remastered set of almost all of their recordings, with the most obvious things missing being never-on-CD 12” mixes of what may be their most famous song, ‘A Way’ and the re-released ‘A Way II’. Also absent are many single edits, though most of those can be had on a previously released compilation CD, as well as the original mix of the Giants EP, most versions of which have never been on CD.

The remastering has been done by Andy Pearce, who usually does very well at maintaining a good balance between loudness while retaining a good portion of dynamic range. The albums are presented in mini LP replica sleeves with nothing fancy. A tri-fold insert is included with some liner notes, though sadly not by Tanner, and includes basic track information. I would have loved to see lyrics included, but since they weren’t part of any of the original releases, I guess I can’t complain.

The Bolshoi’s 1985 debut mini LP, Giants, was a striking gothic masterpiece. The music is very dark and sinister, despite that it’s sometimes catchy. The classic single ‘Happy Boy’ is about a murderous child delivered with Trevor Tanner’s sarcastic wit and a darkly catchy chorus. ‘Fly’ and ‘Sliding Seagulls’ are both highlights, as well as the chaotic and riotous ‘Hail Mary’. But the pinnacle for me is the frightening ‘By the River’. The song is a perfect blend of echo effects, menacing vocals and music that create a tremendously eerie soundscape that is beyond creepy. It gives me chills and I’ve always felt this song could be translated into a fascinating horror movie with this song playing throughout. It should be noted that the versions included in this set are the remixed versions that appeared on the Bigger Giants compilation, as well as on the U.S. edition of the mini LP.

The plethora of bonus material on the Giants CD includes another of my absolute favorites with another bit of insanity in form of the aggressive ‘Sob Story’, as well as that single’s B sides. A true bonus comes in the form of the hook-filled outtake ‘Billy’s New Boots’. The CD closes out with early takes of what would eventually become some of their signature singles, ‘A Way’, ‘Sunday Morning’ and ‘Books on the Bonfire’. The remastering is strong and definitely sounds better than the previous CD release, though is a little louder on a few tracks than I would prefer.

For this package, the decision was made to use the U.S. EP cover, which is a more traditional band photo instead of the multi-colored and obscured walrus cover of the UK edition, though that is pictured on the disc itself. The track listing on the back of the CD is also the rearranged U.S. running order but the tracks still run in the original UK order. Also, the single version of ‘Happy Boy’ has been replaced with the longer 12” single version, which is the way it was on the original UK 6 track version. Correct track listings are only on the back of the clamshell box.

The band’s first full length album, F(r)iends, was released in 1986 and displayed a more cheerful band, though still with an underlying defiance. Despite the change, it does work to good effect. ‘A Way’ is more radio friendly with a catchy guitar riff and slightly pop feel. ‘Modern Man’ is their first super-catchy head-bopping song, and it’s lots of fun. ‘Someone’s Daughter’ is another poppy song that was prepared for a single, though never released. ‘Sunday Morning’ is more akin to The Bolshoi I loved on Giants. Darkly catchy with a potentially controversial anti-religion sentiment. Now that’s my kind of subject matter. ‘Looking for a Life’ is the only real aggressive song, though still shiny and catchy. ‘Romeo in Clover (Call Girls)’ has a great hook, though could have benefited from being edited down a little. ‘Books on the Bonfire’ has a sort of schizo-waltz tempo with some interesting guitar work.

The bonus material is pretty good. ‘Razzle Dazzle’ is a very dark and moody piece, and one of my favorites. This was originally the B side of the ‘A Way’ single. Unfortunately, this remastered track does not sound so hot. My vinyl is clean and clear, the CD transfer shows excessive tape hiss and overdone high end. It may just be due to a master tape that’s been in storage for the past 30 years not being fully revived to its former glory. The album tracks are a definite improvement on the previous CD releases. The unreleased ‘Toys Xmas Party’ is more of a novelty and seems to be clearly influenced by The Stranglers’ well known B side story about Vladimir, at least in structure.

The third release, Lindy’s Party, is starting to show a band running a little lower on ideas, and even moving a little towards the dance floor, but still with some of their eccentricities. ‘Auntie Jean’ is a pleasant album opener, though not particularly stunning or original. Definitely more dance oriented. Adding further to that is the single ‘Please’. Of the various versions of this song, the album version is my favorite. It’s got a very thunderous sound that is tempered on the single release. ‘Crack in Smile’ is where things get really boring for me. Things pick up again with the listener friendly ‘Swings and Roundabouts’. ‘She Don’t Know’ is a bit bland and repetitious. The single ‘TV Man’ has a more pleasantly familiar Bolshoi feel. The album drops off again until the sinister circus that is ‘Barrowlands’. The album highlight is a title track ‘Lindy’s Party’. This longer song starts very soft and quiet but gradually builds to and enthusiastic climax. A great way to end a so-so album. The remastering on this CD is very strong and far surpasses previous editions.

But then The Bolshoi were gone, though news of a shelved fourth release, titled Country Life, circled for years. Was this myth or truth? Well, maybe a little of both. I was always under the impression that Country Life was a fully mixed master tape that just didn’t get sent to production, but what comprises the unreleased album, now represented for the first time in this box set, is a collection primarily of demos from various sources, including master tapes and cassette tapes, complete with heavy tape hiss and the occasional fluctuation and drop out. But at least the mystery is finally solved.

Although, for this listener the revelation is a bit anti-climactic. Country Life shows that the band who started as a powerful and original Gothic force continued their trend towards the bland. I’m sorry to say that out of over 20 tracks from what could have been the official Country Life album back in the late 80s, I only found 7 tracks worthwhile. Two tracks are great but the others are just good.

‘World in Action’ is a great, though misleading way to open the album. It’s a drum heavy, hook filled classic. ‘Country Life’ is a pleasant enough song, though the keyboards definitely give it a dated sound, though I do like it. ‘Too Late’ sounds like a Lindy’s Party outtake, and it’s the other track that really stood out as one of the best. I also don’t mind ‘Delores Jones’, ‘Madame Hecate’, ‘Singing the Blues’ and ‘Rockin’ Bird’, but other than that I found the rest of the tracks devoid of any sort of hook. There was a lot of bland meandering that gives the impression that maybe the band called it a day for a reason.

I’m very happy that Beggars Banquet finally decided to pillage the vaults to bring us what will likely be most comprehensive representation of The Bolshoi material ever to be released. Despite what era of the band that any fan enjoys the most, you will find plenty to enjoy with the wealth of material represented here. Well done.

title: Yes, I'll Have a Bite After All
text:
First impressions of this album were tepid. The opening track doesn't punch you in the face like "The Hollow" did, or ask you what the hell MJK was smoking when he decided on vocals for "The Package."

Then you ease into "Disillusioned," which might be the closest thing to "The Hollow" you could ever hope to expect from a band, and you realize this is in fact an APC album.

And honestly, after at least a dozen front-to-back listens I think this may be my favorite APC album in their catalog (And yes, I did revisit their catalog a couple times while listening to Eat the Elephant).

Sounds like Blasphemy! "Nothing could touch Mer de Noms." Yeah, I understand, I felt the same way before I even went into it. I was almost content with APC hanging it up and leaving their work as is. And that album cover... *shudder*. I suppose I was only feeling what truly APC devout are supposed to going into EtE; "this isn't going to live up to the first 2 albums." Initial impressions after the first couple listens; Billy didn't play the guitar enough, and Maynard is getting too old and sanctimonious, and DAMN this is a dark, depressing album.

But really, when you get past the issue of this "not being metal enough" and move away from what you think APC is "supposed" to be, this is excellent music. Billy laid off on the guitars but more than made up for it with insane choreography and excellent instrumentation. The harmonies, the bridges and choruses; it's obvious these were the product of considerable labor and revision. Movement in "The Doomed" between the harrowing sustain during Maynard's guttural passages transitioning into an angelic chorus of beatitudes, signature change and all, is pretty intense. Or the pummeling you'll receive as the massive wall of sound crashes down during the chorus of "TalkTalk." It seems alien at first and wrong, a bit too slow and lethargic, but after you move out of that APC paradigm, you realize it actually sounds better than anything you expected.

MJK's words are timely in their context while refraining from some of the pretense I felt was a big part of what dragged Thirteenth Step down. It's certainly an improvement from EMOTIVE and AMOTIVE, I hope we can agree there. The lyrics definitely touch on social, religious and political overtones relevant now, but there's enough restraint and abstraction to keep them from being too obvious. They are weighty and fairly bleak with glimmers of optimism. "Delicious" espouses the justice we're all hoping to find in a world that seems unfair, and "TalkTalk" suggests personal agency in an apathetic world. It also helps that Maynard sounds better on this album than he has in years: miles ahead of anything he's done with Puscifer, and really even more impressive than most of what he laid down in 10,000 Days.

I could go on, instead I'll just simply say I'm really am enjoying this album. I don't expect these two to keep up a stream of work going forward, but having them check in every decade or so is very much welcome. Next time however, do something better with the album cover, because the grotesque look doesn't work here and it's badly implemented.

text:
Never a Dull Moment's only problem is that it's too short of an album. Rod Stewart was really pumping out quality songs at this point in his career, and he knew it, which is why this album has become a classic over the years. "You Wear It Well" is NOT the same thing as "Maggie May", haha. Some people think the two songs sound the same, and I agree to an extent. The vocal melodies sure sound similar.

His cover of "Angel" is pretty fantastic, but there's only ONE Jimi Hendrix, baby. The emotions are probably just as strong in this version though. You can tell in the way Rod *really* means it when he sings that vocal melody.

"True Blue" is another great track that many people might recognize... maybe not. I don't know what Rod Stewart songs are played on the radio these days. I highly doubt radio stations these days are willing to go far back in time and dig up some forgotten favorites, but who knows.

I really love Rod's version of "Twistin' the Night Away". There's only one Rod Stewart, because no one else I've ever heard even comes CLOSE to having that same kind of pleasant hoarse voice. He really takes this song to a new level of excitement. It no longer sounds like a party song- Rod turned it into a very pretty track.

A must own for Rod Stewart fans.

title: Slowblow makes excellent music for a beautiful film.
text:
This music soundtrack to the debut feature length film by Dagur Kari is mostly free of vocals. Kari is also part of the band Slowblow, originally from Iceland.
You start arguing with yourself about which instruments are your favorites nearly half way through the soundtrack... is it the piano or five-string guitar?
The minimalism of the music works well this gorgeous full-length film that finally came to the US this year. The first scenes of four feet high snowdrifts permeate the atmosphere of this soundtrack. The introduction of electric guitar ponders and glides like a skater across a frozen pond with a haunting musical saw simulating a winter wind.
Thank goodness we hear more of this saw sound again later into the soundtrack.
"Hillbilly" is a banjo-piano melodic piece calling to old Appalachian memories.
The piano work is dramatic and sometimes evokes a feeling of stark loneliness or the melodies are reminiscent of old time merry-go-rounds.
"Komdu Litla Barn" is a non-Slowblow track by Sigridur Nielsdottir that fits perfectly with the sentiment.
"Elegy" is a string track by a non-Slowblow quartet--exquisitely inspirational.
"Groove" is a rich rock 'n' roll instrumental that takes the soundtrack to a different level temporarily, but at least we hear all the Slowblow potential to be ready for their next release on Bubblecore Records.
Their first two albums, Quicksilver Tuna and Fousque, are now out of print. Quicksilver Tuna contains "Is Jesus Your Pal?" which was later covered by Gus Gus on the album Polydistortion.
If you like "Aim for a Smile"--the last track from Noi Albinoi which is used in the end credits, then you should try to look for the soundtrack album Popp in Reykjavik (a documentary film about the Icelandic music scene from 1999), which contains another pop song from Slowblow called "Flirt" with vocalist Emilionu. "Aim for a Smile" is not actually straight on pop but a very emotional sounding style that is addictive upon hearing.
I think this is a hopeful start in getting this band heard through film because they do have an introspective style that is well-suited to the big screen.

title: THE essential Madonna Album
text:
Ever since I bought this album back in 1998, I can understand Madonna as an artist and respect her artistic and musical credibility. From the mellow, density of the opening track, "Drowned World", you feel the direction the album is headed and can understand why this woman writes and performs music. The song is a poetic commentary on fame and how unrewarding it has been for her.
You then voyage into the realm of "Swim", another slower song about the media and their negative effects on society. Then comes the commericially successful title track that was a dance and a raido hit in the summer of 1998, complete with an award-winning video. The track is an upbeat evaluation of how significant and insignificant our actions and lives are at the same time.
The albums tames itself slightly with "Candy Perfume Girl", a rocky, guitar-heavy song with some firey imagery. Next is the tribal and euphoric "Skin" that builds froma quiet moan to a full out orgasmic frenzy of sound, beat, and heat. It asks a question and makes a demand at the same time. Phenomenal.
Next up is "Nothing Really Matters", another American single releases around Valentine's Day 1999. The song is a slower dance song that comments about the lack of value of the materail world. Next is the anthematic mantra "Sky Fits Heaven", a song that has forever made me think about the importance of realizing that there is no day but today and there is no one looking out for me but me. We are briskly swept into "Shant/Ashanti", a sandskrit chant meets yoga workout hybrid. The heartfelt "Frozen" follows which is a song about learning how to accept one's past and hope for a future.
The techno0savvy ballad "The Power of Goodbye" follows discusses the importance of relationships and how traumatic and inspiring they can be. "To Have Not To Hold" follows along the smae lines, but with a tad more of longing for the one that got away thrown in there.
Onto "Little Star" a lullaby for her then baby daughter. Rounding out the set is "Mer-Girl", a creepy, part dream, part acid trip of a song addressing Madonna's mother's death and the impact of death and life.
All in all, aphenomenal album. If any of you have read this entirely too long review and still think of Madonna as a cheeky twenty-something panting to "Like a Virgin" or wanting us to strike a pose, think again. Reinvent yourself, and if you need a hint, I think there is something else you may need to about Madonna.

title: not an good album...unfortunately
text:
After the massive hit that was "OK Computer" Radiohead decide to surprise listeners even further by relasing this surrealist conceptual "dark side of the moon" fourth album of theirs named "Kid A". Unfortunately, instead of constructing more beautiful music, they achieve this somewhat unfocused unaccomplished kerfuffle of ideas that has in the least, absolutely nothing to do with them. The really dissapointing part is that there is hardly any melody in any of the songs save for the gorgeous but opressing "how to disapear completely" and the depressing "motion picture soundtrack". That's already 2 songs. The rest is just bulls***.
The opener "Everything in its right place" sounds like a guy discovering midi instruments and recording baby voices. A fun track but for an opening surprise, a poor achievement. The next track, Kid A, is unnoticeable, in fact I often skip it.On it, Thom's singing, if you can call that singing, is hardly comprehensible. I heard the lyrics were something to do about "rats and children". It's a shame because the idea of computerised music was good but it should have built up to a climax, instead of dwelling nowhere for 4 minutes. The next song, "National Anthem", one of the highlights of Kid A does however build up to a climax.This un-anthem starts off with a beat similar to "Talk show host", for those who have seen the recent Romeo and Juliet, and kicks off with a funky bass, Thom sings "everyone around here, everyone is so near , what's going on?" , the rhythm keeps going, Thom repeats the same words, then brass kicks in, slowly building to an explosive chaos of trumpets screaming, then stopping, and screaming again.It ends with a distorted real "national anthem" in the background and finally stops there... In other words, what the f***?

"How to disappear" is a beautiful piece, the highlight of Kid A and clearly sounds like it could have been on OK Computer, or belongs to "post-OK Computer", the visions of a buried world clearly arising out of the fading in and out violins and brass that have forever replaced what was once guitars..It is beautiful imagery although the song doesn't hit you quite the same way as the similar "Lucky" did. After five minutes of lament about non-existence, the piece dissolves into an insturmental atmospheric "Eno" esque 4 minute piece of peaceful organ and synths, sounding like a track that could be found on any music to relax at home in your bath, but unfortunately nothing much more. Three minutes, four notes. In other words, compared to how far Radiohead have gone before, another what the f***?
After this comes the earthy "optimistic", where Thom Yorke actually sings, at last, but not very interestingly. He sounds like a genius who understands everyting about the world and the lyrics are kind of simplistic: "big fish eat the little ones" and "animal farms". I just don't know why this track is called optimistic, because it feels very neutral, very observational. A great track to promote nature. Musically, though it is not bad for it actually sees the band playing together, but in terms of depth it could have been a better song. For instance rather than adding organs, they should have kept doing something with guitars, and maybe doing something like Paranoid Android, by speeding up, building up to a climax and slowing down again, you know doing something, dammit. That's what's strongly missing in Kid A: climax. I wish there was one song that got to the top, that was worth listening to but even the "national anthem" dsoesn't do it for me. After changing into a soft "dasnce" track for one minute "Optimistic" becomes "In limbo", an intertwined combination of guitar arpeggios, synth loops, and light drumming with Thom humming soft words such as "I lost my way", "trap doors that open wide". This song flows well but its not a song, really, it's more like an interlude between "otimistic" and the next track, the raw and aggressive "idioteque" kicking off with pounding beats, hardcore electronic chords (that have the same effect as if guitars were there). Its a great piece but the irritating beats, synth noises along with Thom's irritating singing and convoluted voices, make it almost impossible to listen to enjoyably. That's track no 8 by the way so there' only 2 more songs. "Morning Bell" follows. Thom is very plaintive there and the depressing feeling that its the end soon takes over so strongly that by the time "Motion picture soundtrack" arrives, you just can't stand it. It is downright suicidal stuff. Way too depressing for me.
As you see, Kid A does not have a lot to offer for me. Some people say this is "artistic" music. It may very well be, but it is still one of the Radiohead albums I least enjoy listening to, and I think it is highly overrated.

The fact that it was released as an album rather than an-ep is hard to digest, because all inall there is only about four or five songs on Kid A, the rest being interludes, or experimental aqttempts.I guess If I knew Radiohead were releasing an e-p called "Kid A" and sold it as an e-p not an album, then I would consider it to have probably been a nearby masterpiece.

Recovery is Eminem fully evolved into what the game is today.. and this album proves that he is still the man to beat in terms of Rap royalty - No, not Jay-Z.. Eminem is the real king of rap - and long live the king - he's back.

title: A Synesthetic Experience
text:
OK its not easy for me to give a 5 star rating without questioning myself about doing so. To my knowledge there are only but less then a handful of albums I own that command such an honor. After several hundred listens, I question no more... this is a 5 star album.

Firstly it is not an album that everyone will love. Indeed I know many people that hate it! Quite simply, if you are expecting the instant gratification of an 'anthemic' track or the dancibility of a Ministry of Sound Annual album... then you will be sorely disappointed.

Nevertheless, if you want an album to take you on a journey to lala land and beyond then buy this CD now!

Involver breaks the stereotype of a clinical/sterile electronic album with repetitive beats and a catchy hook. Damit this album is what Electronic music is (should be) all about; smashing conventional boundaries and exploring new musical dimensions. Through the use of Ableton Live, Sasha has been able to recreate not just remix... and the results are very very special.

Sasha makes a typically majestic entrance with Grand National's brit-pop infused "Talk Amongst Yourselves". It's a beautifully detached track that gives us the perfect introduction to the album's ethereal like landscape.

The album continuously layers and builds using minimal yet fulfilling vocals, break-beats/rolling beats/no beats!, rock infused percussive elements (along with the occasional guitar chord or two) , subtle tempo changes and all together flawless production. From the dreampop of UNKLE's "What You Are To Me?" cleverly layered over Petter's "These Days" to the orgasmic peak of Spooky's "Belong" and UNKLE's "In a State"... this is one truly mind-blowing journey.

It is not until you hit Felix Da Housecat's cheeky and catchy "Watching Cars Go By" are you in the midst of a track likely to be heard at a club anytime in the near future. When this bows out to the gorgeous "On My Own" by Ulrich Schnauss... you realize that Sasha's Involver is a daring effort in everyway possible. Failing to have these two tracks beat match in any respectable manner... Sasha instead speeds up "Watching Cars Go" By (as Sasha says in the descript) `turning the whole track into high hats' and then goes in for the kill with the standout track of the album, "On My Own"... which is sadly also the final track of this voyage!

Many people won't like this album and perhaps in many ways it fails to fulfill many common elements of what makes a good `dance' album... What those people fail to recognize is Involver's revolutionary nature... setting new boundaries, writing new laws on how to make music and exploring new worlds that only music can take us to.

title: The famous composer Brassy-Mussorgsky
text:
You've certainly heard the old story already: an illeterate radio host announces "and now we shall hear the Pictures at an Exhibition by the composer Mussorgsky-Ravel". When it is over he announces it off: "thanks for the phone calls from astute listeners, you will have all corrected for yourselves, it was of course the Pictures at an Exhibition, composed by Mussorgsky and orchestrated by Ravel. And now, to complete our program of Russian music, we shall hear Scheherazade, composed by Rimsky and orchestrated by Korsakov."

Of course Tableaux were not composed by "Mussorgsky-Ravel", and although Ravel's orchestration is the most popular and commonly played, there are many others. So there is a strong legitimacy for scoring it for brass band, as did Elgar Howarth and as performed by John Wallace and his brass band The Wallace collection (with the Night at the Black Mountain to boot, orchestrated by Alan Wilsthire with a strong array of percussion, and the adagio from Khachaturian's Spartacus, arranged by Jonn Miller). And anyway, even if there weren't any such rationale, the only true legitimacy for a transcription is: how effective and pleasurable is it.

And this one is. The timbres of the brass band are particularly suited to the music of Mussorgsky. There is nothing grey or repetitive about the brass ensemble, it conjures a range of timbral colors that has nothing to envy from the symphony orchestra. The low brass, trombone and tuba, add dark overtones (or shall I write "undertones"?), either suitably gloomy (The Old Castle), ponderous (Bydlo) or threatening (Night, Gnomus, Catacombae, Baba Yaga). The upper range (trumpets) of the ensemble is suitably saucy when needed (just try the beginning of Night, or the lighter numbers of Tableaux: Tuileries, Ballet of the Unhatched Chicks, Schmuyle). You almost get the impression that there is a flexatone in "Cum Mortuis in Lingua Mortua" (track 15). Any amateur of Mussorgsky's Tableaux will enjoy this, and it gives a fresh view on the old warhorse.

title: My *FAVORITE* CD: the rock opera to end all rock operas!!!!
text: I got this CD for Christmas last year and am giving it as a gift this year, 'cause this CD ROCKS!!! As both a fan of the TSO and a lover of all things Beethoven, I was completely blown away!!! Just imagine all the fire and passion of Beethoven's music in all its' glory set within a rock opera in which the devil (Mephistopheles) plots to steal Beethoven's music along with the composer's immortal soul. On what Beethoven learns is to be the last night of his life, the devil appears and informs the horrified composer that he has come at last to collect his soul. He then makes Beethoven (who has just now completed a manscript for hia final and greatest masterpiece, a 10th symphony) an offer:: he will allow the composer to live awhile longer, but the price is the destruction of all of Beethoven's music for all time! Given one hour to make his choice, Beethoven angrily confronts the beautiful embodiment of Fate, in the belief that painful events from his past are the cause for his apparent damnation. Taken aback, Fate offers to change anything that he wishes, but the composer soon realizes that to remove any of these painful events from his life would also remove the inspiration for much of his finest work. And when Fate reminds him of the joy and comfort that his music has--and will continue--to bring to so many, he decides that he would not change anything after all. When the devil returns to find his offer refused, he makes the same offer in exchange for only the unreleased 10th symphony which, he reasons, no one will miss. But then the spirit of his old mentor, Mozart, appears to warn Beethoven that his 10th symphony is the voice of God and that he must not allow this music to be destroyed; Beethoven once again refuses Mephistopheles' offer. The devil, desperate to claim this 10th symphony, then resorts to threatening the life of a little orphan girl who is sleeping outside Beethoven's door. The composer tries to tell himself that he is not responsible for this child, but, in the end, he cannot bear the thought of her suffering at the devil's hands and agrees to give up his final work in exchange for the child's safety.`The devil rejoices in his "victory"...until a twist of "Fate" saves both the man and his musical legacy. This CD is an absolute MUST for anyone who has ever wondered what Beethoven's music would sound like set to a rock'n'roll beat...simply AWESOME!!!

text: Parliament made three fabulous albums from 1975-1977, two of them high concept classics that define the group and establish their enduring legacy and one that is a little bit less serious. A great album all by itself, well worth hearing.

title: Enriching
text: One may question the value of an introduction to Rautavaara's music that does not contain one of his Symphonies.  Nevertheless, this is a highly rewarding set.  The ubiquitous Cantus Arcticus receives a lovely performance, although the composer's tape of birdsong is sounding a little dated and shop worn.  Angel of Dusk is a brilliant work for double bass and orchestra, and it showcases a wealth of differing techniques from the soloist.  The performance here is a tape of the premiere, and it sounds exquisite.  The String Quartet No. 2, from 1958 and the composer's serialist period, creates brilliant atmospheres and subtle tensions.  The Sibelius Quartet's playing is stunning, and they are beautifully recorded.  The works for strings on the second disc are really the heart of the collection.  The Cantos, two serialist and one tonal, are intimate and yet virtuosic.  They are profoundly moving.  The Epitaph for Bela Bartok includes string figurations familiar from the Music for Strings, Percussion, and Celesta and the Concerto for Orchestra.  The Hommage a Zoltan Kodaly is a major work in all of 16 minutes, a sort of summation of Rautavaara's technique.  A Requiem for Our Time, composed when Rautavaara was 25, is a warmly Neoclassical piece, beautifully conducted by Jorma Panula.  Perhaps the first piece of Rautavaara's one should hear is the Seventh Symphony, but after that this set would be a welcome appendage.

title: My Favorite Aerosmith Compilation
text:
O, Yeah! Ultimate Aerosmith Hits, released in July 2002, is an Aerosmith compilation.

Aerosmith is, with out a doubt, "America's Greatest Rock "N" Roll Band." There are many other great classic rock bands, but they were from different countries. Pink Floyd (England), Led Zeppelin (England), Queen (England), The Beatles (England), The Rolling Stones (England), and Rush (Canada). Do we see a pattern here? There are many legendary classic rock bands from England. So Aerosmith isn't the best ever, just in America they are.

Kicking this album off is 'Mama Kin' and 'Dream On', both from Aerosmith's debut album, "Aerosmith." I'm always happy to see 'Mama Kin' on a compilation, because it's an excellent song. 'Dream On' is also here, but that's no surprise, since it's one of Aerosmith's top five songs of all time.

From "Get Your Wings" come the songs 'Same Old Song And Dance' and 'Seasons Of Wither'. This is the full version of 'Same Old Song And Dance' and not the heavily edited copy found on "Aerosmith's Greatest Hits." (Note: I'm going to bash Aerosmith's Greatest Hits, because it has major editing problems.) 'Seasons Of Wither' is a nice song, but not the second best song on "Get Your Wings." 'Train Kept A Rollin' holds that title, but it's not here. Why? Who knows? It's an excellent cover but it's not found on "O, Yeah!".

'Walk This Way', 'Big Ten Inch Record', and 'Sweet Emotion' are the songs from Aerosmith's best album, "Toys In The Attic". This is the full, four-and-a-minute version of 'Sweet Emotion' and not the edited version found on Aerosmith's Greatest Hits. Two excellent songs missing from "Toys In The Attic" are 'No More No More' and 'Toys In The Attic'. It's nice to see 'Big Ten Inch Record' appear on an Aerosmith compilation, but 'Toys In The Attic' would have been a better choice.

From the album "Rocks" come the songs 'Last Child' and 'Back In The Saddle'. 'Back In The Saddle' is one of Aerosmith's best songs, along with 'Last Child'. But where's 'Rats In The Cellar', one of Aerosmith's most underrated gems?

'Draw The Line' is the only song on "O, Yeah!" from the album "Draw The Line". 'Draw The Line' has an excellent riff, and it's a very catchy song. But where in the world is 'Kings and Queens'. It's just one more missing gem, not making the cut for "O, Yeah!".

Now the compilation skips three albums, "Night In The Ruts", "Rock In A Hard Place", and "Done With Mirrors". These definitely are not Aerosmith's best albums, but they still had a few good songs. Songs like 'Remember (Walking In The Sand)', 'Jailbait', and 'Let The Music Do The Talking'. It's not a huge disappointment, but they should have at least put 'Remember (Walking In The Sand)' on "O, Yeah!".

"Permanent Vacation" kicked off Aerosmith return to the spotlight, with songs like 'Dude (Looks Like A Lady)', 'Angel', and 'Rag Doll'. All three of these songs deserve to be here. 'Permanent Vacation' would have been nice, but it's no big deal. 'Angel' was Aerosmith's first major ballad and they would have many more ballads in the albums to come.

Next we come to one of my personal favorites, "Pump". It's just one of those albums where every song is excellent. Making the cut for "O, Yeah!" are 'Janie's Got A Gun', 'Love In An Elevator', 'What It Takes', and 'The Other Side'. Other excellent songs on Pump that didn't make it were 'Young Lust', 'F.I.N.E.', and 'Monkey On My Back'. No huge disappoint about those songs not making the cut.

Now on to the so-called ballad album, "Get A Grip." The album's not all ballads, there are still rock songs, but they are not as well known as the ballads. The songs from "Get A Grip" include 'Livin' On The Edge', 'Cryin', 'Amazing', and 'Crazy'. All but 'Livin' On The Edge' are ballads. The non-ballad songs that didn't make O, Yeah! were 'Eat The Rich', 'Fever', and 'Walk On Down'.

From the album "The Beavis and Butt-Head Experience" comes the song 'Deuces Are Wild'.

'Falling In Love' and 'Pink' from "Nine Lives" made their way onto O, Yeah. 'Falling In Love' was a good choice, but I'd rather have 'Hole In My Soul' over 'Pink'.

Next, from the "Armageddon Soundtrack" is Aerosmith's only Billboard Hot 100 number one hit, 'I Don't Want To Miss A Thing'. This is easily one of my favorite Aerosmith songs of all time, and it deserves to be here with other Aerosmith classics.

From their 2001 album "Just Push Play", come two songs, 'Jaded' and 'Just Push Play'. "Just Push Play" is one of their worst albums ever, and these two songs are no exceptions.

To close the album off, you have two bonus tracks and a rap version of 'Walk This Way'. That's terrible. Rap and Aerosmith just don't go together. It was a bad idea to recorded the song in the first place, let alone place it on an Aerosmith greatest hits compilation. The bonus tracks are ordinary songs, and nothing to get excited over.

In the end, you get an Aerosmith compilation loaded with 30 unedited songs, for a sale price of under 20 bucks. That's not a bad deal considering it's the best Aerosmith compilation out there. I'll end my review with a list of missing songs and a list of excellent Aerosmith albums to start a collection with.

Missing Songs:

1. Train Kept a Rollin'

2. Toys In The Attic

3. No More No More

4. Rats In The Cellar

5. Kings And Queens

6. Remember (Walking In The Sand)

7. Permanent Vacation

8. Monkey On My Back

9. Eat The Rich

10. Fever

11. Hole In My Soul

The Six Albums Every Aerosmith Fan Must Have:

1. Get Your Wings

2. Toys In The Attic

3. Rocks

4. Pump

5. Get A Grip

6. A Little South Of Sanity (Two-disc live album)

title: More is less, I'm afraid
text:
I love Little Feat. I was sixteen when I met them in a small club in Ann Arbor, Michigan, no kidding, and got to hang out with them backstage...this was when Roy Estrada was in the band. They were funny and smart and everything you wished a band to be. They kept calling Creedence Clearwater Revival "Cretins Coldwater." I suppose because they were on some kind of similar "roots" circuit. Richie did say, "they have some good songs." I went back the next night and they were THE best band I'd ever heard live. This said...This record in its re release is the same record I bought a few years later and tossed. Sadly.

One example. People love "Dixie Chicken," but it's a song, not an excuse for an extended synth/electric piano solo. The song is a narrative, and it's a great one, probably one of if not the best ever written in pop. But Payne's solo just wrecks the thing. I love Payne, but... It's a song, not a jam. It's a story, not an excursion to even then arch "sonic frontiers." Other, later and lesser songs had room for the noodling.

This is just one example because I don't want to waste your time. Get the first three CDs, or better the records on vinyl, and maybe the fourth one, because it has a couple of pre-noodlemeister tracks.

Lowell George, god bless him, was one of a kind. Rhythm and booze mixed with pure genius. God bless Little Feet. But I think, if Lowell had sobered up, he'd have cut most of the chatter. Great band, great playing....but Little Feat should never have become a Dreadful Grate Revisited, and this is where it was heading.

You have no idea how much it hurts me to write this, because these guys were the first band I ever admired, the first ever to autograph a record for me. I love Roy's note under his photo: "Chinga or Chingow, either one." True fact. And Hayward drew an airplane with a banner across the blue sky. It was a middle finger, with a banner. First record. You'll know what I mean. Get the first three and glory!

title: King Eno continues his reign
text:
The review of this new Eno album in Rolling Stone has the subheading "The godfather of ambient rocks out -- finally!" When I started listening to Small Craft for the first time, I thought "where's the rocking out?" In fact, there are more ambient style or otherwise atmospheric pieces on this all-instrumental album than rockers, but there are definitely also times where the godfather "lets loose" too. The first such "rocking" place comes four tracks in, with "Flint March" and its tribal beats. Then "Bone Jump" has a nice funky bass tone, but I wouldn't exactly call it a "rocker." "Dust Shuffle" gets a good groove going, and "Paleosonic" even has something like an electric guitar solo. Anyway, I very much enjoyed all of those cuts, but the spacey stuff is what I really go to Eno for, and Small Craft contains some of his very best work.

Take the two bookend pieces, "Emerald and Lime" and "Emerald and Stone." They're beautiful piano/synth reveries - heavenly. For a more classic "ambient" sound, listen to the nearly eight-minute-long "Late Anthropocene" which closes the album. There, sustained tones overlap and weave in and out of each other in a sublime swirl of electronics, punctuated by mysterious artificial percussion noises that add background color to the piece. Marvelous! There are many fellow practitioners of this electro-instrumental genre (ex., Trent Reznor), but nobody does it as superbly as Brian Eno. Long may he reign!

I must admit that this album at first reminded me of Madonna's jump into the Electronic music realm, but there's a big difference. Seal's been there before. Seal has taken a break from his great depressing masterful songs. This time he goes back to the electronic realm. A jump that I like! I've been a fan of Seal since "Prayer for the dying". This album doesn't disappoint. Probably because I'm a huge fan of Electronic music.
I think a lot of people are disappointed because they may feel they're past the whole "Dance music" thing. A lot of his fans have grown older. Maybe their tastes have changed as have mine somewhat. That doesn't mean that this is not a great album. "System", "Immaculate" and "Rolling" are a few of my own personal favorites. All the songs here have Seal's personal touch which is great! Sure, this CD may not have the same type of emotion that the others have, but it's still quite good! Maybe Seal is not dealing with the same life issues that he was dealing with when he did those other albums, but I'm glad he decided to come out with what he thought was appropriate.

title: A Lighter Shade of Brown
text:
Without a doubt, Ween was one of the most creatively wigged-out bands in the history of rock music, recording a series of albums that rival and, in most cases, surpass other records in the whole experimental/freak/weirdo genre. From their early four-track days as a drugged-out duo to their later incarnation as a polished full band, Ween laid down some of the most surreal, demented, WTF? pop ever. However, in recent years the once seemingly infallible band appeared to be phoning it in, becoming increasingly sporadic in both their live shows and the studio. Their 2007 release, La Cucaracha, was by far their weakest, and remains the only blemish on their otherwise top-shelf discography. More disturbing, at a gig in Vancouver during 2011, main man Gene Ween (Aaron Freeman) had an onstage meltdown for the ages, resulting in the rest of the band walking offstage. Confusion and speculation abounded- Had the creative well run dry? Was substance abuse finally taking its toll? Had the brown turned black? Was it just a fluke? Turned out it was a combination of all these factors, and the only band member who seemed willing to face facts was Aaron.

In 2012, Aaron retired Gene Ween, left the band abruptly, breaking it up much to the dismay of fans and other band members alike. It is a shame that Ween ended, but in retrospect it seems necessary as Aaron's health, and possibly, his life were in jeopardy. Having emerged in better condition, Aaron offers up this wildly imaginative solo effort displaying a sense of wonder and vulnerability along with his usual command of melody and song craft, sometimes characterized by a familiar brown, but with some Technicolor moments thrown in for good measure.

Honestly, Freeman is not far removed from later era Ween albums, coming off as a hybrid of The Mollusk and White Pepper. For all intents and purposes it plays like a lost Ween record, in essence acting as the true follow-up to the brilliant Quebec (rather than the flaccid La Cucaracha), despite the absence of Deaner and the rest of the band. Songs are largely in the vein of Ween offerings such as "Exactly Where I'm At," "Tried and True," and "Ocean Man"- effects-laden, breezy psychedelic pop with glimmeringly lush melodies, all capped off with Aaron's distinctive vocals. Standout tracks include the hook-filled "The English and Western Stallion," the nursery rhyme-like "Black Bush," and the soaring "Golden Monkey".

Pondering exactly what the creative roles were in Ween, it often appeared as though Deaner was more the musician and Gene the singer/songwriter. Truth is they probably met somewhere in the middle, but on Freeman, the former Gene Ween proves that he is both a more than capable musician and singer/songwriter on his own, sounding fresh and re-energized with a new lease on both his music and life. Aaron is now indeed a free man...

title: Great album, solidly in the tradition of the original Flying Burrito Brothers...
text:
To tell you the truth I didn't expect much, but I heard a couple tracks on Youtube and they sounded good so I bought the CD. Now that I've had time to listen to the whole album I'm even more convinced.

If you're one of those "if it ain't got Gram it ain't the Burritos" people then you might as well just go away -- but you'd be missing a lot of good music -- the 'refried' Burritos of the 70s, the Nashville Burritos of the 80s, the John Beland groups of the 90s, and Burrito Deluxe in the 21st century. The Burrito line-up on this CD evolved out of the last line-up of Burrito Deluxe after Sneaky Pete died and singer Carlton Moody left for Disney World. Ex-Deluxers Walter Egan and Rick Lonow are joined here by brothers Fred and Chris James. Egan co-wrote 'Carolina Calypso' with Saint Gram himself, and Gram also covered Egan's 'Hearts on Fire' on the Grievous Angel album -- both of those are given a solid outing on this CD. Rick Lonow was a Flying Burritos drummer in the 1980s with Beland, Sneaky Pete and Gib Guilbeau, was a mainstay of Burrito Deluxe, and co-wrote the Poco hit 'Crazy Love'. Fred and Chris James are veteran Nashville players who occasionally backed the 80s Burritos, and also played with the International Submarine Band (Gram's pre-Byrds group) on their reunion album. So these guys have the creds -- but do they deliver?

They sure do. I'm not gonna give you a track-by-track -- I'll just say that the material is very strong, the singing and playing is excellent, it's well recorded and the whole thing is just a pleasure to listen to over and over again. This is among the very best Burrito albums ever. Dare I say it? -- the one it most reminds me of sound-wise is that first holy-grail album 'Gilded Palace'. You can't go wrong here...

Alejandra recorded this album in Italy and what surprised me is that Alejandra didn't choose Desmond Child to produce it as he did on "LIPSTICK" and her Grammy Award winner "SOY", Alejandra now took credit next to Mike Mars and Loris Ceroni.

I wish this album gives Alejandra more commercial success in the U.S and Spain, it really has everything it takes to give Alejandra the opportunity to be on top beacuse she has lots of charisma, delivers her songs flawlessly and her voice is one of the best in the market.

title: An underappreciated gem that has stood the test of time
text:
I first bought this album when I was around ten years old and I have recently purchased the cd. One word review: DAMN! These guys could rock like nobody's business. I feel they are the next step in the evolution of glam that the New York Dolls were such a seminal part of, and which, let's be honest, suffered a horrible death when KISS left the scene (to concentrate on metal) to the likes of Poison, Whitesnake, Skid Row, Bon Jovi and all those other lame hair bands.
As for this album, it is more than "Rock and Roll All Nite" plus some other nice tunes. "Rock Bottom", "C'Mon and Love Me", "Room Service" and even "Getaway" (courtesy of the extremely underrated Ace Frehley) are all solid rock and roll tunes. It is my contention that Ace's departure marked the artistic demise of this band. No longer would his blues-inspired guitar genius be given an outlet and voice. Soon the band devolved into a metallite comic book joke, a situation that they have been trying to right ever since. I place the blame for this squarely on the Lurch-like shoulders of one, Gene Simmons, with Paul Stanley serving as an accessory before the fact. Had KISS stayed the course that this album and the original "Alive" set, they would rightfully be viewed as geniuses. Instead, they are best known for selling millions of records, being on lunch boxes and, worst of all, setting the stage for the corporate presence in music that gave us such underwhelming papp as Styxx, Journey, the aforementioned Bon Jovi, Van Halen and a slew of other bands better known for their marketing machines than the legacy of their music.
Was it really worth it?

title: John Coltrane at his beautiful ballad best… the personnel in the group, their contribution to this music on "Giant Steps"
text:
"Naima' has accompaniment from Wynton Kelly on piano with Paul Chambers (bass) and Jimmy Cobb (on drums)

I was recently looking up prominent East Coast hard bop pianist Wynton Kelly and I did not know that he had died in a Toronto hotel in 1971, I had arrived in Canada 1978. Toronto has had its share of jazz clubs but nothing on the scene right now… though whenever a notable musician comes to town the tickets sell out fast! The audience is here! Anyway, I traced Wynton to the wonderful album by guitarist Wes Montgomery "Full House" with amazing solos from tenor man Johnny Griffin, and of course I recognised Wynton on piano with Paul Chambers (bass) and Jimmy Cobb (on drums) as I have the album. My 1960s jazz friends and I quickly bought up that album in Yorkshire, northern England. Then today I realised … Wynton was also the pianist on Naima with John Coltrane, it was not Tommy Flanagan… with again Paul Chambers (bass) and Jimmy Cobb (drums) I checked my album collection. Sure enough, Wynton had performed the poignant and melodic piano solo on Naima, a composition from Coltrane's beautiful ballad mind. Never mind "hard bop", "Naima" is a treasure of a ballad. It has been frequently recorded and another version I like is by Carlos Santana / John McLaughlin on Love Devotion and Surrender. Miles had high praise for John Coltrane, their "Relaxin "was my very first album and then I got the other three "Cookin" ( with tracks Airegin and My Funny Valentine ) "Steamin" and "Cookin". There were pianists Wynton Kelly, Red Garland, Tommy Flanagan of similar styling, somehow Hank Jones never played in the Miles Davis lineup to my knowledge. The Davis Sextet with Bill Evans on piano was Kind of Blue, a jazz musicians vinyl or CD bible. I also appreciated Milestones - Straight no chaser. Miles eventually adopted the brilliant Wayne Shorter for his tenor player on the remarkable ESP album, as Coltrane had journeyed to a musical heaven in 1967. Fortunately, I had just managed to catch him that year playing a final concert with Pharaoh Sanders in Tokyo, he was considered a god in Japan

title: Refreshing
text: Simply put, there is not enough of this sort of playful Renaissance inspired music around. Ritchie Blackmore is a music legend in his own right, and it is a daring move to seek out a musical niche that acknowledges musical history. There is something refreshingly new about a musical artist not trying to be new, but rather trying to just be exceptional in his craft. Whether the instrumentation is classical or modern, this group manages to transport us to another time when it was not enough to just come out with a new hit song on every album, but rather to engage the audience and entertain with exceptional skill. Candice Night has a wonderful voice to lend to the inspired musical tapestry. This double album contains performance live recordings and I was afraid that perhaps the audience would detract from the music quality. Instead the intimate atmosphere of friendly encouragement from the audience only serves to add to the power of this collection.

title: Follow Up Review
text:
Yesterday I reviewed the Borodin String Quartet's performance of Schnittke's Piano Quintet, with Ludmilla Berlinsky at the keyboard. That CD, I'm sad to say, is available now only at inflated used prices. This performance of the Quintet, by the string ensemble of the Australian Festival of Chamber Music with Irina Schnittke on piano, is remarkably different from the Borodin version - a good deal harsher and fiercer, more angry than mournful - but very skillfully played. At the Naxos bargain price, I recommend it unconditionally. Hey, I'm pleased to have both CDs.

The Piano Quintet was composed in the wake of Schnittke's mother's death; it is dedicated to her memory. This AFCM performance has, to my ears, a powerful concept of the work. The piano is on a path of beauty and resignation, while the strings snarl and mock any easy consolation, reminding us of the harsh joys of life. While the Borodin performance reminded me considerably of Shostakovich, this AFMC version brings the influence of Mahler on Schnittke more to the fore.

Also performed on this CD are works for strings ranging from Schnittke's adolescent (1953) Fuga for solo violin to his Klingende Buchstaben for solo cello (1988). The last and longest work on the disk is a String Trio written in 1985 on commission to be performed in Vienna in commemoration of the anniversary of Alban Berg, whose music also influenced Schnittke. It's a more somber and convulsive work than the Piano Quintet, and one that ends with a haunting diminuendo into silence.

Though recorded in Australia, this performance features several Russian musicians who knew and worked with Schnittke himself before his death in 1998. In particular, the violinist Mark Lubotsky had the privilage of premiering Schnittke's violin concertos. Alexander Ivashkin was the principal cellist of the Bolshoi Theater Orchestra during Schnittke's active years in Russia. Lubotsky and Ivashkin are the performers of the two solo fantasies recorded here, both of which inevitably remind me of Bach's solo string sonatas. The cello work, Klingende Buchstaben, asks the cellist to draw sounds from his instrument unlike any you've heard before; it's a subtle, somber study of sound and silence interspliced.

On the whole, I prefer Schnittke's chamber music to his orchestral works, especially in recorded performances. These Russian fiddlers make him a more tormented soul than I have imagined him to be. Perhaps they're right, though his photos show a man with a gentle, forgiving smile.

I had the misfortune of being a teenager during the "dark ages of Black music" of the 1980s when synthesizer banging high tech drek, jerry curled junk, and computerized crap junktified the airwaves. During that putrid era, Deniece Williams was a welcome breath of fresh air that served as a musical oasis in a barren climate with her angelic tunes.

This album was a fine example of this. "Waiting on the Hotline" is one of the great underrated tunes of all time. The piano intro leads lovingly into Miss Williams' sweet and sassy vocals as her multioctave pipes pound plentifully (I've often wondered why rappers never sampled this catchy beat). "How Does It Feel" is a really sweet tune to a catchy pseudo-reggae beat and the part where she shouts "grab your self-control" sends me into sheer bliss. "I'm Still Waiting" is also rather mellow and relaxing after a hard day.

Sadly, because she happened to come out during a time of such otherwise rotten "music," she did not get the recognition she deserved and a lot of her lovely songs were unheard outside of Black American radio stations and dancehalls in Merrie Olde England. Rectify this situation, rediscover Niecy, and buy this CD!

title: The Way Remasters Should Be Done
text:
For those of you unfamiliar with this recording, the music is excellent. It's easily one of the top 5 albums of the grunge era. With several hits and a grammy to boot, this album has both commercial and artistic cred. The only really grunge thing about it is the production. The original album had an in-your-face guitar attack that I personally would have liked alleviated slightly for this remaster, but they left well enough alone and left the guitars up front with the vocals a little buried behind them. That kind of production gives the album a more indie aesthetic, but I like to hear vocals more up front. That's a personal bias though and is something that does not take away from the sheer brilliance of this album. The flow achieved on this album with the kind of diversity that was ventured forth is really remarkable. The band and producers deserve all the praise and accolades that they got.

The remastering is excellent. There's no loudness wars nonsense here. The only differences I heard were higher clarity and separation with a little extra volume without sacrificing headroom. The remastering is immediately obvious without being intrusive to the original recording. The packaging is vastly improved; going from the clunky original thick, double case to the slim, double jewel case. It was always something that I disliked about the original. I put mine into a store-bought slim case but the booklet barely fits in it. The new booklet is the real gem of this remaster. The liner notes are unusually well written. I had no idea that Billy Corgan was as articulate as what he wrote. He gives us a song by song breakdown of how he came up with each composition and it makes this package a very interesting twist that you don't see with other remasters. Even the artwork has been improved from the original. It gives me a much better idea of where they were going with the art. Excellent addition to an already brilliant album.

Any fans of art-rock, grunge, indie or early 90's rock should not hesitate to buy this. Especially in this great reissue version.

title: The Woman In Shania Twain
text:
1995 would mark the year that Shania Twain would become a Country superstar. Delivering powerful ballads full of emotion, honesty, and meaningful messages, "The Woman In Me" would start a path of super star-dom that Shania walked down and is still walking on it to this day. With songs written by Shania herself along with husband "Mutt" Lange (who produced this album), it just goes to show that when two very talented people come together with great, creative ideas, they can deliver the goods. Shania Twain would then live on to become today's best selling female artist of any genre of music. "The Woman In Me" displays Shania's Country roots. Before crossing over to Pop (and still in Country) and gaining more popularity, her music was pure Country. A beautiful Shania Twain exploded onto the scene after the downfall of her hardly noticed 1993 self titled debut. You have your Patsy Clines, your Loretta Lynns, your Dolly Partons, and your Tammy Wynettes, but when it comes down to Shania Twain, she is one of the best Country artists that has ever lived. By displaying sexuality and attitude in her music, fans of Country instantly caught on to her act and propelled her to the rank of super star-dom. I was just 7 years old when I first heard Shania's music back in 1995. The song was "Any Man Of Mine" - the music video had been playing on CMT when I was browsing through channels, looking for something to watch. I would not be disappointed. I was introduced to a beautiful woman with such a beautiful voice, with big, curly brown hair, dressed in a white tank, light blue jeans, and a matching vest on a ranch, pouring out sexuality and attitude. Her image blended in quite nicely with her very upbeat, very catchy, very fun song. I quickly fell in love with Shania Twain. Now, before I get carried away, let me give you my summary of "The Woman In Me."
The starting song "Home Ain't Where His Heart Is (Anymore)" is a great way to grab someone's attention. With an atmosphere of sadness and heartbreak instantly created, the haunting melody and Shania's voice blend in beautifully with this tearful ballad. With a great starting song, we quickly break away from the sorrow and explode into the more fun side of Shania. Displaying nothing but sexuality and attitude in "Any Man Of Mine", Shania delivers a very fun ballad that you'd easily find yourself singing and dancing to. While she may seem demanding, she is anything but. This is probably what any woman would want in a man. The next two songs are very similar to each other.. why? "Whose Bed Have Your Boots Been Under" turns into a very fun upbeat song about a man that can't stand being attached to just woman for even the shortest period of time. While this song may not be serious, Shania sings about how love is all about commitment. This song is quickly followed up by "(If You're Not In It For Love) I'm Outta Here!" which is another very fun ballad. Shania sure does get her point across - "If you're not in it for life, if you're not in it for love, I'm outta here!". Love is all about commitment.. right? Don't answer that.. But knowing you, I'm sure you're only interested in getting tied down to the right person. "The Woman In Me (Needs The Man In You)" was a quick favorite of Country music fans. Shania is able to deliver a very strong, beautiful ballad with such simple, yet very beautiful lyrics that she was able to stretch for almost five minutes. Now, I'm going to skip some songs because I didn't really care much for them.. (not saying they're bad songs, but I'm only going to give you the goods on the songs I liked!) "You Win My Love" quickly spins Country music around in such a very upbeat, very catchy, fun mood. You can now easily see that Shania is very capable of pouring out great songs with their own unique sense of style. Moving on from that, "No One Needs To Know" is such a beautifully catchy song. Shania's voice really mesmerizes the listener on this song. It was a great pick to be featured in the soundtrack to the movie "Twister" (which I love!) ..."The Woman In Me" closes off with a very sad ballad with no music, but Shania's powerful voice. This short, very powerful poem of unity and sorrow will bring many tears to one's eyes. I was disappointed, however, that the music video version wasn't included on this album! That was such a great song!
Now, with all of that said, I'm pretty sure I've given you various reasons why Shania Twain has become one of today's best selling artists and is adored by millions and millions internationally. "The Woman In Me" brings out the Country in Shania, as well as the woman in her.. of course. All of these songs were written by Shania Twain and husband "Mutt" Lange, showing that being creative and putting two very talented people together can easily give birth to such essential songs. I strongly recommend this album to any lover of music. Now, you can talk about your Patsy Clines, your Martina McBrides, your Reba McEntires, and your Tammy Wynettes - but really, when Shania exploded onto the Country music scene, she would change the face of Country music forever and open the doors for people to express their creativity. The sound of her music was far from what modern Country music was back then in the mid 90's - that is why so many people fell in love with Shania Twain and Country music. She was a rebel who was doing things on her own terms, and it paid off. It's easy to say that Shania Twain is one of the best singing artists to have ever lived.

title: Gilmour's odd duck
text:
"About Face", released in 1984, came out during a low point in guitarist David Gilmour's life. Coming off the nightmarish sessions for the heavily Roger Waters-driven "The Final Cut" (an album in which Gilmour's musical contributions were completely stifled) and the dissolution of his marriage, Gilmour found himself wanting to break away from the trappings of his old band but unsure of exactly where to go with the freedom that comes with a solo project. In the end, Gilmour only got one foot out the door.

The album is a somewhat schizophrenic sounding collection of mostly pleasant but occasionally underwhelming tunes, some of which are very Floydian, while others are out of left field. The production is a true product of the 1980's, including synthesizers-a plenty, big reverb, gated drums, and even a few horns(!). The supporting line-up includes many of the session hotshots that were in great demand at the time.

The album kicks off with "Until We Sleep", which is perhaps the strangest song on the album. A driving beat and relentless pulsating synths are paired up with lazy, reverb-drenched vocals that drift overhead as if they came from a different song. There's nothing terrible here, but there's little in the way of changes in its five-plus minutes, making for a somewhat monotonous listen.

After the odd opener comes "Murder", reportedly inspired by the death of John Lennon. This is one of the album's high-points and one that finds Gilmour squarely in Pink Floyd mode (this would have been a welcome addition to "The Final Cut"). The track begins with a gorgeous acoustic verse followed by a fretless bass solo (another touch that seems to have died with the end of the 1980's). The momentum builds with a rousing second verse, followed by an extended outro jam that is pure Floyd. While another quiet verse would have really made this one to remember, the overall result is excellent.

Another highlight is the piano-driven "Out of the Blue", the first of two songs railing against nuclear weaponry. "You Know I'm Right" contains strong verses but is marred by a very dated-sounding chorus featuring near-falsetto vocals by Gilmour. The closer, "Near the End", is another strong piece that would be at home on a Pink Floyd album. The sparse verses eventually build to a stirring solo that includes acoustic and electric guitars. The closer's lead-in instrumental "Let's get Metaphysical", is another very Floydian piece that has no major faults but is not overly memorable.

"Cruise", the album's other anti-nuke song, exposes Gilmour's weakness: lyric-writing. The folk-ish acoustic guitars are pleasant enough as background music (Gilmour has always had a fine ear for melody), but under close scrutiny, the song becomes almost unlistenable due to the rudimentary & silly rhyming. Mr. Gilmour would be the first to tell you that lyric-writing is not his strongest suit, which is why he's typically enlisted the help of others in Roger Waters' absence. Left to his own devices on this track, the results are borderline abysmal.

Help on this album did come from none other than Pete Townsend, who wrote lyrics for two tracks, "Love on the Air" and "All Lovers are Deranged". The former is a fairly generic ballad that comes off as rather corny. The latter is a hard-rocker that, while somewhat unusual for Gilmour, works quite well and is another album highlight.

"Blue Light", a much derided song by most Floyd fans, is the most obvious attempt to break away from the usual sound. The track begins with a funky echo-drenched guitar riff before settling into a horn-laden R&B rhythm. It's the most out-of-character track Gilmour has ever done, and while I am glad he didn't make any further attempts to become the next Phil Collins, I find myself enjoying the track's infectious qualities, even if it is a load of cheese.

Overall, "About Face" is the weakest overall of David Gilmour's three solo albums. His self-titled debut, while slightly sketchier in the ideas department, holds up better over time and is a more compelling listen. "On an Island", while almost too laid-back at times, is an absolute treat for fans of Meddle & Dark-Side era Floyd.

There's enough good stuff on "About Face" to warrant a healthy three and a half stars (which I've rounded up to four mainly because David Gilmour is quite possibly my favorite musician of all time). The album is essential for fans of the Pink Floyd guitarist, but all those who purchase should temper their expectations a bit.

This score is an ominous, beautiful closing to the trilogy. It focuses on the dread of the forgone conclusion (Anakin becoming Vader). In keeping with the film, the music is less about victory than it is about survival and sacrifice. As far as the recycling of music from previous films - that's the whole basis of "leitmotiv". Pieces of music are connected with specific characters and places. Through all six Star Wars films, John Williams' music has served the story and sometimes exceeded it.

There aren't any cute, Disneyland-sounding passages this time! From this, I gain hope that Jar-Jar Binks has relocated to Florida and the movie isn't sprinkled with warm-fuzzy scenes.

Con: Three tracks use that truncation thing, where they chop two pieces of music and stitch 'em together. Can't we try the "Ultimate Edition" approach again, even though the one for "Phantom Menace" really wasn't?

Williams' "Sith" score yields a few more classics. "Anakin vs. Obi-Wan" and "Battle of The Heroes" share a memorable D-minor horn refrain. "Padme's Ruminations" is similar to Williams' "Anne Lively" music for the film "Minority Report". "The Immolation Scene" is Williams at his elegiac best, worthy of his work in "Schindler's List".

Tibetan throat singing sets the mood for "Palpatine's Teachings," serving as a theme for corruption. The first two minutes of "General Grievous" sounds like a Tarzan movie.

As always, the staccato horns are airtight, and sometimes minor melodies overlap major chords and vice versa. The London Voices choir is all over this cd, and it adds a lot of drama to the music.

"A New Hope AND End Credits" offers a nice, long medley of themes introduced in "Sith" and reprised from Episodes IV-VI. It's sort of the Super Bowl/"last hurrah" of Star Wars music. With this most likely being the last true Star Wars music (and films), there's a sad finality many of us felt after "Return of The Jedi." Well, Sith happens.

title: Strange Artifact of 1970
text:

You like electronic pop? Try this one, you might enjoy it.

title: This is Not Classical Music; It's Also Not Very Good Pop Music
text:
I admire John Adams immeasurably -- I think his 'Harmonielehre,' for instance, is truly a masterpiece -- although I've had some questions about some of his compositions. Many people think his cantata 'El Niño' is terrific. I think it's claptrap. And this one, I'm sorry to say, is much worse. It is lousy pop music, quasi Broadway, and although it shows that Adams can compose music in several pop styles -- gospel, soul, r&b, blues rock, et al. -- none of it sounds very good. The combo that accompanies the singers sounds like someone's garage band. The pop singers in this recording are primarily European and their accents -- although some are fairly good -- are often jarringly European in what is quintessentially American music.

I freely admit that as an old geezer, I'm not particularly fond of the past twenty-five years of American pop music, and you must take that into account when considering my opinion here. But for those of you who are expecting something along the lines of Adams's better-known works, including his operas, this one is a real shocker. Be warned.

Scott Morrison

title: The Best and the Worst
text:
The first CD takes the listener through "Hotel California," the title and leadoff song of the fifth album. This break is significant, for The Eagles became only the eagles with the loss of Randy Meisner and the addition of Joe Walsh. Firing Don Felder was also one of their dumber moves. Note that credits for "Hotel California" list Glenn Frey and Don Henley before Don Felder, indicating that they had more to do with writing the song than Felder, although in the credits on the original album Felder is listed first. In fact, Felder wrote all of the music himself, including the arrangements for each instrument. The stunning guitar duet that ends the song, in my opinion, represents the high point of their career.

Some of the songs have been remastered, unfortunately muting the msndolin and banjo contributions of Bernie Leadon. The song that loses the most in the recorded version versus the live performance is "Take it to the Limit." Again in my opinion, Timothy B. Schmit is a very poor replacement for Randy Meisner, whose range was greater - and voice truer -than any of the others, and Frey's version just doesn't make it. I also have a hard time recognizing some of the songs as "hits," but it is good to hear them again.

In short, if you like listening to The Eagles while you're driving the highway and want to change the CD player as little as possible, this is an excellent compilation. The collection is in chronological order, which none of the other "best of" releases have been. It enables the listener to follow the the changes in the band from the beginning, which I really like.

title: An Excellent "Traditional" Rendition
text: This recording is available as a CD set or as part of a boxed set with Israel in Egypt.  {BTW - The Parrott led recording of Israel in Egypt is among the finest I've heard.}  This Messiah rendition seems familiar - even if you've never heard it before.  That's probably due to the slower pacing and the avoidance of dramatic dynamic and tempo changes some conductors prefer.  Nonetheless it is an excellent recording!  The orchestra is 'spot on'.  The soloists [all six of them!] are excellent across the board.  But the star of the show is the chorus.  They simply nail it.  The clarity, precision and wonderful blending of the voices are all superb.  The sopranos don't oversing in their high range and the choral balance always seems to be as Handel intended.  BTW - I own 9 complete recordings of The Messiah and have sung in more than 40 complete performances.  One curious note:  this recording along with the Layton/Polyphony/Britten Sinfonia recording offers an abridged version of the Pastoral Symphony; as I enjoy this orchestral work I miss the full 3 minute version.  If you want a recording with a lengthy rendtion of the Pastoral Symphony, The Sargent/Royal Liverpool 1959 recording has a 4 1/2 minute version.  This Parrott led  recording is one you can put into your stereo, sit back in an easy chair, close your eyes and simply revel in what your hear.

Symphony No. 14, Op. 135. Galina Vishnevskaya, soprano. Mark Reshetin, bass. Mstislav Rostropovich, conductor. Chamber Orchestra of Moscow, recorded 12 February 1973.
Seven Romances on Poems of Alexander Blok, Op. 127. Galina Vishnevskaya, soprano. David Oistrakh, violin. Mstislav Rostropovich, cello. Moisei Vainberg, piano. Premiere performance recording, 27 October 1967.
The first of Rostropovich's two recordings of Shostakovich's 14th Symphony, employing the same cast as the world-premiere performance (under Rudolf Barshai - Russian Disc) is a record your reviewer has long coveted. title: When alternative music was still considered alternative
text:
The term "alternative" nowadays is anything alternative, especially in music. Alternative music hasn't been remotely good for almost ten years now. The 1990s was the decade when alternative rock was at its peak. One of my favorite alternative rock albums to come out of that decade is Hole's blistering breakthrough hit LIVE THROUGH THIS.

LIVE THROUGH THIS is Hole's finest album with its raw angst-riddled lyrics and Courtney's eviscerating vocals. You can hear the fury in Courtney's vocals as she tears through songs like "Miss World" and the chorus in "Asking For It". LIVE THROUGH THIS isn't the most melodic album I have heard from the '90s and at times I get tired of Courtney's screaming. Courtney really did capture the angst that many people like myself felt at the time in the '90s. There was a raw honesty on LIVE THROUGH THIS that I haven't heard after that album was released. My personal favorite song on the album is the ballad "Softer, Softest". Hearing Courtney turn her rage down a few notches was a nice change. My least favorite track has to be "She Walks On Me". I get a headache just thinking about this noisy, tuneless track. While I do prefer the sounds of L7 and Babes in Toyland, I still enjoyed Hole as much as the next person.

I was fortunate enough to see Wolfstone a few times on their North American tour in 1994 and was immediately captivated by the musicianship and energy of this amazing band. As much as a recording can, this CD captures the spirited enthusiasm of this Scottish band, which singlehandedly turned the Celtic revival on its ear.
I like "Unleashed," their first "official" CD, for its combination of lyrical and instrumental tunes, slow and fast ones, a nice mix. The fiddle power of Duncan Chisholm is awesome in combination with the skilled twin guitars of Stuart Eaglesham and Ivan Drever. Try "Hector the Hero" for its dramatic sweep, "Cleveland Park Medley" for musical wizardry, "Here is Where the Heart Is" for powerful sentiment and truth, "Song for Yesterday" for its beautiful nostalgia.
"Unleashed" features the wonderful songwriting and resonant voice of Ivan Drever, who is no longer part of the Wolfstone lineup. The lineup has changed over the years, especially the pipers (no similarity to Spinal Tap drummers intended!), but, in my opinion, the loss of Drever was the hardest to come back from. Although much of the Wolfstone energy is still there in later recordings, the quality of songwriting has suffered since "The Half Tail."

title: One of Khan's most sublime efforts
text:
The problem with assessing the quality of cd's is that artists often have different phases in their career, or different kinds of output for their talent. Khan, for example, had a "fusion" phase (early Khan material and the band Eyewitness), has a Latin jazz side, is a superlative sideman and session player (look at, e.g., Steely Dan's Gaucho album), and has real bonafides as a "straight ahead" jazz player.
My favorite format in jazz is the trio, particularly the jazz guitar trio. Khan has done several albums in this vein and Got My Mental is my favorite (it's more or less a trio). The songs are perfect examples of trio playing where the interactivity is so complete that one almost forgets there are separate players. Khan's melodies are sing-able (a forgotten art in so much guitar jazz) and his solos speak with phrases both lovely and enigmatic. (Is Khan the Wallace Stevens of the guitar solo? Not a bad analogy.) Here, too, John Patitucci really shines; one of the first albums where he leaves the "hot shot fusion bass player" thing behind and lets Khan's melodism guide him beyond his technical habits. And Jack DeJohnette--what can be said? He is a drummer's drummer, the perfect third point in this triangle.
Without a doubt, this is a "Desert Island Disc." Check it out and you'll be singing it for the rest of the month.
