title: Nilsson and Windgassen Present us with their Youthful Takes on Tristan; Sawallisch lead a lukewarm Tristan
text:
Connoisseurs of Wagner's operas generally speak of the Bayreuth Festival performances recorded during the 1950s in hushed tones, and for good reason. During no other decade since the Festival reopened after the war have the conductors, singers, and directors involved in this enterprise upheld the art of Wagnerian music drama to such a staggeringly high level. It was the decade that introduced us to Wieland Wagner's optically arresting Parsifal, a production dubbed by Ernest Newman (the composer's biographer, and a contemporary of Wagner and the many musicians of his time) as "one of the three or four most moving spiritual experiences of my life." Wieland's first Ring, another visually stimulating concoction of light and shadow, entertained and challenged audiences annually between 1951 and 1958 with Wagnerian singing and dramaturgy of the highest level. In 1952, Herbert von Karajan immortalized the finest Tristan und Isolde recorded on the Green Hill with the potent singing actors Martha Modl and Ramon Vinay. The roster of artists who relived the master's complex characters could not have been more impressive: Hans Hotter, Astrid Varnay, Wolfgang Windgassen, Martha Modl, Birgit Nilsson, Gustav Neidlinger, Josef Greindl, Ramon Vinay, Hermann Uhde, Jon Vickers, Leonie Rysanek, Ludwig Weber, Hans Knappertsbusch, Joseph Keilberth, Clemens Krauss, Herbert von Karajan, and Wolfgang Sawallisch. By virtue of these artists' dedication to their craft, this decade and part of the one that would follow represent a golden age of Wagnerian art that lived by Wieland Wagner's motto "Hier giltst der Kunst" (Art reigns supreme here).

Wieland and Wolfgang Wagner would often trade productions of the canonical ten operas at the Festival during the first two decades after the war (Wieland died in 1967, prompting Wolfgang to switch to the now well known workshop model where the most innovative theater directors in Europe stage their ideas about Wagner's dramas at the summer festival). Critics often lavished praise upon Wieland's stage designs and abstractions, his tricks with lighting as an enhancer of the drama, and his special way of directing the characters onstage. Less successful at the producer's chair was Wolfgang, who was reviled for failing to arrive at a definitive statement with his artistic concepts. While Wolfgang's artistic style was indeed an epigone of Wieland's revolutionary take on his grandfather's dramas, both brothers at least shared the same singers, all of whom turned in performances of the highest calibre. In the absence of recorded video, lovers of Wagner's musical theater could at least revel in the remarkable audio performances we now hear from the Festival’s annual radio broadcasts.

This performance of Tristan und Isolde, recorded during the 2nd revival of Wolfgang Wagner's Tristan, presents us with the youthful heroes of Birgit Nilsson and Wolfgang Windgassen. Both singers' interpretations of these complex characters are best known from Deutsche Grammophon's 1966 recording with Karl Bohm—a document of such febrile intensity and remarkable musicianship that it continues to be hailed as one of the greatest Tristans ever recorded on disc. Karl Bohm there leads a highly theatrical and driven orchestral reading of the score—hailed by some as one of the greatest nights of theater at the Festival, while accused by others of being too fast and lacking in sensuality. Here, the great Wolfgang Sawallisch turns in a more measured take on the score. Timings are broader and in keeping with conventional Wagnerian aesthetic, orchestral textures are transparent, and the pacing is neither too fast or lugubrious. I certainly appreciate Sawallisch’s excellent command of the orchestra in this performance, but the deepest wells of the work seem to elude this most intelligent and musical of conductors at this stage of his life.
In 1958, Sawallisch was the youngest conductor to have been invited to Bayreuth, and while his sense of theatricality and solid musicianship foreshadow the greater things he would accomplish in the future, his concept here lacks the ultimate sense of excess, passion, and love-death (for lack of a better descriptor) that we hear in the great readings by Karajan, Furtwangler, Kleiber, and Simon Rattle. Sawallisch was certainly unmatched in youthful Wagnerian works like Hollander, Tannhauser, and Lohengrin, and in his later life would master the mammoth Ring Cycle and Meistersinger as the director of the Bayerische Staatsoper. But this Tristan I find was caught too early in his career. By any standard, it stands as a vibrant and excellently led performance, but comparing this with the 1952 performances by Karajan, the Wieland/Bohm partnership, and the Everding/Kleiber recordings of the 1970s reveals an interpretation that sits at very good as opposed to great.
On the same token, the lead singers here present more youthful, but ultimately less complete characterizations of Tristan und Isolde than what we would hear with Bohm and Wieland. In 1958, the great Birgit Nilsson already brandished a formidable instrument with a clarion top. While her 1950s instrument was fresher and more feminine as opposed to the clarion warrior sound she developed in the 60s, there are several moments in her 1958 Isolde that reveal a soprano voice that has yet to achieve its true prime. Excerpts of her singing in the Act 1 Narration and Curse and the love duet find her middle voice lacking in strength and resonance, and the high notes, while thrilling, were not nearly as full as the ones we would hear in the 60s. Her interpretation developed with Wolfgang also lacks variety and internalized angst compared to the complex heroine she would commit with Wieland. Make no mistake: Nilsson when measured by all standards remains the most complete and compelling Isolde we have heard from Bayreuth, but her great take on this heroine needed Wieland’s genius to realize its full potential.
Wolfgang Windgassen here presents a far more youthful and lyrical sounding Tristan than the one we hear a decade later. Unlike archetypal Wagner tenors like Max Lorenz and Lauritz Melchior, Windgassen possessed a focused lyric sound that was used intelligently and tirelessly in the theater. In fact, his versatility and intelligence allowed him to become the only tenor in Bayreuth history to have sung major tenor roles in all of Wagner’s canonical operas for two decades. The main advantage to hearing his portrayal with Sawallisch lies in the quality of singing—as an interpreter, he had already developed strong ideas of characterization that would only be slightly refined by working with Wieland. His ravings in Tristan’s third act delirium, for instance, are far more potent in 1966 as opposed to 1958. However, his vocal quality was on several levels superior with Sawallisch, his timbre then fuller and capable of imbuing a heroic aura that would diminish and become brittle with age. Tristan’s exchanges with Isolde in Act 2 are thrown with heroic abandon, and the simultaneous qualities of rapture and despair upon their realization of Brangane’s deception in Act 1 are conveyed with greater immediacy by virtue of his young sound. It is only in Act 3, where Tristan must express a whole spectrum of emotions ranging from desperation to delirium to despondence, that Wieland’s reading emerges as superior.
The supporting cast in this performance represented the high caliber of singing that existed at Bayreuth during the 1950s. Grace Hofmann, Erik Saeden, and Josef Greindl were starred members of a company of exceptional vocalists and dramatists who brought the ultimate in artistic expression and musicality to Wagner’s theater. Hofmann, a fine Amme, Fricka, Waltraute, and Ortrud, here provides a sympathetic companion to Isolde. Greindl is a competent Marke, reprising the portrayal he had committed with Furtwangler in the first studio recording of this great opera. His voice isn’t the most alluring, but one hears such gravitas and nuance in Greindl’s voice when he fleshes out Marke’s monologue. Saeden is by many standards the weak link in this cast, as Hotter and Neidlinger were the Kurwenal’s of choice from the premiere year. While these supporting singers cannot compare with the stellar trio of Christa Ludwig, Eberhard Waechter, and Martti Talvela (who would share the stage in the Bohm production), they nevertheless represented a now gone standard in the art of Wagnerian singing.
Compared with most Tristan’s in the market, Sawallisch’s recording on Orfeo stands as a very good addition to the catalogue, even if it is unable to eclipse the greatest studio and live performances. The sound in this Orfeo release has been cleaned up remarkably by the engineers, and the orchestral image and voices emerge with a clarity and immediacy that cannot be heard in other pirates. For the ultimate in Tristan und Isolde, one must hear the two great recordings from 1952—Furtwangler’s studio document with the great Kirsten Flagstad, and the white hot live recording from Bayreuth with Karajan, Martha Modl, and Ramon Vinay. Tristan’s of an earlier vintage, like the 1941 Leinsdorf from the Met with Flagstad and Melchior, are essential listening for the listener to experience the titanic Wagner voices that once existed during an operatic golden age. The Bohm recording from 1966 is very fine indeed, and fast forward forty years later, one must hear Nina Stemme’s great Isolde’s with Antonio Pappano and Marek Janowski (a finer recording, with the greatest American heldentenor Stephen Gould). Karajan’s 1972 studio reading with Jon Vickers and Helga Dernesch I like very much, but many complain about the recording even as I rank it among my favorites. Kleiber from 1982 must be heard for the orchestral reading and the commitment of the cast, even if the voices are slightly underwhelming. In the face of such competition, the 1958 Sawallisch reading may seem underwhelming, but if one must hear a youthful Birgit Nilsson and Wolfgang Windgassen in the theater, by all means explore this new release from Orfeo.

title: A great introduction to classical guitar music
text:
As someone who was brought up on rock (indie, alternative, shoegaze, punk) I craved something new, so I searched for something different. I'm a complete beginner, so please view this review in its proper context.

I listened to old Segovia recordings and liked them, but I found some of the recordings lacked good sound quality so I couldn't quite apprecitate the music behind the cracks and pops of the recording. I tried Parkening and liked him. His music is so complex and layered but a bit cold to my ears. Sometimes when I listen to his music I feel like I'm in a movie theater. I can't quite describe why I feel this way when I listen to his music, but I just do.

I found Scott's music by accident. I enrolled in a beginning guitar class at Palomar College and he happened to be the instructor. He was a great instructor...very lively, enthusiastic, accessible, and friendly. I purchased his CD mostly because I wanted to support a local artist. When I listened to his CD I found that his music was also....very lively, enthusiastic, accessible and friendly. The recording quality of this CD is top notch. You really feel like you're a foot or two away from him when listening to his recording with no distracting artifacts or veil on the CD.

The selections are upbeat and fun...folksy is how I would describe it. The tempo changes throughout with the CD starting out lively and playful and then mellowing out around Track 9. It gradually picks back up and finally is wrapped up with Track 17...a two-faced song that alternates between peaceful dreams and frentic flurries. Scott made a comment once that people usually like about half of the songs. I liked them all because I appreciated the variety. I usually listen to whole albums and not just single songs and despite it having 17 tracks, it is a very quick listen because of the effort placed in track selection and cohesiveness. Every song has its place and performs its task wonderfully.

I would highly recommend this CD to anyone who is just starting out in this genre. While it may be tempting to purchase a "Best Of..." classical guitar music compilation, the songs will not be intertwined with each other like they are on this CD.

title: great compendium of sonic juxtapositions
text:
The producers "used mainly a cappella recordings from the Lomax Archive, such as field hollers, work songs from prisoners, and a couple of recordings from the Georgia Sea Islands. They constructed instrumental tracks around them, often adding jazzy chord changes, while usually preserving the rhythmic feel of the original recordings. [They used live blues & jazz musicians.] In fact, there are only a few of the remixed tracks that could be considered dance material. One is an unlikely combination of an old fishing song with a reggae beat, while another maintains the sound of the prisoner chopping with his axe in time to the music, and uses that as part of the rhythmic motif. Billington and Reynolds also go further and sometimes combine two very differed field recordings in a single track which ends up sounding remarkably coherent. The result is a very interesting and enjoyable album that can change one's perception of sampling...

"While there are those who think that the remix fad is a great art form, there are others of us who consider the field the realm of plagiarizers and people incapable of coming up with their own music. It's a rare occasion when the concept works as well as it does on Tangle Eye's debut release Alan Lomax's Southern Journey Remixed, especially given the reverence accorded by many to the source material. Of course, folk music purists will likely still consider this a bastardization. But unlike most other remixers and sample jockeys, Tangle Eye consists of real musicians playing real instruments with a respect for the original source material, as well as a sense of adventure. Co-producers Scott Billington and Steve Reynolds are also very creative in their use of the samples of the original recordings, not only combining them with the contemporary instrumentation, but melding disparate original recordings in interesting ways. The result is a very satisfying album that is a great compendium of sonic juxtapositions."

title: Stronger than Saturday Night Wrist
text:
I own all of the Deftones albums beginning with "Adrenaline" up to this most recent album "Diamond Eyes", and I'm happy to say that it is stronger than their last album "Saturday Night Wrist". I personally was introduced to the Deftones with "White Pony" when a friend suggested I give them a try. The only point I wish to make is that my later introduction may skew what I expect out of the Deftones to the "White Pony" sound than say "Adrenaline". That being said, I am a big fan of their first two albums as well.

I must say, I've been pretty disappointed with bands as of recently. Many of the solid groups I grew up listening to put out album after album that slowly signified the decline of an era. Sure I'm biased like every other reviewer out there, and I have fond memories of the music and style that I was introduced first to, but overall I feel I'm pretty open to change and growth. This is definitely not "Adrenaline 2" or "Around the Fur 2" or "White Pony 2" as some people claim (or demand) but it is definitely a Deftones album. When you get that--not only with this band but every band that has ever existed--you can really learn to appreciate it.

The good news, as I said, is that this is a Deftones album. It's got the core of what makes one: those harsh sounding guitars, those groovy drum beats, and lyrics that drive you to understand the message, sung with emotion and unconcern for direction. However, as with every Deftones album it is always those elements that make it so hard to digest at first. This is a CD you need to play through once entirely to first get a sense of what it is about, and then on repeat listens you can start to pull out the gems. It reminds me of when I first listened to "White Pony". I knew there was something so unique about it, but no one part was grabbing me. It's after you can start to predict Chino's sometimes unusual vocal melodies and pacing that you realize how catchy the songs are.

I was somewhat concerned when I heard the first single "Diamond Eyes" off the album. That song by far is the most commercial and outwardly catchy song that I believe the Deftones have ever created. No I don't feel they "sold out" with this song but its almost so catchy that it's corny. It's a different Deftones than I'm used to but that's not necessarily a bad thing. I have nothing against the song as I listen more to the album, but I frequently skip over it to songs like "You've Seen the Butcher", "Prince", and "Risk" which I feel represent some of the real highlights on this album. If you give these songs a chance they will get stuck in your head.

The only real thing I do miss on this album is those real heavy uptempo tracks like Hexagram or Korea. I understand why some people are disappointed by their absence, but I get it. They are getting older and their music is starting to chill like Korn did and Incubus did. You get older and you don't have that same kind of angst and hate for the world as you did as a kid. I personally am glad they were able to move on from that stage. Doesn't mean they can't throw a heavy one in there, but I get that slow and emotional is where they are ending up.

It brings me back to "Saturday Night Wrist", which I feel was the weakest of their albums so far. It didn't have the raw straight-forward sound of "Adrenaline", the more polished yet still rocking sound of "Around the Fur", the complexity and otherworldly sound of "White Pony", or the hard hitting sound of "Deftones". It was kind of just slow and mediocre. I feel this album takes that new introduced sound in "Saturday Night Wrist", adds some Team Sleep sort of flavor, and actually produces real stand out tracks.

If you liked their first four releases, and were maybe iffy about "Saturday Night Wrist", I think you need to give this one a chance. If it doesn't get stuck in your head, then maybe you and the Deftones have hit a fork in the road.

title: Norwegian `80s melodic rock classic!!
text:
This is the self-titled debut album by Norwegian melodic rock/AOR band "Da Vinci" originally released in 1987, re-issued in 2006 by "MTM Music". The line up features lead singer Lars Aass, guitarist Gunnar Westlie, bassist Bjorn Boge, drummer Jarle Maloy and keyboardist Dag Selboskar.

Upon first play one notices the over-produced rhythm section which dominates the rhythmic of the album from the first song to the last. The second characteristic of "Da Vinci" identifiable early on is their melodic orientation. The guitars, complemented by the keyboards, provide the majority of melodies found on this debut not to mention a range of masterful solos. Equally important, as you would expect, is the contribution of singer Lars who can handle just about every vocal melody whether he sings over a keyboard into or leading the band into an intense chorus on top of all instruments.

One could roughly describe "Da Vinci" as a subtler version of "Europe", baring the same thick production but at the same time relying very little on riffs, which is quite remarkable for a rock band by any standards. Clearly, melody is the name of the game for "Da Vinci" and the more one moves along the track list the bigger the melodies and the more intense the performance becomes. Standout tracks include "Forever in my heart", "lookin' for love", "Dreamin'" , "look at me now" and the power-ballad "Ain't no goodbyes"; to be fair each and every of these songs could be regarded as classic of `80s AOR baring the flamboyance of melodic hard rock coated with the subtlety of adult oriented rock. Fans of the genre as well as collectors should definitely grab "Da Vinci"s debut album provided the opportunity.

title: Yo-Yo Ma has the temerity to record the Elgar Concerto; strong Walton Concerto
text:
I say temerity because the Jacqueline Du Pre/John Barbirolli Edward Elgar concerto dating from 1965 is in my opinion one of the great classical recordings ever released. If you are interested in this CD for the Elgar, I recommend you proceed forthwith to that EMI release on amazon. That said, Yo-Yo Ma and Andre Previn have collaborated on a well-performed and successful disc fully deserving of 5 stars. The problem is that the program overlaps a legendary interpretation.

My guess is that this disc was actually intended to present William Walton's Cello Concerto, completed in 1956, based on the fact that Andre Previn has been an advocate of Walton's music throughout his career. I was very much impressed with Walton's effort here. The Concerto is mostly tonal, in three movements, much of it featuring delicate effects. It is not particularly discordant and in fact isn't particularly difficult listening. I've taken in many, many hours of listening to modern concert music and the Cello Concerto is one of the finest post-World War 2 compositions I’ve had the pleasure of hearing. I’m underlining this fact because fans of contemporary music won't highlight this disc as part of the genre - but it is one and is very worthwhile. Ma and Previn are very good throughout. The delicate orchestral effects are perfectly balanced while the cello is played with technical assurance, even in some hair-raisingly high passages.

Likewise, the famous 1919 Elgar concerto gets a well-conceived and able performance. Despite its quality, though, Ma and Previn just doesn't bring the emotional power of the Du Pre performance, nor its striking structural cohesion and sense of architecture.

The release dates to 1985, when Ma was just 30. I am happy to report that the sound engineering is, unlike so many early digital sessions from that decade, very good - it's warm, detailed and not abrasive at all. A good disc, but one really best suited for the contemporary music listener.

title: A Lustrous Art Song Recital
text:
PHIDYLE, the new art song recital by Czech soprano Katerina Knezikova, is a most gratifying disc to hear. Knezikova's sound strongly resembles that of the great Slovak coloratura soprano Edita Gruberova (1946-2021): it is limpid, shimmering, sparkling, flexible, and penetrating; a difference is that Knezikova's recorded voice is fuller of tone than Gruberova's and has a bit more “face,” or personality. Like Gruberova's it is recognizably an Eastern European soprano sound, and it is nice to know that even as the World Wide Web blurs the “boundaries” between the nations, it is still possible to hear in the world of classical singing distinctive “national” characteristics.

Before PHIDYLE, I had only ever heard art song sung (on recordings) by American opera stars like Leontyne Price and Sherrill Milnes; I was therefore in a poor position to judge the subtleties of specialist Knezikova's interpretations. What I can say with confidence is that her voice does not overwhelm the songs and that she always sounds as if she knows what she is singing about. If you often feel, as I do, that “meaning” is wrongly valued over beauty of tone in art song performance, then you ought to appreciate in Knezikova an artist who values equally both aspects of the singer’s art. The sensitive artist with the stunning voice is captured in sumptuous sonics and supported by the superb musicians of the Janacek Philharmonic Orchestra. The oboist is particularly fine.

text: All I can say about this album is "Wow!".  It is a magnificent achievement, very heavy, very intricate, and occasionally melodic, in short, everything a metal album should be.  Okay, so it's a distant second to "Cowboys from Hell", but this album is a work of art in its own right.  Standouts would have to be "Walk", "F. Hostile", and the two "ballads", "This Love" and "Hollow", the latter being the better of the two, and the best song on the album.  I'd also say it's Pantera's second best song, right behind "Cemetery Gates".  It's mainly better than "This Love" because the melody and heaviness blend together better, and the chorus in "This Love" didn't seem very well thought out.  But, they're both great songs, anyone who thinks Phil can't sing should hear them.  He almost sounds like Layne Staley at certain points.  Anyway, if you want an album that's good and heavy, has a bit of slow stuff, and has music that doesn't sound like something any idiot could play, this is the album for you.  And, if you like this album, check out "Burn My Eyes" by Machine Head.  All hail Pantera, one of the heaviest, most awesome bands alive!

title: raw, unburnished honkytonk truth
text: Among the more depressing cultural phenomena of the 1990s is the disintegration of country music into bland Southern suburban pop.  To hear meaningful heart-and-roots music, you'd have to go  to bluegrass, folk, or  blues, genres that have thrived recently in part, I suspect, as one  consequence of Nashville's artistic collapse.  Now, in a magnificent return  to form, George Jones reminds all of us who grew up with country music why  we were drawn to it in the first place.  There's no gloss here, just raw,  unburnished honkytonk soul -- country music like they used to, when (in  Merle Haggard's words) Hank and Lefty crowded every jukebox.  This album is  crowded with songs whose quality ranges from good to superb; in particular,  two of them -- the bone-chillingly uncompromising title cut (by the  underappreciated Jamie O'Hara) and the achingly moving "When the Last  Curtain Falls" -- measure up to any country classic you can name.  And  then there's Jones's performance.  The man is singing better than ever, if  that's possible to imagine.  Though this CD was recorded just before the  accident that nearly killed him, Jones sounds here like a man who's just  returned from the grave and is here to tell us about it.  Country music  doesn't get any truer than this.

title: Check the price and divide by 7
text:
Soundtracks (7CD Box) ~ Ry Cooder (Warner/Rhino)

A very tempting collection of all the seven soundtracks albums issued on, or through, Warner Bros. where the music was produced (and played) by Ry Cooder.

I already had CD versions of three of these soundtracks and rated them all very highly so the question for me was is this box worth buying for the four soundtracks I did not have and had not heard.

Based on one listen I'm certain the answer is most certainly yes!

I can't imagine anyone who likes Ry Cooder being disappointed with any of the easier to find albums here like 'The Long Riders', 'Paris, Texas', and 'Crossroads'. The versions in the box either equal or (in the case of 'The Long Riders') sound even better than the original CD editions. The cardboard sleeves are all very neat too. 'Paris, Texas' has a different sleeve than the one I am familiar with.

'Alamo Bay' was originally issued on Slash Records (1985) and was one title that I have always wanted to get hold of. It has, as a stand-alone album, been out of print for years, so I was well pleased to find it included in this box. This soundtrack has a varied mix of different musical styles, and all have their own special attractions. Although I have only heard it once I like what I am hearing.

'Blue City' (1986) is another album with a varied mix of musical styles. It opens with a rocker, followed by a slow groove instrumental that features some lovely steel drum sounds. I don't think Ry Cooder plays on the third track, a pop song performed by a band called True Believers. The record also includes a Ry Cooder version of the 1958 Johnny Cash song 'Don't Take Your Guns To Town'.

A lot of the very impressive 'Johnny Handsome' soundtrack (released in 1989) was featured on the superb double CD 'Music By Ry Cooder', and after hearing the deep atmospheric pieces that were featured on that compilation getting hold of the entire album became a priority.

'Trespass' (originally issued on Sire in 1992) is the one album here that really will surprise a lot of people. This soundtrack features Jon Hassell on trumpet and is full of what sounds to me like industrial/experimental music (not a musical style you would associate with Ry Cooder). The record is notable for the inclusion of one cracking vocal track with killer lyrics - 'King Of The Street', and ends surprisingly with 'Party Lights', an out and out straight country song with Junior Brown on vocal.

All the CD soundtracks in this box have a great sound so no worries about the mastering.

The box itself is sturdy. There is no booklet - but that's no big deal when you can check online if you want or need any further info / reading material.

If you are after a bargain just check the price of the box and divide by 7 (then check the price of the stand alone CDs).

This collection is an excellent follow up to last year's wonderful 11 CD box >>Ry Cooder<< 1970 -1987.

title: Solid Playing - the Singing . . . . . well
text:
The Sorrows from Coventry in England is known for their one 1965 hit "Take a Heart". The band released 6 solid R&B singles and one album for Pye Records during 1965-66. In late 1966 lead-singer Don Fardon and bassist Philip Packham left the group, and an endless list of line-up changes began.

The group had over 1966 lost ground in England and after Fardons and Packham farewell the group was given the opportunity to take a short tour in Italy. This tour with new member Roger Lomas was quite successful, and the group settled in Milan and began to record singles both in English and Italian. The first "Pink, Purple, Yellow and Red" was a brilliant pop-psych thing with guitarist Pip Whitcher as new lead vocalist - unfortunately no hit en Britain. The group left Pye records and began to record for the small Italian label Miura.

This extended album contains the "Miura" recordings supported by a never completed 1969 album, and a live recording of a 1980 reunion concert.

The earliest recordings on this album/compilation are by far the strongest. Pip Whitcher, though not as powerful as Don Fardon, was a good lead singer, and the 3 soundtrack recordings the band did during 1966-67 "Ypotron" and "Pioggia Sui Tuo Viso # 1 and # 2" are as good as most of their early material.

Pip Whitcher also takes the lead vocals on the Italian version of "Listen to Me" ( "Per Una Donna No" ), but left for England sometime in 1967. Two new members, Kit and Rod ( apparently nobody remembers their last names ) were recruited, and the new line-up began recordings for a new album. Most of these recordings have survived on an acetate only and are included on CD 2 of this release. The guitarist Chuck Fryers, who was also a songwriter had also joined the group. Musically the band still sounded pretty tight and solid but neither Kit nor Rod were very good singer - passable at their best though. The album never was released, and Kit and Rod left the Sorrows in frustration, Kit and Rod wrote some good tunes and one of them "The Makers", survived to get its place on the 1969 album "Old Songs New Songs".

New lead singer for the band was a guy called Chris Smith, and he's the lead singer on most of "Old Songs New Songs". Whether it's bad production or the limits of Smith vocal capeability that makes many of these album hard to listen to, I cannot tell. The harmony vocals are also pretty poor at places; so it does not help much that the playing is pretty solid on most tracks. Chuck Fryers apparently was quite a good guitarist. The most successful tracks are older ones with Whitcher or Kit and Rod as singers.

A 1968 unreleased single "Which Way" / "My Way of Thinking" is listed as a Chris Smith vocal performance. I can have my doubts about this, because this single is among the higlights on the CD - especially "Which Way" is a gem.

With the CD comes 16 pages booklet with detaled information about the band's history - well written and well researched and very nice lay-out.

Though the music rarely reaches the standards of the early Sorrows recordings - they are interesting enough for fans of early British rock.

title: Strong  stuff
text:
I've been listening to "Indy" rock for 20 years now - since the days when originality and experimentation were still essential criteria to be considered part of this movement. While I was initially happy for later bands to build on some of the highpoints of the bands that came before them in the movement, recently there's been little that was either as strong or as original as the artists that first defined the "Indy" or other extensions of the "post-punk" or "New Wave" sounds.

This album however has some really strong tracks on it, and it's amongst the better records of this ilk that I've heard ever. It builds on some as-yet-untapped high points of bands that have been, and which no-one else has been insightful enough to mine yet. In doing so Interpol pass over a lot of ideas that have been run into the ground, and breath life into a musical tradition that is in grave danger of drowning to death in mediocrity.

I should end on a high point though. "Our Love to Admire" is the best rock album I've heard this year, and I look forward to hearing more music from bands like them who tread the high musical ground.

title: Outstanding Monteverdi from Tragicomedia and Stubbs
text:
This 1993 release gives us outstanding early music, with a terrific and consistent performance from the Tragicomedia group led by Stephen Stubbs, presenting several very strong compositions from early baroque composer Claudio Monteverdi, all helped by near audiophile grade sound engineering.

The album’s centerpiece is Monteverdi’s major mini-drama, “The Ball of the Ungrateful Women,” a thirty-five-minute-long composition dating from 1608, when the composer was just beginning to develop the early baroque style which he established in the coming decades, with recitative-like monody, dramatic roles and the accompaniment of a continuo of plucked and bowed string instruments. At the time the “Ball” was first drafted, it would have represented a daring and avant-garde effort. I think the “Ball” remains among Monteverdi’s best works and despite its archaic theme – the ingratitude of beautiful women who reject the wooing of suitors – has many moments of beauty. The avant-garde aspect of the “Ball” is often apparent, with unusual effects. Including a fading-away vocal ensemble conclusion that sounds like no other baroque music I know of.

Tragicomedia does the piece very well. Each soloist is strong. The “Ball” is led by soprano Barbar Borden (Love), Harry van der Kamp (Pluto, lord of the underworld ) and countertenor Paivi Jarvio (as Venus). The casting of a male countertenor in the part of a woman is a misstep, but probably the disc’s only significant one. Why have a man perform a woman’s role when there are so many talented altos out there? In fact, a very good rival recording from the Consort of Musicke (on Virgin Classics) casts an alto as Venus, logically enough, and the results are excellent. Despite this error in judgment, the performance here is excellent. Van der Kamp has a resonant and powerful bass voice that he uses expressively. His solo opening the Entrata (track 4), a somewhat spooky love song emanating from the depths, is presented just beautifully. I also liked the singing from both Borden and Jarvio, a fine countertenor.
The playing of the small band is very enjoyable. The “Ball” is recorded along with the other works with quite a bit of ambient sound, which serves well and emphasizes the luxuriant and often harmonically ostentatious nature of Monteverdi’s writing, the chromatic chord changes caressing us.

The disc also presents two shorter madrigals, both from the 7th book of madrigals, issued by Monteverdi in 1619. Each feature tenor John Potter, as soloist in “Tempro la cetra” (“I tune the lyre”), and paired with soprano Suzie Le Blanc in the longer, dance-like “Tirsi e Clori”. These are not dramatic like the “Ball of the Ingrates” or the other long dramatic madrigal which concludes the disc, “The Combat of Tancred and Clorinda”, a twenty-minute long bore which I don’t put in the same class as the other music here. The two shorter madrigals are beautiful, each very different. “Tirsi e Clori” is somewhat wistful, lighter but with a captivating melody, while “Tempro la cetra” is slower, a more self-consciously arty piece, with a truly sublime main melody in the strings, surging and sensuous.

One of the interesting things about the disc is how each of the compositions – despite their age and remote background – sound very different. Stubbs’ programming succeeds in emphasizing what a flexible and imaginative artist Monteverdi was, someone who could and did change techniques and styles depending on the intent and the text being set, and most times, succeeding brilliantly at it. Getting to know this recording has been very enjoyable for me and, if you are a committed early music fan, you will want to hear it as well.

title: Leaving a Mark On Music History
text: People always say that Leave Home is a slightly weaker album than their debut. I on the other hand totally disagree.  Leave Home offers more of the same music from the first, but turns up the pop sound, the Ramones were pop/rock. What I really liked about the remastered version is that they added "Carbona Not Glue" and "Babysitter".  The live songs were great, but not that necessary.  Anyway, back to the true genious of songs on this album, not only did they give us great pop songs, but they gave us some more lyrics to listen to.  Instead of the same lyrics getting repeated, they give us more of a story to listen to on each song.  The lyrics also get more controversial, "Glad To see You Go" and "You Should Never Have Opened That Door" are some of the Ramones most controversial lyrics since "Now I Wanna Sniff Some Glue". Leave Home definently leaves you in awe.

title: Very lovely music undone by indifferent performances
text: If you are interested in the string quartets of the classical era, you owe it to yourself to dip your ears into the string quartets of Reicha. Read the other reviews below, Scott Morrison's in particular, and you'll get a fine idea of how much delight they can cause and why they're worth hearing. But it must be said that they are also worth being played much better than they are by the Kreutzer Quartet here... which turns in very unlovely performances. They don't sound like a seasoned string quartet, much less like one that adheres to the professional standards common today for such ensembles. Apart from intonation issues (subtle, but it doesn't take much in a string quartet for it to sound off-the-rails), they are also plodding their way through the music like troglodytes at the coming-out ball. Not always, but often enough to seriously hamper my enjoyment of this disc. In fact, except for reference to the music, I will not listen to it again -- hoping instead that they will improve their playing in subsequent issues or, better yet, that a more able quartet takes on this valuable music.

title: Incredibly Creative
text: Ben Allison's Peace Pipe is one of the more ambitious and unbelivably original jazz project's I've ever heard. Allison creates incredible textures and rhythmic patterns by using so many different unusual elements in the music: muted piano, prepared piano, picking bass strings with a subway card, cymbals on the drum heads and of course, the defining aspect of this recording, the traditional Malian kora, a harp made from a gourd. Mamadou Diabate is a stunning musician, but the kora makes a certain thought about this music on this album even more incredible. I had the pleasure of seeing Diabate live once and realized that the kora is actually a diatonic instrument. It can only play in one key at one time. As a result, the writing process of this music must have been extremely difficult in order to make jazz with the harmonic limitations of the kora. The result is music like you've never heard before. The improvisational ablities of the musicians is outstanding as usual. Get ready for a musical treat with Peace Pipe.

title: Great Journey Album
text:
This is an awesome album by Classic Rockers, Journey in 1981. I'll say that this is their 2nd best or 3rd best (Best being Infinity and this is their 2nd or 3rd best depending on how much I like Frontiers.) But this does include some of their all-time best songs: "Don't Stop Believin'", "Who's Cryin' Now", "Escape", "Mother, Father", & "Open Arms". Steve Perry sounds amazing just like any other album, Jonathan Cain makes his Debut in Journey here (Ok he was with the Babys but what I mean is this is his 1st album with Journey), Neal Schon rocks as always, Ross Valory gives us a solid performance, Steve Smith (Best Drummer ever!) is completely awesome here!

Now let's take a look at this music:

1. "Don't Stop Believin'"- I won't describe this because I've never met a person who's never heard this before! (Yes it's that popular! This puts all modern music to shame.)

2. "Stone in Love"- Great tune. I like the opening guitar part and the song that follows said opening.

3. "Who's Cryin' Now"- Mellow but powerful rocker. GREAT guitar solo. This solo really showcases Schon's talent as a guitarist.

4. "Keep on Runnin"- A fun little song that is fast and catchy. I like it a lot.

5. "Still They Ride"- A beautiful ballad that showcases Perry's amazing voice.

6. "Escape"- Best song on the album. As a fan of progressive music, this is amazing. I love the instrumental section between the 2 different parts. And the guitar on the 2nd part is just plain awesome!

7. "Lay it Down"- None of the songs of this album are bad by any means but I don't like this one and the next one as much as the rest. It's just a rocker.

8. "Dead or Alive"- A good song but not too interesting to me. It has a good beat and guitar part but I just don't care for it.

9. "Mother, Father"- A very nicely done Power Ballad about the strength of the family. I love the whole song and I think it's one of their overall best.

10. "Open Arms"- Their biggest hit of the album. It reached number 2 back in the year it came out. I like this ballad but "Faithfully" from Frontiers is better IMO.

Bonus Tracks:

11. "La Roza del Sol"- This is a lame excuse for a bonus track. It's okish but I don't like it. It's like a dance song but it just sounds weird for them.

Tracks 12-14- Live versions of "Don't Stop Believin'" (I like the live version of this one better), "Who's Cryin' Now", and "Open Arms".

Verdict: This is a Classic Rock Classic. This was their biggest selling album (until they released their Greatest Hits) and for good reason. It's mainstream 80's and very awesome. This reissue is just awesome. If you like bands like Boston, REO Speedwagon, or Survivor, then this will please you. If you want to get into this band, then get this or the greatest hits. I'd say this over the GH but whichever you choose I guess. IF YOU DON'T LIKE IT, YOU ARE DEAF!

title: LINDA SCOTT IS EVERY LITTLE STAR
text:
"The Complete Hits Of Linda Scott" is an album of absolute perfection. . . track after track after track! Linda's crystal clear yet powerfully melodic voice presents these songs in a manner that has made them "true classics". If you hear Linda's version, any other singer's version gets compared to hers and probably will not just quite measure-up. Of course her "I've Told Every Little Star" is her theme-song. And she sings a number of songs about "stars". But she has a really unique song about love found and lost called "I Left My Heart In The Balcony" which captures that mood just right.
The artists performance, the musical arrangements, and the recording production of this album is a delight to the ears.
It's a shame that Linda Scott quit recording back in 1968 (she sang background vocal that year on Lou Christy's "I'm Gonna Make You Mine"- a song not on this collection obviously, but it was her last year of recording.) She tends to guard her privacy very carefully these days. . . but still I hope for miracles. . . I hope she records some more. I don't know what a more "mature" Linda Scott's vocal delivery might sound like now, but real talent like hers is always lasting and I believe she probably sings and sounds better than ever. C'mon Ms Linda Scott, give us a little bit of happiness, sing a few more songs to brighten our lives with your "smile". . . a smile that you can hear in your voice when you sing. Thanks Linda for the music you have given us.

One of those covers, however, is a rough and almost psycho version of "Pretty Polly" that makes you long for the old days. And why, oh, why did he go through a phase where he had to keep re-recording the born-bad "Born to Rock 'n' Roll?"

I must admit to liking "Bulldog" a bit, and "Jolly Roger" is just plain fun. The trouble with this double package is that both albums are so disappointing that I think of them as one, although Cardiff Rose is not as commercial sounding. If you want to buy this package as a completist, it's not horrible, and I still play it from time to time--admittedly not much, but I would certainly recommend almost anything in lieu of these two albums. title: Alive with Lifehouse
text: In “Out of the Wasteland,” the band Lifehouse takes direct aim at contemporary American culture and pathos and delivers a sound that is surprisingly real, current, and can one say gritty without being anachronistic.  With titles like “One for the Pain,” “Runaways,” “Firing Squad,” and “Hurt this Way,” the album is not exactly milk and cookies on a Saturday night and yet the overall sound has more to do with honey than vinegar.  It is the flavor of a film by Tennessee Williams, poignant, emotional, slightly dysfunctional but always reeling with hope and a free-wheeling desire.  It is a uniquely American sound, feeling, and vibe being gloomy yet optimistic, tame yet wild, honest yet a false projection of a land that has struggled with all kinds of evils and shortcomings.  There is no better band than Lifehouse to take the triumph and tragedy of the American experience and translate it into music that is, if not epic, at least enjoyable and resonates with our better angels.

title: Wicked, Evil, Sublime- One of Funk's finest...
text:
Venetian Snares is the one-an-only Aaron Funk. This bad mofo hails from Winnipeg, Canada. In the span of a few short years he has produced an amazing body of work. He has released over 15 full length-albums since 2001. In addition, he has also released numerous 12-inches, 7-inches, EP's, and other assorted madness. He never ceases to amaze, constantly reinventing himself, yet maintaining his own distinct sound. `Doll Doll Doll' was one of the first Venetian Snares albums I had the pleasure to pick up, and it still remains one of my favorites. This is some very dark and aggressive music. Funk has easily infiltrated the often boring and unimpressive world of electronic music, assaulting our ear drums with delicious violence, virtuoso editing, dark melodic ambience, and blistering breakbeats. This is not your typical drum n' bass. Anyone who calls it that is sorely mistaken. The music of Venetian Snares occupies its own sonic space, combining power electronics, sinister ambience, free jazz, breakbeats, punk attitude, alien sound creation, and an assortment of other entities (some of which don't even have proper names yet). I find myself increasingly distancing myself from electronic music. Most of the electronic music I have purchased during the past few years I have found to be boring, contrived, and really missing something. However, I find myself increasingly drawn to the sinister, renegade stylings of Aaron Funk.

`Doll Doll Doll' is one sinister monster of an album. Chock full of mesmerizing drum programming, evil samples, and a pervasive feeling of dread. If you are familiar with Funk, you know what to expect. If you are not, this would be a great place to start. I find for some reason, this album is a lot easier to listen to than many other Snares releases. I find this to be paradoxical consider its hardcore, evil, foreboding nature. I think it has something to do with the breaks used throughout the album. They seem to be slightly less chopped and destroyed than on some of his more recent releases. I also love the artwork. Trevor Brown's skewed visions perfectly augment Funk's music. Some people seem to be offended by the artwork and the music. Obviously this wasn't made some people. If you find yourself drawn to the darker side of humanity, you will probably love this release. It is violent, yet beautiful. Evil, yet comforting. It is one of my favorite albums. I highly recommend it to those who love music that is dark, heavy, and scary. Fans of power electronics and breakcore surely already have this...

title: one of the best lyric-driven albums ever yet released
text: The music underlying "All My Happiness is Gone" seems to intentionally recall "Love Will Tear Us Apart". And since Berman is a better writer than Ian Curtis, I end up loving this song more. What makes the album superior to "American Water" and his other, must-hear classics is that every song is a gem, and worth re-hearing multiple times. Perhaps there is nothing as completely catchy as "Random Rules" here, but the lyrics seem rawer, and the throwaway lines don't exist. "Darkness and Cold", a song mostly about a love's affair, does brilliant things with the "light of my life" metaphor, with the words definitely elevating the chorus. I can see lovers of vocals not being super fans of David Berman but when fellow musicians John Darnielle and Stephen Malkmus put his songwriting on a higher level than their own, it's far from mere talk. Lou Reed occasionally reached similar literary heights ("Harry's Circumcision", or his tribute to Delmore Schwartz), but Reed wrote with far more affectation, most of the time; Berman always stayed true. I still would put Randy Newman at the top -- check out "I Want You to Hurt Like I Do", "Miss You", "My Life is Good" --  but how many writers make you go back to the works of his creative writing teacher (James Tate) after listening to his stuff? Anyway, "Purple Mountains" is brilliant. The accompanying videos on Youtube seem to add nothing to the music, btw.

title: The Last of the Great R&H Dramas
text: While Rodgers and Hammerstein went on to collaborate five more times during their career, this was the last of their great musical plays.  All that followed "The King and I" could be more easily described as musical comedy.  Although its age is evident (none of the early recordings on random labels hold a candle to the Columbia recordings), this really is the recording of choice for any "The King and I" connoisseur.  After all, R&H wrote the show for Gertrude Lawrence who came to them with the story.  Granted, her voice may not be the loveliest on Earth, but she's got the spunk and attitude necessary for the character.  The rest of the cast, including the inimitable Yul Brynner (nice try, Ben Kingsley), is wonderful and the songs are performed at their best.  Songs like "I Whistle A Happy Tune," "Hello, Young Lovers," "Getting to Know You" and "Shall We Dance" are sung as well as can be expected by an at-the-end-of-her-life Lawrence.  While they are all among the best songs written by R&H, they pale in comparison (in my humble opinion) to the two real winners in this score: the beautiful love duet "I Have Dreamed" and the score's best song "Something Wonderful."  The latter song really does sum up the entire relationship between Mrs. Anna and the king and is the true theme of the show.  I highly recommend this recording, especially over the abominable 1992 Andrews/Kingsley recording.  At least Lawrence still had some spunk when she performed these songs.  Andrews had already lost her voice and scooped every lyric.  Trust me, they got it right with the original cast!

title: A Fabulous star in the forgotten power pop constellation
text: The commercial failure and critical success of Alex Chilton and Big Star is now a story so well known that the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame telephone call, induction, and display is simply the last chapter of the Dostoyevskian tale. Add to the pile of tragic and undeserved obscurity of Memphis power pop The Scruffs. A worthy pile, it is also inhabited by Big Star, of course, and Tommy Hull, Ricky Branyan, and Randy Chertow's "The Randy Band," and one-time Rolling Stone auditioner, uber-guitarist Robert Johnson (no, not that Robert Johnson, the other one, of "Close Personal Friend" fame), and also tragically, The Grifters. While "Midtown" does not feature the classic Scruffs lineup of Stephen Burns, Dave Branyan, Ricky Branyan, and Zeph Paulson, enough of Burns crystal clear expression is available to satisfy the most linear of Scruffs fans who previously were only familiar with "Wanna Meet...?" From the very first track "Things are Green" we encounter an artfully constructed pop song with lyrics and pacing that in a just world would push everything else off the radio. And the album just gets better after that. This record should be in everyone's collection, for without it you only know a single chapter of the lost generation of Memphis power pop, a musical movement that remains so powerful to this day that virtually no guitar song with a Rickenbacker jangle guitar riff doesn't own its very conception to these pioneers.

title: Great late Goldsmith
text: This is one of those Goldsmith scores, like "Extreme Prejudice," that is often cited - by the critics at Film Score Monthly in particular - as an example of Goldsmith at his nadir: overreliance on the drum kit, bombast over substance, etc etc etc (as the King of Siam probably never said.) It's gotten a bum rap, and has become as rare as wit in a Hollywood blockbuster. I could give or take "Extreme Prejudice," but "Deep Rising" is a score that LIVES. When I first found it, I couldn't stop listening to it. True, it doesn't attain the emotional highs and sonic resonance of "The Omen," "Poltergeist" or "The Wind and Lion." But to these ears, it's one of Goldsmith's most exciting, accomplished and inventive action scores, on a par with "Capricorn One," "First Blood," and "Under Fire." Which is to say, among the best ever composed for a movie.

title: Like no other version
text: If I had to pick one song(not CD) that demostrates the essence of John Coltrane I would pick "My Favorite Things". The alto sax work was a breakthrough that opened the doors for others. Through the years I've played this song hundreds of times and get mixed reactions from people who happen to be listening with me. The overwhelming majority love it. I'm biased but the song itself is worth the price of the CD alone. Recorded relatively early in his career, during his Atlantic years, the CD is pretty mellow in comparison to his later years that were more introspective and exploratory. Cole Porter, Gershwin and Rodgers and Hammerstein penned the songs so that in itself should tell you something, there are no Coltrane originals. The swinging result is that these standards are reworked by Coltrane in his own unforgetable style style. "Summertime," one of the most recorded songs of all time is bluesy and soulful as performed by Trane. The lyrical stylings of his tenor horn is driven hard, fast and furious by drummer Elvin Jones, elapsing into breathless improvisation that winds up through and around a course he takes the listener on winding back into familiar territory where "the living is easy, so hush my darling don't you cry." Coltrane regroups while McCoy Tyner takes his turn, followed by bass before bowing out to the master sax man to bring it all back home. The title track and "Summertime" are easily the best cuts from the CD. This is a good CD for someone just getting into Trane and perfect for those that need to upgrade from their old versions. As a snapshot in time of his career it is excellent. In comparison to other releases from his vast body of  work it falls a little short(A-) but who's compalining, not me. Great stuff by one of the giants of jazz and not to be missed to experience the evolution of greatness, whether for the first time or again and again.

title: It's a trick of hand
text:
It is somewhat unusual to get 20 tracks in one CD without noticing that there are actually 20 tracks in one CD, of course only an experienced trickster - like Diggers - can pull off such a thing. Such slight of hand not only requires talent, but intelligence too.
John definitely knows his music, but to place them so cohesively together as if they were deliberately composed in order to be mixed in the same fashion as found in T3 is unbelievable or rather mind boggling.

Introducing Sasha's Coma as the beginning track sets the mood early for what is to come, which is more of the good stuff. I like everything about "Coma" but I especially like how it comes back in the 16th second of track 2 for exactly two seconds flashing you with the sweet nectar of itself in time when you thought it was over. I know it's only two seconds, but it's worth its time in gold (don't ask me how).

The general feel of the composition is eerie, and although not dark in the sense of (GU Hong Kong) dark, it is definitely darkish in its electro taste. That by itself is a welcome change from the regular electro/minimalism we have been listening to for the past couple of years. To save you on all of the mumbo jumbo, there is really nothing to say that has not been said before in other reviews, so I will not repeat the praise. However, I do have to say this about Diggers third transitions installation in comparison to (transitions1 & 2): 3 is better that 2 but not better than 1.

Enjoy in a dark room with your favorite choice of poison.

title: Sparkles with Originality
text: Shelby Lynne's "Revelation Road" sparkles with originality.  As always, Shelby is an expressive singer who embodies her songs and oozes feeling.  As a songwriter, each track is strong.  Softer songs like "The Thief" also shine, "If I thought a million bucks could make you want to just stand up and walk into my love like before, I'd rob a rich man's diamond mine to make you be my Valentine; Say the word & I'll become a thief."  "Woebegone" churns slowly somewhere between country, folk, & rock with a touch of blues, "Should have seen it coming; A crystal ball says it all; When I wake up and see me crying, woe be gone."  The midtempo rocker, "Heaven's Only Days Down the Road," is a stunning gem that deals with death as a release from pain, "I've been insane since I was nine, never went to crying, was the fighting kind, load up the gun full of regret; I ain't even pulled the trigger yet."  The title track has one of Shelby's best melodies that seems to flow effortlessly with her sparkling vocals crowning the track.  This is a wonderful set with charms that keep enhancing with repeated listening.  Enjoy!

title: Northern Soul !!
text:
Wow, Bruce has really found his calling with his 2022 album, Only The Strong Survive. Who knew that this hard working American roots rocker was actually the best white soul singer alive today?

This album is mostly covers of Butler, Gamble and Huff ravers and Frank Wilson gems, delivered with heart and verve. Springsteen's sandpapered growl is perfectly suited to the task of putting over these soul classics the way they were meant to be played.

This isn't new territory for The Boss. I suspect a lot of these dance tunes were used as closers or encores, when Springsteen's band was playing beach bars on the East Coast in the 1960s and 70s. Now he's dusted them off, given each one a thoughtful new arrangement, and delivered them like a loving gift to a brand new audience.

title: When Fogerty's angry, I'm happy - he makes better music that way.
text: Let's face it, John Fogerty was NOT in a good mood when CCR recorded Green River. No matter what the idyllic title track may lead to believe, this is an enraged, paranoid, defeated record. Not only that, it's an excellent engraged, paranoid, defeated record, loaded with some of the group's best hits. I'd go with the best song being the natural-disaster warning Bad Moon Rising (which, contrary to popular belief, had NOTHING to do with bathrooms on the right). Not to discount the other songs, though. The title track is a favorite of mine, and as I said one of the few songs this disc that's not angry. Even then, it's melancholy. Same with Lodi, a song about a musician payin' dues. Commotion is another warning song, and it's also first-rate. Plus we get a couple of the group's best album tracks: Tombstone Shadow and especially Wrote a Song for Everyone, the latter being my second-favorite on the disc. The album does fall apart on a couple tracks, though: Cross-Tie Walker is at the level of some of Bayou Country's fillers; Night Time is the Right Time throws off the mood and showcases awful faux doo-wap backing vocals that must be heard to be believed. But whatever - this is still CCR's best.

title: just one little annoying thing
text:
Everything others have said about this album is true: it is an excellent album from Neil's phase when he still sought memorable, original melodies and sounds. All I can add is that what may pass for slightly quaint conceits now (although no less listenable for that), such as opening the album with an instrumental, countrified thing, or letting Jack Nitzsche go to town on String Quartet From Whiskey Boot Hill with a contemporary (read: occasionally atonal) chamber music interlude, was innovative at the time of its creation, and made everyone feel like there was still hope for the progress of rock.
Now on to my little annoying thing. The good news is that this remaster is truly a remaster, a warm, "round"-sounding one well worth the money, unlike the myriad remasters where you sit dumbfounded and wonder where the difference with the previous release is, and where your money has gone. The one teensy thing that bothers me is that the loudness levels don't seem to be equal from song to song. Right off the bat, you'll want to hear The Emperor of Wyoming louder than The Loner, which follows it. Granted, the first one is soft and leans toward violins, the second is a pretty hard rocker with a typical Neil-fuzzed electric guitar and the killer 60's organ; they are naturally different-sounding songs, but I'd have thought that was precisely what remasters were for: to find the best possible balance for all songs on the album (among other things).
I don't know if this is the case for all four in this initial series of remasters: I started at the beginning, we'll see where this leads, but I do hope the levels are more consistent on the remaining albums.

title: My response to the complaint
text:
Dear Mr. Brad H. from Ohio:
I am intrigued, to say the least, to learn that what you call the rhetoric is not relevant to the music, for in fact I recapitulate what the artists (Malick and Zimmer) had to think about when making the movie and its score. And, I was offended, to say the least, to learn that in reviewing music, we must either repeat the most conventional sentiments (for these, it appears, are always "relevant") or somehow maintain the on-the-face-of-it absurd proposition that music points nowhere and is noise.
And I am very offended that the moderator of this group at Amazon has inserted your offtopic complaint. Your post is not "about" the music at all whereas there is a rather short chain of relevance between every sentence of my review, and the music.
A thoroughgoing application of "relevance" would mean that there would be one valid post of the form "I liked it" or "I did not like it". This would be useful to market research only, not to real flesh-and-blood listeners.
Your review is "about" your conventionality and authoritarian streak; for Malick's film is a comment about those who, like Steven Spielberg, glorified modern, industrial war as somehow heroic and who are war criminals, responsible for inveigling a new generation into a new "police action" in Iraq.
In my review I provide information that is useful to the listener of the Zimmer score who may very well be ignorant both of the film and the history of Oceania. It is for example not possible to understand the a capella singing in the score without understanding how pervasive Christianity is in Oceania.
I have traveled in Oceania near the islands where the film was made and its culture, and its brutalization by the Second World War, are most germane, most relevant, to understanding the film and the score.
Theodore Wiesengrund Adorno has reflected on the barbarism of deliberate forgetting horror in his comment on the possibility of poetry after the Holocaust. Absent the supplementary "irrevelances" of my post, the danger is that Zimmer's score becomes (as I said in the review) just more Muzak that Americans use to lull themselves to the growing barbarism of our domestic life and our international conduct, safe, or so they think, within their SUVs and with their state-of-the-art sound systems.
Therefore I ask the Amazon moderator to either post this at the Zimmer site, or remove Mr. Brad's comment. It violates the very rules he attempts to apply. My original post DOES NOT.

title: Fantastic
text:
Okay, so I admit it. I was one of the fans who thought she had lost it. Over the last several years, Tori Amos's music seemed to be running low on steam. 1999's ambitious, feisty "to venus and back" album was followed by the birth of Amos's first child. After that, everything seemed to head downhill. The following albums, "Strange Little Girls" and "Scarlet's Walk"; were both commendable efforts, but it didn't take a brain surgeon to acknowledge the fact that they could instantaneously put the listener to sleep. So once "The Beekeeper" was released in 2005, things started to get really fuzzy. Gone was the energetic, piano-humping, red-haired goddess. In her place was a mellow, soft-spoken, almost lifeless performer. Incidentally, the album cover for "Beekeeper" looked like a children's book, with Amos smirking among little plants and cute fonts. This was actually the same woman who breast fed a pig back in the photos for her "Boys for Pele" in '96.

I saw Tori perform in the summer of '05 in Baltimore. The venue was nice, the weather was gorgeous. If only the performer matched the weather. At one point, I started thinking about what I had to do the following day. I remembered thinking about laundry and other things. This was not supposed to be happening to me at a Tori Amos show! After this concert, I had decided that Tori Amos had lost it. I was happy for her in the sense that she was a mother and allowing herself to relax, but I was unhappy that it had taken a toll on her art. So when Tori had hinted to fans in early 2006 that the "warrior woman" was going to come around for the next album, I was anxious to see if she would follow through.

Fast forward to the new year. A photo of Amos was released to the Internet featuring the artist standing in front of a house, arms opened. One arm had "shame" written on it. The other was holding a Bible. Her leg had blood dripping down; a foreshadowing go-ahead for me to welcome the familiar Tori Amos back to the music world.

The photo was a promo shot for "American Doll Posse", the latest release from Amos. Let's begin with the concept. Unsurprisingly, Tori decided to give herself alter-egos (the Posse girls) who "perform" each song. These girls are based on Greek characters. There's Santa, the passionate girl based upon Aphrodite. Isabel is political and based off of Artemis. Clyde is trying to understand her life like Persephone. Pip is the "warrior woman" like Athena. Finally, the character Tori is based upon Dionysus and Demeter and obviously is the artist herself.

Once you know the posse, you can understand the songs. And by songs, I mean all 23 of them (26 if you count the bonus tracks available elsewhere). Tori...I mean, Isabel...opens the album with "Yo George", a short and witty number that takes a stab at none other than our favorite Bush. 'I salute to you commander and I sneeze,' Isabel sings for about a minute and a half before Tori (the character) launches into "Big Wheel", the thumping first single that can have you dancing in seconds. No other moment feels better to hear when she calls herself a "M.I.L.F.", a term that everyone should know by now. We welcome Clyde to the stage on "Bouncing Off Clouds", which is perhaps one of the most gorgeous songs Tori has written yet. Pip shows up for "Teenage Hustling", a shocking return to form as the artist rocks the sh*t out of the song with biting lyrics like 'I've been working it since I was 14' and guitar noise that I never expected to hear again in a Tori Amos song. Santa appears a few songs later with "You Can Bring Your Dog", a rock song which, if done by a male artist, would not sound too shabby coming from Elton John. The next surprise comes as Pip's next appearance with "Fat Slut", a 41 second interlude with overamped guitar (reminiscent of the ones we heard back in '94 with Amos's cover of "If 6 Was 9") and intense vocals. At this point during my first listen, I remember wanting to ask the artist where the hell she had been these last couple of years. The album isn't all rock and roll. Staple Tori Amos ballads are included. "Digital Ghost", "Girl Disappearing", "Father's Son", and "Dark Side of the Sun" are terrific songs. Particularly the latter, which "ends" the album with a climactic segue into the state of the world. The album isn't over, though. "Posse Bonus" is a quick tune that very obviously tells the listener that the experience isn't complete. Afterwards, we get quite possibly the best two songs on the album- "Smokey Joe" and "Dragon". And if you still haven't had enough after the whopping 23 songs, you can pop in the bonus DVD for "My Posse Can Do", a toe-tapping tribute to each posse girl. Venture to iTunes and you can hear a song called "Miracle". Then, find someone who bought their copy of the album at Borders and ask them nicely to hear "Drive All Night", the 26th and final song (to our knowledge so far) recorded for "American Doll Posse".

Sometimes artists throw fans a surprise (whether good or bad) in their career. The Beatles and Tom Waits went wacky in the 80's. Michael Jackson was a worldwide pop superstar and is now the laughing stock of the universe. Madonna and Cher have reinvented themselves more times than Bush has screwed up the country. Tori Amos was the fiery pianist who changed the face of female rock when she was first bestowed upon us. She slipped away for those couple years that I discussed earlier. But with "American Doll Posse", her surprise is that she is back full force, and now there are five of her. And I couldn't be happier.

title: Sprawling
text:
For me this album defines sprawl. 2 cds that go on forever and ever. That is not to say that this is not a fine example of Van Morrison's more recent work, but there sure is a lot to digest here, may be too much.
For me, too much of this album is given over to two of the less interesting themes in Van's recent music--overt (conventional) religion and griping about the nature of show-biz and celebrity. Dropping a few of these songs would have yielded a more compact and powerful album.
Still, the best tracks on this set are as transcendent and moving as Van's recent work gets. "Carrying A Torch", the title track, "I Need Your Kind of Loving", "Hyndford Street", and "Take Me Back" are all masterpieces. "Carrying a Torch" may be the best song Van has done in the last 20 years. None of the rest is bad (except may be "Village Idiot"), and quite a bit of it is good/very good just not truly remarkable (at least by Van Morrison standards). Trim the fat and you'd have a five-star classic for sure.

title: The missing link?
text:
Death From Above 1979 (DFA) blazed across the indie world and into that nether region between mainstream success and credibility. "You're a Woman, I'm a Machine" had some major money behind it, Vice's record imprint is technically part of Atlantic... I should say, major force, if not funds. That album was a short blast of dance-punk/metal noise that was wholly unexpected by most. Jesse's angular bass chops and Sebastian's furious Joy Division-esqe drumming created a heady brew. The mostly tongue in cheek lyrics and occasional analog synth blast just added to the mix.

However, bass and drum noisecore bands are nothing new: Lightning Bolt has been rocking that scene for over ten years. But making the same style music poppy (and sing-a-long) was pretty much unheard of. It's hard to quantify what made them so magic, but their only LP is insanely hard to put down... even over a year later.

Their first EP, "Heads Up" has since been reissued, to help fill in the catalog. Whether this is an opportunistic grab from Last Gang, is immaterial, although the re-release fixes the old textual errors (the original release had the wrong website and "Death From Above" without the 1979 appended... pre-"cease and desist letter") and adds new ones ("Too Much Love" is misspelled).

Since the band broke up, chances are you will pick this up and it's well worth the price. Judging this record in comparison to "You're a Woman..", it gets four stars. However, in the grander scheme it's a little more mediocre. Remember this was originally released in 2002. Jesse and Sebastian endured two more years of sweaty basement gigs before they achieved success.

Of course the record quality is lower, more consistent with self produced home studio albums. If that turns you off, be thankful that "You're a Woman..." is so sparkly... indie music in general, might not be for you. Remember some of the greatest indie records of the last twenty five years were pretty rough (Black Flag's "Damaged I", The Wrens "Secaucus", At The Drive-In's "In Casino Out", etc). If anything, it's more consistent with noisecore... even if DFA isn't technically a noisecore band (Jesse's background is more arty-retro punk). After all, Lightning Bolt tries to make records sound "live".

The album starts out with, what sounds like Japenese or gibberish through a vocoder and rockets into "Dead Womb" (a song that evokes some of the quicker moments on "You're a Woman..."). "Dead Womb" is a quicker step and a little less "dancey" than anything on "You're a Woman", almost more punk. The next song, "Too Much Love" continues like that... actually a little more driving as the song doesn't really break up for a hook. "Too Much Love" actually has Jesse singing too, one of the few times you really hear him doing background vocals. "Do It!" (live) actually is probably my favorite track on the album. It starts with a little synth and breaks up for a long vocoder piece in the middle (laid over some double bass drumming). Except for the intro and outro, "Do It!" sounds just like the other tracks (in terms of production)... that's only mentionable because it's a live album. "Do It!" seems to be more metal too... the drumming is slightly more technical and entwined with the bass. "My Love is Shared" has a pretty big hook, which the earlier songs don't really have. "Losing Friends" starts with pummeling drum work and a very rhythmic bass part, quickly going into the metal-punk-dance style that they would build on for "You're a Woman...". One major distinction is that played with a full band, it would actually make a pretty convincing punk-metal/metalcore anthem. Crazy, eh? The album ends with "If We Don't Make It, We'll Fake It", a longer more screamy song, with a weird synth/vocoder outro.

What makes this different form "You're a Woman..."?

Well, the vocals are more distorted and nothing is double-tracked. While the casual listener interprets this as "poor production", it is actually proof that the band was just as good live as they were in a big studio. Another big distinction is the ability to hear the background vocals.

Overall, this is a more aggressive, less poppy release than their album. Since it lacks the extreme polish it isn't a stretch to say that it might not be for everyone. Yet, you should pick it up, anyway (only 2000 copies were made of the re-issue) and listen to it thoughtfully. DFA was brilliantly punk, self destructing before they could ruin their credibility and this just adds to an album that will become legendary in the future.

Buy it!

title: + 1/2 stars.....Bluegrass Is Alive And Thriving
text:
I have had in my collection for decades the numerous albums the Stanley Brothers cut for Starday, King and Gusto in the fifties and sixties. However, I'll admit it wasn't until Ralph Stanley's resurrection in popularity with the whole "O Brother" phenomenon that I began noticing his more recent labums.
The premise to this 2001 Rebel release was simple: Find some of the best female vocalists in the business and revisit some of the old Stanley Brothers classics. I was skeptical at first, but after the first notes of "Ridin' That Midnight Train" with Iris DeMent, any misgivings I had disappeared.
Although no less moving, Stanley performs "Oh, Death" with Gillian Welch--not a capella, but with the backing of the Clinch Mountain Boys. Other highlights are Dolly Parton's version of "Loving You Too Well," Sara Evans' "Are You Tired of Me, Darling," Lucinda Williams' "Farther Along" and Valerie Smith's "I'll Remember You in My Prayers." Truth to tell, these are are all lovingly performed songs.
As the reigning patriarch of bluegrass, it's encouraging to see Ralph Stanley (who was 73 when these recordings were made) not only receive the recognition he deserves but for helping pass the torch so bluegrass will continue to thrive into the 21st Century. HIGHLY RECOMMENDED

title: Finally, someone reissued these classics
text: The good thing about these overseas compilations is that you get a 2 for 1 deal on the recordings. The bad thing is that with a band like Devo, who constantly morphed from one album to the next, it renders a different feel to the CD half-way through due to the overall tone and attitude of one album to the next. DNFTF exhibits a sound not typical of any other Devo record, not quite as 'punk' as their earlier material and not quite as 'squared off' as their later material. Often with a feel of some other 'progressive rock' emerging at the time, this album explores odd time signatures and new approaches to rock. New Traditionalists falls into the 'squared off' genre. This is post-Whip It, very synth heavy and finely tweezed, as if they had steriled their own safety pin. This features their other siren songs: Through Being Cool and Workin' In A Coalmine (their 'radio songs'?), however there are far more substantial tracks on this record than these. All in all, it seems NT is the destination of Devo's journey....all things prior seem to lead to this point. As usual, both album are laden with prophetic visions of 'de-evolution' and when looking back today it inspires one to say, 'Devo was right'.
