title: Deserves to be a winner.
text:
There used to be a ready market for fanciful, colourful, evocative little orchestral items such as these. You could find almost all of them available in countless versions in the 78s catalogues. Some of the items represented calling cards for Marek Weber and His Orchestra in Europe, and Arthur Fielder and the Boston Pops in the USA.
Well, here they are, marketed now as "classics" in beautifully recorded, slightly English-accented performances. Gounod's own orchestration of his piano piece "Funeral March of a Marionette" is one of the stand out items here, seeming all the more unusual for not being much heard these days. Joseph Hellmesberger's "Ball Scene", a test for the string section of the orchestra, receives virtuoso treatment here. The polka from "Schwanda the Bagpipe Player" stands out too, making one wish there had been time to include the fugue with which it is usually coupled.
Nevertheless, the results of considerable research, long selection processes, program building, two days of recording, and the preparation of excellent notes by Andrew Lamb make this another Hyperion release which deserves to be a winner. My only quibble is regarding the statement in the notes that the Alfven piece included here had wide currency in the 1950s under the name "Swedish Polka". It was the first few minutes of Alfven's "Midsummer Vigil", in a version by Percy Faith and His Orchestra, that topped the charts in the early 1950s, given the title "Swedish Rhapsody".

title: "Instead of celebrating our differences, we choose to fear them"
text:
When you listen to the first demo tape Laura recorded (solo) under the Against Me! name, in 1997, the first thing you hear is the quote, "Instead of celebrating our differences, we choose to fear them". And this new album flows very much with that spirit. Much about this band, and their sound, has changed in the following years. The mainstream accessible sound as of the "New Wave" era was something we fans either got used to, or didn't. For me, White Crosses felt poppy and a bit hollow. I realized that if they continued on the trajectory established by those two albums, a day would come where I would throw up my hands and give up on Against Me!

But that day is not today. Meaningful (as a tremendous understatement) lyrics and powerful delivery in Transgender Dysphoria Blues have put the band back on a course that I'm excited to hear more from. I personally prefer their work up to and including "Clarity", but I can't stop listening to the new album.

title: Not "truncated" versions of the hits--these ARE the hits!
text:
I'm tired of reading about how this compilation sucks because the songs have been "edited" or cut off in the middle. That is simply NOT TRUE. When you see a JB tune with "part one" after the title, that just means you've got the hit single version. Back in the day JB recorded the long versions solely so he could cull 2-3 minute singles from them. Sometimes the track was split into part one and part two--or the A side of the 45 and the B side (or in the case of "Make it Funky" spread over two singles in a part one, part two, part three, and part four). Most often, however, the entire track was NEVER MEANT TO BE RELEASED.

This cd comp is a collection of "hit singles," not a dip into the vaults as most JB cds of the past couple of decades have been. Now I'd never give up my cds with the long versions--I love 'em--but it is also cool to have a cd of the Hit 45 versions.

title: Small label retrospective
text:
For a few years in the mid-60's, White Whale records of L.A. put a stream of singles on the charts, headed by their flagship act, the Turtles. This compilation, with a sampling of the Turtles' best-known tunes, includes eight top-100 songs along with a variety of singles that didn't get as far. While White Whale had its share of avant-garde material, where it succeeded best was with its classy, sophisticated pop productions. One prime example is "All Strung Out", Nino Tempo, with sister April Stevens', Spectorian pop extravaganza. Beyond the well-known Turtles tracks, this CD includes such rarities as Liz Damon's Orient Express' "1900 Yesterday", Rene and Rene's Latin hit "Lo Mucho Que Te Quiero" and Lyme and Cybelle's "Follow Me".

All tracks are mono as they are single versions with the exception of track 17. The eight-page liner notes booklet offers up backround information on the included artists.

Overall, an interesting gathering of tracks from this short-lived but productive independent label. For more detailed coverage of the artists on White Whale, there are several Turtles CD's available and Varese Vintage has reissued Nino and April's White Whale album with bonus tracks.

title: Fear Factory Slays The Naysayers Again
text:
I was pleasantly surprised to hear that Dino Cazares and Burton C. Bell were working together as Fear Factory again last year. This album - despite the petulant whining of some nameless reviews - is a fine return to form for the group. This is NOT a record you can grasp completely upon just one sitting. After three listens I am still hearing things I had missed before. True, as mentioned before the stock Fear Factory guitar assault, keyboard atmospherics and inhuman drumming fill this work from end to end. However it seems the years apart have given Burton and Dino a fresh dynamic, and they're picking up where their better works of [[ASIN:B0008F113W Demanufacture]] and [[ASIN:B000009CEM Obsolete]] left off. They also throw in the brute aggression of [[ASIN:B0002ZYDYM Soul of a New Machine]] to kick the pants off the Demanufacture and Obsolete reminiscings on this record.

What's killer is that they're trying new twists on the old formula, and you can tell it's good thing because it's pissing some people right off! Those who whine about there being a solitary actual lead on this album forget that Dino played a minimalist lead on the song "Messiah" on Obsolete's bonus track edition. I suppose Dino should just stick to root-note rhythms and pretend he doesn't know how to play anything else according to some. In lyrical content Fear Factory ties all their previous work into the ultimate analogy: the state as the machine. In subtle nods to the 9/11 Truth Movement and to futurists predicting a decentralized progression of society, it's nice to see the sci-fi rubber meeting the real world road.

The addition of the 1991 demo shows the continuity of the band. After all these years, oh yes it's true, Burton and Dino are still Fear Factory. It's educational to hear the original arrangements of those 4 bonus songs, especially if you own Soul of a New Machine and the bonus edition of Obsolete. In their final forms half of them were sped up and rearranged on their respective records, but you can make out the intent just the same. Don't believe the hype: you have to hear [[ASIN:B00319ECC4 Mechanize]] for yourself. A good record takes you on a journey, energizes your boring daily routine and inspires you to kick some healthy arse. In my honest opinion this record hits it right out of the park. Don't take my word for it - preview the songs here on Amazon and you be the judge.

title: Accept Me for What I Am---Accept Me for the Things That I Do...
text:
Just a note to my worldwide fans- I have opened up my review site to influential people who may include notes of interest to certain selections. I am busy now, investigating paranormal activity in millionaire's homes (and being paid the current minimum wage!). It doesn't matter people if I have to stay awhile and they put me up in a tent with no running water. I will just dent their Rolls Royce with my Yugo on the way out.
But, at least I found a ghost of a chance to write this review. To begin- this music is a refreshing turn away from selections I've recently reviewed. I like all types of music and the last thing I want all of you to believe is that your beloved Metamorpho is predictable. Besides, sometimes you need softer, beautiful music to get reflection up to snuff. I have, yet, another gem for you all and here it is.
Musically, I think of the 60's as one of the most diverse periods for popular music. We were treated to many new and exciting sounds. One of the most infallable sounds in popular music from that time is captured with this album. I really don't know how to describe the sound - easy-going, orchestrated swing, jazzy, suave, heartfelt? Well, this list could include reflection goal oriented for sure. (!) When you have a superb songwriting duo such as Burt Bacharach and Hal David - the songs approach a spiritual sublime. Add the vocal perfection of Dionne Warwick in with this then you have heavenly sound on earth.
Alot of these songs convey the vulnerability of women at that time. Heartbreak, hurt, and the longing to be loved. The fact that men wrote them is even more astounding. But that is an indication of the talent and the ability to tap into human emotion. There aren't many that measured up to that duo.
But Dionne......ahhh.... Dionne. The inflection in that beautiful voice, the raising and lowering of phrases totally appropriate to the material. Listen to her heartfelt declaration on "Don't Make Me Over", the hurt on "Walk On By", the insistent charge of "Always Something There to Remind Me", or the grace and softness on "Alfie". You all know what she can do by now. All the familiar tunes can be found on your local adult oriented pop music station. But, even the lesser known songs are a pleasure and a treasure.
And the arrangments on these selections are dead on. There is no excess here. The instruments are craftily crafted to add to the sum total of the mood they are trying to create. I love listening to this - how they use the orchestra. Violins lovingly used- a little piano run - the horns coming in at just the right time. This, my people, is a definite joy in life. Of course the atmosphere in which you listen to this is essential. It is your choice certainly. But, for me, I come home from a hard day saving people from ghosts and make myself a martini. Then I put this on, plop down on the couch, take my Seer's hat off, close my eyes and let this music wash over me. It clenses me from the bad energy vibes I picked up during the day. A remedy for sure. But one that works for your beloved Seer.
In closing, this album is righteously good. Essential for my fan club. Essential for new-comers (catch other reviews-the real drift!) and those that need positive uplift in life. Now you must excuse me. My martini is getting warm!

title: Straight ahead jazz, as good as it gets
text:
This was a groundbreaking record when it was released (1961) . At that point, Murphy was 29 years old and was already one of the best jazz singers in the world. The record companies originally tried to market him as a crooner, singing ballads and standards, which he did very well. Had he stayed with that kind of music, I'm sure he would have made more money. But he was a jazz singer to the core, and this record was the one that really established his direction. And he never looked back.

I know that non-jazz people can appreciate Murphy, but I think you have to be a jazz musician to really get it. In his choice of notes and his phrasing, you can hear his intimate knowledge of the chords and harmonies, the rhythms and syncopation, all of the components that make up jazz. And Murphy can interpret lyrics well as as Sinatra or anybody else. In fact, blasphemous as it may sound, I think Murphy sings "Angel Eyes" better than Sinatra. His performance is absolutely riveting. Sorry, Frank!

I'd say this record is the best introduction to Murphy for the uninitiated. Start here and work your way through his scores of recordings. You'll hear his evolution over the decades.

Murphy belongs to an elite group--real jazz singers. Not singers who sometimes sing jazz tunes, but actual jazz singers who improvise like jazz instrumentalists: Betty Carter, Eddie Jefferson, Jon Hendricks, Anita O'Day, et al. Today's most popular jazz singer, Kurt Elling, credits Murphy as a major influence.

We lost him last year, and he was singing great right up to the end.

title: Seventies Savannah Music
text:
This CD is at heart a disco CD, but it combines a large number of elements from other musical styles as well, including swing, jazz, R&B, and Latin elements. It is an impressive attempt at combining all of these elements. That being said though, I just don't feel that it does enough to really distinguish itself from all the other disco music and R&B that came out during the seventies.
August Darnell, who later became Kid Creole of the Coconuts, is the writer behind this music and he has a gift for words, there are quite a few literary and musical allusions contained within this music and half the fun for me is trying to recognize all of them. Miss Cory Daye's singing also really helps out this album and makes it sound fairly good.
My favorite track is probably "Cherchez La Famme/Se Si Bon" which is just a great song all around and gets my toes tapping every time. "I'll Play The Fool" is very retro and Miss Cory Daye really does justice to some of those old time crooners. "Sunshower" is quite opposite "I'll Play The Fool" but good nonetheless, where "Fool" is an emotionally blue song, "Sunshower" is cheery and filled with positive energy.
Overall this is a pretty good album and quite unique in its combination of sounds. title: John Andrew Schreiner more at the forefront here than anywhere else.
text:
It took me a while to learn to appreciate and love this album, but now that I do, I want to recommend this album to any fan of John Andrew Schreiner's deep Christian music. For starters, the first song on the album takes it lyrics from Lamentations chapter 3--you won't get that often (if at all) from "Contemporary Christian Music" artists. I dislike most CCM, or almost all of it, but Schreiner has always struck a chord with me, and spoken to my heart. I'd describe him as "the Pink Floyd of Christian music", but point out that his similarity is mostly with the later (80s and onward) Floyd, and not their earlier stuff. I'm by no means an expert on Christian music, not having the time to sample much of it and being very selective by temperament as it is, but I find I almost always appreciate Christian music that John Andrew Schreiner's been involved with, mostly as producer, arranger, and keyboardist. But on THIS album he really takes the forefront--more so than on any album he's been involved with. Indeed, this is the only album I know of that is listed under his personal name; he seems to have modestly and deferentially kept his name off of the covers of other great albums (like Maranatha! Music's "Celtic Hymns" and "Communion" CDs) that bear his unmistakeable talents and presence.

This album is a journey though, from "the wilderness" of Christian experience (hence the heart-bearing desolation of the opening track) to the "City of God" (which is the name of the last, enraptured song). There are a few beautiful instrumental songs throughout, but most of these tracks are songs with vocals, mostly sung by Schreiner himself. There are also a few joyous "rockers" in the midst, although most of the album is slower and contemplative.

text:
This album reinforces the true genius of John, Paul, George and Ringo. It also reinforces how much George Martin brought to the table and molded the original songs into classics, and what genius Giles Martin is in the studio as well. The fact that the tempos, chord patterns, and melodies can be layered and segued without the music being altered in a detectable way is almost mystical that it could be done and magical that it has been done. This whole album is like finding a new hidden story in the hyroglyphics inside one of the pyramids that we've been studying for hundreds of years.

How does the same vocal track for the original "While My Guitar Gently Weeps" which rocks, transcend into a guitar and vocal intimate ballad as presented here without being re-recorded? "Mr. Kite" morphing into "She's So Heavy" is so great you have to laugh!

Having played this album incessantly for several days, I reckon it's far and away her best album since the stunning Jagged Little Pill - which was in my opinion, a landmark in Rock.
Without direspecting anybody, I simply cannot imagine how some people, presumably Alanis fans, have reacted badly to this exceptional collection of songs.
To me, this is one of those rare albums on which virtually every track is a potential single. Eight Easy Steps, Out Is Through, Excuses, Doth I Protest Too Much, Knees Of My Bees (hey, how about that title?) Not All Me, Spineless, and the actual single Everything, are some of the most murderously singalong songs I have ever heard - and Alanis is SUCH a strong singer, with a beautiful voice, both in lead and harmony vocals.
Lyrically, the utterly haunting Doth I Protest Too Much (borrowed from Shakespeare's "Methinks she/he doth protest too much...") and The Grudge, beautifully revisit Alanis Relationship Territory, yet the whole album is very up tone, presumably reflecting her own worldly yet positive state of mind.
I have loved all her albums, but this goes infinitely beyond anything I was expecting. Like the stylistically different Jagged, this is yet another true work of genius.
Use The Force Alanis... "You don't need to see the bad reviews... Just buy this unequivocal mistresspiece..."
She will be mine... Oh yes...

title: Sloan's Best Effort
text: Sloan's first two CDs are each great in their own way.  "The Song Inside" seems to bring the elements together with her songwriting, singing & its instrumental prowess.  "Too Nice for Too Long" is a breakout bouncer.  "I don't want to be your wife; I don't want to be your mother," Sloan declares on "You Are the Feast."  "Wavelength" floats by in a stream of consciousness.  Sounding like Bonnie Koloc, Sloan rips on "Bridgeburner," "You left town.  What a relief."  "Falling Backwards" is a soft rumination.  "How many millions of pieces can one grown man shatter into?" Sloan asks on the strong title track.  Rhythm guitar thumps with David Mansfield's gorgeous violin on "Less Is More."  "Freedom" has an original melody & a great drums by Joe Bonadio.  If there's a clinker, for me it'd be "Martha."  Sloan's singing is so strong; but the lyric is not affecting unless your best friend also has that name.  "Steven Leif" suffers from lyrics that are also too specific to connect.  Dennis Yeary's Native American flute adds a nice touch to "I Stand Up."  The CD rocks out with "Unseen Guide," "Push the door open into the darkness."  This CD has the right mix of about two-thirds uptempo tunes, Sloan's strong singing and some great original melodies.  Bravo!

title: Elton John: Breaking new artistic ground...
text:
To start, "The Diving Board" is a great success and very much worth a purchase (in "deluxe" long-form if possible). To expand, since "Songs From the West Coast" at the turn of the millennium, Elton John has moved in an encouraging direction with his studio album output. His work between 1976 and 2000 was, depending on where one might cherry-pick: mediocre, brilliant, crassly commercial, directionless, or uneven. The highs were actually still as high as during the first seven years of his career, but the lows were much lower indeed. More significantly, the lesser work popped up at a much more alarming rate during this long stretch.

The aforementioned direction Elton John now is taking has led to efforts that almost completely remove those lows from his offerings. "Peachtree Road" was as uneven as they've come in the last twelve years, and it was still, at least, a decent album overall with some specifically fine tracks. His material in the new millennium has continued to trend toward fully-realized work with notable consistency and craftsmanship. Elton John has used each album as a vehicle to rekindle or reconnect with a past sound lost since his peak commercial and artistic years. While he has succeeded marvelously at bringing back a sense of excellence and quality, he has, until now, not done much more artistically than seek to recreate a sound he already had created.

Now, however, with "The Diving Board", he has taken that next step that so many fans and critics have been waiting for. The new album is just as adventurous and risky as "Blue Moves", but, one would could argue, lacks even one track that could be considered a dud. To extend the metaphor from above, the highs on this album never reach the heights of his greatest songs, but, there are also no lows. "The Diving Board" is unpredictable, amusing, understated, learned, and even, nearly, avant-garde! A few listens through will reveal the hooks for which Elton John is so deservedly famous; the first time through will not be enough in this case. Patience will reward the listener though; his best songs have always been those that take a while to hum because they are complicated enough that once you have them, they don't annoy you two days later (like with most hook-driven pop material). Elton John has finally taken his new consistency and moved it forward without trying to capitalize on taking it back (even if the marketing for this album is unsurprisingly claiming otherwise). "Rolling Stone" gave this album four stars out of five, which, on their rating scale, translates to "excellent". I would tend to concur. However, Amazon's four star review translates to "like"; its five star review to "love". On this rating scale, I am more in the five-star camp (hence my choice). Still, though this album is probably his greatest work since Ford was president, he does have it in him to take this renaissance to an even more brilliant level. I very sincerely hope he continues in this direction. One or two more albums like this, along with his work after "The Road to El Dorado", would lead to a strong case that Elton John as an album auteur may be a greater artist now than he ever actually was before.

text: His show started the year I was born, and ended before I really got into watching television. Now I can barely contain my frustration that the genre of variety television is gone. The best thing about this DVD is that it gets right to the point; it has a modern-day intro by Mr. Williams himself, then segues immediately into the clips (which also make up the DVD's menu of scenes)- and captions everything, from guest star name to airdate and year. Look for the *4* Osmond brothers (sans Donny, but with baby Marie); Pearl Bailey at her most diva; Carlos Jobim performing "Girl From Ipanema" in Spanish [with Mr. Williams doing so in English]; a "clown makeup" fight with Judy Garland; a marvelous duet with Ella Fitzgerald; and a marvelous 'triplet' with Eddie Fisher and Bobby Darin. Most impressive about the show is the star himself: he seemed (and seems) to be a genuinely kind, genial, humble, humorous guy, and I'm not the least bit surprised that his show enjoyed an amazing nine-year run. Hope he reads this someday.

title: Weak Album
text:
Linkin Park is a modern pop-rock band, and as such, they have to cater to a certain need in order to sell albums. Their first album, while showing no musical talent at all, displayed enough pop hooks and the right blend of guitars and rap-rock vocals to do very well and cash in on the rap-rock fad.
This album, however, is a disgrace in many ways. First of all, in the 3 years it took to come up with a sophomore release, Linkin Park was only able to put together 36 minutes of music. Sure, their fans have little attention span, but this is ridiculous. I could buy the 36 minutes if it actually showed progress from their first release, but they just rehash the exact same themes ad nauseum. Which brings me to my second point - there isn't any significant progression. They have the same pseudo-teen angst lyrics to poor turntable work and sloppy and simplistic guitar riffs. Do something new.
And, finally, there is just alot of music out there that is infinitely better than this, yet this will be a platinum album. This album should be proof to everyone of how poor the record industry really is.

title: There is Metal... and then there is Metallica!
text:
There was a saying that I came across a few times in my pursuit of the finest quality music. It's not all that common, or at least it don't appear to me to be so, but it truly applies here, "There is Metal, and then there is Metallica."

This Album does so well, that just a few years ago, it got the 5X platinum rating which is amazing for an album released in 84, now how many albums from how many bands can do that? I personally feel that this album while loved to death by Metallica Fans, especially those who favor Cliff-Era prefer this one over all others, and I do so myself, but it seems that the more casual fans of Metallica get Black, Justice for all, and Master of Puppets before looking at this one. I believe that is a mistake, because this is the most perfect thrash album in their entire collection. It's closer to thrash than any other in their collection and yet holds amazing melodic beauty that is sometimes lacking in Puppets, but found and so loved in parts of Black. This is Metallica, through and through. Now the songs.

*Fight Fire with Fire* starts out with an unusual slow almost like rock kind of strumming that is designed to lull you into one feeling, and then blow you away with the awesome metal that erupts from it's very core of awesome. First thing I notice, is the sound is a major improvement over Kill Em All, because that one did so well they were able to get better quality crew to help turn out their sound, plus Kirk, James, and Lars all show great improvement. This is just a high speed track of awesome overlayed with a vast drumming of incredible finished out with in my opinion, the best voice (at the time) of the Thrash Genre.

*Ride the Lightning* is the first of the three most memorable songs of the album (which follows one after another) and it's slower than the previous song but it's slower than the one before, however it has a much more stable riff that goes almost to the end of song, the only thing that seems to alter is the Drumming which changes pace to match James vocals, naturally. About mid point it jumps more instrumental, including the minute long Solo by Kirk before finally it goes back to James to bring it home, which it does well with a great shorter instrumental part near the end, before going into the last verse and then finishing up with a long but great closer instrumentation. This song is just awesome, someone wants an example of Thrash, Play ride the lightning, it's not the fastest Metallica song, but I dare call it one of the best of Metallica's more Thrash type songs.

*For Whom the Bell Tolls* A requirement for all Metallica Concerts in my opinion. This song slows down even more than the previous song, and yet is still far faster than any of the hair metal, and great on the ears to boot. This song has a hammer effect, even the drums hit that momentary hammer sound between each line of the lyric. Like Lightning, it holds a generally stable feel all the way to the end with bits of instrumentation, and solos. The song fades out in a manner as if it's winding you up for the next song, which is great. It's got some of my most favorite lyrics in the entirety of Metallica's library. Like Lightning before it, this song is one of the 3 choice songs from the album, not to say the others are bad, this whole album is great.

*Fade to Black* Was a song of such a nature in sound that when I was a little kid and didn't know no better, I thought it was on black, which is by far one of their most melodic albums, and much like the best parts of the later black album, this song is one of their best of the more melodic type songs. The previous two songs maintained a general pace, while this one slowly amps up with each moment of the song. I've heard this song so many times, and even listening to it now, it still has a powerful effect over me. At the 4 minute mark, the song changes, and it gets more intense as does the lyrics itself, and from here it starts amping up even faster until it goes into a high speed thrash of metal glory. This is the third of the three most loved songs from this album. This is without a doubt in my opinion, one of the top 5 most beautiful songs in their entire Library.

*Trapped under Ice* this song as an odd opening for a Metallica song. Even as a Metallica fan, I'd never heard this song before until I got this album, (which was the last I got, other than Anger) but this song is all kinds of awesome, it's the fastest song on the entire album. Less notable than creeping death but in my opinion slightly better. This song has not been heard live more than a handful of times, and not until recently at that, it was played live 5 times from Lightning's release until Magnetic tour. It's unfortunate. This song would have been great on the Binge and Purge album. A great song, among Metallica's best.

*Escape* has a very off putting opening that reminds me of a video game sometimes, and I tend to avoid playing it. But it's not a bad song, I'm especially fond of the Chorus here. This song has never been played live in it's entirety. Weakest song on the album, but far better than 90% of the metal that was out there in those years, that's Metallica for you.

*Creeping Death* What's not to love? Great title, great song, awesomely fast, as I said before it's slower than trapped under ice, but that's only barely, and in this case this makes this song second fastest on the album and one of Metallica's fastest songs. My absolute favorite part of the song is the way James' vocals complement the music, and vice versa. It's seems almost in sync, by virtue of this effect, this is without a doubt the only Metallica song I don't like live, however it is very popular live, so we'll leave that is my opinion only, because this effect is very very hard to replicate, even for pros. This is one of my choice songs for a playlist while playing Gears of War.

*Call of the Ktulu* Finally, some people prefer Orion is the classic instrumental song, I don't. This song is better than Orion in my opinion, and as a result, I consider it to be their best instrumental song. This is one of those songs that is actually better on S&M for the record, but this is so great to listen to that it don't matter, it's great studio, it's great live, it's great anyway you slice it. It's powerful, it's amazing, it's incredible. One could argue that this is the 4th choice song from the album. The song itself due to length and complexity would be difficult to describe, so the best way to describe it, this song tells a story of sound without words in such a manner that it far surpasses many songs that tell a story in words. I've actually timed cooking food to this song, LOL. When it's done, certain meals I eat happen to be done.

The Album through and through is one of the best, if not the best Thrash metal, if not Metal album. If you love Metallica, even just the old stuff. You want this album, you need this album. It's my opinion that this second album, though slower than the first album, is superior to all other thrash albums, both Metallica, and other bands. Thank the metal gods for this album.

title: The best album under the Starship name
text: Love Among the Cannibals from 1989 was really the best album under the Starship name. It avoids the bombast of '85's Knee Deep and '87's unrecognizable No Protection and focuses on strong music content.  I still like It's Not Enough, perhaps the first Mike Shipley-produced song I've heard after over a decade of mixing Def Leppard's albums.  It has made me respect Shipley more for his producing or mixing for artists the past 16-17 years now.  Shipley did a few other songs, especially the social message song, We Dream In Color. Some other surprises are The Burn, Trouble In Mind, and the tribal Love Among the Cannibals. That title song would sound perfect on the hit reality show "Survivor" as a theme song. Mickey Thomas is great vocally on here and while I miss Grace Slick on this album, she did her best with the group in the'80s.  A few numbers sound like Bryan Adams or Def Leppard, but that's just the first couple of songs. The rest of the album is solid pop-rock at Starship's most creative.

title: One Be Lo "The R.E.B.I.R.T.H."- 4 Stars
text:
Late in 2007, Michigan emcee, One Be Lo, dropped his highly anticipated follow up to his (IMO) classic album, [[ASIN:B00078FALE S.O.N.O.G.R.A.M.]], "The R.E.B.I.R.T.H". The album title is an acronym (as are all of his albums) for Real Emcees Bring Intelligent Rhymes To Hip Hop, and he sure follows that motto. For those who haven't heard One Be Lo, he reminds me of a mix between Nas, Ice Cube, and Talib Kweli. His lyrical style is really amazing. I personally believe he is one the best emcees in the game today. Anyways, back to the album, 'Lo's lyrics are no doubt terrific throughout. He shows off his lyrical skills, while also being political and a storyteller. Although they may have faded a bit from his previous album, they still hit hard. The production on this album is actually really good, but samples are way overused. The actual beats are fine, but there is over 60 seconds of samples of others speaking on just about every song. One exception of this is the final track, "Hip Hop Heaven", which is a beautifully put together track. One Be Lo doesn't bring along any of his Subterraneous label mates around to rhyme this time around. Or any guests appearances for that matter. Overall, this album is a great listen; it gets even better if you fast forward through the last 45 seconds or so of every song, as that is usually just sampled talking. If you like One Be Lo, or have never heard him before, try this out. You won't be disappointed.

Lyrics- 9/10
Production- 7.5/10
Guest Appearances- N/A
Overall Sound- 8/10

4.08

-Shaun B.

title: Miles' Final "Acoustic" Album Deserves to Stand with His Masterpieces
text:
When reviewers type up accolades of Miles Davis and point out his key albums, a few names are inevitable: "Birth of the Cool", "Kind of Blue", "Sketches of Spain", and "Bitches Brew" to start with. Slightly more adventurous reviewers will grab the First Great Quintet Prestige albums, "Round About Midnight", "Miles Ahead", and "In a Silent Way", or be daring enough to add "Jack Johnson" or "On the Corner". Usually, though, the Second Great Quintet albums are somewhat lumped together, considered more valuable as a whole than the sum of their parts. Some will go ahead and nominate "ESP", since that was the debut of this special quintet and contains a few obvious classics, but to me the album that deserves a place beside the immortals is this one.

Recorded over two months at almost the same time as "Sorcerer", this album shares almost nothing in common with the warmer sounds of the previous record besides the somewhat angular song structures and the playing styles of the musicians. Pushing the ease of the prior album to one side, this album gave its prime real estate to the rhythm section, and the greatest trophy to Tony Williams. Williams received amazing press almost from the beginning for his unique approach to the drums, using them more as an active frontline instrument than a timekeeping one. But here, especially on the opening title track, Williams is thrust to the forefront. With Davis and Shorter playing the hypnotic melody line in the manner that Ron Carter usually played his bass lines (compare what they do here with Carter's bass line on "Masqualero", for instance) Williams is encouraged to thrash, bash, push, and generally tear down the song structure. As the horns rise and fall, Herbie Hancock's piano goads at Williams, spurring him into new territory while Carter, as ever, wraps his bass lines around everything. It's a nine minute blast unlike anything that came before it, and it sets the listener off base almost immediately. Into this, then, comes "Fall", another Shorter penned tune that offers minimal solo spacing and again puts the melody as the anchor, letting Hancock float the song into a dusky dream while Williams and Carter play off of each other.

From there, one might expect the album to fall off, incapable of sustaining such highs, but instead it simply shifts gears. "Hand Jive", a somewhat soulful racket, lets Williams write his most complex piece of music yet, returning the solo spots to Shorter and Davis, who embrace their moments and let it all out. After this, the sequencing of the record gives way to Herbie Hancock's songs, and they may be the two most aggressive Hancock originals ever penned. Honestly, neither may sound as Hancock originally intended: "Madness" is the result of Davis slashing at a Hancock piece, saving only the most aggressive eight bars of the music and tripling its speed, turning this into a not unpleasant assault on the senses, letting Hancock pound his keys as the band falls apart around him. Next in line is "Riot", which was occasionally performed on stage. This song is cut down to a three minute stand, featuring even more of that claustrophobic, maddening piano but presented as a fighter built for speed. To get an idea of how Hancock may have seen this, listen to his version on his own "Speak Like a Child", recorded a year later. That version is slower, less focused in its melodic attack, and sounding nothing like its title. "Pinocchio" then lets Shorter take the album out on a melodic note, a comedown after the attack of the rest of the side but a thrilling piece on its own. It says something that three more Shorter originals, all of which were more melodically close to this piece, were recorded at this time but rejected by Davis (they came out in 1976 on the fine "Water Babies"). Davis knew exactly what he wanted, and there's not a note out of place on the record.

Ultimately, this album didn't start a riot in the jazz world upon its release", but it doesn't mean that it didn't radically shift the music. From here, low sales and Miles' ever changing moods would move him into electronic sounds and then into funk, but that was still several months and one European tour away. It's easy to feel that Davis started something here that he should've continued, that the unique song forms and jagged playing of these tracks should've opened up more such albums, but with the exception of half of the "Miles in the Sky" album, that was not to be. Listening through this agian, I note that Davis rarely repeated himself once he'd reached perfection: he never attempted to follow up "Kind of Blue" or "Bitches Brew" with another record like them. The same holds true here. Once you've reached a peak, there's simply nowhere left to climb.

title: An okay compilation, but certainly not deserving of the title 'Definitive'
text:
Louis Armstrong's recording career spanned five decades and 47 years. 1923 to 1970, Louis recorded albums and singles regularly. As of December 25, 2009, the only collection that has come close to summarizing all of his recordings is the 'Ken Burns JAZZ' collection, with 25 recordings. But that still doesn't do him justice.

So, in 2006, Hip-O Records (owned by the Universal Music Group, or UMG) decided to release the millionth-and-one Armstrong collection. The title was 'The Definitive Collection.' It looks like a nice set, judging by the packaging. There's Satchmo on the cover, with his signature trumpet. And to it's defense, the packaging is incredible. Good liner notes, good information about the tracks. Hip-O did outstanding in that regard.

But other than that, this is a pretty awful collection. A low point in the normally-outstanding 'The Definitive Collection' series.

First of all, while most of the music here is great, it is by no means a 'definitive collection.' To be truly definitive, you need his Hot Fives and Sevens from the 1925-1928 period, his recordings with Earl Hines from 1928-1930, his RCA victor period from 1933-1934 and again from 1945-1947. And while we're on the topic, why not include his early 1923 recordings with King Oliver? In order for it to be definitive, these recordings are absolutely necessary.

What that leaves are his Decca and Verve recordings. 'Struttin' With Some Barbecue' is here, albeit in it's 1938 remake of his recording ten years prior, but still in a smoking version nonetheless.

But all that's left now is the "easy listening" Louis. That means, 'What a Wonderful World,' 'Hello Dolly,' 'Blueberry Hill,' 'A Kiss to Build a Dream On,' etc. And while those are quite nice recordings and are definitive, they are just not enough for a compilation titled 'The Definitive Collection.'

A more appropriate title would be 'Louis Armstrong - The Definitive Decca/Verve Collection.' Because that's in retrospect what this is. It's not truly definitive. In my honest opinion, there is yet to be a truly "definitive" Louis Armstrong collection, and I doubt there ever will be. You'd need at least 12 CDs to do so.

Recommended for the latter day Louis Armstrong fan.

title: An intense performance, from the heart to the heart.
text:
There are many recordings of the German Requiem of Brahms, and I have seven of them in my library.

I cannot recommend too highly Rafael Kubelik's version with the Bavarian Radio Symphony and Chorus, Edith Mathis and Wolfgang Brendel on Audite. Recorded in concert (with no audience sounds) in 1978 and issued recently in glorious sound by Audite, this performance is generous in every way: fine musicianship, deep emotion, and rich sound. One has the sense that the musicians have lived into every phrase of this work and deeply believe in it and its message.

Other recordings I rank at a similarly high level and recommend with great enthusiasm:

1. I always find the performance by James Levine and the Chicago Symphony and Chorus with Battle and Hagegard an overwhelming experience. I have used it in college teaching and student response has been predictably enthusiastic, even from students who "don't like classical music." This recording comes to us on RCA/BMG. It is a 1983 studio recording recently re-released on Universal at a low budget price. Levine and the Chicago deliver a big, heart-on-sleeve sound yet pay loving attention to details and the soloists sing exquisitely.

2. Herreweghe and the Orchestre des Champs Elysees on Harmonia Mundi. This recordng ranks among the finest and is unique in the clarity of voices, whether solo, choral, or orchestral. The woodwinds and brass are never covered by the strings, yet the string sections sound full and play with precision. The soloists are not over-miked and their voices seem to come from the midst of the greater ensemble. Especially impressive and touching is the singing of Gerald Finley (although his command of German has greatly improved since this recording).

3. Rudolph Kempe with the Berlin Philharmonic and the Choir of St. Hedwig's with Elizabeth Gruemmer and the young (therefore not yet fussy and mannered) Fischer-Dieskau. This is a very fine mono recording from 1956 still found on EMI. There are days when I think this is the best of the best in every respect. The playing and singing is exemplary in very way.

4. John Eliot Gardiner's interpretation, with his Orchestre Revolutionanaire et Romantique, the Monteverdi Choir, Charlotte Margiono, and Rodney Gilfry on Philips, is fleet and somewhat light-weight. It is a studio recording from 1990. Gardiner's tempi are the quickest by far yet never seem rushed. I've always liked this performance, but in light of those mentioned above it is relatively cerebral. Four stars, not five.

Now, what about Robert Shaw's recording on Telarc? Amazon states up front that this is the recording people "ultimately" buy. Maybe so, but I wouldn't click on "Buy Now" until I had heard samplings of some other recordings. Yes, Shaw and his musicians are amazing in their dedication to the work. It is a great performance. I have always found it necessary to boost the treble and perhaps reduce the bass to get a clear sound with this recording.

As for the other available versions, many are very fine indeed; yet I think none of them quite reaches the heights of the five I've listed above.

title: Another TD repackaging exercise
text:
This 2-CD compilation set, dating from 2000, is actually drawn from the larger 5-disc compilation set of 1996, "The Dream Roots Collection". Quite why anyone would want this in preference to the larger set (except to save some money, of course) rather defeats me.
All of the works showcased here, mostly in bleeding-chunk form, come from two periods of Tangerine Dreams' recording history. The so-called Pink Years (1970-73) prior to the band's signing with Virgin Records and the Blue Years - the time during which they were signed to New Age label, Jive-Electro (1983-87). The band's five earliest albums are covered here by a total of just seven tracks, taking up about half the first CD of the set. These tracks are not simply extracts from the original discs, however, but are mostly "recomposed" versions based only loosely on the originals. Some snippets of the original material are detectable underneath the drifts of thick new synthesiser textures that have been laid over them but sometimes only just. 'Green Desert' is the only work to benefit from this treatment, in my opinion, although fans of the original will no doubt disagree with me.
In fact, I suspect that most fans of TD's early music will absolutely hate what has been done on these first seven tracks. Certainly, much of the new material seems to have been added with little sensitivity to the original and gives the impression that it has been produced in order to appeal to those who only know Tangerine Dream's later music. I suppose that one almost acceptable way to approach these treatments is to view them as new retrospective mixes, merely based upon ideas from the older works. Even then, though, the whole exercise feels to make about as much sense (and is as sacrilegious) as taking coloured felt-tip pens to beautiful old pencil sketches: it may "update" the medium, but the original message is mostly lost in the process! I do hope Edgar Froese managed to achieve some sort of karmic closure from this revisiting of his roots and that he can now get on with new things!
The remaining disc and a half are given over to a period that is regarded by many as marking the very peak of Tangerine Dream's creativity. The albums included in this period are the studio albums "Tyger", "Underwater Sunlight" and "Le Parc", plus the live sets "Poland" and "Livemiles". All five of these are represented to some degree. The booklet notes suggest that the tracks included here are also studio reworkings of the originals but most sound (to me at least) like live concert versions of the originals. Sometimes, they are more or less identical to their earlier releases but mostly, either the instrumentation is subtly different, or the tempo altered a little, or else some other slight re-arrangement features. All of this music remains faithful to the original, though, and I don't believe anyone who knows any of the previous releases will be at all dissatisfied with the treatment they receive here. They are all identical to the selections presented in the Dream Roots collection, which manages to include roughly twice as much material from these albums as appears here. Interestingly, track ordering here matches the chronological sequence of the original releases, so that the discs do provide something of an encapsulated journey through the band's musical history - or would if the early material hadn't been so drastically altered.
In summary then, this collection will present a good buy to anyone who is just looking for a sampling of the works of Tangerine Dream but doesn't want to fork out for the full 5-disc collection of which this is merely part. Established fans should avoid this release altogether, as it has nothing new to offer them whatsoever. Any such interested in hearing the new treatments should go instead for "The Dream Roots Collection" and so at least gain some new material as well.

title: Introducing Jeff Golub.
text:
This CD was my introduction to Jeff Golub. I heard his version of "Pick Up The Pieces" by Average White Band on the radio in `95, and I had to find out who the guitar player was. After several listens to the radio, waiting for them to play the song again, and eagerly awaiting someone to announce who it was, they finally did, and I bought the CD. I was not disappointed, as there are several gems on the CD. My favorites are: "Pick Up The Pieces" (A cool, bluesy remake of the Average White Band hit), "Gimme Some" (a funky, makes ya wanna dance kinda tune, with Jeff's bluesy licks), "That's The Way Of The World" (a soothing version of the Earth, Wind, & Fire hit), "Nightingale" (a positive, uplifting tune with some very cool jazz/blues guitar melodies), "I'll Be Around" (a nice remake of the soul hit, with Jeff playing octaves and his dazzling licks), and "Moon River" (another soothing jazz remake, with just Jeff and his guitar in the beginning, playing some fat jazz chords).
The CD also features a solid drum and bass section. There are electronic drums on this CD. As a musician, I tend to favor "real" drums, especially when playing in a live band situation, but I also enjoy experimenting with electronic drum beats, so this CD really appeals to me.
I would recommend this CD to anyone who is new to Jeff Golub, or who appreciates some tasty jazz/blues guitar playing and well crafted jazz/blues songs with a modern sensibility.

title: "The biggest pub we've ever played"- Michael Hutchence
text: It's been years since I've put in my VHS copy of this show and I had forgotten how good it is. This DVD is a treasure, not only to see Hutchence and company at the top of their game, but of course just to see Hutchence and be reminded of his charisma and stage presence. It is with admiration and sadness that I watch him take control of the Wembly crowd and perform every song like it was his last performance. What electricity, honesty, ... what a spark he had. Not that the rest of the chaps, especially Jon, don't seem to be having just as good a time. It really is the band in historic form. From "Original Sin" to "I Send a Message" to "Suicide Blonde," it's just about the perfect time capsule for the band (although I happen to think Welcome To Wherever You Are is one of music's great underrated masterpieces and would love a DVD from that era). I swear, when the Wembly crowd takes the vocals from Hutchence on "Mystify" in glorious DTS 5.1 sound I want to sing along. I would have loved an enhanced 16X9 widescreen picture, but how small a quibble is that? I haven't had a chance to go through the bonus features, but they're plentiful. Until INXS release a comprehensive and remastered DVD compilation of their video clips, this will do just fine.

title: EVERYONE get this album
text:
In the world of progressive rock music, one finds shelter from the storm that the industry pounds down on you. Unfortunately, within this shelter (though I do support all prog), we're still getting bombarded. Not with bad music necessarily, but with an excess of "side projects" that get churned out faster than one can write a lyric for the next Matchbox 20/John Mayer bland-o-rama hit. Yes, in the prog world, it's not raining Acid Rain, but it is raining... hmmmm.... let's say candy. This is a good metaphor because there's so much greatness you can't eat it all and you have to pick and choose, unless you are extremely wealthy and/or have a really good pancreas.
When you heard about O.S.I., no doubt you were intrigued, but possibly you (like me) were exhausted that you felt obligated to pick up yet ANOTHER of Portnoy's works. I knew I had to get it but didn't even know when I would get around to listening to it.
So let me tell you; along with Transatlantic and L.T.E., this is one of the great side-endeavors worth anybody's listening. It uses what I consider the PERFECT formula, which is all too sensible to me, yet almost always neglected; commercial sensibilities with a MUSICAL BRAIN and still the power of ROCK.
Yes, kids, what we have here is a minor miracle. There's no 64th note rollercosters a la John Petrucci, BUT, to be honest, I needed an album with some time to breathe (notice I didn't say sleep, which is what one would get in the "real world" of pop fluff).
This album is smart as hell, using poignant sound clips from the news, carefully planned synth layers, and very good lyrics, revealing that SONGWRITING is indeed, not a bad word at all. AND, they get all the more credit for some good "commercial" (for lack of a better word) sensibilities, using nice strategically placed hooks and choruses at times. The songs are kept short, except for one, which is the best song on the album (as it should be). It is called shutDOWN, featuring the brains behind Porcupine Tree, and it is everything I always wanted in a song. Except for the fact that the B section doesn't get a great transition and it could easily pass for another song, that is. But that is excused because of the perfect marriage of mood, music, and lyrics. The rest of the songs all work together to create a similar atmosphere, while doing all of the things that good music should. Remember, writing a really really good pop tune is also a craft and skill, and it's not everyday that musicians master both worlds. I don't see what better criteria one could have for making music. An extra applause goes out to Kevin Moore, as it is clear he put a lot of hard work and effort into this creation. Job well done.
So, if you want to keep up with all the quality music releases out there, but funds do have an end point, take a breath, take a chance on O.S.I., and also enjoy that bonus cd!

title: It's a bore.
text: What a shameful way to destroy a classic score written by two masters at the top of their game.  If the creative team of this production was so afraid of this story appearing salacious, then they should not have picked source material about a girl being groomed to be a courtesan in the first place!  Let the story be what it is and let Collette's satire shine through...don't try and water it down and make it "PC."  Such terrible direction, and an awful adaptation of Lerner's work (and if you are going to augment his lyrics, your last name had better be Sondheim...or you are sure to come up short)...so many bad, bad decisions went into this misbegotten "revisal."  Making Gaston a young man simply rings false...how does a whelp in his early twenties feel so jaded?  Why would Gigi's youthful exuberance so enchant and disarm one who is also so young?  The significance of this man finally settling down for the love of her is completely lost.  Taking "Thank Heaven for Little Girls" away from Honore and giving it to the grandmother and aunt also rings false, and was a cowardly choice.  Was it truly not possible to direct that number as written without it seeming creepy?  And transforming "I'm Glad I'm Not Young Anymore" from a charming star turn into a duet also does not work.  So many other bad choices, too numerous to mention...but re-assigning of lyrics being a constant source of frustration to be certain.  The elder character actors all do their best and Corey Cott is a true find and will hopefully find a better vehicle for himself.  And Miss Hudgens may find success in a show that is more contemporary and American....playing a European is certainly not her calling.  As for this material-please enjoy the Academy Award-winning film or the 1974 recording of the Broadway production written by Lerner.  Apparently the creative team of this show felt they knew better than Lerner and Loewe in how to make this material fly.  The fact that this production was a poorly-received flop should let them know not to mess with the masters.

title: Martin Barre is no guitar hero...
text:
..but he certainly is a hero of the guitar. Never one to seek the spotlight, Martin lets his guitar do the talking, and he can say more with one note, put more emotion into it than any other guitarist I’ve heard. Separated from Jethro Tull after more than 40 years, he is now back to playing the music he loves: that blues-drenched rock that defined the early Tull sound before synths and squeezy things squeezed him to the back of the stage. So here on this live in the studio recording Martin is back with a vengeance, playing a “dirty, nasty, low-down blues” take of A New Day Yesterday, a rocking Song for Jeffrey, and even Fatman from Stand Up, and To Cry You a Song and Teacher from Benefit. We’re also treated to a nice slice of Thick as a Brick, and an excellent version of Robert Johnson’s Crossroads on the mandolin.
I can’t help missing the flute here and there, but Richard Beesley’s sax fills in nicely, without ever dominating. Dan Crisp too sounds out of place at first, as Ian’s voice is inseparable from these songs, but after a few plays you come to realize his Crisp’s voice too is well suited to the music.
While it can be rightly said that Ian Anderson is the creative force behind Jethro Tull, and his quirkiness, humor and eccentricity have kept the music adventuresome and unpredictable, Martin was the engine that powered the band, a guitarist extraordinaire, a true virtuoso who can shred with the best but favors tone and control over speed. It is wonderful to hear him playing the music he loves, and if, like me, you love it too, you will thoroughly enjoy this set.
There are a lot of high profile guitar heroes out there, but Martin Barre is a name few recognize. Give this CD a listen and you will wonder why.

title: Give Me More
text:
There are some great songs on this CD, but frankly it could have been a much song stronger selection. Major omissions would be "Candy and a Currant Bun" ("Let's Roll Another") and "Lucifer Sam" and "Interstellar Overdrive," both from The Piper at the Gates of Dawn. How about more of the upbeat stuff, please? Granted, depression was part of Syd Barrett's life for a while, and it's only logical that he composed his share of downbeat material. Some of those songs are finely crafted too, but considering the pain Syd Barrett lived with I just can't bear to suffer along with him.

My other issue is the packaging. The cover art is totally tacky symbolism, and the back which includes the song list, is so poorly printed with song titles in black printed on a dark purple background. I can barely read it. Okay, inside you get a little booklet on nice paper, and the lyrics for all the songs are given. Syd was a superb lyricist so I appreciate that. What I don't appreciate are the silly cartoon-like illustrations that accompany them. The schlock-like feel of this is off putting, and, given the singular artistry of Syd Barrett, doesn't he deserve better?

title: Wonderful music. Excellent performances. Great Buy
text: This group of sonatas were written and published in about 1773. These are all wonderful sonatas. The F Major is well known and has been recorded by a wide range of artists from Horowitz to Ax. These sonatas are easy to listen to. They are full of what has been described as charm, wit, and beauty. Jando is an excellent pianist. I have enjoyed his Beethoven sonata cycle, Mozart sonata and concerto cycles, and this Haydn cycle. Unlike Beethoven and Mozart there are not many choices if you want to acquire a complete budget set of the Haydn sonatas. The McCabe cycle is another good choice but I think only avaialable as a complete box. Fortunately Jando is an excellent pianist, these volumes are well recorded, and the price is low. The whole ten disc set is available for $[...] and the individual discs are available for $[...] or less on line.Compared to many better known pianists who have recorded some of these individual sonatas his technique and interpretations compare well. As I have stated elsewhere if you are a strong intermediate pianist these are wonderful sonatas to read. They will test your articulation, legato line,and control of dynamics. These sonatas  are in Volume II of the Hinson from  Alfred Publishing. The edition is described by the editor as a "practical urtext-pedagogical" and the fingerings are helpful. They are good inexpensive editions. Occassional pedals marks are suggested by the editor. Listen to Jando play these sonatas and give it a try yourself. If you have never played the piano or have not touched the keys in a long time please take lessons. Playing these sonatas will bring you great joy. If playing the piano is not an option just dream you are the pianist.

title: She's had how many No.1 hits?!
text:
How many artists can you think of that have had so many No.1 singles, that there are enough to make up a "Greatest Hits" type record? The Beatles and Elvis have all done it, and so has Mariah Carey. She was by far the biggest selling female artist of the 1990's, shifting a whopping 130 million albums in the space of a decade. Her US No.1 singles have now totalled 15 - 13 at the release time of this record, #1's. I became very interested in Mariah's music after hearing Heartbreaker and Fantasy, and bought this superb collection of No.1's soon after.
#1's begins with the superb Sweetheart (Mariah Featuring JD) (10/10). This song is a superb one to open such a prestigious record, and has the "R'n'B Mariah" vibe. The song was never released as a single in the UK, but a superb video was made for it. We then move onto the breathtaking When You Believe (From The Prince Of Egypt) (10/10). This duet with Whitney Houston proved all the doubters that Mariah and Whitney were good friends - and not arch rivals like the press had speculated. The song was never released in the US, but peaked at No.4 in the UK in December 1998. Carey and Houston's vocals make a unique combination, making for one of the greatest duets in recent times. Whenever You Call (Mariah Carey & Brian McKnight) (8/10) is another great song. I prefer the original version with only Mariah's vocals from her Butterfly album, but this version is still good. My All (10/10) is a career highlight for Mariah. A superb ballad, the beat is striking and Mariah's voice is so full of emotion. The song earned Mariah her 13th US No.1 in June 1998. Honey (10/10) was released in August 1997 and was the first single from Butterfly. It stormed the charts, peaking at No.3 in the UK and No.1 in the US. Always Be My Baby (10/10) is one of my favourite Mariah Carey songs, because of the sweet and trouble-free lyrics. The song simply swings with simplicity, and became Mariah's 11th US No.1 in May 1996. One Sweet Day (Mariah Carey & Boyz II Men) (10/10) is the BIG song on #1's! The song is a beautiful ballad about lost love with some amazing melodies and striking lyrics. The song peaked at No.6 in the UK in December 1995, and topped the US singles chart for a staggering 16 consecutive weeks! It still stands as the longest running No.1 single in the US. Fantasy (Featuring O.D.B.) (9/10) is the next song. This is not the pop/video version, but the R'n'B Remix. I was very disappointed when I bought this album as it did not have the original version of Fantasy on it, but I've grown to love this version too. The original version topped the charts in the US for 8 weeks in September 1995 and peaked at No.4 in the UK. Hero (10/10) and Dreamlover (10/10) are up next. The former was Mariah's 8th US No.1 single and peaked at No.7 in the UK. The superb ballad is a strong favourite amongst many fans because it's about strength and the power to carry on. The latter is a brilliant up-tempo pop number from Mariah that peaked at No.9 in the UK and No.1 in the US.
#1's continues with the superb I'll Be There (Featuring Trey Lorenz) (10/10). This song is a live version of the Jackson 5 classic, that was recorded at Mariah's special MTV Unplugged concert early on in her career. The live version became so popular that it was released as a single and peaked at No.2 in the UK, and became Mariah's 6th US No.1 single in June 1992. Emotions (9/10) and Someday (10/10) are both superb pop singles with a hint of R'n'B in the former. I sometimes get both songs mixed up, because they sound so alike. Emotions was released in October 1991 and peaked at No.17 in the UK, but became another massive US No.1 for Mariah. Someday peaked at a shockingly low No.38 in the UK, but thankfully was another US No.1! Love Takes Time (9/10) is another brilliant Mariah ballad. The song was released in November 1990 and became Mariah's 2nd US No.1 single. Vision Of Love (10/10) was Mariah's very first single. Peaking at No.7 in the UK and No.1 in the US (surprise, surprise!), the song is an awesome power ballad in which Mariah gets to showcase her stunning vocal range. I Still Believe (9/10) us up next and peaked at No.16 in the UK in April 1999. The song is a great ballad, but can't quite live up to the superiority of ballads such as Hero, My All and this next song.....Without You (10/10). Released in April 1994, the song became Mariah's first UK No.1 single where it stayed for 4 weeks. The song peaked at No.2 in the US - how frustrating! Mariah really sells this song from the depths of her soul, which is why it did so well. The final song on #1's is Do You Know Where You're Going To (Theme From Mahogany) (9/10). This superb ballad has a real classy feel to it with some amazing lyrics, but Mariah's voice is not as good as it could be.
OVERALL GRADE: 10/10
There are 12 US No.1 singles on this version of #1's, but there are 18 tracks. The songs that didn't make it to No.1 in the US were I Still Believe and Without You. The US version of this album has I Don't Wanna Cry on it instead of Without You, as the former made No.1 in the US and Without You did not. The other songs are just bonus tracks. Yes, I know this is very confusing! #1's was the first Mariah Carey album I ever bought, and I suggest that if you're curious to get into her music, you buy this one first too! Well, either #1's or Greatest Hits - both are superb, because, well...how many artists can boast more than a dozen No.1 hits?!

title: A Very Good "Roman Trilogy"
text:
Lorin Maazel is known for his Respighi interpretations. This recording of Respighi's "Roman Trilogy" is a testament for his love of this music. I'm pretty lukewarm about Maazel's conducting, but he has turned in some good performances through the years and one of them is this one. I wish Maazel had recorded the whole trilogy earlier on Decca as those performances are much better than these readings. I often find Maazel's recordings incredibly lackluster. Maazel turns in a great "Pines of Rome" here. The reading of "Fountains of Rome" is also quite good. "Roman Festivals" doesn't capture the magic he did with the Cleveland Orchestra on Decca, so I subtracted a star for this very dry, mediocre reading.

The audio is also quite good, although it seems it could have been recorded at a lower volume than usual and will require you to turn up your amplifier a little more to hear the quieter passages. The Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra play well.

These readings never quite capture the fire that Reiner's readings on RCA got, but they're good enough and the price of this release is also something to consider. It's good, but not as good as it could have been, especially given Maazel's history with this music.

title: INDEPENDENCE FROM BORING METAL
text:
"When in the Course of human events it becomes necessary for one band to revive the art of epic metal songwriting, a decent respect to the opinions of metalheads requires that they should declare the causes which impel them to the recording.
We hold these truths to be self-evident, that all METAL bands are unfortunately not created equal, that they are endowed by their songwriters with certain unalienable qualities, that among these are intelligence, poignancy, drama, guitar harmonies and the pursuit of HEAVINESS. --That whenever any metal band becomes destructive of these ends (*cough*ironmaiden*cough*), it is the Right of the Metalheads to criticize it, and to look elsewhere for enlightenment, laying its foundation on such principles and organizing its listening habits in such form, as to them shall seem most likely to effect their Headbanging and Happiness....
--Such has been the patient sufferance of fans of certain reunited metal bands which can't seem to write good songs anymore, and such is now the necessity which constrains them to alter their listening habits to ICED EARTH. The history of the present "reunited metal gods" (I.M.,J.P.) is a history of repeated injuries and lame albums, all having in direct object the establishment of an absolute boredom over our ears and minds. To prove this, let Facts be submitted to a candid world...."

Having pretty much given up on Steve Harris's songwriting long, loooooong ago, I felt pretty lost on where to turn for an intelligent storytelling epic in the metallic art form. Then I heard about "Gettysburg".
I had heard a few Iced Earth songs over the years, but never got into them enough to purchase a cd. Yet the more I read about the "Gettysburg" epic, the more interested I became and ended up buying this 2-disc edition out of curiosity.
I am extremely glad I did.
Jon Schaffer clearly poured his entire being into the creation of this grand opus. This is the sort of track that allows metal to be the intelligent artform that it is, and we should be grateful to him for bringing back the quality songwriting that this genre has needed for so long. The kind of stuff that makes you THINK!
Not to detract from the songs on the first disc, but clearly the focal point of "The Glorious Burden" is "Gettysburg (1863)" and rightfully so. Schaffer is merely documenting the events which occured there because of his intense fasccination with American history. He is making no judgements on who was right or wrong or who should or should not have won, but simply relaying an important historical event to an audience that, frankly, probably would not have learned about it otherwise.
This edition is put together very beautifully, and features wonderful artwork to represent each song on the album alongside the lyrics. Schaffer also included extensive notes on his impetus for creating "Gettysburg (1863)", and very meticulous details about what the instrumental sections in the song are meant to represent.
The rest of the songs, though they stand in the shadow of Disc Two, are more of Schaffer's observations of historical events which moved him enough to want his listeners to understand the impact they have had on human events--some little, others not so little. Tim Owens--who does a GREAT job on vocals throughout--finally got his shot at lyricism on "Red Baron", which fits comfortably with the theme of the album; "Declaration Day" is an awesomely anthemic fist pumper about America's fight for independence; "When the Eagle Cries" is a somber tribute to 9/11; "The Reckoning" lyrically seems a sort of follow-up to "Eagle" but it is represented by artwork depicting an old western gunfighter; "Attila" is self-explanatory; "Hollow Man" is actually a non-historical piece about overcoming personal obstacles; the album opener "Star Spangled Banner" would give Brian May fits of jealousy with its beautiful guitar harmonies; etc.

This is a profound collection of intelligently written metal which anyone who is not utterly self-absorbed should own.

title: "The Meeting" of two friends at the dusk of their careers, poignant and touching
text:
If you like the song "The Meeting" from ABWH, you'll like this. Most of the music has that stripped down feel. It's just Rick with his cascading keyboard, and Jon singing his usual "positive energy- we are all beautiful" music. Rick stays away from his grand Moog and Organ stylings, and plays it pretty crisp -mainly on the piano. It's a quiet, reverent sound from two heros from the glory days of YES.

There are four Yes songs on the album, I skip them all. Not one of them comes close to the original power of Yes. They sound like forlorn arrangements, thrown in to "kiss" the audience. The rest of the songs, thematically, are like Jon Anderson solo music, with Rick playing sympathetically behind him. 23/24/11 is the oddest of the lot, with some strange lyrical content, However, the Garden, Just One Man, and the Living Tree are all gorgeous in their simplicity. By the end, we reach "The Meeting" which is stunning in essential beauty. It's probably the best song on the album. This is a unique view into a "Yes" what might have been scenario.

title: Maybe not definitive but still a good collection
text: Jerry Lee Lewis redefined rock n roll and boogie woogie during the late 50s, spawning a chain of several top billboard hits including Great Balls of Fire, A Whole Lot of Shakin' Going On, and Breathless. Lee was arguably the second fastest and most flamboyant pianist of the 20th century, only second to Liberace. Jerry Lee could play the piano like he invented it, he knew every trick behind it, what made it produce the most upbeat sound. Lees music was like a slap in the face to classical pianists and his highly controversial piano burnings and rebellious attitude, which only added to his fame. Sure Lee isn't a classical pianist, and his style isn't quite anything you would find in any other pianist, but that is what makes Lewis the genius that he is, he invented his own style, combining the old fashion boogie woogie bass line, with the at the time, new sensation rock n roll. Lee played with the energy and soul of a gospel singer, and incorporated much of this style into his music as well. Unfortunately his success was cut short when his controversial marriage to his cousin was made public, and he was shamed by the public and decided to leave Sun records and stay in the shadows for a few years. Lee was later rediscovered in the late 60s, which was after he divorced his cousin, and started playing country, which might not have been as big as his earlier hits, but it still was good, and showed Jerry Lee was a man of many styles. Of course, Lee did grow up a country boy in the deep south, and grew up with country. Now Lee might have been no Ray Charles, or Liberace, or even Elvis, but he played with just as much enthusiasm and soul, and this collection showcases a wide variety of his songs, spanning his early years with Sun, to his later success in the 70s and 80s. If you are a die hard Lewis fan, you will probably be disappointed, as this is only a small slice of what Lewis produced, but if you are just a contemporary fan who admires his work, this will really be all you need. And honestly if it weren't for his controversial marriage, Lewis may have gained almost as many billboard hits as Elvis. Regardless, Lewis is one of the best pianists of all time, and has a different sound that makes him one of the strongest performers of the rock n roll era.

text:
This CD may as well have been titled "guilty pleasure," because for me, that's exactly what it is. Somehow Mates Of State have made one of the most immediately catchy and captivating albums in recent memory while defying every notion I had of what makes a good "rock album." The songs on this disc are blatent and direct, saturated with unapologetic, childish glee.

The Mates Of State aesthetic consists of a male/female (and in fact husband/wife) vocal attack, shrill, giddy organs and keys, and thankfully ballsy, solid drums holding it all together. The sound here is as blissful as it is ridiculous, a sort of fun-house ride through pulsating organs hammering out bold, instantly hummable melody lines, tight (sometimes shouted) vocal harmonies that resemble Rainer Maria's back-and-forth dynamic, and strikingly upbeat lyrics. The duo manage to cover a broad range of sounds with this seemingly limited setup. The organs hum like bass guitars, squeal like Strats, and spit out all kinds of crazy sounds and textures in between, giving the ultra-sweet pop tunes on Team Boo a truly undefinable sound.

At face value, this approach recalls the gimmickery of the White Stripes girl-and-guy minimalism. But where that duo's shortcomings are apparent (Meg's miserable drumming and a self-conscious attempt to be lo-fi) both "Mates" are very adept at their respective instruments, creating a full, energizing, and completely satisfying sound. And it all sounds completely genuine, devoid of the pretense with which other indie acts of the day deliver their music.

Tunes like "Ha-Ha," "Whiner's Bio" and "I Got This Feelin'" bounce around between absurdly catchy hooks, sing-songy choruses and chaotic organ noise, and ultimately leave you totally disoriented, but wholly pleased with the experience. The Mates ground these bursts of nervous teenage energy with a couple of well-placed mid-tempo pieces. The surprisingly melancholy "Parachutes" finds the duo singing about a couple who sky-dive to their deaths and appreciate the ride together, over a lulling piano line that tugs at the heartstrings as Kori sings "twenty-five seconds to live, and I'm falling." "An Experiment" follows, with a moody, haunting organ fade-in punctuated with analog blips and beeps. A slow build during the verse gives way to a shimmering chorus highlighting perhaps the best lyrical moment on the disc, "I wonder if I could tie the ocean to your knees..." - an achingly beautiful sentiment that feels right at home on an album so overflowing with raw emotion. It's just that the vast majority of that emotion is pure unadulturated bliss, the likes of which is rare in these times of self-consciously serious rock bands and cold, detached electronica. Give this album a spin before you leave for work in the morning, and you're sure to feel somehow a little better about your day.

The performances of many of Joni's best songs are superior to the studio versions with unmatched life and vibrancy and Mitchell is in amazing voice.

I have loved Mr.Petty and his fine band since 1977. Just an amazing performer who has timeless songs. Not just the hits, the B sides are tremendous. Anything thats rock n roll, restless,spike, on and on and on, this band blows Springsteen and that overhyped Northern bunch away.

That said, the decline began 1991. Stan Lynch left because of the Ballads and whiny songs that were increasingly becoming the new music. Sure we would have an occasional hard rocking sound primarily driven by a wonderful riff by THE best lead guitar on the planet. Tom would have to write a lyrics to match. like Running down a dream. But they became far and between. Remember when you would buy Hard promises, your gonna get it, Torpedos, and EVERY single song was a sing along rocking masterpiece?

I think as Tom aged it became way too easy to write boring "room at the top" crap, that even he has admitted is much easier to produce than a guitar driven rocking song.
He got good reviews for Wildflowers in 1994, and it's been downhill ever since. More palply draggy songs with an occasional gem or two thrown in.
Oh well, the stones have done that for years too.
I was spoiled with TP for so long, I expected at least 7 great songs per album. That is long gone.

Either he cannot do it anymore, or doesn't want to. It always amazes me that a band will hit a formula fans love, then decide to "do something different" or as Tom puts it "we were treading water"

So Tom keeps doing the special projects, and the DJ political statements, and the feel good self absorbed Mudcrutch stuff. Bad barn music is all it is. It's not making me happy.
