title: This is okay only
text:
I've been a Pixies fan since I was a teenager and Nirvana were not yet heard of. They are No 3 on my favourite band list after the Beatles (first place) and U2 (second place). I was lucky enough to see them in Sydney a few years ago when Kim Deal was still on bass, and it was a magical night with the band in awesome form.

Indie Cindy is as disappointing as I suspected it might be.

Kim Deal was a very important part of the band, and her absence is noticeable on this record. Frank's genius evaporated suddenly about 20 years ago, and in my opinion he hasn't re-found it here on this release, despite what a lot of fans are saying. These songs sound too simple in their melodic construction to be considered along with the Pixies back catalogue. There are a few nice moments, but there are definitely NO brilliant moments.

I still sit in amazement over how Frank ever wrote the bizarre and unpredictable curve-ball tunes he did for several years between the late 80s and early 90s, and those albums will always captivate me. But Indie Cindy actually bores me on many of the tracks, because Frank has long since lost his creative edge. The Beatles never made the mistake of trying to reheat a souffle, and the Pixies have shown us with this release why it can be an unwise thing to do.

To sum up, Indie Cindy is a good release if you're just a decent band. But if you're a legend of a band like the Pixies, this release is nothing more than a blemish on what had been a spotless career.

Tracks like "Thank You" "That I would Be Good" "So Pure" and, especially, "Joining You" rank as some of the best female pop-rock of the 90's. Yes, I bought her next two (the Unplugged and the Rug Swept album) but neither of them, while good, hold a candle to this great piece of artistry. I still do not own Jagged and will never purchase it (cause I think it was a total phony album) but this record was as REAL as Jagged was NOT. Five BIG Stars. P.S. I'd never heard of Busconi until I read a piece in the New Yorker by Alex Ross. As usual, the investment based on his comments was well worth it, and I highly recommend that whatever Alex Ross recommends, you should consider.

This piece borders on bombastic, somewhat like Liszt showing off, and approaching Liberace with the extra numbers of notes within a measure. The changes in tempo and key are sometimes reminiscent of eastern European composers, and, for those of us of a certain age, perhaps a hint of what prog rock would try in the 1960s and 1970s. The first two sections are especially good, as is the final section, the "Cantico".

In fact, I have to wonder why ELP didn't adapt part of this instead of "Pictures at an Exhibition". Hint to Keith Emerson.

title: A GIANT among Beethoven cycles - and in SIGNIFICANTLY improved sound
text:
It has been a revelation to hear this astonishing Beethoven cycle from Franz Konwitschny and the Leipzig Gewandhaus Orchestra, and it’s quickly become one of my cherished CD acquisitions. The cycle itself is tremendous, and it moves me. These performances remind me of how profound the Beethoven symphonies genuinely are no matter how many times we've all heard them. In this cycle, the symphonies have a humanity to them that transcends whatever jaded feelings one might have about this music. And the playing of the Leipzig Gewandhaus has to be heard to be believed – it’s a testament to an orchestra that had its own incredibly special klang, which sadly is no more (just as the klang of the Berlin Philharmonic during the Karajan era is no more). For the first time I now understand how the Leipzig Gewandhaus was regarded in the past as one of the three greatest orchestra in the world. They play this music as if their collective lives depend on it, and have a richness, depth, and soulfulness of sound that is just hard to put into words. How could any orchestra have been this exceptional? There's a lot here to unpack.

The great news is that this re-mastering from Berlin Classics of the original Eterna recordings (made in conjunction with Phillips – which is why they sound so much better than similar vintage eastern bloc-era recordings) is a stunning improvement over the original CDs (which hardly sounded bad). It’s totally worth the purchase cost to get the re-mastered recordings – and then some.

This cycle was recorded very close to the end of Franz Konwitschny’s life (he died in 1962; these were recorded from 1959-1961). What one hears in these performances is a great conductor at the height of his powers leading an exceptional orchestra that just breathes this music and understands it to be profoundly spiritual. There’s not an ounce of routine in any of this. It’s unbelievable – all these stellar musicians playing as one, with total commitment, with no doubt in the importance of what they are doing, and collectively bowing humbly in front of the master, Beethoven. They understand who the rock star is here: not them, not Konwitschny, but Beethoven. That’s what I hear.

And what interpretations! There’s a supreme confidence and rightness to these readings. Konwitschny doesn’t make cheap interpretive points to remind us who is standing on the podium, but rather, conveys utter respect for this music and a desire to communicate its profound meaning and deep humanity. There are no distractions from rigid adherence to metronome markings or out of tune obsolete instruments. This is big-boned Beethoven without apologies, striving to get to the soul of this music. It’s overwhelming. Could it be that these performances are extra special because during the Communist era (and in particular in highly repressive East Germany) this was the only way for the musicians to protest, by bringing a deep spirituality that could not be spoken of to their “work”? I don’t know, but something very special is going on here.

There’s not a performance in the entire cycle that’s a throwaway. They’re all special. The 5th in particular sends chills up my spine. If there’s one performance I’m less likely to return to it would be the 9th. It’s a solid performance, don’t get me wrong, but Karajan’s 1977 performance is just so definitive it’s almost impossible for me to enjoy hearing the symphony played any other way. That’s not to say there’s anything wrong with Konwitschny’s reading. But Karajan 1977 is so searing (in its original incarnation, not the re-mastering which improves the sound but loses the performance’s soul), it just seems like the final word on the subject.

So here’s my apology to the universe. From what little I knew of Franz Konwitschny prior to actually hearing his music-making, I understood him to be mostly a laughingstock, a conducting apparatchik if you will. He was a notorious alcoholic and reportedly his musicians referred to him as Kon Whiskey. Being stuck in East Germany and behind the Iron Curtain certainly didn't give western audiences the chance to hear his music-making. My first exposure to him was a live recording of Bruckner 2 with the RSO Berlin that I was given as a gift (which I had no interest in acquiring on my own). Yet to my astonishment it turned out to be an AMAZING performance of that under-appreciated masterpiece, even if the sound was less than optimal. So I purchased the Scribendum box set, and was rather surprised to hear first-rate music-making that was actually distinctive. The Beethoven symphonies were clearly excellent, although the Schumann symphonies were more variable than their reputation (but 1 and 3 in particular are superb). But it wasn’t until I got to his Bruckner that I realized Konwitschny is indeed one of the great conductors of the 20th century, even if he doesn’t have that reputation. I’m still listening through his Bruckner and I don’t want to make any overall comments about it just yet, but let’s just say I’m really impressed. From a still-evolving perspective, it seems to me Konwitschny deserves to be spoken of as a great conductor alongside Klemperer, Giulini, and of course Karajan (who is still better than all of them). It’s been a joy and given me a sense of euphoria to discover Konwitschny’s music-making. And the best thing I’ve heard from him yet is this stunning Beethoven cycle.

This gets my highest endorsement. It’s beyond exceptional – it’s profound. I still think I prefer Karajan's 1977 cycle overall. But Konwitschny's cycle more than holds its own and the two might be a toss-up for the greatest Beethoven cycle I've heard, although I'll probably still go with Karajan 1977. It may well represent Konwitschny's finest achievements musically. And for sure, it speaks of a truly great Leipzig Gewandhaus Orchestra which was a colossus during this era, even if that time has sadly come and gone. But these recordings are a profound time capsule, and I personally believe this set (in its re-mastered form) belongs in the collection of anyone who is serious about this music.

title: "All Men are Brothers"
text:
01-27-14 Alan Hovhaness strikes a cord witj me in his mystical and romantic view of the world, indeed of existance. He does so with millions of listeners all over the Earth and, hence his music is generally well recieved in concert halls and recitaL AUDITORIUMS. TROUBLE IS GETTING THESE WORKS PROGRAMED IN THE FIRST PLACE. He has only one consistant champion thatv I am aware of, that being Gerard Schwarz, formerly the Music Director of the Seattle Symphony Orchestra, a very good 2nd tier American ensemble. This maestro has recorded a fair amount of Hovhaness's work, for Seattle, and mopre recently, the Liverpool Philharmonic as well as an occasional European group. But, it's simply not enough. I do believe thaT WHEN AMERICAN AUDIENCES HEAR HOVHANESS, MOST OF THEM FOR THE FIRST TIME, THEY WILL LIKE IT, AND WANT TO HEAR MORE.
The Symphony #11, "All Men are Brothers " was premiered on MaRCH 12, 1961 BY NTHE NEW ORLEANS PHILHARMONIC UNDER FREDERICK FENNELL. THE WORK WAS THEN TOTALLY REVISED AND THE NEW VERSION WAS FIRSAT HEARD ON MAZRCH 31, 1970, IN NEW ORLEANS, UNDER WERNER TORKANOWSKY. I KNOW OF NO OTHER INFORMATION REGARDING THIS SYMPHONY. IT IS, HOWEVER, NOTABLE THAT IT IS IN ONE MOVEMENT, here lasting 32:26.
The music is built on the ternary form of "A/B/A" aND, AS SUCH HAS ANOPENING "MOVEMENT" MARKED "ANDANTE APPASSIONATO", which runs for 08:17 the middle "Allegro maestoso is 12:30 long and then we return to a concluding "Andante con nobilita>" this is it, a fairly good sized work which until this very moment I had note heard a single note of. My very first imporessions are as follows.
The first part, "A" #1 , contaiins some "distant" sounding trumpet calls and slowly heighten the tension of the movement, building as it does, steadily throughout this initial section. This is the fdirst piece of Hovhaness I have with the ROYAL PHILHARMONIC, A GREAT BRITISH ORCHESTRA AND THE COMPOSER HIMSELF IS ON THE PODIUM doing a fine job. It is also the first time I have heard him conduct, as well. The mood here is more a simple "Andante," than necessarily an andante appossionato". tubular bells ring out a bit after the 6 m inute mark and, for some strange reason, this music brings into my mind a vision of the planets as viewed froim a craft in the vicinity of, say, Jupityer. AZ short modedratly forte brass chorale ties a bow atop the first "movement." The second or two pause leads into the "B" section, whic consists largely of a long string dominated agitated theme, with distant timpani strokes each few sdeconds and more of thiose evocative bells here and there. The brass choir enters periodically, often with a slight increase in volume and intensity. But, the strings do control the sxegment, now around the 10-11 minute region, becoming more organized and sounding a bit like a dance. As I listened to this fine Royal Philharmonic, i reall that this is likely the best orchestra I've yet heard playing this composer, though Schwarz did record Mysterious Mountain" yearfs ago with the Rioyal Liverpool on Telarc. THAT is a splendid disk and highly recommended by myself. The middle part, begins moving towards a conclusion with a strong unison statement, headed by the brass choir at about the 18:32 point and by the 20:00 minute mark, we are now concluding this interesting and clever movement.
Pat 3 is the second "B" section, and is another slow movement, majestic and graceful, marked as an "Andante con nobilita." At around 23:22 or so, a beautiful rich string melody enters nobily and moves in a stately and dignified manner. Once again the strings dominate thisa section with that dance like music. In the 28-29 minute range, the bells and other percussion inclding tam-tam join in to the fray as the momentum now begins to slowly build towards the Symphony's climax. The Symphony #11 closes with a noble and grand chorale for full orchestra, swelling slowly and beautifully unter the composer's fine leadership. I am very impressed by his music, his conducting and , of course, the wonderful RPO. Highly ecommended, thnough this is not MAJOR Hovhaness, it is still well worth collecting.
Next is the Armenian Rhapsody #1. A post-script regarding this work will be added as an addendum to this review. The "Rhapsody" lasts for only 4:54 and is a pleasent moderately paced melody in dance tewmpo, based , I presume, on Arrmenian themes. This piece, and the following pair of works are performed by the Crystal Chambert Orchestra, conducted by Earnest Gold. I guess the "Crystal" is name after this recording company, upon whicxh these works were made. Another ternary "A,B,A" piece, the "B" section is fast, whirling delightful and tambourine embellished. If only it were longer.
Another recording of Hovhaness's very popular "Prayer of St. Gregory, " this one with trumpet soloist Thomas Stevens.

But hey, I was seeing Radiohead, and it was hard to give the Jicks much attention despite seeing them 3 times with Radiohead this summer.  However when I arrived home, I had these songs stuck in my head... I had to run out and buy Pig Lib, which I listened to probably a hundred times the first month I had it.  It is hard to explain what kind of "style" or "genre" this music fits into.  The vocals are great, the arrangements are tight, and the music can generally be described as bizarre, wacky, and definitely unpredictable at times.  Malkmus is a GOD on guitar, but doesn't have to flaunt it all the time.  His band is like a tight disciplined jazz quartet, changing tempo, getting into grooves... But Malkmus and the Jicks ROCK OUT!  This album may seem mellow at first listen, but give it time.  Like Radiohead albums and other fine jems of music, this work of genius may require several listening to fully appreciate what Malkmus has accomplished... enjoy....

title: The End of an Era
text:
I began to listen to Argentinean rock only as teenager, and Sui Generis was my introduction. Until that point, I had been obsessed with bands like Guns N’ Roses, Nirvana, Aerosmith, and of course, the Beatles and the Ramones. Rock nacional? No, thank you, I would have said back then, with a sideways glance. Then I met a guy with whom I would get together to play the guitar, and he introduced me to Argentinean rock. Discovering Sui Generis was a turning point in my life. Of course I had heard their most famous song, “Rasguña las piedras,” but listening to _Confesiones de invierno_ (1973) convinced me that my country had much to offer when it came to music. When I had listened to the complete Sui Generis oeuvre, I asked my acquaintance about Serú Girán. Well, he said, it’s different. I listened to a few songs, and that was it: this music went over my head. Two decades would pass before I’d give Serú Girán another chance, and this time I would get it.

Sui Generis and Serú Girán both bear the unmistakable mark of Charly García, the mad genius of Argentinean rock. The former is, for the most part, easily accessible; the latter is deeper and requires more of the listener’s involvement. From our perspective, Serú is a supergroup: Charly García, David Lebón, and Oscar Moro were all talented musicians who had been involved in significant bands such as Sui Generis, Pescado Rabioso, La Máquina de Hacer Pájaros, and Los Gatos, while Pedro Aznar was a still relatively unknown virtuoso. The combination is magical, as the results show.

_Peperina_ (1981) is not Serú’s best album. After much deliberation, I’ve decided to award that title to the band’s eponymous debut album, which was released in 1978. The second and third albums, _La grasa de las capitales_ (1979) and _Bicicleta_ (1980), offer more than the first in terms of scope, but the material is of slightly lesser quality. _Peperina_, finally (the reunion album, _Serú 92_ is another story), is the band’s most well-known album, probably thanks to the title track and the story behind it. It is not perfect. It does not reach the heights explored in songs like “Eiti Leda” and “Serú Girán,” both included in the first album. Why, then, have I given _Peperina_ five stars? Because it is a brilliant album nevertheless, and while it is Serú’s most accessible, this does not mean it is simple or shallow. This is the type of album anyone can listen to and enjoy, but which also has deeper layers the more sophisticated listener will appreciate. In short, it is an album that has something for everybody. This is, then, a great place to start if you’re new to this band, unless you want to go for the good stuff directly, in which case I recommend the debut album.

I will comment briefly on the songs that make up _Peperina_. These are the eleven tracks:

* Peperina: perhaps the band’s most famous song, it was inspired by Patricia Perea, a reporter from Córdoba who was always critical of Serú Girán’s performances. The bleeping at the beginning (of the word “huevos”) was not the result of state censorship, but a joke on Charly García’s part. The song describes the girl of the title, a mediocre, hypocritical opportunist. “Ella adora mostrar la paja de la cara ajena.” “Dentro de su cuento ella era Cenicienta. / Su príncipe era un hippie de los años sesenta.” “Duerme con los visitantes y juega con los locales.” “Su cuerpo tiene pegada grasa de las capitales.”

* Llorando en el espejo: a beautiful, mellow, piano-driven piece. The lyrics are brief and memorable without necessarily telling a story, and the tune is catchy. One can see the link with Sui Generis here. The second half of the song is instrumental.

* Parado en el medio de la vida: like “Seminare” (from _Serú Girán_) and “San Francisco y el lobo” (from _La grasa de las capitales_), this is one of those short but wonderful pieces from David Lebón. The lyrics are not entirely coherent, but the melody works, so we give Lebón a break. He does make a good point with the very first line: “¿Qué estamos esperando para recibir amor?” I always get distracted by the fact that Lebón pronounces his t’s almost like an English speaker. (He lived in the US as a kid.) One of the band’s best songs, if you ask me. “Con los ojos cerrados me ves mejor.” Great stuff.

* Cara de velocidad: the first of three instrumental tracks. It begins with a gentle piano that reminds me of Erik Satie, but Lebón’s guitar and Aznar’s bass soon take over, drowning it. Don’t worry. The initial melody will reappear in the sixth track: “20 trajes verdes.” Excellent, fast-paced bass work and guitar improvisation here. I’m reminded of Queen, for some reason.

* Esperando nacer: this has got to be one of Lebón’s best songs. The opening solo, which anticipates the stanzas and chorus, simply draws you into this slow, soothing piece. “Tengo la esperanza de encontrar un sonido, y un amor tan grande que te pueda mover. Por Dios, escúchame.” Serú Girán were often described as “los Beatles criollos.” This song may give a clue as to why.

* 20 trajes verdes: fulfills the promise that opens “Cara de velocidad.” One may criticize Charly García for many things, but he is a great pianist and knows how to make music. My mother has a rather pronounced dislike for Charly. I would like to play this song for her, ask her what she thinks (I’m sure she’ll like it), then tell her who composed it.

* Cinema verité: enigmatic with somber undertones, like something out of the dark areas of Sui Generis’ _Pequeñas anécdotas sobre las instituciones_ (1974). A song of many sections, each one with its own feeling and color: Charly García’s forte. “Yo nací para mirar lo que pocos quieren ver.”

* En la vereda del sol: one of the album’s upbeat tracks, along with “Salir de la melancolía.” Simple and catchy.

* José Mercado: I read somewhere that the name José was inspired by José López Rega, who was Minister of Social Welfare from 1973 to 1975. This satire is Serú’s strangest song. It begins with a Brazilian-style percussion section. José Mercado is the stereotypical Argentinean who is obsessed with foreign goods. Like Peperina, he is an example of “grasa (vulgarity) de las capitales.”

* Salir de la melancolía: like “En la vereda del sol,” one of those songs most listeners neither love nor hate. A jazzy tune, it reminds me of Spinetta Jade, especially the album _Bajo Belgrano_ (1983).

* Lo que dice la lluvia: a sublime instrumental piece, this is the only one composed by Aznar for this album. (His two other Serú credits are “Paranoia y soledad,” from _La grasa de las capitales_, and “La luna de marzo,” from _Bicicleta_). He plays all instruments in this one. Serú Girán disbanded when Aznar decided to go study music in the US, so in a sense this is “goodbye.”

At first, my intention was to give this album four stars, to indicate that it is not superior to the band’s debut record. Both albums are magnificent. If forced to choose one, I would go with _Serú Girán_, but… how can one put it?… there’s just something about _Peperina_. It marked the end of an era. Soon afterwards, Charly García started to develop his more pop-influenced solo career, and bands like Soda Stereo, Sumo, Virus, Los Pericos, Los Fabulosos Cadillacs, Los Auténticos Decadentes, Attaque 77, and of course the beloved Patricio Rey y sus Redonditos de Ricota began to emerge.

As usual, I intended to write a brief review, but I didn’t have time. I hope these musings resonate with someone here. It does feel a bit strange to write about Argentinean rock in English, but my hope is that readers from other latitudes will profit from these comments. Do I take myself too seriously? Probably. There are worse things.

I’m thinking of reviewing something by Sui Generis in the near future. We shall see.

Thanks for reading, and enjoy the music!

title: Best Interpretation of the American Folk Song

title: a must for any swing-jazz collection
text:
I have tasted a number of swing albums, each with a style different from any other. The one I keep coming back to over and over is " A Night Out With Blue Plate Special "; You will see how crisp and tight the brass section is, while the lead vocal captivates you, and keeps you fixed on the melody. Like a good buffet, there is alot to select from, with no repeated style from one selection to another. With each song, there is a new flavor to get your attention.
"Night out", the first song grabs your attention immediatly, where the lead vocals are clearly in control of the song and keep your attention to the end.

title: Hornsby Enters the Next Phase of His Career
text:
When I put together a review, I normally try to mention something about the liner notes - positive or negative. In the case of Bruce Hornsby's "Harbor Lights", I think it's important to mention this at the beginning. The liner notes for this collection are simply outstanding and go a long way for helping you understand some of the new directions that Bruce takes for this particular collection. These liner notes do include lyrics, musician and production credits - all of which are important things. But, more importantly - there is a 2 panel write-up from Bruce himself that discusses some of the things he did differently. Bruce will give you his insight and context into each of the songs. This goes a long way into understanding this collection. With this particular review, I will try to add some additional perspectives on this collection and try to reference points that Bruce makes in his collection.

"Harbor Lights" marks the fourth album by Bruce Hornbsy. Hornsby pioneered something that has been called "The Virginia Sound". The best way I can describe this sound is a mixture of a lot of different genres of music: Jazz, Classical, Bluegrass, Rock, Country, and Pop. In the past, Hornsby incorporated a wide range of instruments in the songs to give this such a distinct sound: Mandolin, Guitar, Violin, Piano, and even Harmonica. On his first two albums ("The Way It Is" and "Scenes From the Southside"), if I had to pick a strong influence from those genres - I would probably lean toward Bluegrass. For his third album, "A Night On The Town", Hornsby began to emphasize Rock and to a lesser extent Jazz. For "Harbor Lights", Hornsby definitely turns things more toward the Jazz side.

Hornsby does a lot of other things differently as well. As Bruce indicates in the liner notes, this is his first album without his band - The Range. The lone holdover from The Range is drummer John Molo. Bruce also mentions that this is his first album where he took complete control of the Production Duties. He also mentions that this was recorded in his home studio in a very "loose" (i.e. jamming style session). One thing that Bruce doesn't mention is that most of the songs on this collection were written by Bruce and Bruce alone. On the previous three albums, Bruce's brother John would co-collaborate with Bruce on many of the tracks. On this collection, John only is credited with writing the words for 2 of the songs.

Usually when an artist decides to self-produce, work at home, and take on the majority of the songwriting - it sometimes proves to be too much. Phil Collins for his "Both Sides" album tried to make a true solo album in which he did everything (including play most of the instruments) and the end result reflects that it is too much. For "Harbor Lights", Bruce does enlist the help of some top musicians - the end result gives this collection a very good feel. The musicians included are Pat Metheny, Branford Marsalis , Phil Collins (who at this time was working on the "Both Side" project), Bonnie Raitt, and Jerry Garcia. The inclusion of Metheny and Marsalis make sense. Metheny is a legendary guitarist whose Jazz-like style fits very nicely with the Jazz-like theme of "Harbor Lights". Metheny contributes some of this great guitar work on "Harbor Lights", "Talk of the Town", "China Doll", and "The Tide Will Rise". Marsalis also has experience in working in Jazz/Rock fusions. Bruce had done a song with him during the 1992 Barcelona Olympics. It was Marsalis' horn work that played a major role of Sting's Jazz-infused Rock album, "The Dream of the Blue Turtles". Marsalis contributes some outstanding horns on this collection to "Long Tall Cool One" and "Rainbow's Cadillac". Collins contributes both percussion and vocal work: "Talk of the Town" (bongos); "China Doll" (background vocals). Raitt's unique vocals are heard on "Rainbow's Cadillac" and "The Tide Will Rise". As for Jerry Garcia, he had started working with Bruce on "A Night on the Town". Bruce had actually worked with Garcia on some Grateful Dead Shows. Garcia contributes some nice guitar work "Passing Thru" and "Pastures of Plenty".

Hornsby's albums have always had some strong songwriting. His liner notes describe many of these songs beautifully. On previous works, we've seen sociological messages this on "The Way It Is", "Look At Any Window", and "Fire On the Cross". Hornsby is at no loss for this on this collection as "Talk of the Town" deals with an interracial marriage. Hornsby has always done a nice job at a "storytelling narrative" style in prior songs such as "The Road Not Taken" and "A Night on the Town". You'll hear this style on this collection on songs like "What a Time" and "Long Tall Cool One".

While the Virginia Sound might have switched directions, Bruce hasn't totally abandoned it. As Bruce says in the liner notes, the song "The Tide Will Rise" is about the Waterman of Virginia. You'll hear a bit of the classic style from his Range days on "What a Time" (i.e. a bluegrass spin). You will also hear some violin and viola on "Pastures of Plenty" - something that was more of a Hornsby staple in his earlier days. In fact, "Pastures of Plenty" really does a good job at the whole spirit of the Virginia Sound - the fusion of the many genres.

title: Nelly Is Back!!
text:
Nelly Furtado burst into the mainstream about 5 years ago with her carefree, summer anthem "I'm Like A Bird" and fresh debut album "Whoa Nelly". After this initial success she lost her footing with the public and released the commercially failed "Folklore", though this album was a great effort and risk by Furtado, it disconnected her with the charts and she needed something to propell her forward. "Loose" was the ideal start.

Nelly hit back with her first ever US #1 and topped the charts across the Atlantic with another song. This mainstream doesn't make her a sell out. It just proves that the public knows good music when they hear it.

This album is chiefly produced by Timbaland, the master behind Justin Timberlake and Missy Elliot. His production on the album is flawless and gives it an edgier feel.

This album is a refreshing mix of pop, R&B and hip-hop. Standout songs include "Maneater", "Say It Right" and "All Good Things (Come To An End)".

On the latter you can hear Chris Martin's writing contributions very evidently.

I love this new side of Nelly, sexy and edgy. OK, I admit it she is kind of using sex to sell her music but in this instance it is actually a good way to market her music. She herself has said this album is about just letting go and not caring what anyone says.

2006 has been a great year for music and this album is definitely one of the highlights. Even though it has some notable fast songs, it has its share of ballads that show off Nelly's range and talent.

Simply excellent.

title: GIVE THE GIRL HER DUE!
text: I'm sure that many of the so-called critics will dismiss this album in the same way they have dismissed most of the work she has done since she became phenomenonally successful.  Then again, most of them probably had their review written before they even bothered to listen to the album.  One will rag on her because she's not a songwriter.  Another will trash her for being too bombastic.  And yet another will criticize her for singing too many ballads.  I think the most astounding criticism I've read complained that her voice was souless and mechanical!  Yes, her voice is technical perfection but not to the exclusion of a wellspring of genuine emotion.  In fact, I would say that those two things in existence together are what set her apart from MOST singers.  If there's one area in which she CANNOT be criticized, it is that astounding instrument which is her voice.  That voice is the most important criterion upon which her music should be critiqued.  Listen to the amazing note she hits near the end of "Sorry For Love" and answer one question for me.  WHO else can do that??  Incidentally, this song has GOT to be a single. Twenty years of training and discipline have gone into the creation of that voice and it is NOT the result of studio wizardry (I have seen her live in concert twice), so please give the girl her due! Other highlights of the album include the uptempo,life-affirming "I'm Alive", the tender ballads "Have You Ever Been In Love" and "Aun Existe Amor", the shimmering title cut, and the simple, poignant "Nature Boy".  Anyone who appreciates real music as opposed to most of the ... record companies put out these days should own this record...

title: The beautiful Chopin Waltzes played beautifully

Chopin's very beautiful waltzes are, to me, some of the most gorgeous compositions by that composer. Stephen Hough's new (2010) recording of these works is so beautiful and sensitive. His playing of all the Waltzes (8 published and 9 unpublished plus 3 of doubtful origin) especially the melencoly ones in minor keys moved me to tears. He has such fabulous technique and produces the most beautiful tones.

Hough beautifully, rhythmically, gracefully and elegantly plays the Waltzes in chronological order of composition (which finely shows, to me, Chopin's development as a composer) with the ones in minor keys being my absolute favorites. (by the way Hough's use of rubato is sublime). Added to the aforesaid compositions, Stephen wonderfully plays the Nocturne in E flat number two (2) which really sounds a lot like a Waltz in disguise. Whatever form it really is, Stephen plays it most beautifully. I love this album and have listened to it often. Stephen Hough is a real "treasure". I just love how he plays the piano. title: "I don't really wanna stop the show..."
text:
An undeniable masterpiece, The Beatles eighth proper album (in five short years) is an artistic landmark and something that every person should experience at least once. It's the grand extension of their previous album, Revolver; and it owes much of its inspiration to the brilliant Pet Sounds (by the Beach Boys.) Among critics these three albums are most often considered the "best of all time." Which is truly the best is one of the most contested debates in rock music. There is room for all three, but I feel this is the best.
The concept of Sgt. Peppers is famous; The Beatles, tired of the weight that came with their reputation, decided that in this album they would pretend to be another band. The album was supposed to be a concert set that the "Lonely Hearts Club Band" might play. Actually the concept is only followed loosely (though it did inspire the most fascinating album cover ever.) Still, this supposed concept underlies one of the main themes of Sgt. Peppers, which is that the songs are concerned with day-to-day observations on life rather than introspection. Sometimes, the lyrics tell a great story, or produce terrific images. But often the music evokes feelings that the lyrics don't match, as sometimes they are complete nonsense. As other critics have noted, this is sometimes a drawback; but the music more than makes up for this...
The title track is one of the greatest openings ever, complete with the backing symphony warming up and an anticipatory audience. McCartney's searing vocals provide the perfect edge to this killer rock tune, and the backing symphony fuses with the sound seamlessly. This fusion of different musical styles permeates the record, and is part of what makes it so ground breaking and timeless. She's Leaving Home, a thoughtful song about a runaway girl, is completely done with a chamber music strings section like Eleanor Rigby, only more beautiful. Fixing a Hole is another great McCartney song, this time with a harpsichord. Almost every song on the album was conceived with instruments never before used in rock before. But the real genius of The Beatles is that these additions never feel forced; when you listen to the album you can't imagine a better way to do any of the songs.
The music is truly timeless. Even after all these years, the intricate melodies and progression of these songs sounds refreshing and inventive. This was the first album to ever have one track flow straight into the next. It gives the feel that this is more than just a collection of singles; it is an artistic statement that belongs together. No other band could have so effortlessly placed McCartney's 30's tribute (with a great bass and clarinet line, and some delightfully whimsical if silly lyrics) after the sitar-laced, trance-like Within You Without You (which is a very minor Harrison contribution, seeing as his similar "Love You To" on Revolver is a better song.) This cohesion is much more noticeable if you listen to the first half in the order described in the liner notes; the Beatles had intended a different song progression than what resulted (only because the album format couldn't support a "Side A" that ran the first seven songs.)
The classic With a Little Help From My Friends is the only song on the album that John and Paul actually worked out lyrically together. Altogether, Paul deserves most of the credit for Sgt. Pepper's execution, as he came up with the concept, was most interested in the final result and wrote 8.5 out of 13 of the songs (the half coming from his part of A Day in the Life.) Lennon's contributions were integral, but he was somewhat removed from his peak songwriting. At the time, he had been somewhat depressed, and his lyrics suggest a lack of effort: Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds, one of the best psychedelic songs both sonically and lyrically was inspired by his kids' (Sean) drawing; Being for the Benefit of Mr. Kite, a very peculiar carnival-sounding song had it's lyrics copied verbatim from an old poster; A Day in the Life's nonsense lyrics were based on newspaper clippings (even though I think they're some of the most evocative Lennon's ever penned.) The irresistible, ragged Good Morning, Good Morning was written about a day's errands, but does comment on the monotony of living day to day.
This isn't to say that Lennon was in a slump; songs this good couldn't ever be considered a slump, even by his lofty standards. But Sgt. Peppers was the first Beatles album that McCartney clearly directed, and he would continue to do so from this point on. In the earlier records John was generally more of a leader but by this point he had already detached himself from the group to some extent.
The coupe de grace of the album belongs to Lennon, however. A Day in the Life is might just be the greatest song ever written. It's a bewildering musical achievement, and officially heralded the arrival of studio songcraft. It begins with a simple, haunting four-piece melody and some piano chords, and builds to a glorious full-stringed climax- which releases with a most transcendent, sustained chord. Lennon delivers his lyrics about the human tragedies we all read about everyday with an aching and stunned voice, as if numbed by the sadness of modern life. This is accentuated, in typical Beatles fashion, by McCartney's mid-song bit about going through the motions of another day as normal, completely unaffected by the injustice that surrounds him. It's a simply mind-blowing song.
Revolver may have had better lyrics than Sgt. Peppers, but Sgt. Pepper sonic assault is both more varied and more assured. This album changed all the rules about what rock music was, what it could mean to people and where music was going. There may be albums that are its equal, but no one has ever done music better than The Beatles' Sgt. Pepper.

title: "Southside" Steve Marriner Hits a Home Run !!
text:
I was fortunate enough to see Steve Marriner on-tour with Harry Manx at the King's Theatre in Annapolis Royal, Nova Scotia, in the Summer of 2006. As great as Harry Manx was, Steve Marriner totally stole the show, conjuring up the spirits (and tones) of Sonny Boy Williamson during the first half of the show, and Little Walter during the second-half.

Marriner's new album, "Going Up," is a powerful blues tour-de-force, and should be nominated for the best blues album of the year. The production-values are consistently good throughout, the compositions and arrangements are excellent, and Steve's vocals are very good. But the real treat here is Steve's harp playing: he captures the early '60s reverb-and-overdriven tone of Little Walter to a tee. The guitar playing on this album is very strong as well, with fine performances by Garrett Mason and Sue Foley.

As a blues guitarist thoroughly schooled in the styles of Howlin' Wolf and Muddy Waters, I recognize in Steve Marriner a PhD-level student of the Chicago Blues genre.

In sum, a remarkable album by a remarkable talent. I can unreservedly recommend this album for electric blues fans.

title: It's a matter of personal opinion.
text:
And my opinion claims that this album is one of the best this year, right there with the likes of Bloc Party, The Bravery, Maximo Park and Franz Ferdinand. The problem is that The Rosebuds will likely get the least recognition. Which is not fair, as this album could be successfully argued the better album of all the former mentioned bands.

"Birds Make Good Neighbors" starts with what is now the best Rosebuds song to date: "Hold Hands And Fight". The song starts soft and melodic, after one minute however it picks up and enduces one of the most melodic vocal melodies yet by The Rosebuds. The song makes the best use of the expression "whoa" ever.... ever. It's enchanting, really. "Boxcar", the next track, is another really good track. The song starts off a lot similar to "Back To Boston" from "Make Out", but proceeds to differentiate itself with the rest of the song. "Leaves Do Fall" is an amazing song, which has husband and wife, Ivan and Kelly, trading vocal duties. "Shake Our Tree", which is the second best track on the album, has a nice beat with an ambiance of clapping that would in fact provoke clapping. It also has an extremely good chorus. The album ends with "4-Track Love Song", which has a slow 80s sonic guitar sound. VERY nice, it definitely finds itself on multiple repeats from me. Other notables are "Outnumbered", "Warm Where You Lay" and "The Lover's Night".

With only a few months remaining in the year, this album is without a doubt one of the best yet. It's nearly perfect if not for two songs, which is not unlike any other great release this year, but "Bluebird" and "Wildcat", which seem repetitive to me, could have seen a change up or two. In a year which as seen so many great releases, The Rosebuds just proceeded to cemented themselves on the top of the pile.

Pick this one up for sure, and look out for the new releases by Rogue Wave, Franz Ferdinand and especially 31knots.

P.S. 31knots sounds nothing like these other bands, I just wanted to mention them as I am obsessed with their music.

title: She's about more than just movies...
text:
The Essential series is responsible for some of the best compilations yet released. I own several of them. Everything from Dolly Parton & Alan Jackson to Michael Jackson and Carole King. They never disappoint me. No doubt about it whoever compiled the songs on other volumes of the essential series, knows what they are doing. All of the Cd's in these compilations are 2 disc and the compilers do a great job in choosing the photos and songs in this collection.

Doris Day --who just recently passed away-- is the subject of this essentials CD and once again the compilers have done a great job in choosing the tracks. They have cherry picked the best of her sides and some surprising selections that aren't as famous, but are still essential in some way. Doris Day started out in the 1940's as a big band/jazz singer. I'm most familiar with this aspect of her career. She has always been underrated and seems to be remembered today for her "good girl" image and her movies, Which include "Pillow Talk" and "Pajama Game". There's more to Doris than movies though....

Doris possessed a charming and at times considerably powerful vocal instrument. Listen to "Secret Love". Doris starts off the song softly crooning and then alternates this, with a pretty powerful belt at the songs mid section. Doris could be a powerful vocalist, but unlike today's singers, offered tasteful restraint. There's no question that Doris was a good belter, but she communicated a songs message tastefully. She could shade lines at will in almost indescribable ways. Doris had amazing tone, great punctuation and could really put a song over with relative ease. She's a joy to listen to.

I applaud the song choices here and mostly everything's here, but there are a few cuts from the "Columbia: Golden Girl" collection (1999) that would've fit well here. I think "That Jane From Maine" should've been included here as well as lesser known chestnuts such as her rendition of "I'm Forever Blowing Bubbles". These are minor qualms though as the selection here is generally excellent. I love Doris voice and i'm enjoying this collection immensely. The liner notes are written by singer Nancy Sinatra and they are insightful and genuine. Doris music never got the attention it deserved in my book and that's a real shame. Because imo the music was better than the movies, but who can argue with success. Doris will forever be one of the best big band singers and hopefully, in the future she gets the accolades she so rightfully deserves.

title: EP to should satisfy Crimson fans till 2003
text: With the release of a brand new EP and a planned album of all original material slated for a 2003 release date, it is obvious that even after 30+ years, King Crimson is still going strong.  "Happy With What You Have to be Happy With" is a prelude to hold fans over until the release of King Crimson's next full length, the Power to Believe, but it is much more than simply a sampler of forthcoming tracks and holds up on its own very nicely.  The album is full of different styles all siphoned through the traditional sonic-progressive monolithic rock that is King Crimson. The opening track is a Belew vocals only track that sounds annoyingly like Yes, un-accompanied vocal tracks like this are scattered through the EP to provide sort of transition between the major songs, but when track two starts, the listener immediately knows King Crimson isn't just another pretentious prog group, in fact they are anything but.  Crimson takes a more focused, song-oriented approach for the rest of the album playing 3 particularly strong numbers that all strongly display King Crimson's new influences.  "Happy With What You Have to be Happy With", or the title track, sounds a lot like hard rock experimentalists The Melvins, coming across as a dense rocker with the most powerful vocals that have ever fought their way out of Adrian Belew's throat.  Of the two remaining fully developed original songs, "Eyes Wide Open" is a mellow, acoustic prog-esque song that discusses the necessity of being aware in today's modern world and "Potato Pie" sounds like the result of King Crimson spending a day listening to B.B. King with a strong blues roots influence pushing its way through Crimson's traditional sound.  However, just to prove that Crimson hasn't simply become another verse chorus verse band, the incredibly elaborate live version of Lark's Tongues Part IV is simply immense and Fripp's blistering guitar runs midway through are enough to make any fellow guitarist feel insecure.  In addition to the short ambient Fripp/Eno type track of "Mie Gakure" and the Tortoise sounding percussion song "Shoganai", there is also an odd medley of talking and music as a hidden track at the end of the EP presenting a strange juxtaposed overview of the recording of an album in less than three minutes.  "Happy With What You Have to be Happy With" is another well crafted set of King Crimson songs and if their new 2003 album is half as good and consistent as their new EP, then Crimson fans are in for some really great music in the coming year.

title: Sterling and Seductive Debut Album
text:
I return to Diamond LIfe again and again, to enjoy the understated cool vocals of lead singer Sade backed by her talented, experienced band. The album weaves a narrative of young love, the importance of dedication and strength in relationships, meditations on life's challenges (both matters of the heart and economic concerns), support of family and friends.

My favorite tracks are Smooth Operator, Your Love Is King, and Hang On To Your Love. Each of these tracks highlights Sade's seemingly effortless command of velvety lyrics overlaid a percolating, measured percussive bandplay. Sade's phrasings are often at a lower register; some times seductive, other times maintaining a presence of solid observation. The world is complication and large. The beauty of Sade's debut album is the band's ability to winnow down narratives to a human-to-human level, mining universal tales of heartache, dreams, a dose of reality that nevertheless can offer redemption and hope.

Diamond Life is never rough, always refracting various elements common to our collective human experience. At the time of this writing, February 2015, Diamond Life is approximately 30 years old and is as timely today as it was upon its release. This sterling collection of songs is cohesive and benefits from the fine collaboration between vocalist and instrumentalists. The album is relevant, a pure joy to listen to, and is deserving of a place in your music library. I highly recommend Diamond Life.

title: Finally,  New Cornelius To Sink Your Teeth Into
text:
I wasn't going to review this album, but about halfway through the second song this time I said what the hell. This is a great record from beginning to end. I like it better than "Fantasma" at this point. "Fantasma" was/is a great album, but "Point" just seems to hit a little bit better.
"Smoke" starts off with a reminiscent sound familiar to Tortoise and Yes. The bass in this song is the funkiest part of this album. The song is very well rounded with Cornelius repeating the word smoke over and over. "Drop" takes you on an IDM/Folk journey and also begins the "sound effects" portion of the album. Water running and birds chirping give this a bit of an experimental quality that Cornelius is so good at. The next song, "Another View Point," picks up where "Drop" leaves off. It's a little faster pace, but still keeps the integrity of the album.
The real surprise here is the song called "Brazil." It's the theme song from the incredibly bizzare movie by the same name. I'm sure some of you have seen this one before. Nevertheless, Cornelius adds his touch as always making one of the most intimate songs on the album. I absolutely love the vocal effects on this song. Superb.
I can't wait for you to hear "I Hate Hate." I laughed when I heard it.
All in all I believe this is a better rounded album than "Fantasma." Maybe it's just because this album is new to me. I don't know. You be the judge. Either way, if you get this album, I'm sure you'll be happy with it. If not, give it to a friend. I don't think it will make it that far, but rest assured you'll have a great recording for your collection. I'll bet this will be on some "best of 2002" lists at the end of the year.

title: Border Girl
text: Mexico hasn't had much of a roster as far as successful crossovers in the US. Sure, there was Ritchie Valens (who was Mexican-American), Selena (who was ALSO Mexican-American), but much of Latin music's noteable breakthroughs in recent years have come from Cuba or Puerto Rico. In 2002, Mexico City-native Paulina Rubio, hot off the success of 2000's top-selling Latin album, "Paulina", hit the pop charts with "Don't Say Goodbye". This came swiftly after Colombian pop-rock goddess Shakira hit the Top Ten with her English debut earlier that year. Rubio's disc, "Border Girl", didn't quite match the success of "Laundry Service", but it was as equally satisfying, if not more delightful. Fans of dance-pop will no doubt tap easily with "Border Girl", as many of the album's highlights are driven with lush synthesizers and delicious club beats. "Don't Say Goodbye" is a fantastic introduction- bringing to mind a late-night party in the vast deserts of Mexico as well as visions of sweaty bodies in a posh discotheque. "I'll Be Right Here (Sexual Lover)" also benefits from a dance music helping- bringing digitalized vocals with a pulsing dance beat, as does "Fire (Sexy Dance)". "Border Girl's" ambitions for dance-chart domination set it apart from most contemporary pop releases, which look to hip-hop and edge-driven R&B for inspiration. Not to say that Rubio doesn't pull this trick, for she does with the bland "Stereo" and "The Last Goodbye" (which luckily also brings ranchera vibes in the mix and is a standout on the album), but it doesn't work half as well as when she's channeling her inner Euro-disco goddess. The ending tracks are Spanish versions of "Don't Say Goodbye", "Casanova", "The One You Love", and "I'll Be Right Here", as well as the new "Libre". This half of the album allows those unfamiliar with Rubio's phenomenal success south of the border to become acquainted with her sexy vocal stylings that has made her a pop icon and sex symbol in the Spanish-speaking world. "Border Girl" doesn't break too much new ground, but it's undeniably catchy, surprisingly consistent, and shockingly eclectic, unlike most pop albums of today that are focused on the breakout single and then full of filler attempting to capitalize on the initial winning formula. Variety is aplenty here, and ear-catching, body-moving energy is the name of the game.

Valjean: Colm Wilkinson is just, well, good. Javert: Terance Mann was, eh, okay. He's fine in the part, just not as strong and powerful.

This becomes horribly obvious in "Come to Me." Like "I Dreamed a Dream", she sounds a little bored at the beginning, adding a little trill of vibrator (Coseeete, it's tuuuuuuuurned so coooold.) Then she proceeds to belt what just should not be belted ("And tell Cosette I love her and I'll see her when I wAAAAAAAAAAAAAke)

Marius: David Bryant is, just well, not that good. He's overly dramatic. At times in his performance, he sounds as if he is in desperate need of bowel movement.

Cosette: Cosette is just not interesting. Although in this recording, I find her incredibly interesting because Judy Kuhn (who sings the part) is honestly the only one who sounds good in this recording.

Eponine: Yeah, I don't know what everyone is seeing, er, hearing in her voice. She's horrible, nasally, and whiny. At times, she sort of mumbles through her song (see "On My Own": "And now I'm all alone again, no where to turn...")I know the book says that Eponine had a rough voice, but this is a musical, not a book. Frances Rufelle is bad. This is unfortunate, because she sings my favorite songs ("On My Own" and "A Little Fall of Rain")

This is definitely not the best recording there is. I advise you to get 10th anniversary CD or 25th anniversary DVD. The only reason I can see to buying it is if you're collecting all the Les Miserables recordings.

title: Signs of life
text:
Look, it's very simple: Clapton on smack is more soulful, more exciting, more interesting, than most contemporary guitarists on ecstasy. Or mineral water, or whatever it is they do. On this disc he's out of practice, and it shows--if you are a seasoned fan. Badge is played very close to the original, in sharp contrast to the double-time versions he played in the Eighties, with solos polished to a chrome shine. Let It Rain chunks along, with a superfluous conga solo by Traffic percussionist Rebop. But it's all still wonderful, with the cleaned up sound and expanded tracks. Sure, this is of mostly historical interest: Clapton hadn't been ready for the Dominoes to be over, when he went into seclusion, and he hadn't yet reinvented himself with 461 Ocean Boulevard. So this is a glimpse of him hanging between two worlds. Or, trying to climb back into this one.

Trivia: Pete Townshend plays the Gretsch Country Gentleman guitar, a gift from Joe Walsh, that Townshend used to record The Who's classic Who's Next. It wouldn't stay in tune for stage work so this is one of the instrument's only concert appearances.

title: ~ Madonna's debut remastered CD sounds good with extra tracks added! ~
text:
Back in 1983, Madonna made her big official debut with her self titled album. Her main songs that hit the airwaves and did very well on MTV were "Lucky Star", "Borderline", and "Burning Up". I don't recall seeing "Holiday" on MTV, but it was quite a hit also for her. So, I would say these are the 4 main songs on the album, but it's quite good all the way through. The 2006 remastered edition sounds really good on my home stereo with equalizer. On the original CD, there was quite a lot of hiss from the analog. Plus, having been there when CDs first came on the "market" in around 1985, the first ones pressed didn't have a lot of care put into them. So, yes, the sound was better in some cases, the analog "hiss" inherent to that type of recording was still present although diminished from cassette tapes.
In the "autorip" stated above for this CD, it says "Holiday" is not even 4 minutes. Well, it is wrong. That song on here runs 6:08 at least.
Not only do we have the original lineup, probably with the exception of a 3:44 "Burning Up", we have two additional song versions on this release.
BURNING UP (12" version) 5:56
LUCKY STAR (New Mix) 7:15..still sounds pretty much close to the original 5:37.
It's a great CD and does sound better than the original CD put out years ago, trust me on that. I have never owned the LP, so I cannot compare that to this 2006 edition. I don't think the LP has the two "bonus" tracks, either.
The liner notes are wonderful, plus has a Madonna photo I had not seen from this album photo session.

title: Really, this is German Lieder singing?
text:
I was extremely disappointed by this new recording by a soprano whose work I have always deeply admired. To be frank, I do not understand the complimentary reviews. The problems are on two level: vocal and textual. First the goal problem: the tessitura for many of the songs, and especially the magnificent Strauss Four Last Songs, seems to lie too high for Piau: her voice often sounds just plain shrill and inflexible. Next the textual problem: does Piau know German? I can hardly believe so. She splits words into syllables as if they were two words (listen to "jeden Baum," where "jeden" sounds like "je" "den" with no connection. The diphthongs are often mangled over and over again. The German is often so bad that the text is incomprehensible.
I believe that Piau is an extraordinary musician and a fabulous soprano, but this CD is a go mistake.

title: When metal loses its way.
text:
I own every Tourniquet album so I can speak as a true fan of the band. This album is a casualty of the 90's rejection of heavy metal in favor of a toned down, back to rock, approach that Metallica led with the release of the so-called "Black album". As a work of art/music the album is good and full of the typical eclectic experimentation Ted Kirkpatrick (the drummer and main creative force behind the band) excels at. The let down lies in the fact that the overall musical approach is rock not thrash metal which is what the band is known for.

Having said that, the album is worth owning for a number of reason, 1)if you're a fan and you want a complete discography of the band. 2)It makes a good listen when you want something different but still akin to metal (which is how I mostly stomach it). 3)Ted's creativity is still very much present throughout the songs.

Fortunately for us fans Ted found his way back to metal and the last two albums of the band: Microscopic View of a Telescopic Realm(2000), and Where Moth and Rust Destroy(2003) are true thrash metal - Tourniquet style! So be sure to give those a listen because you won't be disappointed.

title: Nearly Perfect Album by TBP
text:
Before popping in a CD by The Bad Plus, you already know to expect that which cannot be expected. This innovative, off-kilter, and outright odd trio from Minneapolis, MN is comprised of pianist Ethan Iverson, bassist Reid Anderson, and drummer Dave King (not our MT writer), and has earned a spot on any eclectic jazz mix tape for their ability to defy the taxonomic containers of genres in lieu of a fusion, if not commentary, on how music translates thought to emotion.

So that is what we are left with - emotions.

Never Stop is an entirely instrumental disc - without Wendy Lewis on vocals as in their previous album, For All I Care. So that leaves us with deciphering the jazz code, translating elements like meter, rhythm, cadence, and chords in to digestible experiences - an activity that requires a strong ear.

What first pops out to me about Never Stop is that it is relentlessly jagged. Ubiquitous throughout the entire album, phrasing stabs in unpredictable bursts that interrupt the listeners' expected flow of each song. Outside the realm of simple syncopation, off-beats of off-beats of off-beats punctuate each song with conviction, trying their damnedest to interrupt your comfortable listening process. Even compared to the jazz genre as a whole, this unpredictable phrasing is considerably avant garde.

I must make the distinction for you that there are important differences between avant garde and absurdest Neo-Dada noise music e.g. Yoko Ono's nauseating brand of art. There is, indeed, many layers of thoughtful construction and musicality buried within each track of Never Stop. They are just woven and layered in a manner that requires some careful listening and decoding.

Nor is it true that this album lacks any discernible structure or beat. In fact, my favorite track, Beryl Loves to Dance, is rooted on a fundamental-funk groove that is absolutely guaranteed to nod your head. Some songs are mellow introspections like Snowball, and some are a little more driving like the title track, Never Stop.

The disc is solid in its transportability; careful listeners will be able to let this album take them places as they examine new and interesting arrangements of three simple instruments.

The Good: The Bad Plus always delivers, and this is likely their strongest work yet. It's fun, it's creative, it's dense and ripe with new ways of looking at the world through music.

The Bad: Some people will never get jazz, especially the avant garde fusion of The Bad Plus.

Verdict: Definitely buy this album. The next rainy day, brew some yerba maté, and think about every note of this disc.

This review was written by myself for use on both the Amazon.com product review page and my music blog, Mystery Tricycle.

title: It hurts me...
text:
...to write this review. It truly does. I'll explain why:

I love Sade to death. I not only own each of her seven prior releases (five studio sets, a greatest hits compilation and a live album) on both CD and vinyl format. I have Sade b-sides, extended versions, alternate takes, remixes, rarities, you name it, I not only have it but love it. There's not a Sade release that hasn't deeply moved me...

...until Solider of Love.

I grinned ear to ear while my heart skipped a beat when I garnered an advance copy of SOL a week before its release. I was ready to fall in love with another Sade album on first listen just as I had with all of the others.

Yet, at the end of SOL's 43-minute duration, I was left wondering what I never thought I'd wonder about Sade's long-awaited return: "I WAITED TEN YEARS FOR THIS?!"

SOL is not a terrible album but any means but it is a surprisingly listless one. The album actually starts out on a strong note with the silky "The Moon and The Sky", which is classic Sade. The brilliant title track follows (for the first time in Sade's musical lifetime, the band hints at a new direction while still sounding exactly like they always have). Yet, after that, the album dives into a slow, samey patch of indistinguishableness. In all fairness, there are some slight moments after the high point of the first two tracks. "Morning Bird" is a minimalistic mood piece, similar to "I Never Thought I'd See The Day", "Like A Tattoo" and "It's Only Love That Gets You Through. The amused good feeling of the raga- influenced "Babyfather" is perhaps the most whimsical song that Sade has ever released. The song is the lone sunny moment on the otherwise dour disc. (All of Sade's prior albums had a nice variation of mood and groove. SOL doesn't- it just remains on one level.) Aside from those tracks, none of the remainder of SOL distinguishes itself. Nothing else stands out and sticks. This is a very first for a Sade album.

I was hoping that SOL would grow on me but almost a month since its release; it still stands as the lone Sade album that just doesn't captivate me.

I will always love Sade to the fullest. I'm very happy for SOL's soaring international commercial success and will root for it to continue. It's a testament to the band's organic talent and Adu's graceful, natural mystique that she can release an album ten years after her last (at the advanced age of 51) and still outsell and outclass younger, lesser talents in an age where people no longer really purchase music.

Yet, the album's success doesn't change the fact that it's the very first Sade album that I do not love.

And that hurts for me to say that.

title: What a Voice
text:
I first heard William Topley when I borrowed this cd from a friend. After I returned it I found that I could not live without it. I had to buy my own copy. I listened to it for three straight months before I was willing to let other cds share the airtime. Three years later this album still gets more than its fair share of airtime in my house, car, and job. Since then, my Topley collection has grown and now includes The Blessing as well.
The first thing you notice when you play this album is the deep, throaty voice of Topley. It's half hypnotic and half addicting. You can hear passion dripping from each word that he sings. It turns the song's lyrics into something more than words --it turns them into feelings. It's more than the way he sings the words but how he sings them as well. In the same song he'll sing a phrase really fast and staccato like, and then slows down the next phase by holding each note. This keeps things interesting, and turns his voice into a real living instrument.
The style of the album ranges from the reggae feel of "Soul Love" to the bluesy "Sycamore Street". My favorite songs of the album are "Song of a Seabird" and "Highway 5", but don't ask me which one I'd like to drop because these are all keepers. Very rarely does one find an album that you love most of the songs on it, but I love every single note of this album. If you like a gravelly voice that can sing with feeling, a good supporting band, and just plain good music, then check out Topley. You won't be disappointed.

title: This Has Not Aged Well...
text:
...and it wasn't great when it came out either.

This is perfectly acceptable music to drive your car to.

Emerging from a long period lost to drug addiction and facing numerous physical difficulties, it is somewhat of a miracle that Davis returned to recording at this period of his life. And though synthesized to death, it sounds as if Davis has his chops back here!

But. There isn't a lot to hear here. In a project where Miles abandons experimentation, abandons composition, abandons being the musical director, we get Davis jamming to some light funk grooves. The whole thing reeks of "studio." With Davis' huge body of "electric" work -- about 25 years of problematic, interesting, funky, pithy, compelling music -- I'm not sure why anyone would choose to engage with this.

P.S. I don't buy the explanation that "Miles didn't compose because he didn't like his contract with Warners." I think Miles didn't compose at this time because he didn't want to compose. (Which is fine...the dude remains one of the most productive musicians of the 20th century!)

title: THIS is "Soul Music"
text:
I first heard Michael Shipp three years ago on a wildlife benefit cd. He was playing guitar for Billy Bob Thornton on a song called "Island Avenue". That song in particular is still one of my favorites and it really opened my eyes up to what a great guitar player he is. Last September when Billy Bob released "The Edge Of The World", I got to hear more of Michael's playing, then I got word that he had put his own album out. After checking out the site and hearing a few samples, I became hooked. This is the real deal.
"The Adventures of Roosterboy" will draw you in from the first note. This is one of those rare albums where you can put it on just about any time and listen to the whole thing without hitting the skip button. Whether you're having some friends over for a few beers or out driving around on a sleepless night, this is a perfect choice for just about any occasion.
The first thing you notice is his voice. Think more of a tuneful Tom Waits and maybe a little bit of Springsteen and you'll get the idea, but what really gets me (aside from the lyrics) is the guitar. I've never heard ANYONE play like that. Just listen to the solos in "Favor" and "If You Had A Soul". If that don't move ya, check your pulse. You're probably dead.
"Blue Malibu" is a story song about a recently released inmate returning to his hometown with an agenda. This song alone would make a great movie. Very vivid lyrics. "Staring at the Wall" is a little number that works great late at night.
As a whole, the album is flawless. To me, it plays almost like a concept-album and it takes me right back to Arkansas every time I hear it. In fact, this is my soundtrack every time I make the seven hour drive back home.
Go ahead and pick it up. I feel comfortable reccommending it to anyone who likes Steve Earle, John Hiatt, or Billy Bob's music. I'd even reccommend it to anyone who doesn't. Bet you can't listen to it just once.

title: This One's a Hoot!
text:
When I was a kid back in the 1940s, there was a group that appeared regularly on radio -- this was before TV and when there was actually good music played on the major networks in the USA; alas, those days are gone! -- who called themselves the First Piano Quartet. Four players at four pianos. And they were marvelous. They have long since faded way; I could find but one recording of theirs here at Amazon, and that was only part of a CD that featured several other artists as well. But the notion of several players at several pianos was not all that odd back then, or further back in the 1800s. Composers like Brahms and Ravel regularly arranged their works for two pianos and there were festivals for multiple pianists at multiple instruments. Lo and behold, then, here is a recording with six Canadian pianists at six pianos. They call themselves 'Orford Six Pianos' because they came together as an ad hoc group at the Orford Arts Center in Québec. Most of the repertoire for this CD was transcribed for them by one of their number, pianist Olivier Godin.

One might be concerned that six pianists would create such a dense sound that individual lines would be obscured but that simply is not the case with these arrangements. Hats off to M. Godin for that!

Saint-Saëns' 'Danse macabre' is given a real workout (and some extra counterpoint) in Godin's transcription. It is followed by three pieces from Prokofiev's 'Romeo and Juliet': the rather formal 'Minuet - Arrival of the Guests', the tender and innocent 'Juliet', and the 'The Montagues and Capulets' with its tensions between the two feuding families. Then comes the swirling 'Waltz' from Gounod's 'Faust', arranged for two pianos, eight hands by Renaud de Vilback. Its entwining counterpoint is a joy to hear.

Rossini's Overture to 'The Barber of Seville' is a complete delight. You will recall that much of the overture is delicate filigree and repeated notes. The 'group of six' handles this impeccably. Marvelous! Rachmaninoff's little character piece 'Polka italienne' was originally written for piano, four hands, with trumpet. Godin has rearranged it for six pianos, twelve hands, and its charm is palpable.

Bizet's Carmen provides the material for a two-piano/eight-hands Fantasy on its themes transcribed by Mack Wilberg, currently one of the directors of the Mormon Tabernacle Choir; it is the longest work here --almost ten minutes -- and includes most of the opera's memorable tunes, mostly reharmonized and freshened with countermelodies above and below. The CD ends with a piece by the nineteenth-century Dane, Eduard Holst (not, mind, the more famous Gustav Holst) called 'Demon Dance', which forms bookends with the Saint-Saëns 'Danse macabre' for the concert. Originally a salon piece for solo piano, Godin has fashioned a piece for what sounds almost like a demon music-box which whirls and dances to a dizzying conclusion.

I hope this isn't the last we'll hear from 'Orford Six Pianos.' I recommend this CD highly for those interested in this sort of thing.

Scott Morrison

title: A More Intimate Album
text:
The good:

1. Phil Spector's overblown orchestral embelleshments are gone, thus giving a very intimate, almost "unplugged" feel to the album.

2. First-rate remastering.

The bad:

1. Song sequencing is not as good as on the original album.

2. Different versions of some songs are inferior to the originals ... "Let it Be," for example, uses a completely different guitar lead which sounds like a basic, pentatonic scale.

3. Deletion of the studio chatter ... that stuff gets into one's musical DNA after listening to an album for over 40 years. Kinda like the record you had as a kid that skipped in one spot ... when you replaced it and the skip was gone, it sounded "wrong."

4. Deletion of "Maggie Mae" and "Dig It." Song fragments, I know, but they ARE part of the album. Similarly, the inclusion of "Don't Let Me Down" seems misplaced as it doesn't really belong.

All in all, "Naked" is an interesting version of what I think is a criminally underrated record in the first place. Is it better than the original? I can't say for certain. I think it could have been had Paul simply cleaned up the tracks and kept the original song versions, sequencing, studio chatter, and song line-up. Nonetheless, it's essential for any Beatles completist.

title: Damaged Goods
text:
It seems as though the recording engineers kicked everybody but Arthur off the sonic stage. Blythe is credited, but so is Bob Thiele (of CTI label infamy) who is my prime suspect. The magnificent drumming of Jack DeJonette is in the next room, Cecil McBee (of Ornette Coleman fame) is down in the basement, and Blood Ulmer is playing his guitar in another building down the block somewhere. The screech of James Newton's flute receives an undeserved prominence (but then, I do have an aversion to that instrument). So, as all these reviewers eloquently point out, the material is lovely and Arthur delights, but this would have sounded so much better if the rhythm section came off as part of a cohesive unit rather than an overqualified backup band.

If you'd like a better recorded and higher energy Arthur Blythe/Blood Ulmer performance, try [[ASIN:B000002B3Z In the Name of]]. He only performs on three of the tracks, but totalling nearly 25 very powerful minutes. And Hamiet Bluiett and Sam Rivers are pretty thrilling substitutes on the rest.

I have both the highlights and the full recording of this version of Figaro. For some reason, though, Amazon doesn't seem to carry the full version, which is too bad. This is one of the few operas I actually think needs the recitiatives.
Anyway, so since the acting doesn't matter too much on a highlights version I won't get into that. The singing is very good, in fact I think it's probably the best version of Figaro out there. The only exception is in regards to Gundula Janowitz's performance of Dove Sono, which seems to be very ill-suited to her voice. The rest of her part is done beautifully. I also think it's sad that Marcellina's aria was left off, since that is always one of my favorite songs and I will never intentionally buy a recording where it has not been included, but due to how frequently it gets cut, I am not surprised.
Anyway, I recommend the highlights version if you are after something you can listen to in the car and don't want to bother with a full three disc set. For all other purposes I would advise you to track down the full-length recording, which is definitely worth it.

title: A Lack of Musical Architecture Indeed....
text: Unlike the reviewer below, I believe that Frederic Chiu was wisely shown the exit after the second round of the Van Cliburn competition.  Certainly his technical powers as a pianist are undeniable, but a thinking musician who allows the music to speak naturally without disruptive and individualistic statements he is not. As is sadly the case with many young performers these days, we are first made aware of Chiu's abilities and only afterward are we allowed to hear the beauty of Mendelssohn's music - and beautiful music it is. Anyone who has heard these works in the hands of a great musician (like Perahia) will hear at once the chasm that stands between such selfless interpretation and the land of Chiu. Menham Pressler said at the competition, "I want to meet another lover of music, I don't want to meet another player." Perhaps this disc is the best explanation for Chiu's failure in Fort Worth - buy it if you want to hear him and not Mendelssohn.
