title: Decent In Parts But Not What Most Fans Will Expect
text:
Most people who remember Boston will remember songs such as "More Than A Feeling," "Don't Look Back" and "Amanda," among others. Are you expecting songs like those on this CD? Well, if so, I would HIGHLY urge you to listen to the samples of this CD before purchasing it.
.
I enjoy lots of new movies, art, and music but this collection of songs did little to stir up the sort of emotions the band used to exert on me. It wouldn't really matter to me if these songs were released by another band, I still can't fathom it having any influence on my enjoyment of them.
The most vintage sounding Boston song on the CD, "I Had A Good Time," is pretty reminiscent but lacks a real hooky chorus, and that's the trouble with the CD as a whole; it's spotty, at least to those who're anticipating something a little more rock, and less pop oriented.
Don't get me wrong, I enjoy pop / rock if it really inspires me, but this just doesn't quite do it for me, unfortunately.
Make no mistake, there are some very decent brightspots on the CD, and it may very well be your thing, but really, when it gets right down to it, it's just not the sort of album most fans who remember the band are going to expect at all and if you're thinking about buying this CD because you're hoping this is another collection of legendary songs that've taken years to compile, then you're only half right, in my opinion. It did take years, but to say it's another collection of legendary songs would be to stretch the definition of legendary beyond recognition, in my opinion.
The songs don't stick with me at all like their earlier material. It doesn't matter that they don't SOUND like earlier Boston songs. What matters is that they don't inspire me like earlier Boston material.
Buy at your own risk. I don't recommend this one. I would recommend "Walk On," their last studio CD, over this. This is NOT in the vein of Third Stage or Walk On. I'm sorry but it's not. This CD is in a class all by itself and can't be compared at all with ANY earlier Boston, with the possible exception of the track titled "I Had A Good Time." Although I'm not a huge fan of "Walk On," I feel it's much more superior, musically, and Third Stage is infinitely more inspiring, in my opinion.

title: A Highly underrated gem of an album!
text: Whitesnake had quite a challenge of following up the megahit and classic "1987" album. I feel Slip of the Tongue comes close. There's been alot said about Steve Vai's playing on this album and the feeling that he wasn't bluesy enough for Whitesnake. I agree that he may not have been the perfect fit, thinking of other high profile guitarists at the time, Coverdale could have used someone more like George Lynch. Steve Vai was given alot of freedom to put his stamp on these songs and maybe the producers should have worked to blend him more with the band. Regardless, he does some great playing. I also have a soft spot for this album because this was the first hard rock concert I went to unsupervised in my junior year of high school. To date is still was one of the best concerts I've been to, in a live setting the lineup of Coverdale, Vai, Vandenberg, Sarzo and Aldridge delivered the goods! Slip of the Tongue sold very well but underperformed in comparison to the 87 album. I blame alot of this on the fact the wrong songs were released as singles. Judgement Day should have been the leead single and video, not the remake of Fool for Your loving (according to Coverdale, it was A & R guy John Kalodners decision). Sailing Ships should also have been a single/video. Deeper the Love is a good power ballad that reminds of the Is This Love feel. Now You're Gone is good but a feel is a weaker track. Wings of the Storm is a monster track that should have been performed live. Kittens Got Claws and Cheap and Nasty rock hard and were done gret live. Coverdales voice is in excellent form on this album. I also blame the underperformance of this album on MTV and radio who didn't promote them as much as they did with the 87 album. I also give thumbs up to the writing team of Coverdale and Vandenberg. Its a shame Adrian couldn't play on this album, I wonder how it would have turned out if he did.

title: Great Slide!
text: Whether you compare this disc to anything else Roger's has released, compare it to other slide guitar releases or compare it to other blues CD's released this year, it is not hard to justify a five star rating.  This release is simply heads and shoulders above the rest.  Like all "solo" releases, this release features an all star cast which serve up a creative rhythmic backdrop against which Roger's works his magic. No stranger to a Rogers CD is Norton Buffalo who performs harp on six of the thirteen instrumental tunes here.  Joining Buffalo on two of the tracks is former Muddy Water's drummer Francis Clay. Freddie Roulette (CD "Back In Chicago"), one of the last of the living blues steel guitarist, appears on two tracks and Joseph Zigaboo Modeliste (CD "Zigaboo.com"), one of the premier funk drummers alive today appears on four tracks.  The CD opens with a slide shred fest called "Avalanche", and then glides into the rockin' "Smoke and Mirrors" before settling down into what most folks will recognize as the blues.  The intensity of the music retains its fairly relentless pace until the rather funkified "Gumbo Funk".  Forget any notion you may have that a slide guitar instrumental CD might be a little mundane and prepare for a wild ride.  This is great music.

title: A Must-Have
text: Of the three main box sets (50's, 60's, 70's) this one is my favorite. The reason is Elvis' voice is in absolutely top form. Especially on songs like "Fame and Fortune"! Not even Bing Crosby could've done that one better. And that's saying a lot. The first couple of discs are simply incredible. Elvis was apparently nervous when he was in the Army waiting an excruciating two years to find out if America still wanted him on the throne. Maybe that's why his performances are so mesmurizing. He wanted to out-perform his 50's records, and without a doubt (vocally) he did. There are some filler songs on disc 3 that are of the same caliber as his movie soundtracks, but at least they are fun. I'm glad they were all included anyway. Disc 4 features many great tracks such as "Suspicious Minds", "And the Grass Won't Pay No Mind", "Anyday Now", "Long Black Limosine" and many more. Disc 5 features a lot of filler (like unpolished versions of songs like "Kentucky Rain") but the best track on #5 is the great duet with Frank Sinatra "Love Me Tender/Witchcraft", a clever combo of the two songs sung together. A lot of critics say Elvis recorded nothing but movie soundtracks during the 60's, but this box set proves otherwise. Only a couple of these songs were from the movies. It's interesting to hear the decline in song-quality in the middle of the box set (in other words in the mid-sixties.) It's obvious that there was a time when he wasn't getting good songs anymore. But the songs from the beginning and end of the decade remain classics and Elvis never sounded better. It is disappointing that "If I can Dream" is missing. But that's forgivable considering the excellent booklet and liner notes that come with this set including tons of great pictures. If you are just getting into Elvis though I would start with the 50's box set first. They are better when heard in order.

title: Xcllnt
text:
This aptly titled effort seems in many ways to be the evil twin of Primal Scream's brilliant 1991 release, "Screamadelica". On a near equal footing quality-wise with that groundbreaking masterpiece, "Xtrmntr" is a much, much darker affair.
Whereas "Screamadelica" played like a sunny, opiated soundtrack to the quintessential hippie commune, Primal Scream is in a full-throttle rage on "Xtrmntr". The message is one of complete dissatisfaction with just about everything, and the music does a remarkable job of conveying that frustration: sampled guitars drenched with distortion; angry, driving basslines; and menacing string synthesizers create a paranoid panorama that is likely to cause injury on the dance floor. title: Haydn Symphonies - Fey & HeidelbergSO: Spicey, Amazing
text:
My recorded standards in Haydn to date have included the complete Fischer Austro-Hungarian cycle, now released total on Brilliant at a good price I believe, plus the older Dorati with the Philharmonia Hungarica, probably now drifting through used bins somewhere. Other supplemental recordings included Bernstein's NYP run of the later symphonies, and Paris cycle sets with Dutoit and von Karajan.

The band at hand in these discs - six or seven to date in a projected complete recorded set of all the Haydn symphonies - is a strange bird, indeed. The Heidelberg SO uses a mix of modern and period instruments, with the strings and woodwinds being modern, and the brass being period originals or rebuilds of authentic period instruments. Why Thomas Fey and friends came up with this mix is difficult to explain, exactly. On the surface, it seems like an odd idea that probably would not work, musically. Yet, against all early odds, Fey and company do make it all work, and brilliantly at that. Fey studied with some of the leading lights of the period instrument performance movement, including Harnoncourt, and the truth of my listening ears is that I would much prefer to hear him, so far, than I like to hear his world-class pioneer and mentor.

As it happens, this mix is just about perfect for Haydn. You get a punch from the period brass that seems obvious, once you have heard it. Beethoven got his sforzandos from somewhere, in this view. Haydn comes off like a pretty vital, cool character. Not missing touches of gallantry and elegance, particularly in the loving care that is paid by these players to slower movements and lightening textures - a touch of very sweet, then. But on the whole, their approach stays so alive and vital that few will get sleepy, even listening closely to Papa Haydn. Tempos are reliably fast, but not rushed to blur the articulation of phrases and chords so important to the harmonic story being told by the composer. Against all odds, the strings, woodwinds, and period brass have a blend - spicy and piquant - all their own. One suspects that Fey and friends relied on their own ears, more than on abstract notions, as they molded their performance strategy.

The sound is regular 16-bit CD in stereo - but very good for all that. And do check out similarly Wow performances of Beethoven - an interrupted complete cycle in progress? - and Mozart. The real deal for music first, and period performance invention, second. Very Highly Recommended.

title: Listener-friendly 20th Century music
text:
At the turn of the century, a man spent the summer in a small "composing shed" near his house writing his first symphony. It's the story of Gustav Mahler, and also of Leopold van der Pals.

Pals had completed studies with Rheinhold Gliere and was inspired to write big works. His first symphony was completed in 1907. Its creation parallels Mahler's first, but that's where the resemblance ends.

Pals' symphony is much more modest in scope. This four-movement work shows Pal to have an original voice. Post-romantic chromaticism mixes easily with impressionistic chord structures.

It was well-received in its day, which isn't surprising. Pal guides the listener along a carefully delineated path. Unlike the Mahler first, Pals' symphony isn't revelatory, but it's well-constructed. And it's enjoyable to listen to.

This release includes other orchestral works written around the same time. Frühling und Herbst (Spring and Autumn) are two tone-poems about seasons transforming from winter to summer (and vice versa).

Wieland der Schmied is symphonic prelude based on a play by Friedrich Lienhard. In these works Pals seems closer to Debussy than Mahler in style.

The Helsingborg Symphony Orchestra, directed by Johannes Goritzki give credible performances. The ensemble sound is warm and blended which serve Pals' fluid harmonies well.

title: A brilliant and edgy album...
text:
While the previous chart-topper "Violator" was released in 1990, and as great as the music on that album is, it was still very much in the confines of what Depeche Mode sounded like in the '80's. Let's face it, the whole of the album was written and mostly recorded in '89, so it was for all intents and purposes an '80's DM album. And so I tend to think of this gem of an album "Songs of Faith and Devotion" to be the true sound of Depeche Mode in the '90's. The music takes on a completely new turn this time around, adding live drums courtesy of Alan Wilder (who really shines on this album) and incorporating more guitars than any past DM album (and yes, there were guitars on "Construction Time Again," "Black Celebration," "Music for the Masses," and "Violator"). Martin Gore's songs take on a new level of maturity and David Gahan's vocals are aggressive and raw (his voice actually sounded deeper and more punchy on this record). Overall, I'd have to say that it is less ambient than the follow-up album "Ultra," but it is no less powerful or atmospheric. It's also the album that marked the farewell of Alan Wilder, who left after the subsequent 18 month tour (dunno what they were thinking taking on that kind of pressure). Now on to the songs...
-"I Feel You": the first single that kicks off the album with that famous tire-screeching sound is reminiscent of "Personal Jesus," only slower and much more sexual lyrically. Here we have the first indication of Gahan's voice adopting a grunge element, which only adds to the force of the song.
-"Walking in My Shoes": a beautiful song that leads up to a powerful climax that fades out to Gore's sliding guitar and a series of synth-string backdrops. Some of the best lyrics on the album are in this song alone. "Now I'm not looking for absolution/forgiveness for the things I do/but before you come to any conclusion/try walking in my shoes." Great stuff!
-"Condemnation": it took me some time to get used to the gospel nature of this song, but I do have to say that Gahan's vocals are truly impressive here.
-"Mercy in You": to me, this is the most underrated song on the album. This song is like "Halo" was for "Violator"...it would've been a great single.
-"Judas": another gospel inspired song that could actually bring tears to the eyes if you're not careful.
-"In Your Room": while the single "Zephyr Mix" is closer to the grunge persona people assumed the album had taken with "I Feel You," this version is far more atmospheric and all the more incredible. With a pulsing bassline that reminds the listener of "Clean" from "Violator," the slow buildup to a gut-wrenching climax is darkly erotic and beautiful.
-"Get Right With Me": if any song on the album was a throwaway, this one should've been it. Not that it's a bad song, but it does little to contribute to the lyrical message delivered by the album as a whole. The B-side track "My Joy" from the "Walking in My Shoes" single could've been in place here, but alas...a great song saved for a B-side. And in its place, a mediocre gospel song...it's alright thought. Listen for the interlude which is a brief excerpt from a Brian Eno mix of "I Feel You."
-"Rush": now THIS is a techno song! This is my second favorite song on the album. Straightforward, aggressive, edgy, with a pulsing techno rhythm and an ambient mix of guitars and synthesizers make this something of a concert showcase!
-"One Caress": apparently Gore's only lead vocal on the album, sung amidst a string quartet. A beautiful song that pretty much fits in with other songs Gore has sung in the past, from "World Full of Nothing" to "I Want You Now."
-"Higher Love": nothing special about this song. After listening to the rest of the album, this one just fits in with the new formula DM had adopted musically, and that just makes it a good song to close the album. Although I wouldn't recommend it as an encore to close out a concert with.
Much controvery has surrounded this album, from the 18 month "Devotional" tour that followed, to Gahan's much publicized heroin addiction, to Andrew Fletcher's nervous breakdown, to Wilder's departure. However, there's no such thing as bad publicity, and ironic as it may seem that so bad a situation was surrounded so successful and so brilliant an album, it only helps add to the ambience of emotion in listening to this album. "Songs of Faith and Devotion" is for DM what "Achtung Baby" was for U2. A chancy yet successful change of direction towards musical excellence. A great album!

"I Don't See You" is a sarcastic look at infatuation ("You won't go away/And I never asked you to stay/You're waking me at night/Away from my dreams"),the non-statement statement of "Ambiguity Song", the mocking Black Flag cover on "Wasted" and the misguided anti-establishment figure in "Opi Rides Again-Club Med Sucks" ("The people there, they are so stupid/They exploit the poor and the weak/I want no part of their death culture/I just wanna go to the beach"). College rock hit "Take the Skinheads Bowling" is also a semi-guilty pleasure. It's not really a great song lyrically, but it's fairly catchy.

The bad: There are entirely too many instumentals (8 of the 17 songs) and most of them really aren't all that interesting. Also, some of the songs here are just strange for the sake of saying "Isn't it cool that we're so odd?". These types of jokey songs really don't wear well with time. title: You Can Take the Man out of Chicago...
text: ...but you can never take Chicago out of the man.  Indeed, Mark Farina successfully reCONNECTs with Chi-town roots in his latest to create a tapestry of house music that is distinctly not Bay Area (which is just fine as far as I'm concerned...okay, so maybe I'm just a wee bit housist!).  I personally tried my best to feel his United DJ's of America contribution - but my  distaste of that album was fully justified once I gave CONNECT a serious gander.  This is house music at its best...jazzy, highly danceable, beaucoup loops, beats you can feel, right from the soul - and let's not forget the introductory latin cuts, which have far more personality than others I've heard as of late.  For the cursory listener, the most attention-getting tracks will likely be Joshua's "Work It Out" with the De La sample (need more house tracks like this); Halo, Penn & Chus' "Vuelve a Casa" (hard, uptempo beats juxtaposed with a dark tech bassline); Andrew Macari's "Seven of Nine" (is he referencing a certain -Borg?  either way, a wonderful jazz surprise); and the list goes on and on.  At times I wished he would play each song for a longer period of time before mixing to the next; I would have to say that this CD is guilty of feeding me a plate of delicious house hors d'oeuvres - each morsel satisfying me in tiny bursts but leaving me hungry for more when it's all over (though disappointed I surely am not).  I'm eagerly anticipating his next installment - I just hope I'll need to pack my knife and fork when the time comes.

title: I have always loved her music but don't recall hearing about anything new ...
text:
Remember Nichole Nordeman? I have always loved her music but don't recall hearing about anything new in some time. When I heard Nichole came out with a new album, The Unmaking, (which released on August 28, 2015), I knew I just couldn't wait to hear it. T

Here's what Nichole Nordeman says about her album, "Before things in our lives can be resurrected and given new life, certain things must die. Before beauty blooms in spring, roots must do the hard work under the hard frozen soil of winter. Before you renovate and re-build, you tear down the parts of the structure that are weak or damaged or dangerous. Before we make, we must unmake."

Nichole Nordeman is a recording artist and songwriter for Sparrow/EMI CMG, with numerous number-one and top ten singles to her credit and cumulative CD sales of over one million. A two-time Gospel Music Association winner for Female Vocalist of the Year, she has won a total of nine Dove Awards, including the best-selling album, Music Inspired by The Story. Her best-known songs include Holy, Legacy, Brave, This Mystery, Why", and What If. She lives with her family in Tulsa, OK.

When I knew I was going to get this CD, I wanted to learn more about Nichole. Although Nichole herself hasn't recorded a studio project in more than ten years, I learned that earlier this year, Prince and 3rdEyeGirl released an electric guitar-heavy cover of Christian singer-songwriter Nichole Nordeman's song, What If, a song that embraces the closely-knit relationship between doubt and faith. Nichole contributed a track called I Will Believe to the Music Inspired by the Chronicles of Narnia album, and she wrote a song for VeggieTales called Sweetpea Beauty.

Nichole's new EP is full of songs written with the same passion and lyrical depth that made her past songs such a success. This EP signals a new season for Nordeman. A recollection of the brokenness and beauty in her own life, she delivers a courageous and compassionate recording that dares us to recognize the process of unmaking in our own lives. I love the third song on the EP called 'Name' - great lyrics and great song!

There are only six songs on this album but when hear it, you'll love it and if you are like me, you'll wish there were six more songs on this album. As a Plumb fan, I loved the fact that they collaborated on the song, Not To Us too, it's a great song.

I am very grateful to have received this product without cost in exchange for my honest review and unbiased opinion.

title: *far* from gentle
text:
Due to contractual obligations, I have to write a review for Gentle Giant's debut album. I tried getting out of it, but I can't. I HAVE to review it. Well gee willikers!

It's not that I dislike Gentle Giant's debut- it's actually a terrific album. You betcha. It's just that the band hasn't developed their distinctive style yet, so in a way (a HUGE way) Gentle Giant's debut is yet *another* debut album by a rock band still searching for their identity. How many times has THIS happened, you ask? Well, lots of times.

Look at Jethro Tull. Did future Jethro Tull albums sound like This Is? Nnnnnnoooooo. Well okay, maybe they do a little bit. Do we remember Deep Purple for their late 60's blues-oriented blend of hard rock? Nopey dopey! Actually in this case *I* do, hehe. Do we remember Yes for Yes. Yes? No!

I'm worried that my review will end up extremely short just like the one I wrote for the Power and the Glory. I couldn't think of any really outrageous rant filler for my Power and the Glory review, and the same situation appears to be the case here. The moral of this story? Attention all aspiring rock stars- don't make ordinary albums! Then I won't be able to think of anything to blab about!

Gentle Giant is still searching for their identity here. Yes, I said the word "identity" again (because you probably didn't pay attention the FIRST time I said it). Everyone used to accuse me of never paying attention all through my 12 years of school, but guess what? How many times have I sat on my duff and seen someone completely staring off into space? Thousands of times by this point. You know what you have to do in order to correct yourself, so do it.

Anyway, what's up with that big freaky head on the album cover? He looks like a jolly old man who appreciates living life to its very fullest and someone who loves playing innocent games! I'd sure trust a guy like that with my kids. If for example I saw him sitting on a park bench reading a newspaper while my children were on the swingset -and let's say I had to walk away for about 10 minutes to play with my BlackBerry or something- I'd be like "Keep an eye on my kids for me", hehe.

Anyway, the first track is simply called "Giant". Here's a question- since it's simply called "Giant", would it still make sense to call it the title song? A HALF title song is probably more appropriate, haha.

My feelings on "Giant" go like this- my favorite team in the division is still the Eagles. Oops, haha. Even though the song doesn't necessarily indicate that Gentle Giant would soon become one of those (underrated) giants in the world of progressive rock exactly one year later, it's still a pretty memorable song (mainly because of the way the vocal melody and guitar riffs compliment each other nicely). Two nice musical qualities complimenting each other. If only they could communicate with each other we'd be living in a perfect world.

Anyway, the song feels entirely rear-stuck in the typical hard rock style of the early 70's with only *extremely* brief moments of weirdness, and those moments mainly come in the way the band plays their instrumental chops. Only a really tiny indication that the band was about ready to move on to bigger, better and more super interesting/creative things. An indication you will soon never forget, just you wait! Acquiring the Taste is right around the corner! Here it comes! "Heeeeeere's, Johnny!"

Let's not discuss Acquiring the Taste though (and all its amazing, creative, original brilliance). It should already be a GIVEN it's a classic album. After all, it's the first album that gives you a perfect idea what Gentle Giant is really like... unlike this pitiful poor excuse of a debut album!

I'm kidding, haha. I like this album quite a bit actually. I just can't think of anything exciting to say about it, so expect a Mount Saint Helens lava flow of unrelated rants on my part in order to fill an adequate amount of space for a readable review!

Is "Nothing At All" that nearly 10-minute slab of those REALLY soft and beautiful vocal melodies? You know, the kind of melody that reminds you of falling asleep with the girl of your dreams right beside you (perhaps in the trunk of a car... while stargazing... right next to a really high cliff where you can see the perfect view of the city lights below)? Do you get my drift?

I can't believe so many movies feature those romantic scenes of a parked car next to a really high cliff. I don't know about you, but making out with a girl in a car that could easily go over said cliff doesn't exactly make for a romantic mood. It makes me fearful for my life.

Or maybe the song (yes, we're still talking about "Nothing At All" believe it or not) simply reminds you of dreaming and/or sleeping? Yes? YES it does! It also features a hypnotic drum solo. Yup, you heard me correctly- that wasn't just nonsense talking. The DRUMS are hypnotic. That's just... completely unheard of, haha. What is this world coming to.

Just throwing in a drum solo in the same track that features a really beautiful vocal melody makes me feel all weird and mushy inside (in a special kind of way). Who else would attempt such a thing? Don't say *you* would either because it's too late. :)

I like how there's a song on here called "Alucard". Don't tell me the video game developers at Konami were actually listening to this song and that's how they came up with the lead character for *the greatest game of all-time* Castlevania: Symphony of the Night (for the Playstation One console)? That would be... absolutely shocking, haha.

By the way, since I'm mentioning it, that really IS one of the best games ever created. I highly recommend you purchase it so you can experience one of the greatest sword-slicing, spell-casting, demonic creature-filled castle adventure games you've ever seen in your entire LIFE.

Anyway, those magical-sounding keyboards you hear briefly in "Alucard" remind me of the first cave area you encounter in an old NES game called Wizards and Warriors 3 Kuros: Visions of Power. This area is located immediately before you have to complete one of those dreaded tests, ugh! No, these aren't like school tests- these are actually much worse, haha. At least when you fail a Wizards and Warriors test you don't get punished by your parents- you just beat yourself in the head instead!

"Isn't it Quiet and Cold?" (no, it's been extremely hot and humid for three weeks now) is another highlight. I absolutely LOVE the sneaky mouse vocal melody that leads way to a highly melodic (and elegant) instrumental break. That instrumental part is REALLY good too. I absolutely love it. So what if it reminds me of Martha Stewart's clothing business a tad. No big deal, we'll recover (like an economy). Otherwise it's awesome.

That vocal melody really does sound like a mouse sneaking in the kitchen past midnight in search of some cheese, crackers, and peanut butter. Darn rodents must have a sweet tooth for the kind of candies children like to eat (and adults who never grew up, haha).

Um, I don't hear anything funny about "Funny Ways". I just hear a terrific vocal melody. Must be British humor. I'm American by the way. I grew up in southeast Pennsylvania home of the Philadelphia Eagles, Phillies, 76ers, and Flyers. I'm a very passionate sports fan. You know what THIS means! I criticize anything that moves, haha.

"Why Not?" is a VERY good Steve Winwood impression. The lead singer sounds just like a Blind Faith or Traffic song. Awesome.

It's Gentle Giant's debut, and it rules. Just don't expect the weird factor of the band to creep into the picture yet. Okay home slice? Wait until Acquiring the Taste is released next year.

title: How Does She Do It?
text:
I saw Crystal perform live in January 2019. I felt so uplifted watching her! I think what makes her face and her voice so beautiful is that she seems to be always smiling on the inside. And her voice is truly changeless. It's like honey,: golden and warm, loving and kind. She knows her craft, that's for sure. I've got all her albums and I honestly can't point to a single musical mis-step she's ever made (although there probably have been a few. Who is perfect, after all?)

This new album is another treasure to add to the collection, and even includes a duet with sisters Peggy Sue and Loretta Lynn. It is produced by her son, Christos. This is music at it's best: enjoyable, melodic, fun, pretty. Crystal always has the best virtuoso musicians work with her. The arrangements are sumptuous as well. After listening a few times, I'm left once again asking myself " How does she do it?" Because she is defying time, people. She really is!

title: A Performer With Flair
text: It was while Regina and I watched a series featuring country performers that she and I were introduced to Doug Kershaw. He did not strum a guitar but plucked at a fiddle instead. He had a rather curious way of holding it under his chi you would have to see as I cannot describe it. His music had an infectious beat to it we could not resist, and started buying his records. Yes, this was in the days before cassette tapes even. One of them was Devil's Elbow, the title song talking about his love for the fiddle. Other songs included Jamestown Ferry about a woman leaving her husband, and I Like Babies where he speaks of father and mother playing with their children. The kids are Roy Rogers and Dale, the mother is Trigger and dad is the bad guy. I liked the line that says "It's babies playing grownups and grownups playing kids." He comes across as a real family man with solid values who doesn't mind singing of those who are otherwise to a rousing Cajun beat with that fiddle going like mad. I loved the album and now I have it on a CD with many other Kershaw releases in my Amazon wish list to buy when I can. This is real feel-good music and will be forever glad I came to know of him.

title: A Fantastic Live Set
text:
I have been looking forward to this CD, since I heard rumors of the release of Neil's archives probably a decade ago. I was very excited a few months ago when I heard that Neil will release the material, one CD at a time.

As soon as I found this one in a store, I picked it up immediately. And I have listened to it a half dozen times already. It is fantastic: the driving guitar sounds of Crazy Horse, the magic of the original performance, the excitement of hearing some of Neil's classic songs early in his career.

I have read a few of the reviews of "fans." I don't understand--and being OCD I should--how grown people can speak of being "ripped off" or "disappointed," because this CD does not have all of the songs of the original set at the Fillmore East. They complain because of one song not being on the CD.

In the first place, this is Neil's artisitic material. And in the second place, being a "fan," I trust and respect his decision regarding how he wants to release it. His musical skill, his artistic creativity, his perfectionism make me interested in his music. The only promise Neil has to worry about is one that he obviously made to himself long ago, regarding the way he creates and releases "his" material without someone spoiling it when so-called experts mix it or put it together.

I don't know a lot about Rock 'N Roll history, but I once read that Buffalo Springfield's first recording suffered because of those very issues. I love the album in spite of everything I have read, and I hope that some of the archival material has some early studio and live things by Neil's first band.

I own everything Neil ever recorded on vinyl, cassette, or CD, most things in all three formats. I purchased everything in his catalogue a second time on CD, except for two albums not yet available. I never felt "ripped off." NOT EVER.

This CD is no exception. You hear the early sounds of Crazy Horse with Danny Whitten, something I was ecstatic about getting and 46 minutes is plenty of material for me, although I would like to hear more.

I figure it this way. I bought it. I enjoy it. I hope Neil will continue to release his material. If I had to encounter the constant negativity from a minority of people who never will be satisfied with anything, I would not release a note for them.

Thank goodness Neil's music is about art and not about making a buck. That's why people have so much passion for it.

I found tracks 1 and 12 quite cheesy. Tracks 2-3, 5-6 and 9 are pretty good. I found tracks 4 and 10 to have some good qualities, but majorly lacking. And I really didn't "get" tracks 7-8 and 11 at all. The tracks seem to rotate between dark/grungy and corny!

This album is quite different than what you might be used to from Neil Young. Unless you are part of a small segment of hardcore fans, you are better off getting something else. Neil Young has a lot of good stuff. If this is the first Neil Young CD you hear, you may be lead to discount him to easily. In that case, do your self a favour and get something else.

These songs were all recorded at the same time of 'Kid A' so before listening, you must understand that Radiohead is not going backwards to their guitar driven pop. Forget all the pre-release rumors of 'like kid a but more guitar' or 'kid a' meets ok computer'. It is neither of these but yet it fits smoothly along their last release...so smooth that you wonder why they even waited to release this as a separate entity. I think the two work better as a whole. title: A great change!
text:
Largo is a very interesting recording in Mehldau's discography for a number of reasons. It is his first recording with a large group, the first time he has recorded vibraphone and the first time he's used a significant amount of effects and engineering techniques making this very much a "studio album". This is in contrast to most, if not all, of his previous albums which have a decidedly live feel whether they were recorded at a concert or not.

Teaming up with an experienced producer such as Jon Brion proved to be a great match, but Brion was skeptical at first. When approached about Mehldau, his initial response was luke-warm at best, because all he knew was that Mehldau was "just another jazz pianist". But after hearing him, Brion quickly changed his mind and became excited about the project. It's obvious that they both felt good about recording together because of the great variety and spontaneity that resulted from these sessions. Many of the tracks were totally improvised and they also cover originals, Jobim, Radiohead, and The Beatles.

What makes this record exceptional even for Mehldau is how complicated yet accessible and simple it is. His level of playing is on par with other outstanding examples of pianistic mastery (such as Art of the Trio Vol. 3) but this time adds simple, yet poignant melodies as well as complimentary drum parts. All of these details seem to catapult Mehldau's playing to the next level and as a result, this is the type of recording you can listen to over and over. Not only can you put it on as background music but you can listen closely and hear myriad layers and themes that will keep your attention even if you listen to it hundreds of times.

title: An unbeatable recipe.
text:
The combination of an all-Broadway repertoire and the greatest voice in American music today is what Linda Eder fans have been clamoring for, and she has given it to us...and then some. For those few who may be experiencing her talents for the first time, "Broadway My Way" will hook you in but good.
Linda newcomers: Linda's voice produces the similar shimmering, Disney-esque high notes similar of a Streisand, and the full, heartbreaking middle-to-low range that sounds even more remarkably like Garland. But ultimately, Linda really sounds like no one else but herself. Once you hear her voice, you'll never mistake her for anyone else, or vice versa. Every melody she touches on this new project sticks in the head like glue. "What Kind of Fool Am I?", a song for which I've never cared greatly, I now cannot stop humming.
She's singing mostly standard Broadway fare here, but has stepped into a whole new arena of interpretation, with daring phrasing, rubato tempos, and unique arrangements. Even that old warhorse "Edelweiss" is fresh-invented with a subtle, almost African rhythm and a chorus of angelic Linda's singing backup. "Some People" makes my heart pound with all her dramatic nuances and inflections. "I Am What I Am" will have listeners throwing open their closet doors across the country.
When I first saw the song-list, I wasn't that thrilled, since a few of the numbers I've heard Linda perform in public or on previous CD's countless times before. But some are stunningly re-recorded, and they fit so well within the pattern of the newer choices, I now can't imagine the CD without them.
Wouldn't it be great if the promoters...could grab the ring and get this gem out there with the current trend of public appreciation for American pop-standards like Diana Krall, Barry Manilow and Tony Bennett?
More, please, Linda . . . and BRAVO!!!

title: Be Prepared - TO LAUGH!
text:
How can you describe Tom Lehrer's work to someone who has never encountered it before?

Satirical? Yes, but only partially.

Biting? Always, but sometimes with a touch of silliness.

Wicked? Definately, but with a twinkle in the eye.

Perhaps the one word to descrobe Tom Lehrer's work is, quite simply, funny.

Having discovered Lehrer through a chance hearing of his most famous song, Poisoning Pigeons in the Park, I became hooked. This box-set presents all of Lehrer's recordings along with a fantastically produced hard-backed book chronicalling just about all of the information there is on the man (he's a very private individual) as well as all of the lyrics.

Taking each of the three discs individually I shall start with the second one. Disc Two features Lehrer's two original recordings from 1959 and 1960 - 24 tracks in all. Each song is a gem but standouts include the aforementioned 'Pigeons' as well as The Hunting Song, My Home Town, Oedipus Rex and The Masochism Tango. The titles themselve point at the very political-INcorrectness of the content! These recordings are live and include the bridging introductions and gags (some of which are even funnier than the songs) and are boosted greatly by the presence of a very receptive audience.

Disc Two is virtually the same set of songs as Disc Two but without the audience and dialogue. These versions were recorded in a studio and suffer badly without the rapport that Lehrer has with the live audience. The only reason to listen to Disc One over Disc Two is for the two extra tracks slipped in at the end. Both I Got It From Agnes (how you interpret this song shows how dirty your mind is!) and That's Mathematics (a riff on That's Entertainment) are little treasures well worth re-visiting.

Disc Three is a mixed affair that is never short of genius. The first 14 tracks are Lehrer's work featured on the US version of That Was The Week That Was. These are all performed with an audience and bridging dialogue and are just as good, if not better than those on Disc Two. Classics here include Smut (my personnal favourite from the whole collection), Pollution and The Vatican Rag (which has the assembled audience in stitches!). The titles here rightly suggest that more satire is apparent in this set of songs than the earlier work. This slightly dates the content, but not so much as to render it redundant. Also on Disc Three are four of Lehrer's earlier works (from Disc Two) with full orchestration instead of the usual self-played piano. These are wonderful to hear, but still lack the audience reaction. Also here are songs that Lehrer wrote for The Electric Company TV show (funny, educational and yet, still a little subversive!) and a few little oddities including I'm Spending Hanukkah in Santa Monica (a Jewish 'Christmas' song) and Selling Out (another personnal favourite).

By the end of the third disc I was a little depressed that this comic genius had not made any more recordings. We must be satisfied with what he has left us, and look at the quality not quantity. Start again as soon as you're finished listening, these songs have great 'repeat appeal'. The only other recording of Tom Lehrer's work available (if it still is available) is the cast album of Tom Foolery, a revue of Lehrer's songs from 1980, performed by a cast of four and produced by (a young) Cameron Mackintosh. Although Lehrer himself does not appear on this recording, the cast work well with the material and the inclusion of a live audience helps too. I own a copy of this recording and treasure it.

Lehrer's final (to date) public appearance was as part of the Cameron Mackintosh celebration Hey, Mr Producer! Here he performed Poisoning the Pigeons in the Park and here is where I took an interest in the rest of his work. This performance is available on DVD, video and CD.

title: I said naked, not denuded
text:
"Some day, one day; somehow--not now!--and you will find, what you lose once you have peace of mind..."

Ahem. Those of you whose only exposure to Blue Six is through the first two Nude Dimensions CDs, with their inferior remixes of "Music & Wine" and "Pure," might not see the significance of an LP full Jay Denes' work. But for those who know Jay from Bare Essentials and Nude Dimensions 3 know just how indispensable this album could not help but be.

What Wagon Christ is to trip-hop, Spring Heel Jack is to jungle, Orbital is (or was) to house, and Rinocerose is to French house, Blue Six is to midtempo. That is to say, something which is unique and at the same time sitting royally atop a heap of wanna-bes. If I knew anything about making music (which I do not), I'd want to make it the way Jay does: combining euphoric chord changes, compelling beats, haunting lyrics and an array of evocative vocalists to sing them. "Let's Do It Together," "Close to Home," "Sweeter Love," "Very Good Friends," and "Beautiful Tomorrow" are all just what you'd expect from the creator of "Pure," the single greatest track in the Naked Music library.

That said, I can only give this album four stars, or maybe three and a half. I don't want to go so far as to say that Jay dropped the ball, but it feels like this album was released before the final mixing was complete. "Love Yourself" is barely a shadow of Petalpusher's robust, booty-shaking remix for ND3; and, tragically, the original cut of "Music & Wine" turns out to be lame (no I am not joking), almost totally deflated without either the guitar that forms the core of Jay's unbelievable "Conga Lounge" remix, or the thundering deep house elements of the "Th'Attaboy Vocal" mix (as heard in The Italian Job!). The minimalist production works on "Very Good Friends," which despite being little more than a vocal and a bassline is one seriously engaging piece of music. But nearly everything else is rather underwhelming, and feels like it needed another layer or two to truly bring it to full life (save of course for "Pure," which is really anything but). In "All I Need," "Yeah," and "Grace," especially, the few good elements are frustrating because they only point to their own squandered potential. I thought these albums were supposed to be "naked" in the sense of being lush, romantic, and uninhibited, not in the sense of being anemic and stripped-down. It's the other way around with ND3 and the awesome Carte Blanche series, where the bass matches the beats and there's always atmosphere to spare. What, did Astralwerks make trouble about a deadline and force Jay to submit an unfinished product? Or is it simply that production is his Achilles heel? If ever there was an album that begged for its own remix album, this is it.

text:
There is no pretense with Devildriver. They are a straight up, honest, grooving, modern metal band. Live, they are a phenomenal force.

In my humble opinion, this album is a great progression in terms of the band's sound. It feels like the logical next step to Beast, and in particular the 'Dead to Rights' side/style of Beast.

At times, though, I would like a little more 'space' for songs to breathe. I love Dez's lyrics, style and delivery. I just feel like the vocal lines are suffocating the songs a little.

There isn't the same kind of space and groove here as on "Last Kind Words", but then there wasn't on "Beast" either. And then, "Pray For Villains" was something different again - personally I think "Waiting for November" is one of their most heartfelt and underrated songs.

But, I would still recommend buying this album. Get into Devildriver! All up, an underrated band and a brutal, brutal album you'll return to many times.

title: Revised Caveat about Which Iteration of SKARA BRAE to Buy
text: The 1971 vinyl release of SKARA BRAE (siblings Micheal, Triona, and Maighread Ni Dhomnaill, plus Daithi Sproule) on Gael Linn Records did NOT offer optimal sound quality. I own both an original issue of the LP and a CD. The latter shows two copyrights: 1971, which is presumably for the LP, and 2004, which is presumably for the CD. To my ears, there is no perceptible improvement in sound quality apart from what you'd normally expect from any CD sourced from original master tapes used for vinyl. So I have no way of knowing for certain if the CD I have is a CD reflecting any Gael-Linn remastering. And just because there is a huge jump in price for one of the listed iterations of SKAKA BRAE is no guarantee that it is the remastered CD. Yes, it's irksome that Gael Linn didn't clarify or assert provenances as well as the year for mastering and remastering so Amazon customers could make a more informed decision about what iteration to buy. That's why I gave it an overall  two-star rating. Nevertheless, I'd agree that buying any iteration of SKARA BRAE is better than having no iteration at all. The album is a bona fide classic Irish traditional album of singing by three siblings and a close friend joined in memorable harmony.

title: What is the Superlative form of Verismo??  % Plus Stars! !
text:
03-09-2015 Back in 1973, I bought my first season pass to Chicago's Lyric Opera, and attended 7 of the 8 productions for that year. First up was the eye-slammer from France, "Manon," by Massenet. After surviving the powder and the fluff , I got hit square in the eyes by Puccini's masterpiece :Tosca." referred to, by the composer, as a verismo (realistic--earthy--gutsy) opus, it tells the tale if a love triangle, set in 1800 Rome, with political rebellion and secret police setting the mood of intrigue, suspense, crime and the struggle for power, influence and, of course, love. More on that night later, but this EMI recording is a boxed set of 2 CDs with full text and valuable background information. Maria Callas is Tosca, Tito Gobbi as the Baron von Scapia, and tenor Carlo Bergonzi, as the painter Mario Cavaradossi. The French National Chorus and Orchestra from Paris under the direction of Georges Pretre. The complete performance lasts for about 1:52:00and was recorded in 1964, in December.

ARTISTIC IMPRESSIONS
I'll get right to the point here. This is a 'DREAM CAST", if ever there was one and the too loud Mario Del Monaco is here replaced by the much more easily digestible Carlo Bergonzi. Callas is, of course, Callas but the key to this opera and, indeed this recording , is the massive presence of baritone Tito Gobbi, as the cunning and calculating police chief. From the very first instant of sound, quite good I must add, the drama is unrelentingly "in-your-face with one big moment after another. The romantic bliss of Act I is totally overshadowed by the threat of Scarpia, even before he makes his crushing first appearance. Under Pretre's powerful leadership the "bad guy" takes all the oxygen out of the room. Maybe his trademark role, Gobbi's Scarpia was better than any I've, EVER! ! For me, he epitomized the concept of the "singing actor", although that is something not all listeners are concerned with. There are millions of opera lover who have never attended a live performance, nor do they care to. And, that's all right, because, the real core of the work IS the singing. BUT, let's face it, opera began as a fairly passive activity---gossip, whispering as to what she or he is up to in a distant box seat, etc. Hence, it caught on quickly with the mass audiences of the day, back in, say, Mozart or Handel's times. Truth is , there are people who "love opera," and those who love "GOING TO" the opera. Agree or disagree----please comment.
The Chorus and Orchestra of the Paris Conservatoire provide a vibrant and powerful accompaniment, as well as some of the finest nuances heard in this visceral offering. As to my personal experience with Tosca, I first saw it in 1973 in Chicago's Lyric Opera with Tito Gobbi as Scarpia and Janis Martin singing the Cavaradossi was Mr. Kraus, either Alfredo or Thomas, I can't recall. The reason being the overwhelming presence of Gobbi, why not call this opera "Scarpia?"
I confess my ignorance of the so called-"definitive" 1954 version with Callas and Gobbi plus the boisterous Mario Del Monaco under, I think, De Sabata (?). This stereo version is leagues ahead of it's famous predecessor, as the sonics make for no contest. In my living room, I felt as if I were back in that main floor seat at "Lyric." Ah, the magic of the CD. WOW! Don't hesitate. Get yourself a copy today and just sit back and use your imagination for the visuals. Enjoy. THE best "Tosca," EVER> Trust me. Best wishes and God bless you all, Tony.
A. M. D. G.

title: Szell's definitive Mahler Fourth
text:
In his biography of George Szell, Michael Charry (Szell's former assistant) tells the story about how Szell kept a cherished copy of the score of the Mahler Fourth with him, and loved to play the four hand piano version with Charry for pleasure. To say that Szell did not have a feel for Mahler, particularly a love for this work, is false.

Even compared to other legendary Mahler Fourths, Szell/Cleveland's is a benchmark recording of this symphony, that catches Szell and Cleveland at the height of their mastery.

The (deceptive) classical garb of this work plays to strengths of Szell/Cleveland (who were pre-eminent interpreters of Mozart/Haydn/Schubert/Beethoven), but there is also an incisive modern edge to this interpretation. Despite its reputation, the Fourth is not an "untroubled" work. Szell's pristine, detailed presentation allows you to very clearly hear the conflict between brightness and innocence, and the macabre and grotesque.

The first movement unfolds with the ideal pace, and the transitions are handled with a dancer's agility, without the clumsy lurches that mar many versions of this work. The clarity, precision and touch of the orchestra is on full display. What makes this recording special is the chemistry between the conservative inclinations of Szell and the subversiveness of Mahler's score. The second movement is a fine example of this. What is very beautiful and innocent dances in front of something terrifying, capturing the Mahlerian "devil dance" perfectly.

To anyone who could ever accuse Szell as being cold, or "not Mahlerian", this performance sets the record very straight that neither was the case. Scores of many newer recordings of the Fourth are more clinical and hollow by comparison.

The bad news is that this treasured Fourth is no longer selling at a bargain basement price, except in used copies. It is available in another CBS edition as well. Regardless, this is a virtually perfect classic recording that is worth finding and treasuring. Search for the best price and grab it.

title: A defining Nu Metal album, but remember Korn didn't invent Nu Metal!
text:
It's all to easy to submit to peer pressure and say all Korn is Crap (I must agree they deserve it now especially after making a single of repeating F*** over and over.) However they were a landmark of the 1990's and whether you love or hate them Korn, you can't say they didn't heavily influence 1990's music, and although most of the decent nu metal bands (if that is 2 words I can put together) were out before Korn.

Yes teeny boppers, Korn didn't invent Nu Metal, two examples are Rage Against The Machine and P.O.D. who existed before Korn.

However Korn's heavy funk/ jazz influence helped to make the band more original. The downtuned 7-string guitars helped make Korn seem heavier than most of the other Nu-Metal. You can definatley see more of late Sepultura vibe in this Album. Jonathan Davies has chosen the root of agonised growls instead of his poor attempt at a poppy singing.

With little good traditional metal (with the massive exception of Pantera.) However along with Rage and P.O.D., Korn helped to make the teen spirit stinking years that bit heavier. However the fact that Korn sold out and the loss of their guitarist has made them a band who are mocked as much as they are respected. They're names have gone down in history however like Metallica and the 'Chillis they seem to have run out of ideas.

title: What a rediscovery of PURE GOLD!!!!  A masterpiece.
text:
I recently purchased "PopArt", which is a must have greatest hits collection like only Pet Shops Boys could release. In other words, worth every penny even at import prices. It's downright criminal that these guys are not ruling the airwaves here in the US. Because of "PopArt" I've gone back to my Pet Shop Boys CDs and put "Alternative" on and I still can't believe that I'd allowed this masterpiece to remain on the shelves for so long without listening to it.
When Pet Shop Boys released "Alternative", which is a double-disc set of The Pet Shop Boys' B-sides, I bought it because I buy all that is Pet Shop Boys, but since I buy so many CDs sometimes some get overlooked and this was one of them. MY LOSS!!
Far from being a superfluous collection of junk that most artists put out (i.e alternative mixes, unreleased mono, dub versions et al), this album contains a wealth of prime material that could have made for 2 consecutive hit releases. There is not a weak track in the bunch. Accordingly, this collection is a MUST not only for hardcore fans, but for casual listeners as the songs are all hit-worthy.
One of the reasons why this release may be so good as that the boys seem to still live up to the concept that, in pre-CD days, many vinyl singles (45s) includes relevant and even essential B-sides as , for example, is the case with Queen's "We Are Tha Champions"/"We Will Rock You"). In fact, during the heyday of single releases, many B-sides were more popular than the A-sides.
In a nutshell, Pet Sh have complilled 30 amazing songs that exempligy the wit, the finesse, and musicality that they bring to what so many of their peers are content to treat as trash. Although I love ALL the songs, among my favorites are "In The Night", "Paninaro", the amazing piano subtlety in "Jack The Lad", "Do I Have to".....
Also, the insert is extremely informative and gives you a peek into each of the songs. This is no rush job, but rather a masterpiece that was snuck into the marketplace. The boys should re-release this in another form to get new listeners to remind all these so-called dance acts that they are mere amateurs when compared to their older, wiser, and talented peers.
I am listening to the first CD right now and I feel downright idiotic as it feels like an early Christmas 2004 present that I happened to buy for myself in 1995.

title: Brilliant, Perceptive Songs That Slowly  Envelop Your Soul
text:
Unlike Miles' extraordinary "Slightly Haunted" that immediately grabs your attention and heart, "Night In A Strange Town" works its hypnotic magic more slowly and deliberately. Its effect on the listener is more profound, more powerful than her previous outing, but the songs require many listenings to truly grasp their ultimate rewards.
The music is deceptively mellow and belie the pain, yearning and irony of the lyrics. Miles yearns for perfection but is resigned to the imperfection of life and love. "I've been hurting so long for the perfect romance but I could not taste the honey for the bees...sometimes it's ok to be brought to your knees," she movingly emotes in "Perfect Romance" The bitter irony in her songs is perfectly represented in the song "Wrong": "Love is not bitter, love is not cold, love is not a weapon." but "love gave you sad answers and a hurt that won't heal..."
Miles has fashioned a moving, perceptive triumph- a collection of songs that slowly creeps up on you and never lets you go. It is, unquestionably, a singer/songwriter tour de force.

title: Early Xenakis orchestral music.
text: This fifth volume in Tympani's series of CD's covering Xenakis' orchestral works includes his earliest works in the medium, all of them top-flight masterpieces.  His exploration of music as statistical sound combinations (never "patterns" as there is no overt repetition, the sound being more "sculpted" rather than "stamped out") was so utterly unheard-of and unique that it rendered his early works well-nigh unintelligible to audiences of the time.  There were often riots at his early performances, which ironically helped put him on the map.  These works still can shock, fifty years after their premieres!  The performances, recordings, liner notes and all are first-rate all around.  Kudos to Tympani for bringing this series about.

I am a Wilco fan that was hooked by "Yankee Hotel Foxtrot", and have been enamored with everything since. "Summerteeth" - ngeh. I listen to it because it is smart and relaxing but I don't love it. I streamed a couple of tracks pre-release from "Sky Blue Sky" and wasn't thrilled - It seemed bland and watered down. Now that I own it and have given it several spins, I find that I am loving it. The addition of Nels Cline is brilliant - he is a master and exhibits a strong technical interpretation of Tweedy's rhythmic drone. title: Most of the Favorites from Her Broadway Career
text:
A double-disk release, "Patti LuPone Live: Highlights," was recorded live at the Westwood Playhouse in Los Angeles, California, on January 15 and 16, 1993. It contains most of the crowd-pleasing favorites from her successful Broadway career, and a good selection of just plain interesting/beautiful songs, too. But it may be just too much of a good thing for some, like me, who actually later additionally bought [[ASIN:B000003FK8 Patti LuPone Live! (Highlights)]], the one-disk release of this material.

It's not as if LuPone, a Juilliard graduate, isn't a greatly talented singing actress, although she stands but 5'2". Furthermore, it just goes to prove once again the acuity of legendary Broadway director/producer Hal Prince's well-known remark that his favorite singers are "actors with voices....A musician who appreciates words, and has the taste, brains and quirky wit to make the most of these wonderful show tunes."

Lupone, a native of Long island, New York, has just now closed her multi-award-winning Broadway run in "Gypsy," with book by Arthur Laurents, who directed its current run, music by Jule Style, lyrics by Stephen Sondheim, and choreography by Jerome Robbins. In it, she played Mama Rose, mother to two famous theatrical sisters of the mid-twentieth century, June Havoc, and Gypsy Rose Lee. Mama Rose was, for your information, famed as the worst backstage mother ever: the part, as is well-known, was created by Ethel Merman. Bernadette Peters played it recently to critical praise - I was lucky enough to catch Peters in that revival. However, the critics raved when LuPone did the part in one of City Center's recital-style productions a while back: after which, it was probably always in the cards that LuPone would get her chance at the part on Broadway. Most particularly now that the famous play's last living creators are aging, and might wish to see their great work again, splendidly done, before they go.

Most of the 2008 theater awards were given Lupone for her performance: she won the Tony, Drama Desk, and Outer Critics Circle Awards for Best Actress in a Musical, and the Drama League Award for Distinguished Performance, too. (She was previously nominated, at least, for most of these same awards for her performance as Mrs. Lovett in the revival of Sondheim's "Sweeney Todd.") However, quite ironically, she audibly tells her LA audience that she'll be leaving that city shortly to perform/tour for two years as the lead in Andrew Lloyd Webber's "Sunset Boulevard." Theater fans with long memories will recall that Lloyd Webber, creator of "Evita," from which LuPone's signature song "Don't Cry for Me, Argentina," comes, soon decided against her performance, at any cost. Anyway, I never got to see LuPone as Rose, as I no longer live in New York. I did, however, catch the actress on Broadway in the non-singing but star part of the housekeeper, Dotty Otley/Mrs. Clackett, in the revival of Michael Frayn's hilarious "Noises Off." Her timing was galvanizingly funny; (I do love funny, and had also seen the original production of that play.)

The actress gives us another top-flight performance, a tight two-handed kitchen scene with Kelly McGillis that was cut from the the film "Witness's" theatrical release. But the interlude sometimes shows up when the movie's on late-night television; I guess programmers then wish the movie to run a little longer. It's also on the DVD "Witness: Special Collectors' Edition," that I own.

On the CD at hand, LuPone is in good form: voice clear, intonation and phrasing flawless, and she sure do swing: catch "I Get a Kick out of You." As to the show's overall timing, the performer once remarked about another live album. that, as she was first hearing those tapes, "I couldn't believe the pace of the show. I thought we must have all been on speed." True enough. Her versions of "Surabaya Johnny," "Argentina," and "As Long As He Needs Me" brim with emotion: her devoted fans should be well-pleased. Mind you, the singer herself once said, "When I'm speaking between songs I sound like a babbling idiot." And there is some of that. But still.

The star once said, "I learned about performing on stage, period. I don't know what cabaret is. I just get up on a stage. I learned how to deliver a song without a mask. There was nothing to hide behind."

title: Another Shift In Sound
text:
I have been a Devin Townsend fan for a long, long time. From Strapping Young Lad through his many individual projects, I own a good chunk of everything he has ever done. I knew that Z2 wasn't going to be like the original Ziltoid album, which was an album I thoroughly enjoyed, but I came in with an open mind as I loved the idea of Devin Townsend taking his music on tour as a big, elaborate play. I'll be honest, I badly wanted to like it, and in the end...I did. Just not as much as I had hoped.

This album is strange. This isn't going to come as a shock to most Townsend fans but...strange in a way that doesn't really click with me. Lets start with the second cd, "Dark Matters", which features the play. It took a few listens but I absolutely love the cheesy, over the top sci-fi story and all the zany turns that it takes. The only issue I have is that only a few of the tracks really stand out on their own, but considering the album is meant to be taken as a whole, that isn't really a major problem.

My issue, strangely enough, is with the first cd "Sky Blue". The title track is incredible, one of the best Townsend has done, but the rest just...doesn't grab me. It isn't bad, I can't think of anything on it I was classify as "bad", but few songs really stand out as "great". Perhaps my expectations got the best of me on this one, as I was expecting a more upbeat version of Townsend's "Ghost" album where this is more of a softer natural follow-up to the Epicloud album (which I have mixed feelings about as well). Overall, if you're a fan of Townsend's work then you won't be disappointed, but you likely won't be blown away either.

title: "Billboard Top R & B Hits 1972".....Compilation....1990 Rhino Records
text:
I rec'd this 1972 R & B Billboard CD, on May 12, 2015. I'd like to volunteer my opinion on ALL of these songs, that are incl., here:

1. "Lean On Me"...by Bill Withers...This hit single went all the way to #1 on the charts, in the LATE Spring of 1972. And it was also his BIGGEST chart hit. This song is excellent. The R & B group, Club Nouveau ALSO took the REMAKE version of "Lean On Me" to the #1 spot in February of 1987.

2. "Let's Stay Together"...by Al Green...Once I heard this ORIG, version, by Al Green, I did remember this song, after all. This song made it to the #1 spot, in December of 1971 & going well into 1972 on the charts. Tina Turner also made a REMAKE version & it went to #26 in February of 1984. I liked HER version, too... but MANY had said to me that they liked Al Green's ORIG. version, MUCH better, though.

3. "I'll Take You There"...by The Staple Singers...While this song had been charting. since April of 1972, I never caught it, on the radio, until LATE July of '72, when I heard it for the very FIRST time. This is ANOTHER excellent song, that I've always loved & enjoyed. And THIS song was also a REMAKE hit single for General Public (of "Tenderness" fame) in April 1994, stalling @ #22 on the charts. However, the Staple Singers took THEIR original version, all the way, to the #1 spot.

4. "Oh Girl"...by the Chi-Lites...This song was always very good & it was the follow-up to their late 1971 hit single, "Have You Seen Her". BOTH of these hit singles are VERY good. I don't think that they did any other hits, afterwards.

5. "If You Don't Know Me By Now"...by Harold Melvin & The Blue Notes...After a COUPLE of musical notes, I could easily get THIS song confused w/ The Eagles 1975 hit single "Take It To The Limit", but then the music changed. But maybe that's only my opinion. Otherwise, I think that this song is GREAT & I've always loved it very much. The music is quite pretty. "If You Don't Know Me By Now" has ALSO been remade by Simply Red who took THIS Remake to #1 in May of 1989, beating out the ORIG. version's chart position, which only hit #3, in October of 1972. But to me, NOTHING will ever compare w/ Harold Melvin & The Blue Notes ORIG. version, though, even as good as Simply Red's version was.

6. "I Gotcha"...by James Brown...I almost had forgotten about THIS song, This song is fun & it also has a comical feel to it.. I like this song, quite well.

7. "Power Of Love"...by Joe Tex...I always remembered this song from the later part of 1972. It was good to hear this song, again.. And I've always liked & enjoyed this song.

8. "Me & Mrs. Jones"...by Billy Paul...The music on THIS song is quite PRETTY. This song deals w/ secrecy & temptation, but I do like it. This song even went well into 1973.

9. "Freddie's Dead"...by Curtis Mayfield...This song appears on the 1972 movie soundtrack, "Superfly". "Freddie's Dead" was the FIRST single released from THIS movie. And "Superfly" was the NEXT hit, from THIS movie, LATER in 1972 & going into 1973. The song "Freddie's Dead" is okay, but I really like "Superfly" which is rather comical & I love it A LOT more.

10. "Get On The Good Foot (Part One)"...by James Brown...This SECOND hit by James Brown, which appears here, is also pretty good.

This R & B music CD, from 1972, is ALSO very good & I also recommend this.

title: Another Masterpiece by Dudley Taft
text: The 7th studio album by the legendary Dudley Taft kicks off with the title track and it rocks! Dudley has become a master of the blues riff, taking it to new and exciting places. Vocal harmonies are rich, riffs are abundant. This album is blues-based but is far more complex in it's melodies and chord progressions than the typical 1-4-5 blues classics. Dudley's lead playing is crisp, creative, and crafty with an edge that is reminiscent of his hard rock days. Left in the Dust is a straight ahead rocker that really satisfies. The Devil is a cool shuffle that has a lot of energy. Goin' Away Baby is more traditional blues but with some tasty double-stops. One In a Billion it tinged with some Robin Trower-like distortion and some outstanding vocals by Taft. The End of the Blues is another example of Taft's excellent song writing and lead playing. Relentless is a beautiful song featuring the very talented Charmae on lead vocals. Fly with Me leans back towards the rock vein with some very cool riffs and bad ass vocals. Hey Hey Hey is a fun song with some more tasty leads by the accomplished shredmeister. All for One reminds me of early Black Sabbath in the beginning with serious heavy distorted tones. It's haunting vocals and guitar are really stunning. I'm a Believer is a clever number again showcasing Dudley's rich vocals and excellent phrasing. I Will Always Love You is a beatiful and melodic ballad that shows Taft's broad grasp of musical styles. This album is superb from beginning to end, a must for any music lover's catalog! Keep 'em comin' Dudley!!

title: Thursday continues to put every other screamo band with a "message" to shame.
text: After rumors of an impending break up, Thursday have returned to the fold with their most unified and dynamic album to date.  Sorry guys, I know that "Full Collapse" is almost sacred territory for emo/screamo enthusiasts but "A City by the Light Divided" is better.  There may not be a stand out single like "Understanding in a Car Crash" on "Light Divided" but the overall delivery is far superior and astounding compared to some of the other garbage out there.  The CD begins with a quasi-sequel to "Understanding" in "On the Other Side of the Crash/Over and Out (Of Control)" and it was the most excited I have been after the first 30 seconds of a record since "War All the Time" erupted with "For the Workforce, Drowning" and the beautiful thing is that, unlike "War All The Time", "Light Divided" maintains the elegance, grace, and raw emotional urgency we love about Thursday for the entire album.  Also, Geoff's vocals have never been richer and his lyrics more painstakingly poetic.  From "The Lovesong Writer" to "Running from the Rain", Geoff hits higher notes with more elaborate ballads than ever before and takes the band into new, occasionally even Radiohead-ish territories.  Furthermore, the accompaniment of Stellastar's lead singer on the track "Telegraph Avenue Kiss", although brief, provides the band with a short female complement to Thursday's hopelessly romantic/political outcries that I didn't realize was so painfully missing from the band's previous albums until I heard it for the first time on "Light Divided".  Overall, there isn't a bad point on this album with the possible exception of "the Light", which was seemingly intended as a short rest but ended up only making me want more of the good stuff--i.e. the first five songs and the last five songs.  If you like Thursday, this album won't disappoint, but then...If you REALLY like Thursday, you already know that.

title: Another elegant, intoxicating work by Basia
text: Basia and Sade both create gorgeous works seemingly irrespective of public taste, what's currently "hot" and "hip," and yet each of their CDs sound fresh and wonderful for many years after its initial release. You never get tired of listening to Basia or Sade, and it isn't just because they each put out new works so infrequently. The first time I heard "The Sweetest Illusion," I was, I'll admit, a little disappointed that the Brasilian influences were a bit more subtle than on previous works. I very quickly realized the power and depth of this album, however, and how much it demonstrates Basia's growth as a singer and songwriter. The songs are a bit longer and less pop-oriented than on the first two CDs. "Drunk on Love" and "Third Time Lucky" are witty and sophisticated, with irresistable melodies. She sings "third time lucky, and you've arrived," and I think that's very true of the artist herself on this CD. "Third Time Lucky" is classic Basia, with delicately-entwined harmonies, exotic, samba-soaked percussion, wonderful piano work by Danny White, and even a jubilant whistling hook, and the song's ending is jazzy and wild. "Yearning" is a long, slow-paced piece about finding a home in the heart of a loved one. It's a gorgeous, unforgettable ballad. "She Deserves it" is a gentle, bossa nova-esque duet with Trey Lorenz, and is juxtaposed with the instrumental "Rachel's Wedding." The link between the two is thematic, and it is a perfect wedding present for the lucky Rachel. "Hug an Olive Tree" is lively, fun, and exuberant, similar to the song "Copernicus" from the "London Warsaw New York" CD. "The Sweetest Illusion" begins with elegant strings before launching into an explosive tempo and intriguing lyrics (by Peter Ross) overlayed with Danny White's keyboard mayhem. The sound recaptures some of the frantic magic of Basia's Matt Bianco days. "Perfect Mother" is another very quiet and gentle number, full of beautiful harmonies, and obviously deeply personal. Next is the very upbeat "More Fire than Flame," which is heated up with lots of brass touches and a very urgent chorus. "Simple Pleasures" is yet one more lush, gentle bossa nova-like piece, evoking "Brave New Hope" from the previous CD. "My Cruel Ways" is, in my opinion, the strongest song on the CD. The lyrics are wise and personal, the strings rich and emotional, and the song brings the haunting bass lines from "I Heard it Through the Grapevine" to mind in places. The final track, "The Prayer of a Happy Housewife," is a simple, heartfelt message of gratitude for a wonderful life. I'm not completely bowled-over by this song, but the soaring, gospel-flavoured choruses anticipate the song "Clear Horizon" from her later greatest hits CD. Another remarkable work by an amazing artist.

title: Finally, something that sounds like good local music

I first heard of the Walkmen when they played a show at a little (emphasis on 'little') coffeehouse in my comparatively small town of Grass Valley, California. I think the reason I enjoyed this show so much was that The Walkmen evoke the same feeling as do the local bands which I've come to appreciate more than the mainstream artists who always seem to have lost something on their journey to stardom. The Walkmen have a style which is delightfully reminiscent of an earlier era in rock and roll, a kind of carefree nostalgia that simply makes you feel good (clearly, a welcome departure from the despairing, depressed style of today's chart-topping rock).
If you ever get the chance to see The Walkmen live, definitely take it, and enjoy the experience of live music the way it should be-small clubs and true sounds. However, until they come to town again, "Everyone Who Pretended to Like Me Is Gone" is a must-have.

title: Strauss in a most unusual combination ,but does it work??
text:
This,the most unusual combination of a Finnish record company,a Czech orchestra and a Russian conductor have here combined to produce just about the best recorded performance to have appeared in years.The opportunities of the beautiful acoustics of the Czech Philharmonic's home,(the Rudolfinum in Prague),have here been used to their full advantage by the recording engineers in capturing this interpretation in sumptuous sound.
This is Ashkenazy's second attempt at this work,his first with the Cleveland Orchestra on Decca,does not really compete either as an interpretation or in terms of sound.His real challenge in this work comes from Herbert von Karajan and the Berlin Philharmonic Orchestra on DGG.This combination was almost always unbeatable in the music of Richard Strauss,and so it proves here.The one thing that let it down was the sound.That has been improved in the latest "Karajan Gold" reissue,making it far more comfortable to listen to,and also making easier to appreciate what a riveting interpretation it was.It would,however, be wrong of me to give the impression that I am "damning with faint praise" this magnificent new perfomance of Ashkenazy's.It is only in comparison with Karajan that it falls slightly short.Taken on its own terms it is a winner and I recommend it highly.
