title: A beautiful musical memoir of an Army Captain and Medevac Pilot
text:
This is another of many albums that have received the production and performing high qualities that one has come to expect from Will Ackerman and his team. However, the most profound performance and creativity is not found in Ackerman et al but rather in the very personal compositions and presentation of pianist Peter Jennison. Titled Longing For Home (Songs From War) this album is not just a tribute to the soldiers and the families that sacrifice their relationships for our homeland but more so this is a musical memoir of Army Captain, Medevac Pilot and intensely sensitive pianist Peter Jennision.

This represents Peter's debut recording album that was written during his second deployment during the Iraqi war. Written back in 2006 and 2007, Jennison expresses that the album is a means by which the listener can experience through evocative music the impact war has on all who are touched by it. And there is no better place than via the opening track "War" that begins with a rather solemn piano introduction that quickens in its tempo followed by subdued percussion from Jeff Haynes that almost sound like bombs exploding in the very far distance as the soldier darts while he attempts to advance.

Though "War" is probably the liveliest track on the album the more mellow tunes to follow do not diminish the visual images that Jennison continues to create. Such is the case on "Time Passage" that begins with Jennison playing on his piano the opening chime of a grandfather clock that you hear on the hour prior to it chiming. Though it reminded Jennison of his own Grandfather the music also effectively marks the extended time a solider spends away from their family. Such a simple musical idea that is profoundly visual. And then there is the more melodic "Longing For Home" that represents the beating heart and quickened pulse of that dedicated soldier right before they return to embrace their loved ones that they have dearly missed. The color yellow on the ribbons surrounding them on that day have never looked so bright.

Where Peter's other songs are not quite as visual but nevertheless no less beautiful, his personal comments on each song assists you as the listener to feel the struggles of our armed forces and their willingness to lay down their life for their country with the hope that one day war will be no more. This is beautifully illustrated by the heart wrenching closer "Anthem (When We All Come Home)" that once again effectively uses Jeff Haynes well placed percussion embellishments.

Pianist Peter Jennison has not only recorded a beautiful and stunning debut but has also shared a deep part of his soul that has faced the brutal effects of war on the soldier and their families in hopes that others will be soothed by his therapeutic music. Peter will begun to write his follow up album next year that will be unfortunately driven by his third deployment to the parched deserts of Iraq. We will wish him traveling mercies and protection as this very heartfelt musician and soldier continues to bear arms and his soul for his country both at and away from war respectively.

title: Four-Plus, Five-Minus...
text:
... but probably the best performance available of this repertoire, the motets of the great German Renaissance composers Heinrich Isaac, Ludwig Senfl, and Paul Hofhaimer. To those names, I would add Thomas Stoltzer, Heinrich Finck, and others -- all scanted by the recording industry.

Ensemble Hofkapelle is an all-male choir of six young Germans conducted by Englishman Michael Procter. Stylistically and vocally, they have many of the same merits as the American male choir Chanticleer. They produce a rich, well-tuned choral timbre, a robust resonance. Their 'weakness' is, however, a king of resonant robustness, in which the polyphonic voices blend artfully but seldom achieve the emotive independence of rhetoric that makes the music more than just beautiful. In other words, there's a bit too much 'evenness' in their style, and on this CD that evenness is amplified by their use of cornetti and trombones doubling or supplanting the voices. Hey, I love the cornetto. I play the recalcitrant little beast. But instrumental doubling was a situational choice in the Renaissance, depending on the acoustic of the performance space, the skills of the chorus, and the magnificence expected by the listeners. It is seldom the best choice for recording in a modern studio.

Another slight weakness of this CD is the 'program', which meanders from instrumental piece to motet and back without quite becoming a unified "concert" of music. It doesn't 'build' affectively; it's just an assortment of extremely fine pieces. Yes, the individual pieces ARE extremely fine, and although two of the motets are by Josquin and one originally by the Italian Costanzo Festa, they do have interesting historical connections to the court of Maximilian I, the Holy Roman Emperor. Those connections are explained succinctly in the program notes.

Here are the items:
Hofhaimer - Salve Regina, for organ
Isaac - Salve Sancta Parens & Virgo Prudentissima, motets
Isaac - Christ ist erstanden, instrumental carmina
Senfl - De Profundis, motet (and a very fine one!)
Josquin - Inviolata integra et casta est Maria, motet
Isaac - Innsbruck ich muss dich lassen, polyphonic German Lied
Josquin - Proch dolor, motet (possibly his last composition)
Isaac - Sancti spiritus assit nobis gratia, motet
Festa/Senfl - Quis dabit oculis (a consummate masterpiece of polyphony; see below)
Isaac - Christus surrexit, instrumental carmina

The "Quis dabit oculis" was composed by Festa as a requiem for the death of Anne of Brittany in 1514. Maximilian and Anne were betrothed but never married. When Maximilian died in 1519, Senfl adapted the text of Festa's requiem, without changing a note, to be performed during the mourning. It's as moving a piece as either Festa or Senfl ever composed, and Ensemble Hofkapelle sings it sublimely well.

title: Spoilt by artless mastering
text:
This CD presents the first 2 CDs by Chér, both produced by Sonny Bono following his estrangement from Phil Spector. Using the same Hollywood studio and engineers and as many of the same production techniques as he could approximate, Sonny Bono's attempts at replicating the sound of his erstwhile boss were rudimentary and low-budget, lacking, for example, strings, horns or even backing singers. Nevertheless, they and the contemporary recordings by Sonny and Chér (I Got You Babe was recorded towards the end of the sessions for Chér's first album) have considerable charm and achieved great commercial success, sparked by the success of the lead single, Bob Dylan's All I Really Want To Do, which outsold the rival version by the Byrds in America in 1965. In my opinion, Chér's best work was that which she did with Sonny in the sixties.

This should have provided a welcome opportunity for me to replace my much loved but long lost vinyl copies, but I cannot wholeheartedly recommend it because so many of the tracks have been artlessly truncated by the re-mastering engineer, often losing between ten and twenty-five seconds. This is a reprehensible practice and quite needless since with a program time of 65:35 there remains almost fifteen minutes of capacity on the disc to accommodate full-length versions of every track. Unfortunately there is currently no CD alternative for acquiring these full albums, though all but three tracks (all dropped from the second album) appear on [[ASIN:B000O5BP6E The Best of Cher: The Imperial Recordings 1965-1968]] 2CD, which from the sleeve details appears to have consistently longer track times; so this would seem to be the better value purchase, unless you must own her covers of Ferlin Husky's Time, Edith Piaf's Milord or Charles Aznavour's A Young Girl.

title: A nearly flawless entry that freshens the post rock/ambient scene
text:
4.5 Stars

Well, it has been a long wait since Eyes like Brontide and Lights Out Asia have finally answered my prayers by releasing an incredible yet different album into the sea-like postrock/ambient genre. How is this album different from their previous entries? Well first off it's a little darker in tone and feel. We are introduced to this new sound with "All these worlds are yours". It's a quiet track that features someone speaking in what sounds like english though the voice continues to be distorted throughout the track as very soft electronic melodies are played in the back ground, creating almost a dreamlike track.

Except Europa is a perfect example of the music on the record, and is one of their most beautiful tracks. Gorgeous ambient melodies over a droning electronic beat; this track hits the spot. Followed by two beautifully ambient tracks "attempt no landings there" and "All is quiet in the valley", this section of the album really allows you to relax. By this point the band has really incorporated a soft sound that i haven't heard in their previous records and that is hard to put into words. Maybe an organic electronica ambiance? Or as i have just now dubbed it "orgtronbiance".

13AM Is a change in sound and leans very much towards the post-rock side of this album. It has a very epic feel and can be very moving. Great standout track. The interlude "Arbres Paisible" leads us into another standout track "Great men from unhealthy ground" which takes us back to the aforementioned orgtronbiance sound i mentioned. Some gorgeously layered piano melodies and waves of soft sounds make this track a treat for the ears. Listening to it while driving was a fantastic experience for me.

Current meets the tide brings their soothing and introspective trademark vocals into the scene and it does it well. This tune is very catchy despite being very ambient without containing any real "hooks" save for some moving sections/lines. By this point you're wondering why i've given it 4.5 stars as i have been raving through my review of the albums unique qualities. "Then i hope you like the desert" is a track that does not really sit well with me. Discordant vocals create almost a dissonant sound with the instrumentals in the back ground and this track just didnt work in my eyes (Or ears).

Luckily the record bounces back with in my opinion one of their greatest tracks "Shifting Sands Wreck Ships". What an epic masterpiece of postrock/ambient brilliance. I hear so much chemistry between the vocals and instruments and the atmosphere of the track is gorgeous. Very moving! Reminds me alot of "Psiu! Puxa!" or "Radars over the Ghosts of Chernobyl".

Unfortunately again the album takes a sour turn and ends with a minimalist way-too-ambient of a closer, "Bye Bye November". This track and "Then i hope you like the desert" prevent this album from becoming a flawless entry by one of the greatest Ambient/post-rock bands i know of. I'm extremely pleased with this release and am interested to see what the world thinks about the record after having given my insight. Sit back, relax, listen and enjoy!

title: Not Down With 'Crazy Love'
text:
If you're a Michael Bublé fan, 'Crazy Love' isn't going to disappoint. He continues to sing the classics as with his past releases and for the most part, stays true to the arrangements that made them American standards with only minor tweaks to the instrumentation to make the songs feel a bit modern. As a casual fan, the album lets you down a bit because this album just feels like a rehashing of what he's already done without many chances being taken. Yes, he's adhering to the classic adage of 'If it's not broke, don't fix it' but at the same time, you get this feeling that the act is getting a bit old because you know exactly what to expect from him and he's not really singing any songs that are surprising or come with any risk.

The Good: Bublé's voice is probably the best thing about 'Crazy Love', as with most of his releases. While there's nothing truly new or daring about the music he's singing (since they were made famous by other artists and are old standards and classics), it's his voice that makes him stand apart. I feel like his best vocal performance is probably on 'Georgia In My Mind' where he's forced to just slow down and focus on putting some emotion into the lyrics to keep it from being a straight karaoke performance. Another great example of him putting some heart into the performance is with 'At This Moment'. It's on these two songs that left me feeling that this was something worth buying and that he wasn't just singing another batch of songs to put out a CD.

The Bad: The fact that he's this far in his career and still singing classics and standards feels a bit tired and worn out by now. I wasn't really impressed with 'Crazy Love' because there's little that makes it feel like a new product and something different than his past releases. There are some songs where I felt he was just performing them without putting in much of emotion or thought, as if this has become his niche and since there's no risk involved, he's just singing to make a buck. "Heartache Tonight" is good and his voice is okay but it just feels like an 'American Idol' performance. "Haven't Met You Yet" is another song that I felt he had no connection with; it just sounds like a performance he spat out. My overall complaint or critique with 'Crazy Love' is that by itself, it's a good cd. The vocals are better than most and the music is decent. When compared with all of his other work and releases, it sounds a bit less authentic and as if it's become so routine that he's just chosen whatever songs and classics he hasn't done before and is spitting them out without any thought or without connecting to the music and slapping it on cd and calling it a day. It struck me as lazy, unremarkable, tepid and just plain boring.

Overall, average songs and nothing surprising in terms of performance from Michael Bublé but it will please his niche and fan base. For the casual fan, I'm not sure it's original or good enough to buy and spend money on. I'm hoping at some point of his career, instead of continuing to sing classics and standards made popular by others, he'll actually take a chance musically and do a full release of some original material fit for his voice and preferred genre. Unfortunately, 'Crazy Love' is not that and is very paint-by-numbers and tame.

title: A FINE CHAMBER OPERA . . . . . AVAILABLE ON-LINE FROM FYNSWORTH ALLEY
text:
Frankly, the reason I purchased this CD is because I didn't want it to disappear before I got a chance to hear it -- and to add it to my collection of show recordings. It took me some time to get around to playing it, and it was only after listening to it for a second time that I read the synopsis. I was able to follow the story easily, without knowing the plot or being familiar with Thomas Hardy's short story. For me, that's a sign of pretty good musical writing.

Since I haven't seen the show, I can only judge its merits by what's on the disc - the music and the performances. As good as the music and lyrics are, I think that Stephen Cole and Matthew Ward have a long way to go before they can be crowned "the new voices of the musical theatre." And although Beethoven's "big and brassy" Ninth Symphony may sell out Orchestra Hall, there's also an audience (perhaps smaller) for his string quartets - in a much smaller concert hall. And, yes, some people find chamber music to be boring, but others can't be dragged to another Beethoven Ninth.

"After the Fair" might not have a lot of hummable tunes, sometimes the the notes seem to bounce all over the place, and sometimes the lyrics are a little trite. But right now I can't recall a melody from "Pacific Overtures" or "Sunday in the Park with George" or "Passion," but after listening to this show only twice, several days ago, I can sing "Every morning I run just to greet you" at the drop of a hat. The ensemble pieces are especially well written, even if Lerner & Loewe ("My Fair Lady") and Harvey Schmidt & Tom Jones ("110 in the Shade") wrote better songs for their leading ladies to express their anger. The five-piece ensemble does a fine job of supporting the singers. I, too, prefer a full orchestration, realizing that a show this size couldn't afford a pit full of musicians. Nor is a full orchestration always right for a show. Compare the expanded Broadway recording of "Charlie Brown" to the original, more intimate Off-Broadway recording.

Nor do I find the English accents offensive. To my ears, Michele Pawk sounds every bit as "British" as Julie Andrews ever did, and English actors have been playing Americans ever since "Gone With The Wind." Miss Pawk is a truly gifted singer/actress, and I hope there are song writers out there somewhere who will write the show that makes her a star, perhaps even Messers Cole & Ward. All the performers are excellent and in excellent voice, even if David Staller pushes his voice a little too much at times.

So, what's behind the negative comments? Perhaps it's the fact that "After the Fair" is not a conventional musical, but rather an intimate chamber opera. And like most operas, it isn't about cheerful stuff. No one dies in this show, but no one lives happily ever after either. And I think the music fits the piece quite well. No, it's not perfect, nor do I predict it will become a dinner-theatre staple like "The Fantasticks" or "I Do! I Do!" That said, I wish a lot of companies would mount this show and prove me wrong. I'd rather see "After the Fair" than the 100th production of "Hello, Dolly!"

title: The 90s Needed This
text:
It would be easy to lump the Cardigans into the mid-90s one-hit wonder category, and perhaps this is justifiable from a certain perspective. Their signature song "Lovefool" was distinctive and catchy, and with contemporaries like Smashmouth, Sugar Ray, and Fastball, whose full albums were radically different from their singles, the music consumer should have been wary. However, I don't think that "Lovefool" is necessarily the best song on "First Band on the Moon." I think that it stands out because, as a single, it received a great deal of production attention. However, it is not in a radically different style than the rest of the album, and I think that several other songs are just as hooky and clever. Suspending the bloated expectations presented by "Lovefool" reveals a pretty solid and enjoyable album.

The Cardigans' sound is pastiched and nostalgic, but at least the styles that they reference are clear. Overall, there is a strong 70s disco aesthetic, complete with strings, to the proceedings, but with a healthy dose of tounge-in-cheek lounge (i.e. the silly "Iron Man" cover). While the presence of a vibraphone probably appealed to my 90's Twin Peaks fanboy side, infectious songs propel "First Band on the Moon" more readily than the specific instruments used. As an example, check out "Been It," which offers chunky riffs and quiet staccato guitar chords, in contrast to "Great Divide," as it dreamily shimmers with mallets and fender-rhodes. If I were to point to a weak tune, it would probably be "Loser," which comes off as two songs that did not quite mesh convincingly into one.

THE LOWDOWN: Even today, people may ask if they "had any other songs." The answer is yes. Purchasing "First Band on the Moon" is not buying a "Lovefool" single with a bunch of B-sides. Instead, it is an album that stands on its own as a consistent and unique example of melodic mid-90s power pop.

title: Uh, yeah. Punk opera. Right...
text:
I'm not a fan of this group at all (other than the album Warning. I like Warning), but I decided I'd give them ONE more chance after suffering through Dookie. Oops, my mistake. Of course, Billie Joe Armstrong STILL cannot sing, but that's not exactly news. He can't exactly make good music, either.

Yes, there's a bit of experimentation - Extraordinary Girl had a cool worldbeat thing going on at the start, but quickly melted (for lack of a better term) into the group's usual unvarying power-trio look-at-us-we're-pop-punkers formula I know all too well. But unoriginality's still the name of the game - Are We the Waiting kicked off with a drum solo lifted from When the Levee Breaks, and Give Me Novocaine has a drum intro ripped off of Are We the Waiting. So they rip off their Led Zeppelin ripoff. Interesting...

Okay, I haven't even gotten to the most annoying parts of American Idiot yet. No, it's not even the four awful hits that are contained here (the unusually political title track and Holiday, whose big statements - America is practically run by the media and the Iraq War is going wrong - aren't exactly big-time relevations; Wake Me Up When September Ends, smarmy even by their standards; the ludicrously overplayed Blvd. of Broken Dreams, an unlistenable self-pity fest in the form of a power ballad), though those are close. No, I'm talking about the two nine-minute "epics" (Jesus of Suburbia, Homecoming) which rummage through a pile of different parts that sound conspiciously alike (as usual, they sacrifice creativity and technical skill for speed and volume) while trying to tell some sort of story. But the story's just plain BORING - more of the "I'm a whiny suburban kid who's mad at my mom because she won't take me to the mall" dreck that makes up a big part of why I hate this band. Sorry Billie Joe, but you ain't Pete Townshend, and American Idiot ain't Tommy. And, of course, none of these guys can play their instruments. But you knew that.

Okay, when am I gonna stop being so negative? Right now. I actually LIKED the closing song, Whatsername, surprisingly tuneful for the band. But to hear it you'll have to suffer through the rest. No thanks...

title: Sappy, poppy R&B "funk" with bad digital sound
text:
Reelased in 1990, this CD has that bad digital sound common in many jazz CDs of the time. It is an all digital recording, so the sound is clear (although not as clear as you might expect for a digital recording) and bright. But, it has that unnatural punchy, pinging sound that was common at the time. It is close to the sound you get if a CD sticks. I am not a vinyl snob, but with sound like this, you can understand why some people were really down on CDs when they first came out. On a high quality sound system this attribute really comes out and makes a CD hard like this hard to listen to over a long period of time. However, it is not as bad as many of the early CDs with the muddy sound and no dynamic range.

The CD is about 45 minutes long.

There are many big Clarke and Duke fans who really don't like these collaborations. I am one of them. It is easy to find these CDs in at cut rates in the used CD bins.

This is mostly sappy R&B with no energy or emotion. Songs like Right By My Side and Find Out Who You Are, that have something to say, should be played with a rough edge, but are defiant songs played like love songs. It is like Celine Dion singing Smells Like Teen Spirit.

The only really good thing on the CD is the cover of P-Funk's Mothership Connection. There are also a few good, but short instrumentals here and there.

This was a bad time for jazz and funk. Jazz Fusion has dying out and everyone was playing either boring Sunday Brunch jazz or getting into lite R&B. I don't like many of Clarke's albums from this time period either. It is interesting to note, now 20 years later, these musicians are revisiting the fusion days and no one seems to be trying to revise the type of music heard here.

title: The Band Played On
text: If Tusk was the thesis in Lindsey Buckingham's post-Stevie-collaboration songwriting career, Mirage is the antithesis in the Hegelian dialectic.  The synthesis was to be hit in 1987's Tango In The Night from which he never looked back.  Without question, this album contains two of the greatest Mac songs with Hold Me and Gypsy.  With it's unique vocal harmonies, structure and guitar work, Hold Me is a song that no other band could have made except this iteration of Fleetwood Mac.  Gypsy is another brilliant collaboration between Stevie Nicks' lyrical sense and direction, and Buckingham's guitar and production.  On these tracks, Buckingham is in fine form working with the other two artists.  With his own stuff, however, Buckingham falls apart.  Oh Diane and a couple of his other songs are a retreat - an unceremonious, full-tilt retreat - back to his childhood bedroom with his older brother's 1950s 45s.  It's annoying.  Oh Diane and Buckingham's other conservative songs on this album are nowhere near as good as his unhinged efforts on Tusk and Law and Order, nor are they comparable to his sublimely different Eyes of the World or rocking Empire State on this very album.  It seems the knives came out and they wanted to bottle-up Buckingham here, and it doesn't work.  It sounds at times like he's doing some sort of tribute to late 1950s post-Elvis rock, but that's not what makes him great.  Despite Buckingham's struggles with some of his own material, Mirage is another great album loaded with creativity, not to mention Eyes and Empire.  It's not as confident as their first three albums, and that's sad, but again they soldiered on and did the write thing for each other despite the stresses.  Again, in total, they made great music.

title: Great
text: I was lucky enough last December to see The Doors of the 21st Century (now called Riders on the Storm) and it was one of the best days of my life. The songs they placed were well chosen, they did a great job of doing it. I met drummer Ty Dennis and new bassist Phil Chen backstage and almost met Ray Manzarek, Robbie Krieger, and Ian Astbury. It was great; So, I was interested to watch the DVD to see them perform a few songs they didn't perform at the concert I went to (like one of my favorite Doors songs "Love Her Madly" & "Soul Kitchen). This DVD is great and does not dissapoint. The way it's filmed and compiled is great and of course the video and audio quality is spectacular as well. At the concert I went to Ray Manzarek was playing keyboards with his teeth and his feet at moments. In this one, he plays with his head. Robbie Krieger looks awesome, wearing a beanie and dog tags. Ian Astbury looks very Morrison-esque, but I did notice that when on camera the band did act quite a bit differently. Astbury spits on stage quite a bit and is literally drinking water every chance he gets. On this DVD, he drinks no water and doesn't spit at all. But he does wail away at every song placed in front of him and that's something I love about Astbury. While there is definitley a resemblance between Astbury and Jim Morrison, Astbury never tries to be Morrison. He uses the same voice he used in The Cult, when he begins to chant Mr. Mojo Risin' during the performance of the song "L.A. Woman" he dedicates it to Jim Morrison. He does do a few things (dance moves, etc.) that are Morrison-esque, but all-in-all does justice to the fallen poet. Obviously, if you're a Doors fan you'll notice that John Densmore does not appear on drums and is replaced by Ty Dennis. Dennis imitates Densmore's every move perfectly and is a great guy to replace him with. Bassist Angelo Barbero replaces Ray Manzarek's hand really and does a great job, but is (in my opinion) not quite as good as Phil Chen. Anyway, this is a fantastic concert DVD and a must for Doors fans/enthusiasts. A+

title: The Measuring Stick for all Masterpieces
text:
Whereupon "Rubber Soul" provided the pivotal turning point in the canon of the Beatles, "Revolver" was their greatest artistic triumph. Although the Beatles would continue to stretch the boundaries of the album, "Revolver" was their most perfected achievement.
From the opening sound of Harrison's guitar on 'Taxman' all the way through the one chord magic of Lennon's 'Tomorrow Never Knows', this album became the latest measuring stick for what was now possible for the genre. The songwriting was more equitably divided than on any other Beatles' album; Harrison notched three songs, and Lennon-McCartney penned the other eleven. (For comparison, Only one of Harrison's songs made it onto their next album, Sgt. Pepper).
Mccartney scored some of his greatest songwriting moments on this album, including 'Here, There, and Everywhere,' 'For No One,' and the timeless 'Eleanor Rigby.' Lennon contributed his usual wit through 'And your Bird Can Sing' and 'Dr. Robert.' In short, everything clicked on this album.
As any great album must, "Revolver" has withstood the test of time; but additionally, as all masterpieces must, it has defined its' time. It is, in my humble opinion, the single greatest album made to date.

title: Epic concerts, fantastic recording
text:
Start of a 70s concert recording revival ?

It's always been something of a puzzle that only The Who (Live at Leeds) from among British rock bands of the late 60s/early 70s produced a contemporary live recording which really did justice to their stellar on-stage reputation. Until now.

Salute Zeppelin's manager, the late Peter Grant, for having the wherewithall to setup venue recording on this 1972 USA concert tour, and Jimmy Page for taking the time to remaster and organise this audio material as a tangential project to the Led Zeppelin DVD (also released in 2003).

No need to repeat what many other comments have already stated. It's a great sounding package. Indeed my only quibble is the near-CD worth of unrecorded space (approx 75mins) spread across the 3 audio CDs. Due to the long length of some individual tracks, the LA Forum/Long Beach concert montage would not quite squeeze on a double CD, without substantial editorial and track listing alteration.

But - unless I've missed some diabolically embedded "bonus" material - given this is not a single "in concert" recording, but a digital meshing of separate concerts (the presence of bass AND mandolin, plus guitar and drums on tracks like That's The Way suggest some additional mixing handiwork), is it being greedy (given the very reasonable pricing) to expect live recordings of Physical Grafitti material featured on the DVD from 1975 Earls Court performances ? (yes, probably)

That said, with the critical and commercial success of this release, no doubt the executives at EMI and Virgin have been sending their archivists and lawyers away to trawl the masters vaults for Pink Floyd and Rolling Stones 70s live recordings. Could be the start of something of a trend. Garage sale Bootleggers beware.

title: What's wrong with everyone?
text:
I am in complete accordance with those who say that 'Mezzanine' is a masterpiece but I also feel that '100th Window' is a worthy follow-up to such a classic. Is it better? Not really, but I hear a definite growth of experimentation in sound. I haven't read any other reviews, however, I notice most of the ratings to be either 3 or 4 stars and I am left scratching my head, wondering why? My guess is many fans are having a difficult time getting into this album simply because the overall tempo is slower paced than the majority of their previous works, and perhaps your not used to hearing that from Massive Attack but, believe me, they've created some brilliant songs here. Just open your mind without any sort of expectation.

The mood throughout is rather somber with dark, atmospheric electronic dubs instead of funky trip-hop ones, and the inclusion of orchestrated instruments provide a cinematic feel that really seems to shade the melodies, accenting them chillingly. But by no means does '100th Window' tread into ambient territory. It would be best described as smooth electronica that will likely appeal to those who enjoy dance-tinged chillout music (visions of ice and snow come to mind when listening to this record). And replacing the sweet female vocalists Sara Jay and Elizabeth Fraser, who both sang on 'Mezzanine' when Andy Horace wasn't (and you gotta love his unique style, which I find to be very sexy...in a strange kind of way), the more powerful yet ever gorgeous Sinead O'Connor guest sings on several cuts here; most notably "A Prayer For England" which comes on after a slightly more upbeat "Butterfly Caught", a personal favorite of mine. My only complaint is that the album starts losing its luster a bit after track 6. However, given there's only 9 songs in all, this evens out to be a winner in my book.

I've had this CD for a long time - longer than I would care to admit - and I still love it like the day I bought it. Without thinking twice, I bought an MP3 replacement off of Amazon, and I'm still planning on replacing the physical disc.

When I say I love this CD, I want it to be understood that I love it despite not loving a small handful of tracks on it. The songs on this CD that are great are *so* great that they totally make up for the few weak tracks (of which I would cite Book of Lies, Death in Detroit, Still Born/Still Life, and Mother) and the smaller group of great, but "have to be in the mood for them" tracks (The Angels, Desperate Hell, and the spectacularly well-done Cervix Couch remixes). This gives a trimmed down list of thoroughly listenable, outstanding tracks in Deathwish (some of the best Christian Death metal sound out there), the all-too-brief perfection of Spiritual Cramp, Sleepwalk, two great takes on Figurative Theatre (though I admittedly prefer the Extended Version over the Klute remix), and the incredible, frantic madness of Lost Minds. With four tracks that I find generally unlistenable, remix CD garbage, this album still pulls in 5 Stars in my book.

And I was never really into the whole Goth thing; I was a post-punk listener to mostly industrial music, I preferred colorful dress over the all-black cliche, and I liked a handful of goth acts that became a smaller and smaller handful as I grew up. I *still* love this CD.

title: No Carrie, You Ain't in Checotah Anymore!
text:
And as bittersweet as leaving your sleepy little town in the heart of America may be, it has only brought you further into the hearts of America!

I was wary of an overproduced product of the American Idol Machine, yet very eagerly anticipated the release of Some Hearts. Very simply, one whole season of the TV show only made me want to see and hear more of this little country girl with the BIG voice! And while I half-expected some slick studio sound to overpower her, she more than held her own. Kudos to the producers for not falling into that trap, and for finding the right material and arrangements to showcase that voice, instead of camouflage it!

The opening cut "Wasted" is absolutely perfectly placed to initially grab the listener; plenty of hooks to keep him hanging; and enough truth to make him self-search. Follow that up with a song that would be cliche for anyone else, but "Remember Me" sounds more like a Carrie Underwood autobiography than ear candy.

I am particularly fond of the one sure crossover hit, should the producers realize the goldmine here. The title track, "Some Hearts" is sure airplay on any FM station. So far superior than the weakest cut on the album, the song AI chose for both Finalists' early release, "Inside Your Heaven"...a song I didn't like on the show and liked less on the radio. The official first release from the album, "Jesus Take the Wheel" will ellicit much airplay and many fans especially in the country market. Having just watched Carrie perform this on a TV Christmas special from Rockefellar Ctr, I see they've finally figured out the correct mix. Carrie can really shine on a sweet, yet vocally challenging ballad with very little musical support. That is my only complaint about this debut album, if it can be called a complaint. I would love to hear Carrie in just that fashion a bit more...with widely sweeping lyrics but carefully subdued acoustic support. We all know the girl can hit and carry powerful high notes with a professionalism that makes one scratch one's head to wonder where she's been hiding for 22 years. But I would also love to hear her just plain sing a sweet country song, too. One or two per album is all I ask. "Jesus Take the Wheel" is about as close as we'll get on this debut.

From first to last, though, this is one terrific debut album and well worth the wait! The more I hear it, the more I find myself waking in the morning with one of it's tunes in my head. Anybody who grew up in a town slightly less populous than New York City can certainly relate to the rousing "Ain't in Checotah Anymore" and it will have you grinning as you recall your hometown experiences. You're right, Carrie...you are on your way, girl! Checotah's loss, America's gain.

title: It's never really over (strong 3.5)
text:
There's been a trend of record companies not wanting to release an artists' material because it might not be successful recently, and Kelly Clarkson is just another mark on the board. Once again, here's proof that record execs should just let an artist live and learn.

My December, Kelly Clarkson's newest offering, isn't as bad as some would lead you to believe, but it's also not as grand as others say. It's one of those CDs that has some great songs and some that you can pass over. Maybe with a bit more time she could've fixed a few songs to be more enjoyable, but this is still clearly KC, so I'm satisfied.

This CD isn't perfect. Anyone who tells you that is most likely a jaded fan or someone who refuses to reason. Point number one...Hole. It's not a good song. It has no rhythm, the lyrics aren't great, it feels like a mess. However, My December does have Kelly's best song to date, Sober. Mainstream pop doesn't get a lot of unflinchingly honest songs (Christina Aguilera's Stripped-era songs are probably the most prominent examples), so to see an artist with as powerful a voice as Kelly's, who always uses it tastefully--yes, that's directed at Mrs. Aguilera--do a track like Sober is long overdue. One Minute is instantly likeable with a certain dance quality that many will love. Haunted finds Kelly the way I like her best, supported by a rock band.

My favorite songs are One Minute, Sober, Haunted, Be Still, and Yeah. All in all, My December proves to be a worthy purchase. The good tracks outweigh the bad and anytime I can support an artist who deserves the attention they get, I gladly will. With vocals like Kelly Clarkson's, it's gonna be downright impossible to make a horrible CD, and My December only further proves the reason why Kelly is in a league of her own.

title: MISNAMED, BUT STILL A COLLECTION FAVORITE
text:
One other reviewer--younger, new-to-Freddy--says it: "It's a little too poppy and silly for me and doesn't rock enough." Freddy might have been "Boom-Boom" but, despite teen slice-of-life themes (Abagail Beecher, Patty Baby, Teen Queen of the Week) Cannon was rarely "Rock `n' Roll."

Cannon came closest to R `n' R with his first two releases in 1959, Tallahassee Lassie and Okefenokee. It wasn't just the arranging that made him "pop", it was the material, too; what other chart-topper of the day recorded vintage songs from bygone eras such as Muskrat Ramble, Way Down Yonder in New Orleans and Chattanooga Shoe Shine Boy? It says some fascinating things about late 50s and early 60s hit music that one of the three (Chattanooga) made Top Ten and the other two made Top Forty, something that rockin' Okefenokee didn't do.

So, this collection is misnamed. But, I can shrug that off. As a kid, I was really fascinated by the SOUND of these records more than the material--Okefenokee really pumps, and Palisades Park--barely 2 minutes long--exists in a sonic world of its own. But Freddy's not responsible for this.

Song writer-arrangers Frank Slay and Bob Crewe (who went on to greater fame via The Four Seasons) deserve the credit for much of what you hear and--if you're my age-- still fondly remember. They get no accolades here, though: Freddy thanks everybody from his parents and DJs to his fans...but not these two guys. Curious, that.

I hunch that Crewe, perhaps especially, was having a good time exploring music styles. It's these explorations that make lesser-known tunes such as Humdinger (#59 ) and The Urge (#60) such a delight. Crewe digs a band and back-up singers and, therefore, allows us to dig them as well. Oh, yeah: Freddy's there, too! So thanks to Frank, Bob and the Indefatigable Freddy Cannon. It ain't (totally) Rock and Roll--but I like it.

title: Interesting.
text:
This album attempts a synthesis of jazz, Latin & (on "Shake 'Em Up") Caribbean musics. The result is an hour of intelligent, interesting music that never really adds up to much more. Byron's clarinet playing is mostly pretty restrained, & his partner, the trumpeter James Zollar, is sometimes downright tepid; it's genuinely bizarre to have an album concentrating on Latin jazz which is (a) lacking in fire & high-note showmanship; (b) oddly introverted & even sombre in hue. It could really have used a musician as sunny & as distinctive as Bill Frisell, Byron's regular cohort: the band is perfectly fine but lacking much sparkle. The subtitle "More Music for Six Musicians" is in some ways misleading--there are a whopping 14 guest musicians on here, bringing it up to an even 20 players in various combinations. Yet the actual texture of the album is virtually uniform, to the point that one hardly notices the added reinforcements.
Worth a listen, but this is yet another Don Byron album that is "interesting", in the weak sense of the word: more of a concept than a fully satisfying musical experience. Get _Romance with the Unseen_ if you want a better sample of recent Byron.
[One sidenote: Byron's packaging is getting ever more pretentious. This album has bizarrely elaborate artwork that has to be seen to be believed; it also has the--consciously?--absurd statement in the linernotes: "DON BYRON IS A MEMBER OF: NATIONAL WRITERS UNION; SCREEN ACTORS GUILD; BLACK ROCK COALITION; MENSA". title: The Resurrection of Lupe Fiasco
text:
Consider this the resurrection and rediscovering of Lupe Fiasco! One of my all time favorite hip hop artists perhaps took a step back in many people's eyes over the past few years. However with this return to form on his new album Tetsuo & Youth, he has vaulted his name back into the conversation of one the best hip hop artists the game has today and quite possibly we have seen in the last 15 or so years. The lyrics and songs are so textured, intricate and multilayered with the production and sound being the best he has had since The Cool that it will grab hold of your ear immediately. But all the while, you will need several listens to consume all that Lu has to offer in his songs.

On this album instead of Lupe going too political as he had on his last effort F&L2, he takes a journey back to the hood and delves into topics such as the imprisonment cycle (Prisoner 1 & 2), how the ghetto gets left to starve (Deliver-CRAZY how he can connect not getting pizzas delivered in impoverished neighborhoods to how the government leaves people with no help or chances to eat), using women's body to move work and them living by the death before dishonor code(I'll just bite my tongue so I'll wear it like a scarlet letter from Body of Work) or the sort of 'barrel of crabs' mentality that happens when one does not get afforded or take advantage of opportunities that another does(No Scratches) and running circles around fans and MCs alike with the eight-minute track Mural. That song can go blow for blow with any MC in the game to me, bar none. And he raps like crazy but still brings focus and a purpose to the song. The sound on the CD experiments with banjos as well as harmonicas (Dots and Lines), guitars(No Scratches) and a futuristic-like heavy synth/drums beat(They.Resurrect.Over.New). But the real sound that Lupe shines on are the crazy jazz samples that are heavily shown on tracks like Body Of Work and Little Death. Jazz is one of the art forms that can capture emotion without one word. Lupe can bring vividness to the ghetto with his crazy wordplay. The two put together form are darn near flawless match! The way Lupe slips and slides on these tracks is pure magic and just brings the songs to life even more with its somewhat melancholy feel. Reminds me of how A Tribe Called Quest or Pete Rock and C.L. Smooth used the jazz in the early 90s, except Lu slows it down with his songs. The CD also goes in sections of seasons starting from Summer where everything feels happy go lucky and can get a feel for how the emotion and direction of it goes in a dark and haunting mood with Fall and finally Winter which might be the two best sections on the album. In the end, he reaches to inspire kids to slow down and be kids while straying away from the street life to be something better than what they see everyday on Adoration of the Magi. Then with what could be a double meaning on They.Resurrect.Over.New looking to bring new life to the hood as well as the game of hip hop itself. It is no wonder those were the last two songs to cap it off to lead into Spring as his words rain down on your brain and brings sunshine to your life(enlightenment).

As a lot of people are saying, this could very well be consider a masterpiece. I won't sit here and compare this album with a couple of my favorite CDs in the last decade in Food & Liquor and The Cool. I will say there were a song or two on each of those albums that I could have possibly done without. Not because of what he was saying on the song or its meaning, but moreso maybe the beat didn't always quite matchup with the feel or his words. This album really has no flaws in that department. So in those terms, it is definitely on par with those albums. Classic is a word that may get a bit overused these days just because we yearn for the frequent classic albums we were blessed with in the golden era of rap/hip hop of the late 80s and throughout the 90s. This CD deserves that claim in every bit of the phrase. It is that special!!! Don't hate or hesitate on this album!! If you need real hip hop or just real music in your life, let Lupe serve you up another plate of food for thought!

(Review after review: Been listening to this album for like a week straight just about non-stop, and it just keeps getting better every time. Picking up more on the lyrics and deep thoughts. Also don't think was intended(or maybe it was, this is Lupe we are talking about) but the seasons kind of mirrored how his career in hip hop has gone. He came in with full of life as you hear the kids on the Summer intro and slowly he saw what the industry can do as he maybe got down and angry as the feelings portray in the Fall & Winter portions. Now he is just doing him and resurrecting himself as you get that feeling was Spring finishes the CD. Just my thoughts that this will be an album that could down not just as a great hip hop album, but a great music album. Period. It is an artwork that is that incredible!)

title: An overlooked classic
text:
To start, the only reason I'm giving this album 4 stars is becuase the review only goes as high as 5 stars. This is not in the same league as Stevie's 70's masterpieces but I still feel that it's one of the best albums of the 80's. The title is basically talking about the world of music being hotter than July. In other words, there's a lot going on in regards to musical taste. At the time of the album release, rock was still going strong, country was becoming more popular, Bob Marley had brought Reggae to the masses, and the world was waiting for a new Stevie Wonder album after the confusing, at least to most of the public, Secret Life OF Plants album. This was it. The album sold quickly and had a top 10 hit with Masterblaster and Happy Birthday. I usually do my reviews by going song by song but this album boast a song so amazing that I have to give it it's due. That song is Lately. First off though, I will mention the other 2 songs that should be given their due too.
Ain't Gonna Stand For It.: Stevie goes country, in a playful way. This song is another romp in the same league as Say it 'Cause I Love Having You Around and Don't You Worry 'Bout A Thing. It's a great dance song and in the middle section Stevie really rocks out. Don't take this song seriously. Just have fun with it.
Happy Birthday: This is basically a sing-a-long. Nothing really special musically going on in it. So why am I including it as one of 3 significant songs on the album? Mainly because of the public importance of the song. Can music actually make laws? This one did. Stevie wrote this in honor of Rev. Dr. Martin Luthur King, Jr. and it was the theme song throughout the efforts to make his birthday a national holiday, which Stevie spearheaded. Within one year of campaigning, President Reagan signed the bill to bring the holiday to life. This song will live on as the soundtrack to the campaign and also as the new way we all sing happy birthday at birthday parties around the world.
Lately: To me, there are 5 songs that made the 80's. I Still Haven't Found What I'm Looking For by U2, Every Breath You Take by the Police, Billy Jean by Michael Jackson, When Doves Cry by Prince and Lately. Of the 5 Lately is the least known, although in the past few years more and more people have come to know it's greatness. Stevie has always been ahead of his time and Lately is just anothe examlpe of that. Let's look at it on two different levels.
Musically: The song is in a major key but yet 90% of the chords heard are minor 7ths. Something never done before in popular music.When this song originally came out in 1980, these chords were so strange I remember my friends asking, what happened to Stevie? Did he go tone deaf because this whole song is out of tune! Twenty-three years later we hear it and it doesn't sound strange at all. Because of this song, these types of chord arrangements have become common when referring to some of the better artist of the last decade. These minor 7ths help the atmosphere of mystery and confusion in the song. Another interesting thing Stevie does, on the piano part, he continually plays these two 8th notes in the bass section. This represents the thoughts that go through our mind when we suspect that we're losing our lover. With these 8th notes he plays with dissonance. He plays the same note even though the chord has changed. The chorus of the song includes a clash if you will, of huge minor 7th chords that climb to a major. For the climax, he holds down the pedal on the piano that makes the note linger as he plays these chords again. This make for even more dissonance. Why so much? How do you feel when you think you're going to lose your lover? Not too happy and in tune I bet. That's why so much dissonance. At the end of the song Stevie changes keys but not the way it's normally done in popular music. He climbs to three keys higher than the original key of the song. The song finally ends in yet another key that could represent either the end of the relationship or a new beginning. You make the choice. Quincy Jones uses this same technique less than a year later on his classic "The Dude album on the song Just Once. Not to mention a number of other songs throughout the 80's and 90's that have used the "key change, you make the call" trick.
Lyrically: The song is about losing a lover to someone else. In other words, it's about cheatin'. Stevie says he has a feeling that something is going on but doesn't have a really vivid reason to suspect anything. In the chorus, he sings "Well I'm a man of many wishes, hope my premonition misses". Stevie is the optimist you know. But in this song he speaks for all of us. We don't want to admit the truth. But, as he says, "But what I really feel, my eyes won't let me hide. 'Cause they always start to cry. 'Cause this time could mean goodbye". A line so simple and yet so powerful. The second verse starts with Stevie wondering why he is with this person, "Lately I've been staring in the mirror, very slowly picking me apart. Trying to tell myself I have no reason with your heart". The "picking me apart" line is really interesting. When you're in a predicament like that, how often have you sat there wondering about yourself? You think, what's wrong with me instead of thinking, why is he/she doing this to me?
Lately is a masterpiece of songwriting. It is an art song in the same league as anything Chopin or Liszt has done. Yet it deals with something that everyone has felt. Whether their rich, poor, educated or not. You will feel this song in your bones. Listen to it again and again. Hotter Than July is a very good album with some good songs on it. Lately brings it up to another level.

title: THE INVALUABLE OFFERING !!!
text:
Incredible double dvd from the masters of norwegian symphonic black metal. Featuring 2 complete concerts and a bucketload of extras.

I used to be into brutal black metal only and someone gave me this to open my mind and boy they did it !! Main feature on disc 1 is 17 tracks culled from a set in Oslo and songs from gigs in Germany and the UK totalling some 80' of live music.

The performance is intense, the stage is dimly lit for effect and the bass player puts out a hell of a show; pity his impressive 5-string Warlock can barely be heard, if at all. He also adds some clean vocals here and there but the lip-sync is dubious, as if they came from a DAT tape or had been heavily pro-tool post-produced . Never mind, since the end result, if a little light in the bottom-end department, is very good. The band has stunning stage presence.

There is a backstage feature (drunken antics) embedded but you have to hit enter whenever a red symbol appears on the low right corner of the screen, which totally detracts from the flow of the live gig and I did try to access this feature separately at the end but didn't succeed.

Pic is excellent for standard def (1.85:1) but the sound is uneven. I could have used heavier bottom end on the main feature and lighter on the extras (Berlin-London, which have little audible guitar and OTT vocals and are there to extend the meagre 40' the Oslo show runs for. The Oslo gig begins with almost no audible guitars, goes on with super-loud guitars with homicidally trebley tone to them and as the show progresses the guitar recorded on the right channel fades till it disappear completely toward the 3-4 final songs. The
2.0 sound is useless because it sounds WAY louder on the right channel so I had to resort to 5.1 which is not my cuppa for live gigs but evened the soundscape. Volume is incredibly loud, making it difficult to adjust.

Disc 2 starts out with a complete set at Wacken Open Air Fest, at night with the exact same lighting. Most of the songs are the same but the mix is now more keyboard-heavy. The cymbals, unlike on the fist disc, are now loud and clear. Bottom end is a LOT weaker; Had to crank my 12¨, 250 watts JBL sub a lot. On some songs the kickdrum sound is well-mixed, but on others it's like an earthquake, as if Laureano actuated his pedal a lot harder. Galder's axe is now more audible on the right channel but has a weird tone. The set goes on for some 75' and can be watched back-to-back with that on disc one without risking repetitiveness due to the aforementioned differences. Start out with OTT vocals though but they're corrected as the show progresses.

Extras are 3 songs from P3 sessions(taped at a huge auditorium-shaped radio studio in Norway designed for broadcasting of live bands). The sound is rawer but both guitars are gorgeously audible and vox has a perfect level.

Then 6 awesome videoclips ensue and to my surprise the studio sound of the songs is VERY different from the live versions. This is almost too much bang for the buck and has made me a fan of the band.

The menus are very elaborated with lots of animations but it's slow and a pain to navigate.

The two dual DVD 9 set comes in a transparent case with a glossy booklet so thick it makes it feel like a brick in your hand. However, other than the lyrics to some songs, illustrations and artsy pics of member of the band, it is uninformative to the point of not even featuring a tracklist. Highly recommendable in spite of the flaws,esp. of you are a fan of the band. In spite of being a clear case of quantity over quality, this is a good release no fan can do without.

title: An extraordinary musical journey
text:
"Smithsonian Folkways World Music Collection" brings together 28 selections of ethnic music from all over the world. There is, in my opinion, something for everyone on this CD. The songs are a diverse group: all instrumental pieces, all vocal selections, and songs that blend vocal and instrumental performances. There are both solo and group vocals. Many of the songs feature striking ethnic percussion.
It is not possible in the space of a short review to go through all of the highlights on this CD. But here are a few of the pieces that made particular impressions on me:
"Ompeh" (track #1), a joyful mix of percussion and group vocals from Ghana; "Animal Dance Song" (#2), an all-vocal selection by the Mbuti Pygmies of Zaire; "Seis Chorreao" (#5), an ebullient instrumental from Puerto Rico; Joseph Spence's "Brownskin Girl" (#11), featuring an amazing guitar performance from the Bahamas; the delicate, graceful "Paloma Blanca" (#15) from Peru; the haunting, tremulous vocal performance on "Mele Pule" (#18) from Hawai'i; and the mystical group vocals on "Shelkovaia v pole travushka" (#26) from Russia. I also want to make special mention of the wonderful "Lithuanian Lullaby" (#27) -- the charming vocal solo on this selection is accompanied by the laughter of the child being sung to.
This is an amazing human journey through music, a journey that moves from the ethereal to the earthy, from the playful to the passionate. Highly recommended.

title: Liszt Played By A Russian Piano Master.
text:
Unfortunately, many reviewers on Amazon did not rate these recordings of Lazar Berman playing Franz Liszt's "Annees De Pelerinage" very favorably. I must respectfully disagree. I found Berman's Liszt interpretations commanding and magical.

It has been a while since I listened to the "Swiss Book" (Book 1) of the "Years of Pilgrimage," so I will add an addendum after I go back and listen carefully.

However, the "Italian Book" (Book 2) is amazing. Berman plays as if he is completely and totally absorbed in the piano music. His touch is very sensitive and emotion-provoking, yet he can deliver pianistic storms when he chooses. The "Petrarch Sonnets" are beautifully played, and the most sensitive listeners will cry upon hearing such deep, beautiful, reflective music. Berman goes beyond the notes and truly delivers musical sonnets. He plays with great lyricism, poetry, control, and nostalgia.

Then, Berman gives a tempestuous reading of the "After a Reading of Dante" (the "Dante" Sonata). He really lets loose and shows his technique, power, and passion. Berman handles the runs and monstrous difficulties well, and he goes beyond just being a mechanical technician. I disagree with people who state that Lazar Berman was merely a "piano technician." The "Dante" Sonata shows him to be that and much more.

The Third Book of "Years of Pilgrimage," untitled, offers some of the most reflective and forward-looking piano compositions of Franz Liszt. The opening work, "Angelus," evokes church bells and a sort of meditation on religious faith. It tinkles, sparkles, and draws listeners away from worldly concerns and planes of thought. Berman really sparkles, shines, and communicates with "Angelus." If you enjoy the piano music of Claude Debussy, you can really appreciate the advancement in Liszt's composition.

The next two pieces are based on the cypress trees that Liszt was impressed by while he and his mistress, Comtesse Marie D'Agoult, saw and admired while they eloped to Italy. Berman plays them beautifully, and the same nostalgic, detached, distant atmosphere of "Angelus" is present. I seem to remember quite a bit of musical turbulence communicated by Berman in the first of these pieces.

Many musicians and listeners are well-acquainted with the "Jeux Deau a La Ville D'Este," the water fountain piece that has been cited as an important precursor to Debussy and Ravel (the latter wrote a beautiful, sparkling piece of the same name--"Jeux Deau"). Berman plays the rapid arpeggios with crystalline clarity and evokes the powerful, upward bursts of water from an Italian fountain. The piece is brilliant, and Berman plays with great technical mastery and evocation.

I will add more about this boxed set later. I listened to it completely a year ago, and then I listened to the Second and Third Books again last week. However, I would like to hear the "Swiss Book" again, as well as the supplement to the Second Book, "Venezia e Napoli," so I can write more about those particular works.

All in all, this is an outstanding set of recordings, and listeners who are interested should not hesitate! Also, if you are interested in Franz Liszt's "Transcendental Etudes," I recommend the Berman recordings. Type in "Lazar Berman" on amazon, and scroll down to the second or third page of listings. Look for a CD with piano keys on the cover and the title, "The Russian School." It is hard to find, and you will most likely have to buy it used, but I recommend it. It is astounding!

title: The hottest R&B/Jazz album in years!
text:
If you are into jazz and R&B music, Regina's seventh album "Lazy Afternoon" is a must listen to. She uses her soothing, unique voice as another instrument, blending rhythm and range into a melodious marvel. Regina is a pure talent, and has put her own imprint on each track on this CD that she was destined to record. Her unique and sophisticated voice is more than perfectly suited to present this great collection of standards.

Regina's sense of style always pointed to the creation of a masterpiece, and that has been realized with this album.

The greatness of this record was born out of the remakable creativity of George Duke, who produced, arranged and played with impeccable taste and profound soul.

The sessions are a study in relaxation.The rapport betweeen Regina and the fabulous musicians is both magical and thrilling.

Simply put, "Lazy Afternoon" is Regina's most solid release of her entire career.

I have read in some of the previous reviews about the similarity between Regina Belle and Timi Yuro, the magnificent blue-eyed soul songstress, whom the world of music unfortunately lost last year. I recently hecked some of

Timi's old records and I agree. There is a striking affinity between the two vocalists and I truly believe that Regina, with a jazz homage record under the direction of the one and only George Duke, is the only singer on the present music scene capable of bringing back to our hearts the magic of those old, unforgettable songs.

I am definitely looking forward to her next CD, hoping that her label "Peak Records" will not make us wait so long,this time.

title: Wow An Amazing Cd Of Dance...But More
text:
Cyndi's first album of all new material since 2001's "Shine". She showcases dance songs here but not your typical mindless dance songs with no real lyrics. There are a few songs created just for fun like "Into the nightlife" and "Give it up" BUT these two also have the best beats on the entire album so it's o.k. they are not deep. On the other side you get a fun yet lyrical song in "Echo" which is easily the catchest tune on the disc. Some dance tracks with pretty meaningful lyrics include "Lyfe",
"Same Ol' Story","Set your heart","Grab A hold","High And Mighty" and a little lighter sound with "Raging Storm" and "Lay Me Down". A real different wacky song can be found in "Rocking Chair" but I enjoy the lyrics and beat alot. For ballads you get one in the beautiful "Rain On Me". If you get the Japan version you get a second ballad...the beautiful and haunting "Can't Breathe" and a fast dance/pop song with "Got Candy".
There really isn't a bad song on the entire disc and it is all enjoyable. I do like some songs better then others. My favorites are:

Into The Nightlife,Echo,Grab A Hold,Rain On Me,Give It Up,Can't Breathe,
Same Ol' Story And Set Your Heart.

Honorable Mentions Include: Lyfe,Rocking Chair,Raging Storm,Lay Me Down and Got Candy.

Yes I only left one out and thats High And Mighty. It's a good song just my least favorite and I usually skip it.

So there you have it. If you are a die hard Cyndi fan you will probably love this Cd...once you get used to the new sound. Those who loved She's So Unusual/True Colors era will enjoy fun songs like Into The Nightlife,Give It Up and Got Candy. Those who loved her ballads like on the A Night To Remember era will love Rain On Me and Can't Breathe and those who loved the deep lyrics of Hat Full Of Stars,Sisters Of Avalon and to a lesser degree Shine era will enjoy tracks like Lyfe,Raging Storm,Lay Me Down,Grab A Hold And Same Ol' Story. There is a little bit of everything here.

title: Spirited rock, a bit murky
text:
Santana III was another successful album by the great Mexican guitarist and his band. Good rock, a little heavier and murkier, as opposed to just dark. Just listen, especially, to those earlier numbers.
A highlight of the album is "Toussaint L'Overture," named after the leader of the Caribbean slave revolt. Sort of orchestral in structure, dramatic, with excellent percussion and intermittent climaxes, and fabulous soloing by Carlos. The other most well-known songs are everything: the hard-driving, bouncy "Everybody's Everything" and the upbeat "Everything's Coming Our Way" (I prefer the latter). "Jungle Strut" is also enjoyable, with its graduated swagger, as the title implies, and more excellent guitar soloing. Of the murky earlier cuts, "Taboo," mystical and intense, is the strongest. "Guajira" and "Para Los Rumberos" are signs that Carlos will in the future revert to the more typical latin sound, without the structure, rhythm, and melodies that typified the songs that had mass appeal to non-Latin audiences.

title: Beyond words
text:
There are certain sonic frequencies known to cause nausea, depression, anxiety, giddiness, and other sensations.

Then comes Naked City.

I bought this as part of the Naked City boxed set--which I recommend much more highly than buying the album on its own. In that compilation, this disc ends in "Leng Tch'e," which, though it stands on its own, does not at all seem out of place here.

Like much of John Zorn's stuff, I let it set, listening to it every once in a blue moon.

Well, it turns out for one occasion, I was asked by someone to produce an album of "horror music" to set a certain mood. I immediately picked "Absinthe." Not only did it work, it stuck in everyone's mind, and they haven't been able to get it out of their heads ever since.

It's what I envision H.P. Lovecraft would sound like in music form. Dark, and oddly beautiful. "Val De Travers" is like alien wind chimes being blown by an intermittent breeze. "Une Correspondance" is the rattling of demons working in some subterranean laboratory. "La Fee Verte" is a quiet walk through a haunted wood. "Fleurs Du Mal" is a bone-chilling subsonic pulse you can't escape. "Artemisia Absinthium" is the squealing of flies and tortured beasts. "Notre Dame De L'Oubli" is spinning plates over a heartbeat--very beautiful and serene. "Verlaine: Part One" brings it all together somehow--the chimes, the pulse, and the frantic machinery, blended and quietly resolved. "Verlaine: Part Two" is that uneasy tension that the monster is always just around the corner. And, finally, "...Rend Fou" is the crackle of white noise that takes away the edge and lets you experience the entire thing over again--an erasure, if you will, only that "Absinthe" is not something you can ever forget.

title: WILL THE REAL JON ANDERSON PLEASE STAND UP
text: After the great Tormato album came out I camped out all night for tickets and got 8th row front and center (although with the revolving round stage it wasn't as important it turned out).  I was flying high on YES then and was ready to go through the routine one more time when I heard Drama was coming!  The first songs that I heard were cool - Tempus Fugit, Does it Really Happen, Machine Messiah - but along side the usual great playing of Squire, Howe & White was this Jon SOUNDALIKE Trevor Horn.  I was indignant and in disbelief...anyone else is just a chipmunk in an off-white wedding dress!  Paaaahlease!  What, ya didn't think radioland would notice, or the real YES fans wouldn't MIND?  I basically dismissed the album, didn't buy it, and decided not to go to the concert when it came through (I ended up in Europe anyway so it didn't matter).  In the back of my mind though I would often think of a few of those songs, they were pretty good, no, damn good hard hitting songs.  Squire is particularly great here and White is really hammering those drums this time...and DAMN, Howe has a fire lit under his butt and almost tilts metal.  Okay, I relent: THE POWER OF YES IS TOO STRONG, even (whisper: without you know who).  There I said it, I do like this album alot, even more than 90125.  It is still not above the 70's albums in my mind, but it has great charms and is one of the best 80's rock albums I would say.  The Buggles really didn't ruin it, in fact I like this variation as a diversion, Horn can sing - just not like Anderson, which is fine.  Sometimes the keyboards sound a little too 80's, but they are cool nonetheless.  The Rhino remaster is absolutely stunning sounding up loud (YES albums are pretty slick, Eddie Offord made sure of that this time).  The packaging is great with lyrics, great track notes, original artwork, essay on the history, etc.  Some of the extras are INDISPENSABLE!  Tracks 9 & 10 are great Howe jam sketches that would have been so cool if fully developed.  14, 15 & 16 are like lost YES songs, especially Golden Age and In the Tower, not perfect but interesting and promising.  Try Dancing Through the Light with Drama, Sorry Trevor, I really don't think you are a soiled chipmunk in a wedding dress, YOU ROCK!  Get this classic, it is a gem.

title: Moving, Brilliant, Timeless....
text:
As the title of my review suggests, I'm quite smitten with Moderat's "II". A beautifully produced, lush album that will not leave your car stereo for some time. While the first effort from the Modeselektor - Apparat tag team may have felt a bit uneven at times trying to appease each member's individual tastes, this record feels very cohesive and confident from start to finish. I love the first album and view it as a classic in the genre, however, it does not reach the heights of its successor. The track "Let in the Light" is a wonderfully composed electro-pop work of art. Extremely well written and very catchy. This track embodies the feel of the album best. Warm synths, soaring vocals from a more confident sounding Sascha Ring, this track brings pins and needles to my body with its intensity.

The album goes through various changes in mood. Near the middle of the record we're hit with the ambient-house 10 minute long "Milk". A gorgeous track that progresses into something quite heavy at the end. This track sets the pace for other heavy instrumental pieces to follow. The album takes a turn with "Damage Done". A song that wouldn't feel out of place on an Apparat record like "Devil's Walk". If you purchase the deluxe album it includes the track "Last Time" which is certainly worth the extra $.

So far, Moderat II is the best work from both Modeselektor and Apparat. Enjoy!

The overall feeling of the recordings is that they are Beatles Elevator Music!  But, in case you don't mind 'easy listening,' they suffer one major difference; where as 'Muzak' is tedious, boring, and purposefully non-engaging (easy to listen to, eh?) Muzak is nearly always VERY well performed, and amazingly tight, and in tune!  BUT these 'Beatles Baroque' are NOT!  The recorder players especially, but really the whole thing is so out-of-tune. Listen to 'Across the Universe' if it is on the sound samples?  My ears hurt, sorry.  And they all just sound so weak, and flimsy, and just plain 'not so in tune.'  And the mics perhaps were all too far from anything, so it always has a very distant, not quite there feel, and sounds also as though everybody had their parts, knew they knew the tunes (we all think we 'know' all the Beatles songs?), and they might have practiced their parts a bit, and click... 'take one'..., etc.  Sort of sounds like these might have been the tapes George Martin tossed out, when his first orchestra at the EMI studio, just didn't cut the cake, and he hired a better one?  AND, really sounds like the director just copied all the Sony Band scores of the songs, cut and pasted the parts, and handed them out.  There is no special anything about the arrangements at all.  Not really 'Baroque' anything except the instruments?  And a look at the CD photos will reveal that the guitarists have electric/accoustic modern guitars(!), probably playing exactly what John and George and Paul played, without any hint of Baroque continuo style.  And the percussion is exactly what Ringo did, which is fine (Ringo was great), but JUST DOES NOT sound very Baroque to me at all.  I was SO dissapointed too, as there are a few really hot players on the CDs, and even they do not shine as they do on their solo efforts.  I do not feel that anyone at the recording had any passionate feel for the actual Beatles songs, or what the Beatles were saying and singing, but only studio musicians playing their parts that are on the music-stand in front of them.  The purpose of these reviews is MAINLY (I think) to let buyers know sort of what they are getting, as we cannot return CDs when they dissapoint us!  My aim is to do exactly that.  I could not even listen to any single song all the way through an any of the 3 CDs, will never listen to any again, and see they even now have a 4th Greatest Hits version?  Perhaps alot of work, and well intended, but these all just plain miss the mark!!!

title: The Ones That You Love Lead You Nowhere (?!?)
text:
The greatest hits package from Del Amitri is appropriately named "Lousy With Love". Surely that title was the brainchild of the Dels voice and bassist Justin Currie, who also wrote all the lyrics to 1992's "Change Everything". If you were to read all the enclosed lyrics before listening to even the first note of this album, you would very likely expect to be bombarded by musical melancholia. Somehow, this is NOT at all the case here. "Change Everything" is arguably the BEST full album Del Amitri has done up through 2001.
Great bands seem to revolve around excellent lyrics and storytelling complemented by brilliant musicianship. Del Amitri's heart and soul has always been Currie's songwriting perfectly paired by guitarist Iain Harvie's stunning instrumentation. Justin steadfastly refuses to acknowledge any deep meaning in his writing but, he is a natural born poet. The lyrics thinly belie a likely checkered and rocky road in a few past romances. Suffering is the germ of brilliance according to many pundits and Justin has apparently traversed that road with his sense of humor and self intact while developing keen insight and observational skills. Most all of the stories throughout this album are fraught with love gone wrong and/or astray but, the final cut "Sometimes I Just Have to Say Your Name" ends it on an uplifting and hopeful chord. The melodic half of the Dels brilliance throughout "Change Everything" is literally in the remarkably capable hands of Harvie. His guitar work and razor sharp timing provides perfect musical counterpart to Currie's words. Listen to the riff Iain launches into on "When You Were Young" after Justin sings "Sometimes your lack of sympathy gets hard to explain, so on your mask of make up you just paint a little parody of pain" and try and tell me the hair on the nape of your neck doesn't stand on end in stunned, giddy amazement! Feel the guitar chords rumble like emotional thunder in the background of "To Last A Lifetime" or the strumming intensity throughout "The Ones That You Love Lead You Nowhere" that could rouse even the long-dead to joyful fits of dancing! Much of the radio airplay this album got (and still occasionally gets) is deservedly from the single "Always The Last To Know". Catchy harmony and riffs abound on this cut which still sounds just as fresh today as it did in the Summer of 1992. The brooding side of the Dels permeate the "Surface of the Moon" with the words and feel of "From the well-swept streets of Jackson Heights to the dockside drudgery, everything's now a replica of what it used to be, and since they tarted up the trenches and painted the bridges blue, it seems less like a home to me than just a place they bury you". The album leads off with almost a warning in "Be My Downfall" admonishing "The bus is pulling out and I guess I'd better go before I make a grave mistake and let my feelings show, and twenty miles away she waits alone for me, but when I try to picture her, you're the one I see, and in another situation I could put up a fight, but you will be my downfall tonight". Double-entendre? You bet! Similar examples are rampant.
Del Amitri has never quite taken off the way they deserve to. Justin, Iain, and the ever changing other members of the band have never been much for conformity. This is often one of the very reasons why the rabidly loyal fan base (myself included) love them so. One can identify with the events powerfully in many (most) of their songs. They are human, like us. And very real. Promoters and elite producers often don't care for those immutable qualities, hence their relative obscurity in my opinion. But, if you are a fan of SUBSTANCE, DO NOT PASS UP ON THIS ALBUM!!! It will grow on you and, you may even find yourself quoting a line or two!
