title: An Admirable Balancing Act (nearly ruined by the Loudness Wars)
text:
[Note: On the issue of the album's sound mix, go to the end of the review.]

ENYA-NESS IS LESS THAN GODLINESS:

There is an additional hurdle (at least for me) in reviewing a 2014 Jackie Evancho album. In the interest of fairness, I have to let go of the iron grip on those projections that were mentally conjured up a few years ago when she was flaunting her supernatural abilities at the age of ten. You know what I'm talking about, don't you? Those projections of what her future musical output would be like.

You see, when Jackie broke out of the gate on America's Got Talent--and later on, headlining her Dream with Me PBS special--her voice was so remarkable, her delivery was so sincere, and her future seemed so limitless and unknown, that it was hard not to go completely off the deep end. "What's she gonna be doing in a few years? Maybe she'll be able to shoot lasers from her eyes! Maybe she'll have a 27 octave range! Maybe she'll hit notes so low they'll cause whales to beach themselves! Maybe she'll put past music icons to such shame that the respective executors of the Mozart and Beatles estates will elect to burn all remnants of their legacies to the ground out of deference!"

Of course, such expectations were just a wee bit far-reaching. So one thing to grapple with in regards to Awakening is that Jackie is becoming her own person with her own particular sound and tastes. She has a management team with their own ideas about what kind of career Jackie should have. And those things might not exactly conform to previous expectations. (And no, she probably won't be singlehandedly achieving peace in the Middle East. Damnit!)

Putting aside 2011-era wishcasting, it seems that at 14, Jackie remains an atypically good singer. She still possesses that trademark, bell-like purity in those high notes, and she's still a bit less assured in the lower registers. Perhaps in an effort to maintain long term health, or perhaps simply the result of a changing body, she seems to sing in a much more reserved way than she did as a child. The results are still nice, but don't quite reach "powerhouse" levels as consistently as when she was in grade school. And yes, that last sentence sounds just as bizarre to me when I read it.

While all of this adds up to just being short of being able to shoot lasers from her eyes, in the more fair and real terms that every other music artist who is not Jackie Evancho is measured by, I guess that's nothing to sneeze at. (Perhaps even more than nothing to sneeze at, when you consider how many "singers" don't do a lot of singing these days.)

It should come as no surprise that Awakening falls in the "Classical Crossover" category. This is how Jackie has always been labelled, and it's what most fans now expect from her. However, for me, Awakening makes me realize is that for all the times "CC" has been thrown about in regards to Jackie, that label never really sat well with me. Even though in the past Camp Evancho clung to the "Classical Crossover" label consistently in interviews and such, I always got the impression they were using the term more like a protective cross to ward off the more self-important and unstable vampires of the opera community who seem to have been threatened by Evancho's existence ever since her AGT debut, rather than because they thought it really encompassed all that Jackie was capable of.

I mean, Jackie had elements of opera, some pop, some classical, some chamber music, some Mario Lanza... but her output never really reminded me of any single one genre. When Jackie was singing, I never thought, "Oh, that's nice. Maybe I should put this on in the background while I do my laundry," in the way that I imagine many people say about other CC singers. No. My only thoughts were, "Holy crap, that kicks a**!" In fact, if I had to come up with a singular genre that Jackie has been performing this entire time, the only real answer would be "That Mind-Blowing Savant from America's Got Talent and Man, Does She Kick A**!" That was Jackie's genre, Bobby Fischer meets Shirley Temple, and she was the only member of the club.

Well, "Awakening" marks a first, because it's the first album of Jackie's that feels like full-on Enya or Adiemus. It is indeed Classical Crossover(tm). And it's ironic that the one album that really lives up to that moniker makes me wish that Jackie was in fact not a part of her chosen genre and that she had the motivation to shoot higher.

What she was originally when she first broke out, I'm not even sure what you would call it. And it might've been too niche to be commercially viable in the long run. But whatever it was, and regardless of how profitable it would've been over the span of a career--damn, was she ever good at it.

THE GOOD:

Having said all that, "Awakening" does deserve much praise. What it tries to do, it does very well. It comes very close to achieving its goals completely. Yes, it would take unconventional courage from team Evancho to full-on push Jackie into being the best operatic or classical performer of her generation (as per David Foster's words). "Awakening" is the polar opposite of such a career choice, but in its own way, it takes chances too. It is the most conventionally "pop" sounding of Evancho's albums, and yet it manages to straddle that line between "let's try to make Jackie sound more contemporary" vs. "let's also not offend her original fanbase." For years, you could almost hear such wheels turning in the heads of Jackie's management. "How can we transition the Dream With Me girl into something more commercially viable without giving people conniptions?"

I've always been fond of the adult contemporary sound from the 90's. People like Sophie B. Hawkins or Maria McKee. I've speculated that if Jackie ever wanted to try to be a "pop star" (without completely descending into desperate Miley Cyrus territory) then echoing the approach of such albums would be the way to go. "Awakening," if not for a particularly muddy sound mix, comes close.

Basically, Awakening attempts to do what "Songs from the Silver Screen" tried--make Jackie radio-friendly. But unlike Silver Screen, it actually pulls it off. (Although the less said about Awakening's Cosmo-like final album cover, the better. What ever possessed them to scrap the cover photo used in the advance copies?) You see, Silver Screen's attempts at mainstreaming Jackie were sad. By having Jackie perform songs like "My Heart Will Go On" and "Reflection" (choices which still to this day cause me to twitch; like seeing John Nash being relegated behind the cash register at Target because he's good with numbers), they not only did not make Jackie sound hip, but also didn't make best use of her unique vocal skill set.

Awakening's attempts at "hipping up" Jackie aren't nearly so lazy. Here, instead of relying on tried-and-true "Top 40 hits" to make Jackie more accessible, they instead take chances in slightly more aggressive (and unique) song choices and more contemporary arrangements (upbeat percussion and synths, etc). This is Awakening's approach to popularizing Jackie, and to my mind it is the most logical route they could've taken in achieving this goal without going Miley Cyrus overboard. It's a mix of some vaguely pop-like songs (that could still be classified as CC) and a few more classical oriented pieces that showcase her vocals, (AVE MARIA and VOCALISE) and it works as a whole. Yes, it's a bid towards mainstream appeal, but it's one that works.

THE SONGS:

I won't mention every single track on the album, but just know that--excluding the issue of the sound mix which I'll get to later--there honestly isn't one song I could call "bad" on the album. Every track is solid. (Although I do think that "Think of Me," from Phantom of the Opera is the least "attention getting" of all the songs, which makes the decision to use that track as early album promotion sort of vexing.)

Even though early album promotion seems to be focusing on THINK OF ME and YOUR LOVE, it's not until the sinister-sounding JE T'AIME, track 3, that things get especially interesting. It's here when it dawns on you just how different this album is compared to her two previous albums.

TAKE ME THERE is the first Jackie track I can remember that sounds like they just flat out decided to "go for it," and produce a catchy, upbeat pop(ish) single. It's Enya meets Lazytown. It works. This could've been a good album opener.

The folksy and light Irish-tinged ballad OPEN FIELDS OF GRACE continues the strengths. Of all the material Jackie has released so far in her career, these tracks are the ones you could most easily imagine becoming radio-friendly hits. OPEN FIELDS also seems arranged to take advantage of Jackie's strong upper registers.

MEMORIES is another pop(ish) song in the vein of TAKE ME THERE. Once again, it goes for unabashed CC/pop, and does it well. I particularly like the use of synth and how this upbeat song somehow ends on a sinister minor key. Any of these last three songs would've promoted the album better had she performed them on her recent appearance with AGT, rather than Think of Me. In fact, I think Memories is possibly the most "marketable" song Jackie has ever done. The melody is catchy as hell, and if they really wanted to give her that "push," a decent-budgeted music video should be made of it.

It's about the time we transition to THE RAINS OF CASTAMERE, that I realize that there hasn't been a bad track yet on the album. While the choice to push Jackie toward a career in this type of lightweight Enya-esque pop may not be fully utilizing Jackie's potential--when one accepts that this is (at least for now) the bed that Jackie has chosen to lie in, it's hard to deny that it's a well-constructed bed.

WITH OR WITHOUT YOU, the famous U2 song, is the diciest experiment on the album. When listened to by itself, it probably doesn't work. Jackie never steps away from her restrained soprano delivery and it makes for some strange bedfellows against the percussive arrangement which is still very similar to U2's original. It reminds me a bit of when the Food Network visits county fairs and they serve garlic ice cream. Two things that are great on their own, not necessarily working together. But you know what? When listened to within the context of the rest of the album, it fits right in.

Having Jackie perform Rachmaninoff's VOCALISE is kind of funny when you think of it. One criticism of Jackie throughout her short career is that she tends not to enunciate her words clearly. With VOCALISE it was almost like the team just said, "Screw it. Let's not have her sing any words at all." You see, vocalize doesn't actually have any lyrics. It's just Jackie showcasing her soaring upper registers to a haunting melody. And if not for the album's soupy sound mix, VOCALISE (along with the equally haunting AVE MARIA) would be a standout track.

***

So in conclusion, as Classical Crossover albums go, Awakening is solid. (Perhaps more than solid, given the catchiness and replay value of most of the tracks.) And even though it departs from what most have come to expect from Jackie, I think most would say it does so gently.

I also think it's accurate to say that if Enya was the one releasing "Awakening" people would consider it the best album she's ever made, with the most impressive singing of Enya's career. Considering Jackie and Enya probably share a lot of the same fanbase, most are probably fine with this. And if you are one of those people, then there's no reason to read on. Purchase the album and enjoy it. Thanks for reading. The End.

***

EXCEPT:

But for those people that don't fit into the above category, that's the rub, isn't it? Making the best Enya album ever would all be well and good, except that ain't Enya on the cover. That's right, bud. Look again. That's Jackie Evancho. Jackie Mother-Grabbin' Evancho.

That's the girl who blew audiences' minds to such a degree when she sang on AGT that some assumed it couldn't possibly be real. That's Jackie Evancho, the girl who's been invited back to the White House so many times they may as well have given her a permanent position in the administration and saved on airfare. This is the girl who at ten years old, asked Sarah Brightman to duet with her, and then proceeded to bend said childhood idol over her knee on national television and spank her like a gassy baby. That's Jackie Freakin' Evancho, whose voice box was such a miracle that the news program 20/20 saw fit to have it analyzed, like she had pyrokinesis or something and we all lived in a Stephen King novel. That's Jackie the Widowmaker Evancho on the cover, who could slay grown men with just the first few notes of "The Lord's Prayer."

Jackie Evancho is a girl who can knock your socks off. Enya, pleasant as she is, never knocked the socks off of anyone in her life. Enya makes music to put on in the background while you *iron* your socks.

And therein lies my issue with Awakening: It's nice. Yes, in the reality of day to day existence, a nice album is a good thing to have. Nice music makes long work commutes more pleasant, and it's good for Pilates classes. But when Awakening is measured against actual greatness--the kind of rare greatness that can only be achieved by savants who remain passionate at what they do and who don't take their innate talents for granted--its goals feel a little too modest.

It used to be that when Jackie performed a song, given the very fact that she was the age she was, and was singing with the sincerity and power that she was, everything had a sense of "edge" to it. So even songs which would otherwise be considered "normal" in the hands of any other performer (Angel, To Believe) felt provocative. However, disregarding those "normal songs," it's also worth noting of this period that while she was younger and lending that automatic surrealism to everything, the material she performed was also more outlandish. (Pieces like "Nessun Dorma" and "Pie Jesu" are outlandish when measured against what's radio friendly.) Now that Jackie is at an age in which the "automatic edge" is wearing off, it seems more important than ever that she truly step outside the box in terms of what material she chooses to perform and give the people something that they don't hear every day from their favorite singers. And yet ironically, at a time when being "niche" would benefit her most, her material has become more mainstream, her vocal delivery less committed.

And you know those decidedly *not* radio-worthy pieces such as Ombra Mai Fu? In my opinion those are still the pieces which shine the most when Jackie deigns to sing them live. That's when socks get knocked off. It's impossible to watch such performances and not conclude that that is what she was born to do. The road less traveled.

I still hold out hope that someday Jackie will go back to fulfilling the promise she showed us when she first broke out. That earnest passion and uniqueness that was exemplified on stage when she'd tackle classical arias or the Lord's Prayer. I hope someday she WILL be shooting lasers from her eyes and assaulting people's hosiery and turning their undergarments into projectiles, just like in the good old days.

But until that day comes, Awakening makes for a well-constructed tide-me-over.

***

P.S.

Special mention has to be made of the SOUND MIX on Awakening. It can't be avoided: It's awful. Like "someone should make a public apology" awful.

Don't get me wrong. For the most part, all the choices in arrangements and instrumentation on the tracks are really great. However, bizarrely, there seems to be little separation between the left/right channels.

Worse still, Awakening also seems to be mixed in accordance with modern trends in regards to volume dynamics. In other words, the highs and lows which in albums of past generations would form crescendos and moments of calm, seem to have been digitally crushed out of the mix. It's so extreme that it threatens to undo all the best efforts of everyone else, including Jackie's singing. It prevents Awakening from actually sounding as good as those adult contemporary albums of the 90's I mentioned earlier. It makes it impossible to judge how good the album "really" is, and it's the fatal flaw that I have to force myself to overlook in order to justify my 4-star rating. Seriously, someone should be embarrassed over this.

This has been a practice in the music industry for several years now. (The most infamous example is the Metallica album "Death Magnetic.") I guess the reasoning is, "Hey, if every instrument and every second of every song is at the same peak loudness, that will make the album nonstop excitement!" It's the recording industry's version of that person who TYPES HIS FORUM POSTS IN ALL CAPITAL LETTERS THINKING IT WILL MAKE PEOPLE TAKE HIM MORE SERIOUSLY!!!111ROFLAMAO! Yeah, you know that guy. And the tactic is even more annoying when applied to music.

Unfortunately, when one considers the concept of relativity, if everything is at the same volume level, then nothing can truly be called "loud." With no valleys, there are no mountains. Kind of like that quote from The Incredibles, "When everyone is special, no one is."

Such compression might temporarily snag the attention of a distracted listener for a scant few seconds when he's changing his radio dial, but in the long run it only does a disservice to the material and unfortunately, the artist. It contributes to the sense of overall muddiness and the sense that songs have little emotional variance. Moments of passion like choruses, when the listener should be pounded right in the heart, lose their power. Different sound elements that should be more prominent than others (like a certain singing savant's vocal tracks) are drowned out amidst the soup. Ironically, by making everything "loud," the result is a mix without any dynamic range--i.e. it sounds small and flat. I'm guessing this is also the main reason why the few negative Amazon reviews for Awakening consistently mention how the songs become tiresome after a while. It's called "ear fatigue."

Also noticeable is the lack of variance in reverb. It's not so much that Jackie sounds like she's singing in a cave as one reviewer put it. It's not quite to that extreme, and a certain amount of reverb/ambience can be great. (In fact, the problem I usually have with modern albums is that there seems to be a complete lack ambience; rather it sounds like the singer is in a broom closet. Although, I think that's usually the result of modern digital recording methods.) However, the mixer seemed to go a little crazy here. This dude apparently set the dial to ten, then cracked open a comic book, ate a Philly cheesesteak and fell asleep while Jackie sang. Let's call this the "Enya Pilates Class Effect." (To be fair, it's possible the reverb only seems so extreme because it's being exacerbated by the volume compression issue.)

It might seem unfair to single Awakening out for the volume compression thing. After all, this is the industry norm now. Well, unfortunately, amongst a personal album collection of mostly rock and pop albums (including the latest Guns n' Roses offering), Awakening is by far the worst instance of sound compression I've ever heard on an official release. By far. It's almost as if they took the completed album, then converted all the audio files into 56kpbs mp3s, then released THOSE files to the public. The mix crosses the line from "just being trendy" into flat-out incompetence.

Consider too that this is Jackie Evancho, who has one of the most remarkable singing voices of her (or our) generation. Suddenly this misguided practice of diminishing the overall sound quality into a cacophonous mush to "get people's attention" becomes infinitely more stupid--much more than if it were just Joe Schmoe laying down the vocal tracks. It's kind of like being lucky enough to get Kate Upton to appear in your advertising campaign, and then photographing her with an early-90's video phone. Dude, when you've got the keys to a Ferrari for a weekend, don't waste the opportunity picking up Fritos and a lotto scratcher at the Circle K.

The mix on Awakening feels so compromised that I think a release of "Awakening 2.0" would be justified. I've read that Metallica's "Death Magnetic" was later made available to Guitar Hero: World Tour players, except it was the uncompressed version *before* all the sound dynamics were crushed out of it; and apparently it sounded a lot better. With an Awakening 2.0 we could really guage how many of the other small risks really paid off in creating a compelling pop/CC album. But, whether or not such a version is ever made available publically, I at least hope it exists in a vault somewhere. It would be a shame if the vocal tracks Jackie laid down during the recording of this album only existed in the soupy form heard on the CD.

title: An interesting DVD that never quite manages to feel necessary
text:
Angels and Airwaves was a really interesting.....idea. I liked We Don't Need to Whisper, but was a bit let down by I-Empire. Not sure why, don't know if it was my growing feeling of resentment towards Tom's attitude and his fake personality in interviews, etc...don't know if it was the fact that it felt more like "more of the same" rather than an ambitious continuation....maybe it was the fact that every song was about the SAME DAMN THINGS....but I sort of lost interest in the band after that CD, even though I thought it had some great tracks on it. Still, though, I like the band, and remembered hearing about this film they had planned. And despite this supposedly going to be a "huge release" it was released with little fanfare right to DVD and I just happened to see it on a store shelf and picked it up.

It's an interesting documentary but never really.....great. This is a very new band, it makes almost no sense to make a documentary about them by this point. Look how long it took Metallica to put out Some Kind of Monster, and they're.... frigging...Metallica. The movie briefly discusses Tom's breakup from Blink, shows the band recording and discussing We Don't Need to Whisper, features Tom talking about his addiction to painkillers, etc. etc. etc. It's all...interesting, but nothing that couldn't have been discussed in a "revealing interview" in Spin Magazine; I have no idea why this thing was produced. It just seems to unfortunately further highlight what I've been noticing about this band; they just think way too highly of themselves. A section on the DVD even is called "Reviews" and shows pictures of magazine articles that praised the CD....really, guys? Could this DVD be any more one-sided?

That said, there is definitely some good stuff on here. 2 of the band's music videos, a commentary with the band and director, a 10-minute explanation of Tom's leaving Blink 182 (wish more of this made the film, instead it's under the special features section,) and the band's CG music videos. I just find it hard, though, to see the point of all this. I like Angels and Airwaves, but to hear Tom call it "the best stuff he's ever made" and see him go on about how emotionally powerful this music is....I just can't agree with it, Blink 182's final CD was much more emotionally powerful to me, both lyrically and musically, than anything on the first 2 Angels and Airwaves CD's, hate to say it. They were good CD's but let's not oversell them. And I think that was this band's biggest mistake from the beginning.

Start the Machine's a documentary about a decent new band with talented people in it that think a bit too highly of themselves for their own good. Still, though, there's a bit here of interest to fans, and it's genuinely well-made and provided a nice viewing. It highlighted Tom's need to be appreciated as a "real artist" other than the jokester he was in Blink, though I wish he'd realize that he doesn't have to abandon who he is in the process. It also explains where the name "We Don't Need to Whisper" came from, and a couple (but not enough) live performances and plenty of studio footage. A decent DVD. I think it would have been better, though, as a bonus disc with their 3rd CD, whenever that comes out, because a full documentary release at this point in time just seems a bit premature.

title: Pure prog-pop pleasure!
text:
After teasing us with a proggy intro to a more pop-heavy album in "Delicate Friction" last year, The Mommyheads really get their prog-pop on this time with "Vulnerable Boy", exploring sounds we've never heard before while at the same time retaining that signature Mommyheads appeal. But to merely label the Mommyheads as prog-pop does them a disservice, as there's lots to explore here. This is a rare album that has both instant accessibility and rewards for repeat-listeners, something for long-time fans and for those out there who might be saying "The Mommy-whos?"

"On A Clear Night" kicks things off with a sparse, beautiful piano melody reminiscent of early Tony Banks. Adam Elk's vocals come in like a lullaby, and we think we know where this is going to take us, but then the drums and guitars kick in and we're happily off in Mommyheads land, where music can be both poppy and experimental, daring and familiar. This track links nicely with the following track, "Gimme Silence", continuing with a new piano theme, leading to a percussion and bass pattern that reminded me of Radiohead's "The Raindrops" but with warmth and funk. This takes us to the 6/4 beat "Science and Reason", showing that pop, rock and prog can peacefully coexist in the same track. Next up is the epic, wonderful "Medicine Show", probably the album's defining track, a fact that the Mommyheads have underscored by using part of the lyrics for the album's title. A lovely acoustic guitar and vocal melody gives way to thumping fuzz bass and layers of keyboards and vocals bordering on chaotic, but somehow the Mommyheads effortlessly steer us through it all and we're happy to be along on the journey.

"My Intruder" and "Skinny White Uptight" highlight the more abrasive side of the band, the former track with dark cynicism and the latter with self-effacing humor. "Devastate Me" takes a sparse keyboard riff and puts some real bounce into it, "Right Where They Should Be" and "Out on the Cliffs" are classic Mommyheads. "Force of Will" features a fun little keyboard trill that should sound dated but doesn't. "Silent Age" has a man-on-the-corner skiffle feel to it, and "Bleed From a Glass" ends on a subdued note, returning to the piano themes of the early tracks. Bonus track "No One Gives a Damn About Your Band" comes off as fun rather than bitter, although god knows the Mommyheads have a right to be. As a fan I will say it's a shame that a Mommyheads masterpiece such as "Hello Friends" has a handful of views on YouTube while Train's "Soul Sister" rakes in millions. Both are good songs but the Mommyheads deserve their recognition too!

Overall, I found "Vulnerable Boy" to be an ambitious, highly listenable mix. In one sense, the first four tracks make up a complete "suite", and we're left breathless and wanting more. And while the rest of the tracks are fine (and at times, great), they lack some of the sonic majesty of those first four tracks. I get the sense that they were really trying to stretch themselves in the front end of the album. In particular "Skinny White Uptight" sticks out as not really belonging here, but damned if the track isn't catchy. And that's one of the reasons I love the Mommyheads. As soon as you try to define them or pigeonhole them, they say "Wait, but what if we did this?" You end up getting the best of both worlds: invention and accessibility, in one great-sounding package. I can't wait to see what these guys do next.

title: It's not a Duran Duran spin-off, OK?
text:
Considering his background as the guitarist of Duran Duran, Andy Taylor can be easily underrated and any project launched by him could be candidate for not be taken into account for lack of seriousness. Don't fall into it.

My first contact with "Thunder" was hearing the opening track -"I Might Lie"- on the radio without knowing who was playing, and it surprised me when I eventually knew. I immediatly recorded in its whole on tape from a borrowed LP. It makes you understand how restrained Taylor was when he was part of Duran Duran.

When Andy left the band, he wanted to prove he was a good guitar player and made an album that let everybody knew his idea of being a Hollywood rocker: its sounds reminds the hair metal bands in their early ages. Althought not a shredder, there's plenty of soul in his solos -just listen "Life Goes On" and "Bringin' Me Down"-, and the songs have a Bon Jovi-esque catchiness. Guitar riffs? Think Def Leppard's "Hysteria". Lyrics have a bluesy-dark feel that gives the whole album an almost depressing mood.

When "Thunder" came out, it didn't get good critics at all, and may be the reason why Andy didn't made a second effort. Maybe it wasn't Durannie enough... maybe it wasn't as heavy or shredding as other contemporary albums... "Thunder" ain't anything of them, that's why it's worth the buying.

If you like his playing out of Duran Duran, you can even get Rod Stewart's "Out Of Order", the 2 Power Station CD's or his collaborations on "Miami Vice" and "American Anthem" soundtracks.

title: Same old story.
text: Depending on who you talk to, Ryan Adams is either the second coming of Springsteen or a precocious self obsesser who has sold his country sound for the sheen and seamstresses of Hollywood. Whatever the case, he is undoubtedly prolific. Since the release of his commercial breakthrough Gold last year, Adams claims to have written enough material to fill four CD's which he had originally intended to release as a box set . Wisely, he decided to refine the collection to a single disc. The result is Demolition, essentially a "best of the rest" compilation comprised of 13 previously unreleased demos. Recorded at four different studios around the globe and featuring Gillian Welch, David Rawlings, lap steel guru Bucky Baxter and long time cohort Ethan Johns, Demolition probably wont do much to synthesise the polarised opinion of Adams' work. Indeed, a more apt title for the record would have been "Hit and Miss." When Adams is good he is exceptional. The frisky blue grass of "Chin up, Cheer Up," the sorrowful lament "Tomorrow" and the brooding acoustic ballad "Dear Chicago" are as fine as anything he has recorded since Whiskey Town. Never straying far from his perpetually fractured heart, Adams can have you calling any number of ex girlfriends and professing that you really do love them.  When he is bad however, Adams is on the shorter side of mediocre. The opener "Nuclear" is mawkish U2 mimicry, "Desire" is pedestrian whine reminiscent of Counting Crow , whilst "Starting to Hurt" sounds like it was written for his much maligned doppelganger Bryan. Ultimately, Demolition, like Gold and Heartbreaker before it , is the work of a talented artist who struggles with his execution. Wunderkind or Wunderbrat, the jury is still out.

title: You should hear what I hear...
text:
While other people will search for hidden drug references and just talk about the Chemical Brothers in general, here's a review that focuses on the actual single. "Star Guitar" is the second single for the Chemical Brothers' "Come With Us" album, the first being "It Began in Afrika", another highly recommended single if you liked "Come With Us". Anyway, on with the review:
1. Star Guitar (Edit) -- a quick little ditty similar to the "It Began in Afrika" edit. It's a nice little tune for those of you who don't like too much repetitiveness.
2. Star Guitar -- the version you've heard off the album. A sweeping tune filled with ambience and trance moods all centering around a faint vocal proclaiming that "you should feel what I feel" and that "you should take what I take".
3. Star Guitar (Pete Heller's Expanded Mix) -- I heard Pete Heller's Park Lane Vocal on Moby's "South Side" single and thought it was pretty boring. It's grown on me since then and so has this remix of "Star Guitar". Unfortunatley, Heller centers on the "you should feel" part of the vocal, so it gets pretty repetitive and at over eight minutes, you might wanna hit the "Skip" button for this one.
4. Star Guitar (Pete Heller's 303 Dub) -- Ah, here we are, a much better attempt by Heller. The 303 Dub is a wild combination of melodies and harmonies from the song and, if I'm not mistaken, there are minimal, if no, amounts of vocals. But, it all pales in comparison to what you hear next...
5. Base 6 -- The No. 1 reason that anyone who already owns "Come With Us" should buy this single. "Base 6", like its cousin "Hot Acid Rhythm 1" off the "Afrika" single, is an awesome dance mix, centering around a computerized voice counting up to six. With more than enough variation to make it interesting, it's a wonder why this didn't appear on the album. It's these little surprises that make buying singles worthwhile.

title: Hard to beat The Real Deal!

title: MUCH MORE than Carlos just "going through the motions"!
text:
I read a review here titled "Carlos going through the motions", that says Santana's feeling just wasn't in his guitar playing in this CD.... Speaking from the perspective of someone who watched this concert in a TV broadcast (and has heard one of the CD tracks so far), I believe I understand what made that reviewer say what he did, but IMHO he truly misses what's REALLY going on here.... Its true that Carlos played this concert in a different style -- there's shorter phrases, and sharp riffs, where you'd normally expect a "Santana flow"... The music has a noticeably, but not harshly, different feel than the hypnotic, easy-going style you typically expect from Santana.
But I believe this was all a very deliberate mission to re-interpret his songs with a bit of the style of the man portrayed on his shirt in that TV concert... Jimi Hendrix. I believe Santana wanted to give us a bit of what HE hears when he listens to Jimi, and what more clear (and fun) way for Carlos to do that than through his language with us,... his own songs!
I don't own this CD (yet), but if it fully matches Santana's performance in the Mexico City concert I saw (as I expect it does), I'd say be prepared for something different, something experimental, something that really makes you listen to these songs again, through a new Carlos perspective. If you are open for something other than a pure recreation of your existing Santana music, and especially if you are a Hendrix fan, I'd say be prepared for Carlos to take you on a new Experience!

title: The selection of guest artists leaves a lot to be desired
text:
The long and successful career of Ronnie Milsap, while filled with chart-topping hit songs and many awards, is often a subject of frustration for me. Few artists with his level of talent have achieved such commercial success while remaining overlooked and underappreciated by the media and the public at large, most especially in the last 25 years as overrated younger stars with a fraction of Milsap's talent continue to overshadow him. Every CD Milsap has released in the last 20 years has been largely ignored by radio and the media while real country music has become nearly extinct as modern pop and rap influences have contaminated the current Nashville scene.

Every few years it seems we are cursed with another useless duet album that consists of a real deal legend of true talent {Ray Charles, Frank Sinatra, Tony Bennett, John Fogerty, Lionel Richie, etc.} sharing the microphone with a selection of inferior modern day stars that anyone who values talent and musicianship should care less about. Ronnie Milsap is my favorite artist of all time, a wonderful man whose music represents everything GOOD about American music. For reasons obvious to anyone who knows and understands REAL country music, I am certainly NOT a fan of any cookie-cutter mainstream record company puppets that have dominated modern Nashville from the mid-90's to the present day. As a music fan who values talent above all else, the last thing I want to hear is today’s inferior artists performing with a true legend who they pale in comparison to.

As a Milsap fan, what qualities does Ronnie represent that I look for in the music I love?? How about honesty, musicianship, powerful singing, a distinctive vocal sound, a great stage show with no gimmicks or booty-shaking, and most of all, TALENT....that dirty six letter word that is no longer acceptable in the mainstream music scene of the 21st century. With the exception of the legendary Willie Nelson, Dolly Parton, Billy Gibbons, Leon Russell, and maybe George Strait, what do any of these cookie-cutter guest artists have to do with the timeless qualities that Milsap stands for??? This CD is obviously another attempt to "introduce" current country fans to a great music legend who should need no introduction. If you don't know who Ronnie Milsap is, you don't know great country music! Sadly, most music fans brainwashed by the bubblegum drivel on the charts today wouldn't recognize a great song or singer if it slapped them in the face. As long as corporate puppets like Luke Bryan and Jason Aldean are the only singers shoved down their throats by record companies, they never will.

Luke claims Ronnie as one of his heroes, but nobody would ever know it by listening to the cookie cutter booty shaking bubblegum crap he churns out year after year. Along with his buddy Mr. Aldean, he has succeeded in turning country music into rap and bubblegum pop for an audience of 20 year olds who would likely think Ronnie Milsap must be the name of the manager at the local Walmart or something. Let's get real here...there's not a Bryan or Aldean fan on the planet who knows or cares who Ronnie Milsap is, nor is there a Milsap fan who would ever waste their money on a Luke or Jason CD. Putting them on the same album with the great Milsap is like Justin Beiber singing duets with Waylon Jennings or George Jones! If Nashville executives believe Luke and Jason have any business sharing a mic with a supreme talent of Milsap's calibre, they should have included Britney Spears and Taylor Swift too! I'm actually surprised they were left off the roster. I can totally hear Taylor butchering Stranger in my House just as effectively as Puke Bryan. Why not?? To take a stand for the REAL DEAL, let me suggest a list of REAL DEAL TALENT that should have graced the line-up for this CD instead.

1. Charley Pride {One of the few country legends who is still alive and well and the man responsible for bringing Ronnie to Nashville in 1973. Charley should have been the first man chosen for this project. Ronnie started his country career as an opening act for Mr. Pride.}
2. Los Lonely Boys {the most talented modern band on the scene today. Anyone who saw their excellent CMT Crossroads show with Ronnie will know why they deserve a spot on this CD! Compare their fantastic performance of Stranger in my house with the inferior Luke Bryan duet here.}
3. JOHN FOGERTY! {The ageless rock n' roll legend is still in top form at 73 and met Ronnie during his early years in Memphis at TJ's nightclub. Ronnie and John on the same record would be a case of TALENT OVERLOAD!}
4. Linda Ronstadt {America's finest female vocalist, but her recent health issues would have prevented her from being a part of this project. Linda and Ronnie should have done a duet in the 80's when both were in their prime. What a great record that would have been and what a shame Linda is no longer able to sing.}
5. Travis Tritt {Probably the best country artist of the last 25 years who can handle country, rock, and blues much like Ronnie}
6. James Otto {Recorded a duet with Ronnie a few years ago and a better choice than Jason Aldean}
7. Hunter Hayes {A better choice than Puke Bryan. Hayes is a rare current country star with actual musicianship who can do more than shake his booty on stage.}
8. Bonnie Raitt {another fine legendary talent compatible with Ronnie's blues/rock side}
9. Tony Joe White {The great country/rock legend who recently passed away after this album was recorded}
10. Larkin Poe {Two up and coming sisters who can play the hell out of blues, rock, and country. These talented sisters {Rebecca and Megan Lovell} recently toured with Bob Seger and Keith Urban in 2017-2018. Look them up on youtube and let’s hope they put Taylor Swift out of business before the year is through...}

Now THAT is a line-up of talent any fan of real music can spend their money on. Ronnie, did it ever cross your mind to include any of these fine performers, all of whom wipe the floor with any of the Nashville puppets chosen for this CD?? Could it be that Nashville big shots behind this project were more concerned with selecting hip, popular stars than worthy talent?? I believe if Ronnie had full control over who would appear on this album, we would have had at least a handful of the great artists listed above. If you love current country music {correction: Nashville bubblegum pop/rap drivel}, this CD might be up your alley. If you value real talent and musicianship like myself {and I realize most mainstream music fans do not}, do yourself a favor and watch Ronnie's great 2005 appearance on CMT Crossroads with Los Lonely Boys on youtube. THAT is the calibre of collaboration this CD should have been! What a shame the Garza Brothers were not included in this project as they deserved to be. It would have been the highlight of the CD for me.

I know this review seems a bit harsh. Make no mistake, I certainly mean no disrespect to the living legend that IS Ronnie Milsap, a true gentleman all his life and one of the finest musical talents of the last 50 years. Somehow by the grace of God, Ronnie Lee Milsap lives on in this nightmare called mainstream music in 2019 when so many music legends have died off in the last three years alone. Thank you always Ronnie for the true musical values and decency you stand for kind sir. If this is the last album we see from him {the man is 76 and getting no younger} I wish him nothing but good health and happiness always. title: 8:30 is Better
text:
After being absolutely blown away by the three live sides of 8:30, the rumor of another live Weather Report release had me intently searching the internet for clues daily ... and the fact that the tracks would be hand-picked by Zawinul himself from recordings spanning the entire star-studded history of the band only cemented my decision to order this disc sight-unseen.
Sadly, the music does not live up to my self-induced hype (nor my memories of seeing a post-Weather Report Zawinul band in concert). The tunes which repeat from 8:30 (Black Market, Teen Town) are culled here from pre-8:30 concert dates, before the band had learned to stretch the tunes into the raucous jams and solo showcases from 8:30 that test the limits of my stereo. The other Jaco- and pre-Jaco era tunes are similarly unspectacular performances (for Weather Report, anyway). Interestingly, it's the Victor Bailey and Omar Hakim material that is the most adventurous music on Live and Unreleased, although it is not enough to save an otherwise curiously by-the-numbers outing.
I have never been a big fan of "best of" or "through the ages" live albums -- especially ones that so unnervingly jump back and forth chronologically. Give me a complete concert from start to finish anytime, warts and all (such as the brilliant Miles Davis Complete at Montreux).
Weather Report was a smokin' band, in all its incarnations ... there must be some more smokin' concert recordings available for release, just waiting to blow my stereo once again.

title: They'd Love To Turn Us On
text:
How can I do this album justice? I was ten years old when I bought my copy and since then I've probably listened to it hundreds of times. To my ears, it still sounds fresh. It still captivates me. It remains a very special place for me to go. It's had a profound influence on me as a songwriter. I adored the Fab Four before the release of "Sgt. Pepper's" but when they began to collaborate more with the 'fifth Beatle'- producer George Martin, they took rock and pop to new heights- a brave new world as it were. From the beginning sounds of an orchestra warming up amid a crowd of people murmuring (on the title track) to the final sounds on the album which consist of 1) the sound of an orchestra playing their instruments from their respective lowest notes to their highest notes and resembling something like the sound of Heaven exploding; 2) the sound of all four Beatles pounding the same chord on four different pianos simultaneously (both from "A Day In The Life"; to 3) the odd loop at the very end which one can hear much better on the CD than one ever could on the vinyl version, this album turned pop music upside down and inside out.

On "Sgt. Pepper's" you get the 'basic' rock/pop songs your growing body needs such as the intro and reprise of "Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band", the classic "With A Little Help From My Friends" lead-sung by Ringo, Paul's "Getting Better" (though John contributed the great "it couldn't get much worse" line to balance things out), Paul's "Fixing A Hole" and "Lovely Rita" (with its weird vocalizations at the end) and John's "Good Morning Good Morning" which was inspired by a TV commercial selling cereal. I grouped these tunes together because they're the least psychedelic songs on the album for the most part. For mental growth through mind expansion, the Beatles give us the lovely John-penned "Lucy In The Sky With Diamonds" which was inspired by a colorful drawing his first son Julian created. The Fabs have repeatedly denied it has anything to do with LSD. We'll leave it at that. Paul's very touching string-quartet melodrama "She's Leaving Home" is complete with gorgeous harmonies by John and George. John's "Being For The Benefit of Mr. Kite!" is one of the most psychedelic songs on the album. What makes this track so awesome is the cut up then looped tapes of calliopes playing in which the Beatles, George Martin and associates of the band all participated in the initial cutting. Mr. Martin is the one that did the final editing of these random sounds and they fit perfectly into the song. It was an astonishing feat especially considering the primitive technology of the time. Listening to this track is like being on acid at a carnival. I just love it! George's underappreciated meditation on universal love, "Within You Without You" comes next. George Martin's string arrangement beautifully compliments the basic sitar & tabla arrangement. My least favorite song on "Sgt. Pepper's" is Paul's music hall-derived "When I'm Sixty-Four" and though it's my least favorite, I still dig it- especially the very clever lyrics. Paul would go on to compose more songs in this style with each of them annoying me more and more. "Your Mother Should Know" from "Magical Mystery Tour" and "Maxwell's Silver Hammer" from "Abbey Road" are cut from the same cloth as "Sixty-Four" but don't work half as well as the original.

The album closes with what may be the Beatles' most incredible piece of music- the one-of-a-kind "A Day In The Life". John begins the song (it's mostly his composition) and Paul wrote and sings the middle part that begins "woke up, fell out of bed...". The unique, soaring orchestral part in the middle and at the end of the song was Paul's idea. George Martin has stated that John's vocals on this song are quite possibly his best. I love how vulnerable he sounds when singing "I'd love to turn you on'. Some folks may quibble about the sequencing of this album but "A Day In The Life" unarguably belongs where it is, as the most amazing 'encore' ever recorded.

On a personal note, one of my own albums titled "The Last Hurrah" (email me and I'll send a sampler of it) from 1990 was tremendously influenced by "Sgt. Pepper's". It was also inspired by "The Velvet Underground & Nico". How's that for an interesting mix?

Turn on to Sgt. Pepper's" today- they'd love to turn you on!

title: Steve Miller Band Anthology, a must for blues/rock fans
text:
STEVE MILLER BAND ANTHOLOGY REVIEW: BY Kristy
Steve Miller has played many different styles of music throughout his long career which is still continuing today. He's most known for his instant gratification songs such as: The Joker, Fly Like An Eagle, Jungle Love, Take the Money an Run, Abracadabra, and Jet Airliner. But I'd like to write a bit about his earlier style which was much closer to BBKing than The Who.
He has an honest sounding, baritone voice, not specatacular, but it does the job he's trying to do...make good music that doesn't have be shout/sung. It is especially effective when he does blues ballads, like many of the standard classics on this album, which when orginally realeased was a two LP set of their best songs from the late 60's to the early 70's which is when he still worked with now famous Boz Scaggs, which helped add a different feel to this album than his later work.
I don't have time or space to write about every single song on these albums, but I'll definately cover the highlights...although all of the songs are great in their own way.
'I Love You' is the romantic opener, subtle yet beautiful...simplistic, but I wish more rock would be like that...I think today's bands should follow Miller's example. Nice harmonica work
'Baby's House' has to be one of my favorites on this album.. you know me and my piano fetish, well this is a gentle mournful song that has this great piano solo in the middle...a little long...but like a great movie, you always wish it could last a little longer...the lyrics are bittersweet...
...
I don't care what I've heard other critics say. Steve Miller was inovative and didn't just copy other styles...that's why I wrote my own review because all of the cynics just smugly diss him, saying he was nothing but a cheap thrill in long technical terms. I strongly ugre this album to be in your music collection..second suggetion if you're new to Miller and want his greatest hits, buy The Steve MIller Band's Greatest Hits 1972-1978.

Unfortunately, it takes more than hard work and a tough Bronx upbringing to make art -- you also need talent and an interesting take on your raw material. Fat Joe may get an "A" for effort, but his new CD falls miserably short of appealing in any way. Monotonous and dull, ALL OR NOTHING relies on explicit lyrics, clichéd production tricks, and a slew of star-studded cameos to provide what little energy there is.

Even appearances by Eminem, Jennifer Lopez, Li'l Jon, Mase, Mashonda, Nelly, R. Kelly and Remy Martin don't help a whole lot. And production assists from Streetrunner, Just Blaze, Cool & Dre, Swizz Beatz, DJ Khaled, and Timbaland don't pull this project out of the mush pit either. There's no musical consistency and the individual songs aren't written well enough to make up for the apparent lack of direction.

Then there's the content. Lyrics are explicit without being clever; violent, racist, and sexist without ever getting to the point. Fat Joe may hang out with the big boys, and hang in there as a recording artist, but he's going to have to work a lot harder to hold his own as an artistic peer.

title: Broken Promises, Frustrated Expectations
text:
I decided first not to be put off by the fact that this artist has been sainted in one of those slumming, breathlessly near-whispered music reviews on NPR. That's a bold entry in the debit column, but it shouldn't trigger an asset sale.

So, giving it a few listens, I came away with this: this CD is uncommonly good on first listen, mainly because of the artist's ear for a good melody. The lyrical quality, though, is uneven, not across songs, but within them; pulling off early, sometimes eye-popping poetic feats, he creates an expectation that he can't sustain, so that virtually every song on the CD becomes finally disappointing.

Here, for example, is a verse from "Lua" (just trust me that the iambs really work with the song's see-saw rhythm):

I know you have a heavy heart.

I can feel it when we kiss.

So many men stronger than me

Have thrown their backs out trying to lift it.

But me, I'm not a gamble;

You can count on me to split.

The love I sell you in the evening

In the morning won't exist.

I love it. But then the song drags on. I forget how it ends. I just remember a verse that starts, "When I'm alone, I can be my own best friend". This evokes the dark side of Paul Simon and sent me lunging for the scan button.

Here's an example from "Landlocked Blues" that illustrates even more perfectly what I'm referring to:

I found a liquid cure

For these landlocked blues,

They will move away like a slow parade,

They're leaving but you don't know how soon.

That simile is inspired, and it gets, if not better, not much worse:

We made love on the living room floor

With the noise in the background of a televised war

In the deafening pleasure, I heard someone say,

If we walk away, they'll walk away.

OK, so no conflict since the Spanish American war has been quite that straightforward, but I still think this is admirably ambitious stuff. Then comes the perfectly unnecessary suicide moment, the vague, brainless scream that warms the hackles of nostalgic boomers who have traded in a worn-out irony for an inchoate earnestness that's apparently an end in itself:

But greed is a bottomless pit,

And our freedom's a joke, we're just taking a piss,

And the whole world must watch the sad comic display

If you're still free start running away

(CAUSE WE'RE COMING FOR YOU!)

Oh yeah? Try warbling that in Pyongyang, you entitled, epicene little prick.

Finally, in "We are Nowhere, This is Now":

Why are you scared to dream of God

When it's salvation that you want?

You see, stars that clear have been dead for years

But the idea just lives on....

Yet another simply arresting setup, followed by a chorus in which Emmylou Harris's crystal drawl promises to charm everything in earshot. I just don't remember where the song goes after this. I really don't.

I don't think this guy's voice is bad. I think it's fake, a memorized sort of tremulous folk castrato that makes you alternately want to laugh and to fatherly remind the singer that he's a man and should sing like one.

title: Critics, you know what you are?
text:
Every time a new Nine Inch Nails album comes out, a huge sect of Trent Reznor fans change their minds about how much they like his music. Something I've always liked about Trent Reznor is his integrity, never sacrificing his own artistic opinion in order to please his critical and demanding fans. With Teeth is not what I was expecting, and that's probably the best thing about it.

Listening to the first track, 'All The Love In The World,' which is minimalist and somewhat repetitive, a fan could be quick to criticize Trent's entire body of work. But after hearing Reznor scream at himself in agonizingly personal songs like 'You Know What You Are' and listening to the reznoresk message in 'The Hand That Feeds,' With Teeth forced itself onto my favorites list.

Reznor changes his style with each album not necessarily for the better, but certainly not for the worse. The absence of the lyric booklet in the case might bug you like it did me, but listen to what he has to say before you toss Nine Inch Nails completely.

It's a good album, more fragile than The Fragile, I think.

title: You Won't Find A Better Loser
text:
I came late to the game in my appreciation of this album, but once it got imbedded in my soul/heart/skull it let me know that it was not going away. Please note that this review is for the 2-CD 40th Anniversary Deluxe Edition (the mix is closer to the original vinyl LP edition and that's a good thing, though my core belief is that you can never have too many versions of this masterpiece).

The band was doomed and if you don't believe me, dig a little deeper into the history, I personally was amazed that there WAS a history, with all due respect, I used to see that LP cover when I was a youngster and thought it looked kind of bland but now the cover art stops me dead in my tracks. There is a heaviness to the soul entwined with the blues (Clapton's most anguished playing/singing) on display here like an open smorgasbord heart that almost hurts to listen to, but if you have been hurt and felt the pain before, it will attract you like a newborn baby needs it's Momma.

Of course, this record had Duane Allman deputized at the last moment to lace the proceedings (all but 2 songs, I believe) with fierce/majestic/transcendent slide guitar, forever associating him as a member here, but the rest of the band is totally playing in cohesion and on all cylinders creating a document to be reckoned with.

Bobby Whitlock has so much soul in every nuance/grunt/howl of his vocals and organ/piano (as well as acoustic guitar) that he could probably be considered as the true heart/center/soul of the band.

Carl Radle's bass is so solid you couldn't separate it from this album with a jackhammer.

Renowned session drummer Jim Gordon is perfection personified and please believe me when I say "perfection" I mean that in the truest organic sense, and NOT in the way much of modern recording robs records of any soul there is to be had by perfection via tweaking any computer-perceived imperfections out of the sound leaving it lifeless and dry and...computerized. Gordon was at the top of his already mountain-peaked game on these recordings, and his downfall was to be the most tragic of all.

The extra tracks are all essential listening, but if you are coming in with new ears to this record, I recommend you play nothing but the first disc (which contains all the tracks from the original 2-LP Set in their original running order) a few times at least to let it sink in good. It is a dense record that some have looked down their nose at regarding the production, but after 3 listens it got under my skin and began to penetrate deeper with each subsequent listen. By the 4th time some of this record moved me to tears, while others had me grinning and feeling gratitude to be still alive and finally hearing this music that I had ignored for 40 years. It's that powerful.

title: Another Ray Lynch classic. Excellent!
text: With Deep Breakfast having already become one of my favorite albums of all time, I was excited to see the release of No Blue Thing, purchasing the CD the very day it was released. I was apprehensive, wondering how Lynch could possibly create anything comparable to his previous masterpiece. When the title track began playing, I was more than impressed, feeling as if I had been reunited with an old friend. This artist conveys many moods in his music, from carefree joy and playfulness to a deep, contemplative reverence toward life. He again captures a wide scope of human emotions on NBT, something he seems gifted at. Ray Lynch music is unique, plain and simple. You won't find it sounding like anything else though if you enjoy Jarre, Oldfield or Tangerine Dream, you'll be pleased. I particularly like Lynch's clever and melodic use of electronic sequences and NBT surprised me with beautiful and more complex rhythms in this regard. If you enjoy clean, crisp sound and a soundstage extending beyond your speakers, this CD will delight you too, not to mention solid deep bass notes that at higher volumes might challenge even the best loudspeakers. Like Deep Breakfast, sound quality is impeccable, if not more dynamic and translucent. I found myself getting lost in this new and wonderful collection of songs, forgetting all else as the Mr. Lynch takes me on another soothing and relaxing musical journey. The tunes are playful (Homeward At Last & No Blue Thing), spiritual, (Drifted In A Deeper Land,) and often inspiring and uplifting, (The True Spirit Of Mom & Dad.) He once again proves he is a master craftsman at integrating traditional and electronic instruments, however the music on NBT is more polished and confident, suggesting that he continues to mature as a composer and musician. NBT is a splendid follow-up to Deep Breakfast, and will delight nearly all music lovers. Listen to the samples and order this CD - you won't be disappointed! HH

title: A Fair Sampling of Recent Commercial Trance
text:
Simply put, this is a cheesy trance album with a handful of exceptions. It's unmixed of course, with tracks from all the familiar faces: Lasgo, BT, Motorcycle, DJ Sammy, Ian Van Dahl, 4 Strings, Darude, and Paul Van Dyk. New trance listeners need not be alarmed. This provides a fair sampling of commercial trance in the 00's.

Alone - Vocal Trance Provolone... this is minimalist commercial trance over rolling drums and aural key sirens. Not very good.
Simply Being Loved - Here's a refreshing track, although it's not your conventional trance. The lower frequencies flutter in this one, and the vocal tweaks are wicked.
As The Rush Comes - I don't know how many different trance mixes this song actually appears on, but there are many versions out there. This is the original radio cut - quality.
Sunlight - Arguably better most of Dj SAmmy's other work, this is one of the good tracks on this album.
Reason - I just have to say that it's cute. If I was a twelve year old girl living in a New York suburb, I might get my rocks off to this song. Either way, I'm not a big fan of it.
Diving - Excellent trance song with a superb driving beat. Great vocal accompaniment, awesome ambient effects. This is classic trance.
Music - Not a fan.
Beautiful Things - The best track on the album. This is the original radio cut and it shines like gold. Awesome string sound and bass line.
Am I On Your Mind - Decent cheese trance. I don't mind hearing this one now and again.
The Way - Like Show Me A Sign by Kontakt, this song sounds like it borrowed elements from Binary Finary's 1998. It's an alright song for cheesy trance.
Nothing But You - A radical release from Paul Van Dyk that just happened to work. This is an extremely uplifting dance track. One of the best on the album.
Get Better - I don't like to think of this as trance. I'd rather think of it as dance. It's decent, but I'm not a fan.
Show Me A Sign - As said before, this song sounds like 1999. It's decent trance cheese, so it's appropriately way over the top.
Is This Love - Ah, cheese.
Désenchantée - Decent, but ultimately... cheese.

If anything, buy this album for the good tracks from BT, Paul Van Dyk, 4 Strings, Andain, and Motorcycle. This is a decent release but it just can't compete with the DJ compilations out there. If you want radio edits, buy stuff like this.

title: Progressive JB on 45rpm
text:
The subtitle of this CD set, on the jacket reverse side, says "The Swingin' James Brown" and at first the longtime fan/student/historian is taken aback - "swingin'"? - what about the "funk". Well, the truth is, that *swingin'* jazz was everpresent in his 1969-1970 singles, as Pee Wee Ellis, Dave Matthews, et. al., understood that James Brown's Jazz was perhaps as important as his Gospel. How can you dissect "Gittin' A Little Hipper, Part Two" [Disc 2/Track 7] components and leave out jazz?
So we are presented here with JB's most intellectual recordings, with few exceptions (recuts of "It Was You" and "Bewildered"), progressive musically and deeply philospohical lyrically. But be assured that rhythms are typically all-involving for the musicians and for the listenes.
For this Reviewer, the chance to have on CD material that was not pressed on domestic l.p. at the time ("The Drunk"; the first studio remake of "Bewildered" - notable as a "G-rated" version in comparison to other JB period renditions); or pressed on domestic CD until now ("I'm Not Demanding - Part 1; "Any Day Now", "World - Part 1/2", "Let It Be Me" with Vicki Anderson). Although "It's Christmas Time" was found on the "Forever Soul Christmas" CD not long ago, those unfamiliar with said release will be astonsihed by one of the most sensitive performances of James Brown's career. I enjoy saying that his Christmas music is exceptional in his catalogue (or anyone's catalogue) Alan Leeds' expert analysis of the tracks is a bright aspect of the package; the sessionography will leave no one disappointed.
If I can pick out two highlights at this juncture, having just listened over headphones to this item, "World - Part 1" and "The Drunk" (instrumental) make the cut. The ballad has traveled through time well, and should be an enjoyable listen especially for those who recall his Music Scene TV Show and Joey Bishop Show performances at the time. On the Bishop Show he was asked to sing it a second time, so as to emphasize the *lyrics*. Strong and weak verses alternate through a full orchestral arrangement and the chart numbers do not suggest a "failure", as implied in the notes. If one studies Elvis' "If I Can Dream", Frank Valli's "To Give", or John Lennon's "Imagine", he'll/she'll find some "naive" sentiments, as well.
Somewhere in the copious notes is mention of...Volume 7. A happier circumstance in Pop music you won't find in '09. Let's work our way up to "Dooley's Junkyard Dogs"!

title: Epic Music for the Tale of Christ
text: Miklos Rozsa was one of the grand masters of epic film music. "King of Kings" ranks high as the best of his scores, a film score that is awesome, inspiring, and powerfully moving. I think "Ben-Hur," is his best score, possibly the best film score ever written for an epic film, but "King of Kings" is also superb. Rozsa, born in Hungary, weaves his narrative themes of the birth of Christ and the music powerfully drives this famous tale. The emotional force of the music is overwhelming, with brutal Roman Marches, choral music and themes, and tender loving themes of Mary and Jesus. Again, this score was out in just excerpts but now the entire score can be listened to and enjoyed for all the power its composer infused into it. Miklos Rozsa was for decades, the high standard bearer for epic film scores. Many musical themes in "King of Kings" echo "Ben-Hur" and this is understandable as they deal with similar stories.Fans of great film music will enjoy this double CD for its religious themes, tonal beauties and great power.Rozsa takes us back into ancient history and brings that history alive. Very few composers have equaled what Rozsa accomplished. Highly recommended and also buy "Ben-Hur" and "El Cid" to listen to Miklos Rozsa at the top of his art of composing film music.

title: Michelle Branch is this year's best new artist!
text:
Michelle Branch is this year's best new artist.
In an age when teenagers are seemingly (and unfortunately) puppets of the industry, churning out sugar pop and mimicking each other's style, it's refreshing to discover a truly talented young artist. Michelle is "only" 18, yet she outshines many female performers more than twice her age.
Michelle writes her own music, plays the guitar, and has one fantastic voice. With her surprisingly mature sound and hook-laden refrains, look for Michelle to quickly develop a large and diverse fan base, from teenagers to baby boomers.
I have over 500 CDs in my collection, ranging from Madonna, Depeche Mode, and Prince to Blink 182, Eve 6, and Outkast. I like all genres of music. Thus far, "The Spirit Room" is this year's biggest breakthrough and most consistent album; the CD has 11 potential singles. I rarely write reviews for Amazon, but could not resist spreading the word on this stunning disc.
Her first radio cut, "Everywhere," is beginning to gain radio exposure, and is featured in the film "American Pie II." It's infectious.
"All You Wanted" is my choice for the second single. Once again an amazing hook.
Other standouts include "You Set Me Free" (as close to the teen pop sound as she gets, while maintaining her integrity), "Something To Sleep To" (one part Fiona Apple, one part the Beatles), "If Only She Knew" (unique song structure), and "Drop in the Ocean" (displays her impressive vocal range).
Look for Michelle to be a critical and commercial favorite this summer and fall. I'll also predict she'll be nominated for Best New Artist at the Grammys.
Yes, it's that good. Don't hesitate on this one.

title: AWESOME Country tinged Power-Pop
text:
Brian Wilson once referred to the songs of "Pet Sounds" as "Teenage Symphonies to God" and Velvet Crush, showing their true allegiance to 60's pop, comes through "big-time" in their tribute to the Beach Boys, the Byrds and all those other influential, jangly bands of the 60's and 70's (If the CD cover ISN'T a dead-on imitation of so many 60's "STEREO" or "DYNAGROVE" jackets I don't know what is!!! By itself it takes me back to my living room floor in the 60's).
The cover of Gene Clark's "Why Not Your Baby" is nearly worth the CD's price! Add in oughta be hits such as "Hold Me Up", "Time Wraps Around You" and "My Blank Pages" (a clever turn on a Dylan "title" covered by the Byrds) along with the other eight pop-masterpieces on this disc and you've got yourself some real toe-tapping, hum-along, rock'n'roll music.
These guys don't record often, and this one is a must have for lovers of rock melody. Put them on your list of 90's power-pop greats along with Teenage Fanclub, Catherine Wheel and some other "retro-pop" bands recording today. Buy this CD then sit back and enjoy, it may be a while before you put it back in its jewel case!

title: High praise, indeed.
text:
"Even if you have such basic sets of the six Brandenburg Concertos and four Orchestral Suites as that with Trevor Pinnock and the English Concert (Archiv 423 492-2Ax3) and that with the Adolph Busch Chamber Players (EMI CDH-7640472), there are still others to be recommended for the insights and vitality of the performances such as that with Pablo Casals conducting the Marlboro Festival Orchestra (Sony SMK-46253, SMK-46254, SMK-45892)—and the list could go on beyond reasonable shelf space or moderate thrift. Yet, there is something winning about these three discs featuring Helmut Winschermann and the Deutsche Bachsolisten. There is an exuberant joy and rhythmic vigor to the opening movement of Brandenburg No. 3, a dulcet poetry in the rendering of the Andante of No. 2 that is never sentimental. Throughout, the tempos are somewhat slower than Pinnock's, Hogwood's, or Koopman's among the original-instruments groups but not quite as spacious as those adopted by Adolph Busch. Often they are closest to those chosen by Casals. Harpsichordist Johann Sonnleitner is positioned sufficiently back so that his instrument never gains undue sonic prominence while always audible. His solo followed by the entrance of the strings in the Adagio of No. 3 is especially noteworthy and his contribution to No. 5 with its extended solos in the opening Allegro rank with the best. There is overall a blending of sonority with clarity and transparency of texture, a roundness of tonality, if you will, but without the crisp precision for which Pinnock strove so assidulously, a more luxurious sensuosity, less disciplined austerity. Christian Altenburger is to be particularly commended for his violin solos in No. 4, and the opening movement of No. 6 is both rapturous and exhilarating.

It is quite the same with the Orchestral Suites, with tempos slightly more expansive than Pinnock's, an energetic élan, lyrical warmth, and once more in the slower movements scintillating solos. Paul Meisen's flute solos in the Orchestral Suite No. 2 are radiant and yet they are always balanced and integrated with the orchestral textures, not invariably the case with this suite. Similarly, the flute and harpsichord interchanges in the Brandenburg No. 5 are quite affecting, poignant, and delicately molded.

Since these three discs are separately packaged, if only one is to be sampled it might well be that containing the Orchestral Suites Nos. 3 and 4 and the two concertos, BWV 1060 and BWV 1063. The jubilation of the overture in No. 3, the delicate gossamer of the phrasing in the Air, and the concluding dance are enthralling. No. 4 is hardly less attractive with flowing tempos and well-sprung rhythmic resilience. Although Ton Koopman and the Amsterdam Baroque Orchestra evoke more grandeur in their recordings of the Orchestral Suites (Deutsche Harmonia Mundi/BMG GD-77008), Winschermann and the Deutsche Bachsolisten are their match for expressiveness and color. The Allegros in BWV 1060 are a bit faster than with Pinnock (Archiv 413 731-2) and the Adagio is a bit slower, but all to very fine effect. Tempos are about the same between the two groups when it comes to BWV 1063, but this performance has a more graceful Alla Siciliana than Pinnock's with The English Concert (Archiv 400 041-2). Such fine performances and vividly defined sound coupled with the bargain price provide what for many might well serve as the basic set for this music. "

Jon Tuska, Fanfare Magazine 1994

His comparison to the incomparable Casals set is apt, but at the give-away used prices for this set, anyone wanting another set of this glorious music can't go wrong. HIGHLY RECOMMENDED!

title: Moderately good singing; poor aria selection.
text:
I bought "Aria" from Amazon.com a couple days ago, and I just listened to it an hour ago. I was surprised at how good Andrea Bocelli's operatic singing voice is. I'd read many reviews giving him a rating of 0 or 1 out of 10, so I was prepared for the worst. But this fellow is actually pretty good. I'd say, 7 out of 10. Not as good as Placido Domingo or Luciano Pavarotti, but then, no one is. On the plus side, Bocelli's operatic tenor singing voice is rich and sonorous, capable of fluid vibrato and good pitch range and dynamic range, and he nicely avoids the highly-nasal resonance so noticable in his pop singing. On the negative side, his highs sound a little forced and a little raspy, and sometimes his vibrato reverts to the fluttery sound he uses in his pop music. All in all, Bocelli is a good, but not great, opera singer.

I didn't like the music selection on this album, though. Whoever selected the music should have put some more emotional, evocative arias in here. None of these arias really move me very much, and none have the emotional clout of truly great arias such as Nessun Dorma from Puccini's Turandot. I'd dearly love to hear Bocelli attempt Nessun Dorma; that would be fascinating. But there's nothing like that on this album.

Bottom line: I give this album only 3 stars, because while the singing is good, the music selection, in my opinion, is weak.
