title: Almost But Not Quite A Worthy Successor
text:
Contrary to the other review, Edita Gruberova singing scenes and arias from the three Donizetti Tudor Queen trilogy operas is not a worthy successor to Beverly Sill's triumphant performances. Edita Gruberova was just one of the many coloratura sopranos who were engaging in dramatic roles in the 60's and 70's revivals of bel canto operas, most of which were Donizetti. Edita Gruberova on this cd sings the entire Mad Scene and finale of Anna Bolena, the tragic story of Anne Boylen and her death at the hands of her furious husband, King Henry the 8th, who executed her for adultery in order to marry his next wife, Jane Seymour. Edita Gruberova's uneven coloratura, shrill vocal styling and seemingly incomplete technique does not measure up to Beverly Sill's masterful performance as Anne Boylen. The same applies to the other roles, Mary Stewart and Queen Elizabeth I. Donizetti's Maria Stuarda deals with the tragedy of the Catholic queen Mary, who, according to the fictitious opera, insulted Elizabeth I and rivaled her as Queen. For this, and her supposed conspiracy, she was executed. The Confession Scene and other lyric arias that are key moments for Mary in the opera should be sung with convincing suffering and pathos, but Edita does not meet the standards of the role. Again, Beverly Sills takes the trophy for a great Mary Stewart.
Roberto Devereaux was Donizetti's last opera. It dealt with the intense unrequited love of Elizabeth I in her old age to the dashing naval commander, Robert Devereaux, Earl of Essex. When she discovers he loves the Duchess Sara, and has betrayed her politically as well, the Queen sentences Devereaux to death. The part of Elizabeth I in this opera is the most demanding and high caliber role for a dramatic soprano, at equal grounds with Bellini's title heroine Norma. The part must be very varied- lyric, expressive in coloratura in the first act when we see how much she loves Devereaux and full of dramatic fire and fury toward the second act and finally, choked with grief and remorse upon failing to save Devereaux from his fate. The arias Edita Gruberova sings here are the final ones for the Queen- "Vivi Ingrato" and "Quell Sangre Versato", which express her lament upon Devereau's demise. Again, Gruberova fails to be convincing and dramatic. She sings purely in the bel canto tradition, all fluff and vocal beauty without the necessary substance and dramatic weight to make the opera greater and as Donizetti intended. For a great Edita Gruberova performance, in a Donizetti opera, listen to her in "Maria Di Rohan", in which she vividly and dramatically portrays another English monarch. For some reason, this obscure opera she revived looks and sounds great at her hands. It would be the only dramatic role she truly made legendary.

text:
I acquired this recording as part of a reissue on the Zigzag label of Italian baroque music featuring Ensemble 415 (led by the famed Swiss violinist Chiara Bianchini). Ensemble 415 has been on the baroque music stage since the ‘80s. They have a sterling reputation in a broad range of baroque, pre-baroque and early classical repertoire. I have many of their recordings and hold them in very high esteem.

Extremely enjoyable, not only because of the quality of the performances (absolutely first rate) but also because of the beauty of the music itself. Albinoni’s sonatas opus 2 are seldom heard or recorded, and bring to light a very different musical perspective of a Venetian composer whose current fame rests more on his oboe concerti and the unfortunately misattributed “adagio in g minor”. Ensemble 415 renders the sonatas beautifully.
I've owned several other recordings of Albinoni sonatas (including two different versions of his op 1.) While these others also have much to recommend them, I'd say this one goes to the top of the heap.

This is a CD you can listen to all at once or dip into as the mood beckons. Highly recommended.

title: As a huge Janet fan, I am profoundly disappointed.
text:
This is a bad album.

I could not be more disappointed in Janet...the decline in quality of her last few albums is astonishing. She can't even out-imitate her imitators.

Seriously, Ciara, Rihanna...pretty much every solo female pop singer with a dance/hip-hop bent owes her career to Miss Jackson. Starting with Control, and on through Rhythm Nation, Janet, and The Velvet Rope, she had crafted a strong catalog of the best pop music heard on the planet.

True, the "Janet" album suffered from too much "sameness", and "The Velvet Rope" album, with it's darker tone, took a little while to sink in.

"All For You" had a few killer singles, but not much else.

"Damita Jo" had one. And it wasn't that "killer". If Britney Spears had released that album, people would have said it would have been bad even for Britney.

We expect more from Janet.

"20 Y.O." opens with a catastrophically generic, melody-free "I'm So Excited." The next song, "Show Me", has the exact same tempo, the same beat...it's the same song.

"Get It Out Me", besides the head-scratching title, is awful. First, the verses are sung in this weak falsetto, with her lower register singing in a voice that sounds exactly and distractingly like her brother, Michael.

I know there have been many jokes over the years about the two of them, but I never agreed with the idea that they were interchangeable. I guarantee you will think immediately of him during this song, and not in a good way.

After four disappointing tracks, it actually gets worse with "Do It 2 Me". It sounds like she's trying WAY too hard to be "modern." And what is it with these song titles? Show me, get it out me, do it to me, call on me...doesn't this show a lack of creativity right there?

"This Body" continues her streak. She did this before, and better. A thousand times. Three times on the "Velvet Rope" album alone.

"With U" is at least pleasant sounding. A standard ballad of hers...think "Again" or "Let's Wait Awhile"...but not as catchy or dramatic. And too long at five minutes.

"Call On Me" is her duet with Nelly, but it's a weak copy of "Dilemma." At least it sounds more organic than the other intrusive rapping earlier in the record.

Then we come to "Daybreak", the first song on the record that'll perk up your ears and say, out loud, "Finally!"

In the same vein as "Escapade" and "When I Think of You", it has a bouncy, easy tempo and a melody you cannot get out of your head, just like all great pop music should be. This is "new" Janet looking back on "old" Janet in a terrific fashion. It sounds classic and new all at the same time. Her voice sounds fine; she sounds happy and comfortable.

AND it's the first song that Jermaine Dupri is not listed as a co-producer. Hmmm.

"Enjoy" is also not too bad...an easy, shuffling, head-bobbing beat...a simple melody, verse and chorus. It would have been the seventh single off an earlier album. Here it glows in comparison.

Also, no Dupri.

Y'know how many of her earlier albums ended with a bunch of slow songs? Here ya get "Take Care" and "Love 2 Love", and they're fine. "Baby-making" music, if you must. But a bit heavy-handed.

There's a reason this album isn't selling well. It's not that good, and they're not picking good singles.

"Daybreak" should have been the end-of-summer hit of the year.

I just don't know where Janet fits in today's popular music environment. I love this woman to death; I've been to her concerts; have all of the records...and will continue to buy her albums the day they come out...but being honest, I am profoundly disappointed.

I guess I want her to blow me away each time a new record comes out, and she hasn't done that in a long, long time.

title: Deep Within is Exquisitely Enchanting
text: This is definitely my absolute favorite of Gary Stadler's CD's. This latest collaboration with bewitching vocalist Wendy Rule takes Gary's enchanting music into a whole new dimension, a somewhat darker place within the mystical Fairie realms. Gary Stadler has made some incredible music over the last decade with some pretty spectacular female vocalists including the late Singh Kaur on the dreamy Fairy Night Songs and Stephannie on the magically inspired Fairy Heart Magic (my favorite until this one). But Deep Within A Faerie Forest is more hauntingly beautiful and more deeply moving and stirring than his previous releases. Rule's vocals are sensuous, lush and quivering with a fantastic intensity while still remaining diaphanously radiant and pure and the lyrics are just extraordinary. And Gary's piano work combined with Lisa Lynne's harp has never sounded better. Each song possesses a unique quality, like individual fairytales woven into a sparkling magical veil, each with it's own distinct feeling, taking you deeper into the mythic. "Midwinter" is my very favorite with lyrics that just want to make me run into the forest and never return. Thank you Gary Stadler for making the Faerie realms more and more real with each new album. Ooops ! Are those wings coming out of my shoulders ! Magick Happens !

text:
For 20 years, I looked at the Division Bell as the final chapter of the greatest rock band ever, and High Hopes as the grand finale of the whole act. Thus listening to the final track had always filled me with sadness and so much joy at the same time.
Today, when I learned that the 15th album of the Pink Floyd is on its way, I am all joy and from this point on The High Hopes would be the bridge that links the Division Bell to the Endless River album.
As much as I love Roger Waters, if he was with the band at time that they were recording the Division Bell, the album would not have been the same. His departure sparked the creativity flame in the band and they no longer depended on him. Wright and Gilmour shine here with their work.
Looking forward to the Endless River release.

title: Hilarious
text:
There are three tracks on this "single", the ceterpiece of which is a remixed "Only Time". I have to admit, the first time I listened to it, my reaction was "wow, that's really awful". Forget the usual layered Enya vocals, the lush synthesizer harmonies, all the usual Enya trademarks, this is just the original Only Time track turned down a bit, with some jerk playing a cheap-o Casio synthesizer a bit too loud. My wife's first question on hearing it was "Did Enya authorise this?". I don't know; she certainly didn't put her name on the "work" for this remix, which is credited to others.
That's as may be, but by the second listen I had firmly latched on the rather obvious comedic value. There is absolutely nothing like this in your Enya collection, I guarentee you. This really is so bad it's good. I can't listen to it without chuckling, and there isn't much in life that will offer such reliable humor.
As for the other tracks, Oiche Chiun has been previously released on the single with the same name, and is a nice rendition of the Christmas classic - although it lacks the usual Enya richness, more a vocal piece like Marble Halls from Shepherd Moons (although not as rich). Willows on the Water is a nice instrumental track that hasn't been released elsewhere that I know of, but had it been included it would probably be about the 8th-best track on A Day Without Rain, if you are torn between purchases.
In all, well worth the offering price - especially for the Enya fan, who really should listen to the remixed Only Time at least once. Certainly not comparable to A Day Without Rain in value, but good nontheless.

title: A Review of the original (NOT the alleged BOOTLEG)
text:
Way back in the early 90's after Tori Amos had released "Little Earthquakes" and was gaining much critical and commercial buzz, I heard about this out-of-print "first album." As has been stated here ad nauseam, Amos had released it with a group of studio musicians and the end result was something less than memorable - a Kate Bush-meets-Starship lite-metal piece of forgettable pop fluff. To be honest, I've always thought Tori Amos was an American version of Kate Bush and Bush's pop eclecticism and brand of Celtic/Tolkien mysticism runs apparent through most of Amos's in-print catalogue. I don't know how much Amos admits Bush as a major influence, but it can't be denied, especially on two songs on "Y Kant Tori Read": "Cool On Your Island" and "Fire On The Side." And the beats on "The Big Picture" could be argued as being lifted from Kate's "The Big Sky" (on Hounds of Love).

One day, I was visiting The Wall (remember that record store?!?) at a mall in a neighboring state, back in the heyday on the infamous long box, when I happened to notice the title "Y Kant Tori Read." I picked it up, paid a measly $13 bucks plus tax for it, and now sit back and laugh that people are willing to spend close to $100 for a new copy. It's always been a guilty pleasure of mine, and I file it in my CD collection under Tori Amos.

By the way, the original album stops with "The Etienne Trilogy." Overall, it's not a great album but it is pleasant to listen to. I do not regret purchasing it. However, I would strongly suggest that you seek out used copies of the original Atlantic release.

title: The right kind of TANNHÄUSER
text:
I agree wholeheartedly with Mr. Foster's review. And, ever since I first bought this recording on LP back in 1977 (and this is certainly a documentable case of CD sound being less than its earlier LP pressing), I too have not hesitated to declare this recording to be the best one available--certainly for all of the reasons that Mr. Foster cites, but for a few others as well.

I continue to be amazed by the vocal characterization that Wolfgang Windgassen brings to the role of Tannhäuser. Certainly by this time in his career some wear and tear were becoming evident in Windgassen's singing, but he more than makes up for it by the unforgettable intensity and insight he offers. The recording stands as an objective lesson for singers in any age that what can make for an exemplary vocal performance is not necessarily technique, heft, or, as is now so depressingly the case, 'looking the part', but musical intelligence and the ability to make a role be more than just a certain singer's appearance in it.

I cannot recommend this recording too strongly: Sawallisch's handling of the score is remarkably free of idiosyncrasy, convincingly musical, and true to both the glories and the subtleties it contains. As for the other singers in the cast, Anja Silja's Elisabeth has its own powerful intensity, and, whether it's medieval ecstasy or resignation, her youthful soprano delivers; Eberhard Waechter's nobly executed Wolfram does not disappoint; Josef Greindl's Landgraf Hermann has a smooth and honest quality about it, and all of the other supporting singers represent some of the best that the New Bayreuth had to offer.

And finally, this is a live recording, and not only does it sound like one but it also sounds like a live recording of what must have been a stupendous performance for those present. There is in any live performance a living pulse, a direction and a momentum that has its own ebb and flow. This recording conveys some of those inexpressible particularities--small pauses, open places where one is left to wonder, and, because it is a recording, points where the imagination gladly works with what the performance is already managing on its own. Some live recordings don't generate much electricity--they sound like studio takes with audience noise added--but this Tannhauser stands as a true festival evening thankfully preserved for the ages.

[Note: This recording did receive the Grand Prix Du Disque.]

title: Five Stars Yes, but Throw Away Two Cuts
text: Disembodied singing heads (Out of Our Heads, after all), "like Bob Hope entertaining the troops," figure prominently in the mostly spoken word Dancing in the Head and Bob Hope and Charity.  They, and the spoken intro to Stonehead, are truly grating.  But the rest of OOOH is terrific, excellent songs of loss, faith, evil, love, resignation and endurance set to music that draws on all the genres the Mekons have made their own through almost three decades, a little punk, a little pop, a good deal of avant-country.  Haunting, unsettling, sometimes flat vocals complete the striking mix.  Favorites: Take His Name in Vain, with its tale of "old familiar vampires," Lone Pilgrim, One X One, and Stonehead with the universal reality -- "one day we'll be gone/leaving no trace/We pride ourselves that our memory/Will vanish from the memory of the world."

title: The Smiths 2.0
text:

And for those of us who selectively tuned out the vocals on Smiths songs to focus on the glorious instrumentation, there's no need to do so here.

title: I really like this album, and I'm not even a hip hop fan!
text:
My review's title says it all. I'm not a huge fan of hip hop or rap. If one were to look through my iTunes library, it would seem as though I don't even know what hip hop is. But there at the near bottom (it's sorted alphabetically) you will find an album named Attention Deficit by a rapper named Wale. And you will find that I've listened to it a fair few times.

I think the reason I enjoy this album so much is that all the songs sound so original. There isn't any cookie-cutter formula that makes Wale sound like every other Top 40 artist you'll hear on the radio. Songs like "90210" and "Shades" have catchy beats as well as smart lyrics, not just some silly garbage about watching the artist 'crank dat.' In fact, I'd say the message in 'Shades' is one of the more important ones I've heard in recent pop music. Other songs like "World Tour" and "Chillin" have that radio/club-friendly sound while still sounding refreshing. It's an album that you can hear in a club, or booming out of a car at 1AM, or in your room as you fall asleep.

I admit these aren't the deepest words one can say about an album, but I do think that anyone who even somewhat enjoys hip hop will like Wale's debut studio album. Hip hop fans will like it even more. Overall it's a great set of songs and I'm glad that Wale is putting DC on the map for a genre besides go-go and hardcore punk.

title: A Passion Play given the masterful Steve Wilson treatment - rebirth indeed! Absolutely beautiful remix, absolutely great!
text:
ANOTHER five-stars for another Steve Wilson remix of a Jethro Tull album? At the risk of sounding redundant, well, quite. Yes! Here indeed is another five-star review for another 40th anniversary remix of a classic Jethro Tull album.
Having bought this a few times over the 40 years since it first came out in 1973 - the year I graduated from high school, the same year that Dark Side of the Moon came out - I can honestly say here that buying it yet again in this set is DEFINITELY worth it. The remix is so good the album sounds brand new, totally fresh. I absolutely love it!
Like all of the 40th Anniversary Tull releases of late the entire thing is packaged beautifully. A little pricey you might say? Perhaps. But definitely worth it. Every penny! The five Jethro Tull albums from 1971 to 1975 - Aqualung, Thick As A Brick, A Passion Play, Warchild and Minstrel In The Gallery - have all been lovingly ( yes I do mean lovingly, for this has no doubt been a labor of love and a gift from Ian Anderson and Steve Wilson to all of us longtime Jethro Tull fans ) re-created and given a completely new life forty years on. I am enjoying all of them as I did when I first bought the albums in the 70s. HIGHLY RECOMMENDED!!!!!!!

title: Though uneven and definitely not for everyone, "Adventures" is an influential album that ambient fans will love
text:
The Orb's "Adventures Beyond The Ultraworld" was essentially one of if not THE first ambient house album (it at least inspired other artists and (somewhat) popularized the genre - "Little Fluffy Clouds" is a very appealing track). It is, admittedly, a little uneven. If you've only heard the song "Little Fluffy Clouds", be prepared for a quick change of pace. The rest of the album is very ambient and very experimental, but for ambient fans and the open-minded it's very interesting stuff to listen to. My personal favorites are the first three tracks, and the rest I don't think are as fun to listen to as a whole (they're definitely very good, though). It's not ambient in a traditional sense - there's definitely a beat in most of the songs which help keep them accessible. What's also great is how you're essentially getting two albums for the price of one (actually more like the price of 1.5 albums)! If it weren't for this fact and its influence on the world of music, I probably would've given it a 4.5. Ambient and electronica fans will definitely love it, though. Even if most people won't like the album as a whole, they'll most likely enjoy "Little Fluffy Clouds". Highly recommended!

text:
Hugh Martin is best known for writing "Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas," but this CD shows that he was also a very talented performer. His version of "Merry Little Christmas" is just beautifully performed --and is especially impressive because he was in his 90s when it was recorded.

I'd also recommend his recent memoir, "Hugh Martin: The Boy Next Door." There, he tells his story of working with theatrical luminaries like Richard Rodgers, Judy Garland, Mickey Rooney, Kay Thompson, and Noel Coward. He started in the early 1930s, worked in Hollywood in the 1940s and 50s ("Meet Me In St. Louis," among other films), and was still working in the theatre in the 1970s and 80s. Mr. Martin is now in his 90s and has told a fascinating story in this book.

text:
Yeesh! This was one big disapointment, especially after paying nearly $[money] for this. If you're expecting another mind-trip like Age Of Plastic, you'll be sorely shot down. The Buggles broke up almost right after this, and it shows. Most of the songs here sound like your everyday 80's new-wave pop.
The only real notable one is the goofy bouncy "On TV". "I Am A Camera" is a reworked wimpy version of "Into The Lens", found on the Yes album "Drama", which Geoff Downes and Trevor Horn worked on, after Jon Anderson and Rick Wakeman took a brief leave from the group. Some of the songs, such as "Rainbow Warrior" and "Inner City", will make you cringe, as Trevor's normally great singing voice turns into a mere annoying whine.
The album does have three bonus tracks: the somewhat catchy "Fade Away", "Blue Nyon" which is the weirdest Buggles song you'll ever hear, and a 12" mix of Camera which is essentially the same song, without the slow piano-driven intro. Even the liner book is a bummer, as its very lengthy and has a huge biography on the Buggles. Unfortunately, you're [stuck] unless you can read Japanese.
Bottom line: If you want a great follow-up to the immortal Age Of Plastic, get "Drama" by Yes instead. It's cheaper, much easier to find, and it rocks much harder.

title: The LotR Soundtrack is great, some reviewers are not
text:
I am shocked by the people that dare to compare the Lord of the Rings soundtrack to John Williams. First of all, I must say that I am a huge fan of film music, and John Williams is without a doubt one of my favorite composers. He is a master at creating melodies that are really masterfully integrated into a soundtrack so that it is seamless and extremely cohesive.
That said, I would like to comment on the unjust comparison that someone said (notably the reviewer from Milwaukee) about how Peter Jackson should have approached John Williams instead of Howard Shore. Certainly, when it was announced that Shore would do the music, many film music fans raised their eyebrows and said "could you repeat that?" But given the results, all harsh critics are (or at least should) be overjoyed at the completed score. I am always happy when an underrated composer (which certainly would have described Howard Shore as of a year ago) gets the chance to stun the audience with an emotional score, which is exactly what Shore did. I am amazed that someone can say the job should have been given to John Williams -- John Williams has huge blockbuster scores to do every year, how many do you think Howard Shore has had in his entire career of over a decade?
And on the subject of the Oscars, I am very glad LotR won, it was without a doubt the best score of the year. In second place would by John Williams' A.I., which is also an exceptional score, even if it lacks the scale of LotR. On a side note, John Williams' second nomination (Harry Potter) should not have been nominated, it was not a very good score.
For those of you wondering why the 4-star rating, it is simply because of the deplorable advertising used including the computer pop-ups screens which were unnecessary and irritating, the over-publicity about Enya used in the selling of the album, and the disgusting "Limited Edition" and wacko pricings that the record company has used with the retailers.

title: Good-Time Party Music
text:
Back in the 1940s, Mexican-American youth experienced a surge in awareness that they were a group of people who were no longer Mexican but who were not yet fully assimilated as Americans either. This cross-cultural tension fueled the pachuco fashion fad and, in the world of music, led to some interesting sounds coming from the barrio.
Pachuco Boogie is a sampling of the different styles then in vogue in the young Mexican-American community and is a hip collection of tunes even a p....e gringo can enjoy. Pachuco music draws not only from Mexican influences, jazz and swing, but also from Cuban mambo and rumba which were popular throughout North America in the late 1940s. The music is simple, down to earth, and is best enjoyed in a party atmosphere as most of it really jumps.
Though there are no real classics here, I like the whole CD. My favorites are bluesy cuts such as Muy Sabroso Blues, Los Blues, the rumba Los Chucos Suaves and the more traditional sounding Las Pachuquitas. Also, there is some great piano work on songs like Guisa Guacha and Chicano Boogie. If your musical horizons are broad, you'll be sure to enjoy listening to this.

title: Shame it's not one of the best Rock en Español albums
text:
Amantes de Lola came first out as the winners of a Battle-of-the-bands type of contest, holding a demo of "La Flor de Bagdad" as their introduction card on the radio. Then recorded a first self-titled album and picked up the harvest of a rock scene with few good options.

This album came out as the 2nd effort of this five-piece group. Would be very hard for them to beat Caifanes or Maldita Vecindad, althought Amantes de Lola were more in comparison with fellow musicians Fobia. "Rock en Español" at that time was at its peak, options to hear were growing, offering also many more opponents stealing attention of the audience.

Sophomore albums' fame didn't apply on "La Era del Terror". Since the intriguing title, and from begining to end, Amantes de Lola proved to be one of the best promises among Mexican rockers, since it features trips to doo-woop ("Preludio"), funk ("Valiums a tu Tia" and "Deseo"), light rythmic ballads ("Hombres y Locos" and "Hotel") and straight-forward rock ("Juego Sucio" and "No Me Dejes Caer"). Unfortunately, all the tracks are overshadowed by the excessively known "Beber de tu Sangre", but don't get caught in the trap, every track has a reason to be placed after each other -listen to "El Dios en la Pared" with heart in hand and feel, like I do, how the tears slowly come out-.

Most of the credit goes to the great voice of Kazz, who I consider one of the most under-rated vocalists in the Mexican rock scene. His voice has an enviable range and sustain that he makes seem effortless; and although across the time the arrangements still sound less 90's than 80's, the results sound cohesive (it's not a band backing up a vocalist, but a real pop rock group effort).

It's a great album, nevermind you're a nostalgic who thinks Rock en Espanol was better made before, or you're young and want to know about the roots of what's made now.

You can never go home again. You can never go home again. You can never go home again. I hate to keep repeating that but in all honesty I could probably cut off the review for Jimmy Eat World's new album "Futures" with that one sentence. Many bands have tried before Jimmy Eat World, and inevitably many more will continue to try and replicate a sound that they did previously, after abandoning it on an extremely popular album. BUT..... very few bands are ever able to pull it off. The example that comes to mind is the last studio Smashing Pumpkins album. It was an attempt to go back to the sounds of "Siamese Dreams", and it was a horrible failure. The album received attrocious reviews, and fans bailed on the band. Jimmy Eat World, thankfully does not fail as miserably.

I, like millions of others was sucked into the "Bleed America" phenomena. I hadn't so much as heard a song off the album, but at the 9.99 price tag and after reading a few solid reviews for the album I bit the bullet and picked it up. And for a while I adored that album, I played the heck out of that album. But I wasn't the only one, their singles were all over the radio, and all over muchmusic and MTV, it was practically impossible to dodge Jimmy Eat World. And yet at the time I was oblivious, I just kept on loving that album. Now, years later. The album collects dust. The radio and tv overkill of the singles makes it impossible for me to throw that album on and not skip tracks again and again. However, during their peak I was so into Jimmy Eat World that I went out and purchased their older catalogue of CDS. What I found, was an entirely different sound. Far less pop, and far more ambience and jams. Much better lyrics, and in general just a better product. "Bleed America" was Jimmy Eat World's sell out album and it worked. Perhaps too well. But there is only one problem..... you can never go back. In spite of this, Jimmy Eat World's new album "Futures" is a throwback to the older more ambient less user friendly sound that they cashed in on with "Bleed America". When I heard this I was filled with some hope that perhaps this album would be great, and when I heard the lead single "Pain" it was a quality enough songs that at 12.99 I was enticed to give the band another shot. In retrospect, I could have spent that 12.99 more wisely.

Don't buy into the hype, I have found a lot of really good reviews for this album and I think those people are somewhat misinformed. Anybody who has actually spent a lot of time listening to old Jimmy Eat World can not honestly say that this album is better or even as good as those albums. However, if you had never heard those old albums and were just going on hearsay you might ASSUME that this album is just as good. But assuming is never a good thing. When you go for broke, and sell out like Jimmy Eat World did you are stuck between a rock and a hard place. If you put out another poppy album like "Bleed America" the hardcore fans that have all your albums will give up on you, but if you go back and try to do an album like the old ones the new fans you picked up with "Bleed America" will lose interest. So inevitably the band ends up releasing something that attempts to do the impossible and satisfy everyone involved. There are some decent songs, but then there are songs I have to skip. And there are as many of those as there are decent songs. "Futures" if it does anything, tells me that Jimmy Eat World doesn't have much of a future. But hey at least they made a nice chunk of change on the last album to support Jim Adkins drug habit.

Tracks I can recommend: "Futures", "Kill", "Pain", "Drugs or Me"

text:
I have a clear memory of hearing "Thrift Shop" back in 2012. It took me a while but I eventually bought "The Heist" and it took me a while to appreciate it. In preparing my review for "Ben" I went back and listened to each Macklemore album in sequence. I'll say this, "Ben" is three stars--good, but also uneven, which is how I also felt about "Gemini" (2017) his last album. I see Ben Haggerty as a singles artist whose albums are typically uneven, but he fared better when he was with Ryan Lewis. Both of those albums stand above Macklemore's three solo albums.

One of my continual complaints about Macklemore albums is their length. "Ben" is no different with 15 tracks when there should only be 10. I tried hard to think of which 10 tracks to keep since there are many disposable songs here. I also felt the creativity was at a low point on this album as he either recycled 80's, old Macklemore & Ryan Lewis, or old school hip hop/rap. There wasn't anything new here even though he tried some new things (like singing on "1984" which doesn't quite work).

After listening for a week these songs were the ones I liked best:

"Chant", "No Bad Days", "1984", "Maniac", "Day You Die", "Sorry" and "Tail Lights" and maybe "Heroes" and "Tears". That's 9 songs out of 15. So, three stars, average. I get Ben Haggerty has been through a lot and is in recovery. I think he's pretty honest about his experiences on "Ben" and has some clever wordplay. However, the songs are quite up to snuff this time. That doesn't mean I don't look forward to his next album, I do. I'd like to see him get back with Ryan Lewis, though.

Here's how "Ben" compares to Macklemore's other works:

2005 The Language of My World: Three Stars
2012 The Heist: Four Stars
2016 This Unruly Mess I've Made: Three and a Half Stars
2017 Gemini: Two and a Half Stars
2023 Ben: Three Stars

title: Very likable early to middle Simpson symphonies with great sound.
text:
Robert Simpson, the modern British composer, openly stated his desire to bring modern music back to some sense of structure once epitomized by the symphonies of Ludwig von Beethoven. Simpson's Symphonies Nos. 2 and 4 aptly reflect that goal. In fact, Symphony 2 is scored for the same instrumental forces used by Beethoven in his first two symphonies. In this Hyperion disc, Vernon Handley conducts the Bournemouth Symphony Orchestra in performances of those two symphonies that were recorded in 1991 and 1992.

Symphony 2 begins with a quiet pastorally-styled introduction in its first of three movements. It is tonal but, as the accompanying booklet describes, driven by two keys. The movement sounds modern with musical expressions that demonstrate more interest than beauty. As is characteristic of Simpson's works, there is much rhythmic vitality interspersed with interludes of respite. The 2nd movement is a sorrowful statement with brass punctuation in theme and variations form. The 3rd movement is aggressive with an intensely driven character to it. It is frequently punctuated by brass and timpani. The coda is even fiercer.

Symphony 4 requires larger forces than the Beethoven-like ensemble of the Second. In comparison to the more modern, less accessible harmonies on Symphony 2, the Fourth is more tonal and agreeable. It is lively with much play between instruments. The 2nd movement is an impressive demonstration of big, explosive orchestration, and the movement concludes with an agitated climax is the movement's icing on the cake. The slow 3rd movement features a cello solo and comes closest to presenting an extended glimpse of an actual melody. The movement has many moments of beauty. It segues into the 4th and final movement which amounts to a turbulent struggle between minor and major mode with the former remaining dominant throughout most of the movement. The coda is pure excitement with snare leading the charge to a simple end.

Simpson is a very impressive modern symphonist with wonderful orchestrating skills. These symphonies are accessible albeit more so in the Fourth. Sound is exemplary. The cymbals of the Fourth Symphony's 4th movement, in particular are unusually life-like. The music is exciting with moments of exquisite beauty in the Fourth's Andante. VERY HIGHLY RECOMMENDED!!!

title: A Definite Must for Diana Fans
text:
This album represents one of her biggest peaks in her amazing career. She was riding high on the success of [[ASIN:B000B5XOSY Mahogany]]and had 3 strong singles from this one album. The cover alone was brilliant--a defining moment in the birth of her true DIVA status...which continued with the covers of [[ASIN:B000008K89 Baby It's Me]], [[ASIN:B00000J2RF The Boss]] and [[ASIN:B00009U5J6 Diana (Deluxe Edition)]].

This album (the vinyl record) had always been one of my favorites, and for several years was unavailable on CD (Motown was really bad about releasing her 70s music on CD in the 90s...I had to hunt for everything at used CD shops before the internet made shopping easier.) Thank you Hip-oSelect for re-issuing all her CDs as expanded editions with lots of extras. Nearly every Diana song is now available on CD except for one of her most beautiful ballads from [[ASIN:B000UTJT5S Ross (1978)]]: Where Did We Go Wrong. All the other songs from that album have been added as extras in other CDs.

Why should you buy 1976 Diana Ross? If you were a fan of the original, you will like hearing the alternative versions. Another reviewer said, "there is a reason they weren't ever released," which I understand. However, although I prefer the versions I am already familiar with, it's FUN to listen to outtakes, and hear some of the other choices she made when discovering the songs. Do you know how many countless bootlegs of Beatles Albums there are out there? Countless! And fans buy them for the exact same reason: to hear the decisions that the band was making for each song, different riffs, different harmonies, maybe even a little laughter.

But the most fantastic track on this 2 disc set for me is the interview with Diana from 1975/6, who sounds the most eloquent I have ever heard. She sounds relaxed and smart and in love with life. I am a huge fan but the first to admit that sometimes she doesn't interview well--because she might misinterpret the question or not connect with the interviewer (but her last appearance on Oprah in 2011 was probably my all time favorite interview with Diana that I've seen!) On this CD she talks about the birth of the Supremes, about working on her movies, about the tracks on this CD, and she exudes confidence and joy being exactly where she is in her life.

So for Diana novice who wants to hear her 70s hits, buy [[ASIN:B00007MB3K To Love Again]] for ballads, or [[ASIN:B00004YWW7 All The Great Hits]]. But for the people who are fans and liked [[ASIN:B00383UBV4 Touch Me In The Morning [Expanded Edition]]] or [[ASIN:B000WQJJ7W Last Time I Saw Him (Expanded Edition)]], definitely get this. If you liked the original 1976 release and want to dig deeper, get this before it goes out of print. It already happened with [[ASIN:B000BPGJIQ Where Did Our Love Go]] (another Hip-oSelect special). If I had to choose my top 20 Diana Ross songs, 6 would come from this album alone: After You, Ain't Nothin' But a Maybe, Theme from Mahogany, I Thought it Took a Little Time, Love Hangover, AND One Love In My Lifetime. SO MUCH GREAT STUFF HERE!

title: The Last 'True' Echo & the Bunnymen Album
text:
Echo & the Bunnymen's self-titled album, popularly referred to as "the gray album" (due to the color of the cover), is similar to "Ocean Rain" in the sense that it has a timeless quality and sounds fresh and new, despite the passing of years. This, their fifth studio album, comes off as a far less earnest attempt than their previous releases. Ian McCulloch's vocals are more restrained, possibly more refined and artful than before.The instrumentation isn't anything epic or grandeur like "Porcupine" or "Ocean Rain", but I think this album is a bit classier and probably more accessible for newer fans' tastes. Though there are a few tracks that stand out ("Lips Like Sugar", "Bedbugs and Ballyhoo", and "The Game", for instance), this album seems to be best listened to as a whole.

This album was really the last one that truly captured the spirit of the band; after this, the band's singer, Ian McCulloch, on to do solo work and the drummer, Pete de Freitas, died in a motorcycle accident. Their next album, "Reverberation", was released in 1990 and featured an entirely different vocalist and new drummer in place of the previous Echo & the Bunnymen members. An album featuring Ian McCulloch as vocalist, "Evergreen", did not appear until 1997. Still, after several more major album releases (in 1999, 2001, and 2005) the band hasn't yet been able to, and probably won't, regain the energy and style of music that they once made in their first five studio albums, especially due to the loss of a very critical member of a band, Pete de Freitas, Echo & the Bunnymen's incredibly talented drummer.

This re-mastered edition includes seven extra tracks: "Jimmy Brown" (an early version of "Bring on the Dancing Horses"), "Hole in the Holy" (an early version of "Over You"), "Soul Kitchen" (Doors cover), an acoustic demo of "The Game", and two B-sides ("Over Your Shoulder" and an early version of "Bedbugs and Ballyhoo").

"Joe's Garage" is a sharply-executed rock opera looking at the  "what-if" scenario of music getting banned, and focuses around  the misadventures of an aspiring rock-star named Joe. The performance of FZ  and his band is amazingly excellent and these musicians are amongst the  most talented ever. Although some may be offended by FZ's sometimes risque  wit presented in the lyrics of many of the songs, he shows off his wit in  good humor and taste, and the result is hilarious. Not to mention that FZ  as always shows off his guitar expertise. An essential Zappa album for any  rock music lover. Album Highlights: "Central Scrutinizer",  "Joe's Garage", "Catholic Girls", "Why Does It  Hurt When I Pee", "Stick It Out", "Packard Goose",  "A Little Green Rosetta".

title: Where Are They Now, And Why Aren't They Still On Top?
text:
Nickolas Ashford & Valerie Simpson have, without debate, written, produced, performed & recorded some of the most timeless songs EVER. Whether for themselves or others. Their track record is full of huge successes. Diana Ross alone owes not one, but two albums worth of kudos to this incredibly talented duo. So why in blazes aren't they still in demand on the radio or television or studio? They are what R&B is AND should be.

Right alongside Holland/Dozier/Holland, or even Stevie Wonder, they are responsible for classics such as "Let's Go Get Stoned," Ain't No Mountain High Enough," You're All I Need to Get By," "Ain't Nothing Like the Real Thing," "Reach Out and Touch Somebody's Hand" and "The Boss" to name a simply stunning five classics that will never be lost to time. Add to that the still remarkable "Solid" and "Found a Cure" from this collection and the question begs: why are they not still on, or at least very near, the top.

Pint-sized Valerie possesses more melodic soul than any wanna-be "idol" franchise may attempt to crank out. Why Motown didn't get behind her early 70s solo albums is a crime against true talent and potential. And the incredibly talented Nickolas, who's talent measures taller than his height, his own voice compares, if not beats anyone of the last 40 years. While, at face value, this collection is excellent it is pitifully short of what could be representative of this marvelous couple.

title: Sheer emotion from Poland
text:
Those who know me well acknowledge the fact that I'm a bit compulsive about the things I like. I have to admit I am that way to some extent. Some things I can't just casually enjoy, I get almost fanatical about them. Fortunately, that's only the case with a few selects things. Another thing that's part of my character, is a strong inclination towards the unconventional, that which hadn't been done yet or that which is extremely original and heartfelt. Right now, I can tell you of at least one band that fits all these bills: RIVERSIDE.

"Out of Myself", RIVERSIDE's debut album, is a concept album about one finding inner peace, understanding of himself and the surrounding world. According to the band's vocalist and bassist, Mariusz Duda, this is the first part of a trilogy dealing with the aforementioned subjects and, let me tell you, if the next two pieces are on par with this one, then I can't wait for them and this trilogy will become a huge classic.

I wouldn't say RIVERSIDE are strictly a progressive band but they surely approach it in a very strong manner. So much so that this album can clearly appeal to 70's progressive rock lovers. The closest they come to being really progressive is right on the first track, "The Same River", an ambitious 12 minute piece which goes through different moods and emotions, always showing a band that's unbelievably tight for a debut, aswell as instrumentally superior. Take for instance, right after the first section of the song, how ethereal the guitar that enters the scene at 04:40 really is. Piotr Kozieradzki's drum work is always precise yet rather complex and Michal Lapaj's keyboards provide a sweet backdrop to the song (and the rest of the album too).

Throughout the record, the idea I got is that RIVERSIDE are the perfect cross between PORCUPINE TREE (in the sense of ever present surprises and unexpected turns in their songs) and OPETH (especially with their "Damnation" album). In fact, Duda's vocals reminded me more than once of Mikael Akerfeldt's clean vocals. Also thrown in for good measure are some PINK FLOYD influences.

Speaking of Duda's vocals, rarely I listened to someone sing with such warmth and feeling. Take for example "I Believe", "Loose Heart" and especially "In Two Minds" which starts with a telephone-like sort of whispered and echoed voice (another PORCUPINE TREE trademark and possible influence) and then becomes crystal clear. This song's arrangement blew me away. This is top notch composition, as far as I'm concerned and Duda's vocals always give me goosebumps. Piotr Grudzinski's guitar work is also amazing and perfectly balanced.

"The Curtain Falls" is a more experimental tune, yet rather good, and "Ok" basically gives Duda singing softly over a sort of trip hop-ish backdrop. Interspersed within the album, are also two moody pieces "Reality Dream I" and "Reality Dream II" which serve the concept purpose of the album making use of interesting samples - the sound of a phone call producing a dial error, an alarm clock going off, a clock ticking. Both are probably the heaviest numbers on the album showing the metal side of the band. I suggest you check the section in "Reality Dream I" from 03:58 to 04:51 for the ultimate demonstration of what this band is instrumentally capable of, in particular the odd time signatures produced by Kozieradzki and of course Grudzinski's guitar work. The whole of "In Two Minds" show just how good Duda is as a singer.

The production is top notch and that's a relief because it would be a shame if such a truly beautiful piece of work got ruined by it. The worldwide release of "Out of Myself" features cover art designed by Travis Smith (of OPETH and ANATHEMA fame) which pretty much suits the underlying concept.

My compulsiveness towards the things I like may sometimes be a problem, but bear with me on this one. Usually when a band debuts with such a great album it either disbands immediately (CYNIC comes to mind) or is destined to great things. I sense RIVERSIDE are on the latter group. I just hope they get that little bit of luck everyone needs to succeed, because the talent, the emotion, the technique, the ability... well, it's all there. Saint-Exupery once said that "perfection is not achieved when there's nothing more to add but rather when there's nothing more to take away". While I don't claim "Out of Myself" to be perfect (despite the hands-down 5 star rating) it certainly comes very close to fitting that phrase.

You want to have this album. Don't say I didn't warn you.

title: Enough's Enough Linkin Park
text:
I'm not quite sure how to express my opinion of this album without being too profane...calling it the worst piece of garbage since Limp Bizkit would almost be a compliment. It truly saddens me that this is what is passing for good music these days and worse over, I've seen LP listed in magazines as being 'metal.' Anyone who has heard the true metal like Priest, Maiden, Sabbath, Slayer, Pantera, Sepultura, or Megadeth likely pukes at the very idea of LP being considered 'metal.'

As far as the music goes, it is pretty much as bland as it gets. The guitar riffs are all down-tuned mindless three-chord drones that completely lack invention or ugency (and solos). Their hack of a guitarist makes The Edge (from U2) look like f***in' Jimi Hendrix by comparison. Continuing on, the bass is completely non-existant, which makes one wonder if the bassist just hangs around the band to look important and collect a paycheck. The drumming is absolute sub-par and does not go beyond anything but keeping a basic 4/4 beat (go listen to Neil Peart, Danny Carey, or John Bonham if you want to hear a REAL drummer). The samples are by far the most pretentious part of the music and are a poor attempt to make these songs a fusion of rap and rock.

I can usually get past lousy musicianship in bands if they can write meaningful, rockin' songs (The Ramones were masters of rock 'n roll simplicity), but LP is forever crippled by the ultra-stupid, pointless lyrics and raps of Chester Bennington and that Shinoda fool. Bennington wails like a teenage girl after going through a junior-high school breakup and Shinoda thinks he's totally badass for ripping off Zack de la Rocha and SA Martinez in each of the songs' magically timed rap sections.

If there is one thing that I truly hate in songs, it is self-loathing lyrics. Yes, everyone has problems...but how many people really want to hear about them? In the past five years, LP have become millionaires, yet still bemoan how hard their lives are. Yeah, traveling the world, making millions of dollars and playing huge concerts must really be the drags (can you hear my sarcasm?)

Rap-rock music is not the problem; rap-rock can work, just listen to 311, Rage Against the Machine, Faith No More, etc. The problem with this band is lack of interesting or dynamic music, whiny lyrics and just the overall corporate image they project.

"Meteoria," and "Hybrid Theory" are two of the worst albums in the history of rock. One star is too good of a rating, but the webpage won't let you do zero stars. Take comfort in knowing that this band will eventually be forgotten 20 years from now and their 'nu-metal' will just be a bad memory.

title: A Journey Through the Mind (and Heart) of AL
text:
I became a fan of Adam Lambert on June 19th, 2010. Yes, almost a year and half after he first appeared on American Idol. But as someone who hasn't watched Idol since season 1 and has a general dislike for all reality TV shows, I really didn't know anything about this guy until just a couple of weeks ago. I remember that date well because I stayed up 'till almost 6am watching various clips of his performance on Idol, of songs on this debut album, and of him in interviews. I really enjoy how articulate and funny he is, BUT MOST OF ALL HIS MUSIC! So let's talk about this album, which I purchased pretty much immediately afterward.

Here is an ecelectic mix of sexy pop/dance songs ("For Your Entertainment," "Fever," "If I had You"), classic rock ("Strut," "Sure Fire Winners"), slow soft ballads ("Sleepwalker," "Aftermath," "Soaked" ) and tear-your-heart-out emotional anthems ("Whattya Want From Me," "Time for Miracles"). There is no question about his singing ability - the voice that delivered immaculate performances week after week on Idol really shines here on these tracks. The simmering energy underneath each song is infectious, and even though Adam only spend 3 months on this album, it doesn't feel rushed at all.

I didn't have the same expectations for him as maybe someone who followed his journey through Idol, so maybe I don't have "as much" investment in him. But I really really enjoyed every track of this album and am hoping to see him on tour. Furthermore, I'm looking forward to his second album already!!! (UPDATED: Spring 2011 according to his latest interview!!! YAY!)

But first, let's get this to platinum!!! I have no doubt this will be hitting the 1mil mark by the end of this year, and it richly deserves so. It's not often I enjoy every single track of an album as I have done here. I might even go get another copy to keep! :D

title: "WHO KNOWS WHERE THE TIME GOES": JUDY COLLINS' FOLK-ROCK MASTERPIECE
text:
Judy Collins' 1968 release "Who Knows Where The Time Goes" is a true folk-rock masterpiece which may very well have set the standard and was the template for the modern folk-rock wave that took hold of the music scene by by dawning of the 1970s. Filled with masterly covers of songs by Leonard Cohen, Bob Dylan, Fairport Convention, The Incredible String Band and Ian Tyson, "Who Knows Where The Time Goes" has a country-rock edge to it and a smattering of her classical inclinations mixed into its folkiness.

The album starts out with "Hello, Hooray", a rousing number about performing, something the hard-working Collins knows quite a bit about.

Next up is Cohen's bizarre tale, "Story Of Isaac", with its religious overtones and its haunting harpsichord accompaniment. On this album, she's also covered (what I feel) is the premier cover of his "Bird On A Wire", done in a countrified style, as is Ian and Sylvia's "Someday Soon", a hit for Judy.

Collins' beautiful soprano floats on Dyaln's "Pity The Poor Immigrant" and The Incredible String Band's "First Boy I Loved".

The title track is by the late Sandy Denny of Fairport Convention and is a shining example of how Judy Collins' artistry can make a song her very own.

The eerie "Pretty Polly" (a "traditional" song and, again, I don't know where Collins digs up some of these interesting things she's recorded over the years) is a staggering account of physical abuse and murder with a moral to it.

Her own composition, "My Father", is truly magnificent and shows what a polished songwriter and keyboardist she is.

"Who Knows Where The Time Goes" really moves and is another album from Judy Collins' pinnacle of fame that has stood the test of time, sounding as modern as ever amidst the new trend of Americana-flavored music which has made headway in recent years and is a great example of the influence she has had on the music world.

This CD of shakuhachi and koto duets by Riley Lee and Satsuki Odamura paints sound-pictures or introspective dreams in an intriguing and rather beautiful way. Sometimes the phrases are simple and slow then suddenly there are bursts of energy as the instruments dance in ecstasy and passion.

title: 3 1/2 stars. I like candy and I like Kandi!
text:
I feel so compelled to say one thing: Kandi has so much potential that it is not even funny. As you may know, she penned TLC's smash hit called "No Scrubs" as well as many other songs for Faith Evans, Pink, and Destiny's Child. She always sounded so fresh and vigilant on all of Xscape's music. Now, on her debut, "Hey Kandi", she really got a chance to shine. As far as vocals and delivery are concerned, Kandi did a splendid job on every single song. I am very impressed with her ability to stay on key and never give too much or too little vocally. She has a beautiful voice and she knows just how to use it. One can't help but wonder why she wasn't given more solos when she was apart of Xscape (her voice is even better than the lead singer, LaTocha Scott's.)

The title of her album is "Hey Kandi." It's simple, but very effective for whatever reason. What really drove me to purchase this album was the lead single, "Don't Think I'm Not." I absolutely love this song's subject matter which is, "If you cheat on me, I'll cheat on you and I will not feel bad about it." The production is great and so is Kandi's delivery. So, why did I begin my review by saying that she has potential? Well, there are a few missteps on this album, but her good material is very good. At her best, she's a very capable artist and I can listen to her music for hours on end, but, there are moments here where she apes others. For example, "What I'm Gon Do to You's" subject matter is exact to Blu Cantrell's song, "Hit `Em Up Style." These tracks are about damaging men's property because they mistreat you. The song is just average; Cantrell's song is better. Further, "I Wanna Know" and "I Won't Bite My Tongue", as far as production and melody are concerned, sound like they could have been on Pink's debut, "Can't Take Me Home." "Easier" features the very talented Faith Evans. This ballad is beautiful; Kandi dedicated the song to her late brother and it is very touching. Kandi speaks at length about cheating throughout this album and it makes the listener wonder just how many men have done her wrong. I wish there was more subject matter on this album, but I can get over it.

Good R&B is found on "Hey Kandi." She does a good job overall and those who enjoy ballads and up-beats should enjoy this album, even if only partially.

title: Kosmiche Tango Elektronische?

Ok this is Ashra not Ashra Temple so its not progressive psychedelic teutonic influenced music nor is this a rehash of Blackouts or New Age of Earth....
Now that has been cleared let me explain this IS still Ashra and a mid 1980's version of the project so in essense Manuel is utilizing more of what was then modern electronics ie. drum machines, digital synths PPG<?> samplers etc to get his creative muse mojo working.
The music is not as grey, minor as his 1970s material nor is this anything rock, blues or even progressive in content.
What you will enjoy is a more lively Ashra in a more major key ie the opener with uplifting chord swells, jingly guitars and a ton of drum machine rhythmic undulations.
I for one enjoy the fact that Manual seems to be riding the creative wave without a nod of concern as to conformity to the older releases and the music is exciting and full of positive forward momentum. At times this does sound very 80s but thats fine by me even in the 21st century. As a side note Pretty Papaya is a really fun almost Caribbean sounding tune with the crystalline Casio bells, Stratocaster guitar and Simmons drumming. Just fun summer music replete with synthesizer warbles and straight-ahead percussion! A nice under appreciated release that should get a second breath of revisionist listening!

title: A traditional and informal jam session
text:
Some combos just make sense. Putting John Hartford, Tony Rice and Vassar Clements together makes sense. Hartford became a major figure in bluegrass with a brilliant progressive bluegrass album in 1971 called Aereo-Plain. Clements, who played on Aereo-Plain, was arguably the most adventurous fiddler in bluegrass, and he often played rock or jazz. Rice, of course, remains one of the most influential flatpickers around, particularly for his early work with David Grisman, and his similarly jazz-influenced group, The Tony Rice Unit. So, putting Hartford, Rice and Clements together sounds like a recipe for boundary-pushing progressive bluegrass. However, this album was recorded around 1988, by which time Hartford had become more enamored of traditional bluegrass and old-time music, and the group takes its cues from Hartford here. So, this is a very traditional-sounding album, albeit a very informal one. It is as though Hartford, Rice and Clements are playing an impromptu gig to honor Bill Monroe.

Hartford was a multi-instrumentalist. In the 1970s, he focused primarily on the banjo, but by the 1980s and 1990s, he played fiddle primarily. However, Clements handles the fiddle here while Hartford plays banjo. Personally, I would much rather listen to Hartford play banjo and Clements play fiddle anyway. After all, Hartford's tone is a fiddle player was never as clean as Vassar's. However, this is not a fiddle/banjo/guitar trio. Instead, the three principals are joined by Roy Huskey on bass and Mark Howard on mandolin. So, the arrangement is that of a standard bluegrass quintet. Again, despite the progressive backgrounds of each of the three principals, this is a very traditional album.

Even the solos are quite restrained. Every once in a while, Clements takes a brief and unadorned solo. Every once in a while, Rice takes one. Hartford rarely every soloed in other contexts, so it shouldn't be a surprise that he doesn't take many solos here. Instead, the group just focuses on playing some old standbys in a straightforward manner, and having fun in the process.

In a sense, then, this album could be viewed as a bit of a disappointment. Hartford and Clements pushed the boundaries of bluegrass together in 1971 with Aereo-Plain, and adding jazz-influenced flatpicker Tony Rice to the mix could have produced still more innovation. It is a shame that these three didn't get together in the 1970s. However, that shouldn't distract listeners from the fact that this is a fine album of traditional bluegrass, played expertly by three friends who were obviously having fun.

title: Really missed this recording!
text:
Recently saw Joe at Villa Montalvo in Saratoga playing Duke Ellington covers with Regina Carter on violin. Ms. Carter has the spirit of the late Stephane Grapelli flowing through her instrument. Joe is starting to have that elder statesman look about him, but the whole concert outdoors behind the mansion was very satisfying, and the band pretty tight. On the way home I realized that all I had available on CD was Jumpin' Jive, so I set out to fill the void with my two favorites: Blaze of Glory, and Big World.

Not being an early fan of Joe, Big World was my point of conversion, with great songs and much stylistic diversity. "Soul Kiss" is such a great song, and obviously underrated as even some hardcore Jackson fans said "huh?" when I mentioned it. With the album Blaze of Glory, however, Joe reached a transcendent place in the echelon of recording artists/composers. No offense to Elvis Costello, but this is the point at which Joe showed his superior chops and left Elvis in the dust. At the conclusion of the final song "Human Touch", you take a deep breath with a tear in your eye, then sit down at the piano and play your own feeble version of it. At least I do :-)

Never heard Hugh Masakela until my 40's, and immediately recognized the heavy influence of "Ha lese le di Khana" on Joe's early tune "Breaking us in Two". All musicians owe a debt to the sounds of their predecessors, which is probably why Joe is recently covering Ellington tunes. But Joe, with his diverse palette of influences continued to grow and stretch as an artist, and I feel that Blaze of Glory is his finest hour.

title: The History-Making Recording of a Lifetime!
text:
Just listen to the opening applause. Even before she steps onto the stage, the audience is already going crazy. Now that's some true magnetism. Magnetism as only Judy Garland could exude. And from the moment she steps onto the stage at Carnegie Hall and starts blasting those wonderous pipes of hers, you just know that the audience is transfixed stone-stolid, because you yourself are, over 40 years later, in front of a CD-player instead of Judy herself. This performance is dated in 1961 and it's still not out of print. And people are still buying it and savoring every minute they can from Judy Garland. The orchestra sounds beautiful, Judy's voice is strong and rich, the audience is so often in ecstatics I've lost count.

With a good mix of pop standards that sound infinitely better with Judy's phrasing and delivery, and hits from Judy's own films, this concert marks one of the (very) high peaks in Judy's career (she had many of them).

Here are some of my favorite tracks (in performance order):

Almost Like Being in Love/This Can't Be Love : Fun, swingin', you can really tell Judy loves singing these songs.

You Go To My Head : There's a halarious moment when Judy forgets the lyrics. An otherwise flawless and upbeat delivery.

Just You, Just Me : Judy's voice is so suitable to this song. She hits every note pitch-perfect.

Rock-a-Bye My Baby With a Dixie Melody : Judy remains the only (other) performer who can successfully sing this song.

Swanee : A definite high point in the whole CD. The audience continually shouts requests for this song and absolutely goes wild when the orchestra strikes up the introduction.

Judy also shows off her finely-tuned raconteur chops, bantering effortlessly with the audience and continually having them in stitches from some funny story or other. (Something about a Parisian hairdresser, her fantastic sweating skills, and some business with a faulty zipper.)

Please please do yourself a favor, buy this CD, pop it into your stereo system, crank up the volume, sit back, close your eyes, and be transported back to 1961 and spend an evening with Judy Garland.

text: Well,  not really. But this documentary comes as close to it as any documentary I've seen. You see and hear it all: preliminary rehearsals, takes and retakes, instructions to the orchestra, frustration, pleasure, triumph, take out food, the works. And some glorious glorious music. The final take of "One Hand, One Heart" is astounding: benevolent Lenny conducts, Carreras conducts himself, Te Kanawa beaming at Carreras, and pulling herself out at the end, and the wonderful sound of their two voices. The middle, orchestral part, is marred by a voice-over from Bernstein, but you learn to ignore it. And that's only the BEST sequence on tape. There's lots more. "Officer Krupke" is a lot fun, as the singers act and gesture in role (some even have 50s-style letter jackets). "Maria" is superb, after Carreras  recovers from a frustrating session where he walked out of the studio in anger. Bernstein chews out someone for not getting his annotations marked on the parts, praises the first trumpet player, throws shoulder moves on the orchestra. And so forth. Get it, now.

Say what you will about Anthrax, but these guys know how to make a metal album. "Sound Of White Noise" is a classic in my book, and "Stomp 442" runs closely behind but with "We've Come For You All", the guys have really out-done themselves.
Every track here is a winner in it's own right and no, you won't find any nu-metal riffs nor will you find any rapping or whining. What you do get is REAL metal the way that it was meant to be played: Loud and fast, with CONVICTION. There is something about their music that never sounds dated and you could take any song from "White Noise", put it on the radio, and people would never know that it came out ten years ago. Did you ever hear "Only"? In case you haven't, it's probably one of the best metal songs ever recorded and it has NEVER managed to get stale.
On, "We've Come For You All", you can tell that these guys have really come a long way. Their (to use a corny cliche) ten years older and ten years wiser. The lyrics are smart and the band has never sounded better. The only thing this album needs is a little airplay.

title: A Must Have For All Linkin Park Fans
text:
When I was growing up, I mostly listened to hip hop music and never really gave rock a try. When I first heard of Linkin Park, I didn't really like them that much. I was like most people that I know today that still don't like Linkin Park. At the place where I used to work, one of my co-workers called them a "boy band with guitars." And admittedly, that's what I had originally percieved Linkin Park as. Mainly because I heard songs like "Crawling" and "In The End" and thought of them as songs "more geared towards teen girls."

After a while, I started getting into a few bands like Limp Bizkit. But after listening to constant yelling about a girl that Fred Durst got screwed over by (which happened like years ago) and songs that had little to no meaning whatsoever (Rollin') I had a desire to seek out a rock band that not only satisfied my hip hop needs, but also brought in some emotion and feeling to their music.

Then, my friend came over to my house with Hybrid Theory in his hands. At first I didn't really care, but then he started playing the CD and all of a sudden, something very unexpected happened. I started liking Linkin Park! I tried to pretend like I didn't like the music, but that CD was everything that I had been looking for the past few years. Not only did it have a good deal of rap in it, but the lyrics were filled with feeling and emotion. I started to realize that songs like "Crawling" weren't just written for teenie bopper girls suffering from depression. A lot of the emotions and feelings of that song, among other songs on the album, described the feelings that I had inside of myself.

Then one day, I came across an import of Hybrid Theory at the local music store. It included two bonus tracks not found on the CD that my friend had. It costed a lot, but there weren't any regular versions of the CD so I figured, might as well get it so I can have something to wave in my friend's face. After getting home, I listened to the entire CD and was extremely surprised by how awesome it was. Here's my thoughts on all the tracks:

Papercut - The first song on the CD, it gives a good impression of what to expect from the rest of the CD. Some hard-hitting guitar combined with some great rhymes from Mike. (5 out of 5)

One Step Closer - The one song that I liked even when I didn't like Linkin Park, and one of my favorites to this day. Great singing and screaming from Chester. A classic. (5 out of 5)

With You - A great example of Mr. Hahn's mad DJ skills, combined with killer lyrics from both Mike and Chester. The great mix of scratching and guitar is especially awesome on this track. (5 out of 5)

Points Of Authority - Another classic heavy rock song. Nice lyrics, especially from Chester. I love the cool effects at the end of the song. (5 out of 5)

Crawling - The classics keep on coming. Didn't really like it back when I first heard it, but now it's one of my faves. Really deep lyrics in this song. (5 out of 5)

Runaway - Another song with some nice DJ work combined with more hard guitar and nice lyrics from Chester. (5 out of 5)

By Myself - Not exactly one of my favorite LP songs, but it does feature some great lyrics from Mike. (4 out of 5)

In The End - Yet another classic song. Really thoughtful rapping from Mike who busts out with some classic rhymes. Chester really pours out on this song too. (5 out of 5)

A Place For My Head - Great rap lyrics from Mike on this song. A little more complex guitar than in some of the other songs. Great song to rock out to. (5 out of 5)

Forgotten - Another one of those songs that's okay but not exactly a favorite. It's still good though. (4 out of 5)

Cure For The Itch - The one stand-out song on the album. A DJ track by Mr. Hahn, and one of my favorite tracks on the album. Some rock fans might not like it, but if you like scratching this track is tight. (5 out of 5)

Pushing Me Away - The CD finishes off with this song, with more great lyrics and guitar. A great song to close the album with. (5 out of 5)

For those who have either the special edition CD or the Japanese import, there's two bonus tracks included. These do not appear on the regular version of the CD.

My December - The whole song is pretty much piano, with no rock whatsoever. Probably why it didn't make the original CD. It's an okay song, but not exactly on the top of my favorite LP song list. (3 out of 5)

High Voltage - A new version of an old song from the Hybrid Theory EP CD. Some of Mike's best lyrics is on this song, although unfortunately it's censored (the S word, which he only says twice). But still an awesome hip hop song. (5 out of 5)

So anyway, you can get either the regular version of Hybrid Theory or the one with the two extra songs (the special edition also comes with some live songs too, but I haven't heard them so I didn't rate them). I recommend the one with the bonus tracks though, they're pretty tight. And it probably won't cost you too much more.

So to end my review, if you're a fan of Linkin Park chances are you already own Hybrid Theory. If you don't, then you should hit yourself in the head a bunch of times. Then get this CD.

I highly recommend people to give this CD a try. You might just like it. Don't let that "boy band with guitars" stuff get in your head, because if you give them a chance you'll see that their music is geared towards all kinds of people, not just girls. It's a blend of all kinds of musical styles, so even people who don't like rock music can probably get into it. Give it a try, you won't be disappointed.

title: Amy Lee and crew saves me from the nothing I've become
text:
evanesce--to dissipate like vapour, disappear gradually, fade away. [Latin: evanescere, to vanish, e (completely) vanescere (to pass away) from vanus (empty, vain)]
The songs on Evanescence's debut album, Fallen, fit in two different categories. One is the blaring heavy nu-metal guitar and industrially-programmed drums over which Amy Lee sings, such as "Going Under." The others are gothic-style ballads of angst and pain that showcase Lee's beautiful voice, which is the real featured talent here. Call Evanescence the Amy Lee Experience, if you will, or an alternative/nu-metal version of Tristania.
The first of two songs that were highlighted on the Daredevil soundtrack, "Bring Me To Life", has some terrific lyrics pleading an ideal to fill up one's dead and lifeless soul, in a gothic Frankenstein's monster kind of motif. "Wake me up inside/call my name and save me from the dark/.../save me from the nothing I've become." And no, I don't mind the guest vocals by 12 Stones' Paul McCoy, nor the fact that it fits the first category.
The other Daredevil song, the painful loneliness piano ballad of "My Immortal" is more like it. "These wounds don't seem to heal/this pain is just too real/there's just too much that time cannot erase" is indeed the soundtrack of my life right there, and Lee's McLachlan-like voice and the strings are like a warm hug I need. The piano melodies are reminiscent of Enya.
Things become more gothic and spooky with "Haunted", and Lee's vocals take on an eerie edge, as industrial synth drums and the pulsing nu-metal guitar kick in. Things take on a disturbing edge, when the second chorus goes "I can feel you pull me down/saving me r-ping me/watching me" and the gothic choir adds to the weirdness.
The suicide song of the metal "Tourniquet". She likens God to her tourniquet and calls for a "return to salvation." At one point, I hear "I want to die!" The angst of Lee's voice is felt when she sings "My wounds call for the grave/my soul cries for deliverance."
"Imaginary" is something that Tristania might do, crunchy guitars mixed with a lovely female voice. I love the dreamland aspect of this song and Lee's vocals really soar: "In my field of paper flowers/and candy clouds of lullaby/I lie inside myself for hours/and watch my purple sky fly over me." I identify strongly with this line: "Don;t say I'm out of touch/with this rampant chaos-your reality/I know well what lies beyond my sleeping refuge/the nightmare I built my own world to escape."
In "Taking Over Me", trying not to think of a lost love is problematic because "who can decide what they dream? And dream I do..." Lee's voice is a powerhouse, as are the metal guitars, which mirror her emotion.
"Hello" is a melancholy piano ballad showcasing Lee's voice and is of someone lost in a haze of daydreams: "Hello. I'm your mind giving you someone to talk to."
Symphonic strings and heavy guitars lead off and continue throughout "My Last Breath" of a dying love. A backing choir and a frantic strings back up "Whisper", of a struggle to stay alive. "Don't turn away/don't give in to the pain/don't try to hide/though they're screaming your name." The choir sing in haunting Latin, backed by strings towards the end.
Fallen is an attempt to mix crunchy nu-metal with lovely soaring Sarah McLachlan/Tori Amos type vocals. The results surprisingly work, but it reminded me what attracted me to groups like Tristania. However, on other songs, we see Amy Lee proving she can sing as well as Sarah McLachlan or Tori Amos. She has so much potential here, that she'll have no problem getting a solo career, and when she does, to paraphrase from a song here--bring her back to life. Just when I thought 2003 wasn't yielding a decent crop, out comes this magical mixing angry guitars and painful angst.

title: Superb performance.  Splendid sonics.  One of the best.
text:
I find myself growing to appreciate this sprawling symphony more and more as I age, and Shipway's account is a welcomed addition to the discography. The SACD version sounds heavenly. I have another CD from these Brazilians and was impressed, but this recording of Strauss's epic nature piece deserves even higher praise. Stupendous? Probably.

The SACD sound is better than most but I don't have the Red Book version to compare. Suffice it to say, I can't find any shortcomings in the sound or the interpretation. Shipway's reading of the Alpine Symphony is exemplary. He seems to find details missing in many other accounts. While I enjoy the details, there is always the danger that the forest (or in this case, the mountains) may be lost for the trees. Fortunately, that is not the case here. The orchestra is knocking at the door of world-class and plays like it. Track 13 "At the Summit" and the Storm on track 19 are incredible, especially the latter that defines the storm better than any recording I have heard.

I was unfamiliar with the accompanying Symphonische Fantasie aus 'Die Frau ohne Schatten.' It is a gorgeous work much in the same vein as Alpine. It makes an excellent addition to the disc and the climaxes toward the conclusion of the work again demonstrate the power of the Sao Paulo Symphony Orchestra.

Interpretatively, the Alpine Symphony does drag a bit at times, but considering the merits of this recording, the occasional slow tempo is no more than a small negative in an otherwise exceptional recording, and that I will be happy to live with. I'm not throwing out my Karajan, Previn, or Ashkenazy, but I am certainly going to have four top choices, now. My favorite, however, is still Karajan. Urgently recommended!
