text: Since Blur is my favorite band, it only makes sense that I would like a Greatest Hits CD, but there are actually a number of things to criticize about the Best of Blur. For one thing, this compilation was made before the Think Tank album came out. Thus, the somewhat significant Blur hit "Crazy Beat" is not featured on the Best of Blur: a shame since I would consider it to be a pretty good song by the band. Also, my three favorite Blur songs are not featured on this CD (I'm Just A Killer For Your Love, Brothers & Sisters, He Thought of Cars). I strongly believe they ought to have been included, though, because these tracks seem to most clearly display Blur's skills in that they all have amazingly catchy rhythms, dandy lyrics, and are completely original and unique. Contrary to what others say, I don't think Blur is anything like Oasis. Sure, they're both British, but Blur has much more originality, more noise, and a bit more cleverness (although I do really like Oasis too). Anyway, the Best of Blur does have its upsides too. It does after all include the non-album song "Music Is My Radar", and compile a few of the band's best songs. There is of course the track that made them famous: "Song 2", as well as their mellow yet really good song "Coffee and TV". Some selections are really crappy, though, such as some of Blur's weakest attempts at soft songs (No Distance to Run, To the End). When push comes to shove, though, this is a quite commendable "best of" CD that Blur fans ought to try out for the hard to find single "Music Is My Radar" (although it's not that great of a Blur song) as well as for the Live C.D. that comes with it, if you choose to check that version out .

title: The Missing Link, so to speak
text: There is one constant in the last 3 decades of Tom Waits' career: he has peddled his astounding wares outside the mainstream of popular music.  His style, however, has not been constant, but evolved from an anachronistic, lounge lizard, hobo promoter of the down-and-out dreamer (i.e. the perfection of "Small Change") to what he is today (i.e. the perfection of "Mule Variations").  Now, in between the two lies the transition, which can be compared to the awkward stage of adolescence.  Ok, you can see where I'm going with this:  "Swordfishtrombones" is the gangly, unsure, disproportionate, pimply, 13-year-old with braces phase of his catalog.  It's hipper and more experimental than what came before it, yet it is still finding its footing compared to what came after.  In "Swordfishtrombones" there is much to love, and there is much you will tire quickly of.  Some of the songs that are throwbacks to his previous style seem forced, uninspired, and brief and the three instrumentals are pure throw-aways.  But in defense of the CD, there is still beauty and strangeness among the songs and it is an interesting documentation of how he got from "Point A" to "Point B" in his musical journey.

title: A unique Des Knaben Wunderhorn
text:
Thomas Hampson's version of Des Knaben Wunderhorn is truly unique. Using an excellent chamber orchestra and just one voice - his own - for the whole cycle, Hampson rejects the mainstream practice to use a whole orchestra and two voices, and also the idea of performing many of the songs as duets. In the booklet, Hampson and his co-writer Renate Stark-Volt claims that Mahler's desire was to use a chamber orchestra for these songs, and also that one voice is the ideal way to perform them. The argument is that these songs "are essentially ballads and demand a narrator who both comments on the events from a distance and participate in them emotionally" (p. 10).

I think this is the correct view: these songs should not be performed as duets. I don't know who invented that common performance practice, but Szell, in his classic recording ([[ASIN:B0007YZU90 Mahler: Des Knaben Wunderhorn George Szell, Conductor/ London Symphony Orchestra]]), is surely among the "usual suspects" to round up here. Of course, it is possible to perform them in the way of Das Lied von der Erde, with a male and a female voice for different songs, as for instance Prohaska did ([[ASIN:B0000023D6 Mahler: Des Knaben Wunderhorn Maureen Forrester (Vanguard)]]). But there is no clear evidence that Mahler intended that as a performance practice. Indeed, there is evidence against that practice in the fact that Mahler described the songs as "songs for voice with orchestral accompaniment". That is, he didn't say "voices". Of course, Mahler did not see these songs as a cycle with a prescribed order, and the different stylistic aspects of them and different publication dates may also indicate that they are not meant to be performed together. But, on the other hand, the stylistic aspects of Das Lied von der Erde are also quite different, even if not as diverse as in the present case.

I sum, Hampson is surely not on the wrong track when he insists on singing all these songs himself. And this is not the first time this happens, at least not when considering the piano versions of the songs. For instance, we have the recording of Fischer-Dieskau and Sawallisch, where DFD sings all the songs: [[ASIN:B0000260PJ Gustav Mahler : Songs from Des Knaben Wunderhorn - Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau / Wolfgang Sawallisch (Orfeo CD)]].

But as far as I know, Hampson is alone in his adaptation with a male, single voice and a chamber orchestra. Regarding the latter, it is unclear how reduced the orchestra actually is. The booklet picture of "Wiener Virtuosen" shows just 11 players, but it is clear that there are many more musicians in Hampson's performances. The booklet text says that the core of this chamber orchestra "is expanded and modified depending on the repertoire requirements for each project" (p. 14).

What about the performance, then? Well, I would rank it as a desert island Knaben, artistically and technically. Gielen's recent recording ([[ASIN:B005KP9E4I Des Knaben Wunderhorn]]), however, is also outstanding, and I don't want to be without either of these recordings. But perhaps that collection would be enough for my desert island experience, since Des Knaben Wunderhorn, in contrast to Mahler's other works, truly "sein wie die Welt" in every way, to use Mahler's words to Sibelius.

Highly recommended!

title: "Fremat Lucifer inter adores . . . "
text:
"Fremat Lucifer inter adores; artibus astibus Ditis minas irredete." (Though Lucifer may rage at you from his flames, you [Carmelites] may laugh at the menacings of the Lord of Hell.)

However Lucifer might rage, this is a stunningly beautiful performance of Handel's Roman, or Carmelite, Vespers - the finest that I have heard.

The recording is clear and crisp and bright but . . . the sopranos' most beautiful runs are afflicted by a crackling distortion. I'm afraid it is in the recording - for I have played my disc on several systems, and the noise always is there. What a shame!

Still, the music is lovely, and the performance sends chills down my spine. I would not want to do without it. This is Handel's music at its best.

Handel aficionados will note, incidentally, that the much-loved air in the Suite in F major from Handel's "Water Music" of 1717 borrows from "Haec est Regina Virginum" of the 1707 Carmelite Vespers. (Compare [[ASIN:B000001G4Q Handel: Water Music]] track 5, with track 7 of this recording).

Whatever its flaws, I far prefer this recording to the one released first on EMI Reflexe, and re-released on Virgin Veritas, with Andrew Parrott conducting the Taverner Choir and Taverner Players - a recording of a performance that valiantely strives for historical accuracy but that sounds relatively dull, even muddy, by comparison to this one. (Compare on Virgin Veritas: [[ASIN:B00000J2Q5 Handel - Carmelite Vespers 1707 / Feldman · Kirkby · Van Evera · M. Cable · M. Nichols · Cornwell · Thomas · Parrott]]; and on EMI Reflexe: [[ASIN:B00000DNL9 Handel: Carmelite Vespers, 1707]]).

title: minor masterpiece
text:
Back in about 1972, a mate introduced me to Italian Prog, through Felona e Sorona. (We didn't call it Prog then, though). I was entranced,and intrigued that people other than the Poms were producing such great music, only to be hidden from the world. I found, in a tiny shop in my home city, this and Uomo di Pezza soon afterwards. So different. Later, I was tempted to buy the English language version, but as an impecunious student, thought better of it. Forty years later, that decision was vindicated. What induced them to get Peter Hammill to write some unrelated gobbledigook, and append it to the instrumentals? Heavens to Betsy...Anglophones have listened to non English vocals for centuries. This offering contains both versions.

The original Felona e Sorona is mostly a sublime dip into what Italian Prog could produce at its best. This dusting off is excellent, and sounds much as I recall it. Crisp production, good sonic balance, and ambience, and the work itself all fits together.

Le Orme were keyboard and percussion based, though the small guitar parts are perfectly competent. However, unlike ELP and other Keys based Prog outfits, the keys don't overwhelm to the point of distraction. I don't care that Keith E played with the Hammond lying on him...it so often ceased to be musical! I had had an Italian mate translate the lyrics, but he found them somewhat arcane. I prefer the metaphysical to the Hammill inanities. Especially as so often their struggle with English interrupted the flow of the vocals.
The music here is at once seductive, beckoning, contemplative at times and rollicks along at others, but always the music had a legitimate reason to be.
The English, Felona and Sorona, is just daft. Similar comments can be directed at other misguided meldings of English Language lyrics with Italian prog instrumentals.
I found it distracting enough.

So...the Italian language original is a must have for Proggers, but the English version is a historical curiosity only.

title: Sadus' Definitive Masterpiece
text:
I got into Sadus when I bought "Swallowed in Black" almost 3 years ago, and upon my first listen I was instantly floored in sheer delight and amazement. This album is one of the most fastest and most brutal yet technical thrash/death metal albums that I've ever had the pleasure of listening to being that I'm such a huge avid fan of old school thrash/death metal. It is also Sadus' definitive masterpiece, no questions asked. It simply rips and shreds like a super angry beast from start to finish. A perfect follow up to the band's amazing 1988 debut "Chemical Exposure" (originally titled "Illusions") which I also own btw, "Swallowed in Black" attacks the listener with it's viciously rapid and unrelenting speed and balls-out brutality, and it is also a lot more technical than the debut as well. The lyrics are also very serious, intelligent, and very thought provoking, and the band's musicianship itself is of course extremely mindblowing in all aspects. Darren Travis (who also plays guitar) grabs the listener right by the throat with his savagely violent, high piercing, shrieking vocals that are guaranteed to pierce right through the throat within a matter of seconds. The guitar work of Travis and Rob Moore is just downright amazing as they deliver an array of fast, brutal, violent, yet extremely technical riffs and wild, screaming solos that are sure to get the adrenaline pumping. Steve DiGiorgio absolutely shines on here with his incredible fretless bass playing especially on cuts such as "Black", "Good Rid'nz" and "Images", and of course Jon Allen's octopus on speed-like drumming is extremely tight and rapidly pummeling throughout with intense hammering beats and excellent fills. The guy is truly like an octopus on speed, he's such an amazing talent, no questions asked.

This whole album is just flawlessly amazing, there is not one bad track on here whatsoever. The first track "Black" is an awesome opener that begins with a haunting intro, and then before you know it, the song kicks into a relentless high speed thrashing assault on your senses that is bolstered with fast, blood pumping drum work, fiery, relentless riffs and furious soloing, plus some killer bass lines, and angry, wild shrieking vocal attacks throughout. The second track "Man Infestation" is another hammering thrasher that boasts more hyper fast riffing and soloing, rapid fire drumming, wicked bass chops, and angry, frantic shrieking. Other blasting, thrashing monsters on here include "Last Abide" and "The Wake" (with the former being a short 2 minute and 17 second thrasher blaster dominated by more intense driven, blasting beats, and insane, high speed riffing, and the latter which includes some extremely tasty soloing especially around 2:20, plus more insane, intense riffing and drumming throughout), and my personal favorite track "In Your Face" which only clocks in at only 1 minute and 3 seconds, yet it's still a wicked adrenaline rusher with rapid hammering drums, rapid riffing and soloing, and violent shrieks. The title definitely lives up to it's name, believe me, it's a real good kick in the face.

Other fantastic tracks on here including "Good Rid'nz" and "False Incarnation" both include very complex structures and unorthodox song structures that even bands like Megadeth would find very difficult to pull off. Another favorite of mine, track eight "Images" features some really amazing technical bass work throughout by Steve especially in the opening, as well as more savage, blistering riffage, and screaming, shredding solos, plus more savage drum work, and super angry vocals galore. Track nine "Powers of Hate" continues the all out savageness with some cool, fast galloping riffage in the intro before slowing the tempos down a bit around the 30 second mark, and then shifting right back to the breakneck, thrashing tempos around the 1 minute mark thus continuing the savage assault with yet more ferocious, firing riffs and wild, careening soloing, and tight, maniacal percussion work. Then there's the 6 minute plus epic "Arise" which is just fully drenched with numerous tempo changes, mind boggling riffs, killer drumming, awesome solos and sick bass lines throughout this 6 minute monster of an epic track. Track eleven, and the final cut "Oracle of Obmission" is a fierce and ferocious closer that is heavily tatooed by yet more of the band's ferocious arsenal of maniacal shrieking vocals, blazing, blistering riffing and soloing, nimbling bass lines, and vicious, blasting drumming abound.

We also have a couple of bonus demo tracks in "Kill Team" and "Fight or Die" both from the band's 1986 "D.T.P." (Death to Poseurs) demo tape which are great as well.

Overall, if you're a serious old school thrash/death metal fan as I am myself, then by all means "Swallowed in Black" is a serious must have in your metal CD collection. Believe me, this is an album you can't ever go wrong with after you've listened to it from start to finish, it is that damn awesome...Highly Recommended!!!

From the soulful screams of "Try(Just a little bit harder)", to her really raspy yet whispery delivery on the classic "Summertime," Janis's voice seemed to channel profound emotions right into your soul. The musicians are also very innovative and solid, be it pure psychedelia (Big Brother) or horn laden R&B (Kozmic Blues). Yes, she got caught up in the climate of the times and died way too son. Nonetheless, we were lucky to have such rare talent among us. No one since has equalled the power, the raw and piercing emotion of Janis Joplin.

title: And people say I'm crazy
text:
Imagine yourself in an insane asylum. You might hear some of this:

"I've been mad for f****** years. Absolutely."

"I've always been mad, I know I've been mad. You have to explain why you're mad, even if you're not mad."

"Here for today, gone tommorrow. That's me. Hahahahahahaha"

"I don't know, I was really drunk at the time."

"Give him a short, sharp shock and he won't do it again. Dig it?"

"Why should I be afraid to die? There's no reason for it. You've got to go sometime."

"There is no dark side of the moon, really. Matter of fact, it's all dark"

Or you might just be listening to the most groundbreaking album of all time, in the comfort of your own room. And I haven't even gotten to the highlights yet, to the music that made it happen.

The album opens with Speak To Me/Breathe. Speak To Me introduces the album with the heartbeat from Eclipse, the clocks from Time, the engine from On the Run, the money sounds from Money, and the screaming from The Great Gig in the Sky. After the screaming subsides, the music starts, as we transition into Breathe, about being born, and advice on how you live your life.

Next up is On The Run, a frenetic instrumental about paranoia. It could be paranoia like that which overtook Stalin, who felt the world was out to get him, or it could just be the simple paranoia a person feels running to get to a flight.

Time follows, and is about people who think life lasts forever, and before they know it, end up to old to live, without having ever done anything meaningful. It ends with a reprise of Breathe, about a funeral.

This leads into The Great Gig in the Sky, the second instrumental on the album. This particular one is about death, as can be seen in the "why should I be afraid to die" quote above. Clare Torry's shrieks of desperation are unrivalable, when anyone else even attempts it, it sounds like sex, the exact opposite of death.

Money follows, with the absolutely amazing technical achievement of the looping cash register/coins clinking/paper tearing sequence, all leading to an almost reggae (although much better) song about the evils of money, with the almost paradoxical line (money, it's a crime, share it fairly but don't take a slice of my pie).

There is a brief interim period in the last fifteen seconds of this song and the first five of the next in which one of the most amazing song lyrics ever appears twice (once in each song). "I don't know, I was really drunk at the time."

This leads into Us and Them, the most moody song on the album. It's about the evils of war, and the little things we never think about, like how the soldiers on the other side are only human, too.

Next up is Any Colour You Like, an instrumental. However, like every song on the album, this too has a meaning. It is about racism, and how it doesn't really matter what color you are, you can still be a productive member of society (and you can still go insane).

Brain Damage follows, the culmination of all of the previous songs. It's about how the person finally cracks, and is sent to the insane asylum (or the dark side of the moon) where he can be with all the other people like him.

Eclipse rounds off the album, summing up all the factors that make you go insane, ending with: "and all that is now, and all that is gone, and all that's to come, and everything under the sun is in tune, but the sun is eclipsed by the moon" (eclipse were thought to cause seizures).

Put this all together, and you have the best concept album ever conceived, about all the factors that lead a man to insanity:

paranoia, thinking about time and growing old, worrying about death, wondering if you have enough money, the stress of war, and racism.

Now imagine yourself in a theatre. Not a movie theatre, but an honest-to-god theatre, where real people do real live acting for your benefit. You're there to see a play. On the stage is a chair, with a table next to it. On the table is a cd player, in the chair is a man, hanging his head, so you can't see his face. The play you're going to see is called "The Soundtrack to Life."

In the play, the man lifts up his head, picks up his arm, and presses one button on the cd player. After five seconds of silence, in which the man returns to his original position, you begin to hear a heartbeat, followed by some clocks, and an engine, the sounds of money, and some shrieks. And then the first note of Breathe comes on.

Who is the man? You are the man. After you hang your head, close your eyes for the next 42 minutes or so.

You'll get your money's worth.

So sit back, relax, and enjoy the show. And please, no smoking. Pink Floyd is not drug music. This CD will take you anywhere you want to go on its own.

title: Hear the depth of experience on all the memorable, powerhouse tracks
text:
There’s every reason to get the blues after hearing Pay The Price, the 2019 CD by Ray Fuller And The Bluesrockers. The 14-track, 48-minute CD features mostly original tracks from Ray, who adds in some spellbinding blues-rock riffs on his electric guitar. Also playing on the album are Tutu Jumper (drums), Doc Malone (harmonica) and Manny Manuel (bass). Tracks covered include classics by Muddy Waters, Chuck Berry, John Lee Hooker, Hank Ballard, Louisiana Red and more.

On the scene since starting his band way back in 1974, Ray Fuller is hardly a newcomer to the American blues-rock scene, having opened shows for legends like Muddy Waters, Stevie Ray Vaughan, Buddy Guy and other legends. You can really hear the depth of experience on all the memorable, powerhouse tracks on Pay The Price. Blues-rock fans will gladly ‘pay the price’ and then enjoy the blues-rock sounds on this modern day classic from Ray Fuller And The Bluesrockers. (Robert Silverstein, Roots Music Report)

title: Is it really that bad, Kelly?
text:
*2.5 stars*

Oh Kelly, I didn't realize you were so depressed. True, she hinted towards that notion in her 2004 breakthrough "Breakaway", but no one ever would have thought that she was in such emotional turmoil. Although, I'm guessing that a very hard break-up didn't help her. And as any hardcore Kelly fan would know, she did endure her parents divorcing when she was young. So she has grounds to be sad, but it's quite a shame that she had to bring her music down with her.
Starting with the album cover, with its portrayal of a lavish house being taken over by vines and leaves, and a somber Kelly looking away at the destruction, it should come as no surprise that this album will be very different than her previous two. Then again, you can probably make that inference just from the album name itself. It should also come as no surprise that the content of "My December" follows suit with the album cover. There is no light this time around, there are none of the glossy pop hits that turned Kelly into a success star, there are no indellible hooks that make you want to repeatedly listen to this set. Quite frankly, there's not a whole lot of anything here. Even though Kelly has such an incredible voice, and she took the reins of her music and co-wrote every song, she does not utilize either of those talents, even though this was supposed to be the defining moment in her career when she finally comes into her own.
But it didn't have to turn out like this. Kelly, I hate to say it, but you really should have listen to Clive Davis this time. Even though this album is the most personal Kelly has been with the mainstream, it's not the side that people want to listen to. But at the same time, I'll admit that this is both an artistic and personal change in sound that she needed to make. If she didn't get all of her emotions out on this CD, then her fans would have to endure multiple albums of her trying to be a hard-rock girl and singing about nothing but break-ups and depression. So it's good that she at least can acheive catharsis by expressing her thoughts. It doesn't do her career or her talents justice, but it definitely will please herself.
But oddly enough, "My December" isn't all doom and gloom. It's true that none, and I mean absolutely none, of the songs are happy in any way, but not all of the music reflects that. Most of the time she has a good track to work with, but then pairs it up with pretentious lyrics that lose all of their depth. The best moments on "My December" come when Kelly is not trying to brighten up the album, when she just goes with the flow and sings like a depressed teenager. These include the lead single "Never Again", "Sober", and the double feature of "Irvine" and "Chivas". Surprisingly, the last two songs are the best on the entire album.
All in all, "My December" is not an overly enjoyable listen. It does just enough to keep you interested, but most of the songs will not resonate past their playing time. And it's quite frustrating that on an album that Kelly spent so much time working on and defending, she displays her weakest vocals to date and does not emote nearly enough to make "My December" worth all of that trouble. She wanted this album to be comparable to "Evanescence", but it ends up sounding like a tiring and dry version of Avril Lavigne's "Under My Skin". However, the bright side of this dark album, is now that Kelly has aired her dirty laundry, a much better album surely awaits.

title: A MUST HAVE FOR ‘FATS’ WALLER FANS
text: This 2 CD set does indeed collect all recordings that Fats recorded for Associated Transcription Service. Fats did two sessions for Associated, the first in 1935, the second in 1939. Both sessions find Fats in fine form at two different junctures of his career. In the 1935 session, Fats plays and sings a few medleys of his recent songs he had recorded under his new contract with RCA Victor. In some instances he is joined by his band mate Rudy Powell on clarinet and alto saxophone. While Powell's tone quality on clarinet is a bit harsh, his tone on alto saxophone is warm and smooth. His ability as a creative improviser is superb. There are some single piano solos as well and these are simply great. Disc two contains the 1939 session. Fats is joined by his regular group. It should be noted that in the years between the two sessions, Fats recorded extensively for Victor but many of the tunes were second rate. Fats' recordings of his own compositions and piano solos became few and far between. Because he had more freedom at Associated, it's no surprise that he chose more of his own tunes as well as standards that he admired. The jazz factor also seems to be a bit higher as well. Disc two ends with five dramatic piano solos. Along the way there are alternate takes and several fragments. There is a printing error. Disc one contains a piano solo simply titled E Flat Blues. Disc two has a track with the same title but it is B Flat Blues. These recordings have been availble in different pieces, on various labels for years and it's really great that they are all completely together in one package. The sound quality is outstanding overall. A highly recommended set.

title: Incredible underrated record
text:
This is a very high-energy album, loaded with killer songs from start to finish. Many of them reflect what John was going through during the Lost Weekend, including a few songs about how much he missed Yoko. There are rockers like "What You Got," songs that are just fun to listen to, like "Whatever Gets You Thru the Night," softer songs like "Old Dirt Road," and contemplative songs like "Nobody Loves You (When You're Down and Out)." The two best-known songs on here are "Whatever Gets You Thru the Night" and "#9 Dream"; the latter song John later dimissed as "a piece of garbage I had around." The album would be 100% perfect if it weren't for "Ya-Ya," which really kills the mood set by "Nobody Loves You." That was the perfect closing track, but John had to cover "Ya-Ya" so that the copyright owner would get royalties from a settlement on the songs he would release on the 'Rock and Roll' album. For revenge, John made it the last song on this album, as well as the worst and shortest. The only redeeming thing about it is that his son Julian is also playing on it, a really sweet moment between parent and child.

My faves are "Nobody Loves You," "Going Down on Love," "#9 Dream," "Whatever Gets You Thru the Night," "Bless You," and "Steel and Glass" (an attack on Allen Klein which John later said didn't work the way he'd wanted it to). It might not be praised as highly or consistently as POB or 'Imagine,' but the songs on here are just as well-crafted, great, and brutally honest and soul-searching.

title: Ridiculously good value for premium recordings.
text:
As a teenager I was lucky enough to see Bernstein conduct Mahler with the LSO in London (and Shostakovitch , Nielsen as well ). At the time he was regarded as a bit too flash - in a London scene with Solti and Kertesz as well! My annual season ticket to the RFH also took in Guilini, Klemperer, Kempe and others. Wow.

Now I can see that this was a golden age for concert goers, record companies etc. Bernstein gave me my first introduction to Mahler 3 and what a revelation that was. I also had his version of the 7th and 8th, though Solti gave me my introduction to the 2nd and, of course Walter, also on CBS, the 5th and 9th. Ormandy and the Philadelphia Orchestra introduced us to the 10th..I still have these records and have been delighted to buy the Bernstein full cycle which I think (hope!) are the original CBS versions. And all very wonderful they are too. Even after all these years I still do not actually like the 8th very much - I heard Bernstein conduct it at the old style Albert Hall in London and you could hardly make out a thing! Bernstein's versions of symphonies 1,2 ,4 and 5 are all new to me and I have been most impressed. They have brought me back to Mahler after a few years of overkill perhaps. All the ghastly publicity of individuals devoting their lives to one symphony...

So I highly recommend the set and I need to follow up with reading a biography of Bernstein. Did you know that West Side Story had a ten year gestation period; originally East Side Story and with Bernstein wanting an opera! During this 10 year period Bernstein had a full work load and was also composing Candide , from which songs migrated to the by now West Side Story. All the principal creators of WSS fell out and, at one stage, were not talking to each other. No producer would back the musical (later a mammoth hit in London and winner of 10 Oscars as a movie) and CBS even refused to record it! Eventually one producer (Prince?) took it on but would not allow extra budget for scenery as everyone was sure they had a flop on their hands. Later Bernstein had the clout to record it as an opera and ,no doubt, had a bank balance to match the success of the show. BTW PJ Proby (am American based in the UK, whom I saw in Liverpool 2 years ago) had the only two hit singles from that show with Somewhere and Maria..Check him out!

OK so I wandered off subject! Get this set - it is ridiculously low priced .If you adjust for time probably less that the cost of a box set Mahler 3 one had to save up for at the time!

Plus - The Best Of Depeche Mode [A Short Film]

So, are we really in need of another Depeche Mode compilation? We have the recent 'The Singles 81-85' and 'The Singles 86-98' releases from 1998 and 1999. So why invest in another DM compilation?

First, these tracks have been remastered by Simon Heyworth @ Super Audio Mastering, Devon. However, I must note that the remastering here on this 'Best Of' release is not as good as the remastering on the 'The Singles' releases. In fact, it's disappointing, namely on the earlier cuts. The difference is that 'The Singles' releases were remastered by Mike Marsh @ the Exchange. The mastering on those CDs is much more punchy and full, whereas the mastering here seems more restrained and flat.

I would have preferred Marsh's work on this release! I never understood the hype over Heyworth's mastering because it often ends up sounding flat and close to the original in many cases (i.e. The Human League and OMD), whereas other mastering engineers are able to bring out more depth in the music. That's not to say that I haven't heard some good mastering come from Heyworth. It just isn't here, unfortunately.

For example, do an A/B comparison between "Personal Jesus" on this 'Best Of' with the same track on 'The Singles 81-85'. The difference is obvious. It's flat on this 'Best Of' and punchy on the 'The Singles' release. The latter era tracks are recent so the mastering differences really can't be heard. Nonetheless, you will be grabbing for your 'The Singles' releases if you are picky about sound quality. I do, anyway.

Second, we have the fantastic new single, "Martyr", included here. Originally recorded for the 'Playing The Angel' album, it didn't really fit with the style of the album and finds a welcomed place here as the single to promote the release. It's a classic DM recording. Check out that U-Myx as well!

Next, and perhaps best of all, 'The Best Of Depeche Mode, Vol. 1' comes with a DVD on certain pressings -- the pink coloured rose pressing has the DVD. This DVD includes 23 promo music videos, some previously available on the DVD 'The Singles 86-98' and some previously unreleased. All music videos are presented with the Heyworth remastered audio and crisp picture. The earlier videos presented here have never looked and sounded better with the remastered audio re-synced as the soundtrack. This is a bonus since some record labels use the original underlying audio track.

Furthermore, an excellent 30-minute documentary is included, highlighting a number of the singles and videos here in chronological order, from 1981's "New Life" to 2006's "Martyr". This is an excellent documentary, which I enjoy watching often.

So what's missing? On the CD, we are missing a bunch of hits, considering the release is limited to 18 tracks. Notably missing from the CD are classics such as "Behind The Wheel", "Policy Of Truth", and "A Pain That I'm Used To", to name a few. The DVD, featuring 5 more tracks than the CD, includes a handful of videos to tracks not presented on the CD.

Music fans have to remember that the title is listed as "Volume 1", more than likely making room for a second installment. I can only imagine that these missing hits will be included on this second volume. My main problem with the DVD is that it's missing videos for a few tracks featured on the CD side. Where are the videos for "See You" and "New Life"? It's a bit odd watching the documentary, which features a highlight of the "See You" video and single, and not have the whole video included in the package. "Martyr" is excusable since it's the new single for the package. However, all the other 15 songs on the CD are featured in video format on the DVD.

So will these videos finally make a complete collection with another set of videos for volume 2? My understanding is that Depeche Mode do not like a certain selection of videos from their catalogue and therefore will never release them on DVD. Such a shame really!

In addition to the excellent companion DVD, the release is presented with nice artwork and informative liner notes. I really like the cover! The DVD is the real treat here, since it features a handful of previously unreleased videos. It's a very enjoyable package overall, despite the flaws, so I'm giving it a generous 4 stars. I'm looking forward to volume 2!

title: Good News: Great Album
text:
After 1989's flawed "Street Fighting Years," and 1991's decidely mediocre "Real Life," Simple Minds bounces back with a terrific, empassioned album. The band has had many different phases, and this album will appeal most to fans of the anthem rock of "Once Upon a Time" and "Sparkle in the Rain."

After losing yet another key member (the incredible drummer Mel Gaynor), the remaining two band members - Jim Kerr and Charlie Burchill - unleash a great album of passionate anthems, driven by big guitars and awesome lyrics.

The highlights are the monster riffs of "She's a River," and the live-life-with-a-passion anthem of "The Band Played On," which includes some of Kerr's best and most inspiring lyrics ever.

There are some low points - "Night Music" is certainly one of Simple Minds' more disposable songs. But the album overall is fantastic. Like the piano-based closer "This Time," this album is driven by refreshingly optimistic lyrics - you feel like life will only become more rewarding and successful with each listen.

title: Another Immaculate Step In His Ever Evolving Catalogue
text:
Almost unbelievably, at this writing there are only 13 reviews written for this incredible album. Recently, critics and fans (including myself) have been falling all over themselves to heap accolades aplenty upon SURPRISE and SO BEAUTIFUL/SO WHAT as if an aging poet laureate of the folk/rock would have been finished by now and is significantly adding to their body of work with always fresh and new creative genius. They call the new stuff “the best since Graceland” as if that monument alone is/was his testament to the world of music history. Well history has been more kind to HEARTS & BONES than the initial sales were and it is actually selling better as a back-catalogue item. Too bad for the miscreants who either missed or dismissed it in ’83. One fool has written their 2-star review here and I see no one deems it helpful at all, and that is because those who really know this album have nothing but greatness to say about it and those who haven’t listened to it…ever…well you get the picture. The main thrust of my initial point is that some Simon fans are probably way too hard-nosed and narrow-minded in their vision of what Paul Simon really is. If you grew up with him, as I did, from Wednesday Morning 3 AM in “the year of the Beatles, the year of the Stones” you can literally watch his accelerated Darwinian evolution take place. The sounds on 1970’s Bridge Over Troubled Water”, songs like Keep The Customer Satisfied, Baby Driver, The Only Living Boy In New York, etc. all pointed directly at what was to come on ‘72’s PAUL SIMON, but not only that, El Condor Pasa, The Boxer, even Cecilia, and others from previous albums, fired arrows into the air which were to land in the GRACELAND period (if you want to call it that), and what really irks me most is that HEARTS & BONES clearly, without any reservation whatsoever, unless you are deef-mon!, is a predecessor to GRACELAND & ROTS with that “world music” infection already taking firm hold and precursory foothold on the kind of music that Paul was already dabbling in. So enough bitterness now, let’s get on with the most overlooked treasure in the Paul Simon discography, an album which should be held as valuable as these in his iconography: PAUL SIMON, THERE GOES RHYMIN’ SIMON, HEARTS & BONES, GRACELAND, RHYTHM OF THE SAINTS, and SURPRISE; these are the true landmark albums, must haves which define the artist. After these of course you would definitely need to grab up STILL CRAZY AFTER ALL THESE YEARS and SO BEAUTIFUL OR SO WHAT to top off the collection, and then you will find yourself trapped in the world of I Need Them All, and then you will be really ticked that you are still missing Slip Slidin’ Away and Stranded In A Limousine because they were only released on a Greatest Hits album, awe shucks!

Okay, many of the 13 reviews here point you at the album’s songs and highlights, so I will point you at the importance of this album as an autobiographical footnote in the career of the American John Lennon, the man who bridges Bob Dylan and The Beatles, who voices the soundtrack of our lives with wit and cynicism as well as with silly humor and love (as in the American Paul McCartney).

Allergies, a flashy showcase for flamenco-jazz guitar virtuoso Al Di Meola (whose own albums are amazing) is on the cover a fun frolic of germaphobia (you know that’s really not a word…), but is a hidden discourse on the past failures with women in his life. Hearts & Bones, the title track, even more specifically deals with the emotional roller-coaster that was his relationship and short marriage with Carrie Fisher (the one and one-half wandering jews). The song is also a wonderful foreshadowing of the title track of Graceland, both dealing with a sojourn that is dualistic in physical and emotional journeying, and they are musically quite similar. When Numbers Get Serious is probably more highly appreciated today than in ’83 as Simon has a prescience of what was too come in this digital age. The song utilizes complex bass and rhythm signatures employed in the GRACELAND album. Think Too Much exists as two songs, one very third-world Africanized and the other modernized 80’s with a flavor of earlier Simon rock, both bookends sandwiched around a spiritual blues based work of art Song About The Moon. The three pieces are pure Paul Simon at his best old and new songwriting and performance. Train In The Distance, another Simon Eulogy on relationships continues this stylized metamorphosis from the One Trick Pony sound to Graceland World. Rene and Georgette Magritte With Their Dog After The War is the only song which can be stylistically compared to the bare-bones Paul Simon of old, yet it employs the soft jazzy feel of 80’s explorations and is a lyrically surrealistic visit on a surrealist painter, complete with homage to classic 50’s early rock-n-roll-R&B artists. Cars Are Cars is the only “real” 80’s wave experiment, you can take it or leave it if you like, but it has a cryptic message dropped in between the lines and is not hard to figure out unless you are a social cretin. Finally, The Late Great Johnny Ace is a real folk rock Eulogy to three dead Jacks. Johnny Ace being the legendary 50’s R&B artist who was incorrectly identified as a suicide. JFK is interpolated in passing as the bridge between the old rock and roll and the new year of The Beatles and The Stones. And at end, of course, John Lennon’s assassination is the finale in what becomes a deadly documentary of our musical life transition from the 50’s to 1980 (when the song was first conceived).

There are also a few bonus tracks which either add or detract from your enjoyment depending on the seriousness of your devotion to Paul Simon. I will leave that up to you.

HEARTS & BONES is, in my opinion, a natural evolutionary link to GRACELAND, and part of a triumvirate of three terrific studio albums, 1983 to 1990. It is miles better than One Trick Pony (1980) which I like but do hold as artistically comparable, and is slightly better than You’re The One. But you be the judge! The cost of this CD is affordable and if you are a fan, you should have this, no question about it. Pick up a nice new copy from a reputable Amazon Merchant. The re-mastered sound is immaculate, but then I had no problem with the original CD releases.

title: I don't like metal.  This is brilliant.
text:
There comes a point in every music fan's life at which you either become the person ranting about how the kids today don't understand music, not like when YOU were a kid, or you pick your head up from the rock under which you have hidden it for however many years and try to listen with open ears. I don't have a philosophy of music, or music appreciation, or anything like that. To the degree that I advocate anything like a philosophy of music appreciation, though, it is that one should always try new things, listen to new developments, and keep in mind that whatever your first reaction may be to any style, there are geniuses and virtuosos working somewhere within it.

I left metal LONG ago, and much of rock not that long after that. My tastes range far and wide, but somewhere along the line, I decided that the genre wasn't for me. But, as I tell other people, listen for new trends, and go back and see what's going on. In my continuing efforts to keep an open ear and appreciation for the guitar, Tosin Abasi has given me the ability to say, I don't like metal, BUT...

I would now say that I am a real fan of Animals As Leaders. This is not the metal that I left behind, or that left me behind, or whichever. This is beyond even where Tosin took the band initially. It is difficult for me, as a guitar snob, to take a step back and listen to something beyond the instrumental artistry, but aside from that, the soundscapes are carefully painted, and I choose my words particularly. The layering of electric guitars, the use of nylon strings, and electronics give me something that I would have hated, lo-those-many-days-ago when I first heard Ride The Lightning, but at this point, as someone generally more interested in the weirdness of people like Steve Tibbetts, this is exactly where I'd like metal to be, for my tastes. Painting a picture with sounds. When you reach a level of technical proficiency like this, that's about what is left for you to do. That's what Tibbetts does, and that's what Animals As Leaders do on The Madness of Many, even more than they did when they debuted.

Tibbetts is likely a foreign name to the metal community, as more of a fringe figure on the jazz scene, but the evocative soundscapes being painted here make me think very clearly of The Fall Of Us All, between the incorporation of blazing-fast guitar work, electronic effects, and unusual musical structures. As I expand my horizons, I encourage metal fans to do the same.

That's an imperfect comparison, of course. It is a comparison being made by someone who is an interloper here. I am not a metal fan. Then again, if someone had told me to think of how metal sounds, before I had heard Animals As Leaders, this is not what would have gone through my head. Times change. Sounds change. All of this is good.

This is a very good album.

title: As good as I remembered it!
text:
I heard "The Well-Tempered Synthesizer" when it was first issued; like many people I was stunned by the strange, beautiful sound created by a "machine". Then I read about the difficulty of making the recordings, which took tremendous time and thoughtfulness, and this made me appreciate the human element more than the technology.

Imagine someone who, to cook breakfast, designs a henhouse, raises chickens, gathers the eggs, grinds wheat to make bread, picks fresh strawberries...all for a breakfast that could be made more easily using traditional sources or methods. Pardon the clumsy metaphor, but this is what Carlos had done: giving me Bach, by creating a new kind of chicken to get to the egg.

The sounds one hears in this recording are not as sophisticated as more modern synthetic voices, but they are still pristine and haunting. There is a sort of lonely, cosmic emptiness to the sound, but this is not discomforting; in fact, the music triumphs over the strangeness that no human hand or throat moved during the process, except at the keyboard and the 747-cockpit looking control panel of the Moog synthesizer.

Having a CD of this music is a joy, and the music delights.

title: Mono mixes are the original hit single mixes!
text:
Yes, it's true. The stereo mixes were remixes by the record company of Brian Wilson's original mono mixes. Also, the pre-1968 stereo mixes were usually nothing more than the instrumentation in mono with the two vocal tracks channeled separately into each speaker. In other words, not true stereo at all. Also, this stereo mix screwed up the sound balance of the recordings so that the vocals ended up often overwhelming the instrumentation. It is true that the mono mixes are a bit muddy, but they are much more stronger and powerful-sounding than the stereo mixes. Also, the mono mixes are the way that Brian Wilson intended us to hear his songs. Also, yes, he was deaf in one ear which made it exceedingly difficult for him to mix in stereo, but before 1967, everyone mixed in mono and stereo mixes were created later to satisfy a few hi-fi enthusiasts. Mono was king until Sgt. Pepper. And lastly, these are the mixes that were on the 45 RPM singles which were the hits that made the BB's famous. Before 1968, singles were only issued in mono! And from the Beach Boys "Today" album of 1965 through 1967's "Wild Honey", all the BB's music was only issued in mono or horrible fake "duophonic" stereo remixes. So please spare me the garbage about the stereo mixes being the original and pure mixes. Capitol has given us the true goods.
Lastly, the music is great, and that's the main thing.

title: Starts out strong but gets very bad
text:
ACOUSTIC VERSIONS ARE GENERALLY BETTER THAN THE ELECTRIC ONES.

This is moe.'s nineth studio album, depending upon how you are counting. The delux version comes with two versions of the album, an electric version produced by John Travis and an acoustic version produced by moe. The electric version is 45 minutes long and the accoustic version is 4 minutes shorter. The sound quality is very good.

I don't like the electric version that much. It is the classic case of a producer creating a sound in his image instead of letting the band be the band. So, the album is aimed more at the masses and has that hard pop, middle of the road sound. It is not interesting, like moe. can be interesting. What is it with jam bands? It seems like most of them, Phish, Widespread Panic, String Cheese Incident, moe., etc. put out one or two really good studio albums that represent what the band sounds like and what the band's vision is and then they bring in a producer on the third album who messes everything up. A very good example of this is the "making of" DVD that comes with String Cheese Incident's One Step Closer. The band is shown playing new songs in the studio and they sound very nice. They producer comes along, and says wait till we strip out that stuff. He does on the final album and the songs sound bad.

The first 4 songs on the albums are very good. I prefer the versions on the acoustic album better for the most part, but the electric album does have some interesting parts. For instance, on the third song, Downward Facing Dog, the first 5 minutes are much better on the acoustic version, but the electric version has some very nice guitar runs at the end.

The second song, Haze, is much, much better on the acoustic album, and the electric version is just bad hard pop. On Haze, the sound a little like Chris Isaak, and on The Bones of Lazurus, they sound a little like Niel Young.

The one song that is truly better on the electric album is Puebla. It kind of sounds like Santana's Fried Neckbones (a song they used to play before they recorded their first album).

The last two songs are just horrible. One Way Traffic is just a very bad pop song. Reminds of the bad jangle rock groups, like Toad the Wet Sprocket. And Suck a Lemon is just bad, bad by anyone's standards.

Chromatic Nightmare is a silly vibe piece. It sounds like it would be the background music to skeletons dancing in Eastern Europe. It might have been OK to stick at the end of the album, but it is really out of place in the middle of the album....I know it is kind of a lead-in to Puebla, but it is just too long and too silly for that.

title: Of drunks, druggies, pixies, and hustlers Or: how Mike Knott stopped worrying and brought a rocket and a bomb to the main stream
text:
The Aunt Bettys. Man. This band. Another Michael Knott project, signed to Elektra Records if memory serves, and it was his biggest and best chance at stardom. Boy, did he get it wrong.

Knott and pals had made a name for themselves in various bands in the admittedly small and limited Christian alternative sub-genre. Knott was willing to go to dark places unlike many, if not most, of his contemporaries yet he always managed to allow his voice to cry out to his Lord and Savior. It’s what made him singular, unique. But the man always had big plans and despite not having big fame he was, in fact, what we would call a rock star. He always wore boots that were too small for his feet and he repeatedly tried to put on bigger ones. He tried multiple times to break into the mainstream music market while bringing some of his friends with him. He made a go of it with The Aunt Bettys (who were originally going to go by the name Aunt Betty’s Ford) and released a power punk album that was loud, often fun and catchy, and populated by some quirky (and disturbing) characters. A popular rumor at the time was that Knott was writing about people he came across in one of the local dives he used to hang out in. As good a story as any when you consider that he sings about drunks, a spaced out girl, a Vietnam vet with a special doll, drug addicts, mental health breakdowns, and other lost and sad souls. While that’s all fine and good, though, his ability to peg and write about quirky people wasn’t what made him stand out. What made him stand out was his ability to connect with those people in an incredibly humble and comparative way and give witness to how God loves them even in their darkest days but there’s none of that on this release. If people were going to fall for this band it would have been for a bit of seemingly meaningless fun, but it was never going to last. His small but loyal built in fan base was split, too, due to the nature of what Knott sang about and some of the language (incredibly mild by today’s standards) he used. Even a lot of regular joes at the time wouldn’t have been overly attracted to admittedly quirky songs about these down and out characters. In short Knott did not carry his vision of hope to The Aunt Bettys and while a few new people managed to enjoy it they were nowhere near enough to even vault him into the shallow end of the mainstream. As it has ended it has slipped into the history bin of obscurity.

But not for me. I really enjoy the energy of this album and really really like several of the songs, but I can’t ever play this in mixed company or promote this as one of Knott’s better releases due to the subject matter. And in some ways I’m real glad that this didn’t turn out to be his breakthrough into the mainstream because then there would likely have been no Cush, no “Life of David”, no “Hearts of Care, and no “Comatose Soul”. So if you don’t already own this and are curious about Michael Knott I’d encourage you to start at LSU’s “Grace Shaker” or even his solo releases “Fluid” or “Rocket and A Bomb”. But if you don’t care about that and are just looking for some irreverent, quirky, character driven songs in the keys of power punk rock then you’ve come to the right place. Below are some thoughts about each of the songs:

Jesus ~ Probably my favorite original song of the album. This song is not an easy one though. It’s agonizing and the music and singing perfectly complement the lyrics. Starting off with Knott’s clear, almost warm vocals and an acoustic guitar with the singer pleading to allow Jesus to let him essentially get drunk, the song starts to wind up with strummed power chords and a thick slab of bass and revved up singing and then explodes with Knott snarling over crashing and kerranging guitars and drums “I’m getting screwed! I’m getting used! I’m getting kicked! I’m getting tricked! I’m getting out! I’m giving up! I’m getting out! I’m giving up! I’m getting’…hi-i-i-igh!” This is an extremely pained song, but catchy at many points, and probably perfectly summed up a lot of things for Knott at that time in his life. The term tortured artist certainly applied to him. And the beauty of this song is that, in spite of its likely nuances for Knott, many people have felt exactly what he expresses. This is also the fiercest song on the album and though the rest of the songs rock they never achieve this level of flat out agression.
Mother Trucker ~ A stupid fun song, but extremely catchy. The word play of mother trucker made a lot of Knott’s Christian followers wince as they believed he was flirting (probably was) with a perverse epithet. But if you needed a palate cleanser from the heaviness of the first track this certainly would do the trick.
Star Baby ~ Another fun, fast, catchy punk ride.
Skinny Bones Jones ~ One of my least favorite tracks and also their lone single off the disc. It’s power punk with supposedly witty lyrics about The Rolling Stones being really, really old and still going but it comes off as crass and insincere. What’s the use of criticizing a band for their success when you’d like to have a piece of it? The song ultimately reeks of bitterness from behind the punk sweat and energy.
Lush ~ Another really fun, catchy song this time about “sexy”, a girl who likes to shake and sweat to the music. Playfully playing with lyrics again Knott sexes up the song “drinkin’ your disco, doin’ your go-go, suckin’ your disco”. There’s a great moment in the song where he stops and cycles through how everyone there watching her is just mesmerized by her. “Needless to say, we were dumbfounded.”
Feel ~ Oh. My. Lord. I’m ashamed to admit that I love this song. What distinguishes it is the subject matter which is a bit caustic and unsettling. It’s about a guy who’s crushing hard on a girl only she’s into girls. But he tells her that he could “do anything” for her, including Bobbit it. The song stops just short of using an extremely offensive pejorative. The song is catchy as all get out and I think it perfectly characterizes how far we can be willing to go and how much harm we are willing to do to ourselves in pursuit of our lusts and addictions. But that’s my take on the song and I’m certain it was never meant to express as much. You definitely don’t want to play this in mixed company.
Rocket and A Bomb ~ This is the first of three songs that can be found originally on previous Knott releases. This is a reworking of the title track off of his superb solo “A Rocket and A Bomb” release. It was a great song there, but he’s made it quite different here, and it’s one of his most meaningful songs on the album. The punk sounds are gone and traded for a more modern (‘90’s) rock sound so this is different from most of the music we’ve already experienced on this release and waaay diff than the mellow, almost acoustic original version. But what’s most different is that this song is a concise lament that wears its emotion completely on its sleeve. The lyrics can relate to anyone who has lived for someone/ something else, who has idolized and worshipped a false god, and who has fallen out with that thing being worshipped either because they’ve been pushed out or have chosen to leave. To my ears this song is about Knott’s chronicles within and criticisms of the Christian music industry. They were painful and disillusioning to him, and became legendary. I can’t help but think that when he sings “I lived your vision for a time until it snapped my spine and bled me from your vein” it’s his account of how he went from there to here, from then to the now of the Aunt Bettys. If this is true then it is one of three intensely personal and autobiographical songs here, the others being “Jesus” and “Double”. Oh, and one more thing. You’ve probably never heard someone repeatedly sing “sh*t” with as much conviction as Knott does here, and it might make you want to sing along.
Addict ~ Back to the power punk ride this is a pretty straightforward song about literal drug addiction. Why it sounds so good…?
Speeder Mode ~ Another catchy song. About a relationship that’s hard to keep up with, on hard on the one in it.
Kitty ~ Another song originally on “A Rocket and A Bomb” that’s had the volume turned up on it. A fan favorite of Knott’s about an one-time apartment neighbor of his in the L.A. area who had a gut wrenching reek coming out of her pad. They joked about and wondered if it was “kinda human”. The song’s like an urban myth, and kind of funny.
Little Fighter ~ Exactly what you think it’s about. Celebrating the spirit that never gives up. This song and “Speeder Mode” feel like different sides of the same coin.
Suicide Sex Doll ~ This track just by virtue of its bass line feels like it might have originally been penned for release on Knott’s solo “Strip Cycle” offering. This ditty is about a fractured vet who takes comfort in the titled doll. It’s not going for much and despite its teasing title is filler.
Jane ~ This sympathetic song trades the punk sound for a gentle steel string acoustic pluck over a solid drum and while it hits some power cords it keeps it clean and clear. It’s a sad feel, married to a brief story about the mentally touched Jane. It could have been a great song excepting for the lamewad chorus (“We miss you! Boo hoo!”—what are we, four years old?). So I really like this song but am frustrated by it because of the chorus. I could have loved this song otherwise.
Cruel ~ There’s a lot of catchy numbers on this release and this short one that drives off to a head by song’s end is another extremely satisfying one.
Double ~ IMO one of the best songs Knott has ever penned. Originally the lead off track to his fundamental “Grace Shaker” release (under his LSU moniker) he sticks fairly close to the original. This is, unfortunately, a lesser version due mostly to the mixing and it doesn’t flow vocally quite as well here. But it is still heartbreaking. It’s an acoustic, sad, and clear revelation of the drunkard barely slogging through life, home, and marriage.
Rock and Roll ~ Capping off the album is another rock number, slowed down a bit and drained of energy, about an unhappily coupled couple. Placed anywhere else on this release it would be filler but closing the album out with it makes sense.

title: More Of the Same

title: Shows its Age, but with Age comes Memories
text:
Ah memories. I bought this recording multiple times. The first time was in the early 70s, because it was relatively cheap. The German Harmonia Mundi version sold for DM29 for two records!! As that version got worn out, there were two RCA Victrola versions, the second a bit less grossly warped than the first.

I studied the notes, and the names of the performers. I can still recite most from memory:

Concerto 1 in F
Erich Penzel and Gert Seifert - horn
Alfred Sous, Helmuth Hucke, Ingo Goritzki - oboe
Werner Mauruschat - bassoon
Fransjosef Maier - piccolo violin

Concerto 2 in F
Edward Tarr - clarino trumpet in F
Hans-Martin Linde - recorder
Helmuth Hucke - oboe
Fransjosef Maier - violin

Concerto 3 in G has no soloists

Concerto 4 in G
Fransjosef Maier - violin
Hans-Martin Linde, Guenter Hoeller - recorder

Concerto 5 in D
Gustav Leonhardt - harpsichord
Hans-Martin Linde - flute
Fransjosef Maier - violin

Concerto 6 in B flat has no soloists

Other names pop up in my mind: The "Koch brothers" Johannes (viola da gamba) and Ulrich (viola, no idea if they were, in fact, related), Guenter Lemmen (viola), Werner Neuhaus and Brigitte Seger sawing away on the violins. Ah, memories! It's a good thing I still have the LPs, because the CD release has none of this information.

Now for a bit of reality. This isn't really an original instruments recording. Yes, the horns are valveless, and the flutes are made of wood, and the violins use gut strings, but all instruments are essentially played in a modern style. The violins may use gut strings, but they are otherwise unaltered, and photographs of the Collegium Aureum in action show the string players using modern bows. It sounds like it, too.

Second, a lot of the tempi are slow. Concerto 1 is the worst offender. It uses the most players, and Maier, who conducts and plays doesn't maintain a very tight ensemble. Concerto 2 is somewhat faster. In fact, this is the concerto that distinguished the Collegium Aureum from the earlier Concentus Musicus recording. Here was a clarino trumpet played at speed (it's still a bit slow). OK, Edward Tarr tried. He tried very, very hard to keep up while playing MOST of the notes. It all gets a bit much for him in the final movement.

Hans-Martin Linde is solidly in his "big vibrato" phase. The string players use lots of vibrato. It's all a bit lugubrious.

That said, there are some real strengths: Gustav Leonhardt plays continuo harpsichord in every piece, and shines as a soloist in concerto 5. While concerto 3 is heavy and "thumpy," Ulrich Koch, Guenter Lemmen (viola), and Angelica May (cello) lead as mournful an opening movement to concerto 6 as you will ever hear. In this case, it works. Play the first movement of concerto 6 with the Collegium Aureum (7:09) and Musica Antiqua Cologne (4:26) back to back for a true sense of whiplash.

I treasure this recording for the memories it evokes. Memory is a funny thing in this case. It doesn't lie, but rather it underscores a love for a rather flawed recording. I harbor warm memories, but am clear eyed enough not to recommend this recording to others. It simply does not measure up technically or artistically to other available recordings: [[ASIN:B000002AQ4 Tafelmusik]], or the [[ASIN:B000EQHRVA Freiburger Barockorchester]].

If you're like me and was born in the late 1970s, then the only Stevie music that you've grown up listening to was probably songs like "Part-Time Lover" and "These Three Words". Well, although those songs are classics, I'd advise you to pick up this collection and get a thorough lesson of Steveland's career.
All of the songs that you've either heard your moms play or heard other artists do bad covers of are on here. My favorites on Disc 1 have to be "Never Had A Dream Come True", "Signed, Sealed, Delivered...", "I'm Wondering", and the list goes on. In reality, your friends will be arguing with you about what's the best song on this box set.
Other notables are the Latin-influenced "Don't You Worry 'Bout a Thing", "Lately", and "Overjoyed" from Discs 2, 3, and 4, respectively. On Disc 4, the songs go from funk and soul to light R&B, as most of the live instruments disappear in true 1980s fashion, but even those songs sound good, like the most recent Babyface song, "How Come, How Long".
Die-hard Stevie fans will of course have their own gripe about which song(s) should have been included in this box set, but all of it sure sounds good to me.

text:
This album is the greatest re-release ever in the history of rock--period! Not only is the studio (original) portion of Second Winter an absolute gem, the live recording newly added here is even better! This package goes right alongside the Allman Brothers Fillmore East recordings as the greatest blues-driven rock guitar music out there--long overdue! Johnny will blow you away with his smoking guitar chops and soulful singing. And when he starts the intro guitar solo to B.B. King's "It's My Own Fault", you would swear you were listening to B.B. himself! The rapid-fire licks he throws off during "Mama, Talk To Your Daughter" are wicked.

A young Edgar Winter joins him onstage for the last half of the concert to show off his own prowess on keyboards, sax, drums, and vocals. Also a talented guy, no doubt. Sometimes his screechy falsetto gets a little old--that's my only gripe on this whole package. But's it's not enough of a blemish to take away from this being the most indispensable release of the past few years!

If you've seen Johnny Winter recently in concert, you know as well as I that he's past his prime, bless him. Well, Second Winter is his prime, for sure, so if you're not too familiar with early recordings of Johnny, you are sorely missing out. Miss out no more, and get this CD package!!!

title: 12 more classics
text: following behind Volume One, this Volume Two offers 12 more smash hits of Conway Twitty. his first country #1 from 1968, "Next in Line", opens things up. Conway's hits were so popular that i'll bet it was tough for MCA to choose which 12 made the final cut. the years for the songs on this CD in chronological order are: 1968 (track 1), 1970 (track 2), 1973 (track 3), 1974 (track 4), 1977 (track 5), 1979 (tracks 6 and 7), 1980 (track 8), 1981 (track 9), 1987 (tracks 10 and 11), and 1989 (track 12). you'll notice the gap between 1981 and 1987. MCA isn't highlighting his Warner Brothers era, of course (1982-1986). MCA, if they so choose, could release at least four MORE volumes of 12-song CDs on Conway and still have massively popular singles to choose from! the guy had 78 Top-10 hits...55 of them hit #1! 18 other singles charted in the Top-40!! giving him 96 Top-40 hits MCA should use in future releases. On this CD, "Julia" is awesome. "A Bridge that Just Won't Burn", a 1980 #2 smash hit, was over-shadowed by his 1980 #1 "I'd Love to Lay You Down" {that extremely popular single has yet to surface on The Millennium Collection series!} but i love the lazy, jazzy piano/harmonica arrangement of "A Bridge That Just Won't Burn" anyway! the CD closes with his 54th #1 hit from 1989, "She's Got a Single Thing in Mind" which deals with divorce...on Volume One it showcased his 55th and final #1 "Crazy in Love" from 1990. After "I See The Want To In Your Eyes", his 1974 #1 hit, the CD jumps up to 1977...3 years worth of #1 smashes are left off!!! THERE HAS GOT TO BE MORE VOLUMES!!!!

title: Essential for your Listening Pleasure!
text:
This CD was my first excursion beyond Mozart's last six symphonies (for those I highly recommend the re-release of Karl Bohm's 2-for-1 budget set on DG), and what a delight it is. All three symphonies were written when Mozart was about 18 years of age, and they have the aura of fully-formed genius about them. They overflow with vitality, and #25 (the only other symphony Mozart wrote in a minor key other than #40) will just explode on you with its urgency and drama. The first movement was actually used in the film "Amadeus," at the beginning when they're rushing the ailing Salieri through the streets of Vienna. Turn up the volume for this one, because MacKerras really lets it rip, and I'd be surprised if you don't recognize it right away. Ditto for the first movement of #29. In fact, all three of these symphonies seem to belong on one recording together, just as Mozart's last three symphonies ideally do, but for different reasons. Here they share a degree of exuberance and willingness for experimentation that makes them instantly appealing.
Years ago I had an old EMI budget recording of MacKerras doing Mozart's final two symphonies, and he really held nothing back on those. If anything, these Telarc recordings ratchet up the intensity, and I really like the extent to which the recording engineers do the little things on this CD, like accenting the horns in the final movement of #29, without in any way undermining the singing quality of the Prague string section. This is an inspirational selection, beautifully performed, and recorded as only Telarc can do it. In other words, a must.

title: When Barney Bigard Held Forth

As I have mentioned in previous reviews of various classical jazz artists I came to an appreciation of that musical art from one source, and one source only- Lady Day, Billie Holiday. Along the way I started to get interested in her various back-up musicians which led me to the likes of Lester Young, Johnny Hodges, Artie Shaw and others. And, of course, when you get to Johnny Hodges you naturally have to think the Duke- Ellington that is. And when you get to Duke then you have to delve into his various formations from trios up to orchestra and along the way, clarinetist Barney Bigard

Now, for those not familiar with the swing era in jazz, or know swing and the place of the clarinet in it mainly through the great work of Benny Goodman then Barney Bigard may not be known to you. However, those who know jazz better than I do say pound for pound Barney was a better clarinetist. I will leave that for the aficionados but in this CD you will get many of his great performances with various Duke Ellington group configurations and a few of his own compositions so YOU can judge. title: Another Broadway Angel title is restored to the catalogue by DRG.
text:
After having been out-of-print for more than 10 years now, Capitol's original off-Broadway cast recording of Rick Besoyan's delightful operetta spoof returns to active service today.

This was Capitol's first off-Broadway cast album, although the 2-piano accompaniment heard in the theatre was replaced by a full orchestra for the recording.

Eileen Brennan shot to stardom as the winsome Little Mary. John McMartin (later in FOLLIES, SWEET CHARITY, HIGH SOCIETY and dozens of TV shows) was her co-star.

Not all of it works on record. Without the exaggerated staging it might come across as just another operetta.

Some of it didn't work in the theatre: "Do You Ever Dream of Vienna" only made people sad.

But then there's the lively title song, the delightful "Look for a Sky of Blue" and the silly (but fun) 3-part sequence: Playing Croquet/Swinging/How DO You Do?" all make for enjoyable listening, and thanks to DRG for the reissue.

At one time (1992-1997) DRG had the London cast album in their catalogue. It's worth tracking down since it contains the First Act Finale "What Has Happened"; as well as "Say uncle" and "Heap Big Injun" all of which were left off the American album. (The London cast does drop 3 other songs, so you really need both Cd's to get the full score!)

title: Superb rendition!
text: I have several copies of The Messiah, either the full work or highlights, and I was immediately impressed with this reading of the work.  As it is in vogue to do the work with period instruments and using Baroque period sized ensembles (not the gigantic Victorian performances we grew up on), this one needed to be special to catch my ear and not be just another "orginal instruments" also ran.  Martin Pearlman does a wonderful job with his pace and the musicians are absolutely first rate.  I felt both the weight and the intimacy of the work, something I did not expect and something very few performances get right, IMO.  This was the first time I had heard Boston Baroque and now I know it is a great ensemble.  After I purchased The Messiah, I purchased some other recordings by Pearlman with Boston Baroque (including Handel's Water Music) and I was quite impressed with these other recordings, as well.  These people are first rate and Pearlman clearly grasps what the Barioque was about.  I am not a believer generally in what is termed a "definitive" performance, but this recording of The Messiah is about as close as I have ever found.  It is a very enjoyable performance and I am very happy to play it.  It is easily my first choice of all of the recordings I have heard of The Messiah.

title: A Great Album despite ... or becuase?
text:
This album is, to me, a classic. There's an incredibly strong emotional energy behind most of the songs on here, of which 'heroin' is probably the most outstanding example. The music is eclectic, range from sweet and melodic, to avant-garde noise, to rhythm and blues. Sometime in the same song. And Lou Reed's lyrics are superb.
Nico actually only sings on a 3 songs (or is it 4, am I missing one?) and the other songs are done entirely without her, so the title is somewhat of a misnomer. Now while I think this album is charming, it is highly idiosyncratic as well, and just because I like it doesn't mean you will. Here's somethings to note:

The production is HORRIBLE, I don't think there's a single song on the album without at least one instrument badly overdriven. This is in fact charming in a way, to me, and I think it adds a nice finish to "Sunday Morning" in particular, but a couple songs, like "Femme Fatale" would really benefit from a cleaner production.

Avant garde noise. Screaching feedback. Screaching, droning violas, unsteady percussion, atonal paino playing. In my opinion the only song made unlistenable by these factors is "European son', which features around 2 minutes of song and 3 minutes of noise. The feedback at the finale of 'Herion' works, and is appropriate thematically, but one could wish it was mixed to be less over-powering. John Cale's screaching droning viola is essential to "Black Angel Death Song" and "Venus in Furs", but it is not a pleasant thing. While I like all of these, it is easy to see why someone else might not.

Distinctive vocal styles of both Lou Reed and Nico. Lou Reed is a bit like Bob Dylan, I can't really think of a simile for Nico though. Listen to the samples, if you don't like their voices, you probably don't want this album.

Extremely simple forms characterize the songs, and some are extended for as long as 'herion's' 7 minutes of the same two chords. (D major and a G variant) Except for "European Son' and "Run, run, run", this isn't a problem for me. The songs have sufficient weight to be repeated out this long. If your attention span prevents you from making it though a song over 3 minutes long, don't buy this album.

Really, the best thing to do is to LISTEN to most of the tracks before you buy this album, because to some, the idiosyncrasies of this album will combine to make it great, and to others they will combine to make it almost unlistenable.
