title: A Legendary Progressive Rock Album
text: Believe it or not, it was my mom that introduced me to this album. She told me that when she was about my age she had it on tape and loved it. Since then I wanted it and I have finally got it. I really don't think to many people have heard of Rick Wakeman's solo projects. I'm sure they know him from Yes and the album he did with Black Sabbath but not of his own works, I could be wrong though. From what I've gathered, this is his third album the first being The six Wives Of Henry VIII and the second Journey To The Center Of The Earth. If this album is any indacation of how good his solo works are, I need to pick those other two up. On to the music. The story is about Arthur and his companions and their many exploits and I think he loosly based this album on Thomas Mallory's Le Morte D'Arthur in particular. This album shows that Wakeman is a master (if not the master) of the synthisizer and keyboard. Each song is distinct from the previous which is good in my book. And while there isn't a whole lot of singing, the songs themselves do a good job of telling the story and characters. I just love the different arrangements that go with the different characters, especially Merlin and Guinevere. Plus Rick is accompinied by an orchrastra and The English Chamber Choir which is totaly cool. I've read some reviews saying that some of the singing isn't that great but I have to disagree. While it's not the best singing I've ever heard it's still pretty good. The use of jazz and fusion jazz is also good and in my opinion really helps this already excellent album out. If I have any complaints it is that this album is too short and that it comes with no lyrics. For the first, it doesn't really matter because even though it is over forty-two minutes, I've got other cds that are good but are shorter. And as for the lyrics, I'll get over it because there isn't a whole lot of singing and what singing that is there is pretty much understandable. Definitely an excellent album that shouldn't be passed up.

title: Rarely Heard But Wonderful: Krenek for Piano
text:
Ernst Krenek (1900-1991) was a composer who had more stylistic periods than even Stravinsky. That is to say, he started out as a member of the Weillian school (out of which came his most famous work, the opera 'Jonny Spielt Auf'), became more and more enamored of the 12-tone school and wrote many works in that style, moved on to a modified neoclassic style and finally came full circle with a return to ultra-simple tonality and folk-like themes. And all those styles are apparent in this marvelous collection of his piano music. The works here span the period from 1922 to 1956, but his Opus 1, a piano fugue, comes from 1918 and he kept writing piano music up to 1988 (the Seventh Piano Sonata). The works on this disc are presented in generally chronological order of their composition.

'Five Piano Pieces' (1926) sound very much like the music in 'Jonny Spielt Auf', which is to say they are a dry, jazzy, rhythmically inventive, and often polytonal style. Particularly attractive are the third number, a furiously fast toccata, and the fourth and fifth numbers, which are played without pause. The latter are a sardonic funeral march followed by a twenties-style jazz one step with dreamy bitonal interjections.

The 'Second Piano Sonata' (1928), in three movements, is reminiscent, oddly, of present-day neoromanticism, but with a fair admixture of impressionist harmonies which, let us not forget, figure heavily in the jazz style of that and succeeding eras (chords of the ninth, say, or parallel harmonic motion). One also hears echoes of the Viennese waltz (à la Ravel's 'La Valse'). Much of the second movement is a three-legged march that both delights and mystifies with its moving downbeat. The finale is again Romantic in tone with distorted near-quotations of Tchaikovsky and Richard Strauss. I liked this work a lot and the first time through I had to go back and listen to it again.

'Sonata No. 4' (1948) is another kettle of fish entirely. By the early 1950s Krenek had found his way solidly into the dodecaphonic method. I am not enough of a devotee of this method to comment much on the structure of the work, but I can say that there appears in the first movement to be a freely evolving variation of what sounds like a tone-row stated at the outset. And the arrangement of this theme allows for more than the expected quota of real or implied triads. The counterpoint is arresting in its variety and inventiveness. The second movement opens with a series of minor triads and ultimately combines a doleful theme with a nervous staccato theme, to great effect. The brief third movement is a rondo based, the composer said, on a 'devilish' 12-tone theme, and has jazzy syncopations and Scriabinesque trills. The finale is marked 'tempo di minuetto, molto lento' and is a set of somewhat meandering variations that ends with rather distracted restatements of earlier material before more or less disappearing into thin air.

The next track could not be more dissimilar to the finale of the Fourth Sonata; 'George Washington's Variations', Op. 120 (1950) -- written only two years after the Sonata -- is a set of variations based on an 18th-century American military march that is surely even triter than that used by Beethoven in his 'Diabelli Variations'. The ensuing six variations become more and more complex and ironic and one can perhaps detect Krenek's tongue planted firmly in his cheek. Whether he is cocking a snook at the jingoistic atmosphere of 1950 America is for the listener to decide. (I personally think he is. And having lived through that era that gave us Senator McCarthy, I rather enjoyed believing he meant it that way.)

'Echoes from Austria', Op. 166, (1958) is a set of six arrangements of Austrian folk tunes plus one of Krenek's own in the same simple style. This is the most innocuously bland of the works herein and frankly I didn't find much enjoyment in it, although the fifth number has some delicious harmonies.

The disc concludes with a 1 1/2 minute 'Foxtrott', taken from a 1922 suite. It takes us back to the Weillian irony of those days, and it acts as digestif after the saccharine of the Austrian tunes.

All in all, I loved this release. Pianist Mikhail Korzhev, of whom I'd never heard, plays these pieces marvelously and one can only hope there will be an ongoing series of Krenek issues in his capable hands.

Scott Morrison

title: Great music from a magical man
text: I only came to Steve Goodman a couple of years ago when I heard tracks from 'No Big Surprise' played on the radio. I have since chased up everything of his that I can find. While Steve was clearly a terrific songwriter, singer, and guitarist, his music is really much more than the sum of its parts. There is a love of life present in all his music which makes it uniquely moving. Steve could make an emotional journey out of comic songs simply through his own unfettered joy in playing them. (Some of the emotion his music generates is also bound up in the sadness of his too-early death.) This is one of Steve's best albums, and contains the best-ever version of 'The Water is wide', a beautiful traditional number that is often recorded. Buy this, and any other Goodman albums you can get your hands on.

title: Let's not get carried away here...
text:
It's crazy how gaga everyone seems to be over this album. I haven't read a single critical review of it yet, and I must admit that made me very excited to hear what I was missing. I always let myself get all excited about new albums that people are crazy about, and I'm almost always a little disappointed. So I'm trying not to let myself get my hopes up as much. I hope that doesn't sound too jaded, since I want folks who read this to take it seriously. Anyway, the point is, I was less disappointed with this than I might otherwise have been, because this album is quite good. I really, really like it. I would recommend buying it if you're into this sort of heavy metal -- I promise you'll like it. But be warned, this is not the album of the year. It's only April, and I've already heard something better. The problems I have with The Varangian Way are a bit small and petty.
One is that there's a little something missing to the sound that I can't quite put my finger on. I think that the general atmosphere of this album is missing something...I don't know what to call it...I guess it's a "bigness" to the presence. I want this album to take its time more, to let itself build, to create some sort of atmosphere. Just a little, mind you. You know what it reminds me of that I think has the same problem? The band Rhapsody. Go listen to Rhapsody and tell me if you can recognize what I'm talking about.
Second, I think that while the music here is really nicely choreographed, I would like to see it balanced with simpler melodies at times. The melody is complex (again, without having a true "fullness") and Turisas sometimes don't give you a chance to get into it before they change it into something else. It makes the music a little hard to follow, and a little hard to get into. I think this CD could be a lot more successful if they'd just hook you with some simple riffs and some catchier verses. I think there's a lot to be said for that, and I think that's what makes bands like Manowar so likeable. There's also another band, Battlelore, from Finland, that does that sort of thing well, and that's why I still think Battlelore is better than Turisas.
There's plenty to like here, though. There's some fun fiddlework in Track 5 that really got me going, and the last song, Miklagard Overture, brings the whole concept of the album full circle and really finishes everything nicely, and I think it's a totally successful way to close the album. It's truly epic. The backing vocals are perfect throughout, as are the main vocals, which I think is very crucial to good music.
So all in all, a great album. I give it a B+. Are these guys going to be bigger than Manowar? I would find that hard to believe. Will I get their next album? Probably. And so should you. This band is way better than lots of others out there.

title: Just What You'd Expect
text:
If you've been a fan of the Ted Leo and the R/x for a while, then you should know what to expect from this album: a remarkably consistent collection of very good power pop and rock songs with two or three standout tracks that will become instant favorites.

If you're not familiar with Ted Leo, here's the quick synopsis: clever lyrics and musical experimentation reminiscent of Elvis Costello, Billy Bragg, or the Clash mixed with the pop hooks and guitar licks you'd associate with Big Star, Thin Lizzy, or the Pixies.

As for the album: it's everything you can reasonably ask for from an album. Leo is one of the few performers in the indie world who's still making the unpretentious guitar rock that defined the early nineties underground scene. The most negative comments I've heard about Leo fall into two categories: either he's not original enough, or he never changes his formula. Both comments are true--Leo owes a lot to the great songwriters who preceded him. And though his influences are varied (albums often have rock albums, pop songs, and songs influenced by folk, reggae, and punk), it's true that his albums tend to be similar in style and structure and there's no real attempt to make a grand, artistic statement.

But it's really hard to criticize a guy for knowing his strengths and sticking too them. There aren't many lyricists today who can turn a better phrase, and nobody seems to write rock anthems anymore. This albums is filled with great tracks. Ranking it against his earlier albums, it's probably a bit beneath the level of "The Tyranny of Distance" and "Hearts of Oak," but it compares favorable to "Shake The Sheets." The album has a decent amount of experimentation and several laid back songs, so it's probably closest to "The Tyranny of Distance" in terms of structure.

If you want a good feel for the album check out "The Song of Cain," one of the albums best rockers, "La Costa Brava," a good pop song, and "Bomb. Repeat. Bomb," a more experimental track with an abrasive, DC-punk sound.

title: Revolutionary and Great
text:
First of all, if you like your music more conventionally minded, do not buy this album. This record is anything but, only for those who like their music more complex. If you like conventionality in music, look for an album that is more suited for your tastes.
Second of all, this album is truly revolutionary and pulls it off flawlessly. It pulls off everything flawlessly. It is impossible not to marvel at the musicianship of the entourage brought on for this album. Omar's vocals are alternately a Robert Plant-ish howl, a Jeff Buckley-ish falsetto, a vibrato rap, and so much else. The guitar picking is pure wizardry, the bass (as played by Red Hot Chili Peppers' Flea) has no unnecessary note played, and the drumming is a thrashing rush of adrenaline at all times.
And let's not forget the songs themselves. The flow between songs is seemless; the songs might as well be one entity because they are so connected. The lyrics are something along the lines of someone getting high while reading the dictionary. This may make this sound like a bad thing but it can't be better. The words are so lyrical and poetic it's astonishing. This could be what happened when the man for who this album was made died, an escape from his demise. It could be inspired by anything, it's still perfect.
If you like your music revolutionary and complex, get this album now. This is among the ten best albums ever in my book.

title: Decent, but skimpy compilation (master tape problems, maybe)
text:
A few points: first, my copy contains the 4:42 "extended version" of Sunshine Superman, not the "shorter single version" as has been suggested here by some (the original album version was about 3:15, ironically). Also, I (unlike some others) have no trouble with mono releases - that's what it was in those days. We listened to this music, often as not, in juke boxes and car radios. The mono/stereo debate continues.

Donovan's UK releases of about 5-7 years ago were from EMI, and supposedly from the "original" master tapes (Donovan was ill-served by Pye and EMI in the 60s - more was released (by Epic, a Columbia subsidiary) in the US and Canada). The album releases in the US in the 60s were more numerous, and very different from the UK, both in selections and in the mixes. Electronically rechanneled stereo was all the rage for a time, especially in North America, and usually sounded pretty dreadful, even then, as strange things were done, like adding echo and reverb. Much of this music (on Disc 1) was released in the US in this form.

The UK re-releases have certainly addressed the sound problems; the Vic Anesini remasters contained in this release may not have been from the _original_ master tapes (almost certainly weren't, because if they were, the booklet would have said so). Having said that, Anesini has done as well as he could, given what he probably had to work with. Remember, a remaster is not a remix, and the "mono" he had access to may have been, in some cases, fold-downs from the rechanneled "stereo" and not true mono. Since we don't know the status of the tapes Anesini mastered from, we can only guess. Most cuts here are at least acceptable in sound quality, and most are very good. I rather suspect this was rush-released to coincide with D's well-deserved induction into the R&R Hall of Fame, otherwise they might have done better in the tape research.

My usual complaint with compilations: even when they have the space, they don't fill it! Donovan, for one, has easily enough "essential" material to fill two CDs @ 79+ minutes each. In general, Columbia's Essential series often falls down, both in shortchanging us and in their sometimes dubious selections. Compare, for example with the usually excellent (in every way) Universal's Gold series - they really do a good job most of the time.

5 stars for the material; 3 for Columbia for shoddy work.

title: A Very Solid Sounding Album.

You can't go wrong with this album. "There's a Kind of Hush" has been covered by many artists, but none is so memorable as the Carpenter's recording. The vocals of Karren Carpenter are so sharp and spot on. The only other version I listen to of this song is Herman's Hermits 1967 recording.
The rest of the album is filled with very great easy listening songs that make you feel just right. The song by Randy Edelman called, "You" is a "You make me happy" song. "Sandy" is a song by Richard Carpenter and John Bettis that is very smooth and refined. "Ooh Sandy, Could we spend the day together?" "Goofas" sounds a little goofas to me, but you have to have at least one song that sounds silly. "Can't Smile Without You" should have been a hit, but was made a big hit for Barry Manilow in 1978. "I Need to Be in Love" is the best song on the album. The orchestration is fabulous. I always come back to this song. "One More Time" written by Lewis Anderson is a get away song to escape to better times. "Boat to Sail" is yet another get away song. There is a reference to "Brian Wilson songs are never left behind" and wonder if that might be one of the Beach Boy's songs or maybe several of their songs. "I Have You" has the interesting lyrics, "I was born to belong to the lines of
a song and make them my home" and also, "I believe in happy endings, though I've only known a few", which leads you to believe that you've got to create your own world of happiness when there is none. The album closes with Neil Sedaka's classic song, "Breaking Up is Hard to Do". This could have been included in their "Yesterday Once More" medley on the second side of the album "Now and Then". I don't know if it is a leftover from that session, probably not.
Now as far as the sound quality of the CD I purchased, I did not get the remastered version. I got a AAD first version of it which cuts off the piano intro to "I Need to be in Love" and sounds like the single version released on the 45. The other thing is that it sounds like a veil is put over the recording with noise reduction. The original recording on the vinyl you can hear right into Karren's mouth with every click of the tongue. The stage presence is more pronounced. I always believe that recordings from A&M records sound better on the original vinyl , even better than the remastered versions. I recommend this album to anyone seriously wanting to complete their library of Carpenters discography.

title: Playing The Game Just Right For The Times
text:
Well the 1980's had arrived. People who happy disco seemed to be dead and that punk entering a new phase. Queen themselves were entering into a very clear minded creative head at this point,even though the "new" rock world couldn't be more confused in many ways. There was so shortage of great rock coming out at this time. But it all started to seem very conditional. In many ways,this mostly existed in the writers/critics world. Musicians,performers and artists of all of sorts still had music to make. Know I said it before but it really seems to need to be said by as many as possible. After having edged out of the theatrical elements of their sound with the previous release [[ASIN:B000000OAH Jazz]],this one just went right for it. While still very much a rock album in many ways,it's all rhythm section based here. And also filled to the brim with pop hooks and craftsmenship. Not only that but Freddie was reaching for his inner soul here on an emotional level,rather than being the "drama queen" (literally) he may have come off as slightly before. The result is big success and a reborn band.

The album opens with "Play The Game",a dynamic piano ballad before going into "Dragon Attack",a fierce rocking funk of the first order that gets right down in the hard of the groove. Of course Chic's grooves are channeled directly on the lean,mean and sleek "Another One Bites The Dust",one of my favorite Queen hits with Freddie letting his inner Michael Jackson/James Brown come out,riding the rhythm break beats and all on some more smoldering funk. "Need Your Love Tonight","Sail Away Sweet Sister","Coming Soon" and the mildly new wave rock synthesizer chsrged "Rock It (Prime Jive)" introduce Queen's possibilities as a mainstream pop/rock band-very well crafted,catchy rockers there all very much radio ready for the time. The ghost of the rockabilly Bill Haley/Elvis Presley sound comes through on another hit "Crazy Little Thing Called Love",complete with the band providing Jordanaire's-like backup vocals. It could also easily work as a country swing piece as we'd much much later from Dwight Yokham. "Don't Try Suicide" is another crafted pop/rock piece dealing with a touchy issue perhaps,but encouraging the character who THINKS no one cares that...people would care even less if she died.

"Save Me" closes the original album with a John Lennon type confessional piano ballad and than it's onto an R.A.K remix of "Dragon Attack",which slickens up the funk groove again with a heavy dose of early 90's hip-hop. Overall this is an excellent beginning for Queen's poppier phase. And because they were always great craftsmen and pop tunsmiths underneath all the instrumental theatrics,they actually always possessed the stuff to make it work when the need arose. And their was need. Progressive/glam/art/pomp rock,or anything in that general area had two basic choices during this era-to go the more mainstream pop direction Queen did or become arena favorites. As with most rock bands who went the poppier route,Queen probably fooled a lot by really remaining exactly who they'd always been. Just made their songs a lot easier to take in. Also the bands transition towards a funkier dance oriented sound went very well along with the new wave era's strong sense of groove and soul. This would become an even bigger part of Queens sound as the decade progressed,providing mixed results for them critically. But for now,they'd "crossed over" in a way that was both acceptable to themselves and most everyone else.

title: Great disc, despite themselves.
text:
I've always felt that the best way to listen to heavy music is while driving long dark stretches of empty post roads far past midnight (alone), and employing that tradition proved once again to be the right thing to do.

The first thing that struck ma about the music was that the musicians could truly play their instruments; the bassist's playing in particular, is full of tasty licks, and frankly, I'm reminded most of Somewhere in Time/Powerslave-era Iron Maiden or early-Nineties Suicidal Tendencies.

While Alex Varkatzas, primary vocalist, probably screams too much and the cadence of his "singing" is rather stilted, he still delivers the good, expressing the agony, escstasy, and rage of the music. The backing vocals and occaional sung choruses/breakdowns complement the music as well and make an excellent counterpoint to the howls.

There are three reasons why, despite thoroughly enjoying this disc, I can't give it a five-star rating: 1) it's exceptionally brief, clocking in at just under 43:30. 2) it's a little bit over-produced--the rawness that seems inherent to their music and to the genre is lost, leaving everything somwhat . . . slick. 3) the lyrics are absolutely horrible, however much conviction is mustered to sing them.

. . . and I can live with the pseudo-goth image--after all, I've been hooked on Queensryche since their "Queen of the Reich" days, and besides, image has nothing to do with talent. The CD booklet is festooned with images of lilies and an intriguing Kate Moss-lookalike with fangs, an impressive webwork of prominent veins on her upper body, and freaky contact lenses, and this will offend the sensibilities of some because they find it creepy, and others because they find it tired and lame, but the music speaks for itself, and should be one's motivation for purchasing the disc.

title: The band's second transition album - take that for what you will.
text:
If what you're used to is the old-school borderline-harsh emo-core Jimmy, this album will in all likelihood irritate you to death, and you will find it as much a sellout as "Bleed American" or whatever that album is being called now.

But this particular album is a natural progression for the band, something all bands eventually go through (ex. Goo Goo Dolls). It trades the harshness for occasional bitterness, the chainsaw guitars for refinement, and the payoff is glittering pop gems like "Work", "Polaris" and the monumental, wistful "23".

And because it is "Jimmy" there is substantially better musical craftsmanship present here than we see for other, younger bands currently higher on the hip scale (it isn't three-chord BS). The album is especially enjoyable for old geezers like me, who have out-grown the need to get caught in the mosh.

title: Let him introduce himself reel good...
text: There is no doubt that `Dr. Feelgood' is Motley Crue's most accomplished and successful album and for good reason. The band made the lifestyle changes (albeit temporarily) that allowed them to produce music that their collective talents were capable of but had been held back by living certain aspects of the rock n' roll lifestyle to the hilt (ie. drugs, drugs and more drugs). Nikki Sixx sobered up (to save his life never mind his career) and wrote a much better album as a result. The pulled off the rare combination of sobriety without losing any of their edge and result (no doubt helped by new producer Bob Rock) was also their best sounding record as well. The hits flowed through as the title track, "Kickstart My Heart" and "Don't Go Away Mad" showed that the Motley's weren't going away, at least not for awhile. Some of the additions which had influenced the previous album, sort of a glam blues thing flourished on `Feelgood'.  Sex dominates such pornographic but fun ditties as "Slice of Your Pie", "Sticky Sweet" and "She Goes Down" while the Crue also shows their sensitive sides with a couple of ballads.  Unfortunately the highly combustible nature of the four personalities would mean that success would not insure stability and within a couple of years the first of several band blow ups would occur as Vince would leave for the first time. Motley are still here today but they said all they needed to say with Dr. Feelgood.

title: ULTIMATE CLASSIC TRIO
text: There was some kind of Creative Harmonic Convergence that Jazz was the recipient of during the brief time The Bill Evans Trio,(Bill Evans (Piano), Scott LaFaro (Bass), Paul Motian (Drums), played together. To listen to SUNDAY AT THE VILLAGE VANGUARD is to become aware of a chemistry, a creative fire present in this trio. A fire that is timeless. The music on this c.d. sounds as fresh and exciting today as the moment it was expressed through these three musical artists. Sometimes I wonder how Scott LaFaro might have evolved musically. There is no doubt of his consummate gifts as a bassist. He seems to me to be exploding with musical expression. Wonder if he had the chance to develop further whether there might have come into his playing less busyness, more economy, silence. Somehow Bill Evans had that quality from the very beginning. I've never had a pianist affect me the way Bill Evans always has. Especially the ballads. This album is mostly up tempo, and yet I love it for the same reason I do the ballads. It seems to me that Bill Evans played from his heart and soul, and that he penetrated into such a depth in the region of his own being, that his own heart and soul becomes the heart and soul of the listener, in this instance - mine, too. Paul Motian's exquisite, understated and refined playing was the perfect support and complement for the trio. This is the trio against which all others have been and will continue to be measured. To listen to this album is to be touched by PERFECTION.

title: Rare delicacy in TPL, in both senses
text:
Years ago I fell in love with Messiaen's "Trois Petites Liturgies" of 1944. Since then I've grabbed many of its rare recordings and this new one is a delight. Myung-Whun Chung conducts a remarkably delicate but solid performance by the strings, percussion and women's voices of Radio France. As ever comfortable with the composer's peculiar melange of low-carb Debussy, birdsong imitations and mid-century steel, Chung allows a few tiny idiosyncracies, like the lengthy crescendo closing the second movement. It's definitely the first time I've heard the vocal part sound so refreshingly young, and Roger Muraro's clear but un-bang-y piano playing effectively seals the nimble approach. "Liturgies" takes half the disc and easily justifies purchase on its own. (Anyone wishing to purchase a comparative reading should try the Bernstein re-issue on Sony, it's segments also available here as MP3 downloads.)

"Couleurs de la cite celeste" is from two decades later and is more rigorously abstract and ornithological, with a deliberately hard-edged tonal palette omitting strings, keeping the piano, and adding brass plus a tangy, quicksilver trio of clarinets. Interestingly, it's the broader-paced brass chorales that sweeten this number.

The wash of strings opening the last selection, "Hymne pour grand orchestre" is a balm for those wishing to re-visit the post-Impressionist emollients of the "Liturgies." Messiaen had to re-compose the music in 1946 after its score and parts were lost, but he seems to have retained the flavor of the 1932 original. So often the case with Messiaen, the piece is ostensibly sacred in inspiration but feels ecstatically Tristan-esque through much of its duration.

I had not heard either "Coleurs" or "Hymne" before, and it's a privilege to add these works to my library. Had you predicted 20 years ago that a German record company would engage a Korean-born pianist-conductor to issue a definitive set of Messiaen's difficult and French-to-the-core orchestral works, I'd have laughed. The joke's on me, since that's indeed the case.

title: Accessible, enjoyable, and falt-out wonderful
text:
Many armchair-jazz pursuists have a few unkind words to say towards the Bad Plus. While others praise the wonderful reinterpretations of pop songs, many cite the fact that this is an old tradition, nothing innovative, and that their original works simply are not up to snuff. They usually end with a mention on how one should go and listen to "true jazz" in the likes of Brad Mehldau or Matthew Shipp.
Don't get me wrong: these critiques are understandable. But accessibility does not translate to "dumbed-down jazz" by any means. (On top of that, Mehldau and Shipp both love pop covers as well, the former attacking Radiohead songs with a fury ["Paranoid Android" & "Exit Music (For A Film)"] the latter taking "Frere Jacques" and sending it to acid-jazz hell and back)
The use of covers is no doubt an imporant part of the Plus' appeal - many alt-rock pursuits caught a glimpse of their beautiful rendition of "Smells Like Teen Spirit" and then bought their debut album, "These Are the Vistas." Electronica kids were stunned upon hearing that a group did a jazz cover of Aphex Twin's "Come to Daddy" B-side "Film". Its parent album happened to make it onto Rolling Stone's Top 50 Albums of the Year list.
Yet, while the covers drew people in, it was the originals that kept them there. "Keep The Bugs ..." had a syrupy and wonderful bassline and wonderful piano work, while the aformentioned "Film" had some very understated and fantastic drumming that any true jazz fan would simply marvel at.
Which brings us to Give. In many ways, this album follows the same pattern as the last one, except with far more diversity and far more success. The covers are still wonderful: the pounding, scary rendition of Black Sabbath's "Iron Man" makes for a fantastic album closer, while revisions of the Pixies "Velouria" and Orentte Coleman's "Street Woman" are just wonderful. Yet, again, its the original compositions that happen to keep you there. Simply listen to the steel drum (!) work on "Cheney Pinata", making for a feel one generally wouldn't expect from a jazz album. And, truly, nothing really matches the heights of the energetic, fun, and almost dancable "Layin' A Strip For the Higher-Self State Line", a song so filled with joy it's impossible to resist. While still adhearing to the same formula, it's astonishing to see the drastic new directions the band is still able to pursue.
If people still think the band is nothing more than a so-so jazz combo with novelty covers to hook people in, they are sadly mistaken. The band recently released three studio outtakes online that didn't make the album. One of which was a cover of "Every Breath You Take". If they truly wanted to sell out, they would've included that, but no - they didn't, leaving room for their glorious new originals.
This, matched with El-P's fantastic "High Water (Mark)" (released on the same day, no doubt), 2004 is already shaping up to be the year for jazz, and in the best way possible.

title: 2 New Songs out of 84 Tracks over a 3 CD Box Set
text:
Rhino Handmade gives the lavish box set treatment to THE MONKEES PRESENT album from 1969, and the fans who love The Monkeees will spend the expensive price tag for it. It's all done expertly well, with renowned Monkees curator, Andrew Sandoval, extracting virtually every surviving alternate mix, take and occasional unreleased track from the vaults. Out of 84 tracks, there are only 2 never before released songs, HOW CAN I TELL YOU and OPENING NIGHT. These 1969 tracks were left unfinished , but as the pickings are slim for totally unreleased songs, they are good to have, both being Davy Jones tracks. The original 12 track album is not their strongest album. In his liner notes, Sandoval explains the denouement of The Monkees in very informative, detailed fashion. It's hard to believe that they actually expanded PRESENT to 3 CD's when not even all 12 of the original album songs were all strong songs to begin with. The tracks by both Davy and Mike Nesmith are in abundance on this set. Micky Dolenz surprisingly has the least songs, with only a handful of bonus tracks in different mixes, all of which have been previously released, such as STEAM ENGINE, MIDNIGHT TRAIN and YOU'RE SO GOOD. ROSE MARIE turns up for the 7th time in another , hard to tell what's the difference in it mix. LITTLE GIRL is the most different as it is without Micky's multi-tracked vocals, featuring only 1 Micky vocal. Davy's songs I think are the most varied and strongest songs across this 3 CD set. Jones really composed a lot of his own songs during this period. The original album songs like FRENCH SONG and IF I KNEW are more mature sounding songs lyrically and musically. They feature more influences from other countries, and are more moody works that would fit perfectly on a film soundtrack. The abundance of songs by Davy include different mixes or takes that sound much clearer than the mixes used on the 3 volumes of MISSING LINKS, which is where virtually all of the " bonus " material on this set were originally issued in the late 80's. Davy's songs such as IF YOU HAVE THE TIME, MY STORYBOOK OF YOU, TIME AND TIME AGAIN, I NEVER THOUGHT IT PECULIAR and a host of others are both moody and joyous examples of Jones' talents. It makes you appreciate what he did in this life, making music that he loved, which a lot of people, millions , still love and listen to. His songs really stand out here as the foundation of this set.

Mike Nesmith's amazing LISTEN TO THE BAND , widely regarded as one of the group's greatest recordings , which came too late in their career to be the big hit it deserved, is here in 4 different mixes. Most of his songs on this set have been previously released as well on the MISSING LINKS volumes. The other original album songs of his, like GOOD CLEAN FUN and NEVER TELL A WOMAN YES, were very weak songs to begin with , with little continuity, sense or melody. He explains in the liner notes how he came to write GOOD CLEAN FUN , which illustrate how some of the original songs on PRESENT were not even strong songs at all. I remember when I was a kid thinking how great it was to finally hear Nesmith do a song that was upbeat with a melody and chorus on Side 2 with OKLAHOMA BACKROOM DANCER [ written by Michael Martin Murphey who wrote the amazing WHAT AM I DOIN' 'HANGIN' ROUND on album #4 ]. Nesmith had stronger songs than the dreadful NEVER TELL A WOMAN YES, and bonus songs like CALICO GIRLFRIEND SAMBA, ANGEL BAND, and DOWN THE HIGHWAY confirm that stronger songs were left behind on PRESENT. DOWN THE HIGHWAY is not an unreleased song, but is actually MICHIGAN BLACKHAWK from MISSING LINKS VOLUME 2. It's a big letdown that on CD 3, all of the unreleased songs except for the 2 Davy songs are backing track instrumentals only that Nesmith didn't record vocals for. The 1969 TV Mixes of KICKING STONES [ TEENY TINY GNOME ], APPLES PEACHES BANANAS & PEARS and other songs may sound enticing , but differ very little than their previously available versions.

Monkees devotees will want this box, as Monkees fans are almost as obsessed to own these elaborate, expanded & expensive CD's as Rhino is for padding them with extra material . In reality, a 3 CD box set that has almost every song previously available, could have easily been a 2 CD set. Rhino released 2 CD sets of the first 4 Monkees albums , which were the Monkees biggest selling albums in their career, and made them available in stores. To keep the continuity of the 3 CD box set that started with album #5, THE BIRDS, THE BEES AND THE MONKEES, and selling the sets only online, Rhino is really exploiting what little they have left in the Monkees vault. This will go out of print, as they manufactured only 5,000 copies. The Monkee faithful will want this, just as I bought it. For fans that aren't into the " everything but the kitchen sink " approach, the 1 CD version of PRESENT that Rhino issued years ago will do, as well as the MISSING LINKS volumes.

title: Signs S&M is selling out???
text:
After getting this album I was thinking (more or less hoping) it would be reminiscent of great albums like Balance and Bad Dreams. I remember when I first heard Swollen (unfortunately I was a little late and was introduced right after Monsters was released). They were far and above anything I'd heard before and the reason I fell in love with their sound was because they "talk about dungeons and dragons" as Mad Child puts it in "Take it Back." They didn't sound like everyone else in the industry talking about expensive cars, women, big chromed out wheels, and how much money they have. This album has some great songs, don't get me wrong, but a lot of it sounds like it's going commercial and drifting away from their famous sound that got me into them in the first place. Porn Star- their major single that has a video isn't exactly sell-out, but some lyrics point to the current downward spiral I fear they're headed. Also there aren't very many original Rob The Viking tracks that blow my mind (such as my favorite of more recent times: So Deadly- originally introduced in the DVD included in Heavy (SE)). This album scares me, I fear that S&M might be headed for a more popularized rap sound, which what would differentiate them from groups like G-Unit and T.I. (which are key reasons I keep my radio turned off and iPod plugged in). Some of the tracks are good- Kyla, Meltdown, My Life and Concerto are among my favorites. Also the Featuring tracks are a welcome mash up, Everlast returns for yet another album (Put Me On was an instant classic in my book). I did like how they invited Tech N9ne for a song, even if that song isn't the best ever it is awesome to see one of my favorite underground solo acts featured on a S&M album.
Main point, if the rest of their albums continue on this trend I might just stop listening to their new stuff and pretend that they broke up after their 3 year hiatus. I really hope this isn't where my favorite group is headed with the sell-out sounds that are hard to differentiate from the rest of the MTV/Clear Channel sound out there. If so, maybe Shane shouldn't have quit the drugs- anyone else think he looked a little chubby in the Porn Star video?

title: Straight Ahead Jackie Mac in Mono
text:
Just for clarification, this review is based on the 2009 reissue of Bluesnik.

First off, this cd contains some great straight ahead blowing, particularly by the leader, the late great, Jackie McLean. The title track, Bluesnik features the best overall blowing of the session with passionate blowing from Jackie and I particularly like Kenny Drew's bright n' bouncy solo. Vastly underrated bassist Doug Watkins owns Drew's Blues with his pulsing walking bass lines setting the groove.

Unlike the previous 1987 release, Van Gelder elected to remaster this new one in mono just like he did with the recent reissue of the classic Soul Station by Hank Mobley. Why? Better ask him. Maybe it's 1950's nostalgia or something. I have the first 1987 issue, remastered by Ron McMaster in stereo and it sounds great. Ok, so we didn't get the extra photos n' fancy back then, but you can find them on the net if you Google Jackie.

Sound wise, for those who would care, it was Hubbard on the left channel, Jackie on the right and the rhythm section in the middle with the drums just slightly off to the right, the typical Van Gelder arrangement back then. I don't think you really miss anything sound wise with the new mono but good stereo just adds more interest and with all the nice sound systems nowadays, I feel cheated otherwise.

Whatever, this is a very nice and most welcome reissue from one of jazz's all time great alto saxophonists that belongs in any straight ahead bop collection.

when I listened to boys noize after reading a positive review about them, esp the first 3 tracks, I felt that it was too much like justice but w/o weird/odd/corny overdubs[ie "let there be light"] that justice likes to use.

SO the question is whether to buy this to listen to more buzz synths & robot voices if you have justice & when MSTRKRFT so masterfully shown how to use buzz synths in a pop or structured way that is so much fun...

Luckily for BN, someone lent me their CD & I listened to it more on a leisurely basis & was blown away by the remix "my moon, my man" & "I-robot" even w/ vocals are in german. Now I dig tracks like "Oh, & down & Lava, lava".

BN is a real good case study to compare mstrkrft's vs justice's approach. Mstrkrft constructs pop songs using only instrumentals & robot voices..it may look easy but it's not[hard to create compelling hooks that are short & sweet].

Justice, on the other hand, does more breakbeats & layers them to the point where the song is sinking under the weight of too many riffs/beats trying to hang on. But justice REALLY knows how to play funk bass which seems to be their sound/hook. That's how I came to like it eventually

BN uses a more conventional approach to song structure ie ravel's bolero version where a beat/hook is steadyly built on. It can be boring but if used more to build a song,then it is very effective ie "my moon, my man" & a song NOT on this album, "feel good tv off", which was a beautiful, melodic song that really moved me.

I think BN has talent..they should study mstrkrft/old chemical bros's approach to creating songs using buzz synths & look less to justice.

But it should be obvious from my above paragraphs that you have to get MSTRKRFT's the looks if you have not[see my review of it]. Also people who liked Daft Punk's human after all album will be able to enjoy this.

title: WWII History Meets Metal
text:
If you have an affinity for history, it is impossible not to enjoy Sabaton. Although it is not technically a concept album, Sabaton's Coat of Arms (the band's 5th studio release and last with original guitarists Rickard Sundén and Oskar Montelius) is almost exclusively about the Second World War. As far as I can tell, the only song that does not deal with WWII themes is the epic "Metal Ripper," a tribute to Sabaton's influences whose lyrics are drawn from classic rock/metal songs including "Highway to Hell," "Mr. Crowley," and "Master of Puppets," among others.

Sabaton's style on Coat of Arms is smooth and streamlined. Similar to many other power metal bands, the keyboards are the prominent instrument on a good number of Sabaton songs. Even when the guitars and bass take on more of a featured role (like on the excellent "Screaming Eagles") the keyboards are still in the foreground of the music. This isn't a bad thing, but along with meaty guitar tones and the occasional use of synths, it does give Sabaton a very distinct European/Scandinavian sound. Fans of European metal will know what I'm getting at here.

Coat of Arms is a very catchy album that contains a lot of good vocal hooks and slick guitar and keyboard solos. While the song lengths and structures are repetitive (a personal pet peeve of mine), the various speeds and tempos mostly make up for this. In addition, the lyrics are outstanding. Lead vocalist Joakim Brodén and bassist Pär Sundström never cease to impress me with their ability to create clever poetry using historical events and characters as their base. Anyone fascinated by history will likely also be fascinated by Sabaton.

Taken as a whole, Coat of Arms is a solid, likeable album with excellent lyrics and strong musicianship. Listening from beginning to end, there is not a single song I would skip; however, I should also note that a few of the tracks in the middle of the album do get lost in the shuffle. Moreover, the fact that every song is essentially the same length and follows the same pattern gets tedious by the album's end. This is really my only criticism, though, and if that's the worst thing I can say about Coat of Arms, then I won't hesitate to recommend it to fans of power metal and classic rock everywhere.

Highlights: "Coat of Arms"; "Uprising"; "Screaming Eagles"; "Wehrmacht"

title: Mark and Travis prove they're more than just Blink one-eighty two-thirds.
text:
The majority of +44's debut album sounds more or less exactly like what you'd expect from Blink-182's former rhythm section: simple yet melodic instrumental arrangements accented by technically complex and innovative percussion, with boyishly idealistic vocals at the forefront of it all. And while it may be nearly impossible to listen to When Your Heart Stops Beating objectively without comparing it to Blink co-frontman Tom Delonge's current project Angels and Airwaves, the two entities couldn't be further apart musically and thematically.

Rather than reinventing themselves as musicians, bassist/vocalist Mark Hoppus and drummer Travis Barker (along with guitarists Craig Fairbough and Shane Gallagher) have extracted the gloomiest, most sonically textured elements from Blink-182's self-titled 2003 album and superimposed them over stuttering electronic beats, factoring keyboards and digital sampling where appropriate, giving their moody brand of power-pop a characteristic reminiscent of 80s darkwave. As for the quality of the music itself, while not particularly enterprising or neoteric, the songs are as enjoyable as pedestrian, radio-ready pop-rock gets. The gloomy verses and sweeping chorus of 'Little Death', along with the urgency and rhythmic consistency of the album's title track are examples of +44 at their most anthemic while 'Weatherman' and 'No, It Isn't' are reminders that depressing melodies and lyricism can be as ear-pleasing as they are mood-lowering.

By the time the album wraps up with the optimistic Jimmy Eat World inspired 'Chapter 13', the listener is left with 12 formulaic but enjoyable pop songs, given added depth by Hoppus' memorable lyrics ("The past is only the future with the lights on" he sings on 'Baby Come On' while relating that "A little death makes life more meaningful" on 'Little Death').

Far less tangential that Angels and Airwaves, and substantially darker lyrically and sonically, When Your Heart Stops Beating is the spiritual follow-up to Blink 182's last album - competent gloom-pop that remains accessable from start to finish.

title: Exotic yet accessible
text: When most Westerners think of Indian music, two things come to mind. On one hand, there is Ravi Shankar style classical music and on the other, there's Bollywood style pop. Being a curious blend of styles, the music of Falu falls somewhere between. "Foras Road" is accessible with regards to global aesthetics but it's also deeply rooted in tradition. Along these lines, the material is a balance of original and traditional songs. Compared to her [[ASIN:B000T4A84U eponymously titled debut]], this sophomore release is on the other end of the traditional-contemporary spectrum. Along these lines, it's not surprising that all of the vocals are in Hindi. This is classy music that expresses elegance and beauty. While featuring Indian percussion like tablas, Falu's group generally plays Western classical instruments like the cello, viola and violin. Special guests add variety. Along these lines, John Medeski of [[ASIN:B008O9V3UU Medeski Martin and Wood]] plays melodica in 'Bahaar.' As in 'Govind,' a few of these songs feature male vocals by Gaurav Shah. In 'Tarana,' Falu performs vocal calisthenics but the result isn't academic, it's pure joy. On songs like 'Jaagne,' Mark Tewarson's guitar work echoes "[[ASIN:B000005L9Z A Meeting by the River]]," a like-minded collaboration between Ry Cooder (Buena Vista Social Club) and V. M. Bhatt. It's hard not to dance to 'Hori.' Featuring a catchy chorus and a great arrangement, the song is pure bliss. Featuring what is for all intents and purposes a haunting Indian yodel, 'Laal Laal' is a mystical highlight. The bookend is 'Alaap,' which sounds like a vocal meditation. The production on "Foras Road" is excellent. The ambitious size and scope of the project is underscored by the mix. While elegant and cerebral, the album is also warm. New York City jazz cats [[ASIN:B002DU0RCQ Chris Wood]], [[ASIN:B00CP4S380 Kenny Wolleson]] and [[ASIN:B00BDSREZC John Medeski]] seamlessly blend in. Falu's vocals have to be heard to be believed. Her singing is sublime, disciplined and utterly amazing. This music will appeal to anybody that has always wanted to appreciate real Indian music yet couldn't quite get into music played by the likes of [[ASIN:B005T4S7H0 Ustad Sultan Khan]] and [[ASIN:B0000009UE Zakir Hussain]]. The appeal to "Foras Road" is broad: while it's both traditional and accessible, it's always enchanting.

title: Ring out the false, ring in the true
text:
This is a most underrated recording. While it won't make anyone's list of greats, Dark Horse contains a bevy of very fine songs. A sense of personal warmth really comes through here--not only in the songs themselves, but in the style they were recorded--as if you are in his house as they are played.
Dark Horse is mostly an album about the breakup of a marriage; all the songs on the first side cover this theme, as well as the second side's "Ding Dong" ("ring out the old, ring in the new!"). Despite the fragility of his voice, "Simply Shady" is, I believe, one of the best vocals he has ever done--sung with great feeling and sincerity. Guys who've been through the breakup of an important relationship may find words that speak to their feelings in "Simply Shady" and "So Sad."
"Bye Bye Love" is the only song that fails on this record; it starts out with great promise, rhythm guitar and synthesizer making a fine blend; but the song falls apart in the middle as George's newly written verses to this F&B Bryant classic don't follow its structure.
George has some crack musicians backing him here--roughly two groups: the L.A. Express (probably most noted as Joni Mitchell's band on "Court and Spark" as well as their own "Tom Cat") and a nucleus of Billy Preston, Willy Weeks and Andy Newmark. The latter combo, along with George and guitar, really hits a groove lick on "Maya Love"--reminding me that many great songs by Lennon, McCartney and (especially) Harrison were not recorded by the Beatles but instead were consigned to solo albums--with sometimes mixed results. But "Maya Love" and other songs here do not suffer for their musicianship.
"Ding Dong" is a Christmasy song and I always remember listening to this album in the winter (in the 70s and now). "It is He" (Jai Sri Krishna) is an infectious mantra, not unlike "My Sweet Lord" and the only overtly religious song on the album. "Far East Man." written with Ron Wood, strikes me as a very personal song--one might write about a close friend.
Those not already sold on George Harrison's music should certainly begin with "All Things Must Pass" but if you know you like his other stuff, "Dark Horse" should not be overlooked. It is arguably better than anything he put out later.

title: Fascinating, Flawed Remix & Solid Remaster of a Masterpiece… with two tragic mistakes
text:
The most interesting of the Black Sabbath Super Deluxe releases, this 45th anniversary of Black Sabbath’s seventh studio album features THREE very different versions of the classic Technical Ecstasy, along with a sixty-page book, tour book, poster, and phenomenal live album (which, although excellent, exemplifies a major flaw of this set, but more on that later).

Starting with the new remaster, the most significant thing worth noting is that—as with prior Super Deluxe releases—these remasters present a complete different-sounding version of these albums than we've heard before. Gone are the days of the Rhino box set's vile overcompression or the subpar CD masters that preceded it. The Japanese pressings are still among the best, so there will be debate as to which best exemplifies each album, but at least you're getting something different with good clarity, dynamics, and spatial distance. It's not quite as bassy as the last pressing from a few years back, and I think I prefer that version of "All Moving Parts (Stand Still)" slightly better than this one (I think this one needs slight more bass). But what Andy Pearce and Matt Wortham have done here is try to bring out the nuances of the instruments rather than attempt to make Technical Ecstasy sound like Sabotage or Vol 4. And in some cases, it's revelatory, such as in the solo of "Dirty Women," which is no longer so trebly and muddy (which was a problem with the previous remaster). So, this is a really solid remaster--one of the better ones, even if we can nitpick--and I think the warmer tone is closer to the original LP.

Then, there’s the Steven Wilson mix, which is going to be controversial. This mix is fascinating and there’s a lot of things to talk about, more than can be put in a review. Wilson has also separated out each instrument, and brought forward Ozzy’s vocals on certain songs, which had been somewhat under the prior mix. If you can get past the mastering, which is problematic, he does a good job enhancing the songs, the best part being the back end of “Dirty Women,” which is not only much more comprehensible but fascinating! No longer a muddy, jumbled mess, the clarity present now allows you to hear for the first time the incredible things these musicians are doing here (some of which appears to have been ported over from alternative versions)! (Oh, and that new ending is pretty cool too!)

On the down side, it's is a far "dryer" mix than I've ever heard for this album and one that appears to have forgotten balancing bass into it. As a result, it loses a lot of its punch and distinctive power that the album should have. Wilson makes Technical Ecstasy sound it came from a modern Indie band, which may be interesting, but is not quite right. I like Wilson's mix, but it sounds like a mistake rather than conscious choice. Andy and Matt should've done the mastering since the utter lack of bass is going to be a huge turnoff to a lot of fans, and that's a shame because there's some great stuff here.

I have to note here that if this wasn't a mistake, then I think it's best we find someone new to do new mixes of the next few Super Deluxe releases. And if it was a mistake, they should supply substitute discs to fans who contact them.

The only composition the label was unable to find was “It’s Alright,” so the original mono single is presented here instead, I think for the first time on CD. This is an interesting story because “It’s Alright” was actually first recorded in 1972 for the Vol 4 sessions, and not used, and that version has yet to surface as well. Fingers crossed that the label will eventually present us with a Lost Songs release, as there's a lot still out there.

Ok, now the Outtakes & Alternate Mixes: This presents what is ultimately a third version of this album—and some of these are wildly different. Unfortunately, this was handled by Wilson and again lacks the requisite bass, but don't let that stop you from hearing these, particularly the last four songs.

“Back Street Kids” features Ozzy without the doubled-vocals and sounds like a live version. “You Won’t Change Me,” “Gypsy,” and “Dirty Women”are similar in that regard. I don’t think the single vocal works terribly well, but for those curious as to what Ozzy might have sounded like without doubling, you’ll now understand now why he and the engineers saw fit to double and even treble his vocals. Since it's also being presented as a new mix, I'd have done something to rectify this (as Wilson could've doubled it and put it further back in the mix). What does work is hearing the different guitar/bass work being played before the final version. Such fascinating and ambitious songs no matter how you mix it!

Now things get completely bonkers! “All Moving Parts (Stand Still)” may be Sabbath at their most psychedelic and hypnotic… and funkiest! In this version, it sounds like George Clinton stopped by to jam with them! This has to be heard to be believed, it’s just nuts, and could easily fit on a Funkadelic/Parliament album! Picture a bluesy harmonica on the main riff and Geezer with a fat dube just going to town and you’ve just scratched the surface! Even Ozzy’s doing weird ad libs and alternate lyrics (as if they weren’t weird enough). While I prefer this song in its full psychedelic mode and am glad they didn’t go with this version, this is a BLAST to hear and should prove beyond a shadow of a doubt how talented and diverse this band could be!

But we’re not done yet! Did you ever wonder what “Rock ‘n’ Roll Doctor” might’ve sounded like if they leaned in more towards the honky-tonk? Did you ever think you’d hear Ozzy sing the words “boogie-woogie”? Well, strap in!

Love Sabbath’s ballads? Well, here’s the haunting “She’s Gone” done with guitar, bass, drums, and mellotron instead of orchestra! While I still prefer the original, hearing Sabbath do what's essentially a proto-power ballad is just cool, even if the lyrics are a bit wonky: “I know I’ve been a bad guy. I know I did wrong, but baby please come home again!”

But that’s not all, there’s an instrumental version of “She’s Gone.” Now hold on! This isn’t just a karaoke version without the vocals. It’s an entirely different song intended to be an instrumental ala “Fluff” and “Laguna Sunrise”! As with the three last tracks, fans had no idea this existed! At 4 minutes, this is going on my extended edition of the album!

Finally, the live album. This where things get sad. This show had been distributed amongst fans as the bootleg called Definitive Ecstasy, Disc 2. So, this is the December 8, 1976 show… and it sounds INCREDIBLE! The positives are many: Ozzy’s voice growls demonically through “Symptom of the Universe”! Tony and Geezer make “War Pigs” sound even heavier! And this is the only live version of “All Moving Parts (Stand Still)” that’s clean—and it sounds amazing!

But the down-side: this show featured four tracks off the Technical Ecstasy album, not three… one is missing—and it’s important, even if you aren’t a particular fan of the song.

For some reason, they left “Rock ‘n’ Roll Doctor” off. While you might be saying “who cares,” this is why you should: the intro and extro to the live versions of “Rock ‘n’ Roll Doctor” featured an extended jam that was the highlight of any Black Sabbath concert in the ‘70s. Cutting most of it grossly misrepresents live performances of the band! I don’t understand the reasoning behind this. From the intro, Ward’s five minute long drum solo was cut down to 30 seconds, while the jam and guitar solo were removed entirely--seven and a half minutes worth of material—leaving only the extro from “Rock ‘n’ Roll Doctor.” Together, we’re talking around 18 minutes cut from this show!

I’m sorely tempted to remove a star for this, as some will, but I don’t want fans missing out on the other great things this set has to offer. Warner Bros and Rhino: STOP DOING THIS! Release the entire original show, not edited versions! And please get some quality control on these releases.

This Super Deluxe set of Technical Ecstasy should've been a home run. As it is, it does finally dispels any notion that this was a band “falling apart,” or “imploding,” as there is plenty of energy, fun, and experimentation going on here. This was a band stretching its creative legs, exploring, and heading off into strange, new terrain. While that can be scary to younger fans who only want more of the same, it’s something that true artists have to do, and if they’re smart (as Black Sabbath were), they’ll retain aspects of their original template. Technical Ecstasy is still a heavy album; it’s also varied, experimental, and musically diverse, as was Sabbath Bloody Sabbath, as was Vol 4, as was every Black Sabbath album since their first.

I sometimes wonder if Black Sabbath remasters are like Star Wars movies on home video. Each version presents something slightly new and interesting, but with flaws that ensure that it's never quite 100% or definitively what it should be. If so, I'll see you in five years to review the next--hopefully improved versions, with a corrected remaster of the new mix.

title: One of the best of the Leslie Howard's Liszt Edition
text:
Leslie Howard performed a important service for music lovers generally, and Lisztians specifically, by recording the complete piano works of Franz Liszt. While the set is uneven in places, this particular album is doubtless one of his better accomplishments.

The relatively well-known Weihnachtsbaum cycle is delightful, but the central work of this album is the piano transcription of Via Crucis, which I had never heard before. I am not a Christian and the story of the crucifixion holds little emotional resonance for me, but Via Crucis is simply astonishing. Even if you are familiar with Liszt's late piano works, you will still be shaken. The sound world Liszt created is both nightmarish and gut-wrenching. The overwhelming sense of foreboding, of grinding horror that something terrible has happened, is happening, and will happen, is everywhere. For me, it was like walking through a concentration camp, or a city that had just been sacked, or a land beset by famine. This piece stayed with me for a long time after my first hearing.

The remaining works are a set of chorales. They are fine enough, I suppose, but I doubt that many people will purchase this album specifically to hear them.

It is a crime that so much of Liszt's greatest music, like Via Crucis, is almost completely unknown. Kudos to Mr. Howard for his wonderful performance.

title: Afterglow Delivers!  Hands Down It Is Easily The Best Of The Three BCC Discs!
text: It only took two albums, but Afterglow finally shows BCC delivering a stellar album!  There are a lot of songs to like on the first couple of albums such as Black Country, Medusa, Save Me, Crossfire, and Song Of Yesterday, but Afterglow really shows the band hitting their stride.  Joe Bonamassa sounds really relaxed and loosened up and his playing is more rock than blues which is a good thing!  On the first two BCC albums, he sounded standoffish to rocking which I think held the band back making Jason Bonham, Glenn Hughes and Derek Sherinian work a lot harder at reminding the listeners that BBC is as much a hard rock band as it is a blues based rock band.  But Afterglow also shows the band taking more musical chances which has improved the songwriting a great deal.  The album reminds me of what Led Zeppelin was doing with Physical Graffiti and what Deep Purple was doing with Stormbringer and Come Taste The Band back in the mid 1970s.  I have listened to Afterglow quite a few times and I am about to start listening to it again.  Glenn Hughes has never sounded better and Jason Bonham has done his dad proud. Derek Sherinian is definitely carrying the torch started by the late Jon Lord and everyone is starting to gell.  I have read about the drama in the BCC camp recently and I hope that it all can be ironed out so that this band can be around for another 4 or 5 albums.  It is hard to pick a favorite song on the disc because each track is a killer!  There are a long list of classic rock artists who are currently making the best music of their careers, and Afterglow is an album worthy of that list.  Pick it up today!

title: Hoot, Howl & Holler: This is a Good One!
text: Steve Arvey and Bill Buchman have been playing traditional gut-thumping, foot-stomping, soul-dragging blues for a long, long time.  And it shows it in every rousing cut of this hour-long collection of winners.  Book-ended by "Good Morning Little School Girl" as an opener and "Ain't Gonna Drink No More Whiskey" as a closer, these guys follow the 3-H style of blues delivery: Hoot, Howl, and Holler.  And it's all done with good humor and authenticity. ... Steve and Bill aren't the only ones to blame for this first-class CD.  Tony Smith's mouth harp is moaning and crying for mama all the way through.  Mike Dempsey on bass and drummer Rick Andre share the load with a rock-solid rhythm that ably supports every note, every groan, every cut.  Bill Buchman's excellent keyboard work provides the ever-melodic and boogie-hued inspiration for everyone else. ...Steering the whole train, of course, are Steve Arvey's rollicking, guttural, humorous and, at times, gravel-voiced interpretations.  Steve has one of the most flexible and variable voices in the business.  Sometimes you're not even sure it's him singing, the style and delivery can be so different from one cut to another.  Since he's the only one listed for "vocals," however, the responsibility falls on him.  But he's got the shoulders and the chops to do it all. ... Each song in this collection comes from a blues man's heart.  "I Wanna Stay Sober" is the eternal quest of bluesmen everywhere; a quest usually abandoned after the second drink.  And when 'love' is spelled 'm-i-s-e-r-y' you know you're in for some rough times. ...This is a fabulous album.  If you like blues.  You'll love this one.

title: The Machines Final Masterpiece...
text:
Little did we know that an unknown masterpiece from Machines of Loving Grace would materialize as a very cohesive and critically important final album. Although sad to say they've since disbanded, GILT is without a doubt their best album.
Getting things cooking with the brilliantly executed subdued rocker "Richest Junkie Still Alive", the whispered tones of Scott Benzel's voice compliments the great backbone from guitarist Tom Coffeen, bassist Ray Riendieau, keyboardist Mike Fisher, and drummer David Suycott. But the strength doesn't stop here...it's only a beginning. One of the highlights of GILT, "Suicide King", charges on full-throttle guitars and pounding drums with the bittersweet anger of Scott Benzel's vocals. It's one of those tracks that prove irresistible to the untrained ear. The soft metal of "The Soft Collision" is soothing and mysterious with soft whisper vocals. "Animal Mass" has that mysterious throbbing energy that also proves to be quite thrilling, and the guitar swings along to the bass and drum lines, making it equally head-banger worthy. "Kiss Destroyer" seems to seethe with intensity and the scathing vocals of Benzel, and throbs with crunchy industrial rhythms, and "Serpico" and "Tryst" also thrive on throbbing industrial pulses...but be advised, this album leans more metal than anything.
GILT is one of those superb masterpieces that you might wish to hear more of from MOLG. Unfortunately, we might never get the chance to hear from them again. But with GILT, their final goodbye is an entirely satisfying affair.

title: One of the best BFer albums and very hard to find
text:
"Pursuit of Happiness" was the first studio album done after Buddy Blue left the Beat Farmers. Joey Harris brought his entire musical toolbox to the band but he was far from unknown. Having played in the San Diego scene for many years, he had been part of Country Dick Montana's side projects (like the Snuggle Bunnies) so he was ready to fit right in.

To me, this is one of the BFers best albums, if not the best. It has a little bit more commercial sound but that was needed if the band ever stood a chance to gain more fans and move forward. The twin guitar sounds of Jerry Raney and Joey Harris play well together and off of each other. Rollie Love supplied a great rhythm section along with the band spark plug and drummer, Country Dick Montana.

As for the songs here, "Hollywood Hills" is a great song and the video is posted on youtube. Jerry Raney's guitar is classic. Joey Harris' vocals shine on "Ridin'", Make It Last" (which was almost a country radio hit!), and "Texas". Jerry Raney stands out on vocals for "Keys To The World" (always great when mixed with "Deceiver" from Van Go in concert) and "dark Light". title: Great Performances of Justly Neglected Pieces
text:
Before I write anything else, I must introduce you to the "pedal piano." Now, you might ask "don't all pianos have 2 or 3 pedals?" Well yes they do, but none of those most familiar to you have a pedalboard like you'd find on an organ. And that's what a "pedal piano" is. It isn't some new instrument invented late in the 19th century like the celesta. It has a noble lineage harking back to 1460, when a harpsichord with a pedalboard is mentioned by the scholar Paulus Paulirinus. Mozart had one built for himself in 1785 by Anton Walter. Schumann wrote much music for the pedal piano and was so enthusiastic about the instrument that he convinced Felix Mendelssohn, who owned a grand pedal piano, to form a class devoted to it in the Leipzig Conservatory. Alkan, too, wrote quite a few pieces for the instrument. Nonetheless, it never caught on, and was mainly relegated for use by organ players to practice on when they couldn't get at the church organ in the evening.

This CD features Gounod's complete works for pedal piano and orchestra. Now, if you think you're going to hear a piano with a very different timbre to what you'd hear in orchestral works for a regular piano, you'll be disappointed. The works on this CD sound just like a regular piano, the only difference being that the soloist can use the pedal to play the left hand parts in octaves.

As for the music... I can't say I've heard much Gounod in my life; this CD is the most of Gounod's oeuvre that I've ever listened to. Yet I know that he was one of the most famous French opera composers in the second half of the 19th century along with Meyerbeer and Massenet.

The pieces in this recording remind me somewhat of Hummel. Not his style, but his ability to write sublime passages intertwined with musical clichés and rubbish. Gounod achieves this in all the works on this CD.

It is hard to pick out great music on this album, but if anything, the Adagio ma non troppo of the Piano Concerto in E-flat major must stand out as a piece of music possessing true beauty which holds one's ears captivated for the duration.

The fine pianist and musician, Howard Shelley, conducts the Orchestra della Svizzera Italiana accompanying the not-so-terrifically-difficult solo piano parts, played by Roberto Prosseda, excellently. The soloist and orchestra all imbue Gounod's music with as much interpretive and technical skill as it contains and generally make it sound better than it is.

The recording quality is quite good technically, except for being a bit in your face unless you adjust your stereo to a higher level of acoustic delay. If you do that, the sound is excellent, albeit the microphone placement puts a bit too much emphasis on the brass section at the expense of the rest of the orchestra (or maybe the conductor couldn't get the brass section to play anything below a mezzo forte, which is something that many an orchestral brass section can't seem to do). Those quibbles said, it is a musically excellent CD which you shouldn't hesitate to buy due to any major faults with the musical performances or recording mastering not being first-rate: On the whole, this CD is wonderfully played and well-recorded.

I give this recording 4 stars; not for the musical performance, which is easily worth 5 stars, but due to Gounod's music. I rarely evaluate music by dead composers in my reviews, but in this case I have to make an exception. Gounod is just not in the same class as Saint-Saens, Massenet, Franck etc. when it comes to composing this kind of absolute non-operatic music. Unless you're a musicologist by profession or madly in love with Gounod's music, I'd recommend you pass on this CD in the otherwise great series of recordings in Hyperion's "The Romantic Piano Concerto" epic.

You can hear him plucking along with the music, textures and feeling type of guitar playing. He plays quite a bit all through the CD. Check out SYMPHONIC YES DVD. (finally a good DVD from YES)
