title: Bolin leaves powerful rockin' legacy
text:
By Jim Clark, publisher, Lee County Courier, Tupelo, Mississippi

One of my all time favorite axe men was Tommy Bolin. So I was excited to hear my friends at 429 Records were putting together Great Gypsy Soul. It's not exactly a tribute album, but instead other artists playing along with Tommy on newly discovered master tapes of Teaser outtakes.
Teaser (1975) his first solo record is considered one of his best.
Tommy opened for Jeff Beck on Dec. 3, 1976. That would be his last performance. He died the next day of a drug overdose. He is buried in Calvary Cemetery, Sioux City, Iowa.
His life was short but his career brilliant. His first band was Ethereal Zephyr (named after a train that ran between Denver and Chicago). They even opened for Led Zepplin.
In 1972 he formed a fusion jazz-rock blues band Energy.
He would play lead guitar on two classic James Gang albums, Bang! (1973) and Miami (1974). His talent would also be showcased with Moxey on their self-titled LP in 1975 and Deep Purple's Come Taste the Band (1975).
On this new killer guitar album some of best show up -- Warren Haynes, Aerosmith's Brad Whitford, Peter Frampton, Deep Purple's Steve Morse, the Allman Brothers' Derek Trucks, John Scofield, Toto's Steve Lukather, Black Country Communion's Joe Bonamassa and Wilco's Nels Cline.
"Many of the guests added after the fact have a close personal connection to Tommy--all share in acknowledging his place in rock history. Watching (and hearing) it all come to fruition some 35 years later was a journey of its own--well worth the travel," Warren said.
Most of my favorites were here, "The Grind," with Peter helping out, "Teaser," with Warren, "Wild Dogs," with Brad and "Lotus," with Joe, Glenn Hughes and Nels.

title: Essential Mahler
text: This Bernstein-led performance of Mahler's 2nd Symphony is undoubtedly the best reading of this piece that has ever been recorded.  This is probably the most accessible of Mahler's pieces, and it is also a great intro to his very unique style.  This symphony is just a fun roller coaster of colors and emotion, composed as only Mahler could.  Of course, no conductor understood Mahler quite like Bernstein did, so nobody could elicit more emotion and tension from Mahler's manic scores than ol' Lenny.  This recording is a perfect example of this.  Mahler's trademark explosive climaxes go off like an atomic bomb.  The music that leads to the climaxes is always long and drawn out in order to maximize the tension.  In the works of other composers, doing this may not be the best idea.  However, with Mahler, maximizing the tension and making the climaxes as explosive as possible is an integral part of expressing Mahler's manic emotions.  The sound is also excellent.  Though this was recorded live, you'd have no idea.  It really sounds like a studio recording with passion.  It's truly an essential CD and a must-have for any Mahler fan or interested casual listener alike.  Essential!

I always had been a Heart fan. I love any group with female vocalists (in case you can't tell by my other reviews).

This project deals both with the Heart Classics and more contemporary songs. I did notice that Heart is going back to their roots, which is included by the song selection. For example, they had five songs from their first two projects, but only one song each from the two albums that revived their career in the mid-80's ("Heart" and "Bad Animals"), those songs being "These Dreams" (I liked "What About Love" and "Never" from the same project better) and "Alone". Furthermore, the music was more guitar based as Heart originally was. And I was happy with the fact that they included "Love Alive".

In addition to their own material, which featured some new songs, they also did a couple of covers: Elton John's "Mona Lisas and Mad Hatters", and Annie doing her best Robert Plant on "Black Dog".

One thing I like is that they took risks of jazzing up a couple of songs. For example, they slowed down the final verse and ending of "Crazy On You" (one of my two favorite "Heart" songs, with "Love Alive" being the other). Also, an acoustic guitar replaced the piano on "Alone".

This Is It is an album compiling the songs of Michael Jackson's songs that were to be done in his London Concerts, and is presented in the order they were to be performed. My one complaint is that these are the studio versions that many fans already own through Michael's albums instead of something new or updated.

Having seen the This Is It documentary it was clear that Michael was singing all his songs live, even while dancing (he often got out of breath) and a live Michael album is what I think fans would really need.

That being said this album does have some good new things.

This Is It - a sweet, moving ballad by the late King of Pop. Probably not good for casual listeners, but if you're a devoted fan such as myself you'll enjoy it.

Planet Earth - the first time we get to hear Michael reading his poetry aloud. It really shows you the deeper side of Michael's personality; a side we often didn't see.

We then get some demos of his classic songs, the best of which is the demo for Beat It; just fun to hear Michael doing the tune and words all by himself.

This is a good collector's item, but don't expect much new if you already own Michael's previous compilation albums or records.

Remember to always think of love - L.O.V.E - when listening to these songs!

title: Megadeth rule in style on Rude Awakening
text:
Rude Awakening (2002.), a Megadeth live concert DVD/CD release

Thrash metal gods Megadeth have enjoyed a long and glittering career. Over that time Dave Mustaine and Co. have gained a great reputation for putting on an excellent live act. However, prior to the 2001-02 `World Needs A Hero' album tour, Megadeth was yet to release a full concert on DVD. Enter 2002's `Rude Awakening' DVD which shows the band in action at a concert in Arizona. Put simply, this is a concert DVD that any Megadeth fan should own. It is a fantastic snapshot of a legendary band on top live form. Granted, you're initial thoughts may be negative about the DVD given that the line-up in action is not the `classic' line-up that featured Marty Friedman and Nick Menza. However, this couldn't be further from the truth as quartet consisting of Dave Musitaine, Dave Ellefson on bass, Al Pitrelli on guitar and Jimmy DeGrasso on drums have great chemistry and perform as a solid unit.

This DVD is an awesome package (note I recommend the DVD for this over the CD version). Not only is there full footage of the concert but there is also band interviews, studio footage of the band recording `The World Needs A Hero' and some bonus live footage. The bonus live footage is especially great as it shows an excellent small underground live set that the band did, the highlights being a punchy performance of out-take classic `Angry Again' and another beautiful version of `A Tout Le Monde'. Returning to the main bulk of the DVD which is the live Arizona concert, there are many reasons why this release is a winner. Firstly, Dave Mustaine's performance at the forefront of the band speaks volumes. Dave never says too much to the crowd whilst on stage but then again he doesn't need to as he possesses a large amount of performance charisma and intensity that keeps the crowd drawn into the music. His vocals are excellent throughout the concert. Al Pitrelli will surprise many who watch this DVD who don't know of his ability on the guitar. He plays many of the band's solos like he's been a member of the group since they began and he trades off plenty of solos and melodies with Mustaine effortlessly. Mustaine himself comments in the interviews how good a guitarist Al is. Dave Ellefson is excellent on the bass and shows why he's been such a vital member of Megadeth through the years. Jimmy DeGrasso gives an insane, brutal and inspired performance on the drums which adds plenty of fireworks to the Megadeth sound.

The set list selection for the concert is a very strong one, mixing all parts of the band's career. Every album up to `The World Needs A Hero' is represented by at least one song except for the forgettable `Risk' album. I could talk all day about each song but instead I'll say what tracks were for me the highlights. `In My Darkest Hour' is performed with great emotion and intensity by the band making it a true stirring performance of the Megadeth classic. The band play an awsome extended version of `She-Wolf' which involves some amazing guitar trade off from Mustaine and Pitrelli that never lose interest or flair. Jimmy DeGrasso's drum solo to finish is MENTAL and sounds brilliant. `Hangar 18' and `Return To Hangar' are performed with power and finesse in vintage Megadeth style. Dave gives his usual speech about the `Mechanix' song before blasting out a high energy version of that timeless classic. The version of `Hook In Mouth' is excellent and the finishing songs in `Peace Sells' and `Holy Wars' make for full out headbanging!

Buying Megadeth's `Rude Awakening' is definitely money well spent in my book. Any Megadeth fan should own this; it is another viewing of a band that are true metal legends. This is a final snapshot of Megadeth before the temporary split due to Mustaine's hand injury and marks an excellent swansong to one chapter in Megadeth's career. I'd highly recommend this DVD as well as the recently released `That One Night In Buenos Aires' which shows the current Megadeth line-up in action on the `System Has Failed Tour'.

MY RATING: 9/10

title: review
text:
And just when virtually everyone including their record label had seemingly given up on The Hollies, they reappeared with a late inning gem in the form of 1976's "Write On". Apparently having settled some of their internal issues, the group seemed reinvigorated, with Allan Clarke, Tony Hicks, and Terry Sylvester teaming up to write most of the ten tracks. The results gave the band a surprisingly spirited mix of top-40 pop and classic Hollies ballads. Mind you this was music as a product, but given how catchy tunes like 'Star', ' Narida', and 'Crocodile Woman (She Bites)' were, it was quality product that should have returned the band to the sales charts. For goodness sakes, there were even a couple of ballads that were worthwhile - the title track and 'xxx' managed to avoid their usual sappy excesses. Highlights ? 'Crocodile Woman (She Bites)' may have been the best rock song they ever recorded - yes it's even better than 'Long Cool Woman In a Black Dress'. Tying for second place were the highly commercial 'Star' and 'Narida'. Unfortunately their efforts came in the face of growing public interest in punk, new wave, and dance music.

- One of their most pop oriented tracks in years, 'Star' had everything nite On' was pretty impressive. Clarke seemed to a knack for country-rockers and this one had a wonderful melody that was perfect for the patented Clarke-Hicks-Sylvester harmony vocals that made The Hollies so special. Even though the 'special effects' are distracting, YouTube has an interesting television performance of the song: [...] rating: **** stars
- Unfortunately 'Sweet Country Calling' pushed the band too far in the corny country direction ... why do British band's seemingly feel the need to delve into American country ? Clarke sounded uncomfortable on the track and the rest of the band sounded like they were just going through the motions. Forgettable. rating: ** stars
- Other than their patented sweet harmonies and some weird synthesizer effects (sounding like an Indian snake charmer), 'Love Is the Thing' never really kicked into gear. rating: *** stars
- Initially 'I Won't Move Over' didn't do much for me. A pouty ballad, the track picked up speed and a bit of energy as it went along. It got better with a couple of spins and Hick's wah-wah guitar was a nice touch. Not great, but one of the better ballads on the album. rating: *** stars
- Yeah, 'Narida' was way too cutesy for their own good (putting them dangerously close to ABBA-styled top-40 dance material, though maybe that was the goal), but with the goofy lyrics, second grader rhyming scheme, golden chorus (na-na-na-na-na-rida), Bernie Calvert's pounding bass, and Tony Hicks guitar solos what wasn't their to love here ? Should have been a massive international hit for the group. rating: **** stars
- A mid-tempo rocker that seemingly reflected a bit of Bruce Springsteen influences in the lyrical department, 'Stranger' was actually an enjoyable effort by the band to reflect a tougher, more contemporary sound. rating: **** stars
- For a band not particularly known for their rockers, The Hollies could occasionally surprise you and 'Crocodile Woman (She Bites)' stood as a perfect example. Kicked along by Pete Wingfield's barrelhouse piano and Clarke's growling vocal, this was a rollicking '50s-tinged number that was easily as good as 'Long Cool Woman In a Black Dress'. Perhaps the best rocker they ever recorded ? rating: **** stars
- 'My Island' was an easy-going, this-side-of-cocktail-jazz radio friendly pop song that really didn't have a great deal going for it outside of Pete Wingfield's cheesy ARP synthesizer lines. The song became a staple in their live show and appears on the subsequent "Hollies Live Hits" collection. YouTube has the band lip syncing the tune for some forgotten TV show at: [...] rating: *** stars
- The lone non-original, 'There's Always Tomorrow' was a classic Hollies big--ballad. Unfortunately, even though it was given the full Hollies treatment (strumming acoustic guitars, waves of harmony vocals, and a catchy chorus), this one wasn't all that good. Someone online described it as "another home alone on a Saturday night song ..." which struck me as the perfect description for the track. rating: *** stars

The album was tapped for a couple of singles. American audiences saw:
- 1975's 'Write On' b/w 'Crocodile Woman (She Bites)' (Epic catalog number 8-50204)

In the UK the single was:
- 1976's 'Star' b/w 'Love Is The Thing' (Polydor catalog number 2058 719)

In wasn't a classic Hollies LP, but song-for-song it was impressive and quite enjoyable. Unfortunately Polydor made no attempt to sell the album in the States.

title: Stylized Bach!
text:
Nathan Milstein (1903-1992) was always a very humble player. Certainly his name was not immersed in the jet set of Szigetti, Heifetz or Oistrakh. His playing was extremely meditative and introspective, though invested of a visible stylized approach. These Bach 's works are the supreme fire proof for any serious violinist.

His vibrato is far to be sumptuous but instead possesses an sense of tune and color, an expansive sound and a innate freshness. It is fair to acknowledge the tempos are faster than the rest of the recordings you have listened, but despite of this fact his phrasing is so clean, so well articulated, with an impressive aristocratic tone, admirable clarity of conception and sparkling imagination filled with remarkable expressiveness and humanity.

His reading of the well known partite No. 2 is simply vibrant. Milstein possessed temperament and personality; brightness and eloquence. The Allemande and Giga specially, are majestic. The Chaccone is impregnated of that mysterious aura with ravishing cosmic breath and impetuous intensity.

In my personal list I have this set in a second choice after the legendary achievement of Henryk Szeryng, in the third place Sandor Vegh, the forth for Szigetti and the Fifth for Heifetz.

Go for these treasured performances.

But please, remember: the primacy belongs to Szerying!

title: Robbie: the natural showman
text:
I've been a RW fan since he split from Take That. It wasn't clear back then whether his solo career would take off; ex-boy band members tend to falter when faced with having to carry off an album, or a concert, all by themselves. But Robbie flew out of the starting gate and never looked back - it seemed as though Take That was a training ground for his real career.

Since then, he has become a huge star all over the world (except, inexplicably, here in the US, where he is all but unknown, although most people are probably familiar with 'Let Me Entertain You'), and has branched out into swing with a legendary concert at the Albert Hall and a fabulous album to go with it. Only Robbie has the cheek and the charisma to pull off something like this. He happens to be a fantastic singer and a gifted performer, and his sheer chutzpah does the rest.

'The Robbie Williams Show' was made to promote his 'Escapology' album. Ostensibly a TV show, it uses a gigantic set built at Pinewood Studios to give it a large feel. There is some spectacular scenery, particularly a huge scaffold on which about 100 dancers gyrate in silhouette while Robbie belts it out in front of them. The colours, lighting, and camerawork are clever.

What shines are Robbie's natural demeanour and strong connection with the audience. This would not have been visible (or even possible) in a traditional concert format; the small stage-in-the-round just for Robbie with the musicians off to one side allows him to make close eye contact and (in both senses) touch people. This lets his humour and charm come to the fore. He's cheeky and a bit lewd, but you just can't help loving him.

On top of all that, of course, the music is terrific. The song list is an ideal mix of his older hits, the swing stuff, and the then-new Escapology tracks. Robbie throws everything he has behind each song. His vocal range and power are top notch, and he doesn't have any of those irritating phony-soulful vocal mannerisms so popular among other solo singers these days. From swing ballads to grunge rock anthems, he can do it all.

Highly recommended.

title: Delightful, Whimsical, Perfect-Sounding Masterpiece
text:
As far as vintage PG-era Genesis goes, this is about as good as it gets (depending on what your opinions are on _Lamb_). In terms of musicianship and band unity, I don't think the members of Genesis were ever tighter and more prominently on display than on this masterpiece. The first two songs pack quite a punch - "Dancing With The Moonlit Knight" starts out with a gentle beginning, before launching out into an all-out assault. Hackett is all over the place on this track, and you'll hear his mastery of polyphonic technique here YEARS ahead of Halen. The song fades beautifully into brooding mystery. The eerie and whimsical "I Know What I Like" rears up next, posessing a great, propulsive, almost funky sitar-led riff at its heart. More traditional prog-rock territory is covered on "Firth of Fifth". Here is found Steve Hackett's greatest moment on guitar as a member of Genesis, highlighted by a long, majestic, legato solo which rides Tony Banks' swelling synths like a sandpiper on the crest of a wave. "More Fool Me" marks the very beginning of Phil's long and disheartening journey into the heart of Adult Contemporary music, however his balladeering here is more minstrel-like, innocent and welcome in the context of the album. (He took a similar pastoral turn on Anthony Phillips' solo album _The Geese And The Ghost_.) Again on the jaunty "Battle of Epping Forest" Genesis choose to display their whimsy - no band ever packed a song with as many sly winks as this band did, seemingly satirizing modern gangland warfare by comparing it to medieval warfare. Peter puts several of his different voices on display here, continuing the tradition of musical theater. After the fine "After The Ordeal" there's another "Suppers Ready"-like exercise, "The Cinema Show." Like "Supper" many elements of Greek mythological imagery are synthesized and contrasted with modern elements - the two-song cycle ends with "Aisle Of Plenty", a musical shopping list.
I like what another reviewer pointed out with regards to the satirical and modern societal elements of Gabriel's lyricism and its parallels to contemporary British events. Im not sure that the parallels and critiques of modern society are as prominently on display as well as they are on _Lamb Lies Down On Broadway_, but there is something to be scryed here between the rubric formed by PG's scattershot mythological imagery and Shakespearean references. "Cinema Show" and "Battle Of Epping Forest" hold especially well up to such lyrical scrutiny.
John Burns' note-perfect production, while reaching an early zenith with the fantastic and bubbling "I Know What I Like", is a bit too sterile for my tastes towards the end of the album. This album also features, IMHO, some of Genesis' more meandering instrumental indulgences. Production quibbles aside, there's no denying Hackett's performance is masterful and this is a mandatory purchase for any fan of Genesis. I think a lot of fans of their later poppier years would do well to start with this one before tackling _Lamb_ or _Foxtrot_. The new edition features both remastered sound as well as song lyrics.

title: Sound Reproduction is Disappointing
text:
I have listened to many old recordings (from classical to blues) and have become accustomed to the various flaws therein. The low-fi sound reproduction and crackle and pop of 78s do not bother me. But for some reason - whether it was the initial recording or the subsequent transfers - these recordings often have severe distortion that render them irritating to listen to. I suspect the problem was the conditions under which they were recorded. (The audio quality reminds me of many of the blues "field" recordings made by the Lomaxes at about the same time period - i.e., late 1930s and early 1940s.)

As I continue to listen to these CDs - there are 66 of them! - I am getting somewhat more used to the distortion and appreciate what are, in most instances, fine performances. The compilation [[ASIN:B00803EXHK Schubert Lieder on Record 1898-2012]] has much better sound quality for the recordings made during the same WWII period, and I highly recommend that smaller (17 CDs) and more expansive (more than 100 years of recordings, albeit from one composer and label) set. But other than perhaps a handful of recordings, there's no overlap (so a Schubert fan could add the 14 Schubert CDs from the Rauscheisen set to the Schubert Lieder on Record CDs - and perhaps even throw in the Hyperion collection - for quite an historical overview of incredible Schubert lieder).

And a word of advice if you do decide to order this. Make sure the seller will FIRMLY package and cushion the set to prevent any shifting of the contents (either shifting of the CDs in the box, which will cause the box to break, or the shifting of the box in the package, which could break the CDs and/or the jewel cases). This is a VERY heavy and fragile item, and the post office gorillas will have a field day with it unless it is packaged appropriately (and then some).

title: Much more than you may expect
text:
From what I understand, Beanie Sigel was discovered by The Roots, and appeared on some of their material. He signed to Rocafella records, and recorded this album, simply titled, The Truth.
The production on this album is well-done, and the beats usually fit the mood of the song. While Beans's flow is not perfect, he spits a lot of introspective lyrics about street life, family, [chemical substances], and such. An example would be "What's Your Life Like". Over a dark horror-movie-esque beat, he questions many of the so-called 'thug' rappers, who insert false details in their life depicting struggle. Most of the lines in the song begin with a provoking question (sample: "What you know about solitary/Locked down, no commencary/And you wild or ready/and you just seen your mom get buried/You got drowns, comin' in all kinds of flurries").
Beans is very much a 'reality rapper', and his topic matter usually doesn't stray from violence and hustling. But the reason why this album is not a completely formulaic release is that he is very straight-forward. He also does what a lot of other rappers like him don't do, and that is critisize. When I say critisize here, I'm not talking about the type of critisism you might hear from anti-Versace rappers or KRS-one about how ...rappers have [imitation] subject matter and poison the mind of the youth who listen. Critisism is used against hustlers or thugs who he think carry out their criminal duties ineptly. Take "Stop, Chill" for an example: He calls out [chemical substance]-smugglers in his area ("Stop , all my young bucks huggin the block/Stop puttin drugs in your sock/You makin it easy for the cops to catch you/They hooked to that stash and that trash and that bag of pretzels"). A lot of other rappers who may speak of hustling or [chemical substance]-dealing are too simple to have any real objection to the way that they do this. You probably notice that a lot of them only cite the many foolish [chemical substance]-dealers in their area instead of taking a closer look into it. While Beans may justify their criminal methods, It is interesting how he doesn't just see it as perfect (at least their dealing with it).
Songs like the title track and (but not limited to) "Ride For My..." are not terribly special, with the subject matter dealing with the usual thug rhymes, violence and [chemical substance]. But Beans is quite conscious of what happens in his society, so he doesn't treat the subject matter cheaply like many ... rappers do.
The guest appearences on this album are pretty good. "Who Want What" is an excellent duet with Memphis Bleek, and both spit tight lyrics. Jay-Z appears on Raw & Uncut, and it works ok I guess. They are quite different, since Jigga seems to talk about more commercialized stuff like gold chains, women and cars....
Speaking of commercialism, "Playa" (also with Jay-Z) seems to be the only huge club track on the album. Since I am not bothered by club/party rap music as much as many anti-commercial people area (it's fun), it's a pretty good dance track with a well-done beat, but it wholy depends on your taste. Unfortunetely, female label-mate Amil also appears, and awful, childish flow and simplistic lyrics almost ruin the track.
Another track of note is the brilliant "Mac Man". Using the Pac-Man theme and beat, Beans uses the game as a metaphor for his life as a chase. I won't cite any examples of lyrics, you'll have to hear it for yourself.
Beanie Sigel is not one of the most creative or lyrically superior rappers around, so if you're looking for someone like Canibus or Raekwon, this probably isn't for you. His Charisma is definetely for a certain taste, so he may not always appeal to you. However, his flow is usually on point, and his lyrics are quite topic-oriented, and the beats are quite good, and it's always important for a rap album to succeed on those levels.
Check this out along with Memphis Bleek's, "Coming Of Age"
(note: there is a bonus track here "Anything" which is a Jay-Z solo track. Really good beat, accompanied by strange "Oliver" samples (I think...))

title: Reaching for the stars!!
text:
Rufus Wainwright is one of those artistes that constantly garners tonnes of critical acclaim, which somehow fails to translate into sales. With "Release the stars", he sets out to right that wrong.

The first I heard of him was on the soundtrack to "Moulin Rouge" (La Complainte de la Butte), as well as his awesome performance of "Hallelujah" on the "Shrek" soundtrack, and I was hooked.

As lush, poetic, and cinematic/operatic as his other releases, this finds him upping the pop factor in his music, and even reigning in Pet Shop Boy Neil Tennant on production.

Lead off single, the stunning piano ballad "Going to a town" is a perfect example, with a forlorn vocal delivery set against a swelling string backdrop as he ponders "I'm going to a town that has already been burned down/I'm so tired of you America". My absolutely favourite track.

"Leaving for Paris no. 2" is a simple piano ballad with a gently caressing vocal delivery, apparently originally written for the "Moulin Rouge" soundtrack.

The title track "Release the stars" has a sweeping jazz feel, and "Sansoucci" ups the tempo a bit, with quivering guitars and sparkling piano.

Other standouts are the humorous upbeat "Between my legs", the sumptuous "Tiergarten (with sixties sounding harmonies), and the soaring classical sounding "Tulsa" (with dramatic strings).

Lavishly orchestrated chamber-like pieces, that awesome nasal/emotive/melancholic voice, and striking the perfect balance between pop and classical, here's hoping this is the album that brings him commercial success.

title: Restraint.
text:
On Gravity, Monolake has released a more stripped down, restrained approach to their sound. The percussion is usually a steady, consistent 124-130 beats per minute which usually consists of a basic basskick and various slight tweaking of hi-hats.
The tracks have a barren, bare feel, and trudge along purposely but they don't really expand or float in any different directions. The accompanying sounds reverberate with the percussion consistently, and they maintain a similar feel throughout this release (except perhaps the dropping chime melody of "Zero Gravity". These filling sounds are low to mid tones, and give Gravity a late-night city-esque vibe.
"Nucleus" closes with a monochrome drone based track, which has no beat whatsoever. Gravity is somewhat cold, steady, dark-edged but it also has an overall decent groove and the sounds off the beat usually work pretty well. It doesn't match the quality of Hong Kong, and it sure is far away from the excellent Interstate release, but it does have it's stronger points. However, don't be surprised that after 20 minutes of listening, you become a little bored with it. This isn't Monolake's top material. 2.5 stars.

text:
As a progressive rock fan, I place Kayak as the perfect progressive pop band and no other album demonstrates their genius better than The Last Encore. This is an album of extremes from mellow and "sad" songs to all-out pop blisterers as well as some genuine progressive rock. In this way it is more adventurous than their previous album "Royal Bed Bouncer" but both albums are 5 star albums.

Some of their sounds remind me of Focus, Alan Parsons Project, and ELP, but the sound is not a copy. It doesn't meander as much as Focus or ELP -- it gets to the point -- and this is, in my opinion, more enjoyable than those bands' music. This group will not wow you with their virtuosity (save for the piano work, which is as good as Keith Emmerson in some songs) because their focus is on the overall sound and structure of the song. Take the vocals, for instance, they are more of an instrument than a lead (kind of like Yes). All songs on here are very well-written and played but they really excel with the songs "Evocation" (possibly their best song ever), "Do You Care", "Still My Heart Cries For You", and "The Last Encore".

It's ironic to me that this album has been the hardest of all their catalog to find on CD.

Something confusing...but then he plays the hymn itself beautifully you just forget about everything else your mind has been on and know you've never heard this played better than what you're hearing here and now.
The other numbers are wonderful too. He avoids the overindulgence and repetitiveness you sometimes hear on gospel numbers where a singer repeats and repeats a phrase or word so many times you want to throw up. text: APRIL 16 Edit to my own review: Now that I've found a copy of this CD at a reasonable price, upon many subsequent listens, I must say it really it is one of PL's best! Careful listening uncovers a lot of more going on here than upon the first hearings, so I'll up my rating to FIVE STARS! Sure, it's a return to form of sorts, but it rates as highly as anything they've ever done - the performances are top-notch, the production KICKS, and the underlying melodic structure of the songs, even amidst the back-to-basics metal edge of the music, puts this band at the top of their game! Why these guys aren't A.) on a major American label, and B.) one of the biggest bands in the world, is beyond me!! MARCH 14 REVIEW:- I'll write a review of this album now because A.) I can complain about the outrageous import price of this album, and B.) because I have heard it, BY DOWNLOADING IT FOR FREE! I hope their record label sees this, too, because charging over 30 dollars for a 50-cent piece of plastic, especially in this day of rampant free downloading is simply arrogant and outrageous. That's exactly why this excellent band is still traipsing around Europe with no presence in the States (although I do lay some blame on the Koch label for signing their last few albums and then not promoting them at all!). Anyways, this new self-titled effort is meant to signal their return to their roots, meaning the glory-days of the "Draconian Times" era, which many consider the blueprint from whence they strayed (did that come out right??). Mixed results. Sure, this is less sample-and-keyboard oriented than their last few efforts - definitely more guitar and therefore more in common with D.T. Yet I find many of the songs to have that been-there-heard-that feel, especially in light of the fact that so many bands have since copied their gothic metal sound, so I am a bit, I hate to say, bored with some of the tracks. Songs like album opener "Don't belong" and "Over the madness" are perfect examples of the doom-laden goth that they have perfected, while other tracks like "Forever after" or "All you leave behind" seem a little bit tired. I guess many fans have complained that they've strayed from their roots, but I have LOVED every album they've done since "Draconian", and while this will grow on me, it's also a bit of a retread. Now if only I could buy the damn thing!!

4700 copies worldwide...ridiculous. (Having purchased this album, I don't claim for a second to be above the frenzy.)
Amazingly, nearly all the remixes on these two discs are better than the original versions from "Empires." It's a head-bobbin' blend of EBM stomp and intelligent sing-along melodies.
Disc One:
"Lastlight" gets off to a slow start, then fleshes out nicely with a "Violator"-era Depeche Mode sound. The addition of vocals is nice, since Ronan Harris has a Peter Gabriel charm without the high notes. "Further" is the big winner, with a driving beat and some of VNV's most yearning, thought-provoking lyrics to date. "Legion (janus)" has a snarlier synth sound than the original, and "Saviour (vox)" has a nice computer effect on the vocals. "Legion (anachron) is a soothing, orchestral closer.
Disc Two:
This is the "Standing" single also sold separately. A good band can do multiple versions of a song without inducing sleep. "Standing (still)" is an easy, low-impact dance track. "Standing (motion)" adds some Lords of Acid energy to the mix. "Radius 2" (I don't know how to type "2" as superscript on here) has a lot of warm synth and reminds me of VNV's "Genesis" or a gentler "Solitary." The original cut of "Standing" ends the CD.
"Burning Empires" is full of dancefloor gems, but it's almost a guilty pleasure given the insanity involved in getting your hands on it.

title: American Classic Rock icon at his best!
text:
This is a live album by the iconic American singer / songwriter / guitarist David Crosby, recorded with a trio called The Lighthouse Band, which comprises of vocalist / guitarist Becca Stevens, vocalist / keyboardist Michelle Willis and vocalist / guitarist / bassist Michael League. The album offers a CD and DVD, both presenting the same sixteen tracks: several Crosby’s classics and the rest new songs co-written by Crosby and the trio members and only one track originating from outside the quartet, a Joni Mitchell classic. The sound quality, which is especially important in this mostly acoustic and delicate music, is absolutely stunning.

The album was recorded in December 2018, following the release of two superb Crosby albums: “Lighthouse” and “Here If You Listen”, which were recorded with the same band, and naturally offers several songs, which appear on these two studio albums.

The music and the performances are absolutely stellar, based first and foremost on the divine vocal harmonies the four vocalists are able to create together, and of course also on Crosby’s unparalleled songwriting. Crosby, who was nearing eighty at the time, seems to be in high spirits and his voice is still steady and strong, and most importantly absolutely clear, with a sense of harmony which led his musical career at all times.

Crosby is a true icon of American Rock, and his combined recorded legacy is certainly one of the most impressive among all his peers. Open-minded and searching, his music is a soundtrack of my generation and I love his contribution deeply and wholeheartedly.

Overall, this is an instant classic album, which encapsulates American Rock at its best. Based on vocal harmonies, which originate in Folk music, and embracing Psychedelia and Rock, this is pure musical ambrosia, which Crosby managed to carry on for his entire life. God bless and please stay with us for many years, singing and playing guitar, as Classic Rock without you, David, would be simply mostly meaningless.

title: The End Of The Ride
text:
Steve Walsh had been gone for more than a few years and Kansas kept on keepin' on with the second record to feature the vocals of John Elefante singing the songs of Kerry Livgren in his place. The band was still doing well but without the violin and vocals of Robbie Steinhardt the greatest link to the glory of what was once Kansas was gone. The band was under the control of the Christians and the course was stuck in the middle of the road like everybody else in music. Kansas had lost it's mojo and Austin Powers cannot save it from itself.

What saves this album from being tossed in the bin is the quality of the songs found here in "Drastic" times. "Fight Fire With Fire" and "Andi" are great Kansas tunes but after those I can get lost in the muck. A certain sameness glosses over what could have been straight forward driving rock Music. I got the impression that this was going to be the final album from Kansas. You have gotta have violin in this band in a few years later the band would return and they would do so with a great fiddle player who (no, not Robbie) would shake things up.

The Kerry Livgren years would end with this record and only once more the band would put out an album with Kerry and his songs included. I wasn't ready for Kansas to be over but in a way it was as it couldn't be the original group any longer as the rifts were too large between the tribes. This is a good record but they call it Kansas and (for me) without Robbie it cannot be Kansas.
Three & 1/2 Stars

title: Fantastic, relaxing CD
text:
Normally, I'm not one for relaxing music. I don't buy a lot of New Age or soft, tinkly things. But this album--wow. I loved it years ago when I had the double album, and when Wendy Carlos remastered it for CD I bought it immediately. It lives on my iPod now, and whenever I'm having trouble relaxing at night or taking a nap, I listen to it. This isn't active music--it's phenomenally recorded spring-summer-fall-winter soundscapes with electronic sounds and music quietly interspersed. Much of the time the natural sound is louder than the electronic additions--which makes this a very unusual example of the genre.
I've tried to find other music like this album, but I've never heard anything so well composed and recorded. The sense of space is incredible, and the compositions are really very nice. The fact that it puts me to sleep shouldn't stop you from buying the album--in fact, I've listened to it when not intending to sleep, and enjoyed the experience just as much.
The extra tracks aren't very interesting to me, and I don't listen to them. But the original recording sounds like it could have been made yesterday--the sound quality is truly amazing considering its age.
Enjoy!

title: One of Miles' best.
text: Miles Davis is a man of many faces. The cool Miles of Kind of Blue and the mad scientist Miles of Live Evil have very little in common, but In A Silent Way has him exploring funk and rock textures like he would in his fusion period within the confines of his laid back, sustained-noted cool jazz format. Chick Corea and Herbie Hancock trade off electric piano duties and Tony Williams shuffles the beat without ever calling too much attention to the drumset. But the true star here is John McLaughlin, whose guitar is just as present on this record as Miles' trumpet. One of the finest jazz or ambient records put to wax.

title: As if we needed more proof . . .
text:
As if we needed more proof that Amanda Shires is the real thing, she has released this gem of an album. Following an album as great as 2011's [[ASIN:B004R2A7DW Carrying Lightning]] is no easy feat, but she has pulled it off magnificently. 'Down Fell The Doves' delivers on the promise of 'Carrying Lightning' and expands on the talents of Ms. Shires.

On this album, Ms. Shires has moved ever-so-slightly away from the Americana/AltCountry/Texas-Fiddle-Music sound that informed her previous albums. This is the work of a premiere songwriter, no qualifiers or genre designation needed. Amanda has been quoted as saying her favorite songwriter is Leonard Cohen, and that fact is borne out by the way she, like Cohen, tackles the darker aspects of life, love and the human soul in her writing. In fact, one of the highlights of the set is "Song For Leonard Cohen," which finds Amanda dreaming about meeting her idol and stating that she would "just listen to you talk." You won't find any feel-good sunshine-laced love songs here; be prepared to face the darkness with songs like "Box Cutters," which examines the myriad ways in which one might end one's own life. "Deep Dark Below" brings us the story of Alicia, who falls prey to the Lord of Darkness himself, because "it's usually the weak ones he finds." Perhaps the centerpiece of the album is "Bulletproof," in which the protagonist fantasizes about what she could do if she were invincible:

"Maybe folks would line up, and show up armed
Excited for a person to try their weapons out on,
And we could charge money . . .
We could charge a whole lot of money."

Shires also shows increased confidence in her voice. While still retaining her signature "quiver," her voice seems stronger and bolder than on her previous albums.

In short, this is a great album that will be loved by anyone who appreciates great songwriting.

I can hardly express how happy I am to have received this in my mail today! This truly is Gene Krupa at his finest. For a long time now, I have hunted down collectors for bootlegged editions of these albums, and even bought vinyl copies on ebay, when I could find them. For years I have hoped, and even contacted the label, that one day these great Krupa albums from the 50's Clef/Verve/Norman Granz era would be issued.

Thankfully, AVID JAZZ has answered my prayers..AND they did it right. To finally be able to hear these great albums in crystal-clear sound is a revelation. All of Krupa's subtle brush work and technique is rediscovered here. The masters used for these transfers are immaculate. The performances are all stupendous and in short, everything is perfect. AVID goes the extra mile by including all original album artwork and liner notes are all here in the cd booklet.

If you are a fan of jazz, 50's jazz or just plain-old great music, this set is for you!

[Note: In 2012, Avid Jazz also released another 2-disc set of Krupa from the 50's entitled: "Five Classic Albums". Like this one, it is essential Gene Krupa from the 50's. I strongly encourage you to purchase that set, as well.]

title: The Album That Began a Legend
text:
Black Sabbath's self-titled album accurately set the standard for what was to follow in their muscially career. The album's opening track (an ominous depiction of an encounter with a demonic spectre) is about as quintessential as it gets; no wonder why the band was able to garner so much religious atttention so quickly. Truthfully, none of the band members worshipped Satan (in fact, the inverted cross indside the album's cover was the record label's idea, not that of Iommi, Ozzy, Butler, or Ward), but the record was still frightening enough to suggest that.
Surprisingly, this is Sabbath's most bluesy album. Influences like Cream and Blue Cheer are evident in both The Wizard (which features an insanely engaging harmonica line and some simple but cool lyrics) and N.I.B. (in which the riff from Cream's Sunshine of Your Love is clipped and played on a heavily distorted guitar). Some other tracks drag a bit, but this problem would diminish with time, namely after the release of Paranoid.
Overall, this is an enjoyable introduction to the Sabbath canon. Over thirty years after its release, it still holds up as an immensely daring and influential recording.

title: You've Never Heard Anything Like This  {5 Stars}
text:
What can I say, when you take into consideration how this album was put together, you can't help but be in awe of the man known as Scratch -- best known for his tenure as a member of The Roots crew. Here's the long and the short of it, this is basically an album of guests like Jill Scott, Malik B., Bilal, Black Though, Schoolz Of Thought (cop their album, they're ill), Floetry, Dice Raw, and the like all getting busy over tracks laid by Scratch. He creates all the tracks with -- get this -- his mouth. The incredible thing about it is the fact that if no one mentioned it or if you didn't know who Scratch was, you'd never know that these are beatbox tracks.

The only thing about this album that may have folks up in arms about this 5 star rating is the lack of uptempo tracks. There are a few, but most of the beats are mid tempo, but the tracks are all produced by Scratch and, again, he does it all with his mouth. He only gets help, according to the credits, on two tracks -- 88 Keys lends a hand on track 6 and Yameen All World helps out on track 11. That means that this dude is literally the embodiment of instrumentation without question. No disrespect to the greats (Buffy, Doug E., Rahzel, Ready Rock C., etc..), but I can't think of anyone better at this beatboxing thing.

The Embodiment of Instrumentation is literally a one of a kind album. Scratch laces every track without the use of instruments. Well, technically, his mouth is the intstrument, but you get my point. Like another reviewer said: "How many beatbox albums come out in a year....or a decade....or ever?" I couldn't have put it any better. Not only did it come out, but it's an excellent gem of an album that shows just how much you can do with this hip hop sh** when you don't rely solely on the rap aspect of it. I recommend adding this album to your library.

Standout Tracks: Sumthin' That U Missin' feat. Flo Brown, Spontaneous, Ciph Born, & D-Ruck, Breath Of Fresh Air (My Favorite), Square One feat. Bilal, We Got What You Want feat. Schoolz Of Thought, U Know The Rulez feat. Black Thought, Malik B., & M.A.R.S. Co-op, What Happ'N feat. Floetry, and That's What We Talkin' About feat. Dice Raw, Calente, & E.S.T

title: Good Nevermore album
text:
I like this album, it's pretty good and warrants several replays in your CD and MP3 player, but unfortunatley (and you'll understand why i say unfortunatley) I feel it necessary to compare this to the band's last effort 'This Godless Endeavour'(TGE) as this was the album that introduced me to Nevermore and hence made a fan out of me and countless others.

Additionally it can be argued that TGE is their best work to date so therefore what better standard is there to rate them against? So though I may not be most qualified to give this album a fair rating, here's my 2 cents nontheless:

While I like this album, one can sum up the effort in one word- 'Unpolished'. It is raw and not the refined gem that TGE was and sometimes comes across to the listener as the recording of a relaxed band jam session rather than a meticulously crafted album.

The album kicks off as if already in the middle of the first track with some great work being exhibited on the part of Loomis. The production is notably great, rich and heavy, however, I thought something was wrong with the track and kept hitting the back button of my cd player to restart the song as I thought it may have skipped forward accidentaly, only to realize that in fact that's how the first track starts. Honestly I felt a little cheated as it seemed that little thought was put into the start of the album.

The main issue that sticks out to me however is the vocals. As great a vocalist as Dane is, (both lyrically and melodically) I found his effort to be somewhat lazy, perhaps a bit uninspired.

In some tracks (notably 'Emptiness Obstructed' and 'The Day you built the Wall')it seems that vocals were either foregone in favor of letting the rhythm section come to the fore or, they were just limited on the whole. Though i've come to appreciate it now , at first listen I found these parts to be almost empty.

Speaking of 'empty', Track #5 'Emptiness Unobstructed' while one of my favourites could have been 10 times more amazing if the effort was put into tweeking the bridge and chorus to vary rather than repeating the same lines over and over.

Some of the lyrics and melody also seem somewhat juvenile (track#2 'Your Poison Throne') and not something you'd expect from the guy who penned the caliber of lyrics on TGE.

Don't get the impression though that the vocals are poor on this album , because that is far from the truth, Dane true to form delivers many memorable melodies and infectious hooks.

Though notably not as complex as TGE, Loomis does fantastic work on this album. But is it just me or is the opening riff of the third track 'Moonrise (Through Mirrors of Death)' a rehashed riff from the title track on TGE? This quirk aside, Loomis does a great job of blending light and dark on this album which continues to push Nevermore's progressive edge, I would however welcome a return to the lengthier arrangements as seen on TGE.

The backbone of the band (bass and drums) does a solid job. Williams is totally solid and really takes it to the skins on the title track. I personally enjoyed his performance on track #4 'And the Maiden Spoke'

Overall, this album is defintley worth the purchase and worth repeat listens. With a little more care and effort I dare say it may have stood equally with TGE.

title: Another impressive effort
text:
Bombino has a sound. He has a sound, and he is sticking to it.

Desert blues is having a kind of musical moment, and that's a good thing, as far as I'm concerned. While Tinariwen get plenty of accolades, I have generally found myself more interested in slightly more southern sounds from Mali's Ali Farka Toure, who has heavily influenced most desert blues practioners, even if that isn't how he is generally classified himself. And here, it becomes important to tell the famous story about Ali Farka Toure. Toure's sound, which is more of a Malian griot sound translated onto guitar than what people today think of as desert blues, is closely related to desert blues, but distinct from it. Upon hearing him for the first time, a westerner once remarked that he sounded just like John Lee Hooker. His response: "who?"

Ali Farka Toure's music developed with minimal direct influence from western blues. West African music is just foundational to western blues, given how the blues developed. So, Ali Farka Toure and John Lee Hooker were kind of like the musical version of convergent evolution.

Then came Ali's son, Vieux, who is a musical genius in his own right. That next generation winds up sounding more western, simply because he takes in more global influences. So, you get a live album with guest spots from musicians like Derek Trucks, and my favorite, Jeff Lang. Vieux took in the influences from around the world, and created something different, but still rooted in Mali's sound, and still rooted in the influences that formed desert blues, like Bombino, Tinariwen, Group Inerane, Aziza Brahim, Songhoy Blues, and so on. But Vieux did it consciously, knowingly, purposely.

Desert blues, of course, is an evolving sound. If you listen to early Tinariwen, it sounds different from Bombino. You can hear them combining sounds the way one would expect from travels, not all of which were voluntary (euphemisms). And in that, you can hear the influence of the Malian griots, which is a better classification for Ali Farka Toure. His guitar style is now a big influence on the desert blues scene. As we get to the current generation, with Bombino, there is more cross-fertilization. As with Ali's son, Vieux, Bombino is taking in more influences. He is not quite as brash and bold with his recombinations as Songhoy Blues, but his guitar chops show an ear for alternative picking styles.

And with a sound built around that, he has established himself. There is now a Bombino sound. It's a good one. He'll branch out a bit, and by the time you get to Takamba on Deran, does anyone notice that this thing is built around a Sly Stone vamp? Go listen to Stand! Track 7 from Stand!

This is what Bombino is now doing.

When that guy asked Ali Farka Toure about John Lee Hooker, Ali really didn't have a clue. Bombino and Sly Stone? Bombino knows Sly Stone at this point. He's making the rounds at music festivals. I guarantee you he's heard that track. This is what's happening these days. It's pretty cool. Bombino's sound is a weird, westernization of desert blues.

title: United Artists Koussevitzky Vol1
text:
A very nice reissue of historic RCA Victor 78 rpm disks that have been transferred to digital from the original discs with minimal remastering. The new transfers leave all the music and doesn't try to remaster them into sounding like modern hiss free recordings.

The slim french/english booklet is informational and has recording info on the original sessions and details like matrix numbers of the 78's used for the transfers and the private collections they came from.

Contents with year of recording.
Mozart - Symphony 34 1940
Beethoven - Symphony 5 1949
Schubert - Symphony 8 Unfinished 1945
Berlioz - Damnation of Faust Op24 1936
Berlioz - Harold in Italy Op16 1944
Tchaikovsky - Romeo and Juliet Overture 1936
Brahms - Symphony 4 1939
Brahms - Academy Festival Overture 1947
Wagner - Hollander Overture 1947
Strauss - Till Eulenspiegal Op28 1945
Liszt - Mephisto Waltz 1 1936
Rachmaninoff - Isle of the Dead Op29 1945
Rachmaninoff - Vocalise Op34 no14 1945
Sibelius - Symphony 2 Op43 1950

There are mainly 2 types of historic recordings available today, ones that try to remove the surface noise and recording limits of the original recordings though digital remastering, usually poorly done and sacrificing music to get rid of the audio artifacts, or transfers like this that give you the best copy of the original 78 rpm disks including the hiss and surface noise, but with the full range of music captured by the orignal recording process.

If you are interested in the latter then this set is one of the better ones out there.

If you can't stand hiss or surface noise then maybe this would be better for you, [[ASIN:B0009AM5PE Koussevitzky]] as they remaster it to try to sound like a modern recording with mixed results.

text:
So, some say it sounds like Rainbow - it doesn't! The guitar playing has nothing in common with Blackmoore's, it's a totally different style. It doesn't sound like UFO either without the exception that Riot has included a UFO cover. Regarding the singer some claim that he sounds like Joe Lynn Turner, but I don't think the comparison is striking. Think of Iron Maiden when the first song begins - it's very similar to the guitar riffs Maiden usually play. Sometimes during the listening I also get to think of Black Sabbath with Tony Martin...
I believe this album has 3 really great heavy metal tunes with good arrangement and harmony: "Turn the Tables", "Through the storm" and "Burn the sun" - all top quality! Then there is 2 decent ones: "Lost inside this world" and "Chains"; 1 rather good cover: "Only you can rock me", and 1 boring semi-ballad called "Let it show". I don't know what Riot try to do with a song like "Essential enemies" - a modern approach? Well, it doesn't work, and the same goes for "To my head". We also get 2 instrumental tracks at the end, and although it's good guitar playing it doesn't get me excited.
If you got lots of money to spend on records and you're a fan of more traditional heavy metal I think this one would please you - the 3 best songs are really great! A few more songs of this calibre, and I would give this one 5 stars... And by the way, if you like this one I advise you to buy Pretty Maids "Red, hot and heavy" - you won't be disappointed!

title: "Crazy crazy crazy for the chicken bone..."
text: This album was voted by anime fans at Anime Expo 2000 to be the best anime soundtrack of the past year.  That's a pretty high honor considering AX is the country's biggest yearly anime convention.  When you hear it, you'll know why.  In my opinion, this is one of the best anime soundtracks ever composed.  'Course, everything Yoko Kanno has put together has been nothing but wonderful, but this soundtrack series, and this album in particular, is a melodic experience that, like the anime series itself, is pure genius.  Just about every genre of music is represented splendidly here, from dance to rock ballad to jazz club to opera to spaghetti western(!), with Ms. Kanno's personal, unique twist on every one.  Most of the songs on this album are from the later episodes of the series, and if you've had the privilege of seeing them, this will make you relive the experience all over again.  Every time I hear the first track ("Blue") and Mai Yamane's haunting vocals, my mind fills with the final scene of one of the most incredible endings in anime history.  Every song stands out, but the ones that stood out the most for me were "Blue", "Call Me Call Me", and the alternate version of "The Real Folk Blues" (the last track).  Whether you're an anime fan or not, this album will appeal to just about everyone.  It's a masterpiece from the master artist herself.

title: The Catherine Wheel: The Complete Broadway Byrne
text: The Catherine Wheel is simply a masterpiece of modern electronic music.  Here we find David Byrne, unfettered by the limitations of the pop song format that constrained his work with Talking Heads, stretching his wings as a modern composer.  The Catherine Wheel combines the best lessons of Byrne's synth-funk and found-vocal Eno collaborations ("The Red House") with quirky and soaring sound scapes ("Light Bath," "Dinosaur"), verbal ellipses and his trademark (and under appreciated!) rhythmic-lead guitar work.  There is no wasted music on this one: every track has something wonderful to offer.  Because The Catherine Wheel was written as a dance score, a number of tracks lack the formal structures of pop songs.  But these are not gratuitous noodlings nor mere sketches of songs that might have been.  Rather, each piece has an integrity and musical interest to it.  And, on a larger scale, the layers of rhythm and instrumental texture throughout draw the ear and the mind into a complete and coherent musical vision.  The Catherine Wheel reveals one of America's great musical minds in full flower.

title: Bowie, Sade, & all that Jazz...
text:
"Absolute Beginners" is a British movie set in 1950s Britain, directed by Julien Temple, and studded with stars like Patsy Kensit, David Bowie, Ray Davies (of the Kinks), and Sade, to mention a few. Released in 1986, it bombed at the box office, but went on to become a cult classic.

The soundtrack, for the most part, comprised music representing that era; Jazz and early Rock. The title song was performed by Bowie, one of the few nods to modern Pop, it appears here in its eight minute entirety (most Bowie compilations feature the 5 minute edit).

"Killer Blow" is big band Jazz by Sade, while "Have You Ever Had It Blue?" is lilting horn rich Latin-tinged Jazz by Paul Weller's The Style Council.

Pianist, arranger, composer Gil Evans provides four beautiful horn-driven instrumentals ranging in mood, the swinging "Va Va Voom", the quicker paced "Boogie Stop Shuffle (Rough And The Smooth)", the calmer "Better Git It In Your Soul (The Hot And The Cool), and the brief "Absolute Beginners (Refrain)".

Ray Davies sings the jaunty Pop song "Quiet Life". Other standouts are the upbeat "That's Motivation" and a Tango-like cover of the Italian hit "Volaré" both by Bowie, a slinky "Having It All" by Eighth Wonder featuring a rather nasal-sounding Patsy Kensit, the Rock & Roll "Selling Out" by Slim Gaillard, the truly beautiful "Riot City" by Jerry Dammers (with mood shifts), the comical Rocking "Ted Ain't Ded" by Tenpole Tudor (warning, pronounced British accents here), the upbeat Cuban-style "Napoli" by Clive Lange, and also upbeat (almost Disco-ish) "So What? (Lyric Version)" by Smiley Culture (with cascading keys).

A truly classy and timeless collection!

This is one of a series of cd reissues of the RCA Victor jazz catalog. text: "Streetlife Serenade" by Billy Joel is the prettiest album of his career. This record (his 3rd studio album) is so underrated. It's sandwiched in between his breakthrough album, "Piano Man" and "Turnstiles" which is considered a masterpiece. Billy Joel did admit that he didn't have a lot of material while working on this album, but there some really beautiful songs here like, "Streetlife Serenader" which has a gorgeous and unforgettable piano melody. "The Great Suburban Showdown" is subtle but has powerful, heartfelt lyrics. "Roberta" is about a "lady of the night" and "Los Angelenos" is an up-tempo track with a killer keyboard riff (the lyrics are pretty cool, too). "Last of the Big Time Spenders" and "Weekend Song" are decent songs, but not as good as the others. "Souvenir" contains Billy's best vocal. Wow. What a voice. It's a short little ditty but it's extremely emotional. It will give you chills. "The Entertainer" (the only single released from this album) contains hilarious and sarcastic lyrics. Such a brilliant track. I love Billy's wicked sense of humor. There's 2 instrumental tracks, "Root Beer Rag" which has a touch of vaudeville, and "The Mexican Connection" which I absolutely adore. It's so whimsical. A lovely album by an even lovelier man. He's a genius and yet so humble. One of the best singer/songwriters of our time. Enjoy!

This is a truly great glossy pop album with a bit of a rock edge to it. Anyways their high pitched voices are pretty much gone, their vocals are much richer, and more beautiful now that they are a couple of years older.

The songs are even more addictive then their last album, and a lot more sincere. Songs such as "Everything" the lead of single is extremely catchy, along with the lush ballads "Wanna Be Where You Are" and "Eventually". There is only one song that didn't hook me and I felt could have been left off of this set and that is "Payphone", its more of a b-side. Some of the best tracks include "Miss Popular" is a very humorous song, ,"Wanna be where you are" a very beautiful and lush ballad, with good lyrics as well, "Eventually" with it's incredibly lush harmonies and deft key changes, "Leave me alone" the melody on this song is what hooked me, and it is definitely influenced by Hanson, whom they toured with and dated.

It is truly a shame that they broke up after the release of this album because of how good these songs were and the improvement over the last album, they could have gone on to be a great power pop duo, but instead they embarked on solo careers that never went beyond Europe. Part of the break up may have been caused by Marit's push to the back, as she has very few lead vocals on the album, and Marion mostly takes over, much in the same way Roland Orzabal took over very nearly all of the lead vocals on Tears for Fears second album. I like this new BK release and have an issue with those who lament the band's move to more straight up rock and therefore trash the Cd. Admittedly, it isn't Brothers. It is what it is. Any Cd can be viewed on its own merits and can be listened to in the context of the artist's discography up to that time, and, in retrospect, in relation to a lifetime's output. Too many reviewers lock into an artist and then cry foul when the artist alters musical course. You can embrace and appreciate the new direction or you can reject the new tack as being not for you. If the new course isn't to a listener's taste it doesn't mean that the product is bad or sub-standard. Of course it can be. It just isn't necessarily so. In the case of artists who live on the edges and who have limited or cult following the reaction to a musical change of direction can be particularly venomous. The cry of "sell-out" is often heard together with the oft repeated criticism that the music has become, heaven forbid, accessible, and worse still, popular!

On the other hand I do agree with those who object to the quality of the sound.I have a volume control of my own. text:

ORIGINAL UPDATED REVIEW 2001

"The Beatles 1" was not anywhere near my introduction to the Beatles, I grew up watching "The Yellow Submarine" and listening to them with my dad in the car. However, this compilation was what really made me aware of just how big of an impact the Beatles made when they were together because it got me researching and listening to everyone of their albums, many of them, borrowed from my father. I don't remember what prompted me to buy this, I suppose it was just a whim, I was 16yrs and I had a paper route, so I did have some sort of income of my own, and with 7 kids in my family (even with 3 of them moved out by the times I was 16yrs), we never had much money, so this was the only way I could by music or books most of the time.

It is hard for me to believe I wrote this 10yrs, well, the writing makes it obvious, but it seems like it was longer and and yet shorter of a time frame then 10yrs. The songs on this set are all immediately catchy, and the only song that still has never grown on me is "The Ballad of John and Yoko", other than that every song, for me, is a gem. If this is your first time thinking about listening to the Beatles seriously, this is a great place to start as it really shows the progression of their music, even through their biggest hits, remember many of their best songs were not #1's or weren't even singles (Sgt. Pepper had no singles at all), but it is a good jumping off point. After this set, I would say, either pick up the blue and red box sets or even better, just start sifting their through catalog album by album, whether you start at the beginning, the middle, or the end, its doesn't really matter, but there is some fun stuff on their earlier albums, so don't dismiss them just because they might have been a little fluffier and sillier.

title: Buy This Album.  It's Still Great After All These Years.
text:
I owned this CD when it was released in 1984 and by that time I was a dedicated Rickie Lee Jones fan. Wel;l, as time passed, I became interested in other genres and artist and moved on from Rickie Lee. Then a few months ago, one of her lyrics got stuck in my head so I looked that up on Spotify, and much to my pleasure, Rickie Lee's music has held up to the years. I logged onto my Amazon account and ordered copies of three CDs from my past all by Rickie Lee. Everything I liked about her music earlier was still true all these years later. The lyrics were smart and well written and the music had a timeless quality to me. So, in many ways, my love affair with Rickie Lee Jones was rekindled. No doubt a bit of nostalgia comes into play here as it was from a time when I was young and just beginning to experience life for myself. I look back on that time with the tinted lenses of time so the edges are softer and the angst and confusion of those days don't occupy the forefront of my memories.
I can remember the good times and old friends from school when I listen to this CD, but I think the recording itself has held up over the years. I have a different interpretation of her poetry as a middle-aged adult, but it's good solid writing.
Did I expect to have such an emotional reaction from hearing the sounds of my youth? It hit me right in every way possible and was like being reunited with an old friend. I hadn't realized how much I had missed her.
So now it's 2015 and there is a new recording from Rickie Lee on the horizon. I'm looking forward to its release and imagine I will be listening to her music for a long time to come.

text:
08-13-2014 Here is he famous RCA recording of the Brahms and Tchaikovsky Violin Concerti with soloist, the legendary Jascha Heifetz and the Chicago Symphony with Fritz Reiner on the podium. Recorded in 1955 and 1957 the Brahms, then the Tchaikovsky are here presented in stereo, with a newer Super Audio version also available for a few bucks more. Just about everyone says this is THE reading to own, but, as I listen to it for the umpteenth time, I do not hear the elite, king-of-the-hill greatness in it. Perhaps, I'm missing the point but aside from the fact that this is a Jewish Russian, with a tendency to play more energetically than, say a German or an American, I simply cannot go along with the herd this time , hence I voice my doubts regarding it's number 1 status. For the Brahms, in my humblest of opinions THE FINEST of all concerti, this is particularly difficult for me. My top choice is, and has been for several years, the Perlman/Giulini, followed by Kennedy/Tennstedt, then Szyring/Haitink and so forth. I admit I need to sample Mutter, Perlman/Barenboim, Shaham/Abbado and Fischer. I do have a surprisingly good Hahn recording with Hugh Wolff, and I would expect good things from both Stern and Oistrakh. The list is, nearly, endless and much the same applies to the Tchaikovsky, however, Brahms, with the invaluable assistance of Joseph Joachim, simply can't be caught by anyone, not Tchaikovsky, or Mendelssohn, Mozart, or even Beethoven.
No, the Brahms is tops and because of it's intense lyricism and "dream-team" blending of soloist and orchestra, and the unbearably wonderful homogenous sound of solo violin with a perfect orchestral accompaniment, makes a combination that is forever unbeatable. Hearing the Brahms Concerto is a special night, indeed, akin to spending hours with Mahler, notably his 2nd , 6th or 8th Symphonies.
So, for this listener, nothing but the very best will do for the Master from Hamburg, and I do love Hamburgers, done medium rare with copious amounts of juices, condiments and a great glass of pop, then a serene afternoon nap. L.O.L. Tchaikovsky is a fairly close runner up, 3rd place behind Beethoven and Mendelssohn.
It has become pleasingly obvious that Tchaikovsky fairs better in this Heifetz interpretation, with the gorgeous opening movement's initial exposition of the main theme taking my breath away and as lovely as any I have heard or are likely to hear. But, overall, these concerti feel a tad pushed, and rushed. Reiner's tempi are no dragging matter, to be sure. Either you keep up, or else! He was, undoubtedly, Maestro "I'm in charge," and that's it. The CSO, plays wonderfully in these pieces and in the mid-later 50's the CSO was on the cusp of being a great orchestra, when Solti, with the aid of that wildly successful 1971 European tour, charged into the world-wide elite circle, and has been a charter member ever since. As an engaged to be wed couple, my wife and I began our lives together with Solti's rise to stardom with CSO concerts beginning in 1973, and so on. At the Orchestra's s annual Summer Ravinia festival in 1973, I even proposed at intermission of opening night's Mahler 8th under James Levine.
In closing, let me be clear. These works get first class readings, yes, but they both could stand a more relaxed pacing and smoother edges, not the razor-sharp crispness from two of the most energetic tacticians, hence, these concerti certainly are anything but droll, or worse yet, ponderous. The sonics for the time, are pretty good and I think I will go ahead and order that SACD version now while I'm at it. This hearing, perhaps only the 5th or 6th one I've done is the best of them all, and I now can tell that these compositions are more worthy of the praise I failed to comprehend in previous years. So, I do recommend them both, but probably save you money and order the SACD version. Wish me luck and for you, happy listening and God bless all, Tony. AMDG!!

Early, classic Elton John music is the artist's peak as far as I'm concerned. His run that began with 11-17-70 and ended with Captain Fantastic is just astounding. But Tumbleweed Connection is possibly the best of the lot.

From a musical, lyrical, and production standpoint, TC is peerless. Every song is a winner. There's the irresistible "Amoreena" and the gorgeously layered (but never over-produced) "Burn Down The Mission" and the bucolic and ever-catchy "Country Comfort." It's been well documented that John and Taupin (his lyricist) were into The Band during the writing and recording of this album. Well, that influence is certainly present.

Each tune abounds with tasteful acoustic and electric guitars, thoughtful and timeless lyrics, and of course John's wonderful piano playing. There are no hit singles on this album. There are no affectations on this album. And there are no duds on this album. A true classic.

title: Where is she now?
text:
Those of you who have been wondering where Gale Garnett is now... I have an answer for you. She's been fairly successful as a writer and an actress the past couple of years, as a matter of fact, she was in "My Big Fat Greek Wedding" in 2002. She now lives and works chiefly in Canada, where she settled after leaving New Zealand. According to her bio on ubl.com, she's written essays, columns, and book reviews, and also written two one-woman plays titled "Life with Gale Garnett" and "Life After Latex." To the best of my knowledge, however, she is no longer recording music or performing, even though "We'll Sing In The Sunshine" won her a Grammy for best contemporary folk recording.
That said, "We'll Sing In The Sunshine" is one of my favorite "oldies" and one of my favorite "one-hit wonders."(The song hit #4 on the pop charts nationally and #1 in Detroit, on the chart published by Motown's leading top 40 station at the time, WKNR/Keener 13.) Radio in 1964 was saturated with the Beatles, and for an unknown folk singer from New Zealand as she was to make a breakthrough was probably quite remarkable, as short as her tenure on the charts turned out to be. (After "Lovin' Place" fell off the charts, she had one more single, "I'll Cry Alone," "bubble under" before fading away.) She had a very distinctive voice - not diva-esque soulful, but warm and rich, good to relax with.
Correct me if I'm wrong on this, but I believe Gale Garnett also has the distinction of being the only artist from New Zealand to ever hit #1 on a Billboard chart ("We'll Sing..." was #1 on the AC charts for an impressive seven straight weeks).
Luv ya Gale, and there still are people out there who appreciate your music.

title: He is Back
text:
Not unlike many dominant '90s rappers whose careers have stretched into this decade, Snoop Dogg appears to approaching something of a crossroads.

While never as purebred a gangsta MC as some other West Coast artists, Snoop nonetheless has always managed to blend just the right amount of gangbanger menace with his wit, charm and taffy-elastic flow. Even though his new album, "R&G (Rhythm & Gangsta): The Masterpiece" (Geffen) certainly doesn't abandon Snoop's 'hood roots, it does find the rapper settling much more comfortably into the avuncular "Renaissance Man" posture the actor/TV producer/fashion designer has been cultivating in recent years.

No longer the street tough who once threatened cop killings on "Deep Cover," he's more the blue-collar uncle. Snoop's cool and street-wise, still pimped-out and not to be trifled with, but also cured by years of hard knocks and ready with words of advice that can be as wise as wrongheaded.

title: Vader trample all over the thrash/death metal line with a great album
text:
Metal to those who are not fans is basically a bunch of noise. Those who do love it, including moi, know it's a vast complex and diverse genre, and in my opinion the last bastion of real rock and roll for the most part, depending on the group. It's been broken down to several sub-genres, and in that respect it has created a noose for its creative output. It's quite the paradox: fans want the band to be what it's famous for, but criticize it for playing it safe. When a band does stretch out, they get lampooned by ignoramuses for not being a carbon copy! Most fans like the diversity, others are just intolerant and stupid.
Which brings us to Poland's greatest metal band, Vader. I have always maintained the line between thrash metal and death is a fine one, and the most furious of the thrash outfits, Slayer, Exodus, Kreator, Sodom and Venom are actually quite close to those on the death side, Sepultura, Obituary, and even Morbid Angel in places. Vader have been around a long time and have consistently turned out the highest quality death/thrash, never disappointing, always crushing and willing to redefine boundaries.
"The Empire" is a relatively brief album, as all their CD's are, around 40 minutes or so. The last couple saw Vader inserting some classical interludes here and there, while "The Empire" visits the more classic thrash formula, making this album just a tad more accessible but still vintage Vader.
Overkill is a proud ancestor and supporter of Vader, and perhaps the influence of NY's best thrash band has rubbed off on Vader. One tune,
"Iron Reign", is thrash all the way, and Peter Wiwczarek, the band's leader and vocalist is as expressive and passionate as ever. The production is a tad roomier, and overall Vader have made another fine metal album. I like Behemoth too, but Nergal's delivery can be a bit oppressive after a while. For those who don't really care about labels though, and want a great solid metal album need look no further than "The Empire" and for that matter, the whole Vader catalogue, including the absolutely crushing "Litany", one of death metal's most brutal albums ever.
