title: Perhaps The Finest Hour of Their 2nd Incarnation
text:
I know they would sell more copies with the upcoming SATURDAY NIGHT FEVER soundtrack and it's follow up SPIRITS HAVING FLOWN both of which I love. However, MAIN COURSE may be the finest moment of what I call the 2nd phase of their brilliant career. The had moved to the U.S. and began recording in Miami, Florida with legendary producer Arif Mardin. He began to move them away from their previous soft rock & pop early career to a more R&B based sound that would soon lead to them topping the charts and releasing a string of albums and songs that would put them in the conversations about the greatest of all time.

I have heard people dog their supposed "Disco" era as being something to be embarrassed about, during this time the wrote some of the most incredible songs the world has ever heard, sold out shows across the world and topped the charts in ways that no one had come close to doing before. The "critics" always had a hard time trying to fit them into a particular category or box. They were multifaceted and multitalented artists who took the music world by storm and more than once which is something you can't really say about most of their contemporaries.

There is absolutely nothing for this band to be ashamed of as a matter of fact, at one point in 1978, the Gibb brothers were responsible for writing and/or performing 9 of the songs in the Billboard Hot 100. In all, the Gibbs placed 13 singles onto the Hot 100 in 1978, with 12 making the Top 40. They also had a string of 6 consecutive number 1 hits at one period from 1978 to 1979.

Now to the proper review of this album, "Main Course" is the beginning of what would be called "Disco" by many in just a few short years. It truly was what is termed "Blue Eyed Soul" from the area I grew up in and truly displayed fantastic songwriting, musicianship and singing. Barry and Robin Gibb are the main songwriters with Maurice co-writing some of the songs and the melodies as well as playing multiple instruments. The albums first 2 tracks, "Nights On Broadway" and " Jive Talkin" were two of the biggest hits of the era and played in clubs and discotech's around the world both then and now.

The album also showcases the variety of their songwriting with ballads such as "Songbird" and "Baby As You Turn Away"; Soft Rock classics like "Fanny: Be Tender With My Love" and "Wind of Change" and even Country influenced songs "Country Lanes" and "Come On Over". One of my personal favorites is "All This Making Love", I love the interplay between Barry and Robin's vocals and Alan Kendall's guitar on that song is gritty and fantastic.

This is a complete album from beginning to end and was a main catalyst to opening up doors for Barry and Robin in particular to start writing for other artists in just about every genre known at that time. This is truly an outstanding display of talent and musical knowledge and this album would solidify their move away from their Robert Stigwood influenced years and they would start taking more control over the direction of their careers.

This album is one of the greatest examples of what made this band great and one of the most influential bands of all time. And let's be clear, they were a band and not just a singing group who all played instruments, wrote and produced songs and sang with a passion that few have ever reached. I read recently that at least 2,500 different artists had recorded their songs. This is the truest testament to the greatness of this band and one of many examples of why they deserve all the praise they have received and in this reviewers opinion, are deserving of so very much more.

title: I thought it was a good idea!
text:
Reviewed By: Natasha Tripney · Mar 10, 2010 · London

Ramin Karimloo and Sierra Boggess
in Love Never Dies
(© Catherine Ashmore)
Sequels are always potentially dangerous ground, and this has certainly proved to be the case with Love Never Dies, Andrew Lloyd Webber's follow-up to his most popular musical, The Phantom of the Opera, now at the Adelphi Theatre. The new show, directed by Jack O'Brien, turns out to be muddled and baffling, and full of moments of unintentional humor. It is also unlikely to satisfy existing Phantom fans nor attract new ones.

The story is set 10 years after the events of the original. The Phantom (Ramin Karimloo) has fled to America -- specifically to Coney Island, where surrounded by freaks and circus folk he has created his own Barnum-style attraction, Phantasma. Meg Giry (Summer Strallen) and Madame Giry (Liz Robertson) have accompanied him across the Atlantic and Meg is now topping the bill there nightly, desperately seeking his approval.

Without revealing his identity, the Phantom invites his former object of affection, the soprano Christine Daae (Sierra Boggess) to perform an aria he has written for her. Not surprisingly, she accepts, arriving with husband Raoul (Joseph Millson) and young son Gustave in tow. She needs the money, as Raoul is now a drunk with heavy gambling debts. Once more, she ends up caught between the two men, and the lack of suspense in who will win out is one of its most problematic elements: Christine's mind seems made up from the start.

Despite the contributions of four different people to the book -- Lloyd Webber and Ben Elton, as well as the lyricist Glenn Slater and the novelist Frederick Forsyth -- the dialogue is peppered with clunky exposition. As a stream of Vanderbilts and Astors spill off an ocean liner, a well-informed crowd member points out Christine and remarks that though she is still pitch-perfect, it's like "the flame has gone out or something." Later, much is made of the significance of little Gustave being 10 years old in case the slower members of the audience have failed to make the connection.

Musically, it's a mixed affair in every sense. There are rock numbers and music hall pastiches as well as the obligatory ballads. "Devil Take The Hindmost," the Phantom's showdown with Raoul, is suitably peppy, and the Phantom's first duet with Christine, "Beneath a Moonless Sky," is fairly powerful, although more for the strength of their joint vocals then for the song itself. Christine's big emotive number, "Love Never Dies" (which is partly recycled from an earlier Lloyd Webber/Elton collaboration, The Beautiful Game), is rather limp in comparison. Worst of all, hardly any of the music digs its way under your skin.

Karimloo has an impressive voice and a measure of stage presence, yet he comes across as more eccentric than menacing. Boggess has a lovely voice, as well, but her Christine never seems particularly conflicted or troubled by the situation she finds herself in. She seems most comfortable in her scenes with Gustave (the role is split between seven young actors; at the performance I saw he was played, with a strong sense of timing and considerable vocal skill, by Harry Child). Saddled with a sliver of a role as Raoul, Millson has little to do but look cross and slink off.

Bob Crowley's projection-heavy design veers from the effective and elegant, in the moon-lit prologue and a later bar scene, to the ridiculous. The Phantom's tower-top aerie is truly a sight to behold; it's a cross between a Bond villain's lair and the Addams Family's attic.

title: Syd?  Crazy, but not crazy!
text:
OK, so there has been a lot said and written about this guy and I've heard most of his stuff. His departure from PF might have been unhappy and or forced, but I seem to think there was something among friends here that nobody wants to recognize.

These guys were all lifelong friends. To see Syd crack up from that perspective would mean to see one of your own peers that grew up with you as a kid go nuts. What would you do if you had a band with him? So they left him out one night on the way to a gig. They were all just kids.

But back to the album. Peel shows a lot more of this friendship as regards Barrett and Gilmour. These two, after all went on the famous busking holiday in France, almost getting arrested and being fast friends through it all.

This comes through all the way in this album. Their guitar playing and harmonizing sounds like they could still be busking together, making a stop with Jerry Shirley somewhere in France again. There is an obvious friendship between Gilmour and Barrett and after all the fallout and Gilmour taking Syds place and Syd glaring at Gilmour on the stage from the front row seems to be just another falling out among friends that know they will work it out.

Of course Syd was half bonkers by then but he made it a few more years - two solo ambums - and he had his confidence back as a solo artist before giving up the music industry altogether. Thanks to Peel, we can see Barrett at the peak of his game before making that decision.

The quality of the mixing is excellent and the all the songs, especially Baby Lemonade, show Barrett and Gilmour sharing a nice vibe together. Yeah it's sad and bittersweet what happened after all was said and done, but I think Syd made his own decision. Probably just in time to go back home and work the excess acid and mandys out of his system.

You might have heard all these songs before, but I really recommend getting this CD. Then wonder what would have happened if Gilmour had been recruited into PF before Syd started losing it. PF would have been a lot different, and, in my opinion, have a happier sound. This CD is a hint of how that chemistry could have worked out.

title: The Floacist proves she can carry an album on her own
text:
This is the second solo album for Natalie Stewart, a.k.a. The Floacist, formerly of the British duo Floetry. For those not familiar with her previous work, Stewart was the spoken word half of the duo, while Marsha Ambrosius was “the Songstress.” Now that they’ve parted company and embarked on solo careers, it’s been interesting to watch them develop over the last few years.
On Floetry Re:Birth, The Floacist proves that she can carry an album on her own. Stewart’s lovely voice, soft and caressing, stays firmly within her comfort zone and though her range is rather limited, it’s perfectly suited to her style of jazzy neo-soul. She’s assisted by a bevy of back-up singers, including her husband Nolan Weekes, who also produced, arranged, and co-wrote many of the songs. The opening track “Start Again” sets the mood, with guest vocalist Raheem DeVaughn weaving in the background vocals, adding range and depth to the mix. Other album highlights include “Soul” featuring the female quartet Debonair on back-up vocals, “Speechless” with its scatting refrain and poetic interludes, and “Roots of Love” with South African singer Thandiswa Mazwai providing the counterpoint to Stewart’s spoken text. Also included is the “10th anniversary edition” of the sultry ballad “Say Yes,” a reinterpretation of the song from Floetry’s debut 2002 album. A seductive and provocative set piece, Floetry Re:Birth firmly establishes The Floacist’s vision and cements her place among female adult contemporary neo-soul singers.

title: Weezer's turn.
text:
In many ways, this album represents Weezer coming full circle. It probably more similar to their first LP (the blue one) than any one released since. But the band doesn't rehash that territory in a vacuum.

Weezer takes some of the best aspects of the bands they've influenced and integrates them into their work. Perhaps more importantly, they take some of the sillier and worse aspects of modern emo and turn it into something that lives between parody and brilliance. If you don't laugh when you first hear Troublemaker, you're listening wrong (I'm teasing); after a listen or three, this song will start to blow you away.

In order to really open up this offering, other band members sing and contribute in more ways. This certainly changes the feel, but the differing vocals add a layer of depth that you never realized was lacking in past releases.

So, if you hear a song that sounds like another band, even a band you're not fond of, take a step back and listen to Weezer's take on the past 14 years.

title: Optimal Needs to Learn How to Center Stampers When Pressing Records
text:
This is a classic album with great mastering by Kevin Gray. Unfortunately while Optimal has cleaned up their act in some aspects, they still can't press a centered record. When the stampers are not properly aligned on the pressing machine, it creates an off-center record. During playback, the tonearm sways side to side creating extra noise and throws off the pitch, making the music sound seasick.

Why we are still having this problem in 2022 I do not know. Take just a little bit of extra time when installing stampers on the machine, punching stampers after they are made, etc. and we wouldn't have this problem. Blue Note - get on Optimal's case and have them fix this.

Unfortunately defects like this mean I have to return these records and hope the next copy is properly pressed. It's a huge hassle and one record buyers shouldn't have to be dealing with after we fork out money for these records.

title: Toe-tapping Traditional Music
text:
First of all, I wasn't sure how I wanted to rate this double album. It would get a 4 or 5 for content, but the actual recording itself, while not horrible, is less than the digital clarity we've gotten used to over the years. Actually, it's not even clear as the typical 60's era LP stereo records would have been (the time these recordings were made). It probably didn't help that I played the music both over my laptop speakers, and a small portable CD player. But the scratchiness, and slight muffled tones are there in various songs.

I definitely have an eclectic taste in music--classical music is my favorite, including opera, but I enjoy folk, pop, Broadway, country, rock, etc. As an amateur singer and guitarist, I also have a deep appreciation for any artist who is obviously skilled in their particular genre. There is a version of "Dueling Banjos" that would leave
the famous version from the movie "Deliverance" in the dirt. The first cd includes songs as well as instrumental pieces, and the second, shorter cd contains all instrumental pieces that would make the dead get up and dance.

The Dillards came to fame on the old Andy Griffith Show, playing the mountain dwelling "Darling" family. The boys didn't say much on the show, but played and sang various musical numbers during the episodes they appeared. Actors Denver Pyle and Maggie Peterson played the Darling father and daughter respectively. Pyle played along on a jug, while Peterson sang (those were her actual vocals on the show). Neither Pyle or Peterson are on this recording, but some of the songs featured on the show are, including the Dillards' original song "There is a Time".
Despite the technical issues with the recording itself, it's really refreshing to hear music that hasn't been over-processed by technology, though I kind of wish it were a bit clearer.
One other thing to mention...there are some jokes during a few actual "live" recordings that may not go over well these days, including an introduction to "Pretty Polly" that has an audience laughing at the thought of a man who rids himself of his pregnant lover by whacking her over the head and leaving her body in the woods. A lot of folk songs, many that go back to earlier equally or more violent British versions, just have a lot of murder in their themes, but I was puzzled why the audience thought it was so funny. I just mention this as a warning to those who might find such themes, much less the attitudes surrounding them, unsuitable for children or sensitive individuals.
Still, I do recommend it for music fans who miss traditional country and bluegrass music , or fans of traditional American folk music. This will be a favorite album to play on long, boring drives or when doing tedious chores around the house.

title: Great work by the young, early Allison
text: First, a warning: though the cover claims all the songs have Mose Allison on vocals, the last three on CD 2, "The Well," "Idyll" and "Stand By," are instrumentals. Now for the good news: I'll never forget the first time I heard Mose Allison, on his first solo album, "Back Country Suite." It seemed like a nice enough jazz piano album, nothing special, until I heard the song "One Room Country Shack." Allison's piano playing was competent but his singing was riveting: at once laid-back and powerful, with a blend of urban sophistication and his real-life rural roots (he was born In Tippo, Mississippi). The first 13 tracks are Allison's vocal recordings for Prestige; the later package is a willy-nilly blend of tracks from his brief tenure on Columbia and his first two records for Atlantic (where he would duplicate Nat "King" Cole's transition from being a piano player to a piano player who sometimes sang to a singer who accompanied himself on piano – though he never took Cole's final step of abandoning the piano almost completely and just singing). All of It is great and a measure of Mose Allison's fabulous talent, both as a singer and songwriter (though a lot of the tracks here are old Duke Ellington compositions or covers of R&B hits). These discs have rarely been out of my player since I got this release!

text:
I was apprehensive to buy this only because there was only one review. I loved Giles Reaves album, 'Sea of Glass' in the nineties and had been craving something of that caliber for quite some time. I think this album is amazing. The compositions as well as the overall sound treatment is beautifully complex. At first I felt it a bit dark sounding but instead it feels very deep. The percussion in the tracks 'Fascination,' and 'Troubled Skies,' is wonderfully intricate and engaging, while 'Enduring Time,' is simply mind blowing with sweet layers of sequencers and drums. The organic elements really blend well with the synthesizers-- 'Feeling Helplessly Drawn,' being another example.

It simply overwhelmed me the first listen, but left me somehow intrigued enough to listen again. By the third time, I just put my high end headphones on and slipped away into The Range, a place quite far from here, and then onto the beautiful synth bass groove of 'The Space Between' and then the trippy finale of 'The Walk,' very reminiscent of Edgar Froese's Pinnacles or Stuntman until it utterly explodes with another killer bass groove (bass guitar--dunno??) that sort of drops the hammer like the old Berlin School greats, Software.

It is a modern New Age/Electronic music classic in my opinion.

title: WHY DID THEY BOTHER?
text:
This is the third recording of Handel’s Messiah by the Mormon Tabernacle Choir, and is probably the least satisfactory of the three. The first, the legendary 1959 recording conducted by Eugene Ormandy, paired the enormous choral resources of the MTC with the full sonority of the Philadelphia Orchestra. It made no attempt to be “authentic” in the forces used and performance style, but the result was a delightfully lush and exuberantly joyous romp through Handel’s most famous oratorio. Its primary shortcoming was its brevity; it was heavily cut—almost one third of the score was omitted, ostensibly so it would fit on two LPs.

The unabridged score was performed in the 1995 MTC recording conducted by noted Handel interpreter David Wilcocks, who made a semi-bold move by employing the orchestration devised by Ebenezer Prout in 1902 to specifically deal with the problem of employing choruses many times larger than those Handel used, reinforcing the instrumental forces and allowing for changes in performance traditions—by 1902, harpsichords were virtually extinct and orchestral instruments had evolved into markedly different incarnations of what they had been. In my review of that recording, I applauded Wilcocks’s decision to let us hear that historically significant edition, but lamented the fact that he employed it only for the choruses; the solo arias were performed with more authentically scaled orchestration, which gave the overall performance a schizophrenic quality as it ricochet between the mid-18th and early-20th centuries. But the performance was spirited and well recorded, and I found it highly enjoyable.

Most recently, in 2016 the MTC took another crack at what be the most-recorded choral work of all time, under the baton of Mack Wilberg, who seems to have carried on Wilcock’s attempt to reconcile two irreconcilable aesthetics, namely more authentically Baroque performance practices and inauthentically gigantic choral forces. But his results are hampered by two shortcomings. One is the recorded balance, which exemplifies what I have come to term “bathroom acoustics,” by which I mean the soloists are recorded in extreme closeup, with the effect being like having the soloist seated next to you on your sofa while the orchestra and chorus are in the bathroom with the door closed. Such extreme boosting of the soloists may be typical in 21st-century pop music, but is just plain wrong here; there is no way on earth that a solo soprano, for instance, would sound so much louder in a live performance than the massed sound of 80 choral sopranos singing in close proximity.

Which brings us to the second shortcoming, namely the quality of those solo singers, each of whom is competent but not in the same league as soloists who can be heard in many other recordings. Sonya Yoncheva, for example, has a perfectly pretty voice, but she is up against such legendary sopranos as Joan Sutherland, Kathleen Battle, Eileen Farrell, Heather Harper, Margaret Price, Elly Ameling, and Elisabeth Schwarzkopf, to name only a few from the more than two dozen recordings in my collection. To be fair, the women in this recording—Yoncheva and mezzo-soprano Tamara Mumford—fare better than the two men, whose vocal shortcomings are only exaggerated by shoving a microphone down their throats. And all four of them indulge in stylistically inappropriate “ornamentation” of the vocal lines. Someone needs to explain to them that ornamenting a vocal line is not the same thing as simply rewriting the melodies crafted by one of the greatest composers for the human voice of all time. I assume the blame can be assigned to the conductor, who also incorporates some highly questionable phrasing and articulation—the mannered performance of the chorus “All we like sheep” is a vivid example.

In short, if you want a Messiah with the Mormon Tabernacle Choir, you would do better to stick with Wilcocks (or, if you don’t mind the cuts, Ormandy). But if you want a truly spectacular and vibrant recording that goes for sonic splendor with no apologies for not being “authentic,” my highest recommendation goes to the legendary performance by Sir Thomas Beecham that boasts a truly stellar quartet of soloists, a sumptuously large chorus, and the deliciously Technicolor orchestration by Eugene Goosens.

text:
I must admit, this is better then Against, its an improvement, but its still very weak at certain points, filler is evident, some parts do not make sense and this is the only Sepultura CD where no lyrics are given. This is Sepultura's version of Soulfy's primitive pretty much with being released a year apart from each other and both having several guests. Derrick still doesn't fit in with Sepultura, but as they progress, he is doing a better job. One reason I feel is that Derrick doesn't play guitar on the songs, where as Max did. Now to me, that's a type of consistency problem, you may see pictures with him holding a Guitar but he only uses that for playing older Sepultura songs live and in music videos. It doesn't label him as playing guitar anywhere within the CD insert.

But the pros, are that the quality has increased (in comparison to Against, which has worse) and Igor's drumming still rules. Andreas and Paulo do a good job too, but are weaker in comparison to past efforts. They showed off their ability to experiment by creating Nation as a Concept album, having Sepultura create this perfect utopia. At times it works and at others it falls flat. For example the opener Sepulnation sounds very Nu-Metal and unfocused. But then there are parts like the song Politricks (my personal favorite) featuring Jello Biafra as a guest. Anyone who likes Jello at all will instantly love this slow, creepy song. Other interesting songs include Tribe to a Nation, and the 2 closing songs Water (a strangely slow beautiful song, where derricks singing actually works) and the song Valtio (Finnish for Union) which features the Finnish cello group Apocalyptica, and is very, very Hypnotizing. Other then that most of the other songs have flaws of some kind.

As far as the Concept part, in between certain songs there are often people speaking in different languages, I know one of them is German, but none are in English, so I don't know what they mean yet, I assume that they are saying what they want in a nation but don't take my word for it.

If you want to get nation, then go with the Import version with the 5 bonus tracks, they are all very interesting, 3 covers, a demo and a live song. Since those are really the reason why you are looking here I will go over them.

Bela lugosi's dead - Interesting Bauhaus cover.

Annihilation - Cool Crucifix cover

Rise Above - Awesome Black Flag cover

Revolt (Demo) - The original is 56 seconds long, yet this is 3:46 seconds, now does that make sense? It almost seems as if they screwed up and inserted the demo as the final product.

Roots Bloody Roots (Live) proving that they will still play the great songs at concerts, this one is definitely the best of the 5 bonus songs and is very interesting to hear Derrick singing this.

Overall, it's better then Against, but still, this is Sepultura we are talking about. This is definitely something for the hardcore fan. Don't pay full price for it and don't pay full price for the import, get it used, I got it for 6 bucks. I think I made a wise decision, so why don't you?

title: landmark deathcore record---Mitch gone, but not forgotten
text:
Although many critics slammed this record as having all the songs
"sound the same," that, in this reviewer's opinion, is a totally
invalid assessment. It would be like saying that the Stooges'
FUN HOUSE or Weezer's PINKERTON are filled with sound-alike songs--
which, on first listening to them, is true. But just as the mastery
of the punk or emo style is more about mastery within one range, that's
also the case with THE CLEANSING. Within the deathcore genre, this is
a really compelling, brutally uplifting record, with not just anger or
"cookie-monster" grunting, but ACTUAL SONGS, whose creativity and fine
construction become obvious to open-minded and open-eared listeners.
"No Pity For a Coward" is flat-out brilliant, probably the ultimate deathcore
song released to date, and most of the other tracks are not far behind; gems
of very dark, brutal, but imaginative music. My only mild caveat is that the
production could have been a LITTLE cleaner, to highlight the late Mitch Lucker's
incredible pipes and the overall awesome musicianship to better advantage. But,
on the whole, a criminally underrated and very cool record. RIP in metal peace,
Mitch.

title: WONDERFUL MID-SEVENTIES CLASSIC ITALIAN POP
text:
Another delightful gem from this legendary Italian diva. Beautifully conceived and executed.

The title song is a fascinating story of a male lover with a big secret. When the secret is discovered, he kills himself, leaving his lady to take the blame for the "crime." The woman thought she'd always have faith in love, but, after 5 years in a sanitarium, her font of love dries up. Powerful and moving! "E' Gia' Finita," "Senza Te," and "Perdersi" are truly beautiful ballads sung to perfection. "Luce" is a moving, "modern" pop ballad, with a great sense of drama. "L'uomo questo mascalzone" is one of Milva's great tangos. "Non arrenderti" is her version of the American gospel classic "Keep Your Hand on The Plow" and loses nothing in the translation. "L'uomo dal mantello rosso" has a circus-y, circular, hypnotic feel, and "Monica delle bambole" (a big hit) is not to be missed for its wonderful performance and sweet, sympathetic treatment.

This set has a wonderful variety (and yet unity) to it. For any fan of great pop music and wonderful, expressive, soulful singing.

title: A hard rock monument that literally made history!!!
text:
`Lordi' is the Finnish shock hard rock band probably known as the metal group that experienced the greatest popularity boom in recent history within the European market, literally becoming superstars overnight. Having established themselves as recording artists since 2002, the band was chosen to represent their home country in the annual European POP song contest `Eurovision' of 2006 (held in Athens, Greece that year). The band was set to perform the track `Hard Rock Halleluiah' from their latest at the time, 3rd album `The Arockalypse'. And it won! Most European countries voted in favour of `Lordi' placing them in the first position, with the rest following far behind.

Without doubt the 10th of May 2006 will be remembered as the metal celebration of the European metal community; and the track `Hard rock Halleluiah', as glorious as it sounds, perhaps was not all that amazing or, put more accurately, was not the strongest track on `The Arockalypse'.

`The Arockalypse' was perhaps the most 80s oriented hard rock album of 'Lordi' and despite the monstrous (yet catchy vocals) featured the biggest choruses than any other hard rock album of that year. Beyond that, the guitars are thick on the riffs and unexpectedly technical during the leads (including twin guitar melodies and shredding). In addition the keyboards add the very essence of 80s AOR to the album making the opening riffs so exciting and the choruses even more climactic. Finally the rhythm section is totally metal with a huge-as it deserves- production.

I have to admit that there are very few albums released in `00s that were as infectious as `The Arockalypse'. Summing the recipe of their success? big song openings straight to the point lyrics, mega choruses, at to that loads of melodic guitar and there it is!

Furthermore this special edition of the album including the original 12 songs plus re recorded versions of 3 of their older tracks is the REAL DEAL; NON STOP HARD ROCK HEAVEN absolutely no fillers allowed on this monumental album! And very honestly, to this day songs like `Good to be bad', `Who's your daddy', `Now it snows in Hell' and `Would you love a monsterman' are amongst my favourite hard rock tunes of all time.

A true monument of Hard Rock.

"Metal Hammer" Greek magazine (issue 259) marks this album with 7/10 commenting: "Old school 80s hard rock to the bone in the style of Kiss, Alice cooper, WASP and Twisted sister"

title: Great metal!
text: A different approach from the far too short lived Enforsaken on this album.  More melodic, occasionally slower with a more epic/folk metal sound than its brutal predecessor, the outstanding  Forever Endeavor.  This new approach, falling somewhere between melodic death, thrash, and folk metal (though still dominated by the death and thrash) is great!  As melodic death tends to vary in style from dominated by death metal to having strong power metal tendencies (read: overuse of synthesizers and all things cheese), I've always appreciated those album that shy away from the power metal.  I can handle it in small doses, and occasionally an album will come along that is strong enough to overcome the cheese, but for the most part it's a turn off.  And that's what's so attractive about Enforsaken.  No power metal, here!  These guys are clearly strong musicians, and uncompromising in their own vision without a desire to make their music more palatable and catchy.  Good stuff!

title: Drug Plan's Only Album Solid But With Holes...
text:
Caramel, the group that brought out the semi-successful radio hit "Lucy", soon disolved into nothing. But soon afterwards, band members Simon Brierly, Virginia Storey, and Andy Curran began to form another band and brought along another drummer, Randy Cooke. Together, these guys formed Drug Plan, and hence the ashes of Caramel were resurrected. While this album is very difficult to find, if you can find it (I got very lucky finding it), you will hear the influence of former band Caramel throughout this self-titled effort.

"I Can't Quit You" has a nice pace to it, very quick and somewhat catchy too, but nothing like "Lucy". Elsewhere, "Breakdown" hints at metal, and is probably the heaviest tune on the album. "Truck Driver" and "Let's Just Stay In Bed" hint at the melodic elements of Drug Plan, especially "Truck Driver", which is probably the most melodic song on the album. "Pig" brings a hint of grunge to the rock palette, and "I'm So Over You" mixes melody and groovy rock. Closer "Born Loser" hints at the pressures of trying to be successful, and the music is pretty good. But tracks like the going-nowhere "Taco Bel Air" and the manic "Apple" mask their hooks with a bit of weakness...not that they're bad tracks, just competent ones. But for most of the album, Drug Plan picks up where Caramel left off, adding a little more in the way of aggression to their music, but retaining some good hooks throughout, making it quite enjoyable.

So for fans of the later resurrection of Drug Plan, Leisureworld, and the former Caramel, you should find plenty to enjoy here on DRUG PLAN. While by no means a ground-breaking collection, it's a solid and entertaining bunch of songs. So if you're finding yourself interested, get your copy now before they become extinct.

title: Souped Up, But Very Average Riddim. . .
text:
An interesting thing is happening on reggae albums these last few years. You can probably count on one hand exactly how many albums have been released by the top level dancehall artists this year, while at the same time, you might need about 3 or 4 to count how many have been released by roots reggae artists at the top, just in 2005 alone (because of Sizzla's, Anthony B's and Luciano's propensities for releasing about 4-5 a year). And dancehall artists don't tour as well as roots artists either.

However, speaking specifically in album terms, by far one of the most successful instruments in all of reggae is the dancehall riddim album. It is released in some form or fashion by every big reggae label in the world. It generally includes the top level dancehall performer and sometimes the up and coming artists as well. And you will see them released by the DOZENS, every year and they sale, if they didnt, Greensleeves would have went out of business by now.

Greensleeves often spends months at a time dedicating its time to strictly its Rhythm Series. For example, 2004 ended with the Slow Bounce riddim, #66 in the series, this year alone has seen all the way up to the Ice Cube riddim, #76 in the series, and as it just so happens, #77, the Justice, was just released this week as well. Greensleeves DOES NOT PLAY when it comes to the version album!

The Ice Cube in particular, produced by previously unknown Mr (Ernie) Wilks Productions is very very different. It is a ridiculously fast paced, souped up riddim that takes a good while to get used to (apparently longer than the 20 tracks here). It is so different and. . . just odd that I can imagine how difficult it might have been getting artists to record on it (which may explain why riddim album CRAZIES Elephant Man, Sizzla, Beenie Man and Bounty Killa all passed.

From those who did brave the unforgiving Ice Cube, General Degree scores the best with Hardcore Reggae, taking the cube just like the vet he is. Oddly enough, Red Rat (well not so oddly, he's kinda odd himself isnt he) also handles the cube fairly well on Curfew as does Kiprich on Kurfew. Also doing a good job is Red Square (minus head men Spragga and Assassin) on Bad From Wi Born, and Spragga himself on Backative Strong.

And that's about it. The rest of the tunes are filled with half of Leftside & Esco's alter ego Dr. Evil on the odd No STD, and even more strange, Kartel on a tune called new with lyrics that are. . . OLD!

Overall, do not buy this one on unheard advice at all. You MUST hear this riddim and like it before you too brave the Ice Cube. Mr Wilks may prove to be a great producer ultimately, but a suggestion to him would be to change the riddim more amongst the artist's tune, that's the next step in such an album, even the hardest dancehall nut (myself included) cannot possibly stand the Ice Cube for 20 tracks with no, or very little, variations.

title: Possibly the best of this period of the band's development
text:
I have been a Rush fan since the time I saw them touring the album "Hemispheres", and "Test For Echo" was one of the only albums from them I was disappointed with upon release. It seemed bland, and the lyrics to the song "Dog Years" seemed goofy without being legitimately funny.

These many years later, my opinion of the CD has changed somewhat.

Rush had, just before this CD, released three CDs of fairly short guitar-oriented songs. They were getting back to their guitar-based roots basically. Looking back at these four CDs now (Presto, Roll The Bones, Counterparts, Test For Echo), I find this to be the least satisfying period of Rush's development. The band seemed to be going through the record-industry-approved motions somewhat: the songs were short, many of the lyrics seemed less than completely convincing but often sappy, and the band was safely staying away from the controversial keyboard excesses of the previous period of their development.

I'll say, with benefit of hindsight, that this is a very good CD. It may be the best of the four CDs in this period of the band's development. While the previous three releases each had some good songs and some mediocre songs, this CD has only 2 mediocre songs, and they are next to each other on the CD's later half, almost as if the band was trying to bury them (The songs I'm referring to are "Dog Years" and "Virtuality", which both have what another reviewer described as awkward lyrics). Besides those two songs the only real fault the CD has is that it doesn't have that one track that most Rush CDs have that could be described as being a strong and obvious single.

The playing is strong throughout and with the exception of the two lyrics mentioned above, lyrically satisfying. If you wrote Rush off after they began experimenting heavily with keyboards on "Power Windows" and "Hold Your Fire", this might be up your alley.

title: Aum is back in Fillmore
text:
Classic rock act from San Francisco, almost totally forgotten now, but with cult status nevertheless , faithful following and superb credentials - that was one of the "in-house" bands during glorious days of Fillmore West, and it was signed by Bill Graham for his Fillmore Records label (by the way, this record label together San Francisco Records were established by Bill Graham, and not by CBS).
This blues-inspired and jam-oriented power trio (Wayne Ceballos, Kenneth Newell, Larry Martin) was around for a long time, since mid 60s at least, working hard and playing small venues, so they were a household name of the vibrant San Francisco musical scene. Initially they were spotted (and promptly signed by Sire) for a debut album "Bluesvibes" (1969) [[ASIN:B00008UE42 Bluesvibes]], built around seven lengthy jams - it's a matter of taste, but I like it.
Aum used to hang around Fillmore, where it was picked up by Paul Baratta for Tuesday Dollar Nights , which was Bill Graham's way of introducing local talents. Later Bill Graham wrote that in 1969 he had Cold Blood* and a band called Aum - "a bunch of good acts but they just didn't break", it couldn't be said better!**
For the deal with Fillmore Aum changed almost totally their approach - the LP released in 1969 had tasteful artwork with a hint of religious inspiration, as well as the whole concept which remains a rather awkward attempt to drag in eternal Christian themes ("And the ghosts of a thousand suns came shining through the trees...)
All compositions were originals penned by Wayne Ceballos (except Pachuko Boogie) under a strong spell of Fab Four - the main element of "God Is Back To Town" was unashamedly borrowed from the intro of "Sgt.Pepper's" and is the best part of this lengthy piece, while acoustic "Only I Know" and sad and melancholic "Today & Tomorrow" definitely got the inspiration from the same source.
I wouldn't insist on recommending the album to everyone - I do admire greatly the musicians of those long gone days, and all their sins should be forgiven. But "Resurrection" is not the most accomplished masterpiece - the opening track is noisy and messy, and when they are trying to imitate tribal chanting (as on "God Is Back..." or "Aum") it could have been impressive at the live gig, on the studio album it sounds rather unconvincing and even annoying - although the voice of Wayne Ceballos (when singing solo) is clear and powerful; on "Resurrection" his voice reminds Jimi Hendrix. Two up tempo hard rocking songs ("Bye Bye Baby" and "Little Brown Hen") are also spoiled by the same unison singing. To my most humble opinion the best composition is "Aum", which starts as prayer-like hymn and develops into virtuoso psychedelia with polyphonic singing.
Aum just didn't break , in 1970 it was no more.
* [[ASIN:B00005LZPV Cold Blood / Sisyphus]]- strongly recommended
**[[ASIN:0306813491 Bill Graham Presents: My Life Inside Rock And Out]] - must buy! Not only excellent reading, but treasure box of first-hand information

title: A Tragedy of Funkadelic Proportions
text:
Between 1970 and 1975 Funkadelic released seven albums on the Westbound record label. All of them are essential. The fifth album, 1973's "Cosmic Slop", is as strong, soulful and funky as any other from this seminal period.
That "Cosmic Slop" didn't end up a cosmic flop is a testament to George Clinton's unparalleled skill as a producer. In 1972, after the release of "America Eats Its Young", things were falling apart for Funkadelic. Ace lead guitarist Eddie Hazel was incarcerated for drug possession and assault, bassist Billy Nelson quit and rhythm guitarist Lucius Ross overdosed on LSD and speed, leaving him incapacitated. Funkadelic essentially lost three of its founding members right before recording for "Cosmic Slop" began.
Funkadelic, though technically a group, was essentially a George Clinton "thang." Determined to make "Cosmic Slop" Clinton reincarnated the band. Nelson and Ross, though founding members, proved dispensable. Hazel was missed (but will return on later albums.) Gary Shider, a guitar virtuoso in his own right, takes his lead, contributing incredible, soulful vocals as well. And keyboardist Bernie Worrell comes into his own. In fact, a cobbled together Funkadelic proved as solid and formidable as any previous incarnation.
"Cosmic Slop" is brimming with classic P-funk essentials. "Nappy Dugout", replete with whistles and duck calls, starts the album in typical Funkadelic style. "You Can't Miss..." sounds like a lost "Maggot Brain" single (a good thing.) "March to the Witch's Castle" is, in my opinion, the saddest, darkest, most honest song ever written about the Vietnam War. (A masterpiece maybe?) "Let's Make It Last" is transcendent and soulful. "Cosmic Slop" is a classic, 'nuff said. "No Compute" sounds like, well, country-funk. The raunchy lyrics about a one-night stand are hilarious. "This Broken Heart" is a heartfelt cover of an old doo-wop number with a hysterical interlude. "Trash A-Go-Go" is a funked-out guitar jam, possibly the funkiest moment on the album. "Can't Stand the Strain" is a joyful Motownish number... Joyful, that is, until the lyrics sink in.
Lyrically "Cosmic Slop" tends to be a sad, bluesy album. Half of the songs are traditional soul tunes about love and heartache. The others deal with war, prostitution and drugs. Even though at times the lyrics are funny, there's a tragic quality to them overall.
Musically it's a soulful, funky, yet brazenly psychedelic album. Funkadelic stands for psychedelic funk, which is what you get on "Cosmic Slop." This album has little in common with late-70s disco-influenced Parliament and Funkadelic albums, like P's "The Mothership Connection" or F's "One Nation Under a Groove." Rather, think Sly Stone and Jimi Hendrix on acid and you're close.
Hope this helped. Funk on.

title: Any album Rahsaan creates is an ultimate gift!
text:
I was pleasantly surprised to learn that Rahsaan Patterson had released a Christmas album at the close of 2008. He is definitely one of my favorite singers and I knew that he would astound and satisfy me with his yuletide LP. Though I did not care for his album "Wine and Spirits", one thing I have to say in his favor is that he never sounds bad vocally. He has amazing control of his vocals; it's easy to know that he was born with that gift, he only enhanced it.

"The Ultimate Gift" truly has an innovative, futuristic sound. It's the type of sound that Rahsaan's group, SugaRush brought forth a few years before this album was released. There are a few tones on the album, but anyone who listens to this album in its entirety would know that he set out to make you sing and dance; most of the tracks are mid-tempo or upbeat. He did a few classic Christmas songs, but he also did some writing and gave us fresh songs to listen to as we deck the halls. The song I was most impressed by was the title track. I listened to it once and ended up repeating it several times. The title track has an absolutely brilliant chorus, a great beat, and fantastic lyrics. It's an instant Rahsaan Patterson classic. It just made the entire album shine. I also enjoyed Rahsaan singing alongside the sound of piano on "This is the Season." His falsetto is heartfelt, but the listener's bliss is cut short because this song is only 2 minutes and 21 seconds, therefore you are forced to continually repeat it. "Angels (Sing)" and "Christmas at my House" are decent tracks, but weak when being compared to the rest of the album.

I was very entertained by "The Ultimate Gift" and recommend it to anyone looking for Christmas songs with a futuristic twist.

Mikeisha's Top 5

1. "The Ultimate Gift"
2. "Holiday"
3. "This is the Season"
4. "Wonderful Christmastime"
5. "Little Drummer Boy"

title: Back to Formulae
text:
Upon a few listens of this new disc, it's become very clear to me that 'Greater Wrong of the Right' must have been a practical joke. Sure, it was fun, accessible and catchy and all, but it simply wasn't the Skinny Puppy I knew and grew to love. T'was too comfortable, really.

Yet enter 'Mythmaker'. Admittedly, like a friend of mine, I hear about an upcoming SP album and hope dearly that it doesn't suck. Such being the case, I proceeded to download a torrent of said album and give it a preview. I bought it the next day, no questions or hesitation.

To call 'Mythmaker' perhaps the most accessible album to date is clearly implying one hasn't heard GWotR, has heard it but doesn't understand better or has heard it and completely omitted it as a SP album entirely. 'Mythmaker' is beyond ambitious - it's a truly virtuosic experience. It's proof that our boys are paying attention to their roots while bolstering them with today's bells and whistles.

As can be expected, some tracks are weaker than others. "lestiduZ" and "jaHer" are both on the weaker side in that they are leaning too far to a spectrum - "jaHer" on the relaxing and "lestiduZ" on the atonal rhythmic. Yet there are songs that find a happy medium in this spectrum, especially "haZe," which I will admit moved me almost to tears with a marvelous combination of beauty and aggression that sounds nothing short of (in)tense emotion. "daL" isn't ranked far behind in this emotional vein, either.

And surely there are the fun ones where fans of old can rejoice and feel some comfort that their industrial idols are still intact after the many years. Certainly "politikiL" takes the cake with many such listeners, boasting plenty of exciting noises and even some catchy (and downright spastic) themes and hooks. "pedafly" doesn't waste much time, and is a much more straightforward work of gritty and groundshaking effects and songwriting. Even the vocally repetetive closer, "ugLi " has it's place, especially to smite the closer of the last album which sported nothing like the noise finales we fans expect and enjoy - but the latest album doesn't fail here, either.

The vocals and lyrics are back where they belong: cryptic and, more importantly, often incoherent. Nivek Ogre's voice is once again used as a powerful instrument rather than a source of easily-caught statements. But have no fear, the statements are still there. The mass distortion is back, so not-so-fans of the very clean and pretty 'GWotR' can rejoice tenfold. Beats are just as intricate and affective as ever, if not much more. The synths and guitar effecting is also at an impressive height in quality. Songwriting is back where it belongs in the spastic and comfy-to-loathesome area.

Just take it from me: Skinny Puppy is back and better than ever, ladies and gentlemen.

title: Excellent 2011 Live CD By Al Stewart and Dave Nachmanoff
text:
This is an excellent live CD featuring Al Stewart and his current guitar accompanist Dave Nachmanoff doing material from Al Stewart's extensive recorded output over his 40+ year career.

This album is somewhat reminiscent of Al Stewart's Rhymes In Rooms CD from the early 1990s, which featured a live performance featuring Al Stewart and his then band partner Peter White on guitar. Both this album and Rhymes In Rooms feature two guitars (Al Stewart with Dave Nachmanoff and Peter White, respectively) and Al Stewart on vocals performing Al Stewart material. Neither album has any back up band behind the two guitars.

One interesting feature of this album is that the material Al has selected for live performance here does not include any of his best known tracks, like Roads To Moscow, Nostradamus, Josephine Baker, Year of the Cat or Song On The Radio.

Most of the material here will be familiar to Al's long time fans - I'm certainly one of those - but it's not his best known material. Most of the compositions on this CD date from 1970 - 1979, with Last Days of the Century from the early 1980s. There's none of his newer material from the 1990 - 2010 period.

But there are also two compositions I haven't heard before: Coldest Winter (about the Swedish invasion of Russia in 1709 - Al Stewart is very good at doing songs on historical topics) and Princess Olivia. Does anyone know if these are older compositions just being released or newer compositions? Perhaps you can post a comment with an answer if you can shed any light on that. (*June 2013 update - I checked Al Stewart's website and found that Coldest Winter and Princess Olivia are from a late 1990s limited release album that was only made available to members of Al's fan club. That's apparently why they're not well known to many long time fans.*)

Overall, this an excellent Al Stewart live CD. The guitar work is excellent and Al's voice has held up well. Highly recommended for Al Stewart fans and for anyone discovering Al Stewart for the first time.

title: Beethoven Middle Piano Sonatas: Stewart Goodyear: Rediscover Beethoven the improviser ....?
text:
Stewart Goodyear is a new piano name to me. I noted his first release of the late Beethoven piano sonatas; yet it is this middle sonatas volume that got me listening. From his web site ([...]) we are given the following background: "Born and raise in Toronto, Canada, pianist and composer, Stewart Goodyear began his training at Royal Conservatory of Music in Toronto, received a bachelor's degree from Curtis Institute of Music in Philadelphia and completed a Masters Degree at Juilliard School of Music in New York. Now calling New York his home, Stewart has performed with the major orchestras of the world, ..."

Now the current catalog has no shortage of meritorious recordings of Beethoven sonatas. We can find complete sets, by famous and not so famous players. We can find excerpted discs, again by really famous virtuosos, ordinary famous pianists, and unknown pianists. Why add Stewart Goodyear to our selection lists? What does his Beethoven sonatas offer us - if anything? - that we cannot find equally among the available recordings?

Let's start with the player's basic physical sound world. Rather like singers, instrumentalists often reveal their own touch. Some are distinctive and recognizable, at least some of the time in some music; others are nearly always instantly recognizable. Aspects of that continuing musical and sonic signature must be credited to engineers; but the expert recording engineer will strive to capture the real sound the player makes, especially if something sets that artist's way with the instrument apart.

It is far better to actually listen to Goodyear's basic sonics, than to try to describe what makes him, himself, on the modern grand piano. The ear immediately notes he is a clean, direct player with a lean, crystalline tone ... a bit in the Wilhelm Kempff mode, but not Kempff. Goodyear often takes tonal or sonic risks that other players might wish to avoid: he can really allow his tone to be plain, naked, exposed ... yet ultimately elegant in phrasing, pacing, and shape. The only pianist who comes to mind with such an x-ray analytic on risky display might be, Glenn Gould playing JS Bach. But that partial insight is misleading, too, as Goodyear remains Goodyear. From the home web site, we may infer that Goodyear is a Steinway artist.

On disc one we get the three middle piano sonatas, 13, 14, 15. Disc two serves up the final three in this set, 16, 17, 18. Thus, all of Opus 27, 28, 31.

At first I was worried. Goodyear is technically quite fluent; but he seems to have little - very little - interest in romantic, push-pull, stop-go, and virtuoso display. Compared to other players taking on Beethoven sonatas, one's initial impression might be that Goodyear is making quite an effort to be self-effacing. Then the sheer genius and elegance of what he is doing begins to sink in.

No szforzando punch is slighted, no drama is starved or thinned out beyond Beethoven recognition. But everything, every single page is just about as limpid and shining as it could possibly be. This misled my ear again and again, so that often I had to remind myself that Beethoven was not pouring out baroque polyphony after all, because we were in the Classical Era. The multiple voices Beethoven unfolds to make any number of narrative, dramatic, and expressive points are simply naked and compelling in these readings. Although tempos and phrasing seem quite straightforward, the barest touches of inflection, rubato, and expressive nuance enrich his playing. Beethoven's piano sonatas catch fire in a very special way, with nuanced and subtle lights, and it is hard to recall another player who quite gives us Beethoven in just this effective yet modestly-composer-focused way.

By the end of the first sonata in the set (Number 13) and through the remaining five sonatas, one grasps in fresh energy and detail Beethoven's well-known public reputation as the great improviser of his day. The flood of variety among musical ideas and across musical ideas is effortless, infinite, and simply mind-boggling. At some moments, a player will suggest touches of fresh improvisatory impetus by somehow sounding as if while a figuration or motif is playing out, the composer is already at work dreaming up the next steps. Goodyear is stunning and marvelous in this regard, because he has little or no need to bother much with any obvious signals; yet he aptly conveys Beethoven, able to invent and vary his musical ideas, textures, and structures - on the very spot as it were - while at the very same conveying that this composer improvising is always in utter, joyous, disciplined control of his genius.

The impression of free improvisation is only matched by the sheer brilliance of structure, color, and all the other elements that go into these six piano sonatas. To hear the real, live Beethoven improvise must have actually been nearly an incomprehensibly overwhelming intellectual and emotional feast, without in the least relying on excess, nor using any looseness masquerading as complete freedom of invention. Goodyear channels a Beethoven who is deeply enacting a mastery that goes from strength to strength to amazing strength .... right off the top of his musical head, as it were.

I was quite pleased, and not a little overwhelmed by the time those last notes of the sixth piano sonata in the set fell into silence. Few other recordings in the current or any catalog have conveyed so elegantly, subtly, yet forthrightly - how deeply and constantly this Beethoven is able (terribly able; winsomely always at musical ease; and never at any sort of intellectual or musical loss) as the composer births a seemingly infinite variety of brilliant and imaginative riffs on the whole existing western classical sonata form or tradition, as Beethoven had received it through Haydn and Mozart and other exemplars.

This Beethoven is heard in the very process of assimilating sonata form in its parts and whole; while also stretching, expanding, shifting, ... playing it all, playing with it all, no holds barred. We have many reports of the composer breaking piano strings, in public and at home. What comes across in this playing is the sheer abundance of path breaking musical ideas, a veritable flood of shattering invention. Thus while showing how deeply he has understood the mold, Beethoven is also revealing endless variations on how it can be managed, varied, transformed. The many figurations which mostly convey appropriate energy and direction in other player's hands, here contribute not only the flow and energy, but also the constant great intellectual and musical power at work.

So these six middle sonatas are keepers, no doubt. The most famous yet most hackneyed of the set, the ubiquitous Moonlight (Opus 27 Nr 2) becomes another sort of creature altogether, than much of what we are used to getting in this work. The iconic first movement shimmers just barely enough, but conveys discipline and structure, too. The middle movement is an interlude, but banks its force, strength, and intellect as if to remind us listeners that the concluding movement will be about something more than blistering virtuosity. Indeed, Goodyear brings out the last movement's force and energy while suggesting a scherzo-like dimension of form.

All along, we are further enriched by apt touches of post-Haydn wit, post-Mozart humanism, Schubert-like song and warmth, always driven by overwhelming, disciplined intellect. Nothing schematic or sketchy about Beethoven's musical thinking mars the communication in any movement of any sonata. Simply everything Beethoven serves up in Goodyear's recreation arrives full-blooded, intact, born alive and feeling and moving in multiple shapes with amazement moistening all ten fingers. This set of Middle Sonatas is a keeper, and I have just now ordered a set of Late Sonatas.

title: Britten the conductor delivers the ultimate recording of the G-minor symphony
text:
Strengths:
- Excellent craftsmanship, articulation, and precision by the English Chamber Orchestra, and Benjamin Britten knows how to get this done the right way. Plus, the Snape Maltings concert hall acoustics enriches the music like no other hall.

Weaknesses:
- Initially, I thought my speakers couldn't handle the loud passages in the G minor symphony. I even thought the perhaps the record was a bit worn off of dirty (however, I always clean my styles and the record before using them). But later I listened to a digital transfer on CD, and to my surprise, there's clipping and distortion in the CD version as well (in the exact same loud passages). This was also a problem in Britten's simple symphony recording also with the ECO. So, it seems that one will have to live with this flaw as far as with this recording.

Additional comments: Britten respects the 40th symphony's repeats to the point where the 2nd movement alone lasts 16' 19", and the fourth and final movement lasts 9' 23". However, Britten and the ECO never miss a beat and you will hardly believe that you will go through almost 39' of the G minor symphony. Moreover, the ECO's sound is the perfect blend of chamber orchestra and large symphonic orchestra. Think a blend between Marriner's 1971 recording with the Academy of St. Martin in the Fields (by the way, Marriner's tempos are roughly the same as Britten's) and Karajan's 1970 recording with the Berlin Philharmonic under EMI. In summary, one cannot go wrong with this recording, to me, this is the ultimate recording and prime example of musical craftsmanship.

title: Pleasing
text: When collections of this sort were popular in the 1950's, by people like Ormandy and Fiedler, they featured virgorous, tense performances that really brought the showpiece quality to the fore.  Eiji Oue, while technically a very fine conductor, has a slightly different take on these pieces.  In Espana, for example, colors are manifold, but there is a lack of snap to the orchestra playing.  Finlandia is not hyperdramatic, but it is well delineated.  Escales is perhaps the best performance on the disc, in part because French music seems especially suited to Oue's virtues.  The Alfven is a full scale, lush performance, while Capriccio Italien, however short on excitement, offers sumptuous string sound and an idiomatic treatment of the themes.  I did not listen to this CD on a CD player with an HDCD chip, as recommended.  Nevertheless, the sound was full and warm, with excellent detail and just a hint of wispiness to the violins.  If you want these pieces in up to date sound, don't hesitate.  But there are more thrilling recordings of Finlandia and the Alfven by Ormandy and of the Capriccio Italien by Bernstein and the N.Y. Philharmonic, all on Sony.

title: Overlooked Glam Rock Gem
text: I can certainly understand that in the world of Pop, you're either hot, or you're not.  After "Zinc Alloy", which many perceived as a lame "Ziggy Stardust"-styled ...(after Bowie spent so much time stealing from Bolan, ironically), I stopped buying T-Rex records.  The reviews at Amazon brought me back to this one.  Purportedly recorded before "Zip Gun" (which most people detest), this would've been perceived as a "Diamond Dogs" ...(complete with spoken intro, half-baked thematic concept, etc.), and perhaps by the time it came out, people hadn't even cared to listen anymore, but I must say, I love this album.  I bought it three months ago, and I still listen to it every week.  It's good, semi-overblown but catchy T.Rex rock.  Start with the single (and bonus track) "Laser Love".  It's a lost glam gem.  Gloria Jones doesn't bother me a bit; this song is a blast.  The first five tracks are solid, especially "All Alone" with its swinging violins (I have this perverse love of pre-Bee Gees disco, especially heavily orchestrated tunes).  It gets a little soft in the middle, and then gets wonderfully odd at the end, especially with "Dreamy Lady", which is this perverse sorta lounge number that would be at home at any karaoke bar.  Am I being facetious?  Heck no!  This album is Bolan having FUN.  It's utterly charming, unpretentious, and wickedly absurd.  This could inspire the next Radiohead album!  Don't pass it up; it's a keeper.

I'd give him the nod over Bjorling, Corelli, Monaco, Pavarotti, though of course they all bring their own virtues.  Hendricks I did not think was so great in this role.  My favorite is the angelic Tebaldi on the Monaco/Borkh recording.  A word too for Ping, Pang and Pong (one of whom is the splendid Francisco Araiza--talk about luxury casting!). title: Extra dry...
text:
Three and a half, actually...Maybe this CD shouldn't even be reviewed. Iverson has gone so far beyond this. But CD's exist as moments in time, edifices...If you're gonna put it out there, then there it sits, waiting - for love, critique,etc...

Ethan Iverson is one the most gifted pianists who has ever devoted him/herself to Jazz/Creative Improvised Music. He never uses technique to blow the listener away. But someone who knows the piano becomes quickly aware of Iverson's vast control of time, tone, rhythm, scalar vocabulary, etc. And he is a gifted musical thinker. I rarely find myself agreeing with his line of thought on his very interesting blog, Do The Math, but I always find his writing stimulating.

All this being said, I don't find this CD very engaging. It "swings" I guess...There are a bunch of strategies borrowed from the Tradition; the title New Chimes Blues is a nice shout-out to King Oliver and early Jazz. And Reid Anderson is a very strong, commanding bassist. But the compositions all seem like sketches - they don't have much feeling of arc. They have lots of notions about vocabulary, but those are not galvanized into real edifices. Take the piece Mystique: It starts out kind of like a piece from Bartok's Microcosmos. Gradually "Jazz Harmony" is inserted. Then we arrive at something which feels like a bridge, which leads to a kind of Bachian counterpoint, the Bartok thing comes back, this time more reminicent of one of the Concertos, then a harmonic cycle which reminds me of the Ellington-Strayhorn Tonk, which leads to some kind of Movie - Music Exotica - a scary ostinato. Then some blowing: very Bill Evans meets Brad Mehldau, with what sounds like an actual Chopin quote inside of it. Then back to the head. And then a well-orchestrated coda. All very interesting, but kind of arid and undigested. The next piece, Hullabaloo 2, has some really beautifully executed hybrid scale passages (Bartok again?). You can enjoy them for what they are, because when have you ever heard an improviser play such scales in such a non - "lick" oriented way? That is really refreshing. Too bad it all doesn't all lead to a more coherent statement. The coda brings us into the world of ironic bombast which would become The Bad Plus.

I think it's time for Iverson to make another CD like this one, without all of that Bad Plus-ian rhetoric. With the help of a Tough Love-ing producer kicking his butt to keep it all out of the realm of the manneristic and the sketchy, I'm sure it would be great.

title: I didn't like the darker sound at first but I think it ...
text: This album really grew on me. I didn't like the darker sound at first but I think it is really cool now after a few listens. Once again Shigeto creates a lush soundscape full of subtle clinking, ratcheting, booming, popping and dinging percussion with really cool patterns. This is one of those percussive albums that is done right. The melodies in the song are really subtle and clearly exist to complement the percussion. I love the use of keyboards in the album. They sound like some real crisp and loosely played Rhodes sounds. I love how all the components of the songs sound so natural and organic, even the synths. Some beats are off beat but it's just not a problem with this album because it creates that human element. It's not an album I would play in a group of people but rather one I would listen to in solidarity out in nature or something where the textures can create an experience with my surroundings. Superb!

title: Great Album, Excellent Remaster
text: The songs on this album really grow on you, in a good way. It's my 3rd favorite Supertramp album behind "Crime" & "Breakfast," and it's not a distant 3rd, it's a close 3rd. I've read that when Supertramp recorded the album, they were pressed for time, short on material, so most of the songs are leftovers from "Crime" sessions, or even older. When you first hear the album you think, "sure that makes sense…sort of sounds like that." But the songs have a charm and a raw quality which I think is fantastic. It's got the good Ken Scott engineering like "Crime," but it's not as dramatic, powerful, or sonically perfect, and Bob Siebenberg's drums sit further back in the mix. The remastering is really good. Yes, it has some compression to make the album pop, but it's tastefully done. The life hasn't been squashed out of it. If you like Supertramp, it's an essential album to pick up.

title: CONTENTS ANALYSIS
text:
Ten CDs devoted to friends of Debussy, and early performances of his music:
- Photo 1: Camille Chevillard and the Lamoureux Orchestra c.1900
- Photo 2: Pierre Monteux (right) and his all-mustachioed orchestra, with Camille Saint-Saëns 1913
- Photo 3: Pianist Ricardo Viñes c.1905
- Photo 4: Mary Garden as Melisande, 1902
- Photo 5: Maggie Teyte as Melisande, 1908
- Photo 6: Hector Dufranne as Golaud, 1902

Part 1 of 5: CONDUCTORS (arranged by birth date)

- CAMILLE CHEVILLARD 1859-1923:
---- Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune: Concerts Lamoureux Orchestra, rec.1922
Camille Chevillard (photo one) conducted the premieres of La Mer and the Nocturnes for Orchestra.
- GABRIEL PIERNE 1863-1937:
---- Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune: Concerts Colonne Orchestra, rec.1930
- ARTURO TOSCANINI 1867-1957:
---- La Mer: BBC Symphony, rec.1935
- HENRI BUSSER 1872-1973:
---- Petite Suite, orch. Büsser: French National Radio Orchestra, rec.1952
Forty years earlier, at Debussy’s request, Henri Büsser orchestrated Printemps and the Petite Suite.
- PIERRE MONTEUX 1875-1964 *
---- Nocturnes: Boston Symphony, rec.1955 stereo
---- Images for Orchestra: London Symphony, rec.1963 stereo
---- Jeux: French National Radio Orchestra, rec.1955 mono
- WALTHER STRARAM 1876-1933:
---- Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune: Concerts Straram Orchestra, rec.1930
- PHILIPPE GAUBERT 1879-1941:
---- Nocturnes (Nuages only) Paris Conservatoire Orchestra, rec.1928
- DESIRE-EMILE INGHELBRECHT 1880-1965:
---- Nocturnes: Debussy Festival Orchestra, rec.1934
- ERNEST ANSERMET 1883-1969:
---- Epigraphes antiques, orch. Ansermet: L’Orchestre de la Suisse romande, rec.1953
- PIERO COPPOLA 1888-1971:
---- Children’s Corner, orch. Caplet: Paris Conservatoire Orchestra, rec.1934
---- Danses sacre et profane: Lily Laskine harp, studio orchestra, rec.1929
---- Estampes - La Soirée dans Grenade, orch. Coppola: studio orchestra, rec.1935
---- Images - Cloches à travers les feuilles, orch. Coppola: studio orchestra, rec.1935
- CHARLES MUNCH 1891-1968:
---- La Mer: Paris Conservatoire Orchestra, rec.1942

* Pierre Monteux (photo two) conducted the Paris-based Ballets Russes from 1911-1914, where he led the world premiere of Jeux, and the ballet premiere of Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune.
Monteux later recalled “Debussy was behind me when we played Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune … When we came to a forte, he said 'Monteux, that is a forte, play forte'. He did not want anything shimmering. And he wanted everything exactly in time”.
Warner’s preference for Monteux’s stereo recordings of Images and Nocturnes over earlier mono recordings seems misjudged.
The closer to Debussy’s time the better.
(the 1955 mono Jeux is unique in Monteux’s discography).
------------------------------------------------

Part 2: PIANISTS (arranged by birth date)

- CLAUDE DEBUSSY 1862-1918
---- Estampes: ‘La Soirée dans Grenade’ 1913 piano roll
---- piano accompanist to Mary Garden, rec.1904 (see Vocalists below)
- MARGUERITE LONG 1874-1966
---- Arabesques, rec.1930
---- Estampes: ‘Jardins sous la pluie’ rec.1929
- RICARDO VINES 1875-1943 *
---- Estampes: ‘La Soirée dans Grenade’ rec.1929
---- Images, Book Two: ‘Poissons d’or’ rec.1930
---- the pianist speaks (in French) about Debussy, rec.1938
- ALFRED CORTOT 1877-1962
---- Children’s Corner, rec.1947
---- Préludes, Book One: ‘La Fille aux cheveux de lin’ & ‘Minstrels’ rec.1919, ‘La Cathédrale engloutie’ rec.1947
- WALTER GIESEKING 1895-1956 **
---- Suite bergamasque, rec.1931
---- Images, Book One, rec.1948
---- Images, Book Two, rec.1948
---- Préludes, Book One, rec.1936
- MARCELLE MEYER 1897-1958
---- L’Isle joyeuse, rec.1957
---- Préludes, Book Two, rec.1956

* Ricardo Viñes (photo three) was Debussy’s favorite pianist.
He played the premieres of Estampes, L’Isle joyeuse, Images Book One (no.1&3), Images Book Two (all), Masques, Pour le piano, Préludes Book One (no.5,8,9,12) and Preludes Book Two (no.4,7,12)
** Walter Gieseking: these 1931-48 recordings predate the better-known 1951-55 recordings in his complete box: [[ASIN:B071P1LWXJ Debussy: The Complete Piano works]]
------------------------------------------------

Part 3: VOCALISTS (arranged by birth date)

- MARY GARDEN 1874-1967:
---- ‘Ariettes oubliées’ with Claude Debussy piano, rec.1904 (dedicated to Mary Garden).
Mary Garden (photo four) was the first Mélisande (see part four below).
- JANE BATHORI 1877-1970:
---- ‘Fêtes galantes’ Second Book, self-accompanied rec.1929
- CLAIRE CROIZA 1882-1946:
---- ‘Ariettes oubliées’: “Il pleure dans mon cœur” with Francis Poulenc piano, rec.1928
---- ‘Cinq Poèmes de Charles Baudelaire’: “Le Jet d’eau” with George Reeves piano, rec.1930
---- ‘Pelléas et Mélisande’: Croiza sang Geneviève in the 1928 recording of excerpts from the opera (see part four below).
- NINON VALLIN 1886-1991
---- ‘Mandoline’ with Gustave Cloëz piano, rec.1928
---- L’Enfant prodigue: “L’année en vain chasse l’année” Gustave Cloëz, Grand Orchestra, rec.1930
Ninon Vallin sang the celestial voice in the premiere of ‘Le martyre de Saint Sébastien’ and was the dedicatee of ‘Trois Poèmes de Stéphane Mallarmé’.
- MAGGIE TEYTE 1888-1976:
---- ‘Trois Chansons de Bilitis’ with Alfred Cortot piano, rec.1936
---- ‘Le Promenoir des deux amants’ with Alfred Cortot piano, rec.1936
---- ‘Fêtes galantes’ First Book with Alfred Cortot piano, rec.1936
Maggie Teyte (photo five) was the second Mélisande in 1908, and premiered ‘Trois Ballades de François Villon’.
- CHARLES PANZERA 1896-1976:
---- ‘Trois Ballades de François Villon’ orch. Debussy (excerpts) Piero Coppola, studio orchestra, rec.1931
---- ‘Pelléas et Mélisande’: Panzera sang Pelléas in the 1927 recording of excerpts from the opera (see part four below).
- HUGUES CUENOD 1902-2010 (not a typo; he lived to age 108)
---- ‘Ariettes oubliées’ with Jacqueline Blancard piano, rec.1951
- CAMILLE MAURANE 1911-2010:
---- ‘Trois Ballades de François Villon’ orch. Debussy, with Jean Fournet, Lamoureux Orchestra, rec.1954
------------------------------------------------

Part 4: PELLEAS ET MELISANDE

Two singers from the 1902 premiere made recordings:
--- Mary Garden created the role of Mélisande (photo four), and recorded “Mes longs cheveux descendent” in 1904, with piano accompaniment by Claude Debussy. PROBLEM: Warner forgot to include it in this box. It's only one minute, 48 seconds, so there was plenty of room for it with the other 'Pelléas et Mélisande' recordings. It was included in Warner's [[ASIN:B076D14CFP Debussy - The Complete Works (33CD)]] which I strongly recommend anyway (it's a steal).
--- Hector Dufranne (1870-1951) created the role of Golaud (photo six), and repeated it in the 1928 recording of excerpts from the opera (see below).

Piero Coppola, Concerts Pasdeloup Orchestra: excerpts, rec.1927
--- Pelléas: Charles Panzéra
--- Mélisande: Yvonne Brothier
--- Golaud: Vanni-Marcoux

Georges Truc, Orchestre symphonique: excerpts, rec.1928
--- Mélisande: Marthe Nespoulos
--- Golaud: Hector Dufranne (created the role in 1902)
--- Geneviève: Claire Croiza
--- Arkel: Armand Narçon

Roger Désormière, Orchestre Symphonique: rec.1941, first recording of complete opera
--- Pelléas: Jacques Jansen
--- Mélisande: Irène Joachim
--- Golaud: Henri-Bertrand Etcheverry
--- Geneviève: Germaine Cernay
--- Arkel: Paul Cabanel
--- Yniold: Leïla Ben Sedira
------------------------------------------------

Part 5: CHAMBER MUSIC
--- String Quartet: Calvet Quartet, rec.1931
--- Sonata for Cello and Piano: Maurice Maréchal, Robert Casadesus, rec.1930
--- Sonata for Flute, Viola and Harp: Marcel Moyse, Eugène Ginot, Lily Laskine, rec.1928
--- Sonata for Violin and Piano: Jacques Thibaud, Alfred Cortot, rec.1929
--- ‘Minstrels’ (from Préludes, Book One) arr. Debussy for violin & piano: Jacques Thibaud, Alfred Cortot, rec.1929
------------------------------------------------

COMPLAINTS?
One major:
Warner forgetting Mary Garden's 1904 recording of “Mes longs cheveux descendent” from 'Pelléas et Mélisande' with Debussy at the piano is unforgivable (even if it was included in Warner's 33 CD Debussy Complete Works box).
One minor complaint:
I wish Warner had limited the collection to musicians who were actually known to Debussy.
Approximately fifty percent of the contents feature musicians who came to prominence in the 1920s and ‘30s, after the composer’s death (the balance is skewed by the youthful cast of the 1941 ‘Pelléas’).
When Debussy died in 1918:
-- Conductor Charles Munch was a 27 year old conscript in the German army.
-- Pianist Walter Gieseking was a 23 year old regimental bandsman in the German army.
-- Baritone Camille Maurane was a 7 year old soprano.
In time, all three would come to be highly regarded as specialists in Debussy’s music.
One inevitable complaint:
The three-page article about Debussy’s interpreters is superficial, and there are no texts or translations for the vocal works, not even a plot summary for 'Pelléas et Mélisande'.
On the other hand, except for a few piano recordings, everything was newly remastered in 2018.
