title: It's good
text:
The indie-rock scene has long been as full of copycats and one-trick ponies as the mainstream (or close to it, anyway), but over the course of their still-brief career the Shins have always managed to stand out as a force for innovation. Along with The Arcade Fire, the Decemberists, and Modest Mouse, they stand at the forefront of cadre of indie bands that have managed to move on to commercial success with little to no help from radio, and deservedly so, as they've consistently managed to find a sound that's catchy without pandering and intelligent without any undue intellectual pretensions. The Shins have always relied as heavily on unpredictable, meandering song structures and off-kilter arrangements as on James Mercer's sunny melodies and enjoyably dorky vocals, and it's as winning a combination here as it was on their classic debut Oh Inverted World! and its even better successor Chutes Too Narrow. Like the first two albums, Wincing the Night Away does take a few listens to get into, probably even more so in this case as the band's sound comes to rely increasingly on detail, but at the same time the Shins' sound has become more inviting since they arrived back in 2001: the big, chiming guitars that sort of float along over the rumble of the bass, with the occasional keyboard accent drifting in and out of the mix, all signal a level of mass appeal that few would've seen coming five years ago.

Right from the start, it's obvious that the Shins weren't slacking off during their three-and-a-half-year layoff since the previous album, as the opener Sleeping Lessons establishes their continued vitality quickly, starting off all dreamy and minimal and lulling the listener into a false sense of calm before the tempo makes a sharp increase and some whiplash riffage kicks in about halfway through. The Shins' well of unpredictable, endlessly listenable indie-pop tunes also hasn't come close to running dry yet: lead single Phantom Limb is a sprawling, expansive epic (by this band's standards anyway) whose hooks keep biting down just when it seems ready to run out of steam, while Australia and Turn on Me are both cut from a similarly shambolic, multilayered and instantly memorable cloth. There are, naturally, some variations on the theme as well, which is where the Shins really put some distance between themselves and the pack. In the hands of a lesser band, the combination of cutting riffs, lilting melodies, and languid talk-singing that makes up Sea Legs would sound like a mess, but the Shins manage to combine these seemingly mismatched elements into an infectious, head-bobbing classic. The album's darkest, hardest-edged song, Spilt Needles, is driven forward by some propulsive drumbeats and icy synth work that wouldn't sound out of place on an old Cure album. The amorphous Black Wave is another interesting tune that sees the band ever-so-slightly expanding their comfort zone, a drumless piece that relies heavily on gently strummed guitars and eerie atmospherics.

The album doesn't end particularly well--Girl Sailor is a little fey for my tastes, and the closing A Comet Appears doesn't do too much--but the bulk of what precedes the last two tracks builds up so much goodwill it's hard to find fault. Fans can debate endlessly about whether this is the Shins' best album, but that's really beside the point. What Wincing the Night Away indisputably is is another step forward for a band that's obviously determined to expand its sonic pallette, even if only by increments. At the very least, if you were a fan of the band's first two albums, you'll probably find it next to impossible not to like this one.

title: Tragic, but essential
text:
It is, of course, impossible to listen to Harry Chapin without thinking of the car accident that took him from us much too soon. That has never been more true than with this great live performance, which took place just six months before Chapin's death.

That said, this is one of Chapin's very best (if not THE best) albums, and the bitter irony of its timing only adds to that. Recorded in an intimate venue on Chapin's old Greenwich Village stomping ground, it features a warm, immediate quality that is lacking on the two live LPs Chapin released during his lifetime. That intimacy is almost certainly by accident - no one knew at the time that this performance would take on historical value, and Chapin wasn't known for spare production - but so what? The band is in fine form, and if the performances are a bit ragged in places, that only plays up their sincerity. (This, of course, was not always apparent on Chapin's studio albums, including the original versions of so!me of the songs featured here.)

As for the music itself, there is a decent cross section of his entire career here, including first rate renditions of "Taxi" (with terrific audience participation), "A Better Place to Be", "WOLD", and the obligatory "Cat's in the Cradle". The latter is one of the weaker performances here - the band almost sounds bored - but if you're a serious fan you already know that one note for note anyhow. But it's on the more obscure numbers - "Mismatch", "Mercenaries" - that this collection really shines. It's a nice reminder that story-songs weren't Chapin's only strong point. Last but not least, if "Remember When the Music" doesn't move you to tears, Chapin's thoughtful, poignant spoken introduction will. That one deserves to be among his most famous songs, and this is the definitive rendition of it.

In a nutshell...if you're already a serious fan, you don't need me to convince you of anything. If you just want to find out what Chapin was! about beyond "Taxi" and "Cat's in the Cradle", this is the best place to start!

title: And the crowd goes wild....
text:
First of all, this is the Deftones record everyone expected after White Pony. Instead we had to wait ten years but thats ok, the albums in between were great as well. I may be biased in this because I love the Deftones, my most favorite band, ever. I even have Deftones tattooed on my arm, that is my devotion. I got it a year before SNW, certain that the Deftones would never fail to blow me away.
This album is almost perfect. I wish Chi had been a part of this, although I think a lot of the songs were influenced by his tragedy. The light found a way in that darkness. Everyone is trying to compare "Diamond Eyes" to previous albums, but it's on it's own, just like every other album. I hear bits of almost every album, mixed with some fresh new Deftones. Chino's vocals sound beautiful and you can hear that he truly put his heart into it. The lyrics are trippy and amazing. Sergio Vega, replacing Chi for now, did a great job I think, and it obviously added to the songs in a way we have yet to hear because we are so used to the five members of the band that have always been there. I have never listened to Quicksand, but Vega proved his worth on this album. Stephen, excellent on the guitar as always, this time tuning it way down.....sounds like it's tuned down to B or maybe A. Very heavy stuff. Abe, one of the most underrated drummers, plays more upbeat for the most part, adding to this beauty. Then finally Frank with his keyboards and samples, I can't imagine the Deftones without him. He gives the songs bigger with more structure.
I have been a fan since ATF (god, so long ago!) and these guys have never ceased to amaze me. White Pony is another classic album. Following was the self titled release, which sounded very rushed and raw, not like White Pony at all. But I still love that record, although it is one of the albums at the bottom of the list of my favorite albums. Except "Hexagram" which is one of the greatest songs ever made period. SNW sounded like the band was trying to go back to the White Pony cd, but not quite. There are some great songs on there, but it was no ATF or White Pony.
Then we thought we were getting "Eros" but since Chi had his accident, we got "Diamond Eyes". When I first listened to it, I was wishing it followed right after White Pony, maybe more fans would have stuck around. But at least we have it now. From the opening track to the last it is just wonderful. I have that feeling I had with White Pony ten years ago, the feeling I was listening to songs created by geniuses. Anyone who says they love or even just like the Deftones, needs to get this album. This album justifies the tattoo on my arm, and my loyalty to the band. I still listen to all the Deftones albums on a regular basis, they just don't get old to me.
Like I said, I am biased because I love every song(except some cover songs) by the Deftones. The one fault in this album is plain and simple album booklet, but at least we get lyrics.

Some songs are still growing on me, but these are my ratings for the songs (so far)

Diamond Eyes 10/10: I love this song and the lyrics, it's a stand out track (it is a single after all) and if only it was a little longer.....but it is still a beauty. Love the lyrics
Royal 10/10: One of the more harder and faster songs on the album. Guitar work is amazing here, and this one does remind me of older Deftones. Some good screams here.
CMND/CNTL: 10/10: This song has Chino doing a more upbeat "rap-like" vocals. It is short and sweet, and Chino offers up some more good screaming. Music is good and bouncy, which flows together well with the vocals.
You've seen the Butcher 7/10: This track I am still getting used to. It is very heavy, with a Tool like sound, sorta. It's not as good as the other tracks.
Beauty School 10/10: I love this song! It is mid-tempo but I love the sound and beat to it, and the lyrics blow me away. One of my top faves from this album.
Prince 10/10: Another of my top faves, this is another harder track, with Chino doing his screaming/singing at the same time. Lyrics are very cool.
Rocket Skates 10/10: I have listened to this track more than any others because of it being released some months ago. This reminds me of ATF, which makes this song badass!!! It's no wonder it's a single. Another of my top faves on the album.
Sextape 10/10: Slower song for sure, but Chino's voice sounds so good, I love it. Another of my faves.
Risk 9/10: Mid-tempo song, great chorus, great lyrics.
976-EVIL 8/10: This song is obviously about Chi, another slower track. It is very good and like people said before me, it flow perfectly with the next song.
This place is death 9/10: Not the greatest ending to a Deftones album that I have heard but it's pretty damn close.

A year from now, this could all look different (but only a little) but this like ATF and White Pony, is an album I can keep listening to over and over again without the urge to listen to anything else.

My favorite Deftones albums (in order) as of now
1. Around the Fur
2. White Pony
3. Adrenaline
4. Diamond Eyes
5. Saturday Night Wrist
6. Self-titled (but remember Hexagram is one of the best songs ever!)
7. B-sides

Congrats Deftones, you are back.

Music I recommend to anyone who may have read this, listen to these bands. They are not the Deftones but they are still good.

Wide Eye Panic

title: Interesting and Different Versions for Elvis Fans
text:
A lot has been written concerning the propriety of artificially creating duets of Elvis with other singers. Some people say that Elvis's Christmas recordings are so well made that they should not be touched. I think that attitude assumes that the creators of "Elvis Presley Christmas Duets" were trying to improve on the originals. It's hard to know what their motivation was, since there's no essay in the CD booklet explaining their reasons for doing this. MY attitude is that the point here is NOT to try to improve on the originals, but rather to provide something interesting and different for Elvis fans to enjoy. That's my perspective when I listen to it, so I'm OK with the idea of altering Elvis's recordings this way.

At any rate, after listening to "Elvis Presley Christmas Duets" at least a dozen times by now, I think it's a good effort. My favorite duets here are (in no certain order) "Here Comes Santa Claus" with Leann Rimes, "White Christmas" with Amy Grant, "Blue Christmas" with Martina McBride, and "Santa Claus is Back in Town" with Wynonna Judd. Most of the others I think are good, and the only ones that I don't much like to hear in these new versions are "I'll Be Home for Christmas" and "Merry Christmas Baby." However, since "Merry Christmas Baby" has been considerably re-edited here, it's interesting to hear parts of the original 11 1/2-minute studio jam of that song that didn't make it even onto the extended versions.

That reminds me, one aspect of this CD that few reviewers have mentioned is that not only have 11 singers been added here to create duets with Elvis, but actually a lot more has been changed. The booklet indicates that on most of these songs both instrumentals and vocalists have been added, sometimes over a dozen of them. And it seems that the original recordings have usually been remixed and re-edited as well. So the entire sound of the originals has been altered. I believe that the result is well crafted, though seldom if ever an improvement on the originals.

I'm actually most impressed with the 3 songs on here that are NOT duets but still are remixed, re-edited, and with performers added to the original recordings. Those songs are "The First Noel," "If I Get Home on Christmas Day," and "Winter Wonderland." I don't like any of the original versions of those songs that were on Elvis's 1971 Christmas album, but I DO like all of these altered versions! Generally, I don't like the idea of someone messing with Elvis's recordings this way, but hey, I didn't like those songs before but I do now, so I can't complain too much.

All in all, I've enjoyed listening to "Elvis Presley Christmas Duets" so I'm glad I bought it. For those who don't like the idea of doing things like this, well, they don't have to listen to it.

title: BTO's best comp
text:
A flawless 2-CD comp. It has 5-6 songs from every album up to Freeways, then the last three songs are cherry picked from their two post-Randy albums from 1978 (Street Action) and 1979 (Rock & Roll Nights). Nothing from their 1984 reunion album.

Now for the important stuff: All their big hits are here. Album versions, no edited singles, no live cuts, just the core songs that made them my favorite band back in the day. As with any comp, there will be a few personal faves missing (I wish it had more songs from Street Action included, and "Sledgehammer"). But the 35 songs included are all their best songs, and it's hard to quibble with the song selection, and since each CD is filled to the max with nearly 80 minutes each, I tip my hat to the compilers.

In a perfect world, BTO's entire catalog would be remastered and sold together in the new "bare bones" format so many other artists are doing these days (Black Sabbath, Deep Purple, Chicago, John Mellencamp to name a few). Maybe one day...but until then, this GOLD comp will easily make any BTO fan happy.

UPDATE: Ignore the last paragraph, there is now a BTO boxset containing all 8 of their studio albums from the 1970s, and the sound quality is great!

title: It's not what you have to think about
text:
I see here too many people who rate E4 too low. From one hand, I can understand them - they're an old fans of Enigma and they got used to it's style very much. And, as E4 is much more different from the previous ones, they're upset. But, I must admit, that Enigma shouldn't be the same in all the albums Cretu makes! What if E4 had the same Greg. chants, low mood's melody etc? We would dislike the music for its sameness. But here we're resting while listening to completely new (though with some old sounds) music.
As for the album itself, I can say that the music became more aggressive and lively. We hear no more so many low-key tracks as in E2-E3. It's only Traces which is the most quiet and serene. Modern Crusaders and Silence Must Be Heard are the most aggressive and solid/dance pieces here.
What is more important is that Cretu (as always) gave us a perfectly mixed compilation. Sometimes, when I listen to E4, I can't even imagine how it becomes possible to combine so many sounds in that order that it's not a mess but a great melody.
The only thing I disliked here (may be you - too) was the repetition of some "words of wisdom". Though they're as always brilliant, repetition makes them less mysterious and attractive. But, again, it happens only in one-max. two songs.

title: So-So Material, Dated Production
text: "Rock a Little" is in many ways the most confusing of Stevie's solo albums. Lacking the charm of "Bella Donna," the sadness of "Street Angel," and the confidence of "Trouble in Shangri-La," this 1985 album gets lost in a haze of over-production and glossy, shallow songs. Stevie was getting burned out after a decade of drug use that escalated during the making of this album and her bad judgment is evident during much of "Rock a Little." Her voice sounds strained and shrill and her lyrics seem empty and forced. Stevie is rarely bad, but when she is bad she is dreadful, as is clearly the case on "Sister Honey" and "If I Were You." Her concert gem "Has Anyone Ever Written Anything For You" works great live but not here on the album, where it seems synthetic and detached. The synthesizer laden "I Can't Wait" and the clunky "Talk to Me" were both big hits but seem ancient today. The rest of the songs are marred by a disconnected, superficial sound that is unusual for Stevie. "Rock a Little" was  a two million seller, but it left a bad aftertaste among Stevie's fans and critics alike that would take years to fade.

title: No comparison
text:
Rush has always been a fantastic band. They have consistently broken the confines of what hard rock is supposed to be. However, their last few efforts lacked that energy and drive that powered their earlier efforts. "Test For Echo" had only one great song on it, and other 90s efforts like "Roll The Bones" and "Counterparts" were still ahead of the learning curve but hardly compared to the creativity and vision of their earlier classics.
Enter "Vapor Trails".
This album restores my faith that Rush can put together a spectacular album. With several years and not just a couple of tragedies behind them since their last studio effort, Lifeson/Lee/Peart have created a sonic vision that recalls their glorious percussively heavy days back during the "2112" era but also includes the lyrical thoughtfulness that characterized their output since 1980. Not that this sounds like old-school Rush, but it creates a musical vision all its own.
Simply put, after listening to literally hundreds of albums over the last year, I haven't heard another yet that has the drive, energy, and passion of "Vapor Trails". That a band that's been around nearly 30 years has put together the best album to date in 2002 is stunning.

title: REM - Around the Sun
text:
I find the reviews of this album very revealing about the sort of people that listen to REM. Most people seem to have very two-dimensional, linear expectations of this band. And so they miss the point completely.

People seem compelled to make comparisons "It's not as good as Automatic for the People!" or even "It's their best since Automatic for the People!". If I want to hear Automatic for the People, I go put it on. People complain that REM have lost the punky, college-radio folksy alt.rock edge of the IRS years. If I want to hear that - I go put on Lifes Rich Pageant or Document.

REM down the years have provided us with an embarrassment of riches, and the widest variety of sounds of any major band I can think of. The point that a lot of people seem to miss is that REM have been on a journey since day one, since Chronic Town, since that gig in that church in Athens. Each new album is a further step along their way - but each album follows on logically from the one before.

They have never tried to forcibly change themselves (Apart from maybe with Monster), yet they have never allowed themselves to stand still. If you listen to the albums consecutively – each album actually sounds a lot like the one before (Again, apart from Monster – that album was a deliberate attempt to sound different to Automatic.. That album was a reaction to what had gone before rather than an evolution.), and yet despite each other album being sonically similar to the one before– they have somehow got from the startled lo-fi of Murmur to to the celestial glimmer of Around the Sun. It’s been a true journey of evolution.

Each album has been a unique and distinct snapshot of where the band were at the time. Around The Sun is a great album, and an essential addition to the REM canon. Stipe's voice has never sounded richer or more assured, the musicianship is consummate as we would expect. The song-writing is some of the most personal and emotional they have released.

REM have done precisely as they always have - they've provided us with the REM album we need today. Not the one we needed ten or fifteen years ago - they already made them.

title: Reliving Great B'way Memories
text:
In "Broadway's Lost Treasures I" we get a chance to see some of the finest Broadway performances in color and in brilliant clarity with the original stars. Various hosts (Angela Lansbury, Joel Grey, Tommy Tune, Jerry Orbach, and Chita Rivera) introduce the twenty-three musical numbers. Some of the numbers were done with very large supporting casts. My favorites were Angela Lansbury singing in her Cockney accent and in the most macabre make-up imaginable about the worst pie-maker in all of London from "Sweeney Todd", and Carol Channing singing and meaning "Before the Parade Passes By" from "Hello Dolly".
Also I loved Zero Mostel singing and clowning through "If I Were a Rich Man" from "Fiddler on the Roof" as well as Yul Brynner doing "Shall We Dance" from "The King and I". No one ever beat Robert Preston's take on "Trouble in River City" from "The Music Man."
Paul Lynde is hilarious in a shortened version of "Kids" from "Bye Bye Birdie". Joel Grey as the M.C. in "Cabaret" leads a large cast in "Wilkommen". He says the horrible mask-like face echoed Hitler. Later versions of this show portrayed the M.C. as a gay Jew and a victim.
Chita Rivera and Gwen Verdon do a great job with "All that Jazz" from "Chicago" while Jerry Orbach does a masterful job with the anthem "Lullaby of Broadway from "42nd Street". Other noteworthy numbers were "Tomorrow" from "Annie" and "Memories" from "Cats.
I wasn't overly impressed by Julie Andrews's rendition of "Send in the Clowns" from "A Little Night Music." She has a certain coldness and emotional detachment that doesn't suit this charged song. Currently on Broadway Roberta Peters is wowing audiences with her interpretation of the song in the 2010 revival. I love Patti LuPone, but her two outings on the disk from "Evita" seemed over-the-top, more shouting than singing.
Composers and lyricists get short shrift in this compilation. The emphasis is on the performers.
Some interesting facts that emerged from the show: Jerry Orbach was a star in more performances of American musicals than any other actor. John Raitt, the baritone, had six decades of performances beginning with "Carousel." Joel Grey and Yul Brynner were two of only seven actors that won Tonys and Oscars for their roles on Broadway and in the movie version.
This DVD will bring back many memorable moments for veteran theatergoers.

title: Great  for those who love Christian or jazz from the 30
text:
Most critics consider Charlie Christian the first important electric guitarist in jazz and an crucial bridge between swing and bebop. For a long time, however, it has been relatively difficult to collect Christian's music because his work was released on several labels and haphazardly repackaged. Definitive Records has addressed this problem by releasing two box sets of his music: the Complete Studio Recordings and Complete Live Recordings . Only the possessor of a definitive discography knows if either set is complete, but the Complete Studio Recordings includes all the sessions I've heard about, including five tracks used to flesh out John Hammond's "From Spirituals to Swing" `live' set, five tracks of studio jams and three alternate takes (all collected on disc four of the set). It does not include a complete set of "alternate" takes, however, and if one expects every note Christian recorded in the studio, this set will disappoint. Definitive, however, is quite open about not offering alternates (both liners and track listings make this clear) and while this policy has historical limitations, musically it has much to recommend it.
Definitive Records has offered a number of such sets in the last couple of years, including a delightful Lee Wiley compilation and six discs covering Louis Armstrong's early years on Decca. These collections take advantage of lapsed copyrights to offer chronological looks at an artist's work, in contrast to official releases, which are usually limited to the label or labels owned by a given corporation. This label-blind approach helps the consumer, since otherwise one has to follow a musician's career in starts and fits depending on which label keeps material in circulation, and it hardly harms artists who have been dead for decades and saw little income from their recordings in any case. Unfortunately, sometimes the quality of the sound suffers, since independent labels rarely have access to original masters. Definitive's record is mixed (scratched?) in this regard. Blessedly, they do not smother their recordings in noise reduction and thus provide lively and detailed sound. The Armstrong discs present his trumpet as vividly as any I've heard: it's a cliché, but that horn really does send chills down your spine. On the other hand, Definitive can be remarkably careless about tracking down clean sources to master from. Their Ellington "Blanton /Webster" set seems to have been taken from 78s used as frisbees, and the Lenny Tristano single disc has similar problems. In the case of the Christian Studio Recordings, the sound is well above the Definitive average. Either these 78s are common or a staffer tracked down a relatively pristine collection. The packaging is fairly minimal, with only a couple of semi-translated paragraphs on the guitarist's career, but personnel is listed for each session and the visual design competes with the majors.
Listeners turning to the set solely in order to hear Christian will be disappointed. None of the included sessions was recorded with the guitarist as leader; he does not solo on every number and often plays only half a chorus when he gets the spotlight. As long as you enjoy the music of this period, however, you'll love this set. Christian kept excellent company. Lionel Hampton, Benny Goodman, Henry "Red" Allen, Cootie Williams and other heavy-hitters from the `30s make sterling appearances. There are very few weak tracks, rare enough in a box set, and any one of the four discs can be listened to from start to finish with pleasure.
On the basis of this material, Christian's greatest contribution to jazz was showing how the electric guitar could be a viable solo instrument. He sounds strikingly different from major predecessors like Django Reinhardt (whose affair with electricity was star-crossed) Eddie Lang or Lonnie Johnson (though Johnson is his closest acoustic cousin) and it's clear how his linear approach could easily be adopted to bop, although harmonically Christian seems firmly swing. He plays unpretentiously, with a countrified edge to his sound that wouldn't be out of place on an early Elvis single. His solos don't feature jaw-dropping technique, and his ideas, frankly, sometimes seem mundane. Of course, Christian had dozens of imitators to ossify his fresh ideas into cliché, so you can hardly blame him for the impression he makes on early twenty-first century listeners. His playing never strains and never fails to propel the listener happily from bar to bar. The recordings he made from 1939 to 1941 offer gems from a period when uncomplicated joy was the reigning aesthetic and small groups the best place to get "real jazz."

title: Still Waiting for some killer Revolver?!
text:
Ever since the stars aligned and this lineup came together. The expectations have been high for something really spectacular to come out. After listening to Libertad a few times I'm still waiting. Libertad follows a more focused direction in it's musical styling's than the debut. Many tunes have that punk vibe going on. Which does nothing for me. One thing that surprised me was that nothing on Libertad really blows you away? Yes, nothing, not one tune! Some tunes are pretty good and others are just alright. But nothing really rocks your socks off?! It's not soft but it's definitely not real aggressive either. No, in your face guitars, nothing with an edge to it. Nothing really makes you want to crank it up to 11! We've always been wanting something from "VR" that will make you say, "GNR & STP who are they"? I wish Libertad did that but unfortunately it doesn't. Contraband had a few highlights that were worth the price of the CD. Tunes like "Headspace", "Slither" and "Illegal i Song". Nothing here has that same intensity. Contraband also had "Fall to Pieces" which reminded me of "Plush, Sour Girl & November Rain". Libertad has "Gravedancer" which just sounds like a rehash of "Fall to Pieces" and not as good. If "Contraband" left you hopping for a little bit more. This will just leave you disappointed. I wish that wasn't the case, I've always liked GNR & STP.

With Audioslave dismantling and leaving a big "Supergroup" whole to be filled. Velvet Revolver unfortunately can't put the pieces together to fill the void.

If you're longing for some old "GNR Like" intensity pick up the 2001 debut by a band you probably never heard of, "Beautiful Creatures". It's an awesome edgy guitar intense ride that won't leave you disappointed. Two other hard rock debuts that flat out smoke are: Loudmouth from 1999 and Injected from 2002.

title: Cotton Candy Confection
text: Five for Fighting has created a sweet mix of sounds on "America Town."  "Easy Tonight" starts slow with piano & guitar and then blasts loose on the electric chorus, "Shotfun fire -- anybody home?  I got 2 dimes in the telephone."  "Bloody Mary (A Note on Apathy)" is a midtempo track with churning guitar.  The blockbuster track is "Superman" with a distinctive melody that builds from ballad to anthem, "I'm only a man in a phony red shirt; I'm only a man looking for a dream."  The title track starts midtempo and ends with thundering lead guitar.  "Something About You" is another distinctive melody; guitars wash over the arrangement.  Another favorite is "Jainy," a slow tune with piano, strings and a beautiful melody.  "Michael Jordan" has a piano-driven arrangement, "I would do anything for you."  (Especially in North Carolina, most would agree!)  Rhythm guitar and organ drench "Out of Love" with its sputtering beat.  "The Last Great American" is a ponderous melody, "for every daughter, every son."  "Love Song" has an unusual lyric, "Put away your raincoat & make you bed; take another bullet right to the head."  The thing I like best about the storm of electric guitar called "Boat Parade" is that at 2 minutes 46 seconds, it's short and ends abruptly.  "Alright" has a nice pop chorus and seems like a Peter Frampton deja vu.  The hidden track "Do U Mind" is nice, although, I really wish this fad would stop and they'd just list it as the last track.  It's annoying when you try to copy to your computer.  All in all, this is a very good CD.  The songs are sweet.  If I were to suggest improvement, I'd want a bit more sense of a whole.  The parts are mostly good, but the overall effect is a bit disjointed.  That said, 5 for Fighting is very enjoyable.

title: A prog masterpiece...keep your minds open

I won't re-hash what the other reviewers have already said so eloquently. To sum it up, this album is indeed wonderful, "a masterpiece," and IMHO should be added to any serious prog rock listener's catalog. There simply aren't many artists/bands out there today putting out this level of quality music. To dismiss Neal Morse because of his lyrics will cause you to miss out on some outstanding, cutting-edge music.

As an open-minded Christian, I would like to offer this up to all the non-religious reviewers. I happen to like the group Pagans Mind (now what is a Christian doing listening to them?). I like them because they totally rock. Yes, they may be singing about aliens, constellations, and other worlds (kinda cheesy), but I can get past that and enjoy the music: mind-bending guitar work, hammering drums, and the soaring melodies.

This helped propel album sales to enormous proportions. The song had a pop remix that became a hit on that radio format as well. The same goes for the second single "The Way You Love Me", which was a huge hit as well. The third Tim McGraw/Faith Hill duet would appear on BREATHE, the ballad "Lets Make Love". The album opens with the country-rock song "What's In It For Me", and goes into "I Got My Baby" which Faith has said is influenced by Motown. There's some nice ballads here like "It Will Be Me", "If I'm Not In Love", and more. She does a great version of Bruce Springsteen's "If I Should Fall Behind" and Bette Midler's "That's How Love Moves". "Bringing Out The Elvis" is a song that Faith dedicates to her fans. Other highlights include "If My Heart Had Wings", "There Will Come A Day" and "Love Is A Sweet Thing". The singles from this album were "Breathe", "The Way You Love Me", "Lets Make Love" and "If My Heart Had Wings". Excellent album.

title: Good collection of Beatles tracks.
text:
The latest and most recent Beatles compilation disc is
probably a good place to start if you want a single disc
that surveys their work. Of course, if you really want to
get into the depth of their work, the best option would
be to buy their studio albums first, and then proceed to
other Beatles albums like compilation and live albums.
This is a good collection of lovesongs, ballads, and rock,
even though the album is slanted towards more pop, which
isn't surprising, given the amount of success the Beatles
enjoyed in this area.
People have to keep in mind the selection of tracks
for this compilation is restricted to singles which made
the top of the charts in the UK, the USA or both.
Personally I feel this is a good overview for a single
CD, and the number of tracks (27) is fairly generous.
If you're a huge Beatles fan, you're better off passing
on this collection. However, if you're curious, or a
beginner, I can't think of a better place to start.
This CD might help you decide on whether or not you
want to pursue purchasing studio albums by this band.
In terms of length, the CD runs approximately 80 minutes.
There are people who are complaining because not all
their most popular songs made the cut on this album.
It's impossible. Even if you buy the Red and Blue
albums, there are tracks on 1 that aren't available
on the Red or Blue albums. The Beatles were a singles
band, whose albums sales were driven by this fact.
Surprisingly, this is the only Beatles album to date
that has earned the distinction of being the top-selling
album of the calendar year. This album earned that
distinction in 2000.
This collection is essentially an updated version of
the 1982 Capitol release 20 Greatest Hits, with 7 additional
tracks. I believe that title is now out of print. For
those of you who are wondering, the 7 tracks you get
on this album that you don't get on their 20 Greatest
Hits album are: From Me To You, Daytripper, Yellow
Submarine, Eleanor Rigby, Lady Madonna, The Ballad
of John and Yoko and Something. The songwriting is
good, and the way the music behind the songs maybe
even better than the lyrics themselves. Of course,
not everyone has the same opinion with regards to
what constitutes quality songs, and what is garbage.
If you want to know why The Beatles are the top
selling act of alltime by far (165,000,000 albums
sold and counting), this would be probably a good
place to start if you're on a budget, and can't
afford to get all their albums.

title: Technically proficient but uninspired performance of Tchaikovsky's trio
text:
Tchaikovsky's Piano Trio, composed in memory of the death of Nikolai Rubinstein, founder of the Moscow Conservatory of Music and Tchaikovsky's friend and mentor, is generally considered to be his finest chamber music composition. It is quite long and consists of two or three movements, depending on how you count them. The first movement opens with an unforgettable melancholic theme that only Tchaikovsky could have written. The movement is in sonata form, with an exposition followed by a development section, but there's a surprise; a slower "moderato assai" section that eventually leads back to the melancholy theme and a recapitulation. The moderato theme reappears in the coda.

The second movement, labeled "IIa" by Tchaikovsky, introduces a serene Mozartian melody followed by 11 variations, including a waltz, a fugue, and a Chopinesque mazurka. The final movement (or section) labeled "IIb," as originally written is cast in sonata form with an extended coda and starts with a lively twelfth variation, but later the composer sanctioned a cut that changes the nature of the movement (or section). In either case, the work ends with a return to the melancholy theme in a funereal mode.

This is a dramatic work that in my opinion calls for a dramatic approach. I bought this CD with the expectation that the Moscow Rachmaninov Trio would be good at imbuing their performance with the essence of the Russian soul, but I was disappointed. Not that the performance isn't quite good in many ways. Technically, all three performers are excellent, especially the pianist in handling his difficult and exhausting part, but the performance lacks inspiration and is somewhat pedestrian. Of the several available recordings, I think that the ones by Argerich-Kremer-Maisky and Lang Lang-Repin-Maisky capture the drama inherent in the Trio's first movement especially. Compare how these two groups, especially the pianist, handle the stretto-like transition section to the second theme. Lang Lang makes it a dramatic and exciting affair; so does Argerich though she's a little more restrained and poetic in her playing. The MR Trio is lackluster here and only rises to mf where the score calls for ff. In the theme and variations, the MR Trio acquit themselves better, though they are somewhat ponderous in the fugal variation. In the finale, the Muscovites are slower than either AKM or LRM. AKM takes this section especially fast, leaving one almost breathless. None of these three groups takes the cut in the finale.

A classic recording by Rubinstein, Heifetz, and Piatigorsky, recorded in 1950 and reissued on CD with surprisingly good monaural sound, is as fine a performance as one would expect from these famous players. They take a fast tempo in the opening movement and take the cut in the finale. Out there on YT but (surprisingly) not available on CD is a splendid performance by Evgeny Kissin, Joshua Bell, and the redoubtable Maisky at the 2009 Verbier Festival in Switzerland. Though not quite as robustly dramatic as AKM or LRM, this is perhaps the best all-around performance, but it does have the cut in the finale.

The other work on the CD is a piano trio, "Pathetique," by Tchaikovsky's predecessor, Mikhail Glinka. This is a short work consisting of four very compact movements, each a marvel of musical economy. It was originally scored for clarinet, bassoon, and piano but is usually performed with violin and cello today. The work's title is supposedly reflected in the slow third movement, though it's by no means tragic. It's a musically delightful piece, reminiscent in some ways of early Beethoven. This comparatively lightweight work is well performed, and it's accorded slightly sharper sound quality than is the Tchaikovsky trio.

In summary, the Moscow Rachmaninov Trio are excellent when it comes to performance expertise but rather tame in performing a work that cries out for a dramatic approach. Some listeners, though, may prefer such a performance to a more emotional one that might be considered "over the top." Musical tastes vary, especially for a work like Tchaikovsky's. The CD comes with a descriptive brochure. As of this writing, it's not available as an MP3 file.

title: A Beautiful Surprise
text:
I've attempted a number of times to listen to Anathallo in passing, mostly because they are from my area and I know a couple of the guys. But somehow, I just couldn't connect. It was too avant garde, too untraditional for me. Then I listened to Hanasakajijii (Part 4: A Great Wind, More Ash)... and nothing changed.

But I found myself hooked on certain catchier parts of the music, so I listened again. And again. And again. Until I started to realize there was a story hidden beneath. I did some digging on the internet and finally I wouldn't be satisfied until I heard it all. And as I dug I found my own treasure.

This is quickly becoming one of my favorite albums both musically and lyrically. The music is a combination of folk, modern rock, and modern orchestra. However, if you are expecting something in the vein of punk or rock, you'll be disappointed. It is very low-key, very thoughtful, often times dischordant, but never without reason. I find most of the energy is bottled in Anathallo's unique chanting and vocal arrangements found throughout the album (not to downplay the unique rhythms and percussion). The lyrics are pure poetry, begging to be picked apart and chewed. The heavy use of Japanese language and culture is an interesting choice, but it fits well. The overall theme even harkens to the band's own name, if you are familiar with its meaning.

I must also comment on the cover. That itself is a work of art. Look carefully at all the black in the image; it is a stencil cutout, with all the colors you see on a secondary cover behind it. Perhaps it's been done before, but I've never seen it, and everyone to which I've shown it is impressed. It's so distractingly pretty that it took me until today to notice the story is captured here, too.

If you're willing to put the time in, I would HIGHLY recommend this album. As for me, I'm off to buy a glockenspiel.

title: Genial, attractive Tchaikovsky 1st in excellent Karajan recording
text:
The "Winter Dreams" symphony opens with two long, programmatic movements, "Dreams of a Winter Journey" and "Land of Desolation, Land of Mists" approaching half an hour in length put together, which are highly attractive and also likable. The symphony has a spirit of innocence and youth about it that is refreshing, a presentation that is at odds with the difficulties Tchaikovsky had writing the work. It is the earliest of Tchaikovsky's works to be played on a regular basis, finished in 1866 when the artist was 26 years old. None of the compositional struggles are evident to me; the music flows smoothly and expansively, as if Tchaikovsky had rattled it off at one sitting.

The 1977 release from Herbert von Karajan and the Berlin Philharmonic found here is downright excellent. Karajan emphasizes the strings in this interpretation and presents a fairly homogenous texture, something often heard in his recordings. This is different from other interpretations of Russian 19th-century orchestral music, where the winds have a prominent role, an approach that I think is supported by the Russian orchestration style, with emphasis shifted from the string section as in German music to a texture making heavy use of winds, often solo winds. That said, I am not about to criticize Karajan's approach as unidiomatic; there are many ways to skin a cat, and Karajan leads a performance that is committed. I have to think that he has a great affection for the "Winter Dreams" symphony. The technical acumen of the Berlin Philharmonic also helps the performance; this is a world-class orchestra in primo form.

Particularly impressive is the climax at the end of "Land of Desolation, Land of Mists" (about 10 munutes into track 2), which Karajan brings out in thrilling fashion. I compared this performance with the Sony release from Claudio Abbado and the Chicago Symphony and found many differences between them, particularly in how the "Land of Desolation" movement is structured. I think Karajan has a much more cohesive and intense conception of this movement than Abbado and in general I prefer the German conductor's interpretation.

The 1st symphony is paired with two dances from Tchaikovsky's beautiful opera "Eugene Onegin" (1878) and the short Marche Slave (1878). The Marche Slave is one of those occasional pieces that I think sully Tchaikovsky's reputation. It's fun at the beginning but noisy and embarrassing by the end. But the performance of both the Marche and the Onegin excerpts are very strong.

Sound quality is also mostly very good (the Onegin dances are less satisfactory than other tracks). This is a consistently well-executed disc marked by a notably inspired "Winter Dreams", a work that I very much like. Recommended.

title: It's not Hurt anymore.
text:
I should have spotted it from the knockoff Pink Floyd title and the imitation Pink Floyd cover art. Hurt shows us they are a band in transition. Gone is the sound that all the Hurt fans have grown to love, and born anew is a band searching for a more popular sound and borrowing from so many others.

Take the song Pills for example. Here's a track that's a mixture of Pearl Jam's Better Man and any number of countless Train songs. The guitar work is plain, the lyrics are forgettable, and the melody sounds like something you could hear on any pop station 7 years ago. I could see someone singing this song on American Idol in the next year or two.

The track Role Martyr X could be compared to classic Stone Temple Pilots. Track 8, Well, has a Glenn Frey solo sound, perhaps something you might catch on Miami Vice, but then there's the chorus, which seems to end one word too soon (why not croon out the word 'you' at the end of it and make it something special?). It simply makes me feel like the song is unfinished and unpolished.

There are some good songs on this album, probably none I would call great. World Ain't Right is a good acoustic track, although it sounds like they ran out of words to rhyme and just repeated the same line in the last couple of verses. While I happen to like the track Wars, I can almost hear the same song coming out of Creed a few years back (hey I admit it, I'm a Creed fan). Okay, so it has a little Tool thrown in too, which gives me that warm and fuzzy Hurt feeling again. Fighting Tao sounds like a track that could have easily been found on one of their first two efforts, and I'm glad to find at least one track in there that I can identify and tell my friends "here is your classic Hurt sound."

Despite the few gems, I find my ears weren't challenged by this effort in the least. I really love the 3/4 time rhythms of the first two CDs, and Goodbye to the Machine said goodbye to that classic style. Gone are those memorable emotions of such classic Hurt tracks such as House Carpenter and Summers Lost, and in their ashes are the sounds of FM radio.

I admire the effort, especially how Hurt sampled the entire CD in analog (if this rumor is indeed true). But I really wish they would have given more devotion to their classic sound, and stayed true to the first two albums. I'm an avid Hurt fan, despite how critical and negative this review may sound, and I'm not going to give up on them because this CD failed to captivate me. I can only hope this type of mainstream effort doesn't become a habit. -SM

title: Funk Me!
text:
3 Stars = Good

In 1989, Sweden's, the Electric Boys, released "Funk O Metal Carpet Ride," another entry into the funk/metal sweepstakes that rose up in the very late 80's to early 90's. Much like another band of that time, Extreme, the Electric Boys performed a competent, & sometimes very inspired version of funk/metal built on the shoulders of 70's seminal acts in this sub genre like Pat Travers & Mahogany Rush. Though no where near as adapt or groundbreaking as those bands, the Electric Boys were still a band that was worth a listen & took the right cues from the right bands to funk it up right.

"Funk O Metal Carpet Ride," had its share of exciting musical passages & time changes, funky rhythms, & tasty guitar. Their singer was pretty good to, & there was a pinch of Beatlesque sound to some of the harmonies & music on this album. The center piece song for me was "Captain of My Soul," a rip roaring Pat Travers like song if there ever was one on this album. Catchy, hook & riff driven funk/metal of the kind I enjoy very much. It's just too bad that the rest of the album was not up to that standard, not that it was bad, it wasn't, but "Captain of My Soul" just ruled! The rest....well they more or less served "Funk O Metal Carpet Ride," to a good extent, being competent, if not always truly inspiring. Even so, if you have a funk/metal Jones like me, you could do a hell of a lot worse than "Funk O Metal Ride!"

After "Funk O Metal Carpet Ride," the Electric Boys put out "Groovus Maximus," which tried to live up to it's name, but just did get the funk/metal out like the first & the band started to dissolve. Then after their third "Freewheelin', disappeared all together, never to be heard of again....

title: Review excerpt from Music and Media Focus
text:
In a departure from the more worldly music that has characterized some of veteran recording artist Hennie Bekker’s albums in recent years, his latest release, Beyond Dreams reflects an otherworldly sonic dimension. Subtitled, “Pathways To Deep Relaxation,” the music is based on the latest scientific research in brainwaves and body response and features dreamy synthesizers, piano, soft rhythmic pulses, and ambient atmospheres to gently entrain the listener into a profoundly peaceful state.

As the album opens on a track entitled “Self Connect,” sustained chords of soft synthesizer pads create a peaceful ambiance to begin our inward excursion. I found that listening with headphones enhanced the experience, particularly in feeling the very deep tones that add an earthiness to the more ethereal sounds drifting above them. After a few minutes, a soft pulsing pattern starts to emerge. It’s a lovely combination that eases us into the first level of deep relaxation. On track 4, “The Calm,” I particularly enjoyed the bell-like tones, which reminded me of Indonesian gamelan music. The blend of these sounds with the dreamy synthesizer atmospheres was particularly soothing.

One thing I found of interest on track 5, “Quiesence,” as well as other places in the album is that while there are rhythmic sequences that are bouncy or bubbly and provide a sense of forward motion, the overall effect of the music is quite calming. I also really liked the little electronic blips and bleeps that drop in and out of the music and create a bit of a futuristic sci-fi feel. The album concludes with the title track that takes the listener deep into the celestial realms. It is an expansive cosmic journey that would be right at home on a Hearts of Space radio program.

According to Hennie: “With this album, I wanted to combine rhythmic entrainment with melodies that listeners could enjoy while preparing for sleep, meditating, practicing yoga, or general self-exploration. As a sound-healing tool, “Beyond Dreams” creates the perfect ambiance for a rejuvenating inner journey. I greatly appreciate having this album as a resource and it’s a journey I know I will take often.

title: Excellent Collection
text:
This review is from: [[ASIN:B005Q6DW9O The Best Imitation Of Myself: A Retrospective [Explicit]]] (MP3 Download)

You know that feeling you have in the fall when you put on a jacket you hadn't worn since the previous winter and you find money in the pocket? It's such an awesome feeling. You don't remember leaving the money there, but you love it anyhow. It's like you traveled through time and left yourself a gift.

That's how this collection feels, like Ben Folds traveled through time and left us this incredible gift.

Like the new found money in your pocket, these songs are all familiar, but they're also from a vaguely forgotten time.

So what's in this collection? Well, in four discs, it's probably easier to ask what *isn't* included. I could be wrong, but I don't think there's any new material included in this set. That was a bit of a surprise to me, but I'll get over it.

I bought this collection on the first day it came out. I had been eager to get it after hearing Folds interviewed on Adam Carolla's podcast. Those two are always hilarious together and they almost never say anything substantial, but I could have sworn Folds said he got together with the guys from Ben Folds Five and cranked out a few new tracks for this album. I must have been mistaken though, because nothing seemed new to me.

So again, what *is* included?

Disc one starts with some greatest hits. No complaints from me. They're all good. But most of them aren't just retreads--there is a good portion of mixes that aren't just the original album versions. There are a couple radio mixes, some previously unreleased tracks, and even an orchestral version of Smoke with the West Australia Symphony. Pretty interesting stuff.

But it turns out disk 1 was just for getting warmed up.

Disc 2 is where it starts to get really good. This is where the live versions of his older stuff comes out. Some of the tracks are with the Ben Folds Five and some are just him. Not a clunker in the batch though.

This continues through disc 3. Lots and lots of old live tracks. Very well done.

Then disc 4 brings out the demo versions of his familiar hits. It's amazing to hear the difference between these original demos and what the songs finally became. It's also surprising to look at the dates on some of those demos (1992, 1994, etc.) and think about what I was listening to at the time. Why couldn't those tracks make it to my radio market back then? Why did it take another eight years for him to pop onto my radar?

Anyway, if you're a Ben Folds fan, then this collection won't disappoint you. If you're not a fan, then why are you reading reviews on Ben Folds albums?

Nice job, Ben, on putting together a real gift of a collection. I'm sorry I didn't get you anything.

title: I feel SOOO good!
text:
I am amazed upon reading through the reviews here that almost no one mentions my favorite track on this record, and one of the happiest songs of all time: I Feel So Good (I Wanna Boogie)!

I have loved this song like mad since the first day I heard it in 1993. Of all the classic and lesser-known blues my friend Freimuth Fischkal in Berlin turned me on to (a fine guitarist and great guy, by the way...gruss dich und vielen danke, Freimuth!), this was a track out of thousands that jumped out and grabbed me in a special way.

Everybody knows the blues are about feeling low-down, but I've always also loved the blues that are about feeling good again. And this track just can't be beat for that purpose. Along with Shuggie Otis' Inspiration Information, it's one of the songs that always gets me back to that good place where life makes sense and it's time to go have fun.

It's just a simple little 12-bar riff, an up-tempo shuffle, but the rhythm section meshes its gears and propels the groove into orbit right off the bat, and never lets up. It's as if Sam's daring us to feel this good along with him...and why not? Jump up and dance your blues away! Now there's a good reason to make music...maybe the best. And Sam's full-on wail of a voice says it all: you can't sing like that if you don't really know what feeling' good is all about.

The whole album is truly solid, and as a guitarist I really dig Sam's compact, clean tone. He mixed his singing and playing beautifully, and his singing is excellent. He can really hit the big note, and my other favorite track here, I Don't Want No Woman, features his large voice in full cry, as does All Of Your Love. (And I guarantee that Plant knew this album insde out; Zep is full of Magic Sam-ish vocal moments.)

What a shame that Sam died at 32, just as he was revvin' up. But he did leave us another great album as well, Black Magic, which is just icing on the cake, for West Side Soul is a killer.

title: Rare renaissance gems
text:
The Blue Heron Choir is on a mission: they want to bring to life music that has gone unheard since the reign of Henry VIII. The Peterhouse Partbooks (stored in Peterhouse College, Cambridge) were compiled in 1540 by Thomas Bull. Written for liturgical use at the Canterbury Cathedral. Since these were performing copies, the music is carefully transcribed with no illuminations or distracting graphic elements.

Bull's collection contains over seventy choral works, fifty of which are unique to the partbooks. The partbooks were only in use for seven years. Under Edward II, professional church choirs were dissolved, and the books stored away and forgotten -- until now.

The center piece of the album is the Missa Spes nostra by Robert Jones. Known more for his lute songs and madrigals, this mass is a masterwork of English renaissance polyphony. Jones shifts back and forth between modes, giving the work a slightly modern sound (at least to my ears).

Also included is a work by Nicholas Ludford, and one by Robert Hunt. Hunt is something of a cipher. Only two of his works are known -- and both only from the Peterhouse Partbooks. His setting of the Stabat mater is expressive and effective, letting the words dictate the course of the music. Perhaps because of that, some of his harmonies are quite surprising, but never out of context. This is a gem that deserves to enter the sacred choral repertoire.

This fourth volume in the Peterhouse Partbooks series continues the same high standards of the previous three. Blue Heron has a smooth ensemble blend, with especially strong sopranos. That's important, as many of these works have wide leaps in the upper registers, which these singers take with apparent ease and hit with laser-like accuracy.

The recording's cleanly recorded, with just the right amount of ambiance to carry the cadences into the following phrases. Yet I never had trouble discerning the various lines as the weave contrapuntally in and out of each other.

title: An essential to anyone's electronica collection
text:
Electronica has got a bad rep for being unemotional and annoying. Autechre is one of those groups/artists which shatters that stereotype with rythmic, intelligent, and beautiful electronica music (the others that I am aware of that are GREAT are Aphex Twin, Boards of Canada, and Squarepusher). Autechre's music may not be extremely easy to listen to, but after you listen to any of their albums 2 or 3 times you relize just how beautiful and flowing it is. In my opinion, Incunabula represents the pinnacle of Autechre's music. Unlike many of their other music, Incunabula is filled with old-school electronica sounds, which is why some people say it sounds out-dated or simple, but in all it is a reason why it is so great. Incunabula's music relies more on percussion and hip-hop beats, which is different but gives the album a sound that is actually rare. As with most of Autechre's music, Incunabula is very mathematical, and its beats are perfectly synchronized. At first, it does sound like it was put together with elementary software using old, out-dated sounds. But once you get used to the album, you see the hidden beauty. Every song in this album has its own characteristic, but all are great. The only song I really grown to enjoy is Bronchus 2.

1. Kalpol Introl- 8/10- Probably the most inriguing sounding song of the album. It doesnt rely on the hip-hop percussion beats like the rest of the songs do, as it uses the strange flowing sounds that are more common in electronica today. The thing is it just drags on without getting somewhere significant. Great sounding in the beginning though.

2. Bike- 9/10- This song sets the ambient/hip-hop beats that are common throughout the album. Not the most entertaining song of the album, but is very good nonetheless.

3. Autriche- 9/10- Probably the most ambient song of the album; it is soft, fairly slow, but has the catchy percussion in the backround. Has plenty of weird ambient noises in the backround, but its all the better for it. Sounds out-dated compared to Aphex Twin's [On #1]- which was made in 1993.

4. Bronchus 2- 5/10- To me, its the weak-point of the album. It's definatly the most abstract of the bunch. I am usually able to appreciate abstract ambient electronica a lot more than this...

5. Basscadet- 9.5/10- Picks the beat and noise level up a notch, but keeps the ambient attitude. It is a lot more catchy, but just as intellectual and mathematical as the rest. I can imagine that some people may not like it because it doesnt go where some of the other songs go; kind of like Kalpol Introl, but not to as big of an extent. In my opinion its a great song.

6. Eggshell- 10/10- Take the best qualities of this album and mix them together, and you get this song. Along with 444, it is my favorite. 9 minutes may seem way too long for any song to last, but once you appreciate this kind of music you'll enjoy every second of this song. Very few, if none at all, can make an old-school song like this and make it an enjoyable and memorable experience out of it.

7. Doctrine- 9/10- One of the stranger songs of this album. It takes a more violent and harsh sound and mixes it in with the old-school electronica sound that flourishes in Incunabula. Fortunatly its a great mix, and is a great song.

8. Maetl- 10/10- Similiar to Eggshell, it takes ambient and intelligent techno and blends them together. Great song.

9. Windwind- 9/10- Definatly the ambient song of the album. It stretches over 11 minutes in length, but just like Eggshell it makes good use of that time. Windwind sounds quite like those from Aphex Twin's Selected Ambient albums. It is long and flowing, and evolves at a slow but noticeable pace.

10. Lowride- 10/10- The most hip-hop sounding song of the group. Has a great beat but retains the mathematical aspect of Autechre's music, and also retains their sense of artistry. One of the best songs of the album.

11. 444- 11/10- Another ambient-sounding song, very broad and flowing. But unlike Windwind, 444 is extremely involving, and is one of those songs that let's your mind free to expand and explore. Probably my favorite song of the album. Doesnt sound as out-dated, as it is very complex. It may take a few times of listening to it to grasp it's greatness, but once you explore the depths of sound that makes up the structure of this song, you will experience one of the greatest electronica songs ever made (in my opinion). Once again, it sounds like a song made by Aphex Twin but with an Autechre-twist. Magnificent blend.

Overall, Incunabula is a must-have for those who listen to electronica history. It is an album that will show you just how far electronica has evolved since it's release over 10 years ago, but it will show you just how beautiful it is for it. In my opinion, it is Autechre's finest work of art and is one of the greatest electronica albums ever released. Go ahead, expand your mind and try it out.

title: CALLAS' ASTONISHING NORMA
text:
Well, I think there are two roles in the history of opera that after the interpretation of Maria Callas it would not be unwise to claim that they should not be performed again: Norma by Bellini (all recordings she ever made) and la Traviata by Verdi (the definition of the role lies in the London 1958 Traviata- unfortunately, her 1953 studio recording with Cetra is almost unacceptable considering how she developed the role of Violetta after 1955).

Although I very rarely sit down to write a review at Amazon, after having read so much on Mme Callas, I feel it is my responsibility as a fan of this great art named opera to make the following points:

a)Maria Callas was not an interpreter. She was a creator herself to be placed at the same rank as Donizzeti, Bellini and Verdi. Had it not been for her I doubt that opera would exist today and if it did it would be a sad, boring musuem exhibit. She recreated the whole of Italian Opera -not just bel canto- and modernised it in a way that will make it last for another 100 years aftet her death. I remind you that opera in the 50's meant German Opera. Italian opera before Mme Callas was something of a joke. Terribly abused by singers and a bad tradition of horrendus vocalising, the music of Italian composers had lost its drama, its sense, its meaning.

b)why do people spend so much time judging the voice of this great artist? Why can they not just relax and enjoy this great artistry? No-one says that there are no other great singers! But no matter how great, they are unfortunately just that:"singers". Caballe, Sutherland, Sills, Price, Fleming, Dessay all have amazing voices and great carreers. But, comparing them with a phenomenon that was for the opera what Mozart was for classical music simply does not do them justice.

c)Whether we like it or not Norma is a dramatic soprano role! A very difficult one as well and it should be treated with some respect. Caballe and Sutherland, because they had these amazing voices, did manage to sing it and they sang it well. But, as they were not dramatic sopranos they conveyed a lyricism in their interpretation that simply does not suit the role and Bellini's intentions. Other attempts however (Sills and -alas- Gruberova recently)should really remain as textbook examples of how inflated egos can ridicule both theselves and a work of art. I repeat that Norma is a dramatic soprano role. In this sense the only singers that approached the Callas perfection are Elena Suliotis (Decca for reason of expediency or stupidity is not reissuing her marvellous 1968 recording with Del Monaco) and Jane Eaglen in the Sony Muti recording. The only singer that seems to have been taught by the Callas Legacy in Bel Canto is Mme Renata Scotto but she was as well inadequate as Norma and wasted much of her talent singing (for commercial reasons, I suppose) Puccini.

d)Callas has been very unlucky as far as supporting cast is concerned. The 1960 Norma recording is the only exception. It features the amazing Franco Corelli. What a voice this man had! Pefect voice, perfect dramatic conviction, beautiful and clear italian diction. Can we imagine a Callas -Corelli partnership in Aida, Pirata, Manon Lescaut?

e)Callas did not lose her voice even though she overworked it in the 50s. The 1964 Tosca recording is the best proof of that. But she did lose her confidence and emotional stability. This fact led her quit her carreer in 1965 and that is the real tragedy of opera. Had she managed to work as hard in the 60-68 period when all her worry was Ar. Onassis we would have been left with at least 10 amazing stereo recordings. And I say 68 because someone like Callas simply would refuse to play young soprano roles after the age of 45. She believed that opera singers are like ballet dansers or athletes (and they are!), they should retire early. Mme Sutherland had a voice till the age of 60. And so? Is it not ridiculous singing La Sonnambula at the age of 59? If Callas did that she would not be the legend she is!

This is all I wanted to note on a woman that achieved a fame in the world of opera (and beyond!!!) in a way that noone else had before and I am afraid no one else will do so in the future. People had to sleep on pavements for three days and three nights to get a ticket for this lady!

I am a fan of change, and by now you probably hate me enough to not believe me, but this change is in the wrong direction. Metal bands should not become punk bands. It doesn't work.

title: Our Copa Runneth Over!
text:
The staggering efforts of Motown Records' crossover dream hit the fast track when Diana Ross proved to be the little engine that could just as Berry Gordy predicted. Less than a year after their first chart topper peaked, Diana Ross & The Supremes made pop culture history with their ground breaking stint at The Copa. Filled with standards, 6 Supremes hits and a show stopping tribute to the late Sam Cooke, this best selling re-issue brings back all the soul and schmaltz plus lost footage of the famed NY engagement. Rave reviews, sold out status and return demand was the instant response to the Herculean efforts of all involved, with everything resting on the fragile looking, but very capable shoulders of young, amazing and uber-talented Diana Ross. It is no wonder that, nearly 50 years later, Diana Ross is still selling out, garnering rave reviews and requests to "come back soon" around the world.
With alternate tracks, additional songs and patter, this limited edition is a must for fans. Just having From This Moment On and Tonight/The Way You Look Tonight finally released is worth the price to me. I really like Incubus (a lot), but this CD is truly one of the biggest disappointments of the last few years. Megalomaniac is, in my opinion, the only song on the CD that doesn't suck in some way, shape or form. Truly, anyone who believes that this CD "kicks like a mule," (to quote the Incubus website) or that Incubus has gone "back to their original style" (to quote a fellow amazon reviewer) should seriously get a CAT-scan; the similarities between S.C.I.E.N.C.E. or Fungus Amongus and this are few and far between.
First off, a good percent of the vocal melodies aren't even melodies - they're more like ramblings. The music is for the most part downright weird, and not in an inspiring "wow that's really weird but cool" sort of way. In an attempt to be original and sophisticated, the songs get complex, but in a manner that muddles and doesn't better the songs. Almost all of these songs could be written by your average crappy high school band, although the lyrics - not the vocal melody mind you - are ok. I sure hope this isn't the result of Dirk Lance's departure, 'cuz if it is, he needs to come back and save this band before they start to suck and never return. Save yourself the money and buy the "Megalomaniac" single instead.

title: Delicious Flavors
text:
This is probably my favorite album by Alanis and at four years since her last one, well worth the wait. Combining Alanis's rock sensibilities with techno courtesy of producer Guy Sigsworth who has previously worked with Madonna and Bjork, this is a masterful work of art. My favorite tracks include the Mid-Eastern/Indian flavored "Citizen Of The Planet" (sample lyric- "I am a citizen of the planet. My president is kwan yin. My frontier is on an airplane. My prisons: homes for rehabilitating.") which I totally relate to. John Lennon's "Imagine" shares this sentiment in that rather focusing on what country one pledges allegiance to (which is all about division), we instead align with all humanity and love this Good Earth without the boundaries. The strings on this song (arranged by Sigsworth and Fiora Cutler) are incredible, sending an already fantastic song into the stratosphere. "I get giddy" indeed. If you liked "Baba" from "Supposed Former Infatuation Junkie" and the title track of "So-Called Chaos", you'll love "Citizen". The angst-ridden "Straitjacket" is one of the songs here that you'll want to (in Alanis's words) 'dance your face off' to. Great beat, more great lyrics that are nakedly personal, and I love the treatment the word 'straitjacket' is put through, giving the song just the right touch of insanity. "Versions Of Violence" gives me goose bumps in its depiction of a relationship that could be interpreted as either personal or universal. I love the way Andy Page's synth bass threads through the song.
After a deluge of sound from the first four songs, "Not As We" simmers the album down in just the right place. Basically just Alanis singing with piano accompaniment by Guy, this is perhaps the most personal and heartbreaking song on the album. But it also has a glimmer of hope reflected in the lyric "From scratch begin again but this time I as I and not as we" which makes it all the more touching. More hope and positivity comes in the form of the subtle beauty of "In Praise Of The Vulnerable Man" which also has a glorious string arrangement. Lyrically, "In Praise" seems to be a further exploration into the territory established in songs like "UR" and "So Pure" from "Junkie". "Torch" is another very personal song concerning Alanis's breakup with Ryan Reynolds. It's musically dynamic, going from relatively minimal instrumentation to full bloom and back again. This woman is fearless when it comes to documenting emotions and her art is richer because of this openess. Another ode to positivity and happiness, "Giggling Again For No Reason" follows. It's sort of a sister song to "Knees Of My Bees" from "So-Called Chaos" and allows Alanis to show a brighter side of herself before the intensity of the swirling "Tapes" which includes the priceless lyric "All these thoughts in my head aren't my own wreaking havoc". The song ends with Alanis singing in an upper register that is heavenly. "Flavors" ends perfectly with the upbeat "Incomplete" with swirls of gorgeous background vocals and other nice flourishes of sound courtesy of Andy Page's 'sound design'. I don't know if it will offend many of her fans but I dig Alanis's perception of God as female in this song. In this white male-dominated nation, I find this notion refreshing and share it with Alanis.
"Flavors Of Entanglement" shows Ms. Morissette continuing to grow as an artist. Girlz Rock!

title: Dreampop heaven
text:
The Doves 1st 2 records were minor masterpieces - at last a quality band that would carry the dreampop banner into the 21st century for many of us that were brought up on the 80's/90's dreampop of Echo & The Bunnymen/The Chameleons/The Church/Catherine Wheel, etc. And while The Doves represent the cleaner sounding side of these bands (at least in the studio), their music has the same transcendental power and ability to take you away.

"Some Cities" isn't necessarily a departure from the previous records, but when everything works as well as it does here, that's not an issue. 4 strong singles highlight this record - "Black And White Town", "Snowden", "One Of These Days" & "Walk In Fire". These 4 songs are worth the price of admission alone. Add in the gentler washes of "The Storm" & "Someday Soon" and you have a near dreampop masterpiece.

If you were a fan of previous Doves records, this is a no-brainer and if you're just looking for some great moody dream pop indulge yourself.

title: MUST BE RE-ISSUED ON CD
text:
The RCA Victor recordings of Gary Burton of the 1960s were all gems. This was the masterpiece, however,of all if them. With Larry Coryell on guitar, Steve Swallow on bass and the renowned Roy Haynes on drums made a one of a kind album. Not jazz but yet it is, not rock but yet it is, not fusion but yet it is .

In fact Miles' Bitches Brew which is the Rosetta Stone for fusion would not be released until 1969 , a full 2 years after "Duster" .

This is the jazz version of the Beachboys' "Pet Sounds". The album where the Beatles supposedly heard and based their Pepper album on.

Ecletic and esoteric but yet it swings mighty fine as Larry Coryell on guitar never sounded so reigned in but powerful still.

I remember when this LP first came out the Downbeat magazine reviewer was astounded of the new musical sounds that was coming out of jazz from this LP other than the "Avante Garde " school of free jazz of Coltrane and Ornette .

...........and he gave the LP 5 stars also.

BMG should re-release all of the Burton Victor albums but if they have to do just one , this is it. Plus it always had the coolest cover for an album ever made.

title: Whole > Parts
text:
New Zealander Ladyhawke has said that she wanted to write new music that would make people feel instantly nostalgic. Well, she has succeeded. When I heard the first track, "Magic" (one of the best), The 80's rushed at me, begging to be recognized. This song, and several others, would be right at home amid the music of Berlin, Laura Branigan, The Pet Shop Boys and Madonna. Ladyhawke's vocal quality sounds very much like that of Terri Nunn of Berlin, more closely than anyone else I can think of. Synth-pop is the predominant sound, but there's more. The very heavy drums and guitar work give some of the tracks - "My Delirium", "Another Runaway", "Love Don't Live Here", "Back Of The Van" and "Morning Dreams" - a "rock" quality, at least as much as the work of Pat Benatar, The Cars or even Journey. (I know that rock purists will disagree, but terms like "rock" and "pop" mean different things to different people.)

Other elements combine with the "synth-rock" to make this album distinctive. One is Ladyhawke's persona. She is mostly cool and confident, but every now and then her intense emotions must erupt. In "My Delirium", obsessing while waiting for THAT PHONE CALL, she shouts, "I won't eat and I won't sleep for you, yeah-eh-eh-eh-eh-eh-eh-eah!", and in "Back Of The Van", whether she is with her lover or alone, her feeling is "You set me on, you set me on, you set me on FI-YURE!" Another feature of her music is eerie background sounds, vocal and instrumental, most strongly in "Magic", "Love Don't Live Here" and "Professional Suicide". That last one is also memorable because it sounds very much like the music of Garbage. "Dusk Till Dawn" features Ladyhawke's deliciously Brit accent. The final track, "Morning Dreams", is a solid power ballad, the only ballad on the CD.

The song that attracted me to this talented new artist is "Paris Is Burning". I am a sucker for anything French, Paris in particular, and Ladyhawke says that she wrote this song immediately after her first visit to Paris, in order to describe her impressions of the vibrant activity that she found there - the champagne, the clubs, the sidewalk cafes, the kids on the streets. To really appreciate it, you should check out the video. But it's not necessary, because the song - with its conversational lyric and melody, mirrored by the "talky" bass line - is a happy but yearning remembrance of that visit, and a delight in itself.

The diverse elements that make up Ladyhawke's music (and it is HER music, because she wrote, arranged and played instruments on every track) make it difficult to put her in a category. Just when you decide to call her music one thing, it changes into something else. Remember that in this case, the whole really is greater than the sum of its parts.
