Jeff Johnson is a man of many musical moods. Instrumental or vocal albums. Chamber music or synth rock. Musical travelogs or accompaniments for reading. New creations or ancient renditions. Trailblazing or traditional. Solo or ensemble. Selah meditation or singer-songwriter composition. And this latest? This evocatively titled album, incidentally NPR "Echoes" December album of the month, is a collection of instrumental, Celtic-tinged, Christmas carols, the latest of six Johnson seasonal projects which stray variously among the styles above. It's just the thing to hear drifting over the scent of bayberry candles on a cold winter night, snuggled with a cup of hot cider under a blanket on the divan, maybe with a good book. It's everything everyone loves about the unique, indefinable, yet always recognizable Jeff Johnson light, deft musical touch, which makes his multitude of fans crave more.

Why then a four? Merely because to always be doling out fives inflates the rating process. This best falls among so many bests that it comes down to simply a matter of taste or style or musical mood as to which are the fives. My favorite Johnson albums range all over the board, some less known, nearly lost to history, favorites of a few, far from the madding crowd. These would include The Memory Tree [[ASIN:B00006959H The Memory Tree]], Pilgrimage [[ASIN:B000024SCE Pilgrimage]], Songs from Albion [[ASIN:B000SXKCDY Songs From Albion]], Icons [[ASIN:B000KNMCWG Icons]], and Great Romantics [[ASIN:B0000288QI Great Romantics]], to name a few. For those avid for more Johnson, there is always more to explore. How glad is this listener that, along with the widely available MP3s, some of these other musical moods have found their way onto Amazon, along with these sounds of the season.

title: Expectations Are Always Hard To Live Up To...
text:
Just over two years ago, Jimmy Eat World finally arrived on the world stage after being one of the most underrated bands of the last decade. They had stacks of hardcore fans (including a little band called Blink 182) but also plenty of record company hassles. That all changed with their self-titled release. It sold well over 2 million copies and the group started popping up everywhere - even commercial radio, thanks to the catchy chorus of `The Middle'. The problem with success like that is how do you follow it up. Well I can tell you 'Futures' is not a bad effort. It lacks the commercial appeal of their previous album but dares to be a little more adventurous - not just up-tempo rock song after up-tempo rock song. Things get slowed down on `Drugs Or Me' and `Night Drive' (the latter having some nice instrumentation), they prove they're still handy with an energetic hook (`Pain') and even pull off a 7-minute epic (`23') to close proceedings. It's all done with a refreshing amount of confidence, leaving `Futures' a very satisfying experience.

Highlights: Pain, Drugs Or Me, Futures, Night Drive.

title: My favorite Erasure CD
text:
Although most Erasure fans might consider THE INNOCENTS their favorite CD, I have to chose this one. Why? Mostly because I believe this 1994 release not only captures the duo of Andy Bell and Vince Clark at their artistic/creative peak, but it also is incredibly easy to listen too, even though it navigates through many different styles of music.

From the opening track "Take Me Back" all the way to the soft ending of "Because You're So Sweet", Andy Bell's vocals are superb-full of nuance, sensitivity and energy. I don't think he's ever delivered a better complete vocal performance on one CD (although he has delivered better individual performances on some tracks of other Erasure CDs).

But what makes Andy's vocals shine so, is the intricate, amazing setting that Vince Clark has created for them. Not since his early work with Yaz and Alison Moyet, has Clark found a better match for his style.

Of course, the track "Always" was a top 40 success, but in my view, it's one of the weakest tracks on the CD. My favorites are "So The Story Goes", "Blues Away", "Run To The Sun" and "I Love Saturday".

Never has this duo sounded more free, more engaged and more adventuresome, and the only other Erasure CD that comes close to achieving what this CD does, in my view, is COWBOY.

So, if you are a new Erasure fan, and haven't heard this CD, I highly recommend it. If you are a longtime fan and have never placed this one at the top of your list, I suggest you give it another shot!

Indie Cindy isn't a bad album and if you're like me you've been waiting for some new Pixies material for quite some time, so anything you get will seem like candy for the soul. But ultimately the latest installment of Pixies music seems far more like Bossanova than Surfer Rosa or Dolittle. It's not bad, it's just generic. Frank Black et al created a sound that was unique and fresh in the 1980's and early 1990's and you can't exactly blame them for their invention becoming stale, but you can always hope that they recognize it. Virtually any other band on the market today would be proud to add Indie Cindy to their catalogue of music, but Indie Cindy feels more like R.E.M.'s "Green" than a bold new direction.

It's unfortunate that alternative rock fans in 2014 will discover Pixies music through this tainted lens and one can only hope that they follow the hype back in time and discover the band that literally turned alt-rock on its head. I don't question Frank Black's musical genius and I have no doubt that Kim Deal's rocky tenure had overstayed it's welcome, but Black without Deal is like Morrissey without Marr. Predictable. Doesn't grab me. An unfortunate blemish on an otherwise impeccable discography.

title: Interesting and well-played: a tip about the "Unfinished"
text:
The standard, finished symphonies in this set are given very standard but glowing performances. It is an excellent set just for that. The special news, of course, is the collection of unfinished orchestral movements included in the disks, including Newbould's conjectural reconstructions of symphony 7 and 10 and a finished Unfinished. The latter two are especially important and beautiful, offering plausible Schubert that bears listening and relistening.

Here is a personal tip concerning the finished Unfinished (8th symphony), which includes the Scherzo that Schubert fully composed in piano score, but only began to orchestrate, and the B-minor Entracte from Rosamunde, often thought to be the intended finale to the 8th symphony.

I recommend making the Scherzo the second movement, and the slow movement the third. There is no precedent for this in the other Schubert symphonies, but there is ample precedent in other classical-period pieces (most famously, Beethoven's ninth symphony). In this symphony, it has the result of making the Scherzo a vigorous palate cleansing between two dreamy movements. I find it works very well, and I much prefer it to the more obvious order. Just a suggestion (but a good one!).

title: A "Buzzard" leaving no stone unturned!  Brilliant!
text:
As the author of the Jefferson Airplane book "Take Me To A Circus Tent" and a former radio disc-jockey, I am often asked to write and or discuss various recordings from the 60's and 70's.

When even the most talented performer is asked by choice or force to work outside their element the normal results aren't pretty. This is only one of the infinite reasons why the self-titled effort from Armageddon is nothing short of spectacular.

Imagine the surprise when Keith Relf a vocalist in the higher echelon decided to branch out from his legendary British Invasion (Yardbirds) singing style for a trip into uncharted waters. Relf had left a permanent stamp of greatness with his contribution to the Yardbirds in the 1960's.

Armageddon (1975) was-Keith Relf on vocals (Yardbirds), Martin Pugh- guitar (From Steamhammer), drummer Bobby Caldwell (Johnny Winter) and bassist Lou Cennamo (Very early Renaissance, Illusion, and Steamhammer).

Unfortunately, for the musical world we lost Keith after the one and only treasure the band would leave us. Clocking in at about forty-one minutes the album is timeless. Every facet is brilliant from the cover that shows the destruction in the background, the musicians selected to record, and the life or death effort put into every note and lyric.

When the words heavy and metal are together to most it conjures up negative thoughts. The preconceived notion that it is all about being loud and how many of the same useless riffs will be repeated is forever branded in the brain. There is also "Intelligent Metal." Records such as this one, Deep Purple with Ritchie Blackmore, Blue Oyster Cult in the early days, and Black Sabbath with Ozzy should never be placed in the same cookie jar as the thousands of groups known for their hair and not talent.

Track 1 is appropriately titled "Buzzard." There is no preparation for what's to come. A vacuum with the power of a tank sucks you through the wall with no escape. You are in a trance as the sonic blast emanates for eight minutes. If the speakers and your body need recovery, there will be brief calm before the next storm.

Track 2 "Silver Tightrope" is beauty plain and simple. The perfect mix of Pugh's guitar (With such clarity he can be in the room with you) and Relf's extraordinary vocals create a song of beauty.

Track 3 "Paths And Planes And Future Gains" continues the theme of the opening cut. Once again a destructive force leaves no stone unturned. The energy and aggression don't dissipate. Pugh's guitar is a machete sparing nothing.

Track 4 "Last Stand Before" features well-written words that are delivered in majestic fashion by Relf. His range is tested throughout, as is inflection. There would be no doubting the outcome. Listen for tremendous production during Pugh's solo, as the sound changes from speaker to speaker. The octane a shade lower than the previous track but not any less stellar. You may even hear Relf pull out a harmonica from the Yardbird days!

Track 5- "Basking In The White Of The Midnight Sun (Warning Comin' On/Basking In The White Of The Midnight Sun (Reprise)" Somehow the band is still standing although the listener has long been rendered unconscious. The conclusion is more firepower and a terrific vocal delivery from Mr. Relf.

There aren't enough superlatives that would give proper justice to the artistry of the Armageddon debut. There is a reason above all others that this should be in the CD collection. Keeping Keith's memory alive with the brilliant Yardbirds reissues and his final gift to us is paramount.

Enjoy the music and be well,
Craig Fenton
Author of the Jefferson Airplane book "Take Me To A Circus Tent"

title: A flawed near-masterpiece
text:
Some may have been quick to throw the label of masterpiece on Source Tags & Codes, but even while it falls short of being an instant classic, there's more than enough reasons to seek it out. It's simultaneously challenging and accessible, a difficult quality to wind up with in indie rock. The song structures and musical rhythms are complicated, there are arty interludes and song switches, and buzzsaw guitars doing as much screeching as thrilling. But strip away those bits and you're left with a melodic rock record that almost anyone could embrace.

There are nearly flawless hooks in "How Near How Far" and "Relative Ways," showcasing the band's edgy pop side. And on a drawn-out epic like "Monsoon," there's an almost tangible unpredictability that keeps the listener on edge (it never truly pays off, but has enough strong moments to rank as one of the albums better tracks). Intro, "Invocation," and the interlude, "After the Laughter," both coast by on a similar simple melody, so pretty that I can't even qualify them as throwaways. The album's best moment comes from "Baudelaire," a relatively straight rock song replete with driving guitars and reverb, both melodic and powerful. "Homage" stumbles and falls over its own mountain of excess and "Heart in the Hand of the Matter" is groping blindly for the gravity it needs to survive after soaring too high into the overkill stratosphere. But they're little quibbles, and abundance isn't so much of a bad thing.

Even with them there, I almost never hit the skip button because the album flows so well. Flaws and all, Source Tags & Codes is a great record, one which time and reflection should be kind upon, and I can't fault those who heralded it as a work of genius. Certain moments do make that promise and falling a few inches short is just fine by me.

Best cuts: "Baudelaire," "How Near Is Far," "Monsoon," "Source Tags & Codes," "Relative Ways," "It Was There That I Saw You," "Another Morning Stoner," "Days of Being Wild"

title: Controlled anger with stellar musicianship
text:
Weight was the Rollins Band's breakthrough into the mainstream and remains their best album. While their previous album The End Of Silence was an unfocused affair with many of the songs tending to drag, Weight cuts out all the fat as every song here is very strong both musically and lyrically.

This album is best known for its memorable video/single "Liar" which starts out as a mellow jazz tune under Henry Rollins' soft spoken vocals before getting heavy during the choruses. While this is the most well known track, many other songs here match its brilliance. "Civilized" and "Step Back" both rely on a killer groove before dropping down in tempo midway through before regaining its original momentum. "Alien Blueprint" is a fantastic tale of a former outcast who doesn't let his past ruin his future. "Shine" is another great tune driven by a groovy riff and more of Rollins' great self-help lyrics. "Disconnect" is a mid-tempo track driven by the excellent rhythm section of bassist Melvin Gibbs and drummer Sim Cain that is also very strong. The momentum slows down on the grinding "Volume 4" and the slow jazz of "Tired" which concentrate more on mood and Rollins' vocals which speak of a man wrestling with his emotions. Other great tracks include the driving "Icon", "Fool", and "Wrong Man" which are all carried by Chris Haskett's killer riffs and wild yet creative soloing. Rarely has an album been released that combines controlled anger with such great lyrics and musicianship. Highly recommended.

title: A unique and disturbing Squeeze CD
text:
A very unique entry to the Squeeze catalog after a long gap. Now actually follow the story told here. This is a sad narrative of a terminally losing "normal" couple that failed their kids and life, trapped by their routines and limited life patterns. Happy days in the past are of no use and there's salvation for the two. My thought here is, this couple apparently never listened and payed real attention to the old Squeeze songs, or any other good music, songs that give us all clues on how to live a better life, and escape the "trap of the ordinary" style of care less living, life that eventually ruins so many around-the-block normal people all over the world (I can't help but think, if only more people over the past half century, since some really good and enlightening music started emerging with the John Lennon side of the Beatles, actually listened to the songs, and were thus motivated to take their lives more seriously in doing so, the world we live in might not be in such sorry shape).

As far as radio-friendly style hooks go, this one is certainly not Squeeze's most memorable set of songs for a release. Nonetheless as I wrote, uncomfortably disturbing, in a good way, and each of the songs here rates and paints a piece of the overall picture. This can cause issues with some cartridges.  A conical needle will not track on this album and depending on the cartridge the needle may not track to the bottom of the groove.  Be sure that your cartridge is aligned properly.  1970's RCA LP's used micro grooves and some were just nasty with distortion and lack of high end.  I had to purchase a copy of Jefferson Airplane's Volunteers mastered at Sundazed to get one that tracked correctly. My point being that some cartridges may have tracking issues with this pressing and some will not.  So try to find a slightly used Very Good+++ rated copy if you have issues.

title: Where are the songs???
text:
When I first heard the news of one of my favorite bands, Pain of Salvation, recording their newest epic with an orchestra, I could hardly sit still. What could be sweeter than one of your favorite bands in your favorite genre of music recording a purposed masterpiece with orchestration?! Much to my dismay, the outcome left a bitter taste in my hopeful mouth. 'Be,' unfortunately, is topping my current list of this year's sincere disappointments. This recording was quite an undertaking I'm sure. As a musician who has written orchestral scores for rock projects, I can relate to just how hard it is to accomplish a successful finished product (hats off to the genius, Daniel Gildenlow!). Throughout 'Be,' there are fleeting moments of greatness with beautiful orchestration (love that oboe melody in 'Imago') and the usual Pain of Salvation impressive musicianship. However, all the problems lie within the songwriting on this CD.

One of the strengths of Gildenlow is his ability to create melody lines and musical passages that leave you weeping in your bowl of breakfast cereal. Yet, the biggest let-down on this CD is the complete lack of melody, memorable moments and simply mediocre songwriting throughout the CD. There are interesting attempts at alternate stylistic experimentation (such as the ala'-Southern Baptist inspired 'Nauticus' or the blues influenced 'Dea Pecuniae'). But truthfully, the willingness to experiment musically, on top of the addition of the would-be-impressive orchestration, does NOT substitute for any lack of poor songwriting. And while we're at it, the lyrics do not help any sort of improvement to the record either. The topic of the concept CD is quite interesting (dealing with the creation, the expansion and the destruction of the human race). However, the lyrics are *SO* over-conceptual and story-telling that it creates Gildenlow to perform gobs & gobs of spoken word, muttered vocal lines and even spoken vocal 'samples' vs. the more poignant melodies we are more commonly exposed to with PoS. There are very limited memorable choruses or musical moments which unfortunately supports/feeds that fire of the anti-progressive folks out there who claim progressive rock artists don't know how to write a successful song. Not to mention the titles of every song in Latin being a sheer annoyance, making it hard to associate personally with much of the content of the CD from anything outside Gildenlow's own personal point of view(s). It makes me wonder if he was more infatuated with the "concept" of this entire project rather than the actual songs that make up the recording.

A close musician friend of mine is not a fan of progressive rock unfortunately. When asked why, he defends his stance by saying that he feels progressive artists "try too hard" to be creative, almost surpasing that goal of being a deep, real artist and moving straight toward being phoney and completely pretentious. Though I don't feel that way about much progressive music and will always be a life-long fan, this recording ('Be') certainly illustrates his theory to a deep extent. Sadly, I'll have to await the next PoS in hope to rediscover the magic of writing a true "song" again.

title: Seventh Star Great, but no live extras w/ Glenn a dissapointment...
text:
Seventh Star is an excellent 80's style Tony Iommi solo metal album. Calling it Black Sabbath backfired as a sales incentive, angering many Black Sabbath fans who would have been more open minded to the records different styles if it had been labeled ONLY as a Tony Iommi solo project. And it would still be long forgotten without the excellent soulful vocals of Glenn Hughes, "The Voice Of Rock". He makes the average songs good, and the good ones incredible! Heart Like A Wheel, Danger Zone, Angry Heart and In Memory are standout tracks because they DON"T sound like Black Sabbath. A unique record in the 'Sabbath timeline.
It's the bonus live tracks that dissapointed me so badly. Glenn was sick/in a fight and got his nose broken/having drug issues (or all of the above) just before the Seventh Star tour, and was in no shape vocally to perform. Glenn stuck it out anyway and sang on March 21, 1986 in Cleveland. It was rough in parts, but the show went over well. After that, Glen fell apart more each performance, and was replaced by Ray Gillen within days.
The live bonus tracks feature Ray instead of Glenn on vocals, and that's where things go wrong. Whether you're a Ray Gillen fan or not,these live versions are nothing like the Seventh Star studio tracks! The first (and best) live show that Glenn Hughes performed with Black Sabbath (Cleveland 3/21/86) should have been remastered and added as the bonus tracks... they are the only ones that compliment the Seventh Star release and would have truly let you hear and judge this unique "Black Sabbath" lineup live before it's brief time was up.

title: An instant Oldfield classic.
text:
Even after 44 years, Mike Oldfield’s music never seems to get stale. Despite a catalogue of 26 albums, he is still best-known for his landmark debut hit in 1973. Indeed, Oldfield seems to be a victim of his own success—“Tubular Bells” launched his career, and he has occasionally issued sequels or revised or updated versions of his monster hit record. “Return to Ommadawn” is the first direct “sequel” that hasn’t been a retread of some sort of the Tubular Bells theme. “Ommadawn,” released in 1975, was Oldfield’s third album, and was in many ways a more concise, thematically-unified musical exploration than “Tubular Bells.” There are aficionados who will readily state that “Ommadawn” stands as Oldfield’s best album. “Return to Ommadawn” shares much of the same structure of its spiritual predecessor. Like its progenitor, “Return” is a thematically tight, two-track exploration of a musical landscape. It is perhaps the most atmospheric of any of Oldfield’s albums. In fact, it could just as easily be a sequel to Oldfield’s experimental album “Guitars” (in which every sound originated from a guitar). Unlike “Guitars,” and some of Oldfield’s recent offerings, however, the sound on this album is less processed; more organic. And consequently, it feels more alive. To further add to this impression, the cover artwork suggests a definite story. It is a far cry from the stylistic, logo-like covers that have previously appeared on the front of Oldfield albums.
In “Return to Ommadawn,” Mike Oldfield has stepped back a bit from the rich processing of his sound that we heard on recent musical forays. Here, his acoustic instrument playing is personal and unfiltered. Even when he adds his signature myriad layers, the music never sounds clinical or overdone, such as it did in “Tr3s Lunas,” “Guitars,” or “Songs of Distant Earth.” “Return to Ommadawn” is rich and evocative, but also manages to stay intimate and personal at the same time.
With acoustic and electric guitars, organs, exotic percussion, world-music vocals, and other acoustic instruments, “Return” is vintage Oldfield. Anyone who enjoyed his first four records should be extremely pleased with this entry. The first track is good, but the second track is better, building upon some of the ideas postulated in the first. While some of the musical themes are direct quotations of “Ommadawn,” Oldfield achieves alchemy on “Return”—transmuting those themes into something entirely new. Mike Oldfield has always demonstrated a clever knack for hiding his themes in plain sight, later bringing them front and center to make the listener experience a kind of musical déjà vu. In “Return,” Oldfield takes both sides to work through some achingly emotional moments, eventually achieving a rousing and satisfying climax. By the final notes, in which we see Oldfield’s optimism and sense of humor on full display, “Return to Ommadwan” seems not so much part of Oldfield’s closing act, but a new beginning.
Mike Oldfield’s two latest albums have been exemplars of his formats of choice. “Man on the Rocks” was a thoroughly enjoyable pop album, with standard-length songs that were catchy enough for top-40 radio. “Return to Ommadawn” with two 20-odd minute length sides, stands as one of Oldfield’s best instrumental new-age albums, rivalling “Tubular Bells” and even “Ommadawn.”

text: Streisand's sophomore release serves up another set of consistent songs, given a strong sense of cohesiveness by the jazzy arrangements and Barbra's revolutionary vocal performances.  A Top Five, Gold-selling record, nearly half of the set is devoted to the material of Harold Arlen.  Streisand proves to a perfect interpreter of Arlen's compositions, giving the definitive performances of many of his songs, especially "Any Place I Hang My Hat Is Home," "When The Sun Comes Out," and "Down With Love."  Barbra even gives the album's only pop number (the single "My Coloring Book") a reverent dramatic sensitivity that allows the number to sit perfectly balanced between the other, more sophisticated material.  Another top-notch effort from a vibrant and essential artist.

title: Ka-Boom Ka-Boom
text:
The "AntiChrist Superstar-Mechanical Animals-Holywood" trilogy is over, and it's time to go back to basics. But, with all this experience, knowledge, and wealth, would Marilyn Manson really produce a second Protrait of an American Family? The answer is no. In fact, the band is just as experimental as ever, and this album shows. Some of the songs sound something out of a 1930's Berlin play, such as the bouncy "Doll-Dagga Buzz-Buzz Ziggety-Zag" and the somewhat depressive "The Golden Age of Grotesque". There's a bit of pop found in "mOBSCENE"; some catchy metal from "Slutgarden" that's reminiscent of early Manson's "Get Your Gunn"; a little Mechanical Animals soft rock in "Spade"; and straight up mosh material in "(s)AINT" and "Ka-Boom Ka-Boom". You might even say that "Better of Two Evils" has a hip-hop influence, although that's debatable.
Despite the many different band line ups and the vast amount of experiments that Manson the band has made over these years, we've come to a point where we expect them to release good music -- and The Golden Age of Grotesque is certainly that. Fans of previous albums might find a slight problem with some of the songs, but listen deep and you'll find that, despite the 1930's and electronica influence, this is still Marilyn Manson at the core.

title: Lost in the Awesome
text:
What's that? You've never heard of Lost in the Trees. Come with me and we'll go on a little trip into the land of music that's better than what you're listening to now...

My friend and I both stumbled onto Lost in the Trees whilst shopping at Amoeba in Hollywood. "What's that?" we asked ourselves. "A mini orchestra? A darling, unpretentious singer with a gorgeous voice? An ensemble with talent? Absurd!" No, dear readers, it exists. Lost in the Trees creates a sound that is nothing short of emotionally exhilarating.

While many groups and singers today build a sound on the concept of distraction, Lost in the Trees is about precision. They know exactly how to describe emotions that in less adroit hands have been ground into cliche. While normal shows and normal music plays AT the audience, Lost in the the Trees plays WITH the audience. It's a cumulative experience; you'll find yourself inspired, your brain thinking more clearly, your senses heightened as if you had suddenly been dealt a swift blow to your nerve endings.

The actual band members are some of the kindest people I've met (granted, I live in LA, so it's exciting when someone puts down their cigarette to talk to me) and their talent is mind-blowing. I mean, come on, Emma plays the glockenspiel, French horn, autoharp, drums, and sings. So, unless you can do the same thing, I suggest you buy the album.

In short, Lost in the Trees feels like flying. And once you start listening to them, you'll want to fly forever.

title: Live At The Apollo
text:
James Brown-Live At The Apollo ****

First I just want to say that James Brown has had better albums, and better live albums as well. I can see why Live At The Apollo receives such high acclaim but for me personally I don't enjoy it as much as most. I love live albums, getting to hear what a legend you may have never seen live is amazing.

Live At The Apollo does not live up to what I always imagined James Brown being like. For one sometimes during the album the lyrics are not that audible, like on 'Think' for example. This is one of his all time great tracks and I don't feel that during this performance he did the song justice. Other performances were better and more memorable. Brown also seems to be out of breath a lot during the performance as well which I know he was a machine on stage but still he was very young during this performance and on later live albums he seems to have held up better.

There are some very good things about the album though. For example the medley during the middle of the album is amazing. Easily the best performance on the album, not a weak point in the long jam. Also James' backing band here is breath taking. This may be the very best his bands have ever sounded live, it is too bad I can't say the same about Brown himself. Lastly for an early performance this is a great set of songs.

What is really cool about Live At The Apollo is that it wasn't supposed to happen. His manager told him not to do it and didn't support him so Brown recorded the whole performance himself. While I'm not saying this is a bad live album, because it really isn't, all I am saying is that Brown has released better, much, much better.

title: Grisman still earns his place at the top
text:
It would be so easy to overlook this album. Quintet/Sextet. If you look quickly, you may not even notice the wording difference. The album cover looks so similar! When David Grisman released The David Grisman Quintet in 1976, the idea was so simple, so brilliant, and in retrospect, so obvious. The Django Reinhardt/Stephane Grappelli approach to jazz would be so easy to connect to American string band music that why not do it? Why did it take so long? Because like so many great ideas, it is only obvious in retrospect. Grisman's concept, eventually to be known as dawg music, became so deeply ingrained in bluegrass that it is now hard to separate modern bluegrass from Grisman's influence. He could have rested on his laurels, and when you look at the album, the title, and even the cover, it would be so easy to assume that that's what Grisman would do here.

There are some instrumentation changes, like the addition of a flute, but how big a deal is that? The key is what Grisman has done in the decades since. He never stopped searching. And in particular, he has collaborated with everyone, not just bluegrass musicians. Most importantly here, he did some interesting collaborations doing work with various European folk styles. That's really what is going on here. And like with the creation of dawg music, it is so simple that it should have been obvious. After all, hot club jazz has an intrinsically European sound anyway! Why not go a bit further? So that's what Grisman and crew do here. They take the basic model of Grisman's style of bluegrass/dawg music, and seamlessly blend in European folk music with instrumentation changes. It just sounds logical, as so many innovations do after you hear them. The real difference here is that having heard what Grisman has been doing along the way, the album just sounds like exactly what you'd expect. The album title, cover, etc. just make it clear what Grisman is thinking. He is thinking back to '76, and thinking back to how he approached that classic album.

Will The David Grisman Sextet revolutionize string band music to the same degree? It can't. That's a bar that can't be reached, except on extraordinarily rare occasions. Yet, the music is fiery, soulful, groovy, and it makes you wonder why it hasn't been recorded before. What else do you want? Grisman never lost it.

title: Essential Folk-Rock Collection - Lovely, and Often Fun
text: The fifth star may have been awarded because I have admired this folk-rock duo since their earliest days, but anyone knowing nothing about Brewer & Shipley is missing some fine Woodstock-era tunes.  The package collects all four of their albums for the Kama Sutra label (their first was for A&M records), which represents their heyday both musically and commercially.  The fourth and fifth albums lack the consistency and zest of the second and third, but are certainly worth having - and, to my knowledge, were never released in the CD format until now.  Brewer & Shipley are most famous for their comedic "One Toke Over the Line" (if you want to experience true hilarity, look up the clip from when it was performed on the Lawrence Welk show!).  There is nothing wrong with the gentle good humor evidenced by this and several other tracks, but it does not constitute much of the duo's oeuvre (particularly the achingly lovely "Weeds" album).  The partners were fine harmony singers and, particularly in the beginning, accompanied by luminaries such as Mike Bloomfield, Jerry Garcia, and Nick Gravenites.  Their rendition of Jim Pepper's "Wichi-Tai-To" (from "Weeds") should have been minted in 24-karat gold.

I was pleasantly surprised with this album and all its' beauty. The album cover and the rest of the album art catch the eye and compliments the overall soul and beauty of the songs. Prism shows a different side of Katy with more mature and meaningful lyrics that bring out Katy's talent. There's not one song on the album that I don't like as most of the tracks are very strong and can definitely hold their own. The only 2 songs that didn't stand out as much to me were "Love Me" and "This Moment." They're still really nice pretty songs but they're not as strong as the rest of the tracks.

I listened to the entire album as I was driving home from work and it just had a very peaceful and relaxing vibe that made the drive home much more pleasant. I loved all of the songs but This is how we do, Unconditionally, Double Rainbow, and Spiritual were amongst my favorites. Unconditionally, Double Rainbow, and Spiritual have very heart felt and hauntingly beautiful lyrics whereas This is How We Do is more fun and upbeat and sounds more like Katy's other pop hits such as TGIF.

I also really liked her song Legendary Lovers. I felt the beats and style of the chorus were unique and not like a typical Katy Perry song. It actually sounds more like a song Shakira would do. Songs like Roar, Birthday, Walking on Air, and International Smile are the dancy, upbeat, fun songs. Birthday and Walking on air kind of have an 80s sound to it which I like.

Another one of my favorite tracks, Dark Horse, is more hip hop with amazing beats and chorus. The rest of the songs are more heart felt, slower ballad type songs. Ghost sounds like a personal song written about the break up/divorce that she just went through. It's one of the more sad songs that add a personal touch to the album.

None of the songs disappoint and will leave you with most of them stuck in your head. It is definitely an album one should sit with and really listen to as opposed to just skipping through the tracks. The first half of the album is more upbeat and poppy while the second half winds down to the beautiful more mellow songs.

This album has a song for everyone and it seems like Katy definitely worked really hard on it and put a lot of heart and soul into the songs. I really love the personal touch to this album but that she also did some songs that reflect her fun quirky side. Overall beautiful and well done.

title: Vittrad Is Hit and Miss
text:
The first full length disc by Swedish folk rockers Garmarna showcase their flare for combining dark, old world ballads with modern rock twists.

This is a band that still has a lot of room to grow and they seem unsure of what to do with singer Emma Härdelin, who was new to the Garmarna fold at the time; most of the brief tracks here are instrumentals (Emma does play fiddle and flute) and only a handful have vocals. The best of those are Den Bortsålda (a classic!) and Straffad Moder & Dotter. Emma's voice is raw and the band play pretty conservatively -- they show very little of the stretching out that would come on later releases.

The brevity of the individual tracks works against the album, but taken on the whole it is a nice listen and is a great step back in time as well. The band would go on to do better things but this album is still worth having for the aforementioned tracks, as well as other tracks such as Vittrad and Klevabergselden.

title: Not just for country music lovers!
text: One listen to "The Best Of The Oak Ridge Boys - The Millennium Collection" will have you immediately hooked on the material, even if you aren't a fan of country music. What endeared many a fan to this legendary quartet is their unique brand of interwoven, finely homogenized blend of vocalization. Perhaps you could call the Oaks' the "Mamas and the Papas" or the "Three Dog Night" of country music. In this collection, you get eleven of their best known country tunes, plus the Oaks one and only crossover country-pop smash "Elvira", which features Richard Sterban's trademark bass vocals. I couldn't sing that low if my life depended on it!  The saxophone playing in "Bobbie Sue" is reminiscent of The Coasters "Charlie Brown", which gives this track a jazzy-bluesy sort of quality. My favorite tracks in this collection would have to be "I Wish You Could Have Turned My Head (And Left My Heart Alone)", "American Made" (which was later revamped and used in a  popular beer commercial), "Trying To Love Two Women", "Fancy Free" and "Make My Life With You". The other tracks featured in this greatest hits collection are worth the money as well, so you'll derive great listening pleasure, as well as get more than what you pay for with this one of a kind body of work from one of country music's biggest legends. This could be a five star review, had MCA included the Oaks' two most endearing favorites "Thank God For Kids" and "Everyday", but MCA sort of dropped the ball on this one. Although The Oak Ridge Boys have enjoyed a rather fruitful career over the years, perhaps their most notorious act was when Joe Bonsall, Duane Allen and Richard Sterban dismissed fellow longtime member William Lee Golden in the mid-'80's for refusing to shave off his trademark shepherd-like, salt and pepper beard. C'mon guys, that's like asking Alex Trebek to do away with his "flavor saver", or even asking Kenny Rogers to  shave off all his facial hair! The group then replaced Golden with a dark haired guy with no facial hair, who, in photographs looked so out of place in this band. By the time the '90's rolled around, Golden was later back with The Oak Ridge Boys, but the group failed to recapture their late '70's/early '80's chart success. This Millennium Collection CD belongs in every country music/Oaks' fan's, and in some cases, pop music fan's CD library. You better not wait too long, because "The Best Of The Oak Ridge Boys - The Millennium Collection" might not be around for the next millennium! As they say down South, "Ya better git while the gittin's good!" In English, that means "Order yours today (while supplies last)!"

title: Simply Beautiful
text:
For those who may not be familiar with contemporary improvisational music, there is a label out of Munich, Germany run by Manfred Eicher called ECM. Since 1969, they have produced some of the most beautiful and in some cases, the most highly influential records the genre has to offer. The records are generally done in roughly 3 to 4 days, leaving little room for studio tampering. Eicher is tyrannically opposed to overdubbing and over-producing, allowing the music to retain a very spontaneous atmosphere, as well as a very organic one. The music in most cases, reflects a wider world influence infusing not only elements of modern North American jazz, but classical European harmony and world folk.

The new record from Grizzly Bear member Daniel Rossen and long time musical collaborator Fred Nicolaus reminds me of one of Eicher's records. It's sparse arrangements coupled with dense harmonies and often-shambolic rhythms, brings to mind early Ralph Towner records. The chord structures used here are certainly not the generic ones found on most pop records, as with Grizzly Bear's Yellow House, chords are often realized beyond their mere 3 note applications and extend into the upper regions of the chord's implied harmony (extended 7th's and 9th's). The vocals are recorded in such a way that separating them from the music is impossible. They almost function as an instrument, that's not to detract from the lyrical content, but instead, enhances the experience by placing you as a listener right there with them throughout the whole record.

Discussing the lyrical content of this record would probably be a disservice, mostly because it really does transcend words for the most part. Having said that, the album was dedicated to Rossen's late father and carries with it topic matter that may not have been suitable for a Grizzly Bear project.

Another great strength of this record (along with Yellow House) is the "repeated listen" factor. It is recorded in such a way that the subtlety of the music will not reveal itself upon first listen. There are myriad vocal effects, reverb, and instrumental textures that are layered in a such a way that warrant this music to be experienced alone with a set of hi-fi headphones.

This is record to explore, live with, and more than likely, will be used as a reference 20 years from now as to where independent "pop" music was at the time and who were it's innovators.

title: My Second Favorite Pentangle Album.
text:
Little did I know that when I eagerly purchased this album that it would be the group's last. It was doubly sad because the album marked a return to the band's roots and even though I find BASKET OF LIGHT a better overall album, SOLOMON'S SEAL has my 3 favorite Pentangle songs. All 3 feature the haunting vocals of Jacqui McShee (THE CHERRY TREE CAROL, HIGH GERMANY, and WILLY O'WINSBURY) and all 3 are traditional in content (Carol, Folk Song, Ballad). The instrumentation is delicate but appropriate and brings each song to life.

This also featured my favorite of all The Pentangle covers although that was no longer a reason for buying the album. Whenever the Autumn & Winter seasons draw nigh I find myself drawn to Pentangle's albums and those of their contemporaries THE INCREDIBLE STRING BAND (at least their early albums). What made Pentangle so unique was not only the totally original sound that they conjured up reflecting their diverse backgrounds but the fact that the same 5 people were there from beginning to end allowing for not only consistency but a chance to chart their progress.

Neither Bert Jansch nor John Renbourn were great singers but their voices suited their material and when you had Jacqui to sing the rest or in tandem it hardly mattered. The group's choice of instruments and the way they used them were never better than on this album. Perhaps they knew it would be the last and wanted to go out on top which IMHO, they did. Renbourn's recorder accompaniment and guitar work are exceptional. Jansch's unique guitar sound and the solid underpinning of Cox (drums) and Thompson (stand up bass) make their sound unmistakable. Too bad it had to end here.

title: Ancient Rome Comes Alive
text:
This CD is a wonderful collection of music for wind instruments from ancient Rome's imperial period played on accurate replicas of various Roman instruments. This is a great buy for anyone interested in ancient music or the study of ancient Rome.

There are unfortunately few direct sources on the composition of Roman music. Most of the work in this CD is a recreation of what the music would have sounded like based on the range of the instruments, various classical sources, and anthropological studies of present Mediterranean cultures. I strongly disagree with a previous reviewer's giving of a low rating on the basis that the music is not the direct product of Roman sheet music. Although there may be certain inaccuracies in the recomposition of such music, the number of different scholars who participated in producing this work from various disciplines probably makes such inaccuracies rather slim. Furthermore, since there is no direct source for such music nor is it likely that we will ever uncover any, it's better to have this than nothing at all. The music is primarily brass and percussion but it also has string accompaniments for certain pieces. The music is charming and makes one feel as if they are reclining on their sofas, eating dates, and drinking wine in praise of Baccus. The package makes this CD worth every penny as it has a very detailed synopsis of all the instruments, the works themselves, and the work that was involved in this music: the pamphlet is also filled with photographs and drawings of the instruments as well as various Roman frescoes from Pompey depicting Roman social life and the instruments in question.

This is a great contribution to the study of antiquity and a valuable tool for teachers of ancient music, antiquity, or anthropology. This also a great buy for anyone who has broad interests in music and its development. For what you get with this CD it's a steal.

title: The Beast is alive and well!
text:
I will confess - after "Scarcity of Miracles" came out I thought that Robert Fripp's career was over; that the old man had finally nodded off into MOR land never to return. Instead that old man came back with a vengeance with the 7-headed beast that is the current King Crimson. The "Orpheum" CD really didn't do justice to the power of the live show; that was rectified with the sublime "Live In Toronto" release. Now we have pictures to go with the sound.

There are many ways of filming/editing a live show - and all of them suck. :) As the liner notes to the package state, it's really impossible. But this movie takes a very interesting approach involving multi-layering that I think does as much justice as possible to a band where everyone is constantly doing something of interest. It's sort of multi-tasking watching, and can be a bit disconcerting at first. But once into it you realize the advantages.

I have only one negative about the movie: they nearly totally ignore Bill's Rieflin's keyboards. You don't get the close-ups you get of others, and sometimes you get nothing. On the mellotron-heavy songs this is quite noticeable and personally a bit disappointing. But that's me. I was told (by a keyboard player) that unless it's flying fingers, that keyboards are boring to watch. But in any case it's not worth downgrading the set for.

I was sort of skeptical when I read the CDs would be the live tracks with no audience noise (and by the way, the CD tracks are the same performances as in the movie, just rearranged). But the live power still comes through, with no applause necessary. Some bands need a raucous audience atmosphere for their live shows to work; KCs music brings its own energy.

The bottom line is that we have a unique but very good movie, outstanding sound, and a great performance. Fripp and King Crimson are alive and well, and it's not a radical action at all to give it 5 stars.

One last comment - some may say that in essence this an oldies band - the King Crimson Orchestra as conducted by Fripp. There are many bands (or what's left of them) from the past that go around playing their old albums. This band does not sound like that. Maybe the very nature of the music, Fripp's idiosyncratic vision, makes it timeless in a way. Or maybe it's what great musicians do. Whatever, the music sounds as vital as it ever has. No, there's not much new material, and what there is breaks no new ground. But this band makes the old ground new. They deserve the name King Crimson.

text:
There really isn't a better word to describe this album- I imagine that, since an American listener would be unlikely to understand the lyrics, he or she would find it somewhat more visceral than the band may have intended. All the same, this is completely unlike well-behaved easy-listening music, cookie-cutter pop, poseur rap, or any other music you are likely to hear on the radio, on television, or in films these days. Garmarna adapts medieval ballads that mix folk tales (talking animals, magic) with everyday fears of the time (slavery, starvation, war)- and if you don't care to read translations of the lyrics, you can enjoy the strange combination of Old Norse tunes played on electric guitars and a jew's-harp.
The music itself is wonderful to listen to- it makes a great car tape, since the music raises your adrenaline and puts you in touch with your inner Viking (so to speak) enough to keep you alert for long stretches on the Interstate. It's usually fast-paced, seems like it was made for dancing, and is a little off-putting, since you're basically putting yourself into another culture. Also, possibly, because a few of the songs- particularly the last, "Klevabergselden"- seem rather apocalyptic and overwhelming, but why else would you listen to a group that has apparently named itself after Garm, the wolf in Norse mythology that swallows the sun and creates endless winter? Unless you explicitly hate all kinds of folk music, you should check this album out.

title: Hitting Their Stride
text:
I am not what could be called a diehard Marillion fan, but I have been completing my collection in a desultory fashion over the years. It seems to me that with this album the "new" Marillion surpasses the old in ambition and musical complexity, just as they did a few years ago in sheer volume. I don't know what Hogarth has against prog-rock: I say we ignore his pleas and rejoice that prog is alive and well. Not big on hooks, this band instead makes complex musical arguments, projects that build on lyrics collaborating with instrumentation, melody, time and distance. Over the past few albums the tracks have been getting longer and deeper... the music won't work as wallpaper, and if you don't sit down and pay attention to it it will have no effect. That said, "Quartz" and "The Fruit of the Wild Rose" have eerie haunting licks that curl around the bassline and build to terrifying heights. "When I Meet God" is a subtle and unsettling indictment of religion and mysticism hinging on the deceptively simple plaint, "If the bottle's no solution, why does it feel so warm?" And the sheer power and pain with which Hogarth wails, "If my heart were a ball, it would roll uphill" is staggering. "This is the 21st Century" brings it all back home with a lingering twist: "The universe demystified, chemicals for God;" yet this is not a refutation of hope: "Magic isn't dead."
And neither is prog-rock. Put on your headphones.

title: Needs a Reassessment
text:
STARFISH, the 1988 album by psychedelic jangle rockers The Church. Regarded by some as the work of one hit wonders (the band is still going strong after 25 years) or as a sell out move (it was produced by LA uber studio stud Waddy Watchell) by some long time fans, STARFISH holds up surprisingly well some 18 years after it's original release. There are not many other works by 80's artists that you can say the say the same thing about these days.

Of course this contains their big "hit" UNDER THE MILKY WAY, but actually is packed with many songs of equal or greater quality. From the haunting opener DESTINATION, to the haunting closer HOTEL WOMB, The Church do what they do best, creating hazy lyrical musings over taut guitar workouts with a subtle but strong rhythmic bed beneath. They can also rock out to good effect as one can hear on SPARK, BLOOD MONEY and the sublime REPTILE. Reference points could easily be The Byrds, Television and Echo and the Bunnymen.

While the bands lyrics are never going to be quoted as great rock poetry, the melodic talents of the band will create music that will echo in ones mind long after the disk has been retired to it's case. STARFISH provides evidence that there actually was good music made during the 80's and some of it was actually semi-popular.

title: Dave Van Ronk: Musical Bio
text:
Even if it isn't exhaustive, this Smithsonian Folkways 3-CD set provides a pretty good representation of Dave Van Ronk's musical life from 1958 to 2001, a year before his death. Known as "The Mayor of MacDougal Street," Ronk in his early Greenwich Village days worked with (and mentored a few) of the up-and-comer folkies like Odetta, Mike Seeger, Jack Elliot, and, yes, even Bob Dylan (before he became a SuperStar). Oddly enough, Ronk never really thought of himself as a folk singer, even though nearly everyone else did. His musical heritage was founded more on jazz and blues than on the folk idiom. A few of his early idols were Bessie Smith, Billie Holiday, Jelly Roll Morton, and Louis Armstrong. A touch of each of those masters can be seen in Ronk's work in one song or another.

Perhaps most people remember Ronk for his unique voice and singing style. It was not a pretty voice or style, not smooth, not mellow. On the contrary, Ronk's singing was about as gritty and gravelly as it could get. And yet, despite its roughness and edginess, his was a voice that could convey the deepest kind of downer emotions: like loneliness, loss, and heartbreak. But it could also convey a rowdy, good-natured kind of humor that was able to replace those emotions with a tongue-in-cheek joy when the lyrics required it.

Known mostly as a performer, Dave Van Ronk also wrote some of his own material. Perhaps the best known -- and most widely covered by the Big Name singers and groups of the folk era -- was "River Come Down" which he wrote with Dick Weissman. A few of Ronk's other compositions included in this set are "Standing By My Window," "If You Leave Me Pretty Mama," and the poignant "Another Time and Place."

This collection also includes a few songs from a handful of other people who were not known for their song writing abilities. For Instance, "Georgie and the IRT" is said to have been written by Lawrence Block, a novelist better known for his prodigious production of crime novels. "Jelly, Jelly, Jelly" was written by jazz and pop singer, Billy Eckstine. "Trouble In Mind" was written by jazz pianist Richard Jones. One song that WAS written by a well-known song writer is "Bucket of Rain," a Bob Dylan composition from HIS folk era.

Over the years, Ronk's unique voice and finger-picking guitar work didn't change very much. If anything, they both got just as bit more gritty and unpolished as the years wore on. While Dylan transformed himself and his sound numerous times during his career, Ronk pretty much stuck to the same persona. "What you see (and hear) is what you get" seemed to be his lifelong mantra. The terms "polished" and "commercial" were not part of his musical vocabulary. And yet tenderness and sensitivity were present all the time, just below the roughly-hewn surface.

To make this a truly representational collection it probably should have included one of Ronk's most popular and well known pieces, "Cocaine Blues."

Overall, however, "Down In Washington Square" is a good solid collection that has been well-produced. The set also includes an informative booklet that provides a lot of insight into the folk era, the performer himself, and the individual performances: dates, locations, composers, etc. If you like Dave Van Ronk and have been looking for a well-rounded, multi-CD collection, this one should fit the bill.

Russ Heitz

title: Solid third album, but not as good as the first two
text:
After two outstanding albums to start their discography, Down to the Bone slipped a little with Album III: Spread the Word. The vibe is still as funky as anything in mainstream contemporary jazz, but it started feeling a tad tired on this album.

In some ways this album is less than the sum of its parts. Although a number of tracks are interesting listening individually, this is a difficult album to listen to straight through and lacks any particularly memorable songs.

Downtown Shuffle features a great piano solo and Soul Brother No. 1 features some great percussion work (although it gets a little monotonous at times). Sound As A Pound is slightly underwhelming, but all other tracks are worth listening to at least once.

As with many other Down to the Bone albums, the songs on this album tend to get a bit too repetitive and drag on 1-2 minutes too long at times. That said, the sound on this album is closer to that of the original two albums than any of the groups other subsequent releases, so if you simply can't get enough of that early Down to the Bone sound, then you'll want this one in your collection. Otherwise, skip this one and try the group's fourth release, Crazy Vibes and Things, instead.

title: The Veritable Archetype of Alt-Rock
text:
I had been a fan of At The Drive-In, and when that band fractured into Sparta and the more popular The Mars Volta, I investigated both new bands. The Mars Volta have certainly become more well known; and their style of bizarre, experimental art-rock/psychedelia/fusion/whatever is interesting, but I seriously think that this album by their counterparts Sparta is one of the great underappreciated alt-rock albums of all time.

Pop-inflected, atmoshpheric, creative, otherworldy, artistic, catchy, gritty, expressive....these are all way I could describe this amazing and addictive album. Both more coherent and more well-written than anything The Mars Volta have ever done; it really is a shame that this album didn't receive more attention from the music-buying public. For me, this band and Sunny Day Real Estate are the veritable apogee of the alt-rock/emo sound, in different ways, without some of the annoying pretense and smug hipness of some of the other bands in the genre. I still can't get this one out of my CD player. A modern obscure classic!

title: A Different Bodom
text:
This album is definitely a lot different from their other albums. It took me a little bit to get used to this album, but now, it gets better every time i hear it. I like how they use keyboards more for an atmospheric effect on this album. However, they still, of course, have the good ol keyboard and awesome guitar solos. Alexi throws out some awesome solos on this album, as well as Roope. I'm also pleased with the lyrics, as they head more towards death, like Hatebreeder and FTR, which Bodom is about.

1. Living Deadbeat - 6/5 - One of my favorites of the album, uses keyboards for an atmospheric effect. Catchy chorus. Second favorite song.

2. Are You Dead Yet? - 4/5 - Catchy Chorus, other parts of song are kind of annoying. Solo's too short.

3. If You Want Peace...Prepare for War! - 6/5 - Very agressive song, and even has a triple solo with Roope, Alexi, and Janne. This is tied with Bed of Razors for my favorite Bodom song. The solos on this song go forever. Perfect song to listen to when you're mad or want to hear loud heavy music.

4. Punch Me, I Bleed - 4/5 - The slow song, has an awesome solo, but other parts could have been better. I like Angels Don't Kill better as far as slow songs go.

5. In Your Face - 4/5 - This song is growing on me. I didn't like it much at first but now it's awesome. more atmospheric keyboards, and chrous is catchy. Only part i don't like is "I don't give a flying f**k motherf****r"

6. Next In Line - 5/5 - Took a little bit for me to like this one too, but the solo just drew me in. My second favorite solo on the album.

7. Trashed, Lost, and Strungout - 5/5 - Awesome awesome song, first song i heard from the album. Alexi's voice is awesome in this song, and i love the guitar in this song.

8. Bastards of Bodom - 5/5 - I love the intro to this song! Typical Bodom themed song. Love the lyrics, especially "Don't need a reason, and i won't tell you why..."

9. We're Not Gonna Fall - 5/5 - The song itself is worth 4 out of 5, but i gave it 5 because of the solo. It starts at about 2:10 and goes for about 30 seconds. My absolute favorite. I LOVE that solo.

Overall: 10/10

I admit this cd is not like the other Bodom albums but if you liked HCDR you will LOVE this cd. It's better in all aspects. Bodom keeps getting better and better.

text:
Bernadette Peters is usually associated with Sondheim. And I loved her in Webber's Tell Me On A Sunday. This BP loves R & H is quite something.
Miss Peters' unique talent comes right through the "live" recordings. The phrasing is not practised like Miss Streisand would in her studio recordings. Mind, I do adore Miss Streisands' talents enormously. BP oozes fun and frivolity in some of the cheeky numbers like The Gentleman is a dope and Mr Snow.
Her guts and emotions are so intact for the performances of these songs here, that she sounds like she's in character on stage!! Only without the usual distractions of a live stage recording. Although at times, her voice is too forwardly placed, but it works as I listen to it again and again. She is right here on stage in my home!! Brilliant!
Miss Peters' rendition and choice of There is nothing like a Dame is rather audacious but appropriate. Do listen to this and enjoy what she is trying to say.... a howling, glaring, gutsy telling of R & H music and lyric!!
The treatment of It Might As Well Be Spring and Something Good is most exquisite. The latter, as pointed out by others here, is a mostly over-looked gem from The Sound Of Music.
In Weber's Tell Me On A Sunday, BP delivered the most individual performance I've heard. And here, now doing R & H, I am in love with Miss BP again....
Jonathan Tunick of course, has come up with some stunning arrangements and never sounding like he is repeating himself even though he has arranged these tunes many times for other artistes. Great work.
Other pieces to really note are, If I Loved You,Out Of My Dreams, So Far....I Haven't Got A Worry In The World, Something Wonderful.... well, the whole CD recording!!!!!!
Get it, a wonderful collaboration of all involved..and of course the fabulous Miss Peters. Don't forget to check out the TATTOO.

title: Pretty darn good even though not their strongest..
text:
Okay, let me start by saying that for me, 'Steamroller' music is now a must-hear Christmas tradition & I have all of their Christmas CDs. As for the new 2007 'Christmas Song', I actually like the record a lot in many respects, but I also do agree with some of the negative comments regarding the quality of the material and some arrangements.

First, the NEGATIVE points:
1) In the liner notes, Chip Davis says this album was actually created `based on popular demand' and I personally feel THAT better-explains the compromise in the quality of the material versus past efforts more than anything else! Of course, I love Nat's `Christmas Song' and Gene Autry's `Frosty the Snowman' as much as anyone, but while a thoughtful gesture on Chip's part, perhaps giving what the typically tone-deaf masses wanted was not such a great idea for a Mannheim recording in a world where talent-free rappers dominate 'popular music' sales... Let's fact it - unfortunately, many listeners will largely gravitate towards fluffy Xmas ditties (e.g., `Frosty', `Santa Claus is Coming to Town) in terms of material versus an obscure Celtic carol like `Wassail, Wassail' or `Carol of the Birds" that made Mannheim's first records so unique. Part of the charm of the older `Mannheim' releases is Chip always managed to dig up beautiful carols like the latter, beautifully arrange & pristinely record them, and then share some of his equally impressive knowledge of their history in the liner notes. Next time, I think Chip should return closer to form and do some beautiful arrangements with HIS material of choice regardless of what he thinks will `sell' the most.

2) Use of Vocalists: I prefer the more Christmassy chorale-oriented vocals on the earlier CDs, but I don't think the presence of vocalists is as problematic as are the arrangements behind them. The vocal tracks on `Steamroller CDS could've all used some more organic-sounding harpsichord, dulcimer and/or woodwind backing, or even some good old acoustic guitar as opposed to the synth-heavy sound, which would make them sound more like classic `Steamroller with vocals as opposed to a more tame Lite-FM'ish sound. The one track where I think the big synths actually work extremely well is `Above the Northern Lights'. The real `Northern Lights' are an ethereal sight and the dreamy arrangement & melody and nice vocal by Gene Nery (to me) evoke images in my head similar to the swirly `Christmas Tree in the sky' on the cover art. And love him or hate him, Johnny Mathis is one of the classic Christmas voices (for me his perennial "It's Beginning to Look Alot Like Christmas" is one of the definitive renditions of that tune). His `Christmas Song' rendition here isn't so bad, but I think his vocal on `Oh Tannenbaum' from 2001's `Extraordinaire' was a bit more robust. Olivia-Newton John is okay on `Christmas Lullaby', but it's too bad they couldn't do something different with the arrangement - The '95 instrumental version is better.

3) Arrangements / Song selection: Alluding to my previous paragraph, as an acoustic guitar player and big fan of acoustic stringed instruments, I wish there was some more of the `Renaissance' sound on here in the arrangements, and I also agree that it's time for Chip to start digging for NEVER-recorded songs for the next outing versus recycling previous instrumentals by adding vocals.

4) Songs I mostly skip:
(Track 10) The `Traditions of Christmas': This music-box style sounds pretty, but at just 36 seconds, why even bother including it? It's the most pointless track here...
(Track 2) "The Christmas Song" - Johnny Mathis sounds pretty good here to me, but the bland Lite-FM-ish arrangement detracts from it way more than he does... It needs some guitar or pan flute in there.
(Track 3) `Santa Claus is Coming to Town': Surely included for the kiddies, I have mixed feelings on this one -sometimes I'll listen to it, sometimes I skip it.
(Track 11) `Christmas Lullaby': Olivia Newton John's vocal is only mezza-mezza here, and the arrangement is not as nice as the 95 instrumental version, which I still prefer.
(Track 12) "Have Yourself A Merry Little Christmas" - not horrible, but just not my favorite arrangement here.

Okay, now for the POSITIVE:

Songs I listen to repeatedly:

(Track 1) `Let it Snow': Has the classic synth-&-pan-flute `Steamroller recordings and is a pleasant start.
(Track 4) `It Came Upon A Midnight Clear': My personal fave on this CD because it features a beautiful finger-style 12-string acoustic guitar-harpsichord combo driving the lush arrangement - beautiful stuff! I wish they'd use that 12-string acoustic more often...
(Track 5) `Feliz Navidad': Of course it ain't Jose Feliciano (I'm surprised they didn't have him sing here since they had almost everyone else on here!), but I found the arrangement to be kind of fun despite a slower tempo than Jose's hit.
(Track 6) `Snowflakes on Your Tongue' - A very pretty original that has a nice harp-driven arrangement and nice flute work.
(Track 7) `Masters in This Hall': NOW they're getting it done! This is by far the most vintage-Mannheim track on the CD! Half Celtic Renaissance/half rocking, this track would fit in very well on their older CDs.
(Track 8) `Above the Northern Lights' - As I said earler, very `dreamy' and ethereal arrangement and vocals... Nice track
(Track 9) `Frosty the Snowman' - Another one for the kiddies that most people on here seem to hate, but I'd dare say that I like this one better than "Santa Claus ICTT". It is a bit out there in terms of the melody, but reminds me of `Rudolph The RNR" from `95's "Christmas in the Aire", which also strayed a lot from the melody but still managed to be fun, so it's not as bad as it could be...

So, the final score for me is 7 out of 12 tracks I really like plus 3 I'll still play once in a while, so it could be much worse.
Well, that's as detailed a review I can give here... let me know what you think. Merry Christmas to all!!!

title: A Journey Into The Mysticism of Sound
text: I found these recordings performed by Cage connoisseur Margaret Leng Tan a wonderful oasis in my several months journey as a complete novice to understand John Cage. These are all early works, rarely seen in performance,  the Sonatas for prepared piano (specific modifications with screws, bolts and felt wraps for each piece) and a wonderful and rare recording of spiritually satisfying "Chess Pieces".  As a contemplative I find them all, each and every piece on this wonderful album, spiritually refreshing. As Margaret Leng Tan explains in a separate documentary ( John Cage: The Works for Piano 6), the modifications designed for each piece in the "Prepared Piano" series really create a unique instrument that is no longer piano.  The "voices" created by these modifications are sometimes percussion ( eg the tingling of a washer against a screw when the key is struck) and always  a haunting journey into the mysticism of sound.  Margaret Leng Tan's pure delight in Cage shines in every sound. This album includes one non Cage piece,also from the 1944 "imagery of Chess" show as a companion to "Chess Pieces" that belongs in this group.

title: An overlooked gem of a Christmas Album
text:
I have to say that I'm a bit surprised to see that no one has reviewed this John Anderson Christmas CD. I've had the CD for about 4 years, and it's among the top ten Christmas CDs I own -- and I own quite a few.

I like this CD first because John Anderson has a wonderful voice, and shines on ballads -- many of the songs he's chosen for this album would be considered Christmas ballads.

Second, because he hasn't included many 'one off' songs, like so many artists seem to do these days. It's not unusual to see newly released Christmas CDs with 50% of the songs as tunes I've never heard of. I like the classics, and I like them well-done. And that's what you get with John Anderson.

Anderson's voice isn't for everyone - you'll hear some folks say it's 'too' country - but if you're a true country music fan, particularly one with a few years on you, you should grab this CD. Other no-brainers to add to your collection: "Let It Be Christmas," by Alan Jackson, "Light of the Stable", by EmmyLou Harris, and "Blue Grass and White Snow" by Patty Loveless. They are among the very best Christmas CDs - by any artist in any genre - you'll find. For what it's worth, I consider Jackson's "Let It Be Christmas" to be the best Christmas CD ever released -- and I like pop music as much or more as I do country.

Anderson's isn't as good as Jackson's, but it's still a fine collection of mostly classic Christmas songs.

title: good for any day of the week...
text: This is the debut album by the Manchester quartet, THE SUNDAYS.  Not unlike Manchester's finest, THE SMITHS, THE SUNDAYS play a similar brand of simultaneously shimmering and jangly brit-pop.  in fact, i wonder if THE SUNDAYS name was taken from the "silent and grey" day MORRISSEY so easily described on this debut solo album _viva hate_ two years earlier.  at it's very worst, _reading writing and arithmetic_ is a worthy tribute to THE SMITHS, with pleasant deviation in direction at the vocal position.  as quirky and snarky and utterly brilliant as MORRISSEY was/is, vocalist harriet wheeler brings her own set of positives.  his voice is cutesy and juvenile-sounding, in that CYNDI LAUPER sort of way.  and yet there's a maturity in her composure.  despite being pushed to the forefront in the mix, wheeler shows a good deal of restraint in never over-singing, but rather doing her part to pump out well-crafted, song-oriented jams.  i find the production a bit stiff and muted-sounding; though it appears other reviewers see this as a high-point.  it has a particular effect on the drums, as they tend to sound like they were recorded with pads on.  wheeler and guitar-player david gavurin are definitely given center stage on the album's mix, while the rhythm section seems to have been ordered to lay low.  nevertheless, it works.  the production is certainly unique and could perhaps boost the perception of a grey, humdrum Manchester and the mixed feelings that go along with that.  but in spite of the strength of the two singles and select others, i find _reading writing and arithmetic_ together lovely and a tad underwhelming.  as mentioned in the editorial review, the album is a bit singular in sound and some songs seem to get lost in the shuffle.  despite the catchy, feasible nature of the music, it's an album that requires a lot more of your attention than you would suspect, lest the album's finished playing and you're left wondering if it's a good as it was made out to be.

title: A dynamic duo!
text: Earl's Chair is the dynamic duo of fiddler, Michael Albert, and guitar/bouzouki player, Henry Lebedinsky, both of The Beggar Boys (try their "The Night the Word Was Born" Christmas album--gorgeous! You'll have to Google it as it is not on Amazon). All tunes are traditional or penned by Albert and Lebedinsky. The sound is smooth and you can tell they have been playing together for some time--the playing is tight and captures their simpatico. My favorites are some of the slower tunes, especially Gladys Maryott's (dedicated to Lebedinsky's wife's grandmother--so sweet)--it makes me cry every time. Albert pulls emotion out of the fiddle and the whistle that taps into the deepest longings in the human soul. I have seen them live and they are fantastic performers and have true musical genius. This album is highly recommended!

title: Great country Christmas album
text:
This is my first Blake Shelton CD and it might not be my last. I am not a huge country fan. I have seen Blake on The Voice, I love Christmas, and the convergence of those two facts convinced me that I should give this CD a listen.

The emotion in Blake's voice really comes through. He feels these lyrics. The most moving song is the reworked Home with Michael Buble. I honestly don't think much about Michael B but I love the two of them together on this song.

I own a ton of Christmas music, and honestly I have enough versions of White Christmas, Winter Wonderland, etc., in every genre to last a lifetime. What makes this CD for me are the unusual songs. In addition to Home, I also love Oklahoma Christmas (with Reba), Santa's Got a Choo-Choo Train, and Time for Me to Come Home. I think Blake does something special with I'll Be Home for Christmas, and I do love his version of Jingle Bell Rock with wife Miranda Lambert. Probably 8 of the tracks on this generous 14-track effort are really special.

It is part of the drill for an artist to introduce a Christmas record with some version of "Since I was a little kid, I have always loved Christmas." Scotty McCreery says pretty much the same thing. Blake proves his love of Christmas with this record - the joy and passion are right there to hear. Scotty's effort is a little more pedestrian, I'm sorry to say.

So far for me this is the best new Christmas record of the season.

title: The Album that seriously put Def Leppard on the MAP
text:
While I love to brag that I discovered Def Leppard before the "Masses" did after Pyromania literally exploded on the scene, it truly doesn't matter when you discover them--only that you do. While 'High 'N Dry' remains (probably) my all-time favorite Leppard release, there is SO much to love about Pyromania that I hardly know where to begin...

To a large extent, 'Photograph' was the song that most people remember hearing first by these underrated English Metal Masters. Sure, it was an enormously HUGE hit, but remains one of my least favorite songs from their repetoire. The song from Pyromania that just *Did It* for me, was probably 'Rock, Rock 'Til you Drop'. It had ALL the ingredients of what (in 1983) I was looking for in a Pop Metal sound. From there I became enthralled with other classics, 'Billy's Got A Gun', 'Comin' Under Fire' and of course, 'Too Late For Love'. Sure, 'Rock of Ages' was a radio staple, but I found so much more to enjoy, the least of which also included 'Foolin' and 'Action! Not Words'.

You have to remember that as I purchased this record (or cassette as I recall my first copy happened to be) I was still jammin' to 'Bringin' On The Heartbreak/Switch 625', 'Mirror Mirror', 'Another Hit And Run' and 'Let It Go'--just a small sampling of what made Def Leppard AWESOME from 'High 'N Dry'...so Pyromania was just a natural extension of what I already LOVED about their 2nd record. Unfortunately their first record, 'On Through The Night' just didn't have that mass appeal they managed to succeed with in their subsequent releases. That isn't to say that they haven't laid more than their share of eggs over the years, but Pyromania is a perfect example of when a band was definitely in the Right Place at the Right Time. I wonder if the same record were produced today, would get the same kind of love that it received when it came out over 25 years ago?

I've been in radio for the better part of 20 years now, and being exposed to bands on a daily basis, some of which have that *IT* sound, and the vast majority that simply doesn't, I have developed an ear (I guess) for what sound works, and what sound falls flat. Pyromania, for the Pop Metal fans out there easily ranks in the Top 10 of ALL-Time. Record sales alone proves this to be true, although Hysteria literally blows it away in that category. Say what you want about how the band has evolved over the years, one thing remains constant: my un-ending excitement every time the beginning riff to virtually ANY song off this cd begins to play.

text: I bought this on CD, but I imagined that there was two very different and distinct sides to this record. It comes on strong and lush and soulful for the first say, half a dozen songs and then Love breaks out the acoustic (not always a bad thing, but it doesn't work here). From there, it was one dull throwaway song after another. "Celebrity Skin" is front-loaded with effective studio wizardry and technology and when it all comes together, it feels pretty good and rocks your socks and even makes you a little wistful with its imagery. However, it seriously runs out of energy in its second half. I'm only guessing, but it's probably not a coincidence that Love shared arrangement and musical duties with Billy Corgan on the first half of the album. When they click, it's effective synergy. But this record is unfinished, as far as I can tell-Courtney alone cannot carry this middling, top-heavy concept record about California.
