title: Successful...and almost famous
text:
How many of us have dreamed about being rock stars? Probably most of you reading this review, huh? I can remember in 1964 when my friends and I badgered our parents into buying us guitars and/or drums and formed a band. What was always a hoot about it all was the emphasis we placed on how we should look and act on stage. Never mind the fact we couldn't play yet; we had to look the role. More to the point, exactly what did being a rock star mean? Well, it was to be like those bands we saw on Hullabaloo and Shindig and - for those of use with UHF convertor boxes - Disc-O-Teen as well as those bands in films. We were going to be bigger than The Beatles.

What didn't enter our minds was that massive success came to few bands and only a portion of those saw longer-lasting success. The Beatles ended their success by disbanding. The Rolling Stones, on the other hand, roll on and on; presumably until Jagger dies or is killed by Keef. Other other groups were only ever able to come up with a single successful record. Like the proverbial shooting star, they were here today and gone tomorrow. So, when all is said and done, you really need to define what the word `success' means before you try to measure it.

I'm rambling like this for a reason. Success is ephemeral and subject to a situational and personal set of criteria for definition. The Beatles were successful to be sure; they set a bar that - in my opinion - will never be exceeded. But, is a not a band that can fill a bar on weeknight in the suburbs also successful? And, can the same thing be said about a touring group that plays a circuit? The answer is, of course, a resounding YES! if you are satisfied with what is happening. Like beauty, success is in the eye if the beholder.

The CD under review here is by The Chains and is titled `The Beatles of El Paso.' It is produced by a relatively new label named 60sgaragebands, which is an outgrowth of a website that collects info bands...like the name says. One might feel anger at the audacity of the group and/or the label to use a title like that. But, the moniker was attached to the band in the 60s by a local DJ who - with likely complete objectivity - believed them to be the best non TexMex band in the area. The story of this band; its predecessors and descendants is at once mundane and surprising. The Pinney brothers grew up in the New York Metro. Both exhibited musical talent and were in various, though separate bands, from 1960 on. One incarnation, The Dolphins, was a surf band that recorded and released two 45s. When older brother Roy went away to college (in New Mexico...talk about a change from the East Coast!), he dabbled in several bands until he and three friends came together in a group called Rasputin and The Chains. They were modestly successful locally, then relocated from New Mexico State University to the University of Texas at El Paso. There, the band name was truncated to The Chains and younger brother Tor Pinney migrated to El Paso to join them. Over the 1965 - 1968 period, the band issued a few 45s, toured relentlessly throughout the Mountain Time Zone; lost Roy Pinney and then moved back to NYC to play in Manhattan. In fact, the band played regularly at the Peppermint Lounge. But, as these stories go, the grind of being a mid-level success was wearing and the band split up in 1969.

End of story.

No!

In a case that utterly is rock `n' roll, Tor Pinney was approached by a record label to form a touring band that would perform a certain hit that was sweeping the country. You see, the song had been written and recorded by session players and the label wanted to profit from the song's success. Tor agreed, called some of his buddies and became Steam of Na Na Hey Hey Kiss Him Goodbye fame. After that success, he worked behind the scenes for a while, and then left music without regret.

So, what about the CD? Well, the music on it is very, very good. The last six songs are from the surf band period and a typical of the genre - they've got a good beat and you can dance to them. The first 14 cuts are by The Chains and include the regional hit `I Ain't Gonna Eat Out My Heart Anymore.' The songs, the band and the production is all very good to excellent. There's a pretty wide range of styles here, ranging from middle-of-the-road harmonies; a stab at psychedelia with a 'Paint It Black' rhythm line; some slightly heravier stuff that might presage Grand Funk Railroad and - in case you forgot where they're from - Lovin' Spoonful cover. As you listen, you know that they were a damn good band, one you would have planned to see if you had the chance.

Successful.

Especially when the music comes at super budget price from a respected label like Naxos. Okay, the Penguin guide is a little dismissive of this disc, saying that Francois-Joel Thiollier isn't as competitive as the big names. Rubbish. He's a fantastic pianist who gives color to any piece he plays, as his recordings of the Ravel concertos and de Falla's Nights in the Gardens on Spain can attest (also on Naxos). The ever-reliable National Symphony Orchestra of Ireland is completely first rate, and the sound is one of Naxos' best. You simply cannot be disappointed by the performances of these works, and though there may well be better versions out there, where can you find all these works on one disc? And they go together so beautifully...

Shamefully, it took me well over 10 years to discover the sheer beauty that is Franck's Symphonic Variations. It's one of the most concise and dramatic works of the century, particularly in a period that was known for its verbosity. It's every bit as passionate as his famous D minor symphony, but unlike that magnificent work, it has dashes of humor and playfulness. The surprise in this program is Faure's Ballade, a gently unfolding piece that reveals its charms slowly, over a few listens. But it's quite dramatic in its way, with a broad, sensuous melody that becomes very compelling. I've heard the solo version of the Ballade, and I think the orchestration, though subtle, adds just the right amount of color and atmosphere. And then there's the show stopper by D'Indy, Symphony on a French Mountain Air, which is right up there with de Falla's famous concertante work. Both works reek of nationalist perfumes, exotic colorings, and exquisite melodies. This work is jaw-droppingly effective, and only gets better with repeated listenings. From the brooding, dramatic first movement, we pass into a tender, mysterious slow movement, and then into the rollicking finale with the most memorable melody in the world. It's irresistable.

So in short, a fabulous disc, beautifuly played, with some of the most engaging piano/orchestra literature in the 19th century. I waited far too long before buying this disc. Don't make my mistake.

text: Fighting the demons that plague most rock n' roll bands; Alice In Chains released their third long player late in 1995. This eponymous LP could be seen as one of the last important grunge discs although AIC were among the heaviest metal that the grunge movement ever produced. Lanye Staley's heroin addiction was hurting the band but to their credit (and perhaps detriment) Jerry Cantrell stayed with his talented but unpredictable front man though AIC would not tour in support of the album. `AIC' the record is as diverse as the group would ever be and proved to be their swan song as Staley would lose his battle with drugs within a decade.  "Grind" was the defiant opener, lead single and received immediate airplay as the LP debuted at number one on the charts. However due to the lack of a tour the sales did not match previous highs. "Again", "Heaven Beside You" and "Over Now" were all blasting out of alternative rock radio stations throughout '96. The album featured slower epic building tracks like "Sludge Factory", crankers such as "Brush Away" and slower oddities like "Frogs". Maybe not for all tasted but `AIC' was a great way to end a legendary band's first act and a suitable way to bid farewell to another rock tragedy.

title: great traditional metal
text:
Armored Saint have been around a long time, most famous for loaning the talents of vocalist John Bush to Anthrax for a couple of albums. However, since comparisons between the two are inevitable, in songwriting quality Armored Saint are far superior to Anthrax. "La Raza" is a great album, full of memorable tunes, intelligent subject matter and great guitar playing. "Loose Cannon" starts off the set, a fine rocker as any, showcasing not only Joey Vera's songwriting chops but the advanced chord work and blazing lead work of Phil Sandoval and Jeff Duncan.
Armored Saint are not thrash, metalcore or other offshoot of metal. They are in the finest tradition of classic bands like Judas Priest, Saxon and Iron Maiden, full of great melodies and lyrics that actually mean something. Perhaps the best track is the title track "La Raza", with its Latin rhythms and congas adding a great atmosphere to a fine tune. This is metal for adults who actually care about the world around them and are still not afraid to rock at the same time. One of metal's most underrated bands.

title: Ritual Coffee Memories
text:
I was just reading an article about a coffee shop in Brooklyn that rotates a selection of specialty roasted espresso beans from small roasters from around the country, including Ritual Coffee on Valencia St. in the Mission. Their sweet, fruity espresso is linked forever in my mind to this album, which featured in 2005-2006 along with Wolf Parade's Apologies to the Queen Mary and Postal Service's We Will Become Silhouettes as the post-punk synth pop genre moved on from Modest Mouse's 2004 megahits.

To me, "The Woodland National Anthem," captures the musical exuberance and playfulness that puts Arcade Fire's more restrained tone pieces and dark lyrics into the context of a group of friends exploring a wonderful new musical terrain. It is exciting to look back at this short album and see the driving sense of rhythm here carried into the intense orchestral tapestry of The Suburbs. I like to think of Sprawl II as the post-apocalyptic realization of the fears expressed in Woodland National Anthem, in which we hear attempts at escaping authority and its destruction, "Trees keep fallin' at my feet/ I guess it's time to build a boat/ Make a raft of our bodies/ Do you think that it'll float?" By the time we get to 2010, there is really no escape, "Living in the sprawl/Dead shopping malls rise like mountains beyond mountains/And there's no end in sight,/I need the darkness someone please cut the lights." The irony of course is that the mountains beyond mountains reference is to a Haitian proverb encouraging hopefulness in the face of ongoing problems.

title: Not Thin Lizzy Wannabes (4-1/2 stars!)
text:
The band started off being a Thin Lizzy cover band, and the melodic twin guitar approach remains, but their songs are not copies of Thin Lizzy. This is just gold old-fashioned classic hard rock, a la Thin Lizzy. Just about every song sticks in your head, with catchy riffs, and fine vocals. Thankfully, the production is such, that none of the songs sounds dated. These guys would have been a top selling band in the late 70's, early 80's, and will hopefully become so, very soon!
While this will cause those of us fans who grew up in the 70's to wax nostalgic, this isn't some retro band trying to copy a sound, or an image. These are timeless songs that will hold up against any of the best of that era, or of any era. In fact listening to a band craft such enjoyable music as this, makes me hate MTV even more, because they won't ever feature a band like this to the mainstream audience (maybe VH1 Classic will actually feature a new band that plays in this style? Yeah, right!)
The only reason I don't give this album 5 stars, is because of the one really slow song 'Tears Of Guilt.' It's not a bad song, and in fact, I really like the lyrics, but when the guitars kick in, it's a very slow and plodding song, that interrupts the great flow that the rest of the album provides. I find myself skipping that track, and I just can't bring myself to give an album 5 stars when I usually skip a tune. 'Inner Light' has a slow, mellow opening, but kicks in to a very nice riff laden song that really rocks. 'My Bleeding Evil' has apparently been moving up the European charts, so maybe they will get the recognition they deserve. Twinball is about the best band I've heard come out of Sweden since HammerFall.
As much of a prog metal fan as I am, I really miss this type of music. I miss having guitar riffs that I can hum along with. I have a very hard time getting this CD out of my player for any length of time, and I really hope that I don't wear out my copy, because the import price for this is a bit steep, but it's worth every penny! For those of you who would rather headbang than mosh, this CD is for you.

If you're one for a soft ballad, try "Forever Love (Digame)" and "In My Head". If you are more for alternative music that has real personality, then "Paper Bag", "In The Rough" and "Consider This" are right up your ally. If you want a touching song that really makes you think, I reccomend "Breathe(2AM)", "Wreck Of The Day" and "Catalyst". And if you want an energized, refreshing song try "Satellite" or "Citadel".

title: They're Baaaaaaack!
text:
After a 5 year hiatus in which drumer/songwriter Neal Peart lost his daughter in a car crash and wife to cancer, Rush returns and sound as good as ever.
During such a length gap, even a major fan such as myself was beginning to have doubts if there would even be another Rush album. Thankfully there is and now I'll share my thoughts, so read on...
Overall, I'd say that their latest effort stacks up pretty well against their catalog of previous albums. This isn't their best or most creative effort, but there are some instant classics and even a couple hidden gems (which take a few listens before you realize how good they are).
Rather than trying to break new musical ground, as they have done time and again over their 25+ years togeather, this disc takes a more direct approach, with the trio focusing on "just making music again."
The opening track ("One Little Victory") is noticably heavier sounding than anything they've done in at least a decade. Standouts include: "Ghost Rider", "How It Is", "Secret Touch", "Earthshine", and "Sweet Miracle." The title track ("Vapor Trail") is solid but not among the best tracks on this disc. The remaining tracks not mentioned above are a bit "samey" in that they are good, but don't stand out from the rest of the bunch.
The three tracks that I'd deem hits (and are very radio friendly IMO) are: "Ghost Rider", "Secret Touch", and "Sweet Miracle." These three are among the band's finest tracks, both lyrically and musically.
If you are a fan of the group and haven't bought this album yet, I will tell you that you won't be disappointed.

title: It'll take you home, out of this chasm.
text:
Unlike many fans, Oldfield came to me in February 1988 via radio in the U.S. By chance, I heard the song "Magic Touch" and was sold instantly as a 15 year old. I went right out and bought this 'new' artist, Mike Oldfield, and his "Islands" cd. I listened to it over and over again. It really was the first album I bought that had a 20 minute instrumental which I though was revolutionary at the time (as I had not anything like it in my music collection, even though I had already bought 1986's "Emerson, Lake & Powell" and "Invisible Touch" by Genesis, so I was familiar with some long-form songs). I also liked the five 'pop' songs. It was Max Bacon on vocals for "Magic Touch", and I knew him from two years prior when I bought 1986's "GTR" and the hit "When The Heart Rules The Mind". Still, "Islands" might have been my first introduction to what could be termed "New Age" music which would be solidified the following year when I 'discovered' Enya's "Orinoco Flow" on her 1988 "Watermark" cd.

It would be many years before I collected most of Oldfield's albums on cd as they were extremely hard to come by in the U.S. in the late 1980's and early 1990's. I'm pretty sure I knew after buying "Islands" that Oldfield had done the theme music for "The Exorcist", but I don't think I knew it was a stand alone album called "Tubular Bells". In fact, I believe I owned "Tubular Bells II" before buying the "Elements" box set in 1993 which exposed me to the original "Tubular Bells". Basically, from "Islands" forward, I bought everything Oldfield did as it was released in real time.

So, in a way, I have been a fan of Oldfield's music since 1988 to the present. I own all of his albums now, and I listened to all of them in chronological order before listening to "Man On The Rocks" and writing this review. It took a few weeks, but it can be said that there is likely a division among Oldfield fans. Those who like his 70's instrumental works like "Tubular Bells", "Hergest Ridge", "Ommadawn" and "Incantations", and those who like his more pop works like "Five Miles Out", "Crises", "Discovery", "Islands", "Earth Moving" and "Heaven's Open". Which most contained some long-form instrumental. I'm sure there are fans like me who enjoyed both sides of Oldfield. But here's the argument: Has Oldfield made a decent album since, say, 1994's "Songs Of Distant Earth"? Or maybe we have to go back to 1991's "Heaven's Open"?

To me, Oldfield's output over the past 20 years has been rather pedestrian and mediocre in my not so humble opinion. To me, his best years were 1973 to 1991 (of course, the Virgin years). Something was lost after Oldfield left Virgin Records. For the past 20 years Oldfield has primarily been releasing instrumental works. So, I'm sure it was a surprising turn of sorts when "Man On The Rocks" contained pop/rock songs for the first time in two decades. But, let's be honest, the music on "Man On The Rocks" is nothing new for Oldfield. It should really come as no surprise. What is different is that Oldfield has selected a young male vocalist to sing all 11 tracks. Oldfield has not tried that before. I am not familiar with Luke Spiller, but his vocals are fine by me. Although, I really prefer the female vocalists Oldfield picks. That being said, the lyrics are pretty good for Oldfield who usually tends to write slight pop songs. The problem here is that the album is once again bloated and over-long at nearly an hour. Trim the fat, Mike. Also, the music is pleasant, but not really memorable. It sounds like Oldfield, to be sure, but it's still missing that 'magic'. You know, like "To Be Free" from 2002's "Tres Lunas". That song was really good, catchy, memorable. These songs on "Man On The Rocks" are just okay.

"Sailing" is a good track, and so is "Man On The Rocks". "Castaway" and "Minutes" are decent along with "Moonshine" and "Dreaming In The Wind". However, the second half of the disc is worth criticizing. "Nuclear" and "Chariots" are repetitive and almost irritating. "Following The Angels" is pleasant enough but goes on for eight minutes and wears out its welcome. "Irene" is cringe worthy and the worst track here. The album closes with a decent number, "I Give Myself Away". So, half an album's worth of decent, not great or fantastic, material.

I like that Oldfield returned to the pop/rock song form here, but the music isn't quite up to par. It has been six long years between this, "Man On The Rocks" and Oldfield's last album, 2008's "Music Of The Spheres", which is the longest gap between albums in Oldfield's career. You know what would be interesting? If Oldfield worked with established artists like Daryl Hall, Lindsey Buckingham, Elton John, Eric Clapton, Paul Simon, or Annie Lennox, Sarah McLachlan, Tori Amos, Kate Bush or even Imogen Heap. Those would be interesting choices to write lyrics and music with. What if Oldfield worked with Phil Collins or Peter Gabriel?

I'm just saying that Oldfield could be taking greater risks musically. He could be more adventurous. He's tried so many genres of music in his career, but he's done very little collaborating with established artists (he did work with Jon Anderson of Yes, for example, and Bonnie Tyler, too).

So, here's how "Man On The Rocks" compares with Oldfield's previous works:

1973 Tubular Bells: Five Stars
1974 Hergest Ridge: Four Stars
1975 Ommadawn: Five Stars
1978 Incantations: Four Stars
1979 Platinum: Three Stars
1980 QE2: Five Stars
1982 Five Miles Out: Five Stars
1983 Crises: Five Stars
1984 Discovery: Four Stars
1984 The Killing Fields: Four Stars
1987 Islands: Five Stars
1989 Earth Moving: Three Stars
1990 Amarok: Four Stars
1991 Heaven's Open: Three Stars
1992 Tubular Bells II: Three Stars
1994 The Songs Of Distant Earth: Three and a Half Stars
1996 Voyager: Two and a Half Stars
1998 Tubular Bells III: Three Stars
1999 Guitars: Two Stars
1999 The Millennium Bell: Two Stars
2002 Tres Lunas: Two Stars
2005 Light + Shade: Three Stars
2008 Music Of The Spheres: Three and a Half Stars
2014 Man On The Rocks: Three Stars

title: Perhaps the greatest Boris ever!
text:
For those who appreciate Russian opera, this recording is an absolute must. It captures the atmosphere of old czarist Russia better than any otherI have heard. This is not the only recording Boris Christoff made of this opera, but it is by far the best. All the czar's torment of conscience for the brutal murder of the child who was the rightful heir to the throne simmers and boils in this performance. Boris' death scene is absolutely blood-curdling. The remainder of the cast were well chosen to support the main focus of the work. The children provide some dramatic relief, but even they seem to be under the shadow of the czar's guilt. Dobrowen's conducting ideally supports this intense drama.

Christoff also sings the lead in both prologue scenes very convincingly.

This is a monophonic recording, but the sound is very good. The vinyl, Capitol version is only slightly superior. The lack of stereo goes entirely unnoticed once the drama begins.

The only downside is the lack of a libretto. This was included in the vinyl performance. For some, a scene synopsis may be sufficient because of the incredible vocal acting. A knowledge of the meaning of Boris' last words though will add much to appreciating this great performance.

Don't miss out on this one!

title: Another superb album from Mexico
text: If you pick up any Mexican compilation in a UK shop you will find it is utter rubbish. This is a real shame because, with Cafe Tacuba, Maldita Vecindad, Los de Abajo, El Gran Silencio and Plastillina Mosh, Mexico produces some superb rock. The country's music is sadly under-rated and, at least in the UK, not well represented. This latest offering from Los de Abajo offers a range of styles (Salsa, Polka, Rap, Son Jorocha, etc). These traditional styles have been up-dated with a welcome input of energy (although the cliche, ever present on Mexican albums, about punk energy is becoming a bit worn). The CD is on David Byrne's Luaka Bop label which should already be enough to give it the benefit of the doubt. The album sets out to celebrate Mexico city and includes various street sound samples. It is also very political containing numerous attacks on the corruption of the Mexican government and offering support for the country's indigeneous Indian population. The beautiful sleeve contains English translations of the lyrics (though sadly not the Spanish originals) and a short piece introducing the band and their songs.

OK OK. I too am an indie-rock snob. But I'm older and wiser now--wise enough to know I don't know everything, but why are people so quick to jump on the "SELL-OUT!!!" bandwagon? People are angry that the album sounds different, that new listeners are actually liking MM. And that this is BAD!?! Why? So they are not as obscure as YOU the indie-rock snob want them to be. Remember Velocity Girl, or even better Tuscadero (not unless you did the early 90's DC scene)? Velocity Girl's debut on Sub Pop out-sold Nirvana's Bleach, and it was sugary and poppy and, well, mediocre. But I digress.
I fell in love with MM on Lonesome Crowded West (that was still indie, so am I a bandwagoneer or not?), and I was AFRAID to buy anything else from them because it was beautiful, and obscure, and must be their musical apex. Well, I picked up Good News this weekend on a friend's advice, and found that if you don't take risks, you aren't rewarded.
This is a record that I instantly liked, which is rare. It won't please everyone, and if you don't like it, be disappointed and move on. But if enough people are buying the record so that MM can make more and share their world with us for a little longer, at least be comforted that we have choices outside of top-40 radio.

title: An Excellent Overview
text:
My interest in the music of Richard Galliano dates back several years to when I responded to a recommendation of one of his albums on this site. That recommendation came to me based on my purchases of quite a few Astor Piazzolla CDs. I bought Passatori just to give Galliano a shot and the rest, as they say, is history. Several years later and many RG CDs since then, I picked this one up so as to have a quick fix of some of his best tunes and to introduce friends to Galliano's musical talents.

I agree with the industry reviewer. Gallianissimo is an excellent overview of his career, covering a lot of ground from tango to jazz and many styles in between. Galliano proves here that he is not a one trick pony, not a Piazzolla clone, but an incredibly talented musician with ideas and a direction all his own. Those interested need only to hear for themselves the sheer elegance and virtuosity of Galliano's play to be convinced.

Its hard to pick favorites here, but if pressed I'd choose the romantic Laurita, the jazzy Waltz For Nicky, the stunning Invierno Porteno, the jumping Fou Rire, the sleek La Valse A Margaux, the driving and frenetic Viaggio, Tango Pour Claude, and the cover of the melancholy Piazzolla masterwork, Oblivion.

I recommend this CD highly not only to newcomers to Galliano's music, but also to those who have already heard a few of his albums. You will be astounded at the breadth of his talent and you will find your money well spent.

title: Not the Right Kind of Release for A Teen Pop Star Like Justin Bieber, 2 stars
text:
[[ASIN:B00AU2B0DE Believe Acoustic]] arrives in 2013, likely aimed at tiding over Justin Bieber's fans until his new studio effort materializes. The main problem with Believe Acoustic is that the concept nor the album itself seems to suit a youthful pop star like Bieber. Throughout the effort, Bieber often overdoes the vocal runs, trying to compensate for a lack of full production; he accompanied either by acoustic guitars or piano. The results are as expected - mediocre overall.

"Boyfriend" holds up surprisingly well under acoustic treatment, perhaps because it was a huge hit for the pop star. With pros come cons and the cons of "Boyfriend" as ultimately its ridiculous songwriting which includes references to Buzz Lightyear and fondue. Even so, "As Long As You Love Me" is clumsier as Bieber sounds rhythmically lethargic on the "l-l-l-love me" lyrics at times and clumsy covering Big Sean's rap verse vocally. "Beauty and a Beat" follows, but seems even more ill-suited to ever be considered an acoustic offering.

"She Don't Like The Lights" helps to redeem the set, yielding sound acoustic guitar accompaniment and solid vocals by Bieber. "Take You" seems almost redundant, given the original's prominent use of acoustic guitar. "Be Alright", a less memorable cut from [[ASIN:B007VT6QSI Believe [Deluxe Edition]]] fails to stand out here in acoustic form. "All Around the World", the opener for the parent album, similarly garners no more love acoustically. Finally, "Fall [Live]" finds Bieber overindulging in vocal runs to atone for the cut's blasé nature. Of the originals receiving acoustic treatment, "Boyfriend" and "She Don't Like The Lights" fare best.

"Yellow Raincoat" is one of three new cuts. Bieber sings it in hushed manner and while his subtlety is appreciated, it does little to reinvigorate momentum for this rather boring affair. "I Would" has similarities in sound to John Mayer's "Waiting on the World To Change". While it is nice to hear Bieber accompanied by electric guitar and drums, the cut has its own imperfections. Vocally, Bieber's is inconsistent; his falsetto is thin, sometimes he changes his tone, and occasionally his diction lacks clarity (mush mouthed). By the time closer "Nothing Like Us" arrives, the listener is happy. Unfortunately, the closer opts for slower, more hushed fare as opposed to given the listener some `bounce' and much needed tempo.

Overall, [[ASIN:B00AU2B0DE Believe Acoustic]] falls short of Bieber's studio work. Even after listening, one wonders why a second acoustic affair was needed. Perhaps if Bieber wanted to tide over fans, a remix album or even an EP would have been a better choice. This is a mediocre, unnecessary release ultimately.

title: NOT "Fritz Reiner - The Complete RCA Collection"
text:
This is one of those annoying, venting reviews one finds too often on Amazon. My particular bugbear is with Sony, not the music. If you want a thorough review of the music, please read elsewhere. My cursory take is these performances are excellent, but often a little soulless. For whatever reason, the lighter fare fares better as interpretations after so many years.

My complaint is that a bit of misleading advertising by Sony becomes false advertising on this website. This is *not*, as Amazon claims, "Fritz Reiner - The Complete RCA Album Collection."

Let me provide an obvious and glaring example. Perhaps the most famous opera recording of all time -- one that all casual listeners over 60 years of age have heard -- is Fritz Reiner's RCA recording of "Carmen" starring Risë Stevens. Is it in this box? Nope. This box contains only those: (1) albums; (2) conducted by Fritz Reiner; (3) on RCA; and (4) with the Chicago Symphony Orchestra. Do you want to hear Vladimir Horowitz play Beethoven or Rachmaninov with Reiner conducting? Those aren't here. Do you want to hear Marian Anderson sing with Reiner? Or William Kapell play Rachmaninov with Reiner? Or the album where Reiner conducts Mendelssohn's Midsummer Night's Dream along with Debussy and Ravel? Not here, and the last contains Reiner's *only* studio recording of Le Tombeau de Couperin. Yet every last one of these are RCA albums. They just happen to feature Reiner conducting the RCA Victor, the NBC, or the "Robin Hood Dell" (really the Philly) orchestras. Of course, RCA also recorded stuff with Chicago that they did *not* release, notably some rather humdrum Bach with Andre Tchaikovsky. That, too, would be a nice addition to this box.

I get that most people who bought this box or are now contemplating it at an obscene price on the resale market really want Reiner with the CSO (but there is more of that, as well). The real problem for *Reiner collectors* is this: what will happen with all the other really fine RCA recordings? Sony lost a chance to fold these in with the recent Pittsburgh Columbia recordings as some sort of "Early Reiner" or "Reiner Before Chicago" box. It seems highly doubtful now that Sony will release a hodgepodge collection, even if the other orchestras were some of the most famous in the world.

So you might think "I love Reiner and I would love to collect his commercial recordings. Except for a few easily available Vienna Phil discs, Sony owns virtually everything." But you will be hard pressed to track down a lot of what Sony has and may never release together in a box.

This is not "Fritz Reiner - The Complete RCA Album Collection."

End Rant. What is here is good stuff. If you want even more Reiner with the CSO (but do not care if it is RCA), try also to track down two big boxes released by the CSO (one is still for sale quite cheaply by the orchestra itself!) and in a series of radio recordings released for WFT pledge drives. If you care about Reiner beyond the CSO, Pittsburgh, and the VPO ... well, it gets more difficult.

title: Haunting Record By An Amazing Artist With An Amazing Past
text:
Roky Erickson and John Lennon have at least one thing in common: The authorities wanted both of them behind bars, if at all possible. It's no secret that Nixon sicked the FBI on Lennon. They were especially interested in his drug use, as that was seen as the easiest way to "catch" him. Lennon, like Erickson, was literally seen as a threat to society. Nixon was really more concerned about Lennon's leftist views because he had such a massive following. The battle being fought at the time was to convince the public that Vietnam was a good idea. In the end, they couldn't ensnare Lennon, so they tried to get him deported.

Erickson didn't have the global reach Lennon did, but he and his band, the 13th Floor Elevators, were huge in Austin. They unashamedly announced that they were tripping on LSD at -every- live gig, and encouraged their fans to do the same. The local authorities didn't like that, and thus began an organized campaign to bust Erickson and put him away. They were successful, and when Erickson was arrested for possession of -one- joint in 1969, his lawyer decided to enter a not guilty due to insanity. The judge obliged, and Erickson was sent to a state mental hospital, then to Rusk State Hospital, which is officially not a maximum security facility, but as a practical matter has all the earmarks of one. Erickson was subjected to electro shock and permanently zoned out on Thorazine for years.

By the time I was living in Austin in the 80s, Erickson was out of the mental hospital, and living in seclusion. His shadow still loomed large all over town. Many of the counter culture establishments from the 60s, both musical and otherwise, were still alive and well, and the 13th Floor Elevators' presence was everywhere.

Fast forward to 2010, and Will Sheff, frontman of another Austin based band, Okkervill river, is sent 3 CDs cointaining Erickson's songs from the early days to more recent ones, and asked to produce a new album with him. In the CD liner notes, Sheff describes how humbled he felt in the presence of Erickson, and after the album's release, wonders whether he should have picked some additional or different songs to re record from the collection he'd been sent. He wisely left some of the songs exactly the way he received them, in very rough form, as recorded on very basic equipment decades ago. Those capture background sounds like a TV in the living room where they were recorded as well as bird and cricket sounds from the backyard.

After a few listens to the CD, I'm hard pressed to describe the songs as beautiful, but as raw as they are, when you hear the brutal honesty of "True Love Cast Out All Evil", there is a beauty which comes shining through.

Erickson is purportedly living in South Austin now in his first own house with his first wife. There's a sense in these songs that he has put all the hurt and torment behind him and is at peace. Here's hoping that lasts and we get more music and live shows from Mr. Erickson in the years to come.

There has been such a deep void of expressive women that have the ability to utter more than what women have been reduced to on radio, we've been reduced to nothing more than begging or whoring around ... in the really popular song, we do both at the same time.

title: Long-Awaited Agalloch Masterpiece
text: Long in the making, "Marrow of the Spirit" was well worth the wait. Agalloch manages to stay true to their roots while expanding the range and depth of their sound, incorporating new elements like the contributions of the incredibly talented cellist Jackie Perez Gratz (Grayceon, Amber Asylum). Not only is this one of the top ten albums of 2010; it sets a new bar for American Black Folk (or Folk Metal - Agalloch defies simple labels), and "Black Lake Nidstang" is one of the best songs - in any genre - ever written. title: Mike's best orchestrated work
text:
(This review is for the 2011 Mercury reissue.) This album was Mike’s first after a hiatus of some two years in the late 70s, and possibly his greatest and certainly most ambitious long-form composition, as well as his most heavily orchestrated. I’d actually become familiar with the condensed version on the live record Exposed, so when I first bought the studio version around 1982, I was amazed at some of the differences, especially the section that takes up a good portion of Part 3 that features one of his best guitar solos.
Sound quality is excellent, as expected. A couple of reviewers complained about a glitch in Part 4 where a brief snippet is supposed to be missing, making it sound like a needle skip and throwing off the rhythm. I couldn’t detect anything of the sort, so maybe newer copies have been corrected. The single Guilty was added as a bonus track, though it would have been nice if they could have added the extended version of Guilty as well.
I’ve complained about the deficient packaging of some of the other Mercury remasters, and this one is definitely an improvement, with a great new cover photo and other rare photos. But credits-wise, why is there no credit for or any acknowledgement of the extract from Longfellow’s “Song of Hiawatha” (sung by Maddy Prior in Part Two) anywhere? It’s beyond me how that could have been overlooked. Mike may have supervised the remastering, but he could have given the packaging a bit more attention as well. But I'm still giving it 5 stars.

title: Luther's most underrated album
text:
Even though this album peaked at a very strong #6 on the Hot 200 and was certified Platinum in sales, NEVER LET ME GO has since been unfairly labeled as one of Luther's lessor efforts. I've personally never understood this assessment. While the album may have a few weak moments (and honestly can't hold a candle to his fantastic eighties' records), it's actually quite good overall, and it has more than a fair share of standout moments. Artistically-speaking, much of the album is in the same early-'90's dance mode as THE POWER OF LOVE, however, when taken as a whole, NEVER LET ME GO is actually even better.

First of all, while it's no secret that Luther has a singing voice that is unmatched by anyone on a technical level, it is worth noting that Never Let Go features some of his finest recorded singing. The soaring ballads "Love Me Again" and "Too Far Down" are vocal tour de forces, and stand as pure examples of what Luther does best. The cleverly-arranged "Little Miracles" (#62 Pop, #10 R&B) and the kinetic "Heaven Knows" (#94 Pop, #24 R&B, #15 Dance) were both excellent single releases that deserved to be much bigger hits. The disc also concludes with a terrific medley of the Bee Gee's "How Deep Is Your Love" and Joe Scott's title track, and remains a reminder of the new spin Luther can bring to worn-out songs.

NEVER LET ME GO's biggest problem is that, aside from the cover medley, all of the disc's strongest tracks are included in the first half - which makes the album feel a little top-heavy. On the disc's second half, there are two dated techno tracks that sound like Power of Love outtakes ("Hustle," "Emotion"), both of which sound almost hysterically overwrought. Also, the song "Lady, Lady" steals the medley from Luther's own superior 1989 hit "She Won't Talk To Me" almost verbatim. However, all of this is perfectly listenable, and, in the end, it's the strong moments on NEVER LET ME GO that really stay fresh in the listener's mind. That's what makes this perhaps Luther's most underrated album. If you're already a fan of his, you won't be disappointed by picking this up.

title: The band that keeps on delivering
text:
It's kind of bizarre watching the Fall keep going, and going. I first picked up a Fall album five or six years ago. They were one of those art rock/noise bands I just never quite got around to. Well, that's OK; by the time I did, I had twenty-five years of material to sift through. And they haven't stopped producing.

By this time, Mark E Smith is almost a reproach, and a dare, to others not only of his own generation, but subsequent musicians. I love that he doesn't really play old material in concert, just the most recent couple of albums. But honestly, when you see this unsexy gargoyle up there at the microphone, with hot wife # 3 playing keyboards, and a rotating crew of new musicians to bully into shape, it seems....well it seems to make perfect sense. And I don't know how much fun it is to BE in the Fall, but it's a hell of a lot of fun to watch. I've taken nay-sayers to Fall concerts and they come away converted. The Fall deliver the goods.

There are some super high points on this album. At other times, they seem to be insisting a little to hard. But that's OK. I hope they come back to the USA this year. I will skip work, travel 500 miles, with a car full of unwilling converts-to-be, to see them do their thing. It'll be fun.

title: :W: Turning Back to "Brutal, Cruel, and Dark"
text:
About the Artist:
Wumpscut (:W:) is perhaps the seminal example of the terror EBM genre. Founded in 1991 by German industrial DJ Rudy Ratzinger, the band quickly became popular both in European and North American gothic and industrial clubs and is easily recognized by its harsh lyrics and imagery accompanied by beat heavy electronics and distorted male vocals.

About the Album:
Depending on how you count the numerous :W: releases, Siamese could be considered the 15th full-length album with new material. Long-time fans often point back to [[ASIN:B000005OPZ Embryodead]] and [[ASIN:B000BKSJHU Music for a Slaughtering Tribe]] (MfaST) has the peak of Rudy's work and often lament that his newer releases failed to continue in that direction. Siamese represents a sincere turn back towards the angrier, darker, and brooding songs of old. To steal from the lyrics from "Crown of Thorns" off of [[ASIN:B0001F7UMK Bone Peeler]], Siamese is "Brutal, Cruel, and Dark ... dark, dark, dark".

My favorite track "Killuh" features Clara S., who voiced the spoken words on "Last Salute" (from Bone Peeler). Killuh is more of a chant and one of :W:'s more somber releases. A bonus to the chant is that the ostinato (i.e. melody) slowly transitions from electronics to violins to close out the entire album.
Another highly recommended track is the instrumental "Ziribit". If you liked the [[ASIN:B000005OQA Mesner Tracks]] (MT) or intensity of songs from MfaST, then I can promise you that "Ziribit" will have you grinning and stomping. Think "Crate" from MT or "Default" from MfaST (two of Rudy's best instrumental pieces) and you will know and love "Ziribit".

Continuing the comparison of Siamese tracks with tracks of old, the opening track, "Falling From Lucifer's Grace", starts with a nice minor chord reminiscent of MfaST's The Day's Disdain mixed with Rudy's raspy lyrics to create a song that would be perfect for a Tim Burton-esque nightmare sequence. As noted in the general amazon description, the title track "Siamese" is slow paced, but like the previous tracks I mentioned, the subject matter and tone of the song easily fits in with early 1990s era :W:.

While this album is not another MfaST (my personal favorite :W: album), all the tracks are solid! The liner notes are well designed, including interesting artwork of a siamese twin skeleton and lyrics. I just keep telling myself, "It's not real! It's not real!" (and please don't tell me if it really is). While Rudy's choice to make use of a german looking (Fraktur perhaps) serif font is appropriate and adds to the flavor of the entire package, the lyrics are a pain to read. Siamese is a solid offering, so I'm giving it 5 stars.

Recommended Tracks:
* Killuh
* Ziribit

title: A Shining Star of J-Pop
text:
Even if you can't speak a word of Japanese, that should not stop you from queuing up Platinum 9 by Morning Musume. It starts with a one-two punch ("Songs" and "Resonant Blue") and progresses to a power-pop finish ("Kanashimi Twilight"). While it borrows influences from many sources, this high-energy musical explosion stands on its own after the smoke clears.
This is by far the most mature release from J-Pop giants MM and producer Tsunku. Formed as a result of a talent search in 1997, Morning Musume is famous for graduating members and bringing in new blood through a process of public auditions; at times there could be a 10 year age discrepancy between the oldest and youngest performers. For the first time since its initial generation, all the members are approximately the same age which allows the material a greater sophistication overall and more authenticity when delivered. Tsunku, who writes and produces all of the material, has become expert at integrating both lead and background vocals into synthesized instruments. As voice and music cross-fade into each other, it harkens back to Brian Wilson's approach on Pet Sounds, though Platinum 9 is much more layered and frenetic.
This record is SO MUCH FUN! There are so many things going on in this tightly woven soundscape that it is dizzying. There is just so much to listen to ranging from silly to sublime. For non-speakers, the Japanese lyrics become symphonic elements. As for the English lyrics which are peppered throughout, they are nice reference points to get the overall gist of what is going on; in particular, track 8, "Mikan" carries a message of hope and encouragement in sharp contrast to American pop music which can often feel like commercially motivated iconoclasm.
Influences include, but are by no means limited to artists such as Kylie Minogue, Beyonce, T-Pain and Robert Schumann (yup, the 19th century composer) and genres like video game soundtracks, 50's rocknroll, techno, reggaeton and latin-pop. It is easy to be dismissive of pop music which sometimes is too cliché-ridden, but the clichés are turned on their ear in this case. Platinum 9 shines.

title: Oblivious: Creating Meaning (2013)
text:
Swedish band OBLIVIOUS has been at it in one form or another since 2003, initially with Oblivion as their chosen moniker but altering it in 2009, coinciding with the release of their debut album "Goons and Master" presumably. Come 2013 and Oblivious returns with their second album "Creating Meaning", and as with their initial production it has been released through Swedish label Transubstans Records.

This fairly short album kicks off with two blues-laden, galloping affairs that has a distinct 1970's touch about them combined with a more contemporary stoner rock sound. Personally both of these gave me associations to the likes of Free as well as Queens of the Stone Age, nice and energetic affairs both that maintains a nice drive and tension throughout and concludes before the theme gets overly explored. The following Deluded Darling a creation that to me sounds closer to the stoner rock band referenced and without as many classic era references, and with a nice little delicate, acoustic interlude midways that allows some breathing space in this fairly intense affair.

Bjälkan i ditt öga is a rather different affair altogether, alternating between a Gary Moore meets Robin Trower delicate blues and a somewhat more distinct Black Sabbath flavored variety of stoner rock, while the following What A Trip is an energetic and somewhat more primitive variety of the 70's blues based hard rock meets 90's stoner rock affair. By the Neck, following an initial frail ballad prologue, kicks into a nice Queens of the Stone Age vibe, and You Are The Wall comes across to my ears as a compositions that blends a Black Sabbath inspired verse segment with a Queens of the Stone Age inspired chorus section. Nice stuff too I might add. When this disc concludes with Entering The Night we're treated to material of a vastly different nature altogether, acoustic guitars and piano supporting the lead vocals in more of a basic roots and Country manner on this one. With a brief hidden track feature appearing at the very end that is another delicate little run.

Strong, melodic lead vocals is a key feature all along, and the band is tight and competent in all areas. And while there's nothing original nor innovative to discover on this occasion, it is an album that should have a wide appeal with a certain easy to like and enjoy attitude incorporated into the sound and atmosphere of this production.

If you find the thought of a band blending 70's blues based hard rock with 90's melodic stoner rock to be enticing, Oblivious second album "Creating Meaning" is one that merits a check. It's not a production that will have all and sundry singing it's praises to the world at large, but it's an enjoyable romp mixing the old with the not so old in a tight and enjoyable manner. Good, old fashioned fun if you like, just as suitable in your cars CD player as it is on a Friday night party with friends.

My rating: 75/100

text: Wilson's debut was a breath of fresh air in a genre that had forgotten what a fiddle should sound like.  Beyond the two bonus tracks (a Kid Rock rocker from Target and a nicely done -- even if she feels the need to brag about it on the CD --  single microphone jazz standard) she sticks close to the first CD's formula. Full Time Job is another tired ode to the housewife (tired because she's no Loretta Lynn -- still the master of such tunes -- and here it's more formula than honest), Skoal Ring can't hold up the fun beyond the first chorus, and the same goes for One Bud Wiser. title: Judy's beautiful, silvery voice in top form...
text: Judy Collins first album of original material in eight years finds her in top form with her silvery voice, and shines best on simple tracks like "Singing Lessons", "I Can't Cry Hard Enough", "Voyager", and "Checkmate", which feature Judy singing with just her piano as accompanyment.  "Sally Go Round The Roses", "You Can't Buy Love", and a Joni Mitchell cut "That Song About The Midway" are somewhat nostalgic of her earlier folk recordings from those idyllic 1960's.  Her self-penned "Wedding Song", while sung acapella and written for her husband and best friend Louis Nelson, is warm and soothing, and recorded with a bit of reverb.  My wife and I love this track so much, we used it as a processional song at our own wedding in 2007!  For devout Judy fans, her voice quality is remarkably clear for her 66 years.  A stunning album of incredibly grace and beauty, Judy's music continues to improve with each release after a rather dry spell of tepid albums in the late 1970's and early 1980's.

If you have come across Nirvana and Pearl Jam chances are that you will stumble onto Soundgarden. the most accessible pre-90's alternative group had their first commercial success with -Badmotorfinger-. To introduce myself to the band i bought -A-Sides-, There was some truly memorable singles on that album. Most of the songs came after Badmotor and i got used to the sound. Badmotorfinger is much different than the sound of A-Sides. it is even different from the two singles, "Rusty Cage" and "Outshined". both singles seem to be tamest and most understandable of the CD. most of the CD is very hard to digest and needs numerous listens to actually understand how everything fits in. title: Excellent release from a timeless band. Best release yet.
text:
Creating and performing music is a fulfilling experience and process. Using the many methods and techniques, musicians have endless options and avenues to explore. Some bands enjoy sticking to a genre, while others bend the "rules" and venture into deeper waters. There's no correct or incorrect avenue to take, since the musicians do as they please. For those who favor the more creative, a more memorable and meaningful product is released. In this case, Swallow the Sun continues on their path previously trodden. A much deeper, and more serious accompaniment is apparent on Songs from the North I, II & III. This is no brutal album, it's not extremely heavy. What it is, though, cannot be expressed in a review.

This triple full-length album Songs from the North I, II & III is Swallow the Sun's sixth album, and it's broken into three separate albums. Swallow the Sun formed in 2000, and has yet to release a boring title. Each release has its own character and beauty. This Finland-based band does what they want, and although much of their music has harsh vocals, there are plenty of instrumental and singing portions through all three album of Songs From the North.

For the purpose of this review, I'll briefly describe each album, as they differ vastly in style and sound. Swallow the Sun can generally be referred as Death/doom, melodic death metal, progressive metal. Even these descriptions fail to encapsulate the broad sound and spirit of this band, it's a starting point for those not familiar with them.

Songs from the North I: This opening album is my personal favorite out of the three. It's what you would expect from the band if your familiar with their previous release Emerald Forest and the Blackbird in 2012. At 8 tracks in total, it's 59 minutes and 20 seconds. There's a strong presence of melodic doom, and the harsh vocals are beautiful. "Rooms & Shadows" combine strong harsh vocals, with melodic deep singing which breaks the song up while fusing it as a cohesive melodic body. "Heartstrings Shattering" is a strong emotional ballad with catchy lead guitar riffs and repetitive beauty that is clean enough to became a favorite track even after the first listen.

Songs from the North II: The second disk is not even metal, but still beautiful. It has a lot of acoustic songs, and basic instruments that make it sound more like a progressive rock album. Although it lacks energy when comparing it with album I and III, it's a very complementing disk. With three CD's in total, there's no need to have every release an intense experience. What disk II brings, is a pleasant balance, and although full of peaceful emotion, there's a pain laden deep within. This CD is 42 minutes and 33 seconds.

Songs from the North III: The third and final album is 51 minutes and 57 seconds. It's, without a doubt, the darkest and most doom-infused of them all. With almost all harsh vocals, long repetitive riffs that descend to the deepest of seas, this funeral doom album is now a standard when searching for a pure endless abyss of misery. The heavy guitar affects, the slow monotonous drums, and the almost guttural deep vocals set a fantastic closures to this epic release.

If you know about Swallow the Sun, you know what you are getting – experienced, emotional metal, that's a must have for the seasoned collector. Mind you, this isn't music you listen to and jam out to, it's an experience you absorb as Swallow the Sun relives the darker side of life in a medium that's brutal, but beautiful.

This album will be released in a three CD wallet booklet, and will also be available for digital download.

*This review was originally written for Metal Injection by Nate. With permission from Metal Injection, Nate has gained the privilege to submit his reviews on his personal amazon account.

title: Stronger - Britney at her most catchy and angry!
text:
Stronger was the third single to be taken from Britney Spears' No.1 multi-million selling second album Oops!..I Did It Again. Released in December 2000, Stronger peaked at an underrated No.7 in the UK - possibly through little promotion and/or heavy competition in the singles chart from other acts. Stronger is a perfect example of a Britney pop hit. Written and produced by pop-wizard Max Martin, the song screams "HIT!" And it was; the song topped charts the world over and is one of Britney's biggest hits to date.
Stronger begins with a brilliant beat and a heavy bassline as Britney breaks out into the song. Her voice has obviously been tampered with, especially on the bits where she goes, "Baby!" The verses are a bit quiet, before building up in the bridge and letting loose in the chorus - where Britney juts lets it go and sings her heart out about how this guy left her for another woman. "Stronger than yesterday, now it's nothing but my way," sings a confident Britney. After the second chorus, there's a bit where Britney goes, "Here I go on my own, I don't need nobody - better off alone," in superb fashion. The song dips, as if sinking under water before re-surfing for the final chorus. This is what makes the song so brilliant and downright catchy for me. The video to Stronger is brilliant as well - one of Britney's best videos. It begins when Britney's finds her ex-boyfriend with another woman. Britney's just like, "whatever" before walking off in true girl-power fashion and telling him where to go. She drives around in cars, runs across bridges in the middle of the night in a storm and dances around on a chair and turning it into a walking stick! As usual with Britney's singles, the extra tracks are amazing. Track 2 is a bonus track called Walk On By. Deemed not good enough for the Oops!...I Did It Again album, it was simply put on the Stronger single as a bonus track. Well after listening to Walk On By, I can definitely say that Walk On By should've been on the album! This song is so amazing! Basically, this song is a mid-tempo pop ballad in which Britney moans over a guy about how he never notices her. Track 3 is Stronger (WIP Remix). This brilliant remix clocks in at almost 6 minutes of pure Britney dance fun! This remix is not Britney's best, but has some excellent and diverse sounds. Stronger is an absolute must for all Britney's fans - take it from me and buy all Britney's CD singles, because the remixes and bonus tracks are absolutely excellent. Buy Stronger from Amazon.com now!

title: Outstanding
text: Oh man, where do I begin.  This cd gave me hope for the musical world again.  In an environment where dime-a-dozen "punk" bands churn out catchy little songs every three and a half minutes, this cd is simply a Godsend.  Green Day has talent; Legitimate musical talent.  Talent is not writing 12 cute little guitar hooks and making an album full of what is essentially the same song on every track.  Talent is being able to mature as you grow as a band, being creative and writing good lyrics, and most of all, having the guts to do what you want to do to express how you feel.  If you listen to old Green Day, and listen to Warning, you will see what I mean about the band maturing.  I read people writing reviews calling them sellouts, blah blah blah.  These people are either ignorant, or have Billie Joe and Co. confused with someone else.  Listen to Misery, or Blood, Sex, and Booze.  How could anyone confuse that with pop?!?!  For God's sake, Misery has an accordian and a marimba in it!  Green Day is not a young group anymore.  They aren't old, but lets face it, they aren't 20 anymore.  They are more mature as people, and as a result, their music is going to change.  Think about it.  If they really, truly are punk rockers in heart and soul, then why wouldn't they put out what they want, and not worry about what anyone else thinks?  In fact, it would be selling out to just regurgitate the same tired songs again and again because you know people like them!  Speaking of the songs, they are outstanding.  From the mechanical, bass-driven "Warning" to the light-hearted, hopeful "Waiting," no song is filler.  Misery is essentially a dirge about drug abuse (and excellent, by the way), while "Macy's Day Parade" provides a nice, mellow ending to the album.  "Church on Sunday" and "Castaway" are both great tracks, and "Minority" describes better than I could ever describe the way Green Day seems to function.  They will do what they want, when they want to, and don't particularly care what people think.  Ten, twenty, even thirty years from now, when people look back at the great bands that have been, Green Day will be remembered, not only as a great band, but as a band that helped define a genre, and a band that expanded what punk music could be.  Buy this cd, and see what I mean.

title: An important CD for serious students of the viola da gamba
text: In his beautifully done CD booklet, Paolo Pandolfo presents the context and rationale for his recording of the De Machy dance suites for solo viol. Every cellist knows the Bach solo suites, most warming up with one or more daily. But what they probably don't know is how the genre of the suite of dance movements for solo instrument came about. Pandolfo traces the evolution of the genre from the lute to viola da gamba, giving us insight into De Machy's place in the pantheon of French viol composers and his role in championing the harmonic and melodic capacities of the instrument. The playing is what we have come to expect from Pandolfo-rhythmic vitality, complex ornaments completely in the service of the underlying musical structure, virtuostic playing and improvisation in the spirit and style of the 17th century. This is a lovely CD in all respects. I especially relished the movements he plucked like a lute, reflecting the fact that many of the viol composers and players of the 17th century were also first rate lutenists.

title: STILL ONE OF THE BEST
text: In 1992, I heard 'To Be With You' and fell in love with the song.  I then listened to the 'Lean Into It' album to which that song came from.  I then purchased their preceding CD and realized that Mr.Big was a hidden treasure  in the world of rock music.  Now nearly 10 years and close to twelve studio  and live album releases later I still find the Mr.Big quartet to be one of  the best.What cannot be said about these guys that hasen't already been  said?  Eric Martin is a phenomenal vocalist and his diversity in how he can  deliver is without question more evident here than any previous Mr.Big  release to date.  Billy Sheehan can't be touched onbass and, like a fine  wine, has only gotten better in time.  Pat Torpey's technique and fire on  the drums is very powerful yet so understated at the same time that I don't  think people really realize how good he actually is.  And Ritchie Kotzen,  who has always been a great guitarist in his own right, has finally found  the chemistry he has both needed and has been looking for to make him  complete and this album is a perfect illustration of how he has found that  and a great deal more with Mr.Big.I do have a bit of resentment for the  loss of Paul Gilbert who I think is more missed than a lot of people would  like to let on.  After close to 10 years together, I felt that as a group  Mr.Big had finally peaked with a defined sound and style on their 'Hey Man'  CD only to lose Paul and have to start over from scratch.  'Get Over It' is  definitley a new experience for both the group and the fans who have known  them from the start as it is both less heavy and ballad driven than all of  their previous releases and stays with a constant sound and theme with a  lot of bluesy overtones.  Fortunately the sound works and, considering it  is the first outing minus Paul, almost works to perfection.  True Mr. Big  fans will not be disappointed as they have not sacrificed their signature  sound and trademark verses that brought them to the dance to begin with. title: Good music!!!
text:
I wanted to buy this CD because I was thrilled by her first album and I bought her second album. I wanted to see her third album so I went into a shop and I listened to it there. In fact, at first I thought some of the songs weren't very rhythmical and melodic, I thought the vocals didn't fit in with the instrumental parts. ... And when I learnt the songs, I really started to like it and now I think that the music is really good, together with some catchy tunes and melodic beats. Britney's voice doesn't go very much in range, but those people who hate her should face the fact that she's got a very nice color to her voice and that's something a few people just can't bear. Anyway, I'll give you the list of the songs.
1. Slave 4 U - an unusual beat that catches attention, together with some sexy base, makes it a really unique blend which you start liking after a few listenings.
2. Overprotected - some typical Britney song, with good vocals and catchy tune. It has also got a sort of teen spirit in it.
3. Lonely - the beginning makes me practice my low range :-) I really like the change in pitch because the verses are very low and suddenly, it goes to the chorus which is set on a higher pitch, creating a good contrast. I really like this song a lot.
4. Not A Girl, Not Yet A Woman - from the movie Crossroads, I think it makes you think about yourself (if you're a girl that is), it makes you realize your true self and it's got a deeper meaning than the rest of the songs. Slow and steady, I think it's a good listening song if you feel like calming down or relaxing.
5. Boys - this song is mainly sexy talk that fits some kind of rhythm and I don't listen to it very much because I mainly like singing along and I can't sing along with this one since it's more like talking. It's ok though.
6. Anticipating - a fun-loving, easy-going song which has got really nice vocals, I like singing along with it, although it took more time to learn the pace. I really like it because it's got more like a "summer" base.
7. I Love Rock n' Roll - good and also sexy, I like Britney's voice color in that song. I really like singing along with it, the music is funky and the beat is cool.
8. Cinderella - I liked this song since the beginning, because it's got a typical likeable melody, the music is catchy and the vocals perfectly fit. One of my favorites on the album.
9. Let Me Be - even though I got the CD for a long time now, I at first didn't sing or listen to this song at all - the beginning seemed to be a bit boring. But recently I decided to listen to it and I think it's awesome - almost the best song on the album, surprisingly. I love the whole concept - also contrast between slower, less rhythmic verse and melodic, beautiful chorus. I like singing along - I basically learnt it in three listenings! :-)
10. Bombastic Love - I also liked this song since the very beginning - a typically catchy melody and verses, I like singing along. Also sort of "teen" style, with some flexible-voice parts so I liked singing those which develop voice flexibility - I think Britney does well in this song.
11. That's Where You Take Me - a sweet gentle song, easy to sing along with, with not much vocal range. It's sort of flowy and is relaxing to listen to. Also a bit of fantasy base in it, kind of dreamy. I like it although I don't listen to it very often.
12. When I Found You - a very beautiful song, with some high notes which develop your vocal range. I really like singing along with it, because it's so beautiful and challenging. Although Britney doesn't sing best the high notes (you can hear the vocalists covering up for her in there), she does have a very pretty voice all throughout the verses. It's melodic and at a slower pace.
13. What It's Like To Be Me - typical N'Sync style song, I like that style (I like N'Sync as well) because it's similar to computerized songs - the rhythm and the beat. It's also very catchy, it sticks in your head. At some places a bit challenging not for the range but more for the "cool" style of the voice color - I think Britney sings it well, especially the coloring in "don't you wanna be my man" when she sings that. So a good song on the album, perfect to close it off.
All in all I think this album was a major hit, I think it wasn't better than the first album (that was fantastic), but she improved from the second album which was sometimes boring or fake but also quite good. This album was better and I was surprised at that - the songs are really worthy of listening to, but some songs require your patience and you should spend more time listening to them so that you find the real taste of the whole thing. You won't be sorry you bought it, though. Check it out!

title: A "moody" Elvis
text: The decline of Elvis in the final couple of years of his life is well documented, many books, film materials have gone into great detail of that period of his life and career. This album definitely reflects the emotional state of his life in 1976 and 1977. Recorded mostly inside the "Jungle Room" inside Graceland (believe it or not with decent sound quality)as Elvis did want to go to a formal recording studio to record, so RCA brought one to Graceland. A few of the songs are from concerts in 1976/1977. The album generally reflects a "down" Elvis singing heart wrenching ballads of life's losses, and anguished pain. His live version of "Unchained Melody" (it is he playing the piano on the tune) is a soaring vocal achievment, as close to an opera rendition as one will get with Elvis, a stunning, towering performance where what was left of the energy he had a few months before he died was poured into every note. Same came be said for "Hurt", the reworking of the Timi Yuro tune of nearly 20 years earlier. Elvis makes it his own, and it became a concert staple for him thereafter often bringing down the house when he performed it on stage. There is some lightweight material on the album like the fumbled "Lil' Darlin'" but the album is redeemed with the Top 20 hit "Moody Blue" and excellent songs like "For the Heart and "Way Down". Believe it or not, there is an Andrew Lloyd Webber tune "It's Easy For You", a bizarre curio for Elvis fans. Then there is the punch in the gut, heart wrenching "Never Again" about the wrenching loss of love. The remaining ballads are well performed, with a nice performance of "The Last Farewell", which Elvis personally loved, you can almost see the misty coast of England in the song. This is not Elvis's best album, not a rock and roll collection. It borders on Tom Jones at time and a bit careless at other moments, but it does show the voice of Elvis, near the end was very powerful, and the emotion layed down in the tracks is very real. If you have not heard it and are a casual Elvis fan, it is somewhat different, but definitely worth a listen. I recommend you purchase it.

title: Classic Albums
text:
Gram Parsons was responsible for evolution of the sound these albums created, which was a mixture of country, rock, and americana music. After a tour with The Byrds, and a few efforts with The Flying Burrito Brothers, he released two solo albums. And now both albums are both available on one album, this one.

Sadly Parsons died a mysterious death in 1973, but without leaving us with another legacy to behold. He introduced us to Emmylou Harris, who joined him on many tracks on these albums. The way their voices intertwined and harmonized, that level of vocal power will never be met again. They lend to each other extremely well and join to create a truly blissful and beautiful sound together. She joined him on tracks such as "Still Feeling Blue", "Hickory Wind", "Hearts On Fire", the heartbreaking "Love Hurts", honky tonk "Cash On The Barrelhead", and more. Linda Ronstadt also lends her vocals, to the closing "In My Hour of Darkness".
This is truly what country music is all about. These are classic albums than more than merit a few listens. Give this one a try, you might be surprised. title: Some problems I have with this soundtrack
text:
Do mind that I'm giving this CD a five star rating - because it really is fantastic. Other than Quentin Tarantino, no director is more aware of the importance of songs in his movies than Cameron Crowe, which perhaps shouldn't be surprising considering his past as a rock journalist, and Almost Famous is one of the best song-based soundtracks I've heard - it's a nostalgic trip through Crowe's youth, as much as the Singles soundtrack was a fascinating exploration of the then-current rock revival, and it has some wonderful, classic songs. There are very few chewed-up mega-hits here; the soundtrack features some excellent, long forgotten artists like Clarence Carter and Thunderclap Newman (whose song, 'Something in the Air', doesn't really appear in the movie, but it's one of my favorites on the album) and some truly grand artists who are not quite as famous as they used to be, like Lynyrd Skynyrd and the Allman Brothers Band. Even from the few huge stars that are featured in the soundtrack, the songs selected by Crowe are not their biggest and most familiar hits, but brilliant and lesser known songs - Led Zeppelin's beautiful acoustic 'That's The Way'; Yes's 'I've Seen All Good People'; David Bowie's performance of the Velvet Underground's 'Waiting For The Man'; and Elton John's 'Tiny Dancer', one of the best songs he'd ever written, which predates his time as a mega-star.

And it's specifically because the music in Almost Famous is so good that this soundtrack is not quite satisfactory. The fantastic songs that appear in the film but are not on this soundtrack are almost too many to list - 'Search and Destroy' by the Stooges, 'Everybody Knows This is Nowhere' by Neil Young , 'Teacher' by Jethro Tull, 'River' by Joni Mitchell, 'Mona Lisas and Mad Hatters' by Elton John, 'Burn' by Deep Purple, 'Future Games' by Fleetwood Mac, 'Voodoo Chile (Slight Return)' by Jimi Hendrix, 'Sweet Leaf' by Black Sabbath, 'Misty Mountain Hop', 'Tangerine', 'Bron-Y-Aur' and 'The Rain Song' all by Led Zeppelin, 'My Cherie Amour' by Stevie Wonder - featured in one of the film's most beautiful moments. And there are more. It seems only natural to have released the soundtrack as a double album, or at least to release a second part with as many of these songs as possible. I also think it would have been incredible appropriate to include 'Cover of the Rolling Stone' by Dr. Hook (written by the great Shel Silverstein), which the band members sing in another one of the film's great scene.

Most of all, I'm missing the original Stillwater tracks, all written by Peter Frampton, Wayne Kirkpatrick and Gordon Kennedy. 'Fever Dog' is the only one that's in here, but the other great songs - 'You Had to Be There', 'Love Thing', 'Chance Upon You', 'Hour of Need' and 'Love Comes and Goes' - all of which run through film's many concert segments - can currently only be heard by buying the 2-Disc Director's Cut DVD, and that's a real shame. These are all fantastic rock songs, with great sound, great musicianship and great production (Frampton's mark can really be heard on them) and they should be released. I would rather see them on the soundtrack than classics that can be found on various classic albums from that time (e.g. Led Zeppelin III, Simon & Garfunkel's Bookends, Elton John's Madman Across the Water).

But hey, these are my two cents. It's still a great album. I love the idea of younger listeners who weren't previously familiar with this great music and are getting into it because of the movie. For those, and for anyone who loved the movie, this soundtrack is a great buy, but also check out some the albums I mentioned above, as well as Jimi Hendrix's Electric Ladyland, Elton John's Honky Chateau, Black Sabbath's Master of Reality, Jethro Tull's Living in the Past, and Led Zeppelin's ZOSO - all of which contain songs which are in the film.
