title: RIGHT ON THE MONEY!!!!!
text:
Neil is just AWESOME!!! I've always loved his work, and I love the fact he does what's in his gut, f*** what the trends are. If he feels like doing an electronic album like "Trans" in 1980, he will do it whether people like it or not. He doesn't care. That, my friends, is punk rock. And Neil, in all his guises, is a true punk rocker, and his latest record "Living With War" is totally vital, angry, on a mission, off-the-cuff, and it really resonates. The fact he wrote and recorded the songs less than a MONTH ago and put them immediately online is as telling as the music itself.

I call it emergency rock & roll.

No, the sound quality is not the greatest (kinda like a live album), but that's not the point. His guitar still cuts through with a noisiness, grunginess, and a clarity he's always been known for. I would compare this as an album-length equivalent of "Rockin' In The Free World" if that song was released right after it was written and recorded.

I completely agree with Neil's politics, and my faves are "Shock & Awe" and of course, "Let's Impeach The President", totally spot on, with direct and correct lyrics, Neil's killer guitar, the power trio arrangements, the Taps trumpet, rightly placed + self-incriminating Bush quotes, and the 100-piece choir arranged within an hour's notice (literally).

I just have 2 questions...

1-- Do we as a people HAVE the power to impeach Bush??

2-- Will Bush actually HEAR this album or will his corrupt comrades in the White House prevent him from hearing it???

What I would do is be like John Cusack in "Say Anything"...go down to Washington, stand on the lawn of the White House, hold a boombox over my head and play Neil's "Living With War" at max volume...over and over and over and over and over again...

title: Another masterpiece of Boney M. magic
text: After the enormeous success of Boney M.'s third album "Nightflight To Venus" that spent 65 weeks on the UK charts, expectations were sky high to Boney M.'s fourth LP, and the release would also be postponed several times  until finally seeing the light of day in September 1979. The group was also  starting to have serious problems within, Marcia Barrett claimed that they  were being paid far too little, and dancer Bobby Farrell was threatening to  leave if producer Frank Farian didn't allow him to sing for real on the  records (Farian had done all the male vocals in the studio himself whereas  Bobby Farrell would only sing for real in their live concerts).  Furthermore, the lead singer of one of Farian's other groups Eruption,  Precious Wilson, had left the group, now wanting to go solo, and although  Farian offered her to take dancer (but not singer) Maizie Williams' place  in Boney M., she declined. Precious Wilson would, however, be featured as a  Special Guest Star on the opening track of the new album, the pounding  disco-rock-stomper "Let It All Be Music" with solo parts by Farian, Boney  M. singers Liz Mitchell & Marcia Barrett, and a goosebumping finale  with Precious Wilson crying out on top of her lungs. Stellar! Right on to  "Gotta Go Home" which was the flagship single with "El Lute" as a double  A-side, another frenetic disco track with oil drums as a hint to Boney M.'s  Caribbean roots. Mastermind Frank Farian would, due to his anger about  Bobby Farrell's threats, show off on this L.P. that the vocals of Boney M.  were only done by himself, Liz Mitchell, and Marcia Barrett (The original  L.P. even features track-by-track vocal credits), thus he would duet with  himself on "Bye Bye Bluebird", a tight, funky disco track with flute and  sax solos, and singing with his incredible falsetto voice as well as his  deep male voice. "Bahama Mama" is a catchy disco track about Bahama Mama  who has six daughters and none of them is married yet, it was released as  the second single flip-to-flip with "I'm Born Again" but not charting as  high as their previous singles due to the disco backlash at the end of the  decade. Next is Precious Wilson's first solo single, a funky cover of "Hold  On I'm Coming" with Farian on the backing vocals, Farian was hoping that  the inclusion on the album would support the single but it did  disappointingly. "Two Of Us" is a surprising reggae-ish version of The  Beatles-song before side 1 closes with one of Boney M.'s most romantic  songs, the country-flavoured "Ribbons Of Blue", penned by their drummer  Keith Forsey. It had been issued earlier that year as the B-side of the  non-album single "Hooray Hooray It's A Holi-Holiday", and due to space  limitations on the album, it is only a 2-min. edit version, sadly BMG  didn't put the full 4-min. version on the CD. Whereas side 1 of the album  is much dominated by a disco beat, side 2 is more diverse, opening with the  magnificent title track, a funky, almost Earth Wind & Fire-esque opus  with Frank Farian singing all the vocals himself! Then follows "El Lute"  (the first single), a beautiful mid-tempo song, somewhat reminiscent of  ABBA's "Fernando". The mood shifts on "No More Chain Gang" with its heavy,  monotonous drum beat, after which the accordion intro of the next song "I'm  Born Again" is effectively surprising. This soft song with Liz Mitchell on  the lead vocal was released in the fall of 1979 as the second single and  was apparently thought as the ideal single for the Holiday season but in  the UK, it reached only a disappointing #35 after a string of Top  10-singles. Marcia Barrett sings the funky "No Time To Lose" about her man  being free again and coming home to her before the album closes with a  Calypso flavoured version of a South African traditional, "The Calendar  Song", a song which is still popular today. Although "Oceans Of Fantasy"  isn't quite as magical as the previous "Nightflight To Venus"-LP, it is  still a bonafide album with an outstanding production and sound. It's a  shame, though, that BMG hasn't made an effort to reproduce the stunning LP  poster cover in the CD booklet.

title: THE Howard Jones
text:
After two noteworthy releases and a vocalist change, Killswitch Engage are back for their third studio album, "The End of Heartache." I was a huge fan of Killswitch's previous two works, so I was defintely looking forward to what this one would be like, especially after hearing "When Darkness Falls" on the Freddy vs. Jason soundtrack.

First part: The Howard Jones
Howard Jones is not Jesse and never will be. They're not extrememly different, but Jesse had more range than Howard and it's evident in old Killswitch songs as opposed to tracks on this album. However, Howard is argueably the best live vocalist in metal today just for his energy alone. His studio performance isn't too shabby either. Tracks like "When Darkness Falls" and "The End of Heartache" are so masterfully crafted to compliment both the bands musical talent and Howard's vocal offerings. The new Killswitch is a different beast than the previous band and it's largely becuase of the differences in each vocalists offerings.

Second Part: The songs
Killswitch Engage definitely tweaked their sound for "The End of Heartache," making it more "user" friendly then "Alive or Just Breathing" was. However, the "user" friendly apporach lacks the originality and brilliance of "Alive or Just Breathing." No song on this album can touch "My Last Serenade" with a 10 foot pole, but they're not bad songs. If you people have no previous exposure to KsE and are wondering why they're heralded for being so incredible, this isn't the album you want to listen to. "The End fo Heartache" is just another album put out in the frey. While the middle of the album is where most of the beef lies, the first two tracks are very dissapointing, and it really leaves the listener hungering for "When Darkness Falls" too early in the CD. A stronger opening track like "The End of Heartache" would've fit the album better. Overall, the songwriting is aveage. Not bad, but not worth dropping your jaw over.

Part Three: The Live Performance
If you like this band, see them live. If you don't like this band, see them live. This CD doesn't even capture their live performances to a degree. The bands biggest strength lies there, and you have to see them live to really understand what KsE is all about.

text: Saravah for Cafe' Apres Midi is a mellow collection of heavily bossa nova flavored French music from the 1960's. Pierre Barouh's compositions are given prominence. The five initial Barouh songs culminate in an extremely low-fi analogue recording of Barouh and Baden Powell where several bossa nova and rising tropacalia stars are mentioned by name. I guess it's an homage that Barouh seems to be paying. The mix occasionally sags into more campy French lounge music before moving to 60's R and B. The C.D. reaches its apex with two Barney Wilen numbers from a 1970 released album entitled Moshi (available from Amazon.Com (Japan) for a very good price! The Wilen tunes contain funky lighthearted chanting by several women who seem to be recounting stories of Wilen's mishaps while trying to record pygmies in Africa. The two Wilen songs have a deep Afro Jazz groove, and Wilen's saxophone playing is definitely loose and inspired. The Saravah CD and other Cafe Apre Midi CDs created by DJ's in Japan contain some very rare and tastefully chosen tracks that avid music collectors would be happy to own.

title: The RajMan (Fan) Review
text:
Glen Campbell, who is in the final stages of Alzheimer's Disease, recorded this, his final studio album, in 2012 just after his diagnosis, and it is among his finest efforts.

Although the photography features Campbell posing with one of his guitars, Campbell leaves the instrumentation to others, most notably his long-time banjo player Carl Jackson, who produced the album and plays guitar, and Campbell's daughter Ashley, who plays banjo and accompanies and backs up her father on vocals. The album also features Campbell's sons Cal and Shannon and guests Willie Nelson and Vince Gill.

This allows the elder Campbell to focus on singing, and he really gives it his all. It would be a cliche to say he has never sounded better, but at the very least, his voice is as wide-ranging, nuanced, and poignant as ever, especially in light of – and in spite of – his personal struggles.

The songs are all excellent, making the album a pleasure to listen to from beginning to end and over and over again. I have developed a particular fondness for "Everybody's Talkin'," "Postcards from Paris," and "A Thing Called Love."

Adios is so good that you wish this wasn't the end. But it's a fitting farewell, as well as a lasting reminder of how good of a musician, singer, and all-around entertainer Glen Campbell was.

title: Their Most Uneven Album
text:
If you're new to the band, save this purchase for last. If you've bought a few albums and like what you're hearing, you should still save it for last.
It's not that it's altogether terrible, but is obviously a transition album. It was the last recorded with their drummer Jamie Salazar, and they knew it while they were recording it, which I'm sure affected the mood somehow. Keyboardist Tomas Bodin, who is responsible for a huge portion of their bombastic prog excellence, was absent for a lot of the sessions due to a divorce. This is also the 2nd album with jazzer Jonas Reingold on bass, and it's obvious he wants to stamp more of his own style on the Flower Kings sound, as evidenced by the smooth jazz-bass/sax jam on the second half of the otherwise boring "Elaine".
This album almost totally does away with the sound they stuck with for all of their previous albums, which was a heavily orchestrated, glorious wash of vintange keyboards and uplifting melodies with just enough of a bit of humor and whimsy for good measure. The Rainmaker has a very dreary and deadly serious feel throughout which doesn't let up, which can be wearing. Even down to the cover art, the album is a very somber and dark affair. Even the more melodic sections of the album have a darker feel to them.
It is a fragmented release which constantly tugs between jazz, mood music, and dark, heavier riffs, which were styles they started experimenting with most on this record. In some places it works very well. "The Last Minute On Earth" is a fantastic piece of schizo prog, with a main guitar riff very reminicent of Black Sabbath or Tull, which was totally out of character for them. "The Sword Of God" is a more straightforward hard rock track with thick, distorted hammond a la Jon Lord and a vocal performance by Hasse Froberg that would have made this a legendary track, had it been released in the 70's. He really gives Paul Rogers a run for his money! Towards the end of the album you get the melancholy pop song "Thru The Walls" and "Serious Dreamers" which as Roine Stolt said himself does kind of sound like Tears For Fears. It's an excellent epic though, with a really great bouncy bass groove towards the end. "World WIthout A Heart" is one of the more straight-ahead acoustic-type numbers which I really like but doesn't seem to impress most fans.
Sadly, the rest of the album doesn't hold up so well. Two of the other epics, "Road TO Sanctuary" and "City Of Angels" are fragmented and do not work well within the format they are presented, which is an overlong song stuffed with way too much junk. "Road To Sanctuary" has a very promising first few minutes but soon meanders off into musak territory. "City Of Angels" just STARTS in musak territory and is one of their grossest and most boring songs, as far as I'm concerned. Hey, an album is entitled to a few clunkers but not ones that go on for 15 minutes.
None of the instrumental tracks are anything noteworthy. They would be good for a film score, but it's not the kind of music that reaches out and says something to you like their other grand instrumentals "The Man Who Walked WIth Kings" or even Tomas's quiet, gentle "Power Of Kindness." They are just background music, and serve no purpose.
However, the experimentation with jazz, darker music and heavier riffs ended up resulting in something magnificent, which was their next double-disc release Unfold The Future. All of the styles they experimented with on the Rainmaker collided with the familiar and wonderful Flower Kings sounds on prior albums, with stellar results and a few of their best-ever tunes.
So in that sense, it's great that the Rainmaker came when it did. It serves it's purpose in their history. It's best appreciated after you own most any of their albums BUT this one first, though.

title: From MainlyPiano
text:
"Etheria" is the new fifth volume of "The Elements Series" that Peter Kater recorded on the Real Music label back in 2005. I loved those albums, which were titled "Air," "Earth," "Water," and "Fire," so it came as a very pleasant surprise that there was a fifth installment created almost ten years later. Kater’s piano and synthesizers are accompanied on some of the seven tracks by Richard Hardy on bamboo flutes, and soprano and tenor saxophones. For the huge body of music that Kater has released over the past 30 or so years, it is truly amazing that he has been able to go in so many different musical directions and still maintain such a consistently high quality of work - "Etheria" is no exception. The music on this album ranges from ambient and, well, ethereal, to approaching a haunting jazz style. Tracks range from more than 7 1/2 minutes to about 9 1/2, so the album flows organically and evolves at a leisurely pace. The album was created to represent the vast environment containing both our planet and its elements - etheria - and the music is suitable for meditation, relaxation, and/or pure listening enjoyment.

"Etheria" opens with “Heaven’s Window,” performed on piano and sax with atmospheric sounds and an angelic choir. Slow, peaceful, and very calming, it’s a beautiful beginning. “Celestial Light” is also very “heavenly” with piano, atmospheric sounds, and wordless vocals. More ambient than melodic, the sound soothes like a gentle breeze on a warm day. “Rising Sun” begins with an anthemic, church-like feeling with the choral voices chanting. The reverb is such that it sounds almost like it was recorded in a big cathedral. In the second movement, bamboo flute enters, casting an air of mystery. As this section develops, the choir re-enters, merging spirits and continuing as one. Breathtaking! I love “Violet Waves,” a peaceful bit of heaven for piano, flute, sax, light percussion, gentle background voices, and some beautiful keyboard enhancements. Sometimes tranquil and sometimes soaring, this is my favorite track. “Awakening Stars” goes much darker (duh!) with twinkling bells representing the sparkling stars and haunting keyboard sounds depicting the vast, black sky. Bamboo flute and piano flow together seamlessly to create feelings of calm restfulness and beauty. “Waxing Moon” begins in a very ambient style, but the sax enters and takes this piece to a more jazz-like place similar to music you sometimes hear in film noir. Intense and even a little scary at times, this piece stands out as quite different from the other six tracks. I really like the piece itself, but it isn’t what I would call “ethereal.” “Luminescence” returns to extreme peacefulness and an ambient, floating quality that soothes and gently uplifts as it brings this very effective album to a close.

"Etheria" was worth the wait for the fifth element of the series and fits right in with the other four. Recommended!

title: The Stones rip US fans off, & manage to insult Brian Jones again in the process! I paid $17 for a $5 reissue
text:
Not keeping at all in the spirit of the previous high standard of The Rolling Stones "From The Vault" series, this is merely the short TV special "The Stones In The Park". The special was something you could get cheaply for about $5 on little budget labels going all the way to the VHS days. It has also been released officially in Europe and Japan with three bonus songs and with the same visual quality. The stereo mix found here is better, but it is simply a straight reissue of a bonus disk from the deluxe version of a recent live collection "Sweet Summer Sun".[[ASIN:B00F0JG7E4 Sweet Summer Sun - Hyde Park Live [2DVD/Blu-ray/2 CD Combo]]]

Bluntly this is a crap release. Where do I start?. OK like I mentioned we just get the original TV special with none of the three bonus songs that have gone on the official European or Asian releases. No commentary, no bonus footage of additional songs that may still be in the archive, no contemporary footage of them on TV in 1969 to fill up the very short disk, zip, zilch, nada. This was fine as a bonus disc on another release, not so fine as a new release on it's own. This goes against the very concept of "From The Vaults" which has always given the buyer a little something extra for their money.

This is beyond a bare bones release. At very least they could have put the entire concert on the blu ray as a audio only feature. I mean a blu ray has so much capacity and they put a paltry hour of footage. It shouldn't cost more than the $5 VHS I got in 1990 they way they did this.

The notes are also pretty insulting to Brian, which shouldn't be surprising being that this is a Mick and Keith special. He's referred to only as their former guitarist, and there isn't one photo of him. No mention of his multi instrumental abilities, no mention of his founding the band, no mention of his early leadership. Keith takes credit for the Johnny Winter song getting played because he bought the album the month before. This is bull, every former account of this show mentions the song was played because it was one of Brian's current favorites.

Of course there is no separate LP/CD of the concert coming out this time either. I guess they don't want to release what was their first, and ultimately their worst, show with Mick Taylor. However that doesn't make sense in light of them putting out the film. Perhaps people would enjoy the show more if heard in it's full context, but I guess we will never know.

As it stands this blu-ray should be recalled and have the 3 songs added. I won't pre order anything Stones I am unsure of content wise ever again. I'm very tempted to send it back. For those who have not bit yet, DON'T BUY THIS VERSION. Get yourself a foreign copy with the bonus songs. Most DVD players will play overseas DVD's if you know what buttons to press.
UPDATE 9-18-2015 Just learned the few who find my review too harsh on the basis of the "new" stereo remix are in for a harsh surprise. This "new" stereo version has been out for two years as a bonus on the "Sweet Summer Sun" 5 disc deluxe version I have the vinyl with DVD for that and did not realize this is simply that repackaged to unknowing fans. How low will they go! I have updated the main review to reflect this.

title: Immaculate; enlightening
text: I came across a German review of this album which I tried to read.  It started out by saying something like: "Beautiful.  And that's the problem."  Well, for me that isn't a problem.  After all, there is an abundance of outright beautiful music here.  The fact that this young man plays these sonatas beautifully, and does so in a way that helps me understand them in a manner I never have before, is why I accord five stars and a solid recommendation.  The clarity of thought present in these recordings is most impressive, and Levit's technique strikes me as audibly immaculate; indeed there seems to be something very special here.  I haven't been as impressed by recorded performances of these pieces since I first became familiar with the (outstanding) late sonatas volume of David Allen Weir's survey of all 32 (on Connoisseur Society).  This set joins Weir's at the pinnacle for me, displacing others in my collection.  My only question is: with Beethoven's late sonatas comprising his first record release, where does Levit go from here?

title: Great content, lousy DVD picture quality
text:
Being a huge Queen fan, if I had to rate this by the songs and the videos themselves I would give it a 5 star rating, but this DVD set is incredibly marred by the absolute worst video compression I've ever seen on a DVD. Whoever is responsible for encoding the video for it should be fired.
The video artifacting is so bad that non-moving objects in the background seem to continuously jump up and down, and large areas of solid color seem to have little squares moving around in them. (This effect is, fortunately, minimized by the fact that usually everything on screen is moving anyway - it is a collection of music videos, after all.) Worse, the widescreen aspect ratio is improperly encoded on the disc, so when I try to watch the videos on my TV with my DVD player, it stretches them out to the full height of the screen, resulting in in an abnormally tall rock band. To view the videos properly I have to view them on my computer, which thankfully figures out whatever the problem is and displays the videos correctly.
Queen fans such as myself will no doubt want to acquire this set anyway for the new audio mixes and just to have some video material of Queen, but I urge you to do so with the understanding that they messed up the video so prepare to be tolerant of the video quality.

title: Vibrant Afro-Influenced Jazz
text: This recording is created by one of the versions of Kahil El'Zabar's Ethnic Heritage Ensemble.  The consistent grouping is drums, horns - tenor sax and trombone, played by Ernest Dawkins and Joseph Bowie, respectfully, with the addition of Fareed Haque on guitar.  The horn players make contributions on small percussion instruments,and Kahil holds down the bottom with his earth drum and other hand drums, and he also plays the drum kit and kalimba on a couple of tracks.  This is vibrant, essential music for those who love Afro-influenced music, and it's a good place to start for those who are ready to be introduced.  Kahil El'Zabar has been one of the central figures out of Chicago who continues to carry the banner of great Chicago jazz.  Parts of this studio recording really swing, and the general mood of the recording is soothing, with substance - nothing thin here - again, this is essential music with depth.  Kahil El'Zabar has always paid deep respect to Chicago jazz musicians and mentors who have preceded him and influenced him, and in recent years he is sharing his passion and gifts for the music by mentoring and influencing a younger generation of musicians.  Also try out the two DVDs of Kahil that are available.  The music alone is great, but it's a special treat to watch Kahil on video, or better yet, live.  His passion is evident, and the experience is very moving.

title: Awesome
text:
There is no real explaining how good this cd is. If I had to destroy all of my albums but one I would probably keep this one. First of all, it's a double album containing over 2 hours of music which I got for the price of a single album, with the greatest consistency of any album I own, except possibly Aenima. Buy it. Buy it now, especially if you don't own any Iced Earth. Now, with that gushing aside I'll go into an actual review.
As stated in an earlier review, I am generally not big on live albums. The problems that plague most of them are not significant here. The fans sing along some, which is occasionally a problem, and their perpetual chanting of "Iced Earth" between songs can be kind of annoying, but they usually don't matter too much. The sound quality is excellent, which it usually isn't, and the bands performances are flawless. Smedley's drumming is particularly good, better than on most of the albums. The one real complaint against the album is that most of the songs aren't substantially different from the original versions, though I consider them different enough that this cd is completely worth owning despite my having the studio versions of every song but one.
Though this album is perhaps the most consistent I own, I will still complain about the track listing a little. The excellent album, Burnt Offerings, is under represented, with only 2 tracks(though one is extremely long, 16 minutes) and none of them being the classic title track or "Diary" or "Brainwashed". A handful of other classics are missing, like "Consequences", "Disciples of The Lie" and worst of all "Scarred", which is especially annoying because it does include the other 2 songs of the "Suffering" trilogy, so it messes up the continuity of it, not to mention it's simply being an awesome song. The thing is, though some other songs should be on here, only one song, "Melancholy", seems like it would be an acceptable loss.
This cd does contain an excellent overview of the bands career up to with just under half of the album being from before "The Dark Saga", and the rest from that point on, which is good because that marked a distinct change in the bands style. Sadly, it of course contains no songs from "Horror Show", since it wasn't even released yet, but there is already too much material from the earlier albums to be compiled here. The earlier stuff is very "Master of Puppets" and "...And Justice For All" esque, except generally even more complex, though with a bit more melody as well. This music benefits from the new recording, because the original versions sound quality is a little flat and sterile, even in the "Days of Purgatory" versions, with the "Stormrider" material being much more intense and powerful. The best stuff from this era are generally the longest ones, such as the 10 minute "Angels Holocaust/Stormrider" the 9 minute "Travel In Stygian" and the 16 minute "Dante's Inferno", with the shorter "Path I Choose" also being particularly strong.
The later stuff is slower, simpler, shorter and more melodic, though with a greater variety of song types, since the early songs are almost all prog-thrash epics. The Ballads, "A Question of Heaven" and "Watching Over Me" are among the best from this era, with the faster, heaviest songs on the opposite end of the spectrum being the next strongest, particularly "The Last Laugh", "Slave to the Dark" and "Burning Times". Thus this album has a great variety of songs, as much so as is possible while having all of them being rooted in 80's underground metal. Lyrically, this all comes off a bit weird, as it has three different storylines from concept albums all interweaved together, but this doesn't matter much, as Iced Earth has alway been about sound, not message.
So what does this all come done to? It's a compilation of most of the best material by arguably the best band ever. So, once again, buy it, buy it NOW!

title: Adventurous Indeed
text:
Glenn Kotche's latest effort is indeed an audio adventure. The major work -- Anomaly -- was written for the Kronos Quartet, who perform in this recording. The concept is intriguing -- treat acoustic instruments (a string quartet) as an extension of a drum kit, shading the drums' indefinite pitches with specific notes played by the paired stringed instrument.

Each of "Anomaly's" seven movements examines this interface from a different perspective, using the building blocks of minimalism to create tension and motion -- with just a touch of rock n' roll.Interspersed throughout Anomaly are short solo works by Kotche. These are mostly electronic, with so much packed into each piece that they actually seem much larger than they are.

I recommend listening to this album two ways -- first, as the composer intended with all the tracks in order. The moving back and forth from "Anomaly" to the other pieces creates an organic and compelling meta-composition. The second way is to just listen to the "Anomaly" movements. The interconnections between the movements become much clearer, and almost assumes a different character when heard as an integrated whole.

The only reason why this  album was not given the "5 star rating" was because of the poor  production (basically the drums sounded like sticks hitting cardboard). title: This is THE progressive metal album of 2011.
text:
I became a ginormous fan of this band after "Tall Poppy Syndrome" and have been adamant about recommending to everyone I know. They are a breath of fresh air in the metal world and this album is an amazing progression in their still young sound. This past month was a great one for progressive metal with releases from my favirote band, Opeth, my other favirote Dream Theater, this album, and the upcoming release of Three's newest record. I've gotten them all so far and, for me, Leprous' new record beats the others by a large margine. Now *that* is saying something because I've been a fan of DT and Opeth for over 15 years respectively.

I don't want to get into a long-winded description track by track. The main thing about this album is that it is more song oriented than TPS was in that each song(except for two of them) are generally much shorter and more focused on a central theme and/or melody. Likewise, the harsh vocal stylings are more sparse and only a focal point of a song in one or two tracks whereas they were more of the focal point before. This doesn't mean they did what Opeth did with "Heritage" though. The music stays pretty much to their style but the distortion has softened up a bit in parts and there are a few more "softer" tracks on this record. The songs are just so dynamic though. One particular song features Ihsahn on the vocals and the entire musical theme of the track is much more "metal" than the rest of the album. I love how it caters to his presence and almost sounds like a track ripped from his solo trilogy, even though it totally fits this album.

Most of this album is still in their avant-garde, ecclectic brand of metal though. There is just so much variety in the riffs and vocal structures that's hard to really pigeon-hole this at all. TPS was more direct in its theme, but this album tends to jump around and offer something new with every successive track, an amazing feat these days. The keyboards are there in spades yet again and add so much to the already full sound. Tor's vocals are killer, moreso than they've ever been and he shines on this album. He puts so much feeling and emotion into his work and it sends chills down my spine on almost every single listen. His melodies generally drive every song on this record and there are many Opeth styled hummed sections that just jump out at you. I love their ability to write music that matches up with his vocal melodies and they do that 7/10 times on this record creating vibrance few can match. Their drummer Tobias is one I consider to be one of the best in the scene in terms of creativity and he shows it once again here with off-tempo rythmes and some great moments in songs like "Restless" where a the jazzy syncopation drives the song more than anything. It's those moments where he is important because you realize that he is bringing something more to the music.

Everything about this record moves Leprous somewhat away from the more metal oriented "Tall Poppy Syndrome" and finds them, I believe, coming full circle into the sound that will define their career in metal. They, like Opeth, have strength in bring truelly skilled musicians who *can* overplay and throw their skills in your face but restrain themselves by using their mature musical acumin to create something truelly "musical". When a song demands harsh vocals, they'll use them. When a song calls for a wonderfully sung clean chorus with light synths in the background, they'll go that way. When a drum solo accompanied by some guitars riffing playing off synthesizer riffing pops up, they'll just flow with it. But one thing Leprous will never do is ruin a song to indulge. I've never heard a Leprous track I didn't like or love and there is nothing on this album I'd consider second-rate. If you're a fan of bands like Opeth, Riverside, Three, or even more extreme bands like Enslved or Ihsahn(the solo artist from Emperor that both help Leprous and uses them as his live band btw), I guarantee you'll eat this album up. If you don't, I will personally refund you your money...maybe.

title: get right with mode
text: This is an excellent collection from the kings of gloom synth-pop. The two-CD set includes the popular tunes such as "Question of Lust," "Personal Jesus," "Enjoy the Silence" and "World in My Eyes." It also includes some of the lesser-known gems of the Faith and Devotion album, such as "Condemnation" and "I Feel You." For all the criticism that DM takes, what music would you rather have playing when the world seems bleak and you feel isolated? But it's not all gloom, DM made some of the most danceable, smart, well-crafted dance-techno-industrial music of the last 15 years. For DM fans, this is a great collection to have in the car or to take on a plane, when you want to hear the hits. For those who aren't quite sure about buying "Violator" or "Faith and Devotion," this is a very good "intro-to-Mode" collection.

title: Manson beat Bowie at his own genre!
text:
This album is musically brilliant! Gary Glitter/David Bowie esque glamrock, with a slight electrosynth tinge.... ITS GOOD!
However, it is in the storyline where we find the brilliance on the record. Manson plays two characters in this, these being the "Marilyn" or good side, called Alpha, and the "Manson" or dark side, called Omega. Even though the caracters are the same person, they represent opposite sides of the personality, with Alpha being naieve, hopeful and somewhat charitable, whilst Omega is a cynical, bitter manic-depressive addicted to every drug in California.
As for the songs....
1. Great Big White World: Genuinely goregous glam track, sung by Alpha, as he is horrified by the conformity of our world.
2. The Dope Show: Musically brilliant, this lets us in on Omega's cynicism, and the emptiness of his fame.
3. Mechanical Animals: Alpha dealing with the mechanical nature of this "Bride".
4: Rock Is Dead: Industrio/Glam mixture, Omega bitching over the agonisingly ignorant criticism he recieves for being controversial. Damn catchy too.
5. Dissassociative: Omega overdoses on drugs (again), obstensibly for his depression, and reverts to Alpha, seeing the world as a "Dead Astronaut". Very Bowie, and very good.
6. Speed of Pain: Omega, now on a come down, vents his angst, and it is here where we first see his despiar.
7: Posthuman: Alpha, infuriated at the superficiality of our world and our religion, reminds us of the Antichrist Superstar and tells us to wake up to our god being a Statistic.
8: I want to dissapear: Omega, full of anger and frustration, blasts us in a punk sneer about how shallow he has become thanks to our screwed up society.
9: I dont like the drugs: Omega makes fun of all those who have supposedly 'given up' their addictions, but really traded in the drugs for the church, ending up with another addiction.
10: New Model: Omega raves about how the media is creating a new type of person, all shallow and "Homopolitan."
11:User Friendly: Omega is distraught, and now the sex is as mechanical as the people, with it being a weapon and not a f**kfest.
12: Fundamentally Loathsome: Omega resolves to end it all, not knowing what is real emotion, and what is preprogrammed.
13: Last Day on Earth: Omega reverts back to Alpha, and confesses his love for Coma White, and pledges eternal devotion. The most moving song on the album, and a good one too.
14: Coma White: The death of our Heroine, exiled from society for the 'crime' of individuality. Tragic ending, but beautiful...
Overall, this is Marilyn Manson's masterpiece. The music is far more sophisticated (and more rock than metal) than any of his previous efforts, and it has some of his best songwriting ever. It is deeply intellectual, it sounds great, and works very well overall.

title: Throwback Classic Country -- not for everyone but for those who like Classic Country, a real gem.
text:
Some of the comments suggest the video quality is low here. Yes it was shot, probably with 16 millimeter film back in the late 50's but if you like classic country this is the real deal. There are some noticeable video splices as they switch between performers and performances but it does not affect the enjoyment of the viewing (and what do you expect from film from 50-plus years ago?). What is amazing is they have this film and it's in clear color. Viewing this sort of reminds me when of when color TV was 'new' and how vivid color seemed on shows like Bonanza. Ray Price and Jim Reeves each add to the color scheme with their bright Nudie suits which is also a throw-back. Ernest Tubb, not featured on the title or pictured on the front of the DVD, performs an equal number of songs. He is dressed in his classic Texas Troubadour attire. The DVD constantly shifts between performances by Ray Price, Jim Reeves and Ernest Tubb which provides a variety show type feel to the DVD.
The song selection for these artists suggest this was some sort of early 'off-label' offering designed to showcase some of their "B" side selections -- as you won't hear the signature songs or the more popular hits associated with these artists -- although Ray Price's tunes come the closest with "Don't Let the Stars Get In Your Eyes" and "You've Done Me Wrong" but for Reeves you won't hear "He'll Have to Go" or Tubbs' "Waking the Floor Over You" and Price's "Heartaches by the Number" But that's OK. They're all readily available elsewhere.
Probably not that many folks out there these days who are looking for a real country classic collection like this, but if you're a throwback like some of us (me!) you'll enjoy this. As someone who thinks that Ray Price's contributions to country music over the years have been over-looked and somewhat under appreciated, I really enjoyed his performances on this DVD.

title: Tremendous Body of Work
text:
Abba's The Albums collects all eight of the group's studio albums, as well as an additional disc of non-album singles and stray random tracks. It's fantastic. The set comes in a modestly-sized box, so it isn't super bulky like many box sets are. Inside, there's a booklet that lists all the recording and touring dates, along with plenty of pictures and other song information, to present a very basic history of the group. Each disc is in a slim cardboard recreation of what the original record looked like. It's nothing too fancy, just a simple way to present the music. (As of this writing, Amazon includes all the mp3s as part of their auto-rip feature, which I love, because you get all the songs instantly and you don't have to rip them from the discs. Also as of this writing, it costs less to buy the CDs and get the auto-rip mp3s than it does to buy only the mp3s, which is great for me, because I like to have both.)

As to the music itself, it's a joy. Abba was of course one of the most commercially successful bands of all time, and they remain well-known and well-liked for their numerous hit singles. But they have a lot of depth and variety in their album tracks, too. From post-60s folk rock to disco to 80s new wave, they explore numerous styles, always with their distinctive production and meticulous attention to detail. The lyrics, too, are often much more interesting and thoughtful than people tend to give Abba credit for.

Some people are only going to be interested in Abba's hits, and that's fine - there are plenty of options for them out there. If you want to go deeper, though, I think it's well worth going all the way and getting this entire set. They had an outstanding career, and this is definitely the best way to get it all.

title: Half of the Time We're Gone
text:
The incredible thing about the "Garden State" soundtrack is how well the tracks blend together. There is a marvelous consistency throughout. The film revolves around a character who has been medicated to curb his emotions since a tragic accident in his teenage years. The music reflects an emotional detachment that includes a pervading sadness and an eventual awakening. In short, the music fits the film exquisitely.

The Coldplay opener "Don't Panic" has languid chiming guitars with the chorus, "We live in a beautiful world." "Chutes Too Narrow" is one of my favorite CDs; so I was delighted with the inclusion of two Shins tracks. "Caring Is Creepy" is a good example of their lyrical complexity juxtaposed to original melodies that are slightly off kilter. Zero 7's "In the Waiting Line" has a great Prozac feel, "Everyone's saying different things to me...Everyone's taking everything they can. Do you believe what you feel?" The Shins' second track "New Slang" starts off with cousin-to-the-Beach-Boys backing vocals and blossoms into an acoustic gem. Australian Colin Hay's sad ballad "I Just Don't Think I'll Ever Get Over You" is a theme song for anyone who's ever carried a torch. I've been spinning Nick Drake since back when he was alive & on vinyl. His "One of These Things First" boasts a classic melody. My favorite new find is "Lebanese Blonde" by Thievery Corporation with its percolating percussion and airy vocals. I remember being at the 1970 World's Fair in Osaka, Japan as a 17-year old a long way from home and hearing a folk singer belt out Simon & Garfunkel's "The Only Living Boy in New York" at the fair. I thought my heart might break with homesickness as he sang, "Half of the time we're gone, but we don't know where, and we don't know where." So its inclusion here shows me fine music remains classic to cross generations; and we can expect the same for much of the music from the GS soundtrack. Iron & Wine's "Such Great Heights" is picked out on acoustic guitar & melds perfectly with the Shins & Nick Drake. Frou Frou's "Let Go" is an excellent track with great energy flowing in its lighthearted melody, "There's beauty in breakdown." The "Garden State" soundtrack is an excellent collection that fits the movie like a glove but also stands on its own as a unified musical experience. Stay cool! :)

title: Better than the other late 70's Wings releases, but.....
text:
This was one of the first albums I purchased with hard earned lawn mowing and car washing income, and I was pumped when I got it. The radio was playing Getting Closer, and his new label (Columbia - who did not get their money out of Macca) was hyping the daylights out of the album. I instantly loved the sound of the record, but my 13 year old brain couldn't get around the lyrics - is McCartney trying to say something? Is this some type of concept album? Why the spoken word pieces? What's the point?

My now 42 year old brain now knows that there wasn't any point to any of it. It was just Paul up to his usual tricks - a wide variety of styles and song snippets from early in the disc showing up at the end (a la Band On The Run and Ram). I still have no clue on the spoken word piece.

This isn't saying Back To The Egg is a bad McCartney album. Chris Thomas (who later produced INXS and handled the excellent Run Devil Run) gives the disc a much more agressive, up front sound than the previous two Wings discs. Most songwriters would kill to compose half the catchy melodies that show up on Back To The Egg, and McCartney seems to toss them off. Getting Closer, Old Siam Sir, Arrow Through Me, even the throwaway Winter Rose all are chock full of hooks. The problem with the disc is that there is nothing to put on the hooks. Strip away the production and the catchy meoldies and there just isn't much there. It wasn't the first time that the lack of a point betrayed McCartney, and it wouldn't be the last. Except for Tug of War, McCartney spent most of the 80's looking for a point.

Despite the hollowness of the disc, it has far more energy than the other late 70's Wings albums, and a few of the songs - see above - are underrated in the McCartney catalog. I still get a kick putting it on and harkening back to my youth. But this is a minor work in the McCartney catalog, and newbie fans are advised to purchase a whole bunch of other discs (Band On The Run, Ram, Tug of War, Chaos and Creation, and Run Devil Run to start with) before getting this one.

title: Finally...after so long a wait!
text:
You better believe I went after this one the moment I learned about it. My copy still has the mail order receipt tucked inside - it was ordered on the Aug. 14, 1993 and in my mailbox the 20th. As you can see from A-com's stated release date, I didn't dawdle.
For years I'd satisfied myself with two vinyl copies of their 1966 "Greatest Hits" on Epic - one in glorious mono, which had to navigate a warp to play, and a pristine copy that carried that notorious moniker "electronically re-channeled to simulate stereo." The latter copy is as shiny as ever; one listen was enough to know that mono was the way. I also had a treasured few 45s: Can't You See That She's Mine, Nineteen Days, You Got What It Takes & You Must Have Been A Beautiful Baby. So I was waiting and longing like every baby-boomer for whom The Five's immortal hits were burned in the brain for their re-availability. Until Mr. Clark let this set out in 1993 you could really pay through the nose for used copies of their Epic LP's and even singles (presuming you wanted copies worthy of better than toy phono equipment). Other reviewers here complain about the high percentage of unnecessary filler in this set, and they're right, but because all the essential hits are present as well, I can deal with it.
What you might not know, was at the time this CD set went on the market, Mr. Clark also let Hollywood Records release a small set of the group's hits again on 45! I won't list all the titles but it was a 7-disc series of double `A' sides spanning the time between "Glad All Over" & "You Got What It Takes," with what you'd except as the obvious choices in between. Though I still hadn't even lost the shrink-wrap yet of this just-released CD set, you'd better believe I grabbed up those 45s too! Sure, I'd rather have the original Epic issues with their picture sleeves, but I'm not quite ready to go up to fifty bucks apiece for a 45, you know?!
I'm very glad that Amazon com typically lists release dates for CD products, but in this case I'd be pleased also if they could tell us when Mr. Clark decided to abruptly change his mind and turn off the availability faucet to this set. It didn't last long, and seemed to be gone as fast as it was here. As I write this review, the info is "1 used & new from $99.50!" I don't understand that kind of eccentricity, Mr. Clark, but it sure as hell must be nice not to need the money!

title: One of the Greatest and Important Albums in Rock History
text:
1965

Rubber Soul was the album that started it all. It was the album that marked the Beatles going from pop stars, to true music geniuses, beginning the revolutionizing of rock music. 1965 was a busy year for the Beatles; they had tours, T.V. shows, songs to record, and also, the movie Help. But not even all this would stop the fab four (who would soon be growing out of their "fab" image) from creating one of the greatest albums ever.

Even the untrained ear can tell that Rubber Soul is different that Beatles' albums that came before it (that is, if their ear has been trained enough to listen to those). The album is much darker and not nearly as upbeat as the 5 previous ones. The drugs were influencing this change along with, maybe even more so, Bob Dylan. Around this time Dylan began having a large effect on the Beatles, especially after they met him, when he introduced them to marijuana. But Dylan was more than just about drugs to the Beatles. His songwriting made a long-lasting and important impression on them. The other famous thing about Rubber Soul is the sitar played by George Harrison, on "Norwegian Wood". Although Harrison would have so many other great accomplishments after Rubber Soul, the sitar has become one of his most famous contributions to rock music. This began the Beatles exploration of new sounds to apply to their already masterful works.

However, nobody would care about any of these things if the music wasn't great, which it definitely is. When I'm listening to this album, I tend to see John as the standout songwriter. After listening to Rubber Soul, it's pretty easy to see why, as he pens "Nowhere Man" and "In My Life". The sophisticated melodies and more introspective lyrics mark a turning point and a great development in Lennon's songwriting, to accompany the Beatles changing style. Paul is sure to make an impact as well. Many people consider "Michelle", a romantic ballad that he has become famous for, to be his best track on the album. It even won one of the Beatles few Grammy awards. McCartney also writes the opening rocker "Drive My Car", and "You Won't So Me", a song reminiscent of the Beatles earlier pop songs, but still fits in nicely on Rubber Soul. George also comes along with his songwriting on "If I Needed Someone"; probably his best work up to this point. He also writes, "Think For Yourself", which is very similar to his earlier songs, and it is by no means bad. Ringo gets his first songwriting credit on the country-ish "What Goes On". Another famous song is John's "Girl": a very simplistic song that's still very good (one of my favorites on the album).

Rubber Soul deserves its place in rock history. It is held in such high esteem for a reason and I highly recommend it, to anyone interested in or likes classic rock. It is also one of the most important albums ever, as it marks the Beatles transition into becoming the greatest band of rock n' roll.

I thought this was touted to be a return to rock music? Outside of "I Can't Stop I Thinking About You" and "Petrol Head" this is a seriously mellow album. I almost fell asleep during track 8. The melodic content that I love about Sting is really missing here. Inshallah is much better. Mellow, but better. Would have been very much at home on “Brand New Day” or “Sacred Love”. The Empty Chair is pretty. A decent album closer. Overall, a surprising number (5 to my count) of average to below average songs. The rest ranges from very good to good.

My warning to fans is, if you've read pre-reviews or promo material promising the most rock album since his Police days, you'll be very very disappointed. If you like solo Sting albums as I do, you still might be a bit let down. His last studio album, 2003's "Sacred Love" was much stronger. I’ll go as far as to say that on first listen this is my least fav of his solo pop/rock albums. As to the bonus trax, LA version of Can't Stop... sounds like an acoustic live in studio version. Not a must have, but a nice bonus. Inshallah (Berlin Sessions Version) is likewise nice. Not really different enough to include both versions. Finally, the live version of "Next To You" is a rockabilly version that is alright I guess but might put some off. Worth a listen but for those debating standard version or deluxe edition, stick to the standard cd. Not worth the extra cost unless you're (like me) a completist.

title: First choice George Lewis
text:
This reissues the 1962 LP "Endless the trek, Endless the search" with the addition of Tiger Rag and Savoy Blues as bonuses .
The sound quality is somewhat distant and hollow but the music easily transcends this. I haven't heard any better late period Lewis, indeed it equals anything he ever recorded. Some of the credit goes to the driving, staccato trumpet of Kid Thomas and the melodically inventive guitar of George Guesnon. The other musicians are Jim Robinson, trombone; John Joeseph, bass and Josiah Frasier, drums.
They all have plenty of room to stretch and some of the final choruses build to high levels of excitment. Lewis himself is in fine form, especially on the blues, with none of the apparent tonal uncertainty which marred some of his earler work.
This is music of rugged beauty and complete sincerity, and anyone with an ear for New Orleans jazz should have it, along with the 1940's Climax sessions on the American Music label

He works wonders with "Pierrot", the second "Carnaval" piece, repeating its second half. In the Brahms sonata, his playing of the scherzo movement has wonderful vigour, light and shade.  For some reason both recordings were withheld from publication until after Solomon suffered a stroke in 1956.  Their remastering and transfer to CD comes with three Liszt pieces Solomon recorded in the early 1930s. title: This Is the Best of All Planxty Albums
text: It's not all that unusual for a debut album to be the best by a band or individual musician. The first Bothy Band album is still the finest ever released by that great group. Music critics are aware that the debut album by any band or individual musician often represents the best of the work-shopped and road-tested material they have up to that point. In general, a first album reflects cherry-picked music by the artist possibly in tandem with the record company. As is the case with many artists whose lauded debut albums sell well, the labels for whom they record want a second album ASAP. That rush or fervor to get another album out--especially with musicians who basically "shoot their bolt" on the first album--can lead to disappointing music not properly developed on the road and/or selected in the studio. Planxty did release subsequent albums of unquestionable interest, but none has the uniformity of first-rate quality and impact that this debut has. All that said, becoming a Planxty albums completist is not a bad thing to be.

title: Enter the Systematic Execution
text:
I'm honestly surprised by how few death metal fans are actually aware of Malevolent Creation. They are one of the best Death Metal bands out there and have existed since 1987. Any Malevolent Creation album with Brett Hoffman on vocals is the perfect place to start. There are few Death Metal bands that stand up to this guy. I like what reviewer Oddity said about this record, in that it is Brett's vocal and lyrical ability that bands like Cannibal Corpse, Deicide, Etc. lack in their music. Those guys probably sit and write the lyrics in five minutes and tend to grunt the words together. As a result, all their songs the same and you can't take it too seriously (seriousness is something I like in my music) and becomes boring. Where as the way Brett Hoffman growls and projects his voice and the way he write the songs, you can tell, or at least get the feel that he is dead serious about it and honestly sounds like he came from Hell (and I don't say that too often). Also the Drums, Bass and Guitar are excellent. Just check out my particularly favorite song titled Mindlock for proof. If you like Death Metal like Vader then this definitely for you.

An interesting thing about Malevolent Creation is that their lineup practically changes on every album, keeping them fresh. It's sad that Roadrunner decided to discontinue most of their Malevolent Creation albums. Get a copy of this as quickly as possible off eBay or something; you'll be glad you did. Hopefully they will re-release these but that doesn't look like it's gonna happen anytime soon. This is difficult to find but the search is worth it. It shreds, it pounds, it screams, it kills, it owns. Just hunt down a copy and you'll be one happy head banger.

Interesting Fact: This album was produced by Scott Burns, who also Produced Sepultura's Arise and Beneath the Remains. His great production shines on this record as well as those.

title: THE CAVALLARO/DUNING STORY
text:
This early-stereo Decca bestseller remains very entertaining despite its stylistic inauthenticity (Eddy Duchin's original piano style is too fleetingly channeled here). A fuller soundtrack could have included more of George Duning's orchestral underscoring and cues, which accompany Kim Novak's third of the film. The keyboard highlights are Carmen Cavallaro's prerecorded tracks for the scenes in which Ty Power convincingly mimes Duchin's fingering and arm movements (to Carmen's personal--and drastic--revisions of Duchin's piano technique). So far so good--Power is memorable visually, the impostor Cavallaro anything but in laying down the piano-hits template.

The problem is one of stylistic integrity, never to be expected from a Hollywood musical biopic: Decca’s middlebrow lounge-piano mainstay Cavallaro plays Duchin charts remodeled for the 1950s in the inapt Cavallaro style (cocktails, candelabrum and vulgar arpeggios ad libitum), now superseded and definitely not due for revival. (True to his own era, Cavallaro doesn't even execute those ghastly arpeggios cleanly, so he's endearingly human and not Hollywood soundstage-perfect.) I'll concede that Mr. Cavallaro plays "Dizzy fingers" dizzyingly fast and finds honkytonk potential in "Chopsticks." His frilly arpeggios are more muted in "You're my everything," "Brazil" and "La vie en rose," and these keeper tracks more successfully evoke the big sound of the full Duchin society orchestra as recreated by the progressive Duning, famous for his Novak-Holden PICNIC score and, years later, a television series, STAR TREK.

Cavallaro groupies will buy this release anyway, if only for the original Kim/Ty cover art and the bonus tribute album. But serious listeners ought check out the REAL Eddy Duchin, possessor of a much suaver keyboard technique than his hapless revisionist imitator. Duchin's Brunswick 78s, well anthologized on ASV's EDDY DUCHIN STORY, reveal the pianist--an expert showman with a magnetic personality--as only one, albeit stellar, component in a very large, very swank society dance band. Cavallaro, dribbling treble furbelows, missed Duchin's pianistic/stylistic point entirely: As the Brunswicks reveal, Eddy habitually voiced the melody, rhythms and cross-rhythms in the baritone and even the bass registers of the king of instruments--a robust, masculine sound--and that solidity, a Duchin trademark, automatically impelled society dancers onto the floor. (There were Duchin arpeggios to be sure, but delivered with more taste and discretion.) Just compare Duchin's quite raunchy original take on Harold Arlen's "Ill wind" with Cavallaro's anemic bonus track for graphic evidence of what this old Steinway frontman is carping about.

The bonus album (here Cavallaro, backed by guitarist and drummist, daringly ventures into lower registers, and Cole Porter, but his lounge-piano overornamentation persists) is a testament to the obsolete Cavallaro style, not to the true, very Art Deco, Duchin style which could make a comeback because of its lightly jazzy inclinations and its seductive danceability. Despite this set's ongoing stylistic gaffes, it is a thoroughly entertaining twofer for Cavallaro followers (with Duning and Duchin fans getting shortchanged). Collectors should buy this anyway, if only for Ms. Novak's sake (in the film Kim as trophy bride Marjorie Duchin hauntingly dies "of the wind"--how cinematically romantic is that?).

For DVD-Audio fans like myself, the DualDisc offers us Advanced Resolution Stereo and Surround mixes on the DVD side of the disc. If you don't have a DVD-Audio player, you still get Dolby Stereo and Surround mixes that still sound better than CD-quality audio.

The 5.1 channel surround sound mix is really nice, though it appears that they mainly only use the back speakers for ambient sounds.

Standout tracks here are "Days of Wonder", "The Beautiful Side of Somewhere", "Back to California", "Nearly Beloved" and "All Things Are New Again".

You're just going to have to purchase Bill Hicks' "Relentless," to find out. In the short amount of time of hearing about this guy and purchasing one of his albums, (time is about three weeks), I have purchased all five of his albums. Or at least the ones I could find. Bill Hicks has grown on me a lot faster than most of the other comics I have listed to. It's just a shame that he went through life without getting the recognition and respect he deserved. How can a brilliant comic genious be so underrated?
"Relentless" is 100% Bill Hicks. Filled with anger and outrageous ideas and theories, Bill Hicks is able to make us laugh and think at the same time. He was a man who did not know any fear, and was not afraid to talk about stuff that other comics wouldn't even dare to think about. He doen't follow the traditonal formula, as in talking about love, marriage, and family. No, he talks about drugs, war, politics, and a whole bunch of other things.
This is by far the best Bill Hicks CD. I really enjoyed listening to every track. Bill will be missed, and it's up to us to make sure that more people know about him. Hicks was, and still is, a comic genius who knew how to entertain. A great commentator and observer, he was.
We miss you Bill! R.I.P.

title: Another successful record with international/worldwide acclaim.
text:
4 albums in, Per Gessle and Marie Fredricksen -- the heart and muscle of Swedish power-pop duo Roxette -- have crafted yet ANOTHER beautifully dance-heavy, feel-good, crunchy guitar, melodic synthesizer, rock-laden album. This time, however, 4 of the 16 songs were performed live from various venues. Moreover, the LIVE versions of "She's Got The Look", "Things Will Never Be The Same", and "Joyride" have only cemented Roxette as international icons! :) I actually love these versions A LOT better than the studio versions because it really flexes Per and Marie's vocal prowess to the max!! In fact, Per's voice was already getting a lot deeper.

The fourth live track, "It Must Have Been Love", is a complete re-working of the 1989 mega-smash which is partly live (with a call-and-response sing along from ravenous fans, no doubt) and partly studio with a melancholy, twangy, gut-wrenching, harmonica-laden country version of said song. Again, I LOVE this version so much more than the "Pretty Woman" version.

1 other song was also completely re-imagined: 1986's "So Far Away" from the "Pearls Of Passion" album has been stripped to the bone and is now a lone acoustic ballad, yet still perfectly led by Marie. 2 more delicious tracks -- the Per-Gessle led "Fingertips" and "Cinnamon Street" -- were also later re-worked and have both been released on this updated re-issue. The latter track, aptly titled "Cinnamon Street 2", is another version that is sung by Marie (instead of Per's original) with a really great guitar outro! :)

All 16 tracks were recorded in various hotels, studios, stadiums, and arenas. There is absolutely no filler on this album; in other words, Roxette fans will have NO problem whatsoever eating this up. :)

title: A 5 Star Winner For Musiq...Bonus Trax Are AWESOME!
text:
Alright, I finally obtained the COMPLETE 'Luvanmusiq' & all of the various BONUS TRACKS make an already impressive CD, even better (IMO). As for the 1st single ('B.U.D.D.Y.') , let me say that I really don't like it (or any of the numerous remixes!)...this song simply rips off (not samples!) Taana Gardner's old school jam 'Heartbeat'. Musiq's song lacks any hint of creative sampling, and I've heard the same lyrics from Musiq before ("Maybe we can do this, Maybe that.." yada, yada!).

THANKFULLY, the CD shows MORE substance after the 1st track and I love 'Ms.Philadelphia' & 'Teach Me', which proves that Musiq still has the ability to sing meaningful songs (when he wants to!). 'BetterMan', 'The Questions' and 'Today' are also impressive tracks that feature great lyrics from Musiq. 'Make You Happy', 'Ridiculous' & 'Millionaire' are cool midtempo jams (Musiq's cool lyrics & vocal arrangements are a PLUS!) for crusing around the town. Now, with 'Take You There', 'Lullaby' & 'Greatest Love', Musiq decides to slow the tempo down and delivers stellar love songs ('Lullaby' is up there with 'Teach Me'!!). 'Greatest Love' is also a triumph, which is sung with sincerity, and you can feel the lyrics sung by Musiq.

**Now if you don't want your CD to end after ONLY 12 songs, simply add the various bonus tracks to your disc. Most of these tracks are pretty good!
13. All About You - Pretty Decent As A 'Bonus'! (7/10)
14. Ride Through - Another Good Mid Tempo Cut! (6.5/10)
15. Slowdown - I'm Not Feeling This...The Worse 'Bonus' Cut! (4/10)
16. Rewind - Cool Midtempo Jam! (9/10)
17. Ooh Baby Baby - A Smokey Robinson Remake (9/10)
18. Reasons - A Earth, Wind & Fire Remake (8.0/10)
19. Struggle No More (w/Anthony Hamilton & Jaheim) - From
'Daddy's Little Girls' Soundtrack (9.5/10)
20. Addicted - Lloyd Banks (feat.Musiq) - Suprisingly Decent! (7.5/10)

In the end, I give 'Luvanmusiq' 4.75 Stars (rounded off to 5), and it's almost as good as 'Juslisen'! Musiq Soulchild's fans are urged to add this CD to their collection! (Look for the Limited Edition sold at Best Buy featuring THREE of the 'Bonus Tracks!)
Peace, SD

title: Classic debut from some r&b revisionists
text: "Derivative" may be the first word that springs to mind, but all  bands have their inspirations.  This first album from some very fine  American rhythm and blues enthusiasts embodies the very spirit of the  genre.  It captivates the youthful recklessness of leather-clad rockers,  while showing a professional grasp of soul and roots music.  They take the  Stones and add their own individual touch, layering it with body-shaking  hooks, raw and raspy vocals as well as gospel-tinged melodies.  This record  shows the power and precision of the original bluesmen, and adds to it a  90's persona.  It is way above average in its entirety, and its wholesome,  rough and ready nature will make you want to get your rocks off.  And if  that's your poison, be sure to have a listen to their next three albums  "Southern Harmony & Musical Companion", "Amorica"  and "Three Snakes And One Charm" to hear a band holding on to  their influences while progressing and scaling new heights with each  successive release.  But for the record, this is the one that started it  all for them.

title: ........wow...........
text:
I have listened to many, MANY, CD's out there, and none of them top this. This is the greatest CD of all time. That is really all there is to this.

This CD hit me at the right time. Up till then, my life had begun to get progressively worse and worse, and NIN was the soundtrack to this (no, i am not blaming NIN, cause only stupid people with no grasp on reality do things like that). At a certian point, i realized i had to turn somet things around. I got the Fragile, and one thing after another, my life turned around. To understand this CD, youve gotta look at the fact that TR went through hell before recording this. His Grandma, who raised him died, his dog died, longtime NIN drummer Chris Vrenna quit NIN, TR's best friend Maralyn Manson and him hated eachother, and that is only the stuff we know about. The guy went through hell and decided to make a CD that would get him out of the hole he is in. And he did. The sheer amount of ground he covers on the CD is amazing. TR also decided to make use of some of his NIN live band, with guitarist/bassist/keyboardist Danny Lohner and keyboardist/theremin player Charlie Clouser contributing to songs like Starf**kers Incorporated and Somewhat Damaged, among others. The CD starts out with each song being denes and extremely negative, and The Day The Whole World Went Away litterally sounds like the most mournful/dense feeling you can feel as your whole world collapses. It sounds like the end of the world. Then, after that song, the whole CD takes a curious yet optimistic turn, and the songs lyrically pretain to getting back up and getting things out of your system that you need to, as well as healing. Lyrically, Trent is doing amazing things. Instrumentally, this is so blindingly amazing-every little thing on here puts so many different colors and things in your head and its just incredible. One of the most amazing things about this CD is that it makes geinous use of organic instruments (Drums, Bass, Guitar...) and geinous use of electronic sounds and melodies. Every single melody, note, syncopation, and rhythm is absolutely amazing. Every note on here is meant to be here. Plus this CD achieves something that no other CD has-it makes the electronic sounds organic. Everything on this CD breathes, especially the electronic stuff, which is something no other artist has done. No other CD has electronic parts that sound alive and breathing as much as organic instruments and vocals. None.

one thing that any fan of Nine Inch Nails, or good music in general has to hear, is the no longer in print EP known as Still. It came with the initial pressings of the NIN live CD for the touring that came after this CD's release, and is amazing beyond amazing. It was written when the touring behind it ended, and is amazing. It consists of super stripped down and incredibly intimate perfomances of a few already-heard NIN songs such as Something I Can Never Have, The Becoming, The Fragile's Title Track, and The Day The World Went Away. It also has about four or five new songs. All of them were written during/after sessions for The Fragile, and all but one are purely instrumentals. The instrumental ones are mostly TR at the piano playing beautifully sad melodies with amazing background textures. The new song with vocals is called "And All That Could Have Been", and is just amazing beyond amazing. It is the best sad/soft song in the entire NIN catalog, totally topping the final 2 songs on With Teeth, Something I Can Never Have, and the various soft songs on The Fragile. It is also one of THE Greatest songs ive ever heard in my life. TR wrote it with Danny Lohner (before he left NIN so TR could do rebab, and now Lohner is in a new band with Wes Borland, Josh Freese, and Josh Eustis called Black Light Burns, which will prolly be coming out in spring with the new Tool, scoop up both of these if you have any respect for real music) and everything about this song is stellar. I can't put it into words in this little review and that is so frustrating that i cannot convey how amazing this song is. It is frustrating beyond frustrating. It is one of maybe like 4 or 5 songs that perfectly frame being at the lowest point of your life.

NIN have gone through some major changes since this CD (and Still). Everyone in the live band has left (except for TR of course) and the new band, while they are great, mostly play the versions of NIN songs that the Lohner/Finck/Clouser era of NIN played. NIN has become, unfortunately, much more accessible, in a sense that well, here is an example-The Hand that Feeds only has one instrumental melody throughout the whole song, excluding the amazing keyboard solo in the middle of the song. TR has scaled WAY WAY WAY WAY WAY back on use of guitars, and use of insturmental NOTES for that matter. The only songs i can fully stand behind on the new NIN are the first two and last three songs on it. There are some other good ones, but i donno. I feel bad saying anything negative about it because of the impact NIN has had on me, but i just don't like it. I could care less if a CD sells or not, its about what it does to me. I dont really like the new NIN even though i am totally glad that TR cleaned up and i think that it's a great thing. Those songs from it that i do like are exactly what i had hoped for, but the rest-i just donno, man. None of those other songs are bad, but they just aren't for me. But every little thing about The Fragile/Still is just geinous. Nothing has topped this CD has topped it, and while there are some CDs out there that defidently deserved to be menntioned in the same sentence as this CD (such as The Great Southern Trendkill by Pantera, Mellon Collie and the Infinite Saddness by The Smashing Pumpkins, Battle of Los Angales by Rage Against The Machine (for starters)), none of them top this.

if you don't own this CD, you have no idea just how innovative and expressive music at it's best can really be. That's all there is to it.

title: Very good...I'm getting more albums!
text:
The Smashing Pumpkins are amazing. Really, they are. Back in the early nineties, when I was about 4 or 5 years old, my older brother used to listen to The Smashing Pumpkins. Now, about a dozen years later, I listened to the sample of "1979" and was blown away by a wave of wondrous nostalgia.

The Smashing Pumpkins have their own sound, and are an amazing part of alternative rock. This collection practically proves it. I have never heard their other stuff before this, but even I can tell that this album is diverse in terms of sound. You have heavy songs such as Siva, Bullet with Butterfly Wings, Zero, and The Everlasting Gaze. Then you have lighter rock tracks such as Cherub Rock, Perfect, Untitled, and Ava Adore. And also, don't forget those slow, sincere songs as well--Disarm, Drown, Rhinocerous, Stand Inside Your Love, Landslide, Tonight Tonight, and Today. Then, of course, there is a bit of dream pop, like Real Love. And the dark, depressing song known as Eye.

Personally, my favorite songs on this collection are Cherub Rock, 1979, Ava Adore, Stand Inside Your Love, Siva, The Everlasting Gaze, Untitled, and Perfect. Cherub Rock has an amazing pillar of guitars polaying, and some of the coolest vocals and lyrics. 1979 has stellar-sounding guitars, and reminds me of the past. Ava Adore is an excellent mix of rock and pop. Stand Inside Your Love is one of the few love songs that I like. and the other 4 of my favorites are just plain excellent.

If you like bands that experiment with their sound, I highly recommend you pick this up. Sadly, The Smashing Pumpkins are no longer a band...but everything they've put out so far is excellent. I will be honest and say that I did not overly enjoy Zero or Bullet with butterfly Wings; but everything else in my opinion is either pretty good or simply awesome. Especially Cherub Rock and 1979. Get this CD!

title: It was *forty* years ago today...
text:
Over the years, the music of The Beatles has been praised, scrutinized, criticized, and listened to by millions of people. This year marks the fortieth anniversary of the acclaimed album Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band, a major landmark in the band's history. For this reason, now is as good a time as any for zealous fanatics to revisit the album, or for younger generations to experience the historical Sgt. Pepper for the first time.

The Beatles formed in 1960 and had gained immense popularity by 1964. When Sgt. Pepper was released in 1967, members Paul McCartney, John Lennon, George Harrison, and Ringo Starr had reached a level of superstardom previously unattained (or even imagined) by any musical group. By this point in their career, The Beatles' immense fame and evolving music style had made touring impossible, but the group's lack of live, public performances in no way hurt their popularity.

Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band is an eclectic mix of tracks, but it is a collection that The Beatles' blended perfectly together. The album gracefully transcends musical genres, and still sounds fresh and new forty years later. For example, the album includes the psychedelic "Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds," the experimental "Being For the Benefit of Mr. Kite," and the cabaret show tune song titled "When I'm Sixty-Four."

The individual influence of each band member is clearly present, such as the drummer Ringo's vocals in "With A Little Help From My Friends" and George's sitar playing on his creation "Within You, Without You." But even though each of the Fab Four contributed new and different ideas, Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band still sounds like a Beatles record, overall.

In conclusion, The Beatles' Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band remains a great album even forty years later. Sgt. Pepper would be a good starting point for any new Beatles fan, and can be recommended to anyone who appreciates sixties culture.
